[The Author: Chapter 002 → I bow to the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Brahmāṇḍa, to Śrī Nārāyaṇa Hari, the inner controller of all, the God who descends in all incarnations. (1)
Salutations to that Anvaya, whose two wives are Śrī and Lakṣmī, whose mouth is considered to be the Brāhmaṇas and the sacred fire, and whose heart is eternally the virtuous;
he who dwells in heaven, in the sacrificial grass, in the three worlds, among the ancestors, and in all beings.

Salutations to that Śambhu, the showerer of bliss, whose very nature is attainable through meditative absorption. (3) On a beautiful peak of the Himalayas, in his own hermitage on that most excellent of mountains, this is the Saṃhitā which was indeed spoken by Nārāyaṇa to Lakṣmī. (4)
Then, having obtained her at the sacred ford of Badarikāśrama, Śvetavyāsa, assuming his original form and possessing divine vision, spoke to his four disciples:
Śvaiti, Suśikha, Śvetāśva, and Śvetalohita.
Those four great souls, most devoted to Brahman and having reached the further shore of Brahman,
attained the abode of Hari from which there is no return. Those wives of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, however, [attained] those [liberated] states.
In the hermitage of Lomaśa, they affectionately questioned their husband Nārāyaṇa regarding the field of Kuṅkumavāpī at Aśvapaṭṭasārasa in Saurāṣṭra.
And Nārāyaṇa indeed imparted this Saṃhitā to them.
The work known as the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, which contains all meaningful subjects, consists of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses;
in it, the number of verses is such that merely reciting it bestows liberation. (1.1.10)

Once, Nārada set out to behold Vaikuṇṭha; by him was seen the assembly seated there, presided over by Śrī Viṣṇu. There were the divine liberated souls known as Akṣara, as well as others residing in Goloka.
The liberated ones dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha, those residing in Śvetadvīpa,
those dwelling in the unmanifest nectar (Avyākṛta-amṛta), those residing in the abode of Śrī Lakṣmī,
as well as those in Badarī, the Ocean of Milk, and those residing in other abodes.
The ṛṣis, the ancestors, the gods, the siddhas, the gandharvas and cāraṇas, the world-protectors, the Manus, the ascetics, and those who are virtuous;
the sages of divine course, possessing divine and unassailable forms. (14)
All of them were present there in that assembly, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
The assembly hall, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas and crowded to its very limits,
was seen by Nārada to be half-illuminated by men.
Where Lakṣmī is on the left side, there the goddesses are stationed:
Muktā, Vāsudevā, Gopī, and other female friends;
as well as the sovereign ladies, the Bhagavatīs, the attendants, and the handmaidens. (17)
The mothers are the divine Brahmāṇīs, the Mānavīs, and those with perfected forms.
Indeed, Nārada beheld that assembly hall, which was half-illuminated by women, [and there he saw] the eternal Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari-Viṣṇu. (18–19)
Nārada joyfully offered salutations to Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Mahāmāyā; then,
having bowed to the entire assembly, the sage Nārada sat down there upon an excellent seat provided by Viṣṇu, being honored by them all.
I am Vyāsa, known as Śveta; Sūta is named Suśikha.
Likewise, there are other commentators headed by Bṛhaspati;
all of them possess divine forms through the will of Nārāyaṇa.
There they engaged in various discourses that increase devotion.
Among them, Nārāyaṇa said: "This great sage Nārada is one who has heard much, who possesses vast knowledge, and is a supreme treasury of traditional narratives."
One skilled in worldly affairs should be questioned for the sake of understanding one's conduct.
Lakṣmī said:
"O ascetic, O great yogi, O portion of Viṣṇu, O great sage!"
Whence have you come, and what is occurring among the creations of Viṣṇu?
(25) What are the vows of the people on earth, and what is the current state of affairs?
Likewise, [tell me] about the holy fords, the virtuous, the brahmins, and the cows upon this earth. (26)
What is the current state of the poor, of those who perform meritorious deeds, of virtuous women, and of renunciants? Is the path to liberation now free from harm?
Does knowledge, accompanied by realized wisdom, shine among the Brahmins? (27)
"Does true devotion to Nārāyaṇa indeed exist among people?
Śrī Nārada said:
"I always revere my parents, who are compassionate and bestowers of liberation."
Indeed, there is nothing, however slight, that remains unknown to my all-knowing parents;
nevertheless, because it is the duty of a disciple, I shall relate it in due order.
Having wandered through many lands and observed the condition of the Kṛta Yuga, [I have come here].

O Mother, beholding people endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu created by Viṣṇu, and subjects devoted to their husbands, I rejoice again and again. Blessed is this Lord Viṣṇu; blessed am I, the Supreme Goddess.
Indeed, by whose majesty liberation is surely obtained by human beings:
through hearing of Viṣṇu, chanting his names, remembering him, serving at his feet, worshipping him, bowing to him, befriending him, serving as his servant, or offering one's very self. (3.2–3)
Whether performed with knowledge or ignorance, because it removes the impurities of saṃsāra, liberation is attained immediately; therefore, what fortune could be greater than this?
Those who recite the mantra even once, or utter the name of Hari—

O Mother, those people who—whether children, the elderly, or others—receive either the ordinary or the primary initiation (dīkṣā) of Viṣṇu through divine contemplation, certainly attain eternal liberation; indeed, they shall become residents of Vaikuṇṭha. (35–36)
Constant conformity to Viṣṇu, the avoidance of all that is contrary to Him,
perfect faith in Viṣṇu in the form of the prayer "I am Thine," and the renunciation of the sense of ownership regarding the body,
senses, mind, vital breath, ego, intellect, and the inner self— [these constitute surrender]. (37)
Entrusting oneself to Viṣṇu, as well as perpetual dependence on Hari for one who is distressed;
the firm conviction that "Hari alone is my everything, and no other"—this sixfold surrender to Viṣṇu is the taking of refuge. (38–39)
Having attained that one [state], being solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa,
he should accomplish either oneness of disposition, oneness of action, or indeed oneness of self;
in such a way that oneness with Śrī Hari arises to the fullest extent possible.
To that extent, one personally experiences the bliss of Nārāyaṇa.
(41) The essence of love is liquid in nature, and the self also partakes in liquidity.
Upon the meeting of these two liquids, Viṣṇu himself becomes liquid. (42)

One who has attained oneness with Nārāyaṇa enjoys all desires—those which are characterized as a mass of bliss, a mass of consciousness, and a mass of pure awareness; as eternal contentment, eternal coolness, eternal happiness, and perfect nourishment. (43)
In some instances he is on the side, in some in the form [of the body], and in some he is dissolved within it.
In some he exists as the liberated one, in some as Lakṣmī, and in some he proceeds as a servant.
He arises like the body, like the senses, and like the mind.
But I, O Mother, am called Nārada, the mind of Viṣṇu;
you, however, are Lakṣmī, said to be his half-body and his very self.
Hari is the manifest object of existence (san-padārtha), while you are regarded as his half-consciousness (cit).
The melting of those two is called great bliss, which is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda).
By whatever means the Self may attain a state of melting,
having reached that melting through that state, it attains liberation consisting of Viṣṇu.
The illustrious Śvetavyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Nārada dissolved into Viṣṇu in liquid form, into that ocean of the experience of bliss which is the ultimate limit of love. 49.
While all those present in the assembly were watching, this wonder occurred, causing great amazement: "Oh, how great is the devotion of a devotee!
Indeed, Lakṣmī herself, who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa, desired to test him. (1.1.50)
She questioned the Supreme Self for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Supreme Self, indeed many devotees have been seen by you."
No one such as this has ever been seen who has undergone such a transformation before you.
I believe, however, that the cause for this lies in your compassion, O illustrious one;
for upon whomsoever your boundless grace falls, O Lord, [such a change occurs].
O Lord, it is my conviction that you are not distinct from him.
Whatever is your intention regarding the attainment of such a self, or whatever you desire to be done by me for the sake of obtaining your grace—[please tell us]. (54)
The illustrious Śvetavyāsa said:
Having heard that, Nārāyaṇa, desiring the welfare of all,
spoke with supreme affection words that were brief yet possessed incomparable meaning.
"By which even common living beings attain such a destination.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Marvel of Nārada’s Liquid-like Devotion in the Assembly of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha," within the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 1.1.
← Chapter 001: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 2 [[Author: Chapter 003 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall declare how grace may be obtained from Me for the sake of attaining the state of melting devotion; understand that according to its true nature.
The Lord is the master over the creation of the liberated, the creation of the Lord, and even the creation of individual souls;
he created all embodied beings with their forms—such is the established doctrine.
The Self, however, is called Indra, the locus of all powers and qualities.
The internal instrument of that [Self] consists of the mind (manas), the intellect (citta), and the ego-consciousness (ahaṃbuddhi).
These four are declared to be the powers of Indra.
Furthermore, there are the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, feet, and hands. (3–4)
Indeed, the organs located in the anus and the genitals are external instruments;
these ten powers truly belong to Indra alone.
They proceed further and further outward toward the objects to be grasped.
Having assumed the form of the grasped, they partake in the appearance of the grasped.
But when all of them undergo transformation, they partake in the appearance of the sustainer.
Indeed, when these [powers], having shattered the internal organs, attain the Self, [they become one with it]. (6–7)
Having assumed the form of objects of enjoyment, they become the experience of Indra;
then this direct experience occurs within one's very own self.
I am directly established as Indra, the fulfiller of all powers.
It is established that Indra, having come into union with me, is the locus of full power.
From the ungraspable up to me, the essence of love is considered to be fluidity;
that indeed is placed everywhere, and by it all forms are made to cohere. (1.2.10)
I am Viṣṇu, full of oil, full of bliss, full of love, and the refuge of happiness; indeed, I am full of fluidity, for through union with me, he too possesses fluidity.
Everything—whether gross, subtle, conscious, or otherwise—is likewise so.
"Everything has been melted by my melting; here, my grace is the cause.
(1.2) "But may this one also become melted"—when such compassion for me arises, then he melts at that very moment, and never otherwise. (1.3)
The means for my grace is considered to be the surrender of one's entire self.
I am always full of grace, compassionate, and an ocean of mercy. Endowed with compassion, I shower the rain of grace through the joy of devotion.
To the extent that the flow of my compassion enters into the steadfast devotee,
to that same extent the Reality repeatedly attains a state of melting.
I alone, without a second, abide in the imperishable abode.
In my form there, my liberated state and even my imperishable Brahman-nature melt away due to the abundance of my love and by the power of my grace.
At that time, I am the sovereign Virāj; nothing whatsoever remains separate from me.
This liberation is attained by those who know its state, through the realization of identity with that [Brahman].
If He, being alone, does not find delight, He desires a second from Himself;
for that Brahman is the Imperishable, manifested from that Great Self. (18–19)
By the will of the Lord, that formless [reality] became twofold: with form and without form.
The formless is the supreme abode from which all abodes were born;
the one with form possesses a form identical to its own, being embodied and conforming to the nature of embodiment. (1.2.20)
That Hari, however, again desired his own manifold form.
From him, who is without beginning, infinite liberated souls have appeared in endless numbers;
they reside there in those spheres within the three-quarters of the immortal heaven.
Muktā, Brahmā, and Parabrahmā—this triad is considered the creation of Brahmā.
All these divine beings possess forms with limbs corresponding to their respective appearances;
indeed, the senses are of the nature of the Self and are non-different from the Tattvas.
However, by way of metaphorical designation, the names consist of the essence of the power of taste (rasa-śakti).
Indeed, they are the mind, the ear, speech, the eye, the skin, and so forth, beginning with taste.
Even when the sign is complete, these remain hidden; there is neither delight in them nor any latent impression (vāsanā) thereof.
Since that [embryo] is not born of a mother, the six sheaths (kośa) are not found there.
Therein, the vital breath (prāṇa) is the power of the Self; space (kāśa) is its unobstructed nature.
Its hair, gold, nails, teeth, and so forth are not at all separated [from it].
Indeed, those divine lights, which are of the nature of pure consciousness and identical with the One, shine forth as their own self.
All those divine illuminations radiate within the divine abode;
this is what is called the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) according to the Upaniṣads.
The body of liberation is Brahmic; it is the state of experiencing the bliss of Brahman.
He eternally enjoys all desires together with Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Possession of Form through Liquid Liberation for the Supreme Brahman, the Liberated Souls of Brahman, and Others in the Imperishable Abode," within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now, [I shall describe] the desire of Hari— who resides upon the left limb of her whose nature is imperishable (Akṣara)— and who,
desiring to make that service fruitful by means of his own form as Vāmā.
Like Nārāyaṇa from his left side, [he manifested] the auspicious one consisting of his own self-power (svātma-śakti),
the locus of all blessings, good fortune, love, and affection;
a form corresponding to [his own], his own support, his own field, and his own refuge.
[The Lord],

the ocean of mercy, desiring for Lakṣmī the fruitfulness of her unerring devotion, assumed a manifested form consisting of beauty, which is the abode of his own qualities, sovereignty, power, passion, strength, and the cave [of the heart], and which is the locus of the quality of delight. (3–4)
Assuming a form endowed with unfailing vigor known as Vāsudeva,
he is this very Nārāyaṇa, called Vāsudeva and Śrī Hari.
He became twofold, bearing the names Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.

Having seen all the liberated persons in the world of Brahmā, Lakṣmī beheld none other there but herself alone, who was identical in form to her own self. Then, with joy, she prayed to the Lord Śrī Hari, her own husband.
O Lord, please provide a suitable place for his wife;
having understood the disposition of that beloved woman, and desiring her welfare,
he fashioned the divine abode known as Vaikuṇṭha, indeed the world of Brahmā.
For the sake of service, the Lord also settled male and female servants there;
for their sake, he created divine enjoyments and divine implements—
a divine creation of his own, complete and with every desire fulfilled.

Śrī Hari himself made her endowed with all means of accomplishment and possessed of prosperity and happiness; he personally recognized her perfection, thinking: "I am he, she is you, these two worlds are ours, and Vaikuṇṭha belongs to us. (11) I am he, you are she, these two worlds, and Vaikuṇṭha is ours.
Having seen this new great yoga consisting of husband and wife,
the unborn Māyā— the eternal power of Hari composed of the three guṇas who gives birth to the principles— desiring Śrī Hari as her husband, [became manifest]. (12)

She requested that very form which is identical to Lakṣmī, which is desired, and which is where creation—consisting of reality—is born and where it dissolves; she then again requested this from the Lord, the Sovereign of All, the Master, Śrī Hari. (13–14)
Commanded by the Lord, she assumed a new form that causes infatuation—
the beautiful form of Rādhā, the vessel of countless delights—
and remained as his inseparable consort by His will. 15.
For that purpose, Śrī Hari indeed assumed the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
the Supreme Person, the refuge of all desires, the showerer of all aesthetic flavors,
possessing unfailing and immeasurable prowess, fortune, beauty, strength, and splendor.
The Lord, assuming the youthful form suitable for Rādhā’s lover, was beheld by Rādhā as a handsome and worthy husband suited to herself;
she then requested a divine and independent residence for herself within that abode. (18)
It was a garden created for my pastimes, a vast refuge for my supreme delight;
it was the pinnacle of my glory, perfected by all my resources, and all its furnishings were of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss. (1.3.19–20)

By the desire of Rādhā, "May everything be present there for the sake of Śrī Kṛṣṇa," everything came to pass, including millions of maidservants. That supreme, divine, and imperishable abode, Goloka, became exceedingly opulent.
That which is perceived beyond the boundary is extended within the world of Brahmā.
Indeed, Śrī Hari, having been commanded by [the Lord], fashioned the beautiful and sublime abode of Goloka, which is graced by Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and honored by Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. || 22–23 ||
That eternal abode, Goloka, is established in the world of Brahmā;
there, assuming the form of Kṛṣṇa, He accepts the service performed by Rādhā.
Furthermore, in Brahmā’s world, in Goloka, and in Vaikuṇṭha, there are multitudes of objects of enjoyment.
They are all equal in their devotion to Śrī Hari and always bring joy to His devotees.
(25) According to their respective emblems, forms, yoga, and honors, according to their pleasure and requirements, they manifest from the desire of Hari. (26)
There, divine pleasure and constant celestial bliss arise for those whose very selves are that [bliss].
Through union with Hari, divine love is eternally born there.
Just as the Lord always delights among His beloved consorts in Vaikuṇṭha, so it is there.
Likewise, even in Goloka, the Lord rejoices with His beloved consorts;
but in the supreme abode of the Imperishable, Hari delights among the liberated souls.
There, the Lord Himself causes His liberated devotees, friends, and female attendants to play.

"Or, just as they worship Me in one form or a pair, so do they approach Me as their Lord, the giver of happiness, and their husband. (1.3.30) Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Establishment of the Two Abodes of Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka for Lakṣmī and Rādhā," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. Chapter 3.
← Chapter 003: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 4 [[Author: Chapter 005 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
That Supreme Self, Hari himself, thought, "May I be born as progeny.
The All-pervading Lord then emanated Mahākāla, His own power, from Himself. (1)
To him, the supreme bringer of the end of all and the agitator of Māyā, Hari issued the command: "Agitate Māyā!
Indeed, having seen that Māyā thus agitated by him, the person was liberated from Hari.
Then another, who was obedient to his command, was joined with that illusion (māyā).
That illusion is primordial nature (prakṛti), the root; but the person (puruṣa) is the Lord.
Thus, nature and the person brought forth their own creation.
From those two, indeed, millions of principal beings (pradhānapuruṣas) were born.
Pradhāna is the Great Principle (mahattattva), consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), and is called the field (kṣetra). Puruṣa is declared to be its lord; thus, they exist as pairs.
All those who were previously merged within primordial nature (prakṛti) have now become manifest as lords (īśvara),
assuming the forms of husbands and wives.
From Pradhāna and Puruṣa, however, Mahāviṣṇu was born.
She is indeed declared to be the ego (ahaṃkāra), and she is also called the Golden Man (Svarṇapuruṣa).
She is the excellent daughter of Pradhāna, remembered as Ahaṃkṛti.
She is Hiraṇyā, the Great Lakṣmī, the companion of Mahāviṣṇu.
Mahālakṣmī and Mahāviṣṇu—that pair is thus proclaimed. That embryo which was produced in Mahālakṣmī from Mahāviṣṇu is called Hiraṇyagarbha; from that, the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) was produced.
The golden egg split in two, and from that was born this Virāṭ. From the Virāṭ also came a woman, who is considered the wife of the Virāṭ.
From the Mahāviṣṇu of the ego-principle (ahaṃkṛti), the sixteen principles (tattvas) arose.
From the *sāttvika* [aspect], however, the ten sense organs (*indriyas*) together with the mind (*manas*) arose.
From the *tāmasa* [aspect] arose the group of subtle elements (*tanmātras*), and likewise from the *rājasa* [aspect] arose their respective deities.
These are: hearing, touch, sight, taste, speech, hands, feet, and the organs of excretion and generation.
The generative organ (upastha) and the others are the senses; the mind (manas) is the internal instrument.
It should be understood that there are five organs of cognition (jñānendriya) and five organs of action (karmendriya).
Among these, the five beginning with the ear possess the power to produce cognition.
However, because of their power to produce action, the five beginning with speech are indeed called the organs of action;
the mind (manas), on the other hand, is of the nature of both.
[The presiding deities are] the Directions, Wind, Sun, Varuṇa, the Aśvins, Fire, Indra, Upendra, and Mitra. (15–16)
And Candra—these are considered the gods consisting of the creation of Īśa;
they dwell within the bodies and the spheres (golaka) of the lords.
And the single mind arises as fourfold through the distinction of its functions.
Those [entities] are called by the knowers of reality mind (manas), ego (ahaṃkāra), consciousness (citta), and intellect (buddhi).
By the will of the Lord, they were joined together in the form of Virāṭ;
nevertheless, when that Virāṭ did not rise up because it was devoid of vital breath (prāṇa) and the soul (śūnya), [the Lord acted]. 18–19.

Śrī Hari, indeed assuming the form of the vital breath (prāṇa), entered therein; for by Him the power of life known as vitality (jīvana) was placed within. This is due to the union of Śrī Hari, the conscious Self of the vital breath, with that [body]. (1.4.20)
In this matter, his form truly became "Vairāja" (the Sovereign) in accordance with its literal meaning.
From the great stalk of the lotus at his navel, Brahmā was born. Then, from his forehead, Rudra appeared as the creator characterized by the quality of *rajas*.
He, however, was the tamasic Viṣṇu who became the destroyer of the heart;
he is declared to be the sāttvika nourisher, endowed with his own power.
Residing within the body of Brahmā, his wife is called Brāhmī.
She who is known as Sṛṣṭi is indeed the half-body of Brahmā;
Rudra’s power is Rudrāṇī, Śivā, Harāṅganā, and Satī.
Vaiṣṇavī, who is the power of Viṣṇu, is likewise remembered as Lakṣmī.

To those three [deities], there are three wives who bestow creation, destruction, and nourishment; they are considered to be identical with them and are regarded as providing assistance for their respective functions. By the command of Brahmā, they carry forth the flow of creation.
From the primordial person (Āmūlapuruṣa) down to the end of their hair, all are remembered as lords;
they possess bodies of pure *sattva*, and that *sattva* is indeed the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Hari.
Therefore, they are all lords, the manifestations of the Supreme Brahman.
There, having entered into all the lords (Īśvaras), the Lord sports.
Among them, Śrī Hari assumed a form worthy of worship;
he indeed became Vāsudeva, the controller of the lords.
O Great King, this Lord, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the lords of lords,
accompanied by his own power Vāsudevī,
created that white abode for his residence within the imperishable realm. (1.4.30)
The Lord made his dwelling in his own divine white abode;
for he himself is Vāsudeva in that supreme abode called Amṛta. Furthermore, Vāsudeva himself [resides] in his own [abode], which was created by the Lord.
For the sake of creation, preservation, and dissolution, he assumed his own threefold form.
Aniruddha was born as the one who brings forth the creation of the Lord;
Pradyumna was born as the nourisher of that very creation of the Lord.
He who is the destroyer of the creation of Īśa was born as Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Indeed, there are three forms of Vāsudeva that exist directly;
yet Śrī Hari himself assumed a fourfold form.
Therefore, those who know the scriptures speak of fourfold arrays (vyūha).
Among them, some lords are four-faced, others have eight faces, and still others have sixteen faces or even a hundred faces. (35–36)

There are those with a thousand faces, ten thousand faces, and a hundred thousand faces, as well as others; there are those with a billion faces and ten million mouths, possessing an equal number of feet and hands.
Therein lie the fourteen cosmic eggs (aṇḍagola) of Viṣṇu.
There are twenty-eight *golaka*s (spheres) belonging to Sadāśiva Rudra;
fifty-six *aṇḍas* (eggs) of Pradhāna-māyā are proclaimed;
and for Mahāviṣṇu there are two hundred and twelve *golaka*s.
There are indeed five hundred Prakṛtis, Puruṣas, and Aṇḍas;
the worlds of Mahākāla are proclaimed to be one thousand.
These are the realms of Vāsudeva, Kṛṣṇa, and Nārāyaṇa.
They are divine, infinite, innumerable, and beyond the range of words.
(41) For all the lords, however, their own powers—consisting of mind, intellect, senses, and so forth—are considered to be identical with their very selves and endowed with pure *sattva*. (42)

Likewise, in the world below that, [it is so named] due to its contact with the lamp of the sun. (15–16)

Likewise, the world of heaven is known as *dyau* (the sky) because of the shining of the stars; below that, in the intermediate space, it is called *antarīkṣa* (the atmosphere) because of the illumination seen from the constellations,
and it is also known as *bhuvar* because it is the hollow of the earth.
Below this level, because of the manifestation of a vast fire,
it is called "Agni" (Fire) and "Pṛthivī" (Earth), as well as "Bhūḥ" (the Shining One) due to its brilliance. Below that, for each of the seven netherworlds (*talas*), there are seven illuminators.

The *maṇis* are the divine objects; they are joined with the initial syllables of their respective names. Listen to me as I correctly state those various names. Because medicinal herbs (*oṣadhayaḥ*) shine there in the lower world, it is therefore called *atala*.
Because of the splendor of the lapis lazuli jewels, Vitala is remembered as being beneath that;
because of the radiance of the multitude of Kaustubha gems, Sutala is considered to be beneath that;
and because of the lamp-like jewels on the tips of the hoods, Talātala is said to be [beneath that].
That great netherworld (Mahātala) was illuminated by the light of emeralds;
that subterranean realm (Rasātala) was illuminated by the light of various kinds of gems;
and [that world] situated on the surface (Pātāla) was illuminated by the light of Puṣparāja jewels.
Brahmā himself indeed gave it the name Pātāla.
Mahar, Jana, Tapa, and Satya are the stones [forming its foundation], born of meritorious principles.
Svar is the layer of fire, and Bhuvar is said to be the layer of wind.
The earth was fashioned from the earth-element, while the regions beginning with Atala are increasingly dense with darkness;
thus indeed was the arrangement of those layers made by Brahmā.
Even within those [lower worlds], there are minute portions of the earthly element for the sake of providing stability.
In some places, there are fiery portions consisting of elements mixed in layers;
in other places, there are watery portions, and even very firm ones belonging to the quality of darkness (tamas).
Indeed, these layers, which serve as the support for living beings, are called "cavities" (vivaras).
Then Brahmā fashioned a pillar as a support for the stars even in the center;
that golden pillar, well-established from Pātāla up to Satyaloka,
indeed became his own abode in Satyaloka.

In the middle world, Śambhu fashioned Kailāsa as his own abode. Viṣṇu, however, who reclines upon Śeṣa, fashioned for himself his own suitable residence beneath Pātāla in the waters of the Ocean of Milk.
It is indeed for the purpose of beholding the great-souled ones such as Nārada and others who are practitioners of yoga, as well as the gods and the perfected beings (siddhas), that they go there;

He envisioned a second such place called Śvetadvīpa, where there would indeed be a favorable rebirth for others possessing divine bodies. That divine island is remembered as being situated in the northern region of the Ocean of Milk.

The gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, who bring security to the world, always strive in this manner for the sake of protection, since they are established therein. Their abodes within this cosmic egg are material and inferior. (36–37)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Production of Innumerable Brahmāṇḍas, the Arrangement of the Stellar Paths, and the Abodes of the Three Deities," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

"Because the day is eternal in the *dhruva* [station], since the creation is distinct [from it].

Such was that city of the one whose emblem is the bull, composed of radiant energy. By his will, a mental ground made of gold was fashioned;
filled with jeweled sands, it exists pervaded by splendor.
Resembling the light of the autumnal moon and like the rising sun,
they were half-white and half-red, as well as golden;
they were the size of chariot wheels, with stalks possessing the luster of emerald.
With a delicate form and an incomparable fragrance,
there were divine lotuses in those groves and parks— some resembling the petals of bees and others made of refined gold. (23–24)
Indeed, there are lotuses that are half-black and half-red with delicate interiors,
equal in size to parasols;
and divine rivers flow there, carrying streams of meritorious nectar.
The best of rivers carry water that resembles a circle of jewels, mixed with the petals of lotuses and lilies, and possessing the form of swirling foam;
indeed, those who are undistracted, well-disciplined, and have conquered their senses meditate upon that very [water]. (26–27)
Here the high-souled ones behold that city of the one whose self is the bull and the bull;
in the midst of that best of cities stands a great, divine palace,
radiant with auspicious splendor and possessing a thousand pillars, made of refined gold.
He was adorned on all sides with incomparable jewels:
with crystals resembling the moon, with lapis lazuli possessing the brilliance of the moon,
with golds having the luster of the rising sun, and with [gems] like fire.
It shone with beautiful pillars made of silver and sapphire,
and it was constructed of massive, firm beams made of diamond;
it was perfumed by waters of various forms that were brilliantly radiant.
The city was adorned with banners possessing the brilliance of the moon,
and it was constantly filled with festivities due to the sounds of golden bells and other instruments.
There were the Rudradāsas, the Gandharvas, the Kinnaras, and the Sutamas and Māgadhas.
They praised the Lord Mahārudra together with his retinue.
This royal palace of Rudra shines with a hundred stories, wherein stands the image of Tryambaka, resembling the Vāsantī flower, in his residence. (33–34)
Rudrāṇī, the power (śakti) of Śambhu, is a goddess endowed with beauty and virtue;
with her fragrant body, she indeed serves the god Rudra.
She is Śrī, Lakṣmī, Māyā, Kīrti, Śobhā, and Sarasvatī.

Indeed, these goddesses are accompanied by the [principal] Goddess; they are endowed with beauty and fragrance, eternal and innumerable, each surpassing the other in qualities. They are the ornaments of all jewels, and the very embodiments of the splendor and grace of the Goddess.
A hundred crores of highly fortunate women, dividing themselves by their own power,
joyfully attend upon the Lord Mahārudra without weariness.
Behind them are another thousand female attendants.
And they were all embodied, endowed with beauty, and lotus-eyed;
accompanied by playful gestures and most captivating emotions,
they rejoiced together with the youthful Rudras, who were like the finest fires.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Sāttvika Rudra and Rudrāṇī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 16. [Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Part 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna), Chapter 17]
[The Author: Chapter 018.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall speak for those who are devoted to many forms of worship.
And the countless female attendants of Rudra, as well as his hosts in the form of weapons—
[2] lovely, gentle, handsome, with limbs of firm constitution, with symmetrical thighs, hips, and shanks, and with symmetrical, slender waists. [3]
Some were hunchbacked, some were dwarfish, with beautiful limbs and auspicious faces;
others were marked with spots, or were misshapen, or terrifying, or flat-faced;
some had protruding bellies, short arms, three eyes, and the faces of horses.
Some had the faces of lions and short feet, while others had the faces of elephants;
some had the faces and bellies of elephants, and likewise others had the faces of lions and tigers.
They were red-eyed, possessed great breasts, were fortunate, and had beautiful eyes.
With short, curly hair, beautiful and with lovely cheeks,
all those excellent women were capable of assuming any form at will;
they possessed firm waists and were always endowed with full, dear, and sweet speech, as well as with graceful gestures and amorous expressions.
The Blessed One, the ten-armed Maheśvara, delights with them,
together with Nandin and the hosts of great-souled beings who possess universal forms,
as well as with the hosts of Rudras who are equal in magnanimity and prowess.
Resembling the son of Pāvaka (Agni), with faces formidable with sacrificial posts for tusks,
he was being saluted by those stationed in celestial chariots and honored by those intent upon him;
he was inhaling a garland of flowers from all seasons that rested upon his chest.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with broad, copper-colored, and elongated eyes;
with slightly protruding and formidable lips, and resting upon a row of sharp fangs;
possessing six upward-facing eyes, difficult to behold, yet beautiful, and clad in divine garments. (1.17.10–11)
Unwearied in battles and the destroyer of all enemies,
his *paṭṭiśa*— placed against his left side with arm locked against arm—
shines, held within the reach of his outstretched left hand.
He possesses a great, terrifying roar and strength with incomparable vigor.
His ten-colored bow is variegated and shines exceedingly.
His trident has the luster of lightning; it is unfailing and the destroyer of enemies.
The axe blazed with its own form, endowed with ten thousand splendors;
likewise the sword, the best among the powerful, and the moon with its cool rays.
In brilliance, form, and luster, they were like the high-souled Lord of the Gods.
Standing before the God is a great, beautiful, and glorious vessel made of gold, which is auspicious and has all enemies as its handle.
And she, wearing white garments, has placed her sword back into its scabbard.
Adorned with a great pearl resting upon her breast, the four-armed, highly fortunate Vijayā is honored by the world;
she is the foremost female doorkeeper of the Goddess, peerless and supreme like Śrī herself. (17)
Radiant, she stood there with her hands joined in reverence before the God.
Following behind her were other women, accompanied by throngs of Apsarases; indeed, they waited upon Śaṅkara with their ever-new charms. (18–19)
Endowed with all auspicious marks and accompanied by musical instruments,
the hosts born of the Gandharvas sing praises to the Lord of the Gods.
He is broad-chested, towering, and possesses the splendor of an autumnal cloud.
And the bellowing Gopati shines in his house;
his son Skanda, possessed of immeasurable heroism, is accompanied by his retinue.
He is glorious, wearing red garments, and has eyes like the petals of a choice lotus.
His disciples— Śākha, Viśākha, and the wise Naigameya— are free from all calamities and devoted to the protection of living beings.
Together with them, that mighty one whose vehicle is the peacock shines resplendent.
The one whose face is everywhere indeed plays with children’s toys.
And there, tigers of golden luster and great speed follow him;
they all move about at will, created by the Lord himself.
They are indeed like death unto death, the destroyers of Yama’s pride;
they are lions, the hosts of Rudra, who abide under the control of Rudra’s will. Possessing strength equal to Mount Mandara and incomparable power, [they stand there].
[They were] with the color of necklaces, jasmine, and the moon, sounding like lightning and clouds;
indeed, they wore crest-jewels, possessed garments resembling clouds, were marked with the Śrīvatsa and the thunderbolt, and held finger-rings and tridents in their hands. (27–28)
Such was the residence of those gods of divine splendor, possessing such beautiful forms,
within the pillars of his principal palace;
indeed, it was there that a thousand lions were stationed by the high-souled Lord.
All those who acted out of anger from their own nature became lions in form.
Then, those by whom devotion to Rudra-Maheśvara was cultivated became modest,
powerful, self-controlled, endowed with heroism, and free from greed.
Those who have taken refuge in Maheśvara with purified action, mind, and speech, and with a pure inner self, having become single-minded,
have attained the eternal and imperishable state that is the same world as Rudra.
Indeed, they were all brought to a state of unsurpassed similarity in form with Bhava;
they were all primarily Vaiśvānara, possessing universal forms, with matted hair, blue throats, white necks, sharp fangs, and three eyes. (33–34)
With uṣṇīṣas shaped like half-moons and wearing crowns of matted hair,
all these heroes have ten arms and are fragrant from within lotuses.
Resembling the rising sun, they are all clad in yellow garments.
All of them held the Pināka bow in their hands and were mounted upon white bulls.
Endowed with splendor, they wore earrings and were adorned with pearl necklaces.
By virtue of their divine nature, they possessed even greater brilliance; they were all-knowing and all-seeing.
Having divided themselves manifoldly and being freed from old age and death,
they sport with various dispositions, attaining enjoyments that are very difficult to obtain. With movements at their own will, these perfected ones (siddhas) are awakened by other perfected ones.
Then many tens of millions of Rudras were created from those eleven.
Together with them, that high-souled Maheśvara, the God of gods, the Blessed One who is compassionate toward his devotees and the true lord of his devotees, rejoices. (1.17.40)
When the terrible dissolution of all beings has occurred,
at the end of the destruction of the great elements, when the final dissolution has arrived—
there are many millions of Rudras as well as numerous hosts of female attendants.
All those great-souled ones, such as Aneka, Gaṇa, Vyāghra, and others, as well as the various Siddhas and so forth,
having gone to the world of Rudra, all attain dissolution into Maheśvara; they all go to dissolution in Rudra, and Rudra dissolves into Brahman.
Having taken refuge with supreme devotion and a mind endowed with knowledge,
one attains the eternal, imperishable state of co-residence with Rudra (rudrasālokya).
This creation of Rudra, the unborn son, is indeed of the nature of Rudra.
She is embodied by throngs of male and female servants, tigers, vehicles, and mounts;
she has as her attendants weapons, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and bards;
and she is adorned with houses, gardens, great palaces, rivers, lotuses, and other jewels. (45–46)
All forms consisting of *sattva* are of the nature of *sattva* and bestow great happiness;
for that which is the fierce state (*raudrabhāva*) of Rudra does not exist here at all.
Therefore, this [goddess], who dwells in Satyaloka, was created by Brahmā.
That Raudrī creation, however, was always made stable by the quality of sattva.
Having seen this pleasure-bestowing creation, Brahmā indeed attained satisfaction.
But those Sāttvika deities—the Rudras, along with their male and female servants—[remained as they were]. (48–49)
Having attained sattvic happiness and acquired all forms of sovereignty,
they remained indeed absorbed in those sovereignties and pleasures, their power of discernment being weak.
Therefore, they were deceived by that which is the ultimate knowledge.
If that were so, there might at some time be an obstruction to the path of liberation;
and from such a transgression, the attainment of misfortune would follow. Reflecting thus, Brahmā himself created a pure creation filled with knowledge, so that this might not happen. (51–52)

He then resolved to create a mental creation that bestows liberation, which is connected to Brahman, is of the nature of the mind, and has the form of Brahman; thereafter, he proceeded to meditate for the sake of its perfection.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of the Sāttvika Rudras, Dāsa-s, Dāsī-s, and Others," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. (17)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having established himself in yoga and attained meditative absorption (samādhi), Brahmā then [saw] his own self directly within Śrī Hari, the Lord in the supreme abode.
Having unified [the self] with effort through identity and having made this request, may creation be such that it bestows peace and men become peaceful;
likewise, may others be granters of liberation, overflowing with the manifestation of Brahman. (2)
They are the awakeners of all, untainted, and preeminent in the quality of goodness (sattva). They are of the nature of Brahman, perpetually nourished by the contemplation of Brahman;
they are bathed in the bliss of Brahman and are constant meditators upon the form of Brahman. (3–4)
O Lord, may there be sons for me who are the gurus of the worlds, the refuge of the perfection of dharma,
equal to the lords of the gods, and who extend their protection from Brahma down to the crawling insects;
and by whom the worlds shall always be made happy.
Having thus understood the entreaty made by the Supreme Brahman,
the four who were liberated were then commanded for the sake of [obtaining] sons;
these four liberated ones, who knew his resolve, [departed] from the abode of the Imperishable Brahman.
Having transcended these worlds and reached the world of truth (satyaloka),
even Brahmā, having emerged from his yoga and seeing those four who were liberated, thought:
"May these sons born of my mind become the cause of liberation for others."
Having thus resolved, he released those beautiful five-year-old calves—
just born, of the nature of Brahman, filled with the bliss of Brahman, supreme,
adorned with circles of light, clad in pure white garments, and possessing the radiant luster of lotuses on dry land.
Having obtained four sons who were divine, always compassionate, and destined to live as long as the universe endures, he attained great satisfaction.
By name, those sons were the mental offspring (mānasa) who served as the cause of the world's welfare.
Sanaka, Sananda, Sanatana, and Sanātana—
these are the virtuous ones, whose nature is goodness; they are meritorious and composed of merit,
always removing faults by their very sight and bringing about the dissolution of suffering and grief.
They are compassionate, patient by nature, and desirous of the welfare of all creation;
they are forbearing, free from malice, tranquil, and have no rising enemies.
They are without envy, free from enmity, devoid of pride, and free from jealousy.
They are always worthy of honor and bestowers of honor, whose speech is always dear and truthful;
they are free from pride, devoid of defects such as anger and greed, and untainted.
They are empty of the notions of "I" and "mine," and have conquered the impulse of desire.
Free from hypocrisy, pure, self-controlled, upright, moderate in speech,
free from the pairs of opposites, vigilant, steadfast, and having conquered their senses;
full of awakening, established in the Self, and possessing no possessions.
They are benefactors to all, resting upon the virtues of faith, conviction in the scriptures, and devotion;
they are noble, steadfast in austerity, and free from worldly attachments. They are devoid of malice and theft, and do not disclose the secrets of others. (18–19)
Having conquered the states of the body, they are contented, firm in intellect,
equal in pleasure and pain, free from craving, endowed with satisfaction,
devoid of censuring others and the like, and established in their own true nature.
Endowed with divine fortune, they dwell within the lineage of dharma (21).
They are like a great reservoir for the flood of Hari’s knowledge, equal to Brahmā himself;
for them, not even a single moment passes fruitlessly without devotion to Hari (22).
Sanaka and the others, endowed with such characteristics, took recourse in hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, and so forth;
with action, mind, speech, and a purified inner self.
With undistracted minds, they indeed constantly practice devotion to Hari.
Having taken refuge with supreme devotion, they possess a splendor joined with knowledge;
their divine forms are radiant, gentle in disposition, and beautiful to behold.

Those who are deeply immersed in the bliss of the Self, whose nature is Brahman, and who bestow liberation, count supernatural powers, accomplishments, and treasures as mere blades of grass. They rain down the nectar of their vision upon those scorched by the forest fire of saṃsāra. (26)
They are the gurus who bestow liberation upon the multitude of future living beings;

they are the ancestors of the lineages of the virtuous, the deliverers of those who have slain Brahmins, the paths for those traveling on wrong ways, and the exemplars for those practicing celibacy. (27–28)
They are the foundations of all branches of knowledge, as well as the seeds of all that is auspicious;
they are the treasuries of all scriptures and the embodiments of those characterized by the quality of sattva.
They are the bases of all spiritual accomplishments and the refuges for those seeking protection.

They grant liberation to those seeking release and bestow fruits upon all who perform ritual actions. They are the inspirers of those with virtuous aspirations and the ornament of those possessing the splendor of Brahman.
They are austerity itself for those rich in asceticism, and likewise self-restraint for those who practice discipline. (1.18.30–31)
They are eternally divine, five years of age, with tender inner natures;
they are devoid of the emergence of youth and free from old age and death.
Though four in body, they are considered children in form but elders in wisdom.
Having bowed to their own father Aja, they said, "What may we do for your welfare?
Then Brahmā consecrated them with the waters of the Vedas;
they were initiated and established as lifelong celibate students (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*).
They were established in the world of Brahmā, in the true, celestial, and well-rounded sphere;
in a meritorious, delightful, and supreme chariot born of resolve that moves at will,
where the city of Mahārudra resides within the expanse of the sky.
On that level ground, for their sake, a well-constructed abode was prepared (36).
It was divine, endowed with all supernatural powers, and provided assistance in obtaining one's own desires;
it possessed trees of rice and clusters of flowers and fruits that arose from mere thought (37).
Arising solely from the mere effort of the reality of merit, it consists of objects such as things to be enjoyed, instruments of enjoyment, food, drink, and so forth;
it is a manifest merit, a dwelling-place, and a fragrance pervading the forest. (38)
It was endowed with gardens, groves, fields, medicinal herbs, and elixirs.
(39) There, the golden liquid was purifying and satiating;
the silver water, produced by the rivers of imagination, brought great happiness. (1.18.40)
The Brahma-pools, the Cold-pools, and the Fire-pools are naturally arisen;
they are eternally free from depletion, destruction, and the like, and they bestow the wealth of the submarine fire (Vāḍava).
There are also great huts made of the large leaves of the Brahma-tree.
There are dwellings worthy of yogis and those constructed for the sake of ascetics.
(42) Therein reside infinite auspicious beings born of resolve, equal to Sanaka and others;
they are rich in the wealth of knowledge and devotion, and possess youthful forms. (43)
Such was that celestial mansion, constructed as a dwelling consisting of gardens; it moved through the air at will, was built upon truth,
was made of gold, possessed a hundred floors, and was vast, measuring a hundred thousand *yojanas*.
Having constructed such a dwelling fit for residence— consisting of distinct areas for the assembly hall, the lecture hall, the monastery, the sacred fire,
and so forth— the Creator, desiring them to have a place to stay, offered it to the four Kumāras.
Then, indeed, Brahmā reflected upon how knowledge might be bestowed;
he meditated upon Hari, the Supreme Brahman, that Lord, for the sake of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).
At that moment, the Veda-puruṣas were dispatched there by Śrī Hari.
Having come from the abode of Brahmā, they stood before Brahmā;
they were themselves divine, embodied forms, filled with knowledge and realization. These illuminators, whose nature is wisdom, attained dissolution within the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
In this [work], all forms of knowledge created by the Creator of all things are indeed contained—
those which bestow liberation here and those which grant happiness in the hereafter. Furthermore,
the four aims of human existence known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are included.

The Unborn One resolved to bestow upon them those various Vedas which always describe the [four] castes; he taught them according to the prescribed rule. Those four sons of Brahmā, having studied the Vedas in their entirety, [became the guardians of the quarters].
They constantly protected the Vidyās and taught the Vedas; furthermore,
they created millions of lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhikas) who were fit for those various studies,
as well as eternal mental disciples (mānasa-śiṣyas) aged five years.
[He saw] those whose wisdom, form, splendor, strength, and other qualities were equal to those of Sanaka and the others;
who possessed dwellings, enjoyments, sovereignty, prosperity, and bodies equal to theirs;
who were devoted to the vow of celibacy, divine, meritorious, and supreme. (54–55)
There, in that abode of truth resorted to by Sanaka, he established all those eternal and virtuous sons—
who were oceans of Vedic knowledge and possessed all the qualities of the righteous and sattvic nature.
With his blessings, he united those immeasurable beings of eternal form, whose qualities and appearances were in perfect equilibrium;
they remained within this cosmic egg from the beginning of creation until its dissolution. (57–58)
"The treasures of Vedic knowledge shall remain with those who protect the Vedas.
Having performed this supreme task, Brahmā attained satisfaction once again;
meditating for a moment upon the Supreme Brahman, he remained established, taking refuge in his own self.
Beholding the creation that bestows happiness, he established the fulfillment of his birth.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mental Creation of Sanaka and Others, Their Qualities, Abodes, and the Manifestation of the Vedas," within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
