Chapter 20 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the excellence of the virtuous, for the good bestow eyes upon me; they are my heart.
By such holy men, the path to liberation is made unceasing for me.
It was extracted and set in motion; by it, living beings are liberated.
(2) Knowledge of the Vedas, the conduct of people, and whatever rites belong to the gods and the ancestors proceed from them;
by that, living beings rejoice. (3)
Through those [virtues], the power of devotion, detachment, and various forms of auspiciousness arise;
then, being detached, they indeed attain liberation.
They belong to the lineage of the virtuous, the lineage of the seers, and follow the path of the celibate student.
By means of those [virtues], they always proceed; therefore, liberation shall be certain.
(5) Divine beings such as Sanaka and others, who have been celibates since childhood, are the virtuous ones who realize Brahman by themselves; they alone are the Supreme Lords. (6)
By the blessings of the virtuous, I indeed became Nārāyaṇa;
by the blessings of the virtuous, you became the wealth-giving Lakṣmī.
If the virtuous were to make a request, bring Lakṣmī to us.
Then I shall indeed bestow you, my beloved Lakṣmī, upon the virtuous.
(8) What else could there be that I have not already given for the sake of the good?
Since I now give you, my most cherished one, to them with such reverence. (9)

Male and female servants, the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, the abundance of objects of enjoyment and the means to attain them, as well as Lakṣmī and I myself—all these belong to Me; they are the objects of enjoyment for the virtuous, without a doubt.
When the merit accumulated over many births becomes manifest in the present, [then this occurs].
Then, by good fortune, the virtuous indeed come to their own home.
If the elders have been satisfied through many lifetimes, then those virtuous ones will joyfully come to the houses of householders for many years. (11–12)
Whatever my virtuous [relatives] desire from me— be it home, wife, wealth, or the like—
I shall undoubtedly offer all of that to them out of love.
Neither the world of Brahmā, nor Goloka, nor Vaikuṇṭha, nor even Ākṛta is [my goal].
Neither Lakṣmī, nor Ramā, nor Rādhā is superior to the virtuous for me.
O Lakṣmī! The virtuous should always be served with body and mind day after day;
the virtuous are my very limbs, and the virtuous are my own forms.
Indeed, from their toenails to the tips of their hair, they become divine in body;
the water from their feet purifies the surface of the earth, and the dust of their feet, when borne upon the head, purifies one. (16)
The soles of their feet purify even that which is held upon the chest;
indeed, the touch of their feet purifies the three worlds.
Massaging their feet, once begun, is indeed easy to perform. (17–18)
When one places the feet of the virtuous upon one's own head,
the entire body becomes purified and becomes a vessel for liberation.
By licking their feet, the self is cleansed of all sin.
By massaging their calves, one becomes a servant to them as a sovereign; by massaging their thighs, one becomes a king ruling over all;
and by massaging their hips, one will certainly become the lord of the three worlds. (1.19.20–21)
By massaging their backs, one shall attain the station of Parameṣṭhin;
by massaging their hands, one shall attain the Vairāja station;
and by rubbing their limbs, one shall attain the supreme sovereignty of Viṣṇu.
Through the fulfillment of the intentions of the virtuous, one’s own everything becomes fulfilled.
(23) The body of the Blessed One is within the bodies of the virtuous; the contemplation of the Blessed One is within the contemplations of the virtuous;
the effort of the Blessed One is within the efforts of the virtuous; therefore, the truly virtuous are indeed to be propitiated. (24)
In the station of the virtuous is the power of Śrī Hari’s feet; in the hands of the virtuous is the power of Śrī Hari’s hands.
In the hearts of the virtuous is the power of Śrī Hari’s abode; in the recreation of the virtuous is the power accessible to Hari.
The mind of the virtuous is considered the very mind of Śrī Hari. (25)
The knowledge of the virtuous is considered to be knowledge of Him;
the desire of the virtuous is held to be the longing for Śrī Hari; and the work of the virtuous is regarded as that which has been performed by Śrī Hari. (26)
The channels of the virtuous are the channels of the Supreme Lord; the blood of the virtuous is the blood of the venerable Supreme Lord.
The bodily constituent of the virtuous is the constituent of the venerable Supreme Lord; the breath of the virtuous is the vital air of the venerable Supreme Lord.
(27) The eye of the virtuous is the eye of the venerable Supreme Lord; the ear of the virtuous is the ear of the venerable Supreme Lord.
The mouth of the virtuous is the mouth of the glorious Supreme Lord; the tongue of the virtuous is the tongue of the glorious Supreme Lord.
(28) The food of the virtuous is the food of the glorious Supreme Lord; that which is to be grasped by the virtuous is what is obtainable from the glorious Supreme Lord.
The enjoyment of the virtuous is the enjoyment of the glorious Supreme Lord; through association with the virtuous, even an ordinary object becomes divine. (29)
The saintly are always equal to the Blessed Lord; they grant liberation to those who have come for refuge.
They indeed instantly cleanse all sins and bestow infinite merits.
(1.19.30) For the skin of the saintly is truly equal to the divine syllable *oṃ*.
The bestowals of joy resulting from tactile sensations may occur;
however, for the virtuous, the attainment of the union of all the sense faculties should be understood as the nourishing factor that grants liberation. (31)
Indeed, he by whom a son— a good son who purifies his lineage— was obtained from among the virtuous,
was himself born from the body of Hari.
He is indeed equal to the virtuous and equal to Hari. (32) He by whom the grace of the lotus-face of the virtuous has been obtained here is a vessel for liberation.
He by whom the entire body of the virtuous has been touched possesses all happiness. (33)
People, placing the gift of food for the virtuous at the forefront,
receive the favor of the virtuous as they partake of most excellent and delicious delicacies presented with their sense of taste.
For those who accept the excellent gifts well-bestowed by their disciples,
every aesthetic flavor (rasa)— whether sweet or otherwise— once accepted, would attain a state devoid of qualities (nirguṇabhāva).
Likewise, form (rūpa), when seen as having a beautiful, fair, and gentle appearance, would indeed attain a state devoid of qualities.
Indeed, that sound which is heard by the virtuous attains divinity through association with the good;
likewise, that touch which is performed by holy men [attains the same].

Indeed, through association with the virtuous, he becomes a bestower of liberation. (36) But the fragrance which is held by the virtuous when they grasp it becomes truly free from qualities and is celestial;
however, the mere intention of the virtuous, once awakened, bestows liberation, grants merit, and is fully prosperous. (37)
Whatever seat is occupied by the virtuous, whatever vehicle, or likewise the bodies of beasts and birds,
and whatever [place] the holy ones occupy to attain a measure of happiness— that indeed leads to liberation.
(38) If the virtuous experience happiness within the bodies of both the insentient and the sentient, [it leads to liberation].
Understand that through union with Him, each respective insentient thing attains sentience and becomes divine, having reached perfect liberation.

(1.19.3) That house in which the touch of the soles of the feet of the virtuous is obtained is a beloved divine abode. That object upon which the touch of the hands of the virtuous falls is indeed a divine thing. (1.19.40)
Speech that is employed in the praise of the virtuous attains divinity and does not lead to bondage.
Through association with the virtuous, the mouth and the breath of one here always become pure and divine.
[4.1] Whatever bodily organ, instrument, individual limb, or the body as a whole—
Whatever may be obtainable through the use of the virtuous, let that indeed be divine and conducive to liberation.
Whether they be excellent golden ornaments for the body to be enjoyed, or silver and other such fine jewels, or whatever garments made of silk or cotton there may be, in all their various kinds— 43.
There are fragrant oils for anointing, sandalwood paste for smearing and worship,
and beautiful, sweet-smelling flowers.
Those things offered to the virtuous obtain a threefold merit.
Oh, what more can I say regarding this distinction?
For the virtuous sanctify all things!
[He perceives] sinful, extremely wicked, impure, deceitful, and base living beings dominated by darkness;
as well as the lords of creatures (Prajāpatis), Manus, gods, sages, and ancestors, each existing separately. 45.
The Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and Asuras;
the Kiṃpuruṣas, Apsarases, Kinnaras, and Uragas; as well as the Mātṛs, Piśācas, Rakṣases, Bhūtas, Pretas, and Vināyakas. (46–47)
Vetālas, those possessed by madness, and Kūṣmāṇḍas, as well as the seizing spirits of the elderly and children;
cattle, wild animals, birds, trees, mountains, and reptiles—
all stationary and moving beings, and those dwelling on earth, in water, and in the sky.
Whether they be of pure nature, mixed nature, passionate, or dark,

all living beings— whether auspicious or inauspicious, and whether overwhelmed by merit or demerit— the virtuous purify through their intentions and lead others to liberation by their very sight. (1.19.49–50)
Through association they make one divine; through service they make one prosperous;
through their words they make one a lord; and through their company they make one peaceful.
Their excellence should be understood according to this sequence, and the sequence is determined by the measure of knowledge.
O Lotus-born One, listen as I explain the sequence according to devotion.
Among these living beings, grass and such are superior to us;
from them, food, medicinal herbs, and so forth are superior; and from those, climbing plants are superior.
Beyond those are the excellent celestial trees, such as the mango and others;
beyond the immobile beings are the mobile ones, which are indeed the subtle creatures.
Among them, ants are superior, and even more so are locusts and the like.
From those [plants] come the bees and others; from them, the sparrows and so forth are considered superior.
From those come the hares and others; from them, the goats and others are superior.
From those come humans, among whom the four castes are the most excellent.

Among them, the Brāhmaṇas are considered the best; among those, the ones devoted to Dharma are the best. Among them, the possessors of knowledge (jñānins) are the best; and among those knowers of truth, ten million gods are the best. The ancestors (pitṛs) are superior to the gods, and the sages (ṛṣis) are the highest among them.
Even superior to the sages is he who possesses exclusive devotion (ekāntika-bhakti).
Among exclusive devotees, the most excellent is the abode of virtuous qualities, who has offered his entire self and is dedicated to the state of being the Blessed One (bhagavattva). ||58-59||
The son born from the lap of Śrī Hari is a saintly person, a vessel of virtuous qualities;
the disciple born from a portion of Śrī Hari is indeed a true person and an heir.
His inheritance is liberation (mukti), and he who possesses that share is a saint; he is indeed Lord Hari himself. (1.19.60)
He is considered to be the lineage of Hari, the clan of Hari, and the very form of Hari.
He is not small nor inferior; he is directly Hari himself, and therefore he does not differ from Hari.
There is no one superior to him, for Hari eternally resides within him.
Having understood this gradation, those who take refuge in Hari are to be highly honored;
for those who have directly taken refuge in Hari are indeed the very heart and soul of Hari.
Those virtuous and gentle ones remain in Hari through a state of non-dual conduct.
The divine ascetics, virtuous ones who are the very embodiments of Śrī Hari himself,
become equal to the inhabitants of Janaloka and always delight the people.
[They do so] during sitting, reclining, eating snacks, dining, and even the smearing of vessels.
Those who please people during amusements, journeys, laughter, play, living together, embracing, looking upon one another, festivals, riding in vehicles,
and in activities that delight the mind— [66] — [they are the true friends].

O Lakṣmī! By always pleasing them, eternal happiness arises. (67) They are by nature inclined toward helping others; they take the welfare of others as their own body; they accomplish the goals of others, bestow liberation, and are the saviors of living beings. (68)
Those devotees of Hari are saintly; they bring welfare to all living beings, are ever-forgiving, worthy of worship, and deserving of honor because they are superior to one's own cherished interests.
By taking refuge in the saintly, even the sinful become possessed of merit.

By serving the virtuous, noble women and men attain the supreme goal. (1.19.70) Through the constant renunciation of body, wealth, and mind before the holy ones, or even by the offering of one's entire being, liberation occurs without a doubt. (1.19.71)
Those who are indeed born under the influence of the virtuous and have come under their sway lead others to the supreme liberation that is to be attained by means of their own power.
Since my two eyes are fixed upon seeing them, and since my mind is inclined toward them, [I am devoted to them].
That my two ears are well-situated for hearing the accounts of divine deeds;
that my nose is esteemed for perceiving the fragrance arising from union with your form; and that my tongue exists for chanting your praises and my palate for tasting them. ||73||
My lips indeed grant supreme bliss during the act of kissing my form; their skin always touches my most excellent and stainless bimba-fruit [lips].
For them, nothing other than embracing me is considered superior.
Indeed, for those very beings who are virtuous, I always provide protection, because they are mine.
I always perform service for them and I also always offer them devotion;
therefore, O devoted wife, I am forever flourishing together with you.
Just as I am, so indeed you must always perform service to them;
for by that very service I shall be served— even more than through the threefold practice of devotion to one’s husband—
whether it be mental, physical, or verbal, just as I have been served.
In that way, those virtuous ones should always be served; it will ever bring you well-being.
Through their words of blessing, there shall indeed be no separation between them and me at any time, O Kamalā! Therefore, they must be served by you.
I bow down repeatedly to those who are always worthy of worship, always worthy of honor, my constant attendants, and who have renounced everything for my sake.
For the virtuous, desire is not for the sake of pleasure, nor is greed for the sake of self-interest.
Anger does not result in agitation, nor does delusion lead to bondage. (1.19.80) Intoxication does not lead to pride, nor does hope produce craving.
Rivalry leads to the acquisition of good qualities, and compassion serves to remove suffering. (81)
Thus, indeed, for the sake of assisting others in every way,
the virtuous possess those natures which always bring about happiness and liberation.
Therefore, the divine virtuous ones are likewise intent upon helping others day after day.
"I declare that I, the Blessed One, dwell within the act of helping others.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Holy Men Sanaka and Others," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 19. *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*).
Chapter 20 [Author:
Chapter 21 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, granter of fearlessness to the worlds!
Just as virtuous groups of celibate men (*brahmacārin*) are to be served daily, are virtuous celibate women likewise worthy of service or not? (1)
By these means, the liberation of living beings shall indeed become certain.
Service to spiritual teachers of the same lineage is indeed the cause of delight;
for women, however, virtuous and truthful female teachers are the givers of liberation.
In bathing, massaging, drinking, eating, reclining, providing wealth,
in conversation, touching, traveling, driving, sporting, honoring,
embracing, adorning, beauty, eroticism, and the movement of the body; ||| 4 || [all these are performed through his grace.]
In jest, in festival, in assembly, and in exile;
in knowledge, in making known, in the heart, in the body, and in worldly estimation;
in the menses, in purification, in a vow, in the acquisition of learning, and in the forest. (5–6)
In the house or in the forest, on land or at night, by day or when alone among people;
during rites for the gods or ancestors, in thick crowds, or while worshipping a deity;
likewise during cleaning, purification, impurity due to birth or death, sleep, fainting, or even while dancing.
In marriage, in calamity, in speech, in solitude, or in exile;
in flight, in meeting with a female companion, in the recitation of Vedic mantras and the like,
in the reception of those seeking refuge, and in remaining in a state of nakedness— (8–9)
"By her gestures, a woman is always to be properly served as a guru;
for a virtuous and faithful wife becomes a great teacher without doubt through her lack of reserve. Therefore, tell me: do virtuous women exist, or do they not?"
"Knowing which, women shall become auspicious to the world and always worthy of worship.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall explain this unsurpassed question that you have asked."
Many virtuous maidens were created by Brahmā as bestowers of liberation.
Indeed, they possess uncut locks of hair, remain unmarried, are eternally twelve years of age, and never experience menstruation. (12–13)
May they always be free from the seasonal menses, eternally devoted to Brahman,
virtuous, dedicated to righteous dharma, and emerged from the limbs of the embodiment of Brahman.
Therein lies the principal Mahāgītā, which is identical in form to Nārāyaṇa.
She is of the nature of Brahman, become one with Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
divine, composed of liberation, liberated, and established within the form of Śrī Hari;
in a liquid state, eternally peaceful, and supremely filled with eternal bliss. (15–16)
The Lord Hari, the self-effulgent Supreme Master,
brought forth from his own heart the singular Gītā-kumārikā,
who consists of all splendor and is beautiful in every limb. (17)
She fulfills all desires and is worthy of the highest human goals;
she is divine, beautiful, twelve years of age, fortunate, and auspicious.
She is filled with bliss in every single limb and is perfectly firm in all her limbs.
She whose form is endowed with all limbs well-constructed and perfectly joined;
she who bestows all illumination, who grants liberation to all, and who is beloved;
she who consists of all knowledge, who is delightful, and who showers the nectar of light.
[She is] endowed with all virtues, entitled to the devotion of all,
the destroyer of heaps of sins, filled with awakening,
possessing beauty proportionate to her form, and bringing happiness to those who take refuge in her. (21–22)
For those who, by whatever means possible, approach their own surrender,
there is the divine refuge of Śrī Hari, which leads them [to Him] and bestows liberation;
[it is for those] who bear the single body situated within the fourteen openings.
She is the embodiment of Brahman, attaining the Supreme Brahman by mere resort to it.
Śrī Hari always abides in the Imperishable Brahman;
there, within that eternal Hari, she shines forth as the form of eternal knowledge.
She indeed goes everywhere together with Śrī Hari;
wherever the manifestation of Hari occurs, there she goes.
Accompanied by Śrī Hari, Gītā certainly proceeds in her embodied form.
Sometimes she abides within the form of the Blessed One, and sometimes she exists outside;
she moves through heaven, earth, and the beautiful netherworld, bestowing supreme liberation.
She always dwells as the radiant one who destroys all sin.
She is virtuous, devoted to the conduct of the righteous, and a perfect guardian of the dharma of the good;
she dwells within the hearts of the wise and is the embodiment of higher knowledge.
She is remembered as one whose character and vows are Brahman, who removes all faults, and who bestows purity.

Eternally pure, always awakened, and possessing a form forever free from defect—she is the supreme Goddess Nārāyaṇī, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa. Indeed, in the beginning, Śrī Hari himself brought forth that virtuous lady from his own self. (1.20.30–31)
It was offered to those liberated ones residing in the abode of Brahman for the attainment of bliss;
thereafter, it was offered to the Lords for the sake of obtaining liberation;
and from that point on, it has been perpetually offered even to individual souls for the granting of release.

As long as the arrangement of the creation, fashioned by Māyā, persists, she—the Gītā—remains there throughout that entire creation, virtuous and well-nourished. When the Blessed Lord sends forth the Gītā, it leads to the lower state. (33–34)
Then, as Gītā prayed to the Lord for her own protection,
Hari said, "Let no one deceive me;
let it be so," and He indeed provides every kind of protection for Gītā.
Thousands and tens of thousands of female attendants of the Gītā were indeed produced;
they were of the same nature as the Gītā, and all of them were identical in form and equal in qualities to her. (36–37)
All songs are indeed liberated; others are celibate students who grant desired boons.
They grant liberation, bestow merit, and are meritorious, pure, sanctifying, and supreme.
These female attendants sing in service to the Great Goddess, the Mistress of Song.
The Mahāgītā, the Gītās, and likewise other Anugītās—
beautiful, world-beautifying, embodied, and exceedingly powerful—
they always wander here in this sphere as virtuous female renunciants.
For women addicted to sin and likewise for male sinners;
for children, Śūdras, and those of the lowest castes who cause the intermixture of castes;
and for those burdened by the sins of ancestors, gods, deities, Yakṣas, spirits, and mortals.

The Gītās, which deliver all beings— including those possessed by spirits, vetālas, kūṣmāṇḍas, nāgas, and serpents, as well as those dwelling in darkness— whether moving or stationary, and whether characterized by qualities, actions, or names,
move about within the sphere of the world as virtuous women.

To those with divine vision, they are always directly perceptible; however, to sinful beings who lack such vision, they consist of knowledge and sound. Indeed, these auspicious [energies] exist as the essence of the scriptures of knowledge and are easily accessible.
Taking refuge in them, they cross the ocean of existence.
Whether situated in sexual union, established in the menstrual flow, in the state of childbirth, or in a state of impurity;
whether resting on their husband’s lap, on another’s lap, or reclining upon a bed of passion. || 45–46 ||
In times of misfortune, they fall into the hands of others or are ruined by their own lack of refinement; dependent on fate and dependent on others, they rely upon the trappings of actors;
they are like outcasts in dance and drama, performing tasks that cause their undertakings to collapse. (47)
They are like groups of celestial nymphs, courtesans, women whose husbands are hidden away, and those who kill their children;

they are devoid of devotion to their husbands and other virtues, lacking in righteousness, blinded by intoxication, devoted to liquor and meat, fallen from their proper state, and swollen with pride in their dwellings and homes. (48–49)

All those women who are enslaved— causing calamities such as poverty, bestowing the enjoyments of others, and giving rise to the destruction of embryos, the loss of husbands, and the ruin of virtue and desire— cross over them by taking refuge in the Gītā. (1.20.50) [And those] born of the destruction of dharma and desire.
Indeed, their defects perish through taking refuge in the Goddess Gītā.
There is no sin whatsoever, nor is there any great defect;
there is no base action that the Gītā would not purify. (51–52)
Whichever body it assumes, that [Jñānagītā] is revealed; indeed, it is considered to be named after each of those [bodies], consisting essentially of the word "knowledge" (jñāna).
And for the sake of the seers (ṛṣis), the sages (munis), and likewise those who know the Supreme Brahman—
Of the gods, of the preceptors of the gods, of the humans who dwell in celestial chariots,
of the incarnations of Śrī Hari, and of the knowers of the Lord—
because they are infinite, no end to these Gītās is indeed found.
There are the Brahmagītā, the Muktagītā, and likewise the supreme Viṣṇugītā;
there is the Gītā composed by Nārāyaṇa, and then the Harigītā devoted to Him.
There are also the Satīgītā and the Vadhūgītā; indeed, such songs exist by the millions.
By taking refuge in them, even a barbarian immediately becomes pure.
Having flung open the door of the heart, she destroys internal desires,
gladdens the self, and elevates that supreme abode.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, the Gītā— which is a purifier of sins for women,
the destroyer of worldly existence, the bestower of liberation, and the grantor of union with Brahman—
should always be served. Thus has it been told to you, O virtuous one, together with its own commentary.
"Bestowing liberation along with her friends who sing other songs, [she is] the Great Song (Mahāgītā).

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Majesty of the Great Song of the Great Satī Sādhvī Who Bestows Liberation," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 20. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*).
Chapter 21 [Author:
Chapter 22 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Are there other virtuous women besides Gītā, or not?
O Lord, Teacher of the World, tell me for the sake of the welfare of the world!
(1) Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Indeed, the Upaniṣads are even more excellent and more beloved than the virtuous Gītās;
they are virtuous and, by providing refuge, they grant liberation.
By serving them, one quickly becomes absorbed in the form of Hari. (2)
They bestow the form of Brahman and bring about non-difference from Brahman.
Furthermore, they were manifested by Śrī Hari himself, who dwells in the abode of the Imperishable Brahman, from the essence of the supreme bliss of his own true nature. (3–4)
Others were liberated, possessing divine forms characterized by their similarity to Brahman:
with golden hair, golden eyebrows, and golden eyeballs;
with jasmine-like teeth and the radiant redness of lotus petals upon their lips. (5)
Their excellent cheeks shine with red lotuses within;
they are enchanting with gentle smiles and the beauty of their golden-hued faces;
and they are exquisitely beautiful with breasts shaped like small citron fruits upon their chests. (6–7)
Their beautiful hands were endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
they had slender waists, narrow middles, firm thighs, and excellent lotus-like feet.
Always practicing celibacy, they remained unmarried and pure.
Those who are called Upaniṣads are the inexhaustible oceans of knowledge.
(9) Likewise, the lords, the individual souls, and whoever else moves within the realm of the self, attain the supreme liberation of Brahman by taking refuge in the Upaniṣads. (1.21.10)
Those who have not yet reached the bloom of youth, who are celibate students and self-sacrificing, wander through the worlds in the form of virtuous women; they are abodes of compassion.
There are countless such women in the form of virtuous wives, as well as those whose very nature is wisdom.
Having known this, those women who have taken refuge attain the supreme goal.
Goddesses, divine beings, humans, and those born of the earth—
even those fallen and sinful— attain liberation by taking refuge in her.
Merely by being remembered, these ones of great power cause one to reach the world of Brahmā.
All the virtuous Upaniṣads should be resorted to by those seeking liberation, through the bestowing of self-knowledge and the imparting of the Brahma-mantra. (14)
By granting refuge, they constantly deliver themselves;
by the practice of destroying craving and by the dissolution of latent impressions, and by bestowing self-contentment, they constantly deliver themselves. (15–16)
By the destruction of the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*), by the burning away of their causes,
and indeed by the dispelling of darkness, they constantly deliver themselves;
through the attainment of direct perception of their own self and through the union of the individual self with Brahman.
By bringing about the state of Brahmanhood, they constantly deliver themselves;
and by bestowing eternal bliss and by maintaining perpetual contentment,
they indeed cause themselves constant happiness through the attainment of the fullness of all rasa.
By bestowing omniscience, by fulfilling all desires,
and by manifesting their nature as the self of all, they delight themselves incessantly;
likewise, by granting residence in the same world as Hari and by bringing about his creative manifestation.
By the very attainment of similarity [of form], they cause their own selves to rejoice incessantly;
and by the very attainment of union (*sāyujya*), as well as by the achievement of oneness, they taste the acquisition of the nectar of Brahman incessantly. (21–22)
Until the realization of the Self as Brahman, through the arrival of the vision of Brahman and through direct experience, they constantly liberate the self;
those virtuous women, whose nature is to assist others, are bestowers of liberation. (23)
In every way, they are to be served by me and by you as well, again and again.
Indeed, those who reside in all abodes are lords created by the Lord;
they are living beings situated within the cosmic egg of living beings, resting upon the Upaniṣads.
Likewise, there were countless divine and virtuous maidservants born of Brahman— various Upaniṣads in diverse forms—
who offered praise to the Supreme Brahman and expounded upon the Supreme Brahman. (26)
They are the entire essence of the supreme Brahman’s purpose, the traditions for attaining the supreme Brahman;
(27) all are divine, beautiful in form, and equal in splendor to the Upaniṣads;
all are twelve years of age and move gracefully through the entire creation. (28)
The infinite goddesses who are the Śrutis arise from each individual limb of the divine form of Śrī Hari; they are considered to bestow liberation through their being held in mind.
They possess manifold meanings and manifold forms; they are both with form and devoid of form.
Golden-hued, tawny, and possessing the brilliance of refined gold;
white, pale, and red, as delicate as lotus petals—
these [waters] are exquisite and destroyers of sin through resorting to them and likewise through hearing of them.
The Gītās, the Upaniṣads, and the Śrutis have always taken up their residence in the supreme, imperishable abode, existing there in their liberated forms.
Nevertheless, they were indeed requested by the Creator (Brahmā) to descend from that abode here [to this world].
Having arrived at the supreme truth, they dwell eternally in the world.
Their creation is indeed infinite, with countless abodes and so forth; their riches are priceless, reaching even to the summit of the highest realm.
These goddesses are always divine, always maidens, and always virgins;
they are to be meditated upon, worshipped, contemplated, and served daily.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Virtuous Woman Consisting of the Upanishadic Revelation," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Likewise, there are other supreme vidyās that grant excellent liberation;
they are innumerable, supremely truthful, virtuous, and twelve years in duration. (1)
The supreme sciences that bestow nirvāṇa, by which Brahmā is attained—
those sciences were manifested by Hari through his two eyes.
They are divine, embodied, brilliantly luminous, radiant, and most delicate.
The virtuous women are filled with the bliss of knowledge and bring about the attainment of Brahman.
(3) They are fortunate, of radiant complexion, and possess great beauty;
they are endowed with a fullness of limbs that is free from the emergence of [adolescent] youth. (4)
They were wondrous, gentle, and peaceful, possessing forms characterized by the quality of sattva;
they bore locks of hair as golden as their nails, with beauty corresponding to their physical forms;
their breasts were concealed, their waists were slender, and their bodies were filled with fragrance.
Unblinking, with gentle smiles, perfectly tranquil and changeless;
(6) having attained eternal omniscience, their minds possess the power of true resolve; they are destroyers of ignorance and endowed with the capacity for attraction. (7)
Awakening all people and destroying inner darkness, they lead them to the imperishable abode; bestowing immortality, they are ever victorious.
Indeed, they bring serenity to the very essence of life.
Beholding the form of the Supreme Self,
marrying their own who have come for refuge,
and repeatedly liberating them, they are ever victorious. (9)
Proclaiming their own nature as bliss,
manifesting their vast essential form,
and causing one to well-drink the desired, excellent nectar of Hari.
They cause [the souls] to enter into absorption in the form of Hari,
manifesting the nature of Hari-Kṛṣṇa and illuminating the lamps of inner wisdom.
Wiping away the webs of subtle dust, they lead [beings] to the state of the world of the imperishable realm;
together with the splendor of the imperishable, they bring about cessation.
Thoroughly satisfying [the senses] with flavors equal to those of Hari-Kṛṣṇa,
bringing about delight equal to that of Hari-Kṛṣṇa,
and causing one to ascend to the supreme goal of the Blessed Lord. || 1 2 ||
The Akṣividyā, Madhuvidyā, Pañcāgnividyā, Daharavidyā, and other such great sciences beginning with the Udgītha— all those which reside in Hari—
became virtuous maidens and appeared throughout millions of universes. (13)
Wandering among men and women, they indeed swiftly bring about liberation.
They should always be worshipped like Brahman, served like Brahman, meditated upon constantly like Brahman, and attained as those who are dear to Brahman. (14–15)
There are indeed millions of attendants to those Brahma-vidyās;
they are called the beloveds of Brahman, for they abide in the imperishable Brahman.
All of them are beloved of Brahman, possessing the form of Brahman, and having the very body of Brahman.
Consisting of Brahman, having the body of Brahman, and united with the identity of Brahman,

these virtuous women, whose very nature is goodness, wander throughout the worlds of the Lord and the worlds of living beings, as far as the Great Abode (Mahālaya), for the sake of liberation. (1.7–1.8)
Their maidservants, female friends, and other female slaves, as well as their attendants—

all of them, numbering in the tens of millions and remaining ever-virgin, are bestowers of liberation. Through service to them they grant prosperity, and by taking refuge in them they bestow the highest good.
Therefore, one should certainly serve virtuous women who are celibate from within their inner self. From the god Śrī Hari, who was entreated by Brahmā,
there appeared from his eye at Naimiṣa millions upon billions of female companions who are dear to Brahmā.
All these female attendants are declared to be the nurturers of the Great Vidyā.

For the sake of liberation, they should be worshipped, honored, and served by women. (22) Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Majesty of the Holy Women Consisting of Supreme Knowledge and Their Female Attendants Who are the Beloveds of Brahmā," in the first section, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (22)

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Beloved of my life, Great Lord!
O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you; I have certainly been delivered by you. || 1 ||
But I see, O Brahmin, that the Blessed One is victorious!
What mantra is being chanted by the Blessed One, the Supreme Self?
(2) Your devotees always chant you; indeed, there is no other vessel for chanting.

"O Lord, you are to be chanted by all; seeing this, the thought arises in me: 'Whom else does he chant? O Beloved, please resolve this for me! Having heard that from his wife, Nārāyaṇa spoke the truth as it is.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess, to my secret which brings about all auspiciousness;
I alone am the true vessel for all auspiciousness, of this there is no doubt.
I myself am indeed the one to be recited by all; there is no doubt that I exist even therein.
Nevertheless, for the sake of instructing the world, I recite my own mantra.
Vāsudeva, Mahāviṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other progenitors of creation [are likewise within me].
As soon as [the mantra] had been correctly generated by me, they in turn requested me for the recitation of the mantra;
therefore, the power consisting of my own form was manifested from my body. (7–8)
Inferior to me, yet identical to my own nature, possessing my sovereignty and having me as her very self;
she is divine, attracting [all] through meditation, and bestowing peace through recitation.
She consists of beauty and splendor, delightful, and beautiful with every form of fortune.

Seeing that twelve-year-old girl, who was endowed with the power of liberation, all those who were liberated as well as the other lords were bewildered; at that moment, they indeed became utterly perplexed as to what should be done. (1.23.10–11)
By me, for the sake of protection alone, this Gāyatrī was chanted by myself as a maiden;
she is thus fully proclaimed as Gāyatrī, and the lords of the gods chant her.
Those who chant and worship my form, which is indeed Gāyatrī—
Having burned away the mine of their own karma, they attain my state.
(12) Gāyatrī prayed to me: "O Lord, do not forget me!
May I always be protected by you and thereby become strong. (14)
"O Hari! If you do not grant me the power to burn away the evil deeds of the wicked, how then will you be able to do so?
Therefore, I granted you this boon: 'I shall indeed always remember you.'"
Then, by my command, the goddess Gāyatrī went everywhere—
throughout the worlds of the lords and even through all the living universes.
That venerable maiden Gāyatrī, virtuous and the radiance of my own body, [pervaded them all].
Visible to those with divine eyes, yet invisible to those with dull eyes,
she exists as the means of deliverance for those who recite [the mantra].
She is well-formed in the shape of a maiden, the embodiment of knowledge, and resides within the heart.
Consisting of sound and suitable for recitation, its establishment is threefold.
(19) But when the Vedas were received by Brahmā from my presence, they were then extracted by me from Gāyatrī and bestowed upon him. (1.23.20)

Therefore, she has attained the status of being celebrated as the "Mother of the Vedas" (Vedamātā). Many other Gāyatrīs and others as well have been manifested by me through a mere fraction of my power for the sake of her service, appearing as if they were my own bodies. (21)
In the various worlds and spheres, those [forms] of mine are considered to have distinct designations,
distinct successions, and distinct forms.
All of them exist as attendants of the primary Gāyatrī by the millions.
Not yet stirred by the agitation of youth, delicate and with their inner selves unblemished, these great virtuous women wander about; indeed, they grant liberation to those who recite prayers.
Endowed with the splendor of Brahman, they are the very embodiments of Brahman and bestowers of the yoga of Brahman.
Those whose nature is Brahman indeed dwell in the supreme truth, the auspicious world;
they are all-knowing and all-perceiving, and wherever people remember them,
they swiftly approach there and purify their own practitioners of recitation (jāpaka).
Whether they be living beings, lords, gods, yakṣas, or even other rākṣasas—
whether they be sinful, addicted to sin, or characterized by the qualities of darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas)—
these [mantras] liberate those various men who worship these women from their evil.
They protect those who travel with them and lead them to nirvāṇa.
(28) Thus, O Goddess, the reason for reciting [your name] has been declared to you.
O Lakṣmī, I always recite you so that you may likewise recite me. (29)
"O Goddess, I, the Blessed One, constantly chant for my devotees;
my devotees constantly chant for me—thus we chant for one another.
Indeed, I perform this chanting for the sake of protecting them. (1.23.30)
"O Goddess, they perform recitation for me in order to attain liberation.
(31) Now, no recitation whatsoever occurs without speech; therefore, speech must be employed. And how can that [speech] exist without phonemes? (32)"
Those who had arisen as lords were indeed unable to speak;
observing the vow of knowledge, they remained silent, devoid of verbal discourse.
Even Brahmā and the others, maintaining their silence, praised the imperishable Śrī Hari.

Having understood this praise of silence, Hari himself, the master of speech, brought forth a divine maiden from the region at the tip of his own tongue. Once born, she asked the Lord, "What shall be my task? || 34–35 ||
To that Goddess, who was desiring to know [him] and who consisted of his own self-power (svātmaśakti),
the Lord gave back the power called Prasāra;
having made her into the very form of speech (vāksvarūpā), she indeed became Sarasvatī.
Taking up a divine lute, she played it again and again;
she went everywhere throughout the world, both among the lords and the common folk. In every manifestation, she assumed various forms in order to enter.
Those infinite millions of female embodiments of speech, the daughters of Śarada— maidens and young girls beyond counting, born from the forms of Hari—
all of them became handmaidens and servants of the Gāyatrīs. (39)
The sounds were sweet, pleasant, resonant, and clear;
they were fierce, loathsome, pathetic, comic, base, and terrifying.
They were divine and non-divine, subtle and gross, and endowed with manifold meanings. (1.23.40–41)
All of them were twelve years of age, having assumed various forms;
they were uninjured, unerring, auspicious, and endowed with wealth. They were of excellent form, consisting of the nature of knowledge, and of the nature of speech—thus they were threefold.
Virtuous women endowed with moral conduct and vows are to be served for the sake of liberation.
Without me, there can be no liberation; the Sarasvatīs are my very self, and they, whose tongues are mine and whose sovereignty is mine, are my own bodies.
Those who consist of the traditional collection of all phonemes and whose essence is Sarasvatī should always be worshipped, always served, and always meditated upon for the sake of liberation.
Just as I am all-pervasive, so too is that Speech (Vāṇī) all-pervasive through her.
One who is proficient in the Śabdabrahman attains the Supreme Brahman.
From my [the Supreme] Brahman arises *vimarśa* (reflective awareness); from *vimarśa* comes the *bindu*;
from the *bindu*, the *nāda* is produced; and from the *nāda*, indeed, the various sounds (*dhvanayaḥ*) are said to arise.
Indeed, the arrangements of syllables arising from sound, which are endowed with the Brahman of *sphoṭa*,
become the Great Goddesses of Speech, the Sarasvatīs, among people.
Endowed with the nature of the virtuous, they truly liberate their own dependents.
Those who have served [the lineage] of Brahmā attain the supreme abode.
In the highest world of Brahmā, in the realm of truth, there are divine worlds, forests, varieties of enjoyments, and indeed infinite objects. (1.23.50)
For their sake, he indeed ordained inconceivable cities,
as well as vehicles, mounts, musical instruments, objects of enjoyment, and inexhaustible drinks;
yet, O Sundara, there is nothing in that world superior to those, so it seems to me.
"O beloved! You have awakened Vāsas in the midst of Sarasvatī.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 25 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, in the past great creation, within the cosmic egg of the Supreme Lord,
while the Lord Nārāyaṇa was reclining upon the Ocean of Milk,
there was a maiden born from his eleven senses who is the destroyer of the Dānavas.
That great virtuous lady was born during the Mahālaya festival on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī).
Subsequently, she attained dissolution into the form of Nārāyaṇa;
[so too did] the splendors consisting of the capacities of the senses belonging to that Lord.
Nārāyaṇa himself always resides within those forms at the commencement of the great creation, for the sake of the vows of the lords.
Those maidens were richly endowed with a golden complexion, divine, twelve years of age, perfect in all their limbs and beauty, and possessed of the splendor of asceticism. (5)
He made them manifest; and those [disciplines], devoted solely to Lord Nārāyaṇa, were offered by the Blessed One to the lords for the sake of the vow. 6.
They are not inferior to Nārāyaṇa; they are of great power in bestowing liberation.
Adorned with liberation, they abide in the supreme, imperishable abode of Brahmā.
Having performed that vow, the lords attain liberation in the imperishable state.
They possess bodies of Brahman, the form of Brahman, and are endowed with the sovereignty of Brahman.

All these women bestow liberation through Brahman; they are the Brahmanīs, the givers of Brahman. When they were requested by the Creator (Vedhas) to come into his own creation, then I, as Nārāyaṇa, appeared in an instant.
I became self-restrained for the sake of destroying the great haters known as Mura.
O Dānava, as long as I sleep there in the Ocean of Milk, a most terrible and powerful one named Mura has arrived. (11)

For the sake of battle and for his destruction, I manifested a spear; it was empowered by the strength of the eleven sense organs. This enchanting and beautiful maiden was increased in splendor by me.

Svarṇasundarī was sent for the destruction of the Dānava. As she was going to bring about his end, the Asura saw her; he fell into a state of infatuation, chose her, and desired her repeatedly. (13–14)
Then, addressed by the maiden: "O wicked one! Having conquered both Nārāyaṇa and me in battle, take a wife; otherwise, your desire shall not be fulfilled. (15)
As soon as that Dānava, having heard this, began to fight in his delusion, his head was already severed by the maiden with her sword. (16)
He fell there upon the earth and died, not rising again.
From that time forward, O Lakṣmī, I have granted this great boon to every maiden:
"Those who perform your vow shall go to the supreme goal."
Those who perform your worship shall attain the imperishable Brahman. ||18||
Those who perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) for you shall attain heaven, which grants all desired things;
those who practice charity for you shall go to liberation, even if they are sinners. 19.
Those who bestow merit upon you shall attain the splendor of enjoyments;
whether they possess desires or are free from them, people have come to you for refuge. || 1.24.20 ||
Whether they be men, women, or others—be they gods, Daityas, or any other beings—they shall surely attain their own desired goal, including heaven and the granting of liberation. 21.
O maiden! Be the destroyer of great sins and even greater evils, the bringer of happiness, the purifier of people, and the bestower of liberation. 22.
Thus, by the attainment of this boon, she exists as the destroyer of all sins and the bestower of the path to great liberation, surpassing all others. (23)
Then that goddess said to me: "O Lord, I have been made by you as one;
yet there are many people and worlds—how can my pervasiveness [be established] therein? (24)
"Therefore, act in such a way that I may become many-formed.
Then, I bestowed upon her a most great power. (25)
From that, the twenty-four principal forms of excellent nature arose, and from them, forms of infinite bodies;
indeed, extending to the vastness of the universe, the eleventh [form] becomes one of immeasurable nature. ||26||
Then, by my own resolve, I manifested from my own form eleven Ekādaśīs again and again, numbering in the tens of millions and even infinitely.
Likewise, I have created their primary and secondary attendants in infinite numbers;
they exist everywhere throughout all the universes, bestowing liberation upon human beings. (28)
But here, in the world of Truth, that abode was fashioned by the Creator;
for virtuous women, performing austerities, dwell there as ascetics. (29)
Always possessing unimpaired auspiciousness, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, these divine maidens of twelve years of age possessed unimpaired power. (1.24.30)

Because they lead one to attain that single, perfectly prosperous state which consists of liberation, these [days] are known by the name Ekādaśī; they are the destroyers of worldly existence and the washers away of sin. //31//
Those [goddesses], whose very nature is divine form, accept worship perpetually.
You must always worship and serve those virtuous women daily, together with me. (32)
And [the power] of the lords, the gods, the sages, the beasts and birds, of humans, the Daityas, and those dwelling in water and on land. || 33 ||
Whenever my manifestation occurs within assemblies, at those times their victory becomes a complete victory along with mine. (34)
Jayā, Vijayā, Ādhānā, and my auspicious daughter Dāsī—Prākaṭyā, endowed with great power and non-different from me, have arrived. (35)
She exists in every way as the divine, auspicious bestower of victory upon her devotees;
that delicate maiden is certainly the giver of liberation to her devotees.
She is celebrated as Nārāyaṇī and Jayantī, and she is my very self.
My form is of the nature of Brahman, yet it is always identical with my own essential nature.
"Without me she does not dwell anywhere; thus, abiding with me, she is the giver of liberation, the victorious one who brings triumph. (38)
And I also bestowed upon her the power to assume many forms; consequently, she too attained the state of having many millions of manifestations. (39)
"Taking birth as these known as the Jayantīs, who are infinite in number, I indeed manifest wherever Śrī Hari is present. (1.24.40)
That Jayantī is born together with [the Lord] as a virtuous woman who bestows liberation;
furthermore, the secondary Jayantīs have been made innumerable by me. (41)
Those maidservants were always accompanied by the principal Jayantīs;
through their service, worship, and the cultivation of the practice of their vows, [they attained success]. ||42||
They liberate all people who are well-established in the creation of the Lord of Life; their dwelling is with me, and wherever I am, they abide there. (43)
In the world of Brahmā, in the world of Īśa, in the world of living beings, and likewise in the world of the Creator,
as well as in the world of truth— the divine worlds of the Jayantīs have been made stable.
Crores of Jayantīs dwell there in every way;
wherever there is a festival of Hari, they come there in their embodied forms. ||45||
They are virtuous in form, beautiful in appearance, and likewise of the nature of a festival;
they are formless and of the nature of sacred vows, and are considered in every way to be bestowers of liberation. 46.
Therefore, those who desire their own liberation must always serve the victorious ones;
likewise, through profound devotion, both men and women shall find that liberation is forever established within the palms of their hands. 47.
Thus, indeed, those who are victorious over birth, being duly honored on their birthdays, nourish their devotees—who are identical with Me—just as they honor Me. 48.
Whether pure or even impure, whoever is a devotee who observes the vow, having propitiated me through that, goes to my imperishable state. 49.
Having heard those various delightful stories, having given abundant gifts,
having performed those respective pure vows, and having worshipped them thereafter— 1.24.50.
By the grace of Śrī Hari, all those [devotees] attain the supreme goal;
they are victorious here, for they bring about the bestowing of liberation. ||51||
Gāyatrī roars constantly, Sarasvatī roars, the Ekādaśīs roar, and the Gītā roars to that same extent. (52)
As long as the Jayantīs indeed do not roar throughout the three worlds, even the roaring of other [deities] who grant liberation is not equal to that. 53.
Whatever roar there may be, it pales before the head of Kṛṣṇa-jayantī;
therefore, Hari’s Jayantī is indeed supreme for bestowing liberation. 54.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness and Other Qualities of the Ekādaśīs and Jayantīs," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. ||24||
