Śrī Lakṣmī said: O Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of the universe, O Sustainer of all, O Great Master! All your forms, beginning with Gītā, are bestowers of liberation. || 1 ||
What has been stated is indeed so; however, that [method] consists of great effort. That which is easy and accomplished without effort will bear fruit quickly. (2)
"Tell me, O Great King, that supreme and most excellent means which might exist without depending on anything else; may it be for the benefit of all. (3)

Whether by children, the elderly, or the young; by women, men, fools, or the highly learned; by the wealthy or those suffering greatly from poverty—by whomever it may have been caused [to be made]. (4)
Just as the supreme deity, the Blessed One, the Puruṣottama, is attained through spiritual practice, so too may He be attained by women; let that [method] be explained. (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: I shall now describe that Goddess, by taking refuge in whom even the Gītā and other [scriptures], though they themselves are virtuous, swiftly attain supreme liberation.

Among all virtuous things, devotion—which is the very form of the head [of the body], which is easily accomplished without effort, and which is beloved by Hari—is the mother who grants immediate and effortless liberation; she is highly esteemed by me. Indeed, at the commencement of the Lord’s creation, Vāsudeva and the others [addressed] me:
The younger brothers made their request with hearts overflowing with love.
O Nārāyaṇa, sustainer of the world, ordainer of the world's welfare!
He who is our primordial form, Śrī Hari, shines resplendent in his abode. (9)
From that form, through divine power, there manifest auspicious female energies possessing infinite powers of goodness for the welfare of embodied beings. (1.25.10)
And for them, as well as for us, the practice of unification with Śrī Hara is the most excellent refuge; whether something superior to it exists or not. ||11||
Thus questioned, I said nothing at that time; rather, it flashed clearly in my heart: "Let us go into the presence of Hari. (12)
Vāsudeva and all the other Blessed Ones, as well as the lords, went to where Hari himself, the Supreme Brahman, shines forth. ||13||
In that supreme imperishable world, having approached that touchstone,
they bowed, offered praise, prostrated like a staff, and sat down upon the ground.

He was asked "Welcome," and with joy hospitality was extended to him; we inquired after his welfare and sought to know his supreme compassion. His father, having understood our inner heart, reported it [to him]. (15)
Indeed, this is for that very purpose for which all of you have come. ||16||
I contemplate my supreme, virtuous form,
which consists of my own birth as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa,
and the Supreme Self; likewise, I create from myself a worshipful body for their wives.
For she is both embodied and unembodied; indeed, she is my auspicious body in its embodied form.

Having thus personally conceived a manifestation of birth—though formless and yet worthy of being the dwelling place for His respective selves—the Lord Śrī Hari Himself, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), [appeared]. ||19||
Having revealed his own male form, he became the embodiment of devotion;
and that goddess was most divine, auspicious, and composed of the Supreme Brahman. (1.25.20)
Gentle, delightful, and beautiful, adorned with all excellent qualities, she is endowed with every sovereignty and accompanied by all happiness—such is the Mother. (21)
The Supreme Brahman himself manifested in the form of devotion.
What deficiency could there be therein, or what could not possibly arise from that? 22.
As long as it is filled with that essence, as long as it possesses auspicious fortune, and as long as it is replete with all sovereignty—that body consists of the Supreme Brahman. (23)
Śrī Hari has assumed the form of service preceded by love;
His entire being is deposited therein, and there is not even the slightest deficiency in it. 24.
And that devotion is considered the mother of the incarnations, as well as of the Blessed Ones; it is the mother of the lords at all times, and is held to be the bringer of liberation. (25)
Devotion, however, exists everywhere as something easily accomplished; it consists of mental contemplation in general, but takes the form of love toward a conscious being. (26)
In the body, that [power] is known as the divine, consisting of oil, having the nature of action;
it is manifold, of various forms, and the binder of diverse purposes. (27)
Devotion is the virtuous Great Goddess, situated everywhere in manifold ways; for the Blessed Incarnations, the Lords, and their consorts are all her manifestations. (28)
Sages, ancestors, gods, humans, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and vināyakas— (29)
Vetālas, ḍākinīs, śākinīs, and likewise yoginīs; as well as sūtas, māgadhas, bards, bhāṭas, and cāraṇas. (1.25.30)
The Vidyādharas, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and Mārutas;
the Nāgas, Sarpas, as well as the Daityas, Dānavas, and those who are Uragas. ||31||
Furthermore, those that are stationary and those that are moving, even the animals;
those that are subtle and those that are gross, those with form and those without form, and some that are divine. (32)
In the creation, there are living beings— both those with bodies and those without bodies— who are born in the worlds,
as well as those residing in the non-worlds, in the realm of Yama, and likewise in the City of Dharma.
Whether in heaven or in hell, in celestial realms or on the earth of truth, whatever living beings exist within creation—whether sinful or meritorious—[all are subject to this]. (34)
Whether they are impure or pure, worthy recipients or unworthy, possessed of knowledge or devoid of it, they are all alike, having cast off the burden of both the knowable and the unknowable. (35)
Devotion toward them is a great saintly practice that bestows liberation; of this there is no doubt.
When that devotion takes the form of love for Śrī Hari, it grants liberation instantly. (36)
She should always be worshipped, honored, served, and held dear in the heart by all;
she should always be maintained, beheld, and meditated upon, for she bestows liberation. (37)
No other supreme goddess like her has ever been born, nor is she being born;
indeed, no other will ever be born. Devotion alone is considered the supreme mother. (38)
"Devotion alone leads all beings to union with Brahman";
having thus resolved, the Lord of All created her in the form of Sadrūpā. (39)
The beautiful beloved of Kṛṣṇa, whose form is the embodiment of supreme bliss and consciousness, the Queen of the Gods, with palms joined in reverence, asked Hari: "What shall I do? (1.25.40)
Then the Lord commanded her, "Nourish my devotees.
She accepted that command, and at that time Hari became pleased with her. ||41||
He gave her Liberation as a maidservant, and two sons, Knowledge and Dispassion;
and Devotion [as a daughter] for the abodes of Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Akṣara, and the Unmanifest. ||42||
She was nourished by attendants in the forms of the Blessed Ones and rendered eternal;
likewise, she was nourished by millions of nourished lords within the worlds of the lords. (43)
In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, she has been nourished by Nārada and others;
wherever she is united with liberation, knowledge, and dispassion, there that devotion abides in great bliss. (44)
In a time consisting of truth and untruth, in an age consisting of dharma and adharma.
Devotion, however, is considered in every way divine, powerful, and the giver of liberation;
it increases among the virtuous in every household and among every person throughout the creation. 46.
Taking liberation for himself, he indeed bestows liberation upon his own [devotees];
and those living beings who shall be endowed with devotion in age after age. (47)
Even sinners shall go to that fearless abode of Hari, in whose hearts devotion in the form of love always resides.
Those of pure form do not behold the Destroyer (Yama) even in their dreams. (48)
Neither a preta, nor a piśāca, nor a rākṣasa,
nor even an asura would be able to prevail even by the mere sight of those whose minds are endowed with devotion;
[neither] by austerities, nor by the Vedas, nor by knowledge, nor by ritual action.
Hari is attained through devotion, for Hari is the very form of devotion;
through the power of the meritorious deeds of living beings, love for devotion increases. (51)
May Hari grant devotion; Hari is devotion; through devotion, Kṛṣṇa stands before one.
Those who commit acts of hostility toward devotion perish within the three worlds. 52.
Enough with vows, enough with sacred fords, enough with yogas, and enough with sacrifices;
enough with discourses on knowledge—devotion alone is the giver of liberation. (53)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Devotion," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 25.
← Chapter 25: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā - Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 26 [[Author:
→ Chapter 27
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In brief, devotion (bhakti) should be understood as service preceded by love;
that service is always declared to be for Hari, the Lord of the abode of Brahman. 1.
Devotion performed by living beings out of desire, affection, fear, greed, pride, self-interest, or for any other reason, certainly grants liberation.
Likewise, devotion to one's wife, devotion to one's husband, and devotion toward the family circle [attain the same result].
Devotion to the country, devotion to the deity, and devotion to the Self are the forms of devotion. (3)
Indeed, devotion to Hari excels all other forms of devotion;
for the various types of devotion are many and infinite, yet they are all servants of devotion. Those millions of various devotions take refuge in devotion to Hari.
Devotion to the ancestors, devotion to the guru, and devotion to the divine beings;
(5) devotion to the Lord, devotion to the world, and likewise devotion to cows—all these forms of devotion are indeed services to Hari; such is the established truth regarding devotion. (6)
Because the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) are infinite, the forms of devotion (*bhakti*) are diverse due to the differences in their respective channels,
and also because of the differences in the degree of esteem [accorded to them].
Now, just as a maidservant, so does liberation always arise from devotion.
For in this way, service is considered a form of propitiation, and even servitude is regarded as worship. (8)
The waving of the lamp is another maidservant, and circumambulation is also a maidservant;
praise is a maidservant, meditative absorption is a servant, and salutation is a maidservant. (9)
Dhāraṇā is considered a maidservant, and Prārthanā is likewise another;
Puṣpāñjali is considered a maidservant, and all perfections (siddhis) are maidservants.
Indeed, all these are maidservants who manifest the form of Hari.
All [these forms] consist of the very form of Hari, and they arise with power equal to devotion. ||11||
Residing in the abode of Brahmā, all twelve of them are divine; some are liberated souls, and these others are indeed the very forms of Hari himself. (12)
Those who are filled with joy should always be served, honored, and respected;
for such indeed are the forms of devotion found among the lords in the worlds. (13)
Those who dwell in various abodes exist in innumerable forms;
however, those belonging to this world reside in the supreme Satya-loka of Brahmā. (14)
The various modes of worship, the services, and the commands that are prescribed—these too are well-established with the Mistress in their respective abodes. (15)
In the case of female slaves, service for the sake of propitiation serves as the means;
therefore, worship is considered to be of various kinds, well-known as honor and hospitality. (16)
The *nīrājanā* (lustration) is the *ārārtrika* (lamp-offering), which always provides protection;
for the devotee, circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*) is the movement of Hari to the right. ||17||

Praise (stuti) is said to consist of singing the multitude of virtues; hymn (stavana) is of the same nature. Samādhi is the state of remaining as if dissolved in identity with his essential nature. (18)
Salutation is the internal state of the self manifested outwardly through speech.
Concentration (dhāraṇā) is the one-pointedness of the functions of the intellect upon Śrī Hari. (19)
Prayer is considered the choosing of one's desired objects; likewise, the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) manifests the love of the heart through the medium of flowers. (1.26.20)
The supernatural powers (siddhis) are indeed aṇimā, mahimā, and likewise garimā;
laghimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitā, and likewise vaśitā. ||21||
Reasoning, verbal instruction, and likewise practice—these three are the destroyers of suffering;
as well as the acquisition of a friend, generosity, and the spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) are also considered [means].
Tārā, Sutārā, and then Tāratārā, Ramyā, Pramodā, and then Modamānā.
Indeed, [the goddesses] Sudā, Tathā, Muditā, and Salīlā are considered to possess many varieties of supernatural powers (siddhi). ||23||
Worship before Hari is a pure action for the sake of dwelling [in His presence];
obedience there is the fulfillment of His will through constant compliance. (24)
O Blessed One, all these forms have indeed been manifested by the Blessed Hari himself; they are considered to be identical with his own self and bestowers of liberation. (25)
These maidens are pure, auspicious, and the source of all blessings;
they are remembered as bestowers of divine vision upon those who take refuge in them as soon as they are called to mind. (26)
As soon as they were all born, they performed divine austerities, with the aim that their Lord Hari might always remain pleased. (27)
But by their love and austerity, Hari, the Lord and Master of the Abode, became exceedingly well-pleased and urged them toward the boon. ||28||
By means of them, auspicious boons were obtained from the presence of Śrī Hari:
namely, the fulfillment of the devotees' desires and eternal imperishability. (29)
Possessing both embodied and unembodied natures, she is the virtuous practice of dharma;
she is the imperishable state of maidenhood, existing in the form of Hari’s will. (1.26.30)
May there always be the state of being twelve years of age, the protection afforded by the service of devotion, and a supreme desire to dwell wherever the residence of Hari’s devotees is found. (31)
Residence forever in the form of Hari, possession of Hari’s own power, and the capacity for movement at will as far as the imperishable realm (akṣaradhāma). ||32||
The nature of being a divine woman, as well as being stainless—this also means being free from the fetters of māyā and being eternally liberated. ||33||
They possess the granting of great prosperity and perpetual purity;
thus, through the attainment of such boons, they rejoice and cause others to rejoice. //34//

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Attainment of the Devotion of Female Servants through Worship and Other Means," in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 26.
← Chapter 026: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā - Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 27 [[Author: → Chapter 028
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, hear now of those eternal forms of mine, which are eternally non-different from my own nature and consist of my very self. (1)
Mahālakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Rādhā, Satī,
as well as Vṛndā, the Mothers, and the maidens beginning with Gaṅgā—
having separated them from myself, I have personally sustained them as my own limbs. (2)
All these are non-different from me; like me, they are considered to be bestowers of liberation. || 3 ||
The supernatural powers reside in Śrī Hari, who is my own form, the imperishable abode;
they, being the very nature of Mahālakṣmī, have been manifested by me alone. (4)
Likewise, those supreme prosperities that exist within my very form there have indeed been manifested by me in their entirety in the form of Lakṣmī. (5)
Likewise, that very loveliness which exists there in my own form—having separated it from myself, I have made those goddesses manifest. (6)
Furthermore, whatever desires for perfection I have regarding that form of mine, those very desires have been manifested by me myself as Rādhās within my own form. (7)
Likewise, the universal existence that resides within my form there—being of the nature of reality—it is by me alone that all these have been made manifest. (8)
Likewise, my capacity for bestowing boons resides there within that form;
having separated that capacity, all the Vṛndās have been manifested. (9)
Likewise, those nourishing powers that reside within my form there have all been separated and manifested as the Mothers. (1.27.10)
Likewise, within my form there, all those [energies] whose essence is the rasa of love are to be perceived;
having indeed separated them all, the Gaṅgā and the others were manifested. (11)
All of them are free from passion (rajas), all have unimpaired wombs;
all possess eternal bodies, and all are remembered as my own forms. (12)
In my supreme, imperishable abode, they exist as truly liberated women;
and everywhere within the creation of the Lord, they exist as truly sovereign women. (13)
In the world of living beings, in the supreme reality, those women exist as goddesses; likewise, they dwell in every layer, having the nature of their respective functions. 14.
Mahālakṣmī is the embodiment of prosperity; Lakṣmī is the form of gold and other riches;
Ramā is the very nature of wealth; Rādhā is the perfection born of action. ||15||
Vṛndā is the fulfillment of blessings; likewise, Tulasī is the embodiment of the virtuous wife and the true power of the chaste woman; and the Mothers are the powers of nourishment. ||16||
The Gaṅgā is renowned for its flowing water and is considered by Hari to be the giver of liberation;
the lakes such as Puṣkara and others are but drops of the nectar of His love. (17)
Furthermore, sacred fields such as Haridvāra and the Naimiṣa forest indeed originate from portions of Hari’s imperishable abode. (18)
Indeed, virtuous divine women dwell in those meritorious fields;
for they are considered to be born from portions of Brahmā, who resides in the imperishable abode. (19)
In all those places, the maidens beginning with Lakṣmī indeed reside;
they are perceived through divine vision, and they bestow divine liberation. (1.27.20)
Having taken birth as women, Mahālakṣmī and others are sometimes born as auspicious maidens among householders. ||21||
These maidens, having remained chaste from childhood, become virtuous;
once initiated, they become yoginīs who practice yoga. (22)
Some indeed become female renunciants by taking up renunciation, while others become free from passion through the destruction of attachment. ||23||
Some indeed, through the investigation of Sāṃkhya and through the yoga of Brahman, become Sāṃkhyayoginīs, ever devoted to celibacy. 24.
Those who are lifelong celibates become bestowers of liberation upon creation;
pure and having the nature of fire, those Brahmāṇīs deliver men. 25.
They were virtuous, upholding moral conduct and vows; they possessed the splendor and beauty of the sun;
their faces were composed of lunar tranquility; and they were the destroyers of the three kinds of suffering. (26)
They destroy suffering through the mere sight of them; they bring happiness through service;
they remove poison through prostration; and they bestow purity through hearing them. //27//
By chanting their names, they grant desired fruits; by remembering them, they take away the god of love (passion);
by worshipping them, they lead one along the path of light and bestow liberation. 28.
By giving service, they grant the state of being a servant; by friendship, they bestow companionship;
and by the offering of one's self, they cause the devotee to be established within the Self of Hari. (29)
Those who have been honored with a complete abundance of food, clothing, garments, and articles [attain] the imperishable abode of Śrī Hari by the power of Hari. (1.27.30)
By massaging the feet, limbs, and so forth, they cause Hari’s state to be attained;
indeed, through the performance of whatever specific rites a devotee desires, he shall surely obtain his own desired object. (31)
Wearing saffron robes, they were bound by love for the sake of Hari;
practicing celibacy for the sake of Brahman, they were lifelong students established in devotion to Hari. ||32||
He is called Mukta because he is liberated from death; Brahmāṇya because he originates from Brahman;
Mokṣāṇya because his very form is liberation; and Brāhma because he is dedicated to Brahman. ||33||
They are true because of their continuous succession of chastity; they are virtuous women by being the refuge of the qualities of the righteous;
they are goddesses through the attainment of a divine state; and they are gurus by means of the instruction of knowledge. (34)

The female servants (dāsyaḥ) are considered to be "servants of Brahman" (brahmadāsyaḥ) because they always follow the conduct of servants; however, those who take refuge in the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) should be understood as "mistresses of the Lord" (īśvarāṇyaḥ). ||35||
These wives of Hari should be understood as devoted to their husbands (pativratā) because of their attainment of the Protector;
they are called "wives" (patnyaḥ) because they lead the fallen one to the supreme abode. ||36||
Women are to be understood as "saviors" (saṃtrāṇa) because they lead men to the state of Nṛhari;
they are "queens" (samrājñī) because they enter the vehicle of the Lord of the Kings of Kings. ||37||
They are called *tyāginīs* because of their renunciation, and *svāminīs* because of their offering of self-ownership.
They are called *muṇḍinīs* because they shave their hair for the sake of Brahman and Hari. (38)

They are called *ācāryāṇīs* because they promote proper conduct (*ācāra*). They are called *āravālyas* because they cause the sound of Hari to resound. And they are also called *liṅginīs* because they go toward Hari, who is the dissolved object.
And they are called *avadhūtīs* because of their shaking off (*avadhūnana*) of illusion (*māyā*). 1.27.40.
And they are called Bhagavatis because they bestow the sixfold sovereign powers (ṣaḍbhaga-aiśvarya); they are also called Mothers (Mātṛs) because they grant the measure of liberation. 41.
And they are called *dīkṣitāṇīs* because they bestow knowledge and destroy sin;
though they are weak, they are to be understood as being empowered by the strength of this Viṣṇu. 42.
They should always be understood as *ārṣyās*, because they take refuge in the sages (*ṛṣi*), the Vedas (*veda*), and so forth;
they should be understood as *āryās*, because they remain far removed from Hari;
and they should be understood as *nārāyaṇīs*, because they lead men (*nṛ*) toward Nārāyaṇa. 43.
And those female deer are also to be understood as such; he leads those who have taken refuge in him to Hari. 44.
In the same way, the glories (śrīs) of Śrī Hari also exist; by taking refuge in Him, they become divine and, through association, always bestow divinity. (45)
Their supreme, divine form arises from dwelling within Nārāyaṇa; having received initiation from Hari, they become the attendants who bear the mark of Hari. (46)
Waiting for Hari, they go to the abode of Hari;
they lead those who endure, who have taken refuge in life, and who walk the path of devotion. 47.
These virtuous women should always be served by kings, lords of men, and others;
indeed, they should always be served, honored, and saluted with devotion by women. 48.
The Lord, the divine Śrī Hari, always shines as one who is absorbed in that [state];
there, in the assembly of virtuous women, I always abide with a divine form. 49.
O King, having assumed the beauty, disposition, virtue, and very form of virtuous women, I always abide among them myself in embodied form. (1.27.50)
The virtuous women are indeed not different from me, nor are they inferior to me, nor are they born of material elements; for they should be understood as rubies, being my very own forms. (51)
Not even an atom's worth of their bodies is considered illusory;
their bodies are indeed my body, for they are my very forms. (52)
Form, grace, beauty, attraction, nectar-like sweetness, desirability, gentleness, visibility, mildness, consolation, coolness, and so forth. ॥53॥
Humility, dependence, service, modesty, contentment with one's refuge, wretchedness, fortitude, goodness, affection, gentleness, and so forth; ||54||
Affection for the grove, skillfulness, endurance, and compliance;
faith, trust, truthfulness, purpose, non-possessiveness, protection, and so forth. 55.
Giving, nurturing, surrendering one's entire being, and treating friends as equals; providing support through fortitude, acting as a friend, and equanimity toward pleasure and pain. 56.
Fortitude, lack of fickleness, devotion, service, constancy, renown, praise, secrecy, profundity, magnanimity, modesty, and other such qualities are [the marks of a friend]. (57)
All my [qualities] have been surrendered by me into my own form and bestowed upon them;
for I dwell only among virtuous women after having granted all my attributes to them. 58.
That clarity which has been attained by them is considered mine;
they are indeed the Yoginīs of Sāṃkhya, virtuous women who are the abode of noble qualities. (59)
O beloved, you should honor these women—who destroy ignorance and sin, who bestow immortality, and who are the authorized recipients of Śrī Hari—just as you honor me. (1.27.60)

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Various Etymologies and Attributes of Mahālakṣmī and Other Virtuous Women Embodied as Forms of Nārāyaṇa," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||27||
← Chapter 027: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā - Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 28 [[Author: → Chapter 029
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
My divine qualities always reside within them.
O beloved, listen as I describe those meaningful qualities to you. 1.
A disposition for the welfare of all beings is proclaimed there as truth (satya); and purity (śauca) is proclaimed there as being the state of being an adversary to that which is to be abandoned. 2.
Compassion is proclaimed therein as the absence of form [of aversion] toward the suffering of others;
forbearance is proclaimed therein as the endurance of offenses. (3)
Disregard even for one's own interests is renunciation; contentment is the state of having all desires fulfilled.
Uprightness toward all people is proclaimed as straightforwardness. (4)
Tranquility is the non-subjugation of the afflictions; self-restraint is the control of the senses;
austerity is the cessation of desire; equanimity is the state of being without distinction toward all things;
forbearance is the endurance of power; and learning is the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures. (5)
Cessation, however, is proclaimed to be the non-arising of effort. (6)
Knowledge is traditionally defined as the thorough acquaintance with reality exactly as it is;
dispassion is proclaimed to be the state of being entirely devoid of attachment. (7)
Sovereignty is the state of being a controller, the nature of being the lord of all. Heroism is victory by one's own nature; splendor is considered to be invincibility.
Power is the capacity of the body and the self; memory is eternal manifestation.
Independence is said to be freedom from subservience to others and lack of dependence on anything else. Skill is proclaimed as proficiency in all undertakings.
Radiance is considered to be innate beauty that captivates the minds of all. (1.28.10)
Fortitude is highly esteemed as the absence of agitation when success is not quickly attained;
gentleness, however, is considered in every respect to be the lack of harshness in one's natural disposition. (11)
Boldness is the flash of inspired intelligence; profundity is proclaimed as depth. Humility is to be understood as modesty, and character is the purity of one's conduct.
Concord, however, is the complete ripening resulting from total restoration.
Ojas is the intensification [of energy] through the successful accomplishment of an undertaking once it has been begun.
Bhaga is considered to be the excellence of the manifestation of knowledge and so forth at all times.
Gāmbhīrya is proclaimed as the unfathomability of one's intention even when it is being directed toward an object. (13–14)
Fame is that which is sung by the people of the world; the state of being a vessel for glory is what is called renown.
Silence is the absence of idle chatter, and steadfastness is freedom from fickleness. (15)
Faithfulness (*āstikya*) is proclaimed to be confidence in the meaning of the words of a reliable authority;
freedom from pride (*agarva*) is indeed recognized as the absence of self-conceit regarding one's own virtues. (16)
Freedom from pride is considered to be the state of being empty of egoism; freedom from hypocrisy is the practice of a virtuous conduct that is unassailable and free from deceitful results. (17)
Moderation in food is defined as taking only what is necessary to achieve satisfaction;
skillfulness is said to be the ability to see through to the completion of tasks that have been interrupted. (18)
Loving-kindness is considered the foundation of trust for all living beings;
it consists of providing assistance, being indifferent to receiving anything in return, and offering help with joyful enthusiasm. (19)
Non-malice is indeed the avoidance of harming others by any means whatsoever;
it consists of bestowing honor as is appropriate and performing every act of hospitality. (1.28.20)
The conquest of the six waves is proclaimed as the complete victory over the six;
hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death are the six waves. (21)
The state of being a protector of those who have come for refuge is proclaimed as "refuge-ness" (śaraṇyatva);
while the state of being free from the threads of craving is proclaimed as "effortlessness" (anīhatva). ||22||
Just as non-acceptance is said to be the refusal of more than what is required, so too is the total avoidance of serving and nourishing living beings in every respect. (23)
For these qualities always exist in Śrī Hari, and they grant liberation;
through the power of worshiping Hari, they become attainable by devotees. (24)
Endowed with those very same six virtues, I dwell among virtuous women;
therefore, virtuous women are always worthy of worship, pure, and sanctifiers of the assembly. 25.

The daughters of Māpu, who are practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, are truthful and the refuge of virtuous qualities; likewise, those women who have taken refuge in me are virgins whose resolutions are true. (26)
They lead one to the supreme abode and likewise grant happiness;
they gladden me and offer themselves to the embodied form of Hari. (27)
Because they have performed my work, because they have served me virtuously, and because they have worn my garment, they are not considered inferior to me. (28)
Those powers of yoga which reside in me within the supreme, imperishable abode—having separated them from myself, I have manifested them as the Yoginīs. (29)
Those infinite female servants indeed always become my own very form;
by my command, they wander through all the divine worlds. (1.28.30)
Divine, possessing divine wonders, and eternally twelve years of age, they dwell forever in the Satya Brahmaloka, not born from a womb. 31.
These deities are proclaimed to be the *ātivāhika* (conveying) ones;
they alone lead the one destined for liberation along the path to liberation.
They should be understood as being innumerable, possessing powers appropriate to place and time.
In whatever manner a task may arise, they perform it accordingly. //33//
Whatever quality has been relinquished by me in every respect, having separated that quality [from myself], I have thereby become one who has renounced it. (34)
They too, possessing divine forms, constantly move about during creation;
divine and twelve years of age, they lead embodied beings to liberation. 35.
However, that detachment which exists within my creation has been separated from its qualities;
therefore, by my will, those who are free from passion have been made manifest. (36)
These twelve-year-old girls bestow divine liberation;
just as I exist eternally, so too do they exist eternally. (37)
Likewise, in that imperishable abode, which is my own form, there exists the knowledge of Sāṃkhya;
similarly, the capacity for Yoga is also present—indeed, both of these exist therein. (38)
Then, having separated them, twelve divine maidens were produced—gentle, beautiful, and endowed with a form resembling my own. ||39||
Filled with the essence of all selves, overflowing with all bliss, their youth had not yet reached its full bloom, and their bodies were composed of total nourishment. (1.28.40)
But these Sāṃkhya-yoginīs are in every way contemplations of Brahman;
they always possess the body of Brahman, because they consist entirely of Brahman. 41.
They move through all creations in a divine form;
they always liberate living beings or lords from within the darkness. 42.
But whenever they manifest from the womb of any woman,
then signs appear upon their hands and feet.
Those who are worthy of refuge should be recognized by seekers of liberation through divine marks.
O Lakṣmī! Listen before me as I describe those marks. 44.
But for those women between whose breasts there truly appears upon the heart of Nārāyaṇa a vermilion line known as the *tilaka* above his feet. (45)
Below the navel, in the region of the hips, there should be a line of beautiful golden-piṅgala;
on the forehead, it should have the shape of an arrow and the form of a crown.
Furthermore, on the right cheek and then on the forehead in the middle region, there shall also appear a red spot, which is equal to the Sudarśana [discus]. //47//
On her chest there should appear the four-hasta Viṣṇu-rekhā,
and on the left side of her arm-band there should appear the mark of a mace.
If there should be the mark of a sandal upon her left thigh, and if there is a golden line on the chest of the Vaijayantī [necklace], [she is a woman of high status]. (49)
She who holds a lotus in her hand and has an elephant in her palm should be known as Lakṣmī herself, a maiden in human form. Now,
I shall describe other natural marks as well.
Those women whose feet or hands [bear such marks] are to be known as the consorts of Nārāyaṇa. || 51 ||

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Display of Divine Marks on the Divine Chaste Women Whose Nature Consists of the Qualities of the Blessed Lord," in the first section, the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 28.
← Chapter 28: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 29 [[Author: → Chapter 30
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe the marks upon your feet;
by these, people will recognize you when your birth occurs in the world.
On the right foot, however, the mark of a lotus bud (*phaṇaka*) below the base of the big toe is the *vara* (boon-granting) mudrā;
the mark of a conch (*śaṅkha*) is to be understood at the base of the [other] fingers;
and the mark of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) is on the base of the little finger. (2)
Likewise, there is the mark of a boat, as well as the marks of a conch and a mace positioned below it.
(3) Below that is the mark in the shape of a sea-monster (makara), and beneath that is a pinnacle.
Then, on the heel, there is a line of fish, and in the middle, a betel vine. (4)
There, at the base of the left thumb, the mark of a barley grain is proclaimed;
beneath that is Mahān, where the Prāsāda is proclaimed to be. (5)
Below that, however, there should be a parasol; the upward-pointing line is eternal.
There, at the base of the two fingers, a lotus is considered to be on the hood.

Below that is the line of the banner (dhvajarekhā), and by its side the goad (aṅkuśa) is said [to be]. Below that is the white water-lily (kumuda), on the side the bilva fruit (śrīphala), and likewise the jar (kalaśa). (7)
Below that is a land-lotus; on the heel is a second moon.
There are ten full wheels above the hoods of the golden line. 8.

O Lakṣmī! whenever these signs are seen by me, then that which is called Śrī-Lakṣmī should be known as the Supreme Brahman; of this there is no doubt. Whether they appear as two, or three, or four, or five— || 9 ||
O Goddess, portions of you are seen in every foot; thus, you are considered to be human.
On the forehead is a golden necklace and a golden line as a mark;
on the right cheek is a red dot, and there is a dot on the chin. (11)
On the right breast is the line of a hand; on the left breast, however, is a wheel.
On her neck is a golden necklace, and I am her four-armed thief. (12)
Above the vulva is the emblem of Kāmadeva with a bow;
there are lines on the two thighs representing the *kumuda* [lotus], and a *svastika* on the right hand. (13)
Dhvajā, Matsyā, Vaṃśī, Dhanuḥ, Matsyakā, and Kalaśā—these should be known as the daughters who are portions of Nārāyaṇa. (14)
Whether one, or two, or even more than that, when such a mark is observed, they should be understood as the daughters of Brahmā’s incarnations. (15)
When the glorious Nārāyaṇa appears as a human being in the form of a man,
then in his right hand there are a banner, a thunderbolt, a lotus,
and a flute; likewise, a svastika, a bow, an arrow, a trident, and a fish.
The lotus, the conch, as well as the discus, the sun, the elephant, and the peacock; ॥17॥
In my incarnation, there will certainly be one, two, or three auspicious marks of the goddess Lakṣmī, consisting of golden lines, upon my chest. (18)
On the chest, there should be an auspicious line of a golden necklace upon the skin;
on the abdomen, there should indeed be a hanging line of three folds.
On the penis, there should be a black mole, and on the forehead, there should be a *tilaka*.
There was also a single line extending across both sides of his forehead.
On the left thigh there may be a large, pale-brown mole like a *bhallātaka* fruit;
likewise, a black spot may appear upon the right calf. (21)
The two soles of his feet will be auspicious with the mark of a lotus;
his body will be golden-hued, delightful, and graced with beauty.
His eyes, filled with love for the lotus, have reddish corners and are endowed with compassion.
With a frown and side-long glances, possessing waves of beautiful, curved, and broken brows. ॥23॥
The svastika, banner, barley-corn, goad, staff, octagon, eight-petaled lotus, conch, half-moon, jar, cow’s footprint, pit, triangle, hoof-print, moon, and bow. (24)
On the right petal, there are those nine [symbols] beginning with the svastika;
on the left petal, there are indeed seven lines beginning with the half-moon. 25.
He in whom one, two, or even three [qualities] are seen is Acyuta;
he is indeed an incarnation of Hari, the Blessed Lord, born from a portion of Hari. ||26||
He should be known as untainted, the destroyer of sin and suffering;
even amidst great enjoyments such as women and wealth, he remains unimpeded—he is indeed the Lord.
Though existing within *māyā*, he renders that *māyā* divine.
He purifies even the most sinful who have come to his own yoga.
Those who worship him out of desire, anger, fear, greed, or envy—all of them attain liberation from rebirth through his majesty. (28–29)
Just as fire remains free from soot after burning up healthy fuels, so Kṛṣṇa remains free from attachment after burning away all karmas. (1.29.30)
Just as impure metals and the like, when cast into fire, become clear, so too, by surrendering impure desires and the like to Hari, one becomes pure. (31)
Through connection with Hari, whose power is immeasurable and whose nature is pure, men and women are purified by that Lord who consists of [divine] portions. 32.
He whose palms possess two excellent conchs between the middle fingers, and likewise six wheels on the other [fingers] as well as on the two thumbs; ||| 33 ||
He himself is indeed the Blessed One; he possesses two wheels at the extremities [of the hands], and those two hands are marked with lotuses, likewise upon the palms of the left hand. (34)
He in whose center there is a long vertical line is indeed the Blessed One;
for whatever he places his hand upon becomes truly inexhaustible. 35.
This embodied soul, endowed with one or another of the aforementioned signs, may be in the form of a woman or a man, and may be either a householder or a renunciant. ||36||
Thus, I am Nārāyaṇa himself, eternally performing the human drama; though appearing like an ignorant man, I uplift all beings. (37)
In some instances, I manifest only a very slight degree of sovereignty;
this is solely for the sake of the devotee’s purpose, and not for the sake of establishing my own greatness.
For worldly people are sinful and strive only for their own self-interest.
Those who cause me harm depart far away after accomplishing their own ends.
Therefore, I do not display any miraculous power to them;
for true devotees attain Me even without such wonders. (1.29.40)
Those by whom the Blessed One has been ascertained through the marks declared in the scriptures should not seek for wonders, nor should they grasp at any deformed defects. //41//
The partial incarnation (aṃśāvatāra), having accomplished all his tasks, sees, smells, destroys, enjoys,
sleeps, embraces, kisses, and even consumes the Lord;
he beholds the divine and becomes the master who wields the eight wheels and the husband of ten million women.
For he is served by the fortune of the sovereign of kings just like a king himself.
(43) This one is the omniscient Vyāsa in form, an ocean for all branches of knowledge;
though a human being, he is the Lord himself, surpassing even Bṛhaspati. (44)
O Lakṣmī! Having observed these signs described by me with certainty, and having recognized [the person] as either Nārāyaṇī or Hari, one should practice surrender (prapatti). ||45||
One should serve with one's whole being and practice the offering of all one's possessions;
through devotion, love, and passion, such a person shall quickly attain liberation. 46.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Divine Marks and Other Characteristics of the Incarnations of Nārāyaṇa and of Men and Women" in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. 29.
← Chapter 029: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 30 [[Author:
→ Chapter 031
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O compassionate one, O Supreme Bliss, O God of gods, O ocean of mercy!
Everything that characterizes Brahman has been told in an unprecedented manner.
Indeed, through great merit and compassion, it is possible to hear this;
for who else but you is capable of discerning the marks of a deity? (2)
When you are encountered by one's offspring while bearing a mark, whether in the form of a woman or a man, then there shall be the liberation of those [women]. (3)
"How can there be your presence for people devoid of fortune?
Until liberation is attained directly, one should not depart [from this world].
In this world, among all householders, there are virtuous men and women."
How could they proceed with respect toward such dreadful dwellings? || 5 ||
Furthermore, because the virtuous and the most excellent are indifferent toward all things, householders would find no gain; how then could liberation occur?
Moreover, due to the differences between the ages (*yuga*), the householder’s life has become manifold and full of deception.
It is increased by improper conduct, falsehood, unrighteousness, deceit, and so forth. (7)
One who is intent on nourishing his family, greedy, and indeed of evil conduct;
one who inflicts injury upon others, achieves his own ends, and is impure in heart. (8)
Requiring great effort yet yielding little enjoyment, it is a deception regarding the nominal essence;
it is always obscured by offspring, food, wealth, clothing, and vehicles. (9)
"Grinded by the afflictions of acquisition and occupied day and night, drawn away by desires and other objects—how can such a person attain liberation? (1.30.10)

Tell me that by which the household life of a family member, though devoid of the company of the virtuous and likewise lacking in the performance of good deeds, may nevertheless attain liberation. (11)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, you have spoken the truth! For a man devoid of merit, even if he has attained the company of the virtuous, it indeed departs far away due to his lack of fortune. (12)
Envy, lack of trust, lack of faith, absence of devotion, atheism, and the constant conceit that oneself is superior to all others; //13//
Furthermore, he always and in every way perceives only faults;
and he constantly avoids the pursuit of excessive greatness, honor, and respect. (14)
Ignorance, foolishness, hypocrisy, and a tamasic nature;
as well as censoriousness, demoniacal character, enmity, and an accumulation of sins—(15).
Lack of meritorious blessings and being deprived of divine fortune—these faults always destroy one's association with the virtuous. (16)
A wife is obtained through merit; a husband is obtained through austerity;
a son is obtained through charity; and prosperity is attained through sacrificial fees. (17)
Vision is obtained by means of a lamp, and indeed, life is obtained through ghee; the bodily constituents are obtained through juices, and knowledge is attained through the scriptures. (18)
Success is attained through effort; knowledge is attained through practice;
heaven is attained through sacrifice; and pleasure is obtained through a wife. (19)
Happiness is attained through righteousness, and indeed, a lineage is obtained through women; fame is acquired through good deeds, and favor is attained through devotion. (1.30.20)
A master is won over by service; a greedy man is won over by wealth;
a hungry man is won over by food; and a proud man is won over by honor. (21)
The arrogant man is overcome by doubt; the hero is overcome by haste.
Yet, despite all those various efforts, the company of the virtuous is not attained. (22)
O virtuous lady! It is said that the company of the righteous is difficult for all to attain;
yet it is especially so for those unfortunate householders who seek only their own self-interest. (23)

For the sake of protection, for the sake of liberation, or indeed for the sake of the next world, one should offer oneself to me, established within my form, while completely setting aside anything separate from me. 24.
I have created divine *pātivratya*, which accomplishes all goals.
The service rendered by a woman to her husband is here called *pātivratya*. (25)
Service consisting of devotion to her husband took the form of a maiden;
she held heaven and liberation in her hands and placed merits at his feet. (26)

Having placed the gods within his body and concealed the sacrifices within his womb, he placed all the sacred fords (tīrthas) upon his palms and the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) upon his thighs. ||27||
He placed the wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu) upon her breasts, the thought-gem (cintāmaṇi) upon her heart, the creepers of merit upon her hair, and the moon and sun upon her eyes. || 28 ||

Having grasped the Dharma along with its lineage in his mind and speech, as well as all spiritual accomplishments, and having seized the four aims of human life by the hair on his head, [he should act]. 29.
Having properly placed the guardians of the directions in his two ears, the lords up to Īśvara on his forehead, and all the incarnations of Śrī Hari within himself; || 1.30.30 ||
Having placed the two *sat* syllables on the tongue and likewise the word "ānanda" in the belly, one should hold the two very beautiful paths called *arci* and *dhūmra* upon the lips. 31.
She was beautiful, divine, and brilliantly radiant, adorned with a halo of light;
she possessed blossoming youth and breasts, and was twelve years of age. ||32||
Having reached the stage of the arousal of passion, she is moist yet not yet menstruating;
with the golden line of fine body hair, she captivates the beauty of desire. ||33||
Modest, rich in truthful conduct, possessing a form like that of Nārāyaṇa;
the imperishable, eternal Goddess, worthy of the best offerings, whose movement is hidden. 34.
That virtuous woman, known for her devotion to her husband, having bowed with palms joined in reverence, stood before Hari and requested his instruction. ||35||
"Command me, O Lord Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Teacher of the World!
For what purpose have I been born, and what task is expected of me? (36)
I, Nārāyaṇa, have also ordained that she shall be joined in every way with the company of women; you must indeed always remain together with her. (37)
In Rādhā, in Ramā, in Lakṣmī, in the Śrīs, and in the Satīs;
in the Īśās, in the Jīvanārīs, in the Sādhvīs, and in those who bestow liberation. ||38||
O fortunate one! Always dwell among the womankind;
O passionate lady, dwell among the wives in the homes of married couples. (39)
By your dwelling [there], that family—whether it be impure or even sinful—shall, being purified, go effortlessly to the worlds known as heaven and liberation. (1.30.40)
By those [means] through which you are propitiated, you too must remain present there;
O sinless one, you must always remain in the house of the performer of a thousand sacrifices.
O sinless one, you must always remain in the house of those who serve their parents;
O sinless one, you must always remain in the house of those who know the Self as Brahman. 42.
O sinless one, you must stay in the house of a devotee who offers himself to you; O sinless one, you must stay in the house of a brahmin who performs the six duties. 43.
O sinless one, you must remain within the body of a woman perfected in the lifelong vow;
O sinless one, you must always remain within the bodies of women who are practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. 44.
O sinless one, you must remain within the bodies of these virtuous women who have ascended to yoga;
for those whose husband is no longer alive with the sacred fires, I am considered their husband. (45)
O sinless one, you must always abide by the duties of a widow;
by my power, these worlds shall be led to the imperishable state.
Saying "Om," she accepted this and requested him once more:
"May my form be distinct for every individual body. (47)
"Otherwise, my attainment of all virtuous women would not be possible.
"So be it," Hari replied; thereafter she assumed an infinite form. (48)
And that maiden, remaining devoted to her husband, was brought in again and again;
wherever she was assigned a dwelling, there she remained in every case. (49)
She does not manifest as a single self among the many women created in various worlds;
yet she grants excellent heavens to those with desire, and liberation to those free from desire.
The goddess Nārāyaṇī, the consort of Śrī Hari, bestows [her grace] in every house;
in age after age, throughout the worlds in the cosmic egg, she is the one who carries her devotees across the lowest depths. 51.
Therefore, a devoted wife must be served and indeed worshipped as my own body;
she is to be looked upon, fed, honored, and bowed to at all times. (52)
She too must be awakened as a virtuous woman; she is not inferior to my own body.
For the sake of uplifting the lowly, she was created by me in this world. (53)
Virtuous women devoted to their husbands are indeed my very own forms;
for them, desire is not for the sake of pleasure, but rather for the service of their husband. (54)
Their passion was not for the sake of passion, but for the delight of their husband; their pleasure was not for the sake of enjoyment, but for the perpetuation of their husband's lineage. ||55||
Their enjoyment is not for her own pleasure, but for the delight of the husband;
their touch is not for the sake of coolness, but for the husband's tranquility. ||56||
Their menses do not lead to bondage for the husband, but rather bring him satisfaction;
their pregnancy does not lead to suffering for the husband, but indeed brings about what is desired by him;
their religious observances do not serve their own ends, but indeed bring about liberation for the husband. (57)
Their lifespan was not for the sake of creation, but indeed for the husband's attainment of the further shore. ||58||
Their death was not for the sake of grief, but rather to remove the grief of their husband; their blessing was not for the sake of delusion, but rather to remove the delusion of their husband. (59)

Their home is always a vessel for merit; their body is always a vessel for the gods; their dharma is always a vessel for happiness; and their attainment is always a vessel for the divine abode. (1.30.60)
Their destiny leads to the abode of the Imperishable; their intellect is a night of beautiful form for the sake of Brahman;
their action brings about the state beyond the qualities (nirguṇa); their fortitude attains union with Śrī Hari. 61.
Thus, O Lakṣmī! this means of purification for sins has been declared by me for householders; let it be understood that it should also be practiced. 62.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Power of Origin and Other Qualities of the Chaste Woman," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. ||30||
← Chapter 30: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā - Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 31 [[Author: → Chapter 32
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Great Goddess Lakṣmī; you indeed previously worshipped the great goddess Pātivratyā, a maiden, with divine fragrance.
Then, with saffron and unbroken grains of rice, feed her with a pure heart,
along with excellent food, sweets, betel-leaf, and fruit.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Blessed One, grant me the materials for worship and for the meal, by which I may worship the goddess Kanyā Saubhāgyamaṅgalā. (3)
Having heard this request, Śrī Hari himself manifested coolness and fragrance from his own body in the form of liquids.
That fragrant sandalwood was indeed produced in a golden vessel.
Then Nārāyaṇa manifested blood from his own lip. || 5 ||
The liquid, transformed into powder, was the divine and wonderful saffron;
it shone when placed in the vessel intended for the worship of Lakṣmī.
Then, the nectar was manifested from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
That was held in a vessel of excellent gems; from it, grains were produced which became unbroken rice-offerings (akṣata). || 7 ||
Having obtained those very riches, she performed worship to Lakṣmī;
and her mind was set upon providing food for the virtuous daughter who embodies devotion to her husband.
Then Nārāyaṇa also made his own lute immortal.
That supreme, divine nectar was white as it emerged outside;
by his will, a physical body (piṇḍa) was produced right there from it.
From half of that body, a beautiful cow, one that yields milk well, was born. || 10 ||
A white cow, perfect in all her limbs, four-footed and three years of age, auspicious and fragrant, Lakṣmī milked with the utmost reverence. (11)
Having obtained the milk, which was sweet, he thought, "What shall I do?
At that moment, fire was manifested by Nārāyaṇa from his own eye. (12)
By his command, she threw grains of rice into the milk-pudding as it boiled over the fire.
Then, while she was herself wondering what her task should be next,
Śrī Hari took nectar from the tip of his own tongue.
That supreme essence arose in the form of liquid, white and sweet;
by the will of Hari, it attained the state of sugar.
When these three were combined, cooked, and properly boiled, [it became the elixir]. 14–15.
That which is produced from that is called *paramānna*; it is described as a cooking with milk.
Therein, for the sake of another fragrance, [one should take] from the right nostril. (16)
The subtle cardamoms, possessing fragrance and flavor, were manifested from the left nostril; likewise, the nutmeg was produced therefrom. (17)
That indeed is considered the drying [process] for the purpose of striking away the agitation of the wind;
furthermore, for the sake of imparting the luster of gold and mercury, it was [given] again by the illustrious Hari from his own [being]. (18)
Indeed, from the portion of Hiraṇyaśmaśru, the filaments were manifested;
all of that was placed appropriately within the supreme food. 19.
Having entered a state of perfect meditative absorption, he mixed it like milk boiled with excellent sugar;
then, by the will of Hari, his mind was set upon turning that milk into curds. (1.31.20)
Buttermilk consists of sweet and sour elements, whereas nectar is the opposite of that; he made it with a loud gurgling sound and poured it into a vessel of milk. (21)
Through its union with that [nectar], however, delightful curd was produced, both sweet and sour;
therein, by the will of Hari, mature butter was manifested. (22)
Then, by the command of Nārāyaṇa, the goddess Lakṣmī prepared ghee that was supremely fragrant and divine; how could it not be useful? (23)
While she was thus reflecting, Nārāyaṇa transformed the remaining mass of grain into wheat ears and kernels. (24)
Then, by the mere movement of his own eyebrows, the glorious Hari fashioned two beautiful discs; that auspicious one is considered to be the grinding stone. 25.
That very thing again became the essential nature of Kālacakra;
Kālacakra always crushes living beings with extreme velocity. (26)
From the fierce frown of his brow, Cūrṇikā was created as a woman;
yet even Cūrṇikā, at her very birth, bore the name of "Calamity. (27)
Through misfortune, all living beings are ground to powder moment by moment.
By that very powdering, the wheat is made soft and kneaded into dough. (28)
Therefore, the auspicious *polikā* was prepared by Lakṣmī, anointed with ghee;
she then caused the devoted wife, the goddess, to partake of that auspicious meal. (29)

By means of the remaining alms-food, the Brahmin was created as a person; he is indeed declared to have the body of Brahmā, for therein the mantras are always sustained. He placed the sacrificial oblation (havis) into the cows; by that, the sacrifice is produced.
That cow was given to a Brahmin for the sake of constant sacrificial attainment. ||31||
In all the worlds, the lineages of Brahmā were manifested from the Brāhmaṇa.
Originally, all were Brāhmaṇas because they were born from Brahmā. (32)
Through the creation of Surabhi by Hari, the lineages of cows were made manifest;
through the goddess known as Pātivratyā, the devoted wives (pativratās) were made manifest.
From Kesara, kesara bushes are born here forever.
Likewise, from the *jātiphala* tree, trees are born here that bear fruit of that same kind. //34//
From the seeds of cardamom, small groves of cardamom plants were produced;
from the juice of sugar, long stalks of sugarcane appeared in the world. (35)
Indeed, that which is born everywhere within creation is called the immortal (amṛta). From the presence of fire, many fires are considered to arise for the sake of cooking. ||36||
Indeed, from his unbroken [teeth] were born the rice grains of the *vrīhi* variety;
from the fluid of Hari’s lips was born the red-colored turmeric. (37)
From that, the world always produces saffron which is tawny in color;
and from the nectar and the essence of sandalwood, trees as cool as sandalwood arise. (38)
From that, the [sages] fit for enlightenment were born as the manifestations of Śrī Hari;
then, sweet water was revealed there from the mouth of Hari. (39)
As long as he stands having drunk water and rinsed his mouth with a handful, Lakṣmī thinks: "What fruits should be given? (1.31.40)
Then, by Śrī Hari, nectar was manifested from his own mouth;
from that [nectar], trees with sweet fruits such as mangoes, pomegranates, and santurās came into being. (41)
Coconuts, *aṅgudī* fruits, mangoes, bananas, and sugar;
*navaraṅga* fruits, *amṛta*, rose-apples, citrons, grapes, and *khārikā* fruits. ||42||
The *saphala*, *añjana*, *kadalī*, *puṣpa*, *panasa*, and *kharjūra* trees came into being;
then, having gathered an abundance of their fruit, it was offered. (43)
"What cleansing agent for the mouth should be given to her who has thus remained standing?"—while Lakṣmī was thus reflecting, Śrī Hari [offered] from the nectar... (44)
The auspicious betel vine, along with its leaves, which stimulates fragrance, was placed by him upon a leaf-cup prepared from his own cheek for the sake of coolness. (45)
A reddish powder made from khadira wood was produced, and likewise a white powder was prepared from his teeth along with a stimulating agent. 46.
Having smeared the leaf with powder and placed it within, he offered the betel;
at that moment, a drop of sweat fell from the brow of the illustrious Hari. (47)
Indeed, the betel nut that has grown instantly purifies the mouth;
the excellent grass that has grown is like a drop of nectar for the face. (48)
Having taken those two [ingredients] there, well-prepared betel-leaf was made;
and from that other drop, the skin and cloves were made pungent. ||49||
Then, after that fine betel leaf had been crushed once more, auspicious betel, smeared with gold-leaf, was offered to them. (1.31.50)
And that was chewed by her, the girl devoted to her husband;
likewise, the supreme [act] was performed by Lakṣmī and also by Nārāyaṇa. (51)
That which is swallowed and chewed within the mouth is the supreme essence born of betel;
that great essence is poured as a mouthful throughout all the worlds. 52.
For he exists in the world during creation, having undergone manifold divisions;
he is that very same sweet and red juice which is present when the fruit is ripe. (53)
Whatever redness there is in fruits, that too is indeed flavor;
whatever redness there is in the bodily elements and in colored minerals such as red ochre, [that too is flavor]. (54)
The redness of the twilight, the redness of fire, and the redness of bodies; likewise, the redness of the lips and the cheeks, and of the flowers that partake of the seasons. (55)
Whatever redness there is that is beautiful and sweet in rasa—that is the goddess Rati; for she has arisen from rasa, and she is fond of dalliance. (56)
She is red, endowed with red blood, and the locus of all red qualities;
she is a maiden, Rati, beautiful in form, who has attained fresh youth.
Filled with fullness and redness, golden-hued and beautiful in every limb, she was Rati, devoted to her husband by the command of Śrī Hari. ||58||
When they had arrived here and were established everywhere throughout the world individually,
those two came to this world and spread that knowledge.
The khadira tree was born as Kathaka, while the betel nut tree became the king of grasses;
likewise, whatever other grasses were produced arose from that sap. (1.31.60)
Thus, those cows possessing the fragrance of lotuses, born from the form of the illustrious Hari, as well as the Brahmins therein, are my most excellent body. (61)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of Substances such as Saffron, Grains such as Unbroken Rice, Creepers such as Betel, Fruits such as Coconut and Mango, Red Ochre, and Pleasures such as Passion," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 31: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 32 [[Author:
→ Chapter 33
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O all-pervading inner self, O Self of the self, O Lord of the imperishable!
O Master Nārāyaṇa, you are the one to be sought; O Lord, you fulfill everything. || 1 ||
"Cows are indeed declared to be cattle; how then can they deliver people?
One who is capable may deliver others, but one who is incapable cannot do so by any means.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The noose is said to be bondage; bondage is considered to consist of Māyā. Wherever Māyā exists, there indeed all that is designated as "bound" (paśu) resides. (3)
Indeed, the body of both beasts and humans is essentially the same, dependent upon food and drink, and pervaded by self-interest characterized by desire and greed. (4)

O Blessed One, that person who truly attains the divine mantra of Manu is indeed called a human being; otherwise, he is merely the lowest of animals. As for my cows in Goloka, they are in every way identical to my own form.
Chanting "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," they indeed rejoice, being absorbed in that Brahman.
Those who constantly and firmly chant the mantra "Nārāyaṇa" perform a pilgrimage to heaven and grant me liberation. (7)
Even in Vaikuṇṭha, those cows and other liberated beings indeed reside,
worshipping my name and overflowing with all-encompassing bliss.
Indeed, those are not beasts; for beasts are ignorant men.
But in Vṛndāvana, they remember Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, day after day with devotion. 9.
Those goddesses who reside in the heavenly realms and other such places are considered to be providers of breast milk for the sake of Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, they dwell there having become cows in order to fulfill His every desire. (1.32.10)
They are omniscient, knowers of all languages, and are always considered to be bestowers of liberation;
they are the embodiments of the Blessed One’s mouth, the mothers who are the receptacle of nectar. (11)
Since they are born from my own body, they are considered worthy of worship at every single pore;
for I myself dwell within them, as does Dharma in the form of the Bull. (12)
I dwell within the cows as the cowherd; the cows are my Brahman-body.
Upon the forehead of the cows is the abode of Brahman; there I dwell.
My two horns are the flagstaffs, and between them is my lion-throne.
My two eyes are considered to be the two abodes of Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha. 14.
My nose is the unmanifest abode; my mouth is of the nature of Māyā.
My teeth are the sixteen principles (tattvas), and the tongue is the intellect (buddhi), for that is indeed the Great One (mahat).
The syllable *praṇava* is their resonance (*rāmbhaṇa*), while the two lips are considered to be Rajas and Tamas.
In the vast Śvetadvīpa, his two ears were [the two banks], and his dewlap was golden.
Sadāśiva was their throat, and the four Vedas were his feet.
The four aims of human life were his breasts, and the stalk of the lotus of Vairāja was his navel. (16–17)
The belly of those [deities] is considered to be Vairāja, and Mahāviṣṇu is regarded as the chest.
The stomach is the fire of Brahman’s splendor, while the back of the Creator is Truth itself.
Divine Ganges water is considered the urine, and Lakṣmī herself is regarded as the feces.

The menstrual flow is the water of the Sarasvatī; the womb is the oceans. The opening of the vulva is the Aṇḍakaṭa [mountain]; the root of the tail is the Janaloka and others. The tail is heaven, and the tuft of hair is the celestial sphere of the gods and so forth. (1.32.20)
Śiva and Viṣṇu are his two hips; Brahmā is said to be his abdomen.
Goddess Pārvatī is his womb, and the gods are his body hairs. (21)
"Their bones are the ancestors, and their hooves are the beings born in the netherworld; having thus resolved, I then fashioned that funeral cake. (22)
May cows be my manifestations, for within them dwell the nectars;
by partaking of the morsels made of nectar from their mouths, all beings are satisfied through me.
Cows am I, and I am the cows, regarded as the mothers of the worlds.
Because they nourish, rescue, and lead one to Brahman, they bestow prosperity and liberation.
Through worship they are said to bestow merit; through the offering of grass, they grant prosperity.
Through giving, they lead one to liberation; through service, they bestow heaven.
Through giving, they burn away sins; those who offer water attain immortality.
By warding off gadflies, they destroy poverty in every respect. (26)
Circumambulating them is declared to be the circumambulation of the earth itself;
for embodied beings, the constant use of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) by them leads to heaven. (27)
The water from their tails purifies the wicked and the sinful;
the dust from their hooves is a sacred ford that washes away the deceitful.
By giving a cow with two faces, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
For that which occurs at the time of the calf's birth is considered to be "two-faced" (ubhayatomukhī). ||29||
For the hungry ghosts, the rākṣasas, and those born as spirits who have no means of refuge, the gift of a cow provides a destination that is preceded by the destruction of their sins. (1.32.30)
For a deceased person burdened by evil who has gone to the abode of Yama, the crossing of the Vaitaraṇī river occurs with certainty through the gift of a cow. ||31||
In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, as well as in the realm of the lords, they are providers of assistance;
they should always be honored, saluted, given gifts, and fed by people. (32)
They are always to be served, honored, protected, bowed to, and touched.
If a great sinner should sacrifice his own life in the midst of cows, he indeed attains a divine state, and the messengers of Yama depart far away. (33)
But here, one who serves cows is protected by them in the next world. //34//
One who has obtained the grace of the cows here shall possess the grace of all;
nothing else whatsoever has been performed, but rather the service of the cows has been rendered. (35)

The fruit of that is the world of Brahmā and other realms; for that purpose, it shall be eternal. Both the propitiation of cows and the propitiation of Brahman are considered equal in this world and the next by Hari himself. (36)
In this world, he who [acts thus] toward cows, a woman, a maiden, a sister, or likewise a mother; ||| 37 ||
One who causes suffering to those who have sought refuge or are dependent becomes a partaker of suffering himself.
Indeed, the householder is he who protects the calf and the cow, the bull and the cow. (38)
By him indeed the earth was protected, and he obtained the fruit of being a protector of the earth.
They say that wealth is not merely material riches; the wealth of cattle is called true wealth. (39)
Here he bestows flavors; in the next world, he acts as a companion.
They eat grass upon the ground and always dwell below. (1.32.40)
They endure cold, heat, and other hardships; they offer many flavors [to others];
they nourish their own family and satisfy the gods and ancestors. 41.
Cows are remembered as divine beings who rescue one from falling into the lower realms;
Brahmins are declared to be saviors through the recitation of Vedic mantras and other such acts. (42)
Even those overcome by great sin cross over by the power of cows;
for cows and Brahmins are indeed a single reality manifested in two forms. (43)
For the mantra is deposited in one place and the oblation is offered in another;
through the mantra and the oblation, the sacrifice comes to be, and from the sacrifice, rain then arises. (44)
From rain comes food and water; from those, the elements; and from those, living beings. Through progeny one attains heaven, and from heaven comes happiness and celebration. (45)
From festival to festival go those who serve cows; therefore, they should be served every day.
What need is there for much speaking? Cows are indeed my path to the state of Brahman. 46.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Cow," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. ||32||
