Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord, my mind rejoices from chewing betel;
from tasting the flavor of betel, intoxication arises in my heart. (1)
The taste spreads through the channels, and the flickering mind runs forth. What does it remember? It plays with that which is dear to the heart, reaching into the very core of the heart. (2)
The transformed essence (rasa) excites the blood within;
it makes known its most beloved heat and produces, as it were, a fever in me. (3)
"It causes moisture to flow from my limbs and indeed produces a burning sensation.
O Lord of Compassion, grant me peace; what is this disease that has come upon me? (4)
Then, having heard of Lakṣmī’s fickleness regarding the flavor of betel,
Nārāyaṇa generated from his own mind the god named Kāma,
who was an ocean overflowing with the blossoming of beauty, loveliness, and youth.
Wearing a thick, glossy mass of matted hair that was black with tawny tips;
bearing a sword with the luster of a peacock feather and a lightning-flash crest-jewel;
and wearing upon his forehead a beautiful gem from which radiant light emanated.
Bearing a slightly darkened, slightly golden, and curved frown,
he repeatedly cast streams of the bliss of passion from his two eyes.
Constantly pouring streams of love from his two red lips,
he joined his two beaks to the middle of her lips with the effort of kissing and pressing.
Manifesting a faintly dark and subtle line of beard, he displayed a gentle disposition with eyes flowing with full love. (1.33.10)
Both [of them], having begun with a gentle smile drawn from their hearts and having made their cheeks crimson, cast side-long glances at the goddess Rati;
in some places, they seemed to indicate the union of the two through the act of lovemaking.
Repeatedly performing the act of closing at the outer corners of his eyes. ||12||
Having fashioned a bow from his knitted brows, he first took up an arrow made of mango blossoms. (13)
The second arrow is fragrant oil and the like;
and the third is the *trāṭaka* [meditative gaze] intensely attached to all states of being. (14)
The fourth is called the attraction by the sight of the limbs of the youth;
the fifth is the agitation of delusion, which likewise serves as a touchstone for the arrival [of the goal].
Then, there is the sight of the growth of body hair upon a body that resembles shining gold.
Wearing a golden-colored garment as fine as the thread of a spider's web. 16.
Displaying his form as a sixteen-year-old youth that causes the transformation of the elements, the wise one bowed down to Śrī Hari. 17.
"What service may I perform for you, O Lord? he asked.
I said to him: "Becoming present in every individual, enter the heart of Śrī;
you are indeed the producer of *rajas*, so always remain there for the sake of passion."
Having entered therein, become in every way a producer of such vigor. //19//
"Entering into others during my creation, act everywhere as its executor, so that this creation may always remain stable, bound by each respective state. (1.33.20)
Having thus received this command, he took it to heart;
at that time, O Lakṣmī, you were the first to embrace him. (21)
"O Lakṣmī, by contact with my body, your fever was indeed pacified.
Because of your dwelling within my seed in your womb, Dhanam became your son. (22)
Wealth was well-concealed by you at that time, for it was the appointed moment; indeed, this was due to our union being brought about by a third desire. (23)
Likewise, through the arrival of good fortune for both of us—myself and my son on the third day—and along with wealth, we three have attained an auspicious state. (24)
The tenth is known as Putravatī (the one possessing sons), and the thirteenth is considered Dhanatrayodaśī (the wealth-thirteenth).
Those who desire wealth and perform worship to you during this [period]— ||25||
Bring them wealth consisting of gold, silver, jewels, and so forth.
Then, at my command, Kāma, accompanied by Bāṇa, was dispatched. (26)
Go forth into creation; enter into all youthful bodies, bringing about the production of passion and seed, acting as an assistant to the process of creation. (27)
Requested by Kāma, I gave my companion, Youth, who goes before him, as a precursor to Kāma. (28)
Then, once a dwelling had been established there, I created my second companion, Rati, the beautiful wife, and gave her to Kāma, O Rāma.
I have offered this servant, who speaks for his own sake, to that Kāma;
yet he is the younger brother of Kāma, my own mind-born son. (1.33.30)
Likewise, O son, Hāva and Bhāva were created by me as my mind-born sons;
they were given there to Kāma as your two constant companions. 31.
Then, having again produced two sons named Premākhya and Mānasa, I gave them to him; he too became his companion.
Then, from Gupta, a son named Saṃśleṣa was begotten and handed over;
he too became an assistant to Kāmadeva in the matter of guarding the senses. (33)
Therefore, a servant named Jāgara was given by me to this Jāgrat;
and having produced two sweet enjoyments, they were also presented as his servants. (34)
Then, a son named Śrāva was produced by me and likewise entrusted [to him];
he too became there an assistant to Bindu in the matter of the impulse of desire. (35)
Then, the son named Ānanda was manifested by me from the root *dhā*;
he too was indeed bestowed upon him as an assistant in accomplishing the task. (36)
Likewise, the son Uddīpana was begotten by me and handed over; for a long time, he has been my assistant through his wakefulness, strength, fullness, and firmness. (37)
And I have surrendered even my maidservant Nirvṛti to him;
she, arriving after the emission, causes the two embodied beings to separate. (38)
Then, having produced slackness [in the mind], I have surrendered that servant [to it].
There, for a moment, he remains as a signifier of the cessation of desire. (39)
"Thus, O Goddess, this maṇḍala was undertaken by me for the sake of creation;
it has been performed, bestowed, and protected in the two pairs of the Īśa and Jīva [mandalas]. (1.33.40)
Contemplating all this as consisting of me, one does not incur bondage;
by me the five fires were fashioned and revealed from my own self alone. (41)
Man, woman, desire, vigor, and passion—these five are declared by me to be the five fires revealed from me. (42)
Likewise, these five fires are the states of the constituent element (dhātu).
For the first fire is the Person (puruṣa), and it is called the "personal" (pauruṣa) element. 43.
The second fire is that of the *liṅga*, and its constituent element (*dhātu*) is called the *laiṅga*. Then the third fire is that of the *yoni*, and its constituent element is called the *yauna*. 44.
Then the fourth fire is the *garbha* (womb) fire; it is called the infant (*bāla*).
The fifth is the *apatya* (offspring) fire; it is called the embodied (*mūrta*) fire. (45)
Thus, from the seed of the elements, creation certainly proceeds;
having realized that those [elements] consist of me, the composed individual worships them. (46)
Through the thorough contemplation of my true nature, one neither comes to me nor goes to bondage;
however, desire arising from affection between two embodied beings is fashioned as a bond. (47)
That very affection for Brahman is considered to be fashioned for the sake of liberation;
for from the perspective of Brahman it is a virtue, whereas from the perspective of duality it is a defect. (48)
Because Hari is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), all actions arising from Hari, joined with Hari, and originating from the procreative source of Hari are likewise devoid of qualities. 49.
For Kāma is called a god, and Rati is a goddess because she rests upon him;
therefore, the divinity of the God [Śiva] arises from his power over all the gods. (1.33.50)
Kāma should be understood as the embodied form of Hari, bestowing the bliss of the body's delight;
bliss is the very nature of Brahman, and when viewed through the perspective of Brahman, it does not cause bondage. //51//
O Lakṣmī! Those two sons of yours are indeed Vyāja and Vyavasāyaka;
I give them to people so that, through them, they may become enterprising and find refuge in happiness. (52)

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Arising of Desire Caused by Betel and the Subsequent Lineage and the Agnis," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. 33.
← Chapter 33: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 34 [[Author: → Chapter 35
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Hari! Tell me, where did that Brāhmaṇa who was born from the body of Nārāyaṇa go, and what did he do? Speak of that to me."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: There was a divine Brāhmaṇa, the primordial Puruṣa, sixteen years of age, who had been instructed by his father and was proficient in all branches of knowledge. (2)
Equal to Nārāyaṇa in body and equal to him in virtues as well, he was like another Nārāyaṇa in appearance, age, and form. (3)
He praised the divine Nārāyaṇa, his own father and instructor:
"O Nārāyaṇa! O Lord of cows! You are the father of the worlds and their teacher. (4)
"Tell me, what task should I perform? I shall protect it, of this there is no doubt.
He who protects is called a father, and a son is one who carries out his commands. (5)
The father is Viṣṇu; the father is the deity; the father is Aṃśa, born of Vāsudeva.
The father is Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman; therefore, the father is worshipped.
The father is the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha), the savior, the bestower of merit, and the most excellent.
The father is God, the father is the supreme deity; the father is the eternal Brahman.
He who is the father, the provider of the seed, the nourisher, the protector, and the one who offers everything of his own—what other is considered superior to him? (8)
By him who has satisfied his father, Hari is satisfied;
by him who has served his father, Hari is served. (9)
Charity, merit, vows, hospitality, sacrifice, fire-offerings, self-restraint, and so forth—even if unperformed, these become as if well-performed by one who serves his father. (1.34.10)
Even one who is a great sinner, an extreme evildoer, a killer of animals, or a suicide,
is glorified in the world of Brahmā after drinking the water used for washing the feet of his father.
He is the Father, the Supreme Brahman, the refuge for those seeking shelter; he is the giver, the nourisher, and the Lord of the body, knowledge, wealth, and all else. 12.
By him who has carried out his father’s command, everything has been accomplished; nothing else remains to be done, for there is no duty remaining beyond the father’s blessings. (13)
Whether refined or unrefined, a son who is looked after by his father becomes fearless, worthy of honor, and in every way esteemed even by the great. (14)
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Mahādeva, nor Vairāja, nor the Īśvaras are equal to a father; for the father alone is considered the father. 15.
He who serves his father in old age by providing water, food, clothing, vehicles, and the like, by massaging his feet, and by attending to him as his personal attendant;
he who, when called or commanded, does not reply with a "no. (16)
One who performs his desired rites with the thought "Om" alone will partake of liberation; of this there is no doubt. ||17||
He who performs no action whatsoever without his father’s consent, and who acts only by his command, shall indeed partake of the fruit in every way. (18)
He who is being led away by calamities, he who is crushed by sufferings, and even he who is overcome by obstacles—such a person is indeed protected by devotion to the ancestors. (19)
A father is truly considered to possess a son only through such a virtuous son;
indeed, a father does not possess a son at all through a son who does not obey his commands. (1.34.20)
Therefore, father, I shall carry out your command so that the fruit of birth may be attained; by this, all merit will be accomplished. Thus, grant me your permission immediately. (21)
While he stood thus with palms joined in reverence, demonstrating his devotion to his father, Nārāyaṇa himself appeared as his father and spoke to his good son:
"O son, live long! You have been nourished by my auspicious blessings."
Devoted to his father, he prospers daily through righteousness toward his son. Such is your reflection, and your conduct is performed out of devotion to your father.
O son, I abide in the discernment of filial devotion, which indeed bestows perfection.
He indeed should be known as a true son by whom his father is well protected—constantly saluted, served, honored, and revered.
That son who, having risen in the morning, [honors] the ancestors, the gods, and likewise the teachers... (25)
The noble ones who praise and bow down [to them] partake in imperishable wealth.
Indeed, for them the worlds are imperishable; for them there is imperishable immortality;
for them there is indeed imperishable spiritual welfare, and for them there is supreme prosperity. (25–27)
Their wives were always virtuous, devoted to their husbands,
sweet-spoken, providers of sweet food, and likewise bestowers of sweet enjoyments.
Their homes were divine and possessed millions of riches.
And there are delightful abundance of flavorful substances and materials for those people who serve their ancestors with clothing, food, and water,
as well as through service, compliance, obedience, and attendance. (1.34.30)
For them, there shall be inexhaustible worlds and inexhaustible powers;
there shall be imperishable divine happiness, free from obstacles and long life.
The supernatural attainments abide where the ancestors are honored.
And there, all prosperities arrive, brought about by the blessings of the ancestors:
gold, silver, wealth, grain, and various kinds of jewels;
soft beds like the foam of milk, fair women, and likewise the [six] flavors.
For those who serve their ancestors, there shine vehicles, mounts, and palaces;
gardens, groves, dwellings, lakes, and grounds for recreation;
celestial chariots, cows, and slender-waisted female servants. (34)
Servants become gentle and obedient to those who serve their parents.
Service to one’s parents is an inexhaustible gain; there is no other gain like it, by which sons rejoice both in this world and in the next. (35–36)
By those who previously served and satisfied their father with devotion,
the state of Brahmā and other higher realms were attained, as well as the state beyond rebirth.
Yama does not approach one who has become a vessel for his father’s grace.
Even Time flees from one who is a vessel for the father’s favor.
For one such as Hari, who is a recipient of his father’s grace, there is the state of being a vessel for [divine] favor;
but for those devoid of their father’s favor, the destination is miserable and brings endless suffering.
The lineage of those who have obtained their father’s favor never perishes anywhere;
the well-being of those who have attained their father’s favor never decays anywhere.
For those who have attained their father’s favor, all afflictions depart far away.
Indeed, internal sufferings are never, never seen at all.
For their sense organs always remain free from disease.
The father, the provider of the seed, is worthy of honor; the mother, who nourishes the embryo in the womb, is likewise venerable.
In childhood, the mother who serves as a nurse should be served just as one's father is;
the father should be understood as Nārāyaṇa, and the mother as being the very form of Lakṣmī.
By him who has performed service to his mother, millions of deities have been served.
Abiding in her vow for the sake of conception, the mother indeed places the embryo within her womb;
even while renouncing desired objects of enjoyment, food, drink, and the like, she protects it.
She endures the supreme suffering in giving birth, including death and fainting.
She makes the child, who is covered in urine and excrement, stainless.
Even when she has abandoned sleep, she remains seized by anxiety for the sake of the child.
She meditates upon the child like a lord, and she serves and nourishes him as well.
She protects everything she has earned herself and always gives it for his sake.
Indeed, does the debt of a mother toward her son ever become light? A son is truly unable to repay that debt even in hundreds of years.
Whatever kind of parents they may be, they are regarded as equal to Brahmā;
they should always be honored, served, and saluted by sons who desire merit.
Even if they are blind, diseased, poor, wretched, or unchaste—
"Even if parents are thieves or intent on violence, they are worthy of worship.
You are fortunate, my son, that you always carry out my command; for my command alone is your dharma. Be a soul of dharma at all times. (1.34.50–51)
"O son! I shall bestow upon you that which is renowned as the *patnīvrata*.
You alone are the one who observes the vow of devotion to his wife (*patnīvrata*), a Brahmin endowed with divine perfection.
Since you are my very form, O Kṛṣṇa, you are exceedingly dear to me. (52)
"O son, become an Ācārya known by the name Kṛṣṇavallabha!
You are indeed my own incarnation, a Lord who grants liberation to all.
Become the sole and true husband of the countless virtuous women created by me."
In every creation, having assumed a divine form and being all-pervading, dwell within every man and become endowed with ten millionfold virtues.
Listen; I shall instruct you in the vow of a devoted wife according to its true essence.
Likewise, behave toward men in such a way that you may become a bestower of liberation.
She who brings a portion of her husband into her own womb for his protection is called a *patnī* (wife); she is one who has him as a witness before the fire and is his companion.

"For that purpose and for her happiness, conduct directed toward that [wife] alone for the sake of human goals is called a *vrata*; thus it is termed 'the vow of devotion to one's wife' (*patnīvrata*).

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Brāhmaṇas Consisting of Service to the Ancestors and the Vow of Devotion to One’s Wife," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*. 34.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The true meaning of the term *patnīvratā* has been correctly explained by me;
now I shall tell you what various deeds were performed for the sake of your wife.

First comes the state of a religious student (brahmacāritva), and afterwards indeed the state of a householder (gārhasthya). Having first been a religious student, one should thereafter live with a wife.
"Take up the life of a religious student and also the sacred thread (yajñopavīta)."
"Understand the meaning of the Vedas, and afterwards become one with a wife.
Having thus instructed his son, a Brāhmaṇa who was approaching youth,
he waited for an auspicious moment and proceeded with the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
Thus, with a mind eager to perform the son’s investiture ceremony,
he of great prowess prepared all the necessary materials.
At that time, auspicious musical instruments were sounded again and again.
Then Lakṣmī and the others sang songs there in joy.
This excellent rite was performed for the sake of giving away three cows as an atonement for the three hardships,
and for the pacification of impurity caused by eating according to one's own will.

One should eat in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, eat food obtained unasked for three days, and for the final three days one should not eat at all; this is declared to be the *kṛcchra* (penance).
Furthermore, the worship of the *mātṛkās* and likewise the *nāndī-śrāddha* [should be performed].

He performed the recitation of benedictions (*svastivāca*), the ritual for domestic peace (*gṛhaśānti*), and the feeding of the twice-born; furthermore, Śrī Hari himself personally established the fire produced from the *araṇi* wood upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and performed its worship and other rites. (1.35.10)
Having bathed, eaten, shaved his head, and adorned himself,
he consecrated his son who was seated on his right side;
[he gave him] a loincloth, a waist-thread, and a new sacred thread.
Having performed the oblation of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*), the Lord granted him threefold [status] and said:
"Sāma shall be your Veda; Śrī Brahmā is your lineage (*gotra*);
and your three *pravara*s are Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Hari."
"Indeed, this branch shall henceforth be known by the name *Patnīvratā*. Understand now that you have become a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).
(14) Listen; I shall explain to you in brief the duties appropriate for you."
Offer oblations into the fire at the beginning of the morning; perform the *āpośāna* rite, and act accordingly.
(15) Always perform service to the guru and likewise engage in the recitation of the Veda.
Receive this Gāyatrī mantra and perform its recitation constantly. (16)
"Oṃ, we know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva.
May that Viṣṇu impel us"—with this, one should rotate the rosary.
"Accept this staff of Brahmā, as well as this deer-skin."
Perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti), and avoid anger and falsehood.
Likewise, protect your celibacy (brahmacarya) and never enter into any state of mental distortion. Do not engage in impure eating or drinking, nor ever commit an act of killing.
O Brahmin, do not fall into distress; do not engage in censure anywhere.

You should daily perform these eight: bathing, the twilight prayers (sandhyā), chanting (japa), fire-offerings (homa), Vedic study (svādhyāya), libations to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa), self-knowledge (ātmajñāna), and the worship of Hari.
Having uttered the words "Om," he likewise approached the Sun;
he circumambulated the fire and received alms from his mother.
Śrī Hari [received] cows, gold coins, garments, and ornaments.
He gave [offerings] to the lords who had assembled there;
having given them food and sacrificial fees, they were fully satisfied.
Hari taught his son, whose soul was filled with the praise of knowledge, the Veda.
Wearing matted hair, a water-pot, a staff, a deer-skin, and bark garments,
he reflected upon the marriage of his son, named Pativratākhya, with a girl named Pativratā, who was full of beauty and youth. (24–25)
Nārāyaṇa indeed arranged the marriage of the girl;
having observed the birth-constellations of the two, he determined the auspicious time for the wedding.
Having also considered the moment and the strength of the stars, he wrote out the horoscope.
Having indeed caused auspicious songs and the recitation of benedictions to be performed,
and having likewise sweetened the face of the bridegroom with a drop of unbroken rice,
she massaged the body of the bridegroom with flour-powders and worshipped him.
Having erected the pavilion and set up the pillars of rubies,
and having performed the installation of Gaṇeśa as well as the worship of the Mātṛkās,
he established the water-pot and caused the sacrificial pit to be prepared.
Having tied the *kāmaphala* (mīṃḍholaka) in his hand, he led the bridegroom to the pavilion.
Having brought the bride there, she placed the bridegroom’s garland upon him. Then, having established the *gārhapatya* fire in the sacrificial pit, he offered oblations.
Having joined their hands, he caused sweet food to be given into her mouth;
having tied the knot of the garment, he indeed caused the circumambulation to be performed. Having made the sound of Vedic instruments, he had auspicious songs sung.
Having delighted [the deity] with mudrās and other offerings, he presented the ritual materials from his hands.
Having said, "May you practice the Dharma together," he completed the rite of the auspicious conjunction (lagna).
Having removed obstacles from the head, he joined [the couple] with blessings.
Having given away the bride and groom according to the Brāhma rite, he indeed led them away. Then Nārāyaṇa there instructed the couple:
"A wife is certainly not separate from her husband, nor is a husband separate from his wife."
Because the two loves are non-different, the unity of the two is born of their very nature.
(36) Indeed, the wife bears in her womb the husband’s secret and great potency;
and because those two limbs are one, the unity of the couple is born of their limbs. (37)
The father’s portion remains within the womb and is nourished by the mother’s portion;
thus, the child becomes one for both, and therefore there is a unity between the two.
When misfortune befalls one, the suffering of both is equal. (38)
When one attains the perfection of happiness, the happiness of both becomes equal.
Loss and gain, pleasure and pain—these are experienced equally by both.
Since the self is attached to itself in both, therefore there is oneness for the two as well. (1.35.39–40)
When wealth is acquired by even one person, the ownership of another is established;
when merit is performed by one, a second person partakes of the fruit.
For, when a task has been accomplished by one, the other places his trust [in that result].
One indeed enjoys the food acquired by both;
by day and by night, there is oneness between the two bodies as well as the two minds.
"Mine" and "I" are not distinct; therefore, there is unity between the two.
In weeping, one enters into weeping; likewise, in rejoicing, one enters into rejoicing.
In fainting, one enters into fainting; in thinking, there arises thinking.
Because of the unity of these two, all this occurs; it does not arise from things that are distinct.
Therefore, in every respect, the supreme unity of husband and wife must be understood.
Thus, by the power of this unity, there is even unity in merit;
likewise, there is even unity in endurance regarding the enemy's punishment and the king's punishment.
In matters of pilgrimage, charity, service, auspiciousness, merit, and righteous duty,
the share of husband and wife is equal, both in this world and in the next.
Therefore, half of one's own body belongs to the other.
The left half of a man is indeed his wife, and the right half is the husband;
for the husband always resides in the wife, and the wife dwells in the beloved husband.
Therefore, the wife is considered the half-body of the man, and the husband is likewise considered the half-body of the woman.
Therefore, having abandoned one's own self-interest and recognized the welfare of both,
one should remain for the sake of the livelihood of both,
acting as a helper toward one another by recognizing each other’s own reflection.
Even after overcoming the conflict between the two, one should perform one's daily duties every day.
Just as a husband is to be served, honored, and worshipped like a god by his wife,
so too should a virtuous wife be served, honored, and revered like a goddess by her husband.
In eating, clothing, conversation, recreation, festivals, and play;
in adornment, laughter, honor, sitting, and mounting vehicles;
in conduct, livelihood, ownership, worship, hospitality, and reverence. (53)
Indeed, a wife must always be counted as foremost by a man.
Where women are honored, there the gods dwell;
where women are satisfied, there prosperity resides.
Where women rejoice, there indeed do prosperities increase;
where women find satisfaction, there are prosperities drawn forth. For women bring joy here, and there the supernatural powers (siddhis) arrive.
Women should neither be terrified nor beaten, for they are the upholders of the lineage.
But as for her who, having abandoned her father, has come to the house of her husband—she is subject to her husband and shares his fortune; what wise man would terrify her?
She who lives like a maidservant, indeed existing like a slave-girl; having become wretched and miserable, she follows after her husband alone;
or where she is driven like a cow, there she indeed drags herself along in misery.
Who indeed would cause suffering to her who is like the shadow of the body?
(60) She consumes what is given and what is eaten; she devours the remainder when others are occupied.
Dependent on another, she clings to her husband—what wise man would not protect her? (61)
She who performs her household duties even while enduring hunger and thirst; she who carries out her husband’s work even while suffering through difficult times;
and she who, having abandoned sleep and idleness, disregards her own mind— ||62||
She stands upon the ground below for the sake of fulfilling her husband's desires.
She who, being powerless, endures everything—beating, scolding, shouting, reviling, and even abandonment—who could inflict suffering upon her? (63–64)
In such a virtuous wife, Lakṣmī is established:
Rādhā, Ramā, Jayā, Padmā, Śāradā, Sarasvatī, Ekādaśī, Rati, Sandhyā, Mohinī, and Jayantī as well. (65)
Indeed, these and other great goddesses dwell there among the wives:

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe the many mental sons of the Pitṛs.
As Brahmā was creating his sons, the Pitṛs were indeed born to him.
Madhu and the others—the six seasons—were born as the Pitṛs.
The Agniṣvāttas and the Bārhiṣadas were indeed the Mānasa Pitṛs;
these Ājyapas and Somapas were also Mānasa Pitṛs. Among them, there were those who did not perform sacrifices as well as those who were householders.
Those ancestors who have not maintained the sacred fires are indeed the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs;
those among them who were performers of sacrifices are the Soma-drinking Pitṛs;
and those who were maintainers of the Agnihotra fire are the Bārhiṣat Pitṛs.
For these—the Ṛṣis and the Pitṛs—were indeed born from the creative resolve (saṃkalpa) of Brahmā.
Madhu and Mādhava are anointed with sap; Śuci and Śukra are full of vigor;
Nabha and Nabhasya are full of life; and Ūrja and Saha are overflowing with nectar.
Sahasa and Sahasya, Samanya, Tapas, and Tapasya— these are the formidable pairs of seasons, whose nature consists of cause and effect.
Among them, those who are the mind-born sons of Brahmā are the presiding deities (abhimānins).
The sphere of action consists of the divisions of time such as the *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, months, and years.
Those who possess consciousness and awareness of these are indeed the Pitṛs (Ancestors).
The Great Time (*mahān kālaḥ*) is the Year; its sons are traditionally known as the Seasons (*ṛtavaḥ*). (8–9)
The ages (*yugas*) and the cosmic cycles (*kalpas*) are indeed the Mahattaras and Mahattamas;

they are the Pitṛs, born from Brahmā, whose nature consists of cause and effect. The seasons (*ṛtus*) are their offspring, as are the days and so forth; from them arise the lunar phases (*kalās*) and the rest.
The sons of Ārtavī are the Sthāneśvaras, who are also of the nature of *sthā* (abiding).
Prajāpati himself is Brahmā, assuming the form of the year (*saṃvatsara*) and so forth;
the year itself is Agni, and it signifies the meaning of *ṛta* (cosmic order).

From *ṛta* come those *ṛtus*, and from them the months are considered to arise. Whatever flower belongs to bipeds, quadrupeds, birds, reptiles, and likewise to stationary beings, that indeed is considered the seasonal (*kāla-ṛtava*) manifestation.
"And because there is no difference between the effect and the cause, the identity of names serves to inform the fathers.
Thus the fathers are to be known, as well as the seasons (*ṛtu*) and the seasonal products (*ārtava*).
Then, from them, at the time of the seasons, all beings were born. (14–15)
Therefore, these Pitṛs were also created by Brahmā from the Ṛtus.
Then two daughters, Menā and Dhāraṇī, were born from the Pitṛs;
they were both Yoginīs and exponents of Brahman, and were highly esteemed by the Pitṛs.
The Bārhiṣads gave that Menā as a wife to Himavat. Maināka was born from Menā, and from Dhāraṇī, Mandara was born thereafter.
Furthermore, the daughters Velā, Niyati, and Āyati were also born.
Dhātṛ’s wife was Āyati, and Niyati is remembered as the wife of Vidhātṛ.
From Sāgara, Velā gave birth to an auspicious daughter, Sāmudrī.
And Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Sāvarṇi.
To them, [the gods] gave ten verses beginning with "O Prācīnabarhis, may these [oblations] be yours, O wise ones" (RV 10.62.1–10). Then, after that, the Vṛkṣas gave their daughter Vārkṣī to them.
Dakṣa became known as Prācetasa; the Pitṛs are remembered as ending with Dakṣa.
And those many wives of his dwell indeed in the world of austerity (tapoloka) as ancestors;
all of them were born of his mind (mānasī), yet in the Manvantara they are born from a womb.
Furthermore, those sages who are said to reside in Satyaloka—
Those who were born in their lineages are also celebrated as the Pitṛs.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha—these eight are the sons of Brahmā. (23–24)
Then, impelled by Brahmā, these mental sons produced the Pitṛs who dwell in Tapoloka;
they were the Bhārgavas, the Āṅgirasas, the Mārīcas, and others as well.
The Paulastyas, the Paulahas, and likewise the Krātavas;
the Ātreyas and the Vāsiṣṭhas—these are the groups of Pitṛs renowned in the world, who dwell in the Tapoloka. || 26–27 ||
Among them, some are formless and luminous, while others are likewise radiant; indeed, those ancestors are full of light.
Furthermore, there are the sons of Dakṣa known as the Haryaśvas and the Śabalāśvas.
Numbering ten thousand and five thousand— indeed,
all one thousand five hundred— they are all endowed with the splendor of Brahman.
Having entered the path of austerity, they abide established in penance.

Following the instruction of Nārada, intent upon seeking Brahmā, they arrived at the world of Tapas and remain there, possessing divine splendor. These are the Pitṛs, all of whom bring about the welfare of their progeny.
R̥bhu, Sanatkumāra, and others remain in some places as ascetics (32).
They stay there for the sake of performing their duties through austerity, yet they are established in meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu [are among them] (33).
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and others were first produced from the Brahman together with the mind; thereafter,
having established the progeny, they take refuge in the act of procreation itself.
All the hosts, beginning with the Yāmas, dwell in Maharloka.
But when Maharloka is destroyed, they take refuge in Janaloka alone;
having gone there, they all indeed exist with subtle bodies. (35–36)
Possessing equal powers and likewise assuming identical forms,
they dwell in Janaloka for as long as the night of Brahmā lasts;
even there, they remain endowed with the power of the merit and renown of their previous kalpas.
Those who were Prajāpatis, having ceased from their lordship,
and whose activities have ceased— being self-abiding and well-disposed—
they abandon the Janaloka and, together with them, attain the Tapoloka. (38–39)
The manifestation of the Manvantaras beginning with Svāyambhuva occurs within the world;
the deities whose offices have ceased abide in the realm of light (mahas). Those who are the Manvantaras, beginning with Śukra and ending with Cākṣuṣa, likewise exist.
Residing in Maharloka, they were born from the mind of Brahmā:
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, as well as Svāyambhuva Aṅgiras,
Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and others such as these.
Indeed, for the sake of maintaining the flow of worldly affairs, all the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) go even to Maharloka; they remain there together with them.
Even those established in Satyaloka frequently come here for the sake of their duties.
Once their task is accomplished, they all return once more to their own homes.
These worlds are named Somapada and are known as Maharloka and Janaloka; there dwell the ancestors, namely the Agniṣvātta and others.
The Vasus also exist; they are Amāvasu and the others.
Those extremely subtle sparks of fire are indeed the Pitṛs, the deities.
And those who are the sons of Virajā are the groups known as the Vairājas.
There, the ancestors known as the Agniṣvāttas are remembered, possessing radiant splendor.
Likewise, those sons of Svadhā and sons of Svāhā who shine with light—
those Marīcigarbhas are the ancestors there, indeed having the form of fire.
The ancestors known as the Ājyapas are those who are birds;
their worlds are called the Mānasas, where they reside.
The sons of Viraja, however, are considered to be the Vairājas by name.
Those hosts are radiant, consumers of merit, and indeed formless.
Those who are considered the daughters of the Pitṛs and their grandsons are the Pitṛs themselves;
they should be understood as the expansion of the lineage, residing in separate dwellings.

On earth, they dwell in the forms of virtuous women and holy men; in the intermediate space, they consist of the nature of the wind; in heaven, they are of the nature of the gods; and in the realms of Mahar, Jana, and Tapa, they are mind-born.
Thus the Pitṛs, possessing both embodied and unembodied forms, reside together.

All those primordial gods are great beings of immense power; they grant all desires when satisfied, but are considered to take everything away when enraged. Therefore, they must always be propitiated with every possible effort. (53–54)
"For those who abide in Mahar and the worlds above, their perfection is indeed mental;
for them, everything desired arises immediately by the power of the mind.
Thus, O beloved Lakṣmī, all the great ṛṣis abide."
In the world of heat (Tapoloka) and the world of men (Janaloka), the ancestors are stationed in every way.
In Maharloka, the world-protectors, the Rudras, the lords of creatures,
the Manus, and the ancestors themselves are all established there according to their respective functions.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Mental Creation of the Pitṛs in the Mahar, Jana, and Tapa Loka-s," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. Chapter 39.
[Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Part 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna), Chapter 40]
[The Author: Chapter 41.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
How many kinds of ancestors (pitṛs) are to be understood, what is to be given, and likewise, what is the fruit?
Intending [the offering] for the father, the father’s father,
and likewise the father’s grandfather— by name, across these three funeral cakes (piṇḍas)—
what śrāddhas are to be given, and how indeed do they reach the ancestors?
Whether on earth, in the intermediate space, or in heaven— whether they are suffering or happy—
the ancestors who have entered a body may or may not become *pitṛs*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Gods, sages, and indeed numerous living beings,
having come together in the world of action and performed manifold deeds,
are born as those very ancestors who dwell in the worlds of earth and the other realms.
Some dwell upon the earth, while others remain in the intermediate space of the atmosphere.
All of them, however, are born with latent tendencies (vāsanās) and meet with sudden death.
Yet some indeed go to heaven—those who are solely devoted to merit (puṇya).
Some, through merit, go to the worlds of Mahar, Jana, and Tapa;
others likewise go to the world of Soma, the world of Sūrya, and the world of lightning.
Others go to the world of Agni, the world of Indra, and to the stars, planets, and constellations.
They go according to their merit; those gods are known as the ancestors (pitṛs).
They become ancestors as gods, and gods again as ancestors.
The worlds of the ancestors are known as the Sāntānika worlds, which are considered radiant.
Wherever they may be situated, the ancestors whom those born in the lineage remember—
those ancestors who desire progeny must certainly come there.
And among the ancestors, Soma, Aryaman, and likewise [the others], shall be the king.
Aryaman daily stimulates the Soma with his rays;
and the Soma, indeed, nourishes the entire world with its rays.
And from that [nourishment], all the ancestors become satisfied by partaking of the Soma.
By satiating Soma, their father, with *śrāddha* offerings, they shall attain satisfaction.
Those ancestors who dwell in the world of Soma and subsist on Soma—
Soma, being satiated by the *śrāddhas*, will in turn cause the world to flourish.
The entire world, including its mountains and forests, is filled with all things moving and unmoving.
(14) Those men who, desiring prosperity, perform ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) here, to them the ancestors will always grant both prosperity and progeny. (11)
Those ancestors who, residing everywhere, shall receive the three rice-balls offered at the *śrāddha* ceremony according to name and lineage— including the great-grandfather—
will cause their progeny to prosper through that offering of the *śrāddha*.
Whether they be happy or suffering, the ancestors possess latent tendencies (*vāsana*).
Therefore, water and food must necessarily be offered to them by their descendants according to their capacity;
by that, the ancestors—whether possessing form or formless—shall become satisfied. (17–18)
Seven groups of them are proclaimed, worshipped throughout the three worlds.
Among them, three are formless and four possess form.
Of these, the three that exist above possess the form of pure being.
Beneath them exist four subtle forms;
those whose forms consist of pure being (bhāvamūrti) are satisfied by faith and contemplation.
Those whose forms are subtle (sūkṣmamūrti) become satisfied by the merit derived from food and other offerings.
Moving with the speed of thought, devoted to their own *svadhā*, and possessing all desirable things as their wealth,
they, having obtained food and *soma*, nourish themselves with satisfied minds. There, at that *śrāddha*, they are gratified by the offerings of water and food through the power of those gifts.
Those wise devotees of Viṣṇu, through acts such as the offering of all to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa),
are born as exponents of Brahman at the end of a full thousand yugas.
Having cast off their physical bodies, they become formless and attain liberation.
The deities with their forms are satisfied by ritual action and the worship of the guru;
once satisfied at the *śrāddha*, those ancestors drink the *soma* again.
One should feed thousands of virtuous brahmins, as well as children.
The ancestors of those virtuous women are satisfied by their food;

[they are satisfied] by a thousand Brahmins who have completed their studies, by a hundred *snātaka*s, by a thousand who are without protectors, and by a hundred forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*s). (26–27)
There was one virtuous woman and one virtuous man; indeed, they were distinguished in their eating.
For the virtuous man and the virtuous woman were the children of Hari, consisting of knowledge and meditation.
Divine, bestowing liberation, contented, yogis, they were absorbed in Brahman.
"His son, grandson, or great-grandson shall feed those two children;
his ancestors will be satisfied, just as farmers are by a good rain.
In the absence of virtuous men and women, one should feed two celibate students. (1.40.29–30)
But in the absence of that, one should feed a daughter's son or even a guest;
for perfected beings (siddhas) wander in many forms in secret every day. (31)
One should always honor that guest who possesses the nature of a virtuous man or woman;
for such a person is like the earth bounded by the oceans, or like the gods and the masters of yoga. (32)
Moving about in various forms, these protectors of the dharma of living beings—accomplished ones, holy men, and virtuous women—wander upon the surface of the earth. (33)
One should perform their worship in the form of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and offer them delicious food, side dishes, and fruits. (34)
The gods, the ancestors, and Agni indeed consume [the offerings] by entering into those who appear in the form of guests; therefore, one should always honor such guests. (35)

One should always regard children, those who have arrived [as guests], the weary, virtuous men, and virtuous women without support, as well as devoted supplicants, as being of the very nature of guests. ||36||
A beggar is one who has arrived as a petitioner; a guest is one who has arrived without asking. [One should offer hospitality] to the thirsty, the weary, the wandering, and the extremely hungry. (37)
To the learned, to the virtuous man, to the virtuous woman, to the child, and to the one who has no other refuge—to him it should be given with due honor by one desiring the fruit of sacrifice. (38)
And the virtuous, high-souled ones, being honored and worshipped at the śrāddha, grant liberation, yoga, and sovereignty—these are the grandfathers (pitāmahas). 39.
Whatever is given by all of them in silver vessels, or even in those adorned with silver,
while placing the word "svadhā" before it, truly gratifies the ancestors.
Through devotion, one indeed pleases the ancestors, and the ancestors in turn please him;
this is so for one who desires prosperity or, again, for one who desires to perform worship. ||41||
They bestow nourishment, progeny, and a good heaven, without a doubt;
as well as thousands of celestial chariots yoked with hosts of apsarases. (42)
The ancestors bestow all desired objects, as well as wisdom, nourishment, memory, intelligence, sovereignty, and even health. (43)
Grandfathers bestow pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, tens of thousands of horses and elephants, and even jewels by the millions. (44)
A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is said to be fit for the ancestors;
however, a vessel of silver or one coated with silver is the most excellent for the ancestors. (45)
Even a mere mention of silver, or its sight, or its gift—such a gift to the ancestors is said to be infinite, inexhaustible, and leading to heaven. (46)
Moreover, by this gift, sons born of daughters (dauhitras) rescue their ancestors when they are worthy recipients;
[the gifts include] gold, silver, copper, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds. 47.
Clothing, purifying substances, and even a virtuous woman are called "good" (sādhu);
likewise, whatever food is delicious by which the ancestors are pleased [is also so called]. (48)
I shall describe those [foods] to you, which indeed grant all desires;
they are excellent foods for the Śrāddha ceremony, truly for the satisfaction of the ancestors. 49.
There was rice cooked with milk (paramānna), milk-based preparations, pūrikās, and likewise polikās; there were apūpas with a hundred holes and sweet pūraṇa-polikās. || 1.40.50 ||
Rutalyas, as well as ghāripūrikās, praroṭakas, phāphaṭas, and sthirakas, along with ghee-flour cakes and rice mixed with jaggery. (51)
Śaṣkulīs, khājakas, saṃyāvas, and likewise modakas; kaṃsāras, parpikās, khaṇḍas, piṇḍakas, and likewise granthakas. (52)
There were also *kalikālaḍukās*, as well as *kalikās* and *sevikās*;
*sohālikās*, *maṇḍakas*, *vaṭikās*, and *ghṛtapūraṇas*. ||53||
There were cakes and pearls, as well as garments and threads of cotton;
there were pleasant rice-flour preparations, along with mung-bean dumplings and *ghurghara* sweets. (54)
Sesame rings, *gundrapāka*, yellow essences, and candied sugars;
the auspicious *mohana* platter, rice, and flower-balls. (55)
Rice, barley, and likewise rājagava and other grains;
water chestnuts, red lentils, bottle gourds, and pulses of various kinds. (56)
Vhālā, parpaṭas, parpaṭyas, kvathikā, and curd;
green gram, mung beans, tuvaryas, and milk. ||57||
Vegetables seasoned with cinnamon, cloves, and cardamom; honey;
*gavāhāra* beans; *bhiṇḍaka* gourds; and red *cirbhaṭa* cucumbers. ||58||
Karkaṭī, kāravella, kūṣmāṇḍa, and likewise sūraṇa;
vṛntāka, śarkarākanda, śimbikā, and likewise kharbuja. (59)
Paṭola, gaṇḍaka, ghṛtaṣoḍha, parāvala, lūnikā, methikā, rājñī, jīvantī, and suvamūlaka. (1.40.60)
Tāṇḍulīya, ājyā, hyamlalūnī, rājagraha, dugdhikā, kunarā, śarkarā, tiktā, and various kinds of patravallī; ||61||
Frying eggplants, eating *caṭanyo*, and butter are likewise [forbidden] for those lacking the wisdom of *dhānyāka* and *kauthumī*. (6)
[One should offer] grapes, *khārika* dates, plantains, and various bitter substances mixed with mustard; [as well as] curd-smeared mustard, and many kinds of fermented gruel (*āranāla*). (63)
There were sweet foods that were fresh, excellent, and fit for consumption;
there were drinks mixed with sweets, fragrant, and flavorful. (64)
Sugarcane, *nāraṅga*, banana, citron, *iṅguda*, and *santura*;
the *setu*, the nectar-like fruit-bearing *jambava* tree;
*iṅgudī*, coconut, mango, jackfruit, and *lipsikācikā*.
Likewise, jujubes, mangoes, cakes, bananas, and emblic myrobalans [were offered]. (66)
The fruits of the *rāmaphala*, *pāpanasa*, *sītāphala*, and *subilvaka*, as well as these fruits of *tāmbūla* and the excellent bark of the *pūgī*—[these were offered]. (67)
Water originating from sacred fords and highly fragrant flowers should especially be offered during a śrāddha ceremony for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors. 68.
That by which, to whom, for the sake of whose satisfaction, and where the gift is given—
in these three, the Blessed Lord himself is directly the giver, the recipient, and the leader.
By the sacrificer, the nature of the pervasive Hari should be understood as the giver.
Having meditated upon him as Hari in the form of the recipient, it should indeed be given.
That glorious Hari, the all-pervading one, is also well-established within the father.
Through the union with Hari everywhere, the ancestors shall attain satisfaction.
Having uttered the names of the ancestors, the offering should be given with the thought that it is for Hari.
That satisfaction shall become inexhaustible; even a very small amount shall become incomparable.
Maidens, widows, women, the elderly, and those without a protector—these should be fed with auspicious intent at a śrāddha; the fruit thereof is infinite. (73)
A village is to be consumed by one seeking the fruit [of merit] through the suppression of smoke;
his reward exceeds that of a sacrifice, yet it is consumed by beasts and birds.
Likewise, it is consumed by aquatic creatures and even by insects where such exist.
"The faithful one, the inner self of all, is called the Universal Sovereign (Sārvabhauma).

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "Description of Various Ancestors, Their Vessels, the Fruits of the Food Given to Them, and the Fruits of Attaining Those [Realms]," in the first section on the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 40: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā - Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 41 [[Author: Chapter 42 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I shall proclaim for you their auspicious hymn of praise, which grants all desires, by means of which the ancestors are pleased through recitation and observance. (1)
At the time of the *śrāddha*, that [account] should be recited for the satisfaction of the ancestors,
by the sacrificer, by his son, or by a virtuous Brāhmaṇa—
[the account] of the ancestors who are formless, those who possess forms, and those of radiant splendor. (2)
I always pay homage to those contemplative ones who possess the eye of yoga;
(3) likewise, I bow to those givers of desires, the progenitors of Indra and others, as well as of Bhṛgu and Mārīca, and of the seven seers and the ancestors. (4)
I bow to the ancestors who bestow well-being, the progenitors of Manu and the other lords of the gods, as well as of the sun and the moon. (5)
With palms joined in reverence, I bow to the ancestors of the constellations, such as Carā and the rest, as well as to their grandfathers, and to the ancestors of heaven and earth;
and to the progenitors of the divine sages, who are honored by all the worlds.
With palms joined in reverence, I bow to those who always grant fearlessness. (7) To Prajāpati Kaśyapa, to Soma, and to Varuṇa, and to the Lords of Yoga, I bow with palms joined in reverence. (8)
Salutations to the seven groups of ancestors in the seven worlds.
Salutations to that Self-Existent One, to Brahmā, who possesses the eye of yoga. (9)
By means of this supreme hymn of praise, a person obtains three boons;
the blissful ancestors bestow food, long life, and sons. (1.41.10)
Whatever is cooked in the house, whether it be solid food, soft food, or otherwise, one must not eat it without first offering it to the gods and the ancestors. (11)
He who always offers garlands and fragrant substances of every kind to the ancestors shines, endowed with prosperity, like the sun. (12)
He who offers incense such as guggulu and other fragrances to the ancestors, combined with honey and clarified butter, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. (13)
One who offers incense endowed with the quality of fragrance— beloved and dedicated to the ancestors—
obtains offspring through women both in this world and in the next for both [the giver and the recipient]. Furthermore, he who, being self-restrained, always offers a lamp to the ancestors...
He obtains in this world an incomparable eye that bestows divine vision. ||15||
By means of splendor, fame, beauty, and strength,
he becomes self-luminous and shines resplendently in heaven.
Surrounded by Apsarases and rejoicing at the forefront of the celestial chariot (vimāna),
one should indeed offer perfumes, flowers, incenses, and oblations of clarified butter.
One should bring satisfaction to the ancestors with offerings of fruits, roots, and prostrations;
for at the time of the śrāddha, the grandfathers are always present in the form of the wind. (18)
Seeing virtuous brahmins and virtuous women, they enter them with joy, [honoring them] with gifts of clothing, food, and likewise with various kinds of eatables and dainties. (19)
One should honor those residing in the sacred vessels with drinks, cows, and villages; and likewise the kāśas, the punarbhavas, the barhiṇas, and the upabarhiṇas. (1.41.20)
Those very ancestors are the gods, and the gods are again the ancestors.
One should diligently offer *darbha* grass and funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) facing toward the twice-born.
Then, having brought the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the fire-oblation (*homa*) is prescribed to be performed.
"Oblation to Agni Kavyavāha, and homage to Aṅgiras!
Oblation to Soma Pitṛmat, and homage to Aṅgiras!
And to Yama Aṅgiras, oblation and homage!"—thus he should speak. (22–23)
Especially in a well-kindled fire that is smokeless and flickering, one should offer many oblations for the successful accomplishment of the rite. //24//
If one should offer oblations into a fire that is unkindled and smoky, the sacrificer will become blind and shall also remain childless. (25)
If the fire has little fuel, or is dry, or emits sparks in all directions, or if its flames and smoke move to the right, that fire does not lead to success. (26)
Where the earth is particularly foul-smelling, blue, or black, one should know that defeat is at hand. //27//
Radiant, with a compact flame, originating from clarified butter and gold, smooth, and moving clockwise—such a fire leads to the accomplishment of one's purpose. (28)
Having been permitted by those best of the twice-born with the words "Do so," he should take his wife and sons and offer oblations into the sacrificial fire.
The *samit* (sacrificial fuel) for the sacrifice consists of *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, *vikaṅkata*, *udumbara*, as well as *bilva* and *candana*. 1.41.30.
The *sarala*, the *devadāru*, the *śāla*, and likewise the *khadira*—
these trees are especially recommended for the purpose of sacrificial fuel (*samidh*).
Furthermore, those who are called the Viśvedevas are indeed the ancestors (*pitṛs*).
One should diligently offer them clarified butter and rice balls into the fire.
Likewise, having taken the first portion of all flowers, fruits, and edible foods,
one should sacrifice them into the sacred fire.
At a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should respectfully perform the fire-oblation (homa), the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), and the ancestral rite (śrāddha).
Likewise, temples, the residence of a guru, mountains, rivers,
sacred trees, ponds, or wherever a Brāhmaṇa may be present [are suitable places].
Those various places shall be worthy of ancestral rites (śrāddha); there, merit is incalculable.
Divine and virtuous persons always wander here upon the earth bounded by the shores of the ocean in various forms; through their yoga, indeed, comes liberation. (36)
The Siddhas, the virtuous, and the saintly women constitute the most excellent of all sacred fords;
here, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa dwell incessantly within those very forms. (37)
To one who is thirsty, weary, hungry, or destitute, one should give something with due respect; thus one shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice. (38)

In the ancestral rite (śrāddha), the gross [self] eats the gross; the ancestors eat the merit (sukṛta). Through the offering associated with Brahman, the Self (ātman) itself experiences satisfaction. ||39||
In the world of action, having indeed performed [deeds] and having indeed given [gifts] again and again, they are obtained in the next world; therefore, one should especially give. 1.41.40.
To those for whom the kinsmen offer three rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) according to their names and lineages upon the ground covered with *kuśa* grass, following the procedure prescribed by the Brahmins—
those balls, wherever they may be located, truly gratify the ancestors.
Whatever food a living being may have, that very food becomes his [sustenance]. 42.
Just as a calf finds its mother who has wandered lost in the cow-pen, so does the mantra lead the person to wherever he abides. ||43||
The name, the lineage, and the mantra lead him to the food that has been given;
even if they have entered a hundred wombs, satisfaction follows them. (44)

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Hymn, Fire-offering, Sacred Tree, Location, and so forth," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 41.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now I shall describe the arrangement of the gods in brief.
All the mind-born gods of Brahmā are well-established in heaven. (1)
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall now tell you what happened after that.
[The ancestors] were those who nourish with the splendor born of their excellent penance. (2)
Kings are required as the protectors of their subjects;
likewise, even the Manus are the guardians and observers of the worlds.
For their sake, there are dwellings that are luminous and conducive to nourishment.
Having reflected thus, Brahmā himself performed meditative contemplation.
Recalling the supreme Nārāyaṇa, he resolved upon what was to be done.
First, indeed, there appeared a great radiance that causes both ripening and illumination.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he joyfully prayed to Śrī Hari for that second great splendor which likewise bestows power and nourishment.
At that moment, it first emerged from the right eye of Śrī Hari.
Kaṇa was born from Tejas as the illuminator of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
From him were born countless Kaṇas, most fierce;
they too were introduced into the respective cosmic eggs of the various Virañcis.

And in each of those places, at sunset, they became composed of light. Thus, having approached the Sun, he was established by the Creator Parameṣṭhin in heaven for the sake of illuminating the worlds.
And Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, commanded him.
May you always be the Sun in the three worlds by your splendor;
may you be the mere eyes for living beings, not the perceivers of objects. 11.
Where there is no light, how can there be the perceptibility of objects?
Therefore, the state of being a seer will indeed arise through contact with light.
By that means, all the worldly course of life is rooted in vision.
Therefore, you shall indeed attain [that state]; go forth, O Sun! (13)
Thus commanded by Sūrya with the gift of his splendor, [the Sun], fearing his own destruction, addressed Brahmā. ||14||
O God of gods, O Creator of the universe, I shall obey your command;
yet, through the loss of my bodily luster, my destruction may indeed occur. (15)
"I shall soon meet my destruction; therefore, become my protector.
Employ a means of protection here for me, so that I may remain uninjured. (16)
Having heard that from Brahmā, the imperishable Śrī Hari was remembered:
"Become yourself the fulfiller for the sake of fulfilling the Sun. (17)
Nārāyaṇa Hari, having accepted that request of Brahmā, spoke to the god Brahmā in a manner that fulfilled his purpose. ||18||
"O Brahmin, may it be well with you; I give to you the eye of my sun.
May its form be such that it becomes full and possesses an inexhaustible nature. (19)
Having uttered this, Hari himself—masses upon masses of splendor, the person known as Hiraṇmaya, with golden hair and likewise a golden beard—[appeared]. (1.42.20)
From his hair to his nails, he was entirely golden;
at sixteen years of age, he was adorned with ornaments of gold. (21)
He whose forehead alone emits a thousand rays, and he whose head alone emits a hundred thousand rays upward; (22)
His entire body indeed emitted millions of rays, and on every single hair it was filled with a mass of golden light. (23)
Endowed with beauty of form, sweetness, and auspicious qualities;
wearing a crown, earrings, and a garland, and clad in a golden mantle. (24)
A mass of inexhaustible splendor, illuminating with the brilliance of the sun, the Blessed One, having become such as this, entered the orb of the sun. (25)
Filling all splendors with the streams of his own radiance, together with the Sun, Brahmā, and others dwelling in Maharloka and the higher realms. || 26 ||
The god Sūryanārāyaṇa was worshipped and saluted with sixteen types of offerings; such was his worship of the golden man. (27)
The Eye of the World performs this without ceasing for the sake of bestowing [vision];
he recites this hymn of praise during his petition for the fulfillment of that splendor. (28)
Oṃ, salutations to You, the progenitor of splendor, the Great One of imperishable luster;
salutations to Brahman, the giver of imperishable luster to those who possess splendor. 29.
Whose bulls, many-horned and tireless, shine upon the rain-clouds; and whose radiant descendants followed after their lords as they ruled over the lands. (1.42.30)
Homage to that radiant one, the possessor of cows, who spreads forth with his rays; homage to you, the divine God, who dispels the darkness of the heart and possesses celestial splendor. ||31||
Salutation to the sovereign illuminator who makes himself manifest;
salutation to the wise one who has realized existence, the sage of the awakening of knowledge. 32.
Salutations to you, the ordainer of nourishment; salutations to you, the eternal self of the self.
Salutations to the radiant one who, playing, bestows the seven vessels.
Homage to the one who dwells on earth, the red one; homage to the celestial one, the lightning;
homage to the sun and the fierce one; homage to you, the golden-hued one. ||34||
Salutations to the one whose true gold is the void; salutations to the splendor of the stomach;
salutations to the power of the moon; salutations to the self that is as vast as the sky. ||35||
Salutation to the one whose nature is the effect, salutation to the one whose form is the cause;
to the golden-hued God, to Brahman, the Supreme Self. //36//
You are the creator, you are the nourisher, and you alone are indeed the destroyer;
you alone are the supreme splendor, the foremost among the radiant.
O Supreme Lord, always protect me by bestowing your splendor upon me;
and may all those who possess sight worship the Lord of Light. 38.
You alone, O Radiant Lord, are the entities and their powers;
you alone are the possessor of eyes, the protector, the savior from distress, and the imperishable one. (39)
O Great-Eyed One, O Eye of Heaven, O Eye of the Mid-Region, You alone are indeed the Eye of the Earth, the Eye of All; salutations to the Eye of eyes!
Om Om Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Tat Om, that desirable splendor of Savitṛ.
We meditate upon the splendor of the divine; may he impel our thoughts. 41.
Whoever, free from sloth, should recite this mantra and meditate upon it, the supreme golden deity appears visibly before that person. (42)
By reciting it ten thousand times, the great lord Sūrya himself becomes the bestower of boons upon him and grants him divine power. 43.
It makes that eye divine and opens up the inner space;
it rouses the self and brings about that Brahman.
Therefore, becoming intent on meditation, one should always recite for one's own welfare this hymn composed by Sūrya for the purpose of his own worship of the Golden One. (45)
Then indeed, by Brahmā, the golden Sun was endowed with a male form;
he became the bestower of all splendor within the midst of everything. 46.
Thus established in heaven, he alone is indeed the eye of the world;
for in his absence, those who possess eyes truly become sightless.
By means of subtle atomic forms of light, the deity of the eye also comes into being;
he proceeds as the filler of the minute particles of its own radiance within the eyes.
Whatever living being there may be, by day or by night—||48||
Whether it be very slight or abundant, the eye possesses the brilliance of the sun.
By day its light becomes dense, but at night it becomes sparse;
that light is born from the sun and consists of the radiance obtained from the lineage of authoritative teachers.
Water, leaves, flowers, and likewise fruits should be offered to Sūrya;
salutations should always be given, for he is indeed Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World. || 51 ||
The golden Puruṣa, together with his own golden-bodied Lakṣmī,
always protected [her] there within the solar orb.
And when the destruction of heaven occurs at the end of a kalpa, then—
Sūrya is golden, and Lakṣmī and the goddesses are Sūryāṇīs. ||53||
They go indeed to the world of Brahmā, the supreme, imperishable, and immutable;
for their residence there, it was personally created by Śrī Hari. ||54||
In the imperishable abode, his own divine realm known as Hiraṇya, there dwells the golden Person together with the golden Lakṣmī. (55)
Attended by hundreds of billions of gold coins and male and female servants, the supreme lord, the king of kings, shines forever. (56)
That divine, supreme abode is said here to be gross within the sun;
that shadowy orb of the sun is the root-abode situated in Brahman.
That Puruṣa is the Supreme Brahman, the golden one, the sun, and the visual [perceiver].
This very [Self] is attained by those desiring liberation through the knowledge of the eye of meditation. ||58||

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Mental Sun, His Hymn of Praise, the Golden Person (Hiraṇmayapuruṣa), and Other Matters," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
When Brahmā beheld that singular, fierce radiance, which would have burnt everything, caused destruction, and left nothing to nourish or sustain; ||| 1 ||
Then, for the sake of pacification and prosperity, he prayed to the Lord,
the god Nārāyaṇa, who [arose] from the mind of Nārāyaṇa.
From his resolve, a small measure of light emerged from his left eye—cool, nourishing, satiating, and raining down nectar. (3)
Therefore, from a single atom, atoms of many millions and billions were created;
indeed, by the will of the Creator, they became those great spheres. (4)
They were indeed protected by the creators within their respective cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
Born there as moons, they cause coolness to flow forth from that source. || 5 ||
When he requested the Lord for the sake of fulfilling his splendor, the Blessed One said: "I, who always dwell with the sun through my rays, shall provide nourishment there;
thus your splendor will be complete."
Therefore, the Golden Person bestows his splendor day and night.
This nectar, which brings about peace and nourishment, should be drunk;
it is filled with bliss, moist, dripping with joy, and is the cause for the cessation of all suffering. (8)
Because it rescues one from the suffering of heat, that splendor is indeed the *tāraka* (the Savior);
and because it binds together coolness, that splendor is also the lunar (*cāndra*).
Having thus fashioned the supreme moon consisting of such splendor...
Brahmā protected [the moon] in heaven for the sake of the sweet bliss of embodied beings.
The moon, moreover, was always full and remained eternally constant;
later, however, due to its partiality toward women, it fell into decline.
Furthermore, Śaṅkara also rescued him from that disease;
likewise, because of his fitness, he was then granted partial protection. (12)
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O treasure-house of mercy! Please relate to me that story concerning the moon’s partiality toward women, which resulted in his waning. (13)
Who were his wives, how many were they, and in what manner did he show partiality toward them?
How did the curse come to pass, how was there liberation, and how did it result in the destruction of half [the body]? (14)
Listen to all of this, which is a supreme marvel to me:
O Lord, even for a god such as you, there is such suffering because of your form! (15)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen to his wonderful story, born from the impulse of desire, along with its full details;
having heard it, even though you suffer from the pain of rivalry with co-wives, you shall certainly not act in this way again.
In ancient times, Dakṣa, the Prajāpati and mind-born son of Brahmā,
mentally conceived twenty-seven daughters for the sake of creation;
these were the twenty-seven maidens, headed by Rohiṇī.
He gave those who became the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) to Candra:
by name, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣā, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, and Puṣya. (18–19)
Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvāphālgunī, Uttarāphālgunī, Hasti, Citrā, Svāti, Viśākhā, and Anurādhikā; 1.43.20.
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, as well as Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā;
Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and likewise Śatabhiṣaj;
and indeed Pūrvabhādrapadā and Uttarabhādrapadā. (21)
And Revatī—these are the twenty-seven wives of the Moon.
All were divine, golden-hued, and red, twelve years of age;
even among them, she was preeminent for her beauty, grace, charm, and excellent virtues. (23)
Rohiṇī is always skilled in fulfilling desires, yet she is life-destroying;
just as the moon wanes, so too does Rohiṇī remain. (24)
His eye, which captivates the heart, displays an abundance of love for him;
his gentle face, filled with the weight of smiles, possesses the splendor of all erotic charm. (25)
Even when displaying the knitting of her crooked eyes and eyebrows, she captivates the heart;
likewise, by showing her red lips and blossoming cheeks, she bestows peace. (26)
Holding a beautiful flower garland in her hand, she offers it as well;
her breasts, though small, are well-formed and have become firm beneath her bodice. (27)
The young woman also displays her two beautiful breasts, richly colored with saffron; her belly is golden-hued, and her waist is slender and very delicate. (28)
Her hips resemble two jars at her waist, revealing the looseness of her garment; she even displays her hairless, slender middle, which has the luster of gold. (29)
She even reveals her slow-moving anus at the base of her two golden thighs;
having approached the two cheeks, she gives them a slap and departs in haste. (1.43.30)
Turning back again, placing her hand on his neck, and kissing him, she touches his private parts, offers her face, and manifests her amorous play. (31)
Having become devoid of clothing in some places, she even revealed her own body;
casting aside all shame, she captivated the mind of the Moon. (32)

Although Candra was only sixteen years of age, he was an inexhaustible treasury of virility; he took his pleasure, he took his pleasure again, he took his pleasure, and with complete satisfaction, he took his pleasure again and again. //33//
He always took delight with Rohiṇī, and he delighted with her again and again;
Rohiṇī, too, repeatedly assumed a fresh and lovely form. (34)
Even after sporting with them, the Moon did not remember other women; yet at some time or another, he did sport with others as well, though even then he remained mindful of those [primary ones]. (35)
For, like Rohiṇī, they do not find satisfaction from occasional dalliance;
yet, even though the moon’s youth is fully developed and equal for all, he does not treat them with impartiality because of his attachment to Rohiṇī. (36)
Then her husband, having arrived for their mutual pleasure, was entreated by them.
Nevertheless, Rohiṇī did not consent to their happiness;
intent solely on her own interest, she showed partiality. (38)
At that time, however, others remained indifferent and felt no grief for themselves;
for what indeed is the use of a fixed marriage-rite for those who do not possess the happiness of a husband? (39)

If the yoga [of union] that is permeated by desire—abounding in the youthfulness mounted upon passion—does not provide sensual pleasure for both the man and the woman, what is the use of that marriage?
For both the man and the woman, there should be the complete satisfaction of desire according to their wish. (1.43.40)
It would not have been so, had he performed that [rite] with an auspicious moment sought in vain. //41//
If she whose body is filled with desire and who possesses fresh youthfulness does not obtain happiness from her husband, what indeed is the use of having performed the marriage? Therefore,
it is said that widowhood or maidenhood is better than that.
While her husband is alive, the unfortunate woman does not obtain the pleasure of desire. //43//
Better indeed is falling into a well, better is being consumed by fire, and better is swallowing poison than the suffering caused by the burning of desire. 44.
Better is dwelling in one's father’s house, and better even is the state of being a virtuous wife;
but it is not right to burn oneself with the fire of passion while a husband is alive. (45)
May no woman anywhere ever have a husband who is a eunuch;
nor may she have one who is ill-disposed, devoid of love, or even for a single moment. (46)
"Or let there be no rivalry, not even the slightest suffering born of enmity.
Having lamented thus in many ways, they all [remained] in their father's house. (47)
Having gone there, they reported their husband's distress again and again:
"O Father, a daughter must not be given to one who is devoid of love and full of wrath. (48)
We must never go anywhere in the palace of the Moon for one who has fallen into partiality, for one who is ill, or for one who lies with others. (49)
The moon never treats us with impartiality;
it regards my father’s house as dry, and my husband’s house as even more so. (1.43.50)
Everything becomes parched and withered, O Father, when fullness is devoid of the bliss of delight! We speak the truth exactly as it was experienced in every way. 51.
But your son-in-law constantly and repeatedly favors Rohiṇī;
if he does not do so even occasionally toward us, then even that would not be complete. (52)
Therefore, we shall not go again to the abode of the Moon;
one must certainly not go where there is nothing but suffering, for that is where death must be met. ||53||

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Birth of Candra and Subsequently the Complaint of the Other Wives to Dakṣa Regarding His Partiality for Rohiṇī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Listen, Lakṣmī! Hereafter, I shall tell you what occurred after that.
Upon hearing this, Dakṣa, his father, fell into great distress.
Slowly releasing his breath, overcome by compassion, he said to the daughters:
"Let us go to Candra; I shall instruct him further."
"One should not act in this way; rather, one should maintain equal affection toward all.
Thinking thus, they all departed with reverence for the abode of Candra.
Dakṣa said to Śaśin: "O Lord! O you of noble vows, you are my disciple!"
"You are wise; indeed, what need is there for much instruction for you?
(4) All these maidens, equal in age, have been offered by me to you.
Having observed that they are all devoted to you, they shall become your wives. (5)
"Serve all equally and abandon partiality;
serve all women with the desire for equal pleasure and love.
Do not be attached to one alone; remain devoted to all."
O Moon! May all those desires be fulfilled exactly as they are wished for.
He alone who can bring peace to the burning desire of women possesses prosperity, heaven, and manifold divine powers.

Those who please their wives, who give them life, always increase day by day, remaining inviolate and virtuous; through pleasing them, one attains constant delight. From the heart-born suffering of those women, a man may fall into hell.
The true dharma belongs only to men; for women, it is the pacification of desire.
Therefore, one should not perform that [marriage] at such a time; a marriage performed then leads only to death.
Better for a woman is a marriage with another woman, one devoid of the burden of passion.
If there is no fruit of the ascendant (*lagna*) upon the union of woman and man,
then for either the woman or the man, the ascendant serves only as a burden.
If, even when the ascendant is properly established, a person does not obtain the bliss of the bodiless one (*anaṅga*), [the ascendant is of no avail].
Then, that union which was formed for the sake of a couple did not result in sexual union.
For how could there be a coupling of two women or two men from such a union?
And how indeed could the Lord Hari fashion a man and a woman [from them]? (13–14)
How is it that a woman is offered to a man, but not a man to a woman? Or how is it that there, a man receives a woman, but not a man? (15)
Thus, O Candra, having reflected, you should always serve all these wives of yours, who bestow happiness, so that they may be endowed with every form of conjugal fortune. 16.
Having mentally resolved "Oṃ Candra," and having worshipped Dakṣa with devotion,
he took all his wives and delighted them in many ways; again, taking them all together, he delighted them in many ways.
When a great deal of time had passed, he once again displayed an abundance of affection toward Rohiṇī alone in every respect, while showing only a small amount toward the others, just as before. (18)

Then, having been properly and repeatedly informed by them, Dakṣa became enraged and spoke for the benefit of Candra: 19. Then, having been properly and repeatedly informed by them, Dakṣa became enraged and spoke for the benefit of Candra.
"Candra! You have been properly instructed, and you shall be instructed by me once more:
you must always behave with impartiality toward all my wives. (1.44.20)
Then, may you always be prosperous and powerful like a yogi,
possessing inexhaustible heroism and splendor, and bringing satisfaction to all.
Thus, out of affection for your daughters, I grant this grace to you.
If I were to cast a curse upon you, it would become a source of suffering for my daughters. //22//
Therefore, I shall instruct you: be impartial toward all;
enjoy them all properly, and be a bestower of happiness according to their desire. (23)

through the loss of both power and splendor, you will encounter suffering. (24)
"You shall indeed live with but a single portion; of this there is no doubt.
