But Rohiṇī, the passionate woman, would forcibly restrain him within her own home in many ways, her mind unsatisfied by desire. (27)
Other wives waited for the path of the moon in the courtyard;
when their lord did not come, they wept as they uttered curses. (28)
While we have a protector, we do not obtain the state of being granters of desires;
otherwise, however, at that time, even though she has a protector, the maiden is like one who is unprotected. (29)
"If our protector were not [with us], may he be no protector even for Rohiṇī!
Having thus cried out, they all reproached their protector again and again. (1.44.30)
O Moon, always go toward your waning! Your power and vigor are subject to decay, whether you possess vigor or lack it, O you who dwell within the fortnights of existence. (31)

This Rohiṇī causes excessive enjoyment, yet she may become afflicted by disease;

Then, at that time, when a hundred years had passed in the world upon the earth—
Without the nectar of the moon, all medicinal herbs have gone to ruin.
Grains do not arise at all within husks or flowers; likewise, the essence of the earth does not grow within bulbous roots or roots. (41)
Nourishment was then forever lost, and living beings were consequently distressed;

"Choose a boon; may it be well with you; be forever happy, O Śaśin.
Then Candra said to Nandīśa: "O Lord!

In Saurāṣṭra, on the western frontier, in the vicinity of the shore of the ocean. ॥46॥

"O God, O Mahādeva! I shall perform your installation; having summoned Brahmā and the others here, I shall conduct a great festival of sacrifice. (48)
Having thus resolved, Candra [invoked] the deities beginning with Brahmā, as well as the ṛṣis, the munis, and the lords of progeny (prajāpati) there. ||49||
The Manavas, Devagandharvas, Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Nartakas were summoned for the purpose of the installation of Śaṅkara and arrived there. (1.44.50)
That region situated in the southern direction, extending from the river Bhadrāvatī as far as the ocean, is a field that brings liberation to human beings. 51.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is indeed an incarnation of the Supreme Brahman.
By the command of Brahmā, he caused the installation of Somanātha to be performed. After the installation was completed, Brahmā then spoke to the wielder of the trident (Śiva).
By the waning of the moon, as many medicinal herbs as there were have gone to their destruction.
All creatures, whose very root is that [moon], repeatedly go to their destruction;
therefore, O compassionate one, the waning of the moon must be prevented by you. (55)
Śambhu said to them all: "Let us go to the distressed Dakṣa;
let us speak for his benefit so that the world may become very happy. (56)
Having addressed him thus, they departed for the abode of Dakṣa.
Dakṣa welcomed them, and they sat down in their respective places.
Dakṣa inquired after their welfare and also made inquiries regarding their purpose.
There would be no purpose for me in [the company of] those great-souled ones who are free from desire. ||58||

Having thus announced himself, Dakṣa remained with palms joined in reverence, offering salutations;
then Śambhu spoke these words to Dakṣa for the sake of Soma.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction and Curse of Candra by Dakṣa, the Disease, and the Installation of Somanātha," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 44 ||
← Chapter 44: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 45 [[Author: → Chapter 46
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then Śambhu said to Dakṣa, "Destroy the disease of the moon.
Dakṣa replied, "O Śaṅkara, I shall indeed remove my curse for you."
Who, other than the Moon, can ever remove that perpetual sorrow born of hopelessness for daughters, which arises again and again from the moon? (2)
Who indeed could ward off the curse uttered by his virtuous wives to burn away their grief? Let Śaṅkara do as he pleases. (3)
Having heard these words of the self-restrained Dakṣa, Śambhu then spoke to Candra: "May the curse of Dakṣa be annulled;
O cool-rayed one, regain your virility and do not remain thus diminished for half the month."

Then, in order to destroy the curse uttered by his wives, the Lord Śaṅkara begged Revatī and the others for forgiveness. And at that time, it was proclaimed by the wives: "Let the disease depart! (5–6).
The disease of the loss of vigor was destroyed, yet the loss of its digits was not;
it was atoned for in order to eliminate the fault of partiality.
Thus, the Moon abandoned his attachment solely to Rohiṇī.
The falling away of his vigor was destroyed by Śambhu;
[yet] the moon accepted the state of being present in all [phases], while the waning of its digits was not destroyed by Śambhu. (8–9)
Then Candra spoke again to the god Brahmā:
"The loss of one's luster causes suffering that is more distinguished than all other sufferings.
Luster is the very soul of the radiant; luster is said to be honor. (1.45.10)
Splendor, fame, renown, wealth, and greatness are established upon splendor. //11//
He who is devoid of splendor in this world is excluded from the count;
however, one who possesses splendor is reckoned among the glorious.
Even if he is destitute of other virtues, if he is endowed with the form of splendor, [he is counted]. (12)
Likewise, the flower born of the *kiṃśuka* tree is indeed pleasing to the eyes. (13)
Even if endowed with many qualities, that which is devoid of beauty and splendor would not be pleasing to the eye, just as blackness pervaded by darkness;
likewise for white, blue, yellow, red, and green.
And "kapīśam" and "karburam"—these they extend as the seven forms. ||15||
Among all those, the white form is indeed said to be the most excellent;
after that, the yellow, then the red, and immediately following that, the brownish-red.
Then green is proclaimed, and after that blue is counted;
then variegated, known as "spotted," is said here to be dear;
and white is the radiance of Brahmā, indeed of the Supreme Brahman.
The form of those who are liberated, designated as Brahman, and who dwell in places such as Goloka,
is held to be eternally white and pleasing to the eye.
My own form is always considered to be white and the support of splendor.
"Without that splendor, even I, Kṛṣṇa, am equal to iron or clay.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, grant me my eternal splendor! (1.45.20)
"O elder brother! Deprived of splendor, I truly do not wish to remain;
for everyone treats me with total contempt when I am devoid of luster. (21)
Even my own women will no longer honor me as they did before.
Previously, through the abundance of my splendor, I shone in the assembly of the gods;
now, deprived of that splendor, how shall I go to the abode of the deities?
Deprived of my splendor, I would not live; I shall die, I say, in your presence.
While he was thus imploring Soma, various medicinal plants originating from different worlds arrived there. 24.
There, some medicinal herbs have one part of nectar for their life; some medicinal herbs there have two parts of nectar for their life. (25)
Some drink the nectar of three kalās; some possess the nectar of four kalās;
some are enjoyers of five kalās; and some possess the nectar of six kalās. ||26||
Some enjoy seven digits; some are nectar from eight digits;
some enjoy nine digits; and some are nectar from ten digits. (27)
Some have eleven digits, some have twelve excellent digits;
some have thirteen digits, and some are fourteen digits of nectar.
Some, having attained satisfaction through the enjoyment of the nectar of the fifteen digits, consume their own respective nectar on those particular days as they arrive. (29)
Thus, possessing diverse powers and diverse immortal lives, nourished by various portions [of the divine], they indeed arrived there together. (1.45.30)

A life seeking one's own interest is distinguished by various medicinal herbs; if the moon, possessed of the digits of waning and waxing, were merely fortnightly, [what would become of the world]? (31)
Then our life would proceed nourishingly, fruitful, flavorful, and prosperous, like well-nourished sustenance according to one's needs. (32)
If the full moon were always to remain as it is—possessing its seed, according to its growth, its nourishment, and its season—then those [women] would likewise remain so forever. (33)
Unable to endure even a fraction of this nectar of immortality, we would surely perish; for we are incapable of withstanding its coolness, which consumes like fire. (34)
All these delicate maidens would perish day and night;
therefore, she was unable to endure the constant cold of the moon. (35)
"Let these creepers, so tender even as sprouts, not meet their destruction.
Having heard this prayer of theirs, Brahmā and Śaṅkara [responded]. (36)
They both spoke these words, which bring happiness, to Candra, the lord of medicinal herbs:
"O Candra, you must indeed take to heart this request made by the creepers. (37)
I accept this by force here, for no other path is seen;
the life of these worlds has been made entirely dependent upon medicinal herbs. (38)
The life-force of plants is considered to consist of sixteen digits (kalās). Since those various distinct digits sustain each respective part day after day, they are so designated. ||39||
"You have been declared the repository of all arts; if you were not to show compassion, everything would surely perish through their constant mutual conflict. (1.45.40)
Therefore, upon obtaining the essence of fire, speak and act accordingly:
"May you increase during the waxing fortnight and meet with decline during the waning fortnight. (41)
The fault of partiality has been placed by you in the *kalās* alone;
indeed, there would be a depletion of your *kalā*, yet your *vīrya* would remain inexhaustible. (42)
Indeed, by whom can the thunderbolt of a curse bestowed by one's wife be warded off?
And what cherished object desired for the sake of those to be supported is not sacrificed for their sake? 43.
Those whose nature is to assist others, for the sake of the happiness of others, ultimately renounce their own interests and what is favorable to themselves. 44.
O Candra! Bestow your pleasure equally upon all your wives;
do not indeed take their breath away, but remain happy. 45.
"O bearer of wings, accept the merit of the life-force of the medicinal herbs.
Having thus addressed the Moon, Brahmā and likewise Śaṅkara [spoke]. 46.
Then the gods established the waning and waxing of the digits (kalās) in that very manner;
from that time forward, the moon has always been fully endowed with complete potency. ||47||
He sports with his wives who have the forms of the lunar mansions, remaining impartial toward them.
As for the waning and waxing of the digits, these remain subject to the requests of the horses and the medicinal herbs. 48.
Brahmā and the other gods likewise returned to their own abodes.
Then Śambhu requested that moon to serve as his forehead ornament. 49.
Brahmā gave him that moon born from the ocean as his first portion;
the second was the moon born of Atri, who became the king as the third. (1.45.50)
Each of those moons is indeed to be understood as distinct, arising from differentiated functions;
as many as there are Śambhus, and as many as there are cosmic eggs (aṇḍas). //51//
"There would be as many moons as there are [lunar days], yet they are infinite due to the distinction of kalpas.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have explained to you the cause of the waning even of the moon. 52.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Causes for the Waning, Waxing, and Stability of the Lunar Splendor," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 45.
← Chapter 45: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 46 [Author:
Chapter 47 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the mental creation produced by the God;
there, the Unborn One created the mental gods who possess self-consciousness.
Learn from me their names according to how they endure until the dissolution of all beings:
water, fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, and likewise the quarters.
In heaven are the celestial realms, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, the trees, and the creepers;
likewise, they are the very selves of the medicinal herbs and the selves of the trees and shrubs.
Lava, kāṣṭhā, kalā, saṃdhi, muhūrta, day, and night—these too are his manifestations.
Half a month is an ayana, a month is a year, and [a cycle] exceeding that is a yuga. 4.
The Unborn One created these gods who take pride in their respective stations;
he also created the presiding deities of the lunar mansions, planets, and stars,
as well as twenty-eight crores of those whose natures are perfected by merit.
But those who dwell in the world of the gods are called the Vaimānikas, the celestial inhabitants.
The gods, the ancestors, the sages, and likewise the Manus,
as well as their followers and the sons of Manu—
by calculation, they number three hundred and ninety-two million.
And there are indeed seven hundred thousand and eight thousand [verses]. 8.

For these are indeed the presiding deities of those respective spheres; though they resemble the unborn (Brahman) through their sovereignty, they are truly [mere] possessors of the conceit of "I" without actual overlordship. || 9 ||
These moving and stationary beings are the mind-born offspring of Brahmā;
[so too are] the Tuṣitas, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the lightning-spirits.
The Stanayitnus, the Bhānus, and likewise the eight Vasus—
namely Droṇa, Prāṇa, Dhruva, Āgni, Doṣa, Vasu, and Vibhāvasu.
The Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Asuras, and likewise Rākṣasas;
the Apsarases, Cāraṇas, Piśācas, Pretas, and Bhūtas. ||12||
Vidyādharas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and Aśvamukhas, as well as Kinnaras, Vetālas, Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, and likewise Yoginīs. ||13||
And the Vināyakas, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Vetālas, and the Grahas as well;
the Yātudhānas, the Unmādas, the Mātṛs, the Guhyakas, and the Cāraṇas. (14)
The Prajāpatis and the Ṛṣis, as well as the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Uragas;
the birds, wild animals, domestic beasts, trees, mountains, mortals, and reptiles;
the Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Bandins, as well as Bhāṭṭa, Indra, and Yama.
The Unborn One created Varuṇa, Kubera, Īśāna, and likewise Nirṛti;
he also created the eight Siddhis, the nine Nidhis, and the eleven Rudras,
as well as the Daityas and Dānavas who were born of his mind.
Sacrifices, meritorious beings, the vehicles of the gods, and even animals—such as the cow, goat, buffalo, black [animal], boar, gayal, and ruru deer. ||18||
These animals with cloven hooves are likewise the camel and others;
the donkey, horse, śarabha, gayal, and camari are those with solid, single hooves. (19)
The dog, jackal, wolf, tiger, cat, hare, and porcupine;
the lion, monkey, elephant, tortoise, iguana, crocodile, and so forth. (1.46.20)
Kanka-vultures, crows, owls, hawks, eagles, bhallas, peacocks, swans, cranes, cakravakas, ravens, owls, and cocks; ॥21॥
Thus the Unborn (Brahmā) created those mental [beings] by name;
he created the first creation, the Great Principle (mahat-tattva), which is the differentiation of the qualities (guṇa-vaiṣamya).
He created the second [ego-sense] as the agent of substance, cognition, and action;
but the third he created as the subtle elements (tanmātras), which possess the potentiality for substance.
He created the sense organs as the fourth, consisting of the nature of knowledge and action;
as the fifth, he created the mind and the gods; and as the sixth, he created that which is characterized by ignorance. 24.
He created the seventh creation, that of stationary beings, namely the trees and plants;
but the eighth he indeed created as the animals, such as cows and others.
He created the ninth creation, that of mortals, and the tenth, the divine creation; and in each of those, he then created the secondary creation (gauṇasarga) as required. ||26||

That Grandfather (Brahmā) created ten kinds of vital breaths (prāṇa) from the mind: substance (dravya), action (karma), intrinsic nature (svabhāva), as well as vigor (ojas), strength (bala), and life-force (prāṇa). ||27||
Hunger and thirst [are the presiding deities] of the palate and the tongue; Fire of speech;
the Nose of the sense of smell; and the Eyes and Ears of the ten directions. (28)
The hair, the lord (the heart), the hand, the foot, movement, bliss, the generative organ, passion, the womb, wind, Mitra, sacrifice, and the companion. 29.
The anus, the rectum, the seed, the semen, and the blood;
the navel, the downward breath, death, the belly, the vital organs, and the channels;
contentment, the rivers, the oceans, nourishment, and even the heart.

In that [creation], the Creator of the Universe first fashioned these mental [beings] during the initial creation: Mind, Moon, Volition, Desire, Skin, Hide, Flesh, Blood, Fat, Marrow, and Bone, which were born from the elements. (31–32)
In each of those respective locations within his own abode, he installed various deities. He installed Agni, the guardian of the world, in the mouth, and Vāṇīdeva in the speech.
There, on the palate, he installed Varuṇa, and he installed Jihvādeva in the tongue. (33)
He established the two Aśvinī-kumāras as the deities of the nose;
in the Mahat-tattva, he established Vāgīśa as the deity of the intellect;
and likewise, he established Viṣṇu as the deity of the feet at the two feet.
He established Tvaṣṭṛ as the Āditya and the divine Eye in the eye;
he established Indra for the sake of livelihood and the divine Hand in the hands.
He established Anila for the sake of breath and the divine Skin in the skin. (36)
He established the deity of the ear in the ears, each in its appropriate place.
In the anus he established Mitra, the lord of excretions;
and upon the skin, wherever itching arose, he established all medicinal herbs. (38)
He established the god Brahmā in the secret organ for great bliss;
he established the moon in the heart for the sake of mental transformation. (39)

He placed the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) in the Mahat-sattva, the sense of ego (abhimāna) in the ego (ahaṃkāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) in the mind (citta); he fashioned those mental faculties. From his mouth he created the Brāhmaṇa, the Brahman; from his arms, the Kṣatriya, the protector. (1.46.40)
He ordained the livelihood of the Vaiśyas from his two thighs and the service of the Śūdras from his two feet.
Brahmā then recalled the mental creation within his own body:
"Indra and the others are my arms; the directions are my ears; sound is my hearing. (41–42)
The two *nāsatyas* and *dasras* are his nostrils; the eyes are heaven and Aryaman;
both day and night are his eyelashes; and the yawning of the earth is indeed his palate.
Water is his tongue, taste is his sense of flavor, and the *chandas* meters are likewise his head. (43)
Yama is the fangs; O twice-born ones, the slight intoxication of affection is laughter (hāsya).
This emission is the sidelong glance; shame is the upper lip.
Greed is the lower lip, and likewise, Dharma is considered to be the breasts. (44–45)
His back is unrighteousness; his penis and testicles are Mitra and Varuṇa;
his belly is the oceans; his collection of bones is the mountains; his breath is the world;
his veins are the rivers; his body hair is the trees; and his movement is time. (46)
The flow of qualities would be action; hair, clouds, mind, and the moon [would be its manifestations]. //47//
The Unmanifest is the heart, the dwelling; the Twilight is knowledge, the Great Principle; Giritra is the internal organ; and horses, camels, and elephants are the nails. 48.
The hips are the deer, the wings are the cloven-hoofed animals, the intellect is Manu, the mortal is the dwelling, and the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Apsarases are the musical notes. 49.
The Brahmins are his memory and vigor; the Kṣatriyas are his mouth and arms; the Vaiśya is his thighs and shanks; and the Śūdra is indeed his feet, as well as various objects and actions. (1.46.50)
The tongue is the essence of the oblations to gods and ancestors, the nectar-food, and so forth; the mind is the heart.
Valour is the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, and the Vedic meters are the seven constituent elements (dhātus). ||51||
The sacred fords (tīrthas) are the channels (nāḍīs); the attainment of desires is the feet; the belly is indeed death.
The sheath, the beard, and the nails are the stone, iron, cloud, and lightning respectively. 52.
The penis is the rain-cloud from which flows the semen of the bliss of sexual union;
the anus is likewise the friend who grants liberation through self-restraint, and this is the mental [state]. (53)
Violence is Nirṛti, hell is Death, and the anus is the Earth;
darkness is unrighteousness and defeat, while the bones on his back are the mountains. (54)
All these mental [beings], whose tastes were unmanifest, were first meditated upon within the Raktas;
thus, having meditated on the Supreme within one's own self, this is the mental creation. 55.
Having prepared suitable abodes for them and having bestowed those upon them as well, he indeed caused the gods, the stars, the planets, and so forth, to dwell within that creation. ||56||
On earth, she caused the yakṣas, rākṣasas, numerous pretas, and piśācas,
as well as the Rudras, the hosts of Rudras, and the gaṇikās to dwell together;
likewise, she brought together mortals, beasts, flocks of birds, and countless other creatures upon the earth.
On mountains and in great forests, [he saw] Gandharvas and Cāraṇas, as well as Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Vidyādharas, and birds. ||58||
In the five worlds beginning with Atala, he [subdued] the asuras, dānavas, and daityas;
and in Mahātala, the sons of Kadrū—the serpents and the pannagas.
In the netherworld (pātāla), Brahmā caused the great serpents to take up residence.
This entire great creation was mental, occurring in the first age.
In whatever manner a purpose is required, in that manner the creation is conceptualized;
having thus conceptualized everything, Brahmā then manifested it from his mind. (61)
And here, the lords born in Satyaloka are the masters of the stream of sovereignty;
and here, the stainless, wise sages are the masters of the stream of cognitive discernment (saṃprajñā);
and here, the ancestors who are satisfied by ancestral rites (śrāddha) are the masters of the stream of contentment.
And here, the gods possess a stream of accumulated merit, endowed with the wealth of merit and other virtues;
(63) the pretas possess a stream of meditative concentration, born from the meditation of latent impressions;
and the rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas likewise possess an upward-streaming flow. (64)
On this earth, humans always possess downward-flowing currents and are characterized by passion (rajas);
likewise, animals, insects, and winged creatures here possess horizontal-flowing currents. (65)
In this context, the nagas, serpents, and so forth are considered to be the stream of darkness (tamas);
and the mountains, trees, and shrubs are considered to be the stream of ignorance (avidyā). //66//
In this manner, Brahmā properly established those ten creations produced by his meditative concentration in various locations throughout the world;
he fashioned their food from his own body.
But for the sages, he prepared milk consisting of the Vedic meters as their food. 68.
The food of the ancestors is called *kavya*; the food of the Siddhas is their supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Wine is said to be for the Daityas, while liquor (*āsava*) is for the Dānavas. (69)
He [perceived] the music of the Gandharvas, the beauty of the Apsarases, the sky-faring knowledge of the Vidyādharas, and even the invisibility of the masters of illusion. (1.46.70)
The flesh and blood of yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and other pretas;
the venom of serpents and the like; and likewise the fodder of cattle—71.
The flesh of fanged creatures, the various juices of trees and creepers, the split minerals of the mountains, and likewise the nectar of the gods. (72)
Brahmā alone fashioned for humans wheat and other grains, for birds the trees,
and for aquatic creatures all things composed of the five elements—
each according to whatever was required by each.
Thus, this worldly course proceeds until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus, in the first age, having performed the entire creation along with its limbs and sub-limbs,
all of which was mental, the Grandfather ceased his activity.

Creation only increases; indeed, nothing new is born. Just as it was, and of whatever nature it was, so exactly does it continue to exist. (76) Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Demonstration of the Creation of Gods, Yakṣas, Humans, Animals, Birds, Daityas, Dānavas, Nāgas, Serpents, Immovable Beings, and so forth, along with their Presiding Deities," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The forty-sixth chapter. ॥46॥
← Chapter 046: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā - Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 47 [[Author: → Chapter 048
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O beloved! At the very beginning of creation, on the first day, that which is called mental creation was indeed characterized by the Satya Yuga. || 1 ||
Having created the various abodes for those who pride themselves on their stations, as well as the abodes themselves,
he indeed fashioned the condition of the Yugas for the soul of the abode.
At the beginning of the Kalpa, during the Satya Yuga, he created through his mind the progeny belonging to the ages of Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali.
The Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand divine years;
its two twilight periods (sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa) are eight hundred [divine years] in number.
Three thousand years are considered the Tretā Yuga;
its two junctions (sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa) are six hundred divine years in number.
Two thousand years are called the Dvāpara Yuga.
Its two twilight periods (sandhyāṃśau) are four hundred divine years in number.
A Yuga consisting of one thousand such years is called Kali;
its two twilight periods are two hundred divine years in number.
The Unborn (Aja) fashioned the cycle of four ages (caturyuga) consisting of twelve thousand years.
In that Kṛta Yuga, O Lakṣmī, the subjects attained their goals through the mind alone;
virtue and vice did not exist among them, for those subjects were without distinction.
In that Kṛta Yuga, their lifespan, happiness, and physical form were equal.
In that age, they indeed frequent rivers, lakes, oceans, and even mountains; they consume water that is both cold and warm as they roam about. (1.47.10)
Abiding in mental perfection, they move at will in every respect and partake of sweet food produced by the power of their minds. (11)
There is no obstruction for them, nor duality, nor even succession;
they are free from sorrow, abundant in goodness, and always exclusively happy.
Even the beasts and birds have minds that are eternally joyful.
This time brings all sensual pleasures and grants whatever the mind desires. 13.
Indeed, by means of those [meditations], the tastes and other qualities arise upon the earth;
they bestow strength and beauty, and their accomplishment is the destroyer of disease. (14)
Those subjects had firm and well-nourished bodies and were firmly established in youth.
At that time, truth, freedom from greed, patience, contentment, happiness, and self-restraint prevailed. (15)
All those [women] were indeed indistinguishable from one another in terms of their appearance, lifespan, conduct, and gestures;
yet, based upon truth, the social dealings of the subjects arose spontaneously. (16)
But when there was no engagement of living beings in auspicious or sinful actions, then there were neither the regulations of caste and stage of life nor any intermixture of them. (17)
Free from passion and hatred, they interact with one another;
all possess equal success and lifespan, being devoid of the distinctions of low or high. (18)
Abounding in happiness and free from sorrow, they were full of great energy and great festivals;
their minds were ever-joyful, and they were beings of great courage and great strength. (19) Gain and loss, friend and foe, and the pleasant and unpleasant—none of these existed for them.
The object of those desireless ones proceeds by means of the mind alone. || 1.47.20 ||
They did not desire one another, nor did they show them favor;
indeed, everything on earth ripened without being ploughed, even without the water of rain. (21)
There, food is obtained without effort and possesses a naturally excellent flavor;
likewise, there is neither the pain of childbirth nor the burden of carrying a fetus. (22)
There, women have no menstrual flow and men have no emission of semen;
all cows are yielders of every desire, and all are the fulfillment of one's intentions. (23)
In the fourteen worlds, all prosperities are indeed indistinguishable;
all modes of movement are unimpeded, and likewise, all forms of speech are familiar. (24)
The celestial beings (vaimānika) are without celestial chariots (avimāna), possessing the power of yoga-perfections and austerity;
they are all indeed lords, as if their desires were already fulfilled. ॥25॥
Meditation is supreme in the Kṛta age; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, sacrifice is practiced; and in the Kali age, charity is best. (26)
Sattva is established as Kṛta, Rajas as Tretā, and both Rajas and Tamas as Dvāpara; Tamas alone is to be known as Kali—these according to the influence of the conduct of the Yugas. (27)
In the Yuga-dharma, however, everything remains as a mere remnant of a quarter;
when the Satya-yuga has completely vanished, that perfection indeed disappears.
In that age, there was another kind of perfection; then, in the Tretā age, it occurred again.
When the subtlety of the waters had perished, they then [reappeared] once more in the form of clouds. (29)
When rain, having issued forth once from the thundering clouds, had flooded the surface of the earth with that single downpour; (1.47.30)
Then indeed the waters appeared, and the Kalpa-trees stood within their homes;
from them, all objects of enjoyment for those beings were produced. (31)
At the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, living beings subsist by means of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*).
Then, due to the nature of *rājasa* and its reversal,
a state consisting of passion and greed arises among them quite spontaneously.
That which occurs for women at the end of their life is the *ārtava* (menstrual flow). //33//
In Satya-yuga, he established for each individual among the thousands of pairs created by his mind that which now constitutes the menstrual cycle of living beings.
Then, having attained great joy, those beings became paired; possessed by mutual desire for one another's hearts, they proceeded to engage in sexual union. (35)
From that time onwards, during the Tretā age, the birth of twins is said to occur;
for at the end of their lifespan, women experience menstruation only once, which arises for the sake of sexual enjoyment and for the easy bearing of a fetus. (36)
At that time, they did not conceive, even though they engaged in sexual intercourse. ||37||
At the end of their lifespan, they give birth only once to twins;
they have equal birth and appearance, and they also die together. (38)
When that [Kṛta age] has been exhausted and its purpose fulfilled, by the law of time, during the Tretā age, the mental perfections, asceticism, learning, strength, and lifespan all diminish. (39)
And at that time, those who have performed their duties gradually diminish, their strength, essential nature, capacity, happiness, and majesty reduced by one quarter. (1.47.40)
Then, when Vṛtra had been slain by Indra, the impurity consisting of the murder of a Brahmin was cast forth in four parts upon women, trees, the earth, and water. (41)
From that time forward, for women, that which constitutes their life-span—their menses—began to recur month after month. (42)
Then, as they lived together in that very union, because of their state at that time, they approached [their husbands] month after month. (43)
Indeed, the onset of menstruation and the conception of a fetus occurred out of season, due to the reversal of the natural time and their own physical deficiencies. ||44||
Indeed, all the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) situated within every house have perished;
however, here and there some remain, bestowing supernatural powers (siddhis) upon those who take refuge in them. 45.
When the wish-fulfilling trees had perished, they wandered about with their senses in turmoil; having gone to some remaining wish-fulfilling trees, they longed for material goods. (46)
Then garments, fruits, and ornaments are produced;
from those very things, their fragrance, desirable tastes, and so forth arise. (47)
"Beeswaxless and of great potency, honey in every single cell;
thus all the preparations proceed with great effort. (48)
By that [means], they lived happily during the middle of the Tretā Yuga;
thus, being joyful, well-nourished, contented, and free from all anxiety, they were sustained by the wish-fulfilling trees. 49.
Then, as time passed, the creatures were again overcome by greed;
they seized those trees, taking their honey, fruits, and other products by force. (1.47.50)
Due to their misconduct and likewise by the power of time, those wish-fulfilling trees perished; the subjects were thus left without any support. (51)
Then, greatly afflicted by intense cold, wind, and heat, and being tormented by these pairs of opposites, they constructed shelters. ||52||
Having provided remedies for the dualities, they indeed took refuge in dwellings;
they occupied dwellings and grain-fields as was appropriate. (53)
While the Maruts were bowing down before the mountains and the rivers,
they took refuge in strongholds and regions with perennial water.
According to their requirements and as they desired, on both level and uneven ground, they indeed began to construct dwellings to ward off cold and heat. (55)
And they established agricultural fields for crops on the outskirts, and there they settled both villages and cities. (56)

Having thus measured out the villages and likewise the inner apartments according to their pleasure, they then constructed the palaces and other buildings using their own fingers as the unit of measurement. ||57||
The span from the little finger to the thumb is said to be twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
and twenty-four such finger-breadths shall constitute a cubit (hasta). 58.
A bow-staff is four cubits long, and an arrow is said to be two cubits; two thousand bows are proclaimed there to be one *gavyūti*. (59)
Four *gavyūtis* are proclaimed to be one *yojana*.
By this King Pṛthu, indeed, even the settlement [of the earth] was established. (1.47.60)
A magnificent royal highway, ten *dhanus* in width, was constructed; it was spacious and easy to traverse for men, horses, chariots, and elephants. (61)
One who belongs to the middle class has a house measuring ten *dhanus*;
for a king it is one hundred *dhanus*, and for a sovereign emperor (*samrāj*), it is one thousand. (62)
Thus, for those living in houses and palaces when the wish-fulfilling trees had perished, the loss of their livelihood was contemplated;
indeed, the waters of rain were made to flow from excavations into rivers.
From the conjunction of water and earth, herbs came into being within them.
Trees and shrubs produced flowers and fruits according to the seasons, and grain grew spontaneously, ripened without being tilled by the plow. (65)
At that time, during the Tretā Yuga, living beings subsisted on medicinal herbs;
then, however, passion and greed arose among them again due to the passage of time.
Then they seized the rivers, fields, and mountains, as well as the trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, by force according to their strength. 67.
Having made [the property] their own, those who are powerful forcibly and by violence seize it from those of little luster. //68//
The earth was indeed made their own by those who were both powerful and very strong;
at that time, those of little strength sustained themselves only through service to them. (69)
Those who were then born as Śūdras became devoted to service; others, living by cultivating the land through plowing, became Vaiśyas;
and still others, ruling over the earth by force, became Kṣatriyas.
But those who are peaceful and characterized by sattva there are merely begging for alms. (71)
Those Brāhmaṇas were such great-souled beings with pure intentions;
thus, through their actions, the social classes (varṇas) originated from the Brāhmaṇas. 72.
When human beings had thus fallen into mutual conflict,
by that very fault, those medicinal herbs vanished from their sight at that time.
Being carried away, they were utterly destroyed and became sapless once more;
deprived of leaves, flowers, and fruits, they withered completely on all sides. (74)
Deprived of food and wandering in every direction, the subjects, overcome by hunger, went to Svāyambhuva, the Lord Prajāpati. (75)
Knowing that [the earth] had been requested for the sake of sustenance, Brahmā reflected thoroughly;
having made Sumeru his calf, he milked this earth.
Then the cultivated and wild plants were born again:
rice, barley, wheat, millet, and sesame.
Indeed, there were priyaṅgu, udāra, kāruṣa, and satīnaka grains;
as well as mung beans, green gram, lentils, flat beans, and horse gram. (78)
Āḍhakī, caṇaka, śyāmāka along with gavedhuka, kuruvinda, veṇuyava, nivāra, and likewise jartila; ||79||
Monkeys and uncultivated plants are all considered auspicious; so too are trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing vines, spreading plants, and species of grass. (1.47.80)
All medicinal herbs here were born with their flowers and fruits in season; yet when those herbs, having been released, did not sprout again, [the world was afflicted]. (81)
Then Brahmā established the means of livelihood for the sake of their growth;
through agriculture as a means of subsistence, those [plants] were indeed born as crops ripened by cultivation. (82)
The Vaiśyas there were farmers, the Kṣatriyas were protectors,
the Śūdras were attendants, and the Brāhmaṇas were dedicated to the offering to Brahman.
The status of the Brahmins who perform their duties is the state of being a guru;
the status of the Kṣatriyas is sovereignty over those who do not flee from battle. (84)
The place for Vaiśyas, who live by agriculture and similar efforts, was established on land;
the place for Śūdras, who subsist through service, was established at the edge of the village. ||85||
Then, while the social classes were established, he established the stages of life:
the householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant.
The first and great stage of life is the householder, consisting of the four social orders (cāturvarṇya). It is the foundation and the very source of the other three stages of life.
For those established in their respective duties, Brahmā himself has ordained their stations.
I shall now describe those very things as they are conceived; understand them from me.
For householder Brāhmaṇas, the Prājāpatya is considered supreme;
for Kṣatriyas, it should be the Aindra; and for renunciants, it is the abode of Brahman.
Truth is for those practicing celibacy who have reached the stage of forest-dwellers;
the realm of the Maruts is for Vaiśyas, and the realm of the Gandharvas is for those honored as Śūdras.
These are the paths for traveling to the gods, and the Sun is known as their gateway.
In the same way, the moon is said to be the gateway for those who travel by the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna).
Thus, at the beginning of the Tretā age, this entire creation came into being.
At the end of the Tretā, there was a reduction by two quarters in strength, vigor, and the quality of life.
In the Dvāpara age, all living beings possess strength, vigor, and so forth, diminished by three-quarters; in the Kali age, indeed, all creatures subsist by any means whatsoever.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Number of Years in the Yugas, the Attainment of Siddhis in the Kṛta-yuga, the Diminution of the Foot-measures, the Creation of Couples, the Dimensions of Cities and Other Matters, the Establishment of Foods, Medicines, Castes, and Stages of Life," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 47.
← Chapter 047: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā - Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 48 [[Author: → Chapter 049
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord, how did Indra come to incur the sin of killing a Brahmin? A great curiosity has arisen in my heart; please tell me that story."
Tell me, when was the earth leveled by Pṛthu?
O Lord, what was the goddess Earth like before that? (2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall indeed relate from the beginning that auspicious narrative, which, when heard through the yoga of the Blessed One, becomes a destroyer of sins. (3)
Marīci was the son of Brahmā, and Kaśyapa was indeed his son. From Aditi, the auspicious Tvaṣṭṛ was born as the son of Kaśyapa. (4)
Tvaṣṭṛ begot Viśvarūpa upon his wife Racanā;
there, Viśvarūpa became the family priest (purohita) of the gods. (5)
Once, Bṛhaspati arrived at the assembly of Indra;
however, Indra did not offer him the customary honors, such as rising from his seat to greet him.
From that time forward, Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, [became resentful].
Thereafter, he abandoned the office of priest for the gods;
after that, Indra gave the office of priest to Viśvarūpa.
When the sacrifice had been performed by Indra, Viśvarūpa served as the domestic priest.
Having offered the *bali* to the gods, he gave it to the Asuras in secret;
for the Daityas were his maternal uncles, therefore he gave the *bali* covertly.
Having learned that the *bali* was indeed given in secret, the King of the Gods [acted].
He became enraged, seized a weapon, and cut off those three heads.
One of his heads, however, was that which had drunk the Soma;
from the act of cutting it off, birds indeed arose, the Kapiñjala partridges. (1.48.10–11)
His second head was indeed used for drinking boiled decoctions;
upon its being cut off, the Kalaviṅka birds were born.
His third head, moreover, was the one that performed the act of eating food.
Upon its severance, birds known as tittiris were produced.
With the cutting off of the priest’s head, that Brahmahatyā (the personified sin of killing a Brahmin) came into being—
blood-red, alkaline, green, black, terrifying, and multiform in appearance.
She indeed leaped toward Mahendra, and he became Citravarṇa;
then the gods, having assembled and divided her into four portions, [took them]. ||15||
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, he clearly proclaimed:
"Indeed, let those individual manifestations accept a fourth part of the sin of killing a Brahmin as their share in exchange. (16)

A boon should be granted to them, for it is surely desired by them; of this there is no doubt. Having heard [the request], the boon sought by the women for the sake of satisfying their desire was requested [by him] regarding sensual enjoyment and indeed the practice of much sexual intercourse.
Even when [the world] has been created, there is no effort; let there be the constant enjoyment of desires according to one's will. (18)
When the gods had thus granted the boon, the fourth portion of the sin of killing a Brahmin was assigned to women; that blood indeed became the menstrual flow. ||19||
From that time forth, for women, the god of love became ever new; month after month, the attainment of the menses became like the appearance of flowers, even while bearing a fetus. (1.48.20)
Furthermore, wherever on this earth there may be a depression for me, or wherever there may be a hollow, let there always be a filling of those places. (21)
Having granted this boon to the Earth, namely a fourth part as her share, the excavated regions of the earth are filled by its very nature. 22.
The result of that is that there is an alkaline portion here and there;
or rather, trees and other things are desired there because of their spontaneous presence. (23)
When a wound is inflicted, a limb is severed, or a member is broken, there shall be healing once again;
by giving [trees] to the trees, one obtains there a quarter-share of the merit of a horse-sacrifice. ||24||
And that which was given to the *drubhas*, namely the exudation of the black *gundra* plant—
that insect, which consists of the fruit of the sin of killing a Brahmin, is indeed not eaten.
Then, at the source (*udgama*), a desired boon was requested there with water.
"May there be a fullness of water from springs and the like on all sides;
wherever water is poured upon a substance, may there always be an increase in it. May our residence therein be in the form of rasa (essence/flavor). || 26-27 ||
Having indeed struck out one-fourth of the slaughter from those [sins], such a boon-giver grants it;
by that, fulfillment is always observed in both water and on the earth. (28)
In water, the forms of killing are moss, foam, and bubbles.
Thus, the four portions of the sin of killing a Brahmin have been described. (29)
Having bestowed them upon those who desired them, Indra indeed attained purification;
from that time forward, the lord of the gods performed various principal sacrifices.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, whose son had been slain, offered an oblation into the fire with mantras for the sake of Indra’s defeat and to obtain the ransom of his son. (31)
"O Indra-destroyer, grow strong! Slay Indra here with all haste!"—by means of this oblation, a man of terrible appearance appeared right there. (32)
A massive body arose, assuming a form resembling the color of time; it was constantly increasing with a thousand hands, possessing a foremost hue of smoky grey. (33)
In splendor resembling the clouds at twilight, he stands brandishing his trident;
with matted hair as dark as copper, he possesses eyes as fierce as the midday sun. (34)
Roaring and making the earth tremble, as if licking the sky;
devouring the light before him, as if vomiting forth blinding darkness. (35)
The worlds were completely enveloped by him in the form of darkness;
that terrible being was indeed summoned by Tvaṣṭṛ under the name Vṛtra.
The gods, having rushed toward him, struck him down with divine weapons.
He himself swallowed all the missiles and weapons from every side. ||37||
Then the gods were struck with wonder, despondent, and deprived of their luster;
with their efforts frustrated, they praised the Lord God who dwelt within them. (38)
Salutations be to you, O Śrī Puruṣottama, the supreme deity of Brahmā, higher than the highest;
salutations be to you, the self of Brahman, who abides within the bodies of the liberated; protect us who are shrouded in fear! 39.

In this scripture, offer salutations and protection to the lords such as Śrī Vāsudeva and others—the sovereigns of the abode of Vaikuṇṭha and other realms—and to the millions of lords beginning with Sadāśiva. (1.48.40)
The mountain was borne upon your own back, yet the boat was held fast upon your horn;
the earth was supported by your teeth—may that very God grant us protection.
We have been sent forth for the sake of preservation, yet we are utterly distressed, blinded by the darkness of ignorance.
May the God of gods, the destroyer of distress, provide protection for those who are repeatedly afflicted by enemies and deprived of weapons and missiles. 42.
Having praised him thus, the gods, led by Brahmā, ceased their chanting.
Thereupon, the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari appeared there, bearing his weapons. (43)
Captivating with his divine object of meditation and the beauty of every limb, the gods prostrated like a staff; rising once more, they offered praise. (44)
"Protect us, O Lord, from the great terror of the demon Vṛtra;
O Hari, we have indeed sought refuge in you, the infallible Lord and our protector. (45)
Śrī Hari said: "O Indra, go; may it be well with you. Ask the yogic sage Dadhīca, whose body consists of knowledge and austerity, and he will grant it to you. (46)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari vanished right there;
then the gods, having gone to Dadhyañc, repeatedly requested his body. 47.
Indeed, at that very moment, Dadhyanca, being exceedingly serene and devoted to the welfare of others, abandoned his body by resorting to yoga. 48.
Taking up that thunderbolt fashioned from his bones, Indra joyfully rushed toward Vṛtra to slay him, gladdening the host of gods. (49)
Therein are the gods—the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Agnis, and Vāyus—as well as the Pitṛs, Ṛbhus, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and Kumārakas. (1.48.50)
And other deities gathered there, intent on going to battle; likewise the asuras situated with Vṛtra, who had fallen into the camp of Vṛtra’s faction. (51)
Namuci, Śambara, Anarva, Dvimūrdhan, Ṛṣabha, Kāla, Hayagrīva, Śaṅkuśiras, Vipracitti, and Svayomukha; ||52||
The Dānavas Puloman, Vṛṣaparvan, Heti, and Praheti, as well as the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, let out lion-like roars. ||53||
They indeed bore every kind of weapon;
with maces and iron clubs in their hands, and with arrows, javelins, slings, spears, tridents, axes, swords, other weapons, missiles, *śataghnīs*, and *bhūśuṇḍis*—with these they were armed. (54)
Out of anger, they showered a tumultuous rain upon the preeminent gods from all sides. ||55||
The weapons of those [demons] were shattered into a thousand pieces by the gods;
the followers of Vṛtra fled, and the gods regained their composure.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fourfold Distribution of Viśvarūpa’s Slaughter, the Birth of Vṛtra, and the Battle with the Thunderbolt fashioned from Dadhyañc’s Bone for the Destruction of Vṛtra," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 48.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Vṛtra laughed and spoke to those who were broken and fleeing:
"O Vipracitti, Namuci, Puloman, Śambara, and the rest! (1)
Death is certain for all embodied beings who are born, even for the brave.
There is no remedy for that which has come as one's very nature.
(2) Indeed, for the brave in the midst of battle, [death occurs] upon the chests of their enemies.
How indeed is death not to be honored for the sake of fame or for spiritual welfare?
(3) For two types of death alone are considered certain givers of liberation:
that of yogis through the aperture of yoga, and that of heroes through the aperture of weapons. (4)
Although she was thus being exhorted, Vṛtra’s army fled;
with her mind terrified for her life, she did not heed those words of Dharma.
Then Vṛtra, enraged, spoke again with reproach:
"What is the use of these wretches who kill their mothers, who are mere destroyers of names and abodes? (6)
For those who have brought death upon their backs and who mock the milk of their mothers, there is no glory in flight, no higher world, and no supreme goal.
This fleeing from battle is not praiseworthy; it causes distress like that of petty men.
"May they be well and secure; may they achieve victory in my presence.
Having heard this, those [demons], having regained their strength, then turned back;
terrifying the gods, those fierce ones began to afflict them with their weapons. (8–9)
Vṛtra indeed hurled an iron mace at Indrabhakuṃbha;
by the force of that blow, the elephant retreated seven bow-lengths. (1.49.10)
When Indra seized that thunderbolt which slays the brothers of the Daityas, Vṛtra, becoming extremely enraged, said: "By good fortune, he has come before me! ||11||

"By good fortune, this slayer of a Brahmin, a slayer of his teacher, a slayer of my brother, and likewise a slayer of a disciple, has been struck down by me with a trident; thus I am freed from my debt. (12)
Having slain with a sword a Vedic scholar, a teacher, a child, one who trusts you, or an initiated twice-born man—what destination will surely await you? (13)
May vultures devour you on the ground—you who are devoid of shame, prosperity, compassion, and the like—a corpse pierced by my trident yet untouched by fire. (14)
If I am destroyed by the thunderbolt, I shall attain the destination of heroes;
if you are destroyed by the trident, my position will certainly be that of Indra. (15)
Or rather, what use have I for sovereignty or even for hell?
May there be no passion or hatred in me; may Śrī Hari be gracious unto me. (16)
Slain by your thunderbolt, he shall become a servant of servants;
may I be liberated by you from the ocean of suffering, the snare of saṃsāra. (17)
I shall serve the feet of the Blessed One and perform service with devotion;
what is the use of this perishable body, worldly status, and the like? (18)
May my mind have no attachment to home, children, and the like; may my dwelling always be at his feet. (19)
While Vṛtra was thus boasting, Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, then hurled at him a heavy mace that resembled a mountain. (1.49.20)
Vṛtra, as if in sport, seized that mace with his hand;
at that moment, Indra hurled his own thunderbolt for the destruction of Vṛtra.
Then Vṛtra, for the sake of destroying Indra, hurled a trident made of iron with a hollow at its tip to swallow that thunderbolt.
"O wicked one, you are slain here today! Go to the abode of Yama! Thus he spoke.
Then Indra, with his hundred-edged thunderbolt, instantly shattered the trident.
Just as Vṛtra was about to seize a second trident with his hand—
At that moment, Indra severed his arm and trident with another vajra.
Then, with one hand Vṛtra swiftly seized another trident and hurled it at Indra; then, seizing yet another iron club, he spoke to him. (25)
"You are dead, O Indra! You have gone, O Indra, to the place where your ancestors dwell!
Having uttered this terrible roar, he struck Indra on the jaw with his fist. (26)
The thunderbolt fell from his hand and even Maghavan was thrown into a whirl;
the gods, the Siddhas, and the heroes cried out loudly, "Alas! Alas! (27).
Then Vṛtra said to Indra: "Take up the thunderbolt with your hand!
For those who have entered the field of battle, what shame is there in a marketplace where strength is weighed?
Life, fortune, fame, sovereignty, home, wife, and all such riches—"
Abide on the field of battle with the firm conviction that they do not exist at all. 29.
Knowing that pleasure and pain, life and death, honor and dishonor, victory and defeat—all are composed of illusion—move about upon the field of battle. (1.49.30)
This is called the "Battle-Seat" (raṇāsana), the "Weapon-Eye" (śastrākṣa), and the "Seizer of Life" (prāṇagla). When life has departed, whose victory will there be? Who shall attain it? (31)
Having heard these words of Bhagavān uttered by Vṛtra, he was supremely pleased with him and took up his thunderbolt in his hand. (32)
Just as he hurled it at Vṛtra, the king of the Daityas quickly pressed his lower jaw against the ground and raised his upper jaw toward the sky;
at that very moment, Vṛtra swiftly seized Indra along with his thunderbolt.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the great seers wailed aloud.
Then Indra, having split that vajra-scarred belly with his own thunderbolt and emerged from the womb, cut off the head from there.
When Vṛtra’s great body was indeed severed, it fell to the earth;
the celestial drums resounded, and the great ṛṣis rejoiced in the path of the gods. (36)
The Gandharvas and Siddhas sang, and the Apsarases danced with joy;
then the gods showered flowers and sang songs of victory. (37)
The soul of Vṛtra, who was hidden there within the splendor of Brahmā, was seen by those looking on.
When Vṛtra was slain, the worlds then became free from their feverish distress. || 38 ||
The gods, headed by Brahmā, returned again to their own respective abodes;
but Indra was distressed by the sin arising from the slaughter of Vṛtra. ||39||
He did not obtain even the slightest peace; therefore, in order to destroy the slaughter, he entreated the great seers, "Where shall I cleanse myself of this slaughter? (1.49.40)
The sages said to him: "Perform the horse sacrifice;
having worshipped the god Nārāyaṇa, you shall be liberated from the heap of sins. (41)

The killer of a Brahmin, the killer of a father, the thief of a cow, the killer of a mother, and likewise the killer of a guru—such a person is purified by performing sacrifices for Him, and by chanting His name and serving Him. ||42||
Thus impelled and pursued by the sin of Brahman-slaughter, Indra took refuge in the northern direction at the lake known as Mānasa. ||43||
For one year, indeed, he dwelt in that great lotus stalk, afflicted by heat.
There, that terrible black Caṇḍālī woman, dressed in red garments and smeared with entrails and fat,
followed him even as she moved about the lake, emitting a foul odor on all sides.
The sages, having summoned him, [prepared] for the horse sacrifice in every respect. ||45||
They initiated her according to the prescribed rites through the propitiation of the Supreme Being;
and when the horse sacrifice was completed, the sin of slaughter was likewise destroyed.
Indra, having shaken off his sins, returned once more to the kingdom of heaven.
O Lakṣmī! This divine story has been composed by me in a subtle form. (47)
O Goddess! By means of this gross description, the power that bestows the movement of the planets beginning with the Sun has been shown to you for easy comprehension; it is called Indra. (48)
The power (śakti) that abounds in the obstruction of the manifestation of water is called Vṛtra.
Due to the capacity for the manifestation of water, the planets (grahas) always possess a good course. 49.
Vṛtra, in the form of darkness, indeed creates an obstruction to movement;
for his destruction, the great Indra constantly wages war. (1.49.50)
"Especially in the autumn, Indra then slays the Asura.
Thus, everything has been told to you regarding the fruit of killing, which bestows undesirable results.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of the Horse Sacrifice and Other Deeds that Destroy the Brahman-murder Following the Destruction of Vṛtra," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Mahālakṣmī, I shall tell you how the leveling of the earth was indeed performed by Pṛthu; this narrative bestows the gift of Brahman.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since his abode (*ayana*) was in them, he is therefore the Virāj, Nārāyaṇa. (2)
From the navel of Virāj, indeed, there arose a great lotus;
there Brahmā himself was born and beheld [the world] filled with a network [of forms].
That lotus of his, however, lay in the water in the form of mud.
The earth is pervaded by moisture; no dryness is seen there.
Without dryness, how could the dwelling of those born from the earth and the growth of trees and creepers possibly occur? (4–5)
Then a hymn of praise was uttered by Brahmā to Nārāyaṇa:
"O Nārāyaṇa, ocean of compassion, support and nourisher of all!
Without your vast presence, indeed, what living beings could remain in the waters?"
Therefore, O Lord, having brought forth from the water that which is moist, subtle, and in the form of mud,
bring it to a gross state and assume the form of earth;
for without that, the human creation would be impossible in its fourfold manifestation.
"Where will they stay, or from where will they obtain food?"—even this [he asked].
Homage to the one whose nature is infinite; homage to the upholder of Dharma.
Homage to the one whose nature is gross; homage to the one whose nature is subtle.
Salutations to the one whose nature is the lineage; salutations to the inner controller of all. 1.50.10
Salutations to you whose nature is the imperishable syllable; salutations to you who are the liberated self;
salutations to you whose nature is the emanation; salutations to you who are the embodiment of time.
Salutations to Him who takes the form of Kṛṣṇa and others; salutations to the Golden One;
salutations to Him in the form of Vairāja; salutations to the Dweller in Goloka. 12.
Salutations to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha; salutations to the one who abides in the unmanifest;
salutations to the divine, peaceful one, the inner self whose essence is subtle. (13)
Salutations to the one whose nature is the effect; salutations to the one whose form is the cause. Salutations to the one whose nature is the woman; salutations to the bestower of the seed. (14)
Salutations to the one whose nature is vast; salutations to the one who reclines upon the waters;
salutations to the one whose nature is fire and sun; and salutations to the one who consists of sacrifice. 15.
"Have mercy, O Lord of Mercy! Manifest solidity from the water!"—thus was Janārdana, the God of gods, being praised. (16)
For the sake of accomplishing his purpose, the thousand-faced god assumed a divine, white, and gentle form, with a thousand protruding tusks. (17)
He has a thousand snouts for a face, a thousand hooves for feet,
two thousand great eyes, and a body covered in great bristling hair;
he possesses the power of a thousand tails and two thousand ears.
In an instant, it became there like the great Mount Meru. ||19||
Laughing, he himself said to Aja: "By the power of my splendor, I shall indeed make the earth solid; I will bring forth that which arises from it. (1.50.20)
While my mouths and fangs were hanging down in every way, I acquired the power to draw out sourness and form it into balls. 21.
There, my teeth will soon become free from the impurities of tartar, and their whiteness will become distinct. (22)
By the power of the clods of earth becoming solidified, they became uneven;
having caused all those lumps to be formed, he then unified them entirely.
They will, in an instant, bring before you the earth, which has attained a state of solidity and exists in the form of a globe situated above the waters. 24.
"O Brahmā, let the residence there be easily accessible to everyone.
Having thus addressed him, the Lord Varāha, possessing a white form, departed. (25)
Beholding all that water and the masses of thick mud within it, he formed them into lumps and deposited them by the millions upon his own trunk. ||26||
Having unified all of them and fashioned them into a sphere, he held it between his nostrils and emerged upon the water. ||27||
Having placed the globular great mass of the earth upon the waters, the Supreme Lord, the Great Being in the form of a boar, desisted. (28)
Brahmā, all the sages, and the lords of munis headed by Nārada, praised that gentle Hari, the upholder of the earth, who had accomplished his task. (29)
Salutations to You whose form is sacrifice; salutations to You who have the sacrificial altar as Your mouth.
Salutations to You who have the Vedas as Your feet and fangs, and the ritual acts (*kratavaḥ*) as Your chest. 1.50.30.
Salutation to the one with the tongue of fire, whose hair is *darbha* grass, the ascetic;
salutation to the head of Brahman, who wears the Vedas and their auxiliary branches as a garland. (31)
Homage to him who maintains the moments of day and night, whose snout is the sacrificial ladle;
homage to him whose nose is the clarified butter and whose voice is the resonance of the Sāman chants.
Obeisance to the Great One, whose nature is truth and righteousness; obeisance to the one endowed with valor, who is the chariot of atonement, Oṃ, the Terrible One, and the Knower of the Soul. 33.
Salutations to you, the deity who is the lineage of the Udgātṛ priest, whose characteristic mark is the oblation;
salutations to the deity who is the seed of the sacred sites, the great and excellent medicinal herb. ||34||
Homage to you, the vast one who is struck by mantras; homage to you, the inner self within the altar;
homage to you who touch the clarified butter; and homage to you whose blood is the Soma juice. ||35||
Salutation to you, the tranquil one who is the trunk of the Vedas, whose fragrance is the oblation;
salutation to him whose speed surpasses that of the offerings to gods and ancestors, and whose body is the eastern sacrificial hall.
Salutations to you who possess radiant splendor, endowed with various initiations;
salutations to you whose heart is toward the sacrificial fee, the yogin whose form is the perpetual sacrifice. ||37||
Salutations to the Great Soul, adorned with the Pravargya-vitta and other ornaments;
salutations to the Lord, the source of all, who is the radiant Brahman of the Upākarma sacrifice. 38.
Salutations to you, the vital breath that traverses the various paths of meters and states of existence;
salutations to you, the sacrificial session whose seat is the secret Upaniṣads. 39.
Thus praised, the Supreme Lord, having granted his blessing, vanished;
and upon the vanishing of the Boar, the Unborn One himself beheld the earth.
He constantly contemplated [the ground] on all sides: in some places it was provided with peaks, in some places it was low-lying and excavated, and in other places it was a mountain of stone. ||41||
Having reflected thoroughly, the Creator again remembered that Lord;
then He appeared in a vast form, equipped with a bow. 42.
The mark of a discus and a bow was seen on his right hand;
then Brahmā concluded, "This is indeed the Blessed Lord. (43)
"O Lord, level the earth by dividing its uneven parts.
Thus entreated, the god Pṛthu then [acted] with the Saṃvartaka fire. ||44||
He caused the Bhūtuṇḍas to be burned; they were shattered into heaps of ashes.
All of them became earth, and that is what is celebrated as "mṛttikā" (clay).
Having leveled the entire earth, which was beautiful with a covering of clay...
Having sown seeds in that field, he brought about an abundance of crops.
Where there were stones that had not been burnt, there he fashioned mountains;
where there were low-lying regions, there he fashioned lakes.
Thus was it done by the venerable Pṛthu, the great-souled Nārāyaṇa.
By his own [power], he created fields, forests, villages, cities, and market towns. 48.
Having observed the proper time and according to necessity, he created lakes and oceans, as well as rivers and great torrents of water;
and having fashioned the worlds, he brought forth the creation of living beings.
Pṛthu, having established his supreme sovereignty, provided a system that granted security of residence.
Having fashioned it and given it to Brahmā, he himself disappeared.
From that time forward, the entire ground became level and possessed of a uniform surface. (51)
The great goddess Pṛthvī became the appropriate resting place;
then, upon her destruction, the god Hari himself became Pṛthu once again. ||52||
Having become king, he will repeatedly level the earth;
indeed, at the end of Brahmā’s kalpa, the earth consists of the ten worlds. ||53||
When the earth sinks into the water, then Hari himself, becoming Pṛthu, will repeatedly level the earth there. ||54||
"Sometimes I am born as Pṛthu from the mind;
at other times, however, I take birth from sages or from kings.
Thus, I have related to you everything regarding the form of Pṛthu assumed by me.
Now, indeed, I shall tell you what occurred at the end of the Dvāpara age.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Elevation of the Earth by Nārāyaṇa in the Form of the Boar while Reclining upon the Waters, and the Leveling of the Earth by Pṛthu," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 50 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! As for those subjects who are born from the law of sexual union, while Brahmā was meditating, a husband and a wife came into being. 1.
And before that, Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā, his wife,
caused progeny to increase through the practice of union as a couple.
Having obtained his wife, Svāyambhuva took delight with her repeatedly.
First was that union which came into being at the beginning of the kalpa.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were their two sons; and two daughters, Ākūti and Prasūti, were also born. (3–4)
He gave Prasūti to Dakṣa and Ākūti to Ruci.
From Ākūti, a pair was born: Yajña and Dakṣiṇā.
From those two, twelve gods known as the Yāmas were born.
From Dakṣa, through Prasūti, twenty-four daughters were born.
All of them were exponents of the Veda, yoginīs, and mothers of the world:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Medhā, and Kriyā; || 7 ||
Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapu, Śānti, Siddhi, and Kīrti as the thirteenth—Dharma indeed accepted these as his wives. (8)
From them were born eleven beautiful-eyed daughters of Yavīrya:
Khyāti, Satī, Saṃbhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, and likewise Kṣamā.
Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā—
these eleven were then received by the great sages:
Bhava, Bhṛgu, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Pulastya, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, the Pitṛs, and likewise Agni.
Satī gave Khyāti to Bhava and likewise to Bhṛgu;
she gave Saṃbhūti to Marīci and Smṛti to Aṅgīrasa.
He gave Prīti to Pulastya and Kṣamā to Pulaha; he gave Sannati to Kratu and likewise Anasūyā to Atri.
He gave Ūrjā to Vasiṣṭha and Svāhā to Agni; and he gave Svadhā to the Pitṛs. From sexual union with them, offspring were born:
Śraddhā indeed bore Kāma, and Darpa is recorded as the son of Lakṣmī.
Niyama is said to be the son of Dhṛti (fortitude), and Saṃtoṣa (contentment) is said to be the son of Tuṣṭi (satisfaction). ||15||
From Puṣṭi comes gain as well as a son, Medhāputra, and likewise Śruta;
from Kriyā, however, Naya is said to arise, as well as Daṇḍa and Samaya. ||16||
The son of Buddhi is Bodha, and Apramāda is her other son; Vinaya is the son of Lajjā, and Vyavasāya is the son of Vapus. (17)
Kṣema was born from Śānti, and Sukha was born from Siddhi; Yaśas was the son of Kīrti—these, indeed, were the sons of Dharma. (18)
Harṣa was born as the two sons of Kāma by the goddess Rati;
such indeed was this creation of Dharma through sexual union, which results in happiness. (19)
Bhava created countless Rudras who were fierce;
yet when he was told by Brahmā, "Do not create," Hara remained with his vital seed drawn up. (1.51.20)
From that time forward, Śambhu indeed produced no offspring;
remaining as a celibate student (brahmacārī), he stood firm as a pillar (sthāṇu) until the dissolution of all beings.
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forgiveness, fortitude, the power of creation, self-awareness, and likewise the power of presiding; ||| 22 ||
These ten sovereign powers always abide in Śaṅkara; because he is eternally endowed with them, Maheśvara is a yogi possessed of yoga. (23)
Indeed, by the grace of Maheśvara, a man becomes a Tridaṇḍin;
these three are the staff of speech, the staff of action, and the staff of mind. (24)
He whose staffs are thus disciplined is indeed a triple-staffed ascetic who is liberated;
having himself recognized the omens of misfortune, he beholds his own death. (25)
Listen, Lakṣmī! In this context, I shall indeed describe them in their entirety.
When one recognizes these signs, then one's own death should be known [to be imminent]. (26)
That man who does not see Arundhatī, Dhruva, the shadow of the moon (Soma-chāyā), and the white path (Sitam-patha) shall not live beyond one year.
He who sees the sun as being without rays, or the purifier (fire) as being with rays, shall certainly not live beyond eleven months. 28.
He who vomits urine or feces, or likewise gold or silver—whether witnessed directly or in a dream—lives for ten months. (29)
If one's footprint should have a gap in front or behind,
whether on dusty ground or in mud, that person lives for seven months.
If a crow, a dove, a vulture, or some other flesh-eating bird should perch upon one's head, that person will not survive beyond six months. (31)
Or he may be bound by a flight of crows, or again by a shower of dust;
or he may see his own shadow distorted—he lives for four or five days.
Or he may see lightning in a cloudless sky, appearing to be situated in the southern direction.
If one sees a rainbow in the water, whether three or two [colors appear], he lives for three or two months respectively. Or, if one does not see one's own reflection in water or in a mirror,
or likewise sees oneself without a head, one will not live beyond a month.
If his body should have the smell of a corpse or the smell of fat, death has indeed approached him; he lives for only half a month. (35)
If, immediately after bathing, one's heart or feet wither away, or if one sees smoke emerging from the head, that person does not live for ten days. ||36||
If one's vital airs are disordered and they cut through the vital points (marmas), and if he does not feel a thrill when touched by water, death has arrived for him. (37)
If one travels toward the southern direction in a dream on a chariot yoked with bears, goats, and monkeys, one should know that death has arrived.
If a woman wearing black garments, or one who is dark-complexioned, or a female singer,
leads a man toward the southern direction in a dream, he does not survive.
Furthermore, the man who wears a torn garment or a black garment in a dream [does not survive].
Or seeing his ear broken, he should know that death has arrived.
(40) But he who sinks into a sea of mud up to the surface of his head—having seen such a dream, he does not live even for a moment. (41)
He who sees ashes, charcoal, hair, a dried-up river, or serpents for ten nights shall not live. (42)
He who, in a dream, is struck with stones by hideous black men with upraised weapons, does not live long. Furthermore,
he for whom a jackal appears visibly at dawn or at sunrise—
If she approaches crying out directly in front of him, that man's life has come to an end. ||44||
If, immediately upon bathing, one's heart is severely distressed and a tingling sensation arises in the teeth, one should declare that person's life-span to be exhausted.
He who breathes more and more frequently, whether by night or by day,
and does not perceive the scent of a lamp, should know that death has arrived.
If he should see a rainbow at night or a circle of stars during the day, [he should likewise know his end].
And he who does not see himself in the eyes of others does not live.
He whose one eye flows with tears, whose ears fall from their sockets, and whose nose becomes crooked, should be known as one whose life has departed. 48.
He whose tongue is black and rough, whose face has the luster of mud,
and whose cheeks are flattened and red— for him, death has arrived.
That man who goes toward the southern direction with his hair disheveled, laughing, singing, and dancing— his life ends there.
For one whose sweat repeatedly arises resembling white mustard seeds, death has indeed approached. //51//
If in a dream one sees camels or even donkeys yoked to a chariot, that person is inauspicious;
indeed, he shall not live if he travels facing the south.
One does not hear sounds in the ears, nor does one see light in the eyes;
vision does not reach far, and a red circle is seen. (53)
One whose navel is drawn upward by a hot breath from the mouth does not live;
nor does one who falls into a pit in a dream and finds no exit.
He who does not emerge from the pit has his life at its end.

Whether by day or by night, he who is struck down before his very eyes shall see his slayer; thus struck, he does not survive. Furthermore, that man who enters fire at the end of a dream [is likewise fated].
Nor does he regain consciousness until the end of his life,
that man who sees his own white upper garment.
If one sees blood or even blackness in a dream, death has arrived for him. Furthermore,
he who sees in a dream a woman dressed in a single red garment, or naked, bathing him, or embracing him, does not live.
Having seen a terrifying black messenger in a dream, one does not live.
If a heroic soul sees himself in a dream going into battle carrying his own severed head in his hand, his death is considered certain.
Whether amidst the force of the wind, a flood of water, or a fire on the earth;
whether in a machine, a tree, an animal, or a palace—there may be entry or falling. (61)
If a man sees either being crushed or fainting in a dream, his death should be known to be imminent, just as it is for one struck by a lightning bolt. 62.
If, while traveling abroad, one sees a black snake facing them, it brings about death or bestows suffering equal to that of death.
Furthermore, if a washerman goes ahead and a barber comes from behind, [it portends misfortune]. ||63||
One must never go into the middle [of a funeral procession], for there may be death or the ruin of one's undertakings.
(64) If one’s chosen deity, father, or even mother weeps in a dream, great suffering will arise, or indeed death will be imminent. (65)
The king shall fall from his throne and the divine images weep;
the rising of Dhūmraketu causes the destruction of countless people. (66)
A crow caws upon the throne, and a dog barks while standing directly in front;
the agitation of cows and other animals portends immediate danger. (67)
Indeed, when setting out on a journey, visions of a blind man, a black snake, and one with a severed nose repeatedly indicate death. (68)
Having thus fully recognized these signs and having ascertained one's own death, one should unite the self with Brahman and become devoted to the form of Hari. (69)
The body is merely an object of enjoyment for the woman, whereas the man is himself considered the Self (ātman).
By abandoning the woman with devotion, the man attains Nārāyaṇa.
He should not contemplate anything else, nor should he imagine any other mode of conduct.
One should contemplate the supreme Self as one's own innate self through the practice of identifying with it.
One should not cause fear to anyone, but rather become a source of fearlessness for all;
for fear, malice, and violence are in every way nothing but sin.
Non-violence is the supreme dharma; it is that which assists one in the next world.
Indeed, violence is fear and is not dharma; it causes one to fall from the next world.
Because Vasu Uttānapāda proclaimed the sacrifice as involving violence, he quickly fell from heaven and met his dissolution upon the earth. (74)
Therefore, one should renounce both hatred and attachment in the same manner.
Taking refuge in the Self by means of the Self, one should wander forth upon the path of Brahman.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Dreams Indicating the Creation of Pairs and Death," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
