Śrī Lakṣmī said:
When did that sacrifice commence? Who was the evildoer there? By whom was it performed? How and from where did the fall of Vasu occur?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the first age, known as Tretā, there was a king named Vasu,
the son of Uttānapāda, who bore the marks of royalty.
By a portion of Viṣṇu, universal emperors are born upon the earth;
they have arms reaching down to their knees, hold bows in their hands, and are marked with the bull. (3)
Their lips and teeth have a coppery luster; they bear the *śrīvatsa* mark and have upward-pointing body hair.
Their eyebrows rest upon their hair, they have tufts of hair on their foreheads, and their tongues are long enough to wipe their faces.
They possess the girth of a *nyagrodha* tree, shoulders like those of a lion, and well-formed private parts.
They possess the gait of lordly elephants and indeed have great jaws;
by means of sovereignty such as the powers of atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, by their lordly power, by strength,
by food, and by austerity, they truly surpass even the sages.
By means of policy and austerity, as well as through yoga and the powers bestowed by Viṣṇu, they overcome gods, dānavas, and humans.
On the feet are the wheel and the fish; on the hands are the conch and the lotus;
on the arm is the bow, and on the thigh is the parasol—these are the lines of universal monarchs (cakravartins).
The wheel, the chariot, the jewel, the sword, and the bow-jewel as the fifth [are their emblems].
And Ketu and Nidhi—these seven are the most excellent jewels, yet they are insentient.
The queen, the family priest, the commander of the army, the charioteer, the minister, the horse, and the elephant calf—these are the conscious beings who are the most excellent of jewels. (1.52.10)

These fourteen divine [treasures] belong to all universal monarchs (cakravartins). Among them, four have gone unhindered into the atmosphere, the ocean, the netherworld (pātāla), and the mountains. (11)
A portion of that glorious Supreme Self becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin).
By that [means], powers indeed manifest within his progeny—both divine and worldly—which bring about the realization of the boundaries of the kingdom. (13)

There are instruments for hearing from afar, for seeing from afar, and for measuring time; there are rays that transmit speech over great distances, and numerous divine lenses that reveal forms from afar. (14)
It is the accomplishment of lightning that reveals the bodies and removes the veil of ignorance. 15.
There were excellent lamps with the brilliance of lightning, which maintained their filaments through the power of mineral elements;
there were numerous water-machines produced by the application of fire-engines,
as well as vehicles for traveling beneath the water and vehicles for traveling through the sky.
Indeed, there are countless celestial chariots (vimānas), some of which possess the power of seeing from afar;
there are also numerous terrestrial vehicles, controlled by the power of sound perceivable through vibrations of the wind-threads, as well as propulsion and transport mechanisms. (17–18)
Water-discharging machines, powers for generating clouds, soldiers capable of moving through the air as well as within water;
smoke-vehicles, steam-trains, and likewise chariots. (19)
The substances for deluding and slaying, and the numerous eggs of dissolution.
The movements of the churning of the ocean and the great powers of medicinal herbs;
the movement within the planets and the movement within fire; and the observation of the interior of the earth. 21.
Furthermore, the assumption of other forms, as well as becoming invisible, entering another's body, and so forth— these elemental powers indeed accompany him.
Devas or humans become possessed of those respective powers.
By those [qualities] manifested as belonging to earth, water, and fire respectively; ||23||
By means of both physical elements and mental accomplishments, the Cakravartins sustain and move the burden of sovereignty over worlds in other realms or over other continents. (24)
He rules his kingdom, though separated by the ocean, as if it were right before him. ||25||
He sees, hears, touches, smells, speaks, and experiences [the deity] as if it were situated in his own home. (26)
All the subjects of the universal monarch shall be equally endowed with good fortune and possess enjoyments equal to his own,
by the power of their union of merit.
The son of Uttānapāda will be King Vasu, who travels through the sky.
He became a universal monarch through his devotion to the truth of the Dharma, his worship, his generosity, and his asceticism.
Then Viśvabhuj and Indra commenced an auspicious sacrifice together with all the gods, as well as the munis and rishis. (29)
By the ancestors, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and uragas;
by humans, rivers, oceans, sacred fords, and mountains. (1.52.30)
By means of the constellations, Daityas, Dānavas, virtuous men and women, and the true nature of sons; by those moving in water and on land, by trees, creepers, shrubs, and climbing plants;
and also by Sāttvika Manus, as well as Rājasa humans and men.
Accompanied by the Tāmasa gods and goddesses, he performed a sacrifice. ||32||
There, all those of mental and sexual creation arrived with joy;
then, while the horse sacrifice was being performed, the tāmasas and ardhatāmasas also came.

Those who were fond of eating meat performed sacrifices with animals fit for offering after having themselves partaken of them, while the officiating priests remained occupied with the continuous sacrificial rites. (34)
Then, while those sacred scriptures were being chanted in such a melodious voice,
and while the swift and preeminent Adhvaryu priests were moving about, ||35||
And when the high-souled gods, who partake in the sacrifice, had been invoked with oblations,
and likewise when the sacrificial herds of animals had been consecrated for slaughter.
While the oblation was being poured into the fire by the divine hotṛ-priests for the sake of the gods—
those deities who consist of the senses as well as those who partake in the sacrifice— (37)
At the beginning of the kalpas, the adhvaryu priests worship those gods;
at that time, however, during the moment of the *praiṣa*, they are indeed the great ṛṣis who are characterized by sattva.
Seeing the groups of sacrificial animals standing there dejected, the Adhvaryu priests rose up and, having gathered together, asked Indra: "What is this sacrificial rite of yours? (39)
This unrighteousness of yours is indeed powerful, for you desire an act of violence;
O best of gods, this slaughter of animals in your sacrifice is not desired.
Adharma has been commenced by you, who are like beasts, for the destruction of dharma.
This is not dharma; this is indeed adharma, for violence is never called dharma. ||41||
Violence is defined as the destruction of a living body;
for all embodied beings, no other suffering exists like that. (42)
Just as suffering arises for living beings from an accidental stroke of a weapon,
so too that suffering which arises through one's own action is proclaimed to be sin.
Therefore, merit never accrues to anyone whatsoever through violence.
"How is it that you, having become a god and the lord of the gods, commit such evil? ||44||
O Indra, do not commit the act of harming those who are innocent, silent, and live dependent on others; for this deed is indeed censurable. 45.
Then Indra said to the sages: "Violence in sacrifice bestows happiness;
these living beings offered as oblations in the sacrifice shall go to their desired heaven.
Furthermore, liberation awaits those whom Hari, whose mouth is fire, consumes. (46)
And there is even liberation from birth as an animal, which is filled with an abundance of suffering. ||47||
The sages said to Indra: "From such a sacrifice and from the oblation comes liberation, the destruction of suffering, and likewise heaven! Who could obtain such happiness? (48)
In a future age, O twice-born ones, during a snake-sacrifice, they will perform a fire-offering together with a deceiver; at that time, your instruction shall take place. (49)
The station of Brahmā (pārameṣṭhya), the station of Indra, the universal sovereignty (sārvabhauma), the netherworld (rasātala),
the realm of Virāj, the abodes of the principles (tattva-dhāmāni), the primordial nature (prākṛta), and the assembly of worlds—
all these are like foam produced from the illusory power (māyā) of Brahmā and Hari; they are all hells.
O Indra! even your state is likewise nothing other than hell itself. //51//
This world appears to us as something that causes suffering, abounds in afflictions, and is like a herd of cattle.
Therefore, O Indra! Abandon this body and even your status as Indra.
Becoming a sacrificial animal yourself in a sacrifice, perform the oblation of your own self.
If you have fear regarding your own fire-oblation, you will not perform your own oblation. (53)
"We, however, are sages who shall indeed offer you as a sacrifice; remain steady and undisturbed.
By that oblation, O King, the supreme heaven shall be yours. (54)
O Hari, that which they call the station of Brahman, the unsurpassed abode of liberation—to that place you shall go; come now, for we offer you this oblation today. (55)
"O Lord of Sacrifice, you will become pleased by means of your own flesh;
it is your view that merit shall also accrue to us through the oblation of your flesh. (56)
O Indra! Upon your being slain, there shall be the attainment of sovereignty over food, cattle shall become well-fed, and indeed, very great gains will come to pass. (57)
"Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, come; may you be offered as a sacrifice.
When the sages had spoken thus, Śacī indeed raised a cry of lamentation. ||58||
Even Indra was seized with terror at the sight of the moment of death;
and within the pavilion, among the members of the assembly, a great clamor arose.
Indra was invoked by the ṛṣis, fearing that much harm might come to pass.
Upon hearing of his own death, Indra’s face turned dark;
his radiance turned to gloom, and in an instant his mouth became parched. (1.52.60)
From fear, there was a trembling of the heart, and a shivering arose within his body.
Indeed, his limbs became devoid of strength upon hearing of his impending death.
Or rather, it was said by the sages: "O King of the Gods, let this sacrifice not be yours! (61–62)
There are many Hotṛ priests; let there be an oblation for them as well.
Let there be Adhvaryu priests, Ṛtvij priests, Hotṛ priests, and members of the assembly (Sadasyas). (63)
"May many beings be present; let them be offered as oblations. By this, may Kṛṣṇa be pleased today, and may the animals be protected. (64)
All those who have offered oblations shall go to the imperishable abode of Brahmā;
from the states of gods, humans, and hell, they shall attain final liberation.
Having heard this, Indra somehow regained his composure, though his hope for life was fading;
meanwhile, the Adhvaryu, Hotṛ, and other priests were then plunged into anxiety.
"Alas, what misery! they cried; "we do not desire liberation," they declared.
"Neither release, nor indeed the fire-oblation, nor food, nor sacrificial fees—nor do we desire any object whatsoever from you; let everything be yours. (67)
We shall not remain here; for whom indeed is death dear? ||68||
"We shall go to our respective homes; we have no sacrificial materials left.
As they spoke thus, a great clamor arose from those who were overcome with terror.
Just then, King Vasu Uparicara arrived there.
Descending from his celestial chariot, he arrived at the sacrificial pavilion.
Honored by Indra and the other gods, he sat upon the central seat.
Then the sages declared: "A sacrifice involving violence is not Vedic."
If you desire it here, always perform sacrifice according to the scriptures, by means of a sacrifice seen in the injunctions, which is the cause of imperishable dharma. (72)
O best of gods! [I shall perform the sacrifice] with sacrificial seeds in which no violence exists, which have been stored for a period of up to three years and have not sprouted. (73)
O Great Indra, having reflected for yourself, let this great Dharma be accomplished;
thus did Indra, the enjoyer of the universe, [act] along with the sages who perceive the truth. ||74||
The divine great seers, distressed by that dispute, reached a consensus and questioned both the animal and the lord Vasu. (75)
O King Vasu, how was the sacrificial ritual seen by you?
O son of Uttānapāda, tell us; O Lord, sever our doubt. (76)

Having heard everything from both sides and without deliberating upon their relative strengths and weaknesses, he spoke the true nature of sacrifice in accordance with the Vedas and the Śāstras. ||77||
And by taking refuge on the side of Indra, the lord of the gods, through passion and without opposition, and by the power of his kṣatriya portion; ||78||
"One should sacrifice according to what has been taught," said the king;
"one should sacrifice with pure animals, as well as with seeds and fruits. (79)
This [Veda] shows me that sacrifice has violence as its inherent nature, just as the mantras of the Saṃhitās here contain signs of violence according to the great seers. (1.52.80)

"Because it has been taught by me on the authority of those [scriptures] such as the *Tāraka*, which possess long-standing austerity and direct vision, you ought therefore to hold me in high regard. (81)
O twice-born ones, if those very great sentences (mahāvākya) are indeed authoritative, then let the sacrifice proceed; otherwise, our word would be false. (82)
Thus having received this reply, those ascetics, whose souls were disciplined, remained with their faces turned downward and said to the Earth, "O King, do not speak. (83)
The meaning of the Veda was not grasped by you with a mind that touches only the surface;
for the purport of the Veda is never considered to lie in violence. (84)

Your statement that one should refrain from violence that occurs by its own nature is based on mere logic; for you have declared that violence is not [inherently] violence when it is performed according to scriptural injunction, and thus you are a liar. (85)
"This Vasu is a speaker of falsehood; he does not speak the truth at all.
As soon as this was said, the king entered the subterranean realm. (86)
Vasu was one who moved in the upper regions, yet he became a dweller of the netherworld (rasātala).
By means of a false word, he came to have his eternal residence below the earth. (87)
Therefore, even by one who is highly learned, it cannot be stated [with certainty] because of doubt;
for the path of Dharma, which has many doors, is subtler than the subtlest.
Thus, Dharma cannot be spoken with definitiveness by anyone.
Therefore, non-violence is never a gateway to dharma.
Having given leaves, roots, fruit, vegetables, the food of sages, and even milk in sacrifice, those whose wealth is austerity are glorified in the heavenly world. (1.52.90)
Absence of malice, absence of greed, self-restraint, compassion for all beings, austerity,
service to the Brahmanas, truthfulness, doing good to others, forgiveness, and fortitude—
these are in every way the roots of the eternal Dharma.
"Therefore, do not commit treachery; release the animals from the sacrifice.

O Lord of the Gods, perform the sacrifice with offerings of fruits, food, and other substances. Having heeded these words, Śakra [released them] along with the milk-rice that had been prepared. (92–93)

After that, sacrifices were performed; indeed, from then on, sacrifices characterized by goodness (sāttvika) always prevailed among the Vaiṣṇavas, who were entirely free from malice during the Tretā age.
From that time forward, the sages performed auspicious and excellent austerities.
And they performed Vaiṣṇava sacrifices, which were characterized by the dharma of non-violence.
(95) Regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice with an *aja*," the *aja* refers to rice that is three years old.
That grain is called *aja* because no sprout ever grows from it. (96)
The inclination toward sexual intercourse, intoxicants, and meat arises from the very nature of those characterized by *tamas*;
therefore, a rule for its restraint is prescribed.
If the desire for sexual union is intense, let it be pacified through marriage.
If there is a desire for meat on the tongue, let it be appeased by sacrifice alone.
If there is a desire for intoxicating drink, let it be appeased by the Sautrāmaṇī rite.
May they, having experienced these in some way, become desisted from them.
A prohibition preceded by a prescription is not itself a prescription within that triad; he who is not overcome by liquor, meat, and sexual union is indeed liberated.
Non-violence is the supreme dharma, and celibacy is the great austerity.
Beyond this, one attains supreme purity through the three [stages] and finds the Brahman.
(101) Nevertheless, due to the force of time, the mixing of tamasic food, the lack of obtaining food and other necessities, and the tongue’s longing for flavors, (102)

The *tāmasī* mode of conduct is adopted by those characterized by *tamas*, consisting of those three qualities (*guṇas*). For the purpose of inflicting punishment upon them, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, exists as the dispenser of justice by the will of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa. (1.03)
He performs that purification which is contrary to dharma in the world of Yama.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fall of Uparicara Vasu and Other Matters Concerning the Sacrifice of Mahendra and the Symbol of the Universal Monarch," within the first section, the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O beloved of my life, O knower of the three periods of time, when did the snake-sacrifice take place?
How and for what reason was Indra offered there by the great twice-born ones?
"When did Yama Vaivasvata come into being, and what does he do?
What is the world of Yama like? Tell me this, if you are dear to me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, my dear, to that delightful story concerning the snake-sacrifice, which took place in the first Dvāpara age; I shall relate it to you in brief. (3)
When the Tretā Yuga has arisen and declined, the Dvāpara Yuga sets in.
Indeed, those perfections of the people that existed in the Tretā perish;
at that time, defects such as lack of fortitude and greed arise.
Likewise, commerce, warfare, and the lack of determination regarding the knowledge of reality. 5.
In that Dvāpara age, there occurred a confusion of the castes regarding their own duties, as well as uncertainty concerning their obligations;
furthermore, there was killing, gambling, punishment, intoxication, hypocrisy, intolerance, and weakness—
this was the activity characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*.
Because of that, a division of the Dharma arose, and passion and hatred occurred moment by moment.
Due to the impairment of the sense organs, the uncertainty regarding causes, and the observation of defects, there was then a divergence of opinion among men. (7–8)
Through action, mind, and speech, livelihood is achieved only with great difficulty; moreover, there is much physical suffering as well as a confusion of the dharmas. (9)
The destruction of the system of castes and stages of life, lust and hatred—both exceedingly powerful—and self-conceit and the contempt for others were indeed present as mighty evils. (1.53.10)
Speaking untruth is generally found in business and legal dealings;
likewise, the preoccupation with filling one's own belly is almost always present. (11)
Due to the influence of such a Dvāpara age, people possessing houses became intent on establishing their own sense of ownership. (12)
Fields, houses, extensive gardens, small groves, livestock, trees, ponds, excavations, forests, moist jungles, and lakes; ||| 13 ||
"Those for whom [the mind] is covered by the sense of 'mine' become their objects of enjoyment at that time.
Thus, one should always [cultivate] this mental state which is inclined toward contraction. (14)
Upon merely beholding human beings, truth has indeed dissolved;
the essence of the earth has gone to ruin, and the trees bear no fruit at all. (15)
In that Dvāpara age, the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) were no longer seen, nor was desire fulfilled; likewise, cows that yield all desires (kāmadughās) were not seen at all. ||16||
The wish-fulfilling gems have vanished; the rain of desires no longer falls.
The trees do not bear seasonal fruit, nor do the crops yield grain. (17)
At that time, whoever consumed the strength there became powerful;
thus, indeed, a great decline occurred during the Dvāpara age. ||18||
The king was full of hatred and pride, showing contempt for Brahmā, and his subjects were intent only on their own self-interest; what more need be said when the turn of time had come?
Indeed, as time thus proceeded, talk centered entirely upon the snake-sacrifice.
Listen, Lakṣmī! It has begun—that which liberates one from the bonds of worldly existence. (1.53.20)
Having heard that delightful story—a verse that bestows propitiation of Hari and purifies the world—those who listen with devotion are purified. (21)
The son of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu was known as Priyavrata. He had a son named Raivata, who was supremely righteous.
From his very childhood, he was devoted to austerity, yoga, and the service of the Lord with devotion.
Performing the three daily ablutions and being devoted to the twilight prayers (sandhyā-vandana), ||23||
In the morning, having bowed to his parents, having bowed to the elders and the Brahmins,
and having performed the worship of the cows, he offered water-libations to the ancestors.

Having offered clarified butter and oblations into the fire, and having fed those dependent upon him, as well as guests and Brahmins, he then ate his own food, which had been dedicated to the deities. (25)
Making his own birth meaningful by means of the rosary and worship throughout the remainder of his entire life, he instructed everyone in the practice of devotion. (26)
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, O Mādhava, O Lord of the virtuous!
O Vāsudeva, O Supreme Brahman, O Inner Controller, protect me always. (27)
While he was thus engaged in worship, Nārada arrived there by chance; he was received with honor by Raivata, who offered him a welcome, a seat, and other courtesies. (28)
Having washed the feet of the sage, he who desired his grace spoke to him:
"O compassionate one, O divine-eyed savior of the living beings of the world! (29)
"You yourself have been declared to be Brahmā, born from the mind of Nārāyaṇa.
A yogi who knows Brahman like you is considered equal to the yoga of Hari. (1.53.30)
For those who are free from desire, there can be no longing for anything from one such as me;
nevertheless, the compassionate ones act for the welfare of others. (31)
"Surely, the highest good will certainly come into my hands;
otherwise, it would not be possible to quickly behold the vision of the Blessed One. (32)
"Instruct your favorable disciple and grant me grace as your servant," said Nārada, playing his lute and chanting the praises of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (33)
He said: "O Raivata! You are blessed that you worship Keśava even from childhood.
What other gain could there be for a living being than this, which surpasses even the common mud? (34)
The word for Brahman is "sat" (Being); those who possess that [Brahman] are therefore called "santaḥ" (the good).
Because they attain ultimate union with Brahman, they are designated as "santaḥ. (35)
One should always be such a virtuous person and never one who is not;
for among the virtuous there may be a cessation of association with the virtuous, but never among the non-virtuous. //36//
O Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, being yourself pleased by your devotee’s disinterested and true devotion, you have urged me to speak that which must be told. (37)
The glorious Hari Nārāyaṇa himself, the lord of the abode of Brahmā, desiring to come to the earth, has become the Lord Dāmodara. (38)
He desires to bring the region of Brahmadhāma for his own residence;
hear the reason for that, O King, regarding the western land of the earth. (39)
A gap a hundred *gavyūtis* long exists along the path to Suratrāsa; through that opening, millions of Daityas emerge from the netherworld (*atala*).
Having gone to heaven, they terrified all the gods despite being innocent;
there was a fissure a hundred yojanas wide that caused terror among the gods. (41)
I must complete it there and I shall dwell there forever; for that purpose, I will indeed grant a portion of the imperishable realm to Raivata. (42)
It was a divine, prosperous, and bliss-bestowing realm, one hundred *gavyūti*s in extent, where there were wells of liquid gold and likewise rivers of golden sand. (43)
The life-restoring [herb], the remover of arrows, the healer of wounds, the antidote to fainting, the blood-stopping, the pain-reliever, and likewise the suppressor of hunger and thirst. (44)
Various medicinal herbs will be there along with me, where my wife Bhadrā Subhadrā is, by the river Bhadrāvatī. ||45||
Wherever my wife Ūrjā is, there let she be full of splendor;
wherever the moist saffron of Lakṣmī has been sprinkled, there is the Kuṅkumavāpikā [pond]. (46)
There a brahmin devoted to his wife, who is a portion of myself, shall come into being;
there the Sarasvatī, flowing toward the ocean, shall take up the Vāḍava fire. (47)
Where I shall dwell for a moment in the shade of a Plakṣa tree, where the beautiful city of Svarṇapura shall be located within my island. (48)
Where King Khaṭvāṅgada shall be your son, and where the god Someśvara, Mahādeva, shall be. ||49||
Where, indeed, because of the destruction of Tala, it shall become Talaśyāma;
and where, due to the sacrifice performed in secret, it shall also become Prayāga. || 1.53.50 ||
There, indeed, my great devotee named Dāma will arise;
there, three sages—one, two, and three—will come into being. (51)
On that mountain where Dattātreya, who loves austerity, resides, I shall dwell;
there the Gaṅgā, though appearing mad, shall flow for my sake.
Where the lions, the vehicle of the consort of the Lord of Beings, shall stand;
where my path of devotion, which bestows all things, shall come to be. ||53||
Where Jayā and Lalitā shall become my Rādhā and Lakṣmī, and where the Sun shall take birth in the form of the Arka tree. (54)
There the goddess, having conquered her enemies, will take the form of a river;
there King Ānarta will likewise go to engage in ascetic penance.
Where the city shall dwell, obstructed by serpents and poisons;
where Kṛṣṇa, marked by the bow, shall appear in the guise of a virtuous man.
My parents shall be born upon the shoulder of Gopālaka;
there my incarnations shall take place, O great sages.
Where those who were the counselors of my kingdom shall become my sharers;
where Devānīka shall be the one to consecrate the king;
and where Rajikuṭṭa shall be my fixed residence. ||58||
There, Kṛṣṇa himself will establish my pair [of attendants].
That divine abode of mine shall be without beginning or end;
this divine island shall become the bestower of liberation through Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Future Reality, Beginning with the Arrival of Nārada at the House of Dharmarēvata during the Dvāpara Age in the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, and the Bringing of the Portion of Brahmā to Fill the Chasm in the Western Region," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 53.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Where is that region known as Vivara located?
It lies to the east of the region called Abrikta and to the south of Kaccha.
To the west of the Narmadā and north of the Siṃhāraṇya forest, that region shall become Surāṣṭra, ruled by a Suratrāṇa. (2)
Extending from the Malaya mountain in the west to the Avrikta region in the east,
the land is five thousand yojanas long and wide in every direction;
it is known as the Siṃhāraṇya country, possessing uninterrupted terrain.
To the north of Siṃhāraṇya is the region known as Devadamanasaṃjñaka.
One hundred *gavyūtis* to the north of the region of Devadamanabhū, there exists a great cavity in the earth;
and for its filling, Śrī Hari will grant you His own portion as required. (5)
Come with me to Vaikuṇṭha, O sinless one! (6)
"Take this gift to the land of Saurāṣṭra and return to the surface of the earth;
having filled that opening, make that ground divine. (7)
O Protector of the Earth, remain steadfast in that land of Saurāṣṭra.
In that region stands the great Brahma-giri, composed of jewels and gold. (8)
Establish Soma-Bhadrā in the middle country as your own dwelling;
because of your residence on Raivata, that mountain shall also be known as Raivata.
It shall be called Revatācala, a divine and great Brahma-mountain.
Of Revata, there was his own daughter, named Revatī.
There, the place known as Tīrtha shall remain forever, even though it is situated in Goloka;
and Raivata, a devotee of the Lord, shall dwell there for a long time. (11)
Becoming the fifth Manu, you shall dwell there once again;
that Raivata mountain shall become a great sacred site (tīrtha).
Where Dāmodara Kṛṣṇa resides, where Śambhu, the Lord of Existence, resides, and where Brahmā, the Self-born, resides—what indeed can be called illusory there? (13)
Through union with Kṛṣṇa, the earth is eternally divine, dark, and full of essence;
likewise, it is so called because of the ploughing away of latent impressions (vāsanā) and because of leading one to Vaikuṇṭha. ||14||
He is known as Kṛṣṇa of Saurāṣṭra by name, appearance, and vigor;
and there is also Mount Kṛtasmara on the western side of Raivataka Hill. (15)
A great conflagration, like the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), will arise;
then the goddess Sarasvatī, having led [the mountain] along that path, will go toward the great ocean for the purpose of casting it in. At that time, Smaragiri himself—
Having risen, he will bring about a cessation in its vicinity.
Then the enraged submarine fire (vaḍavāgni) will reduce the mountain to ashes;
even the stones of that ash-bed become soft and white. (17–18)
By those artisans, palaces with white grounds shall be constructed;
the white lime for the plastering material will then be produced from the firing of the kiln. (19)
Then the sages, the ancestors, the perfected ones, the gods, the virtuous women and the virtuous men, the yogis, the ascetics, and the devotees shall dwell upon the Raivata mountain.

Encircled by ten mountain ramparts and graced by the splendor of the palace of Lakṣmyambā, it is circumambulated on the full moon day of Kārttika by a multitude of devotees eager for the festival of ten million pilgrimages. ||21||
Clouds gather upon its slopes; it is frequented by divine sages on its peaks;
its base is crowded with dark-skinned people; and its sides provide a noble path for celestial chariots. ||22||
To the east is Śatruñjaya, and Vārāṇasī is four yojanas further;
the holy site known as Kuṅkumavāpī is three yojanas beyond that. ||23||
To its north lies the river named Bhadrā at a distance of two yojanas;
to its south is Somatīrtha at a distance of four yojanas.
To the west of which, protected by the very shadow of the Yoginī mountain, there is a long region of high ground extending for one krośa in width. (25)
There, you must indeed construct for yourself a city named Raivata;
from that, a son named Khaṭvāṅga shall be born to you. (26)
Becoming a second moon, he will dispel the darkness of night;
by his name, that city shall be known as Khaṭvāṅgada. (27)
In his lineage there will be a king named Hāṭaka, a sovereign of devotees;
he shall bring forth from the netherworld (pātāla) the great god Hāṭakeśa Mahādeva. ||28||
That city shall be known by his name as Hāṭakeśapura;
in his lineage, there will be a king named Maṇimān, who will become an attendant of Śambhu.
That city shall become famous by his name as Maṇipura;
moreover, at that time, upon seeing the ancient fortresses, men— ||| 1.54.30 ||
In the course of time, they shall proclaim that city by the name Jīrṇadurgapura.
Then, after some time has passed there, the Lord’s attendant Vijaya [will arrive]. (31)
There a kingdom will manifest, and he too shall rule over it; it shall acquire the name Vijayapura after his own name. (32)
Virtuous women and virtuous men, embodiments of Brahman who bestow liberation,
shall dwell there forever for the sake of the world’s welfare.
Marvels shall occur on that ground in age after age.
In each successive age, there will be divine persons who act as protectors of the earth and establishers of dharma;
and through the repeated dwelling of Kṛṣṇa and Dāmodara, even the gopīs [will become so]. ||34-35||
In various places there will indeed be women of great vows;
having become virtuous, they shall worship the auspicious and majestic Kṛṣṇa. ||36||
Men, women, beasts, and birds who thoroughly cultivate that support shall be liberated from the snare of saṃsāra; such is the nature of that stage. (37)
Then, at the end of the eon (kalpa), during the final birth of Kalki, this Raivata will arise as a refuge for the Mlecchas on all sides. ||38||
Indeed, from the wrath of his eyes, he shall become Jvālāmukha (the Flame-faced);
scorched by the flames, even the region, tormented by the essence [of fire], shall turn into liquid. (39)
Having reached Vaikuṇṭha, Rasa will become as he was before;
Saurāṣṭra, born of Vaikuṇṭha, shall return once more to Vaikuṇṭha.
Furthermore, it shall be exactly as before even at the end of the kalpa.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, come with me to Vaikuṇṭha.
"Śrī Hari will indeed grant you the region of Surāṣṭra";
having addressed him thus, Raivata departed for that place along with Nārada. ||42||
Having arrived together at Vaikuṇṭha and prostrated before the Lord Hari, he bowed his head like a staff and offered praise with palms joined in reverence. ||43||

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Specification of the Holy Tirthas and Other Sites that Filled the Cavities of the Earth," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 54.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! The Manu named Raivata attained Vaikuṇṭha and, with great love, praised me, the compassionate one, who am accompanied by you. || 1 ||
Homage! To you whose nature is existence and consciousness, the ocean of the mass of bliss;
homage to you who are of a single nature and yet of both natures. 2.
Salutation to the one with golden hair, salutation to the one possessing a beard upon a beard.
Salutation to the one possessing milk and non-milk, salutation to the one who sustains both seed and non-seed.
Salutation to you who are marked externally, salutation to you who are unmarked within.
Homage to You who are like a universal coral sprout; homage to You who are, in some respects, like a mere child. 4.
Homage to the Being of the Right; homage to You, the Being of the Left.
Homage to the one whose nature is above; homage to You, whose form is not above. 5.
Salutations to you whose form is that which is supported, salutations to you whose form is the support;
salutations to you whose form is the two-fold petals, salutations to the source of the sprout. (6)
Salutations to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha; salutations to You who dwell beyond all limits.
Salutations to the one whose form is the mind; salutations to You whose form is devotion. 7.
Salutations to you, O ocean of compassion; salutations to the prosperer of Saurāṣṭra;
salutations to the dweller of Raivata; salutations to you, Dāmodara. (8)
Salutations to the one known as Patnīvrata; salutations to Kṛṣṇa, to Viṣṇu;
salutations to the one whose nature is infinite, to my inner controller (antaryāmin). 9.
O Great Viṣṇu, you are independent; I do not know what you desire.
You ought to accomplish that for which a devotee has been summoned. (1.55.10)
O Viṣṇu, by Your grace, may this servant be led to the further shore of the path of worldly existence;
for wherever Your two feet reside, that place shall indeed be my refuge. (11)
O Lord of Compassion, this servant who has come for refuge must certainly not be abandoned;
since he has been accepted out of mercy, you ought not to forsake him. (12)
"Whatever is desired that brings security in this world, let that be provided"—having praised him thus, Raivata, the best among devotees, fell silent. (13)
The glorious Lord, the sovereign of Vaikuṇṭha, said to him:
"Accept this, which is like an atom, my portion of Vaikuṇṭha. (14)
Within your sphere, O Brahmā known as the Self-Existent One, lies the great western aperture in the earthly kingdom of Priyavrata. (15)
The path of the Suratrāṇa, a gap extending for a hundred *gavyūtis*, must be filled by you alone with blossoming earth. (16)
By that [act], he shall become a protector (suratrāṇa), and thus it shall attain the name Saurāṣṭra;
there, endowed with glory, I shall dwell for your sake. (17)
"Whatever else was spoken by Nārada, I shall ordain that as well;
having said this, the Lord bestowed upon him a particle of Vaikuṇṭha. (18)
Taking that [atom] by the command of Viṣṇu, Raivata returned;
he desired to place that minute atom into the opening exactly as described. ||19||
It expanded to such a vast extent that it was a hundred *gavyūtis* long; in its density, it was equal to the surface of the earth, and that divine [space] consisted of five qualities. (1.55.20)
The gap situated according to its requirement and its proper place has been filled.
From the non-divine mixed with the divine, the junction consists of white and red.
The white unexcavated earth is white and turns back the circle.
That mandala was one hundred yojanas in extent, dark and pale in color.
He ruled over the divine and unbroken land of Surāṣṭra, acquired by Raivata;
and in its central region, having meditated upon Viṣṇu, he established him there. (23)
For Nārāyaṇa himself, casting aside all that is illusory, remains ever intent on propitiating him; he bestows upon him a compassionate glance. (24)
Then Hari gave him a thousandth part of his own jewel;
that [part] indeed attained bulkiness and assumed the supreme form of a mountain. (25)
Thus, this mountain established in the center of Surāṣṭra became famous by the name of its leader as Raivatācala. ||26||
There, Raivata built a city named Raivata;
Raivata was always engaged in the remembrance, chanting, and hearing of Viṣṇu. (27)
For in service, worship, praise, servitude, and the offering of all things, that great devotee remained engaged throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. (28)
In the burden of sovereignty, in legal affairs, in eating, and likewise in sleeping—in every way, O Lord of the gods, he worshipped Nārāyaṇa. (29)
Once, while lying upon a great couch in yogic sleep, meditating on Śrī Hari within his own self, he indeed entered into samādhi. (1.55.30)
By the will of Nārāyaṇa, the golden armlet of his right arm became liquid and fell onto the couch. (31)
The youth became golden-hued, possessing a white luster like that of the moon;
a halo of cool, white radiance appeared all around him. (32)
The palace, the city, and the entire country were pervaded on all sides by white rays, becoming one undivided mass of milk-white luster. (33)
While he sat upon his couch dispelling all darkness, the great devotee Raivata happened to become awake by chance. (34)
Upon her bed, she received a prince born from her own body—one who was as bright as the moon, gentle, radiant with splendor, and auspicious. (35)
White-washing the entire world in all directions and intermediate points, appearing as soon as he was born, perfectly refined, sixteen years of age, and eternally radiant. ||36||

Having recognized that Raivata was virtuous, possessed the mark of a universal monarch’s bow, and was endowed with the wisdom of formal proclamation, [the father] gave him the royal throne on Mount Raivataka. (37)
He went to the Viśālā cave for the purpose of worship; there, Raivata remained constantly absorbed in meditative concentration upon Hari. (38)
Remaining as a single self until the fifth Manu comes into being, he himself [remains] thus in each successive great aeon (kalpa) thereafter. ||39||
It is established that he will abide in the truth known as Mahāvibhūti;
in various places within his lineage, there will be kings such as Khaṭvāṅga and others. (1.55.40)
They shall be rulers of the earth for tens of millions of years.
Born from the club Aṅgada, he was named Khaṭvāṅgada. (41)
On his forehead there was a vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) like a golden line, and on his skin there was a natural tilaka with a drop in the center that appeared reddish. (42)
A golden garland was upon his neck, and there was a natural luster upon his skin;
the mountain (king) was the refuge of all sovereignty, dispelling the darkness with his splendor. (43)
Then, having ascended his celestial chariot, he moved repeatedly through the atmosphere, perceiving from afar and even further away the darkness of the night in the eastern quarter. ||44||
Wherever there was a region devoid of the moon, there he came through the sky like a second moon, destroying all darkness;
wandering month after month in the void of the directions within the sky of the Lord of Night.

She creates the worlds along with their light, spreading forth cool rays. (46) Then, when that had been done, the oceans there became constantly full like those at the change of the moon; the earth was agitated, and the waves repeatedly overflowed the shores. (47)
The waves rise up and do not indeed recede;
at that time, the lands were repeatedly overwhelmed by water. (48)
At that time, medicinal herbs were generally nourished for only one, two, or three kalās;
due to the accumulation of extreme cold and indigestion, they perished. (49)
Having thus observed this loss, he withdrew his own celestial chariot;
he became such a great divine sovereign, consisting of cool radiance. (1.55.50)
He performs devotion to Śrī Hari and causes other people to do so;
he proclaims at dawn that Viṣṇu is always to be worshipped by all people. (51)
A forehead mark (puṇḍra) with a crescent moon should always be made, and food should be offered to Hari.
Having gone to the house of Viṣṇu in the evening, the Lord Janārdana should be praised. 52.
Virtuous women and holy men should be highly honored with gifts of food, drink, and other necessities;
one should offer oblations into the fire and give to the gods with devotion. (53)
He who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa and always worships Nārāyaṇa—my hand shall never be taken by him. (54)
Thus, while he ruled, the entire land was adorned with Vaiṣṇavas;
indeed, there was no one who was not a devotee within that kingdom.
While the circle [of his subjects] was thus endowed with devotion, King Khaṭvāṅga remained peaceful.
Having abandoned all anxiety for the kingdom, he constantly remembered the Blessed One.
Having stationed his celestial chariot in a mountain cave, he himself became intent upon propitiation;
for when many arbudas of time had passed, he set his mind upon asceticism.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Lakṣmīśa, the Acceptance of Maṇibhūmi as a Follower, the Filling of the Earth-Cavity, the Spreading of Radiance that Becomes a Second Moon, and the Enjoining of Devotion," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 55.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! Then the king, overwhelmed by the force of dispassion, [went] three yojanas further east from Mount Raivata. 1.

Having recognized that the delightful Aśvapaṭṭa lake in the great tiger forest was a place of unbroken waters, surrounded by trees bearing roots and fruits, solitary, and free from all disturbances, that king [decided to settle there].
Then King Khaṭvāṅgada went to a secluded place not very far from Aśvapaṭṭatīra;
having seen a region filled with cool shade,
abounding in excellent trees such as *badarī*, pomegranate, rose-apple, tamarind, and *guṇḍrā*.
In that region, which was pervaded and endowed with subterranean waters and ponds,
the water from the pond constantly flowed in the form of a spring;
indeed, flowing over the surface, it proceeded toward the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
There, at the foot of a banyan tree situated near the edge of the pond,
Khaṭvāṅga performed austerities on the surface of the earth, keeping a śālagrāma stone before him;
for a thousand years, he subsisted on the eating of jambu fruits.
He performed the consumption of *guñjā* seeds for a second thousand [days],
and he performed the consumption of pomegranates for a third thousand.
He performed the fourth thousand [fasts] by eating jujube fruits;
the fifth thousand he performed by eating the sour tamarind fruit;
and then the sixth thousand he performed by subsisting on tubers.
In the seventh thousand, he made the consumption of leaves his food;
in the eighth thousand, he made the consumption of water his food;
and in the ninth thousand, he made the consumption of air his food.
For the tenth thousand [years], remaining without food and staying fixed on his big toe, he remained at Śālagrāma meditating upon Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, his guru,
and constantly contemplating the glorious Lord Viṣṇu.
Obeisance to you, O Lord of Lakṣmī, the glorious Nārāyaṇa!
(13) Then, indeed, a great fire emerged from his head;
its smoke and great flames pervaded the three worlds. (14)
Setting ablaze the gods, daityas, humans, and others situated in the sky, the goddess Earth trembled and the oceans were likewise agitated. (15)
There, a great forest fire arose from the fire of his ascetic penance;
when that forest fire had spread, the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa [appeared]. 16.
Out of compassion for him, who was performing penance and was devoid of physical luster, he indeed arrived there to protect him and sprinkled that nectar upon his head. ||17||
By that [act], the fire from his head and the forest fire were extinguished;
Nārāyaṇa, won over by his devotion, said to him: "O devotee! (18)
O Khaṭvāṅgada, you shine forth while practicing great devotion;
by performing penance consisting of devotion, you shall bring about the welfare of all creatures. (19)
"Desist from such austerity and grant me an audience, O sinless one!
For there is nothing that I, a devotee free from desire, would not give to you. (1.56.20)
"O King, what do you require? Choose whatever you desire and I shall grant it.
Having thus commanded, the glorious Hari remained silent at that time. ||21||
Opening his eyes, he beheld Nārāyaṇa standing before him;
filled with affection, he exclaimed, "Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune! (22)
He performed a dance by beholding [the Lord], bearing the dust of His feet upon his head; he rolled about repeatedly at the feet of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. (23)
Having become a servant, that sovereign of the discus always chose to serve at his feet, in the presence of both himself and his own form where penance was performed. (24)
Lakṣmī chose Nārāyaṇa, always desiring a vision of him;
then, by the command of Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī replied, "So be it. (25)
Having spoken thus, he placed an auspicious crescent mark moist with saffron upon his forehead;
and drops of the moist saffron held in Lakṣmī’s hand [also fell there]. (26)
Many had fallen into the pond; likewise, having washed his hands, drunk water, bathed, and given water to the king to drink, [he departed]. || 27 ||
The Lord made his eternal dwelling in Śālagrāma;
there the great lord Nārāyaṇa, the leader of the auspicious caravan, resides forever. (28)
From that time on, that pond became known by the name Kuṅkumavāpikā;
and there, by that king, a temple of Śrī Nārāyaṇa was built. (29)
He himself constructed a seven-storied palace and personally performed service for him;
and she, bearing what happiness indeed, was truly Kambharā, who was Lakṣmī herself. (1.56.30)
Śrī Hari is indeed that Gopāla who always takes and accepts King Khaṭvāṅgada as his protector—the guardian of the earth, which is like a cow—within his own refuge. ||31||
They are called Kambharā and Gopāla, who are Lakṣmī and Narāyaṇa;
their son, born from a portion of Narāyaṇa himself, was devoted to his wife. (32)
In that very place, during the Prakalpaka Kalpa, he remained performing austerities;
the son, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, sat meditating upon his two divine parents. ||33||
In the auspicious holy site known as Kuṅkumavāpī, which bestows liberation upon those who take refuge there, he dwells with a divine body, even though he is all-pervading everywhere. (34)
This is the divine Aśvasara lake and the vast Vyāghrāraṇya forest;
there is the divine Kuṅkumavāpī and the temple of Kambharā-Gopāla. ||35||
In the region of Surāṣṭra, there were the holy ford of Patnīvratadvija, the city built by Khaṭvāṅgada, and the delightful place known as Kuṅkumavāpī. ||36||
Taking with him all the requisites of Vaikuṇṭha, as well as hosts of male and female servants,
along with prosperity and sovereign power, Kṛṣṇa shines forth there.
Every particle of dust from that place is pure and bestows liberation;
it is a divine land with celestial waters, resembling the divine Vaikuṇṭha. (38)
It bestows liberation through sacrifice, ancestral rites, vows, charity, and sacred pilgrimage sites;
there, whether it be a woman or a man, whoever has entered any kind of womb— (39)
Abandoning the body, he attains supreme liberation known as the imperishable Brahman;
all those men who are on that ground are indeed the attendants of Hari. (1.56.40)
The women who dwell there are all followers of Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, all the beasts, birds, and so forth, as well as the trees, creepers, and the like [are his devotees]. (41)
Those liberated souls residing in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha are not to be perceived by one with human vision;
they are to be beheld with divine sight, and certainly not with the eyes of the flesh.

(42) Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Direct Vision of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa through the Austerities of Khaṭvāṅgada at Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, the Flowing of the Bindu from the Formation of the Saffron Moon, the Sacred Site of Kuṅkumavāpī, and the Abode of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa in the Form of the Cowherd Kambharā," in the first section, the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Chapter 58 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The son of Khaṭvāṅga was indeed called Barhiṣāṅgada;
peacocks would come and stand upon his head as he performed penance.
There they shed their feathers, yet he did not perceive it;
for when that mass of peacock plumes had appeared,
his wife’s vow had indeed turned their broom into something great.
While she was guarding the image near the temple during the work of cleaning,
she was seen by Khaṭvāṅgada when he seized her by the hands;
just as he began to wipe it down, rain fell from the sky.
Taking that broom, he entered a hut and remained there.
Day and night, a great rain occurred, with heavy downpours. ||5||
The broom-handle was warm, smooth, and likewise very soft;
it was variegated, pleasant to the touch, and likewise dispeller of cold. (6)
Then, having laid [her] at his side upon the bed, he became subject to sleep;
there, by the will of Hari, he beheld the form of an Apsaras.
Thereupon, an emission of his vital seed occurred upon those sacrificial grasses.
A son was born to him instantly; by the time he looked [at him] in the morning, [he saw him].
Seeing that his son, a great adept, possessed youth as soon as he was born, he then gave him the name Bāliṣṭhāṅgada.
Consecrated as king in that realm, he was proud, heroic, and a wielder of the bow;
honored in the beautiful capital city of Khaṭvāṅgapura,
that pure devotee once went into the forest accompanied by a limited number of followers.
Wandering about, he roamed through his father’s divine tiger-forest. ||11||
Then he arrived there at the excellent holy site of Kuṅkumavāpī, at the hermitage of the brahmin devoted to his wife, in order to see those twice-born ones. ||12||
And having beheld his gurus and his parents, who were the very embodiments of the divine Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, he returned to the presence of his true spiritual teacher. ||13||
At that time, the Guru was established in meditative absorption nearby;
he did not perceive the King’s sudden arrival while remaining within his inner state.
[The King offered] a welcome, as well as honor, a seat, and due respect.

That royal sage did not obtain even a moment’s respect in the hermitage devoid of people; when he found no honor there, his mind being dependent on pride and his intellect ruined, he conceived a base self-interest. (15–16)
"Alas! This mendicant, who eats our grain, treats us with contempt;
even in speech he offers no honor, for he considers himself a Brahmin. (17)
Having closed my eyes in deceit, what kind of meditation have I undertaken?
For if I were awake, it would lead to the king bestowing honors upon me. (18)
"Therefore, having placed this deception before me—that one must remain established in meditative concentration—this twice-born man indeed treats me with contempt. (19)
"Therefore, such a brahmin must certainly not be neglected"—thinking thus, King Bāhiṣāṅgada [tried to remove] the great dead serpent from his throat. (1.57.20)
Having entrusted [his wife] to Patnīvrata, he departed toward his own city; meanwhile, Brahmavrata arrived at that sage's [hermitage]. (21)
Accompanied by the sage’s disciples, Svayamprakāśa and others, he remained there;
having seen a dead snake around the sage’s neck, he understood through meditative absorption (samādhi). ||22||
The king threw a dead snake at the wicked man, thereby invoking that curse:
"Alas! A dog, indeed, by barking at its master and insulting him with its paws [is acting like this]. (23)
"This is a great and extraordinary anomaly:
that a Malakīṭa, consecrated by Brāhmaṇas, has indeed attained the state of a serpent. (24)
He bites those very people who brought him there; what kind of unworthiness is this!
For by whom was this mouse, overcome by fear, joined with the state of a lion? (25)
What indeed could be more base than his desire to devour that [virtue], like a sinful dog seeking scraps, violating the innocent vow of his wife? (26)
Disregarding her venerable father, who was like a god, she threw a serpent’s carcass around his neck; she certainly deserves punishment. (27)
"Furthermore, those dogs shall not cause you any disrespect.
Having thus addressed them and taking water in his right hand, the son spoke. (28)
"May he by whom a snake was thrown around my neck through trickery meet his death within this very month," saying thus, he released water upon the ground. (29)
Having pronounced a curse upon his fellow students while observing the vow of celibacy, he wept before his teacher; at that moment, the teacher arose from his meditative absorption. (1.57.30)
When he saw the carcass of a dead snake around his own neck, he heard his own circle of sons and disciples weeping. ||31||
Then the teacher, devoted to his wife, consoled them all:
"Understand this: for what reason are you all weeping here? (32)
Since a serpent was indeed worn as a necklace upon the corpse of a human body, it should certainly be considered a *hāra* (necklace) during the worship of the corpse.
There is neither loss nor fault here; indeed, I shall perform my ablutions.
Purity indeed comes from mere bathing; for what reason do you weep so bitterly?
Peace must always be protected, and forbearance must be protected in every way;
it is through peace and forbearance that all sages have attained a state of worshipfulness. (35)
Truth, virtue, austerity, meditation, self-study, peace, forbearance, and patience—these we always consider to be our divine and supreme wealth. (36)
That must never be abandoned, for it is our very deity;
forgiveness, indeed, is the supreme weapon that destroys the weapon of anger. (37)
"By means of forgiveness, all the Vāḍavas shall receive honor from the gods.
O sons! I ask you: have you perhaps contemplated something harmful toward him? (38)
Thus, at that time, the sons informed the sage there regarding the king who had transgressed the bounds of propriety; and within a month, the king of serpents [arrived]. (39)
"An impostor has indeed been raised up against us; he will surely bite us"—thus it was proclaimed.
Having heard that a terrible thunderbolt made of adamant, the destroyer of kings, had arisen, the sage, for a moment, remained silent, brooding deeply within his own heart. (1.57.40)
He said: "Indeed, that which is self-luminous and cannot be taken away has been stolen by you. (41)
A great punishment for a minor offense is certainly not just; you have acted unjustly.
O Queen, when there is a ruler, even thieves and the like do not oppress the subjects.
When the land is devoid of a king, the subjects kill one another and bandits plunder them.
"O dear one! You, with your immature intellect, have uttered a terrible curse. (43)
The Blessed One should forgive the fault committed out of ignorance;
even when there are thousands of offenders, he does not grieve at all.
The devoted person suffers but does not seek recompense.
They were insulted, beaten, reviled, and treated with contempt. ||45||
Even when reviled, cursed, mistreated, or struck down—even in times of calamity—the virtuous do not retaliate against the wicked. (46)
Therefore, O self-luminous one! Go quickly and report this:
"Within a month, a rogue will surely bite you. (47)
Thus urged, the disciple went to Barhiṣāṅgada;
the royal sage, overcome with grief, reflected upon his own wickedness. (48)
"Alas! Even a non-Aryan would not have committed such a sin as I have;
I have accumulated a great evil against a Brāhmaṇa who is worthy of worship. (49)
Prosperity, youth, pride, existence, and lack of discernment—these they call the causes of misfortune; yet they have found their true meaning in me alone. (1.57.50)
"Alas! What world shall be mine, having become so arrogant as a hater of Brahman?
May there surely be the destruction of this sinner as its direct adversary. (51)
Furthermore, I shall certainly not act in such a way toward the Teacher, the Lord of Men;
rather, [I shall act] for the welfare and prosperity of kings who honor the Brahmins. ||52||
"Nevertheless, the Blessed One ought to inflict a great punishment upon me.
While he was thinking thus,
the voice of his disciple— which had been gathered for the purpose of a Brahma-punishment— arrived through a deception, foreboding death.
Having heard this, one endowed with discipline should undertake the vow of fasting.
Having paid homage to the Brahmin, he merged his own self into Brahman on the plateau of Mount Raivata, to the east of Khaṭvāṅgapura. (55)
Then, in the middle of the Bhaveśa lake, upon an island consisting of water,
he performed the vow of fasting and sat down facing the north.
Having realized this through the practice of meditative concentration, the sages, as well as the Manus, the ancestors, gods, gandharvas, asuras, yakṣas, and human beings;
the brahmins, virtuous men, virtuous women, sacred fords, and likewise the mountains—[all attained their respective states]. (57)
The divine planets, constellations, and stars, the medicinal herbs, the wish-fulfilling trees,
the cows that grant all desires, the Surabhis, the Mothers, and the guardians of the worlds arrived;
having honored them, he prostrated himself like a staff before them again and again.
When they were comfortably seated, the king, perceiving that his purpose was near its fulfillment, announced what he intended to do:
"O, [you who are] compassionate, givers of liberation, and possessors of merit! || 1.57.60 ||
But your vision leads to the destruction of ignorance and brings about confidence in the next world.

That the arrival of you both served as the pretext for the brahmin’s curse has become for me a source of grace; it has given rise to the root of world-weariness and acts as an impetus toward liberation. (61–62)
Whether sweet or bitter, that which is spoken by a wise man leads to well-being in every way;
for you have come within the range of my vision at the very moment of death. (63)
The compassionate ones should remain steadfast and likewise sing the *Daśa* of Hari;
let the deceiver bite his own desire, for today I have no concern. (64)
May my vital breath go happily into the midst of the assembly of the virtuous who delight in bliss;
wherever I go, may I shine there in the service of those who delight in Brahman. 65.
Having done this and having bowed down at the lake of Bhaveśvara,
the lord of the earth sat down on the central island, abstaining from food.
Then, the gods, sages, and apsarases repeatedly praised him and offered a rain of flowers accompanied by shouts of victory. At that moment,
Vyāsa himself arrived there along with the sage Śvetavyāsa.
He who was born in the first kalpa, assuming a white form—
resembling the sun in brilliance, radiant with knowledge through his learning,
equal to Brahmā in yoga, and Hari himself in sovereignty. (68–69)
Those who were there rose and paid homage to him upon his arrival;
they then seated him upon a great, worthy throne.
As he sat there, the king bowed down to him with palms joined in reverence.
Out of discipline, he asked this auspicious question that leads to the highest good:
"We are indeed heirs of the Kṣatriyas, yet by our actions we have become base; having encountered those such as you, we have been elevated above the world. (71–72)
Merely by the chanting of his name, even palaces become sacred pilgrimage sites;
for when properly served through sight, touch, proximity, attendance, massage, and prostration, holy men indeed purify their servants. (73)
By obtaining even the dust of their feet, householders are purified;
even their homes become pure—how much more so from being in their actual company?
How could the sight of you be mine except through your compassion? (74–75)
"Therefore, my liberation will surely be eternal for years on end.
Now, what indeed should be done by me as I am about to die in every respect?
Shall I ask about listening [to scripture], chanting, or worship, whichever is appropriate? (76)
Or let some other auspicious rite, such as the offering of oblations and so forth, be demonstrated. (77)

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Barhiṣāṅgada in the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Arrival at the Hermitage of Patnīvrata and the Failure to Receive Honor; the Casting of a Live Snake around the Neck of the Great Sage out of Provocation; the Death of that Sage’s Son from the Bite of a Deceptive Snake within a Month and the Subsequent Curse; the Sage’s Knowledge of the Truth, His Vow of Fasting unto Death, and the Meeting with Other Sages; and the Arrival of Śveta Vyāsa and the Inquiry into Questions Concerning One’s Own Spiritual Welfare. || 57 ||
