Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! Understand from me what happened there after that.
Then the sage Śveta Vyāsa spoke to Hāṭakāṅgada.
O King, such a hermitage as yours yields only meager spiritual benefit; the realization of the true nature of the self cannot be attained through sleep, sexual intercourse, or worldly activities. (2)
Life passes away through desire; nights depart in sleep;
and days are spent in the mockery of exertion for the sake of filling the belly. (3)
The observer perceives incessantly the world dissolving moment by moment;
yet, seeing his house, children, wife, and so forth as dead, he does not truly see.
What was acquired yesterday may perish today or tomorrow;
yet the world does not realize that its own destruction has arrived.
A frog, half-seized in the mouth by a serpent, [does not perceive] the one approaching nearby.
One strives to eat a fly; the hope for life is difficult to overcome.
(6) Only someone rare, through a spark of compassion, understands the liberation of the self;
only someone rare, being a vessel of compassion, strives again for the highest good. (7)
Even there, some fortunate person remains solely for the sake of liberation.
O King, you who desire liberation have indeed made a perfectly firm resolve.
The Lord Śrī Hari is to be heard, glorified, and remembered, for the sake of attaining the perfection of yoga-practice and maintaining the wisdom of Sāṃkhya. (9)
Likewise, from the study of the scriptures, there is the attainment of the certain determination of liberation;
and from the birth of a human being, there is the attainment that at its conclusion brings the remembrance of Śrī Hari. (1.58.10)
O King, the virtuous generally delight in the ocean of Hari’s qualities;
even those devoid of qualities engage in the narration and glorification of Hari. (11)
Indeed, the chanting of his deeds, the remembrance of his form, and the meeting with his devotees bestow the highest spiritual welfare. (12)
Listening to His stories and understanding His divine manifestations, as well as meditating upon Him residing in the heart, indeed bestows supreme liberation. (13)
By the power of the grace of Śrī Hari, I am the first Śveta Vyāsa Muni, born from the rays of Śrī Hari; I am devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and I am Hara, who has taken refuge in Hari. ||14||
I meditate upon, remember, and glorify the stories of Hari;
those stories were heard by me from the mouth of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (15)
Through them, I have attained that state which is beyond the gunas and is the very form of liberation;
nevertheless, I cause these to be heard by people for the sake of supreme liberation.
This *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* is indeed of the nature of Brahman.
Indeed, the most blessed speech makes [all things] take on the form of Brahman. ||17||
In whatever place her hearing [of this] occurs through a month-long recitation, that place indeed becomes the divine Vaikuṇṭha, the very essence itself. ||18||
Those men in whose ears this Saṃhitā has entered and who have established it within their own selves, they should indeed be known as eternally liberated, even though they bear a body. (19)
O King, your father Ṣaḍaṅgada heard this compendium from them at Kuṅkumavāpī and went to Hari for fearlessness.
This Saṃhitā was indeed heard by Brahmā together with the Ṛṣis, and in the Tretā age, it was heard in Satyaloka together with the Devas and the Pitṛs. ||21||
Indeed, in Vaikuṇṭha, the goddess Lakṣmī herself recites this;
this complete recitation is considered superior even to all the Vedas. (22)
From the very beginning, this scripture emerged from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, the incarnations of the Supreme Brahman and millions of His manifestations [are described herein]. (23)
These [teachings] have indeed been described according to their true meaning, heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa;
this well-composed Saṃhitā is the first scripture of them all. (24)
This [earth] was indeed made manifest by the first Vyāsa, Śveta;
taking this as his foundation, other Vyāsas and others shall compose collections of scriptures and Purāṇas,
consisting of ancient traditional narratives.
This is supremely worthy of being heard, and it brings about the attainment of the state of Nārāyaṇa.
With a one-pointed mind alone, one should contemplate its supreme meaning,
by which liberation— consisting of reaching the world of Brahman— may occur immediately.
Indeed, one should practice the withdrawal of the senses from their objects.
And one should practice the dissolution of the mental fluctuations into the inner reality every day. 28.
One should practice stability within one's own internal functions and cultivate a very firm union of oneself with Hari.
For one whose character is thus fixed in Brahman, liberation is immediately held in the palm of the hand.
Seated in the svastika posture, he was devoted to the practice of breath control.
Having withdrawn the functions of the senses, one should first indeed fix the mind upon the gross, embodied form of Śrī Hari, consisting of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. 31.
His face was slightly smiling, a fountain of nectar, serene, a torrent of love, beautiful, captivating, gentle, radiant, and white.
A seeker of liberation should wear these two separately as food:
the two eyes of Hari, which are as long as the petals of a blue lotus. (33)
As if mocking the form of the God of Love, it was wide, white at the edges, and beautiful to behold, as if burning with a stream of the nectar of love. (34)
The seeker of liberation should meditate separately on the desirable object of meditation for each of them: the pair of eyebrows, which are slanted, smooth, and gradually tapering;
[and] the peacock-feather-like tuft at the end of the line of fine hair, extending as far as the ear. (35)

In the center, however, it was enriched by the moon of desire, exceedingly radiant as if it were a beautiful form. (36) Then there were the curls—slender, glossy, curved, and shimmering—which, being brilliantly bright, supported the path of Brahmā situated in their midst. (37)
These two should be meditated upon separately, adorned with golden crowns, their hair either braided into a topknot or gathered into a crest-jewel or a lock-jewel. (38)
One should fix one's mind upon the two cheeks, which are adorned with strings of pearls, or else one should fix the mind of oneself there upon the crescent moon [mark] above. ||39||
Their lips, with their mustaches emerging and unemerging, were like ripe bimba fruits;
slightly joined together, curved, they revealed the moment of a kiss. (1.58.40)

One should devoutly hold those two [hands], which are pleasing to the heart, marked by the lines of the bow and the bearer of nectar, separately; then one should gradually bring them into a state of oneness there. ||41||
Their ears, adorned with golden ear-rings, should be held so that they touch the chin, which is made beautiful by a shining golden dot of excellent jewels. 42.
With ear-ornaments, crest-jewels, garlands, and beautiful, shimmering earrings, the face of Lakṣmī is thus desirable and lovely—the very face of Nārāyaṇa. (43)

Then, having drawn it into the activity of the self through meditation, one should again place the object of meditation there—[the form] which is shimmering, sweet, pale-white, and perfectly circular with the luster of nectar. (44)
In that state, the absorption of both the mind and the self is brought about by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Thus, one should unite the self with the Self, which is the Supreme Brahman. By him who has accomplished this union, everything that is his own has been accomplished. (45)
Thus, [he worshipped] the throat, heart, arms, belly, waist, and hips;
the thighs, knees, calves, shanks, ankles, forefeet, and heels—
these are the limbs of Mahālakṣmī and of Mahānārāyaṇa.
One should always maintain, meditate upon, and concentrate upon each one individually. ||47||
By that [means], liberation occurs immediately, characterized by non-return;
however, in that regard, the cause of bondage is merely the obscuration of the thing-in-itself. (48)
If there should be any contradiction regarding his presence within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), one should then perceive him there as well:
his two feet in Pātāla, the two heels in Rasātala,
his two ankles in Mahātala, and his two shanks in Talātala.
His two knees were on the surface of the earth, and likewise his two thighs were in the vital region.
His penis is in the netherworld (atala), the base of his thighs is on the surface of the earth;
the pit of his navel is in the sky, and likewise, his heart is in heaven. (51)
One should indeed show his throat to a great sage, and one should show his mouth to a common person;
one should show his forehead to an ascetic, and one should show his head to one established in truth.
One should observe his arms among Indra and the other [directional deities] in the quarters, his ears in the [region of] sound, and his nose in that of the two Aśvins. (53)
One should perceive his breath in the fragrance, his mouth likewise in the fire;
one should see his two eyes in the sky and observe that eye in the sun. 54.
One should perceive his eyelashes during day and night, his eyebrows upon the seat of Brahmā, and likewise his palate in the waters; one should perceive the tongue of Hari in taste,
his head in the Vedic hymns, his fangs in self-restraint, and his teeth in affection.
In Māyā, there is the laughter of Śrī Hari; in the creation, the casting of side-long glances. ||56||
In a state of shame, one should gaze at his upper lip; in greed, at the lower lip;
in righteousness, at Hari’s chest; but in unrighteousness, at his back. (57)
He placed the penis of that very [Viṣṇu] within the creator (Brahmā), the two testicles of Hari within the two Mitra gods,
the intestines of Hari within the oceans, and likewise the masses of bones within the mountains;
he placed his channels within the rivers and the hairs of his body within the trees.
In the wind, he perceived the breath of Śrī Hari;
in the air, his movement; in the flow of the qualities (guṇas), his activity; in the clouds, his hair; in the twilights, his garments; and in primordial matter (pradhāna), his subtlety. || 1.58.60 ||
One should perceive the mind of Hara in the moon, the state of greatness in consciousness, that internal organ in Rudra, and indeed the nails in horses and other animals. 61.
He placed his hips and back upon the beasts, his dexterity among the birds,
his intellect within the self-born leaf-hut of Hari, and [his] human form among men.
His memory resides among the Gandharvas, and his strength among the hosts of Asuras;
his mouth is among the Brāhmaṇas, his two arms among the Kṣatriyas,
his two thighs likewise among the Vaiśyas, and one should see the Śūdra in his feet.
One should perceive his resolve regarding desires as the divine body of Hari;
his vigor among men as his bliss consisting of the contemplation of Brahman; the subtle within the gross, and the small within the great, as Kṛṣṇa in the Vairāja state. (64–65)
Thus, in every instance, one should perceive the glorious Nārāyaṇa;
through that, one should bring to completion there the acts of hearing, reflection, and meditation.
Then, his bliss, his happiness, and his sweet essence are indeed constant.
"Always, by worshipping anything else, one should lead it all to absorption in That.
Thus, O King, that which must be performed for the sake of liberation has been shown to you.
By that path, Hari indeed becomes directly present. (67–68)

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction Given by Śveta Vyāsa, the Direction for the Recitation of the Saṃhitā, the Meditation on the Form of the Lord, the Manifestations of Power, and the Meditation on Identity with Hari," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||58||
← Chapter 058: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 59 [[Author:
Chapter 060 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Even so, if due to a trace of latent impressions (vāsanā) and the delusion of many births, the mind should again fail to attain stability, [then one must act as follows]. (1)
Then, however, one should maintain the conviction that "this mind alone is Brahman.
Whatever arises within it—whether white or even black—that too is indeed Brahman;
for there is no other object whatsoever.
Thus should the wise person who is about to die reflect; he should not pray for anything else.
Moreover, even if there should appear there various manifestations for embodied beings—
such as cattle, wives, sons, wealth, houses, and prosperity—
one should conceive of all this as indeed Brahman alone, and not long for anything else.
In this way, by means of that state of Brahman, those very forms indeed become of the nature of Brahman;
therefore, they certainly do not cause bondage.
Nevertheless, a person, having themselves made that mind into the form of Brahman— || 6 ||
One should see everything as consisting of Brahman and perceive nothing else;
neither by the external senses, nor by the internal ones, nor even by the rays of latent impressions (vāsanā).
For one should indeed perceive that nothing else exists apart from one's own Self, as anything other than that would not be composed of it.

One should consider one's own mind to be of such a nature as to have the form of Brahman. Then, having made that very self into the supreme Brahman, one should indeed meditate upon the supreme Brahman with an uninterrupted flow. Just so, having made oneself into the supreme Brahman, which is the beautiful embodiment [of that reality]— 8–9.
One should meditate upon that Lord in His gentle form, subtle and the size of a span,
possessing four arms and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
His lotus-face being exceedingly serene and His eyes as long as lotus petals.
Clad in a garment as tawny as a saffron filament, beautifully adorned with ornaments set with jewels;
wearing on his head a crown and earrings whose edges were embellished with great gems;
bearing the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, and graced with a forest garland and the Kaustubha jewel. (11–12)
Her waist was adorned with a girdle, her lotus-feet graced with golden anklets,
she wore delicate golden leaf-patterns, and was draped in a choice outer garment.
Adorned with golden chains, finger-rings, and bracelets;
possessing glossy, curved, dark hair; with a face like nectar and a gentle smile; His eyes overflowing with the essence of love, and supremely compassionate with the playfulness of His eyebrows.
Thus one should meditate upon [the deity] within oneself as possessing divine splendor and beautiful form. 15.
In the same way, one should gaze upon each individual limb, starting from the nails up to the hair, until it reaches a state of steadiness; one should practice for that long. ||16||
Seated in a comfortable and steady posture, desiring to leave this turbulent world behind,
one should restrain the vital breaths, restrain the mind, and restrain the intellect within the self;
one should restrain the self in Brahman, and Brahman in the Supreme Self.
Thus, gradually obstructed by the supreme [state], it becomes tranquil and attains that very nature. //18//

One should gradually withdraw from activities; for qualities do not bestow bondage. What else could it be but Time, Māyā, and so forth—that indeed is the state of Viṣṇu. Contracting the navel and the anus, one should successively leap over the cakras.
Having meditated on the Guru at the root of the eyebrows, he ascends by way of the *suṣumṇā*;
then, having pierced the aperture of the crown of the head, he departs together with the liberated ones.
Having gone to the white Vaiśvānara, he proceeds to the Sun, the Moon, and the stars.
Having transcended the station of the ancestors and the circles of the sages,
having transcended the world of truth (Satyaloka) and the eight coverings of the Lord (Īśvara),
one should then transcend those and go to the Lord Virāṭ Nārāyaṇa.
Having transcended Hiraṇyagarbha, one then reaches the station of Mahāviṣṇu;
having completely abandoned even that, and having cast off the primordial state of Pradhāna,
one attains the eternal abode, the world of Brahmā.
There is neither death nor old age there, neither time nor sorrow;
neither affliction nor agitation—this is called the world of Śrī Hari. (25)
Through that form, one who is composed of bliss attains supreme bliss;
thus does the seeker of liberation [attain it] through ritual action, meditation, or worship. (26)
Having worshipped and meditated in that manner, one attains the Supreme Brahman;
thus have two paths been shown by the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari to Lakṣmī. ||27||
Through the yoga of action and the yoga of devotion, by which the self may attain liberation:
Hari is eternally present everywhere, and everything is considered to be within Hari. 28.
Therefore, one should meditate with one's whole being upon the Seer within the inner self;
hence, by means of one's entire nature, one should always [meditate] on Hari everywhere. //29//
Those who have taken refuge in Hari and who daily drink the nectar of this narrative—by hearing it, reciting it, and meditating upon it—one attains identity with that very essence. (1.59.30)
With their hearts ablaze with longing, they go to his lotus feet;
thus the connoisseur of aesthetic flavor (rasika), having taken recourse to the tongue of discernment (vijñāna-rasana). 31.
Having made the earth his ball, his two arms his pillow, his folded hands his noble vessel, and having fashioned the directions into his garment; ||32||
Obtaining alms from trees, water from rivers, and likewise a cave for a dwelling,
and finding contentment in Nārāyaṇa, the sage delights in the Self. What else, and for what purpose, would he desire, other than Nārāyaṇa?
Whether possessing desire or being free from desire, one should meditate upon Hari with that very self.
Whether in symbols or in the non-symbolic, one who is absorbed in that becomes identical with it.
By that very same one God, his own manifestations have been revealed for the sake of satisfying the desires of various worshippers. (35)
For not every person becomes free from desire at the time of death. (36)
Furthermore, even at the time of death, he repeatedly seeks many objects;
therefore, by means of that very [seeking], he should repeatedly practice the contemplation of Brahman upon them. ||37||
Having reflected with discernment, that very Brahman indeed bestows what is desired;
one who desires the splendor of a Brahmin should worship Hari through the vow of a devoted wife. 38.
One desiring prosperity should always worship you, Lakṣmī, the bestower of gold;
one desiring excellence of the senses should worship Indra, the lord of Śacī. (39)
One desiring offspring should worship Dakṣa and the other Prajāpatis here; one desiring invincibility should worship Agni; one desiring wealth should worship the Vasus;
one desiring virility should worship Rudra; and one desiring food should worship Aditi.
One who desires heaven should worship the Sun, while one who desires sovereignty should worship the Viśvedevas.
One who desires mastery over progeny should indeed sacrifice to the Sādhyadevas;
one desiring long life should worship the Aśvins, and one desiring nourishment should worship the Earth. 42.
One desiring a firm foundation should sacrifice to the Sky and the Earth; one desiring a wife should sacrifice to Urvaśī.
One desiring beauty should sacrifice to the Gandharvas, and one desiring fame should sacrifice to the Kratu.
Furthermore, one desiring sovereignty over all should sacrifice to Brahmā alone.
One who desires the accumulation of wealth should indeed worship Varuṇa;
one desiring knowledge should sacrifice to Śambhu; one desiring righteousness should honor Viṣṇu;
and one desiring the love of a husband and wife should always worship Satī Umā.
One should worship the ancestors with diligence for the sake of increasing one's lineage;
in every way, one should perform sacrifices again and again for the destruction of suffering. 46.
One desiring power should worship the Maruts; one desiring sovereignty, the Manu-deities; one desiring enjoyments, the Moon; and one desiring the destruction of enemies, the Rākṣasas. ||47||
But a person desiring liberation should constantly worship the Supreme Self, the Lord, as a devotee, with a mind consisting of either desire or desirelessness. 48.
One should pray to that very Supreme Self, the bestower of all one's own possessions.
Through that, there shall be the fulfillment of each respective desire; upon its fulfillment, there is contentment and the cessation of thirst. 49.
Thereafter, one should pray for the mass of eternal existence, consciousness, and bliss during recreation, eating, drinking, decoration, urination, and sexual union. (1.59.50)
Indeed, time passes separately even for axes; what then [is surprising]?
For even trees live, and even bellows breathe.
Have you not heard such stories in your ear regarding people of that sort?
Without hearing the story, Vālmīki’s two ears are considered to be mere holes;
without the chanting [of his name], his physical tongue is like that of a frog.
Without bowing to him who is worthy of a crown, the head is merely a burden. (53–56)
Without service to Hari, hands—though worthy of gold—are but fuel;
eyes that do not behold Hari are like the eye-spots on a peacock's tail-feathers. (54)
The two feet resting in the temple of Hari are indeed like mere tree-trunks;
a mortal who lacks the attainment of the dust of Hari’s feet is dead while yet living. (55)
Without the fragrance of the flowers of Hari’s Vṛndāvana, even the nose is not truly functional;
in the absence of melting devotion for Hari, the heart is like a stone. (56)
When there is water in the eyes during the narration of Hari’s stories, horripilation on the body-hairs, a thrill in the limbs, and melting in the heart—that is the state of sattva. (57)
I myself dwell directly within the hearts of the Sātvatas as Nārāyaṇa. Salutations to that Supreme Lord; salutations again and again to Him who is the source of all beings. 58.
Salutations again and again to you, whose inner self is the locus of infinite power;
salutations to the Brahman, whose form is invisible and whose path is imperceptible. 59.
Salutations to You, who destroy evil deeds and whose form is that of all living beings;
salutations to the Lord of the Sāttvatas, whose name is "the Dispeller of the Non-existent. (1.59.60)
Salutations to you, the kinsman of the distressed; salutations to him who shall rejoice in his own abode;
salutations to the one possessed of sovereign power whose qualities and supremacy are beyond all comparison or equality. ||61||
Salutations to You, who abide within one's own heart, yet remain far beyond the reach of those lacking yoga;
for whom hymns of praise, consisting of recollections worthy of being seen and heard, are in every way appropriate. 6.
Salutations to that doer of good, by the worship of whose feet those who have sought refuge shake off their impurities and cast away even the touch of the material elements. 63.
Free from desire, they attain the state of Brahman; salutations to Him.
(64) Those who practice morality, charity, ritual action, mantras, sacrifice, renunciation, austerity, and vows—salutations to Him, without surrendering to whom they find no security.

Dog-eaters, fish-eaters, leather-workers, Yavanas, Ābhīras, and mixed castes; Kaṅkas, Śabaras, Jhallas, Dāsas, Pārādhis, Gaṇikāpis, Kirātas, Khasas, Ghātas, and other sinful creatures as well. (65–66)
Salutations again and again to Him, by depending upon whom and through whose support they are swiftly purified;
this Lord consists of incarnations and is composed of virtuous men and women. (67)
May the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who consists of the lords, Īśas, and the unborn ones, and who sustains the sages, ancestors, gods, humans, asuras, and nāgas, be gracious. (68)
May Lord Nārāyaṇa, who consists of his consort as his very self, be gracious;
he is the Lord whose nature is both man and woman, and who is composed of the king and the queen. (69)
May my Lord—the Lord of the world, the abode, the earth, the intellect, modesty, and fortune—be gracious to me;
for when the heart is cleansed by meditation upon His feet, one perceives that Lord in whatever form He appears through a virtuous intellect that is woven throughout Him. (1.59.70)
In this way, the seers describe him in the world as higher than the highest.
In the language of the Vedas he is the form of Brahman; in the language of the world he is the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);
in both languages he is both sweet and bitter. May he, the granter of desired objects, be gracious.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Meditation on the Lord, the Journey to the World of Brahmā, and Meditation on His Various Manifestations," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī! Thus, every day King Hāṭakāṅgada listened to these stories from the mouth of Śveta Vyāsa, together with his listeners.
Impelled by the curse uttered by the sage against the child, the deceptive serpent approaches from the western quarter with the intent to bite. (2)
Having assumed the form of a brahmin on the bank of the river named Vratadā,
while the king of serpents remained resting in the shade of a banyan tree,
another twice-born man arrived there in the guise of a physician.
This very physician Dhanvantari, taking the medicine that destroys poison, goes to where her recitation has been undertaken. "I shall remove the king's poison and obtain much gold. (4–5)
Thinking of it as a reward,
he too went there beneath a great banyan tree to guard that golden bracelet.
Having reached the very cool shade and the auspicious water of the Kaṅkalāsā river, she sat down at the foot of a banyan tree there to drink and to rest. (7)
Then Dhanvantari, having been questioned by Kuhaka,
spoke out of fear caused by the curse of a brahmin upon the royal sage Hāṭakāṅgada,
and due to the obstacle consisting of poison produced by the bite of Kuhaka’s snake.
"I am going there with the desire for a reward to set him free.
Having heard that, listen, O twice-born one, as Kuhaka spoke:
"How will you ward off the potent poison of Kuhaka? (1.60.10)
"Go from here, O friend, and perform a test of that very banyan tree.
Burn it with fire, and then make it sprout once again. (11)
As soon as he had spoken thus and bit the banyan tree,
that very tree withered from the root upward due to the effect of the poison.
Then Dhanvantari, taking water and medicinal herbs from the river, sprinkled them at his [the tree's] root and proceeded to perform the watering. ||13||
Just as the banyan tree had previously been covered with sprouts and a profusion of leaves and sap, it suddenly became green once again.
Having observed this marvel, the conjurer said to that brahmin:
"Do not go, O best of the twice-born! Tell me, who are you? ||15||
"I give you a parārdha of gold as wealth; go there and do not [delay].
The twice-born Dhanvantari said: 'I am born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa. (16)
"O giver of honor, I am going to protect my devotee Hāṭakāṅgada.
To this, Kuhaka replied: "By good fortune, O Brahmin, you have received this curse!
Why do you wish to commit such a falsehood? (17)

"Because his lifespan has come to an end and because of the exhaustion of his merit, let the lord of the earth meet his destruction through the fulfillment of your agreement. Accept this wealth consisting of gold and jewels, indeed worth a parārdha. (18–19)
"Go away, O Great King; I am going to see him.
Having spoken thus to the king, Kuhaka took his own jewel from his head. (1.60.20)
Since gold indeed becomes infinite from iron through touch, Dhanvantari took the wealth and departed for his own abode. (21)
But the rogue, due to his future union [with his wife], went quickly to the place of the story;
the boy, however, having obtained the nectar-herb, immediately attained immortality.
Rich with white and green leaves, he shall remain for the duration of a kalpa.
He will indeed attain fame in the world as Dhanvantarivaṭa.
To the southwest of Mount Raivata,
at a distance of three yojanas, there stands a small banyan tree, marking his location.
To the west of Mahālayakṣiti, at a distance of one gavyūti, there is that holy site (tīrtha) which removes poison; it is highly praised for the mere act of bathing there. 25.
Merely by touching the *vaṭa* tree, the poison of embodied beings is destroyed;
this mantra, which removes poison, was proclaimed by Dhanvantari. (26)
"O poison, depart; may you be blessed! Go away from here quickly, O poison!
Remember the power of Dhanvantari for the sake of protecting Hāṭakāṅgada. (27)
Having recited this mantra, whoever administers the poison—be it most virulent or even exceedingly fierce—the poison immediately goes to its destruction. (28)
Then that rogue, assuming the form of a brahmin, would quickly and secretly approach the assembly and constantly listen to the discourse. (29)
When the thirtieth day had arrived, specifically in the evening,
at the conclusion of the *pārāyaṇa*, following the worship of Vyāsa— (1.60.30).
When the preceptor Vyāsa went to King Hāṭakāṅgada, the patron, to bestow his blessing,
at that moment the king of serpents assumed a subtle form like a slender rod.
He was indeed absorbed in the flowers of his necklace, like the sun within a flower of its own color. ||32||
While the necklace remained upon the king’s neck by his desire, the king also said: "O Vyāsadeva, salutations to you!
By your grace, I perceive that my obstacle has indeed vanished. (33)
At that moment, the rogue indeed inflicted a subtle bite upon his neck;
he injected his own fierce, potent, and minute venom through his fang.
That [venom] quickly entered the king’s *brahmarandhra* via the channel.
At that moment, the cry of "Alas! Alas! reached as far as the tips of his nails, and a great lamentation arose among the members of the assembly, whose minds were agitated by grief. (36)
But the king, whose mind and self were entirely absorbed in Kṛṣṇa like a sovereign of yogis,
assumed a divine form and departed for the supreme city of Brahmā.
Kuhuka, however, having revealed his own true form and then concealed it, [remained behind].
He ran away quickly and went to his own abode. ||38||

Then, by the king’s noble son, Svarṇāṅgada, a sovereign sacrifice was performed—a snake-sacrifice in which the serpents were offered into the fire. It was undertaken for the sake of avenging his father and to bring an end to his wrath. (39)

Then, for the destruction of the serpents, those who were experts in serpent-mantras quickly summoned the twice-born brahmins and performed a snake-sacrifice; having kindled the fire and recited the names of the serpents, they proceeded. (1.60.40–41)
He offered many snakes into the fire, and they fell into it in great numbers.
Then Kuhaka indeed sought refuge with Indra.
He said, "Protect me, O Lord of the Gods; have mercy on her lest she die."
And having heard this, Indra, the king who protects the three worlds, then [acted]. ||43||
The king of serpents did not indeed fall, for he was protected by his own side;
however, the brahmins then recognized through meditation that he was guarded by Indra.
Then, the brahmins there quickly uttered mantras.
Those foremost of birds, the Suparṇas, having forcibly summoned the serpents, [spoke]. 45.
They offered into the fire both primary and secondary oblations on all sides;
and having uttered the *kuhaka* mantra along with Indra, he likewise made the offering.

"Om, svāhā to Agni! I offer this *kuhaka* along with Indra," he recited the mantra. As soon as he had uttered it and offered mustard seeds into the fire, Indra, joined by *Kuhaka*, indeed fell from his own seat to the ground. (47)
Having fallen into the fire with a snake still clinging to him, he quickly blazed up as far as his waist. 48.
He was indeed restrained by Brahmā: "O god, do not act so transgressively!
Then Suparṇa, the twice-born, and other twice-born beings of great strength, having heard the words of the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), desisted from that action.
Dhanvantari approached Indra and treated him with medicinal herbs.

Seated there upon a fixed, auspicious throne was the Blessed Lord Dharma.
Ten yojanas in extent and resembling a dark blue cloud,
Yama— knower of dharma, whose nature is dharma, and who is devoted to the principles of justice—
is the giver of fear to those joined with evil, yet the bestower of happiness upon the righteous. (6–7)
At the entrance into the middle of the city, indeed, is the house of Citragupta;
it measures twenty-five yojanas in extent.
Ten stories high, magnificent and divine, it was encircled by an iron wall;
it possessed hundreds of thoroughfares and was adorned with hundreds of banners.
It was crowded with hundreds of lamps and filled with the sound of singing.
Indeed, the house of Citragupta was painted by those skilled in painting.
Seated comfortably upon a divine and most wonderful throne made of jewels and pearls, he bestows long life upon Gaṇapati, upon human beings, and upon others as well. 11.
He is not deluded in any way regarding his good or evil deeds; he knows all that has been acquired throughout his births, whether it be virtuous or non-virtuous.
He records the karma performed by means of the body, the senses, and the mind.
To the east of Citragupta’s house is the great abode of Jvara (Fever);

to the south is that of Śūla (Pain), as well as Lūtā (Scabies) and Visphoṭaka (Erysipelas); and to the west is that of Kālapāśa (the Noose of Time), as well as Ajīrṇa (Indigestion) and Aruci (Loss of Appetite). ||13-14||
Various types of cholera are to be known in the north of the central seat;
in the northeast there is headache, and in the direction of fire (southeast) there is fainting. ||15||
In the southwest there is dysentery, and in the northwest there is the affliction of burning;
Citragupta always remains surrounded by these. (16)
Whatever action is performed and by whomsoever, all of that he records;
at the gate of the abode of Dharmarāja, messengers stand by the millions. (17)
Indeed, the path between the world of Yama and that of humans is difficult to traverse; through great suffering, sinners travel along the road of Yama, which is exceedingly hard to pass. ||18||
Yama, having become four-armed and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, summons all the sinners through his messengers and indeed inflicts punishment upon them. (19)

With a roar like the clouds at the time of universal dissolution, possessing a luster like a mountain of collyrium, mounted upon a buffalo, difficult to propitiate, and having a brilliance equal to the splendor of the sun. (1.64.20)
His body is three *yojanas* in extent; he is cruel and inspires extreme terror. Holding a staff in his hand, he is formidable, with a noose in his grasp and a hideous appearance. (21)
With bloodshot eyes, causing extreme terror, a person the size of a thumb emerges from the corpse, crying out "Hā! Hā! as he appears before the sinners. (22)
When one is led by the messengers of Yama to the city of Yama, the messengers indeed display intense fear and threaten him:
"Move quickly, O evil-souled one! You shall go to the abode of Yama! (23)
"Quickly perform [this], for we shall lead you to the Kumbhīpāka and other hells!
Indeed, as a *preta* you will travel along a path filled with forests of sword-leaves, thorns, gravel, heated sands, and poisonous mud. (24–25)
Day after day, that preta travels two hundred and forty-seven yojanas in a single day and night. (26)
On the thirteenth day, that deceased person is led away by the servants of Yama;
on that path he travels like a captured monkey.
For seventeen days, he proceeds alone along the path of the wind.
Within eighteen days and nights, one should first proceed to the city of Yama.
The first is said to belong to Yama; the second is Sauripura;
the third is Surendrapura; and after that is Gandharvanagara. (29)
The fifth is Śailapura, and the sixth is Krūrapura;
the seventh is Krauñcanagara, and Citrapura is the eighth. After that is Bahvāpannagara, and the tenth is the city of Duḥkhada.
Then there is Daśaikamākrandapura and Sutaptanagara. ||31||
The thirteenth is Raudrapura; the fourteenth is Payovṛṣṭa;
the fifteenth is Śītapura; and the sixteenth is Bahubhaya.
The seventeenth is the city of Dharma, and the eighteenth is the southern city;
these cities indeed exist on the path for the sake of obtaining rest. (33)

A sinner who dies becomes a *preta* and acquires a *preta*-body; that *preta*-body, however, is fully formed within nine days and nights. For the sake of achieving the completion of the body, funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) should be offered individually.
By the rice-ball offered on the first day, the head is produced.
On the second day, however, the neck and shoulders [are formed]; on the third day, the heart comes to be;
on the fourth day, the heels; and likewise on the fifth day, the navel.
On the sixth day, the waist; on the seventh, the private parts are produced in their entirety.
On the eighth day, the two thighs; likewise, on the ninth day, the two knees and feet.
Having attained a body through nine [days], on the tenth day it becomes hungry;
possessing a physical form and feeling hunger, it stands upon the roof of the house. (38)
On the tenth day, one should offer that rice-ball which satisfies hunger;
on the eleventh and twelfth days, the deceased partakes for two days. (39)
On the thirteenth day, the deceased is indeed led along the great path;
until the seventeenth day, he travels by way of the wind.
On the eighteenth day and night, he first proceeds to the city of Yama.
There, on the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river, was a great multitude of pretas. ||41||
Under the shade of a great banyan tree, a preta finds rest;
yet, afflicted by thirst and oppressed by fatigue, he cries out with piteous words. (42)
Śambala, the governor of that city, bestows [the offering] upon the preta, whether it has been given by sons or grandsons out of affection or compassion. (43)
Having consumed a mouthful of food once a month, he then goes to Sauripura;
there, indeed, the king named Jaṅgama assumes the form of Time (Kāla). ||44||
Indeed, one who gives him a triple-portioned ball of food for a good meal,
having consumed that water and food there, goes beyond that city;
within two months, he indeed reaches the city of the Lord of the Gods.
Surendra Bhīṣaṇa, the presiding deity of that [thread], indeed bestows it upon him. 46.
If the funeral ball (piṇḍa) or food offered within two months is bypassed, that [offering] goes to the city [of Yama], and another [is required] in the third month. 47.
Having reached Gandharvapura, he eats a morsel of food for three months;
then, in the fourth month, the deceased spirit goes to Śailapura. ||48||
There, stones fall upon the back of the preta.
Having consumed the fourth-month *śrāddha*, he goes to the city of Krūra.
In the fifth month, staying there, he consumes the fifth-month *piṇḍa*.
Having eaten, he goes to the sixth city, Krauñcapura, which is inhabited by Krauñcas.
Having eaten the funeral cakes and other offerings given at the śrāddha ceremony for a period of five and a half months, or slightly less than six months, he rests and proceeds on his way.
Citrapura is the seventh; its king is Citraka.
He is indeed the younger brother of Yama, the presiding deity of the six-monthly rice-ball offering and water. (52)
Then, having eaten his meal, he proceeds ahead on the path.
There, thousands of fishermen come toward him and say:
"We shall ferry you across the great Vaitaraṇī river."
Extending for a hundred yojanas and filled with pus and blood. ||54||
By him who has given a cow there—a cow protected by birds, snakes, fish, and crocodiles from falling upon her flesh—the deceased is swiftly delivered. (55)
If a cow has not been given as a gift, he sinks into the Vaitaraṇī river;
therefore, while his body is still healthy, he should observe the vow of the Vaitaraṇī.
And a cow should be given to a learned man by one desiring to cross that river;
having eaten there at a *śrāddha* performed for the six-month period, one proceeds forth. (57)
When the seventh month has arrived, he goes to a city full of many calamities; there, he enjoys whatever was given that arose during those seven months. 58.
Having passed beyond that city, he reaches a city that brings suffering;
having experienced great misery there, he cries out, tormented by heat. (59)
That which was given in the eighth month, having eaten there, he departs;
he stays in the city of Nānākranda and eats the food of the ninth month.
There, this empty-hearted one, suffering in grief, cries out;
having abandoned that city, the deceased goes toward the city of Tapta.
Having reached Sutaptanagara in the tenth month, he enjoys [the fruits of his deeds];
for the merit obtained there arises from the offerings of food and the presentation of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) given at that place. ||62||
When the eleventh month is complete, he goes to the city of Raudra;
having consumed the rain of milk for ten months, he departs.
There, clouds pour down rain that causes suffering to the pretas.
And at that annual śrāddha performed before the completion of a year, the deceased (pretaka) partakes [of the offerings]. //64//
Then, when the year has fully elapsed, he goes from there to Śītapura; afflicted by intense cold, the insentient preta wails repeatedly. (65)
Having passed beyond Śītapura, one should go to Bahubhītipura;
there, scorched by the fear of hunger and thirst, one then proceeds to Dharmapura.
There, scorched by heat and with tears flowing, he becomes dead;
the messengers of Yama devour him to dispel the fatigue of his journey. (67)
Bahubhītipura and Dharmapura, as well as Dharmakheṭaka—these two are neighboring branch villages of Dharmarājapura. (68)
Then these [messengers] lead the deceased to the supreme city of Yama’s Dharma, which is presided over by eighty-four hundred thousand beings, both embodied and formless. (69)
O messengers, you who have come as most cruel tormentors, place the deceased here in the Hall of Justice. (1.64.70)

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the State of the Dead," concerning the journey through the eighteen cities along the path to Citragupta’s palace and the expanse of Yama’s city, within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 64.
← Chapter 64: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 65 [[Author:

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! In the city of Yama, there are twelve Śrāvaṇas who are followers;
they are the sons of Brahmā and serve as gatekeepers who observe the activities of human beings.
Having deliberated again and again upon whatever action was auspicious or inauspicious,
they then indeed report it to Citragupta and Yama;
whatever karma has been performed by men, whether in a state of contentment or anger.
They reported everything exactly as it was and in its true nature:
the knowledge of hearing from afar, the range of vision from a distance, and the awareness of the activities of those dwelling in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld from afar. (3–4)
Thus they possess the power to awaken [the deceased] secretly within the mortal world and elsewhere;
for as long as they sing there the *karma* of the departed spirit, so long does it remain.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Whose sons are those Śrāvaṇas, and how did they come to reside in the city of Yama?
O Lord, how do they know the karma performed by those dwelling in the three worlds?
How do they all hear? From where has this knowledge come? And when did they arise? Tell me everything, my beloved. (7)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the beginning, the world was produced; indeed, it was created by Brahmā.
It was protected by me, and Rudra is the one who effects its destruction.
The King of Dharma was created by me together with Citragupta;
these three deities carry out their respective duties independently. (9)
In the first age, the Satya Yuga, all people were indeed independent;
all were like the three gods, and there was no one among them to exercise authority over another. (1.65.10)
Likewise, in the Tretā age as well, they performed actions independently;
where, then, would the teachership of those teachers be meaningful if it remained unknown to them? (11)
Then the gods and ṛṣis gathered there for reflection:
"If we do not possess knowledge of the karma of living beings who are independent, [how can we act]? (12)
"We do not know how living beings should be instructed at that time.
Having reflected thus, they deliberated: "Sons of such a kind must be created. (13)
Then Brahmā, having adopted the opinion of Śiva and Viṣṇu and being joined by the mantra, took twelve kuśa blades and sprinkled water there. ||14||
He gave twelve conscious kuśa grasses with water to Dharmarāja;
Yama, taking them in his hand, consecrated them as his sons. ||15||
Masses of splendor, large-eyed, with the power of hearing and seeing from afar; seers of the self, knowers of gestures, and perceivers of the intentions of others. (16)
He created twelve sons who were invisible yet possessed visible forms;
these are the sons of Yama in this world, present everywhere within ears and eyes. (17)
Whatever anyone in this world speaks or whatever auspicious or inauspicious deed they perform, those [messengers] swiftly bring it to the range of Yama’s hearing. (18)
The faculty of hearing from afar and the range of vision from afar—those who hear everything from that very [distance] are all considered "Śrāvaṇas. (19)
Moving in the form of wind while stationed in the path of space, they perceive the activities of living beings and report them to Yama. (1.65.20)
After death, they [reap] according to their actions and according to what they have done—whether it be virtue, wealth, pleasure, or liberation, as it was performed. ||21||
Likewise, they quickly report everything concerning all living beings to Citragupta, and afterwards, they indeed inform Yama.
Those disciples are capable of assuming many forms;
they move through the fourteen worlds in manifold guises. (23)
Those people who practice the Dharma go seated within celestial palaces;
those who bestow wealth go seated within celestial palaces, being honored by Apsarases. (24)
Those who bestow gifts of desire travel in excellent chariots yoked with horses;
indeed, those destined for liberation proceed in celestial vehicles drawn by swans and elephants.
But those who act unrighteously travel on foot along a path that is extremely difficult to endure, for it is afflicted with stones and thorns and consists of forests of sword-leaves. (26)
Bound by nooses, they indeed proceed across a path covered with heated sand;
for their comfortable journey, one should give gifts according to one's ability. (27)
An umbrella, sandals, garments, a signet ring, and a water-pot;
a seat, a vessel, a vehicle, ornaments, and water;
food, clarified butter, a sacred thread, and wealth such as cattle and buffaloes. (28)
It should be given for the sake of the deceased, so that his path may become one of happiness. (29)
O beloved, whatever is given in one's own home for the sake of the deceased has water as its essence; Varuṇa, acting as the witness, knows that in every way. (1.65.30)
Varuṇa accepts the gift; he places it into my hand.
I, Nārāyaṇa, then offer it to the sun-god Bhāskara. ||31||
And because that deceased spirit indeed seizes and eats from the sun, O beloved, various kinds of gifts should be given for the sake of the deceased's happiness. (32)
But he who has performed a religious act yet does not subsequently give the gift, and has not earned merit for himself, goes to terrible hells.
There are eighty-four lakhs of such hells that inflict suffering. (33)
Among them, the most eminent and preeminent leaders are twenty-one. (34)
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, Kumbhīpāka, Kālasūtra, and likewise Asipatravana. (35)
The Boar’s Mouth, the Blind Well, and the Food of Worms; the Pincers, the Heated Iron Bed, and the Śālmali Tree with its diamond-hard thorns. (36)
The Vaitaraṇī river of pus, the suffocation of life-breaths, the tearing apart, the drinking of iron, the Avīci hell, the devouring by dogs, and the eating of one's own flesh. (37)
Thus, these are indeed considered the primary ones in Yamapurī;
hear now the names of the other seven that exist below them. (38)
One is the mire of caustic matter, another is the devourer of the hosts of Rākṣasas;
likewise, there is the one impaled on a stake, the one bitten by serpents, and the one confined in a pit. (39)
Paryāvartanaka and Sūcīmukha are each distinct;
now learn of those other villages of hell that exist there. (1.65.40)
Talapāta, Mahājvāla, Śabala, Vikartana, Adhaḥśiras, Rudhirāndhas, Cakṣuḥśūla, and Prapācana. (41)
The falling from a mountain, the iron stake, the goad, and likewise the fetters;
the iron machine, the kākola, and the tortures of reviving the dead. (42)
And likewise, other hells exist according to their various divisions and subdivisions;
they have indeed been created for the purpose of atonement for those who commit evil deeds.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Twenty-eight Hells Beginning with Śravaṇā," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
