Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Those whose ancestors have indeed spent hundreds of years in a terrible hell, and for whom no progeny exists, they indeed go to serve as messengers.
Sent indeed by Yama, they seize day after day the lamps, food, water-pots, and other offerings from the deceased human being;
for they offer these to the departed spirit itself, who desires food and is thirsty.
They all attain satisfaction every day for an entire year.
First, there is the city of Citragupta, extending for twenty yojanas; there, the scribes behold all their sins and merits in every respect. (3–4)
The city of Vaivasvata extends for twenty-four yojanas;
having gone there, the messengers and servants indeed speak to the doorkeeper.
The gatekeeper Dharmadhvaja speaks of his auspicious and inauspicious [deeds];
meanwhile, the terrifying messengers of Yama, the servants of Yama, [are present]. (6)
Terrible beings bearing nooses and staffs, numbering sixteen thousand,
stand before each individual city, one thousand for each.
The King of Dharma himself administers justice to this sinner;
listen now as to how he experiences various hells. (8)
Those who forcibly seize the wealth, wives, children, and so forth of others,
fall into that Tāmisra hell, severely tormented by hunger and thirst.
Those who, having deceived others, enjoy their wealth, children, wives, and so forth, fall into the Andhatāmisra hell, their vision and intellect destroyed. (1.66.10)
Indeed, those harmful embodied beings fall into the Mahāraurava hell;
having become flesh-eating ruru deer, they cause their own slayer to be killed. (11)
Those who nourish their families through injury to living beings go to the Raurava hell;
for those beings, having become *ruru* deer and serpents, indeed strike back at their oppressors. (12)
Indeed, those wicked ones who have been slaughtered as cattle and the like fall into Kumbhīpāka;
there the messengers repeatedly roast them in boiling oils. (13)

Those who commit violence against living beings such as gurus, parents, Brahmins, virtuous men, and virtuous women, indeed go to the realm called Kālasūtra, which has a circumference of ten thousand yojanas. ||14||
They cause him to roll upon a copper floor heated by fire and burn him;
the heretic who destroys his own dharma goes to the forest of sword-leaves. ||15||
They are repeatedly cut and crushed by double-edged swords;
those who inflict unjust punishment go to the machine known as Sūkarāsya (the Boar’s Mouth). 16.
There, indeed, the limbs of lice, mosquitoes, and birds—whose modes of existence are ordained by the Lord—are crushed and reduced to powder. (17)
Indeed, those who cause the destruction of living beings fall into a blind well;
there, messengers in the form of creatures, having been wronged by them, in turn inflict harm upon them. (18)
Those who consume food without sharing it fall into the Kṛmibhojana hell;
there they are devoured by worms for hundreds of thousands of yojanas. Those who steal or forcibly seize the gold, jewels, horses, and other property of others [suffer likewise].
They go to the Sandaṃśa hell, and there the servants of Yama cut them with iron pincers.
Those who, out of lust, have forcibly approached men or women who should not be approached, are made to embrace a red-hot iron pillar or a red-hot iron image of a woman. (21)
Indeed, they forcibly place lustful men upon *vajra-kaṇṭaka* śālmali trees and have them cut to pieces by beasts and other such creatures. ||22||
Those who follow the conduct of beasts, who have lost their purity, and who consume phlegm, feces, urine,
and pus— these indeed fall into the hell named Pūyoda, where they likewise eat that very filth.
Having become devourers of those they were meant to protect, these instillers of fear destroy their charges;
they are made to carry their own excrement, urine, pus, and blood across the Vaitaraṇī river. 24.

Those who were addicted to hunting and killed animals and other creatures by obstructing their life-breaths— the messengers of Yama pierce them there with arrows. Those who slaughtered and tore apart animals, birds, humans, and so forth, [are likewise pierced].
They tear them apart, devour them, and drink their blood once more. ||26||
The Yamas forcibly compel those people who cause the drinking of liquor—which arises from the destruction of countless living beings—to drink molten iron dross. (27)
Furthermore, the servants of Yama repeatedly cast those who give false testimony down from a mountain two hundred *gavyūtis* in height into the Avīci hell. (28)
Those wicked ones who administer poison or set fires are devoured by dogs;
those who cause the consumption of semen are made to drink it by the messengers of Yama. (29)
But one who commits a transgression against the worship of those worthy of worship falls headfirst into a mire of salt; there he experiences the fruit of that action. (1.66.30)
The followers of Yama devour beasts, birds, men, and women;
they eat their blood and drink it as food for the hosts of Rākṣasas. (31)
The servants of Yama repeatedly pierce living beings with thorns, needles, and spikes; they impale those already transfixed on stakes with sharp-pointed instruments. (32)
And those with hundreds of faces, who cause agitation among living beings, tear apart and repeatedly devour the biting serpents. (33)
In caves, hollows, granaries, pits, and the like, they obstruct those who confine living beings with smoke and other substances, as well as with fire and molten lead. (34)
The hungry messengers devour those who eat meat and other such foods; when they are touched by their hands, [the victims] are restored to fullness, and the messengers devour them again. (35)
Having cast the one who is conceited about his wealth, who looks askance, and who is an evildoer, into the Sūcīmukha hell, they sew him up with threads. (36)
If he looks upon a wretched, weak, and worthy recipient with an angry eye, birds with diamond-tipped beaks tear out his eyes. (37)
But as for others who commit theft of tree fruits, the followers of Yama lift them up by the palm tree and cast them down upon the ground. (38)
Having cast those who have burned the forest-dwelling fields into the great conflagration, the messengers of Yama indeed roast them in the fire again and again. (39)
For they cause the one who feeds the impure to fall into sin;
there, the followers of Yama feed him that which is impure and foul-smelling. (1.66.40)
Those fierce ones cast into Vikartana those who, having cut open a chest or a bundle, steal the goods;
they hack them apart and drink their blood.
And those who, having made a hole in a wall or similar structure, steal wealth— [they too are cast there].
They weigh them in the sky with their heads downward by means of the fire at their base. 42.
Men do not serve animals with milk, grain, or water;
instead, they cast them into the hell of Rudhirāndha, where those animals drink their own blood. ||43||
The attendants of Yama inflict punishment upon the one who employs his evil eye toward that which is unworthy of being seen;
indeed, they cause a spear to enter his eyes.
Furthermore, those living beings roasted by fire cook him as well.
Those who kill living beings with stones are indeed made to fall upon rocks.
The one who binds an innocent person is bound by the yokes of iron fetters;
the one who grinds a creature to powder, having been identified, is ground by iron machines.
But he who inflicts suffering upon living beings is tormented in the Kākola hell;
likewise, he who causes misery throughout one's life and he who utters false accusations. 47.
Having killed, devoured, and restored to life, the followers of Yama—those very Yamas—cut him to pieces, tear him apart, and devour him. (48)
He who causes suffering to his wife, she who causes suffering to her husband, and those who cause suffering to their dependents—these indeed fall into the Raurava hell. (49)
Thus, wherever there are guards who are devourers living by plunder, they are all born as hell-beings and are torn apart by the servants of Yama. (1.66.50)
Thus do these hells exist for living beings who have not purified themselves, wherein the most wicked are cleansed;
from there they proceed to rebirth, according to the nature of the birth and the karma previously accumulated by each. (51)
By that very same path, Yama leads him to rebirth. ||52||

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Sin for Those Going to the Forty Hells," in the first section, the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 66. [Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Part 1 (Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 67]
[The Author: Chapter 68.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having experienced the great suffering of the hells, the denizens of hell...
And indeed, by means of the portion remaining from their own karma, they obtain a body—
whether divine, ancestral, human, or even infernal.
Having attained such a birth, liberation occurs thereafter through the power of dharma.

In whatever manner a person performs an action, they shall enter that very same womb; experiencing the results exactly as they were performed, they wander through all wombs. By whatever ripening of karma one becomes a partaker of hell in such a way—
O Padmaja! Listen as I describe to you their subsequent births.
At the end of their torments, those who have been liberated pass through many successions of lives and are born in human wombs bearing the marks of their sins. (4–5)
In that regard, one who utters falsehoods has a drooping throat and a half-exposed tongue;
or rather, he becomes mute, being a reviler of the gods and others.
One who takes life suffers from consumption and leprosy, while a drinker of intoxicants has blackened teeth.
A stealer of gold becomes one with deformed nails; one who forcibly enjoys a woman becomes one with diseased skin.
Even from envy, one becomes blind from birth; one who plucks out another's eye becomes blind from birth.
A stealer of fruit becomes a monkey, and from eating food stolen by theft, one becomes a crow.
One who reviles another's lineage becomes one devoid of lineage and childless;
a stealer of wealth becomes a monitor lizard, and a giver of poison takes birth as a serpent.
Furthermore, one who acts with violence and force is born here as a *piśāca*.
The cātaka bird is a stealer of water, while the mouse is a stealer of grain. || 1.67.10 ||
One who diverts the flow of water will become a fish in the water;
indeed, a living being who commits acts of deception is born repeatedly as an owl. (11)
One who eats by snatching from others is reborn as a dog;
a living being who, having given his word, does not fulfill it, is born as a jackal in the forest.
Having committed theft and constantly consuming [stolen goods], one is born as a village pig;
indeed, by insulting those worthy of worship, one obtains the body of a tortoise. (13)
Indeed, one who treats everyone with contempt is born here as a *cāṇḍāla*;
one who takes loans from others becomes a bull, a horse, or a donkey;
one who creates obstacles to sexual pleasure becomes a eunuch; and one who eats the flesh of others becomes a cat.
One who strikes another's property is indeed born as a partridge in the forest.

Those who forcibly bring women under their control shall surely take birth as women. Those who engage in sexual pleasure by force become afflicted with diseases of the female and male organs and so forth.
Those who rob others of their homes and dwellings are born as wild animals;
and those who slaughter animals here are born as animals that are themselves slaughtered. (17)
Those who steal the property of their master become impoverished;
those who practice the censure of the learned become fools and simpletons. (18)
Indeed, those who deceive living beings and act as their captors or killers are born in the wombs of animals and birds confined in cages. Furthermore,
one who insults human beings is born here with a deformed mind.
One who nourishes deceit, hypocrisy, and cruelty shall become a gambler.
In this world, he is born as a killer of men, a holder of nooses, and indeed a traitor.
Having become a slayer of animals and a butcher, he shall indeed become a goat for a hundred births.
One who eats fish will be born as a fish; one who eats all kinds of food will become a large fish.
One who steals the food, clothing, house, or other possessions of others will become a tree in a desert wasteland. (22)
One who steals fragrant sandalwood is born with a deficient nose;
one who listens to the disparagement of gurus, parents, or those worthy of honor will indeed become deaf in this world. (23)
One who seizes another's feet shall become lame; one who strikes with the hand shall have his hand cut off. One who causes suffering to women shall become a donkey belonging to a potter.
A woman who causes suffering to her husband is likewise reborn as a female donkey; one who steals the wealth of a laborer becomes a poor monkey. (25)
One who destroys living beings becomes a lizard that eats the creatures living in walls;
one who is impure takes birth as a fly, and one who is prone to anger attains the state of a serpent.
One who is full of hatred becomes a village dog, and one attains birth among ants.
One who lusts after another's wife shall become a castrated bull, and one who cuts off the testicles [of another] shall become a eunuch-bull. ||27||
One who steals the food, grain, or wealth of others shall become a distressed dog;
those who consume the food and other belongings belonging to others shall attain the womb of a hen. (28)
One who destroys an undertaking is a *ghūka*; one who obstructs an undertaking is a *śṛgālaka*.
One who steals from those whose vessels have been served is a *vṛkṣavāgulī*. (29)
A stealer of women is a *rākṣasa*; a practitioner of mantras is a *piśācaka*.
A seller of perfumes is a *bhūta*, while one of cruel gaze is a *śākinī*. A *ḍākinī* is full of envy, and a *piśācinī* is a practitioner of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).

One who destroys the embryo becomes a prostitute; one who desires her husband becomes unchaste. Even if she is capable of bearing offspring, she remains childless here [in this life] because of her lack of desire for children.
However, one who does not accept the ritual offerings during her fertile season (ṛtu) certainly becomes a eunuch in every respect.
Furthermore, that which cuts off others becomes the destroyer of itself;
those who bring about the destruction of the sleeping [soul] are slain in the house of the slayer. (33)
Those who steal another's grain become those whose livelihood is not on their own land;
those who destroy another's work are born into wombs of non-action.
One who steals oil becomes a consumer of oil, while a slanderer has a foul-smelling mouth.
One who steals grain has an extra limb, while a slanderer has a putrid nose. (35)
A killer of a Brahmin becomes a dog, a donkey, or a camel, and in the end even becomes mute.
A thief of wealth becomes a worm or an insect, while one who destroys his guru becomes an eater of grass. (36)

One who steals gold suffers from consumption; one who steals cooked food has black teeth and deformed nails; one who steals food is deprived of nourishment; and one who steals dyed cloth becomes mute. (37)
One who falsifies weights and measures shall become a *vaṭavāgulika* (a small, insignificant creature);
one who mixes counterfeit goods for sale shall become afflicted with labored breathing. ||38||
One who deprives others of their lives will indeed suffer from the disease of consumption (kṣaya);
one who practices deceit in buying and selling will suffer from hemorrhoids;
and one who pours out water while still impure will suffer from urinary disorders and similar ailments.
In this world, one who takes away the livelihood of others becomes a beggar who is treated with contempt.
One who is excessively intolerant toward others and wicked becomes a *caṇḍāla* or a *vāghghari*.
One who practices deceit and fraud becomes a fisherman (*dhīvara*) or even a *śabara*. (1.67.40–41)
A weaver may even be one who practices deception in the sale of cloth; an outcaste (antyaja) is one who creates filth at the crossroads and drains away impurities. 42.
One who forbids bathing and purification becomes a washerman, a cleaner of clothes;
and one who desires what is undesirable for others becomes a thief, being reborn as a crying cat. (43)
He shall be a provider of counterfeit medicines in a secluded forest;
he shall be a creator of fraudulent goods, and indeed, he shall be a false wife and son here [in this world].
(44) He who, through deceit, mixes gold, silver, and other such materials—
He shall be born of mixed castes and likewise suffer from oozing leprosy;
he shall be a corrupter of maidens and a rogue for as long as he lives.
A barber who performs the work of shaving shall be a speaker of falsehood toward his master.
The maker of weapons is born as a leech;
those who eat the flesh of beasts, birds, cows, horses, and so forth, become vultures and scavengers of excrement. (47)
Those who sell meat are born as lions, tigers, wolves, and hyenas;
those who sell their daughters are born as worms in the womb;
and those who adulterate liquids are born as worms in filth. (48)
Those who milk the unestablished become parasites of the virtuous;
one who breaks the row and fills only his own belly becomes afflicted with intestinal disease. (49)
Dancers become those who cause distress to couples;
indeed, Vṛndalas are born as those who separate people who are attached to sensual pleasures. (1.67.50)
Those who abandon the pleasures of desire and find delight in the solitude of the forest become deer;
likewise, men who possess delight and envy are born as frogs. (51)
One who commits treachery against virtuous men and women shall become mute or deaf among people;
for those who fail to nourish those who ought to be supported, the state of being a filthy rat shall come to pass. //52//
For those who kill defenseless animals for their milk, rebirth occurs with a headless body upon a waterless land;
for those who pierce the vital organs with the arrows of speech, birth occurs as a porcupine or a lizard. (53)
Those who commit the theft of flour are born as rough bears;
those who commit great thefts are born among blind serpents.
Likewise, one who betrays deities, sacred fords, and gurus, as well as a reviler of the Dharmas, [is reborn in such states].
He would be a cause of distress to his family, like a lamp lit in the wilderness. //55//
One who subsists on liquor and meat becomes a lion in the forest or a king; one who eats from nets, traps, and snares becomes a many-horned deer. ||56||
One who is lazy about bathing becomes the animal called the rhinoceros;
a stealer of flour becomes a bear, and one who eats in secret becomes a bat. (57)
Citrapicchā is chalakartrī; śilakī would be svatantriṇī.
Guptapibā is the house-lizard, and the gavaya is guptabhojana. ||58||
Or just as, through the connection with latent impressions (vāsanā), diverse embodied beings are born repeatedly—those who perform various crafts, numbering eighty-four thousand. (59)
Those who commit insults against the elderly are born as dark beings such as insects, trees, or those dwelling in grass; they are born as buffaloes or bulls. (1.67.60)

Those who cause the separation of husband and wife shall be miserable in birth after birth; being excessively greedy for filth and with defiled senses, they shall always become worms dwelling in excrement. (61)
The Guptaghātas, Jhallādas, Pāśins, Śvapacas, and others [are the subordinates].
One who has impaired his senses is "Indriyahā," being devoid of sense-faculties and afflicted by injury. (62)
Those who go about as assassins, constantly inflicting pain with their bodies bent in cruelty, are born as Tamasic Yavanas, Daityas, and Rākṣasas. (63)
Women who kill their husbands are born as widows in birth after birth;
a woman who causes suffering to her mother-in-law is born as a lean female donkey. (64)
A female cat becomes a hater of the bride and suffers from leprosy and other such diseases;
a female dog becomes a creator of hatred toward co-wives and suffers from mange. (65)
One that causes partiality leads to a state of poverty like that of a beast;
one that destroys undertakings becomes a "ghūkī" (an owl-like female), and one that causes affliction becomes a "kābarī" (a variegated, ill-omened female). ||66||
She who tastes food that has not been offered as an oblation becomes a vulture and a shrieking jackal;
she who behaves with deceit within the home becomes a hawk and a crane. (67)
A black female crow becomes a rogue; likewise, a female jackal becomes a barber’s wife.
A female snake becomes a hater, and she acts with malice toward her offspring. (68)
One who performs malevolent rites such as *abhicāra* is a *ṣaṇḍhā*, whose nature is the destruction of the sexual organ;
likewise, one who employs mantras for malevolent purposes is a *bhūtī* or a *piśācikā*. (69)
A woman who kills children, destroys fetuses, or destroys seeds becomes a *rākṣasī*;
a Yavana woman or a *khasī* woman causes internal burning and bestows suffering.
In this way, people become inhabitants of hell for many births.
Furthermore, through karma, one is born again among the hundred thousand species of living beings.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Signs of Rebirth for the Denizens of Hell," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 67.
← Chapter 67: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 68 [[Author: → Chapter 69
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall describe the physical characteristics of people;
what kind of appearance a person has, what kind of actions they perform, and what kind of qualities they possess.
I shall explain that briefly for the sake of the world’s understanding:
the bodies of men, women, and gods are indeed identical;
the difference in form is merely indicative [of their specific nature]. (2)
The distinction between signs, however, serves to characterize their respective functions. (3)
The feet of one devoid of wealth are shaped like winnowing baskets and veiny;
they are crooked, rough, and withered, with pale nails, soles, and toes.
Feet that are turned upward and reddish-brown are destroyers of one's lineage.
The feet of a slayer of a Brahmin shall be [marked] near the ankle-bones (śaṅku).
In the case of a pauper, there shall be only a single hair in each hair-pore;
for a king, a Vedic scholar, and likewise for those possessed of fortune and wisdom, there shall be two hairs in each.
Indeed, those with hair on the forehead and other such parts that is thin become destitute, partakers of suffering, and subject to reproach.
He whose hair is curled will surely die while abroad.
But he whose knees are fleshless shall be a person possessed of good fortune.
A person whose knees are sunken and small should be known as one who is always devoted to women.
(8) One with uneven knees is poor; one with well-developed knees will be a king.
One with large knees is long-lived, while one with crooked knees is lustful. (9)
His feet have soft soles resembling the interior of a lotus; his toes are closely joined, his nails are copper-colored, his heels are well-formed, and they are free from prominent veins. (1.68.10)
One whose feet are warm, elevated like the back of a tortoise, and have hidden ankles shall become a king;
however, that man whose male organ is small shall indeed be childless. (11)
He who has a thick penis, even if he has offspring, will be destitute of wealth;
he whose penis is curved will be devoid of sons and riches. (12)
He whose penis is bent downwards will always suffer from poverty;
he whose penis is curved to the right is considered by people to be a man possessed of sons.
If the penis is joined with thick knots and covered in veins, one will have many sons;
if the generative organ is concealed within a sheath, one will be a king and possess many sons. (14)
He will always have a long penis, a curved sheath, and be destitute of wealth; he will be weak, have only one testicle, or have uneven and unstable testicles. (15)
A king is said to have symmetrical [shoulders], while one with drooping [shoulders] shall live for a hundred years.
A man with a lion-like waist becomes a ruler, whereas a man with a monkey-like waist is destitute. (16)
Those with serpentine bellies will be poor; those with thick sides will be wealthy.
Those with even armpits are rich in enjoyments, while those with sunken armpits are devoid of wealth.
Kings have prominent armpits, whereas those with crooked or uneven armpits are dishonest.
One who engages in sexual intercourse slowly has a short life, while one who engages in sexual intercourse quickly has a long life. ॥18॥
One with a broad navel shall be happy; one with an excessively deep navel shall be miserable.
A navel situated amidst folds of skin indeed causes suffering from colic. (19)
A man with a right-turning whorl on his head is wise; one with a left-turning whorl is self-controlled;
one with a whorl extending toward the side will have a long life; and one with a whorl above will become a lord of wealth.
A man with one line on his forehead shall live for a hundred years; one with two lines will enjoy prosperity;
one with three lines will be a lord of the earth; and one with straight lines will be a teacher and happy. (21)
One whose body hair curls to the right will be a great teacher of men;
one whose hair curls to the left or in other directions will be a servant and a person of suffering. ||22||
People with fingers that are not protruding and are tapered become fortunate;
those with fingers that are protruding, uneven, long, and yellow-tipped are poor men. (23)
The heart of kings is even, elevated, unshakable, fleshy, and broad; whereas that of the base is rough, hairy, and veiny. 24.
One with a level chest will be wealthy; one with a broad chest will be the lord of Lakṣmī (prosperity);
one with an uneven chest will be destitute and shall meet death by a weapon. ॥25॥
One with uneven collarbones is poor; one with thick collarbones is a lord of wealth. One with a flat throat is destitute, while one whose neck is veiny and dry is happy. (26)
One with a buffalo-like neck will be a hero; one with a deer-like throat will be an ender of the scriptures;
a king with a conch-like neck will be a glutton who eats excessively. (27)
The *kakṣā* with *aśvattha* leaves is excellent, as is the fragrant *magaromikā*;
otherwise, it is devoid of merit and a cause of poverty. (28)
The arms that are symmetrical, broad, well-knit, slightly curved, fleshy, rounded, and reaching down to the knees belong to those destined for divinity and royalty. (29)
The hands of those who are wealthy possess hair, are short, excellent, and resemble the trunk of an elephant; moreover, the fingers of the lord of wealth are golden in color. (1.68.30)

Furthermore, those of the intelligent are known to have slender fingers, while those of servants have flattened fingers; those who are destitute have very thick fingers, and likewise, those with hands like a monkey's are poor. (31)
A person with a sunken palm will be a destroyer of his father’s wealth;
one with a concealed wrist will be granted a kingdom, while one with a well-rounded wrist will be a giver of riches.
With hands and palms that are copper-colored, red, and soft—
Those with yellowish and rough nails will always be gurus and bringers of death.
Those with nails like chaff are eunuchs; those with cracked or discolored nails are considered poor and intent on the schemes of others. (33–34)
The gods are considered to have copper-colored, rounded feet with elevated nails; a king has a big toe marked by a barley grain, while one who has sons has toes with full joints. (35)
A man who provides a shelter for travelers shall have hands marked with the yoke and the fish;
the thunderbolt is the sign of the wealthy, while the fish’s tail belongs to the learned. (36)

The conch, the parasol, the palanquin, the elephant, and the lotus appear on the forehead of a sovereign; the frontal globes, the goad, the banner, and the lotus stalk appear on the forehead of a lord of treasures. (37)
A line resembling a small drum indicates one who is rich in cattle; a swastika indicates a lord of kings.
A wheel, a sword, a spear, a bow, or lines resembling elephant tusks indicate a lord of kings. (38)
Lines resembling a mortar are considered to be on the hand of one who performs sacrifices;
many circles and lines like a sacrificial altar belong to the maintainer of the *agnihotra* fire.
A line like a divine pond or river and a triangle are found on the hand of a righteous person. (39)
The lines at the base of the thumb bring happiness and indicate the birth of sons. (1.68.40)
The line extending from the base of the little finger to the base of the forefinger is the "life-line"; if it is broken, it shortens one's lifespan, and there is danger from trees. 41.
Those who are destitute will have many lines on their faces, while those who are impoverished will have thin chins;
however, one with fleshy and red-colored lips shall be wealthy.
Those with lips that are like a bimba fruit, yet cracked, parched, uneven, and split, will be devoid of wealth; however, teeth that are glossy and dense are auspicious. (43)
Sharp teeth are excellent when even; a red tongue is auspicious when even;
it should be known that a smooth and long palate is favorable, whereas a white palate indicates the loss of wealth. (44)
A tongue that is black, rough, and red-tipped is considered indicative of disease;
whereas the mouth of a king is said to be gentle, symmetrical, smooth, and well-proportioned. 45.
The opposite, however, pertains to those who suffer, the unfortunate, and those who do not see the higher worlds:
the face of the wealthy is round, while that of the destitute is long. (46)
A face that is fearful indicates a doer of evil; a square face belongs to rogues;
a sunken face belongs to those without sons; and a short face belongs to the miserly. 47.
A full, beautiful, smooth, auspicious, and soft beard,
which is dense and has uncracked tips, as well as a red beard, belongs to a thief.
Kings have spike-like ears (*śaṅkukarṇa*), whereas those with hairy ears (*romakarṇa*) have short lives.
Those with large ears are wealthy kings, while those with small ears are miserly.
One with sunken cheeks is indeed a seeker of enjoyments; one with full cheeks is a counselor (minister).
One with a parrot-like nose is said to be happy, and one with a parrot-like nose lives a very long life. (1.68.50)
One with a nose that is cut at the tip will have sexual relations with many women;
one with a long nose will be fortunate, while one with a crooked nose will be a thief. (51)
One with a flat nose will be cruel as well as devoid of fortune.
A nose that has small nostrils, well-formed cavities, and is not crooked is considered [auspicious] for a king.
If it is crooked toward the right, it indicates cruelty; if it is crooked toward the left, it bestows misfortune.
Those with eyes that are curved at the corners, resembling lotus petals, are partakers of happiness. 53.
The wicked-souled are sinful with eyes like those of a cat, tawny as honey;
the cruel have squinting eyes, and the defiled have greenish eyes. (54)
Those with squinting eyes are brave; those with eyes like an elephant's are army commanders;
those with deep-set eyes are lords; and those with large eyes are ministers. Those with eyes like blue lotuses are learned, while those with dark eyes possess good fortune.
Those whose eyes have black pupils will be uprooters [of others]. (56)
Those with circular eyebrows will be sinful, while those with thin eyebrows will be destitute and dejected in appearance.
One with long, closely-set eyebrows will be wealthy, whereas those with uneven eyebrows will be poor.
Those with broad, high, and curved eyebrows like the crescent moon will be rich in happiness.

One with a broken forehead is poor, as is one with eyebrows resembling those of a young boy. Those with broad foreheads are likewise destitute, while people are considered wealthy if their foreheads are shaped like a half-moon. ||58-59||
Those with broad, prominent veins are teachers; those with sinuous veins are evildoers; those with raised, cross-shaped (svastika) veins are lords of men;
and those with depressed veins are fit for execution and devoted to cruel deeds.
Those with concealed foreheads are miserly, while those with prominent ones are kings.
A smile that is without trembling is excellent; one with closed eyes brings misfortune;
a laugh repeated often is wicked; and one accompanied by pride leads to destruction.
Those who have three lines extending to the forehead shall live for a hundred years;
he who has four shall be a king, and one lives ninety-five years.
If the lines are interrupted by ninety marks, the lifespan is half of that;
and if they reach the hairline, the man's lifespan shall be eighty years. (64)
With five, seven, six, fifty, and many [veins], as well as with forty and thirty red ones that reach up to the eyebrows. (65)
With twenty teeth that are curved to the left, one's lifespan is short;
however, with heads shaped like umbrellas, one becomes a king, equal to Bāṇa, and wealthy.
The king has a pot-shaped head, a fondness for sinful deeds, and a flat nose; his hair is black, curled at the tips, glossy, and without a parting.
The queen’s soles are soft, marked with fish, goads, banners, and lotuses.
Those whose secret organs bear the marks of a vajra, a lotus, or a plow, and whose ankles are well-concealed, are considered excellent.
The supreme secret organ is broad like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree;
a concealed penis is auspicious, as is one that is fleshy and rounded at its opening. (68–69)
The navel is spiraled clockwise; the waist is adorned with three folds.
The lower lips are excellent and slightly reddish; the face is fleshy and round. The hair on the head is glossy, dark blue, soft, curled, and auspicious.
Or these [lines] may be on the soles of the feet or on the palms of both hands of women. (71)
Horses, elephants, śrīvṛkṣa trees, sacrificial posts, barley-corn, tomara-spears, banners, chowries, garlands, mountains, earrings, and altars; ||| 72 ||
Those [lines] that appear as conch shells, umbrellas, lotuses, fish, svastikas, excellent chariots, goads, and so forth, belong to goddesses; they are beloved by kings. (73)
The auspicious marks are the swastika, the bow, the trident, the banner, and the fish.
That line which arises from the wrist and extends to the middle finger and the palm is called the "upward line" (*ūrdhvarekhā*);
it may appear on either the hand or the foot.
For both women and men, such [a sign] leads to sovereignty and happiness.
A woman possessing male marks, and a man possessing the form of a woman—neither of these two brings about auspiciousness; rather, both produce the opposite result. (75–76)

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Physical Marks of the Divine Bodies of Nara and Nārī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 68. [Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna), Chapter 69]
[The Author: Chapter 70.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! O my beloved, I shall describe your characteristics to you.
Behold your navel, which spirals to the right and is endowed with profound depth.
(1) Behold the three folds [of the abdomen], free of hair; behold the heart and breasts, likewise devoid of hair.
Behold the waist-region, enriched by every power, and observe the firm circular muscles within. (2)
Look at the reddish-brown line below the navel of Svarṇabāṇa;
likewise, look at the mark of a sandal on his left thigh.
Observe the line of a foot between his breasts upon his chest.
Behold on my forehead the form of a crown, and on my cheeks, the mark [bindu].
(4) Behold Viṣṇu, who am I, upon my chest in the form of four arms;
O beloved, observe the sign of the mace on my left arm. (5)
O sinless one, behold the golden line upon her heart;
behold the elephant with a lotus in her right palm.
And behold the auspicious conch-mark upon her right foot.
Behold at the base of the finger a line resembling a celestial chariot (vimāna).
Behold beneath the base of the little finger a well-drawn boat;
likewise, behold the lines of a conch and a mace, and the drawing of a sea-monster (makara).
Likewise, O beloved, observe the beautiful line on the peak [of the foot] in the middle;
see the fish-line on the heel and the betel-vine in the center.
See the mark of a barley-corn at the base of the left big toe, marked by a beautiful line.
Below that, behold indeed a great palace by means of a line.
Below that, behold an umbrella joined with an upward-pointing line. Behold the lotus-line on the hood and the banner-line as well.
Behold the mark of the goad, the white water-lily, and also the *śrīphala* fruit; observe the lines of the lotus on the ground and the lines of the jar.
Behold the crescent moon of the second lunar day and the ten wheels.
Behold the golden line upon the hood, the mark of a spider's web on the forehead, a dot on the chin, and a circle on the left breast;
on the right breast, the lines of the hand, and a beautiful, deep-orange necklace around the neck. (13–14)
Behold indeed a golden line like a bow upon her hips, as well as a svastika on the palm of her right hand, along with a fish and a banner. (15)
Behold the bow, the lute, the fish, and the line; behold the jar-line, the goad, the mandala, and the discus upon the palm of her right hand. (16)
Behold the line of the rampart and the archway there as well;
behold also the mark of the plow, O beloved, right there upon the hood.
"Behold, Lakṣmī, his hidden penis and likewise his two slightly reddened lips;
behold the upward line on his right hand and likewise on the left. (18)
O my beloved, behold the upward lines upon the soles of my feet; there,
on the foot, see the horse, the elephant, and the great auspicious tree,
as well as the sacrificial post, the arrow, the barley grain, and the javelin within the line.
Behold the line of the rosary on his hand, as well as the lamp and the fly-whisk.
Behold the mountain and the earring; behold the altar by means of the line. [Behold] the face, eyes, eyebrows, forehead, lips, nose, and cheeks. (1.69.20–21)
Behold them, radiant, fair-complexioned, and enchanting with their golden hue; likewise, the goddesses, distinguished by their respective marks, are beloved of the Blessed One. (22)
Indeed, the women who are devoted to me become embodiments of Lakṣmī;
by the power of my worship, I make them dwellings of the lotus.
Those who dwell in the world of Brahmā, those who have made their home in Goloka, those who have attained residence in Vaikuṇṭha, and those who have gone to Śvetadvīpa; ॥24॥
Abiding in the abode of nectar, situated in the midst of the circle of fire, dwelling in the world of the sun, and established in the orb of the moon. 25.
Those who dwell in Satyaloka, those born from the creation of Īśvara,
those who have entered the progeny of the Pitṛs, and likewise those who are the wives of the Ṛṣis— ||26||
Then the goddesses, as well as the human women and those who were not goddesses but beloved by the Nāgas and others—all of them, having approached me with supreme devotion, became Śrīs. (27)
And I, O Mahālakṣmī, in the form of Nārāyaṇa, do not delight those [goddesses] in the many worlds as I do you here in this abode. ||28||
Indeed, all those [women] who possess devotion in their minds certainly become Lakṣmīs; however, those others who do not worship me do so because of their sinful karma. ||29||
They go to various forms of pits in this world and the next, even after experiencing great sufferings in birth within the realm of Yama. (1.69.30)
Those women who belong to the city of Yama do not arise as givers of merit; rather, they come into being for the sake of suffering after having experienced torments. //31//
Those births characterized by even a trace of evil are declared to be nothing but givers of suffering;
listen, for I shall describe them to you briefly as the occasion arises. (32)
She whose little finger or ring finger does not touch the ground, or whose forefinger extends beyond the thumb, is an unchaste woman. (33)
She whose shanks are hairy, excessively fleshy, and overly veiny, and whose private parts are sunken, small, and curved to the left, indeed brings suffering. (34)
With a short neck she is destitute; with a long one, there is the destruction of the family;
and with a broad one, she becomes fierce—of this there is no doubt. (35)
If her eyes are squinting and tawny, and her dark pupils are restless, she is unchaste; if there are pits in her smile and on her cheeks, she is certainly an adulteress. (36)

A woman with a lock of hair hanging down upon her forehead kills her husband's younger brother; one with such a lock on her abdomen kills her father-in-law, and one with them on both buttocks kills her husband. (37)
A woman who has hair on her upper lip is certainly not auspicious for her husband;
likewise, breasts with hair and uneven ears are inauspicious. (38)
Teeth that are jagged and uneven lead to suffering;
those with blackish flesh and are long lead to theft and the death of the husband. (39)
With hands resembling those of flesh-eating creatures, like those of wolves and crows, and which are veiny, uneven, and withered, those women become destitute of wealth. (1.69.40)
She whose upper lip is excessively elevated speaks harshly during quarrels;
she with long ears, a harsh voice, and a beard has *kālikā* on her foot. 41.
One with red eyes, a sharp chin, and a very small forehead is a killer;
one with many lines on the forehead, much hair, excessive talkativeness, and extreme fickleness [is likewise so]. 42.
Having many attachments, much sleep, great indolence, and excessive expenditure, he deliberates upon poverty and total destitution in every way. (43)
Therefore, one should always perform good deeds and never an evil deed.
From the merit produced by performing excellent deeds, a body endowed with auspicious marks is obtained,
as well as wealth, grain, servants, houses, gardens, and other such superior things.
Time waits for no one; what has been done by this [person], or what has not? //45//
A living being dies, is born, and thrives again and again;
yet that death, birth, and thriving which are ordained for the sake of liberation must indeed be accomplished by oneself, or else by one's sons and family members. (46)
One should conduct oneself day and night in such a way that it results in the welfare of living beings.

The earth provides a dwelling, water provides satisfaction, the wind provides tranquility, the body provides labor, and food provides sustenance; why then should one not accomplish what is beneficial?
An excellence exists everywhere, provided one investigates again and again;
and likewise, having investigated, one finds that there is no excellence in dependence. (49)
Having cast off his own body with whatever comes by chance, he should carry out the affairs of the world with a mind free from excessive attachment. (1.69.50)
O lotus-eyed one, he who does not constantly worship Nārāyaṇa as you do has neither happiness nor spiritual welfare; for him, even liberation is exceedingly remote. (51)
One should worship me in the form of virtuous men and women by offering everything to them;
one should joyfully serve me in the form of the poor, guests, and the helpless. (52)
O Goddess! I wander in various forms—such as a student, a child, a young woman, an old man, or a teacher; may someone serve me in whatever form I happen to have assumed. (53)
Abiding there, I shall personally bring about the supreme good;
indeed, I carry out initiation in order to always effect the welfare of my devotee. (54)

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marks of Lakṣmī and the Marks of Other Women," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 69.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! Without liberation, the journey to the next world is always miserable and brings only suffering, for one’s life is lived according to the merits and demerits one has personally acquired. (1)

If one does not offer the appropriate funeral cakes and other rites even for the sake of the deceased, there will be an obstruction of their future progress, and an abundance of suffering will befall them. (2)

Therefore, as one who is about to depart upon the course of karma and is himself about to die, one should, while still alive, perform meritorious deeds without sloth for the sake of one's own happiness. (3)
Whether a man or a woman, through the union of body and senses,
they naturally perform virtue for the sake of happiness and non-virtue for the sake of suffering.
(4) One should indeed practice virtue for the sake of happiness, and non-virtue leads to suffering.
Nothing at all has been done by oneself; what can one who comes later do?
Nevertheless, people are affectionate and such is the nature of humanity;
sometimes, even toward a person who comes later, one acts out of dependence on affection.
When a living being indeed departs from the body for the next world, then that body, deprived of the vital breaths, is designated as a corpse. (7)
It quickly becomes untouchable, designated as worms, excrement, and ashes.
From the moment of the soul's departure for the deceased, one should offer six funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in succession.
In the place where death occurred, a funeral cake (piṇḍa) called Śava is offered;
by that, the earth and its presiding deity become satisfied. (9)
If a traveler should be at the doorway, an offering is given by that name;
by that which is thus given, the presiding deities of the house and its site are satisfied. (1.70.10)
At the crossroads, there is one named Khecara; by means of that [mantra] given by his name, the multitude of spirits flees from there to cause harm. (11)
This offering, designated for the spirits (bhūtas), is presented with reference to that place of rest;
as well as for the piśācas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and whatever others dwell there. (12)

For that body which is to be offered as an oblation, there are no factors that cause its unfitness; rather, the practitioner offers the deceased, known as the *preta*, to it upon the funeral pyre. (13)
Thus, by means of these five lumps, the corpse becomes fit for the oblation; thereafter, the fire shall ignite the funeral pyre to destroy the defects of the body. (14)
Having swept, smeared, and then scraped [the ground], and having removed the altar-mound (vedikā) and sprinkled [the site],
one should establish the fire there according to the prescribed rule.
Having worshipped the deity known as Kravyāda well with flowers and unbroken rice grains, and having said, "Lead the deceased to heaven," one should perform the oblation of the body. 16.
When half of the body has been thus consumed, one should then offer an oblation of clarified butter (ājya) to Yama,
to Antaka, to Mṛtyu, and likewise to Brahmā. Indeed,
one offering should be given into the mouth of Jātavedas (Fire), and likewise one into the mouth of the deceased (Preta).
Then one should cause the fire to blaze upward over the funeral pyre in the eastern portion [of the site].
"This purifier blazes for the sake of the heavenly world; svāhā!
Having thus offered an oblation of clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds accompanied by the mantra, ||| 18–19 ||
Then, it is said, the son must certainly perform the cremation;
he must weep intensely thereafter, for in this way his happiness will come to pass. (1.70.20)
Immediately after the cremation, having performed the rite of collecting the remains there,
one should indeed offer the *pretapiṇḍa* (the rice-ball for the deceased), which truly serves to pacify the suffering of the burning.

Then, having performed a bath with their clothes on along with their sons, they should offer water with sesame seeds and strike the stone with their hands while pronouncing the name and lineage [of the deceased]. (22)
One should say "Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu"; then people, having gone to the right of his door, [should apply] cow dung and white mustard seeds. || 23 ||
Having placed the god Varuṇa within his own house and concealed him, one should eat neem leaves; having consumed clarified butter, one may return home. //24//
One should not shed tears after offering the handful of water;
for the deceased, being powerless, consumes whatever phlegm and tears are consumed by the kinsmen. (25)
For three days, one should offer milk and water in an earthen vessel;
by looking toward a cremation ground, a crossroads, or one's own home, one is led away by the messengers of Yama. (26)
For ten days, one should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) into the pit day after day;
furthermore, handfuls of water should be offered constantly, intended for the deceased.
A son, a wife, a disciple, or a brother may indeed perform the rite;
however, half of the daily offered *piṇḍa* bestows a body. (28)
The third [portion] he lives upon with the messengers of Yama, and by the fourth;
after nine days and nights, the deceased attains completion.
In the tenth month, hunger arises for the living being whose body has been fully formed;
possessed by hunger, he remains upon the house as one whose very body is hunger. (1.70.30)
Staying there, they then proceed along the path of Yama to the abode of Yama;
experiencing sufferings, they later lament when they obtain rebirth. (31)
Alas! While in good health, I did not perform even the slightest act that bestows liberation;
I neither chanted the names of Hari nor listened to His sacred narratives. (32)

I have not performed the chanting of praises nor the singing of songs, nor have I practiced the remembrance of Hari; I have not performed His worship, nor the massaging of the feet of the virtuous. (33)
There is no hymn of praise and no prostration performed with the body;
for that body is not mine, which has been so extensively nourished by me. (34)
Though protected, cherished, and served repeatedly and properly, it was abandoned by him in vain; thus, his purpose was not accomplished. (35)
Having closed my eyes along with my senses, this body has been led to futility;
the time for attaining liberation was not made meaningful by me. (36)
The wife was compliant, the husband was dear, and the sons and servants were likewise favorable; yet even so, the self was deceived. (37)
I possessed abundant wealth and various kinds of goods for the purpose of giving;
yet, due to mere greed, I did not attain liberation.
I did not perform service for virtuous men and women;
I am now reaping the fruit of my misdeeds—what indeed could happen now? (39)
Human birth is obtained through a great accumulation of merit;
yet that has not been made meaningful by me, for much else has been done instead. (1.70.40)
Childhood was spent in play, youth was wasted in sexual pleasure, and old age has been cast away in anxiety; what can be done by one who is powerless at the time of death? (41)
That body, which possesses the splendor of the wish-fulfilling tree, the cow of plenty, and the wish-granting gem, has been exhausted in other tasks; I have not accomplished my own true purpose.
Completely dependent on others, I am excessively tormented by servants; what can I do?
Indeed, no gift was ever given by me, nor was any austerity performed;
no vow was ever observed, nor was an oblation offered into the mouths of the virtuous.
No pilgrimage site was visited, nor were any ponds or similar works of merit ever constructed.
No sphere of activity was ever undertaken; who will provide assistance?
No service was rendered to others, nor were preparations for the next world made.
The religious observances were not properly honored—what indeed will happen now?
I have never performed service to my guru, nor to my parents.
(46) This female body is a source of great suffering, always dependent on others and impure;
I have certainly not made it meaningful through devotion or service. (47)
This human body is a great burden, inauspicious and carrying manifold cravings;
yet, through neither devotion nor merit has it been made purposeful by me. (48)
Thus that *yātanā-preta* speaks, grieves, and weeps;
he is tormented and beaten by the messengers, and cries out again and again. (49)
Afflicted by suffering, he remembers the happiness derived from his wife, wealth, home, and land; he grieves deeply for his servants, friends, sons, grandsons, and family. (1.70.50)
Indeed, one who is unable to proceed on the path is dragged downward by messengers;
they merely lament piteously, crying out, "O beloved! O son! O wife! and so forth. (51)
"May they come together and liberate me from this unbearable torment!
May my son, grandson, or kinsman perform meritorious deeds on my behalf;
O my dear son, may he indeed make a gift of a cow for my sake! (52)
I shall cross the Vaitaraṇī river; otherwise, my immersion there is certain.
I have not brought even a small amount of provisions for the journey named "merit";
neither has it been practiced through austerity, nor offered in sacrifice, nor recited as mantra, nor given in charity—whence then could it come? (54)
When one travels by a path that is hot, damp, or cold, one who is fainting or terrified there grieves only within the heart. //55//
If some kinsman of mine were to offer a gift of clothing or the like, then this suffering would be destroyed; otherwise, alas, there is only enjoyment [of my misery]. (56)
The servants then say to him, "Where indeed is such merit of yours?
At that moment, crying out, "Alas, O Fate!", he regains his composure for a brief instant.
[He thinks: "If indeed I should obtain a human body once again..."
"I swear that I shall certainly take refuge in the path that grants liberation. (58)

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Rites for the Corpse, the Offering of Piṇḍas, Grief, and the Sorrow for the Departed Spirit," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 70.
← Chapter 70: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 71 [Author: Chapter 72 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having experienced the miseries of Yama’s city, listen to how the denizens of hell emerge from hell and wander about. (1)
But those hungry ghosts, being uncertain as to whether they might attain some form of birth, searched for their own family among their wife, their son, and other relatives. (2)
Or, having established themselves among relatives or household members, they dwell within the family;
moving about bodilessly, they are intensely afflicted by hunger and thirst.
At times and in certain places, they forcibly obstruct and delude them.
"They cause us pain, they cause us to faint, and they afflict us again and again.
(4) Why indeed was liberation not achieved by you for my sake?
Therefore, having become ghosts, we shall afflict you most severely. (5)
Agitated by intense rage, they afflict them again and again;
likewise, those who obstruct that path block the gates of the ancestors.
Like thieves seizing travelers, they seize the shares of the ancestors.
In one's own home, on a ground rendered impure by the discharge of feces, urine, and so forth; || 7 ||
Having stayed there, they observe which person might be diseased;
they afflict them with forms of fever and devour their food.
They also drink their blood, though only in minute and very small quantities here and there.
Remaining in places such as where food scraps are left, they constantly contemplate what is undesirable.
There they drink water mixed with the leftovers of their food;
they constantly plot deception against their family members, such as their own children.
Thus, with such evil intentions, they inflict suffering upon their own kin.
A *preta* torments its own family, but it torments others through their vulnerabilities.
While alive, he was full of affection; once dead, he indeed becomes malevolent.
Having found a vulnerability or impurity, he repeatedly inflicts suffering.
A hungry ghost (preta) shall torment that person who is devoid of all ritual actions, who neglects the worship of the gods, and who consumes impure food. 13.
For one there may be the loss of a son, while another does not obtain a son at all; one may be devoid of progeny, for indeed, in that case, there is the fault of a *preta*. (14)
The lineage shall perish from the womb, and that which has been born will be destroyed;
there will be the loss of livestock and wealth, as well as conflict with kinsmen. (15)
The natural state undergoes transformation, as does strife among sons;
there is the sudden onset of calamity, and that suffering arises from the deceased.
Indeed, there is madness, insomnia, indigestion, and fever.
17. Eructation, stomach-ache—this affliction arises from a *preta*.
18. A fondness for theft, domestic strife, poverty of wealth and grain, and the gradual decline of prosperity—this suffering arises from a *preta*.
Even wealth that has been acquired slips from one's hand;
there will be a failure of crops despite a period of plenty, and failure in one's undertakings. (19)
There will be the undertaking of base actions, fear from thieves, fire, and kings, as well as the onset of great diseases and affliction of one's own body. (1.71.20)
First she becomes a servant and later a wife, yet she is like a dog;
her mind is constantly intent on the ruin of the household, and her suffering arises from the spirits of the dead.
She lacks devotion and mindfulness, and her actions are devoid of mental discipline.
There is daily strife among one's own kin, and that suffering arises from the deceased. 22.
For women, there may be miscarriage and likewise no menstruation; or even if menstruation is seen, no fruit at all is seen. (23)
There is a gradual loss of life-span, constant quarrels over teeth in the home, and a lack of satisfaction during meals due to anger, agitation, and the like. (24)
Quarrels and even murderers—sons who are like the offspring of an enemy—neither find joy nor true happiness; that is the suffering born of the deceased. (25)
One who does not obey the words of one's parents, nor serves one's own wife;
and a wife who does not look upon her husband with the eye of a spouse—that is the suffering born of a preta. 26.
Those who cause sudden death become suffering pretas;
likewise, one who performs actions contrary to dharma or performs rites devoid of the prescribed rules becomes a preta. (27)

At that time, due to association with the wicked, or because of the failure to perform the rite of releasing a bull, or even by falling under the power of an evil death, his body remains undissolved. ||28||

O beloved, due to the omission of cremation rites and other ceremonies, and because of the fault of dying on a bed or similar surface, one is born as a preta through the affliction of hunger, thirst, burning heat, and death. (29)

Due to the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), one may become a preta in some state, devoid of speech and movement; once that state of a preta has become firmly established, one should practice the liberation of the preta.
He who indeed thinks of the deceased as ghosts shall himself, upon death, attain the state of a ghost.
In that family where there is the defect of ghosts, no happiness is found. (31)
Intelligence, joy, pleasure, wisdom, and fortune—these five are destroyed;
when the third or fifth house is occupied by a male planet, the cutting off of the lineage occurs. (32)
Poor, destitute, and indeed a doer of evil deeds in birth after birth—thus do the hungry ghosts (pretas) torment themselves through their own cruel disposition. (33)
Tormented by hunger and thirst, the pretas shall enter their own homes;
having entered, they shall lie down with bodies of wind among those born of their own respective lineages. (34)
In dreams, they show their own forms as sons, wives, and so forth;
having become elephants, horses, or bulls, they appear with distorted faces. (35)
A cat, a woman, or a snake may repeatedly appear for a moment;
or the bed may be inverted, or one's own self may appear distorted. (36)
He who, having risen, looks around, is indeed tormented by a *preta*;
he is bound with fetters in a dream; this is wrought by a *preta*, of this there is no doubt. (37)
If one begs for food in a dream and is slain by many weapons, or if one slays a person oneself—all that is shown by a preta. (38)
Taking cooked food from one who is eating, he indeed flees;
or, afflicted by thirst, he forcibly drinks the water of himself or another. (39)
Mounting a bull in a dream, or wandering together with bulls;
leaping up and traveling through the sky, or going to a sacred ford out of hunger. (1.71.40)
One may see one's own wife, kinsmen, children, husband, or teacher as being present and yet dead; all such things are shown by a preta. 41.

For the sake of the liberation of that deceased person who, overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, begs for water in a dream, one should have funeral cakes (piṇḍas) offered at a sacred ford (tīrtha). ||42||
At night, as he departs from his house, he sees in a dream his sons, as well as his cattle, fathers, brothers, and wives, due to the affliction caused by a *preta*. (43)
For the sake of pacifying that [evil], one should perform libations at home, at a sacred ford, or under a banyan tree;
having honored black grains, one should give them to a master of the Vedas. 44.
For one who, having abandoned all obstacles, undertakes the means to liberation, the fruit of that action is excellent: eternal satisfaction for the departed spirits. 45.
The self alone shall be united with the highest good, and the deceased shall attain long-lasting satisfaction;
for those who are satisfied always desire the welfare of their own kinsmen.
Otherwise, however, evil-minded people cause suffering to those born of their own lineage, through mere sight, conversation, conduct, or even by causing pain. (47)
He does not attain a good rebirth, but is tormented by the curses of hungry ghosts;
he remains childless, without cattle, as well as poor and diseased. (48)
In birth after birth, one shall be destitute of livelihood and wretched;
therefore, liberation for the deceased must always be effected through libations (tarpaṇa).
When satisfied, they ward off the calamities that would otherwise befall their own descendants.
Later, when the time has come, they attain liberation through their son.
They always bestow prosperity, growth, and wealth upon their kinsmen.
He who performs the auspicious Nārāyaṇa-bali rite dedicated to the ancestors [attains these benefits].
By performing that, obstacles are destroyed and one is not afflicted;
one is certainly liberated from the torments of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and the like. //52//
Having performed the Nārāyaṇabali, one should carry out the rite of releasing a bull and other such ceremonies;
thus, one shall attain freedom from all calamities and obtain every happiness. //53//
In this world, there is no other supreme deity equal to one’s father and mother;
the father is the lord who brings about the birth of the body and is the manifest deity. (54)
The teacher who instructs one in what is beneficial is a visible deity;
therefore, the father, the teacher, the mother, the elders, and likewise the husband, are to be honored.
One's body, wealth, wife, sons, and eternal worlds [depend upon them].
By whose grace these things are obtained—who else could be more worthy of worship than he? (56)
Since he protects his father from the hell named Put, he is therefore called "putra"; thus, one should deliver one's father. //57//
If the father and mother of anyone should die of an untimely death (apamṛtyu),
one should perform the funeral rites (dharma), pilgrimage (tīrtha), marriage and other ceremonies, as well as the annual śrāddha.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Residence of Pretas on Impure Ground, the Various Torments Caused by Pretas, the Signs in Dreams Caused by Pretas, and the Means for Their Cessation," in the first section, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 71: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 72 [[Author:

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall describe those who have become ghosts due to untimely death—those who were heretics, those who died of greed, and likewise those who died without the performance of purificatory rites.
Those who die from a caṇḍāla, water, a serpent, a curse, a tree, lightning, or from fanged and horned animals, become pretas. (2)
Those who died by hanging, those struck down by poison, weapons, and the like, and those who committed suicide through malevolent rites (*ābhicāra*) and so forth—[these are excluded]. (3)
Those who have died from great hardships or diseases, those killed by bandits, those struck down by cholera or fire, and those who have perished in landslides and similar calamities; || 4 ||
Those who died untimely deaths, those who were defiled, those whose deaths were caused by impurity,
those for whom the funeral rice-ball offerings were omitted, those who lacked the rite of releasing a bull,
and those who died from falling from a mountain, from the collapse of a wall, or by traveling through the sky; || 5 || [these are the ones who remain].
Those who die while a woman is in her menses, or during sexual intercourse, or while engaged in purification;
those who die in the intermediate space of the atmosphere, at a boundary, or in a desolate place;
those who have perished from malignant darts and the like, and those who die during periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka) and so forth.
Those who, out of thirst, fail to provide water and those who fall under the power of an untimely death (kumṛtyu) are indeed born as *pretas*; they wander upon the surface of the earth.
They are those who seize cattle and livestock, and those who destroy water sources and groves.
Those who corrupt the conduct of the gods, those who destroy the livelihoods of the distressed,
those who obstruct acts of giving, those who ruin meritorious deeds,
and those who cause suffering to many— by virtue of their sins, they become pretas. (1.72.10)
Those wicked ones who delight in harming others, having fallen under the power of a sinful death and being constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, attain the state of a preta. (11)
Neither mother nor father is considered the cause at the time of birth as a preta;
rather, the state of being a preta arises from karma and the decree of Yama. (12)
There indeed were some of deformed appearance, with hanging lips and distorted faces;
some had large bodies and teeth, while others had crooked mouths. They possessed the faces of serpents, the faces of cats, and various other kinds of faces.

Whatever kind of karma they have performed to become hell-beings, such indeed are the qualities of a preta at those various times. Whatever sin a human being has committed to attain the state of a preta, such are his characteristics. (14–15)
In that very manner, his hunger and thirst arise repeatedly;
yet neither pure food nor even pure water can be obtained anywhere.
Indeed, there is no access to pure food or water anywhere at all. (16)
Your food is pure by virtue of the Vasus, and the water is pure by virtue of the Vāruṇas;
it is always protected there, yet it is not even a portion for the pretas.
It is filled with phlegm, urine, excrement, and impurities along with the evacuations.
Food that has been left over, as well as that which is leftover from a meal, becomes the sustenance of the pretas;
the pretas always consume whatever is devoid of purity and is defiled. (19)
In whose house there is no purity nor any offering to the gods,
that wicked house filled with liquor and meat is frequented by hungry ghosts (pretas).
Greed, anger, intoxication, laziness, sleep, sorrow, and fear— 1.72.20.
Illusion, strife, and deceit; impurity and the lack of bathing; (21) the failure to purify the impurities of the bodily constituents and so forth; a garment smeared with dust and semen;
a wall plastered with lime; and a tube filled with urine. (22)
In whichever house there are hungry ghosts (pretas), they indeed eat there;
that food of the pretas constantly flows from the linga and the bhaga.
Death is always better for a living being than to ever become a preta.
He who dies with the food of an outcaste still remaining within his stomach.
Indeed, that man who falls under the power of an evil death is born as a *preta*; he who seizes the property of the gods, the wealth of others, and so forth, is born as a *preta*. (25)
One who misappropriates the property of a guru or the wealth of another is born as a preta;
likewise one who betrays trust, a deceiver, or a person who sells a maiden. (26)

One who seizes his brother's property, a slayer of people, a killer of cows, a killer of animals, an adulterer, a stealer of gold, a usurper of land, or one who speaks falsehoods—such a person is born as a preta. ||27||
The man who abandons his mother, sister, wife, daughter-in-law, daughter, son, or father is born as a preta.

Those who are devoid of the conduct of the cultured, those who lack devotion to their parents, those who are addicted to liquor and meat, and those who perform acts such as the slaughter of animals; ||29||
Those who commit acts of malice against others and cause them great terror, who constantly seek out vulnerabilities and bring about the end of others' prosperity; 1.72.30.
Those who are addicted to excessive sexual intercourse, who eat the flesh of the heart and other such things, who are cruel, given to vices, wicked, and delight in performing prohibited acts; 31.
Furthermore, for others who are like them, there indeed occurs a wasting away of their lifespan;
having abandoned their short-lived and wretched bodies, they become *pretas*.
With such a body, one should accomplish what is beneficial for oneself.
By means of meritorious action, one may achieve either heaven or even liberation.
Through the ripening of past karmas, one experiences both happiness and suffering;
therefore, in this life, one should practice that dharma which bestows happiness. (34)
Whether a man or a woman, having accomplished their own purpose on this earth,
they should always strive for the sake of others— that which is the supreme good and brings about liberation. One may indeed forget other things at will, but one must never forget liberation.
One might forget any other task, but one must never forget the Dharma.
One may forget other objects of enjoyment, but one must not forget the bliss of the Self;
one may forget artificial yoga, but one must not forget Hari who dwells within the heart. (37)
But he who, abandoning the Lord who bestows happiness, worships one who bestows suffering, shall find suffering as his fruit; he does not attain any other welfare. (38)
Therefore, O lotus-eyed one, the denizens of hell are to be known as threefold:
some reside in the city of Yama, while others have the form of pretas. ||39||
But all other hell-beings are exceedingly miserable in every house, for in their homes there is no happiness whatsoever due to the lack of the abundance of food and drink. (1.72.40)
Because of their women, sons, wealth, and grain, those who have large families but are destitute in providing for them are here [in this world] like those in hell manifest before their eyes. (41)
Their clothes and food are never sufficient; they are hell-beings manifest in this world.
He who has even one woman in excess as his wife is a hell-being manifest in this world. (42)
He who commits adultery in his own home experiences hell visibly;
one who is devoted to the wives of others, to prostitutes, and the like, experiences hell visibly. (43)
One who is counted as a dog by an ignoble woman is a manifest hell-being here; she whose husband is like a dog is likewise a manifest hell-being there. (44)

Those for whom hatred, affliction, and anxiety toward their household members have become habitual—lacking both sleep and happiness despite their affection—they are indeed hell-beings manifest before our eyes. (45)
Where one's own kinsmen are thieves, where one's own kinsmen are murderers, and where one's own kinsmen are deceivers—that indeed is hell manifest before one's eyes. //46//
Sons and others do not obey commands, nor does a wife bestow affection;
the family provides no honor—it is indeed a visible hell.
Food is always coarse, preceded by the giving of insults and the like.
Seeing with the eye of hatred, he is here a hell-being in his very presence. 48.
Torn clothes, a house, and a courtyard on the street;

Servants are always dependent on others, and likewise, they are prone to insults.
One's own kin are like dogs, yet he is a hell-being before his very eyes.

it is a refuge for vulnerabilities, cruelty, rogues, and deceit—a hell visible to the eye. (51)

a husband who bestows pleasure is not one who strikes, for he is a source of bliss here. ||52||
Those who are wounded by birth, afflicted by diseases of birth, and tormented by the miseries of birth—those who are rich in suffering from birth itself are indeed visible hell-beings.
For the body is truly hell; one is a denizen of hell because of dwelling therein.
Indeed, saṃsāra is hell; one is a denizen of hell (nārakī) because of dwelling therein. 54.
Indeed, one who brings about welfare through devotion is surely liberated from hell;
however, all those in hell are not liberated until that very moment. ||55||
Resorting to the gates of hell, of impurities, of the throats of those addicted to minerals, he truly sports here as a denizen of hell in person. (56)
Having emerged from the hells, one clings to them once again;
in this state of nourishment, one is of the very form of hell—what indeed is more hellish than this? Insult is great suffering, but bondage is even greater than that.
Dependent on others and possessed of great terror—one who has these very [qualities] is a hell-being right here. //58//
He who is attached to that which is called the hell of craving is considered a denizen of hell;
thus, this third hell exists here in every single house. (59)
Impurity, decay, and excess constitute the threefold defect;

These are the *pretas*: those who are living yet dead, the *pretas* in the abode of Yama, those invisible ones, those in the form of wind, and the three types of departed spirits (*paretakas*). (61)
All indeed are experiencers of suffering, and all likewise are givers of suffering;
all are devoid of devotion—what difference is there here among those who have passed away? (6)
Those three— the Yāmyas, the Vāyavyas, and the Mānavīyas—
if they do not perform what is beneficial, then all three are equal to ghosts (pretas).
Therefore, by means of this human body, that which brings about liberation must be accomplished.
Indeed, those who proceed toward liberation through that [means] never go to the state of a preta. But if a woman is a ḍākinī, or if one's husband is a source of terror to spirits,
or if one's sons are slayers of rākṣasas, the preta flees from him.
The womb is that which grinds [the embryo], moistening it with urine and semen; its body becomes like mud, and he who enjoys it is a denizen of hell. (66)
Outcastes (śvapacas) who dwell outside the village are impure and baskets of faults;
what fault can be attributed to a fault? What can a *preta* do there?
Just as one *preta* should neither terrify nor torment another *preta*, [so should one behave].
Likewise, what could one possibly gain by tormenting a wicked person who is like a hungry ghost? //68//
Having indeed abandoned such a family, those who have died depart;
they dwell in a sacred ford, a forest, or elsewhere, perpetually afflicted by suffering. (69)

At the beginning of all births from every womb, happiness is ordained in varying degrees;

Nine kinds of sons are recognized, including those who are not biological (anaurasa).

When the year is complete, one should perform the introduction of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-praveśana).

Because of the infinity of family customs and because of the exhaustion of the lifespan of men. (1.73.20)

With sesame seeds and *darbha* grass upon the ground, his mind shall be fixed there in Vaikuṇṭha.

Everywhere the earth is holy, for even though it is smeared, it is indeed free from stain.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śrī, and Hutāśana (Fire) themselves abide within the maṇḍala; therefore, one should construct a maṇḍala. Otherwise, he who dies there or plays [with the corpse] is carried away by the wind.
O Lakṣmī! These sesame seeds produced from my body are purifying.
Asuras, Dānavas, and Daityas flee when sesame seeds are present.
Darbha grass arose from my hair and sesame seeds from my sweat; therefore, one should place them [there].

Brahmā resides at the root of the *darbha* grass, Keśava in its middle, and Śaṅkara stays at the tip; thus the three gods are established in the *kuśa*. Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, Gaṅgā, Tulasī, the Brahmin, and the cow [are likewise sacred]. (34–35)

In this essence-less and difficult saṃsāra, these six steps grant liberation; they ward off the miserable state for one who has fallen into distress. For the salty taste indeed originated from the body of Viṣṇu.

A gift should be given there; by that merit one is protected.
Likewise, sesame seeds, a cow, land, gold, cotton, and salt [should be given]. (37–38)
Likewise, by giving each of the seven grains and the metals, one purifies that [sinner].
Through the gift of gold, there is happiness and attainment of heaven; through the gift of land, one becomes a king.
By means of the seven grains, one obtains grain, and the servants of Yama are satisfied.
By the gift of iron, the messengers of Yama do not come to the house of the deceased. Indeed,
the axe, the pestle, the staff, the sword, and likewise the dagger,
the noose, the whip, and the mallet are the weapons held in the hands of Yama.
The *kuriṇas*, *sārvasūtrāpas*, *śūṇḍās*, excellent *markas*,
*śabalas*, and *śyāmadūtas* were gratified by the gift of iron.
Indeed, one should uplift oneself from the accumulation of sins through the gift of iron.
Indeed, a cow can ferry one across the Vaitaraṇī river and lead one to heaven and liberation.
Mahādeva even repeatedly performed service to cows in Goloka,
and Śrī Hari indeed performs service to cows at all times.
Cows are all forms of prosperity; I dwell eternally within cows.
Through the gift of gold, one attains the world of the Sun, as well as the splendor of the Moon and Fire.
Furthermore, salt given as a gift opens the very gate to heaven.
The gift of sesame seeds for a mortal destroys even great sins.
Other gifts as well, including various articles and utensils,
should be given for the sake of the deceased’s attainment of happiness and liberation.
Seeing his father on the ground with eyes half-open and his breath faltering as it moves from its natural place, he is said to be one afflicted by death.
At that time, whatever son causes all kinds of gifts to be given, [he gains great merit].
"Nārāyaṇa, Hare, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī, Lord of Kamalā;

"Śrī Hari is my refuge; Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you are my goal.

Viṣṇu is mother, Viṣṇu is father, Viṣṇu is one's own kin and kinsmen. (54)
Water is Viṣṇu; dry land is Viṣṇu; the earth is Viṣṇu; the *kuśa* grass belongs to Viṣṇu.
