By whomsoever the virtuous have been seen, bowed to, and served at the time of death.
"Once they have been propitiated, he indeed attains liberation immediately; there is no doubt about this.

likewise, by the gift of food, he shall wander happily, free from hunger.

A lamp should be placed facing east or north within the temple of the deity.
(3) One should provide a seat and a vessel that bring benefit to the next world; one should offer water from a water-pot, thinking, "May he who is thirsty drink this water. (4)

likewise, the gift of a bed with its coverlet and other gifts should be made according to one's capacity,
for the sake of attaining the satisfaction, happiness, and peace of the departed spirit.
When that self, mixed with the vital air, departs from the body—
through the hair-pores above the waist as well as from the spheres of the senses—
the life-force (*prāṇa*) of the doer of merit goes upward, while for another it flows from the lower part. (8)

There are twenty-one lakhs of womb-born beings,
and an equal number of sweat-born, soil-born, and egg-born beings.

Having gone here and there as a ghost, he becomes miserable again and again;
he dwells once more in the womb, and birth and death recur repeatedly.

Therein shall be born a righteous son, a treasure-house of virtues and fortune.
Sons are born from women on even nights, while daughters are born on odd nights.
On the fifth day for women, there should be a meal of sweet *gaulma* (barley-based) food.

For a woman, however, exposure to the sun must be avoided; she should consume only cool things.

Just as at the time of conception, when the semen and blood are mixed,

When the mind of desire and the semen attain a state of oneness, then the man reaches a state of fluidity within the womb of the woman. If there is an excess of blood, a female is born; if there is an excess of semen, a male is born.

Within one day and night it becomes a *kalala*, and after five days a *budbuda*.
On the tenth day it is like a jujube fruit (*karkandhu*), and on the twentieth day it reaches the state of solid flesh (*ghanamāṃsatā*).
Likewise, when the month is complete, one should retain the five elements.
In two months, however, the skin and flesh [are formed]; likewise, marrow and bone in three;
in the fourth, the ankles and hair; and in the fifth, the ears and nose.
In the seventh [month], the throat, the private parts, and so forth [are formed]; in the eighth, there is the completion of the limbs;
in the ninth, there is the desire to go outside; and in the tenth, one is born.
[Furthermore,] the earth [element] consists of the fivefold set: skin, bone, channels, hair, and flesh.
The fivefold [functions] of water are saliva, urine, semen, marrow, and blood (27).
The fivefold [functions] of fire are luster, hunger, sleep, thirst, and laziness.
The fivefold [functions] of air are respiration, movement, contraction, expansion, and excretion (28).
Or else, passion, hatred, fear, shame, and delusion are the five qualities born of air;
while sound, resonance, cavities, and depth are the qualities of space perceived through hearing.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumṇā, Gāndhārī, and Gajajihvikā—
Pūṣā, Yaśasvinī, Alambuṣā, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, and Nāḍikā are the channels (nāḍīs).
Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna are the vital airs (vāyus).
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkala, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya are [the secondary vital airs].
Prāṇa is in the heart, apāna in the anus, and samāna in the region of the navel.
Udāna should be in the region of the throat, while vyāna pervades the entire body.
The function of the nāga wind is yawning, and that of the kūrma wind is considered to be contraction.
The trident, the tortoise-shell, and the "god-given" [bow]—beginning with the eructation [of Arjuna].
For the sake of expansion, Dhanañjaya remains in the third heaven even after death.
Indeed, there are nine: the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, anus, and private parts. (33–34)

The womb-cavity in the secret place of a woman is the twelfth; the two breasts are the fourteenth.
Likewise, there are three crores and a half of body hairs.
It is taught that there are thirty-two teeth and exactly twenty nails.
There are three hundred thousand hairs on the head and those located on the face; such is the established state.
Furthermore, three [elements] arise from the mother, namely those known as hair, blood, and flesh.
From the father come the sinews, bones, and marrow, as well as the sixfold sheaths.
Flesh is one thousand palas, and blood is likewise one hundred palas.
Fat is ten palas, and marrow is twelve palas.
Blood is said to be three palas, and semen likewise two kuḍavas.
Blood is one kuḍava; phlegm is six [palas], and feces and urine are half [of that].
Mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness—this is the internal instrument.
All of that, produced within the body, is expelled by the wind of birth and goes outside; indeed, fainting, it undergoes birth.
For the entire form of the universe is situated within the body.
Satyaloka is the aperture of the head; Tapoloka is the forehead.
Janaloka is said to be the mouth, and Maharloka is declared to be the throat. One should know that Svarloka is in the heart, while Bhuvarloka is within the belly.
The region of Bhūrloka is the navel and the lower part; Atala is situated in the hips.
Vitala is said to be the private parts, and Sutala is at the roots of the thighs.
Talātala is the two thighs, and Mahātala is likewise the two knees.
The thighs are considered Rasātala, and the feet are called Pātāla.
Urine is the salt ocean here, while milk is the Kṣīroda ocean.
Phlegm is situated as the Surā ocean, and marrow is the Ghṛta ocean.

The ocean of sweet-tasting water is in the blood; the ocean of curds is in the [stomach] region; the ocean of sweet water is in the part of the abdomen; and the Garbhoda ocean is situated in the semen.
The sun and moon are in the two eyes, while Mars is said to be in the lips.
Budha is to be awakened in the heart; Guru is established in knowledge.
Śukra is in the penis; Śani is in the navel; Rāhu is established in the mouth;
and Ketu is situated in the private parts. Thus, the physical body is declared to be the Brahmāṇḍa.
Longevity, knowledge, wealth, fame, and even death—
these five are created for the embodied being while still dwelling in the womb.
Then, with face downward and feet upward, he indeed emerges from the womb to the outside.

Protected by his mother who gave him birth, and himself protecting others who depend on him, and later protected by his sons—he, that very same person, indeed dies again. Therefore, one should worship Hari constantly, without sloth, at every moment, with devotion. (51–52)
Then liberation will surely be attained, as well as heaven, the abode of all happiness—that which is unmixed with suffering and not immediately swallowed by it;
that happiness brought about by desire is the locus of the word "svarga" (heaven). //53//
"He attains all desires together with the wise Brahman.

While the king was thus bringing happiness to his kingdom and subjects for eighty thousand autumns, Śambhu then set his mind upon residing in Vārāṇasī, desiring to effect a remedy.
Having approached Bṛhaspati, the gods held a consultation with him:

"Though we have been highly honored by that king through sacrifices, we ourselves shall become the very ones who bring about his misfortune. (1.81.30) Even though the gods were well-honored by that monarch with sacrifices.
Nevertheless, humans are not truly considered friends.
Even if no harm is done to us by him, the nature of the gods is an intolerance for the excellence of others. (31-32)
In the kingdom and the household of Divodāsa, there was not even the slightest accumulation of unrighteousness.
No one at all was able to bring about the defeat of this king.
And all the men within his realm were devoted to the vow of having only one wife.
In his realm there are women devoted to their husbands. In that kingdom, there is no Brahmin who is ignorant, nor any Kshatriya who is not a hero;
likewise, there is no Vaishya lacking diligence, nor any Shudra who fails to perform service.

In his kingdom, there was no student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) devoted to the vow of Brahman, nor was there anyone who failed to show honor toward him; even within his realm, there was no one who neglected the duties of a householder.
Furthermore, there were no forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) who lived by improper means, for they were free from all worldly desire.
And those who followed the path of renunciation were never devoid of detachment.
Likewise, others in his kingdom did not wander aimlessly from the right path;
on his land, there was no one without offspring, none who lacked devotion, and no one who was destitute.
There were none who failed to serve their elders, none who died untimely deaths, and none who harbored malice toward others.
There were no flatterers, nor those who were loquacious, nor the deceitful, nor the fraudulent.
There were no heretics, no jesters, no widows, and no liquor-sellers.
In his kingdom, everywhere there was the study of the Vedas, the Shastras, and other sciences;
everywhere speech was auspicious, and there was an absence of liquor, meat, and the like.
There were no gamblers, no debtors, and no thieves. (1.81.40–41)
Even the worship of the ancestors, gods, and others was never interrupted;
in that kingdom there was no violation of vows, nor likewise any neglect of visiting sacred fords (tīrthas).
There was always affection between husband and wife, and the family was not a source of suffering.
Those worthy of worship are worshipped by those who offer praise; the supreme ones are honored by those who perform rites of adoration.
There, the learned are always respected by the subjects;
and among the learned, those preeminent in austerity are honored by the ascetics, as are those who have conquered their hunger by the practitioners of penance.
By those who have conquered their inner selves,
the knowers of Brahman perceive all reality as the very form of Brahman. Through the mouths of Brahmins, virtuous men, and virtuous women, the food of the gods is offered.
The clouds in the northeast always pour down water that fills the ponds, wells, and lakes; the earth is ever covered with grain and clothing,
and both classes of his subjects are always pure, joyful, and well-nourished.
Even though they were searching for even the slightest vulnerability in his kingdom, the gods did not find any at all.
Then Bṛhaspati said to those gods:
"Defeat will by no means occur without a vulnerability."
By employing the stratagem of sowing dissension, even one who is invulnerable may be overcome.

Even those belonging to our own side will possess the wealth of happiness therein; nevertheless, in the work of creating division, those who hold a different opinion may provide assistance. (1.81.49–50)
Having thus reached this conclusion, all the gods then informed Agni of those who move within and without him, and they all paid homage to the god of fire.
Indra then said to Agni: "You are now firmly established in Kāśī."
"In that place, you shine forth there in embodied form from that realm of objects.
Withdraw that [form] quickly; in this way, victory shall indeed be ours.
For in a state devoid of form, the officiating priests would be deprived of the offerings to gods and ancestors. || 52-53 ||
Under that king, the subjects will become destitute of wealth;
and perceiving that the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) of the word "king" has been lost,
the subjects there will become disaffected, and the treasury and military force will be depleted.
The king, too, would have his means of subsistence exhausted, and the three aims of life would perish of their own accord.
Thus Divodāsa will be weakened and either perish or depart;
consequently, our residence here in Kāśī will indeed be free from thorns.
Thinking, "He must arise entirely unmixed with defects such as excessive pride," Agni, having approached Indra's words and remembering them in his heart,
withdrew his own form from that spot.
He seized the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, and Dākṣiṇaka fires— this triad—
as well as the digestive fire within the subjects there. Consequently, the people could not find their king during the morning and midday rituals.
Then all those ritualists and cooks reflected upon that formidable fire: "What indeed can be done without fire?
Having performed his midday rites, the king entered the kitchen.

While he stood there, having arrived for the Vaiśvadeva offering and the meal, the trembling cooks informed him of his state, afflicted by hunger: "O King, if you would grant us the gift of safety, we shall announce your presence. (6.1–6.2)
"Then we shall report the truth of what occurred.
Having been thus commanded by the king, the cooks spoke slowly:
"O Lord, we do not know how the fire departed."
Once the fire had vanished from the city, how could vessels and such things possibly exist?
"Let us bring whatever has been cooked by solar heat.
At that moment, the king understood that this was indeed the work of the gods.
Having understood this through the power of asceticism and having reflected upon it, he then said:
"When the fire has gone out, there is no loss for me; indeed, there is only a loss for the gods.
The kingdom was not obtained by me from them, but was obtained from my grandfather."
By the power of my own self, I shall create wind, fire, water, and earth;
and light, and whatever else is required here—I shall create all that from consciousness. I have no need for the insentient.
While he was reflecting thus, the people of the countryside arrived;
they were ushered inside by the doorkeeper to raise that very clamor.
Having presented suitable gifts, they sat upon seats of honor.
Then they spoke of the extreme suffering caused by the fire procession.
Having heard that, the king, bringing happiness to everyone, said:
"O citizens! It was I myself who previously desired to perform this task. (1.81.70–71)
Thinking, "Let there be no harm, for [the fire] has mostly been neglected," he said with the desire that it might depart:
"O Anala, may you go; may even my life-breath depart quickly from here!
May the Moon, the Sun, Varuṇa, the Earth, and the Sky also depart from here! (72)
Through the power of union with the Blessed One, I become fire;
in fourfold form as fire, I take up and digest whatever there is.
Having myself become the vital breath (*prāṇa*), I shall give life to embodied beings.
Becoming the great wind myself, I shall support the spheres;
becoming the moon myself, I shall nourish the sprout that is the world;
and becoming the sun myself, I shall always heat this earth.
Becoming a cloud myself, I shall bring rain; I shall also become Varuṇa.
I shall abide here in the form of water, and I shall also become the earth.
I shall support the entire universe and I shall become the ether.
Having spoken thus and having consoled his own subjects, the king indeed became so;
and having manifested in many forms, he carried out various tasks. Through the yoga obtained from the Blessed One, though being one, he became manifold.
Then the king of the gods indeed assumed the form of Śalya.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Śaṅkara’s Residence on Mount Mandara after Receiving the Boon, the Arrival of the Gods from Kāśī, the Description of the Qualities of King Divodāsa’s Kingdom, and the Formulation of a Plan to Expel Divodāsa from Kāśī," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 83 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Although Mahādeva was provided with every kind of comfort in his palace on Mount Mandara, he found no happiness due to the separation from Kāśī.
To him, even the pleasure-giving Mandara mountain became a source of dullness and misery.
For the purpose of plastering, sandalwood became his fuel of dust;
at that time, lotus stalks became his bracelets, and gravel became his bangles.
The moon on his forehead became a spark from the fire of separation. (2–3)
By him, for the sake of pacifying the supreme agony of separation from Kāśī, the Gaṅgā was held within his matted locks; she was not abandoned, but was protected by force.
Furthermore, even the gods did not know that the Lord was like a fire of separation.
Absorbed in meditation, he remains as before on Mount Mandara.
This indeed is the sport of the Lord,
who, as the eight-formed one (*aṣṭamūrti*), himself performs ascetic penance through his own form while heating the entire world.
The Hālāhala poison, though it has reached his throat, does not torment him;
rather, the ever-increasing heat of separation from Kāśī torments him.
Indeed, he wears upon his chest a garland produced from cool moonstones.
Due to her separation, she brings about the illusion of a sun-gem because of her fasting for nine days;
for although this fire arising from the casting of her sidelong glances brings the pleasure of worldly enjoyment,
surely even that mind-born fire (Kāma) was reduced to ashes by the [cosmic] fire and is now tormented by it.

Even though he has rushed along the path of the Vedas, he who bestows the happiness of his own devotees becomes one whose speed is stilled and is tormented by the fire born of separation— this indeed is a tragedy.
Even the wind, having gathered droplets from the beautiful Gaṅgā at Kāśī, returns [only to find her gone].

If that supreme bliss were to touch me while I am separated [from my beloved], then happiness would arise within me. (11) Even if the dust rising from the streets of Kāśī were to come to me, carried by the blowing wind, that alone would be sufficient to forcibly ward off the unbearable suffering born of separation. (12)
Having thus beheld Śaṅkara submerged in grief, Pārvatī bowed to her husband, the god, and spoke these words that dispel inner sorrow:
"O Lord, O Mahādeva, O Protector of the worlds, O Īśvara, why [are you thus]?"
O Śaṅkara, remover of the world’s distress, you burn within my heart!
(14) I, who am beautiful and of lovely form, abide here for the sake of worshipping you;
O Lord, why do you cause me such torment? (15)
O You whose forms are the earth, water, fire, wind, ether, moon, and sun;
who are manifest through direct perception, inference, analogy, verbal testimony, postulation, tradition, and presumption;
and who possess non-apprehension, impossibility, effort, and the intuition born of yoga! 16.

O master of all yoga, how can separation from Kāśī afflict you? O omniscient inner self of all, who assumes the form of Brahman like Kāśī itself, Kāśī resides upon the tip of your trident; what distress could there be for you caused by it? (17–18)
Nevertheless, by the power of the divine, that city is celestial and bestows liberation;
herein, no limitation caused by time, space, or substance exists.
There is no manifestation, no transformation, no destruction, and no nature of unreality.
There is neither dissolution nor disappearance for one who has attained union with You, like the city of Kāśī.
O Lord! Kāśī—endowed with divine hosts, possessing divine holy sites, purifying, and bestowing divine liberation—must be visited by all means. (1.82.20–21)

There is no happiness equal to Kāśī, no stability equal to Kāśī, and no peace equal to Kāśī; Kāśī is the bestower of all goals. What is that "ka" by which happiness (*sukha*) is obtained? It is "śa. Therefore, from this "śa," happiness (*sukha*) is attained; hence it is "śī. (22)
Therefore, Kāśī is composed of bliss and is to be served by all.
Indeed, because of the residence of Brahmā, the refuge of Viṣṇu, and the dwelling of Śambhu, Kāśī possesses the form of the three deities. (23–24)
Kā is said to be Sarasvatī, while Ā is Lakṣmī herself, Ramā;
Śī is indeed the goddess Pārvatī—thus Kāśī is the embodiment of these three goddesses.
There is neither Mandara nor Himavat, nor are there gardens or forests.
Just as the celestial regions bring happiness, so too do the lands upon the earth; [yet none can punish the people dwelling in Kāśī].
Neither a god of action (karmadeva), nor Adharma, nor Yama, nor even the one born in heaven (Indra) would be able to inflict punishment here upon the people residing in Kāśī. (26–27)

Where there is the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), there is no rebirth after death; where, through dwelling, there is no stain of karma—O All-pervading Lord, when indeed shall I behold that [state]? There are many ancient cities and likewise many towns.
Indeed, at every step there are no places as prosperous as Kāśī.
All lands established in truth do not become equal to Kāśī. Just as you, so too do I suffer from the heat of Kāśī. (1.82.30)
My birthplace does not possess such power to remove suffering as Kāśī does; for liberation is not attained there through penance,
sacrifices, the fulfillment of desires, charity, dharma, vows, and the like,
in the same way that it is attained in Kāśī by the casting off of the body.
Neither through Yoga, Sāṃkhya, Vedānta, nor the knowledge of the self derived from the ritual sections of the Veda;
as eternal liberation occurs through the falling away of the body in Kāśī,
such a goal is not attained through the study of the Vedas nor even through the Brahma-vow.
Neither in the world of truth, nor in the realm of Indra, nor even in the abode of the sages,
nor in the subterranean regions such as Atala and others, is there happiness anywhere like that which is found in Kāśī.
By remembering Kāśī with the mind, one obtains the fruit of the practice of yoga.
Indeed, for a human being, the state of an animal in Kāśī is always considered superior.
Liberation occurs simply through death; what further need is there for the birth of knowledge?
Therefore, act in such a way that I may go to the Forest of Bliss (Ānandāraṇya) in Kāśī. (35–36)
Śambhu said: "O Goddess of gods! You know my vow:
I consume no object that has not been previously tasted by another, nor anything else.
Urged by Brahmā, Divodāsa took that city through righteousness."
How can it be understood that there is another teacher established there?
(38) Just as Divodāsa departed from the city of Kāśī, so too should one act; having closed one's eyes, dwelling thereafter brings happiness. (39)
Obstacles arise for the unrighteous, but not for the righteous.
He who would create an obstacle for one established in dharma meets with ruin.
Without a flaw, how indeed can one endowed with dharma be uprooted from his position?
Neither old age, nor great time, nor death, nor unappeasable diseases [afflict him];
neither obstacles, nor illnesses, nor malevolent planets, nor piśācas; neither the ways of the world (nīti) nor spirits (bhūta) cause harm to one who has gathered the Dharma.
"Therefore, O Sovereign, whom shall I dispatch so that he may put him to flight?
As Śambhu was thinking thus, the circle of Yoginīs appeared before him;
and when that wheel had arrived, Hara spoke these words:
"O Yoginīs, go quickly to where that most righteous king resides;
he is known as Divodāsa and rules Kāśī with dharma.
By means of your illusory power (māyā), act in such a way that he will swiftly abandon Kāśī. ||44-45||
"I shall return there quickly after having renovated the auspicious city of Vārāṇasī; let everything be prepared.
Having received this command with their heads bowed, they departed in eager anticipation.

"Proclaiming, 'We are most fortunate, having been graced by the gods,' we were sent for the sake of a mission to the glorious Ānandakānana. Having flown from the valley of Mount Mandara, we remained steady in the sky above Kāśī. (47–48)
They beheld a city rich with divine palaces, like another heaven;
with its banners, it seemed as if calling out to travelers standing on the road.
By means of the great lattices of white jewels, even the stainless blue sky appeared [as if covered].

They whiten everything with streams of splendor ascending to heaven. (1.82.50) Then, even in the sky, they performed various transformations of their own forms; and those women followed diverse paths of knowledge. (51)
Indeed, in various places throughout Kāśī, women appeared in diverse guises;
beautiful yoginīs descended there for the sake of accomplishing the task.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Dispatching of the Circle of Yoginīs by Śambhu to Obstruct Divodāsa Following His Intense Suffering Born of Separation from Kāśī in the Cave of Mount Mandara," within the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 82: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 83 [[Author: → Chapter 84
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Behold, Lakṣmī! To what an extent women are intent on their own self-interest;
they assume many forms until their own purpose is accomplished. (1)
Having abandoned her state as a Yoginī and concealed her divinity,
one became a female renunciant (saṃnyāsinī), while another was a human ascetic (tapasvinī). One became a maidservant (sairandhrī), and likewise, another was a female mendicant (bhikṣukī).
One was a garland-maker, another a barber, and one became a midwife;
one was a distinguished physician, another a seller of scales, one a seller of vegetables, and another a protector against snakes and other [venoms]. (3–4)
One became a dancer, another a nurse and a servant;
another became a singer, and yet another a player of musical instruments. One became a keeper of the rhythm, and another became a giver of magical spells.

One was skilled in weaving garlands, another in selling oil and such; one was knowledgeable in the rules of gambling, while another was the beloved of a cowherd. One was an actress, and yet another was a sweeper of streets and courtyards.

Another was engaged in the work of honey-making and the like; another sought out rags from the streets for clothing; another became a *śvapacī*, the daughter of an outcaste, working as a leather-worker;
and another was a virtuous woman who worked as a farmer’s wife, taking up the labor of milking and processing milk products.
Another was a resident of sacred fords (tīrtha), another was a shaven-headed nun (muṇḍinī), and yet another lived in a village hut.
One was an observer of lines and marks, another was a practitioner of writing and painting; one knew mantras for subjugation, and another was a healer of fevers.
One was skilled in the application of collyrium and possessed the power of alchemical pills;
another was adept at mixing metallic ores and the like, or at creating protective coverings from cloth.
One could enchant men and assume many forms, while another possessed the knowledge for the immobilization of speech and fire.
The mantra-giver [bestows] invisibility, the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*), the assumption of other forms, and so forth;
she knows how to perform eradication (*uccāṭana*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*); she deludes the minds of the young;
she grants desired objects; she is the knower of light (*jyotirvijñā*); and another is the protector of cattle (*paśurakṣikā*). || 12 ||
One woman was a provider of tooth-sticks, another was a collector of cow dung,
and yet another Nāgarī woman was a seller of clay.
Having become laborers and maidservants, they went from house to house.
Those yoginīs entered [the city] and wandered about day and night;
though they searched for even the slightest opening for the sake of creating obstacles, they found none.
Then, having returned to the bank of the Gaṅgā and gathered together, they remained unsuccessful. (15–16)
"What must be done? Where should we go regarding Divodāsa and his subjects? Can we find even a slight vulnerability in them? How can we put ourselves far away from them?
We must not return to our master without having achieved the success of our mission."
Having deliberated thus, they remained there and did not go to Mount Mandara.
"Who would remain near [his master] without having accomplished his master's task?
Even without our lord, we shall indeed live here in Kāśī forever. (18-19)
"Prabhu, when enraged, may take away one's livelihood; Kāśī, however, takes away the fourfold aims of life.
Therefore, one should reside in Kāśī and never go to Mandara.
Beginning with these words, the Yoginīs always remain in Kāśī.
Having wandered through the cardinal and intermediate directions, they indeed returned and remained there;
worshipping Nārāyaṇa, they bowed to Divodāsa, and they always considered him their supreme gain. (21–22)
"By virtue of the merit earned from serving Kāśī, even Īśa will come to us;
without Kāśī, he would remain distressed even there, so he must have come here.
Having thus resolved, the Yoginīs [remained] in the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana) of Śambhu.
Standing there, they remembered Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
O dweller of the lotus, listen as I recount their names here:
Gajāsyā, Siṃhavaktrā, Gṛdhrāsyā, and Kākatuṇḍikā.
Camel-faced, horse-necked, donkey-necked, boar-faced, and jackal-faced;
owl-eyed, making a terrible sound, peacock-feathered, and with the face of a sharabha;
hollow-eyed, eight-faced, humpbacked, and with a hideous countenance. (26)
Śuṣkodarī, Lalajjihvā, Śvadaṃṣṭrā, Vānarānanā,
Ṛkṣākṣī, Kekarākṣī, Bṛhattuṇḍā, Surāpriyā,
Kapālahastā, Raktākṣī, Śukī, Śyenī, and Kapotikā. (27–28)
With noose in hand and staff in hand, she is Pracaṇḍā of fierce valor;
the slayer of children, the destroyer with the noose, Kālī, the drinker of blood;
the drinker of fat, the devourer of the fetus, holding a corpse in her hand and wearing a garland of intestines.
Ṛkṣakeśī, Mahākukṣi, Nāgāsyā, Pretapṛṣṭhakā;
Dandaśūkadharā, Krauñcī, Mṛgaśṛṅgā, Vṛṣānanā;
Phāṭitāsyā, Dhūmaśvāsā, Vyomapādā, and Ūrdhvadṛṣṭikā. (1.83.30–31)
Tāpinī, Śoṣiṇī, Sthaghoṇā, Oṣṭhā, Koṭarī,
Vidyullolā, Balākāsyā, Mārjārī, Kaṭapūtanā,
Aṭṭahāsyā, Kāmākṣī, and Mṛgākṣī— these are considered to be them.
Sixty-four yoginīs are worshipped during the nine nights;
they destroy the afflictions of the wicked and protect the fetus, children, and others.
Neither ḍākinīs, nor śākinīs, nor kūṣmāṇḍas, nor rākṣasas [can harm them]. ||33-34||
Whoever should recite these names shall cause affliction to him [the enemy];
they grant victory in battle, in the royal court, or even in legal disputes.
[This is achieved] through offerings, worship, oblations, and the presentation of incense and lamps.
The yoginīs, being quickly propitiated, shall grant one's heart's desires.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the best of men, having observed a fast,
should perform an oblation with the names [of the deities] preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending in the dative case.
For each of these, a hundred and eight oblations are prescribed,
using guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter in the measure of a small jujube fruit.
With a one-pointed mind and being purified, one should contemplate one's desired object in every way.

Whatever accomplishment a person may desire, that he easily attains. (39) Then the Lord, thinking that it would be a long time before the circle of Yoginīs arrived, dispatched the Sun to ascertain the progress of events in Kāśī. (40)
Śambhu said to Sūrya: "O Ravi! Let your residence be in Divodāsa’s [city] for the sake of the preservation of dharma; act accordingly, O Divākara!
For here, there is the disparagement of a devotee who stands upon the path of dharma."
O Bhāskara! For him who does so, there shall be the destruction of all his possessions.
As long as the intellect remains firm in dharma and devotion to Mādhava persists, so long no obstacle arises; nevertheless, perform your endeavor.
By the word of Śambhu, Ravi came to Kāśī like a human being;
moving within and without Kāśī, among King Divodāsa and the subjects,
he did not perceive even the slightest impairment in the flow of dharma and devotion.
Wandering for a year, the Sun became his guest and made a request of him;
subsequently, he obtained everything and assumed many forms.
He became a beggar, a generous giver, a wretched man, an astrologer, and even a counselor.
Sometimes he may be an atheist, a rogue, one with matted hair, or a naked mendicant;
a snake-charmer, a physician for poisons, a heretic, or even one who professes the Vedas (brahmavādin).
He may be a performer of vows, a master of magic, a storyteller, or one who carries a skull-bowl.
A twice-born man who is wise, a knower of the elements, an expert in astronomy, and a master of excellent mantras;
a virtuous man who indeed follows the dharma of renunciation and assumes the form of a female ascetic;
a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra; and one who is a celibate student or a householder. (48–49)
Whether appearing as a forest-dweller, or in the form of a commoner, or even assuming the guise of a *caṇḍāla*,
he wandered thus through Kāśī, yet he found no opening anywhere.
Then, his task unaccomplished, he prepared to return once more to Mandara.
Neither out of fear of insult nor due to the power of Divodāsa did he make his dwelling in Kāśī alone, with the inner core of his heart fixed in devotion;
through that devotion, the sin arising from not having offered [the fruit] will be destroyed.
For by him who has protected the Dharma, everything has been protected;
indeed, this very True Dharma arises from serving Kāśī.
Sons, friends, wives, fields, and wealth— [are all protected thereby]. (53)
In this world, some things are obtained in every birth, while others are not obtained at all. (54) A devotee equal to Divodāsa would never be found anywhere else.
Having thus resolved that he must dwell here alone, Divākara [stayed]. (55)
Having manifested in twelve forms, he is established in the city of Kāśī:
Lokārka, Uttarārka, Sāmbāditya, Khakholaka,
Drupadāditya, Mayūkhāditya, and likewise the one named Aruṇa.
Vṛddhārka, Keśavārka, Vimalārka, and he who is called Yama—
these twelve forms of Gaṅgāditya are established in Kāśī.
They constantly worship Śrī Hari during the assembly of Divodāsa.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Sixty-four Yoginīs assuming various forms to seek a vulnerability in Divodāsa, the Sun’s residence in Kāśī itself for that same purpose, and his dwelling in Kāśī in twelve forms," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 84 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*)
— Chapter 84.
[The Author: Chapter 85.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī! Whichever lord the god Mahādeva sends forth, [he goes].
He did not return again; Haras was submerged in anxiety:
"The yoginīs have not yet arrived, nor has the sun yet appeared.
If my residence in Kāśī were not certain, by what means would my time pass? (1–2)
"I have burned away my passion; let not passion torment me further.
Whom shall I send from here to seek news of Kāśī?"—having thus reflected, he addressed the Creator with great respect.
Śiva said: "O Yoginīs, Sūrya was sent by me;
yet even now they have not returned from Kāśī, despite learning of my condition. The poison did not afflict me as much as the separation from Kāśī does."
"O Creator, ordain my task; go to Kāśī and strive there.
I must depart this very day, yet I must do so righteously.
I cannot, however, bring myself to transgress against King Divodāsa."

"One should not dwell in another's kingdom, nor should one eat what has been left over. (7) "Go with well-being; may your path be auspicious and lead to a happy result. Having received this command, Vidhi immediately departed for Kāśī through the sky. (8)
Seated upon the swan, he beheld the auspicious Ānandavāṭikā of Kāśī,
where the Gaṅgā, the trees, the people, and the palaces were eternally filled with bliss.
Indeed, those very senses by which the land of Kāśī was perceived still remain.

"Indeed, those excellent grasses and grains that fall here in Kāśī—today my life has become fruitful; oh, how great is my good fortune! Today the tree of my body has borne fruit, since I have beheld Kāśī."

"I have created this entire universe, preceded by great skill; yet Kāśī has been fashioned by the Lord himself in an entirely different manner. With a joyful heart, Brahmā, assuming the guise of an elderly brahmin, [proceeded].
Descending from the swan onto the earth, he beheld Divodāsa.
Honored by the king and likewise treated with hospitality, the aged brāhmaṇa sat upon a beautiful seat and bestowed blessings upon the monarch.
"Increase of the treasury when wealth is real; increase of happiness in the next life;
increase of progress on the true path; and increase of *kāśa* grass within your own interior.
(15) The King said: "O venerable Brahmin, why do you speak with double meanings?"

Where there is an increase in righteousness and devotion, there true prosperity always increases. (16) But when it occurs toward one who lacks substance or follows an improper path, prosperity brings fear;
for when it is with one lacking substance, it results in the birth of a son, yet when on an improper path, it leads to running away. (17)
Indeed, during the interval between years, no unhappiness shall befall the righteous person;
however, for the unrighteous person, unhappiness will arise within that same interval.
In praise, there is an increase in manifest prosperity, whereas in the interval, it is not otherwise, being turbid.
"What do you desire, O aged brahmin! Deprived of wealth and treading a wrong path, what is it that you wish for?
Is it the increase of hypocrisy in my heart, or that I become Divodāsa after a year of suffering? What is it that you desire? (1.84.20)
"Do you wish for my escape from Kāśī? What do you desire?

Where there is a Brāhmaṇa of deceitful speech, where the protector of the earth (the king) assumes a false guise, and where there is a false dharma—there may you be one who utters false blessings. (21)
Brahmā said: "In this matter, there is deception, hypocrisy, and the pride of the horned ones (the Śṛṅgiyas).
Wherever a Brāhmaṇa is a merchant in speech, a 'protector of the earth' (king) in dress, and follows the dharma of a merchant, there my blessings shall be excellent. (22-23)
If there is indeed deceit, it is certainly hypocrisy and nothing else. Where a Brahmin is a hypocrite in speech and a priest who wears a hypocritical garb,
there the dharma will be hypocritical and the blessings he utters will be hypocritical.
Then the king said to the Brahmin Brahmā, who was a hypocrite of dharma:
"If you are thus the very embodiment of dharma, why do you engage in deceit?
In deceit, defeat is inevitable; one whose feet are in deceit falls downward."
"Come, O Brahmin! I shall offer you a welcome according to the dharma of sincerity. Accept the water for the feet, food, fruit, the water of the Ganges to be drunk, and the unguent.
Take all of these, O best of Brahmins! Choose whatever dwells in your heart."
Brahmā said: "O King, you have accepted that with devotion; thus you flourish!
O King, you triumph through knowledge that awakens the truth and through righteousness.
Many kings have been seen by me who were performers of sacrifice and givers of abundant sacrificial fees."
O King, though there are those who are learned in the Vedas, skilled in ethics, virtuous in character, and masters of their senses—
grounds of forgiveness, compassion, profound depth, courtesy, and gentleness—
nevertheless, O King, you possess two or three qualities that are particularly superior even to theirs.
Your subjects alone are your family; the Brahmins alone are your deity.
Devotion and righteousness are your companions, and the ascetics are your helpers.
These qualities are not seen in others; indeed, you are blessed and worthy of honor among the virtuous.
"You are worthy of worship for your six virtues; you flourish through devotion and righteousness.
O righteous one! Even the gods fear to commit an offense against you.
As for me, O King, I am a brahmin who has come here to perform sacrifices."
"Having found a devotee such as you, let my residence be here.
As for that other [place] consecrated by mantras, let it remain far away forever.
O King, there are three sacred sites (tīrthas) here: you, the Gaṅgā, and the Earth—the highest of the high. || 34-35 ||
"Where there is no exhaustion even at the dissolution of the world for deeds performed,
let that wealth which has been accumulated with effort be employed in sacrifice.
To the Brahmin who remained silent after saying this, Divodāsa spoke.
"I am your servant in every way, O King, who now desires to sacrifice to Hari.
Take from my treasury whatever sacrificial materials you require.
[Know that I possess] the sovereign, the ministers, friends, the treasury, the kingdom, the fortresses, and a strong army. (37–38)
Appoint him to his necessary duties, but not even slightly for his own private interests.
A king should delight his subjects with his sons, his wives, and his own person.
The fire born from the suffering of the subjects is more terrifying than even a thunderbolt.
The thunderbolt may destroy two or three—suffering, kingdom, family, or body—but with the dust from the feet of brahmins, I always perform my purificatory bath.
That which is offered into the mouth of a brahmin, I consider to be superior to any sacrifice. (1.84.40–41)
Even today, there remains but one aspiration for the sake of the Brahmins:
that even one's own body may become fruitful through its offering for their sake. Today my life has borne fruit; let us conquer! Perform sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees.

"Sacrifice to the gods; know that assistance must be rendered with all available materials. (43) Having heard the king's words, the Brahmin Brahmā gathered the necessary provisions and performed ten horse-sacrifices on the banks of the Gaṅgā. (44)
At that spot, having abandoned its former name Rudrasaras, that sacred ford (tīrtha) attained the renowned appellation Daśāśvamedha; thus,
it found no flaw whatsoever in the devotee Divodāsa.
What would the Creator say upon going to Mount Mandara before Śambhu?
Therefore, having installed the Daśāśvamedheśa Liṅga as well as the Brahmeśvara Liṅga and his own image, Vidhi (Brahmā) dwelt right there.
Through the company of the virtuous, Divodāsa became a perpetual devotee of Hari.
Whatever bliss known as liberation exists in Satyaloka, Vairāja, Vaiṣṇava, and Śāmbhava realms, that indeed is obtained by serving Kāśī.
Having bathed on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one shall be released from bondage.
(49) Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, libations to the ancestors, twilight worship, worship of the gods, and ancestral rites performed there become inexhaustible. (50)
Having bathed on the Daśaharā day and worshipped the Liṅga,
one obtains the merit of ten horse-sacrifices and shall not enter a womb again.
Brahmā remains there in the form of a Brāhmaṇa until the arrival of Śiva.
Divodāsa, however, caused a Brahma-shālā to be built for Brahmā;
there, the city of Brahmā (Brahmapurī), made by Ahalyā, was most beautifully adorned.
Thus, this land is eternally sacred to Brahmā and bestows the world of Brahmā.

"O beloved! What kind of great devotee was Divodāsa to me, such that even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were unable to repay his kindness? Thus ends the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Following the dialogue after Śambhu had sent Brahmā from Mount Mandara—who, in the form of a brāhmaṇa, offered blessings through deceptive verses—the [account of] Daśāśva—
The eighty-fourth chapter, titled "Having performed sacrifices of wisdom, one should dwell in Kāśī," etc.,

Chapter 85.
[The Author: Chapter 86.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, O Great Goddess! Hara was dwelling on Mount Mandara.
She grieved there in many ways: "They have indeed gone and do not return again.
Are they perhaps staying in Kāśī, their purpose unaccomplished and their vigor destroyed? Why do the Yoginīs, Sūrya, and Brahmā not return? Whom shall I dispatch? (1–2)
Thinking thus, the Lord of the Gods summoned his hosts in great numbers and dispatched them, saying: "Go quickly to Kāśī to dwell there!
[He summoned] Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahākāla, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and Mahodara.
Nandiṣeṇa, Somanandin, Kāla, Piṅgala, Kukkuṭa;
Kuṇḍodara, Mayūrākṣa, Bāṇa, Gokarṇa, Tāraka;
Tilaparṇa, Sthūlakarṇa, Dṛmicaṇḍa, and Prabhāmaya. (4–5)
Sukeśa, Vindati, Chāga, Kapardin, Piṅgalākṣa, Vīrabhadra, Kirāta, Caturmukha, Nikumbha,
Pañcākṣa, Bhārabhūta, Kṣemaka, and likewise Lāṅgalin.
Śaṅkara dispatched Tryakṣa, Virādha, Sumukha, Āṣāḍhi, and Skanda; as well as Mahāśākha, Viśākha, Śākha, Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and Naigameya. (7–8)
These highly fortunate hosts, devoted to their master and firm in their vows,
being skillful and assuming many forms through various illusions,
remained with unblinking eyes, longing for a vulnerability in the king.
In matters of dharma, truth, and compassion; in punishment and the protection of subjects;

in guarding [the realm], in the duty of charity, and in the duties of kingship; according to the Śruti and Smṛti; and in the duties concerning the castes, stages of life, calamities, place, time, and so forth.
Having performed the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), recitations (*japa*), and service with devotion and hospitality,
and having never incurred any loss, deficiency, or flaw whatsoever;
and having honored King Divodāsa, who was incapable of being defeated.
All the Gaṇas, their own tasks unaccomplished, were deeply ashamed.
Having installed Mahādeva under their respective names, they took up residence in Kāśī itself and remained there free from all distress. (13–14)
They did not turn back from Mount Mandara until they had understood the greatness of Kāśī.
Vārāṇasī must never be abandoned; it is more precious than even heaven.
Nothing else is equal to the bliss obtained in the Garden of Bliss (Ānandodyāna).
Here Kailāsa itself exists, and Vaikuṇṭha is also found here. How can one abandon Kāśī and adopt a parched state of existence on Mount Mandara? It is called Vārāṇasī, Kāśī, and also Ānandodyāna.
For him by whom this has been proclaimed from the mouth, there is no fear of Yama.
His body, measuring five *krośas*, is born of the three gods;
it belongs to those who have not accumulated merit and whose wealth and lifespan are exhausted.
For those who are devoid of all other means, the city of Vārāṇasī is their refuge.
Those wise ones who dwell in Kāśī with the firm resolve to remain until death are to be known as liberated while living; they alone are indeed worthy of salutation and worship.
In that Kāśī, where a dying creature is bowed to with great effort by Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and others, who stand with palms joined above their heads;
where death is auspicious and where divine manifestation is the ornament.
Where even a loincloth is made of silk from Kāśī, how can anything else be compared to it?
(22) Having abandoned brothers, wife, son, field, home, and wealth—even accepting death—one must indeed dwell here [in this land]. (23)

Thus, having reached this conclusion, they remained right there in Kāśī. Then Śambhu, perceiving that his Gaṇas had gone to Kāśī, stayed there, and had not yet returned, dispatched Heramba, the elephant-faced one.
"Go, my son! Indeed, without you, no one else will be able to deal with the king.
Having devised a plan according to your intelligence, the proper time, and what is appropriate, expel Divodāsa and bring Kāśī under your control. (25-26)
"Even while remaining there, strive for complete success together with your hosts;
ensure that we are free from obstacles, and create an obstacle for the king.
Having received this command, he bowed his head and prostrated before Dhūrjaṭi.
Gaṇeśa set out quickly for Kāśī for the sake of his father’s success. Meanwhile, the Brāhmaṇa remained there, contemplating the means for Śambhu’s arrival at Kāśī;
he wore thick wrappings and the five-fold marks of ashes while indicating auspicious omens.
The knower of constellations, a master of the great circle of luminaries, entered the city;
the elder moved through the inner apartments, indicating [the future] by means of lines.
He examined the lines on the hands, auspicious omens, fortune, and the letters of birth.
Having observed them closely and performed calculations, he became filled with joy for the citizens. At night, he himself would show a dream to the people;
then, having gone to their houses in the morning, he would tell them of their good and bad fortune.
Having set aside those questions, he declared to them his dream-result:
"In a dream last night, while you were bathing in the water, you reached the bank;
having become submerged in the mud on the bank, you sank down again and again. (33)
The fruit of this dream is evil; there shall be an injury to you by water.
Furthermore, having gone to another’s house, you indeed described the dream-fruit [there].
Then, in the dream, you saw a shaven-headed man wearing garments of *kāśa* grass.
The result will be either suffering equal to death or death itself;
or, if a solar eclipse is seen in a dream, the result is death or something equivalent to it. If two rainbows are perceived at night, one's conviction [regarding the outcome] is certain.

"In the west, the sun itself, having reached its rising, caused the moon—just as it was emerging from the path of the sky—to fall to the earth. This was seen by you in a dream; the loss of your kingdom will certainly come to pass. (37–38)
Two comets were seen fighting in the sky;
that too was a dream-omen portending the destruction of the kingdom and bringing about ruin.
Furthermore, one tooth fell out and was carried away toward the south. (39)

That you saw yourself [in that state] was the terrifying death of your family. That you beheld in the latter part of the night the breaking of the palace flagstaff is a great portent foreboding the ruin of the kingdom and calamity among the subjects. (1.85.40–41)
This city that you saw has been flooded by the ocean;
within just two months, there will be a great destruction of its inhabitants.
In a dream, you traveled toward the south on a vehicle drawn by monkeys.
Therefore, your destruction or your departure from this city is certain.
That woman whom you saw weeping at night, naked, with disheveled hair, traveling through the sky—the fruit of that omen is the overturning of the kingdom. (43–44)
Since you have seen the pinnacle of the temple falling,
the destruction of the kingdom will certainly occur very soon, within just a few days.
Deer, jackals, and other such animals will repeatedly come from all around the city.
They are seen crying out piteously; therefore, one should not abandon the city during that month.
46. Owls, hawks, cranes, and vultures are flying all around the city;
they portend great suffering for those dwelling here. 47.
If Hanumān takes up his mace and strikes the back [of the image], destruction is certain. The messengers of Yama are seen stationed upon buffalo-drawn chariots;
they depart taking the subjects with them, and the destruction of the subjects will be certain.
Moreover, soldiers from a foreign kingdom will come here and strike them down.
The result of this will be the destruction of Kāśī and the slaughter of the people.
Therefore, one must certainly depart for another place within a month.
"Indeed, staying here for more than two months will not bring happiness.
Thus he caused them to depart, addressing many of the subjects;
for roughly half of the population then went toward other lands.
Furthermore, having observed the movement of the planets, he spoke again to the people:
"Venus, Saturn, and Mars are situated in a single zodiac sign and are bringers of destruction.
This comet, having pierced the circle of the Seven Sages in the sky," ||| 52–53 ||
If Saturn goes toward the western quarter, he becomes the destroyer of Vaiśyas. When Saturn, having transgressed his zodiacal sign, moves in retrograde motion,
conjoined with Rāhu, Ketu, and Mars, he indeed causes great destruction.

At evening time, however, an earthquake will certainly bring about destruction. (55) A meteor moving from north to south across the sky, accompanied by thundering, and even one that vanishes as it falls, likewise portends ruin. (56)
Even though the sacred tree at the shrine of the four crossroads has been uprooted by the wind,
it nevertheless portends a great slaughter of the people of Kāśī.
At dawn, with the rising of the sun in the east, the crow cries out that there shall be danger.
Two wild deer from the forest, having entered the heart of Kāśī,
escaped the gaze of the people and departed as omens of the city's desolation.
In autumn, the blossoms of the mango and *śāla* trees and the sprouts of their fruit are seen.

"I believe there is a great and untimely danger in this city. Having thus instilled fear by means of the Brahmin Gaṇeśa, those wealthy men and even the landed gentry were driven away along with their families. (1.85.60)
Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*,
Śaṅkara dispatched forty-two Gaṇas and sent Gaṇeśa; by him [Gaṇeśa] was described various dreams, direct perceptions, auspicious omens, portents, and so forth.
The eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Expulsion of the Subjects from Kāśī," [Chapter 85].

Chapter 87 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then, having first ascertained the news through meditative concentration for the sake of gaining the women's trust, Gaṇeśa indeed entered the inner apartments.
By speaking only of matters already perceived, he became the object of the women's confidence.
Whatever had previously occurred, he recounted it all:
having approached one [woman], he said, "Ninety-three sons were born to you; among them, one fell from a horse and died. (2–3)
"By good fortune, this pregnant woman will give birth to an auspicious daughter;
whereas she was unfortunate until now, she has become truly blessed today, for the King has bestowed upon her this most beautiful pearl necklace. (4)
"O Queen, she is indeed worthy of honor, for she lives as if she were you yourself.
The King constantly regards her as one who is the object of his great affection;
moreover, two villages have been declared to be granted to her by his grace."
Then the prince said to another queen: "If a son is born, I shall indeed grant you ten villages for your livelihood.
Thus was it promised by the king on his bed in your presence.

Then he said to another: "If you are my good daughter, I shall grant you half the kingdom. To that, the good daughter replied: "At the time of [giving] affection to another, the king spoke for my sake. (8–9)
"Give me that betel which you have kept; I shall grant you the three cities.
Thus did the Lord of the Gaṇas speak, appearing visibly before them.
He even spoke of their dreams, whereby he became the object of their trust.
And the queens describe his many virtues in his absence:
"Oh, there is a certain elderly Brahmin who discerns the truth;
he speaks of past events exactly as they occurred, according to all valid means of knowledge."
Free from greed, of virtuous conduct, contented, and perceiving the past and future;
with a serene countenance, pure, and proficient in the scriptures, the Vedas, and the legal codes—whatever he declares through his inner light, all that proceeds as truth. (13)
No other such dream-interpreter was seen, yet the one who spoke it directly appeared before their eyes.
(14) O Great King, Queen Līlāvatī herself, whose limbs were as fair as a royal turban, spoke to the king: "The Brahmin is a treasure-house equal to Brahmā. (15)
Someone from Kāśī should be sought out for the purpose of awakening the planets;

he knows everything—what the planetary period (daśā) is, what kind of dream it is, what the time is, and what the omen (śakuna) may be. Therefore, one should indeed ask him regarding whatever is yet to happen.
Having heard this, the Lord of the Gaṇas was then summoned by the king;
he approached the royal sage and, having received his hospitality,
sat upon a seat and greeted him with blessings.
"May there be safety and well-being for you, as well as spiritual merit and worldly prosperity.
May auspicious dharma be yours, and may your dwelling be in the palace, the abode of Hari.
Having heard this, the king said to that brahmin, "O twice-born one!"

"Whatever has been acquired, whatever has been protected, whatever security and auspicious happiness exists on this earth—all that may go to destruction (laṃ layaṃ yāyāt); such is your desire. May my welfare and prosperity be for the sake of Śiva’s auspiciousness. (20–21)
"May even that which is prosperity and auspiciousness become unrighteousness for me! May there be the kingdom of Śiva in my palace, and liberation in Hari!
O best of the twice-born, what do you desire from me other than destruction from this place?"
Having realized the omniscience of Divodāsa, he was struck with wonder.
Then Gaṇeśa, having taken the worthy [child], went to his own abode.
At that time, the king said to the queen: "This brahmin is a seer of the three periods of time."
The subjects flee to other lands; dreams appear terrifying;
a clamor is heard; and a state of being on the verge of imminent destruction prevails.
In the morning, he should clearly be summoned and asked: "What will happen? (25)
"I think that even the god Śaṅkara has turned against me and is no longer my benefactor (aśaṅkara).
Whatever is destined to happen will surely come to pass by the will of Nārāyaṇa.
In the morning, having summoned him and honored him, the king asked what was on his heart.
This entire earth has been governed; enjoyments and prosperities have been experienced;
and indeed, the kingdom and its subjects have been protected by me without weariness as if they were my own life.
Service to the twice-born has been performed fully; nothing remains incomplete for me.
"Having observed the flight of the subjects and the wickedness in dreams, I am indeed bewildered as to what is to come; tell me the truth.
Gaṇeśa replied: "Kings are generally flatterers of the ears. (29–30)
They listen only to what is sweet and punish those who speak harshly;
yet I speak both the sweet and the bitter truth—let it be endured.
One who is valiant, fortunate, heroic, renowned, meritorious, and highly intelligent—
Indeed, even the Lord of the Thirty-three gods does not equal you in heaven.
In wisdom you are like Bṛhaspati; in grace, you are like the moon;
in splendor, you are like the sun; and in majesty, you are like fire.
In strength you are equal to Vāyu, in prosperity you resemble Kubera;
as a teacher you are like the god Rudra, and in battle you are like Nirṛti.
You are Varuṇa in your noose for the wicked, and you are Yama, the King of Justice, in your rod of punishment.
In forbearance you are like the earth, and in maintaining the bounds of propriety, you are like the lord of rivers.
In greatness you are indeed like Himavat, and in statesmanship you are like Śukra to a king.
You are a king comparable to Manu, and in removing distress, you are considered equal to the rain-cloud.
Pure as the Gaṅgā, you grant a happy rebirth like Kāśī;
you are the source of creation, nourishment, and destruction, and you embody the purposes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
Sarasvatī resides in your mouth, and Kamalā dwells in your lotus-like hand.
Poison resides in your anger, while nectar dwells in your speech.
Nārāyaṇa is in your heart, yet my disciples are not in you;
indeed, I have come to your courtyard to provide for their livelihood.
I speak what is true and not what is untrue; I speak what is concealed and not what is false.
I speak for my own sake, yet it is rich with the welfare of others; I speak sweetly, though the fruit is bitter.
O King, from this day forward, on the eighteenth day, a Brāhmaṇa...
Someone from the north will surely come and instruct you.
You must act exactly according to that; then you will attain what resides in your heart.
Today I am going to my own home; wait for his arrival.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Gaṇeśa remained right there in Kāśī.
For the sake of his renown, the names of the illustrious Gaṇeśa are as follows, corresponding to his various forms:
Ḍhuṇḍhivināyaka, Arkavināyaka, and Gaṇādhipa.
Dūrga, Bhīmacaṇḍa, Dehalināyaka,
Uddaṇḍa, Pāśapāṇi, Kharva, and Siddhivināyaka— these eight Vināyakas reside in the outer enclosure at Kāśī. 44–45.
Lambodara, Kūṭadanta, as well as Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa,
Kūṣmāṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Vikaṭadanta, and Rājaputraka,
along with Praṇava— these eight Vināyakas are in the second enclosure.
Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadanta, Kapisiṃha, Dvipānana,
Pañcāsya, Heramba by name, Vighnarāja, and Varaprada—
these eight, who are fond of sweetmeats (modaka), are situated in the third enclosure. 47–48.
Abhayada, Siṃhatuṇḍa, Kūṇitākṣa, Gajānana,
Kṣipraprasādana, and then Cintāmaṇi-Vināyaka;
Dantahasta, Piciṇḍila, and the one known as Uddaṇḍamuṇḍa.
These eight lords of the Gaṇas are situated in the fourth enclosure (caturthāvaraṇa).
Sthūladanta, Kalipriya, Caturdanta, Dvituṇḍavat,
Jyeṣṭha, Gaja, Kāla, and Nāgeśa are in the fifth enclosure (pañcamāvṛti).
Maṇikarṇa, Āśāvināyaka, Sṛṣṭigaṇādhipa,
the one known as Yakṣa-gajakarṇa, Citraghaṇṭa, Sthūlajaṅghaka,
Maṅgala, and Mitranāyaka— these eight are considered to be surrounded by the sixty [Gaṇas].
Moda, Pramoda, Saṃmoda, Mahāmoda, Arthada,
Jñāna, Dvāra, and the one called Vimukta— these eight reside in the seventh enclosure.
These fifty-six Gaṇeśas are stationed all around Kāśī.
Even by merely hearing these names, one is liberated from sufferings;
one shall never be obstructed by impediments and is freed even from sins.

(55) Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, Gaṇeśa related to Divodāsa the previous events, dreams, and so forth, for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the women of the king's inner apartments, as well as the future calamities and other matters.
The eighty-sixth chapter, titled "Description," in which the abiding of the fifty-six Gaṇeśas and other matters have been told, [ends].

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord of my husband! Salutations to you; Gajānana has indeed become one whose soul is Kṛṣṇa.
Was he previously established in Kāśī and later on Mount Mandara?

In the same way, you too should not act as those who went before have done.

That indeed is celebrated as Pādodakī Gaṅgā by the foremost among devotees.
(5) Hell shall not touch a man who has performed the ritual bath with its water, who has drunk its water, or who has offered its water for drinking. (6)

Drinking the water from the washing of the feet with water [from elsewhere], one shall attain immortality. (8) At the sacred ford of Viṣṇu’s foot-water, one should drink the water from Viṣṇu’s feet; thus, he will deliver seven times seven, and then seven more, generations of his own lineage. (9)

The great holy site of Matsyodara, the beautiful temple of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa,

This [Self] manifests by itself and dissolves by itself alone.

The five organs of action and the five organs of cognition, along with the mind and the intellect—this auspicious twelvefold field of perception (dvādaśāyatana) is to be worshipped. There is neither merit nor demerit, nor indeed heaven or hell. (1.87.30)

"An act consisting of violence must never, under any circumstances, be performed; it must never be performed. To destroy that [violence], one should go to mountains, forests, and open lands.

He said: "The body of human beings is indeed obtained through one's own karma.

Thus, due to the instruction of the Noble One (Āryā), the noble ones no longer performed service; furthermore, rites such as giving and fire-offerings (homa) were obstructed and ceased to occur. Consequently, the entire ritual procedure for bathing the deity also vanished.

Dispassion has arisen in my mind, and I desire to depart for the forest. (47) The entire kingdom has been properly governed, and all enjoyments have been experienced by the power of Hari. There is only one offense, however: I have treated the gods as if they were mere blades of grass. (48)

"Expelled from the kingdom by me, who have attained power through the strength of asceticism, tell me now whatever you wish; I shall do exactly as you say. Furthermore, all my subjects remain devoted to their own respective duties."
In ancient times, the three cities were reduced to ashes by you with ease;

For the sake of its pacification, you must subsequently install a single *liṅga* named Kāśī-Viśveśvara on the seventh day from today; then,

he constructed a great pavilion and summoned the subjects,

the domestic priest, the chamberlain, the officiating priests, the astrologers, the twice-born, the feudal lords, the princes, the cooks, and the physicians. (1.87.59–60)
She spoke with deep emotion to many foreigners, as well as to the children, cowherds, and the elderly, and to the queen and all those in the inner apartments:
"From this day until the seventh day, my death will certainly occur."
I shall consecrate Prince Samarañjaya as king in my realm.
Let the artisans build a palace for the sake of Kāśī Viśveśvara,
and I myself shall listen to the seven-day recitation of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
"Let that very same wealth be given to me repeatedly for the purpose of expenditure.
Then Śambhu himself led his entire retinue to Kāśī,
having assumed the form of a brahmin and arrived there in connection with that very story.
The Brāhmaṇa himself was Viṣṇu, who had reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras;
at that time, he was the expounder there, while Hara was the reciter.
The sages were the chanters there, and the gods were the members of the assembly.
A great Dharma-sacrifice has arisen, such as has never occurred before nor will ever occur again;

On the completion of the seventh day, in the temple resplendent with gold—
Then, having installed Viśveśvara according to the great ritual procedure,

with a gracious countenance, he was charming as he broke into a smile. (71–72)

Divodāsa, through supreme devotion, forgot everything else, O Lord! || 73 ||

Saying "I am coming," he assumed that very same divine body. (74) But with his body intact, having been sprinkled by the waters of Brahman from Mahālakṣmī, he became a great liberated one—divine, possessing a body, and equal to Viṣṇu. (75)
He ascended that celestial chariot and indeed entreated Hari:
"O Bestower of Liberation, lead even those subjects who are devoted to you.
Hari said: "O Divodāsa, by whomsoever and by whatever means one desires [to attain me],"
"Let those who wish to come to Vaikuṇṭha approach without being hindered.

then, shouts of "Victory! arose throughout Kāśī and the three worlds.

Whoever reads or even hears this story is indeed liberated.
For through devotion, he is truly capable of delivering many living beings;
for one equal to Divodāsa, Vaikuṇṭha is attained both here and in the hereafter.

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
In former times, Śambhu went away at the request of Mount Mandara.
How indeed did that offense against the gods by Divodāsa come about?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! to this divine story of how enmity arose.

Due to the rain, the destruction of Kāśī, and the upheaval of the region,

Then the god Mahādeva summoned clouds from all sides.
Having bound them all with his matted locks, he became invisible through meditative absorption.
Having gone to the peak of Kailāsa and stationed the Gaṇas as guards,
he remained in meditative absorption for ten years and did not wake up.
At that time, due to drought, the lands fell into utter ruin.
At that time, Divodāsa was his devotee, established in severe austerity.
At that time, the earth was bereft of its kingdom and the gods had departed for heaven;
no humans were to be seen as a universal upheaval descended.
There is no fixed order among the four modes of birth; sacrifices and other rites do not exist there.
Neither edible food nor sacrificial offerings are found, nor are leaves or flowers to be obtained. (8)

Men, as well as Rākṣasas, gods, living beings, spirits, Piśācas, and forest-dwellers, were running hither and thither. (1.88.10)
Indeed, everything on the surface of the earth became unsettled and filled with great terror.
Young women were carried off by others, and food and wealth could not be obtained.
At that time, in a land without a king, both gods and humans were miserable.
Having propitiated Brahmā, the king who was possessed of great majesty, ||12||
They chose to provide assistance to the gods so that there might indeed be rain. While they were searching for a king equal to Viṣṇu, Brahmā spoke to them:
"Go; I shall employ every means to destroy their suffering."
Having himself ascended a celestial chariot, he went to the Himālaya mountain.
Upon seeing Divodāsa performing most formidable austerities, blazing with splendor like a flash of lightning, Brahmā spoke these beneficial words. (15)
Behold, O King, that I, Brahmā himself, have come here for the sake of protecting the world; what do you, being an ascetic, accomplish here?
Neither penance nor human prowess is equal to the service of others.
There is neither meditation, nor fire-offering, nor even any other ritual action. //17//
If Hari is propitiated by penance, what of it?
If Hari is not propitiated by penance, what of it?
If one has attained desirelessness through penance, what of it?
If you have fallen into a state of craving for existence, then you shall obtain the fruit [of that action]. (18)
When the fruit comes of its own accord and falls into one's hand, who else would be more senseless than he who neither takes it nor enjoys it? (19)
The gods are pleased with whomever they favor for some purpose; since he does not respect them, who else has such fruitless exertion? (1.88.20)
O King! Having completed your ascetic penance, understand my beneficial words:
no one other than you is capable of warding off this terrible drought. (21)

I consider you to be Viṣṇu, you to be Mahārudra, and you to be Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures; for by virtue of performing those respective functions, you are their emblem and identical with them. (22)
For those such as you, the dharma of asceticism is not appropriate during a national upheaval.
Accept the dharma of service and rule the kingdom bestowed by me. (23)
"Come, I shall indeed place this crown upon your head;
I shall perform your consecration with the water from my water-pot. (24)
Now Lord Śaṅkara, having abandoned the great forest of Avimukta, bound the great clouds and led them away, going to a cave. ||25||
"Accept this great kingdom and the capital city of Kāśī; once your consecration has taken place, rain will immediately fall. (26)
May all living beings be happy, and may Hari be pleased;
through this, the fruitfulness of one's birth will be achieved even more than through ascetic penance. (27)
When this had been said by Brahmā, the king closed his eyes, prostrated himself on the ground like a staff before the Creator, and indeed paid homage with his heart. (28)
"O Grandfather, salutations to you; I shall obey my father's command.
When one's father has arrived with a gracious countenance, who indeed would not be satisfied? (29)
When the opportunity for the gods or the ancestors has arrived, a person who does not carry out their command is undoubtedly a seller of his own fortune. (1.88.30)
Whether it be the father, the grandfather, or even the great-grandfather, whatever he may command must indeed be carried out by the wise son. (31)
Those very three are indeed the gods, and they are also the Vedas;
they alone are the bestowers of liberation, devoted to the granting of blessings. //32//
However, if any obstacle whatsoever is seen for the son who is carrying out the task, it must be destroyed; therefore, I shall report something to you. (33)
In the divine worlds of the gods, among the Daityas, Dānavas, and Bhogins, there exists no established order of dharma such as that which has been ordained here for human beings. (34)
If some being other than a human were to dwell upon the earth, then there would be an obstruction of human attributes among women and others. (35)
The gods consider the duty of devotion to one's wife as something not even to be thought of;
therefore, if they were not within my domain, I would rule a righteous kingdom. (36)
Brahmā said: "O King, you whose disposition is pure, you are increasing in excellence.
Accept this crown from the Gaṅgā, the water, the sword, and the garland. (37)
The foremost gods, having been summoned there, arrived in an instant;
in a moment the consecration was performed, and a proclamation was made in the assembly. (38)
Let the deities and others dwelling here, as well as those residing in other worlds, hear this: no non-human beings must enter the kingdom of Divodāsa. (39)
All those gods who dwell there must go elsewhere;
whoever does not acknowledge my authority is excluded from the gods. (1.88.40)
"He must be excluded from my creation"—this is the firm decree of the Creator.
All the non-human gods, as well as the dwellings of Atala and the other netherworlds, [are likewise excluded]. (41)
Then, having emerged from Kāśī, they went to other mountains and such places in the celestial realm where there was no human habitation nor any mixture of gods.
Śaṅkara, however, had previously gone [there] when he was entreated by Mandara.
The three gods, whose abode is the thirty [heavens], have gone to the dwellings of their respective lords. 43.
By expelling the gods, Divodāsa became a great enemy; indeed, he inflicted the punishment of exile upon them for their offense. (44)
"Gods must never at any time come to my kingdom—those who are intent on their own interests, those greedy for the wealth of others, and those who are deeply attached to the wives of others. (45)
"Let them not enter my kingdom, and once they have entered, let them meet their destruction"—from this proclamation that arose, the gods became enraged. (46)
The sun did not shine at all, nor did the moon provide coolness;
fire did not cook food, and Indra indeed did not send rain. 47.
The wind did not blow there, and the seasons were then adverse;
likewise, all of them were enraged, as was Divodāsa himself at that time. ||48||
Through union with Nārāyaṇa Hari, he shines assuming the form of the sun;
and becoming the moon, he nourishes the medicinal herbs and bestows nectar.
Becoming fire, he cooks; becoming a cloud, he rains; becoming wind, he blows; and becoming the season, he brings forth blossoms. (1.88.50)
And wherever any task was dependent upon the gods, he himself, assuming the form of those respective deities, would swiftly accomplish it. (51)
Having himself become the sacrifice and having become that circle of deities, he himself offers it to Nārāyaṇa and himself eats what remains. 52.
No other god whatsoever, not even Nārāyaṇa, would call out to anyone else;
therefore, those gods, being exceedingly enraged, do not come there at all.
The fault caused by Avagraha was destroyed by Divodāsa;
because he conquers his enemies through the power of Nārāyaṇa, he is called Ripuñjaya. (54)
Having attained such renown as both "of heaven" and "servant of Nārāyaṇa," his name became truly meaningful as Divodāsa. ||55||
Truthfulness, moral conduct, celibacy, non-violence, renunciation, and straightforwardness;
the vision of the Self in all as Brahman, and likewise the realization of the Self in all beings. (56)
Service to the virtuous and the chaste, and oneness with Nārāyaṇa—such excellent qualities, preceded by moral conduct, exist there. (57)
These—wish-fulfilling cows, wish-granting trees, and thought-fulfilling gems—were constantly present in every house of the subjects residing in that kingdom. 58.
The king, however, worshipped Nārāyaṇa Hari with ninefold devotion;
the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself became the granter of his desires. (59)
Lakṣmī herself became the manager of the household duties, and I became Nārāyaṇī;
that kingdom flourished with splendor like Vaikuṇṭha itself. (1.88.60)
What indeed could be lacking for one upon whose forehead dwells Śrī Hari?
For in his kingdom, from children to youths to the elderly, the sound of the drum resounds everywhere. (61)
May all worship Govinda and perform no other rite without Him;
may they honor Govinda and listen to the stories of Śrī Hari;
may they meditate on the form of Śrī Hari and behold the image of Hari. (62)
Let them touch the feet of the virtuous and let them eat what has been offered. ॥63॥
May they smell the flowers of Hari, may they serve him with devotion;
may they chant the names of Hari and sport in his abode. (64)
May they find joy for the sake of Hari; may they renounce [worldly ties] for the sake of purification;
may they sleep upon the bed of Hari; and may they remain awake in the service of Hari. (65)
Let them do whatever else falls within the domain of Hari;
let them not undertake any other exertion while Divodāsa rules.

Whatever may be desired by anyone, for the attainment of that very thing, one should stand before the form of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, utter his name, and pray: "O Lord, Sustainer of the Universe, may such-and-such be mine. (67)
May Śrī Nārāyaṇa grant [this] to me through the devotion of Divodāsa. 68.
"By whomsoever this is thus prayed for, by him it shall be attained in every way;
otherwise, I would certainly be worthy of death"—such is the instruction. (69)
On his neck was a garland of *tulasī*, on his forehead a sandalwood tilaka;
a crescent moon mark enriched with saffron, and a rosary on his hand for the purpose of recitation.
A golden image of Śrī Nārāyaṇa was always worn around his neck.
"In this way, one should indeed protect the five marks of Nārāyaṇa.
He who does not honor them thus is to be slain by me with a sword.
Indeed, he for whom there are animals, trees, creepers, birds, or living beings [that have been killed]... (71–72)
"Let them all become Vaiṣṇavas; this is my command.
Let there be no subject of mine who is not a Vaiṣṇava, nor any land of mine that is non-Vaiṣṇava. (73)
"There shall be no object that is not Vaiṣṇava; such is my great teaching.
