May they always gladden, cause to dwell in happiness, and delight the subjects. ||75||
When these two meet, it must be said that Hari is victorious, and not otherwise;
whatever may be spoken of this, it is indeed the very conduct of Hari. (76)
"The sword shall roam upon the neck of anyone who transgresses my command.
Thus did Divodāsa indeed rule a Vaiṣṇava kingdom.
Everything became like Vaikuṇṭha; there was nothing lacking whatsoever. The subjects always sported in the sky with celestial chariots that fulfilled all desires. (78)
In every house there were celestial palaces that yielded all desires; in every house were wish-fulfilling trees, and at every home were wish-granting stones at every spot.
For every individual, there was a golden Hari, such that Vaikuṇṭha became manifest before everyone's eyes.
Such was the power of that king; having led his subjects to take refuge in Hari, he went to Vaikuṇṭha in his physical body—who else could go there in such a manner?
Whatever gods and followers of Śaṅkara arrived there did so through deceit. (1.88.80–81)
Protected by Viṣṇu, they did not receive even a blow from his sword.
Such is this divine illusion (māyā), O Blessed One; for he is indeed both the doer and the one who causes others to act. ||82||
Whatever dwells upon one's forehead, all that shall abide there;
whatever departs from one's forehead, all that indeed departs from there. (83)
That very act of forcibly expelling the gods from the abode of the Creator is itself his transgression, since the fruit of it is his own liberation. 84.
"Even an offense would yield the fruit called liberation, for that [offense] is indeed auspicious. Thus has the majesty of devotion been described; what else do you wish to hear? (85)

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Expulsion of the Gods from Kāśī as an Offense Following King Divodāsa’s Ascension to the Throne, His Own Competence for All Divine Tasks, and the Propagation of Vaiṣṇava Dharma and Devotion," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, dweller in the hearts of all, omniscient one who assumes many forms, how was Dhanvantari indeed born as the third from the ocean of jewels? 1.
O Lord, O Nārāyaṇa, O Teacher of the World, cause me to hear that story;

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
At the end of the Dvāpara Yuga, when all people become of little intelligence, intent solely on achieving their own selfish ends, and unsatisfied in their respective occupations; || 3 ||
At that time, in that age, both gods and humans were pervaded by unrighteous elements such as greed and pride; even Indra possessed the conceit of sovereignty.

As the Dvāpara age approaches here, mental resolves do not bear fruit;
nothing desired is attained, and what is difficult to obtain arises repeatedly.
"Let there be no fault among the subjects here; as is the king, so are the subjects.
Therefore, having summoned the guardians of the quarters, I shall punish them for the purification of Time. (8)
What fault, moreover, is there in the king, for kings are governed by their preceptors?
Yet here, the preceptors themselves are seen to be greedy and devoted solely to their own interests. (9)
Therefore, the elders are to be punished, and from that comes the purification of time;
as are the elders of the kingdom, so are the protectors of the kingdom. (1.89.10)
Therefore, having summoned everyone under the pretext of some festival, I shall make this request for the sake of happiness: "You must remain [here] as you did in the Satya Yuga. (11)
"Time should not be allowed to fall into impurity; let things proceed exactly as they are.
Having reflected thus, Śakra summoned the assembly in heaven. (12)
And it was proclaimed throughout the three worlds, even in the celestial assembly hall of Indra:
"The lords of gods and sages, along with humans and celestial beings, must assemble here; a great festival for the gods shall take place in this gathering."
But for the celestial nymphs born of men, there will be a new dance. (14)
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who were born to Dharma from his wife Mūrti, having received the command of their parents, set their minds upon performing austerities. (15)

While those two were performing penance, Apsarases were dispatched by Maya-Indra to create obstacles; then, at the command of Nara, Urvaśī was manifested with mango blossoms for the sake of enchanting them.
16. By means of the mango flowers of Nārāyaṇa, Urvaśī was made manifest.
She was beautiful, pervaded by youth, and radiant with supreme beauty.
She before whom the others, dark-complexioned as they were, appeared as if devoid of luster—she alone has been granted to me; she indeed shall perform the dance. (18)
"Everyone must indeed assemble to behold him.
Having thus proclaimed, Indra convened a great assembly in heaven. (19)
And Urvaśī performed a dance, enchanted by his dancing and his beauty; she became so absorbed in the melody of his voice that the entire assembly was captivated. (1.89.20)
The world-protectors and the gods, as well as the sages and the apsarases;
likewise the gandharvas, the siddhas, the vidyādharas, the cāraṇas, and others. ||21||
At that time, all the goddesses were likewise infatuated, their minds fixed upon him;
meanwhile, the wise preceptor of the king of the gods arrived.
Surrounded by many disciples, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati [was present];
therefore, while this dance was being performed, there would be a disturbance in the assembly. (23)
Seeing the twice-born Vācaspati, his preceptor, arrived there, the dull-witted Indra did not utter a single word of greeting, being full of pride. (24)
At that time, he offered him no invitation, no seat, and no hospitality;

Then Urvaśī herself, recognizing Bṛhaspati as her preceptor there, abandoned her dance and bowed; at that moment, a commotion arose in the assembly.
O Indra, having arisen, as long as the time may be auspicious, and if the king should be auspicious, and if the preceptor should also be auspicious; ||27||
"The king, the subjects, and time are considered auspicious when they are heavy with virtue"—thus did the preceptor of the gods instruct him, filled with indignation. (28)
Having realized that Śakra was negligent due to pride in his sovereignty and possessed of a wicked mind, he vanished;

When that preceptor of the gods had departed, the deities, the yakṣas, the nāgas, the gandharvas, the apsarases, and the foremost of the twice-born were filled with despondency. (1.89.30)
At the conclusion of the dance and song, Hari then said to the gods:
"Where has this preceptor of the gods, Nārada, gone? To him, he [Nārada] then replied. (31)
For you have indeed shown contempt for your guru and failed to honor him;
through such disrespect toward the guru, the kingdom dissolves and fear has arrived. (32)
A person strives for the sake of happiness, yet that very thing becomes a source of suffering. This is the agitation of Time; the king is not the cause of Time. (33)
Neither a guru nor offspring is the cause; the age is the cause of time.
It is the age that turns the minds of the great-souled ones. //34//
Nevertheless, you must strive according to your strength for the sake of a virtuous continuity;

Then, filled with anxiety, Śakra returned to his own abode, mounting Airāvata with the desire to search for his preceptor. ||38||
As he was traveling swiftly from the path of the sky toward the earth, on the way, the sage Durvāsas—born of a portion of Rudra—was filled with great wrath. (39)
Having taken a garland of *pārijāta* flowers, he arrived [there] due to the delusion born of thinking of his preceptor and because of the exhaustion of his future fortune. (1.89.40)
Due to the force of time, Turāṣāṭ did not bow to him there;
nevertheless, the sage [honored] the king out of respect for the duty of hospitality. ||41||
The garland was offered to Indra’s neck by way of the sky alone;
but Indra, having removed it, placed it upon the head of his elephant. (42)
Having seen that she had been split by the trunk of an elephant, cast down at his feet, trampled, and crushed, the sage was filled with rage toward her. (43)
His limbs were enveloped in the flames of wrath; he was hideous and terrifying.
Biting his lips and showing his fangs, he opened wide and rolled his eyes. (44)
The wicked one said: "O Lord of Gods, let honor be far away;
on the contrary, even though you are honored, you do not even acknowledge the garland. (45)
Even though you are the King of the Gods, whom I have recognized and indeed worshiped, the King of the Śaṭhas, having become powerful, casts my garland upon the ground. (46)
You cause this humiliation by trampling me with the foot of an elephant;
yet in every flower, there dwell jewels and fortunes through my power. (47)
The gift from the temple of Śrī Hari, obtained from Vaikuṇṭha, was offered here to you.
That very gift has been given away by me; why then do you squander it upon mere pieces of paper?
Out of folly, you bring about the destruction of both jewels and fortunes. (48)
Therefore, may your sovereignty over the three worlds perish in every way, along with your riches, prosperities, fortunes, and various kinds of jewels. (49)
"May they go to dissolution in the great ocean; you, be free from sleep for a moment.
Having been addressed thus, Durvāsas then departed for Kailāsa.
Then Ambālikā’s banner fell right there upon the ground;
likewise, the crown fell from his head, and at that moment the elephant sneezed.
The goad indeed slipped from the hand of the elephant-driver.
In that interval, undesirable omens appeared instantly in heaven;
even though Airāvata was urged, he would not proceed toward heaven.
Being thus intoxicated, he indeed puts the king of the gods to flight on all sides.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Bṛhaspati’s Insult, Durvāsas’s Insult, and Indra’s Curse that Destroyed His Royal Fortune," occurring during the festival of Urvaśī’s dance produced by Nara and Nārāyaṇa, within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 89.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The preceptor of the gods himself went to the northern bank of the Kāverī and performed a fire sacrifice for the sake of Indra’s ultimate loss of his kingdom.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, O Ṛkṣakarṇī, four-armed one!
O you with hair standing erect, O Kālarātri, consumer of fat and blood! 2.
Of Indra, whose time has come, O Death, huṃ phaṭ! Strike! Strike! Burn! Burn! Cook the flesh! Cook the blood! Svāhā! 3.
Thus, while he was performing the fire-oblation, a cruel *kṛtyā* was created. Having gone to destroy Indra, she was seen by Indra, who became distraught. (4)
Having fled from the path of the sky, she went to the abode of Brahmā;
the Kṛtyā turned back from there and approached Bṛhaspati. (5)
Then, by the command of Bṛhaspati, they all went to heaven to destroy the jewels of Indra; indeed, they fled here and there, terrified with fear.
Seeing her, who was destructive, most terrible, radiant like the fire of time (kālānala), with her mouth wide open and bearing weapons, they fled. || 7 ||
The curse of the sage Durvāsas became a massive, terrifying body, resembling a black mountain, licking the clouds with its tongue. 8.
Widening his eyes, which resembled the sun and the moon, the devourer of light first went to heaven for the destruction of the three worlds. (9)
That man Karālaka and Kṛtyā also [attacked] Ṛkṣaśravas;
they destroyed the treasures of heaven on all sides. || 1.90.10 ||
Then the lotus-eyed Śacī vanished, as did the great elephant Airāvata and the horse Uccaiḥśravas. ||11||
Likewise, it is said that other jewels fled from heaven when Bālin, residing in Pātāla, learned of Śakra’s dire plight. ||12||
War was waged against the army of the Daityas for the sake of attaining heaven;
by him Amarāvatī was won and jewels were seized. (13)
All seven constituent parts of that Indra were brought down to the Talātala hell;
through the grace of Śukra, the Daityas then became victorious. (14)
Then Uccaiḥśravas and Airāvata fell into the ocean, along with many other various jewels in great abundance. ||15||
The Daityas carried them from heaven, but we seized those from the Daityas;
having fled from the Daityas, they fell into the ocean. (16)
The moon, having become liquid water, and the wish-fulfilling cow, having become milk;
the Kalpa tree and the Pārijāta tree became invisible through their transformation into seeds. (17)
The Apsarases took the form of rivers, as did diamonds and gravel;
meanwhile, that liquid became nectar, possessing the essence of water. (18)
Having become fond of the delights of supernatural power and assuming various forms, they went beneath the surface of the ocean and found rest there. (19)
"The jewels are indeed fit for the enjoyment of gods, not for the enjoyment of Daityas.
Then, filled with wonder, Bali spoke to his preceptor: || 1.90.20 ||
The jewels, won by force, fell into the great ocean.
Śukra said: "Having attained the status of Lord of the Gods through a hundred horse-sacrifices... (21)
Whosoever remains seated upon the throne of the king of the gods, he shall indeed enjoy those jewels;
having performed a hundred horse-sacrifices, there is no doubt that he is their consumer. 22.
"Nothing pertaining to heaven can be enjoyed at all without horse-sacrifices.
Having understood the words of his preceptor, Bali then spoke to the preceptor: (23)
"I shall strive when the time has arrived; that time is not now.
Then Indra was also instructed by the venerable Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
Placing Brahmā, the world-protectors, and likewise the gods and sages at his head, he went to the ocean, the milk-sea.
Having reflected, they all reached the conclusion and began to praise Hari, who dwells in the Ocean of Milk, regarding both the sorrow and joy of the gods. (26)
Salutations again and again to that Inner Controller who lies asleep;
great suffering caused by Time has befallen the gods. (27)
And you alone are endowed with the power to dispel that suffering;
O God of gods, protector of the world, Supreme Self, salutations be unto you! (28)
O Blessed One, being compassionate, quickly protect your own gods from the contempt shown toward their preceptor and from the insult offered to Durvāsas. (29)
Śatakratu has been deprived of his kingdom; indeed, rescue him!
Then the Blessed One said: "Pride is the cause of downfall. (1.90.30)
Through disrespect toward the guru, one's entire personal merit goes to ruin;
likewise for [disrespect] toward one's parents, the guru, a husband, a virtuous wife, and the righteous. (31)
There would have been a great destruction for those who insult cows;
indeed, Indra once committed such an act, and because of that fault, the entire world [was afflicted]. (32)
Let it be observed that suffering is encountered in an instant;
when the time turns adverse, then everything comes to an end. (33)
At such an adverse time, the wise person, maintaining fortitude through conciliation, should accomplish his own purpose even by uniting with an enemy. (34)
Therefore, O Indra, you must enter into an alliance with the Daityas;
by uniting, the lost jewels will be recovered once again through their combined effort. (35)
"I shall be your helper in the churning of the ocean every day.
By uniting as Daityas and Devas, we shall regain our own wealth once more. (36)
Thus commanded, Indra then went to Sutala to Bali;
becoming humble and assuming a posture of discipline, he bowed down to the mighty Bali. (37)
Then even Bali saw the king of the gods devoid of splendor, lusterless, free from pride, without envy, shorn of majesty, and afflicted by great suffering. (38)
Seeing that supreme being free from pride, Bali was then moved by compassion;
with skill and as if smiling, he spoke to Indra in a conciliatory manner.
"O Śakra, tell me why you have come here to Sutala; [speak] to Bali, who is desirous of knowing, who knows all, and who understands the proper time. (1.90.40)
Indra said: "O Bali! Indeed, all the jewels have vanished.
Just as we are, so too are you—deprived of jewels and possessed by the Kali age. (41)
"O King! My kingdom has been taken by you through the force of time and through conflict;

Even though there were very many jewels in the hands of the Daityas, those very ones which belonged to that place [of the king] went away, for they were deemed unworthy. ||43||
"O Lord of the Earth! I am now deprived of my kingdom, jewels, and other possessions;
therefore, you must make an effort to recover those jewels. (44)
"I have come into your presence along with the gods for the sake of seeking refuge.

In that matter, I shall grant you each your own rightful share arising from the attainment [of the nectar] as is appropriate.
The gods and the Daityas, having joined together, repeatedly churned the ocean. (46)
"Whatever [beings] have indeed gone there, we shall then act;
you are our refuge, and it behooves you to grant us assistance. (47)
Thus addressed by Indra, Bali, the lord of the Daityas, himself—
being skilled in discerning what ought and ought not to be done— reflected with supreme intelligence.
He honored Śakra with great respect;
Śakra, meanwhile, recalled the words of Viṣṇu regarding the accomplishment of his own purpose. (49)
"O hero, you shall obtain very many jewels indeed;
O Daitya, exert yourself quickly in the churning for their extraction! (1.90.50)

Then an auspicious voice from the sky, whose essence was Viṣṇu, spoke to the gods and demons: "Churn the Ocean of Milk! (52)
"Having made Mount Mandara the churning stick and Vāsuki the churning rope,

Then, tens of millions of gods, likewise tens of millions in number, joined by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, set out and went to Mount Mandara. ||55||
We bow to that [Meru] whose peak touches the moon, whose feet rest upon the surface of Bali, and whose hips rest upon the earth, while Mandara serves as its base. (56)
We bow to Mount Mandara, the abode of many gods, a mine of all kinds of jewels, and strewn with every medicinal herb. 57.
"O friends! We have come here for the sake of assistance.

"O you who are born of the mountain! Become the churning-stick for the sake of producing the nectar of immortality.

"O Lord of the Gods, my wings have indeed been clipped by you with the thunderbolt!

They sat down right on the path as Mandara fell to the earth;

Devoted solely to grief for the deceased, they are truly unable to bring them back;
for when these have passed away, how indeed will they ever obtain jewels again while living? (64)
"We must not exert ourselves to take his life, for he is here out of hope;

"We shall each go to our own respective abodes of comfort.
Having thus become hopeless, they remained silent; why did they not look on? (66)

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of How Heaven was Overpowered by the Personification of Durvāsas’s Curse Produced by Kṛtyā Created by Bṛhaspati, and How the Jewels Went into the Ocean, and How Brahmā, Indra, and the Others, Having Led Viṣṇu [Along], Made an Alliance with Bali and the Daityas, and Exerted Themselves to Bring Mount Mandara for the Churning of the Ocean," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 90.

he went directly to Vaikuṇṭha; at that time, the gods, Daityas,

Having abandoned that place to that extent, the gods and Daityas, awakened by Viṣṇu and Nārada and remaining undeluded, approached Śaṅkara. ||22||

"Indeed, the accomplishment of your purpose shall not come to pass as it has for you.

The bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), as well as the immersion of the consecration (abhiṣeka), the wiping with a cloth, the garment, and the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). ||33||
Abīra, gulāla, vermilion, and saffron;
likewise unbroken grains of rice, sprouts of dūrvā grass, incense, and lamps. (34)
Sandalwood paste, flower garlands, ornaments, excellent food, drinking water, sweetmeats, betel leaf, and likewise lamps for the arati ceremony. (35)

It was dried up by Śambhu through the power of his yoga while he remained in meditative absorption;

Biters and serpents, scorpions and chameleons;
monitor lizards and water-dwellers, as well as thorny shrubs and bitter creepers. (43)
From that [churning], these [oceans] became equal; then they churned Mount Mandara, and from the coldness of the water and other conditions, the moon was born with a body of frost.
Then, from the second [digit], it took the form of a crescent filled with nectar;

Śambhu, pervaded by the heat of the poison, took the cool-rayed moon upon his brow.
Then Bhṛgu spoke to the gods: "All the planets, too, are most excellent. (46)
They praise the accomplishment of one's purpose; therefore, exert yourself with ease.

The Sun, Venus, Saturn, and Mars as well—therefore, the strength of the Moon is the most excellent for the accomplishment of any undertaking. (48)
"And this Muhūrta named Gomanta is a bringer of victory.
Having heard this, your forces, having gained double their strength, roared. (49)
Meanwhile, they quickly churned the ocean; at that time, the cow Surabhi, ever-yielding her desires, appeared as a tawny Kapila, bearing her udder slowly due to its great weight. (1.91.50)

and it was decided that she should be led away by those for whom milk would be available for their enjoyment. (51)
They were appropriated by the sages for the sake of the gods' rites and for the purpose of sacrifice.
Meanwhile, there were others that were white, yellow, black, and pale-red. (52)
From that, cows of yellow color and variegated colors were born in great numbers;

Then, all of them, being well-exerted, churned the Ocean of Milk;
likewise, the Kalpavṛkṣa, the Pārijāta, and trees such as the mango.
Then Acyuta brought all of them forth and established them upon the shore;
furthermore, from the ocean being churned once more, the great-radiant gem named Kaustubha emerged.
They gave to Viṣṇu the Kaustubha gem, the most excellent of jewels, endowed with the power of a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) and produced together with diamonds. ||56||
The *cintāmaṇi* was given to the Lord of the Gods, while the Daityas gave diamonds;
nevertheless, from that [ocean] being churned, the wonderful Uccaiḥśravas emerged. (57)
They gave to Hari that which was produced from many species of horses;
moreover, from the churning, it was indeed accompanied by sixty-four elephants. (58)

moreover, from the churning itself, the intoxicating liquor Vijayā likewise emerged.
Kaṭuśṛṅgī, ahiphena, gṛñjana, and likewise laśuna,
as well as dhattūra and tamāla— these were then [drugs] that cause madness;
and they were indeed seized by force by the Tāmasa Daityas.
Then, indeed, as it was being churned, Lakṣmī manifested herself—
beautiful, with a smiling countenance, adorned with garments and ornaments,
fair-complexioned, with a divine body, and possessed of breasts beautiful with the budding of youth.

The fruit of sexual union is happiness, for indeed both [happiness and a son] may arise.
However, joy without the fruit of a son becomes a source of suffering in old age. (8)
A mere pleasure devoid of sons leads only to future distress. Indeed, by what means can a woman pass the time without offspring? (9)
When the delay in sexual union with her husband is very brief, the offspring born to women at that other time shall be male in this world. (1.94.10)
When the time of women passes in the nurturing and protection of their children, and in activities such as playing with them—that very time is called heaven. (11)

The first [type of heaven] is the happiness of one's master; the second is that born of one's wife; the third is the heaven consisting of the joy of offspring; the fourth is the heaven arising from wealth and grain;
and the fifth is the heaven of health and fame.
These indeed are the very pleasures of the worldly heavens. 13.
Thus, constantly filled with such thoughts, she took delight with her own husband.
Śambhu, perceiving her inner heart, questioned that devoted wife.
"What do you desire, my beloved? What dwells constantly in your mind? What indeed do you contemplate during our union? Speak, and I shall fulfill your wish. (15)
Pārvatī said: "O Lord of Gods! What is lacking for me in your presence, since I have obtained you, the creator and the giver of everything to all the worlds? (16)
Wherever the Blessed One resides, there shall be great prosperity;
there shall be no deficiency, nor lack of peace, nor failure to obtain that which is most dear.
For women, the husband is the most beloved, followed by the son, and then the season.
Although I have obtained a husband who is the lord of the three worlds, I have no son.
The desire for a son awakens within my heart even as I behold you.
O Lord of Gods, whenever I look upon you, at that very moment— ||18–19||
From delusion, a thought arose within her due to her power and her preeminent worship:
"When shall I have a son who is equal to my husband as a god? (1.94.20)
The separation from beloved ones is said to be the first suffering;
if there is no beloved present, the absence of delight is said to be the second suffering. (21)
And the third sorrow, exceeding all others, is childlessness:
"Though I have obtained you, my beloved, who are the delight of the three worlds, I have no son. (22)
For a woman who is bereft of sons, her life is meaningless;
[only] the merit performed in previous births through austerity, charity, recitation, and so forth [is of value]. (23)
Then a son shall be born who bestows happiness both in this world and the next;
a good son is a portion of his own father and bestows happiness equal to that of his father. (24)
But a bad son is a charcoal-brand to the family, causing nothing but mental anguish;
therefore, people pray, "May I have a good son. (25)
The husband shall certainly obtain birth from his own portion within the womb of a virtuous wife;
for a chaste woman is like a mother and is always a benefactor. 26.
"Unvirtuous, like an enemy, and constantly causing me torment—what remedy shall I employ? Tell me, O bestower of the fruit of sons! (27)
When the goddess Pārvatī had spoken thus and remained silent,
the god Śaṅkara smiled and enlightened Pārvatī.
Listen, Pārvatī! I shall speak; it will be for your welfare.
Indeed, through diligent effort, the accomplishment of all goals arises. (29)
I shall tell you the heart-pleasing means that bestows all accomplishments:
having performed the worship of Hari, O fair-faced one, observe the vow. 1.94.30.
For one year you shall perform that vow known as Puṇyaka, a rite that is a wish-fulfilling tree for the mind, bestowing happiness and granting sons. (31)
That meritorious vow of Hari is the most excellent among all vows, just as the Gaṅgā is the best of rivers and just as Hari is indeed the foremost among the gods. (32)
Just as I am among the Vaiṣṇavas, and you, O Great Chaste One, are among goddesses;
just as the Brahmin is indeed the foremost among the castes, and Puṣkara is the best among sacred fords. (33)
Among flowers, the pārijāta is supreme; among leaves, the tulasī leaf;
among lunar days, Ekādaśī is the best; and among days of the week, Sunday is the most excellent. (34)
Among months it is Mārgaśīrṣa; among all seasons it is spring; among years it is the Saṃvatsara; and among the ages it is the Kṛta. (35)
And as a learned man [shows] toward those worthy of worship, and as a wife [shows] her inner heart toward her mother and elders, and as one shows it toward benefactors and trusted friends; //36//
Just as jewels are among riches, as a husband is among beloveds, as a virtuous son is among kinsmen, and as the wish-fulfilling tree is among trees; (37)
Likewise, the vow of Hari is the most excellent among all vows and meritorious;
it is like the mango fruit being the best among fruits, or like Vṛndāvana among forests. ||38||
Just as Śatarūpā is among women, and Urvaśī among the Apsarases;
just as Kamalā is among mothers, and the Sun is the best among those possessing splendor. (39)
Among those who give delight, he is like the moon; among the beautiful, he is like the god of love;
among the most excellent, he is like the Vedas among scriptures; and among the perfected ones, he is like Kapila. (1.94.40)
Just as knowledge is supreme among glories, as a sovereign is supreme among those who pervade, as the eye is the best among the limbs, so truth is the most excellent among meritorious deeds. (41)
Austerity is service to Śrī Hari; among products of the cow, ghee is supreme;
among foods, nectar is best; and among pure things, fire is preeminent. 42.
Just as gold is the best among metallic substances, sweet speech among pleasant things, Garuḍa among birds, and Airāvata among elephants,
so too is the vow of Hari the most excellent and meritorious among all vows.
Among the celestial sages he is Nārada; among yogis, Sanaka and the others;
among the Gandharvas, Citraratha; and among the principles (tattvas), he is like the conscious principle (cetana).
Among poets he is Śukra, and among those possessed of forbearance, he is like the earth.
Among gains, liberation is indeed the best; among prosperities, devotion is supreme;
as the virtuous man is among the pure, and as the syllable Om is among the castes. (46)
Among mantras, the mantra of Śrī Hari is supreme, just as the wish-fulfilling cow is among cows;
among the Vedas, the Sāmaveda is supreme, and among blades of grass, the kuśa is the best. (47)
Just as knowledge is among pleasant things, as Vāsuki is among serpents,
as the letter *a* is among syllables, and as my father is among those who wish one's welfare;
just as the lion is among quadrupeds, and the Śālagrāma is among sacred images.
Just as the intellect [presides] over the powerful organs, and as Hari [presides] over them; //49//
Among perishable things, the dyad (the atom and its product) is foremost; among givers, Dadhīci is the best.
Just as the Brahmā-weapon is supreme among weapons, and the Sudarśana is supreme among discuses. (1.94.50)
Just as Kṛṣṇa is the essence of all things, so is the Puṇyaka vow among vows;
O Great Goddess, quickly perform this vow which bestows one's own desired objects! ||51||
"Your son shall indeed become the most excellent of all through this very vow. Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the Lord and Sovereign of Goloka, is to be propitiated by means of vows. (52)
When he is pleased, that giver of all things bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
by serving him, a person is released from bondage along with ten million ancestors.
Having uplifted ten million persons, he attains happiness in Goloka.
[He should protect] his brothers, servants, companions, dependents, wives, sons, and so forth. ||54||
A devotee of Kṛṣṇa, having been uplifted, goes happily to the abode of Hari.
Therefore, O Girijā, accept the supreme mantra-vow of Hari! (55)
"Observe the vow and recite the mantra; success will soon be yours.
Having said this, he took water and bestowed the excellent mantra upon the Goddess. (56)
Śambhu whispered the mantra into the ear of Girijā on her left;
Pārvatī meditated upon that mantra being given, yet held this one within her heart. (57)
“Oṃ, salutations to Hari-Kṛṣṇa, who assumes the form of a husband;
to the seed, to the one in the form of an embryo, to the one in the form of an offspring, and to Śambhu. (58)
Salutations to the one whose heart is the womb of intention, and salutations to the bestower of sons.
Salutations to the conqueror, whose form is worthy of foremost worship; grant me a virtuous son.
Grant me a son who is victorious over all and worthy of being worshipped as the foremost by all.
"O Kṛṣṇa, this meritorious vow is being performed for your pleasure.
May it be free from obstacles and bear fruit; O giver of sons, be the bestower of a son upon me.
Grant me a son equal to yourself, one who shall live long—salutations, salutations! (1.94.60–61)
O virtuous lady, having received this mantra from Haradatta, Śambhu went with Pārvatī to the purifying bank of the Jāhnavī.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Bestowal of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, Accompanied by Many Illustrations, Given by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī Who Desired a Son," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. 94.

Chapter 96 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having heard what was to be done regarding the vow, Pārvatī, with a delighted mind,
again questioned Śaṅkara concerning the entire procedure for the vow.
O Lord, that meritorious vow has been undertaken by me with self-restraint;
in what manner should it be performed, and what materials are required therein? (2)
Let it be considered that other fruits are to be given;
whatever object is required, provide and arrange that. (3)
The husband is considered the provider of all needs for women who observe vows.
In her maidenhood, the father always protects the daughter;
after the wedding, the husband is her protector, and in old age, it is the sons and others.
The father, having given his daughter, who was as dear to him as his own life, to a virtuous husband, became happy.
A husband should find happiness only after entrusting his wife to his own sons;
a woman who acts thus, endowed with these three qualities, is considered fortunate in this world. (6)
One deprived of one [of these] is middling; one deprived of all is miserable.
One protected by these is fortunate; another, residing with a different protector, is censured.
My maidenhood, which was worthy of being protected by my father, has now passed away.
And her youth, which is fit for protecting her husband, will soon pass away.
"But without a son, who will provide protection for me in my old age?
Therefore, O Lord, grant me a son, the cause of my peace."
In the presence of the Omniscient One, even erudition appears turbid.
I have nothing else to ask for from you, the father of my son, except for your true compassion. (1.95.10)
Having heard this from Pārvatī, Śaṅkara said to Pārvatī:
"Listen, O Goddess; through the Kṛṣṇa-vrata, one's heart's desire shall become fruitful.
O beloved, the auspicious commencement of the vow occurs on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha."
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the vow shall reach completion. ||12||
This meritorious vow, lasting for one year and bringing satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa, should be performed according to the prescribed rules by a woman desiring a son. 13.

Having fasted on the twelfth day and performed the consecration of the head, as well as the purification of the body and the purification of the garments, one should meditate upon Hari during the night. 14.
At the time of Brahma, having risen from his bed after overcoming sleep, he should remember Hari and perform purification and the like, as well as the cleaning of the teeth and bathing. (15)

Having performed these acts and sipped water (ācamana), having offered the arghya to Hari and put on two washed garments, and having sat down and again sipped water, [he should apply] sandalwood paste. ||16||
Having applied a drop or a sectarian mark made of saffron and meditated upon Hari,
and having performed his daily obligatory rites, he should choose a qualified domestic priest.
Having established the water-pot according to the rules, preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana), [he should proceed].
Having caused the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) prescribed by the Vedas to be performed, one should observe the vow.
Lord Hari himself is to be worshipped with sixteen services:
invocation, the seat, water for the feet, and the offering of honor (arghya) thereafter. (19)

Likewise, the sipping of water (ācamana), the bath (snāna), the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), as well as clothing (ambara), sandalwood paste (candana), ornaments (bhūṣaṇa), flowers (puṣpa), incense (dhūpa), a lamp (dīpa), and the food offering (nivedana). || 1.95.20 ||
The sacred thread and betel leaf should be offered with a spirit of devotion;
one must not perform anything deficient therein, for that causes a loss of the fruit. 21.
Gifts should be given according to one's ability to Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu. Listen as I describe what specific attainment results from each particular gift. (22)
A flower of the pārijāta tree should be offered for the sake of a beautiful form;
a white campaka flower, however, should be offered for the sake of beauty. (23)
A lotus should be given to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of the splendor of his face;
a mirror rich with jewels should be given for the sake of the brilliance of his eyes. ||24||
Likewise, a blue lotus should be given for the sake of the beauty of the eyes;
a white fly-whisk, however, should be given for the sake of the beauty of the hair. (25)
A small box smeared with jewels should be given for the sake of the beauty of the nose;
and Bandhūka flowers should be given for the sake of making one's own lips red. Pearl ornaments should be given for the sake of the beauty of the teeth.
A mouthful of jewels should be given for the sake of the beauty of her cheeks. //27//
Likewise, jeweled nooses should be given for the sake of the chin;
and earrings adorned with jewels should be given for the sake of the beautiful ears. (28)
Honey-wine or sugarcane wine should be given for the sake of sweetness of voice;
sweet nectar-like ambrosia should be given for the sake of sweetness of speech. (29)
A jewel-lamp should be given for the sake of the purity of vision;
water-vessels and the like should be given for the sake of strengthening one's power. (1.95.30)
Lotus stalks should be offered for the sake of strengthening the arms;
red lotuses should be offered for the sake of the beauty of the hands. (31)
Finger-rings should be given for the sake of the beauty of the fingers;
white gems should be given for the sake of the beauty of the nails. (32)
Likewise, jeweled necklaces should be given for the sake of the beauty of her chest;
and when they are ripe, auspicious bilva fruits should be offered to him for the sake of the beauty of her breasts. (33)
Likewise, a golden leaf should be offered for the sake of the beauty of the body;
a navel fashioned from jewels should be offered for the sake of the beauty of the navel. (34)
Two wheels inlaid with jewels should be given to her whose hips are well-formed;
and plantain pillars should be presented for the sake of the beauty of her loins. (35)
Land-lotuses should be offered for the sake of the beauty of the feet; golden fish should be offered for the sake of the grace and swiftness of the gait. (36)
Golden swans and lordly elephants should be given as gifts for the sake of a good rebirth;
and a golden umbrella should be offered for the sake of the beauty of one's head. (37)
A *mālatī* flower should be offered for the sake of gentle smiles and the like;
priceless jewels should be given for the fulfillment of the vow and the attainment of happiness. (38)
Stainless crystal gems should be given for the sake of tranquility of mind;
coral gems should be given for the increase of affection for one's beloved. (39)
Rubies should be given for the sake of the master’s good fortune, as well as a pumpkin, a nine-colored object, a citron, and a bilva fruit. (1.95.40)
Precious gems should be given to Hari-Kṛṣṇa during worship for the sake of obtaining a son;
precious gems should be given to the Master for the increase of wealth. 41.
For the sake of increasing prosperity, one should have musical instruments played during the vow while reciting the glories of Śrī Hari;
likewise, one should offer milk-rice, flour-cakes, clarified butter, sugar, and saffron.
One should devotedly offer things to Hari for the increase of the Master's enjoyment;
garlands of flowers should be presented to Hari for the furtherance of devotion. (43)
Sweet-tasting food offerings should be given for the attainment of sweet foods; Tulasī leaves and flowers should be offered for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa. (44)
One should feed virtuous men and women, as well as the poor, for the increase of the harvest;
and prostrations with handfuls of flowers should be performed for the increase of devotion. (45)
Remaining established in the vow, she should eat sacrificial food for six months, fruits and the like for five months, clarified butter for a fortnight, and milk for a fortnight. (46)
One should maintain an unbroken lamp before Acyuta for a full year;
one should always sit upon a seat of kuśa grass and perform a vigil at midnight. (47)

Celibacy (brahmacarya) must always be observed for the attainment of the fruit of the vow. If it is violated, an expiation (niṣkṛti) must be performed: a fast and one hundred and eight recitations (japa). 48.
One should undertake the preparatory rite for the sake of attaining unbroken observance of the vow;
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, that great festival should be performed. (49)
According to one's capacity, gold and silver coins should be given;
likewise, three hundred and sixty garments and the same number of silver coins. (1.95.50)
There should be that many gold coins, that many portions of food, and one should perform three hundred and sixty oblations of sesame seeds. (51)
This is the daily duty, or it may indeed be performed at the end of the year;
thus the son shall become equal to Hari, a conqueror, and worthy of the highest honor. ||52||
Beauty, supreme good fortune, sovereignty, abundant wealth, and the accomplishment of all desired goals arise for her through the power of this vow. (53)
At the conclusion of the vow, one should enjoy the bed of one's husband, but not in the interval between vows.
During the year of the vow, a woman must never engage in sexual pleasure.

If one engages in sexual pleasure during the midst of a vow, the vow will be broken; therefore, that which is a fault—namely, not engaging in intercourse during the fertile period—is here a virtue. 55.
"O Maheśvarī! Perform this single vow for one year;
O Pārvatī, let there be a son for me who is not born from a womb. (56)

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Annual Vow Named Puṇyaka for the Sake of a Son and the Description of the Gifts to be Given," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 95. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).

Chapter 97 → Śrī Śvetavyāsa said:
O Suśikha! Śaṅkara spoke to the Goddess regarding an ancient event:
"Śatarūpā, the wife of Vaivasvata Manu, was indeed childless;
she grieved that her birth, as well as her wealth and sovereignty, were fruitless. (1)
The opulent home of householders does not shine without a son. (2)
The merit arising from austerity and charity performed in previous lives shall manifest;
then, for men, the sight of the faces of daughters and sons occurs. (3)
The fruit of having a son is remembered as being the deliverance from the hell named Punnāma.
O Suśivā! Even the sages, though possessing nothing themselves, desire a good disciple.
Indeed, the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself does not remain without a disciple.
For one without a wife, a disciple is indeed a son; for one with a wife, a son is his wealth. (5)
The sons of Menā and Śukā and others were born to those who were perpetually barren and widowed;
therefore, for one without a son, the life of an ascetic is better.
Sovereignty, noble lineage, and prosperity are all meaningless without a son;
men do not look upon the faces of those without sons at dawn. A man without a son experiences shame when he attempts to show his face.
Thus, tormented by grief, she then informed Brahmā.
Brahmā said: "Listen, my child, this is the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha;
from that time forward for a full year, it is fit for a meritorious vow."
"Perform the vow exactly as prescribed, and you shall obtain a son equal to Viṣṇu.
At these words of Brahmā, she performed the vow according to the ritual injunctions.
Having performed her vows and received a boon from Nārāyaṇa, Devahūtī obtained two charming sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda. ||11||
She obtained as her son Kapila, a perfected sage who was a portion of Nārāyaṇa;
and Arundhatī, having performed her vows, obtained a son named Śakti. (12)
Śakti’s wife, having performed this vow, obtained the son Parāśara;
and Aditi, having performed the vow, obtained as her son Vāmana. Śacī also, having performed this very vow, indeed obtained the son Jayanta.
Having performed this [rite], the wife of Uttānapāda obtained Dhruva as her son.
Anasūyā, having observed a vow, obtained the auspicious Candra as her son;
likewise, Bṛhaspati was indeed obtained by the wife of Aṅgiras through her vow.
Having performed a vow, Khyāti obtained Śukra as her auspicious son from Bhṛgu;
likewise, by the power of that very vow, Nārāyaṇa himself was born as a son in the house of Kaṃbhārā— he shall become your son.
Having spoken thus to the Queen of the Gods and having given her abundant wealth and many attendants, [he departed]. ||17||
Having explained the means of accomplishment, Śiva established himself in meditation, intent on the worship of Hari, contemplating the ocean of the bliss of knowledge. (18)
Then Pārvatī, having brought all the necessary materials for the sake of her vow,
chose the brahmin Sanatkumāra for the performance of the rite.
The lords of the gods arrived, having learned of the great festival of the vow;
Brahmā came with his wife, accompanied by Lakṣmī, in his four-armed form. (1.96.20)
Then, leaving his meditation, Śambhu came to the place of the vow;
Sanaka, Sananda, Kapila, and Sanātana were there as well. (21)
Āsuri, Kratu, Haṃsa, Voḍhu, Pañcaśikha, Aruṇi, Yati, Vasiṣṭha, Sumati, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Bhṛgu. (22)
Agastya, Atri, Aṅgiras, Durvāsas, Cyavana, as well as Pracetas who is devoted to his wife, Kaṇva, Marīci, and Kaśyapa. (23)
Gautama and Jaratkāru, Bṛhaspati and Saubhari;
Utathya and Jamadagni, Jaigīṣavya and Devala. (24)
Saṃvarta, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, Vibhāṇḍaka, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Pāribhadra, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Lomaśa. ||25||
Gokarṇa, Mṛkaṇḍu, Puṣkara, Pippalāyana, Kautsa, Dvīta, Ekata, Trīta, Vatsa, and Lekhana. (26)
Śaṅkha, Śaṅku, Āpiśali, Svayaṃprakāśa, Āruṇi, Dakṣa, Kaṇāda, Bālāgni, Aghamarṣaṇa, and Pāṇini. (27)
Kātyāyana, Nārada, Nara, and likewise Nārāyaṇa;
those who have taken the vow of Brahman, Mahāśveta, Vyāsa, and other great ṛṣis. ||28||
Gītā, Jayantī, Gāyatrī, Lakṣmī, Vidyā, Sarasvatī, Stuti, Ārādhanā, Pūjā, Bhakti, Nīrājanā, and Ramā. (29)
The Ekādaśīs and the Yoginīs, as well as the Sāṃkhyayoginīs, the Sādhvīs, the Vītarāgiṇīs, the Nyāsīs, and likewise the Siddhis. || 1.96.30 ||
Mothers, rivers, cities, and various other women came there, eager for the festival of Pārvatī’s vow. (31)
The guardians of the quarters, as well as the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, kiṃpuruṣas, and cāraṇas; the mountains with their divine forms;
and Himālaya, overflowing with joy, together with his children and his wife. (32)
He arrived with his retinue, carrying materials, jewels, and gems.
Having gathered all the gifts obtained during the vow, he returned;
those were given to Pārvatī for the sake of fulfilling the completion of her vow. ||34||
The mountain Anantaratnaprabhava gave much to his daughter;
likewise, the Brahmins, Manus, Siddhas, Nāgas, and Vidyādharas [gave much]. (35)
Virtuous mendicants, bards, genealogists, and panegyrists;
as well as Vidyādharīs, female dancers, and male dancers and Apsarases. (36)
They arrived for the sake of pleasing Pārvatī, who was performing her vow. Blessings were bestowed by them [upon her], and she said to them: "May you become mothers of sons. (37)
"Welcome to all! Here is service, food, hospitality, and honor.
Thus honored by Śambhu, they were all satisfied and gave their auspicious blessings. (38)
Having been bowed to, honored with hospitable service, worshipped, and fed, those gods were gathered together in the great assembly hall on Kailāsa. ||39||
To Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, who was seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, Mahādeva said this: "O Lord, O Abode of Śrī, listen!
You are the deity who bestows the fruit of vows; you are the one who bestows the fruit of mantras."
But Pārvatī, while engaged in her vow, did not desire even a son who would grant her happiness. ||41||
Viṣṇu, the teacher of the world, Nārāyaṇa, spoke thus, O Mahādeva:
"The Lord of devotees, whose very life is his devotees, who bestows grace upon his devotees—the Blessed One is indeed subservient to devotion; he will grant every spiritual perfection. (42)
The Kṛṣṇa-vow and the Kṛṣṇa-mantra bestow the fruit of all desires.
When the vow is completed and you have united with Pārvatī,
a noble son shall be born to you from the semen that spilled outside your womb.

"He shall be the conqueror of all armies and the bestower of auspiciousness upon all undertakings; of this there is no doubt. O gods, you desire such a son. While these words were being spoken in the presence of the gods and others, [the gods said: "O Lord, we shall do as you have commanded. Thus they spoke, and at that moment, the gods, led by Brahmā, joyfully honored the Great Lord with various hymns of praise. Then, having been thus addressed by the gods, the Lord of the World, the Supreme Soul, spoke these words to Viśvakarman: "O Viśvakarman, you must fashion a divine chariot for me, which is swift, beautiful, and capable of traveling through the sky. Hearing these words, Viśvakarman, filled with joy, fashioned a celestial chariot of incomparable splendor. It was adorned with gold and jewels, possessed the speed of thought, and was equipped with every kind of weapon. It was furnished with a divine seat and a canopy, and was yoked with horses as white as snow. Having completed the chariot, Viśvakarman presented it to the Lord. The Lord, pleased with his work, bestowed upon him the boon of immortality. Then, having mounted that divine chariot, the Lord of the World set forth to the battlefield, accompanied by his hosts of attendants. As he proceeded, the earth trembled, and the sun grew dim. The gods showered down flowers from the heavens, and the celestial drums resounded spontaneously. Thus did the Lord of the Universe advance, intent on the destruction of the enemies of the gods. || 45 ||
Pārvatī arrived to bow at the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Having bowed and washed his feet, she spoke to Viṣṇu Janārdana: "O glorious Nārāyaṇa, the wish-fulfilling tree for devotees! Salutations be to you! (46–47)
"O Lord! Since I have become a mother by virtue of your meritorious vow, please grant me the resolve and grace so that it may truly come to pass. (48)
Kṛṣṇa then said to the goddess: "The vow must be performed by you with full attentiveness; I shall see you again once the vow is complete. (49)
"May you be blessed with sons who will assist you in performing the duties of the gods.
I am now departing for my own Goloka; do not be negligent in your vow. (1.96.50)
Honored and worshipped by the gods as well as other celestial beings, the goddesses then offered their blessings and departed for their own abodes. (51)
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the virtuous Pārvatī performed everything for the purification of her body along with a fast. ||52||

On the thirteenth day, having performed that morning rite which constitutes the daily observance, [one should offer it] together with all kinds of jewels, gems, grains, wealth, clothing, and so forth. ||53||
Having arrived and taken her place in the pavilion, she worshipped her gurus; having bowed to all those present there, she prostrated to Hari with her inner soul. ||54||
Having firmly established a jeweled pitcher upon white grain, it should be joined with five types of sprouts and adorned with fruits, unbroken rice, and other offerings. ||55||
Adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, saffron, and other [fragrances], and likewise having bowed to and worshipped the family priest and the three deities; ||56||
He began the worship preceded by the recitation of auspicious prayers (svastivācana), having invoked his chosen deity, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, into an auspicious water-pot (maṅgala-ghaṭa). ||57||
With devotion, he offered the sixteen types of ritual services (upacāras) in their proper sequence—those which are prescribed for the vow and those materials which are to be given. (58)
Having offered all [the oblations] with Vedic mantras, he caused the homas to be performed;
at that time, three hundred thousand homas were performed with sesame seeds and likewise with clarified butter. ||59||
Performing the recitation of mantras and likewise remembering Kṛṣṇa, she fed many Brāhmaṇas according to the prescribed rites every day for a full year. (1.96.60)
On the day of completion, Kṛṣṇa, the soul of all, is repeatedly remembered:
"May Kṛṣṇa himself, being pleased, come to the place of worship. (61)
Then they all praised him, who was armed and four-armed, possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids and the power to enchant ten million Manmathas. (62)
He seated that god Kṛṣṇa, whose face was serene and whose radiance was equal to ten million moons,
upon an excellent jeweled lion-throne.
Brahmā, Śakti, Śiva, and the others bowed their heads to him;
Hari, who is worthy of worship, was honored with a welcome and bathed during his vow. (64)
He said, "O Goddess! Your vow is complete; it has become a bestower of a virtuous son.
Then Pārvatī spoke, "O God of gods, O Great Lord! (65)
"Grant me a son who shall be a conqueror and a son who is honored as the foremost of all.
Then the Lord Kṛṣṇa said to the goddess, "So be it," speaking thus. (66)
Therefore, the gods repeatedly entreated him for the destruction of the Daityas and the slaying of the Asura Tāraka; thus, he is the crest-jewel of victors. (67)
"You shall have one son, and a second son who will be auspicious;
he shall be the foremost object of worship for all the gods and the bestower of all blessings upon you. (68)
"Two sons shall be born to you from my seed, both miraculously conceived; they shall indeed become the sons of Śaṅkara. O beautiful woman, please your husband! (69)
Then Śivā spoke to Viṣṇu, the bestower of the fruits of actions:
"Some yogins meditate upon You as peaceful, wonderful, and possessed of form—wearing yellow garments, wielding four weapons, the beloved of Lakṣmī, and having four arms. (1.96.70)
Some [saw him] as a beautiful youth with two arms, adorned with jewels. (71)
I meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, the infallible Lord, who is dark-complexioned, beloved by the cowherd women, the master of illusion, and enchanting—the God who bestows sons. (72)
O Lord! By Your inspiration, I—who am born from a portion of Your splendor—am Your Māyā; having deluded the Asuras in the past through Your Māyā, ||| 73 ||
Having slain them all, I went to that Himālaya, the king of mountains.
Then I was praised by the gods who were oppressed by Tārakākṣa. (74)
In the birth of Bhava, I was born as the wife of Dakṣa;
having abandoned my body at Dakṣa’s sacrifice due to my censure of Śiva, I became Śivā. (75)
I was born of Śailajā, while Kālikā was born of Menakā.
Even in this birth, Śiva attained [me] through manifold penance;
the Yogin took my hand, having been repeatedly entreated by Brahmā. (76)
And that splendor born of passion could not be attained by me through divine illusion. (77)
O Lord of Gods, being distressed without a son, I praise you alone;
at this moment, I desire to obtain through my vow a son such as yourself. (78)
O Ocean of Compassion! Having heard all this concerning the conqueror of all armies and the one who is supreme among all those worthy of worship, you ought to show me mercy. (79)
Having thus entreated her, the goddess Pārvatī remained silent;
then Kṛṣṇa showed two divine sons to the goddess within himself. (1.96.80)

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Examples of Women Performing Vows for the Sake of Sons, the Arrival and Blessings of the Celestial Sages, and the Vision of Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! That merciful Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion, first revealed His own form, which enchants all beings. (1)
Indeed, he is the very essence of celibacy (brahmacarya), the supreme treasury of form itself;
he has six faces, is accompanied by a peacock, and is endowed with many weapons.
Possessing great knowledge, great strength, and great skill, in the full bloom of youth; sixteen years of age, he was endowed with the divine marks of a worthy commander of armies. (3)
Then, his own second form is gross, the supreme progenitor of the lineage;
dark-complexioned, adorned with a garland of forest flowers and jewel ornaments,
youthful in age, and beautified by a serpent as a sacred thread.
Seeing the Lord of All, who possesses the beauty of ten million Cupids, whose mount is a steady mouse,
who is exceedingly joyful, and who bestows grace upon his devotees—
[she saw] two sons of beautiful form who were worthy of him. (5–6)
Having obtained that boon at that very moment, he chose it with his mind.
Then, having granted the boon, Kṛṣṇa caused that splendor to vanish.
Delighted that she had obtained two sons, the Mother of the World, though previously childless,
bestowed gifts upon Brahmins, mendicants, and bards.
He fed them in that manner and worshipped Śaṅkara;
he caused the drum to be beaten and had auspicious rites performed. || 9 ||
Having completed her vow, the daughter of the mountain, after feeding those who were dependent upon her, caused a melodious musical performance concerning Kṛṣṇa to be sung. (1.97.10)
She ate milk-porridge and fried cakes together with her husband;
she partook of betel-leaf, richly endowed with fragrance, together with Śambhu. (11)
Having sent away all her guests, she, being purified, again prepared the household articles and her own body for the sake of pleasure. (12)
Upon a beautiful bed with a frame of excellent jewels, resembling the foam of milk,
scented with flowers, sandalwood, musk, and camphor,
the Supreme Goddess lay down in secret with her Lord.
Made fragrant by a breeze rich with sweet-smelling flowers. ॥14॥
In the delightful sandalwood forest on the border of the abode of Kailāsa, filled with the humming of bees and the songs of male cuckoos,
she enjoyed amorous dalliance with her husband on the slopes of Mount Gandhamādana.
That Ambikā dallied with Śaṅkara;
as the two engaged in sexual union, there occurred a great and wonderful emission at the first discharge of semen. ||16-17||
That semen is of the nature of fire, causing fear and possessing great brilliance;
having faltered at the vaginal opening, it was discharged outside. (18)
Then, by the will of Hari, for the sake of producing a son not born from a womb, [the seed] appeared in the form of a stream and in the form of a flame. (19)
In the sky and upon the earth, living beings fell into a swoon due to the nature of the heat produced by that fiery splendor. (1.97.20)
For the sake of pacifying that [calamity], Brahmā himself, Viṣṇu, and the other inhabitants of heaven mentally invoked Agni; he too arrived with great haste. (21)
And with the consent of the gods, he entered the pleasure grounds;
having reached the courtyard, he spoke these words: "Give me alms. (22)
"O Mother, give alms to me who have a bowl for my hands; I am going.
Then his mother gave him alms that had appeared in the form of milk. (23)
When the milk-rice (paramānna) was placed in his cupped hands,
then the seed of Śambhu flowed forth, falling from the path of the sky.
The sweet, fragrant, and delicious alms, having fallen into the fire held in his cupped hands, were swallowed and consumed by the Fire-god himself in person. ||25||
Deluded by the taste of the fluid, Agni even took up the semen of others;
indeed, he obtained it from the sky, from the intermediate space, from the earth, and from his own bed. (26)
Out of greed for flavors and through delusion, he took all of that himself along with the alms-food, and mixed it together again and again. (27)
Tasting it with devotion, he swallowed the milk-preparation and its potency;
indeed, nothing remained on Pārvatī’s lap for the sake of her son. (28)
Then Gaurī, overcome with anxiety, cursed Agni—who had been enticed by the tasting of the flavor—saying: "O Agni, because of this corruption through tasting the flavor... (29)
"Even the seed that was in the form of your son, which was situated in my bed, has been eaten by you.
Therefore, O mendicant, by my curse, may you indeed become a consumer of all things immediately! (1.97.30)
A curse was incurred, and great suffering arose in the mind of Vahni, because his potent seed did not waste away, as its energy was exceedingly intense and hot. ||31||
On the contrary, that semen caused the fire to blaze up even more intensely.
Indeed, the fire, burning fiercely, went to the great pool of the Gaṅgā. ||3||
The Fire-god vomited all of that and then became restored to health;
however, Gaṅgā was then scorched and consumed by the heat of his virility. (33)
The waters that had surged upward could not endure that heat at all;
cast off by Gaṅgā, the mineral fell indeed upon a thicket of Śara reeds. ||34||
There, the intensely blazing element caused the illusion of fire. At that time, the wives of the Seven Sages arrived there at the Gaṅgā to bathe. (35)
Seeing that [fire] blazing there, the Kṛttikās, who were afflicted by the cold, desired to bathe; however, they were restrained by Arundhatī. (36)
Furthermore, six wives of sages indeed arrived at that place; and as they all performed penance there, the atoms of semen [were produced]. (37)
They quickly entered the hair-pores of those women right there;
they became pregnant with six embryos each and blazed intensely. (38)
And they lamented: "From what cause indeed have we become pregnant?
What is this that burns our entire bodies, as if it were fire? (39)
And right there we abandoned him, not because he had swallowed the medicinal herbs of Alakhaṇḍa;
rather, having drunk his semen as a juice, they discharged it upon the surface of the earth.
In a single moment, that semen became a six-faced child with the luster of gold—an offspring who was instantly beautiful and very delicate. (41)
The powerful Kārttikeya was born on the bank of the Gaṅgā;
indeed, when the six-faced son of Śaṅkara was born from the Gaṅgā, [he was so called]. (42)
At that very moment, Girijā’s breasts began to flow with milk;
beholding Śiva, the slender-limbed maiden said, "O Śambhu, there is a flow from my breast. (43)
"O Mahādeva, he has been born; let it be seen for what purpose.
Having understood through meditative absorption, Mahādeva said, "A son has been born. (44)
Then Nārada arrived and related that birth to Śiva and Śivā: "A most beautiful son has been born. (45)
Having heard those words, the Brahmins, the sages, and likewise the Pramathas,
adorned Kailāsa with canopies, banners, and arches.
Then, with banners and plantain pillars adorned with auspicious and propitious decorations,
the celestial sages, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, hosts of Apsarases,
Yakṣas, serpents, and humans went to the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, Śaṅkara mounted his bull in order to see the son of Gaṅgā. ||48||
Accompanied by Pārvatī and his attendants, he arrived at the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, conchs and kettledrums, as well as many musical instruments, resounded.
Some danced, sang, and praised that ocean of virtues.
They gazed upon the son of Gaṅgā, who resembled Śaṅkara himself.
They beheld the boy pervaded by splendor, with a radiance equal to the sun;
he was fair-faced, possessed of great beauty, lovely, with a fine nose and a smiling gaze. (51)
Then the gods paid homage to that youth, who was serene, possessed of beautiful teeth, lovely in all his limbs, and had glossy locks of hair. 52.
All the Pramathas and Gaṇas, as well as Vīrabhadra and the others, and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahendra, surrounded Kumāra. ||53||
Likewise, others stood nearby on the left and right sides;
then Śambhu, firm in his vows, descended from the bull together with Pārvatī. ||54||
He beheld his son and was overwhelmed with affection;
there, Pārvatī, flooded with love, embraced Guha.
Placing him upon her lap, Pārvatī indeed caused him to drink the milk flowing from her breast;
Pārvatī kissed her son, while his father Śaṅkara licked him. ||56||
Indeed, joined by all with blessings, sugar was then caused to be given;
various kinds of gifts were indeed caused to be bestowed by Hara.
Then the couple shone there, moving together in a single file;
meanwhile, Kumāra took pleasure in holding Vāsuki around his neck. 58.
Then Gaṅgā, the Kṛttikās, and the deity Agni, having arrived there, beheld the child of magnificent form, endowed with strength and the splendor of the sun. ||59||
"This child is mine and not yours," they argued with persistence.
Then the boy spoke directly: "Because of my gaze upon her breast... (1.97.60)
"I am her good son, [drinking] the milk she has milked out of affection"—having uttered this, he first bowed to his own parents, and then to others. (61)

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Vision of the Two Sons Granted by Śrī Kṛṣṇa to Pārvatī, and the Birth of Kārttikeya through Śaṅkara, Pārvatī, Agni, Gaṅgā, Śara, Stamba, and the Kṛttikās," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 97.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Śiva spoke to the gods: "This Kumāra is powerful;
though born as soon as he was conceived, he is divine and young, and is considered the one who shall accomplish the work of the gods."
"Therefore, he who is powerful and skillful should be appointed by you as you wish.
Then all the gods said to Śambhu for the sake of the happiness of everyone:
"O Lord, there is indeed fear of Tāraka for all the worlds. (2)
"Therefore, this son of yours should be consecrated to the office of commander-in-chief.
When Śaṅkara had thus given his consent at an auspicious moment,
he drafted the festive proclamations for the bestowal of the command.
The Gaṇas departed, taking fourteen auspicious leaf-plates to the fourteen worlds, [to reach] the sages, the ancestors, and the celestial dwellers,
as well as the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Bhūtas, Pretas, and flesh-eaters.
Of humans, asuras, and serpents; of kinnaras, uragas, and kings.
By the command of Śiva, they distributed the parchments to every house;
meanwhile, the sages arrived from Satyaloka together with Brahmā.
And likewise, from the world of austerity (tapas), there are the Pitṛs, such as the Agniṣvātta-s,
the Barhiṣad-s, the Ājyapa-s, the Somapa-s, the Vatsara-s, and others.
All the purifying fires, Yama, the pretas, and the lords of the directions, as well as the Manus and the Maruts, assembled at that place. || 9 ||
Indra, Kubera, Varuṇa, Yama, as well as the hosts of Yama, all the Bālakhilyas, the seven Ṛṣis, and the Nairṛtas. || 1.98.10 ||
The continuities of non-dharma and dharma, the wise ones, the thunders, the seasons beginning with spring, and Kāma accompanied by his arrows and other [attributes]—[these were born]. (11)
Viṣṇu, the lord of Lakṣmī, arrived together with Lakṣmī and his attendants;
so too did the virtuous goddesses who adorn the domestic life of the fourteen worlds. (12)
Courtesans, dancers, and devoted female servants arrived;
and the gods on earth, the rivers, the streams, and the mountains also came together. (13)
There were forests and sacred fords, cities and abodes, as well as embodied forms; there were elemental beings and living creatures, along with Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards. (14)
Human beings, nāgas, and serpents; trees, creepers, and birds;
those dwelling in the sky, those moving in water, and those on land—both the stationary and the mobile. (15)
Possessing divine bodies, they assembled for the great festival of the generalship:
singers, dancers, jesters, experts in drama,
musicians, attendants, and others belonging to the classes of gods and non-gods.
All those who had been invited there arrived, seeking the festival. ||17||
Eager to see the boy who was worthy of the position of commander-in-chief, they gathered to witness the rite, as if generally coming to see their own protector. (18)
And almost everyone gathered there to witness that assembly;
meanwhile, Kailāsa was beautifully adorned by Śaṅkara. (19)
Indeed, a great pavilion was constructed with gold, jewels, garments, and other materials;
it was adorned with plantain pillars, water-pots, archways, and festoons. (1.98.20)
There were hundreds of thousands of pavilions, tens of millions of leaf-huts, delightful assembly halls, pleasure groves, gardens, and city gates. (21)
There were infinite varieties of solid and soft foods, millions of kinds of foods to be licked and sucked, and hundreds of thousands of delicious, sweet, and fragrant drinks. (22)
Indeed, there were countless objects for the delight of the mind, as well as various kinds of nectars and numerous sweet fruits. (23)
Indeed, there were most divine cooked foods containing sugar, nectar, and ghee;
likewise, there were betel leaves and other items that provided extreme satisfaction. (24)
Seats, carpets for sitting, and jeweled lion-thrones;
as well as many fine palaces with curtains and celestial chariots (vimānas). ||25||
There were millions of vehicles capable of traveling through water, air, and on land, as well as various articles of enjoyment and mirrors with jagged edges like hair. (26)
Abundant flowers, oils, perfumes, and sandalwood; saffron, incenses, lamps, and musical instruments in great abundance. (27)
In every place, beautiful banners indicating the leadership of the armies fluttered in the sky, and songs of victory were sung. (28)
When the Muhūrta of Abhijit arrived, the gods on earth and the sages performed the recitation of auspicious blessings (svastivācana), followed by the chanting of the Vedas.
Then the noble-minded Bṛhaspati caused Skanda to wear the sacred thread for protection, as well as the Jayamaṇi amulet. (1.98.30)
An auspicious *tilaka* was made with unbroken rice grains, moon-fragrance (*candana*), and saffron; and the Guru performed an auspicious sprinkling with the waters of the Gaṅgā. (31)
There, mantras that bestow strength are applied into the right ear;
a blade of darbha grass is placed upon the ear, and likewise an auspicious mark is placed on the head.
The substance [of the crown] was sprinkled upon his head, and the crown was offered by Brahmā;
then the two auspicious earrings were given by Kubera to his ears. (33)
Then the ocean placed necklaces of jewels upon his neck, and Himālaya indeed offered him ornaments of gold. (34)
The guardians of the directions presented various objects produced in their respective regions.
At that time, Varuṇa offered a white umbrella, equal in brilliance to the moon. (35)
There, Gaṅgā and Yamunā held chowries in their hands, and Indra gave him armor that protects one in the position of commander-in-chief. ||36||
The attire of a commander-in-chief was indeed bestowed upon him by Viṣṇu himself;
and the Sun-god gave him a chariot with firm parts that remained unscathed in battle. (37)
Viśvakarman indeed gave him a firm sword and shield;
Śambhu, however, gave him a bow and two inexhaustible quivers of arrows. (38)
The discus was indeed given by Hari, and the mace and staff by Yama;
the thunderbolt was then given by Agni, and the spear was offered by Vāyu. (39)
Peacocks, horses, and elephants capable of traveling through the sky were given by the mountains;
as well as missiles, weapons, arms, implements, nooses, spears, lances, and so forth. (1.98.40)
Various [powers] were bestowed upon him by the diverse gods who had assembled for that festival;
various inexhaustible *śaktis* were granted to him by the goddesses. ||41||
Pārvatī bestowed her blessing, saying, "Be ever victorious!
Then the retinue was presented by the sages as a support for the army. ||42||
Then everything that was deficient was fulfilled by King Dakṣa and the other monarchs;
thereafter, there arose the proclamation of victory for the high-souled Kārtika. 43.
Musical instruments were sounded and shouts of victory arose;
fierce hosts on the side of the gods stood ready, having been rallied by their general.
Various auspicious signs appeared for the celestial women;
an assembly gathered there from the fourteen worlds. (45)
Well-satisfied with various foods, sweet drinks, and fragrant scents, both men and women offered praises to the son of Śaṅkara. ||46||
Then the world-protectors also appointed a general who was immensely powerful, invincible, and superior in every respect, as well as well-prepared armies. ||47||
Having bestowed upon others provisions for the journey as well as gifts, they were all sent forth by Śambhu and departed for their respective abodes. ||48||
Then the assembled gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, deliberated: "This very day, whether by day or by night, the great Asura [must be dealt with]. (49)
"The one of great strength known as Tāraka terrifies the inhabitants of heaven;
yet this Skanda, a being of great courage, shall slay Tāraka. (1.98.50)
Seven days had passed since his birth when he indeed became a mighty commander of the great army, powerful through the forces granted by the gods. ||51||
"Therefore, this very day we shall go forth, prepared to slay Tāraka.
Thinking "So be it," they immediately set out against the asura Tāraka. (52)
Then kettledrums, clay drums, paṭahas, ānakas, and gomukhas, as well as various other musical instruments and trumpets, were sounded. (53)

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Kārttikeya’s Appointment as Commander-in-Chief and His Corresponding Weapons and Equipment," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 98.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! At that time, fear and fearlessness arose in the world. Having learned of the endeavor of the gods, the powerful Tārakāsura [prepared for battle]. (1)
Accompanied by ten million asura troops, he went forth to fight against the gods.
There, the asuras, rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas gathered together;
shouting with great pride, they marched out with a desire for battle.
Then a great army of Tāḍaka arrived in the presence of the gods.
At that time, a voice from the sky, filled with favor, spoke to the gods:
"Placing the victorious Skanda at their head, let them advance; victory shall be theirs."
That son was manifested by Pārvatī for the sake of victory;
for those whose leader in battle is Skanda the fierce, their victory is indeed certain. (5)
Upon hearing this, the gods rejoiced, becoming fearless and desirous of battle.
At that moment, a certain maiden was urged there by Brahmā;
she was the daughter of Death, who then arrived with an army called Mṛtyusenā.
She resorted to supreme asceticism for the sake of choosing the prince as her husband.
That beautiful daughter of Mṛtyu, the slayer of enemies,
chose the youthful Kārttikeya there with a choice garland.
Then Skanda, joined by her, indeed arrived as the commander-in-chief;
at that time on the field of battle, there were terrible ones with faces like bulls, blood-stained and fierce. || 9 ||
Great kettledrums resounded, along with wonderful ḍiṇḍima drums;
war-hardened trumpets, mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, and ānakas were sounded.
Harsh-horned conchs and fierce bherī drums were played.
And all at once, the gods and asuras rose up, desiring to fight.
Having mounted the prince upon an elephant, the Lord of the Gods (Indra) indeed took the lead, surrounded by a vast army of deities and the guardians of the world. ||12||
Yama was there with his own attendants, as was Samīraṇa (Vāyu) with the Maruts;
Varuṇa was there with the aquatic creatures, and Kubera was surrounded by the Guhyakas. ||13||
Śaṃkara was with his Pramathas, and Nairṛta was with the diseases;
all of them stood within the sacrificial altar-ground, situated between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers.
And those who lived under Tāraka arrived from Pātāla—the Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and Asuras. (15)
Elephants, camels, sheep, horses, mules, and birds;
various chariots and numerous celestial vehicles;
and many foot soldiers with their weapons shone forth at that time. (16)
With swords, javelins, iron arrows, nooses, mallets, and battle-axes; ॥17॥
With arrows, iron clubs, and discuses, as well as spears, tridents, and axes—when the armies of both the Daityas and the dwellers of heaven were thus fully equipped, [the battle commenced]. (18)
Beheld by the crooked glance of Mahākāla, those two shone brilliantly; seeing them as the banners for the commencement of battle, they then released their arrows. 19.
They rained down extremely sharp arrows from all sides—razor-edged shafts, crescent-headed ones, and those with three or five edges. || 1.99.20 ||
The sky was covered with arrows as the warriors pierced one another with shafts;
the severed warriors shone like blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees. (21)
In the army, shrouded by one another’s arrows, those warriors roar;
some have fallen upon the ground, while others indeed roll about with their heads severed.
The arms of some were severed and their necks torn asunder;
the hearts of others were pierced through, and the hips of yet others were crushed to powder. (23)
With nooses, bhallas, goads, and spears, as well as by the sages, many warriors there became bedded upon the earth in an instant. (24)

Kujambha was with Vāyu, Jambha indeed with Yama;

Yakṣas, piśācas, uragas, pataṅgas, as well as pitṛs;

Indra himself, Nimi, Vahni, Kālanemi, and Yama;

Thus oppressed, the gods, together with Mahendra,
then went to the abode of Svāyambhuva and praised the Supreme Lord.
"Salutations to you, the progenitor of the world; salutations to you, the cause, the protector, and the destroyer. Grant us protection from [this] torment.

And even today, no man has been born in this world who could slay him. ||45||
And that Daitya chose his death at the hands of a child seven days old;

Kālarātri is my body, as is Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa;

"Indeed, my son, who is of my own essence, has been chosen by Pārvatī as the one to be worshipped first;

To a Brahmin who was begging, wretched, and oppressed by old age. ||18||

One who is devoid of all prosperity suffers the burden of sin;
a Brahmin said, "May there be auspiciousness for you through your state as a guest; O Brahman, [may there be] peace for you. (28)
