Gaṇeśa, in the form of a son, bowed repeatedly to those who had arrived;
he was honored by all the gods with blessings for long life. ||49||
Then, having been granted [the boon], Viṣṇu spoke to the virtuous Pārvatī:
"From Brahmā down to the smallest insect, every being experiences the fruit of its own karma. (1.104.50)
Whatever good or evil one has committed, that one encounters in the corresponding rebirth; O virtuous lady, even Indra may take birth in the womb of a worm through his own karma. (51)
Even an insect may indeed become Indra through the fruit of its past karma;
likewise, even a lion is unable to kill a fly without the influence of prior deeds. (52)
A mosquito is capable of killing an elephant through its past karma.
Happiness, suffering, fear, sorrow, and joy are the fruits of karma. (53)
Those of virtuous deeds experience happiness and joy, while others of evil deeds do not;
the fruit of actions is experienced both in this very life and in the hereafter through their auspicious and inauspicious nature. (54)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, who is Himself the most perfect Supreme Being, has been born as your son; having heard this, Pārvatī was indeed pleased. (55)
Having bowed down to that wielder of the mace (Gadādhara), she gave her breast to the infant;
with palms joined in devotion, she praised Viṣṇu, the Lord of Kamalā. ||56||
Viṣṇu bestowed a blessing upon both the child and the mother of the child;
he also placed the Kaustubha, his own ornament, around the neck of the boy. ||57||
Brahmā gave him a crown, and Dharma indeed gave him jeweled ornaments;
Dharma gave him the Siddhāsana posture, and the Creator gave him a water-pot.
Śaṅkara gave him a yogic belt and the very difficult-to-attain knowledge of reality;
Śakra gave him a jeweled lion-throne, and the Sun gave him two jeweled earrings. (59)
Candra gave him a garland of rubies, Kubera a crown,
and Hutāśana gave him a garment as pure as fire.
Varuṇa gave a jeweled parasol, and Vāyu a jeweled ring;
[Indra gave] a superior bracelet fashioned from excellent gems produced in the Ocean of Milk. (61)
Lakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, gave him anklets and armlets;
Sāvitrī gave a neck ornament, and Bhāratī gave a radiant necklace.
In due order, all the gods and goddesses likewise gave wedding gifts.
The sages, as well as the mountains and various kinds of jewels.
Vasundharā gave him a mouse for a vehicle;
in due course, the gods, goddesses, sages, mountains, and others [did the same]. (64)
Gandharvas, kinnaras, yakṣas, Manus, and likewise Mānavas [offered] various kinds of substances that were savory and sweet. (65)
And they all performed worship in due order with devotion;
Pārvatī, the mother of the worlds, had a smiling lotus-like face. (66)
He seated his son upon the jeweled throne as if he were his very life,
and then proceeded to perform a special worship for him.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how, in the first section concerning the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, when the ethereal voice announced that this Śrī Kṛṣṇa was Gaṇeśa, Lord Hari joined him with an elephant's head and Brahmā and the others presented him with gifts."

Chapter 106 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then,
with all the waters of the sacred fords collected in jeweled jars and accompanied by hymns of praise,
the sages bathed him according to the mantras prescribed in the Vedas.
And Satī joyfully gave him two garments purified by fire.
She offered water for his feet from the waters of the Godāvarī and the arghya offering from the waters of the Gaṅgā,
accompanied by dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and sandalwood paste.
Having brought water from the Puṣkara lake, he offered it for sipping (ācamanīyaka). ||3||
Honey-mixture (madhuparka) served in jeweled vessels, along with excellent drinks mixed with sugar, and bathing oil for Viṣṇu prepared by the two celestial physicians (Aśvinīs). || 4 ||
A multitude of beautiful ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels, and hundreds of other blossoms from the pārijāta tree. (5)
Various flowers such as mālatī and campaka, as well as leaves suitable for worship, together with tulasī. (6)
With reverence, she offered sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron,
as well as a multitude of jewel-lamps and incense on all sides.
One should offer as an oblation what is dear to Him: mountains of sesame sweetmeats (laḍḍukas), and mountains of sweetmeats made from the flour of barley and wheat.
And mountains of cooked foods, most delicious and charming, as well as mountains of *svastika* sweets endowed with exquisite sugar. (9)
And mountains of parched rice grains smeared with molasses, and mountains of flattened rice; mountains of śāli rice and flour cakes, together with various side dishes. || 1.105.10 ||
And with joy he gave a hundred thousand jars filled with milk, and a hundred thousand jars filled with curd for the purpose of worship. (11)
And Pārvatī respectfully [offered] three hundred thousand jars of honey and five hundred thousand golden jars of clarified butter. ||12||
There were also countless fruits of pomegranates and bilvas, as well as various kinds of dates, wood-apples, and rose-apples. (13)
And the fruits of mangoes, breadfruit trees, and plantains, as well as other ripe fruits produced in their proper seasons and regions. (14)
The Great Goddess gave those foods, which were savory and sweet, as well as water that was clear, perfectly pure, and fragrantly scented with camphor and other substances. (15)
Ganges water for the purpose of drinking, and again water for sipping; and excellent, beautiful betel-leaf, well-scented with camphor and other fragrances. (16)
She gave a hundred golden vessels filled with food;
the ministers of the beloved of the King of Mountains honored the son of the Mountain-born Goddess. ||17||
Viṣṇu himself worshipped him with unsurpassed offerings:
"O best of gods, worship was performed by me for you even before all others. (18)
"O child, become a lord of yogis, worthy of worship by all," he said to him;
and he gave him a forest garland and the knowledge of Brahman, which bestows liberation. (19)
Having bestowed all success, Hari made him equal to himself;
he gave him beautiful articles and the sixteen modes of worship. (1.105.20)
Together with the sages and the gods, he performed a hymn of praise using these names:
Vighneśa, Gaṇeśa, Heramba, and Gajānana. (21)
Lambodara, Ekadanta, Śūrpakarṇa, and Vināyaka—these eight names bestow all spiritual accomplishments. (22)
Whatever task there may be, whether it be small or great, the worship of Gaṇeśa must always be performed first of all. 23.
"Then there would be worship of other gods for me as well;
no practitioner whatsoever would perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and so forth. (24)
If one performs any other rite, it will certainly not be successful; this is indeed certain for the sake of the sages, the ascetics, the ancestors, the gods, the Manvantaras, and so forth. ||25||

By the guardians of the directions and the guardians of the worlds, by the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, by those dwelling in the earthly realm and the intermediate space, and by humans born from the subterranean regions such as Atala; ||26||
"By all those residing on the fourteen stages, Gaṇeśa must always be worshipped first; such is the instruction of Brahmā. (27)
Thus was his status as the foremost object of worship bestowed upon him there in the assembly by the Creator;
and there, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself worshipped him first. (28)
Then, following the worship, the divine benedictions were bestowed;
Viṣṇu, the Lord whose knowledge is equal to Śiva’s and who possesses long life, spoke. (29)
"And in prowess, be equal to me; become the lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
Brahmā said: Be unsurpassed by means of glory, fame, and renown. (1.105.30)
"May worship be offered to you before all others; it is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Dharma replied, "Be as righteous as I am, and be full of devotion. (31)
Śambhu said: "Become a devotee of Hari, a giver equal to me;
always be rich in knowledge, intellect, and great merit, and be peaceful and self-controlled. (32)
Lakṣmī said: "My abode shall be in your house and in your body;
let your beloved wife be equal to me in her devotion to her husband. (33)
Vāṇī said: "May poetic skill, retentive power, memory, discernment, excellent intelligence, and true spiritual power always be equal to mine for you. (34)
Sāvitrī said: "O child, may you be a knower of the Vedas and a practitioner of silent recitation (japa).
Śaila replied: "May you always have devotion for Hari Kṛṣṇa. (35)
"Be virtuous like Śrī Kṛṣṇa and devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
you are like the ocean in depth of mind and possess a form like that of the God of Love. (36)
"May you be endowed with glory, equal to Śrīsvāmī, and like Dharma in righteousness.
The Earth replied, "May you be equal to me in forbearance and possess all jewels. (37)

"O auspicious one, become a refuge, a destroyer of obstacles, and a protector who grants success in great yoga; O Father, you are equal to [the gods] and the bestower of the fulfillment of goals. Umā said this. (38)
"May the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya be exceedingly proficient," so said all the ṛṣis, munis, and siddhas as they offered their blessings. (39)
The Brahmins and the bards performed every auspicious rite;
there, Pārvatī gave ten million jewels to the Brahmins. (1.105.40)
There he bestowed hundreds and thousands of horses and elephants, as well as various other gifts, upon the bards. ||41||
He fed the brāhmaṇas, the virtuous, the virtuous women, and the children;
he had them study the Vedas and performed auspicious rites.
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ! To Gaṇeśa, who is the form of Brahman and is beautiful.
Salutations again and again to Vighneśa, the bestower of all accomplishments. 43.
Having worshipped with this mantra and having offered the ritual substances with devotion, all those present there—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others—were filled with joy. (44)
This thirty-two syllable garland-mantra grants all desires;
it bestows the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and grants all spiritual accomplishments. 45.
Indeed, by merely reciting the mantra five hundred thousand times, the practitioner attains mastery over the mantra;
and all obstacles flee simply by remembering its name. (46)
Whoever travels during the time of the pilgrimage after reciting [this] with devotion to it, for that person all desired goals will surely be accomplished; there is no doubt. 47.
A bad dream seen at night turns into a good dream; moreover, through the recitation [of this], even a terrible affliction by malevolent planets shall never occur. (48)

There shall always be the destruction of enemies, the increase of intelligence, and the growth of fortune; likewise, mental anxieties, physical ailments, sorrows, and fearsome terrors shall cease. (49)
Through the worship and hymn of Gaṇeśa, they neither perish nor come into being;
the armor of Vināyaka wards off all calamities. (1.105.50)
O Mahālakṣmī! I shall tell you that which brings peace to all the worlds;
it is the enchanting [hymn] spoken in the Sāmaveda, within the Kauthuma recension. (51)
Death does not approach those who wear this armor out of fear;
there is no depletion of their lifespan, no inauspiciousness, and no defeat within the universe. ||52||
By reciting it one million times, this armor-mantra (kavaca) becomes perfected;
Prajāpati is the author of this armor that deludes the world. (53)
The seer is Bṛhatī, the metre is Bṛhatī, and the deity is Lambodara himself;
its application is proclaimed for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (54)
Oṃ gaṃ huṃ śrīgaṇeśāya svāhā—may this protect my head;
may the thirty-two syllable mantra always protect my forehead. (55)
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ gam—may this indeed protect the eyes constantly;
may Vighneśa protect the palate constantly upon the surface of the earth. (56)
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīm—may this supreme mantra constantly protect my nostrils.
Oṃ gauṃ gaṃ śūrpakarṇāya svāhā—may this protect my lower lips. (57)
May the sixteen-syllable mantra protect my teeth, palate, and tongue:
Oṃ Laṃ Śrīṃ Lambodarāya Svāhā. May it always protect my two cheeks. (58)
Oṃ klīṃ hrīṃ, svāhā for the destruction of obstacles; may this always protect the ears.
Oṃ śrīṃ gaṃ, svāhā to Gajānana; may this always protect the shoulders. (59)
Oṃ hrīṃ vināyakāya svāhā—may this always protect the back.
Oṃ klīṃ hrīṃ—may this protect the spine and the supreme chest. (1.105.60)
May he who destroys obstacles always protect my hands, feet, and entire body.
May Lambodara protect me in the east, and Vighnāyaka in the southeast. (61)
May Vighneśa protect [me] in the south, and Gajānana in the southwest;
may Pārvatī’s son protect [me] in the west, and Śaṅkara’s offspring in the northwest. (62)
May the portion of Kṛṣṇa in the north, and that of the Most Perfect One (Paripūrṇatama), protect [me];
and may Ekadanta Heramba in the northeast protect me from above. 63.
May the Lord of the Gaṇas, who is worshipped by all, protect me from every side;
may the Guru of the yogis protect me both in sleep and in waking. 64.
Kṛṣṇa himself gave this armor to me in Goloka;
it was bestowed by me, Nārāyaṇa, here in the presence of Yama and the other gods. (65)
That which was offered to Śanaiścara is the deliverer from all calamities;
that very same [mantra], O Mahālakṣmī, has been proclaimed by me to everyone. 66.
He who, having worshipped the Guru according to the rules, wears this armor (kavaca) either on his neck or on his right arm, shall become equal to Viṣṇu. (67)
By the mere act of grasping it, one becomes victorious everywhere and worthy of worship.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and brahmarākṣasas—[are all overcome]. (68)

The ḍākinīs, yoginīs, yakṣas, vetālas, Bhairavas and others, as well as the child-seizing spirits (bālagrahas), the planetary spirits (grahas), and likewise the field-protectors (kṣetrapālas) and so forth. 69.
The timid flee at the mere sound of the armor;
one should reveal it only to an upright disciple who is devoted to the guru. (1.105.70)
Now I shall recite the eight-verse hymn of Lord Gaṇeśa, which bestows happiness;
by its recitation, Gaṇeśa himself always protects one. (71)
Oṃ, salutations to you who possess supreme inner being; salutations to you, the essence of auspiciousness.
Oṃ, salutations to you whose form is Kṛṣṇa; salutations to you, the body of the Daughter of the Mountain. 72.
Oṃ, salutations to the aged Brahmin; salutations to you who are established in pure being. Oṃ, salutations to the one whose form is the body; salutations to you whose mind is stilled. (73)

Oṃ, homage to you who are the foundation of accomplishment; homage to you, the knower of all sciences. Oṃ, homage to you, the protector of the city-gates; homage to you, the one who fulfills the mother’s command. (74)
Oṃ, salutations be to you whose father is unperceivable; salutations to you who are praised by the ancestors.
Oṃ, salutations to you in the form of Skanda; salutations to you whose face is a crow. 75.
Oṃ, salutations to the son of Śiva; salutations to you who are worthy of all worship.
Oṃ, salutations to the one worshipped before [the deity]; salutations to you who are fond of sweetmeats such as *laḍḍukas*. (76)
Oṃ, homage to the destroyer of obstacles; homage to you who sit upon a mouse. Oṃ, homage to the one who attains the cause; homage to you, the long-lived one. (77)
Oṃ, salutations to you of divine stature; salutations to you whose armor is auspicious.
Oṃ, salutations to you who are the nourishment of the armor; salutations to you, the imperishable word.
Oṃ, salutations to you who are rich in auspiciousness; salutations to you, the firmness of devotion.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa; salutations again and again to the illustrious Kṛṣṇa. ॥79॥
Having praised him thus with devotion, a person becomes immortal and attains liberation.
This is called the narrative of Gaṇeśa; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Gaṇeśa’s Special Foremost Worship, Benedictions, Mantras, Armor, Hymns, and so forth," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 105.
[Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (Continuity of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 106]
[The Author: Chapter 107.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: How indeed did the head of Gaṇeśa perish, and by what action?
How indeed, and by what karma, did the joining of the elephant's head take place? 1.
The most perfect, glorious Supreme Self, higher than the highest, the Lord of Goloka, assumed the state of being Pārvatī’s son through his own partial incarnation. (2)
It is a marvel that the head of that glorious Hari was severed and so forth;
how could obstacles arise for Vighneśa, who is the Supreme Self? (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen attentively, O Lakṣmī! This ancient account, along with its traditional history, is as follows:
once, Śaṅkara struck the Sun in eight supreme ways.
Then, as Sumālī was striking him with a trident, Rāvaṇa immediately lost consciousness and fell from his chariot. ||5||
Kaśyapa beheld his son with upturned eyes, as if dead;
placing him upon his breast, he lamented intensely and repeatedly out of grief.
The entire world became blinded and filled with terror.
Seeing his son rendered lusterless, Kaśyapa cursed Śiva:
"Just as my son's splendor has been severed by your trident in the chest,
so shall your son's head, though possessed of splendor, be severed."
And Śiva, his anger having subsided, restored that Ravi to life;
he joined together his chest and filled it with splendor.
Having regained consciousness, Sūrya then rose up before his father.
Sūrya departed for his own abode, having been granted auspicious blessings by Brahmā.
But the two Daityas, Mālī and Sumālī, became afflicted by disease;
they turned leucodermic, their limbs withered away, they were rendered powerless, and their luster was destroyed.
Then Brahmā spoke to those two who were soiled by Sūrya’s anger:
"Oṃ hrīṃ namo bhagavate sūryāya paramātmane svāhā.
With this mantra, he [addressed] the Sun-god with full attention.
Having worshipped with devotion and offered the sixteen types of ritual services (upacāras),
you will certainly attain liberation within one year.
Furthermore, for one who wears this armor of the Sun, no diseases shall exist.
Prajāpati is the seer, Gāyatrī the metre, and Ravi the deity;
its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the destruction of disease and for the attainment of beauty.
Oṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, may the Śrīsūrya mantra protect my head with svāhā.
May the eighteen-syllable mantra always protect my skull. May Ravi (the Sun) eternally protect my chest; may Sūrya always protect my navel;
and may he who is saluted by all the gods always protect my skeleton.
May Bradhna protect my hands always; may Prabhākara protect my feet;
may Vibhākara, the Lord, protect all my limbs constantly.
By wearing this armor, you two shall indeed become free from disease.
The hymn to the Sun, declared in the Sāmaveda, destroys disease;
it is the essence that removes all sins and is supreme in bestowing wealth and health.
Then those two Rākṣasas went to the excellent holy site of Puṣkara. (19–20)
Having donned their armor and worshipped the Sun with devotion through hymns and mantras,
they then obtained a boon from Sūrya and returned to their own original forms. [Thus ended] the obstacle caused by the severing of Gaṇeśa’s head and the curse of the Sun-god.
"The reason why he was born as Śaṅkara has been told to you.
Now I shall relate the story of the elephant, which illustrates the connection with the head—how it came to pass for the elephant even though many other creatures were present. (22–23)
O Lotus-born One, hear the reason why his head was joined [to him].
Once, the king of the gods indeed went to the Puṣpabhadrā river;
on its bank, in a very secluded place, there was a fragrant flower garden.
He beheld the lustful Rambhā, who had arrived from the world of the Moon.
Seated upon his elephant, Indra spoke to her who was restless with amorous gestures, coquettish movements, perspiration, and sidelong glances, as if she were summoning him to sport with her. (26)
"O lady with thighs like plantain stalks! Having embraced you, I do not wish to depart.
Rambhā said: "I am not considered by you to be one who produces satisfaction. (27)
What friendship can there be with rogues who have already achieved their ends?
A woman goes to the best man, just as a fly leaves honey once it has tasted its sweetness. (28)
Like a female crow, the lustful woman, having enjoyed the fruit, indeed departs from the young man who is full of aesthetic flavor, peaceful, well-attired, handsome, and dear. (29)
A passionate woman desires one who is virtuous, wealthy, pure, and handsome;
she does not at all desire one who is ill-behaved, diseased, old, devoid of sexual vigor, ungenerous, or ignorant. (1.106.30)
"Accept me here as your servant, ready to obey your commands, according to your pleasure. (31)
Having spoken thus, she returned and embraced the Lord of the Gods;
there, on the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā, their union of love took place. ||32||
In the meantime, Durvāsas was seen by Indra as he traveled along that path from Vaikuṇṭha to the abode of Śaṅkara, and he was honored by him. ||33||
Durvāsas gave a *pārijāta* flower to Hari;
indeed, Lakṣmī never leaves that person in whose house this flower resides. (34)
Therefore, always protect this unfading [mantra], which increases prosperity,
removes all obstacles, and is obtained through the grace of Nārāyaṇa.
For him upon whose head it resides together with the garland, there is perpetual victory.
He shall become the foremost of all the gods, receiving worship before them all.
Like its own shadow, Mahālakṣmī never leaves him, owing to his knowledge, splendor, intellect, prowess, and strength. (37)
Glorious and superior to all gods, with prowess equal to Viṣṇu, that man who does not bear [him] upon his head out of devotion, but out of egoism; 38.
And there, Durvāsas, having lost his fortune, was excluded from his own caste from the offering made to Hari;
thereafter, he departed from that place for the mountain of Śiva.
Indra, being impetuous, hurled that flower garland at the elephant near Rambhā; the elephant placed the garland, which had fallen upon its two frontal globes, upon its own body. (1.106.40)
Śuṇḍha seized it and crushed it; seeing that, Śrī departed.
Likewise, Raṃbhā went to heaven, and the elephant entered the forest. ||41||
The purifying head of that elephant, having been severed in connection with the flower garland,
Hari took it and joined it to the child.
Thus, the head of this white elephant has always remained fixed upon Gaṇeśa.
O Lakṣmī! What indeed is that which has become worthy of worship for Airāvata? 43.
Then, impelled by the curse of Kaśyapa, Śanaiścara—the son of Saṃjñā and the Sun, possessing a crooked gaze and a giver of suffering—[appeared]. (44)
Arriving there by way of the sky, he beheld the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇanāyaka), who had been stationed at the city gate for the protection of the Goddess. 45.
A battle took place between that Gaṇeśa and Śaṅkara;
with the corner of his left eye, he gazed upon the face of the infant. (46)
By the mere glance of Śani, Hara severed his head; such was the cause there: the gaze of Śani and the curse of Ravi. (47)
An elephant's frontal globe, a garland of *pārijāta* flowers, and the goddess Lakṣmī—these three, though belonging to a single person's fortune, are difficult to obtain even for the gods. (48)
O virtuous lady! All beings enjoy various fruits according to their own karma;
even after millions of eons, karma does not fail the doer. (49)
By their own actions, humans such as Brahmā and Rudra, as well as beasts and birds, kings and servants—even those dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha—are [conditioned] by their respective karmas. (1.106.50)
Possessing disease, sensual objects, beauty, wealth, and poverty; having the happiness of a good wife and sons, yet being thorned by kinsmen and family. 51.
People are born burdened with the suffering of wifelessness and childlessness due to their past actions;
Śanaiścara himself is the personified form of those diverse karmas. (52)
In accordance with those various karmas, he looks with a crooked gaze; even Saturn lives in misery due to his own karma. ||53||
Then Citraratha gave his own daughter to Śaniścara;
having bathed after her menses and adorned herself in beautiful attire, she was tormented by the god of love.
She remembered Śani for the sake of a gift, yet Śani did not even remember her;
due to the loss of her season and the failure to obtain sexual pleasure, she cursed him out of anger. (55)
"Since you did not see me and thus failed to protect the sacrifice, therefore your sight shall never again be a source of happiness. (56)
"Whatever object may be seen by you, let all of that indeed perish.
Thus, by this curse, Śani looks upon whatever with a crooked gaze. (57)
Indeed, all that perishes instantly through the application of those respective karmas;
Saturn, with his naturally humble face, does not look upon anything without [the influence of] karma. (58)
"Driven indeed by karma, he perceives a creator.
Thus everything has been told to you; what else do you wish to hear? //59//
The cause of his having the face of an elephant is profound and great;
by knowing which, one is not deluded regarding pleasure and pain, or the auspicious and the inauspicious,
[due to] a portion of Kṛṣṇa, who dwells within the self, acting from within the self.
Karma has no capacity to smear; rather, it is the inner self that experiences what has been done.
O Lotus-born One, all incarnations are always untainted;
that Self in which they have descended is the one that experiences the fruits of karma. 62.
There are two friends, inseparable companions, both birds established upon the tree of karma.
Of these two, the one who performs action eats [the fruit], while the one who does not perform action does not touch it. (63)
Therefore, Kṛṣṇa experiences no pain from the act of having his throat cut;
for that [pain] would belong to another experiencer there, since it is held that he is a different self. (64)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Saturn’s Gaze upon Gaṇeśa, Śiva’s Curse upon the Sun, Indra’s Crushing of the Auspicious Flower Garland Given by Durvāsas by the White Elephant, and the Subsequent Restoration of Gaṇeśa’s Head and His Sanctity through the Contact with the Touch of those Flowers," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||106||

Śrī Lakṣmī said: O Lord! I have heard the story of Gaṇeśa, whose prowess is wondrous.
It concerns the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, during the first watch of the night at moonrise. (1)
At that time, Gaṇeśa was born; his vow is considered [as follows]:
"Whether with limbs or without limbs, which deity is to be worshipped? Tell me that. (2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Gaṇeśvara should be worshipped together with his wife, sons, and vehicle;
indeed, Gaṇeśvara is always to be honored as equal to one's mother and father.
Skanda and Gaṇapati—these two sons were dear to their parents.
For the sake of their marriage ceremony, Śivā and Śambhu spoke together. (4)
And how should the auspicious marriage of both sons be performed?
O Six-faced One, you have arrived with your army, yet Gaṇeśa has been abandoned by my beloved.
An auspicious effort must be made for the sake of Gaṇeśa’s marriage; this is my considered view.
Furthermore, Kārtikeya likewise has a desire for marriage.
The heart's desire was for the giving of two daughters to the Prajāpati Viśvarūpa;
since two daughters were to be given to the two [brothers], it should be so. (7)
However, it was best to give the two excellent daughters to Gaṇeśa;
then, having summoned them at some point, they spoke to them. (8)
"Listen with affection, my two good sons; I shall tell you the truth as it is:
one of you, Gaṇeśa, is married and is the elder, while the other is without a wife. (9)
Indeed, a rule has been established for the happiness of your marriage:
both sons shall be equal; no distinction is to be found here. (1.107.10)
Therefore, a wager was made regarding both sons: "Whichever of you two shall first return after traversing the entire earth. (11)
"His marriage, characterized by auspicious signs, must be performed first.
Having heard these words of his parents, the mighty Kārttikeya— ||| 12 ||
Mounted upon his peacock-vehicle, he departed swiftly from the temple in order to circumambulate the earth with great speed. (13)
Gaṇanātha, having reflected well right there, said:
"Indeed, my vehicle does not run upon the earth with its speed. (14)
Where am I, traveling by the path of the earth, as compared to him who travels through the path of the sky?
What should be done, and where should one go, while still possessing this gross physical body? (15)
When one has gone only a *krośa* ahead, one is unable to proceed further due to exhaustion; how much more so when, having traversed the entire earth, one’s hope for victory is merely a mockery? (16)
Having reflected thus, the Lord Gaṇeśa bathed, entered his home, prostrated before his parents, and spoke to them. (17)
The earth is my mother, heaven is my father, and the cow is said to be the universe.
Goddess Pārvatī is my mother, and Lord Śaṅkara is my father. (18)
The vehicle for those two is a cow; this bull is the king of the Sudharma assembly hall.
The cow is the very form of the earth, my mother, who is also the embodiment of Ilā. (19)
"Śaṅkara is my father, and his body is considered to be the earth.
For the successful completion of my journey, worship must be performed by me for these three. (1.107.20)
And since these seats have been prepared here for the worship of you both, O Gurus, please remain here and fulfill the desire of our hearts. (21)
Having heard those words of his, the two of them stood upon their seats to receive his worship, and the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇanāyaka) performed that worship for them.
The son performed seven circumambulations of the two of them with great reverence; likewise, he offered seven prostrations and then presented [the gift]. (23)
Gaṇeśa said, "O mother, perform my marriage ceremony quickly.
The mother replied, "Quickly, my son, perform a circumambulation of the earth. (24)
"Come before the prince; let the marriage be the first.
Gaṇeśa said, "O Mother, listen to my words. (25)
"I have traversed the earth seven times, again and again.
His mother asked, "When, my son, was the earth traversed by you? (26)
Gaṇeśa said: "I have performed circumambulation for you both;
by that very act, the entire earth bounded by the oceans has been circumambulated by me. (27)
The Earth is the mother and the Sky is the father; the nature of both is Dharma. Dharma is his vehicle, and the Bull is its mount. ||28||
Having spoken thus, he performed a circumambulation of his father, the bull, and his mother;
by that act, the circumambulation of the entire earth was then accomplished. (29)
The parents said: "We are delighted, my son; you have done well.
By this, you have obtained the fruit of circumambulating the entire earth. (1.107.30)
Through faith Dharma is attained; through faith Hari is attained;
through faith perfection is attained; through faith the fruit is attained. (31)
The mother and father are the sacred site in the home, and the wife is always the Gaṅgā;
if there is no faith in that, everything performed becomes futile. //32//
But for him who, having performed the worship of the Pitṛs, performs the circumambulation (prakrānti), the fruit resulting from the circumambulation of the earth is indeed attained. ||33||

He who indeed departs for a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha) after abandoning his parents at home shall not partake of the fruit of the pilgrimage; rather, he shall become a partaker of the fault of neglecting them. (34)
In this matter, the lotus-feet of one's parents are a great sacred ford for a son;
this proximate ford is easily accessible and a means for accomplishing dharma.
The husband is said to be the sacred ford (tīrtha) for the wife, and likewise the parents for the son;
the devoted wife is the sacred ford for her husband—these are indeed the means of liberation.
If it is true that circumambulating the earth is always prescribed by the scriptures, then Gaṇeśa has told me so; otherwise, the scripture would be false. (37)
Devotion to one's father would be untrue, and all such devotion would become fruitless; likewise, devotion to one's mother and devotion to cows would be entirely fruitless. (38)
Therefore, I have circumambulated the earth in every way;
let my auspicious marriage be performed quickly, for it must soon take place. (39)
Having heard these words of his, his parents were pleased and said to him:
"O son, knower of the scriptures, your intellect is directed toward the scriptures. (1.107.40)
No one is able to alter the boundaries of the scriptures; however, when an inaccessible task presents itself, faith born of the scriptures indeed prevails. //41//
And it is likewise appropriate that for one whose intellect is distinguished regarding suffering, his suffering shall perish through the power of that intellect and wisdom. (42)
He whose intellect is his strength—how can there be strength for one devoid of intellect?
A lion, intoxicated with pride, was cast into a well by a jackal. (43)
Well done by you, my son; the circumambulation of the earth has been accomplished. By treading upon the cows, your mothers, and your fathers, the protection of Dharma has been performed. //44//
But Kārtika did not come; he ran away with great speed.
On the path ahead, he saw his younger brother going along, mounted upon a mouse. (45)
When Gaṇeśa performed the circumambulation of his parents, by the merit gained from that act, another form of Gaṇeśa [was manifested]. 46.
Having become so, it indeed ran ahead with great speed toward Kārttikeya;
but Kārttikeya, seeing that, then grieved most deeply. (47)
"Aha! This rat is so small, yet there Gaṇeśa is so large;
with what kind of speed does he run right ahead of me! (48)
Indeed, all the peacock feathers were struck down by me with a whip or by the wind; he was repeatedly beaten for the sake of increasing his speed. (49)
Even though the peacock now flies up with all his might, he still cannot reach Gaṇeśa; who indeed could surpass him? (1.107.50)
"Even in a dream, no crossing over or proceeding forward is seen;
therefore, I swear to you that I shall not perform this marriage nor any other. (51)
Having thought thus, he turned back and went to where his own home was;
having become calm and entered, he dispelled his fatigue with the army. ||52||
Then the parents set out for the sake of Gaṇeśa’s marriage, waiting for the path of Kārttikeya as they departed. ||53||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Gaṇeśa’s Circumambulation of His Parents and Cows for the Sake of the Fruit of Circumambulating the Earth," within the section on the marriages of Gaṇeśa and Kārtikeya, in the first part of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā* concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga. || 107 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Pārvatī, the mother of the world, was greatly delighted;
she performed that most auspicious rite for the two who were to become her daughters-in-law. || 1 ||
In the meantime, Prajāpati Viśvarūpa,
having brought his two daughters who were worthy of being given away, arrived there as impelled by destiny.

One [daughter] should be given in marriage to Gaṇeśa, the ocean of virtues; the other should be given to Skanda, or else one should follow the opinion regarding daughters that is held by tradition. (3)
Seeing Skanda accompanied by his bride, the two did not choose him;
but seeing Gaṇeśa, the two maidens chose him for his beauty and excellent qualities.
Siddhi and Buddhi both became the two wives of Gaṇeśa;
then a great festival for their wedding took place, causing immense joy.
The gods, gandharvas, vidyādharas, kinnaras, guhyakas,
and others dwelling in the three worlds, being well-pleased, assembled for that wedding.
The words of the family priest, beginning with "May you two practice dharma together," became fruitful there at the wedding of Gaṇeśa.
Gaṇeśa indeed obtained supreme and constant happiness from those two;
for in this world, the state of being a rival enemy certainly gives rise to suffering. (8)
He whose fortune is shattered in this world shall have two wives;
it is a certainty that a man with two wives is as good as half-dead. (9)
Indeed, enemies do not slay him who has died with two wives;
for while one sleeps, the second indeed hates her with wrath. (10)
One woman performs service here while the first becomes envious out of anger;
for one with two wives, every moment the house is considered a chamber of wrath. (11)
One regards the second [attainment] as straw compared to the first attainment of a son;
yet the first indeed regards the second attainment of wealth as straw.
One does not consider the second [attainment] a festival compared to the first attainment of beauty.
The second [type of woman], through her perfection of affection, treats the first as contemptible.
(13) In sleeping, eating, traveling, amorous play, wearing clothes, in gestures, expressions, in pride, and likewise in festivals—the two [types] are like hell. (14)
Even in that case, if those two women born of the same womb were of the species of crows or dogs,
then they would indeed fall directly into the hell named Kumbhīpāka;
and if they were wives belonging to the household, born from the same seminal infusion, then [the same applies].
In that state, there would be no affliction whatsoever; it is considered a home worthy of the name "heaven.
These two are mutual allies, performing the same actions in both pleasure and pain;
they bestow upon one another and do not remain apart from each other. (16–17)
They did not differ from one another in their actions or their thoughts;
they assisted each other, shared the same character, vows, and goals, were equally devoted to their offspring, and likewise possessed the same requisites. (18)
There, the husband enjoys the bliss of heaven, delighted by those two.
Siddhi and Buddhi became such wives of Śaṃda. And after some time had passed for the high-souled Gaṇeśa... 1.108.20.
From Siddhi, the wife of Gaṇeśa, a son named Kṣema was born;
from Buddhi, a beautiful son named Lābha was born. Then the illustrious Nārada came to the wonderful abode of Skanda.
He said: "I speak neither out of envy, nor is it false, nor with deceit.
No one else will do for you what has been done by your parents;
having cast you out, they created such a pretext as that circumambulation. (22-23)
Ganesha’s marriage was performed with two women;
from those two wives, this Ganesha obtained two auspicious sons.
With the consent of his mother and father, he enjoys constant happiness.
The earth was traversed by you through the deceptive act of those two.
O dear son, if a mother or a father deceives their child through the practice of deceit, what can be said of other people who follow such a deceptive way? (25–26)
Indeed, that deed was performed improperly by those two, your parents;
let it be considered by you here as well, for it is not deemed auspicious in my mind.
Even if a mother were to give poison, or if a father were to sell [his child].
The king seizes all one's possessions; who else would be a protector?
Who, being peaceful and wise, would dwell in the house of such a father, by whom this deed born of partiality toward his own son was committed? (28–29)
"Thus has this policy been declared by me; do as you wish.
Having spoken thus, Nārada departed from there for Satyapura.
Then Skanda, overcome with grief and agitation, left his home.

Having departed and bowed to his parents, he, filled with rage, went to Mount Krauñca even though restrained by them, thinking: "If such deceit has been practiced toward me, abandoning affection... (31-32)
The task of Gaṇeśa, who was well-established, was performed with ease;
however, I was then driven out from the house for the sake of a terrible journey.
Indeed, I must not remain in this house for as long as I live.
Having abandoned his army at his father’s house, he mounted his own peacock and went to the great mountain Krauñca; devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa,
having become a supreme Vaiṣṇava, he worshipped Acyuta incessantly.
Having attained lordship, he thereafter adopted the state of a holy man;
remaining ever steadfast in the vow of Brahman, he conducts himself with virtuous character.
Known by the name Kārtikasvāmin, he is worshipped on Mount Krauñca.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, the gods, the sages, and the great seers always go to behold Kumāra; likewise, the lords of munis depart for that purpose.
Then Umā, fallen into grief at being separated from Skanda, [remained behind].
Distressed, she said to Śaṅkara, "Go there with me.
For her sake, Śambhu himself went to the mountain by means of his own partial incarnation;
that Śambhu, named Mallikārjuna, dwelt there together with Satī.
Kārttikeya, having understood that vow, became detached and was about to go elsewhere;
however, being entreated there by the gods and others, he indeed remained.
Skanda, possessing excellent character, stayed there at a distance of three *yojanas*. (1.108.40–41)
Afflicted by love for their son, Śiva and Pārvatī, being full of affection, go there on every auspicious occasion (parvan) to behold Kumāra.
Indeed, on the day of the new moon (amāvāsya), Śambhu himself goes there.
On the full moon day, Pārvatī herself goes forth accompanied by her army.
Thus, O beloved, the worship of Śrī Gaṇeśa should be performed together with his two sons, Siddhi and Buddhi, as well as Kṣema and Lābha. ||43-44||
O Mahālakṣmī! This sinless narrative, which bestows fame, increases happiness,
prolongs life, leads to heaven, is incomparable, enhances devotion to Śiva,
and promotes service to one’s mother, has been told to you.
"It has been declared as bestowing liberation; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Bestowal of the Two Daughters Named Siddhi and Buddhi by Prajāpati Viśvarūpa upon Śrī Gaṇeśa through the Marriage Rite, followed by the Birth of Sons Named Kṣema and Lābha, and the Constant Departure of Kārttikeya toward Krauñcādri," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
