Chapter 109 [Author: Chapter 110 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, you have narrated this most wonderful account of Gaṇeśa as well as that of Kārtikeya. O Blessed One,
I have a certain inquiry regarding this which I wish to pose to you.
"I ask you, O Lord of the gods; having heard [the reason], please pacify that doubt, O Master.
That Kārttikeya should have abandoned his parents and gone far away is not fitting for this world, nor could it possibly occur even in the scriptures. (2–3)
Service to one's mother, father, and guru is auspicious and bestows liberation;
having abandoned service and gone far away, the sin committed against them would arise.
For that evil, which is sin, there is likewise atonement and its destruction.
Why would that fruit not have occurred in the case of Kārttikeya?
(5) Service to one's mother brings liberation; a mother is considered to be of many kinds:
the giver of breast milk, the bearer of the fetus, the giver of food, and she who is dear to her elders. (6)
The wife of one’s chosen deity, the wife of one’s father, and daughters;
likewise, a pregnant sister, the wife of one’s son, and the mother of one’s beloved;
the mother of one’s mother, the mother of one’s father, and the wife of one’s uterine brother. (7)
The mother’s sister, the father’s sister, and likewise the maternal aunt—
these sixteen are remembered as the mothers ordained by the Vedas for people.
Indeed, they are to be honored, saluted, served, and praised by good sons.
Even their words of blessing protect one’s son from sin here;
he by whom service is rendered to them goes to the eternal Brahman.
Through service to them, a son certainly becomes fortunate.
By the grief of their hearts, their auspicious fortune is indeed consumed;
their merit perishes and their excellent prosperity, abandoning him, goes elsewhere.
How then have I, the sovereign of the world, been abandoned by Kārttikeya? (11–12)
O Senāpati, how could you abandon your own dear wife, who is devoted to her husband?
By abandoning a devoted wife, a man shall fall into hell.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, everything has already been ordained by me in this way.
By me, the cosmic egg—the abode of Brahmā, Śambhu, the Pitṛs, the Ṛṣis, and the gods—was fashioned.
In the first age, Satya-yuga, all were Brāhmaṇas endowed with Brahmanic splendor.
For they were indeed equal to the Supreme Self, and their desires were fulfilled by mere thought.
In the Tretā age, however, their powers became diminished due to the difference in time. But in the Dvāpara age, they specifically fell into a state of lacking power.
Power has its root in austerity; it perishes when austerity declines. Due to the decline of austerity among the progeny, there came about a loss of power.
And as power diminished, so too [did everything else].
The power of the lineage of unrighteousness increased more and more slowly.
Through unrighteousness, the subjects there—possessed by falsehood, greed, and pride—became givers of suffering to one another due to the force of time. (18–19)
Having seen this, Brahmā then remembered Śrī Hari, the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of finding a means to protect his subjects;
he, who resides in the abode of Brahmā, was personally invoked for the purpose of protecting the world. (1.109.20)
Having understood the intention of the Creator, Hari arrived there instantly.
Then Brahmā, having bowed and praised the Lord again and again, said:
"O Great King, ocean of mercy, you who deliver even the lowliest!"
Due to the division of the ages (yugas), people who were once devoted to austerity no longer practice it correctly.
Because of the absence of austerity, merit does not exist, and consequently, there is no capacity that bestows happiness.
And due to the absence of that [merit], human beings are devoid of divine grace and are filled with suffering.
O Lord, how am I to protect my devotees who seek liberation?
Even that which is moist is consumed along with the dry, even if it is innocent.
O Blessed One, what means indeed shall I employ for their protection?
O Supreme Lord, through devotion, austerity, and yoga, as well as through worship,
all living beings certainly become truly happy;
yet, due to the influence of time, devotees indeed become devoid of the means of austerity.
If living beings exist [in such a state], by what action are they protected?
(27) Therefore, devise a means for the sake of the happiness of all creatures, by which devotees may always be happy throughout all the ages. (28)
Having heard this method of worship, which includes the protection of the vital breaths (*jīvarakṣā*) performed through piercing (*vedha*), the glorious Nārāyaṇa himself, Hari, the Supreme Brahman,
said to Brahmā: "O Lord of Gods, O Lotus-born one, do not harbor anxiety."
"I myself shall provide protection here for the living beings of your universe who desire liberation;
no one else can be like that. Having reflected upon this by myself alone, [I shall do so] as long as the universe endures. (1.109.30–31)
For that long, however, protection must be provided, since my devotees are dear to me.
If I were to appoint another protector there,
he would instead fall away through the force of time and encounter only suffering.
Therefore, I myself am directly the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest.
Having brought the Imperishable Brahman along for the sake of the protection of all beings,
I dwell here in this world so that there may be the supreme welfare of the worlds.
"From Dharmadeva, my birth shall occur through his mere will in a physical form; having accepted this, I shall become here in the nature of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
For as long as life lasts, I shall remain a celibate student, established in the austerity of Brahman."
"Protecting my subjects through austerity alone, I shall perform service with devotion.
Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, and Nara is remembered as the Imperishable Brahman;
both are indeed rich in the vow of Brahman, having set their minds upon austerity."
"I shall abide"—this is the supreme means of protection.
This vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is always dear to me, indeed most dear. I truly maintain that vow at all times in the world of Brahmā.
In that very same divine Badarikāśrama, I protect [the world],
always established in austerity for the sake of guarding the lords.
Having come here as well to the peak of the Himavat, I am established in yoga.
Established in austerity, which consists of the restraint of all the senses, I shall protect my people by bestowing the merit of that austerity.
O Lotus-seated One, do not worry; the world is protected by austerity.
Indeed, various kinds of austerities exist for the sake of protection.
Not smelling what should not be smelled with the nose—this is called austerity.
Furthermore, not touching with the skin what should not be touched is distinguished as even more so.
Beyond that, it is distinguished by the fact that nothing else is to be seen with the eye;
beyond that, it is distinguished by the fact that nothing else is to be heard with the ear;
and beyond that, indeed, it is distinguished by the fact that nothing else is to be tasted with the tongue.
Therefore, one should not speak with words; indeed, austerity is said to be supreme.

With hands raised, standing on one foot, abstaining from food, and established in austerity—a practitioner who has undertaken such hardship is declared to be superior even to one who maintains silence.
Even better than that is one who abstains from water; even better than that is one whose actions are unconditioned by desire.

Even better than all these is the one who is free from desire and possesses upward-directed vital energy (ūrdhvaretas). One who has upward-directed energy is a celibate student (brahmacārī), and he is distinguished by the absence of sexual pleasure.
The restraint of the subtle body from all the senses is powerful austerity (tapas).
The restraint of the tongue, the restraint of the mind, the restraint of the bodily constituents (dhātu), and the restraint of the skin—these four restraints are proclaimed. 48–49.
Indeed, these four types of restraint arise within the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Therefore, there is truly no other restraint more difficult than this, nor any that is more powerful.
He by whom the vow of Brahman is fully observed, with all its limbs and ancillaries, [is truly successful].
Hari is indeed the embodied Supreme Brahman; there is no doubt in this matter.
For one established in the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), no other duty remains.
The entire world is encircled by the golden thread of the beloved.
He who is dispassionate toward those [objects] and those [senses], the two-armed Supreme Lord,
saves the entire world here by the power of his celibacy.
I, the Lord composed of pure *sattva*, dwell within food.
I dwell within the stomach as the Lord who bestows supreme satisfaction.
I dwell within the bodily constituents as the Lord whose nature consists of *rajas* and *vīrya*.
By whomsoever protection is afforded to Him, by that very person has My protection been performed. (94–95)
One should never, under any circumstances, form a mental resolve for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
nor should one listen to talk concerning the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, one should not utter words regarding the enjoyment of sensual pleasures at all.
One must never, under any circumstances, engage in contact with sensual enjoyment.
(5.7) For the sake of sensual enjoyment, one must certainly not look upon a woman with desire;
for the sake of sensual enjoyment, one must certainly not make a secret appointment. (5.8)
One must never, under any circumstances, indulge in attachment to sensual pleasures;
nor should one ever allow the emission of semen.
Thus, this very practice of celibacy is considered difficult for all to perform. (59)

For living beings who have become united in marriage, such a practice of celibacy is difficult to perform even for those who are not ascetics. Except for Nara and Nārāyaṇa, such brahmacarya does not exist elsewhere; therefore, assuming their form, I shall maintain supreme austerity.
"By means of that vow, I shall protect all my progeny and my own body;
I shall deliver them from evil and bring them happiness in every respect.

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, titled "The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga," it is told how Nārāyaṇa declared to Brahmā the necessity of the descent as Nara and Nārāyaṇa for the sake of protecting his progeny and performing penance through celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
The One Hundred and Ninth Chapter, titled "The Manifestation," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga.
Chapter 110.
[The Author: Chapter 111.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Thus indeed, O Lakṣmī, was my promise made to the Creator."
Then, from that place, I immediately vanished from sight.
(1) Established in the vow of celibacy within my supreme, imperishable abode, I abide in every respect exactly as I abide in the Badarī forest. (2)
Then, having likewise resolved upon it at that hermitage on the outskirts of the abode of the Imperishable, he entered into Dharmadeva.
Together with the Imperishable Brahman, he entered into the embodied form of Dharma.
Then, by my mother Mūrti alone through the power of her mere resolve,
those two boys, who were in essence Nara and Nārāyaṇa, were manifested.
As soon as they were born, they appeared sixteen years of age, handsome, and capable of enchanting even the gods with desire.
With all their limbs well-nourished and joyful, holding a garland and a book in their lotus-like hands,
the two Supreme Lords are intensely radiant, resembling millions upon millions of suns;
their heads are adorned with matted locks as fine as threads of gold.
Clad only in a loincloth, they dwell under trees, in huts, or wear rags;
they carry water-pots and sacred threads, having fulfilled their vows of celibacy as ascetics.
Yet, just as the female portion exists within a man, so too do these two exist elsewhere than in a man.
In a human being, the left side would be the locus of deficient power;
however, in me, Nārāyaṇa, there is not even the slightest deficiency of power in the left.
All powers in both the left and the right are indeed equal.

"The female portion, characterized by diminished power, does not exist within me. Those two marks, however, which are upon my chest—namely, my breasts—are indeed mine. In the absence of the mark of the breasts, there would be a deficiency in my form. (1.110.10–11)

There would not be completeness of all the limbs; therefore, while the mark is preserved in the man who possesses my form, breasts are indeed absent from him. Thus, in that man, there is a deficiency of even a trace of the state of womanhood by me.
The relative strength or weakness of both limbs has not been shown [in that manner].
(1.3) A man should be understood as having no breasts, whereas I, Narāyaṇa, have six breasts.
Since Lakṣmī is always to be protected by me, my breasts are therefore well-guarded. (1.4)
"In a human form, there is no need for Lakṣmī in one of such excellent character;
in my nature as a celibate student, there is no need for a wife.
For this reason, this human form of mine is considered supreme celibacy.
Seeing that their lotus-like arms had grown to such a form as to reach down to their knees,
the parents became truly delighted;
they performed the purificatory rites for the sake of complete purity and commanded them to engage in ascetic practice.
At that time, those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, paid homage to us;
yet service for the sake of spiritual austerity is indeed difficult to obtain from one's parents.
Good sons must always conduct themselves properly in the service of their parents.

In this world, during the process of creation, a mother always protects her son within the womb. For that purpose, the mother constantly endures great hardship; there is suffering at birth, and likewise suffering in the nurturing of the child. (1.110.20)
Day and night she attends to him, cleansing his excrement and urine;
she constantly protects him as her own life and nourishes him with the drinking of her breast milk.
She carries him on her lap and on her hip, and sustains him by eating before herself.
Loving care, affection, and service are always provided by the mother alone.
Even through such service from birth until death, a son can never be free from his debt to her; what then can be said of one who does not serve her?
The debt toward one's mothers does not cease for a son who is devoid of service;
therefore, it is our firm conviction that service must be performed.
Indeed, a son who is devoid of service to his mother is not called a son at all.
"He is indeed called 'sonless,' for he merely burdens his mother.
"Therefore, both of us shall always perform service to our parents;
for a son who does not serve them has a certain destination in hell."

Bound by the noose of time, one becomes a preta and likewise undergoes various births and torments for the sake of repaying debts. Having discharged these three debts, one should fix the mind upon liberation.

For one who possesses craving, there is no goal— neither heaven nor liberation from rebirth. Having procreated a son to discharge the debt to the ancestors, having discharged the debt to the gods through sacrificial rites,
and having discharged the debt to the seers through sacred learning, he should apply his mind to austerity.
Therefore, let us both serve them; otherwise, we shall fall into a low state of existence. Parents who have grown old must be protected by their sons in every way.
Younger brothers must also be protected, and sisters likewise must be guarded.
One should always provide assistance arising from wealth to those who are to be married.
One must perform the maintenance of the family and exert effort in the acquisition of riches.
Furthermore, both happiness and suffering should be borne equally by the kinsmen residing in the household.
"Those two [parents] are indeed considered worthy of service until their residence in heaven;
then, when the son has become young, he will protect us both.
'We shall surely be happy'—such was the parents' expectation. (33)
"Having broken [the rules], one should go to the forest; he is not a son, but a Rākṣasa.
Indeed, there would be no fruit for him in the forest, but rather sin—for he who does not acquire the masses of merit joined with the words of blessing from his parents. (34–35)
Even if he were established in heaven or in sovereign rule, he would be considered a denizen of hell;
therefore, we shall serve you both in every way.
By him who has performed service to his mother, everything has been accomplished.
By him, charity, sacrifice, austerity, fire-offerings, and even the study of the Vedas have been performed;
likewise, the deities have been worshipped, all forms of meditation have been practiced, various types of penance have been undertaken, and the knowledge of Brahman has also been acquired. (37–38)
By him sovereignty was established and heaven was brought into his hand;
by him who served his mother, the state of supreme lordship was attained.
By him the ancestors were gratified and likewise the sages were honored.
Guests have been honored by him by whom his mother has been well-served.
Indeed, sacred fords, holy fields, and shrines have been visited, and sacrifices and works of public utility have been performed by him by whom his mother has been served. (1.110.40–41)
There is no merit equal to service in the practice of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth;
there is no goddess equal to a mother, nor is Hari equal to a father.
Indeed, even a child at the point of death, when gazed upon by his parents, [is saved].
Nevertheless, one would attain heaven; who could abandon these two gods?
Indra, Sūrya, Śaśin, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, Śaṅkara, the Lotus-born (Brahmā), Varuṇa, Agni, and likewise other gods abide within the father.
The son of Janaka obtains every day, through perfect service,
inexhaustible and excellent fruit that is ten million times greater than the fruit of worshipping the gods.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Sandhyā, Sāvitrī, and Satī likewise [bestow this].
Gāyatrī, Rohiṇī, Saṃjñā, Vāruṇī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī—
all these are honored by him who has served his mother well.
Through the merit of performing their worship, ten million times that merit resides in the one who honors the mother.
All of them reside indeed within the form of the mother and not separately;
therefore,
remaining at the feet of our parents, we two shall perform service to the mother and likewise service to the father.
Nara and Acyuta, fully aware of the greatness of serving one's parents, [spoke thus].
(49) Indeed, the messengers of Yama have no power over the eyes of a son who is devoted to serving his parents, even if he is overwhelmed by great sins. (1.110.50)
If, at the time of death, the eyes of the parents are joined with the eyes of a virtuous son by that excellent son, then even in that case, they shall attain a good state.
At the time of death, a virtuous son [should place] water and a lotus leaf in the mouth.
Moreover, by giving even that much, the parents shall attain a happy state;
in whosever house there is a son, the ancestors are well-pleased.
But the ancestors indeed curse a family that is destitute of a son.

Not seeing one who performs the *śrāddha* for their lineage, the great-grandfathers sigh hot breaths, tormented by the prospect of future hunger; and sisters likewise sigh, thinking, "He has no brothers. (54)

"Even our brother is not a giver of a bodice to us," they said. (55) People say that childlessness is an inauspicious sight; they say a girl without a brother is unfortunate, and people would say such a person is without lineage. (56)
A mansion devoid of sons is like a palace or a celestial chariot turned into a cremation ground;
the abundance of food, drink, ornaments, and other riches, when lacking sons,
should be understood as being like the venom of a black serpent— they do not lead to true happiness.
Gods, sages, serpents, and species born from eggs—all desire virtuous sons; a birth without a son is useless.
Therefore, one must always strive to be a good son and a devoted servant.
"Therefore, we two shall always perform service to our parents;
therein lies the highest good, for service bestows liberation.
Having thus spoken of the greatness of their parents, Nara and Nārāyaṇa—
When they remained silent there, devoted to the duty of service,
Mūrtidharman and Śubhāśīrvādayojin— both filled with devotion for their father and resolved to serve their mother— were deeply gratified. (61–62)

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Duty of Serving One’s Parents after Birth," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
[Chapter 111] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna),
Chapter 111.
[Author: Chapter 112.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then Dharmadeva [spoke] regarding the two firm resolves for service.
He spoke to his two sons: "That which is the supreme dharma, beyond which nothing higher exists;
wherein all dharmas converge and which is established as the foundation of dharma—that dharma was first revealed by Hari in the primordial abode. (1–2)

I have heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa the Dharma which brings about all that is most auspicious, which cannot be obstructed by debt, which grants liberation, which bestows salvation, and which is the supreme means of attainment.
Dharma said: "Listen, my two sons, who are most excellent."
"Since you two are virtuous and devoted to your parents, what has been said is most fitting.
Such is the characteristic of a good son: the excellent service rendered to one's mother and father.
Now hear from Hari that which is even more meritorious than that. (4–5)
There is no dharma equal to celibacy; indeed, there is none at all.
All other dharmas are not worth even a sixteenth part of it. Celibacy is the dharma of Brahman; indeed, it is considered to be Brahman itself.

He is the form of Brahman, the embodiment of Brahman, whose very self is Brahman, and who bestows the form of Brahman. (7) When Brahmā, the Lord of all, is pleased, everything becomes eternally satisfied;
before him, services, debts, and gifts are of only slight significance. (8)
That which is said to be attainable through sacrifice is obtained by means of celibacy;
therefore, sacrifice is established in celibacy in every respect.
That which is attainable through sacrificial rites and works of public utility is obtained by means of celibacy.

Therefore, one should always remain firmly established in the desired practice of celibacy (brahmacarya). This form of Brahman which is known as celibacy is superior to all other duties; through it, liberation is attained.
Dharma is established in celibacy; austerity is established in celibacy. Those who are established in celibacy are considered to be established in the abode of Brahman.
Through yoga, perfection arises; through perfection, fame proceeds.
Fame and accomplishment come through austerity; austerity comes through practice within the Brahman.
(13) The restraint of the senses, which is otherwise unattainable, is accomplished through celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Indeed, the world of Brahmā is attained through celibacy and austerity. (14)

For one who has entered the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), even the world of Brahmā grants his desires; how much more so the worlds of the gods and others? For that [world of Brahmā] is indeed founded upon that [celibacy]. Whatever is attainable through the *sattrāyaṇa* sacrifice is obtained through celibacy.
The lifelong vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is established in every respect within the sacrificial session (*sattrāyaṇa*).
That which is to be attained through the vow of silence (*maunavrata*) is attained through celibacy;
therefore, the vow of silence is established in every respect within celibacy. (16–17)
It is attained through the practice of fasting; it is gained through celibacy.
One who stands entirely in celibacy practices the path of fasting.
It is to be reached by wandering in the forest; it is gained through celibacy.
Even the path to the forest is established here within the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya).
That which is to be attained by the path of renunciation is gained through celibacy;
renunciation regarding both the seen and the heard is established in celibacy. (1.111.20)
That which is to be attained through non-violence and is obtained through celibacy—
that non-violence which is universal is established in celibacy.
That which is to be attained by the vow of truth and is obtained through celibacy—
Therefore, truthfulness is established within celibacy in three ways.
(22) That which is to be attained through non-stealing is obtained by means of celibacy;
thus, non-stealing in its twofold form is established within celibacy in every respect. (23)
That which is obtainable through non-possessiveness is obtained through celibacy;
indeed, non-possessiveness itself is established in celibacy.
That which is attained through purity is indeed obtained through celibacy.
Purity is twofold; through the yoga of Brahman, one is established in celibacy (brahmacarya). That which is obtained through contentment is obtained through celibacy;
contentment is entirely one's own when established in celibacy. (25–26)
Whatever various practices of austerity are fulfilled through celibacy,
therefore the great section on austerity is completed within celibacy.
And that which is obtainable through the study of sacred texts is obtained through celibacy.
Self-study pervades everything and is established in celibacy.
Devotion to the Lord proceeds from celibacy;
therefore, devotion to the Lord is established in celibacy. (28–29)
Postures such as Gorakṣa and others indeed bear fruit through celibacy;
therefore, one who has mastered the postures is firmly established in celibacy.
That which is attainable through breath control is also attained through celibacy.
Therefore, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is fourfold and established within the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya).
Withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), however, bears fruit only when the vow of Brahman is present;
thus, the restraint of the senses is indeed firmly rooted in celibacy.
That which is to be attained through meditation is attained through celibacy;
meditation, which is the one-pointedness of the mind, is established upon celibacy.
(33) Where concentration (dhāraṇā) is to be practiced, that too is attained through celibacy.
Therefore, all forms of concentration (dhāraṇā) are established upon celibacy (brahmacarya).
Wherein samādhi is to be practiced, it is accomplished through celibacy.
Thus, whether twofold or fourfold, that [concentration] is established in celibacy.
That which is attained here through self-restraint, tranquility, forbearance, cessation, and so forth, is indeed obtained through celibacy; of this there is no doubt.
O All-pervading One, it is likewise obtained through discernment, inquiry, practice, and virtuous action.

Whatever arises from auspiciousness, from the absence of dejection, and from the absence of elation—all that is obtained through celibacy; there is no doubt in this. It is likewise obtained through knowledge, through dharma, through higher realization (vijñāna), and through various forms of devotion.
Whatever may arise from the knowledge of reality and from the cessation of false cognition—all that is obtained through celibacy; there is no doubt in this.
One who is proficient in the Brahman of sound attains the Supreme Brahman.
The Śabdabrahman, through its expansion, is established here in brahmacarya.

Furthermore, the contemplation of Brahman, the *sadbindu*, the *nāda*, the paths (*adhvan*), and even speech—all these proceed from that Brahman; this is considered the fruit of brahmacarya. (1.111.40–41)

The supernatural powers (siddhis) are: atomization (aṇimā), magnification (mahimā), extension (prāpti), heaviness (garimā), lightness (laghimā), as well as irresistible will (prākāmya), lordship (īśitā), and sovereignty over all (sarvavaśitā).
[42] They produce sounds such as tāra, sutāra, tārātāra, and ramyaka-salila.
And there are also the supernatural powers (siddhis) characterized by joy, gladness, and exultation;
likewise, the three destroyers of suffering— reasoning, oral instruction, and study—
as well as the acquisition of friends and the attainment of knowledge, which are the eightfold siddhis.
Hearing from afar, seeing from afar, taking [objects], moving through space, invisibility,
and likewise all other supernatural powers (siddhis) are obtained through celibacy (brahmacarya).
[These are achieved] by means of *neti*, *dhautī*, *bastī*, and likewise the *kuñjarakriyā*.
Whatever is attained is indeed attained through celibacy in every respect.
(46) Whatever is attained through the libations and *śrāddha* rites for the ancestors, that too is attained through celibacy;
for the *śrāddha* and other such rites are established upon celibacy. (47)
That which is attained through the birth of a son, through sacred knowledge, and through the Agnihotra sacrifice—
that is certainly attained through celibacy alone.
Whatever gain is obtained through the Śruti and the Smṛti, that gain is obtained through celibacy.

That abode which is indeed held to be attainable through the worship of symbols (pratīkopāsanā) is certainly reached by means of celibacy (brahmacarya); of this there is no doubt. And that [abode] which is attained through service to one's mother, father, family, and the worlds— || 1.111.50 ||
That is obtained through celibacy; there is no doubt about this.
It is obtained by serving cows, Brahmins, gods, virtuous women, great souls, and holy men, as well as through celibacy.

The worlds attained by a devoted wife are obtained through celibacy. That goal which belongs to those who are diligent in action, those who possess happiness, and those who are most righteous is indeed attained through celibacy in a state even higher than that.
The auspicious destination that arises for those meritorious souls who are generous,
an even higher attainment than that shall be reached by one who observes celibacy (brahmacarya).
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, vaināyakas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and mātṛs—
Piśācas, pretas, and vetālas tremble before celibacy (brahmacarya).
Likewise, ḍākinīs, śākinīs, śūlinīs, yoginīs, and tālikās flee by the power of the practitioner of celibacy; there is no doubt in this matter. (55–56)
All human prosperities as well as the riches of the gods are indeed obtained through celibacy; they are firmly established in celibacy.
Whether it be the station of Indra, Varuṇa, Kubera, or Soma—
The state of Surya, of Ganapati, of Bhumi, of Svarga, and of the Pitrs;
the Vairaja, Aiśvara, Varṣa, and Pārameṣṭhya stations—these are obtained through celibacy; one is firmly established in celibacy.
The worlds of Agni, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śambhu, as well as the golden realm,
the Prākṛta, the Pauruṣa, and the Muktaka, are attained through celibacy (brahmacarya).
Likewise, the unmanifest (avyākṛta), Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the immortal realm (amṛta) are likewise reached.
Through celibacy, one attains the states of Kṣaira, Śvaita, and Bādrika.
By the power of celibacy, even the individual soul (jīva) attains the nature of Śambhu—
this very Self which is free from evil, devoid of sorrow, and exempt from death.
Free from hunger and thirst, ageless, and one whose desires are realized,
he indeed becomes one whose fruits are true through the power of celibacy (brahmacarya).
Having become equal to the Supreme Brahman, he is permeated by that state in all things.

Through the power of his celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he enjoys all desires. From the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) down to the individual soul (*puruṣa*), the entire circle of attendants, servants, and followers becomes the slave at the feet of the practitioner of celibacy and falls before him. (64–65)
For one who never falters from the [spiritual] element, who always practices celibacy,
and whose vital energy is drawn upward, the gods become his servants and attendants.
The eternal worlds exist perpetually for the sake of the practitioner of celibacy.
By whichever path a person practicing celibacy (*brahmacārī*) then proceeds,
obstacles, sorcery, malevolent planets, demons, spears, and inauspicious things— all ill omens— depart from afar through the majesty of Brahman. (67–68)
On whichever path the powerful celibate ascetic proceeds,
the gods and others approach him nearby for the sake of welcoming him;
so too do the world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, the lords of creatures, and the Manus.
The years, seasons, months, days, and nights approach the celibate practitioner to pay homage to the power of his celibacy. They approach him who blazes with the power of celibacy to offer a welcome.
The Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Vidyādharas, the Kinnaras, and others,
as well as the goddesses, approach him who is radiant through his celibacy.
The sacred fires, those who offer sacrificial fees, and the people residing in household dwellings likewise attend upon him.
The Sādhyas, Kimpuruṣas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and others approach the celibate student who is strong through his vow of chastity;
even the Brāhmaṇas approach the person practicing celibacy with joy. (73–74)
There are millions of couples of men and women within the cosmic egg;
they attain purity by taking refuge at the feet of the celibate student (brahmacārin).
Indeed, through the power of celibacy, the brahmacārin is himself Brahman.
He is capable of transforming the principles of earth, water, and the rest;
likewise, as a celibate student, he himself is indeed able to protect his own vital breath and to release it—for in that matter, Time is certainly not the master. (76–77)
Mahākāla went far away; who were Yama and his followers?
There were the Vālakhilyas, Sanaka and the others, as well as the Siddhas and the lords of yoga;
the Haryaśvas, the Śabalāśvas, and likewise the virtuous men and women.
Through the power of their celibate discipline (*brahmacarya*), they have attained the state of Brahman.
Hanūmān and Kārttikeya remain as celibates;
likewise do the blessed and highly fortunate goddesses, such as Sarasvatī and the others. (1.111.79–80)
These women have indeed become practitioners of celibacy (brahmacāriṇī) and have attained the state of Brahman;
therefore, let your two sons remain in celibacy and perform austerity.
Through the power of celibacy, every debt is discharged.
There is no austerity more difficult to perform than celibacy (brahmacarya).
Indeed, Brahman itself truly dwells within the body of one who observes celibacy.
By honoring the practitioner of celibacy, the Supreme Brahman is honored.
By feeding a celibate student, the Supreme Brahman is well-nourished;
by seeing a celibate student, the Supreme Brahman is revealed;
by touching a celibate student, it is considered that the Supreme Brahman is touched. (84)
In bowing to a *brahmacārin*, one bows to the Supreme Brahman.
(85) Service to a *brahmacārin* is considered to be service to Brahman.
When drinking water from the hand of a *brahmacārin*, the water is drunk by Brahman himself. (86)
Dwelling by the side of a *brahmacārin* is called dwelling in the Brahman;
through the *brahmacārin* and the leader, one truly perceives the Brahman itself.
Indeed, with the nose of the *brahmacārin*, one joyfully smells the Brahman. (87)
Indeed, by means of the tongue of the celibate student (brahmacārin), one speaks the Brahman in every way.
By means of the palate of the celibate student, one even tastes the Brahman;
through the gateway of the mouth of the celibate student, one always partakes of that which is supreme Brahman.
The feet of the Brahmacārī are the hands of Brahmā; born from the hands of Brahmā, he perceives Brahmā in every way through the mental activity of a Brahmacārī.
That which is enjoyed by the Brahmacārī is considered to be the enjoyment of Brahmā.
The dwelling in the practice of celibacy is always considered the abode of Brahman.
The perpetual celibate (naiṣṭhika), the lifelong student (upakurvāṇa), and Hari himself—by him the mother is honored and likewise the father is served. (91–92)
Whatever vow of celibacy has been protected by one who is of the nature of Brahman,
and whatever has been performed as a student of sacred knowledge, all that is indeed performed by Brahman.
Therefore, there is no dharma superior to Brahman, nor does anything remain beyond the practice of celibacy.
Those who are indeed the incarnations of Hari are always celibates (brahmacārins). For the celibate, liberation is forever held in the palm of his hand.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa remained established in celibacy as their sons.
Having received this command from their parents,

Nara and Hari bowed to and saluted Himavat, the mountain of coolness, and went there to perform difficult austerities upon a peak that was eternally adorned with the banyan tree and other features. (96)
Indeed, those two perform penance beneath Badarī for the sake of the happiness of the world.
Likewise, this Kārttikeya also performs intense penance; having undertaken the vow of celibacy, he worships Viṣṇu constantly. (97–98)
Therefore, there is not even a trace of fault in that;
indeed, in the scale of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), non-service is considered to be of no consequence.
That which is non-service should not be understood as such; it is truly service in the form of austerity (*tapas*). 99.
That which uplifts one's own parents through the practice of celibacy and austerity—that service is considered incomparable and unsurpassed;
for by performing it, one always brings about the satisfaction of mother and father. (1.111.100–101)
Service rendered by him is always superior; no other service is distinguished.
The service performed by Kārtika consisted of the vow of Brahman and austerity.
Likewise, the desired austerity was certainly performed by Pārvatī and also by Śambhu.
In the world and in the scriptures as well, there is the renown that austerity (tapas) must be practiced;
O Lakṣmī, the vow of Brahman is austerity, which bestows liberation and does not bring about sin.
Mother Śivā was pleased, and Father Śambhu was gracious. (103–104)

Having attained the position of commander-in-chief, the destruction of the demon Tāraka was accomplished; that was the supreme service of his father’s command. Furthermore, this unsurpassed stationing of Skanda was ordained by me alone.
Thus has it been told to you, O Lakṣmī! What else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Sinlessness of Kārttikeya and Others, Preceded by a Description of the Greatness of Celibacy," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 111: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Age)*

Chapter 113 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of my life, O Great Master!
You have stated that Mahādeva is in every respect the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas.
How is he called a Vaiṣṇava? I am eager to hear that account.
"O my beloved! Tell me today: where and when was he born as a Vaiṣṇava?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, O Goddess, to this divine story which makes one a great Vaiṣṇava."
I shall relate in brief that which bestows liberation and is connected to Viṣṇu.
(3) There are mountains on earth that provide dwellings for gods and others;
among them, this one is the most beloved, bestowing coolness as well as liberation. (4)
The Himalaya is eternally peaceful; there lies the hermitage of Badarikāśrama.
Both the two persons, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, reside there.
Of them, one is white in form and the other is black.
The younger brother is said to be Piṅgala, while Kṛṣṇa is Nārāyaṇa himself.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa are respectively two-armed and four-armed.
The gods dwell there, as do the auspicious hermitages of the sages.
Where the divine Gaṅgā and the Alakanandā flow eternally,
there Maheśa performed austerities for one year.
At that time, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who grants fearlessness to his devotees—
Being well-pleased, he said to Śambhu, "O Śaṅkara, choose a boon!
Whatever you desire, O Lord, that very wish I shall grant.
Then Śambhu spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the compassionate one.
"I shall accept them, O Lord, if you wish to grant them.
Let two boons be given to me, O Janārdana, for you are well-pleased!
May I have eternal devotion to you, and may I become a king among devotees."
May I be renowned throughout the entire world as a great devotee of Śiva.
O Viṣṇu! O Nārāyaṇa! O Lord of the Universe! May my fame as a devotee of Viṣṇu arise forever among the worlds and all the realms. (12–13)
Now, those who will worship me, who will accept my refuge— by your grace, I shall become the giver of liberation to them.
For him to whom I am the bestower of boons, liberation shall be certain.
"May I be a devotee of Viṣṇu and a bestower of liberation; grant me these two boons.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa himself said to Śambhu, the mine of virtues:
"O Śambhu, become my devotee and become a bestower of liberation."
Having thus obtained the boons, Śaṅkara then said to that Hari:
"O Lord, grant me initiation, so that I may become a Vaiṣṇava.
A devotee who is not a Vaiṣṇava cannot bestow liberation, nor can one who is not a Vaiṣṇava. (17)
"Enjoyment and liberation are certain for you once you have attained the state of a Vaiṣṇava through yoga.
Therefore, you must become a Vaiṣṇava; grant me initiation and show me mercy.
Having heard this, the Lord Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, spoke to Śaṅkara.
"O Śambhu, this resolve you have formed for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds is excellent.
O Śambhu, first accept this auspicious jewel of a mantra:
'I am Brahman; I am a devotee of Brahman; chant this incessantly.'"
This jewel of a mantra named [the one beginning with] "Śrī" protects those who have come for refuge.
(21) The mantra "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa" bestows all fruits;
the mantra "Śrīman-Nārāyaṇa" accomplishes all aims. (22)
The mantra *svāminārāyaṇa* is remembered as the bestower of liberation;
the mantra *naranārāyaṇa* is the bestower of the state of Brahman;
and the mantra *harinārāyaṇa* is the destroyer of suffering. (23)
The mantra "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa" bestows prosperity;
the mantra "Vāsudevanārāyaṇa" bestows sovereignty;
and the mantra "Rāmanārāyaṇa" destroys sin. (24–25)
Oṃ, the mantra of Śrī Nārāyaṇa bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This mantra, "Śrī Hari is my refuge," grants total surrender.
Thus, this supreme set of ten mantras should be imparted to devotees.
"Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva"—this is the king of mantras.
(27) O Śaṅkara! Grant these twelve mantras—the king of mantras, the jewel of mantras, and the ten mantras—to your disciples. (28)
I am eternally and exceedingly pleased by the mere utterance of the mantra.
All those who are entitled to the mantra—my devotees seeking liberation, the wise, the yogis, others, the dull-witted, women, and likewise those who have taken refuge in me—are dear to me. (29)
All human beings endowed with devotion and faith are indeed qualified.
Those beginning with the gods who dwell here within this universe are also qualified;
for their own welfare, one or another mantra should be imparted to them.
O Śambhu, likewise take up the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus in your two arms;
and receive this heated branding mark or even a mark made with sandalwood paste on your arms,
which bestows the very form of Viṣṇu.
"Accept indeed this Gāyatrī of twenty-five syllables:
'Oṃ, let us know Nārāyaṇa; let us meditate upon Vāsudeva;
may that Brahman inspire us. This should be recited by you every day."

Meditate upon me as having a beautiful form, either with two arms or four arms. The two-armed form is the form of Brahmā, established in the abode of Brahman—auspicious, consisting of the Supreme Brahman, and the sustainer of all incarnations. (35)
With a discus in one hand and likewise a hand granting fearlessness in the other, possessing two hands;
adorned with necklaces, earrings, garlands, bracelets, and a crown;
clad in yellow garments; sixteen years of age; gracious; the Supreme Lord.
Meditate upon my form within your heart, four-armed, endowed with hands holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, together with Śrī seated upon your left lap.
Then, worship me with the sixteen divine offerings.
Invocation, a seat, water for the feet, and then the offering of honor (arghya);
likewise, water for sipping (ācamana), as well as the bath, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and clothing;
sandalwood paste, ornaments, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the food offering (nivedana). || 1.112.40 ||
Give me the sacred thread and betel with a spirit of devotion;
give me fragrant arka flowers, camphor, and sweet-smelling incense, O sinless one.
Perform circumambulations and prostrations like a staff.
Offer praise and a handful of flowers; likewise, ask me for forgiveness.
Having dismissed me from outside, establish me within your own heart.
[Perform] hearing, chanting, remembering, and service at the feet. (42–43)
Perform worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender;
practice meditation, absorption, and oneness through these spiritual disciplines.
O Śaṅkara, apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and the tilaka upon your forehead.
Apply the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark and the *tilaka* on your two arms and also upon your heart.
Use fragrant sandalwood paste mixed with *kesara*,
and in the center of that, apply a circular spot (*candraka*) using either that same paste or saffron.
Place this auspicious two-stranded tulasī necklace around your neck;
it should always be worn and never discarded.
Furthermore, wear the tulasī garland filled with one hundred and eight beads.
Take this [rosary] made of gems and the like for the purpose of recitation.
I shall give you a name ending in "Īśvara," namely Maheśvara;
and by Pālaka and Ramā, you have been made "Parameśvara."
And by me, through my supreme fortune, you have been made the "Supreme Lord" (Parameśvara).
He who measures and worships Viṣṇu (represented by *paṃ*), Ramā (represented by *raṃ*), and Ma (*ma*)—you are called the refuge of sovereignty, Śambhu, the "Supreme Lord. (1.112.50)
"O Śambhu, may these names ending with 'Īśvara' truly belong to you.
(51) "Thus, O Lakṣmī, initiation was indeed bestowed by me upon Śrī Śaṅkara.
From that time forth, Śambhu has always worshipped me with undivided devotion. (52)
Having received initiation from Śambhu, he went indeed to Gandhamādana;
in his own abode on Kailāsa, he worships me day and night.
Whatever may be available—leaves, flowers, fruits, bulbs, or water—that is what should be accepted.
Śaṅkara does not take any of that at all without first offering it to me.
He applies his forehead mark (tilaka) in my place and performs his recitation (japa) with my rosary.
Free from desire, he remains absorbed in meditation upon my form.
Having thus observed the devotion to Viṣṇu, Pārvatī said to Śaṅkara:
"Whose meditation, recitation with garlands, and the application of tilaka and other rites are being performed by the Lord of the World, who possesses the form of the Supreme Lord? (56)
"You yourself are indeed the Supreme Brahman, the Self-existent One, higher than the highest.
Having heard these words—"Of whom, then, can there be meditation and recitation [of mantras] regarding such a one who is of perfect form?"—Mahādeva spoke this truth to Pārvatī. (57–58)

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowal of Vaiṣṇava Initiation by Nārāyaṇa upon Śaṅkara at Badarikāśrama in the Kṛtayuga Era, along with the Demonstration of its Ritual Components," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 112. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*).
Chapter 113 [Author:
Chapter 114 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Pārvatī, Maheśvara, a devotee of Viṣṇu, began to speak in order to dispel her desire to know [the truth]:
"Listen, O Satī! I shall declare: I worship Viṣṇu directly."
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord—
he is to be worshipped, adored, and chanted upon at all times.
Indeed, I have received initiation from him in the forest of Badarī.
"I indeed meditate upon and worship that Supreme Lord eternally with devotion.
Pārvatī said: "O Lord of Gods! Tell me all that in detail, exactly as it is. Let me hear everything, if it is something I may receive."
By which means I too, by taking refuge in Govinda, may attain the highest good.
O Lord! Why has that not been told to me even until now? Indeed, for all this time, I have remained without the worship of Śrī Hari.
All my days have passed entirely in vain without Hari.
O God of gods! If I am indeed considered by you to be a worthy recipient, then, O Lord, initiate me as well into the path of devotion to Śrī Hari.
The Guru is Brahmā; the Guru is Viṣṇu; the Guru is the divine Janārdana.
The Guru is declared to be one’s own husband, for everything is established in the husband.
Service to the husband is the supreme service; devotion to the husband is considered the highest devotion.

The duty toward one's husband is the supreme duty; grant that duty, O Śaṅkara! For if a man is a Vaiṣṇava, yet his wife is not a Vaiṣṇava, then all service and devotion performed by her who is not a Vaiṣṇava is fruitless.
Food prepared by one who is not a Vaiṣṇava is impure; it is not purifying.
(11) Indeed, the water from the hands of one who is not a Vaiṣṇava is undrinkable; it is not purifying.
The entire house of one who is not a Vaiṣṇava is proclaimed to be a cremation ground. (1–2)
"Lakṣmī departs from the home of one who is not a Vaiṣṇava in every way.
Therefore, I desire to adopt the supreme, purifying Vaiṣṇava dharma of my master; please explain it to me in detail according to its true essence. (13)
Having heard this song of Pārvatī, Śambhu said to Maheśvarī:
"Even until now, you have not attained the state of being a worthy recipient; therefore, it was not told by me.
Indeed, the state of being a worthy recipient is attained through the merits of many births. (14–15)
In this very life, the state of being a worthy vessel attains nourishment through listening to the sacred narrative;
and by serving the virtuous, the self becomes eternal like heaven.
Through devotion to one's husband and service to him, the self shall attain strength.
That person who is strong, fortunate, and a servant of the virtuous,
for him alone does pure conduct arise, both internal and external.
Indeed, O beloved, purity is in every respect the seed of faith.
From that, the desire to know arises, and by that, one possesses the qualification. This being so, when there is union with a Guru, everything that is performed bears fruit.
Now, for you, all of that has arisen and has been applied.
It has now arrived and come to pass; therefore, you are the most excellent vessel.
O Great Goddess, you have been born today, and I am pleased.
Oh, my dear wife, you desire the state of Viṣṇu!
"What indeed could be a greater fortune for me than this?
O beloved, having heard your heart, I am exceedingly pleased. I shall surely grant you everything, since you have become a Vaiṣṇavī. (22)

O Goddess! Whatever food and drink was offered from beginning to end, I indeed consumed it only after first offering it to Viṣṇu. What can I say, O Queen of the God of Gods? For today I am filled with great bliss.
"The rising of the sun for my gold has occurred in every respect;
O dear friend! may you obtain all the fruit of service to a husband.
May my entire household become Vaiṣṇava, and may I be fortunate. (25)

"O Goddess! Today, in the bright fortnight of Kārtika, on the tenth day, perform a fast without food for the purification of the body, O beloved! And for the sake of bodily purification, take the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) here."
Construct a beautiful pavilion for the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
adorned with plantain pillars and archways of Aśoka leaves.
Within it, prepare a *sarvatobhadra* mandala made from the seven types of grain.
O highly fortunate one, prepare [the vessel] and place an auspicious jar there.
Then, place eight new jars at the sides in the eight directions.
Wrap cloths around their necks and place five fresh sprouts upon their mouths.
Place eight coconut fruits, as well as Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī,
there within a golden vessel in the middle of the jar with devotion.
Having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, one should then perform the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Perform the worship of Lakṣmī together with Nārāyaṇa.
Offer excellent gifts and the sixteen types of ritual services.
Keep a vigil at night, and likewise perform your bath in the morning.
Worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa with the sixteen types of offerings. First, take refuge in me as your preceptor (ācārya), who is well-versed in the rules of initiation, for the sake of attaining refuge in Hari.
He gathers the meanings of the scriptures and establishes others in right conduct.
Since he practices them himself, he certainly teaches the Veda;
he knows the mantra of Viṣṇu and performs devotion in every way. (25, 36)
He who knows the wisdom of the Śrīmannārāyaṇa Sampradāya and delivers his own disciple is considered a teacher and a true Guru.
A disciple should have full confidence in his words and be devoted to him with supreme devotion.
One should receive that jewel of mantras on the eleventh day of the month of Kārtika.
O Goddess, receive the conch, the discus, and the auspicious mudrās as part of the initiation;
having bathed [the disciple] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and having worshipped the conch and the discus.
Having established the fire according to the rules, one should offer clarified butter into it according to the injunctions.
Perform one hundred and eight oblations of ghee and milk-rice.
Then, O Guru, place the heated conch and discus into the fire.

"I am Śambhu, the Guru; I shall indeed mark you on both arms with the discus and the lotus. Having worshipped those two again, perform here an ablution upon your head with the water contained in the pitcher."
Having put on a new garment, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with water;
apply a tilaka and an upright mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with a crescent moon upon your forehead.
Then, using sandalwood and saffron, receive my mantra.
"I am Brahmā, I am a devotee of Brahmā"—accept this from me three times. Then, O Daughter of the Mountain! worship me and bow down to me.
Accept this Tulasī necklace, O Adrijā, and wear it around your neck. (44–45)
"O Daughter of the Mountain, receive this mantra: *lakṣmīnārāyaṇa*.
Your names shall be *Maheśvarī* and *Parameśvarī*.
Then, you must meditate upon Śrī Hari as having two arms."
Always hold the divine Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa within your meditation.
There is no deity higher than Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman;
and his other mantra is: "Śrī Hari is my refuge. (47–48)
"O Śivā, accept her today; you have become a venerable and true Vaiṣṇavī.
Practice devotion to Hari constantly, and perform service to my guru.
Cause the branches of disciples and grand-disciples to flourish by bestowing the mantra. (49)
"The abode of Lakṣmī has come to you, and that of Nārāyaṇa has come to me.
We two shall always practice devotion to Nārāyaṇa;
we shall perform service to him by which liberation may become certain. (1.113.50–51)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Subsidiary Sections Granted as Śrī-Vaiṣṇava Initiation by Śambhu to Pārvatī on Kailāsa," in the first section, the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 114 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga)
