Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī was prayed to once again.
"I shall speak before Śambhu that which is supreme and worthy of being heard.
Pārvatī said: "O Lord of Gods, O Mahādeva, O Sovereign of the Suras!
Tell me again in detail about devotion to Viṣṇu, which grants liberation."
The essential nature of Nārāyaṇa, as well as the procedures for mantra and worship,
his manifestations, qualities, and so forth, the means for attaining his abode,
the nature of that abode, its characteristics, and its majesty.
"Out of affection for me, tell me everything in full detail.
Thus questioned by the Great Goddess, Śambhu— the best among the Vaiṣṇavas—
bowed to Nārāyaṇa Hari and spoke with supreme love.
Well asked, O Great Goddess! O you who desire the welfare of all living beings!
O foremost of devotees, endowed with character, beauty, and virtue! O Maheśvarī!
I am well-pleased by your question; you are indeed blessed, O Vaiṣṇavī, my dear one!
"You have performed meritorious deeds and you are a devotee of the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
O Goddess, I shall explain to you the supreme devotion to the Blessed One,
as well as the true nature of Nārāyaṇa and the ritual procedure for mantra-worship."
He alone is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, and the Supreme Lord;
the Lord of all, the Lord of the Great Liberated, the Master who transcends the Imperishable.
He is the Supreme Person, the Highest Puruṣa, Śrī Hari himself.
The Blessed One is beyond the syllables, Vāsudeva, the infallible, the Supreme;
Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods, Viṣṇu, the Eternal; the Lord of Lords, the Lord of the Great Māyā, the Witness, Sadāśiva.
The glorious Hiraṇyagarbha, Śrīyajña, Nārāyaṇa, and Nara;
the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Sovereign Ananta, who rejoices in the Self and transcends all qualities;
he who is the eye of all, the knower of all, who dwells within the hearts of all, and is the Controller.
A mine of virtues, possessing a divine form, dark-complexioned, and heart-pleasing;
he dwells eternally among his devotees and protects his own people.
[He is praised] by Śeṣa, the Vedas, the Upavedas, and others, along with Bṛhaspati and the gods.
Indeed, it is not possible to fully describe the majesty of that God;
O beloved, listen as I speak to you separately of the multitude of His devotees.
(15) The form of Hari should always be meditated upon repeatedly within one's own self.
The marking of that discus and conch is considered the first [duty].

Then there is the wearing of the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the undertaking of their mantras, their worship, their recitation, meditation upon them, and the constant remembrance of their names. (16–17)
Chanting His names, hearing of Him, offering obeisances, worshiping His feet,
drinking the nectar of those feet, eating what is offered to Him,
serving His virtuous devotees, and observing the vows of Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī. (18)
The planting of *tulasī* and devotion—these indeed constitute the sixteenfold [forms of worship].
(19) Now, in his glorious temple, there is sweeping and likewise smearing;
washing, fumigation, swaying, and likewise lighting [the lamps]. (20)
Fanning, massaging, dyeing with colors, applying collyrium,
perfuming, and likewise providing articles according to one's vow;
laughing, conversing, and sleeping— these are the sixteen others.
Various forms of devotion indeed arise for the sake of Hari in the form of ritual action.
(22) Through these various modes of service, bondage to worldly existence is destroyed—for all the gods, for the goddesses, and for me as well. (23)
Hari is to be worshipped constantly by the virtuous, by brahmins, and especially by Vaiṣṇavas; indeed, one should worship Him according to the prescribed rites.
[One should mark] the base of the upper arms with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Having worn [the marks] according to the rule, one should perform the worship of Brahmā;
having washed away his sins, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Worship performed by one who is devoid of the branding of the discus is fruitless.
A Śrāddha offering consumed by one who is devoid of Viṣṇu’s discus is fruitless;
seeing such a non-Vaiṣṇava, the ancestors depart disappointed.
Indeed, cows, land, gold, and other gifts should be given only to one whose arms are marked with the discus.
The asuras forcibly seize whatever is given to one who is devoid of the discus.
Those whose upper arms are marked with the heated discus go to the abode of Hari;
indeed, all sacred fords and sacrifices reside within devotees who bear the mark of the discus.
A Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the mark of the discus is considered to be a mere commoner;
one should not eat anything from him, even if he has performed a thousand sacrifices.
The discus belongs to Nārāyaṇa alone, and it is the destroyer of the wheel of saṃsāra.
Or, for the sake of the successful accomplishment of one's actions, the heated sandalwood disc should be worn.
It is for the sake of accomplishing the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, for the sake of the perfection of mantras,
for the sake of accomplishing the worship of Hari, and for the sake of attaining the status of a Vaiṣṇava.
For the attainment of knowledge, one should especially wear the *cakra*.
One should avoid from afar a Brahmin who does not wear the *cakra*;
having placed him upon a vehicle, one should expel him from one's own city.

One should not look upon a brahmin who is not a Vaiṣṇava in this world, just as one would avoid a dog-eater (śvapāka). O Supreme Goddess, it should be understood that a brahmin should bear the Sudarśana disc on his right arm and the conch shell on his left.
"O lady of beautiful hips! that twice-born who bears Govinda’s weapons upon his body shall attain the fourth, most exalted abode of Viṣṇu"—
thus did the Ṛg-veda verse beginning with "camūṣacchyenaḥ śakuno bibhrat" declare.
In the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, it is stated that a heated discus should be worn on both hands;
this indeed becomes the Agnihotra sacrifice, bestowing the liberation of Brahman.
A heated discus should be worn on the arm, and one shall attain the realm of Viṣṇu.
One should wear the *sudarśana* mark, which is also known as the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*;
it consists of two lines, and by knowing this, one attains union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*).
One who desires union with Brahman should wear the heated discus (*taptacakra*) on the arm.
Indeed, the heated discus should be worn on the arm by one who is devoted to the Supreme Person (Tatpuruṣa).
For with that Sudarśana, by which arm the gods and ancestors were shaken [of fear], and marked by which, one goes to the world of heaven through diligent effort.
Indeed, men marked by Him expand the creation of the world;
they should wear the heated discus on their arm and draw the vertical *puṇḍra*.
By that [mark], it becomes double-lined, and there is no returning again.
That discus, consecrated by Viṣṇu as its deity, should be worn upon both arms.
(43) Having worn the consecrated discus on their arm, the gods go to Keśava;
the Brāhmaṇas wear the vertical *puṇḍra* with two lines, which grants lordship. (44)

May those people bear by day and night this Sudarśana of Viṣṇu, which casts down the lowly, is auspicious, shatters that which is being split in the middle, bestows strength upon the arm, grants much, and possesses great splendor.
It is the purifier; Agni is its felly, and it has a thousand spokes—by means of that felly.

A Brahmin whose body has been heated [by the discus] shall indeed attain union with Brahman. He who bears upon his body the blazing discus of the infinite Viṣṇu, the strength of the gods, goes to the celestial realm (nāka), shaking off all evils; even those ascetics free from passion go there.
"Marked by these signs of the one of vast strides, shall we indeed become fortunate in this world?
That supreme abode of Viṣṇu is called the Imperishable."
Those who go forth marked by these [symbols] reach the other shore.
O Viṣṇu, indeed, for the sake of crossing the ocean of birth, the lords of men resort to your pure lotus and discus.
Others, the ancients, bear at their roots and on their arms your lingas placed upon their limbs;
they wear the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and carry the discus.
That great soul who always meditates with his voice and mantra upon Viṣṇu— the one situated within the heart,
higher than the highest, greater than the great. (1.114.5)
A person who constantly wears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark as well as the discus (*cakra*)—
by that, his inauspiciousness is destroyed and his auspiciousness increases.
The conch, discus, mace, and other symbols are to be worn bound by the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and so forth.
The great protectors guard him, like Viṣṇu with his weapons.
(52) He whose body is always marked with the Sudarśana—Hari himself, endowed with Śrī, shall dwell eternally within that person's body. (53)
Seeing one marked with the discus-weapon, even Yama feels apprehension in his heart;
having offered salutation from afar, he indeed departs from that devotee of Viṣṇu.
[He leaves behind] all cattle, sons, and so forth, as well as the household utensils.

One should mark [the body] with the conch and the discus and give him a Vaiṣṇava name. When the wife and husband perform the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras), they should mark [themselves] with the conch and the discus and give him a Vaiṣṇava name. (55)
Then they shall become fellow-practitioners and devotees, and not otherwise.
All the Vaiṣṇava sages are sealed with the Sudarśana;
by drinking the water from their feet, one is liberated from all sins.
Having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, who is attainable through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, a man who has applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark shall be liberated from all [bondages].
Having donned the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and bearing the insignia of the discus (cakralāñchana), he worships Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī here in this world, transcending the snares of saṃsāra. ||58||
With offerings such as *arghya* and with the mantras of the *Puruṣasūkta*,
that great-souled one shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu—
for the sake of His pleasure, for the sake of auspiciousness, for the sake of protection, and for the attainment of liberation.
A true devotee should always wear the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, which removes all fear.
Marked with the signs of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, and Śārṅga bow,
and anointed with *tulasī* and sandalwood paste, he should perform his twilight devotions (*sandhyopāsana*).
Bathing, charity, recitation, fire-offerings, the twilight devotions, and the rite of self-study— these,
along with fame and ancestral rites, are considered fruitless without the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
One whose body has not been heated by it does not enjoy that [fruit], for only those who have been cooked [by it] truly partake of it.
Carrying this [name], they have attained that state; we place our trust in its long-established conduct.
May those whose bodies are purified by this Viṣṇu cross the ocean of sins—the holy foot [of Viṣṇu], the rim of Hari’s discus, and the Sudarśana.
Having formed a long vertical *tilaka*, they go to the supreme state;
those whose bodies have been heated by that [fire] go to the supreme imperishable (*paramākṣara*).
The thousand-spoked [wheel], which destroys material nature, is the gate of Brahman (*brahmadvāra*), possessed of great splendor.
O Agni, purify our sacred prayer (brahman) with that which is radiant and pure; by that means, cleanse us.
(66) By that filter through which the gods always purify themselves—that thousand-streamed Pavamāna—may they purify me. (67)
That purifying filter belonging to Prajāpati is golden and has a hundred supports;
by means of it, we who know Brahman purify the Brahman that has been purified.
The wheel of the great-souled Imperishable is ever-rolling with its rim intact.
In that body encircled by the wheel, the state of supreme exaltation shall shine forth.
On whose right arm the vast and pure [discus] of the Lord of Heaven rests, his ritual actions never fail; indeed, they truly flourish. (1.114.70)
Those people who, according to the prescribed rite, bear the discus and the conch for the sake of enjoyment—even if they stand in opposition to others—those dear to Hari protect them.
Indeed, Vaiṣṇavism is said to be of two kinds: external and internal.

Protection by Hari is both external, through the conch, discus, and other [emblems], and internal; formerly, the Vaiṣṇava mark was the branding of weapons such as the discus upon the limbs. Furthermore, there is the constant and devoted service to the glorious Nārāyaṇa within the heart. (72–73)
"Thus, by being endowed with these two, one becomes a Vaiṣṇava on this earth.
In this way, the greatness of the discus is manifold, nourishing the meaning of the Vedas.
Therefore, O Great Goddess Pārvatī, that Sudarśana must be worn!"
By which both protection and liberation are certainly produced.

(75) Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Sixteen Kinds of Devotion, the Heated Discus, the *Puṇḍra*, and so forth," in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 1.14.
← Chapter 114: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā - Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 115 [[Author:
Chapter 116 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O beloved! Then Śambhu spoke to his dear wife, the goddess Pārvatī:
"Listen, O daughter of the snowy mountain, to another [account of] his majesty."

I shall now describe the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*); liberation is held to result from its wearing. It bestows the supreme world of Brahman upon man for the sake of final release. Furthermore, that mark is declared to protect one from the bondage of the world.
In the middle [of the mark] is the moon, and the deity Janārdana resides in the *puṇḍra*.
He on whose forehead-tip these two are situated partakes of imperishable liberation.
Merely by seeing him in the morning, the mountains of his sins are consumed by fire.

He on whose body there is the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is the abode of Nārāyaṇa. For one who has the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* upon his forehead, there shall be the fruit of all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the fruit of all sacrifices, and the fruit of all rites of charity and public works (*iṣṭāpūrta*). (9)
Furthermore, it shall yield the fruit of all acts of charity and the fruit of all yogic practices.
Indeed, upon seeing one who has an *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* on the forehead, one is liberated from sins;
by offering salutation, one ascends to a celestial chariot and goes to the supreme abode of Brahmā.
The person who feeds one wearing the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* at a *śrāddha* ceremony— indeed,
for ten million kalpas, the ancestors become truly satisfied and joyful.
By performing a *śrāddha* for the gods with one who wears the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, one obtains the fruit of [performing it] at Gayā.
Sacrifices, charity, recitation, hospitality, honoring guests, fire-offerings, and austerities—
when performed with devotion while wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), their merit is infinite.
Any sacrifice or other rite performed by one devoid of the vertical mark is in vain.

A body without the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* becomes like a cremation ground. For one who lacks the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, the merit of their twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and Vedic recitation (*japa*) is seized by Rākṣasas; indeed, he is himself defiled by that very fault.
One who goes out without the vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* shall not escape the inexhaustible punishment for his own sins.
(12) One should apply it with sandalwood paste rich in fragrance and filaments, or with white clay, or with yellowish-red *kuṅkuma*. (13)
That ornament for the forehead is indeed to be understood as fourfold:
the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, the *puṇḍra*, the *paṭṭapuṇḍra*, and the *tripuṇḍraka*.
The *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* consists of two lines, while the *puṇḍra* consists of a single line.
A thick line made with silk-cloth, a mark of silk-threads, or a triple-mark consisting of three sleeping lines—these are the forms of the *tripuṇḍra*.
For the worship of deities and other divine rites, a double-lined mark is prescribed.
At royal consecrations and similar occasions, the *tilaka* is remembered as being like a lamp.
For the sake of making the forehead non-empty, one should wear a cloth-band (paṭṭa) day and night;
however, during the worship of Śṛṅgāra, Hāsa, Liṅga, and others, one should wear the Tripuṇḍra.
Indeed, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) made with sandalwood paste or the sectarian mark (tilaka) made with saffron is considered [the standard].
With white clay one should make the mark called *paṭṭa*, and with ashes the *tripuṇḍra*;
indeed, the vertical *puṇḍra* should be made by men who are devotees of Viṣṇu. But the Ekāntins, the highly fortunate Mahābhāgavatas, and the Sātvatas always [wear it] thus.
Above that, they form the shape of Hari’s feet with an intervening space;
in the center, it is marked with a *candraka* (moon-motif), for that is remembered as the temple of Śrī Hari.
It should be straight, gentle, well-proportioned, captivating, and most beautiful.

That vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with a single line of saffron filaments and a dot of sandalwood paste above it should be worn by men and women; its sight brings auspiciousness. In that vertical mark, there should be an interval between the lines, and a dot of saffron in the middle representing the moon.
In the center, Śrī Hari shines there, joined with Lakṣmī.
Because there is no intervening space [between them], Śrī Hari departs from that place.
That which has no intervening space is devoid of Śrī; that which has an intervening space is endowed with Śrī.

Taking white or reddish-brown clay from a mountain, a river, a pond, or the pool known as Vaikuṇṭha, one should apply the vertical *puṇḍra* mark. One should take earth from a sacred bathing place or a temple and purify it.
The earth from the root of a *tulasī* plant is praised for the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*; so too is the soil from the ground where Śrī Kṛṣṇa was born, and from the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Furthermore, the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* made with earth from the banks of the Gomatī bestows the merit of sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*).

The ashes of the sacrificial fire and the *agnihotra*, the earth from the sacred fields of Hari and other such sites, saffron, or the earth from the *vāpikā*—these are indeed purifying, equal to the earth of Dvārakā.
Bilva, *pippala*, *tulasī*, banyan, *āmalaka*, and *udumbara* trees [are likewise sacred]. (27–28)
The divine trees, the ground beneath them, and that which is pure and fit for the *tilaka* rite;
those situated on mountain peaks, those abiding in rivers, those within the waters, and those born of the ocean (29);
those in anthills, those in temples, those in sacred fields, and those dwelling within the earth.
Sprinkled with the waters of the gods' ablutions and nourished by rain while situated in the forest, this clay— born from all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), from abodes, cities, and groves—
is the ground produced by the descent of Hari and is the dwelling place of the Lord and the yogis.
And with that [earth], one should apply the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, which bestows excellent liberation.
Indeed, the black [mark] grants peace; the red brings subjugation; the white grants liberation;
the yellow is said to bestow prosperity; and the grey destroys fortune.
Whether it be interrupted, very thick, curved, or not visible from the side; likewise, with unequal intervals, or minute, or with uneven gaps;
or having lines that are short, long, and so forth, or lines that are thick, thin, and so forth. (33–34)
A vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra) that is attached at the edges with a wide gap in the middle, whose base is severed,
which is half or three-quarters of its length, hanging down, dry, lusterless,
stretched out, difficult to see, or circular, is said to bring about misfortune.
Starting from the base of the nose, there are indeed two lines joined at the eyebrows;
they are one finger-breadth in width and extend to the ends of the hair. At the low point at the base of the nose, the second [line] is joined like a crescent moon.
One should apply the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, for that bestows the abode of Brahman:
the Supreme Brahman on the forehead, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa on the heart, Vāsudeva on the right arm, and Nara-Nārāyaṇa on the left. (38)
Having remembered [the deities], one should always perform the rites with substances dissolved in Viṣṇu-water (Viṣṇujala).
One should meditate on Nārāyaṇa in the navel, Govinda at the collarbone,
Viṣṇu on the right side, and Vāmana on the left side.
Having remembered Trivikrama at the neck, Dāmodara at the nape of the neck, Padmanābha on the back, and Vāsudeva on the head—
one who is a great devotee of the Lord should thus apply the twelve *puṇḍra* marks.
On the forehead, the two arms, the nape of the neck, the throat, and the back, [the measurement] should be four finger-breadths;
on the two sides, ten finger-breadths;
and on the neck, the head, the abdomen, and the chest, one should make it eight finger-breadths. (42–43)
The seed-syllable accompanied by the intermediate space and joined with saffron and moon-cream belongs to Śrī.
For Kṣatriyas, however, there are four [marks]: on the forehead, the two arms, and the heart.
For Vaiśyas, there are two on the forehead and the heart, and one on the forehead for Śūdra women.
O Girijā! For your devotees, [the vision] is like the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree;
for my devotees, those of Śambhu, it is like the bud of a lotus; and for the great devotees of Gaṇeśa and others, it is like the leaf of a bamboo. 45–46.
Above that, the mark in the shape of Hari’s foot,
and above that again, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) in the form of a ray, always bestows liberation.
In its center, a drop of turmeric or saffron is the abode of Lakṣmī.
In the middle of the forehead, a mark that does not touch the two lines, level and uniform,
yellow or saffron in color, bestows prosperity like the moon.
One should understand that the dot (bindu) and the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) are always Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
"Victory is always for him who has [the mark] on the forehead, the heart, and the two arms;
for one devoid of it, there is defeat both here and in the hereafter.
Thus, O Gaurī, the determination regarding the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* and other marks has been told to you.
That which was told to me by Nārāyaṇa is entirely auspicious.
Those who are devotees of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, the Goddess, the gods, and ascetics—
though they may appear unrestrained— they will be regarded as playful jesters.
But even those men, possessing faces identical to women’s and wearing their hair in braided tresses, will perform the domestic duties of women;
they will wear garments like women and display their own nature as that of women. (53)

Women who stand in the dress of men, displaying their own forms as those of men, will be devoid of their respective duties and so forth; they will be destroyers of their own liberation. Lacking the [proper] marks, yet possessing false marks, they will indeed go repeatedly to the hells. (54–55)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Urdhvapuṇḍra and Other Marks," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 115. [End of] the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Book 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna), Chapter 116.
[Author: Chapter 117.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then Śambhu [spoke] of the supreme majesty of the mantra.
He spoke to Pārvatī concerning the goal of all things, with its seed and in full detail:
"Liberation or even any desired task is never accomplished by means of a mantra taught by one who is not a Vaiṣṇava; therefore, one should indeed take refuge in a Vaiṣṇava. (1–2)
The mantra bestowed by a Vaiṣṇava Ācārya is indeed the accomplisher of all goals.
One should accept a Vaiṣṇava as one’s guru, never one who is not a Vaiṣṇava.
Through association with a Vaiṣṇava guru, human beings become purified.
The Vaiṣṇava teacher is declared to be the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa.
(4) The divine teacher, equal to Nārāyaṇa, indeed delivers people;
the teacher is Nārāyaṇa himself, the giver of liberation through the mantra. (5)
Indeed, there is no one inferior to Nārāyaṇa who bestows the bliss of Nārāyaṇa;
none is equal to Nārāyaṇa in bodily form, none is equal to Nārāyaṇa in virtue,
none is equal to Nārāyaṇa in liberation, and none is a giver of wealth like Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, the excellent mantra should be received from a Guru who is foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas.

(7) Even one who has studied the thousand branches [of the Veda], who is entitled to perform all sacrifices, and who possesses the birth of a Brāhmaṇa or other [high caste], cannot be a Guru if he is not a Vaiṣṇava. (8)
Having taken refuge in the guru, the meaning of the mantra must indeed be understood correctly.
Marked with the signs of the conch and discus, having applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and the crescent moon-mark,
and wearing a garland of tulasī around his neck, the wise one should contemplate the meaning of the mantra.
The Nyāsa is the eight-syllable mantra: "I am Brahman; I am a devotee of Brahman.
Other Vaiṣṇava mantras as well, such as "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa" and others, constitute the Nyāsa. This mantra, which is the very form of the mantra, is considered the supreme [teaching] of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Other Vaiṣṇava mantras are indeed the saviors of embodied beings.
But once the purpose of the ritual placement (nyāsa) is fully understood, nothing further remains to be known.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, listen to the meaning of this jewel among mantras.

"I am Brahmā, a devotee of Brahmā; in that regard, there are indeed four quarters. (13) Because of its greatness (*bṛhattva*) and because of its expanding nature (*bṛṃhaṇatva*), it is called the all-pervading *Brahman*.
That *Brahman* is indeed twofold: with form (*sākāra*) and formless (*nirākṛti*). (14)
In the abode of the Dharma of service, there dwells the imperishable Brahman, possessing form and embodiment, like a servant; he exists with his attendants as if they were his own retinue.
At times he is known as Mukta, and at times he is the very embodiment of Śrī.
At times he has the form of a man, and at times the seat of a lion.
His dharma is service to no other; his service consists in devotion through *pātivratya*.
This dharma of service is the dharma of Brahman, and likewise, he is the excellent embodiment of Brahman.

The second, however, is formless and is called the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka). It is described as the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma), the celestial realm of Śrī Hari known as the Abode of Space (vyomadhāma).
It is composed of supreme splendor, tranquil, delightful, and bestows the bliss of joy.
That region is composed of light and is called the all-pervading abode.
As the dwelling place for the liberated souls to reside in the Supreme Brahman, that divine ground exists as an eternal form at all times. (1.116.20)
That reality of existence, consciousness, and bliss is indeed what is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
Therein dwells the divine Hari himself, known as Puruṣottama,
in the supreme abode called the Imperishable (akṣara), which is the refuge of happiness.
The nature of that abode is indeed dharma, consisting of being untainted. It is all-pervasive throughout all the principles of *māyā*, yet it remains untainted;
there is no staining by the attributes of *māyā*. Therefore, it is celebrated as "untainted" (*alepi*).
Thus, there are these two kinds of dharmas: service and likewise stainlessness. One who serves while remaining stainless is said to be the meaning of the word "Brahman.
Furthermore, the word "I" (ahaṃ) makes known the Self as the embodied one.
Having attained a specific body, the conscious one is called "I" (25).
Such a self, desiring liberation, distinct from the body yet dependent upon it,
characterized by name and form, is to be understood by the word "I" (26).
"I am the self within the bodies of both male and female, untainted and your servant"—
let this be understood as the intended meaning of "I am Brahman.
In the state of the devotee of Brahman, Brahman is the Supreme Lord, the one beyond the state of the Supreme Brahman.
The Supreme Self, who is beyond the Imperishable, is called Puruṣottama.
His devotion is indeed manifold, known as *pātivratya* (faithfulness).
A devotee who always takes refuge in Him is one who has surrendered and sought shelter.
Devotion, surrender, taking refuge, trust, choosing [the Lord], renunciation, wretchedness, and firm resolve— these six forms,
along with subsequent service, should be understood as the sixfold nature of *śaraṇāgati*.

The wife is the body and the husband is the soul; their living in oneness constitutes the dharma of wifely devotion (*pātivratya*). That service to the husband is *bhakti*—namely, hearing of him, chanting his praises, remembering him, and serving his feet. (3.1–3.2)
Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender—such is devotion preceded by love; indeed, service is the service of one's master.
Prostrating at his feet, whatever he may do, do that for me.
Thus, that surrender is the offering of everything in every way; it is the offering of one’s very life.

(34) I, who am characterized by qualities such as being pervaded, dependent, and incapable, and who am the substratum of the word "I"—such as I am, I perform service to my Lord and Master, who is dearer to me than life itself. (35)
"I am performing [service]"—thus, I became one whose refuge is service that is unimpeded throughout the three periods of time.
For the sake of the collective whole, however, I am born of the mantra: "I am Brahman; I am a devotee of Brahman.
Pervasive, dependent, and devoid of attributes such as incapacity, I am the servant of Hari.
Being untainted and possessing devotion through such acts as hearing the *pātivratya* hymns, I became an inhabitant of the eternal abode; this is the meaning that has been declared.
Having reflected upon this very meaning of the jewel of mantras again and again, [one attains this state]. (37–38)
A devotee should by all means remain deeply immersed in the bliss of Brahman;
for there is no one other than Nārāyaṇa who bestows both happiness and liberation.
Therefore, having surrendered everything, one should offer one's entire being to Him alone.
At the beginning of a mantra, the name of Brahman should certainly be employed as "Om.
Indeed, the three Vedas consist of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*.
By the letter *a* is Viṣṇu himself denoted, and by the letter *u* is the Daughter of the Ocean (Lakṣmī) expressed.
By the syllable *ma*, those two are their devotees; thus, they are indeed the three *om*s.
*A* is Vāsudeva, and *u* is the awakener of Śrī.
By the syllable *ma*, those two are their servants; thus, they are considered the three *om*s.
The letter *a* is the Supreme Brahman, and the letter *u* is said to be Brahman.
By the letter *m*, one who is devoted to those two is remembered as a servant (*dāsa*) through service.
His light is like that of the sun; therefore, it is eternally inseparable from him.
Lakṣmī is the body of Nārāyaṇa, the enchanting wife of Viṣṇu;
she is the eternal sovereign of the worlds, the mother who sustains the universe.
Knowledge itself, possessing the quality of knowledge, the locus of knowledge, subtle, and residing in the heart.

I am indeed considered to be the Self, the locus of the mass of bliss consisting of volition (cetanānanda). I am regarded by the illustrious Hari as His remnant, His servant, and His devotee; having surrendered my own sense of ownership to Hari, my life and self are dependent upon Him. || 46–47 ||
By the power of Nārāyaṇa, nothing would be unattainable for himself.
Indeed, the multitude of men (*nara*) are the *nārāḥ*, and they are his very self (*ātman*).
Since he has them as his abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
He is Śrī Hari, the all-pervading one within all sentient and insentient entities.
(49) The water produced from *nara* is called *nāra*; because he moves (*ayana*) therein, he is Narāyaṇa.
It is said that at the time of dissolution, he is the refuge (*ayana*) for all *nara*s who have entered into him. (1.116.50)
Therefore, the divine Nārāyaṇa is the agent of creation and destruction;
he in whom all is, from whom all comes, and who is all—Nārāyaṇa.
He possesses infinite eyes and feet, infinite heads, and is the sovereign lord of immortality.
Hiraṇyagarbha is indeed Viṣṇu, the Lord of the past, the future, and the present.
He abides in the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśvara, and even in the creation of individual souls.
That Hari, who pervades the three worlds with but a single foot, remains established there.
He is the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable Brahman, Vāsudeva, the Golden One;
he is Vairāja, Viṣṇu, the Lord of Lords, Sacrifice, Savitṛ, and Śiva.
And he indeed stands pervading all, having overspread the earth.
From him were born Diti and Aditi, as well as all those who have two rows of teeth;
from them were born the domestic and wild animals, the Sādhyas, and the Ṛṣis.
Likewise, from him alone came the sacrificial threads and those without threads, as well as the fires.
By him the enclosing-sticks were made; by him this entire world, from the nails to the crest, as well as the guardians of the quarters and the guardians of the worlds beyond, was created.
Since he is born from him, I am his devotee.
Having thoroughly understood this meaning, the practitioner attains perfection.
(58) The world is always composed of devotees, servants, and embodied beings;
one should take refuge in that Embodied One who is to be worshipped and served. (59)
Now listen, O beautiful one, to the secret of the true meaning of another mantra:
Lakṣmī is the sign that causes delusion, and she is the compassion that extends from shore to shore.
Endowed with that [compassion], she is indeed proclaimed as the Great Power (Mahāśakti), the Goddess Lakṣmī.
Nārāyaṇa joined with her is the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Śrī is said to be divine prosperity; he who possesses that is the Lord. He is called Śrīman-Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of wealth through his grace. (61–62)
His own sovereignty is unimpeded, being sixfold and also eightfold;
it consists of omniscience, eternal contentment, fruition of desires, formlessness,
eternal bliss, and the state of being the controller— these six indeed exist therein.
Freedom from sin, freedom from sorrow, freedom from hunger,
likewise freedom from thirst, as well as freedom from old age and freedom from death,
the power of true resolve, and the attainment of true desires— this is the group of eight qualities. (64–65)
Wherever He is present, that very one is the master, the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa.
That Lord Nārāyaṇa bestows celibacy upon the man who does not possess it;
indeed, that Hari-Nārāyaṇa removes the sufferings of His devotees.
For that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa indeed leads [the soul] away, having stripped off its illusion (māyā). He who dwells within, who sports as the inner controller (antaryāmī), and who is the illuminator—
he is truly Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who bestows the highest good.
Indeed, that is Rāmanārāyaṇa, wherein yogis delight.
That which is called "Oṃ" is the Supreme Brahman; that which is called "Śrī" is the beloved of Hari.
Joined with those two is the assembly of men; therein lies the inner rulership of Hari.
Sovereignty, as well as heroism, fame, fortune, wisdom,
and dispassion— these six are indeed proclaimed to have the designation "bhaga.
Be one who offers supreme homage to that Vāsudeva who possesses these qualities.
In whom knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor reside—
he is the glorious Lord, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest.
For the sake of taking refuge in the Self, I know and meditate upon Hari, who dwells within.
That all-pervading Lord shall set us forth in the work of liberation.
O Goddess, for one who worships Hari having understood the meaning of the Gāyatrī mantra,
liberation has forever taken up residence within his very hand.
"Śrī Hari is my refuge; I offer this surrender, fully prepared with its purpose.
Thus ends [the section on] the various modes of taking refuge bestowed by Vaiṣṇava gurus within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the first book of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
The one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of Mantras," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).

Chapter 117 [Author:
Chapter 118 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Pārvatī said to the Lord of Gods, Maheśvara, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas:
"O Lord, tell me how the majesty of the form of Nārāyaṇa is such that even after drinking the nectar that grants liberation, the mind is never satiated. (1)
How is it that even after such a long time this has not been awakened?
(2) This supreme nectar of the immortal Supreme Brahman is most worthy of being heard;
it must be heard by me eternally, ever new with every hearing. (3)
Then Śambhu spoke to the goddess Pārvatī, the supreme sovereign:
"Listen, O Goddess! This narrative of mine, consisting of Nārāyaṇa, is also new and delightful;
it shines forth and increases my joy. (8)
I shall relate it according to my memory, for although it is indeed beyond the reach of speech.
(5) The Supreme Brahman himself, the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa, shines eternally in his own abode as the King of Kings. (6)
The Puruṣa has infinite heads, infinite eyes, and innumerable feet;
having pervaded the entire creation, he remained [standing] upon the mere tip of a hair.
Indeed, he shines everywhere, the Lord of liberation, possessed of supreme prosperity.
There is no other superior to Him, nor is there anyone equal, nor even one who shares in His inheritance.
(8) In this world, all creations of the Lord of Life occupy a fourth part;
however, the world of Brahmā constitutes three parts here, while the Brāhmaṇas indeed reside in the supreme ether. (9)
Therein, neither hunger nor thirst arises;
the illusion based on hunger and thirst expands below that level.
And in his abode, there are indeed supreme abodes.
Holding within himself the minds of the liberated, the lords, and the incarnations,
that divine, singular God shines forth;
thus, this one of vast form shines together with Brahman.
He is attended by hosts of attendants numbering infinite crores,
and likewise served by sovereign goddesses, Śrīs, and Śaktis;
he possesses a divine and auspicious form, enriched with boundless celestial enjoyments.

The youth, the great being Acyuta, whose limbs were delicate and tender, possessed a youthful form that was like the full moonlight of the Mother of the World; he was filled with the beauty of ten million Cupids and an inexhaustible love. (14–19)
For the sake of fulfilling the desires of Śrī, He established the realm of Vaikuṇṭha;
for the sake of bestowing happiness upon Rādhā, the Dark One resides in Goloka.
The abode that grants the bliss of liberation is eternally considered to be the imperishable Brahman.
For the sake of enjoyment, Vaikuṇṭha and the world of cows exist in the supreme sky;
for the sake of divine play and for the dwelling of devotees, the entire universe has been created threefold.
These manifestations are the stages known as the enjoyment of happiness, divine play, and liberation.
There are three [powers] belonging to that very [Lord]; they are indeed his threefold manifestation (*vibhūti*).
The first is called *līlā*, which is the entire creation for the sake of enjoyment; the second is the abode (*dhāma*);
and the supreme abode exists for the purpose of bestowing the bliss of liberation.

When Janārdana withdraws his play, the great creation, then indeed there exists the eternal state within the realm of enjoyment (bhogavibhūti). Beyond even that is another state, consisting of the supreme form, which is characterized by great bliss.
Play (*līlā*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and bliss (*saukhya*)—these three are His very powers.
That supreme abode is three-footed, eternal, and the perpetual domain of the Lord.
At its extremities, other abodes exist eternally.
He manifested those [abodes] everywhere for the sake of the enjoyment of service by his devotees:
the abode of nectar (Amṛtadhāma), the abode of Badarī, the unmanifested (Avyākṛta), the abode of Lakṣmī, and the white abode (Śvetadhāma). He manifested them for the sake of the enjoyment of service.
And for the sake of penance, as well as for the purpose of protecting the world, he manifested [the universe];
three-quarters of it are indeed eternal, while one quarter is non-eternal.
That which is imperishable, rich in the form of Brahman, is Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of cows.
Amṛta and Śrīpura were likewise created for the play of Rādhikā and Śrī, as well as for the other wives of the Lord. There, the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari eternally abides in the prime of youth.
This Mother of the World, Lakṣmī, and likewise Rādhikā, are eternal.
Just as Viṣṇu is omnipresent, so too are Lakṣmī and Rādhikā.
She who is the sovereign of the past and the future is likewise the sovereign Maheśvarī.
Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Rādhā are indeed the inseparable consorts of Viṣṇu.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides,
she is Nārāyaṇī, Kṛṣṇā, the wife of Viṣṇu, and the embodiment of the universe.
Mahāmāyā is the creator of the world, the performer of its emanation and reabsorption;
everything consisting of a mixture of the insentient and the sentient is situated within the corner of her eye.
The world, composed of dissolution and emergence, is produced by her opening and closing of her eyes.
She is eternal, unborn, the left-hand portion, the Great Lakṣmī, the Supreme Sovereign.
She is unmanifest yet possesses manifest form; she is established as all-pervading.
On earth she is *rasā*, in heaven she is *sudhā*, and she is the meritorious one in the abode of the ancestors.
In water there is sweetness, in fire there is cooking, and Lakṣmī in the form of wealth; beauty, splendor, good fortune, physical form, and even charm—
all of this belongs entirely and completely to her alone.
By her, the prosperous abodes of Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and Yama,
as well as those of Sūrya, Kubera, Agni, and Candra, were beheld.
She is Mahāmāyā, Mahālakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Śrī, Rādhikā, and the Beloved.
Kamalā, Śāradā, Padmā, Vidyā, Mā, Paramā, Ramā,
Abdhiputrī, Satī, Śyāmā, Mahādevī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Nārāyaṇī, Mahāvidyā, Viṣṇupatnī, and Maheśvarī. (357)
Gaurī, Sarasvatī, Śānti, Prabhā, Svāhā, Svadhā, Rati, Sāvitrī, Kambharādevī, and Pārvatī—these are her sixteen names. They should be recited every morning for the attainment of prosperity. (38–39)
May Nārāyaṇa bring to me Lakṣmī, who is golden-hued, tawny, composed of gold and silver, lunar, made of gold,
the embodiment of wealth, grain, cattle, vehicles, and the Supreme Person.
O Nārāyaṇa, bring to me Lakṣmī, who never departs;
bring to me the radiant Śrī, who is full of contentment, brilliant, and whose ramparts are of gold.
O Kṛṣṇa, bring to me divine, majestic fame, which is as enduring as a tree.
May Nārāyaṇa bring to me Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of all, who is rich in fragrance, invincible, eternally nourishing, and full of abundance.
May Hari bring to me the perfection of intention, thought, and resolve.
I invoke here that Śrī who bestows gold, male slaves, and female slaves.
For those by whom Lakṣmī is thus propitiated, she never departs;
she is eternally attained upon the chest of Hari—that Hari who is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 44-45 ||
Nārāyaṇa is the Lord of all, the Master of all, the mine of virtues;
he is omniscient, enriched with all powers, one whose desires are fulfilled, and who is a well-wishing friend and happy.
He is an ocean of compassion, the glorious one, and affectionate toward those who have come for refuge.
I perform service to him, the source of the splendors of heaven and liberation.
At all times, in every way, and in all conditions, I worship him;
I indeed perform service to him, for this entire world has become the servant of Hari.
The glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa is to be served and attained; He is the supreme, beyond the Imperishable.
He alone is the mother, the brother, the father, the son, and the kinsman.
He is the refuge, the shelter, the dwelling, the goal, and indeed the final dissolution.
Endowed with all divine qualities and devoid of the qualities of Māyā and the like, Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme reality;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Self. (1.117.50–51)
The meditator is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; meditation itself is Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever exists in this entire universe—whether it is seen or even heard—Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all of that, both within and without.
That Supreme Self is established within the heart, in the midst of the individual soul (jīva).
Indeed, in that supreme abode, Śrī-yuñ-Nārāyaṇa resides;
by His power, Śrī—the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti)—the Great [universe] was fashioned.
From that, Virāj came into being—the earth, and the living beings of both village and forest.
Indeed, from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, the social classes (varṇas) were produced;
for he was the sacrifice itself, and from him were born the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
He is the oblation to the gods and the ancestors, the priest, the enjoyer of the portions, and the sacrificial fuel.
The gods worshipped Nārāyaṇa as the sacrifice, and those ritual acts existed even before; indeed, the supreme duties such as devotion through worship and so forth were already present.
Those liberated ones in the past indeed dwell in majesty in the supreme abode;
those who practice devotion as servants of Him go to the station of Nārāyaṇa.
They are indeed divine, eternally perfected, and liberated, dwelling in that abode.
Beyond Māyā, in the supreme world, they abide in a state of similarity with Brahman.
Indeed, that imperishable abode of Hari is such that once one has gone there, there is no return, nor is it subject to Māyā, Mahākāla, evil karma, Yama, and the like. (1.117.59–60)
She is Māyā, consisting of the universe, eternal, and the primordial nature (prakṛti) composed of the three qualities (guṇas).
She is ignorance (avidyā), the yogic sleep (yoganidrā), the primary matter (pradhāna), the unmanifest (avyakta), and the everlasting.
She is the very form of the shadow of the Abode (dhāma), yet her essential nature is a mass of pure knowledge.
Indeed, she makes the universe impermanent like the thread of a spider;
by her the entire world is enveloped, yet she herself is enveloped by the splendor of Brahman.
The connection between Māyā and Brahman is declared to be the boundary of the Abode.
That [reality] is all-pervading and limitless, yet it appears to have limits through metaphorical designation.
(62) Everything within the sphere of Māyā undergoes contraction and expansion;
it indeed vanishes and reappears, while devotees go beyond it. (64)
Then, having bathed at the Brahma-lake on the boundary— the seat of splendor, bliss, and consciousness— they attain the body of Brahman through the majesty of the supreme light.
Thereupon, their selves are manifested as embodied forms in their own true nature.
When a man or a woman goes with devotion to the Imperishable (Akṣara) and bathes at the boundary of the Brahma-lake, their body itself becomes Brahmic;
there is no longer any connection with the power of other substances within that body.
The Self, possessing excellent vision and conforming to the form of Hari, is perceived by itself;
there is neither conjunction nor division, nor the appearance of substances belonging to a yogi.
By means of its own form as the essence of the single Self, that Self is well-formed, just like Hari.
Mahāmāyā, however, is stainless; she belongs to those who go to Vaikuṇṭha.
Between the Māyā of Vaikuṇṭha and [the other], she is seen there as the essence of Nārāyaṇa’s fluid, like Śrī and like the attendants after they have bathed therein. (1.117.70)
In that way, male and female servants are produced eternally in Vikuṇṭha.
That which is the supreme light, the ether, the imperishable, eternal Brahman—
that divine reality known as Brahman is indeed the essence of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
It has a single hair-pore like the fire of ten million suns; it is undecaying and free from dissolution.
It is empty of dreams and the like, a cooling ocean of bliss that brings peace.
That imperishable reality, hidden by the Vedas, is where millions of liberated ones have entered.
The seers do not know that; the knowers sit there. That is the supreme station of Viṣṇu, which the wise behold.
Even the Vairājas do not see that world, that state.
Where the many-horned cows are ever-extending and always bestowing happiness—
that indeed is the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa, which brings happiness to the cows of Kṛṣṇa;
those who know that go to it, which is like the sun in color and beyond darkness.
In that place, indeed, dwell the liberated ones who have been so since beginningless time.
All the gods, having transcended the universe, being liberated, enjoy that bliss.

(77) Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Glory of the Supreme Brahman, the Abode of the Imperishable, His Manifestations, Līlā, the Brāhmī Form, Nārāyaṇa, Nārāyaṇī, Gaurī, and Others," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 117.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then Śambhu spoke to the Goddess: "O daughter of the mountain, listen! I shall describe to you in brief the manifestations of the glory of the abode of Brahman."
The imperishable abode, the supreme Brahman, the eternal and highest ether,
shines everywhere as a mass consisting of white light.
Even if all the stars and all the suns situated in the sky were to become one, [it would still not equal that splendor].
The earth, well-composed for creation, would consist of divine glass.
And from the mutual conjunction of those two, whatever kind of light might arise—
such a dense and great light exists indeed in the realm of Satya, belonging to the Creator.
From that true piercing light, the luminous splendor is ten million times greater;
it exists within the single neck-jewel of Vairāja, and even beyond that,
the great radiance of Mahāviṣṇu in his crest-jewel is indeed ten million times more vast.
Then, the splendor of Vāsudeva within that jewel is indeed ten million times greater.
And such infinite jewels exist in the unmanifest realm (avyākṛta-stara),
as well as in Badarī, Amṛta, Śveta, Śrīpura, and Vikuṇṭha.
If one were to take the splendors from Goloka and form them into a mass at the site of the Areca nut (pūgīphala) of the abode known as the Imperishable Reality (akṣara-dhāman),
would that [mass] truly attain dissolution, and if so, what would it become? It would be complete.
When the collection of such syllables, abodes,
and splendors of the liberated beings dissolves into even a single hair of Śrī Hari,
then what kind of great splendor would exist there in the complete Hari?
Even it is not possible to infer that inaccessible, sovereign splendor;
for I am indeed not its direct seer, but [I know it] through meditative absorption (samādhi).
[I know] the Lord Śrī Hari, who resides in the abode called Brahman within the cosmic egg.
Having unified [all things] within my own self, I indeed perceive through a super-mundane means.

At that time, by virtue of that proximity, even that which is beyond the highest limit is seen. This which is beyond the range of perception cannot be grasped, reflected upon, or understood. || 12–13 ||
How then, O beautiful one, can it be described? Understand this:
he is one of infinite splendor, an ocean of boundless virtues, a shoreless great sea of beauty, form, gentleness, and a slight smile. (14)
With eyes like cakora birds fixed in a steady gaze upon the moon that is his single-pointed concentration,
the Lord— the supreme king of kings, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest—
shines resplendent upon the great lion-throne, appearing sixteen years of age. (15–16)
His limbs were proportioned to his form, and his face shone with a gentle smile;
he wore ruby earrings that eclipsed millions upon millions of suns, moons, and fires.
His crown and neck-ornament were bound with countless jewels and gems. (17)
Wearing divine diamonds, excellent jewels, priceless gold, and necklaces;
his throat radiant with the Kaustubha gem, which is a mine of splendor; and adorned with a circular ornament produced by the spreading rays of his manifold luster. (18–19)
He was brilliantly radiant in the center of his forehead, made magnificent by a divine light;
his locks of hair were fashioned with ever-dark curls like a mass of clouds;
and he was endowed with eyebrows that served as the curved ends of the bow of the god of love.
His eyes are adorned with rows of eyelashes like fine golden threads;
his eyeballs are divine, white, and shaped like excellent hexagonal crystals; and his lateral pupils possess the luster of fine red filaments. 21–22.
His form is radiant with the shimmering luster of a divine central gem,
and even there, his black pupils are vividly manifest through the power of the object to be perceived;
his eyes, reaching to the ends of his ears, possess the brilliance of autumn lotus petals.
With ears as yellow as soft *saptaparṇa* shoots;
with ears flowing like the fragrance of divine golden cloths and full-blown campaka flowers;
with cheeks as soft as balls of cotton enriched with *golaphulla* blossoms. (24–25)
His nose was curved at the tip like a sesame flower and tinged with a pale yellow;
his mustache was adorned with lines resembling fine golden threads.
His upper lip was marked by a curved line at its tip, shaped like the bow of a fish.
His lower lip is like a vessel for the stream of love, a place of desire, and a reservoir;
both lips are like the red petals of a lotus and possess the sweetness of nectar. His chin is well-formed, deep-set at its tip, and free from protruding veins. (27–28)
His teeth were as white as jasmine, extremely sharp, prominent, closely set, and firm;
the surface of his teeth gleamed like the seeds of a pomegranate rich with red juice.
His nape was like a conch shell adorned with gold and the finest jewels.
His neck was as thick as the base of Mount Meru;
his collarbones were positioned upon shoulders as broad as the crescent moon at the end of an eon;
and his well-nourished, elevated shoulders were bound by the strength of the flood of the [twenty-five] principles.
His flanks and the caves of his belly are the constant seats for the meditations of yogis;
his well-nourished arms are like the coils of Śeṣa, and his beautiful hands possess the luster of gold, well-fleshed and radiant with consciousness.
32. His navel is a shining, deep red, like a well-nourished golden lotus, and his arms are truly beautiful.
With a steady pivot, revolving wheels, stable pins, and knuckles;
with well-formed, gradually increasing limbs and two hands skillfully joined;
wearing beautiful chains, bracelets, and armlets made of refined gold. (33–34)

His fingers were adorned with rings enriched with jewels, diamonds, and gems; the circle of his devoted followers was illuminated by the radiant luster of the moon-like nails upon them. He was a protector of the body of Makhamalla, who was exceedingly handsome and possessed of excellent limbs. (35)
His shoulders were adorned with an upper garment beautified by golden borders;
his chest was well-marked with the Śrīvatsa, shining with divine golden lines;
and his girdle was richly set with gold and gems, fashioned from twenty-seven strings.
The expanse of his three folds of skin flowed forth like the Brahma-well;
his thighs were as radiant as the trunk of a gradually swelling elephant, rich with the fullness of desire;
and his hips were well-developed, worthy of being fashioned into the frontal globes of an elephant.
He possesses the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*) and the mark of a perfectly circular *liṅga* with inexhaustible vigor;
he bestows the essence of passion and the nectar of bliss upon the multitude of young women;
his belly is like a golden cloth, shining with a line of golden hair.
His knees were firm, radiant, and endowed with the beauty of perfect roundness;
his shanks were well-proportioned, tapering like the stalk of a lotus, and possessed of the appropriate joints.
His ankles were symmetrical on the inside and outside, and his wrists were well-formed.
His body is inclined downward like a pearl necklace, curved like the bow of a crossbow,
and beautiful with the moon-like luster of his golden-red nails;
he has a well-developed back, is protected by auspicious marks, and possesses a most excellent form.
Hari shines in his great abode, seated upon a throne;
endowed with all sovereign powers, the energy of action, knowledge, yoga, and so forth.
The throne has four legs, is made of gold, and is most beautiful. (43–44)
It stands with seven steps, adorned on all sides by *kammānikā* ornaments,
and resplendent with *takkiya* designs alongside the great *makhamaḷa* motifs.
Above it, an umbrella is held aloft, encircled by twenty ribs.
A divine, delicate cloth of gold was fixed upon the umbrella.
It featured a pitcher fashioned from gold and a handle adorned with jewels and other ornaments;
likewise, gems were set all around it, as were golden bells.
On all sides, it was provided with seven divine, material jhallarikās;
there were white chowries, fans, and likewise mirrors.
Divine pearls were also present, well-established in the service of dharma.
Released from beneath the umbrella, adorned with a thousand hoods,
that great serpent assumed a massive form and, having fashioned a canopy with his hoods,
stood behind Śrī Hari, serving him like a great pillar. (1.118.49–50)
There, at the rear of that lion-throne, there was a divine great cloth made of golden threads, adorned with various colors and designs;
it was fashioned in the shape of a preeminent lotus, and likewise, divine pillars stood there.
Indeed, there were circles of pearls and gems upon them;

and there, within the pillars, parrots, cranes, and peacocks—whose forms consist of existence, consciousness, and bliss—as well as trees, creepers, and other plants, were established in well-arranged places. (52–53)
All conscious beings shine when they are devoted to the Supreme Brahman;

[the world] is delightful with its various arts and crafts, possessing soft carpets upon its pedestals, and the visible realm appears like an ocean of splendor, resplendent with millions of jewels. (54)
The lion-throne, which is the self-existent abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara) and nothing else, is illuminated by the infinite rays of light from the moon-like luster of his nails.
There, upon that form, there exists a great, circular halo of supreme splendor. (55–56)
With his sides pervaded by infinite cows of sweet, cool, and gentle luster, he possesses seven forms and seven grounds; that enclosure is also liberated.
The splendor of Hari is on all sides in the great lion-throne in the ten directions.
It pervades everything and there is no end to it; those cows have many-horned heads.
Where that lion-throne is, there indeed is a pavilion extending for a *yojana*.
There, the divine great pillars are indeed the imperishable ones made of plantain trees.
Yellow-hued, with green leaves and auspicious green plantain trees,
they possessed a hundred pillars of golden color, beautified by being draped in cloth. Their archways were variegated, adorned with the mastery of artistic crafts.
Various kinds of elephants, white ones, crocodiles, swans, cranes,
peacocks, parrots, white pigeons, cakravākas, and cātaka birds—
all these indeed become liberated, their very forms consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
In that pavilion, auspicious songs composed with the sweetness of divine melodies are sung in the Sanskrit language, extolling his virtues; indeed,
there are mandalas of many millions of great liberated souls.
They stand upon the ground as if on firm land—amidst, above, and within.
Indeed, all those forms that were sustained by Hari during the intervals between creations have been established here in this pavilion. (64–65)

The manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of the Blessed One shine forth in various forms, marked by diverse signs of sovereignty; they serve as the causes for awakening to His various births, incarnations, and deeds, appearing in forms that communicate those historical accounts. (66)
All of them reside right there, in the upper, middle, and lower parts of the pavilion.
Having become mirrors for the sun, moon, and other luminaries with their heads released [from bonds], they indeed dwell within those various pillars. (67–68)
There, the stars consisting of liberated souls shine forth clearly, rich with the light of that [liberation] and radiating cool splendor;
and there are arched gateways made of pearls, gems, and diamonds.
Producing the luster of glass, they were like many divine lamps and moons;
from the pavilion, brilliant rays went upward, downward, to the sides, and in all directions and intermediate points, traveling along the path of the sky.
Such a pavilion or such a throne as that does not exist in other abodes; how can its wonder be described?
Even divine splendor is not found elsewhere, and it cannot be described by me.
"O beloved, hear now of that palace atop the pavilion belonging to Śrī Hari!

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Pavilion and the Lion Throne of the Supreme Brahman Residing in the Imperishable Abode," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*). Chapter 118.

Chapter 120 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Śambhu spoke again to the Goddess above the pavilion of Śrī Hari:
"Listen, O auspicious one! There has never been, nor will there ever be, a temple such as this.
It is a hundred thousand yojanas in extent and a thousand yojanas in height."
There was one row of a thousand pillars, and likewise thousands of rows;
auspicious structures with four archways rose up everywhere.
In the center was a great dome (*ghūmmaṭa*), and there were exactly four in the cardinal directions as well.
Indeed, four peaks shine upon its four corners;
and having reached that very Dhūmmaṭa, there are seven peaks:
three on the right, three on the left, and the greatest one in the middle.
Where there was a pavilion in Koli, beneath it was a lion-throne.
(5) Even atop the palace was a chamber rising a thousand yojanas;
above the chamber was a pinnacle measuring one thousand five hundred yojanas. (6)
There stands a lotus-stone slab measuring five hundred yojanas;
there also exists a ground-stone slab rising a hundred yojanas high.
Above that are exactly one hundred divine golden jars.
Above that is a single water-jar; its weight is considered to be the same.
Beyond that, the flagpole is five hundred yojanas in height, and the bamboo shaft is likewise one thousand yojanas in height.
There, the banner was five hundred yojanas long from its base to its tip;
it had seven colors, two tails, and was as brilliant as ten million suns.
These beings were conscious, liberated souls who had assumed forms for the sake of service.
Always liberated, they remain in that state of service with bodies marked by signs.
On the peak dwell the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, and indeed the Yoginīs reside in the cardinal directions. Furthermore, there are lions and man-lions; these are indeed the incarnations.
In the windows on that summit, pearl-eyed beings indeed dwell;
likewise, other figurines and others who are pearls dwell there.
On the flagstaff, the virtuous Pāṭalikā dwells, and she is considered to be a pearl.
Those [other] bell-bearers were liberated; they were divine attendants of Śrī Hari.
There, the lamp was the Great Lamp, Mahāmukta, and no other;
for that lamp, greater than the great, is indeed the most excellent of all.
Moreover, all the liberated ones indeed dwell upon the other peaks as well.
Even atop the palace is a pinnacle (ghummaṭa) rising a thousand yojanas high.
This great celestial palace is indeed divine, moving through the sky, and composed of light itself.
Moving according to its will, the glorious Hari indeed goes everywhere at his pleasure.
There, the aerial chariots of the sages, which travel according to their desires, truly circumambulate the temple with devotion. (17–18)

There are divine showers of cool and warm water, and eternal fire-pits; there are impermanent cool fragrances, lights in the form of milk, lamps whose intentions are realized by will, and vessels produced according to desire. (19)
Clothing, food, ornaments, and the like, as well as drinks and vehicles, arise from desire.
Houses, domestic furnishings, male servants, and female attendants—these are divine beings with celestial forms; they are indeed liberated souls in embodied form.
In his own magnificent palace, his beautiful lion-throne is situated in the center;
on its sides, the residence of Dharmadeva and Bhakti is certain.
On the left side, however, the residence of Muktī and Ratī is certain.
On the side of knowledge, detachment dwells permanently;
on the side of liberation, devotion and the Command dwell permanently.
On the side of the Command, the desire for liberation and surrender dwell permanently. (23–24)
On the side of knowledge (jñāna) dwells the discourse of sacred stories;
on the side of worldly affairs (vārtā) dwells the initiation into servitude.
Thus, I have described to you the dwelling beneath the seven peaks.
In the *ghummaṭa* (the circular enclosure), there is a circle of clans (*gotramaṇḍala*) during the circumambulation.
Indeed, there are seven families of householders residing there.
At the circular gate (*gopura*), the Supreme Knowledge (*parā vidyā*) is attained by means of which [that state is reached]. || 26–27 ||
The great, circular, divine golden rampart is thus described.
There, all around, shine the palaces inhabited by those who are eternally liberated.
Indeed, those palaces of theirs are like sentient celestial chariots (vimānas). ||28||
Moving at will and acting according to their desire, they are completely filled with all supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
They are the abode of all pleasant tastes—of food, drink, ointments, and offerings—and are ever radiant, divine, liberated, and possessed of the form of Śrī Hari. (1.119.30)
O Pārvatī, listen with steady mind as I shall declare the names of those who possess all powers at will and whose meditations produce whatever they desire:
Guṇātīta, Gopāla, Brahmā, Mukta, Śuka, and Śata. (31)
He of noble vows, the one without lineage, the Infinite, the Ordainer, the son of Vasudeva;
the Eternal, the Inconceivable, the Tranquil, Kṛṣṇa, Renunciation, and likewise Mercy; the Supreme Swan, Dispassion, the Consisting of Consciousness, the Imperishable, and the Lord. (32–33)
Self-luminous, solitary, dispassionate, and likewise conscious;
of the nature of consciousness, the person (nara), and the venerable feet, the purifier;
steadfast, the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa), auspicious (śiva), and indeed the support.
He is indeed consciousness, the devotee of Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, and truly devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
He is the wise one, the auspicious, the Lord of lords, formless, and immortal.
He is also known as the Cowherd, the Holder of the Lotus, Śveta, Vaikuṇṭha, and the God.
Prakāśa, Prasāda, Sudharma, Sukhāśraya, Sukharūpa, Santoṣa, Jñāna, Vijaya,
Badrika, Nivṛtta, Naya, Dhyāna, and Śāntanu. (37)
Śama (Tranquility), Sukha (Bliss), Mahāsukha (Great Bliss), Acintya (Inconceivable), Amogha (Unfailing), Pramodaka (Delight);
Gavendra (Lord of Cows), Anubhava (Experience), Āditya (Sun), Acala (Immovable), Viśvarūpaka (Universal Form);
Prajña (Wisdom), Bodha (Awakening), Vedānta (End of the Vedas), Mukunda (Liberator), and Kṣema (Security). || 38–39 ||
Puṇḍarīka, Vidhātṛ, and Agrāhya; Śāśvata, Dhruva, Ameya, Pavitra, Sthaviṣṭha, and Ṛṣīkaka;
Prabhūta, Niyama, Yoga, Jagadīśa, and Dayālaya.
Sura, Dharma, Muni, Nara, Balabhadra, Prakāśana;
Siddha, Sukhakara, Viśrāma, and likewise Keśava; Kapila, Svayaśas, Draṣṭṛ, Sajjana, and Sāṃkhya as well. (4.1–42)
Bhāskara, Prabha, Ṛṣabha, and likewise Saguṇa;
Nirdvandva, Nṛsiṃha, Videha, and then Deva;
Nirālamba, Viśvāsa, Nirvikāra, and Pradīpana.
Nirapekṣa, Niranna, and the being named Lakṣmaṇa; Nirmoha, Bhūdhara, Bhadra, and Mānada;
Haṃsa, Pradyumna, Ānanda, Mañjula, and Pratoṣaṇa. (44–45)
Bhajana, Nirmala, Śānta, Praśānta, Dhanya, as well as Savitā, Dharaṇa, Sujña, Satyeśa, Jyotiṣas,
Prabodha, Prabhu, Padma, and Tāpasa. (46)
Turīya, Svarūpa, Viveka, and likewise Vāmana;
Nivāsa, Maṅgala, Akṣaya, and Suvrata; Abheda, Turīya, Kṣemaka, and Dṛḍhavrata. (47–48)
Nirviśeṣa, Vicāra, Jiṣṇu, Madhu, Vaiṣṇava, Avyaya, Muktiga, Varada, Saṃśita,
Vallabha, Suparṇa, Viśvadhra, and likewise Durlabha.
Dhana, Prasāda, Śyāma, and likewise Dahara;
Aiśvarya, Avadāta, Rādha, and Dharmarūpaṇa;
Vraja, Bhāgavata, Bāla, Upaśama, and Svastika.
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Śrīdhara, Amṛta, Yajña, Hiraṇyaka;
Īśāna, Prabhava, Pūta, Bhūgarbha, Prāṇada, Praṇa;
Saṃvatsara, Kṛta, Śiva, Kṛtajña, and Sureśvara. (52)
Budha, Vṛṣa, Vasu, Sāma, Guṇa, Adhyakṣa, Pravedana;
Loka, Vyūha, Sarvaga, Bhrājiṣṇu, Caraṇa; Sahiṣṇu, Catura, Anagha, Urjita, and Kāraṇa. (53–54)
Upendra, Dhṛta, Sattva, and also Sāttvata;
Utsāha, Viśruta, Anirdeśa, and Animeṣaṇa;
Udāra, Subhūṣa, Anila, and likewise Vikrama.
Satkāra, Saṃvṛta, Vṛtta, Viśiṣṭa, Siddhimat,
Vardhana, Vivikta, Bṛhadrūpa, Pṛthuśravas,
Aśoka, Sudāman, Sānukūla, and likewise Atula. (56–57)
Ādideva, Śrīgarbha, Nirvāṇa, and likewise Bhājana;
Vyavasāya, Santoṣa, Virāma, and then Nanda;
Sthira, Sudarśana, Viśāla, and also Dakṣa.
Dharmayūpa, as well as Ijya, Makha, Sūkṣma, Pramāṇaka;
Brahmaṇya, Vatsala, Śubhāṅga, and Purātana; Sandhāna, Pramoda, Nandana, and Supuṇyaka. (59–60)
Durjaya, Kumuda, Sulabha, and Śuddha;
Yogīśa, Suvidya, Sākṣya, and likewise Dhanañjaya;
Akhaṇḍa, Triloka, Suhṛd, Bhūmā, and Hiraṇmaya.
Bhava, Bhāva, Kratu, and also Samārādhana;
Vatsala, Vātsala, Susneha, and Kubera-jit; Soma, Alarka, Śūra, Mantra, Mañca, and Mūla-jit.
Tilaka, Kuṇḍala, Kirīṭa, Kaṭaka, Aṅgada,
Naktaka, Kaustubha, Prāvāra, and likewise Kañcuka—
these were the attendants who took up their positions there upon the rampart.
Indeed, they always reside in the palaces within the first enclosure;
(65) and those beginningless liberated ones who serve Hari dwell there as well.
They are also innumerable within the second enclosure. (66)
All of them possess forms identical to the [original] form, and their lordly powers are equal to that of the original form.
All of them behold the temple of Śrī Hari equally in their hands;
there is no state of deficiency or superiority regarding their lordly powers and other excellent qualities.
Just as they desire, they indeed become possessed of eternal omniscience and divine vision.
(68) For that first rampart has an extent of ten million yojanas;
the second rampart has an extent of one hundred thousand yojanas. (69)
The third wall is one *parārdha* yojana in extent;
there indeed dwell those liberated ones who have come from the worlds of the Īśvaras.
The fourth [wall] is as long as a *parārdha* multiplied by a *parārdha* yojanas.
There, within that wall, there are creations of liberated beings who have attained [liberation].
Beyond that, however, is the fifth enclosure, which is infinite;
therein lies Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and also Amṛta, which are boundless.
Likewise, Avyākṛta, Śveta, and Badarikāśrama; Mātsyaloka, Kūrmaloka, and Vārāhaloka;
the abode of Kapila, Hāreya, and the dwelling of Vāsudeva.
The station of Pārthava, the abode of Dattātreya, and Hāṃsaka;
the abode of Nṛhari, as well as Āryama and Vāmaneyaka; the world of Paraśurāma, and likewise Yājña and Sāketa.
There is the abode of Kaumāra, the abode of Hayagrīva, and the abode of Nārada;
there are also the abodes of the kings of kings and those which have Vyāsa as their refuge.
Likewise, there is the abode of Buddha, and indeed there are countless other abodes.
For the incarnations are indeed infinite, as are the millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
Therein, the creations are infinite, and there is no numbering of the incarnations;
therefore, there is truly no numbering whatsoever of those respective abodes.
The number of the fifth enclosure is neither one nor many.
Therein are forests, rivers, mountains, and infinite peaks;
gardens, monasteries, and grounds known by imperishable names. (79)
The minerals, the mines, the excavations, the elevations, and the peaks;
all the celestial chariots (vimānas) and the various classes of their attendants;
the musicians, the dancers, the storytellers, and those who provide genealogical accounts. (1.119.80–81)
Servants, sacrificial priests, chanters of the *sāmans*, those engaged in worldly endeavors, artisans, and those who have attained liberation from the circle of existence—
these are innumerable; no one except Nārāyaṇa is able to count them.
He too replied: "There is no numbering of the liberated souls in my abode;
likewise, there is no counting of my incarnations and my divine manifestations.
Thus it is in the divine, imperishable abode, within the threefold manifestation of my glory. (83–84)
From that, through the divine play (*līlā*) of Śrī Hari, various abodes manifest;
thus, by means of the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), a creation arises consisting of millions of lords.
Indeed, there is no end to it, for it is impossible to reach its limit even through description.
"How indeed can I possibly complete the description by its end?

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The General and Particular Description of the Temple of Śrī Hari, Its Surroundings, Its Enclosures, Its Liberated Attendants (Pārṣadas), Their Incarnations, Abodes, and So Forth," in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
