Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī, Śaṅkara, the friend of the world and the benefactor of the people,
spoke to Pārvatī regarding the description of Goloka.

O Queen of the Gods, understand that Goloka, the abode of the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Hari, is possessed of infinite servants, maidservants, and all other opulences, as well as every kind of prosperity and splendor—
just as it was revealed to me in meditative absorption.
On the far shore of the great river Virajā is the mountain Prākāravān.
And there is the mountain Śataśṛṅga, which is fifty crores of yojanas in circumference;
it is one crore yojanas in height and ten crores of yojanas in width.
On its single peak is the Rāsa-maṇḍala, ten yojanas in extent;
beyond that is Vṛndāvana, and likewise thirty-two forests.
Further ahead is the Akṣaya-vaṭa tree, and there the emanations of the Gopas, Gopīs, and others.
Above that, in the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), is Goloka, and beyond that, the Imperishable (akṣara).
Indeed, that wonderful and auspicious abode removes old age and death;
it is maintained by Brahmā and created by the will of Hari.
It is impossible to describe it; nevertheless, I shall describe it briefly.
By means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), I beheld the vast banks of the Virajā river—resembling pure crystal, exceedingly wide, and enchanting. (8)
Endowed with mines of pearls, rubies, and supreme jewels,
they shone with rows of black, white, yellow, and red gems;
in some places, those two were exceedingly beautiful, possessing brilliantly radiant corals.
O beloved, they are adorned with rows of mines of supreme, priceless, and excellent gems; they possess otherworldly and wondrous deposits of gold mines;
and in some places, O dear one, they are mines of rubies and sapphires.
And in some places, they were endowed with rows of emerald-like forms.

In some places they take the form of the Syamantaka gem, and in others the form of the Rucaka; possessing the luster of priceless yellow gold, they are endowed with mines of various rows of jewels. ||13||
In some places they are mines of jewels, in other places mines of the Kaustubha gem; in yet other places, they are auspicious mines of those gems that are beyond description. ||14||
In one place, two excellent and beautiful divine hermitages are situated;
there is such a delightful river, Virajā, beautifully adorned with its banks, which encircles Mount Śataśṛṅga in a circle. (15)
It was made of divine gold, blazing with a radiance like that of ten million suns.
It was resplendent with long groves of pārijāta trees, pervaded by various kalpa-trees, and beautifully adorned with the wish-fulfilling cow, Kāmadhenu. (17)
Its height is ten million yojanas, and its width increases tenfold at each stage;
the length of the mountain range there is measured at fifty crore yojanas.
Upon its single peak, there is a supreme, circular Rāsa-maṇḍala, ten yojanas in extent, shaped like a rampart.
The circle of the rāsa dance was perfumed with the fragrance of millions of gardens of various flowers, and it was adorned with objects and other things that stimulate desire. (1.120.20)
Therein were tens of millions of jeweled pavilions, such as palaces for pleasure, adorned with staircases and ladders, and consisting of many stories. (21)
They were beautifully adorned with golden jars made of the seven precious gems and pillars of jewels; upon those pillars, enchanting emeralds were inlaid. (22)
There were rubies the color of vermilion, radiant sapphires, various kinds of bound gems, and beautiful varieties of jewels. (23)
Of that excellent pavilion, four gate-towers were likewise seen—divine, kissing the sky, and enriched with the beauty of their door-panels. (24)
There, from the very beginning, clusters of plantain trunks shone forth, adorned with mango sprouts tied together by cords. 25.
In every place here, within the pavilion, ever-new splendor was fashioned, provided with nets of white grain and leaves, fruits, and sprouts of durvā grass. (26)
Anointed with the liquid paste of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron, groups of cowherd girls indeed sport here by the millions. (27)
Richly adorned with jewel ornaments, they shone with garlands of gems;
they were decorated with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and jeweled anklets (28);
and their cheeks were made radiant by jeweled earrings, nose-ornaments, and other finery.
Their fingers were graced by hands adorned with beautiful jewel rings;
their toes were exquisitely beautified by ornaments of jeweled anklets;
they were decorated with precious gemstone ornaments and resplendent with crowns of excellent jewels. (1.120.29–30)
Their beautiful noses were adorned with ornaments of pearls from the lord of elephants;
on the region below their forelocks, they bore bright crescent-marks of vermilion;
they possessed the luster of the color of yellow campaka flowers and were anointed with liquid sandalwood paste.
Clad in yellow garments, they were enchanting with lips like the bimba fruit;
their lotus-faces shone with a luster arising from the full moon of autumn;
and their eyes possessed the beauty of the finest petals of a blossoming autumn lotus. (32–33)
Intoxicated by the thick kajjala clinging to their two eyelids,
adorned with the beauty of garlands of full-blown mālatī flowers draped over their shoulders,
and enchanting with a slow gait like that of the best of elephants or swans; (34)
Endowed with the union of curved brow-contractions and gentle smiles, they were resplendent with rows of teeth resembling the seeds of ripe pomegranates;
their beauty was further adorned by prominent noses as magnificent as the beaks of the king of birds. (35–36)
Bowed down by the weight of their golden breasts, which resembled the temples of lordly elephants;
bowed down by the heavy burden of their firm and swelling hips;
their minds sporting with the pride of Kandarpa and overwhelmed with passion.
Eager to behold the beauty of the faces of the full moon [Kṛṣṇa] in a mirror, their hearts were intent on the service of the feet of Rādhikā and Kṛṣṇa;
these beautiful women were sixteen years of age, with the arrows of youth at their peak. (38–39)
They dwell in a great divine pavilion adorned with circles of lotuses;
there are hundreds of thousands of lakes of ritual action and tens of millions of flower gardens,
indeed filled with tens of millions of lotuses possessing red, white, and crimson hues.
And [the place] was filled with the humming of divine bees resonating along its banks;
it was beautified by millions of bower-cottages containing flower-beds, and the pavilion was radiant on all sides with the rays of jewel-lamps. 41–42.
Then, after that, the beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍapa shines forth, provided with enjoyments, wealth, camphor, betel-leaves, and garments,
as well as white chowries, mirrors, and various flower garlands.
A forest exists that is wondrously beautiful, delightful, and truly divine.
Named Vṛndāvana, it is dear to Rādhā and Mādhava; for the sake of their playful pastimes, it is supreme and composed of wish-fulfilling trees. 44–45.
The grove always shines with the gentle trembling of a soft breeze;
it is fragrant with the scent of lotuses, lilies, musk, and other perfumes;
and it is enchanting with the warbling of cuckoos and fresh sprouts.
It was exceedingly beautiful with groves of *kadamba* trees for the sake of pleasure,
and it was made fragrant on all sides by *bakula*, *kunda*, *mandāra*, *candana*, and golden *campaka*— those various excellent flowers of sweet scent. (47–48)
It was delightful, filled with oranges, jackfruit, mangoes, palmyra palms, wood-apples,
dates, rose-apples, jujubes, aguru, hog-plums, pomegranates,
citrons, plantains, and coconuts.
It was crowded with various trees— *śālmali*, *aśvattha*, *tintiḍī*, *nimba*, *pippalī*, and *sarjaka*— which bore fruit and flowers at all times,
and was filled with *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *svarṇā*, *ketakī*, and *mādhavī* vines.
It was adorned with fifty crores of beautiful bower-huts, resplendent with canopies of climbing vines such as *yūthikā* and *citrapuṣpī*;
there were millions upon millions of jewel-lamps and fragrant incense.
Scents of erotic substances waft from all sides on the winds.
Here and there are flower-beds anointed with fragrant *arka* and sandalwood, resounding with the humming of bees that have assumed divine forms and are adorned with pearls. (53–54)
In the beautiful Vṛndāvana, fifty million gopīs adorned with jewel ornaments dwell by the command of Rādhikā. Within that interior ground, there are indeed thirty-two forests.

There are forests in that circular region consisting of various specific trees known by names such as Kalpadru, Pārijāta, and Kadamba. Beyond that is the abode of Vṛndāraka, where the cowherds and cowherd-maids have built their dwellings.
Indeed, cities dwell for the cowherds and cowherdesses of the pastures,
and there are thousands upon thousands of flower gardens;
these are even more excellent than the homes of the fifty crores of cowherdesses.
Each of the palaces was like Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself in form.
(5.9) And all the twelve-year-old girls were equal in beauty to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; numbering in the hundreds of millions, they were each a perfect embodiment of beauty beyond compare. (1.120.60)
Indeed, innumerable gopīs and gopas dwell in Vṛndāraka,
which possesses grounds of jewels, diamonds, rubies, gems, gold, and so forth.
In that divine Vṛndāraka, there are infinite opulences.
From that time forth, Goloka remained within the abode of Brahmā.
Indeed, all around it were the circles of cowherds and cowherdesses; likewise, these were situated all around Vṛndāraka and all around Goloka.
Indeed, the Vasatis dwell in Vṛndāraka, which is circular;
and in the midst of the abodes of those Vasatis is the supreme Goloka.
To the eastern part of Vṛndāraka, there is indeed the Akṣayavaṭa tree.
It was five yojanas wide and ten yojanas high;
it possessed a trunk a thousand [yojanas] in girth and was endowed with millions of branches.
It was rich with ripe red fruits and beautified by fresh sprouts. (65–66)
Below that, there are jeweled railings with shadows cast by frequent contact;
there, dark-complexioned cowherd boys take their delight.
Wearing yellow garments, their minds are fixed on play and they are full of aesthetic bliss.
Their bodies were beautiful and endowed with the exquisite fragrance of the finest sandalwood;
those attendants, radiant with forms and youth equal to Kṛṣṇa’s, richly adorned with all ornaments, took delight and sported together. (68–69)
Next to that, on the side, is the one known as Bhāṇḍīravaṭa;
indeed, it is here that the union of Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā takes place.
That banyan tree has an extent of five yojanas and a height double that.
That divine tree has thousands of trunks and millions of branches and twigs.
Beneath it, there are indeed pleasure-pavilions for the young maidens of the gopīs, constructed with golden altars inlaid with jewels.
And all those cowherd girls, radiant with forms like that of Rādhā, play and delight together; they are all twelve years of age.
They constantly await Kṛṣṇa and come and go by the millions.
Having obtained Kṛṣṇa, who is dearer to them than life itself, and having served him, they indeed depart.
Between those two banyan trees lies a charming royal road that leads far toward the great palace of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
On every side there were altars fashioned from rubies;
in some places they were constructed from sapphires, as well as from emeralds and diamonds;
and in other places, the altars were made of rubies and crystal.
In some places there were pavilions for rest and law-halls on the sides;
in some places it was beautified by the liquid paste of sandalwood, musk, and saffron;
and in others, it was adorned with parched grain, fruits, flowers, curd, *durvā* grass, and so forth.
Flanked by golden campaka, mandāra, pārijāta, and other trees,
it shone, adorned with trees abounding in fresh sprouts, flowers, and the like.
Plantain groves were beautiful, and fruit-bearing trees were magnificent.

Adorned with fine jewels, the beautiful water-jars placed upon their heads shone as the gopīs went about the task of fetching water. Those golden jars, set upon the slopes of their hips, gleamed as they were filled with water. (1.120.80–81)
Anointed with vermilion and saffron, scented with fragrant perfumes,
and adorned with floral ornaments, the cowherd girls proceed from one path to another,
moving along the thoroughfares.
In their own delightful palaces, upon paths with stairways of jewels,
wearing garments purified by fire and adorned with golden ornaments,
they sleep upon flower-couches with white chowries and mirrors.
By that path, the cowherds and cowherd girls went to their own most beautiful mansions situated at the side, which were adorned with flower garlands and excellent archways,
and were surrounded by walls provided with sixteen gates. (85)
Surrounded by moats and guarded by gatekeepers—thus was that royal road, beautified on both sides;
having entered the city gate, it leads to the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (86–87)
Likewise, there dwell within the enclosure walls beings by the tens of millions.
The wall is circular in shape and extends for ten million yojanas.
This is the most divine Goloka, known as Mahāgoloka.
The cowherds and cowherd girls introduce him by the names "Nijagoloka" and also "Rādhāgoloka. Now,
O Śivā, listen as I describe that primary Goloka to you.

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "Description of Goloka, Virajā, Śataśṛṅga, the Rāsa-maṇḍapa, Vṛndāvana, the Akṣayavaṭa, Bhāṇḍīravaṭa, the Royal Road, Vṛndāraka, and other sites," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 122 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī! Mahādeva spoke auspiciously to Pārvatī:
"Goloka is indeed surrounded by a wall and endowed with temples and other sites.
The extent of its wall is said to be ten million yojanas. (1)
It was endowed with four gates and rested upon celestial aerial chariots in the sky;
it was richly protected by hosts of cowherds and provided with gatekeepers. The palaces were inlaid with jewels and filled with many objects of enjoyment.
The fifty million cowherd girls who surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa—
those beloved ones reside there within the palaces of that place.
Furthermore, there are hundreds of millions of hermitages belonging to the devotee cowherds.
Providing happiness filled with various objects of enjoyment from trees and creepers,
there are ten crores of hermitages belonging to the attendants (*pārṣadas*), which are even more extensive than those and resplendent with jewels and gems. (5–6)
All perfections are fulfilled therein, and not even the slightest deficiency exists.
There are maidens twelve years of age and youths sixteen years of age;
even beyond them are the excellent attendants who bear the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
They dwell in palatial residences, and there are others by the millions as well.
Because they reside where Śrī Kṛṣṇa dwells, there is not even the slightest deficiency in their own abode.
From the palaces, they are joined by the gopīs who are pure devotees of Rādhikā.
There are another thirty-two crores of houses made of jewels, gems, and gold,
as well as ten crores of wonderful mansions belonging to the maidservants of the cowherd women who are devotees of Rādhā.

All the palaces within Goloka are divine, made of gold and fashioned with jewels, gems, and diamonds; they are fulfillers of all desires. Those who have been purified by the penance of a hundred lifetimes and are devoted to the service of Hari [dwell there]. (11–12)

Those who have surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa and who constantly chant "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa" go to the abode of Goloka and dwell within its ramparts. Their residences are constructed of excellent gems, jewels, and rubies.
Adorned with flower-beds, flower-garlands, and white chowries;
rich in the splendor of jeweled mirrors and graced by emeralds;
their crests filled with clusters of priceless jewel-pitchers. (14–15)

The hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, devoted and possessing divine bodies nourished by the accumulation of unfailing vigor, dwell there in their millions upon millions, adorned with fine garments and ornaments,
and enjoying various kinds of nectar.

Then, in the center of that great garden, there exists a supreme and vast hermitage belonging to Rāseśvarī; it is fashioned with exquisite beauty by Rādhā—the goddess of gods, the most excellent of gopīs—and is filled with the memory of her. (17–18)
Belonging to Kṛṣṇa, who is dearer than life itself, it was captivating with its beautiful materials,
exquisitely lovely and circular in shape, measuring six gavyūtis in extent,
endowed with a hundred palaces, and blazing with the luster of jewels. (19)
It was a magnificent city, constructed from heaps of the finest priceless jewels;
it was beautifully adorned with moats that were deep and difficult to cross;
and it was surrounded by *kalpa* trees, with hundreds of flower gardens interspersed throughout.
It is well-encircled by a wall inlaid with jewels of great value;
it is beautifully adorned with seven gates containing altars made of excellent gems.
There, surrounding it on all sides, lies a very large circular garden.
Everywhere there, even amidst the trees and creepers,
another wall exists within the inner garden;
it is provided with sixteen gates at every point.
Rising a thousand bows in height, adorned with pinnacle-pots,
blazing with splendor, beautiful, and graced by hundreds of celestial chariots;
and surrounding its wall were structures resembling the palaces of Kṛṣṇa.
The hermitages of the cowherds and cowherdesses numbered as many as hundreds of palaces.
Within the enclosure wall there was a garden endowed with divine fruits, filled with celestial flowers, and containing beautiful basins of divine water. (26–27)
To the south there exists a beautiful, divine lake;
on its shore stands the king’s palace, where dancers perform.
There is the charming music of the daughters, which is imbued with the virtues of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
The instrumentalists and singers likewise sang songs that were like nectar.
And there, charming cowherd girls, wearing various costumes and longing for the grace of Kṛṣṇa, were seen in every place.
Some held mṛdaṅga drums in their hands, and some likewise held vīṇās;
some held chowries in their hands, while others had their palms clapping in rhythm. Some held musical instruments in their hands, and some were adorned with tinkling anklets.
Some cause the pavilion to resound with the ornaments of tinkling bells;
others, having taken water-pots in their hands and likewise upon their heads, dance there as female leaders dressed in male attire in many ways. (32–33)
Some assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa, while others assumed the form of Rādhā; some stood at a distance, while others were intent on embracing Kṛṣṇa.
Those gopīs, absorbed in play, thus worshiped Kṛṣṇa.
Beside it, on the shore of the lake, there are excellent and magnificent palatial mansions.
(35) Those houses belong to the companions of Rādhā; they are beautiful to behold.
Those thirty-three friends of Rādhā are in the full bloom of youth. (36)
In beauty alone, in virtue alone, in dress and in youth,
as well as in good fortune and age, they were the equals of Rādhā.
O Girijā, hear their names, thirty-three in number, according to their prominence.
Candrakalā, Suśīlā, Yamunā, Mādhavī, and Rati;
Kadambamālā, Sukuntī, Jāhnavī, and Svayaṃprabhā;
Padmamukhī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Sumukhī, and Sudhā. (38–39)
Padmālayā, Pārijātā, Sugaurī, Sarvamaṅgalā,
Kālikā, Kamalā, Durgā, Bhāratī, Sarasvatī,
Gaṅgā, Ambikā, Madhumatī, Campā, Aparṇā, and Sundarī.
Kṛṣṇapriyā, Brahmasatī, Nandinī, and likewise Nandanā—these are her [wives].
Indeed, their palaces are equal to Kṛṣṇa’s own palace;
they truly abound with jewels, minerals, articles of enjoyment, and golden pitchers. ||41-42||
Wherever there were maidens, cowherd girls, female companions, and cowherds who had surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa— in every single house—
Kṛṣṇa, assuming many forms, dwelt and took delight with her.
And with each respective beloved, in every possible way, [he dwells].
(44) Regarding the sixteen gate-towers (*gopura*) on the wall of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa’s palace, the first gate-tower there is made of jewels and gems. (45)
Joined by a pair of railings and possessing doors of vajra-jewels,
there dwells the youthful Vīrabhānu as the guardian of the gate;
he sits upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with ornaments of precious gems.
Wearing yellow garments, his head radiant with a jewel-encrusted crown;
indeed, by whose command two and a half lakhs of cowherds abide.
Then, at the second gate there, which is even more beautiful than that— 47–48.
The gatekeeper is indeed the youthful Candrabhānu, who is dark-complexioned;
he holds a golden staff and is seated upon a jeweled throne. Under his command stand five hundred thousand gopas, who are like lords themselves. (49)
Then, at the third gate there, which was exceedingly radiant with jewels,
stood the gatekeeper Sūryabhānu: a youth holding a flute,
his hand grasping a jeweled staff, and resplendent with golden gem-studded earrings.
At the fourth gate, which is adorned with ornaments distinct from those of the nine hundred thousand cowherds who abide by his command— those Śyāmasundaras—
the youthful Lord of Vraja, Vasubhānu, stands as their gatekeeper.
Holding a jeweled staff, seated upon a throne of precious gems, with lips like a ripe bimba fruit, and adorned with every ornament;
by whose command there are nine hundred thousand charming cowherds. (53–54)
At the fifth gate, on a wall variegated with diverse diamond carvings,
stands the gatekeeper Devabhānu, seated upon a beautiful lion-throne;
he has a crest of peacock feathers and wears jeweled necklaces and fine earrings.
Under whose command one million cowherds are stationed;
and at the sixth gate, which is adorned with diamond walls and doors, stands the gatekeeper Śukrabhānu, decorated with all ornaments. (56–57)
At whose command one million cowherds are stationed;
at the seventh gate, which is exceptionally beautiful and distinct from the other six, stands the youthful gatekeeper Ratnabhānu, the most beloved of Śrī Hari. (58)
Adorned with flowers, sandalwood paste, and ornaments, he sat upon a lion-throne holding a staff;
indeed, twelve hundred thousand cowherds abide under his command—
at the eighth gate, which is distinct even from those seven.
The gatekeeper is Supārśva, beautifully adorned with jeweled staffs,
enriched by the splendor of jeweled earrings, and possessing lips like the bandhujīva flower.
Under his command always stand twelve hundred thousand cowherds.
At the ninth gate, which is rich with diamonds and jewels and adorned with variegated garlands,
there is the gatekeeper Subala, whose form and ornaments are graceful. Under his command likewise stand twelve hundred thousand cowherds.
At the tenth beautiful gate, which is beyond description and supreme,
stands the gatekeeper Sudāmā, as enchanting as Kṛṣṇa himself;
by his command, twenty lakhs of cowherds stand with staffs in hand.
At the eleventh gate, which is most beautiful with its fine paintings and likewise wonderful, stands the gatekeeper Śrīdāmā, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne;
he wears yellow garments and is adorned with priceless ornaments and sandalwood paste. (65–66)
Resplendent with earrings, bracelets, flower garlands, and a crown,
he was like a sovereign king of kings, under whose command millions of cowherds served.
At the twelfth gate, there were four altars made of priceless jewels.
In that place, which is enchanting with the murals on walls of various wonderful and excellent vajras,
there are indeed female gatekeepers adorned with ornaments,
endowed with fresh youth, and graced with heavy braided hair. (68–69)
Clad in yellow, red, and other colored garments, with their hair braided with fragrant flowers,
they were adorned with ornaments of gems, gold, and jewels, and wore golden bracelets;
their forms were graced by excellent armlets, anklets, and earrings.
Bowed down by the weight of their full hips and moving slowly under the burden of their buttocks,
seven hundred gopīs— the most beloved and excellent of Hari— stand at the city gate; and they have ten million gopīs as their attendants, who are likewise dear to Hari.
In the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth gate-towers,
there are female gatekeepers who have reached the full bloom of youth;
they are excellent, captivating, delightful, noble, blessed, and most beautiful.

The beloveds of Rādhā are richly adorned and possess the auspicious fortune of Kṛṣṇa. Indeed, there are ten million crores of such gopīs who carry out her commands. At the sixteenth gate, however, there are thirty-three principal gopīs.
But they have gatekeepers whose form cannot be described;
they are neither Pārvatī, nor Lakṣmī, nor Urvaśī, much less Rādhikā.
Such are they—adorned with jewel ornaments and in the full bloom of youth.

Adorned with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and golden anklets, they were beautifully decorated at their waists with girdles of tinkling bells. Their cheeks shone brilliantly with the luster of jeweled earrings. (77–78)
Adorned with garlands of full-blown mālatī flowers, strings of jewels, and necklaces; their faces graced by mandalas worthy of the full autumnal moon;
their breasts radiant with garlands and necklaces of pārijāta blossoms and the like.
With lower lips like ripe bimba fruits and lotus-faces smiling,
they possessed rows of teeth as white as the finest seeds of the ripe pomegranate and kunda flowers;
their complexion was like the beautiful hue of the golden campaka, with slender waists and slim hips.
Their noses were like golden sandalwood sticks adorned with elephant-pearls;
their nostrils were as slender as the beaks of parrots;
they possessed firm breasts and heavy hips, yet their minds were fixed upon Kṛṣṇa’s feet. (82)
In the gateway (gopura), which has arches and long panels adorned with golden stars,
and which is provided with a sacrificial altar (vedikā), the beloveds of Hari reside.
The entire area within the gateway is decorated with jewels, gems, and other precious materials.
It was adorned on both sides by walls set with emeralds and rubies,
and made fragrant by garlands of *pārijāta* flowers;
within it, there lies a great garden of blossoms.
Therein, the great mansion of Rādhā is indeed the very temple of Kṛṣṇa.
Standing in the midst of the temples is that enchanting palace with a hundred halls;
it is reached from the halls by means of seven desirable celestial chariots.
It was truly divine, fashioned from the finest essence of jewels alone;
it was adorned with pillars of various gems and jewels set with diamonds,
and it shone with clusters of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers.
It was enchanting with walls fashioned from pearls, rubies, and diamonds;
it was provided with white chowries, mirrors, fans, and water-jars;
and it was adorned with sprouts of sandalwood tied with knots of silk thread.
Adorned with a beautiful courtyard featuring clusters of jeweled pillars,
it was infused with the liquid essences of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
and [further] furnished with dried grains, white flowers, coral, fruits, and rice.
Adorned with leaves, durvā grass, unbroken rice, parched grain, water-pots, and garlands, and made fragrant by winds infused with various scents;
whatever in the universe is unseen, unheard, foremost, and difficult to attain—[all that was present there]. (92–93)
And for the sake of Rādhikā, the palace was adorned with various objects;
there were exquisite jeweled couches covered with fine fabrics,
and indeed millions of jeweled jars and jeweled vessels.
Adorned with various priceless and beautiful objects,
it resounded with the sweet sounds of diverse musical instruments;
it was made resonant by lutes and stringed instruments, and was filled with the melodious singing of the gopīs.
Enchanting with the sounds of musical instruments as well as the songs of female singers,
he was surrounded by throngs of cowherds equal to Kṛṣṇa himself,
and graced by the numerous groups of cowherd girls who were the companions of Rādhā.

O Daughter of the Mountain! One who has heard the beautiful music of the verses extolling the overflowing virtues of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa hears sweet singing, beholds excellent dancing, and attains supreme bliss—the essence of Kṛṣṇa’s divine play. (98–99)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Walls, Palaces, Gardens, Inner Apartments, Wall-Gates, Palace-Gates, Gardens, Sixteen Gate-Towers, and Door-Guardians of Goloka," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 121. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*).
Chapter 122 [Author:
Chapter 123 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved! Then Śambhu spoke to his dear Satī:
"In the palace of Rādhikā-Kṛṣṇa, there is an excellent jewel-throne, measuring one hundred bows in size and circular in shape on all sides. (1)
It was adorned with various high and low golden jars upon its peaks and other parts;
it was graced by divine female attendants who were like loving slave-girls;
and above that, it was pervaded by a brilliance equal to ten million suns, reaching as high as seven palm trees.
It was marvelous, more beautiful than all radiant objects;
it was a garment of splendor, a mass of splendor, and the very first mine of splendor.
That divine lion-throne indeed moved through the sky at will.
The lion’s paws, the variegated creepers, Ananta, the cowherds,
and the cowherd-maidens (5); likewise the cows, the calves, and the heifers— these beloved devotees [are placed] upon the throne, on the steps, on the pillar, at the door, and on the archway (6).
Musicians, dancers, and singers were positioned at the sides;
fashioned in the form of puppets, they all shone resplendently.
Peacocks, cranes, swans, cātaka birds, parrots, and mainas [were likewise present].
These auspicious figurines are situated in their respective places.
(8) Upon a divine throne, a mass of splendor, Kṛṣṇa shines resplendent—the most excellent, the one worthy of choice, the giver of boons, and the cause of all givers of boons. (9)
He is the bestower of all auspiciousness, the most auspicious among all auspicious things;
he is untainted and desireless, the abode of divine sovereignty and qualities;
he is eternal, possesses a form, and sustains the manifestations of his power in the Kali age.
He is the support of all, possessing all forms, the seed of all, and indeed beyond the senses;
he is both the body of the insentient and the sentient, yet possesses an independent, divine form;
he is the witness of all, the seer of all, the Lord who is existence, consciousness, and bliss. (11–12)
He is the Lord of all, without beginning or end, the Ordainer, the progenitor, and the Father;
in every single pore of whose vast body there is one entire universe.
That Kṛṣṇa is born from but a sixteenth part of that great Viṣṇu.
Those who know yoga meditate upon Him and serve Him, having attained a state of servitude.
He is a youth, most beautiful, the beloved of lovely women;
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, the excellent one clad in yellow garments.
Two-armed, with a flute in his hand, smiling and most enchanting;
with a crest of peacock feathers and adorned with garlands of jasmine;
anointed with the liquid paste of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron. (16)

Adorned with the essence of priceless, supreme jewels as his ornaments, he shone with a crown and diadem fashioned from priceless gems. With the moon of his face eclipsing the luster of autumnal blossoming lotuses, he was radiant. (17–18)
He shone with a lower lip like a ripe bimba fruit, enchanting with rows of teeth resembling the seeds of a ripe pomegranate;
he possessed the supreme delight of a beautiful smile and was the captivator of the hearts of the three worlds. (1.9)
With makara-shaped earrings blazing from his cheeks and temples,
and adorned with lotus-like feet graced by excellent jeweled anklets;
he shone in garments of priceless cloth, the color of pure fire-refined turmeric.
Adorned with excellent divine ornaments such as jewels and gold, he is enchanting with his bimba-fruit-like lips joined by a playful flute;
full of graciousness, he bestows grace upon his devotees. (22)
With his chest radiant with armor set with beads of excellent gems,
and blazing with the brilliant splendor of the great jewel Kaustubha resting upon him, that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman in the form of an eternal youth, shines forth.
To his left stands Rādhikā, her limbs exquisitely beautiful;
she gazes at her beloved with a smile through her sidelong glances, while her row of teeth shines with the supreme excellence of a string of pearls. (25)
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, her eyes were like autumn lotuses;
her countenance was enchanting with a luster surpassing that of the full autumn moon, and her beautiful face was made radiant by lips whose excellence rivaled the bandhujīva flower. (26–27)
Her lotus-feet were resplendent with a pair of tinkling anklets;
she was adorned by rows of nails that eclipsed the luster of the finest gems.
Covering her complexion, which shone like saffron, her feet were further embellished with red lac.
Adorned with a girdle made of the essence of priceless jewels, her hips were graced by it;
she wore garments purified by fire, blazing and radiant with the brilliance of priceless gems, and was joined at the waist with tinkling bells made of the finest great jewels.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and anklets made of the seven precious gems;
her cheeks radiant with earrings fashioned from the finest essence of jewels;
and above her ears, further embellished by ornaments of the most excellent gems.
Adorned with the pearls from the lordly elephants at the tips of the beaks of the lords of birds;
beautified by the weight of her curly tresses with a garland of *mālatī* flowers;
and her chest beautifully adorned with a necklace of the finest *kaustubha* gems.
Her garments were radiant with the glow of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers;
her fingers were adorned with clusters of jeweled rings.
She possessed the luster of molten gold, her form resplendent like refined gold.
Graceful with her hips and loins, beautifully adorned by her full breasts, she was embellished by all forms of beauty and decorated with every ornament;
her long eyes were like lotus petals, and she moved with the languid grace of one burdened by the weight of love. (35–36)

She is the treasury of Kṛṣṇa’s desires, an ocean of all youthfulness, and the ultimate pinnacle of every form; she is white yet radiant with redness. She captivates the heart of Kṛṣṇa as his mind flows forth in a stream of love.
Without the touch of Kṛṣṇa, she does not remain for even a single moment;
without her beloved Kṛṣṇa, the beloved woman does not stay alone.
Thus, endowed with such mutual splendor, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa proceed together.
Upon that divine throne, with the splendor of a king of kings,
what indeed was lacking in the union of the Blessed One and the Blessed Goddess?
What incompleteness could there be in the union of the Full Brahman and the Full Brahmāṇī?
Indeed, for those residing in Goloka, even a single moment passes as a source of supreme bliss;
yet on this earth, they experience only the equivalent of seven manvantaras.
For such a place is a realm of eternal and profound joy.
There were fragrant cows, wish-fulfilling cows, and dark-blue bulls;
and four-tusked elephants, white and adorned with gold and other ornaments;
[there were] sixty-year-old [elephants] that showered down joy and could travel through the sky.
There were horses with black ears, and winged steeds that travel through the sky;
there were peacocks, garuḍas, swans, parrots, cranes, and peahens;
various birds were there, as were numerous trees and creepers.
There were hundreds of palanquins borne by men, as well as vehicles moving according to their own will;
there were also various types of weapons, and the elements of air, water, and fire served as attendants. (46)

The seasons, as well as those who serve [the senses of] taste, smell, sound, form, and so forth, attend upon [the Lord] in Goloka for the attainment of desired enjoyments. Divine chariots that travel through the sky and such divine manifestations likewise attend him. (47–48)
What indeed could be non-divine about the divine Kṛṣṇa at that time?
Kṛṣṇa is the divine Great King, and Queen Rādhikā is divine.
Virajā, the flowing river, and the attendants—the cowherds and cowherd girls—are truly divine.
Indeed, all the divine palaces situated upon the summit of the mountain are inhabited by them. There, the chariot of Śrī Kṛṣṇa shines with a divine form,
adorned with diamonds and the finest essence of precious gems.
He was adorned with a hundred thousand white chowries and ten thousand mirrors;
he was embellished with fine saffron-colored robes purified by fire;
and he was made exceedingly beautiful by a thousand jars filled with excellent jewels.
He was resplendent with multitudes of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers;
he was joined by the foremost of his attendants, auspicious and composed of gold.
He was the very embodiment of splendor, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns.
In some places there, Kṛṣṇa remains in his chariot having become the four-armed Nārāyaṇa; indeed, he goes from one world to another.
Then that person is dark-complexioned, beautiful, and charming.
Holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, clothed in yellow garments;
wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with a divine forest garland;
anointed with the liquid paste of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
Four-armed, with a smiling countenance, ever eager to bestow grace upon his devotees,
adorned with ornaments that are the very essence of the finest jewels and gems,
he is constantly served by the great goddess Mahālakṣmī.
He possesses sovereign power and is praised by all the gods and goddesses.
And on his beautiful left chariot stands a woman of white complexion,
richly adorned with the splendor of jewel ornaments and graced with yellow garments.
Her face is like the full moon of autumn, her eyes are like autumn lotuses, and her lips are like ripe bimba fruits;
with a smiling countenance, she bestows all desires.
Holding a flute, a lute, and a book in her hands, she is ever-eager to show grace to her devotees.
And the presiding goddess of knowledge is Sarasvatī, whose form is wisdom.
On the right side, indeed, she possesses a radiance equal to a hundred moons;
she has the luster of molten gold, is smiling, and is exceedingly beautiful.
She was graced by beautiful cheeks with two earrings of excellent gems;
she was adorned with priceless garments inlaid with jewels of inestimable value;
and she was beautified by armlets and bracelets set with priceless gems.
She was accompanied by the sound of anklets made from the essence of the seven precious gems;
her waist and hips were adorned with the tinkling of great jewels and small bells;
and her chest was radiant with necklaces of flowers such as the *pārijāta*.
She is adorned with braided hair interwoven with garlands of full-blown *mālatī* flowers;
she is beautified by the orb of her face, which possesses a splendor surpassing that of the autumnal moon;
and she is endowed with a *tilaka* of vermilion in the center of a dot of musk.
Her lotus-eyes were embraced by very beautiful collyrium;
holding in her hand a great lotus rich with the splendor of a thousand petals,
she gazed at Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, with sidelong glances.
Even while standing in the middle of the chariot, all three of them move about freely; furthermore, another excellent chariot was fashioned for him by Viśvakarman,
fifty yojanas in height and four yojanas in width.
It was fashioned from the essence of gold and adorned with various precious gems;
it was joined with the finest of great jewels and provided with garments purified by fire;
it was accompanied by white chowries, decorated, and furnished with mirrors. (7.1–7.2)

Adorned with a garland and necklace, its pinnacle made of the essence of the seven precious gems, it was equipped with a thousand wheels, traveled at the speed of thought, and was captivating to the mind.
Sudarśana possessed a splendor equal to the midday sun of summer.
Resplendent with pearls, rubies, diamonds, and other gems, it is adorned with variegated mechanical puppets, flower-lakes, and groves;
joined by women fit for dalliance, it shines with pleasure-palaces. (74–75)
There, for the sake of serving Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Mahāmāyā also resides;
she is adorned with ornaments of jewels possessing the most excellent luster from the essence of gold, exceedingly radiant with great splendor, and like unto a treasury of majesty. (76)
Endowed with a thousand arms, she holds various weapons and other implements;
her face is bright with a gentle smile, and she stands for the sake of Krishna’s sport;
golden and jeweled earrings rest upon her cheeks and temples. (77–78)
She was made charming by the tinkling anklets fashioned from the essence of the finest jewels;
her waist was graced by a golden girdle set with excellent gems;
and she was adorned with golden bracelets, armlets, and chains inlaid with jewels.
She was adorned with rows of garlands of Mandāraka and Kalpa flowers;
her hips were firm, her waist slender, and her breasts full;
her face was like the full moon of autumn, radiant with an aura of splendor.
Her lotus-eyes were adorned with lines of excellent black collyrium,
and her forehead was decorated with leaf-patterns made from sandalwood and saffron paste;
she shone with beautiful teeth that were as white as pearls, pomegranate seeds, and jasmine flowers.
She was slow-moving due to her braided hair-tufts adorned with clusters of various flowers;
she was graced by the downward curve of her nose, which resembled the beaks of parrots and Garuḍa;
and she wore garlands made of ocean foam and pearls from the Siṃha mountain.
Other goddesses are also present for service, wearing brilliant garments and bodices, adorned with fine golden crescent-moon ornaments, and having vertical tilakas applied to their foreheads;
among them are Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and the beloved Jāmbavatī.
Kālindī, Mitravindā, Satyabhāmā, and another,
Bhadrā, and Lakṣmaṇā— these indeed were the queens there.
There was a great circle of sixteen thousand and one hundred wives.
One who performs service to Kṛṣṇa truly shines in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
there is no end to other [forms of service], for the entire world is under Kṛṣṇa’s control.
Indeed, the gopīs of the twenty-one lotuses belong to Kṛṣṇa alone.
And there are others as well, beyond counting, for everything there is like a servant.
Indeed, the thirty-three companions, the eight noble ladies, and Rādhā as the foremost, are the beloved ones in Gokula. (1.122.90)
Vasudeva and Devakī, Nanda and Yaśodā,
as well as Uddhava, Sātyaki, Garga, Akrūra, and other Sātvatas,
were struck down in Gokula upon those various ramparts and grounds.
Indeed, they dwell in great divine palaces within the gardens;
their enjoyments are equal to those of Kṛṣṇa, for there is nothing lacking.
Furthermore, there is a great chariot for the wandering of the friends who have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa.
Four yojanas in width and five yojanas in height,
it resembles pure crystal and is fashioned from the essence of jewels;
it is resplendent with networks of garlands of unfading pārijāta flowers.
Adorned with ornaments of *maṇi* and *kaustubha* gems, [the mountain] was graced by a pinnacle of priceless jewels and resplendent with necklaces of diamonds;
it was embraced by thousands of millions of enchanting palaces. (95–96)
He possesses two thousand wheels and two thousand horses; he is covered with fine garments and surrounded by ten million gopīs.
What else can I describe of that Lord Kṛṣṇa, the glorious Hari?
There were delightful kitchens and dining halls;
bathing rooms, perfumery rooms, and dressing rooms; pleasure chambers for friends, as well as assembly halls. (98–99)
There were dance halls and assembly pavilions for festivals,
pleasure houses and gardens for recreation and delight;
there were bedchambers and moon-lit galleries with a thousand stories.
Whatever [beauties] exist here that do not exist in other abodes,
those indeed were created by Śrī Hari himself in the form of Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of happiness, for the sake of granting happiness to his devotees, and especially to women. 101–102.
The form assumed was indeed characterized by *rajas* and possessed unfailing potency and strength;
what, then, could possibly be said to be lacking or even slightly deficient therein?
For how could there be any incompleteness in that which is perfect in every respect?
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you a small portion of the Goloka-maṇḍala;
indeed, even Kṛṣṇa himself is not able to describe it in its entirety.
Whoever shall hear or read this account of Kṛṣṇa’s Goloka [shall attain the highest goal].
Indeed, he shall obtain firm devotion toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which is very difficult to attain;
as well as the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, the fourfold liberation beginning with *sālokya*, equality with Kṛṣṇa in this very life, perfection of speech, and great fame. (106)
A son, knowledge, poetic skill, and likewise unwavering prosperity; a wife who is devoted to her husband, virtuous, well-behaved, and steadfast;
progeny, and long-lasting fame—and finally, at the end, a destination in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Jewel Throne, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā, Their Prosperity, the Four-Armed Form of Sarasvatī, the Form of Mahāmāyā as Mahālakṣmī, the Hundred Thousand and Eight Noble Ladies, and Their Palace," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 122. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*).
Chapter 123 [Author:
Chapter 124 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard of the location of Goloka, Pārvatī was greatly delighted;
desiring to hear the divine narrative, she spoke these excellent words to Śaṅkara:
"I wish to hear about Vaikuṇṭha, the divine abode of the form of Ramā."
Having heard this, Mahādeva, the lord of disciplined yogīs, remembered Hari, Nārāyaṇa, who was indeed fashioned as divine by Śrīdhara;
and having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa for a moment, he beheld the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
He described all of that in due order with a spirit of devotion:
"Listen to me, O Vaiṣṇava wife; in the description of [the Lord], the aesthetic flavor (rasa) is truly tasted. Without the nectar of devotion to Hari, other flavors are considered false. (4)
Indeed, the worlds of the threefold manifestation are truly innumerable.
(5) They all consist of the abode of Brahman, are the refuge of the bliss of Brahman-joy, eternal, changeless, and entirely free from the defects to be abandoned. (6)
All of them possess a divine golden luster and a radiance equal to ten million suns;
they are nourished by the true nectar of devotion to the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa, and are considered bestowers of perfect bliss through the singing of the Lord’s Sāman hymns and other such acts. (7)
They are described in the Vedas, Shastras, and other texts by the manifested attendants;
they are presided over by divine women who are the very essence of knowledge and by Brahma-males;
and they are graced by lakes of the pure nectar of love and wisdom.
In the worlds of Brahmā, they are always nourished by the women known as the Śrutis, by the female attendants known as the Smṛtis,
and by the divine beings known as the Śāstras; indeed,
there they enjoy every kind of supreme pleasure and sustenance.
Consciousness alone exists, arising from the reality of Brahman; it is indeed pure sentience.
There is no illusion, no insentient matter, no suffering, and nothing subject to destruction.
It is neither darkness nor something produced, neither perishable, but eternal.
Just as the abode of Goloka exists within the limit of the imperishable Brahman (akṣarabrahman), so too does the abode of Vaikuṇṭha exist within the limit of the imperishable realm (akṣaradhāman).
Beyond Māyā resides the great divine consort who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha.
She who was considered the perfect vessel for the love of Nārāyaṇa,
having bathed in the supreme bliss through devotion to the delight of Nārāyaṇa,
forgot her own nature and indeed became liquid. (14–15)
Through union with Nārāyaṇa,
she who has dissolved into the essence of desire joins Lord Hari— the Master— with streams of ten millionfold bliss, either through her own forms or through the forms of Nārāyaṇa himself.
She remains eternally dissolved, abiding in the pinnacle of bliss.
Hari unites her with the streams of bliss within his own self;
consequently, she was born as the river Sarayū in Vikuṇṭha, taking the form of that river.
And on the far shore of Māyā, that divine, circular, great river flows;
it is filled with the essence of Brahman, carrying a current of eternal bliss.
It abounds with golden fish and possesses sands of the finest silver.
It was covered with divine *kāśa* and *kuśa* grass, blazing with a brilliance equal to the splendor of the sun;
it was enchanting with the shimmering luster of jewels, diamonds, mother-of-pearl, and other gems,
and through its union with divine rays, it possessed a radiance equal to ten million suns.
With its steps fashioned from excellent gems, diamonds, and other precious materials,
it provides a landing place suitable for extensive bathing; it is adorned with countless ornaments and bestows the happiness of residing in Vaikuṇṭha, bathing, and sporting.
Resplendent with its two shores resembling pure crystal,
it shines with black, white, yellow, and red variegated gems;
in some places, it is adorned with bright, gentle coral and fine silken cloths.
In some places it was a repository of minerals such as silver and gold; in other places it was beautifully adorned with mines of sapphire and ruby;
and in yet other places, its surface was fashioned from the finest emeralds.
In some places it was adorned with sites for monasteries, bathing pools, and the like;
in other places it was delightful with lush grass and graced by rows of forests; and in yet other places it provided rest for herds of wish-fulfilling cows.
With various divine boats of many kinds,
frequented by celestial birds such as garuḍas and swans,
living beings were indeed sprinkled with its water and rendered eternally protected. (28)

The liberated ones, residing in the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, become eternal inhabitants there. On its beautiful bank, indeed, lies the Kausala forest; and along the Sarayū, that very forest is circular in shape.
It was composed of celestial trees, with many excellent trees such as the *pārijāta*,
and it shone with vast forests of *kalpa* trees and *kalpavalī* creepers.
Its length was measured at one hundred million (*arbu-da-arbuda*) yojanas.
In some places there are wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas), and in others indeed pārijātaka trees;
in some places there are creepers with the essence of soma, and in others mango trees (rasālaka);
in some places there are indeed madhuka trees, and countless jambu trees.
In some places there are *karmada* trees, and in others *ṭimburu* trees;
there are clusters of *śrīvṛkṣa* trees and *tilaka* trees that touch the sky.
In some places, moreover, there are varieties of nine-colored *jambīra* fruits.
In some places there are indeed plantains, and in some places pomegranate trees;
in some places grapevines, betel creepers, and bitter cucurbit vines;
in some places bark trees, coconut palms, date palms, and *khārika* trees.
In some places there were *setu* and *apuṣpīya* trees; in others, *rāma*, *phala*, and so forth;
as well as *badāma*, *badarī*, *sarja*, *pippalī*, *bakula*, and the like.
In some places there were *kesara* trees, along with *kadamba*, *nīpa*, and *nimba*.
Panasa trees, campakas, aśoka trees, sandalwood trees;
śrīphalas, śālmali trees, tālas, tintiḍīs, mādhavī creepers;
mallikās, mālatīs, golden yūthikās, aśvatthas, and kunda flowers. (38–39)
There are indeed various trees, all of which are united with Vaikuṇṭha;
in some places there are lakes, excellent wells, sprouts, and oblong ponds;
in other places there are various rivers carrying milk and desirable waters.
In some places there were mountain peaks, and in others, the plateaus where forest-dwellers reside;
in some places, there were dwellings constructed for the pleasure of sporting with celestial nymphs.
There, in that forest, exist infinite creations of forest-dwellers.
In connection with Nārāyaṇa, those living beings— be they animals, birds, or reptiles— who have attained liberation in this kalpa or in other kalpas,
having been liberated, dwell there eternally in that forest of Kosala.
Indeed, by the will of Nārāyaṇa, they possess the power to assume any form at will.
Sometimes they travel in vehicles or celestial chariots through the atmosphere;
sometimes they appear as gods, sometimes as liberated souls, and sometimes as various noble beings.
There exist indeed, and dwell therein, divine objects of enjoyment, drinks, essences, and various fruits that provide satisfaction through their consumption;
these were created by Viṣṇu for the sake of those residing in the forest region known as Kauśalyā.
In that forest, there were many beautiful groves of trees—
of banyans, *gundraka* trees, and auspicious *āmalakī* trees,
as well as clusters of *kiṃśuka*, *udumbara*, and *pippala* trees. (47–48)
Beautiful, golden-hued, and tawny creepers,
clinging to the trees, shine forth like canopies fashioned for the sake of the forest groves.
There are pavilions with floors made of excellent gems, jewels, and diamonds.
Those celestial chariots possess staircases of divine materials for the purpose of ascending the excellent path;
they have a thousand floors, their beautiful banners extend into the sky,
they are equipped with sun-bright domes, and they are surrounded by various gardens.
Abounding with pools of cold and warm water and adorned with circles of fire,
the crystal lamps are delightful by their very nature;
there, wish-fulfilling cows roam and graze.
Likewise, there are divine dwellings for those who reside in the forests of Vaikuṇṭha;
there are beautiful women equal to Lakṣmī, in the full bloom of sixteen-year-old youth, possessing exquisite forms, accompanied by their husbands, and joined with their own families. ||53-54||
All those belonging to the lineage of Acyuta dwell there with devoted minds;
their couches, seats, and small platforms are delightful for play and recreation,
and they are indeed fit for sleeping, strolling, and amorous pastimes.
Enclosed by walls and provided with palaces, they were equipped with water and fire-suppression systems;
they were furnished with fans and fly-whisks, adorned with many mirrors,
and decorated with food, clothing, conversation, dance, and instrumental music.
There are palatial mansions and pavilions with the brilliant luster of jewel-lamps;
indeed, fragrant incenses are burning within those chambers. Cool, pleasant, and delightful breezes, carrying the scent of camphor, blow there.
The forest of Kausala is a place of skillful charm for the delight of beautiful women.
There, fifty crores of bowers, huts, and pavilions exist.
Having bathed in the Sarayū and become one whose body is liberated, one should then proceed from there.
If he desires to remain in that delightful forest of Kauśala,
he takes up residence right there and rejoices as if liberated.
Beyond this, furthermore, lies the divine enclosure wall of the great place of protection.
That excellent great wall is eighty thousand *yojanas* [in circumference].
It is circular in shape and rises one hundred thousand *yojanas* high.
Within its height, there are many millions of magnificent divine palaces.
All travel through the air in golden palatial chariots (*vimāna*).
These mansions, reaching a height of one hundred *yojanas* and a width of a thousand *yojanas*,
are like celestial chariots that move through the sky.
All the men and women were like those in Vaikuṇṭha, moving according to their will.
The young women and young men were twelve and sixteen years of age respectively;
they were enriched by the beauty of their braided hair and likewise wore garlands of flowers.
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, necklaces, chains, and crowns, they were embellished with rings, the Kaustubha gem, and golden ornaments;
their brows were intensely arched with desire, and they carried a flowing stream of love.
Well-nourished, white and reddish in hue, with their limbs draped in golden garments;
golden in form, ever delightful, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, and as cool as the autumn moon, they were like mines of all happiness. (68–69)
Indeed, they become exactly fifty crores;
those devotees are likewise eternal, and they too number fifty crores.
Furthermore, others also dwell there within that circular enclosure.
It indeed has four gates in the four directions.
There, the attendants of the Blessed One have been appointed as gatekeepers—adorned with ornaments of rubies and radiant with crowns of excellent jewels. (71–72)
The four gates were protected by all divine beings bearing celestial weapons, adorned with crowns and bracelets, and appearing as youths of sixteen years;
thus was that supreme fortress pervaded, circular in shape.
At its end lies the divine city named Sāketa, with excellent grounds.
Known as the eternal abode of Sāketa, it is not confined to a single residence.
There are many gardens there, as well as countless groves. (74–75)
There were great rivers of the essence of Brahman, numerous mountain peaks,
countless fertile fields, forests, and groves,
all for the pleasure and amusement of the Vaiṣṇavas who were accompanied by their consorts.
And for the sake of providing dwellings for his wives, he established residences there;
there are villages with fortifications numbering many hundreds of millions, and indeed wonderful cities numbering hundreds of thousands of millions. (77–78)
The villages and towns of Sāketa have grounds paved with excellent gems and jewels;
there are pavilions of precious stones and fine houses made of diamonds. There are palaces of pearls and rubies, with walls and stairways of crystal.
There were divine cows, calves, and beautiful heifers; likewise,
there were palaces, turrets, numerous pinnacles,
countless moon-chambers, and resting galleries.
Local roads, royal highways, celestial chariots, and vehicles;
garuḍas, swan-drawn carriages, bulls, elephants, and horses;
all kinds of riches, and women, both common and most excellent.
All of them were twelve years of age, their youth having just begun to blossom.
Those women of Viṣṇu’s retinue dwell in groups of hundreds upon hundreds;
they are radiant with the excellence of the arts of love and are adorned with fine substances that stimulate desire.
Richly adorned with precious ornaments, they were resplendent with jeweled garlands;
they were decorated with jewel-encrusted bracelets, armlets, and various gem-studded decorations.
Their cheeks shone brilliantly with excellent jeweled earrings and other such finery.
The radiance of their fingers was held by gold rings inlaid with jewels;

they were adorned with ornaments of pearls, mother-of-pearl, fine silver, and refined gold; and beautiful crescent-moon marks were fashioned upon their foreheads with red sandalwood, saffron, and other pigments. (86–87)
Adorned with necklaces of pearls and strings of beads, their forearms were beautified by bracelets and joined by chains of *baṅgiḍī*;
their waists shone with girdles, and they wore tinkling bells and anklets. (88)
With faces like the full moon at the new and full phases, with eyes as beautiful as lotus petals,
adorned with fragrant flower garlands bound within their braided hair,
and endowed with slow, languid movements and the graceful arching of creeper-like eyebrows that stir the mind.

They possessed firm, small, and excellent breasts; they were endowed with the grace of Nārāyaṇa; they had the luster of yellow sandalwood and gold; they were clothed in yellow garments and fine coverings;
they had beautiful teeth, melodious voices, and gentle countenances; indeed, they were the very vessels of Hari’s love.
The women belong to the same class as Ramā; their heads are equal to those of Ramā.
All the women have forehead marks (*tilaka*) and are marked with the seven sacred impressions (*taptamudrā*).
All the men are four-armed, holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Adorned with the Kaustubha jewel, garlands, ornaments, and the like, they are white and pale,
eternal, sixteen years of age, and in the full bloom of youth. There, the Siddhas reside, and in every house there are Kalpa trees.
There in Sāketa, wish-fulfilling gems were bestowed;
and all divine prosperities were present—food, drink, and ointments, as well as bathing, giving, recreation, dancing, sporting, and music. (95–96)
All festivals, assemblies, worship, honors, and ceremonies become divine, flowing like streams from a pool of nectar.
There are mountains of fruits, flowers, excellent juices, fragrances, and liquid substances.
There is nothing lacking whatsoever for the residents in the abode of Sāketa.
By the command of Mahālakṣmī, the entirety of Sāketa is perfumed by devotion;
it is worthy of being seen with divine vision, but it is not perceived by the eye of *māyā*.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Divine Sarayū, the Kauśala Forest, the Residences therein, the Circular Fortresses within them, the Sāketa Region, the Gardens, and the Abodes of Vaiṣṇavas and Others," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 123. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Kṛtayuga-Santāna).
Chapter 124 [Author:
Chapter 125 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Śambhu spoke to Mahādevī regarding its further description:
"In that city of Sāketa, within the circular area,
there is a royal highway one crore yojanas in length, which leads to the abode of Nārāyaṇa."
On both sides there are indeed infinite forests filled with wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadruma).
There are also dharma-halls, peace-halls, and resting grounds.
On both sides, moreover, there are wells, ponds, and oblong lakes.
In some places there are white palaces and likewise lofty mansions;
there are excellent houses, richly endowed and worthy of all honors for travelers.
All of them are made of jewels and gold, with golden domes upon their peaks.
Delightful with the essence of nectar-like flavors, adorned with betel vines and the like,
(5) and possessing gardens, enjoyments, and residences for excellent maidens,
the mansions of the Vaiṣṇavas and Vaiṣṇavīs indeed shine on both sides. (6)

Indeed, those palaces shine forth, endowed with various means of enjoyment: banners, arches, flags, couches, mirrors, and lamps; with gentle and soft furnishings; and augmented by foods, drinks, and other delicacies. (7)
There is indeed no deficiency whatsoever in the manifestations [of power] compared to Vaikuṇṭha.
Starting from Sāketa, the divine realm of Vaikuṇṭha exists as the supreme,
situated within the intermediate space in the abode of Brahman.
Indeed, all around it dwell the inhabitants who are entirely devoted to Viṣṇu;
for they reside together in Sāketa within circular dwellings.
In the midst of those who make their homes in Sāketa stands the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
In the eastern part of Sāketa, there was a Brahma-panasa tree,
five yojanas in width and ten yojanas in height;
it possessed the beauty of a thousand trunks and an extensive spread of ten million branches.
Abounding with ripe yellow fruits and adorned with green sprouts,
it provides excellent shade and comfort;
beneath it are square altars where the children of Ramā and Viṣṇu indeed delight.
Equal to Nārāyaṇa in form, they wear yellow garments and possess four arms;
their bodies are perfumed with fragrant sandalwood, musk, and other excellent scents;
enriched with the beauty of all auspicious marks, they take delight and sport. (14–15)
Next to it, on the side, stands a second *panasa* tree belonging to Lakṣmī;
it is five *yojanas* in extent and twice that height.
It is indeed the place of rest for Ramā while she sports there.
There are circular platforms made of the essence of the seven precious gems and rubies (17).
And there are indeed pleasure gardens for the Vaiṣṇava maidens;
all those maidens are the abodes of beauty, qualities, and virtues equal to Lakṣmī’s. (18)
Radiant and divine, those maidens of twelve years of age took their delight;
awaiting Nārāyaṇa, they went forth and returned again and again.
Having served Nārāyaṇa, the lord of life, they indeed departed.
Between those two *panasa* trees lies a captivating royal highway that leads toward the palace of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. On both sides of it are altars made of jewels, rubies, and gems.
Divine mansions and palaces, adorned with the dwellings of Vaiṣṇavas, appear;
and Vaiṣṇava maidens go forth, carrying vessels for worship, with garlands and crest-jewels made of flowers from various gardens in their hands. (22)
Having worshipped Nārāyaṇa, they indeed return there once more.
Clad in garments of molten gold and possessing bodies of refined gold,
their faces enchanted by millions of desires, they serve Śrī Hari within his abode.
The path leading both inside and outside for the residents of Vaikuṇṭha as well as those of Sāketa is always crowded;
in some places along its sides, there are indeed groves of mango trees.
In some places beautifully adorned with groves of fruit-bearing trees such as the jackfruit and the rambhā,
and endowed with the splendor of flower gardens and enchanting lakes,
he now enters the easternmost gateway of the outer wall.
Everything within the enclosure wall is Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Hari.
Within the enclosure wall there are tens of millions of dwellings for the devotees.
The enclosure wall is circular in shape and extends for ten million yojanas.
Situated in the ether of the abode of Brahmā, it is called Mahāvaikuṇṭha;
it is also known by the names Nityavaikuṇṭha and Paravaikuṇṭha. There, the Vaiṣṇava people indeed provide this identification by name. (1.124.29–30)
Upon the ramparts dwell celestial chariots by the millions;
they proceed to the abode of Brahmā and sport in Sāketa.
Having gathered their own devotees from within the cosmic eggs, they return to that supreme realm.
All those attendants, servants at the feet of Nārāyaṇa,
dwell in divine palaces and great mansions within the enclosure wall; their beautiful chambers are filled with excellent jewels, gems, rubies, diamonds, and the like.
In various places there, beautiful palaces exist,
filled with many enjoyments and wealth, and providing abundant sources of happiness.
Within those ramparts and palaces, they become increasingly magnificent as one proceeds further and further.

There dwell fifty crores of beloved consorts of Śrī Hari— Vaiṣṇava maidens who have offered all their wealth for the sake of Nārāyaṇa. Their hermitages are situated there within the circular enclosure across seven levels.

There are millions of divine abodes belonging to Nārāyaṇa, where his eternal attendants have made their dwellings; their splendor is only slightly less than that of Śrī Hari himself. They are celestial gardens, mines of nectar, and natural reservoirs of bliss.
Indeed, one hundred crores of the best of Vaiṣṇava devotees dwell there;
all are four-armed, sixteen years of age, and like Nārāyaṇas themselves.
All those maidens are twelve years of age and like Kamalā herself.
Furthermore, at the end [of that], there are millions of other great devotees, the Sātvatas who are of the very form of Hari, dwelling in palaces;
and there are another thirty-two crores of handmaidens of the goddess Lakṣmī.
There, they dwell within the palatial mansions of the ramparts, which are composed of emerald.
Having realized Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman and thus attained transcendence over death,
their residence shall be there in the great sphere of Vaikuṇṭha.
Through supreme devotion to Nārāyaṇa and likewise through service to Ramā,
they go to Mahāvaikuṇṭha itself, from which there is no return.
For their sake, those dwellings constructed of jewels are situated within the rampart.
Their abodes abound in the riches of flower-beds, flower-garlands, nectar, food, and the like;
they possess umbrellas, chowries, mirrors, golden jars, and ornaments, and are enriched with the splendor of garments and jewelry. (44–45)
Imperishable, possessing unfailing potency, and having attained bodies that are joyful and robust,
crores upon crores of Vaiṣṇavas dwell in their own palaces.
There are eight great gate-towers (gopuras) on the rampart there.
Indeed, the fourteen higher planes were guarded by gatekeepers:
those of Indra, Agni, Yama, and likewise Nirṛti;
as well as Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna. (47–48)
This role as gatekeeper of the gods has been eternally ordained;
all those gods who dwell there are indeed devotees of Viṣṇu, eternal and liberated.
They are truly the lords of the gates, and not merely the guardians of heaven and other realms.
Indra, Pāvaka, Yama, and likewise Nirṛti;
Varuṇa, Pavana, Kubera, and Īśa as well—
those who bear these names are the liberated ones dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha.
Under their command in Vaikuṇṭha are indeed ten billion (*koṭyarbuda*) Vaiṣṇavas;
all of them stand within the enclosure of each one of those [leaders].

This, however, is the seventh array; within that, moreover, is another. There are eight weapons—the conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, Śārṅga bow, plow, and pestle—and the attendants (pārṣadas) bear their respective names.
Having formed the sixth array, they stand in the eight directions in succession, four-armed, embodied, and equipped with mantras, weapons, and missiles.
Under the command of each one, there are indeed tens of millions of Vaiṣṇavas.
Now, indeed, in the fifth array, when the sixth [array] was stationed within,
there were eight attendants: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, Sāvitrī, Garuḍa, Dharma, and Makha.

Residing in Vaikuṇṭha, they dwell there in embodied form with divine opulences; indeed, crores upon crores of Vaiṣṇavas remain under their control. Then, in the fourth manifestation (vyūha), those of divine forms abide.
Satya, Acyuta, Ananta, and another named Durga,
as well as Viṣvaksena and Gaṇeśa— these are remembered as the divine liberated ones (mukta).
Indeed, there are crores of Vaiṣṇavas who are under their control.
Then, when the third array was formed and the fourth stood within it:
Matsya, Kacchapa, Vārāha, Narasiṃhaka,
Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāmacandra, and Kalki.
The divine manifestations of Nārāyaṇa are indeed the Vaiṣṇavas;
likewise, there are crores upon crores of Vaiṣṇavas who are dependent upon Him therein.
Now, in the second manifestation (vyūha), there are Prahlāda and Nārada.
Parāśara, Puṇḍarīka, and Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana; Ambarīṣa and Dhruva, as well as Vālmīki and other great sages—
there are indeed millions of such divine devotees who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha.
In the first arrangement, Vāsudeva’s temple is indeed in the east;
Lakṣmī resides in the southeast, and Saṃkarṣaṇa’s abode is in the south.
Sārasvata is in the southwest, and likewise Pradyumna is in the west.
The world of Rati is in the northwest, the realm of Aniruddha is in the north, and the world of Śānti is in the northeast;
such is the first maṇḍala.
All of these [worlds] are accompanied by billions of their respective devotees, numbering as many as an arbuda and a pārārdhya.
Others dwell in the great Vaikuṇṭha in the presence of Hari;
there is no deficiency in these divine manifestations, nor in their palaces, nor in their riches, objects of enjoyment, foods, drinks, and pleasures. (68)
Of women well-attired, soft to the touch, and full of passion;
of fragrant, excellent drinks, pleasant to the touch, and flowing through the channels of the ears;
and of visible divine enjoyments and gardens for those seeking the nectar of immortality. (1.124.69–70)
Of sweet foods such as curd and milk, of beds, seats, and vehicles;
of cold and hot condiments and the like, and of fans, mirrors, and lamps;
of those who sport with their consorts, and of those adorned with palatial mansions and towers.
Of ornaments, collyriums, pigments, and likewise of flavors;
of things to be plastered and edible foods, as well as of vessels and artisans;
of female and male servants, and of the Vaishnavas who serve him well. (72–73)
Of the female servants of the auspicious worlds, of the trees, gardens, and forests abounding in fruits, flowers, and beautiful leaves; of the honey-lakes, rivers, and excellent ponds;
and of the material and divine beings with skins as smooth as glass or woolen cloth.
Of mouth-perfumes and other such articles, of celestial palaces and their inhabitants,
of servants and gods, of playful lovers and their mistresses, of delicate forms, and of things that provide a dwelling place. (75–76)
Of musical instruments, chants, and dances; of assemblies and festivals;
likewise of thrones, grass mats, vessels, and arrows;
Indeed, there is nothing inferior to Nārāyaṇa, nor is there anything inferior to Lakṣmī. (78) All the devotees are equal to Nārāyaṇa, and the women are equal to Ramā.
In the residence of Mahāvaikuṇṭha, there is certainly no deficiency compared to Nārāyaṇa. (79)
Just as there is no distinction between Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, so too there is no difference within oneself.
There is neither physical decline nor old age, neither graying hair nor emaciation;
there is no loss of vigor, nor lack of luster, nor grief—and how could there be death? (1.124.80)
Indeed, there is no loss of one's resolve; whatever one desires, that shall come to pass.
Everything is pervaded by the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), with the tree of resolve (saṃkalpa-druma) as its constant fruit.
Everything brings about inexhaustibility, being filled by the abode of Brahman (brahmadhāma).

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Royal Road, the Brahma-Plantain Tree, the Great Wall of Lakṣmī-Plantains, the Palaces, the Gate-Towers, and the Seven Enclosures in Mahāvaikuṇṭha," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 124.
