Chapter 126 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī concerning the description of Mahāvaikuṇṭha:
the creations of the abodes of the imperishable Brahman belonging to the Tripādvibhūti are pure, peaceful, supremely blissful, and consist of the nature of the bliss of Brahman. (1)
They are eternal, immutable, and devoid of anything subject to abandonment;
they are golden, innumerable, and possess the splendor of ten million suns;
they are filled with the true essence of devotion to the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, wherever there are Sātvatas who offer hymns of praise,
that very place is the supreme abode known as Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
The highest good is called Nirvāṇa, Kaivalya, and Mokṣa.

Indeed, high-souled and most fortunate Vaiṣṇavas dwell there, greatly nourished by the enjoyment of the nectar of Nārāyaṇa’s feet. The female servants, the foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas, are ever devoted to the service of Hari.
That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, Vaikuṇṭha, that is the station of Hari;
it is filled with various regions and bestows the bliss of Brahman, which is existence and consciousness.
It is exquisitely adorned with rubies, sapphires, and many other jewels.
Resplendent like ten million fires, great and composed of all branches of knowledge;
(8) surrounded by many *mandāra* trees that produce fragrance, and joined by tens of millions of divine celestial chariots made of various jewels. (9)
That world is vast, meritorious, pure, consisting of the Self, and auspicious;
it is simultaneously illuminated by the radiance of thousands of millions of suns.
This eternal world of Viṣṇu is not dissolved at the end of Pradhāna.
It cannot even be seen by me or by the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
It is filled with wish-fulfilling trees, kalpa-trees, and nectar-creepers; it is auspicious, adorned with long ponds featuring divine stairs and sweet water.
There, the maidens delight amidst lotuses that are golden-hued, ever-unfading, and uniform in form; they sport there and travel about in celestial chariots.
Endowed with millions of beautiful ornaments that resemble blazing fire, they shine with splendor.

There, a pavilion for dancing was adorned with fragrant substances; it was praised by throngs of birds releasing their songs in unison, and it was filled with divine men and women who were slightly less than sixteen years of age. (14–15)
Richly adorned with the splendor of all auspicious marks and divine, radiant ornaments,
he shines perfectly everywhere, completely filled with bliss.
Indeed, there is constant dancing there, accompanied by high-pitched melodies and other such sounds.
By that, Ānanda arises again and again for the residents of Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, in these delightful regions, the women who are dear to the Sātvatas worship Nārāyaṇa together with their joyful husbands.
They always enjoy the happiness obtained through the grace of Nārāyaṇa;
they sing of the divine pastimes and the auspicious deeds [of the Lord].
These women have lotus-like eyes and limbs as tender as lotuses.
Adorned with divine garlands and garments, they were auspicious and resembled Padmā herself.
They stood together with their husbands, who bore conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses, were decorated with ornaments, wore garlands, and were clad in yellow robes.
They serve Śrī Hari Nārāyaṇa and worship that divine one.
For those who take delight in one another, the blissful rasa of devotion to Hari increases at all times;
it becomes even more intensely fluid.
Thus, the inner circle within the array is pervaded by the dwelling.
Within that circle there exists a great wall, provided with four gates and equipped with lofty gate-towers. (23–24)
And there, even within that fortress, are celestial palaces and mansions.
At the eastern gate are Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa; at the southern, Bhadra and Subhadraka;
at the western, Jaya and Vijaya; and at the northern, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ.
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana,
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanidra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita—
these eight are indeed the lords of the ramparts stationed at the secondary gates. (26–27)
Within that enclosure, there were indeed palatial buildings,
radiant like ten million fires and adorned with jewels;
they were filled with divine men and women who had reached the prime of youth.
For they are situated in contact with a circular wall.
The wall is circular in shape, measuring ten million yojanas;
it is seven-storied and stands circularly all around in the great sky. (1.125.30)

In the twelve gate-towers there are well-suspended royal roads; within the enclosure wall there, indeed, the royal palaces extend. Following the royal palace within the fortress, the auspicious city lies all around.
For Ayodhyā is divine and auspicious, fashioned by Nārāyaṇa;
it is surrounded by rows of houses as radiant as infinite jewels and suns,
and is filled with lovely divine men and women in the full bloom of their youth.
It is endowed with divine rivers and streams, with fine cascades of the water of love;
it possesses divine food, drink, and clothing, with all means arising from mere volition.
It is adorned with countless divine palaces and the dwellings of Vaiṣṇavas.
The men who took refuge in the great devotee Sāttvata, offering themselves to him, were excellent Vaiṣṇavas with four arms, possessing the very form of Nārāyaṇa.
The women were like Lakṣmī in appearance, radiant with garlands and the Kaustubha jewel. (35–36)
They are permeated with the fragrances of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron;
they are adorned with various gardens of flowers, celestial vehicles, mounts, and palaces.
Here and there, numerous groves of *kalpa* trees abound.

By the will of Nārāyaṇa, there exist divine quadrangles, moon-chambers, and pavilions for rest, as well as celestial palaces with a thousand stories. Standing beneath the shade of the wish-fulfilling trees, those lotus-faced women remain there.
Adorned with various flowers that possess divine fragrance and exquisite beauty,
they are seated upon smooth couches covered with auspicious rugs;
resembling ten million moons and decorated with celestial ornaments.

There, the Vaiṣṇavas— whose forms are existence, consciousness, and bliss— dwell with faces graced by smooth noses and pairs of beautiful golden eyebrows. The female devotees of Viṣṇu always serve Nārāyaṇa with great devotion.
In the divine city of Ayodhyā, there are indeed numerous temples belonging to the goddesses who are Nārāyaṇīs and Vaiṣṇavīs;
nevertheless, there are also the inner apartments themselves, complete with their surrounding walls.
Indeed, [the city] is provided with gardens and all the means for desired enjoyments.
In the eight directions, there are eight lofty palaces with surrounding walls.
Here, the eight Śaktis, who are the embodiments of Lakṣmī, are stationed all around.
May Ramā, Rukmiṇī, Sītā, Padmā, Padmālayā, Śivā,
Sudakṣiṇā, and Suśīlā grant me delight and the fulfillment of desire.
May the conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, Śārṅga bow, and other weapons [protect me].

All of them possessed ever-new and beautiful forms, were filled with the bloom of youth, and resembled molten gold; adorned with every ornament, they were united with Nārāyaṇa within their respective circular palaces. 47–48.
They were adorned with rows of very glossy, dark blue, and curly locks of hair;
they shone with divine flowers such as the Mandāra and Pārijāta;
they were enriched by the beauty of jeweled ear-ornaments; and their tresses resembled a swarm of bees.
Adorned with armlets, bracelets, necklaces, and other ornaments,
those Vaiṣṇava women, possessing full breasts,
were constantly sporting with Hari, the ocean of unfailing potency, who is Nārāyaṇa himself.
That Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is eternally captivating to the minds of his women,
sports here within the inner apartments as long as they remain free from ornaments;
that Lord of gods finds manifold delight with those sovereign ladies.
Resembling ten million moons, adorned with divine ornaments, he possessed a pair of beautiful golden eyebrows and a face graced by a smooth nose;
he shone with two cheeks of smooth, long, and exquisite loveliness. (53–54)
Abounding in dark, curly hair, with eyes like the petals of a red lotus,
his locks fashioned into a braid adorned with *mandāra*, *ketakī*, and *jātī* flowers;
his lips possess the luster of a smooth bimba fruit, and his lotus-face bears a beautiful smile.
He was resplendent with a row of teeth shining like priceless pearls;
his limbs were anointed with yellow sandalwood paste and marked with a tilaka of musk;
and he was graced by four divine, elevated-shouldered arms. (56–57)
Adorned with hand-sprouts resembling hibiscus flowers, and graced by shimmering armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings;
he was further adorned by the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha upon his broad chest.
Adorned with divine garments richly beautified with pearls, he was enveloped in yellow cloth resembling the radiance of the rising sun; his lotus-feet shone, graced by ruby anklets. (1.125.59–60)
He is resplendent with rows of nails shining like the stainless moon;
his pair of lotus-feet are smooth, auspicious, and resemble red lotuses.
His two arms are adorned with the Pāñcajanya conch and the discus.
With his two auspicious lotus-feet as smooth as refined gold,
the eternal Lord of Gods, Nārāyaṇa, sports with them; he,
the glorious one who assumes many forms, is well-served by manifold splendors.
That sovereign of emperors shines as the refuge within his inner apartments;
their splendors are equal to those of Nārāyaṇa and Mahālakṣmī.
Not even by an atom are they inferior, for they are indeed Nārāyaṇīs.
They have Nārāyaṇa as their sole husband, they have Nārāyaṇa as their sole refuge;
indeed, they have Nārāyaṇa as their sole true life-breath and they are identical with Nārāyaṇa.
They possess sovereignty equal to that of Nārāyaṇa and are devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa. (65–66)
Constantly immersed in Nārāyaṇa, they perform their own duties for the sake of Nārāyaṇa; they worship Him with affectionate intimacy, laughter, playful gestures, and amorous sports,
as well as through the contemplation of the mutual massaging of limbs in the play of the bliss of love.
Within the circle of these eight, beginning with Ramā,
there is a great and divine garden of trees as cool as the moon;
there are trees of pleasure, trees of sweetness, and likewise creepers of bliss.
The excellent sites feature landing-stairs made of jewels and diamonds descending into bathing pools;
the regions are enriched with cascades of nectar and variegated flowers;
they possess sands of pearls, grounds of gold, and oceans of milk.
With soft carpets and comfortable dwellings, and possessing beautiful rows of divine groves (71), there are small celestial palaces as well as excellent pathways;
there are water-spraying fountains and lovely swinging trees. (72)
There are numerous groves with bowers formed of creepers as their natural enclosures; there are delightful places for reclining and grounds suitable for resting.
There are many sites for dalliance and secluded spots within the terrain.
Indeed, that [nature] arises according to the will of Nārāyaṇa, as it is required:
invisibility, visibility, luminosity, and its opposite;
according to what is required, each of these changes by His will.
In the center of such a circular garden stands the palace of Nārāyaṇa, possessing a hundred peaks and exceedingly brilliant; it is great,
consisting of divine jewels, and has six hundred floors.
Extending for a hundred yojanas and adorned with excellent archways (77),
it was filled with many palaces resembling houses and numerous dwellings,
featuring beautiful floors inlaid with gems, rubies, fine jewels, and crystal (78).
Resplendent with divine staircases and beautifully adorned with windows like eyes,
it was furnished with various globes and displayed banners and flags;
it shone with the brilliance of many moons due to its numerous golden finials.
Adorned on all sides by hosts of divine female attendants,
this palace belongs entirely to Nārāyaṇa, the inner apartment of Mahālakṣmī; indeed,
it is the principal inner apartment itself.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Interior Wall of the Great Vaikuṇṭha, the Dwellings Within It, the Residence of Ayodhyā Inside That, the Palaces of the Eight Original Female Servants, the Garden Within Them, the Palace of Mahālakṣmī in the Center of That, and Her Appurtenances," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 125. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (The Continuity of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 126 [Author:
Chapter 127 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī, Mahādeva described in its entirety that beautiful and independent inner apartment of Mahālakṣmī. Indeed,
there are staircases made of gold and jewels in the four directions.
There are millions of small pillars and shrubs that radiate the luster of jewels.
On both sides of the staircases, there are creepers adorned with fresh sprouts and shining with gem-like flowers. (2–3)
There were also thousands of decorative friezes fashioned from red and green gems,
complete with mirrors and mother-of-pearl;
and the walls were constructed of powdered jewels, rendered variegated with paintings.
The sides of those bold women were fashioned from crystal;
even the dry grounds appeared like water, and the waters appeared like dry land.
The courtyards at the front of these dry grounds repeatedly deluded their female companions.

Upon the pillars there were auspicious figures of goddesses, adorned with wings and holding excellent garlands; they were like Rāmā herself, possessed of exquisite youth, appearing as if they were twinkling.
Possessing consciousness, they seemed to beckon and to offer respectful welcome. (7)
Holding golden vessels in their hands, they increase [the merit] with parched grain (lāja).
Clad in fine golden garments, possessing golden splendor, twelve years of age,
those Narasiṃhas stand at the base of the pillar, assuming the form of Nṛhari.
Gentle and with smiling faces, they are conscious beings like protectors; indeed,
dancers wearing a single cloth dance amidst the *karmāṇikā* flowers,
repeatedly contracting [their limbs] for the sake of propitiating Nārāyaṇa.
The musicians, taking up various musical instruments,
repeatedly played them for the sake of Hari's pleasure until the end of the festivities.
At every station above the gate stood the *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, and bards.
The Vaiṣṇavas, bearing tilaka marks upon their foreheads, joyfully and repeatedly sing the praises of Hari and his various wonderful deeds as incarnations. Likewise,
the Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and the noble species of Kiṃpuruṣas [do the same].
Before creation, they always sing of the virtuous deeds of Śrī Hari.
In some places, twelve-year-old maidens bring drinks mixed with cool, fragrant, sweet, and other substances for the satisfaction of Hari. (14–15)
Elsewhere, all the beautiful maidens dear to Hari cook more than one hundred and eight varieties of food for the meal of Śrī Hari;
in another place, however, the loving women prepare a bed for Him.
Likewise, others, equipped with materials for bathing, go to that husband for the sake of Śrī Hari;
some indeed go taking the finest articles for worship,
while the Gaurikās go taking fragrant substances and liquid unguents.
Taking collyrium, fragrant substances, rich oils, flowers with excellent juices, and fine items for chewing betel, they go toward their beloved;
taking fruits that are to be licked and sucked, they go toward Hari.
Taking with them objects that are beautiful to see, touch, hear, taste, and smell,
the lovely women go to delight their own husbands;
and the beloveds of the Lord, adorned with the crowns of Kalki, also go taking these things with them.
Clad in golden garments that flash like lightning, with golden bodies and slender waists,
they proceed for the sake of sport, adorned with the tinkling of small bells.
Indeed, at every spot along the streets, there are divine moons.
In the balconies and windows, the cool suns indeed blaze;
conscious breezes, gentle, fragrant, and cool, blow;
and subtle clouds rain amidst the pleasure-groves to alleviate the heat.

In that dwelling, the divine sky shines forth in every direction. There, in every house, reside the most excellent Siddhas, who possess instruments for seeing from afar, tablets for hearing from afar, and the power to perceive things at a distance.
Indeed, musicians play well-tuned instruments for the sake of awakening [the Lord].
In every place, in every mansion, Hari exists in a thousand forms;
delighting his male and female servants, he rejoices along with them.
Bathing chambers, sleeping quarters, pleasure pavilions,
as well as pavilions for adornment, pavilions for worship,
houses for drinking, unguents, and fine sports, and pleasure-houses for play.
Therein were the assembly halls for monasteries, legal proceedings, and other such matters;
as well as kitchens, armories, and stores of weapons;
and treasuries for gold, gems, pearls, diamonds, rubies, and crystals. (1.126.29–30)
Wherein the Guptas are established, he stands above them all,
endowed with many principal palatial mansions and temples,
and adorned on all sides by hosts of divine Apsaras and women.
There is a preeminent royal palace that has never existed before and will never exist again.
In the center of Nārāyaṇa’s own place, there is a magnificent royal hall for great festivals,
auspicious, made of jewels, and adorned with a thousand pillars of rubies.
It was filled with divine Vaiṣṇavas and graced by the chanting of the Sāmaveda;
in its center was a beautiful and auspicious throne composed of all the gods.
Its four legs were the embodiments of virtue, knowledge, sovereignty, and detachment.
It is established upon the knees of those whose forms are the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas;
it is pervaded by Śraddhā-śakti, Ādhāra-śakti, Cit-śakti, and Śiva-śakti,
as well as by the sun, moon, fire, lightning, and the moon of nectar.

Kūrma, Śeṣa, Garuḍa, Haṃsa, the Vedic meters, and the mantras—these become the forms of the seats; in the center, however, is the lotus of Brahmā. It has eight petals, and Sāvitrī is situated within its pericarp.
Here Nārāyaṇa resides, perfectly united with Mahālakṣmī;
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with jewel ornaments, and beautified by jeweled armlets, bracelets, and anklets. (38–39)
Adorned with a pair of jeweled earrings that grace his cheeks,
clad in yellow garments, and embellished with a forest garland;
he is peaceful, the beloved of Sarasvatī, whose lotus feet are held by Lakṣmī.
Possessing the playful charm of ten million Cupids, with a smiling face and four arms,
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste and radiant with a crown of supreme jewels—
he is the embodiment of supreme bliss, the one who bestows grace upon his devotees.

Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns, he is a youth, a prince with glossy limbs and endowed with delicate features. He has the luster of a full-blown red lotus and possesses tender, lotus-like hands and feet. 43.
His lotus-eyes were fully awakened, and he was marked by a pair of beautiful, creeper-like eyebrows.
He possessed a fine nose, was endowed with handsome cheeks, and his lotus-face was most radiant.
His teeth were as brilliant as pearls, and he was beautiful with a smiling lower lip.
Resembling the full moon of ten million rays, with his hair gathered into a braid,
he is graced by very glossy, dark-blue, and curling locks;
he is adorned with the Kaustubha gem, which shines like the thousand-rayed sun rising at dawn.
He was resplendent with a conch-like neck adorned by a necklace and a golden garland;
he shone with high, thick shoulders resembling those of a lion, and was graced by four long, rounded hands like fish-tails. 47–48.
Adorned with rings, bracelets, and chains, he shone with his feet resplendent with anklets variegated with various gems;
he was brilliantly illuminated by rows of nails resembling the moon with its light.
Acyuta is a treasury of beauty, heroism, charm, nourishment, and other such qualities;
he is resplendent with his two uplifted arms holding the conch and the discus,
and beautifully adorned by his other two hands which grant boons and fearlessness.
Seated upon her left lap was the goddess Mahālakṣmī Maheśvarī—
golden-hued, deer-like, adorned with garlands of gold and silver,
endowed with divine marks, and possessing a form in the bloom of youth.
Their limbs were anointed with divine sandalwood paste, and their hair was dark and curled.
They were enriched by the splendor of jeweled earrings and adorned with divine necklaces and garlands;
their beautiful tresses were decorated with mandāra, ketakī, and jasmine flowers.
She has beautiful eyebrows, a beautiful nose, and lovely hips; her breasts are full and elevated.
Her face is like the full moon with a gentle smile, and she is adorned with earrings of the sun.
She is golden-hued, wears golden ornaments, possesses four hands, and holds a lotus in her hand.
She was beautifully adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings;
her forehead was marked with a golden streak, and she held two lotuses in her hands.
Her palms were graced by golden citron fruits.
She whose gateway is fragrance, who is difficult to overcome, ever-nourished, and rich in sacrificial offerings;
she who is the beautiful ornament of the ears, nose, and other limbs, and who bears the auspicious *puṇḍra* and *candraka* marks;
she who bestows the yak-tail fan, *uśīra* root, betel-leaf stalks, and moist betel—she belongs to Viṣṇu. (58)
She indeed rejoices with Nārāyaṇa in the realm known as Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
Thus the Lord Nārāyaṇa rejoices in the eternal Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme ether, together with the ever-present and inseparable Mahālakṣmī.
On the south [side] are Dharmadeva, Nanda, and Sunanda;
likewise Śrutadeva, Jayanta, Vijaya, and Jaya;
as well as Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Puṣpadanta, and Sāttvata.
Viśvaksena, Vainateya, Prabala, and Bala;
Kumuda and Kumudākṣa—these are his eternal attendants. They are divine Vaiṣṇava servants, ever-ready to perform the work of service.
On the left, however, are Dharaṇī, Līlā, Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Kriyā,
Yogā, Saguṇā, Prahvī, Jñānā, Satyeśanī,
Padmā, Jayā, Pāñcālī, Bhārgavī, Lalitā, and Ramā.
Pārvatī, Prabhā, Māṇikyā, Lakṣmī, and Mañjulā;
Ūrjā, Dhaneśvarī, Dīpāvalī, and Premaraseśvarī;
Devā, Devavarā, Bāleśvarī, Ojasvatī, and Śubhā. (65–66)
Kāntā, Śāntā, Caturā, Haṃsā, Amṛtarasā, as well as Mūlikā, Kastūrikā, Sāvitrī, Mauktikeśvarī,
Jayadā, Muktidā, Hemamālā, and the excellent Godāvarī.
Raṃbhā, Jāhnavī, Kāntīśvarī, Lāḍgalikeśvarī,
Nandā, Damayantī, Nirmalā, Ratnapuṣkarā, Maṇīśvarī, Rāliyantī, Campāvatī, and Dayā. (68–69)
Ramā, Jayeśvarī, Pāneśvarī, Savitā, Pramā,
Śānti, and Sukhakarī are the consorts of the Supreme Self;
having taken up the materials for worship, they serve their Lord, the Master.
Five hundred principal groups of divine apsarases, beloved of Hari,
dwell in the inner apartments; they possess the splendor of ten million fires,
and all these Ramas are equal, with faces like the cool-rayed moon.
They serve the Great King, the glorious Nārāyaṇa Hari,
who is that very Supreme Self (Paramātman) established in the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāman),
possessing a divine form and appearing in His own essential nature through His incarnations.
Mahāmāyā praised me, saying, "O Great Lord, accept me!
Then, becoming Nārāyaṇa, I constructed an eternal abode named Mahāvaikuṇṭha at the edge of the Akṣara realm.
Having made his own left-born daughter Mahāmāyā into Mahālakṣmī,
Śrī Hari himself rejoices in the abode of Mahāvaikuṇṭha;
likewise in other incarnations wherever [he appears] with Nārāyaṇa.
Taken along with himself, he indeed brought those *ramā*s into existence;
and they all devoted themselves to their supreme lord, Nārāyaṇa.
He alone was the husband even of those millions of female attendants.
Nārāyaṇa accepts service here in Vaikuṇṭha with devotion;
and other great devotees (mahābhāgavatas), whatever beings they may be, truly dwell here in the palaces of Hari and worship Hari, their Beloved.
Having indeed worshipped Nārāyaṇa with manifold devotion,
those who have gone there do not return; established together with Viṣṇu,
those knowers of the Self eternally attain a bliss equal to his.
For one who follows Nārāyaṇa, liberation alone is the bestower of happiness.
One should constantly remember Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign who grants eternal bliss;
by the mere utterance of His name, one shall attain the supreme state.
Therefore, O Gaurī, one should always pray to the world of Nārāyaṇa.
With unswerving devotion, one should worship the compassionate Lord;
for he, the omniscient one, knowing [the devotee] as his own, protects them in whatever way is necessary.
Having performed that *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, its mantra, its necklace, its rosary,
devotion to Him, and His name, one indeed goes to Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
For the sake of Mahālakṣmī, this Mahāvaikuṇṭha is imperishable.
One of these supreme abodes was created by Hari alone;
the second, Vaikuṇṭha, which is beyond the eternal (dhruva), was created by Viṣṇu, the son of Vairāja, for the purpose of dwelling there with Lakṣmī.
Beyond the fourteen worlds of truth, upon the expanse of Vairāja,
at the edge of the watery veil, lies the second [world], the radiant Vaikuṇṭha.
It exists for the purpose of the gods and others to go there and to offer prayers again and again.

Furthermore, for the sake of attaining union with Him, the third Vaikuṇṭha known as Śvetadvīpa was created, which is easily accessible and provides union with Himself. Beyond even that, there is the realm reached by yogis, which serves as His own bed and bestows supreme peace. (1.126.89–90)
The fourth, Vaikuṇṭha, situated in the midst of the milk ocean in the form of the one reclining upon Śeṣa, was created by Himself for the attainment of peace.
Therein, O Goddess, that which is first described is Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
"Or rather, hear me as I proclaim the second [section], which stands within the enclosure of the waters.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Service Rendered by Mahālakṣmī in Her Various Forms of Ramā Residing in the Great Palace, the Service at the Throne and Those Occupying It, and the Service of Nārāyaṇa, Mahālakṣmī, Their Attendants, and Other Consorts," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, O Great Goddess, Śaṅkara spoke to his beloved Satī concerning that second abode situated at the edge of the watery covering.
That abode of Viṣṇu, the son of Vairāja, is known as Vaikuṇṭha;
it is resplendent like ten million fires and is endowed with all things.
It is beautifully adorned with many fragrant kalpa-trees.
It is endowed with tens of millions of celestial palaces made of excellent gems, jewels, and rubies;
it resembles the great Vaikuṇṭha and is surrounded by five lotus-pools extending for many yojanas.
Following that, the most divine Deva-Gaṅgā flows in a circular course.
Possessing every splendor, radiant with divine milk-water,
it was fashioned from gold, gems, jewels, shells, rubies, and diamonds.
Its descents and its banks shine with rows of forests.
Liberated beings endowed with manifold sovereignty dwell there as lords.
There, divine birds such as Garuḍas, swans, cranes, parrots, peacocks,
and cuckoos possess melodious voices.
The beautiful cātaka, peacock, sārasa crane, sārikā bird, and others,
as well as the golden deer, the great divine lion, and the elephant,
are considered to be of variegated horses possessing great speed that travel through the sky. (8)
There are various kinds of vehicles, forests, and groves;
there dwell beautiful serpents, millions of divine lords,
and Rohita fish as well as golden fish and others.
Indeed, those born of the lineages of tortoises, crocodiles,
and fish are golden-hued, possess backs of jewels, and are capable of assuming any form at will.
They roam through the world of living beings, the worlds of the lords, and the various enclosures.
They possess the strength of Śeṣa and Nārāyaṇa, and are free from pride.
Along the river flows that circular [region],
and situated within it is a forest named Devajayārāma, measuring one yojana in extent.
There, with mangoes, jackfruits, rose-apples, wood-apples, and oranges;
with jujubes, plantains, *puṣpī*, grapes, dates, and *setu* fruits; and with cardamom, betel nuts, cloves, and various excellent trees of nectar-like fruit— (14) —[the place was adorned].
With *kundas*, *aśoka* trees, *sthalapadma*, *jāti*, *kamala*, and *campaka*;
with *ketakas*, *bakulas*, and other fragrant flowering creepers; and with *śāla*, *sarja*, *tāla*, *kadamba*, and *devadāru* trees. (15–16)
The great forest named Devajayodyāna was beautifully adorned with many species of grasses, trees, creepers, lotuses, and crops, including the *pippala*, *udumbara*, *vṛnda*, *khadira*, and *kiṃśuka*.
Therein are monasteries, dwellings, bathing places, and grounds for pleasure;
(18) abodes for health, palatial mansions, and various fields;
and for those dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha, there are delightful gardens and fruit-bearing trees. (19)
Divine and auspicious things indeed prevail there for those whose consciousness is under the control of the Lord.
Within that forest, a great royal road is considered to exist;
it leads toward the Vaiṣṇava city of Devavatī.
There, upon a circular golden couch belonging to Hari, men and women— sixteen years of age and in the full bloom of youth— bow down to Viṣṇu. Indeed,
the grove is circular in shape, and the region as well is circular.
There, extending for ten million yojanas, are indeed regions belonging to Viṣṇu;
there are many various cities of the Vaiṣṇavas,
and those dwellings of the Vaiṣṇavas are filled with every prosperity.
All those Vaiṣṇava women travel through the sky by means of vehicles, mounts, chariots, celestial palaces, Garuḍas, and so forth. Within that [city], there is a seven-storied wall.
It is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent, possessing four gates and eight gate-towers;
it is presided over by the most excellent Vaiṣṇava attendants and Vaiṣṇava women;
it is well-protected by Caṇḍa and other doorkeepers, as well as by Kumuda and others.
It was adorned with rows of divine houses made of various kinds of jewels.
Within that region, however, was the city named Devavatī,
extending fifty-five thousand yojanas in every direction.
It is circular and situated along the perimeter of the wall;
it is filled with millions of palaces rising a hundred yojanas high,
and it is graced by divine men and women who have reached the prime of youth.
Men and women of equal form were the very images of Śrī Viṣṇu;
they wore divine garlands, garments, and fine ornaments, and were anointed with the finest sandalwood paste.
They were the grounds for bathing, eating, reclining, strolling, and amorous play. (1.127.30–31)
Theatres for entertainment, halls for song and instrumental music,
areas for bathing, jesting, and ball games,
grounds for recreation, pleasure groves, gardens, resting places, and gaming saloons.
There are thousands of enclosures there for the sake of dispelling fatigue, featuring elephants, horses, bulls, Garuḍas, swans, and excellent birds; likewise,
there are delightful stables for maidens and other halls for devotion.
There were various kitchens for cooked food and beautiful sleeping quarters;
there were pleasure chambers and palaces delightful with jewels.
All these diverse structures, including the main royal roads and side streets, came into being. (35)
The various groups of gentle abodes become individually enriched with the beautiful splendor of trees and endowed with auspicious jars and banners;
and here, both women and men are graced with all auspicious marks. (36–37)
O Queen of the Gods! There, those Vaiṣṇavas who mutter the mantra of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa rejoice with devotion, delightful joy, and charm;
having entered the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, they rejoice according to their heart's desire.
Having gone there, they do not return, remaining established together with Viṣṇu. At the time of the primal dissolution (prākṛtika-laya), they, along with Viṣṇu, go to Brahman.
Their path is uninterrupted, and their association with Viṣṇu is auspicious.
Those Sātvatas also enjoy happiness equal to that of Viṣṇu;
there, the men and women have four arms and are not inferior to Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī. Wherever the worlds of Hari are, there those people go.
Having gone there, they do not return again; they go to that abode.
Just as Bharata, Śatrughna, Lakṣmaṇa, Śeṣa, and Śarada—all having gone to the world of Viṣṇu—become entirely divine in every way. || 42–43 ||
If they return to the cycle of existence from their own desired world according to their will,
their movement or bondage is certainly not caused by karma;
just as they came, so do they go to that supreme, eternal state.
For the Vaiṣṇavas, there is no birth bound by karma;
indeed, service to Viṣṇu is considered liberation therein.
Since service to Viṣṇu is eternal, there is no other bondage whatsoever.
Freed from all bonds, the mighty servants of Hari worship the Lord, that ocean of compassion, with unswerving devotion;
He, possessing all knowledge and virtues, surely protects His own people. 47.
Having chanted the supreme mantra of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, which consists of bliss,
they attain the highest Vaiṣṇava world, which grants all desires. Indeed, within this circular city of Devavatī— 48–49.
The Vaiṣṇava palace is a magnificent mansion adorned with a hundred peaks;
indeed, it appears in the sky like a great celestial chariot. Therein, the pillars are made of jewels and possess the radiance of a thousand suns.
The walls and pillars consist of divine jewels, and the grounds are celestial;
adorned with golden peaks and the like made of diamonds, gems, and other precious materials, the regions and the moon-chambers shine like the abode of Brahmā. (51–52)
Endowed with all prosperity and possessed of every form and flavor,
men and women there dwell who are less than sixteen years of age;
they are all indeed Vaiṣṇavas, the preeminent attendants of that Lord Hari.
And all the fortunate divine attendants of Hari, who are dear to Him—

there is not even the slightest deficiency in their status, for they possess divine prosperities such as food, drink, worship, objects of enjoyment, and touch, and their wealth is perfectly fulfilled according to their desires. (54–55)
There, in the center of the palace, was a divine and auspicious lion-throne;
its pedestal, made of gold, shone like a celestial flower-chariot.
It rested upon a mandala of an eight-petaled lotus presided over by the primordial power (Ādhāra-śakti).
In that excellent seat of a jeweled lion, rich with tunnels of various colors, the divine and glorious Lord Hari, Nārāyaṇa, was seated;
his radiant splendor was like millions of suns rising at dawn. (57–58)
His limbs were proportioned to his form, and he was as beautiful as ten million gods of desire;
richly adorned with jewels and gold, and decorated with necklaces, garments, and other finery;
he was honored by women devoted with love and served by celestial damsels.
Adored by all the Vaiṣṇavas, the Supreme Person shines resplendent.
On His right side is the Mother of the World, golden-hued,
endowed with all auspicious marks, divine, and twelve years of age.
Adorned with garlands, ornaments, fine garments, and other auspicious substances, she is radiant, her hands holding a lotus, a fan, and a chowrie;
she holds in her hands a vessel of nectar, a vessel of wealth, and a citron.
She always shines and performs service to Nārāyaṇī.
To her left is the goddess Pṛthivī, beloved and lotus-eyed, adorned with ornaments, garments, perfumes, and the like, and graced with all artistic elegance. (63–64)
With his two upper hands held together, he holds two beautiful and auspicious red lotuses;
with his other two hands, he holds a vessel of grain that bestows blessings.
Thus, Hari is attended on both sides by Pṛthvī and Lakṣmī.
There the Lord of Gods shines, his worship performed by Vimalā and the others:
Vimalā, Sumati, Śyāmā, Suśīlā, and likewise Kuśalā;
Dīpāvalī, Jayantī, Ramā, and likewise Bhāgīrathī. (66–67)
Sukhā, Kanakā, Vidyullatā, and Candrakalā—
these hundred thousand women, adorned with every auspicious mark,
served their beloved Hari, who stood in their midst as their lord. (68)
He shone, resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with great armlets and the Kaustubha gem;
with anklets, bracelets, bangles, crowns, and finger-rings; and with the splendor of earrings, chains, and garlands. (1.127.69–70)
The Supreme Lord, served eternally by the thirty gods residing there,
dwells in the city of Vaikuṇṭha within the Vairāja realm, enjoying eternal bliss.
Thus, O Pārvatī, this world of yours is known as Vaikuṇṭha.
The second [Vaikuṇṭha] has been shown; now I shall describe the third—listen!

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Deva-Gaṅgā, the Devajaya Garden, the Royal Road, its Splendor, the Walls, the City of Devavatī, the Vaiṣṇava Temples, the Manifestations, the Vaiṣṇava Devotees, Male and Female Servants, the Jewel Throne, Nārāyaṇa, His Beloved Consort, and Others," in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 127.
← Chapter 127: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 128 [Author: Chapter 129 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Then the god Śaṅkara, the husband of Pārvatī, spoke to his wife concerning the third, most excellent manifestation (vyūha).
This third Vaikuṇṭha is called Śvetadvīpa;
it is the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, the ground of Śvetadvīpa, for the purpose of being seen by the great-souled lords of yogis such as Sanaka and others. (2)
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
Sanatkumāra as the fourth, as well as Sanatsujāta,
Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha— these were the mind-born sons of Brahmā.
There dwell the eight Ṛbhus, beings of pure essence and great majesty,
who experience the singular flavor of bliss arising from the vision of the Blessed One;
and other sages as well, such as Tanu and the rest, truly reside there.
And Nara and Nārāyaṇa dwell upon Śvetadvīpa.
The ascetics residing there are indeed liberated and abstain from food;
some subsist on fruits, while others subsist on air alone.
Some subsist on roots and water, while others subsist on vapors; some take smoke as their food, and others consume the rays of the sun;
some drink the rays of the moon, and others are entirely devoid of any intake of food or drink.
Some wear garments made of śāla bark, while others dwell naked;
some wear the *puṇḍra* mark on their necks, and they all bear mantras and mudrās.
They all worship Nārāyaṇa Hari and perform austerities.
Detached from all enjoyments and free from passion and hatred,
subsisting on food offered with devotion, performing their duties with devotion, and taking refuge in the true company of Kṛṣṇa—
both men and women likewise destroy their own inauspiciousness through austerity.
All are meritorious and most meritorious, white and renowned for their white deeds;
they are sattvic, free from anger, desire, and the like, and partakers of liberation.
Indeed, those infinite Vaiṣṇava people dwell there for the sake of austerity.
For the sake of appearing before them, Hari remains present in Śvetadvīpa—
a beautiful place resembling ten million moons, adorned with various excellent jewels and gems,
auspicious, and frequented by great yogis.
Nārāyaṇa himself dwells there for the sake of being seen by yogins. There are delightful gardens, vast forest lands,
palaces like Mount Raivata, and rivers equal to the celestial Ganges.

And those grounds are considered to be filled with *pārijāta*, *āmraka*, *kalpadru*, and *kalpavallī* trees, as well as fruits, flowers, tubers, and leaves. Among the fourteen classes of beings, there are the *ṛṣis* and likewise the *munis*.
Other virtuous women and virtuous men come and go for the sake of being seen.
There are many *sāntānika* creepers and many sandalwood trees;
likewise, there are lotuses in full bloom in the lakes, as well as land-lotuses and the like.

The *kundabakula*, *śṛṅgāra*, *mālatī*, *mallikā*, and others; the *tṛṇarāja*, *nāgaranga*, *nārikela* fruit, and others; the *pūgī*, *lavaṅga*, *jāvaṃtrī*, *jīvaphala*, forests, and so forth. (1.128.20)
There are jujube trees, plantains, rose-apples, karmadās, amṛtas, and citrons;
throughout the forests there are various reservoirs of water,
as well as wells, oblong ponds, and cool mountain cascades.

There are indeed hot springs, sweet wells, and excellent medicinal herbs for sustenance throughout the center of the island and at its very edges. Here and there, hermitages belonging to liberated ascetics are found everywhere.
And there dwell the Sātvata sages together with their families;
they subsist on forest produce and are devoted to the practice of vision [of the deity].
Divine, moon-like, beautiful, gentle, and of radiant form, they shine brightly. (24–25)
They dwell in the White Abode; there is a beautiful city there to be known as Airāvatī, crowded with many palaces,
filled with divine men and women, and adorned with jeweled celestial chariots.
There indeed dwell devotees—men and women together with their families. All prosperities here arise from mere thought;
there are celestial chariots, pleasure gardens, couches, and riches.

Indeed, various things exist here on earth that are obtained through the power of asceticism by means of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*); for they appear just as one might encounter them by chance.
In Vaikuṇṭha, however, there is nothing at all inferior in terms of prosperity or splendors.
Even the sages dwelling in Satyaloka on Airāvatī,
the deities residing in heaven who inhabit Maharloka and the other realms,
as well as other ṛṣis on earth and those in sacred regions such as Meru— [all came there].
For those Daityas who went to Pātāla and were considered to have been devoted in soul,
there are indeed numerous palaces for their residence;
they are as high as the rising sun, circular, and exist by the millions.

There are tens of millions of celestial chariots, ocean-going vessels, and watercraft; hundreds of thousands of vehicles for traveling beneath the sea and vehicles for traversing the paths [of the sky];
and there are also tens of millions of vehicles for mountains and forests. (33–34)
The royal highways, broad and expansive, with excellent elephants and horses as their mounts, are always divine, most beautiful, and sprinkled with ichor.
In the very center of such a city, there is indeed a great pavilion.
It was fashioned from jewels and gold, resembling a celestial garden;
it was perfumed with the fragrances of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron,
and was beautifully adorned with various flowered archways and canopies.
It was the dwelling place of divine apsarases, adorned with the singing of the Sāmaveda; it resounded with the sounds of dancing, song, assemblies, festivals, and cries of victory;
and its grounds were prepared with thousands of naturally delightful pleasure-halls.
It possesses an excellent ground for the purpose of worshiping through the ninefold devotion and good deeds;
it has many locations for the requisites of the worship of Nārāyaṇa, and it is a house prepared for drinking, eating, massaging, and anointing. (1.128.39–40)
Having constructed another house for the purpose of accepting the service of the Vaiṣṇavas,
he was in no way inferior to Vaikuṇṭha in terms of material objects;
indeed, even the celestial chariots of the gods come and go by means of the wind [before him].
Crowded with hosts of gods, the king of kings shone resplendently.
There, in the center, was a lion-throne prepared for Nārāyaṇa;
it possessed the brilliance of ten million suns, and in its center was a lotus with the luster of the moon.
There, amidst soft *gaddīkas*, cotton, and other such soft materials,
Hari himself shines resplendent upon a golden-colored, tender couch.
Golden-hued and adorned with necklaces of gold, gems, and pearls, he is radiant there.
His hands are radiant, joined with the weapons of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
he is beautifully adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings;
and he shines with a pair of lotus-feet resplendent with gold. (45–46)
He was resplendent with very small nails as white as the full moon; he possessed a most beautiful appearance, endowed with the beauty of youth and a form like that of a sixteen-year-old;
he bore an upright *puṇḍra* mark, which was beautified by a fragrant *candra* in its center.
He is resplendent with beautiful, curling hair that moves within his glossy braid;
he is wrapped in fine garments possessing the luster of milk-foam and the moon; and his ears are adorned with earrings set with pearls, gems, diamonds, and other jewels. 48–49.
Having assumed the auspicious lotus posture, he sits resplendent.
On the left lap of that Lord Nārāyaṇa is Lakṣmī, possessing a divine form;
twelve years of age, she is exactly like him in beauty.
She shines, beautiful with the ornaments appropriate for all happiness;
her form is like the filaments of a lotus, endowed with the vigor of youth, possessed of all auspicious marks, and the refuge of a multitude of virtues and moral conduct. (51–52)
Clad in garments of gold and silver, adorned with fragrant necklaces,
her hair was decorated with land-lotuses, *mālatī* flowers, and excellent blossoms;
she shone with four arms, graced by armlets and bracelets.
Adorned with pearl necklaces and wearing crests fashioned from mandāra flowers; possessing a prominent nose and jasmine-like teeth, her ears were graced by shimmering earrings;
she bore a tilaka mark made of musk and wore fine pearls upon her nose.
Her well-formed breasts were like delicate golden jars;
her body possessed a divine fragrance; she was adorned with flower garlands and the like; she was beautiful, holding lotus flowers and other blossoms, and captivating to the mind. (56)
Holding in her hands a mirror, a citron, a golden lotus, a conch, and other objects,
she who fulfills the heart's desires of her husband Nārāyaṇa shines eternally as the beloved of Śrī Hari, occupying half of his left lap.
Likewise, other Śaktis similar to her and suitable for Kṛṣṇa shine forth in service,
being solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
These include the Great Goddess Īśānā, Jāhnavī, Kamalā, and Ramā.
Sāvitrī, Śāntā, Kāntā, Brāhmī, and Sarojinī were there, as well as the handmaidens Prajñā, Medhā, Dhṛti, Kṣamā,
Śraddhā, Dhāraṇā, Śānti, Śruti, Manīṣiṇī, and Smṛti. (1.128.60–61)
Vṛṣṭi, Vṛddhi, Mati, and the forest-born Śris who perform service—beyond these, indeed, Nārāyaṇa has millions of other wives.
Furthermore, Ananta, Vainateya, Haṃsa, Karī, and the excellent Vaiṣṇavas [are his attendants]. 62.
There are infinite servants devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
The Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, the Viśvedevas, the Kinnaras,
the Vidyādharas, and the Gandharvas are likewise devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Male and female servants dwell here in this abode of Śvetadvīpa—
in palaces, celestial chariots, houses, and cities;
in forests and groves, as well as in domestic gardens and the sky.
In the walls, in the groves, on the banks, and at the river-sides,
they sport, ever enriched with bliss and devoid of useless things to be abandoned;
they are delighted by divine enjoyments obtained through the grace of Nārāyaṇa.

Those who mutter the mantras of Viṣṇu, who are intent on the remembrance of Viṣṇu, who observe the day of Hari, and who are equal to Nārāyaṇa in form, qualities, appearance, age, and feet— they go to that imperishable state. 68.
The eternal realm of Viṣṇu is attainable through exclusive devotion alone.

Chanting the praises of Hari, reciting His names, meditating upon Him, the muttering of His mantra, offering libations, and performing fire-oblations dedicated to Viṣṇu bestow the station of Viṣṇu. (1.128.70)
The men and women there, seeking happiness dependent upon the bliss of devotion to Viṣṇu,
go at the end of their lives to Mahāvaikuṇṭha.

Thus ends the section on the splendor of the sages, munis, ascetics, jewel-like men and women, gardens, the city of Airāvatī, the pavilions, the throne, and Lakṣmī’s attendants in the first book, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, concerning the third Vaikuṇṭha known as Śvetadvīpa.

[Author: Chapter 130.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O beloved! Then Śambhu spoke auspicious words to Pārvatī.
The fourth realm is indeed Vaikuṇṭha, situated within the Ocean of Milk.
For the protection of the inhabitants of heaven, the Supreme Lord,
the God eternally devoted to peace, remains in the Milky Ocean through a sleep known as yoga.
Hari himself, blue as a lotus, established in his own self,
dwells within the innermost chamber fashioned for his divine residence in the vast Vaikuṇṭha, which is resplendent with the manifestations of the Fish and the Tortoise incarnations. (5)
On the surface of the earth within the ocean of milk, by the splendor of Nārāyaṇa,
the expanse of the milky sea was solidified by the Sudarśana discus;
here, lands were produced with ground as white as milk.
There were four walls made of cooked milk,
and a divine canopy and pavement fashioned likewise from milk.
The walls, gate-towers, palaces, mansions, and rows of groves were all composed of the same substance.
Highways, bypaths, and roads; trees, creepers, and forests;
(7) jewels, ornaments, garments, and foods; drinks, beds, vehicles, and mounts (8).
By the will of Nārāyaṇa, all products derived from milk—
lamps, jewels, fruits born of milk,
as well as flower garlands, sandalwood, and whatever fragrant substances there may be— [were produced]. (9)
Substances for good fortune such as collyrium and others were indeed produced from milk.
A pavilion, one hundred thousand yojanas in extent,
was constructed of milk and fashioned from milk-crystal, rubies, gems, jewels, and the like.
White like the splendor of Brahman, divine like the manifestation of Brahman,
it bestows happiness and peace like the Great Vaikuṇṭha, and like the world of Brahmā.
Therein are many colorful palaces for the residence of the devotees.
By the will of Śrī Hari, divine and magnificent prosperities come into being.
(13) There is no means of enjoyment or instrument lacking here;
in the midst of that stands the thousand-faced Ananta Śeṣa. (14)
White, soft, glossy, and warm, he held authority over the bed;
there, for the sake of Hari, he made his bed with the coils of his body.
And for the sake of Hari, he formed a canopy with his thousand hoods.
For the sake of Lord Hari, he has fashioned a staircase there with his tail;
for the sake of Lord Hari, he has provided lamps there with the jewels upon his hoods.
Upon that couch of Ananta, the Lord of Kamalā lies.
Hari is a fresh youth, dark-complexioned, and clad in yellow garments;
his head is adorned with a crown and hair, and he is resplendent with necklaces and the Kaustubha gem.
He possesses the sacred thread, sectarian marks (puṇḍra), the lotus, water, the earth, the discus, and weapons.

He is accompanied by Gadā and Garuḍa, and is resplendent with a forest garland (vanamālā). His feet are massaged by Lakṣmī; he is adorned with bracelets and armlets, and his palms and soles of the feet are beautified like shimmering red lotuses.
Adorned with ornaments such as a girdle, sandals, finger-rings, and chains;
equipped with a sword, shield, bow, spear, iron arrows, and a mace;
and honored with the finest sandalwood paste, saffron, and musk.
He possesses the flowers of the *kalpavṛkṣa*, *mandāra*, *bakula*, *pārijāta*, and other celestial trees;
he is adorned with a well-proportioned, elevated nose, shoulders, knees, and forehead;
he possesses the beauty of feet, nails, and anklets held by a network of tinkling bells.
His lips were as red as *aśoka* flowers, his face resembled the full moon, and he was enchanting with a smile that shone with teeth like pearls;
having reached the fullness of youth, he is the refuge for those seeking shelter. (24)
He always lies down as if exhausted, as if at the end of a rest;
having engaged in great battles with the Daityas, he sleeps again and again.
His splendor is indeed equal [to his enemies] in terms of beauty, character, virtues, and other qualities.
Possessing a beautiful form resembling gold and adorned with ornaments of refined gold,
she always remains there on the couch in attendance upon him.
That large-eyed, fawn-eyed young woman has a slender waist.
Endowed with beauty, grace, sweetness, splendor, and the virtue of moral conduct;
adorned at night by a bodice and a garment with the luster of milk-foam;
her hair decorated with mandāra, ketakī, and jasmine flowers. (28–29)

Her hair was fragrant with oil, fashioned into a flattened crest and braided into a topknot; she bore a tilaka mark made of musk and was beautifully adorned with strings of jewels. (1.129.30) She was further embellished by ear-ornaments rich with various pearls and gems.
She possesses lips with the radiant redness of a ripe bimba fruit or coral;
she is adorned with long, dark, and glossy hair falling to her waist;
and she has slightly elevated, firm, and full cheeks, hips, and breasts.
With her slightly raised, radiant, and soft cheeks that delight the world,
she shines with four arms, flowing like a river of love;
with her two upraised arms, she holds a pair of auspicious golden lotuses.
Sometimes she stands embracing her husband with love;
the goddess Lakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, remains constantly engaged in his service.
Likewise, there are others of equal beauty, such as Narmadā and Tapatī.
The Tuṅgabhadrā and the Kāverī, the Gaṅgā and the Godāvarī, as well as the Sindhu, the Phalgu, the Gaṇḍakī, the Tāmraparṇī, and the Sarasvatī;
the Karatoyā, the Karmanāśā, the Sābhramatī, and the Gomatī.
The Ojasvatī, the Bhadrāvatī, the Sarayū, and the Svarṇarakṣikā;
Indradyumna, Puṣkara, Nārāyaṇasara, and Aśvapaṭṭasara, as well as whatever other lakes there may be. ||37-38||
The Mānasa lake, Rāmasaras, Kṛṣṇasara, Matsyasara, as well as the Śoṇa, Brahmaputra, and Gargara;
likewise rivers, streams, lakes, and oceans.
Krauñca, Maināka, Himādri, Vindhya, Mandara, and Raivata—these mountains; the goddess Earth; Varuṇa and other Vaiṣṇavas;
Mārkaṇḍeya, Bali, Bāṇa, Aśvatthāman, Hanumān, and Varāha.
Nimi, Bibhīṣaṇa, Paraśurāma, Vyāsa, Manu,
as well as Satyavrata, Nanda, Gaya, and Tala—

Being praised by Garuḍa, the Lord of Gods,

Thus, O Goddess Pārvatī, everything has been explained to you.
When the functions of the senses become dulled,
at that very moment Vaikuṇṭha is to be realized by one who desires liberation.
"You are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and you are devoted to Puruṣottama;
thus you know the manifold majesty of the divine manifestations (vyūhas).
O Queen of Gods! I worship that Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Hari.

I have declared to you for the sake of liberation the practice of taking refuge, together with its mantras, its mudrās, its sacred necklaces, and its vertical sectarian marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra). Liberation does not come through knowledge, meditation, austerity, yoga, sacrifice, renunciation, chanting,
or hearing [the scriptures] as it does through offering [everything] to Me;
O My beloved, accept self-surrender in that same way.
By that [initiation], liberation shall become certain for her through the grace of Brahmā, Śrī, and Hari.
Thus Śambhu bestowed the Vaiṣṇava initiation upon his own wife;
from that time forth, she indeed constantly [worshipped] Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed worship and having made an offering, they partake of food and water;
thus those two devotees of Viṣṇu, Pārvatī and Parameśvara,
are solely intent upon my propitiation and have dedicated their very selves for my sake.
"They are my very own attendants and disciples, identical with me, and dear to me.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"If those two divine Vaiṣṇavas have indeed surrendered their very selves to you,"
"How is it that Śaṅkara wears the triple mark of ashes and rudrākṣa beads?
This doubt has arisen within me; O Truthful One, dispel it!
One who knows [the truth] would not abandon his status as Viṣṇu; there must be some other reason."
Having heard this, Hari spoke to Lakṣmī regarding that narrative:
"Why does Śaṅkara wear the Tripuṇḍra made of ashes and other such external marks?

Thus ends [the section] in the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the divine enjoyment in the pavilion of the fourth Vaikuṇṭha on the couch remaining from the bed of the Milk Ocean, where Lakṣmī resides.
Chapter One Hundred and Twenty-Nine: Showing Doubts Regarding the Wearing of the Tripuṇḍra and Ashes by Long-Living Vaiṣṇavas, Śambhus, and Others, as Well as by Devotees of Viṣṇu and Others.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Exactly as you have asked me, so shall I speak.

Then Śambhu spoke to the Goddess a delightful ancient tale;
listen to that, which has its own cause and which deludes the Asuras.

out of affection for me, explain it, for a great doubt exists within me.
The wearing of skulls, ashes, skins, and bones is highly censured."
"O Śambhu, for what reason do you maintain that which is censurable?

Thus questioned by the Goddess in secret, away from people,
Hara spoke that which was most secret— whatever he himself had practiced.
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme mystery, more secret than the secret."
"O lady of virtuous vows, because the body is not separate [from the self], I shall speak to you.
You must never, under any circumstances, speak of this to others or among people.

When those gods, led by Indra, were afflicted and broken by them— who possessed great armies, great heroism, and great majesty—
they approached Viṣṇu and requested his protection.

"O Keśava, you alone are worthy to conquer these great Daityas, who are invincible, most heroic, and whose sins have been washed away by austerity. Having heard this, Hari perceived that fear had come upon those gods.

"O mighty-armed Rudra, for the purpose of deluding the enemies of the gods,
perform some heretical practice— a dharma that causes confusion."
By whichever path the Daityas have gone, may they become weak and fallen;
may they be utterly deprived of strength and luster,
so that they are fallen from their own duties, like those who are dead.

O gods, having achieved victory, may you be happy and free from all thorns. Compose a Dharma that is the foremost of heresies, consisting of books fabricated by heretics—books that delude the Daityas and are preeminent among those hostile to Viṣṇu. (15)
Even though these signs are impure,
fashion them in such a way that all of them may appear very beautiful to those of a tamasic nature,
through your instruction, through that scripture, and through the conduct you have fashioned.
Those who are dominated by tamas will indeed perish by their very nature.
I, Viṣṇu, and likewise the gods [have come] for the purpose of instilling confidence in the Daityas.
And all that was done by you has been so for a short time, merely outwardly.

"Having gained confidence through him, we shall encourage [the Daityas] to accept all that he has devised—that heresy which is the cause of sin. Then, with the conviction that it is truth, they will embrace it, and from that our victory shall come. (1.130.20)
Thus, in order to receive his command, he then spoke to Śambhu: "O Lord, if I were to do on earth this which has been spoken by you, O God,

Constantly remembering me in your heart, chant the mantra dedicated to me:
"Oṃ haraye namaḥ. Practice this mantra as the Supreme Brahman.

Whether it be desire, anger, greed, deception, hypocrisy, cruelty, or even what is inauspicious or harmful—if it is spoken by me, that is indeed dharma. (28–29)
That which has been spoken by me is indeed said to be the Veda itself.
Whether manifest or hidden, that which is spoken by me is the Veda alone. When I command, "Do this," then Dharma consists of that very act.
"When I restrain you, then let there be no dharma;
[let] dharma be my command, and its opposite the lack of command.
Do it, O Śambhu! What has been done by you, I shall worship in age after age."
Therefore, the Daityas and those of the nature of darkness (tāmasa) will worship what has been performed by them.
Just as I am, so indeed are you—the Lord who is forever free from decay.
Swiftly perform what is beneficial; I shall destroy your obstacles.
"O Śambhu, you shall have no devotion to any deity other than me.

Having thus instructed me, O Goddess, she dismissed the hosts of Maruts.
Thereupon, I too reflected: "To what extent must I fashion this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), so that the Daityas may be deluded and rendered powerless by my foot? (36)
Then, for the sake of the welfare of the gods and for the purpose of destroying the Daityas,
I indeed undertook the wearing of skulls, skins, ashes, and bones;
I indeed undertook the wearing of the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra) and rudrākṣa beads.

I ward off all those things from the outside, but not from within. O Queen of Gods! Having entered within, [I ward off] the garland around the neck of Tulasī, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), as well as the Vaiṣṇava hand-gestures (mudrās) and all other marks in every way.
I maintain these [teachings] in secret so that the Daityas do not know them.
By the command of Nārāyaṇa Hari, my eternal duty is indeed to present them as mixed with heresy for the purpose of deceiving the Daityas.
He composed the *tāmasa* Tantras of the Śaivas and Pāśupatas. Having relied upon these very works of mine and having observed me,
all those *tāmasa* Daityas become averse to the Blessed One.
Having smeared themselves with ashes and the like, they worshiped me alone with meat, blood, sandalwood, and other offerings; being shrouded by a great and most terrible darkness,
they had fallen away from all dharma and were possessed by desire and anger.
Having received boons from Me, those who dwell in the realm of sense-objects,
being devoid of goodness and lacking in vigor, gradually go to a low state.
Those who, being dominated by darkness (*tāmasa*), accept My doctrine of smearing ashes and so forth on their bodies—
Indeed, those who are devoid of all dharmas behold hell.
All the Daityas are characterized by tamas, as are others who hold that same view;
always defeated by the gods, the Daityas perish in every way.
"Thus, O Goddess, my conduct for the sake of the gods' welfare has been censured.
Having placed the command of Viṣṇu before me, I have undertaken the wearing of ashes and bones.
This external mark, O Goddess, is intended to delude my enemies."
I shall always meditate upon Nārāyaṇa Hari within my very heart; and while chanting His name— the source of eternal bliss and virtue—
I indeed enjoy supreme happiness with you, for that is Brahman.
Then those devotees who are established in non-existence (asattva) offer ashes and other such things to me;
those who are tamasic know that ashes and the like are dear to Śambhu.
Such people likewise consider me to be a tamasic deity.
They offer me things that are *tāmasa*, such as hemp and ganja, which are *tāmasa*.
But I, O Goddess, am a Vaiṣṇava; I do not accept what has not been offered.
Therefore, I accept only that which is meritorious and offered to Viṣṇu, and nothing else.
Do not fall into delusion, O Goddess! Do not grasp that which is characterized by darkness (tamas).
Worship that which is characterized by goodness (sattva), O Goddess, for you are in every way a Vaiṣṇavī.
Indeed, nothing is ever taken by me without first being offered to Nārāyaṇa.
However, I have made a vow before Hari with devotion:
"Whatever object is to be enjoyed by the master must not be enjoyed by the servant.
Adhering to this principle, one does not eat without first offering it.
If one consumes substances such as dhattūra or saffron that are to be enjoyed by the Lord, it is done by His command; thus, there is no fault in the offering of oneself.
Indeed, the wearing of ashes, bones, and so forth, which are bodily impurities and inauspicious, [is likewise permitted].
That purification is also auspicious through the chanting of its name by his command.
Thus, O Great Goddess, I have fully explained to you the wearing of the *tāmasa-aṅka* and other marks, along with their reasons; having understood this, you shall not be deluded in this matter.
That which involves impurity, violence, killing, eradication, and so forth,
as well as mantras and worship characterized by darkness— that is indeed *tāmasa*.
O Great Goddess, that should never be accepted by those seeking liberation.
"Because it ends in destruction, bestows suffering, and is entirely characterized by darkness (tāmasa).
Thus [ends the section] in the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*,

Chapter 131 [Author:
Chapter 132 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"No one here in this world is truly able to know the reality of the incarnations and the glories of Śrī Hari in every respect.
(1) Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Indeed, who were the Daityas, by whose power did they flourish,
and for what reason were they created and then slain by Viṣṇu?
[Tell me] this story related to Viṣṇu, which is purifying and destructive of sin.
"I wish to hear of the incarnations of Śrī Viṣṇu, the Supreme Soul.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the eternal form of the Fish."
In the first act of creation, Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, created the lords of progeny:
Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, Dakṣa, and Kardama;
as well as Pulastya, Pulaha, Aṅgiras, and Kratu. (4–5)
There, the Blessed Marīci begot Kaśyapa;
and from Kaśyapa were born four wives of different species:
Aditi, Diti, Kadrū, and Vinatā.
May all the sons of Diti, the gods of auspicious appearance, indeed prosper.
The sons of Diti are the Daityas, who are characterized by darkness (tamas) and are asuras and rākṣasas.
Once, while seated with her husband during the summer heat, Diti [fell asleep].
Having ascended the excellent celestial chariot, she arrived at the shore of the ocean;
there, together with Kaśyapa, she sat down upon the surface of the earth.
Due to the contact with the cool breeze mingled with the waters of the ocean, [she felt refreshed].
Afflicted by the force of desire, the goddess longed for her husband as her own lord.
She served her husband with such acts as massaging his feet, on that shore endowed with very soft sands and adorned with the sight of trees, creepers, and other plants.
On that pleasant bank, cooled by breezes moistened with drops of cold water,
she, overwhelmed with passion, performs service for her husband. Whenever she bestows the manifold bliss of love upon her lord, || 1-2 ||
Just before sunset,
the aquatic creatures— crocodiles, water-horses, tortoises, and water-men—
go to the shore and sit there for the sake of air and to escape the heat. (12–14)
Due to the conjunction with the evening sun, they shone like gold upon the sandy bank there,
amidst crocodiles and water-fowls.
At that time, during the era of Kaśyapa’s disciples, a quarrel accompanied by physical conflict broke out.
The aspect of Diti and Kaśyapa was upon Makara and Ghoṭaka.
At that very time, the impregnation also took place successfully on land.
Whatever the aspect at the time of impregnation may be, such will be the intellect. (16–17)
Such a fetus is born, possessing such formative impressions (*saṃskāra*);
by that [cause], the body becomes like a crocodile and the head likewise like a horse.
Having attained those formative impressions within the womb, he indeed remained there as a child.
The couple, having ascended their own celestial chariot, returned toward their home;
remembering that crocodile,
the aquatic creature, they saw it enter the water as soon as it beheld the chariot.
At the proper time, Diti gave birth to an embryo permeated by that [divine] nature;
it had the form of a crocodile in its body, but was like a horse in its head.
This Makara-Hayagrīva was then consecrated with the sacred rites by Kaśyapa.
Although he was a dweller on land, he indeed became especially a dweller in the water.
Initiated by Kaśyapa and sent by his mother to receive alms, the boy,
capable of assuming any form at will, went forth with the desire to study the Vedas.
Assuming the form of a brahmin, he went to the Grandfather (Brahmā);
having prostrated and presented an offering of oceanic jewels, he,
assuming the guise of a brahmin, deceitfully requested the knowledge of the Vedas.
Brahmā questioned his parents regarding [the boy's name] starting from the naming ceremony (*nāma-saṃskāra*).
He said to his great-grandfather, "I am the descendant of Kaśyapa.
Brahmā also [inquired] concerning his own son, the son of Marīci.
Then he gave the Vedas to the son of Kaśyapa as his great-grandson;
having taken the Vedas, Hayagrīva went to the house of Kaśyapa.
Father Kaśyapa was indeed very pleased with his learned son.
Having observed this, he said, "Son, you must indeed teach others.
Then Hayagrīva replied, "O Father, I shall not teach;
the knowledge of the Vedas must by no means be given to anyone at all."
The gods, nourished by the Vedas, repeatedly oppose the asuras.
However, the Vedas must never be destroyed; they are indeed never to be fostered [in this manner].
Through the Vedas, sacrifices proceed, as do the rituals of dharma.
O Father, since sacrifices and religious rites are false,
and because I have repeatedly observed injunctions and prohibitions in the Veda— which always bring about restraint— such restraint does not please me. (3.1–3.2)
All food, as well as drink, intoxicants, and objects of enjoyment may be used according to one's desire.
For us who are powerful, there shall be neither injunction nor prohibition.
Therefore, I will not cause others to recite [the scriptures], nor will I conduct myself according to ritual rules.
I shall destroy the knowledge of the Vedas and utterly ruin the reciters;
I shall afflict the people devoted to the Vedas and slay those established in the sacrifices.
I shall perform the ritual sections [of the Veda] and shall not proceed otherwise than that.
Having heard his son speaking thus, Kaśyapa grieved for that demonic nature which rendered him unfit for his own abode—
a nihilist, a destroyer of knowledge, and a ruin of Vedic learning.
Considering him to be a thief of the Vedas, resembling a mere beast, an adversary to the nourishment of the gods,
a fever of envy that bestows no future happiness, a destroyer of all possessions, and an unworthy recipient of asceticism and learning, Kaśyapa [reflected]. (37–38)
He had Diti cast out from his house after taking leave of her in every way;
that Daitya Hayaśiras, moreover, having assumed the form of a crocodile,
dwelt indeed in the great ocean, devouring those who lived in the water.
Having gone again and again to the sacrificial sites in the mountain regions,
he indeed destroyed the sacrifices, the Brahmins, and the dharmas repeatedly.
In the assembly of Brahmins, he devoured those who dwell upon the earth.
Assuming a divine and beautiful form, he went to heaven;
he swiftly seized the wives, children, and homes of the gods.
Having destroyed the dwellings of the sages as well, he committed acts of torment against them.
Then the celestial sages went and petitioned Brahmā for its destruction.
Brahmā remembered Hari, the Lord of Gods, the destroyer of the Daityas,
who was reclining upon Śeṣa in a pavilion made of excellent jewels within the Ocean of Milk.
Then Nārāyaṇa, leaving Lakṣmī behind and grasping his discus,
took up his mace, sword, and spear,
and came forth for battle to where Brahmā was stationed on the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
There, Viṣṇu himself, assuming a form for battle, saw the unborn Brahmā.
Seated upon Garuḍa, the Lord said to Prajāpati: "O Brahman, how indeed have you been reminded? Speak quickly; I shall do it."
Brahmā said: Salutations to you, O Acyuta, who are composed of the Vedas and the gods!
You are the one who rides upon Garuḍa, the upholder, and the author of creation, preservation, and destruction. You alone assume a form for the sake of protecting the world.
For you alone are the protector of the Brahmins, the Vedas, sacrifices, cows, the earth, and dharma.
O Supreme Person, you alone are the refuge of all dharmas;
you alone are the sacrifice, you are knowledge, and the Vedas have their origin in you.
The entire world has you as its support; the great seers depend upon you;
we all, following the path of prohibitions and injunctions, depend upon you. By your command alone shall we guide people everywhere.
Relying upon this very path, you abide as the Supreme Person.
Impelled by you alone, the worlds proceed in their right and wrong deeds.
The boundary established by you must be protected, for it is certain that "dharma is ours."
"Having studied the Vedas from his guru, he should then teach them to children;
he should establish the duties rooted therein—this is the eternal command of the Supreme Lord.
Having transgressed that boundary, the Asura Mākara, the son of Kaśyapa,"
That horse-faced one, who brings suffering to the gods, indeed acts according to his own will.
O Daitya, having carried away the Vedas, he has entered the great ocean;
for this entire world has the Vedas as its foundation, and the refinement of dharma is achieved through the Vedas.
From the performance of rites shown by the Vedas, all satisfaction is produced.
Therefore, having struck down that Asura, the nihilist who destroys the sacred law, you alone, O Keśava, ought to bring back the Vedas! (57)
Thus addressed by Brahmā, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Supreme Lord, said:
"O Brahmin, bring about peace; let Garuḍa remain here.
I shall go to the ocean, assuming a form suitable for the water."
Having bowed to the sages, Nārāyaṇa himself became a fish;
indeed, he was an unprecedented being with a sharp snout, a devourer of great timiṅgilas.
In an instant, his body became as vast as the Himālaya mountains.
Devouring sea-monsters that resembled mountain peaks, he entered the waters.
By him the ocean was agitated and the earth trembled repeatedly;
then clouds fell from the sky and the planets were thrown into turmoil.

The gods and great sages, having arrived there, praised Hari. Nārāyaṇa, having entered the depths of the ocean on all sides and searched for the great Daitya, seized him by the throat after mounting upon him.
Then that great illusory asura, indeed becoming invisible, assumed the form of a fisherman equipped with a mace and a net;
having become like the Himalayas, he desired to seize the fish. (64–65)
Nārāyaṇa, too, assuming a fierce form resembling the fire of the great dissolution (mahākālānala),
struck the fisherman with his mace.
At that moment, he abandoned the form of the fisherman and became a massive mountain.
His head, feet, and so forth could not be found anywhere.
Having made his back as hard as a diamond, he fell asleep resting upon the surface of the earth.
Then, by Nārāyaṇa, a spear was indeed hurled with great force. (67–68)
Having reached the further shore and shattered that back which was like a diamond,
the Daitya then assumed another form— that of a fish— and stood in another place,
thinking: "He will not kill me, for he considers this creation to be born of his own kind."
Or rather, I shall deceive him and then kill him. Having deceived Hari there, he was struck again with the tail;
he fled into the midst of the water to enter the mud.

Having mounted that seat, the Lord Hari seized him again by the throat; tearing him open with the tip of his beak, he struck him. Then, from within his heart, [he extracted] all the Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs, as well as his own self.
Having completely withdrawn those whose forms were knowledge and concealed them by all means,
she brought them forth from the ocean by means of her power and meditative absorption;
then, casting the demonic self into the darkness of ignorance, she emerged.
Having cast [the world] into the realm of Yama, Hari arrived at the shore of the ocean;
and beholding that fish-form, which resembled the snowy mountain,
the gods, sages, and seers stood there transfixed by wonder.
Having displayed that form for a moment, he became a tiny fish.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa, of auspicious appearance and the destroyer of the waters, assumed a human form; praised by all, he possessed a gentle countenance.
The omnipresent Lord gave all the Vedas to that Brahmā, the Parameṣṭhin;
indeed, the All-pervading One offered all knowledge consisting of the Vedas unto Brahmā. Having offered all benedictions and accepted the worship performed by him, [he departed].
Mounting his Garuḍa vehicle, he vanished into the ocean of milk.
(79) Thus, O Lakṣmī, the account of the first Dvāpara age of the Fish incarnation has been told; now hear the second, the Mātsya [incarnation]. (1.131.80)
