Chapter 133 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Mahālakṣmī! Whenever it becomes evening for the Creator (Brahmā), at that very time,
during the eternal dissolution, the ten worlds beginning with Svarga and ending with Pātāla go to their dissolution,
just as they were in the previous creation.
In that very manner, at the time of dissolution, for the sake of preserving the seed,
Hari indeed assumes the form of a fish that moves within the waters.
First, there shall be a drought lasting a hundred years of Brahmā’s evening.
Due to the absence of rain and because of severe famine, embodied beings go to their destruction;
all water dries up, and plants go to their destruction.
By the heat of the sun, the earth becomes parched in every way.
Then, the seeds will gradually become parched;
the tubers and roots will perish, and the multitude of living beings will likewise perish.
For a hundred years, the land will be scorched by heat, devoid of rain, as time passes.
Consequently, the oceans indeed dry up on all sides;
then, the entire multitude of living beings dwelling therein perishes in every way.
Furthermore, twelve scorching and fierce suns heat everything completely.
Thus, at the end of these hundred years, this earth, together with its seven mountain ranges,
is entirely consumed by fire and reduced to ashes on all sides;
from the netherworld (pātāla) up to heaven (svarga), all living beings have perished.
Then, accompanied by their subtle bodies, they go to Maharloka;
and there in Maharloka, they all remain, sustained by rays of merit.
Then, clouds rain down continuously for a hundred years.
Up to the tenth world (bhuvana), everything shall become composed of water. Indeed, from the heavens down to that point, the waters swell greatly during the dissolution;
thus it continues from the evening until the morning.
This destruction of the ten worlds is called the daily dissolution (nityapralaya).
Again, at dawn, Brahmā himself creates the ten levels of the earth;
having created [the realms] from heaven down to the netherworlds (pātāla), he performs the work of creation.
Then, recollecting each preceding stage in its proper order, he fashioned them just as before.
When evening arrived once more, there would again be dissolution;
at that time of dissolution, the Lord himself, Nārāyaṇa Hari, [would preside].
For the sake of protecting all the seeds of virtue, that ocean of compassion himself assumes the form of a fish; at the end of the dissolution of the Vedas, having arrived,
he protects them with his grace, ensuring they are well-guarded.
At the close of day, at evening, Brahmā indeed arose for the sake of the twilight rite;
taking his own water-pot, he went toward Puṣkara.
Having bathed and filled his water-pot with water, he sat down upon the bank.
While he was taking water from his water-pot for sipping,
he then saw a very small fish-form upon the palm of his hand;
it was as tiny as a barley grain, short in stature, like a minute creature.
Just as the Grandfather (Brahmā) was casting handfuls of water into the water, that [lotus] became the size of a span, leaped up, and fell upon the bank.
It said to me: "O Grandfather of the gods, protect me in your water-pot."
The Unborn One acted in such a way until [the serpent] could no longer fit within my water-pot.
Then Timi said to him, "O Lord, it is truly not enough for me;
my body grows so rapidly that you must cast me into a well."
Then, although he was cast into a well by Brahmā, he grew;
he became too large to be measured within the well and then spoke to the Creator:
"O Father, this well is not sufficient for me; cast me into a lake."
Having been drawn from the well by Brahmā and placed upon the Puṣkara lake,
this body of Puṣkara instantly became so vast that it could no longer fit within the lake;
he then spoke again to the Grandfather.
"The lotus-stalk born from me is not sufficient for you; O maker of bricks, cast me into the ocean!
Then Brahmā, having taken him, threw him into the ocean and said:
"Who are you that are here? Tell me, for you perform a marvel for me."
The fish, having grown large in the ocean, then spoke to the Grandfather:
"I am Nārāyaṇa himself; for the sake of protecting the world, I have assumed this form of a fish. Therefore, it is now evening."
The ten worlds, parched by heat, are considered to be quickly submerged in water.
Therefore, let this fourteenth Manu take the principal seeds located in the four oceans and board the ship.
Even a ship a hundred million yojanas long, with a deep foundation,
firm with a hundred decks, and filled with seeds ready to sprout;
[and] sages, ascetics, as well as gods, cattle, elephants, carriages, and mounts.
The seeds of plants that sprout from the soil, the Goddess Earth, and the Brahmins—whatever else may be required by you in the morning, let all that be produced in the form of seeds;
having taken it all, place it upon the boat. (32–33)
"Establish Manu there in truth and then go to your own realm;
thereafter, I shall indeed bind Nāda,
adorned with chains, to my horn and wander through the great waters in Satyaloka."
During droughts, the heat of the sun, and rains lasting a hundred years,
he brought a boat to the reservoir of waters in the great netherworld (Mahāpātāla).
And I shall protect them all until the end of the dissolution at nightfall.
"Until morning, I shall nourish them with my divine power;
do not grieve, O Brahmin, for I will give you wealth again at dawn.
After that, he will indeed perform that very creation of the ten worlds."
Thus commanded, Brahmā then spoke to the fourteenth Manu:
"Having offered the seeds, as well as the seeds of the gods and sages, he presented the boat to the fish, who was Keśava. (38–39)

Brahmā indeed went to the world of truth, and night fell at that time, during the twilight at the end of a thousand yugas, when the age was perishing. Then a constant drought arose, lasting for a hundred years.
Having become a chariot with seven rays, the Sun indeed rose up.
Those seven rays of his drank the water from the great ocean.
Then, by their intense heat, the earth was scorched.
Together with its mountains, rivers, and oceans, everything became devoid of moisture;
indeed, through the sharp and blazing rays [of the sun], it became a single mass of flame.
Then the terrible fire of universal destruction (saṃvartaka) consumed the worlds.
Having utterly consumed all the subterranean realms, he indeed burned the heavens above.
Then, terrible clouds of the *saṃvartaka* type, shaped like herds of elephants and adorned with flashes of lightning, rose up in the sky.
Blue, white, collyrium-colored, smoky, and yellow clouds—
terrible in form and making a terrible sound—
filled [the sky] with showers and extinguished that most dreadful and inauspicious fire.
When the fire has perished, the vault of the sky remains filled with water for a hundred years.
Thus, when the world is enveloped by water, the entire universe becomes a single ocean;
at that time, indeed, nothing whatsoever can be discerned apart from the water.
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, the Lord makes night;
the Blessed One, in his incarnation as a fish, protects the boat in every way during a hundred years of terrible famine amidst the fire of the great dissolution.
That Lord protects the boat by means of his own power of nectar.
And he protects it at night within the waters of the single ocean of darkness.
Then, when the end of the night has arrived, the Lord of Creatures awakens.
He created the various ten worlds according to their respective inhabitants; indeed,
he brought about dissolution every evening,
and he always performed creation again at every dawn.
This is declared to be the daily dissolution (*dainandinapralaya*) of the ten worlds.
Thus, at the end of a hundred years, the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) together with Brahmā perishes;
that is proclaimed as the other, the occasional dissolution (*naimittikalaya*).
Then, even the twenty-four forms of the root-māyā dissolve; at that time, one should understand that the great dissolution of primordial nature (prākṛta-pralaya) has occurred.
However, for the individual soul, through the perfect yoga with the Lord and through devotion born of true feeling—
When liberation occurs, that very thing should be understood as absolute dissolution (atyantika-laya).
During that dissolution at night, because there is no creation, there is no protection;
nor is there any necessity for the protection of the Manus. ||56-57||
Therefore, during the night of the manvantaras, no creation occurs.
The final Manu who has been proclaimed, as well as the sages who are the seeds,
remain upon a great ship while they abide in the state of sleep.
By the power of Viṣṇu’s desire as Nārāyaṇa, death does not exist for them.
They live until the end of the world, remaining as the seed of creation;
indeed, all those who live long do so through their devotion to Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa.

Having created the world again at dawn, Brahmā himself indeed causes those beings to dissolve back into that very creation, and never otherwise. In this manner, thousands of my forms as Fish are born.
"O Lakṣmī, I know those incarnations according to their respective purposes.
Thus, he who was the great Asura Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti,
at the beginning of creation, [established] the state of Kardama."
He enjoys the great earth situated within the waters like a sovereign emperor;
having emerged from the nose of Brahmā, I shall indeed destroy him and,
assuming the form of a boar, lead him to the abode of Yama.
Having slain that Asura at that time and made the earth well-compacted,
I do not go above the waters, but establish it firmly.
In this way, thousands of my forms as a boar come into being.
"Whenever necessity arises, I shall become the Crocodile (Kroḍa).
Thus everything has been told to you; what else shall I say after this?

Thus ends [the section on] the assumption of the Fish Incarnation by Brahmā in the first book, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the preservation of the seed-vessel at the daily dissolution in the evening, and the recovery of the earth stolen by Hiraṇyākṣa.
The one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Assuming the Form of a Boar and Other Matters," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga),
Chapter 133.
[The Author: Chapter 134.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: How Hiraṇyākṣa was born, and how he seized the earth.
"When did the Lord once again become a boar for the sake of his destruction?
O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, tell me this divine story of Viṣṇu, which bestows the essence of its own connection; I am not satiated by hearing such tales."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Kaśyapa’s wife, Diti, who was authorized [to bear his children], performed severe penance for the sake of obtaining a son.
At first, she mourned her deceased son for many days;
repeatedly remembering Hayagrīva, she became emaciated.
She did not eat well-prepared foods, nor did she desire water or other drinks.
She never rejoiced at anything pertaining to Śrāṅgārika.
Whenever that beautiful woman beheld the face of Kaśyapa, streams of tears fell from her eyes out of grief. (5–6)
Whether exiled, driven out, estranged, or even separated;
whether renounced or deceased—such a son causes his mother to burn with grief.
Even Hayagrīva, though driven from his own home and dead, [caused his mother to suffer].
Having heard this, she grieved in many ways, for her affection for her son was such.
She set her mind upon the destruction of Viṣṇu, who had caused the loss of her son;
she strove in various ways to obtain a remedy for the loss of her child.
"May my two sons become powerful enough to destroy Viṣṇu,
so that I may obtain manifold retribution for the eldest of the horse-faced ones.
Indeed, without the perfection of ascetic penances, this desire of mine could never be fulfilled."
Having reflected thus, that goddess performed penance for a hundred years.
For fifty years she subsisted on a diet of bulbs, roots, and fruits;
likewise, for twenty-five years she lived on water alone.
Furthermore, for fifteen years she subsisted on only vapors;
likewise, for ten years that goddess remained without food.
Diti, moreover, propitiated Brahmā again and again through her ascetic penance.

The fortunate woman sees no other, nor does she touch anyone else in any way; (14) she performs no other amorous adornment, remaining at all times established in austerity. She always sleeps upon the ground and never desires the massaging of her body. (15)
"Oṃ, salutations to you, O Brahmā; salutations to the Lord of Creatures.
Grant me offspring, grant me offspring, endowed with prowess equal to Viṣṇu.
Thus she performed the recitation of this mantra daily according to the prescribed rule.

She indeed spent a hundred years performing penance without any obstacles. With her body withered until only skin and bone remained, she performed the great worship and offered ten lakhs of oblations while reciting the prescribed mantras.
Then Brahmā approached and spoke to that ascetic bride:
"O Goddess, what may be obtained by you? Speak, and I shall grant it; do not practice penance.
Quickly choose whatever you desire, and I will fulfill it through the power of my austerity."
"There is nothing here that should not be given for your sake; choose quickly.
Diti, bowing to that Creator, spoke with modesty to the Mind-born one:
"Welcome! I shall perform the hospitable rites for my venerable father-in-law."
Having bowed at the feet of my great-grandfather, I salute my venerable ancestor.
I beg forgiveness for any offense should there have been any lack of discipline on my part.
If these elders, the protectors of the lineage, do not show me favor... [22]
In that case, where indeed could the suffering descendants go for supreme refuge?
(23) If the elders of former times were capable of fulfilling the desires of their descendants, yet did not do so, then who else could be the saviors of those descendants? (24)
Therefore, having reached a decision, I shall obtain the complete fulfillment of my desire by remaining thus engaged in austerity from my venerable grandfather, the Great Ancestor.
I choose two powerful sons, endowed with the vigor and prowess of Viṣṇu.
"By these two, there shall be honor shown to your eldest son according to my intention.
Brahmā said, "So be it; let Nārāyaṇa do that.
You shall have two virtuous sons whose prowess will be equal to Viṣṇu."

Neither Viṣṇu nor one devoted to Viṣṇu possesses prowess equal to Viṣṇu; nowhere else, at any time, is there anyone with valor like that of Viṣṇu. Therefore, having gone to Vaikuṇṭha, I shall pray to Nārāyaṇa.
Having bestowed this very blessing, Brahmā vanished right there.
Then, with great speed, he quickly went to Mahāvaikuṇṭha,
where the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa, the protector of devotees, resides.
The king of kings, the benefactor of all, shone resplendent.
Having bowed down, offered praise, and sat upon his seat, he spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"O friend of the distressed, O ocean of compassion, You are the one who effects the liberation of the world."
O Acyuta, you are always capable of granting the fruit of Diti’s ascetic penance.
She has requested two sons equal to Nārāyaṇa in prowess;
O Mādhava, please consider how you may grant them to her.
"Act in such a way that she may indeed have two sons who are dear to her.
Then Nārāyaṇa reflected in his heart on how to make the words of his elder brother, the Creator (Brahmā), come true.
Having produced some pretext, I shall fulfill my desire:
that pretext by which I may go to the earth, and under whose guise I may perform the playful deeds of men. (35–36)
The Geyas shall meet with him, and by that they will attain liberation.
Therefore, for this purpose, let it be a source of happiness for my devotees;
let them be equal to me in devotion to me, and possess prowess not inferior to mine.

"Having caused these two good sons to commit an offense against me, the fruit of their penance must be bestowed; in this way my purpose will be fulfilled. Having reflected thus, Hari [directly addressed] his two attendants regarding their misconduct. (38–39)
The two gatekeepers named Jaya and Vijaya, at their own will,
admitted Sanandana and the other three sages; meanwhile, they sent them forth to behold [the Lord],
while a great conversation with Brahmā regarding Viṣṇu was taking place.
Meanwhile, the sons of Brahmā— Sanātana, Sanaka, and Sanandana as the third— possessing the greatest power of resolve, arrived to behold Viṣṇu. (41–42)
Sanatkumāra and Turya—all of them possessed the splendor of Brahman.
They were the mind-born sons of Brahmā, omniscient and embodiments of knowledge.
Having treated detachment as if it were a blade of grass, they wandered about naked.
They were five years of age, gentle, and truly embodiments of Brahman;
indeed, in them there were no defects whatsoever pertaining to the bodies of men or women,
and apart from the Blessed Lord, their activities did not wander toward anything else.
Those whose vision never arises anywhere except for the vision of Brahman,
and into whose hearts nothing else enters except the form of Hari—
chanting His names, they come along the royal road.
Many Vaiṣṇavas residing in Vaikuṇṭha follow after them.
And they praise those boys, saying: "Aho! Behold these Vaiṣṇavas;
in form they are equal to Kṛṣṇa, and their faces are moons with gentle smiles. (47-48)
They were golden-hued, equal to the sun, and beautiful with a halo of radiance;
their well-developed limbs were captivating, and their bodies were as tender as land-lotuses.
They possessed locks of hair that were not too long, golden-colored, glossy at the ends, and adorned with curls.
Stealing away the minds of people with the beauty of their emerging rays,
their steady gazes— resembling the petals of autumn lotuses— penetrate deeply into the heart;
and with lips as crimson as fresh sprouts, they captivate the mind.
All of them bore the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* marks and wore flower-earrings as ornaments;
they held garlands used for worship by the gods and shone with the brilliance of ten million times ten million suns.
With the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) over their left shoulders and girdles of *muñja* grass at their waists, [they appeared].
Their limbs were proportioned to their forms, and their palms shone with a golden luster.
(53) Wearing divine garlands of *tulasī* on their necks and hands, the great goddess Lakṣmī, appearing as golden lines, was seen dwelling upon their chests. (54)
Equal to Nārāyaṇa in beauty and form, they resemble Kṛṣṇa;
in whiteness and meditation, they have the form of Śambhu; in their bodies, they are equal to Brahmā;
and in devotion, they are equal to Lakṣmī—who among these people could even compare to them? (55)
"Let the Vaiṣṇavas behold these marks of the Great Person!
By the power of our good fortune, we behold these divine beings.
Thus did the Vaiṣṇavas dwelling in the second Vaikuṇṭha indeed address them. (26, 57)
They praise him, they behold him, yet they find no satiety in the sight of all those naked ones who have arrived in the form of children;
where he has come to the city gate, two doorkeepers indeed guard the entrance.
Jaya and Vijaya, carrying their staffs, rose up.
Before they could take leave and depart, those two with their staffs said:
"Who are these naked ones going there? How do they enter the inner apartments? (1.133.60)
"Let them stay, let them not go at all, let those who have gone return!"— thus,
overcome by impetuosity, they repeatedly forbade them;
yet even so, disregarding them, those whose minds are fixed on Brahman continued on their way.
What is the door, and who are the gatekeepers that yogins do not perceive?

(62) For those for whom there is no other [object] than the reality of the Self, and in whose vision there is indeed no impurity—what rule or prohibition can there be for them? What indeed is their restraint? (63)
"Let them not go, let them not depart—what are these deaf ones?
O stiff ones, you who look like maidens, who are you, burdened with buttocks and loincloths?
Where indeed do these unknown people go? Victory! Go, turn them back! (64)
"Who indeed are these sons of a female donkey? Why are these sons of a bitch come here? Let the people bind them;
let them strike them with stones and tie them up along with trees. ||65-66||
Shameless and free from worldly stain, they are indeed seen wandering about without regard for others.
"O deer! Do you have parents? Or are they dead?
How is it that you roam about naked and without possessions, searching for whom? (67)
"There are no mothers here; run quickly from this place!
(68) "If they do not turn back, place a staff at the anus.
When Vijaya speaks thus for the sake of victory, then again— (69)
Having turned back and stood still, they heard all that was inauspicious;
they did not move forward nor did they offer any reply.
Jayo, having gone up to them, struck them gently on the back with his own staff.
In the middle of their hips, she pressed them with a staff;
having given them a slap on the cheek, she struck them upon the head.
Seizing their lingas, she threatened them, saying, "Cut these off!"
Having thus rebuked and insulted them, and having seized all four by their forearms, he bound them with a single creeper-cord and would not let them out.
Having thrown dust upon their backs, he forced them to eat charcoal from his own mouth.

Thus, Jayā and Vijayā, deluded by their lack of discipline, treated them with contempt and committed various offenses, regarding them as mere children. Meanwhile, Ramā, Jayā, and the other friends were eager to go out for recreation. (74–75)
Having emerged through that city gate, they then beheld those four Nārāyaṇas, who possessed the form of Viṣṇu and were well-known to them;
falling at their feet, they offered them worship with prostrations.
They repeatedly shook off the dust, released their bonds from the ropes, kissed his feet, and performed acts of cleansing.
"Alas! By what wicked person has this oppression of our lords been committed? (77–78)
Whose hands and feet have been broken, and whose fortune has utterly perished?
Or whose food from this place has indeed come to an end?
Whose water has been destroyed, as the sun rises with its scorching heat?
Whose line of merit has been severed today that it has fallen to the earth?
By whom has such an insult been committed against these holy men?
They shall have no dwelling here; let them not even know it.
"Indeed, as long as Nārāyaṇa himself does not know [of this], so long shall the status of the one who has shown contempt remain here; but afterwards, there is no [such] existence.
Seeing them speaking thus and seeing them weeping again and again—
In the meantime, Lalitā went and informed Nārāyaṇa.
As soon as the Lord of Gods heard this, he rose from his lion-throne and, running swiftly with his feet uncovered, learned of it immediately.
Just as Śrī Hari himself was arriving at that very gate,
hundreds of thousands of wives and millions of Vaiṣṇavas gathered at that spot and bowed down to Sanaka and the other sages.
Śrī Hari prostrated himself like a staff before those four holy men.
He asked about the cause of their distress: "What has been done, and by whom?
By whom has such an insult been committed against holy men like you? (86–87)
He does not deserve to dwell in my gateway nor in Vaikuṇṭha,
if his feet or his hands have committed an offense against me;
I would cut off those two, or I would pluck out his eye or sever his tongue.

"I shall indeed abandon my own Lakṣmī, who has committed a grave offense. (89) "Even children, untouched by the world's wind and with minds unpolluted by sin, sport for the welfare of those who desire a home. (1.133.90)
Indeed, even children are not considered children; they are regarded as fathers regarding liberation and other goals.
For they wander about as sanctifiers of sinners and as purifiers of the world.
May they, showing compassion toward me, forgive my offenses.
"Let them enter the inner palace and accept the service of a slave!
Having thus entreated them, he placed the dust of their feet upon his head.
Then, having led them away, Nārāyaṇa arrived at the city gate.
Then Nārāyaṇa beheld his two attendants, Jaya and Vijaya, bereft of their luster, with pale faces and trembling limbs.
At that moment, those boys spoke there in the abode of Hari, which is beyond all attributes (nirguṇa).
In this purifying realm, which is entirely peaceful, bliss-bestowing, and the ground of liberation;
which is changeless, exceedingly serene, divine, and the abode of Hari—such gatekeepers as these are not suitable, for they cause suffering and destroy liberation. (95–96)
Possessing passions, likewise wrathful, using vulgar speech, and stubborn;
devoid of refined conduct and performing deeds like those of Asuras—
therefore they are fit to resort only to an Asura womb.
Yet you two are not fit to serve the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, which is composed of pure goodness.
These two cruel ones are certainly not considered fit for the feet of Śrī Hari,
since you both, fallen from your station, have entered this sinful, demoniac womb.

Then, as they were falling from their place due to the power of the curse, their eyes filled with tears and they entreated the brahmins for forgiveness. By the will of Nārāyaṇa, those compassionate ones became humble.
The sages and the children said to them: "That triple birth shall indeed be so.
Then you two shall abandon this state of being asuras and complete [your course];
we shall undoubtedly return once more to the office of gatekeepers.

Thus cursed, the two sons of Diti fell from their own abode in the realm of Viṣṇu; they were born as two great Daityas of immense strength. And in Vaikuṇṭha, in their place, [there appeared] Aja and Ajaya.
Hari then appointed two gatekeepers until his arrival.
[He was honored] with the gift of millions and billions of male and female servants, as well as gardens, groves, and the like;
with hospitality, worship, food, and the washing of his feet.
Having performed various services— drinking, massaging, and attending to the beds and so forth—
for the four [sages] beginning with Sanaka who were devoted to Śaṃbhu,
and having properly offered them their vision [of the Lord], he himself received their vision in return. (106)
Having taken and bestowed the merit, they returned to the world of truth;
together with Brahmā, they indeed went to their own ancestral abode.
Then, from there, they went to Meru to see Kaśyapa.
Having bestowed blessings upon their two sons, Hari and Samaya,
they departed for the divine abode of Hari, Śvetadvīpa, the eternal seat.
Then Jaya and Vijaya indeed assumed an asuric nature.
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the younger.
Remaining within the womb for a hundred years, they did not undergo birth, thinking:
"If we were to be born, we would surely encounter suffering."
Thinking that birth should never be accepted again, they did not depart;
however, Nārada then arrived there and enlightened them both.
By the very act of taking birth, at the end of three lifetimes, their own [true nature] was once more [realized].
"You shall both attain the abode of Viṣṇu and become his attendants.
Having thus instructed them, he then further commanded the mantra;
having caused them to hear "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa," he then gave the order.
Out of a spirit of enmity, you two shall indeed worship Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa;
in your second birth, you shall likewise worship Sītā and Rāma;
and in your third birth, you shall also worship Kṛṣṇa and Nara.
"Then you two shall attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the divine Nārada departed for his own three worlds to wander.
As for the two attendants, they indeed took birth as demons.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Account of the Births of Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa, Beginning with the Departure of Sanaka and Others for Vaikuṇṭha at the Behest of Hari, Their Disrespect by Jaya and Vijaya, and the Pronouncement of the Curse of Asuric Births for Three Lifetimes," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. In this chapter, it is related how Brahmā performed penance for the sake of sons for Diti; how he went to Vaikuṇṭha and, having prayed to Viṣṇu there, received a boon from him to obtain a son equal to Nārāyaṇa; and how, upon the departure of Sanaka and others for Vaikuṇṭha as prompted by Hari, they were insulted by Jaya and Vijaya, resulting in the curse that led to their births as asuras, beginning with Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa.
← Chapter 133: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 134 [Author: Chapter 135 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Those two sons of Kaśyapa, as soon as they were born, were possessed of great strength; they had a complexion like the color of gold and were arrogant with great heroism and power.
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder brother, and Hiraṇyākṣa was his younger brother.
His body became immeasurable in size, and his eyebrows were like mountains.
Indeed, he could travel through the great waters and move through the circle of the wind.
He travels again and again through the earth, the intermediate space, and the heavens;
he wanders through the sky like a planet, goes to the netherworld like Śeṣa,
reaches Mount Meru like a bird, and moves through the air like Vainateya.
Indeed, he crosses to the further shore of the eight enclosures like Kṛṣṇa’s celestial chariot;
possessing a massive body and golden eyes, he holds nothing in any account.
Just as he desires, he expands his body at will, like the mountain Śrīparvata.
Whenever he goes to another world for the sake of dwelling there,
he indeed thinks of his own birth-house:
"If someone should ever carry off my golden house," (6–7).
Thinking, "I shall become supportless," he turned back again.
Hiraṇyākṣa had his own palace built by Viśvakarman on the slopes of Mount Meru,
in the intermediate space, and throughout the entire earth.
A thousand *yojanas* above the earth, at an equal interval, is the house; its circumference is indeed ten thousand *yojanas*, and its height is likewise made to be one thousand *yojanas*. (1.134.10)
Whatever prosperities belonged to Indra, Sūrya, Soma, Varuṇa,
and the wise Bṛhaspati, they all became his.
Indeed, whatever is new in mind, auspicious, or beautiful— [all that was his].

If it should come within the range of his vision, even for the great, he would forcibly bring it home and enjoy it without any obstacle. Thus, his prosperous house was like another Meru on earth. (12–13)
Thus, having abandoned his prosperous home, he went to the forest retreats;
then, indeed, the enemy began to harbor anxiety, fearing him from afar.
Consequently, at one time, he grew perfectly great like Mount Meru.
Having raised his thousand arms and uprooted this earth—
including its islands and mountains— and having detached the palace from Mount Meru,

On the thirteenth day, as the earth was being destroyed, there arose a great cry of "Alas! Alas!

he carried them away like myrobalan fruits in his hand and cast them down into the great waters.
Thereupon, all the hosts of gods, afflicted by fear, cried out.
They went for refuge to the Lord Nārāyaṇa-Hari;
having reached the shore of the Ocean of Milk, they praised him at great length.
Crying out, "Protect! Save! O Hari! Preserve us! they fell upon the ground at his feet.

he inspired confidence in all of them, having perceived a great marvel.
Janārdana, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, who possesses a universal form,
assumed the form of a boar and stood there together with the gods;
his body was without beginning, middle, or end, and he possessed great tusks and mighty arms.
Uttering a great cry of "Hā! Hā!
and causing his body hair to bristle, Hari—who has hands, feet, and eyes on all sides and who consists of all sacrifices—became dark-hued like a rain cloud, resembling Mount Meru in stature.
With a face in the form of a boar and a body consisting of Nārāyaṇa,
the Lord— bearing the conch, discus, mace, sword, spear, shield, and other weapons—
swiftly went through the sky downwards, downwards, downwards, toward the great waters. 25.
As he moved along, the great wind became agitated and bewildered;
even the houses supported by it were dragged behind him.
When the god entered the great waters, the asura [followed].
Though overwhelmed by fear and haste, he remained intent on battle.
Then the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa, having placed the earth within his belly,
assumed a body like Mount Meru and took up a mace resembling the Śailācala mountain.
Having whirled him around, the great Daitya fought with the Lord of the Universe.

Then Hari, in the form of a boar, became as vast as Mount Meru.
His fangs grew long, as hard as a thunderbolt or even harder than a thunderbolt;

Then Hari, the Supreme Lord, manifesting the power of his Vairāja body,

At the moment of death, a terrifying, great roar was let out by the Daitya.
Causing terror to the external creations dwelling in the realm of Vairāja,

With his great body crushed to pieces, that lowest of the sons of Diti died.

Having properly joined the earth just as it had been attached to me,

Salutations again and again to you, whose form is the entirety of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Salutations to the one with a thousand hands; salutations to the one whose nature is the universe. 1.134.40.

Salutations to the Lord of Śrī, Bhū, Līlā, Ramā, Lakṣmī, and Kaṃbharā.
"Salutations to the one whose nature is peace, salutations to the inner controller of all.

(42) Having thus offered praise, she, along with the gods, sages, seers, and the Earth, performed the worship of Hari in his boar-incarnation with garlands, sandalwood paste, and other offerings. (43)

Having spoken thus, while being sung of and praised there by the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and great sages, he vanished on that very spot. In this manner, these incarnations as boars occur in every Kalpa and within its intervals.
"When a great task involving the waters arises for me,

"All of you go to the earth in the forms of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others. Repeatedly destroy the Brahmins who perform austerities and sacrifices;

"O members of the assembly, make a solemn vow here, having raised your weapons:

resolving thus with persistence, he performs austerities difficult to practice.
Therefore, act according to what is right and quickly protect the gods and the others.

"Indeed, he has held his life-breaths for a hundred years within a heap of bones without water.

Shaking off from his body the dust of trees, pillars, ants, and clay,

Then Rudra said to the Daitya: "What is pleasing to your mind?

Salutations to the one who transcends all beings, salutations to the inner controller of all;

Homage to Marīci, and likewise homage again and again to all the sages!
(74) May you all be the bestowers of auspiciousness upon me at all times.

Of the gods, asuras, and humans; of the gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas;

"What deficiency could there be for a servant who has performed devotion, even regarding the loss of his status,

Whatever one desires, even more than that is bestowed upon him.

Therefore, one must always and in every way cultivate a state of being free from attachment;
for he indeed attains both enjoyment and liberation, while the other falls downward.
To the extent that the fool indulges in the mountains of sense objects, [he sinks further].

In that very way he became greedy, set ablaze by the noose of delusion. Consuming at will the objects of sense belonging to a universal monarch, that great fool was not satisfied; on the contrary, he went astray.
That man of darkness agitates the world-protectors with fierce punishments;

Then the guardians of the worlds, the seers, the sages, and the brahmins, having lost their protection, fell into supreme misery and were deeply distressed.

"Obeisance to the one worthy of refuge, whose nature is peace; obeisance, obeisance!"

Salutations to the one whose dwelling is transformation, and whose very self is transformation.

"O Viṣṇu, perform a transformation; the unbearable time has arrived.

Having received a boon from Nārāyaṇa as well as his word for protection,

"O chief gods and others, your task shall be accomplished; a fortunate future will surely come to pass for your sake. (46–47)
For all beings, the rising and the setting of the wheel of time (kālacakra) likewise constitute their destiny;

The wheel created by merit and demerit is the bond that binds everyone.

Indeed, the merit of Hiraṇyakaśipu was truly very great;

Wickedness, the disparagement of those worthy of honor, unrighteousness, and likewise the violation of one's wife’s vows—

Thus, blinded by the intoxication of wealth, he indeed practices these many [vices].

"Therefore, his days are for all intents and purposes almost entirely finished.

Having remembered Śrī Hari and bowed down toward that direction with full prostration (daṇḍavat),

Hari, observing Prahlāda, resolved to destroy the demons.

he became entirely devoted to the service of the Supreme Person, having abandoned everything else in every way.
Devoted to the Brahmins, perfected in virtue, and with a mind fixed on the practice of truth;
he was as dear to the hearts of all people as their own selves, and he conducted himself like a servant in the service of the feet of the great. (4–5)
He is gentle, a remover of the suffering of the distressed, and one who has served Mādhava;
indeed, from birth he is enriched with learning, devotion, lordly power, and prosperity.
He is devoted to his guru, cows, and Brahmins, and is free from vices and the like.

Knowing the truths regarding the body—that it is impermanent, impure, and suffering—he was not attached to it; he was free from the effects of illusion such as envy and the like, and he did not find even the slightest pleasure in childish playthings. (7–8)

For him, play is with the form of Hari; Hari himself is his friend—[this applies to] one who is devoted to Hṛṣīkeśa even while dwelling in the womb, in all states and in all activities, through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (9)
He knows no one other than Viṣṇu, the eternal Nārāyaṇa;
his mind is naturally fixed upon Vāsudeva, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, in whom all the great qualities esteemed by the Sāttvatas always reside. (1.137.10–11)
He is deeply asleep toward the world, yet he remains awake toward Śrī Hari.
Whether sleeping, breathing, rising, moving, or turning onto his side;
whether leaping, seeing, tasting, smelling, speaking, or touching—[he remains ever conscious of Him]. (12)
While drinking, washing, eating, meeting others, or reflecting on anything, he has no other occupation;
protecting his devotion to Hari, chanting "Hare Hare," he meditates upon, remembers, and contemplates the Lord at every moment. (13–14)
In some moments, remembering Hari, he sheds tears out of love;
in other moments, seeing the divine Lord situated within his heart, he laughs. In yet other moments, he himself sings the names of Hari with exceeding devotion.
In some moments he dances, his very soul filled with love for Hari, and in others he melts away;
sometimes, touched by His divine form, he dissolves and falls into a state of numbness.
Thus, immersed in the nectar of Brahman, he dwells perfectly within Nārāyaṇa.
For him there is neither hunger nor thirst, no concern for ornaments nor grooming of the body; there is no desire for clothing or other such things, nor does anything else dwell in his mind.
Viṣṇu resides in his eyes, Kṛṣṇa in his face, and Hari indeed in his tongue.
Whether in external or internal affairs, Hari became his refuge.
In due time, that wise youth was initiated and lived in the house of his preceptor.
His preceptor was the family priest Kāvya, who is worshipped by the Asuras.
That poet Śukra had two sons who were masters of the scriptures:
the first was Ṣaṇḍa and the other was Amarka. To them, the king entrusted his son, and they taught him the subjects to be studied that were imbued with the nature of the Asuras.
And thus he grasped the essential meaning of the Sāmaveda and other scriptures, but not anything else.
Many divine and non-divine great sciences were all recited for him;
indeed, he heard everything spoken by his guru and mastered it through repeated recitation.
He correctly grasps with devotion that [wisdom] by which liberation occurs,
and from within he abandons another knowledge that relies upon false attachments.
Even after having studied all the Vedas and various treatises, [he realizes this].

Then, at a certain time, the son of the Daitya, having come into the presence of his father along with his preceptor, prostrated himself, falling at his feet. Embracing that son of auspicious mind with both arms, [the father spoke].
Placing him on his lap, his father Hiraṇyakaśipu asked:
"Prahlāda! You have been residing in the house of your preceptor for a long time.
Tell me properly what excellent instruction you have received from your guru."
Prahlāda, being delighted, bowed and spoke this:
"A man who knows the Self, having abandoned the great snare of the household,
should worship by means of the self, embracing the garland of the Self which lies within the heart."
The venerable Supreme Lord, who moves through all branches of knowledge, is indeed the all-pervading, virtuous Reality; any other object is purposeless.
Having heard the words of his son, which were filled with a stream of devotion to Viṣṇu...
But the Daitya, laughing, said to his preceptors regarding the instruction of his son:
"How has this child-like intellect of his— clear as a white cloth and resting upon its side—
fallen into a state of discernment brought about by the partisan of Viṣṇu?"
"In such a way that his immature intellect does not become divided from the truth,
you, O venerable ones, must instruct him so that he shall never speak thus again.
Then the gurus, having brought him to their own home, [instructed him] with conciliatory words.
They asked: "By whom was this purpose of Viṣṇu taught?
This purpose brings no happiness to the side of the Daityas; abandon it!
From where does this purpose, which is permeated by Viṣṇu, come to you—whether from yourself or from another?"
Prahlāda, the soul of all, the supreme lord Nārāyaṇa, the inner self of all, commanded: "Worship Nārāyaṇa always.
The Guru said: "The Nārāyaṇa of whom you spoke is your father."
"There is no other Nārāyaṇa; worship Him and be happy.
(37) The disciple said: "O Guru, it is true that through devotion to Nārāyaṇa, devotees indeed become equal to Nārāyaṇa himself; yet my father was not so. (38)
Because he dwelt among a multitude of men, even my father was Nārāyaṇa;
however, he was not the divine Nārāyaṇa, the devourer of time and lord of the imperishable.
There is a great difference between those two, like that between a common moth and the sun-moth (the firefly).
"I falsely knew my father Khadyota to be the sun;
O Guru, I truly know Nārāyaṇa, who illuminates himself.
Nevertheless, I regard him as my father, and my father alone."
"Because of your hatred for Nārāyaṇa, you do not show me great honor;
nevertheless," the Guru said, "you must carry out your father's command.
Always perform the worship, service, attendance, and obedience due to your father."

Having returned home in the evening, Prahrāda, who had completed his studies, was embraced by his father and seated affectionately upon his lap. Then, with gentle words, the father asked him: "My son, what have you studied here today?"
"Speak, and having heard it, I shall become happy; let me know the lore appropriate to our lineage.
Prahlāda, having bowed to his father, said: "I shall declare what has been studied by me:
You are indeed Nārāyaṇa in truth, and not falsely so from the perspective of the kingdom."
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is the Truth, served by the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha.
I worship Him; you too, my father, should worship Him.
[The means are] hearing, chanting, remembering, and serving the feet of Viṣṇu.
Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender—these ninefold modes of devotion are supreme; all else is mere mockery.
One should practice this ninefold study; what is the use of any other mockery? (47–48)
Having heard this supreme speech full of devotion, the lord of the Daityas then became enraged and spoke thus to his preceptor:
"O evil-minded one, why has such speech, filled with praise for Hari, been taught to my son?"
"Why have you spoken of this improper act for our family, which is so pleasing to you? O son of the preceptor, what indeed is this instruction directed toward an enemy?
You are hidden, a nourisher of Viṣṇu’s faction, wearing a deceptive disguise."
"The time for even those who are hypocrites in name but wicked has not yet passed;
punishment shall fall together upon the son of the preceptor's son.
Then the preceptor's son said, "I have not taught him such things."
"Let not his innate intelligence cause us distress!
Nevertheless, the lord of the Daityas said: 'But you have not studied under a teacher.
Tell me, child, as is fitting, why indeed have you mastered this? (53–54)
Prahlāda said: "O Lord of the Daityas, this wisdom has been granted to me by Kṛṣṇa;
yet, without a body consecrated by even a speck of the dust from the feet of a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, such wisdom cannot arise except through the company of the virtuous and service to the saintly. (55)
"By the grace of the God of gods, the Lord Hari, I have been instructed.
There is no other teacher for me; that very Hari is the impeller.
He exists everywhere as the hearer, the thinker, the speaker, and the seer. (56–57)
Hari alone is the imperishable teacher; He, the Lord, is also the giver of intelligence.
Then Hiraṇyakaśipu, filled with rage, said to his son:
"I alone am considered the Lord in the world, the sovereign of the three realms."
"Worship Govinda alone; abandon that enemy, the infallible Acyuta.
Or else, worship the god Śaṅkara, Rudra, the teacher of the world, the Lord, the presiding deity of the gods, the auspicious one who bestows all sovereignty. (1.137.59–60)
Prahlāda said: "The Rākṣasas have fallen into this delusion of the Lord’s Māyā; they even think, 'We alone are the lords.
Even Śaṅkara himself is a devotee of Viṣṇu and stands at the forefront of the Vaiṣṇavas."
"Does this Daitya not know? How has he fallen into such delusion?
O Father, you do not understand this because your mind is shrouded by the pride of intoxication.
Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; the Reality is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme. (62–63)
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditator; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditation. He is the eternal Lord, the refuge of the entire universe, the supreme one.
Vāsudeva is the eternal creator and ordainer of the world.
The Puruṣa alone is everything here; he lives upon that very universe.
He has a golden body and eyes like lotuses;
by him alone were Brahmā and Īśa created, and they abide under his command.
Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises.
Out of fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run forth.
There was but one God, Hari, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme.
Neither Brahmā, nor likewise Īśāna, nor the moon and sun;
neither heaven and earth, nor the stars, nor the dwellers of the celestial realm—only the wise ever behold that supreme station of Viṣṇu. (68–69)
Having abandoned that Śrī Hari, why should one worship the father Śiva,
whom the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā, Īśa, and Śakra worship,
and whom the high-souled yogis such as Sanaka and others meditate upon?
By the half-glance of whose grace the inhabitants of heaven—the lords Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Varuṇa, Yama, Soma, and Kubera—are filled with joy;
and by the mere chanting of whose name eternal liberation is attained. (71–72)
I shall worship that Lord of Śrī, the God of gods, the infinite Puruṣottama,
whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, who bestows eternal bliss and happiness—
the protector Hari, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
I shall attain with ease that supreme abode of Viṣṇu—
Lord Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in consciousness, the imperishable, the supreme Lord,
eternally beyond the universe, the universe itself, Hari Nārāyaṇa. (74–75)
Nārāyaṇa should always be known as the soul of the universe, the supreme refuge;
Nārāyaṇa is the form of the highest light, whose very essence is Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever exists in this entire world, whether it is seen or even heard—
Pervading all that is within and without, Nārāyaṇa stands firm.
I bow to Nārāyaṇa, who is the eternal, the truth, the supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, dark and tawny, whose conduct is exalted, and who is the very form of the universe.
Having thus heard his son’s words, Hiraṇyakaśipu was then possessed by a great rage; his eyes turning bloodshot,
he cast his devoted son from his own lap onto the ground.
Glancing around at the Daityas, he spoke, overcome with rage:
"By my command, let them slay Prahlāda—who stands on the path of transgression and is intent on honoring his enemies—with a multitude of terrifying weapons. (1.137.80–81)
Let this lowest of men be executed immediately— he who, abandoning his own kinsmen and friends,
worships the feet of Viṣṇu like a servant of his uncle-killer.
Furthermore, a limb that is diseased and beyond the reach of medical treatment must indeed be amputated.
Even that which brings a multitude of benefits from another should be accepted, like bitter medicine and the like.
(83) It is said that Hari alone is the protector;
therefore, by all means, may I behold the protection of Hari this very day, so that my birth may become fruitful. (84)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Death Sentence and Other Measures Motivated by Hatred Due to the Manifestation of Divine Knowledge in Prahlāda, the Son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, Who Had Mastered All Sciences," in the first section, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Then, O Lakṣmī! the Nairṛtas—holding spears in their hands, with sharp fangs, terrifying mouths, and copper-colored beards and hair—came toward my devotee, uttering fierce cries and shouting, "Cut him! Pierce him! (1)

Surrounding him, they struck him with spears, javelins, and pikes. But there, O auspicious lady, because of his remembrance of Hari, Prahlāda’s body became like a diamond; thus, their blows were rendered fruitless.
Having reached and touched that body, the great weapons of the rākṣasas were shattered and fell to the ground like the withered petals of a lotus.

The soldiers stood near the king of the Daityas, astonished and with their faces cast down.
"Against the Supreme Brahman, the indefinable Lord who is the self of all, and against his great devotee whose soul is united [with Him]—whose weapon could possibly be effective? (5–6)

Hiraṇyakaśipu was then struck with supreme astonishment;
blinded in his heart by great sorrow and as if swooning from rage.

such as Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and others, saying, "Devour them! Having received this command, those Nāgas, fierce with poison, then [acted accordingly].

those serpents of venomous weapons devoured that mighty one, the servant of the one whose banner is Garuḍa;

With their vital organs and limbs severed by Garuḍa, who was impelled by Viṣṇu,

Seeing even the great serpents and his sons rendered fruitless, he,
filled with great rage, commanded the world-elephants (*diggajas*) who were irresistible.

They struck him with their massive tusks; nevertheless, he whose body was like adamant was not wounded even slightly on a single hair by my grace. On the contrary, the tusks of the elephants were severed at the root and fell down.
Deprived of their tusks, the elephants fled in great distress;
yet, even upon witnessing such a marvel, he did not desist.
"O fair-browed one! Alas, the illusory power of Hari causes even the lowest of the low to fall! (19)
Seeing his son snatched away by the great serpents, he cast his own son into a kindled great fire out of rage. A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the village, the hamlet, and the kingdom.
Even though he was the god Agni, he did not burn that devotee who is dear to Hari as he reclines upon the waters;
instead, the fire remained extinguished like the moon.
Nevertheless, the fool did not realize that his protector was present there.

by the power of Nārāyaṇa, even the poison became nectar.
Then, seeing his son uninjured and just as he was before,
he caused a much larger pit to be dug in the earth there;
having cast him into it, he filled the ground level with massive rocks.
Prahlāda had been severely tormented by Nārāyaṇa in the royal palace.
Seeing him returned alive and resembling a god, seated there upon the great throne of the Asura, the king was filled with fear.
"This one is my enemy, Māraka," the king of the Daityas decided and said;
"Lifting him up, let the Rākṣasas throw him quickly into the ocean.
All of them did exactly so, for he had previously come to their homes.

Having seen that great fire on the Himavat mountain, they then cast it [there]; Nara and Nārāyaṇa protected it from being extinguished by the snow. But he, having been seen by the Rākṣasas, reached the palace of the Daitya.
There are indeed means for death, yet they do not bear fruit here.
What should be done? Where should one go, so that death may not come to me? (3.1) Has a boon been obtained by me for my own sake, which has now borne fruit here?
Father and son are both equally praiseworthy; however, devotion to Viṣṇu alone bestows relief from suffering.
(32) What is yet to come shall be granted by Him; therefore, must my death indeed occur?
Nevertheless, I shall make a decision: what power can even the ultimate limit of devotion not overcome? (33)
Having reflected thus, he said to his son: "It was stated by you before me that because Viṣṇu pervades all beings, he is so named;
therefore, demonstrate to me through direct perception his existence everywhere."
And that God who is omnipresent is indeed the Supreme Lord.
His sovereignty, power, splendor, knowledge, heroism, and strength, as well as his form, prosperity, majesty, excellent qualities, and conduct—[all these belong to him]. 35–36.
Having seen Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods, correctly [as you have described him], I then consider him to be superior to me;
for if he is my elder, let him obtain sovereignty here by conquering me through his strength and valor,
and never by any other means.
"There is no one in the world, nor among the gods, who is a match for me.
Indeed, by the granting of a boon from Rudra, I am invincible and cannot be slain.
Hearing these words of his father, Prahlāda then laughed.
He related in every way the power of Hari and the Daitya;
for he who is indeed Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest—
he is called Nārāyaṇa because his abode (ayana) is among men (nṛ) and in the waters (nāra).
Because he dwells within all beings, he alone is Vāsudeva;
because he nourishes the entire world, he is also Viṣṇu due to his pervading presence.

In the midst of all that is conscious and unconscious, His very form exists.
His pervasion is three-quarters in the supreme abode, while His pervasion by one quarter is within the realm of *māyā*.
He is this very one, holding the discus and mace in His hands, who is to be perceived through devotion in every way.
It is not seen through base qualities such as anger, envy, and pride.
It abides pervading all beings among gods, animals, humans, and even stationary things—whether they be small or great. (44–45)
Even as Prahlāda was speaking thus, at that very moment,
the left eye, lip, shoulder, and other limbs of Hiraṇyakaśipu throbbed;
meanwhile, a crow shrieked repeatedly upon the king’s flagstaff.
Then the banner broke, and it fell down of its own accord due to his stumbling.
His heart trembled because he recognized these as ill omens;
for Dhūmraketu was seen in the path of the sky, brandishing a sword.
A black goat-cart was seen traveling toward the southern direction;
his own wife, dressed in a single red garment, was seen for a moment embracing him;
and for a moment, his own head was seen separated from his body and held in his own hand.
Then, during the day, Śukra was seen in heaven, and the quarters of the sky were covered in dust.
As soon as he saw this, he thought, "My death must come about because of this conflict.
Then he perceived him [Śukra] with his splendor somewhat faded and his face cast downwards.
Śaṇḍa and Marka, the sons of Śukra, said to him, "For the sake of conciliation:
'Do not grieve, O Indra among kings! For you alone are the conqueror of the world.
We two shall instruct him so that he may follow the dharma of his lineage. (5.2)
"Having bound him with the nooses of Varuṇa, we two shall protect him in our own home.

That very [māyā] in its uneven state is saṃsāra, the embodiment of reality.
Those transformations of māyā which possess destruction are considered [transient];

The body, however, is born later; it grows through abundant food, undergoes transformation, wanes, perishes, and is false.

The body and so forth are indeed insentient, while the Self is truly sentient.
The body and so forth are of the nature of suffering, whereas the Self is always composed of bliss. He is called Existence-Consciousness-Bliss; he is neither a Daitya nor a Dānava.
He is neither a god nor an asura; he is neither female nor male;
he is neither neuter, nor passionate, nor devoid of passion—he is indeed pure. But the ignorant one, though free from affliction, is sometimes possessed of a sattvic disposition.

In some cases there is the nature of passion (rāja), and in some cases the nature of darkness (tāmasa). I consider goodness (sattva) to be the bringer of happiness; passion (rajas) would be the creator of attachment;
and darkness (tamas) is declared to be the cause of affliction. Therefore, one should cultivate the quality of goodness (sattvaguṇa).
Even *sattva* is considered beneficial for the self, as it brings about gain;

That indeed shall always be the bringer of gain and the bestower of liberation.

As long as the distinction between the self and that which belongs to the self has not been made here,

He indeed is the nourisher everywhere, the giver of happiness, and likewise the giver of liberation.

Then, from that pillar, the immensely powerful Mahāgiri emerged,

Having meditated upon Nṛsiṃha in his heart, he, with a concentrated mind, praised Hari:
"Obeisance to the God of gods, whose form is dissolved in pure being (sattva). Obeisance to Him whose form even Brahmā and the other gods fear. (8.1)

Salutations again and again to you, who are not satisfied with noble lineage, physical beauty, austerity, learning, strength, and the like, nor with prosperity and eloquence of speech. Even a Brahmin who is averse to your feet, though endowed with restraints (*yamas*) and observances (*niyamas*), [is not equal to one devoted to you]. (82–83)
Salutations to You, who accept even a small offering from a devotee;
salutations again and again to You, who are pleased with one who is humble and devoid of pride.
Salutations to Hari, who bestows happiness upon those who have taken refuge in the path of devotion.
Homage again to the giver of protection, supernatural power, prosperity, and great happiness!
(85) Even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, desiring the vision of peace, praise you, the Supreme Self; therefore, manifest your peaceful form. (86)
"O Lord of Gods, I do not fear the cruel form of Narasiṃha;
I fear desire, anger, and the like—therefore, grant me protection from those.
That protection from the asura was merely the protection of the body."
Indeed, I have no protection; therefore, grant me protection.
O Lord of the Universe, grant me protection from the bondage of the unborn [Māyā] consisting of afflictions, karma, its fruition, and so forth; that alone shall be considered true protection.

The desires for children, wife, wealth, power, and the like, O Lord of Heaven, are never fulfilled; protect me from them. I have seen the opulences of the lord of the Daityas, yet they were not protective.
Indeed, these sovereign powers have been seen by me, yet they do not protect at all;
nor do the supernatural attainments (*siddhis*) of the gods provide protection.
But you, assuming many forms, exist for the sake of protecting your devotees.
O Soul of the Universe, you lift up all beings; likewise, grant me deliverance.
For kingship is said to be a bondage, a great evil, and an even greater sin—that which creates obstacles to serving the virtuous through defects such as pride and the like.
In their wretchedness, they resort to asceticism and desire objects born of craving;
having subsequently obtained enjoyments, they forget you—this indeed is their sin.
Therefore, [there is no such thing as] being the God of gods among wives, children, wealth, and the like.
O Lord, grant me yoga; grant me [union] with the lotus of Your feet.
Grant me yoga among the servants of Your servants.
These [beings], by day, long to behold Your gentle form.
"Therefore, O Mādhava, show me your gentle and bliss-bestowing form.
Thus entreated, the Blessed One withdrew that exceedingly terrifying and wrathful splendor and became pleasant to behold.
Resembling ten million autumnal moons, with eyes like white lotuses,
his radiance was like a mass of nectar-filled manes and like ten million flashes of lightning;
he was adorned with bracelets, armlets, rings, and other ornaments rich with excellent jewels.
He is resplendent with his two upraised arms holding the conch and the discus,
and beautifully adorned with his other two hands granting boons and fearlessness.
His chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and he is decorated with a forest garland.
Then the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarī) shone, adorned with earrings, necklaces, girdles, jewels, and gold; he was joined by Śrī, who stood upon his left side.
Seeing that Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha, the deities along with the great sages [were filled with joy].
Having sprinkled him with tears of joy, they offered continuous salutations.
O Lord of the Self, they presented divine worship with flowers and other offerings; having consecrated the Eternal One with jeweled jars filled with nectar, [they honored him]. 103–104.
Having worshipped Janārdana with garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, delightful incenses, divine offerings, and lamps,
they praised him with excellent divine hymns and bowed down to him again and again.
Having bestowed his desired blessings upon all who had fallen at his feet,
he made Prahlāda the eternal king of all the Daityas;
then the Lord, being pleased, urged him once more to request a boon.

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Clear Manifestation of Nṛsiṃha, the Pervasion of His Splendor, the Tearing Apart of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Hymns Offered by the Devas and Others, the Gentle Appearance Following Prahlāda’s Praise, and the Hymn of Lakṣmī," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 140. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Continuity of the Kṛta Yuga).

Chapter 142 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī, that Nṛsiṃha, indeed for the purpose of testing his devotee and to compel him to accept boons, said:
"Accept the sovereignty of the earth as far as the oceans and be happy."
"Accept the earth consisting of seven islands and be happy.
Or, O bull among devotees, take possession of the kingdom of the seven netherworlds;
likewise, rule over a realm comprising the seven heavens and the station of Dhruva."
Accept this new kingdom and the entire universe, O beloved;
whatever you desire, O devotee, I shall grant that happiness to you.
(4) [I give] vehicles, women, female servants, male servants, elephants, and horses.
Celestial palaces and the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*,
the state of piercing (*vedha*), the state of Śiva, the state of Viṣṇu, and the state of Virāṭ—
I shall grant these as something entirely new; accept them if they please you.
Indeed, there is not even the slightest calculation of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) before me;
they exist in incalculable numbers within my own teaching.
The worlds, the guardians of the worlds, and likewise the protectors of the cosmic eggs [are all under my authority].
Indeed, there are countless Brahmās, Viṣṇus, and Maheśas under my control.
Likewise, I shall bestow upon you even the Īśvara, Vairāja, or Vaiṣṇava abode; for you are truly independent—take whichever you desire, O sir!
Thus, even while wandering about, he remained free from desire for worldly objects;
he did not beg Janārdana for anything other than the feet of Hari.
"Whatever you wish to give, O Govinda, let that remain yours alone; I have no longing for it. (1.141.10)
I am not one who desires what is perishable, for that which is perishable is already lost. This [Self] is indestructible and eternal; how could I desire that which ends in destruction?
That entire kingdom is artificial; indeed, the Uncreated is never attained through the created.
One who has not acted [for liberation] shall never be liberated by means of performed action;
rather, eternal liberation is indeed obtained through the self by taking refuge [in it].
Here, [the distinction is made] between *prakṛti-puruṣa* or *pradhāna-puruṣa*.
The worlds, kingdoms, splendors, and prosperous abodes of Vairāja, Mahāviṣṇu, Viṣṇu, or likewise of Brahmā; of Rudra, the world-protectors, the gods, and the serpents—[all these he beheld]. (14–15)

All those that are material (prākṛta) consist of rajas and tamas; even those characterized by sattva are called secondary hells, for they are indeed hells. Indeed, apart from the supreme abode, the Imperishable (akṣara), all those states are hells.
I have no desire for anything anywhere except the feet of Hari.
Therefore, O Lord, always grant me Your lotus feet within Your abode;
grant me constant service to You, as well as service to Your devotees.
Always grant delight in the virtuous; grant me a dwelling in Your abode.
Grant me love for You as its foundation, and always grant me single-minded devotion to You alone.
Grant me the supreme, eternal bliss produced by the Self, which resides in You alone.
I do not seek any other pleasure here or in the hereafter, for it is impermanent and subject to decay.

Whatever I might desire, wherever, for whomsoever, from whatever cause, for whatever purpose, by whatever means, toward whomever, or as whoever—I am "I" only because of You; in reality, all that belongs to You alone. (1.141.20–21)
May everything related to you be offered to Kṛṣṇa for me at all times.
My body, senses, mind, intellect, and vital breaths are never satisfied;
O Lord, may there be eternal satisfaction in You—may I choose that, grant it to me!
"Bestow upon me a garden forever; tear asunder everything else besides you.
Grant me liberation, O bestower of refuge, and grant me service to the virtuous.
Having thus petitioned, Prahlāda, the foremost among the wise, ceased speaking.
The Blessed One said: "I shall give that food to him who does not desire it;
I do not give it to him who desires it—such is my reversal of fortune.
By my command, accept this kingdom which indeed belonged to your father."
In that regard, you shall not go to bondage at all by my command.
Without offering [the fruits] to me, even a real object must not be enjoyed;
always remember me in action, whether it pertains to the body or the mind.
"You are a child, yet you possess the wisdom of the aged; you are devoted like one eternally liberated.
Therefore, indeed, accept this kingdom comprising the seven netherworlds.
I do not truly favor that person who worships me out of mere desire."
A devotee who worships with a desireless heart receives my respectful offering (arghya) before me.

I am the master; seeing a desireless devotee, yet seeing another devotee who possesses desire, I go far away and certainly not near him; however, toward the one free from desire, I approach in every way.
Therefore, enjoy that kingdom of the Daityas for the duration of a Manvantara;
listen to and narrate my stories which bestow liberation,
and while offering all actions unto me, rule your kingdom free from thorns.
Always keeping me in mind, indeed perform only the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).

Exhaust what has already been done by experiencing its fruits, and whatever is new, exhaust that by means of offering it [to Me]; thus bring about a future in which there is nothing to be experienced.
"When the body dissolves in due time, you shall attain Me with immediate glory.
Prahlāda said, "O Lord of Gods, grant me this boon: the purification of my father.
He committed an offense against You out of contempt, yet he was compassionate. (34)
"He has indeed committed an offense against you and against me, your devotee. Therefore, I choose this: that he be purified immediately from this sin by taking refuge in your grace.
I choose nothing else, O Lord; salutations be unto you."
Hari said: "By you, the best of devotees, twenty-one members of your lineage have been delivered; what praise is there for this?
Wherever my saints reside—those who are tranquil and possess equal vision—"
The people of that region follow the customs of the Mlecchas;
yet even those humans dwelling there are purified by the yoga of devotion such as yours—of this there is no doubt.
Perform the funeral rites for your father, and he shall go to the world of Vidhātṛ.
Furthermore, O sinless one, in the third birth as Kṛṣṇa, when Rāma is born in the Satya-loka, he will become a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa;
thereafter, as Śiśupāla, he will be an Asura and then attain liberation.

"O Prahlāda, those two attendants of mine, Jaya and Vijaya, became two brothers due to their offense against Sanaka and the others. Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was his younger brother. (41–42)
Those very two— Rāvaṇa as the elder and Kumbhakarṇa as his younger brother—
shall become Dantavakra and Śiśupāla.
Then, liberated from that curse, they shall attain the side of the attendants (of Viṣṇu).
Through the union of these two devotees, people shall sing my life-story consisting of the account of my births;
by that, they shall attain liberation.
And through your devotion, the firmness of devotion in other devotees shall increase.
Thus pleased, the Lord of Lakṣmī granted him his desired boons;
thereafter, the Lord of All, who is affectionate toward His devotees, together with the hosts of gods,
made the imperishable Prahlāda the king of all the Daityas.
Having comforted his devotee Prahlāda and consecrated him by the foremost of the gods,
and having bestowed upon him unwavering devotion characterized by dispassion (naiṣkarmya),
Hari, the man-lion, was praised by the hosts of deities.
Scattered by showers of flowers, he went to the forest of lions.
There, he engaged in battle with Śambhu in the form of a śarabha;
having abandoned their bodies to one another, they both became invisible.

The lion, the stone, and the Nārasiṃhī shall exist as long as Śambhu remains the lord of the śarabha; indeed, they will endure for as long as creation itself persists. Thereafter, all the hosts of gods returned each to his own abode.
Furthermore, with delighted minds, they partook of their sacrificial portions;
meanwhile, Prahlāda ruled the kingdom according to the Vaiṣṇava dharma,
having then worshipped Hari with numerous sacrifices, gifts, and other rites.
In the end, he will go to the eternal abode of Hari, which is accessible only to yogis.
(53) Those people who hear this account of Prahlāda’s life shall all be liberated from sin and go to the realm of Śrī Hari. (54)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the majesty of Hari as Nṛsiṃha;
his descendants, who have lion-like heads, dwell in the Raivata forest.
Now, O beloved, I shall describe to you his form as Vāmana; listen!
On the divine mountain Raivata, Vāmana himself came as Hari.

(56) Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Granting of Boons to Prahlāda by Nṛhari, the Coronation of Prahlāda in the Kingdom of His Ancestors, and the Disappearance of Nṛsiṃha in the Forest," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
