Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O beloved! I shall relate to you clearly and exactly as it happened everything for the sake of which the form of Śrī Hari became Vāmana.
In the western region of Saurāṣṭra stands the great mountain Raivata,
where hosts of gods have their dwellings and hundreds of thousands of Siddhas reside;
there the Yoginīs and sacred fords (tīrthas) also dwell perpetually.
Prahlāda had a son known as Virocana.
His son was the mighty-armed and powerful King Bali.
By him, many excellent sacrifices were performed on various lands.

A single sacrifice was performed there on the plateau of Mount Raivata, where the Lord Vāmana himself came and requested [the earth] from Bali. Listen to that supreme, divine, purifying, and liberating narrative. (5)
I speak, O Mahālakṣmī! There is no satiety in the nectar of this narrative.
Where there is the Dāmodara Tīrtha as well as the Nārāyaṇahrada, what is the use of many other holy sites? By bathing in those two, one is liberated.
To the north of Siṃhāraṇya, on the ground at the beginning of Vyāghrāraṇya,
near the presence of Somanātha, there is a great mountain called Udayānta;
it is known as Kṛtasmara, having been reduced to ashes by the submarine fire (vāḍavānala).
On its very flank, however, is the mountain known as Raivata;
it is considered to be a portion of the Kaustubha gem of Śrī Hari that has attained a massive form.
The Manu named Raivata resides there in the state of its inner self (adhyātmatā).
This very divine Raivataka mountain resides within Kṛṣṇa’s heart,
just as a pair of golden bells rest upon the neck of a great elephant;
likewise, at the close of the full moon, both the moon and the sun seem to alight there.
Its height reaches as far as heaven, and its middle portion rests upon the atmosphere.
(11) Siddhas such as Dattātreya indeed dwell upon its peak;
all the deities reside in the hollows of its ridges. (12)
On the middle slopes of the mountain dwell the venerable Arhat, Nātha, Gautama, and others— those holy sages who are practitioners of yoga.
On the lower slopes of the mountain, however, reside the Gandharvas and the Kinnaras.
Indeed, gentle Vidyādharas and Kiṃpuruṣas dwell there.
On the knee-like portion of the mountain reside the Yoginīs, who are dear to Śaṅkara,
as well as the goddesses Kṛttikās, the Ābhīrāṇīs, and the Sādhvikās.
On the thigh-like slope of the mountain were indeed herds of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus),
as well as gods and divine elephants, white and possessing four excellent tusks;
likewise, lions, tigers, and divine beings who were the family members of Narasiṃha.
Celestial beings, possessing a splendor equal to the sun, dwell there moving through the sky.
(17) At the foot of Mount Raivata reside the auspicious Gopīs, the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa;
though they are divine, they indeed wander about in human form. (18)
There is the great cave of Mucukunda, which extends into the netherworld (pātāla);
there is the beautiful palace of Rādhā situated on the river Svarṇarekhā;
and indeed, it is the royal capital of kings such as Rukmāṅgada.
And there are wonders belonging to the brahmin named Patnīvratā:
where there are groves of wild mango trees, forests of *kṣīrikā* trees, and slopes of *karmada*, *ṭimburu*, and *jāmbū* trees. (1.142.21)
There are forests of golden plantains with fruits as sweet as the *sītā* fruit,
and plateaus of sugarcane with roots as sweet as sugar-candy.
In the great region called Boriyā, the goddesses bathe and dwell.
And the yoginīs roam about in the region of Nārāyaṇahrada;
the goddesses wander through the forest and at the sacred ford (tīrtha) as carriers of wood.
[They gather] the flowers of the Pārijāta, the kunda, and the kalpa trees.
In this place, forests exist that are fragrant for hundreds of yojanas;
having carried [the scent] all around by means of the wind, they create fragrant grounds.
And while there are hearths of fire that are hot, in some places there are reservoirs of cool water.
The rivers, possessing the luster of gold and silver, flow with pure waters;
they carry delightful streams whose essence is mixed with medicinal herbs.
Having drunk their waters, even men become gods and goddesses.
The kings and their womenfolk, who subsist upon that water and its medicinal herbs,
remain forever sixteen years of age, joyful and well-nourished, radiant with the mastery of their desires;
with moon-like faces, they sport about, causing one to mistake them for inhabitants of heaven.
Nowhere is there a scarcity of fruits such as the nine-colored *panasa* and others;
indeed, there are clusters upon clusters of dates, *śrīphalas*, coconut trees which are like nectar, and *āmalaka* and *triphalā* fruits. (29)
And the forests of *guṃdraka* and *iṅgudī*, of the pods, leaves, fruits, and bark [of these],
as well as the forests of trees such as bamboo, *māla*, *bilva*, and *tinduka*, and of *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, *sarja*, and *tilaka*.
There are forests of *tulasī* trees here, as well as branches of *devadāru* trees;
likewise, there are vines of grapes, betel leaves, and bitter plants.
There are also *mālatī*, *mallikā*, white jasmine, *jīvantī*, and golden creepers.
Indeed, here they shine, resplendent with an abundance of fruits, flowers, and leaves.
In every clearing, streams of water flow forth without obstruction.
Furthermore, there are goldsmiths, copper-workers, and likewise those who fashion the body and its ornaments.
There are also creepers that destroy hunger and thirst, and there are trees as well.
Divine ponds exist there; by bathing in them, one becomes invisible.
Likewise, there are ponds with golden water, from which iron becomes gold.
Leaves and grass are indeed present; even a severed body is well-sewn together.
Blood flows as a stream, and the Saṃjīvanī herb exists there.
There are likewise pools of water; having bathed therein, a woman becomes a man.

Whether one is born as a man or a woman, from that point on one’s destination is the mountain; it is not otherwise. Such efficacy is observed on Mount Raivata. By bathing in a certain pool, wings for flying arise.
Indeed, by bathing again, one's human state shall surely return to its natural condition.
By the gift of a wooden trough (*droṇī*), women become goddesses;
by the gift of a linga, men are born with perfected wombs (*siddhayoni*).
In some places, through the application of medicinal herbs, a person may take on the form of a lion;
having hunted deer and other animals, he becomes a human once again.
On that mountain, there are small pools whose waters grant the fulfillment of desires.
Whatever form one desires, that indeed arises for the bather here;
all the inhabitants there enjoy nothing less than heaven.
There are truly various forests that fulfill every desire.
The clouds there are always fruitful and possess leaves, flowers, and so forth; they dwell constantly in the middle of that region, bestowing rain upon the hips.
And at night, the lightning gradually imparts its brilliance to this [region].
In some places there, the stars remain fixed as they dwell in the sky;
there are silver mines and gold mines mixed with various minerals, as well as mines of diamonds, rubies, crystal, gems, and coral. 44–45.

Divine elixirs that extend down to the very foundations of Pātāla exist here on Mount Raivata; they are obtained by those who possess great merit. Apsarases, like those of heaven, come here to bathe and then depart.
Indeed, during the month of Kārttika, hundreds of thousands of gods, humans,
and virtuous people— both men and women— perform the great circumambulation. Even the Gaṇas and Gaṇikās attain purity through the gift of their bodies.
There is the Parīṣa lake for the bathing of the Parīs;
likewise, there is the Indrasarovara for the bathing of the goddesses. There is also the Rohas lake for the immersion of the gods.
Dātṛ-sarovara is in Droṇī for the sake of bathing for donors;
Vīra-sarovara is in Droṇī for the sake of bathing for ancestors;
and Satī-sarovara is the most excellent, for the sake of bathing for virtuous women.

On that mountain, there is the Bhaveśvara lake, which is a rejuvenating elixir containing all medicinal herbs; likewise, there are divine ponds. Rivers flow out from all sides there with inexhaustible waters.
Standing on Mount Raivata, they all behold the earth, the quarters,
the oceans, the mountains, the countries, the villages, the worlds, and the regions.
Whenever there arises a desire to go to heaven while still in the body, [then...]
Having gone to the peak of Mount Raivata, one attains perfection through bathing;
from there, one may depart and shall not fall again, provided there is no longer latent desire (vāsanā).
By merely bathing in the Gaumukhī and by immersing oneself in the water of the *kamaṇḍalu*, [one achieves this].
Indeed, by drinking a drop of water from Dattātreya, one becomes a perfected being (siddha).
Having found rest upon its peak, the planets depart for other quarters;
and the celestial chariots of the dwellers of heaven, having rested there, proceed on their way.
From that peak, people indeed travel along the paths leading to the realms of Brahmā, Īśa, Viṣṇu, and likewise to Mokṣa and Īśvara, as well as to Yama and heaven.
Having reached the place named Bhīrūvajapa, a human being—
He falls into that very forest, yet even there he attains heaven.
There, certainly, there is not even the slightest deficiency compared to heaven;
indeed, many sacred fords of the gods exist there. (56–57)

The deities, sages, seers, celestial beings, ancestors, and likewise yogis; the perfected ones (siddhas), the knowledge-holders (vidyādharas), the bards (cāraṇas), and those of divine origin—all come to perform circumambulation of Mount Raivata. (58)
Gods and Siddhas wander all around him in the forms of holy men;
and goddesses wander all around that mountain in the forms of virtuous women.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Rāmacandra, Dattātreya, and Nṛhari [reside there].
Kapila, Vāmana, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, as well as Nārada; Paraśurāma, Vyāsa, Kumāra, and even Buddha;
all [the sages] beginning with Sanandana, as well as the manifestations (vyūhas) such as Brahmā and the others.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, during the Prabodhinī festival, as long as [the rite continues],
all the gods, sacred fords (tīrthas), holy sites (kṣetras), abodes,
mountains, rivers, oceans, and likewise all lands must be honored.
They come and dwell here on the Raivata mountain at every spot;
these gods dwell in every leaf in order to perform the circumambulation.
Indeed, by him who has performed the circumambulation of the Raivata mountain at that time, [the merit is secured].

By him, indeed, has the circumambulation of the earth been performed according to the prescribed rites. (65) At that time, those humans who cause the Raivata mountain to be circumambulated are not to be regarded as mere men; rather, they are to be regarded as tens of millions of gods. (66)
By obtaining the dust of their feet, millions of births are liberated.
Whether they be children, youths, the elderly, men, or even women,
those who circumambulate Raivata at that time become purifiers, having taken refuge in Hari.
The virtuous man and the virtuous woman, the male renunciant and the female renunciant, the dispassionate one;
whether they be Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, or Goddess-worshippers, or even devotees of Gaṇeśa—those who have set out upon the path to liberation are indeed deities. (68–69)

To them indeed, whatever food, gift, clothing, or other personal possession one may have, all that should be given; through such service, it becomes a bestower of heaven. Whatever object is in front of whomsoever, that should be given to him in every way.
The virtuous and saintly ones are to be propitiated even with body, speech, and mind.
Indeed, Nārāyaṇa Hari himself bestows everything belonging to him upon the devotee who offers all his own possessions, provided that devotee is of the nature of Brahman.
Those who die at the supreme sacred site of Dāmodara, wherever that may be, indeed dwell in the abode of Hari and never again fall into worldly existence.
The first gift is the offering of oneself; the second is the offering of wealth.
The third is the field and so forth, and the fourth is one's own self-surrender.
All of this is the fruit born from circumambulating that mountain; there, sins are incinerated and indeed do not arise again. (74–75)
Whatever merit one has performed— whether called assistance to others, for one's own sake, or for the sake of others; whether pertaining to the body, the senses,
or the heart— that which leads to liberation conquers the state of being the self as Brahman, while the state of identifying with the body brings about defeat.

One who is free from doubt shall be liberated; one whose soul is consumed by doubt perishes. (77) Therefore, O Mahālakṣmī, even this mountain Raivataka is extremely pleasing to me; there I dwell as Dāmodara. (78)
I indeed dwell as Trivikrama in the temple at Rukmadurga;
I also dwell in the middle of the city in the form of Nṛsiṃha.
I am present on dry land, in trees, in flowers, in leaves, at their roots, in dust, and on mountains.
In rivers, on the earth’s surface, in wells, in ponds, in forests, and in water;
in the lotuses and lilies found there, as well as in land-lotuses, stones, crevices in the ground, anthills, trees, and thickets of shrubs. (1.142.80–81)
Wherever Raivata exists, there I dwell everywhere.
Indeed, I am the Raivata mountain; I am Raivata, there is no difference between us.
His ornament is my body; Raivata is the supreme purifier.
The messengers of Yama do not indeed behold the homes of those who dwell in Saurāṣṭra.
Having performed austerities in Ānarta, that very portion of the jewel which was obtained from Kṛṣṇa by the Kṣatriya has been established here. 83–84.
Saurāṣṭra is renowned as a place where those residing there have nothing to fear; how much less, then, can there be fear for those who have gone to this divine mountain?
For there, indeed, the minerals are red, white, blue, and likewise pale.
There are other stones shaped like elephants, made of gold and silver;
others are shaped like chickpeas, and the sands are as large as *gokṣura* seeds.
There are divine trees, creepers, shrubs, and *saṃtāna* trees. (86–87)
All gold—its root, flower, fruit, and leaf—is composed of light;
the sinful soul does not see it, but one liberated from sin beholds it.
That mountain is constantly frequented by those seeking veins of minerals and other ores.
There, people of the various castes and stages of life wander about and dwell.
There are many birds there— cranes dwelling in the sky,
cuckoos, cātaka birds, peacocks, swans, and likewise mayūraka birds.
Garudas, vultures, pigeons, far-sighted birds, ruddy geese, cocks, partridges, and other divine species—all speak auspicious words; they are ever auspicious and bringers of well-being. (91)
Deer and lords of monkeys, tigers and likewise lions,
bears and elephants, as well as divine horses and the Sātvatas—
by the power of that sacred ford, they do not behave wickedly at all.
Even beasts, birds, and reptiles that meet their death at the proper time all ascend celestial chariots and go to the abode of Viṣṇu;
as do leaves, flowers, fruits, and the like, when they fall by the force of the wind.
In that water of Svarṇarakṣā, everything indeed attains liberation.
The wife of Hari named Suvarṇā always exists in the form of a river through her fluid of love for the service of Dāmodara. ॥95-96॥
The river Suvarṇarakṣā, joined with golden sands,
shines as if it were made entirely of gold, and it turns other things into gold as well.
There, the Naga king Vāsuki, having pierced the earth, came to bathe.
Indeed, he arrived by that path through the root-opening.
And Indra, having come from heaven after performing abundant sacrifices and taking with him merit for the sake of liberation, departed for the stainless heaven.
Furthermore, those people who observe a fast for even a single day shall,
by the power of Śrī Hari, attain the abode of Hari.
Vāsudeva, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Sankarṣaṇa—
Likewise, other lords by the hundreds, lakhs, and crores indeed dwell there;
their beloveds always sport before Dāmodara—fair-complexioned women with faces like the beautiful moon, as well as dark-complexioned ones with slender waists. (10.1–10.2)
There were women with shapely hips and beautiful hair, with fine noses and long eyes;
they had graceful ankles, lovely eyebrows, beautiful waists, and full breasts.
They possessed handsome faces, shapely calves, and likewise beautiful feet, toes, and bellies.
On that mountain named Raivata, they sport and laugh.
There is the Revatī-kuṇḍa; having bathed there, a woman who gives gifts such as gold shall become possessed of sons and fortunate.
In the month of Kārtika, beautiful women who speak the local dialects remain awake before Dāmodara, repeatedly performing songs and dances;
having become embodiments of Ramā and Lakṣmī, they go to the abode of Śrī Hari.
Having constructed a beautiful and lovely temple of Hari consisting of five stones,
or having fashioned a divine pinnacle endowed with many forms,
one transcends all desires and attains the Supreme Brahman.
One should offer a five-colored banner above the house of Dāmodara;
for as many years as there are threads [in the banner], one goes to the divine realm of Viṣṇu.
Here, Vāmana shines forth in the form of Dāmodara.
His auspicious field, Vastrāpatha, measures six *gavyūtis*.
From the ascent of the mountain up to Vāmanasthalī in the west,
the intermediate region of Vastrāpatha is six *gavyūtis* in length.
King Gaya, a devotee of Hari and a follower of Viṣṇu, came there once;
together with his subjects, he performed a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
Having given many gifts and having offered oblations into the sacrificial fire, [he completed the rite].
There, in the vicinity of Mount Raivata, he performed a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
At that time, during that sacrifice, some drank smoke with their faces turned downwards;
others subsisted on dry leaves, and still others indeed lived on fruits.
Other twice-born ones were eaters of roots, while others subsisted on air;
some practiced the penance of the five fires, and some remained seated in water.
Some muttered the divine Gāyatrī, and others [muttered] Sarasvatī.
Some recite the *sūktas*, and others recite the twelve-syllable mantra;
likewise, some recite the eight-syllable mantra, while another chants "Hari.
Similarly, they observe eating once a day, eating only at night, eating unasked food, or fasting.
Having performed such meritorious deeds before Dāmodara,
they became fulfilled in that great sacrifice dedicated to Viṣṇu.
King Gaya, however, shone resplendent together with as many sages and others as were present.
Thousands upon thousands of celestial chariots arrived there;
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras came together with the attendants of Viṣṇu to lead him to Vaikuṇṭha.
Then the subjects, headed by the sages, ascended celestial chariots;
together with all his kinsmen and his wife, that king,
having mounted a celestial chariot, went to the stainless realm of Viṣṇu.
In that sacred field, Vāmana begged Bali for alms.
Such a supreme field has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again,
where liberation occurs simply by residing there, and nothing further remains to be done.
In that place there are many sacred fords (tīrthas), which I shall describe.
For a location becomes powerful through a powerful person;
therefore, O Lotus-born One, the sacred fords come there for the sake of their own purification.
"Having first recollected those [deities], I shall then describe Trivikrama.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Wondrous Majesty, Prosperity, and Splendor of Dāmodara— the Vāmana incarnation— along with the Residence of Pratāpadeva and Others on Raivatācala, the Divine Dwelling, the Kārttika Circumambulation, and Sacrifices Performed by Gaya," in the first section, the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 144 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī! He who undertakes a pilgrimage there at Vastrāpatha on the full moon day of Kārttika becomes one whose liberation is already accomplished. 1.
In Dāmodara, the auspicious river named Svarṇarakṣā is proclaimed;
there is the Brahmakuṇḍa holy site, as well as Śiva as Brahmeśvara. Kālamegha is also proclaimed there, as are Bhava and Dāmodara.

Two *gavyūtis* away, upon the summit of Mount Kālika, is Indreśvara in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest), near Bhava, at Mṛgīkuṇḍa. In the Kṛta age, the sacred site was Sāraṇika; in the Tretā age, it was Hemamāraka.
To the west lies the field called Unnabīla, extending for a distance of one yojana.
There are many sacred sites there, including sixteen places of spiritual accomplishment (siddhasthāna).
Among them is the Sūryakuṇḍa tīrtha, as well as Gaṅgeśa and Maṅgala.
The great god Siddheśvara is one *gavyūti* to the west of the city.
At Indreśvara is Cakratīrtha; Hāṭakeśa is to the west, and beyond that is the great goddess Yakṣeśvarī, followed by a mountain.
Somaliṅga is the central region where there are numerous sacred fords (tīrthas).
There, at that very spot, is the footprint of Gajendra and the well of nectar (rasakūpikā).
There are also a hundred ponds (kuṇḍas) there, and Ambikā resides upon the peak.
Pradyumna, as well as Sāmba and Gorakṣaka;
Gaṇeśa, Hanumān, and Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Mādhava—
they dwell in the midst of the forest, and the forests are named after each of them.
Bhava arrived there, and I shall relate this story:
once, on a beautiful peak of Kailāsa, in the presence of Śiva, the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the others—quickly came to that place. (11)
Viṣṇu spoke to that Śambhu, who was granting boons to the Daityas:
"O Maheśvara, I am not able to protect [the world] while you grant so many boons to the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas. (12–13)
"Later they will undergo transformation and become difficult for me to slay.
Then Śambhu said, "If I do not grant you this boon,
then by their ascetic power the Daityas will surely reduce everything to ashes."
"I have been appointed by you, O Brahmā, and by the gods, for the granting of boons.
This, however, is my own nature; how can I bring myself to abandon it?
By whatever means possible, O Lord, the subjects must be protected by you. (15–16)
My act of granting this boon must be forgiven; it shall indeed yield great fruit.
O Śrī Hari, O Viṣṇu, who else indeed could be the destroyer of the Daityas except for you?
For they have been empowered by me or even by Brahmā through the granting of boons.

Whether they be Daityas, Dānavas, or even Rākṣasas—whosoever they may be—they must be slain by you through strategic means; otherwise, no success will be achieved. Your offense must be forgiven, for you are an ocean of compassion.
Jālandhara, Hiraṇyākṣa, and likewise Hiraṇyakaśipu,
as well as other preeminent among the Asuras, were slain by you alone through your strategic skill. No one else knows such a strategy as you do.
"But we are the bestowers of boons upon them, and you are their bringer of peace.
Thus was the great wheel of saṃsāra set in motion by us;
it continues to turn in that very same way. Forgive this, O Puruṣottama.
I wander manifest, and for that reason the deities and the Daityas come to me in order to obtain boons; thereafter, I become unmanifest.
Protect the goddess Pārvatī, and I shall go to an unknown place.
Having said this, Mahādeva vanished right there.
Abandoning Kailāsa, he went to Mount Raivata;
leaving behind his two divine garments, he stationed himself in the midst of the mountains.
Having abandoned and left behind the invincible elephant of beautiful form,
Śambhu, having pierced the surface of the earth, became manifest in the form of Sthāṇu.
Since he himself came into being, the Lord of Existence (Bhaveśvara) is himself Śiva.
The Self-Existent One was indeed born as Bhava in the lake of Bhaveśvara.
In the meantime, on Kailāsa, they did not see Śaṅkara;
then the gods set forth, placing Gaurī at their head.
All the gods, beginning with Nandibhadra and likewise Indra and the others,
as well as the Goddess herself mounted upon a lion, went forth together with her son;
and the eternal Viṣṇu, having mounted Garuḍa, departed.
The Blessed Lord Brahmā, mounted upon a swan, follows behind.
The King of the Gods himself has gone forth, having ascended Airāvata;
as have the goddesses Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Yamunā, and Śaradvatī.
All the deities, nāgas, yakṣas, and kinnaras arrived;
having ascended the mountain peak, Ambādevī took her stand there.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise the gods searched for the Lord.
They beheld Maheśvara upon the low ground of the pond.
[33] "For what purpose and in what manner have the gods and others arrived here?
I must dwell right here, assuming the beautiful form of Bhava. [34]
"O sirs, if you gods and rivers are satisfied to be servants,
then Viṣṇu, Ambā, and all others shall be the carriers here on Mount Raivataka.
Let even the lions and other beasts remain here as if Kailāsa itself were present."
Suvarṇā, the wife of the Blessed One, is considered the river Svarṇarekhā.
May the Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and others dwell there forever.
On the mountain she is Svarṇarakṣā, but on earth she is Svarṇarekhā. (6–37)

Thus, Śambhu known as Bhaveśa, Viṣṇu himself as Dāmodara, and Brahmā as Svayaṃbhū are present there; and Indra is stationed at Indreśvara. Other various [deities] are established here and there according to their respective natures.
Therefore, this great sacred ford is the deliverer from the cycle of death.
Having performed the destruction of the Daityas there for many nights, Hari,
that ocean of compassion, returns and indeed bestows rest upon them.
Viṣṇu sported on Mount Raivataka until the dissolution of all beings;
having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu and gone to Mount Raivata,
he mounted the auspicious Śarabha and released the Nārasiṃha form.
Having likewise slain Hiraṇyākṣa and gone to the Raivataka mountain,
the Lord indeed leaped upon a tiger in the forest and released the boar;
having made the earth level, Pṛthu dwelt on the Raivataka mountain.
The *jayamālā* was placed by Pṛthu upon the shoulder of Dāmodara.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a killer of an embryo, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—
by bathing in the Svarṇarakṣa water, one is liberated from all sins.
By the sight of Bhava, Āmodara, and Ambā, one goes to that abode.
Vāmana, having obtained Bali and conquered him, remained on Raivataka;
leaving Mount Kailāsa along with the Goddess and the assembled gods. ||45–46||
O Lakṣmī! On the fifteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha, Bhava emerged after piercing the earth;
on that very same day, Vāsuki obtained the path that destroys all sins from the waters of the Svarṇa-rakṣā river.
The great mountain Ūrjayanta was trampled by the foot of Airāvata. Pure water, produced by the elephant’s foot, flowed forth in many streams.
O Padmaja, hear now the measurement of the sacred field of Vastrāpatha. 48–49.
As Hara was wandering upon the earth, his garment and ornaments fell;
that very extent of land was made into Vastrāpatha by the gods.
To the north is the Bhadrā river, and to the east is Kuṅkumavāpikā.
To the south, along the river Ūrjayantī, is the abode of Bali;
to the west, between the two rivers before Vāmana, is the confluence.
This is the field of Vastrapatha, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The width of the field should be known as four yojanas,
and the length of the field is considered to be twelve yojanas.
Moving step by step, he proceeds while rolling on the ground like a staff.
Or, one might traverse a distance equal to the length of a staff while carrying dust;
having ruled the earth with its seven oceans,
he then proceeds to the abode of Hari with a divine body, seated in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) possessing a hundred stories.
Having bound his arms or having slowly bound his feet,
a man should go in silence to Dāmodara, the Lord of Bhava;
he shall be liberated from all sins and shall indeed attain liberation at the end.
In the great field of Vastrāpatha, at the city of Vāmanasthala, the venerable Vasiṣṭha came there to perform austerities;
he went to the waters of the Svarṇarekhā river in the northeast corner of the city. (57–58)
When the sage, having bathed and meditated upon the god Hari, prostrated himself,
then Hari and Hara arrived there and said to him:
"Indeed, you have remained here for a hundred years engaged in terrible austerity."

"O Great Sage, since we are pleased with you, tell us what you wish to request. Vasiṣṭha replied: "O Lords of the Gods, if a boon is to be granted to me, then you two should remain right here as long as the moon and stars exist."
May my vision and service be yours both at all times. Furthermore,
for those sinful people here who drink the water or even rest for a moment,
there shall be a dissolution of their sins.
Thus, this sacred ford (tīrtha) shall forever be renowned by the name Vāsiṣṭha.
Having uttered the words "So be it," the two gods remained there in part,
in the city of Svarṇadurga, on the northern bank of the Kṛṣṇā.
The Sudarśana discus was indeed dispatched for the destruction of the Daitya Dātā; having burnt that asura, it returned.
Then, Hari Nārāyaṇa reached his place of rest.
There, the god Trivikrama and Śaṅkara as Siddheśvara,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhā, Gaṇeśa, and likewise Hanumān,
as well as other gods, arrived out of a desire to behold Nārāyaṇa. (66–67)
The pure mountain-dwellers, traveling along the most auspicious path,
beheld those gods who had arrived there with divine vision.
Those gods were worshipped by those foremost among devotees, the Sāttvatas.
Thus honored, the gods were pleased and spoke to them:
"We are satisfied by your devotion; tell us what you require.
Then they said to the gods: "If a boon is to be granted," [1.143.70]

May the mountain-dwellers as well as those who live in the forests dwell here in this place for the welfare of embodied beings; through the sight of you, they shall indeed attain liberation. Therefore, please grant that boon.
Having granted the boon, saying "So be it," they remained in the temple with their partial manifestations (aṃśas).
It was built here by King Suvarṇasiṃha, being most magnificent,
adorned with golden domes and golden doors and seats.
Upon a floor fashioned from red, yellow, white, and blue jewels,
and within a circular enclosure of walls and well-constructed stairways made of crystal and other precious stones—
those people who come here and perform acts such as gazing [upon it], [shall attain merit]. (74)

For those people who shall perform charity, meritorious acts, recitation, fire-offerings, libations for virtuous men and women, ancestral rites, festivals, and divine worship, their merit shall be infinite. This applies as well to those who perform the concluding ceremonies (*udyāpana*) and the restoration of dilapidated structures (*jīrṇoddhāra*). (75–76)
Those who shall offer food oblations, gifts of fruit and the like, service to the virtuous with wealth and other means, and even with their own bodies, will go to the imperishable state.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Causes for the Dwelling of Various Tīrthas, Bhava-Īśvara, Dāmodara, Svayaṃbhū, Trivikrama, Vāsiṣṭha, Svarṇarakṣa, and Others in Raivata-Vastrāpatha," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. Chapter 143.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
For the sake of uplifting the world, I dwell in sacred pilgrimage sites;
yet I abide everywhere as well, for the purpose of acting as the inner controller (antaryāmin).
In every form, I am always present for the sake of accepting service;
I dwell in those various places here for the sake of affection toward my devotees.
Sometimes, due to the insistence of a devotee, or else by reason of my own resolve.
In some places I dwell here and there due to the necessity of certain tasks.
(3) Indeed, throughout the western region of Bhārata as far as the ocean, there exists no other divine holy site equal to Mount Raivata. (4)
In that very place, in the southern forest, is the abode of Somanātha; in the northern Golden City (Svarṇanagara) is the abode of Anādikṛṣṇa;
and in the east, at Kuṅkumavāpī, is the abode of Gopālakṛṣṇa.
In the west, at Vāmanasthalī, I abide as Trivikrama.
Thus, I dwell everywhere in that region, at every sacred spot;
indeed, in the great capital city, I abide as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
In every corner [of the world], I dwell for the sake of uplifting the people;
yet at the end of the age, my palaces shift here and there.
Those that have decayed dissolve away, while new ones are constructed.
Just as they become my devotees, so do I manifest myself again.
There is no end to my divine abodes according to the divisions of the ages;
those very lands shall be mine, and I shall indeed be present there as well.
Due to the excellence of the priest’s asceticism, the power of the devotee’s devotion,
and the extreme beauty of the forms, I abide as if visibly present.
Having observed Bali’s devotion as well as Kaśyapa’s asceticism, [I appeared].
Though tall, I dwelt indeed upon Mount Raivata, having become a dwarf. Kaśyapa performed most formidable penance on the riverbank,
to the north of Ojasvatī, surrounded by mango trees.
Having drunk the water of the Ūrjayantī there for a thousand years in a secluded place where Vāmanasthalī is situated,
Hari himself appeared before Kaśyapa and Aditi for the sake of a son.
Having been propitiated and adopted as a son, I therefore became Vāmana.
O Lakṣmī, listen as I tell you the reason for that which is in my mind:
after slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Lord himself became Nṛsiṃha. (15–16)
He gave the three worlds to Indra and the regions beginning with Atala to Prahlāda.
In due time, Prahlāda, the foremost of the Sātvatas, attained the abode of Hari.
The excellent son of Prahlāda was known as Virocana.
Having ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years, he indeed went to heaven.
His son was the mighty-armed Bali, the best among the Sātvatas;
he was true to his promise, most righteous, devoted, and the dearest to Hari.
Having conquered the world-protectors and the guardians of the quarters on all sides,
and having brought the three worlds under his own control, King Bali became the lord of the three worlds. With his great strength, Bali made the earth subject to a single umbrella.
The earth yields crops without being ploughed, bestowing abundant grain and fruit.
(21) The flowers are fragrant and the fruits are succulent;
the trees bear fruit up to their very branches, and there is honey in every leaf-cup. (22)
While Bali rules the kingdom, all cows yield milk at will;
all men are devoted to their own duties and are free from sin.
Indeed, the subjects of Viṣṇu constantly worship Hṛṣīkeśa.
Indra and the other thirty gods stood before him as his servants.
Arrogant in his strength, he enjoyed sovereignty over the three worlds.
In his kingdom, the twice-born who were masters of the four Vedas performed sacrifices and other rites.
The Kṣatriyas were devoted to protection and were experts in the meaning of the treatises on warfare;
the Vaiśyas were intent on service to the cattle; and the Śūdras delighted in performing service.
Freed from the sufferings of poverty and death, they lived for a long time.
Since the light of jewel-lamps exists there even at night as if it were day, all the family members are joyful and happy with their desired objects;
and the sacrificial pavilions constantly resound with the booming of wedding instruments. (27–28)
The gods were satisfied by the sacrifice; hence there was no mutual conflict. Even among the animals, birds, and other creatures, there was no strife born of rivalry.
The entire world, both mobile and immobile, had come to a state of friendliness.
At that time, however, Nārada saw no war anywhere in the three worlds.
Just then, a great pain arose within his belly.
[He thought: "What is the use of libations, ritual bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, and the like? (3.1)
That is my beloved bath where elephants fight with the clashing of their tusks;
where the twilight is crimsoned by the blood of headless trunks, making the earth pale-red;
and where the flesh-eaters find satisfaction—that is my dear libation.

O Pūjā, Kṣatriyas are slain in battle by the floods of Kṣatriya weapons. That is my sacrifice where these bulls among men are offered as oblations. Without war, the three worlds appear empty to me every day. (33–34)
"I shall do so, but a conflict with Indra will arise.
Having reflected thus, Nārada went quickly toward Indra.
Indra saw Nārada approaching, remaining indifferent.
Leaving his lion-throne and rising, Hari stood before him;
having greeted him with a welcome, he then spoke to Nārada:
"O great sage, are you well today? From where have you come?"
"Is he indeed skilled in bathing, congregational worship, and fire-offerings?
When asked thus, Nārada laughed and then spoke to him:
"As long as Bali remains a great universal emperor, all-pervading..."
"In that regard, what merit do I possess? I ask you that as well, though it may be false.
However, if there is indeed merit for me, it should be asked whether I shall behold the victory of the gods in battle, as well as the downfall of Bali."
All the planets, beginning with the Sun, being joined together, offer tribute to Bali;
likewise, through Bali’s sacrifices, the clouds rain down oblations upon the earth.
There is no disease nor death; what, then, is the purpose of Yama?
The Lord of the three worlds, the great Indra, the guardian of the quarters and protector of the world—[such is Bali].
Even humans praise you today as the sovereign of the gods;
yet the lords of the Daityas laugh at you and speak disparagingly of the powerless gods.
Having brought the golden earth entirely under his control,
Bali himself did not consider you to be the Lord of the Gods at all.
All the gods were subservient to Bali, being well-fed by the offerings of Bali’s sacrifice.
Rambhā stands at the head of the offering; Menakā does not even think of you.
Tilottamā goes toward Bali, as does Urvaśī, who is under Bali's sway.
Sukeśī and Manjughoṣā always gaze upon Bali.
Pulomā does not experience a thrill of horripilation without Bali;
Paulomī praises Bali and the heavens always bow to Bali.
Nārada, Parvata, Hāhā, Hūhū, and Tumburu likewise [do so].
They praise the kingdom of Bali; what need is there for you?
That which Bṛhaspati declares must not be spoken by me to you.
But Indrāṇī, regarding Bali as Indra, beholds him every morning.
Having heard this, Mahendra, his mind ablaze with anger, said to his two charioteers: "Bring the elephant and the thunderbolt quickly;
likewise, make the chariot ready with Sūrya, Rudra, Yama, and Vāyu."
"Let the war-drums be sounded; let the warriors march forth with haste!
Seeing Indra thus enraged, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati said:
"Bali is to be conquered by means such as conciliation (sāma), and not otherwise."
"Let them summon Viṣṇu, the protector of gods and asuras, upon whom the entire world depends; let them deliberate and carry out what is beneficial for him.
Or rather, Viṣṇu is already present on Mount Mandara for the sake of this task."
"Let us go there, O sages, together with Indra and preceded by Brahmā.
Gautama, Atri, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, the Bālakhilyas, and Nārada [shall go]. (54–55)
Then Viṣṇu, Hari, having seen all the dwarf Bālakhilyas who were no larger than the joint of a thumb,
laughed due to the power of what was destined to happen.
Then all the Bālakhilyas spoke loudly among themselves:
"Because you laugh at us, you shall indeed become a dwarf (vāmana).
After accomplishing the work of the gods on Mount Raivata at Vastrāpatha,
you will cast off your dwarfish form and dwell as Dāmodara."
Thus addressed by the Bālakhilyas, Viṣṇu offered them a welcome.
Indra declared that the sovereignty over the three worlds was extremely difficult for Bali to endure;
yet, having been brought under control by Bali, the Daityas were made partakers of the sacrifices.
"Therefore, let Bali, fallen from his kingdom, dwell in Pātāla;
let some king of the solar or lunar lineage rule upon the earth.
Having heard this, Hari himself said, "I shall do so."
"Let the sages go there and perform the great sacrifice;
I shall arrive there and accomplish that offering.
Having been thus addressed, all the sages then departed for their respective abodes.
Waiting for the right time, they awaited the birth of Hari.
And Kaśyapa, seeing that his son Indra had been deprived of his kingdom,
performed austerities consisting of a milk-diet together with the Ādityas in Saurāṣṭra.
They worshipped Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, Padmanābha;
meanwhile, their bodies there were covered with ants,
and a great radiance then pervaded Saurāṣṭra on all sides.
The people, however, were struck with wonder and praised them again and again.
At the end of a thousand years, Hari, the eternal one, being pleased by their ascetic penance,
appeared right there together with his Goddess.
Having seen that lotus-eyed one, who bears the conch, discus, and mace; who is dark as the petal of a blue lotus and adorned with all ornaments;
and who is endowed with a crown, necklace, armlets, earrings, and chains— 68.

With a heart overflowing with joy, Kaśyapa praised Hari, the Lord of the Universe— He who wears yellow garments, whose chest is marked by the Śrīvatsa and adorned with the Kaustubha gem and necklaces, who is joined by Lakṣmī, who is seated upon Garuḍa, and who is gracious. (1.144.70)

Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of All, Sovereign of the World! Salutations to the bestower of happiness upon those who take refuge in you, who accomplishes the tasks of your devotees.
Salutations to you whose eternal form is devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
Salutations to the one who provides protection everywhere, whose eyes are the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, who are subtle yet possess a gross form. Salutations to you, the Supreme Self, who are filled with auspicious qualities.
Salutations to You, who are accessible to yogis, who fulfill the desires of Your devotees, who possess the singular enjoyment of eternal liberation, and who are the Lord of the supreme abode.
Salutations to You, the fourfold self; salutations to You, whose nature is the cosmic manifestation (vyūha).
Salutations to the one whose nature consists of five times five, who performs the five purificatory rites.
Salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Vāsudeva;
salutations to you, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the universal form, the creator, and the protector.
Salutations to you, Viṣṇu, the Victorious One, who are of pure essence;
O Mādhava, destroy that great strength which has arisen in Bāli.
It is my prayer that the gods may then be happy.
Although this King Bali is a devotee who assembles the gods,
O Mādhava, let there be no transgression against the gods by the Daitya;
therefore, let the sovereignty over the three worlds always remain with Indra alone.
"Let the kingdom of the Asuras and Pātāla and so forth belong to Bali;
whatever you desire, that is what I am to be requested for—do as you wish.
Having spoken thus before Hari, Kaśyapa then became silent.
Aditi, having bowed to and praised the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign of the Universe, said:
"O Protector, if the authority to rule over the gods were to belong to the Asuras, then there would be no purpose whatsoever in the great number of our sons. (8.1–8.2)
If jackals and crows were the manifestations of Your majesty, O Lord, then what would be the use of the lion or the swan? Indeed, what would Your greatness be [then]?
If the Daityas, who are sovereign rulers, were Your brothers and Your servants; [what then of Your power]?
"Enough then with life, with your speech, and with your splendor!
(84) If you, though a Daitya, were to possess such great sovereignty, then enough of the Blessed One; indeed, the Daitya would become Mādhava! (85)
Therefore, prosperity should indeed be bestowed according to the capacity of the recipient, and not otherwise.
If an iron ornament placed around the neck shines with a radiant form, then gold has been made in vain;
for the creation of refined gold was indeed purposeless.
If Indra were to become a Daitya, then the Asuras would indeed be rendered useless;
if the mothers of kings and the Rākṣasīs were to become Indrāṇī, then she would likewise be surpassed.
What need is there for much speaking, O Lord Keśava? Establish a proper order!
Thus entreated, the Supreme Lord, the Consort of Śrī, spoke to them for the sake of granting a boon; then Kaśyapa spoke to him:
"O Lord of Gods, having attained the state of being my son, which is beneficial to the thirty deities..."
"O younger brother of Indra, become Upendra, my beloved;
by whatever means possible, having effortlessly conquered Bali,
give the three worlds to the god Śakra and bring him happiness."
Thus addressed by that brahmin, Janārdana said, "So be it.
Aditi and Kaśyapa honored him greatly.
While being praised by the gods, Śrī Hari vanished from sight.
Then Aditi and Kaśyapa went to the Middle Country;
they dwelt for some time on the land of the Himalayas.
At that very time, of the high-souled Kaśyapa... [93–94]
The blessed Mādhava himself entered the womb of Aditi;
that deity manifested with a body three fingers in height.
At ten years of age, he became one whose body was a span in length.

At that time, Aditi spoke to Kaśyapa, her beloved as her own life:
"Bali, having indeed conquered the gods with his army, will seize our prosperity.
What should be done? My son is still only the size of a span."
"Protection for him is difficult to find; how indeed could it be provided even by the gods?
Let it be as it must be, whatever is destined to happen; Hari will provide protection.
Having heard these piteous words of his mother, Guptamādhava [replied]. (1.144.100)
Then, within her auspicious body the size of a span,
she displayed to her mother infinite millions of cosmic eggs of creation, each as subtle as an atom; indeed,
these cosmic eggs, complete with their seven coverings, were seen to fly upward.
Therein are shown the Lokāloka mountain, Meru, and other mountains;
as well as rivers, oceans, the lunar mansions, planets, and stars; clouds, forests, the netherworlds (pātāla), and the dwellings of those [beings]. (102–103)
Indeed, all the various high and low terrains were shown to him;
there was the Snowy Mountain, its forests, and there was Kaśyapa,
as well as Aditi herself, and Kṛṣṇa, whose form was only a span in height.

having manifested that body of his as exceedingly long,
he then became two spans in height, vanishing from that place in an instant.
Then, when this vision had arisen, there was indeed consolation for his parents:
"When the time arrives, he shall become the remover of the fear of the gods.
Thereafter, at sixteen years of age, he was only the size of a hand.

He possessed golden lines upon his eyes, was resplendent with the Kaustubha gem, and had a beautiful head with a mass of glossy hair like a cloud edged in gold. His eyes resembled lotus petals, and his face shone with the brilliance of the moon. (108–109)
His body was perfectly mature yet tender;
in his hand he held a small parasol, a staff with a jeweled pommel,
and an auspicious garland made of white gems that rested upon his palm.
On his forehead was an upright *puṇḍra* mark of sandalwood and a crescent-shaped spot of saffron;
on his shoulder was a small, golden-colored sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*);
on his head was a cloth of red wool, and on his chest was the Kaustubha gem. || 11.1–12 ||
A white upper garment with golden borders and a bodice;
around her waist, a beautiful, soft, and moist girdle made of muñja grass;
yellow garments, a golden complexion, and sandals adorned with gold.
In his hand is a wooden water-pot and ropes made of cotton;
in his hand is the manuscript of the Puruṣa-Nārāyaṇa-Sūkta;
and for the purpose of worship, a bamboo vessel strung together shines in his hand.
Having placed his seat and deer-skin at his parents' feet and bowed at their feet, and having received their blessings for victory at the auspicious moment of Abhijit,
Acyuta departed from that place for the purpose of his journey.
Then that King Bali, having conquered the earth as well as heaven,
returned to the beautiful land associated with Mount Raivata;

Having beheld the mango grove, the powerful river, the land of beautiful foliage, and the entire comfort of shade provided by trees on both water and land,

That region where the pit was dug became renowned as Balikhāta. Having had that ground prepared and constructed a sacrificial pavilion,
he commenced a great twelve-day sacrifice accompanied by all the prescribed priestly fees.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārāyaṇa’s Residence at a Holy Tīrtha, the Praise of Bali’s Virtues, Nārada’s Departure for Indra, the Counsel for Bali’s Fall, the Austerities of Kaśyapa and Aditya in Saurāṣṭra, the Attainment of Boons from Nārāyaṇa, the Birth of Vāmana, Bali’s Conquest of the Quarters, and the Commencement of Bali’s Sacrifice in Saurāṣṭra," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (Chapter 144, Book 1: The Continuity of the Kṛta Yuga).

those who know the terrestrial sphere, those who know the celestial sphere, the astrologers, and likewise the mathematicians; as well as the auspicious moments (muhūrtas) and all the astrological conjunctions (yogas)—they all arrived.

Mountains of clarified butter, coconut, plantain, grapes, and other fruits;

Harītakīs, kandarālās, vaṭas, and aṭarūṣakas;

Listen, Lakṣmī, to my wondrous account of the Dwarf’s appearance.
Having seen him, who was distinct from all others, curiosity arose within me. (1) A great clamor broke out: "Someone very short has arrived!"
In appearance and splendor equal to Viṣṇu,
he remained there, assuming a disguise and reciting the Vedas along with many Brahmins.
When Daitya youths entered and saw him, they reported it to the Daitya king.
"This dwarf Brāhmaṇa has indeed come to witness the sacrifice.
Delighted, Bali spoke these words: "This is truly the dawning of my good fortune;
the desireless Lord Vāmana asks for nothing at all."
"I shall worship this best of Brahmins and give him whatever he desires.
Viṣṇu himself has arrived as a guest; to him, one should give whatever he wishes.
One vessel is composed of Vedic knowledge, and another vessel is composed of austerity."
The worthy recipient, having arrived, will take away my offering.
While the sacrifice is underway, a sacrificial fee must be given by me;
indeed, this is my final sacrifice, which completes the full thousand.
In this matter, one's entire possession should be given to beggars without hesitation.
A hundred sacrifices are considered necessary for the attainment of Indra’s station,
while the attainment of the supreme station of Brahmā (Pārameṣṭhipada) occurs through a thousand sacrifices.
Therefore, let this great sacrifice not suffer the corruption of the syllable "na.
Indeed, one must give, one must give, one must give under all circumstances.
The word "no" must never be uttered regarding the body, one's wife, or one's children.
"I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose; my life is fruitful.
Having seated him upon a seat of flowers according to the prescribed rite, he prostrated himself, paid his respects, and spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
"O best of Brahmins, having worshipped you, what dear service may I perform for you?
O foremost of the twice-born,
tell me quickly, O best among the knowers of the Vedas, the purpose for which you have come to me."
Hrasva, with a joyful mind, spoke to that lord of the earth:
"O Lord of Daityas, give me the ground of the fire-pit;
you ought to grant me the earth measured by my three strides."
Of all gifts, the gift of land is the most excellent. O King, he who gives even a piece of land the size of a thumb to a destitute Brahmin shall indeed become a lord of the earth.
In this world, no benefactor is found equal to the giver of land.
(17) He who accepts land and he who bestows land—both of them are performers of meritorious deeds and are destined for heaven. (18)
Therefore, O Great King, grant me a three-footed plot of ground.
O Lord of the Earth, do not hesitate to give this small amount of land.
O King, it shall be known as the "Gift of the Three Worlds."
Then, with a joyful heart, the lord of the earth said, "So be it.
He intended to perform the gift of the earth to him according to the prescribed rites;
however, at that moment, his preceptor Śukra restrained Bali.
"O King, let another gift indeed be given; let not the earth be given.
But hear this other thing, O King: you are performing an improper act.
Those twice-born ones who are worthy of honor should be honored externally, as should the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others. (22)
The deaf, the dwarfs, the hunchbacks, the maimed, the crippled, and the cruel—
these eunuchs do not deserve worship at the edge of the sacrificial pit.
A dwarf should be worshipped with gold, silver, and garments, but only outside [the sacred area].
The birth of four types of people is in vain, and sixteen kinds of gifts are likewise in vain:
the birth of those without sons is in vain; the birth of those who are unrighteous is in vain;
the birth of those who subsist on the food of others is in vain; and the birth of those who consort with the wives of others is in vain.
A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin is fruitless, as is a gift to one who is unmarried,
to an outcast, to a Brahmin who neglects the twilight prayers, to a crooked man, to a thief,
to one who causes displeasure to his guru, or to one who has turned his back on his father and mother. (26–27)
To a mere nominal Brahmin, to an ungrateful person, to a seller of the Vedas,
to a beggar in one's own village, to one conquered by women, to the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī),
to a snake-catcher, and to a slanderer— these are the sixteen for whom gifts are in vain.
In the meantime, Bali said: "O Preceptor, you should not speak thus.
Whoever studies the Vedas is, in my view, equal to Viṣṇu.
No delay should be made when a learned Vedic scholar has arrived at one's home. (1.146.30)
With rising from one's seat, with words of welcome, and by washing his feet,
a householder should provide food according to his ability.
When Vāmana departs unperturbed from the sacrificial pavilion—
Then this sacrifice, in which one's entire possession is given as the sacrificial fee, goes to waste.
Therefore, [conceal] this twice-born man, Vāmana, who is the very form of Viṣṇu—
though his body is manifest, tawny, and resembling the sun.
"I shall indeed grant him whatever he desires; what does he not wish for?
Blessed am I, for in my sacrifice a twice-born one equal to Viṣṇu has arrived.
Thinking thus, he offered him the sixteen types of service.
He quickly offered him the madhuparka and a cow.
Having smelled the madhuparka, the cow, having been saluted by [Vāmana] with a low bow,
and Vāmana himself, having paid homage to the sacrifice and all those present at the sacrifice, departed.
"I have come as a seeker; tell me, O Bali, what shall be given?
O Lord of Daityas, grant me three paces of land for the sake of my dwelling, and having constructed a divine cottage, I shall teach my disciples. (37)
"Three steps have been granted to you," Vāmana said.
"Do not give [any more]," Śukra replied. "This is the eternal Viṣṇu.
Then Bali said to Śukra: "What could be a greater recipient than this? || 38-39 ||
Having placed the sacrificial grass (darbha) with grains of rice in his right hand, Bali performed the ritual;
yet the Guru neither executed the formal procedure nor poured water into his hand.
The members of the assembly, the Hotṛ priests, and likewise the ṛṣis were filled with wonder.
The Brahmins, the gods, the worlds, and the Daityas are his family members.
When it is said, "It has been given; it has been accepted," why does he not release the water?
Water is offered into the hand for the sake of Vāmana, for the sake of auspiciousness.
That gift which is given only in words but not followed by action casts the giver into hell and destroys his family.
Uśanas said this to the lord of the Daityas: "This Vāmana is Hari."
This Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord Hari, having been entreated by the gods, has come here by some stroke of fate to see you;
he has come to this place to deceive the entire earth and to obtain [her] from you. (44–45)
I do not know whether he will do something unpleasant or even pleasant;
therefore, O King, this earth must not be given to that great-souled one.
Accept some other object instead, at my word, O Lord of the Earth.
Then, laughing, that king spoke to his preceptor with composure:
"I know, by the power of destiny and likewise through the grace of Viṣṇu, that the sacrifice shall reach completion; it will indeed be made complete by the twice-born."
"I am Indra, a twice-born brahmin, and Viṣṇu; my substance is the deity Āditya.
Therefore, why should I not give this to Viṣṇu so that he may be pleased?
Having said this, Bali poured water into the hand of Vāmana.
"Hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ! O King, what is this being done? It is certainly not appropriate.
Having spoken thus, Śukra then stood outside the pavilion, saying:
"For the pleasure of Vāsudeva, every meritorious act has been performed by me."
"Today I am blessed, for Viṣṇu has come here in person. To him must be given today my very life and great happiness;
therefore, I shall certainly grant him even the three worlds. (52)
Having led [him] around, paid homage, and devoutly washed his feet,
Bali placed the nectar of those feet upon his own mouth and head with a joyful heart; then, having indeed bestowed the gift of wealth as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), [he departed].
"I am blessed; I have fulfilled my purpose," he said then after giving the earth.
"O best of Brahmins, take this earth as you desire.
Whether you wish for a kingdom, gold, or diamonds and the like."
And various kinds of jewels, hundreds of male and female slaves, wealth in cattle, and other things besides— palaces,
mansions, and vehicles— I give these to you if you so desire. (56–57)
"O Lord of Gods, I give myself as the king's wife, and whatever sons, grandsons, and so forth I possess—all that which belongs to me, I offer for your sake.
Even through penance performed over infinite births, the Supreme Person is not attained. (58)
"If he has been obtained through my compassion, what need have I for wives, wealth, and other such things?
Having spoken thus, the devoted Bali prostrated at the feet of Vāmana.
Vāmana said: "O lord of devotees, everything is contained within three paces. (1.146.60)
"O King, I am pleased with your devotion;
today, in your very presence, I shall measure out the earth with a single step while you look on.
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord cast off that form of a young brahmin boy.
Vāmana grew exceedingly large, assuming a four-armed form.
Seeing Hari increasing in size, the brahmins, sages,
and gods praised the Lord Janārdana, who had appeared in the sky.
Victory to you, Viṣṇu! Victory to you, Viṣṇu! Victory to you, O bestower of grace upon devotees!
Victory to you, the Short One! Victory to you, the Long One! Victory to you, the mendicant Vāmana!
Victory to you, the performer of grace for the gods! Victory to you, who are accessible to the devotee!
Victory to the sacrifice, victory to the oblation, victory to the fire, victory to the Infallible One!
Victory to You, the seeker, the giver, and the leader; victory to You whose form creates the universe!
Victory to You, O Fish; obeisance to You; victory to You, O Tortoise, the upholder of the earth!
Victory to You who assume the form of the Boar! Salutations be unto You, O Nṛsiṃha!
Victory to Kṛṣṇa! Victory to the glorious Nārāyaṇa! Salutations be unto You!
(67) Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd son of Kambharā; salutations again and again!
Salutations to you who are known as Patnīvrata, salutations to you, the Lord of Lakṣmī!
That which has been described in many ways in the scriptures but was never seen before, is now beheld by those dwelling upon the fourteen worlds through a mere fraction of your grace. (68–69)
Having seen that great Vairāja form of yours, we are delighted and delivered;
those yogis, Sanaka and the others,
praise Janārdana as Kṛṣṇa ascends to the midpoint of the sky before the city of Bali, his power increasing.
All stood with their faces turned upward, gazing at him who had gone to heaven.
The umbrella, the staff, the deerskin, the water-pot, and the sandals—
all these that had been before Hari increased in size along with him.
First appearing in the form of an umbrella, Hari then ascended upwards;
the sun shone like a crest-jewel upon the head of Hari.
Thereafter, it grew further until it appeared as a tilaka-mark upon his forehead.
Moreover, Hari, having grown, acts like the sun with his earrings;
having risen high, Hari therefore acts like the sun with his *kaustubha* gem.
Having gone forward, Mahendra placed a forest garland around his neck. (74–75)
The earth trembles from the weight [of his strides], and the host of planets situated in heaven shall meet their destruction;
terrified, those Daityas behold Vāmana.
Yet Kṛṣṇa continued to grow, and the sun-like lotus extended to his navel.

Madhusūdana, the Supreme Person, grasped with a single foot the earth— extending fifty crores [of yojanas], together with its oceans and mountains, its seas and islands, and including gods, asuras, and humans. (77–78)
O lotus-born one, having stepped across the entire earth,
that auspicious foot became an extra [span] extending for a hundred yojanas.
The Eternal One granted divine vision to that lord of the Daityas.
Having beheld that universal form of the God, Bali, the lord of the Daityas,
attained incomparable joy, his eyes overflowing with tears of bliss;
and having seen the God, he paid homage and praised him with hymns of praise.
With a voice faltering and with a heart full of joy, he said:
"I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose by beholding you, the Supreme Lord.
O Supreme Lord, accept these three worlds yourself. (82)

Then Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, the Infallible One, extended his second foot upwards as far as the world of Brahmā. O lady of auspicious countenance, that foot of the Infallible One was not yet fully extended.
Hurled with great force by Hari, he was carried to the summit of the cosmic egg;
the cosmic egg became shattered by the strike of his big toe,
and the external waters entered this [egg] and the three worlds.

Then the Gaṅgā, originating from Viṣṇu’s foot, flowed forth from that place. Having recognized the foot of Hari, marked with the signs of the discus, lotus, and other symbols, the Grandfather (Brahmā) filled his water-pot with those waters from it. (86–87)
He repeatedly washed the lotus feet of Śrī Hari;
by the power of Kṛṣṇa, that water became truly inexhaustible.
That auspicious water, having become a sacred ford, fell upon the peak of Mount Meru.
Indeed, for the sake of purifying the world, it was caused to flow in the four directions:
in the east it is known as the Sītā; in the south, it is celebrated as the Alakanandā; in the west, it is called the Cakṣus; and in the north, it is considered to be named the Bhadrā.
And there, at that time, the Ālakanandā also came to have three names:
in the upper region she is called Mandākinī, in the middle she is celebrated as Gaṅgā,
and when she reached the subterranean realm (pātāla), she was known as Bhogavatī.
In heaven she is called Svardhunī; having gone to the earth (Gā), she is Gaṅgā;
and having gone to the netherworld (Pātāla), she became known by the name Tripathagā as well.
When served, worshipped, seen, touched, drunk, or bathed in, [she grants liberation]. || 92–93 ||

Having kindled it, she grants liberation to the embodied being after burning away all sins. O lady of auspicious countenance, who could sustain her as she flows from the center of Meru with exceedingly rapid currents?
Seeing the great force of the flood and fearing it would tear her asunder,
the Earth prayed to Śambhu to hold her within his matted locks.
For the sake of her own purification, Śambhu held her upon his head.
For a thousand divine years she remained fixed within her matted locks.
Then King Bhagīratha and the great ascetic Gautama,
having propitiated Śambhu through their penance, requested Gaṅgā for his sake.
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, she was bestowed by Śambhu upon those two [the Gaṅgā and Yamunā].
Brought down by Gautama, she is celebrated as Gautamī;
and having come down with Bhagīratha, she is called Bhāgīrathī.
While being drunk by Jahnu, she was revealed by Jahnu;
thus she is celebrated as Jāhnavī, the purifier that reaches to the ocean.
[She saw] the many sons of Sagara who had been burnt in the hermitage of Kapila.
Having pulled out sixty thousand [beings], he cast them into the ocean.
Thus Viṣṇu grew in size and seized two feet;
there was no space for a third, and the entire cosmic egg was taken over.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Vāmana’s Entrance into the Sacrificial Ground, His Request for Land, Bali’s Granting of Three Paces of Earth Despite Śukra’s Prohibition, the Growth of Vāmana, and the Emergence of the Gaṅgā from the Cosmic Eggshell by the Second Pace," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 148 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then a great and supreme dejection came upon the Asuras. O Ramā, he strode across the earth with one step;
with the second, the seven heavens; for a third, there was no space remaining.
Then Brahmā, Marīci and the others, and the yogins such as Sananda and the rest;
the Vedas and the Upavedas, the observances (niyamas) and the restraints (yamas), the Purāṇas and the Saṃhitās; the ascetics, the sages, and the celibate students whose vital energy is drawn upward.
They worshipped the feet of the illustrious Vāmana, which were stepped upon by Satya,
with water, flowers, sandalwood, and divine-scented ointments;
with fragrant incense and lamps, and with parched grain, unbroken rice, fruits, and other offerings.
With hymns of praise, shouts of victory, and the sounds of conchs and drums,
as well as with dances, instrumental music, and songs imbued with his power,
they worshipped him and proclaimed a great festival for this victory.
But the Asuras, burning within their hearts, could not endure this at all—
the deceitful Vāmana and his course of untruth;
for they held that death alone was the punishment for one who has fallen on the side of the gods.
Thus the Daityas, the Asuras, and the Dānavas seized their weapons;
fierce, with weapons in hand, and devoted solely to their own interests,
they fled in anger, unwilling to submit to King Bali.
Against them were the attendants of Viṣṇu, holding weapons and missiles in their hands:
Bala, Nanda, Sunanda, Prabala, and Kumuda;
as well as Viśvaksena, Kumudākṣa, Garuḍa, and Sāttvata.
Jayanta, Śrutadeva, Puṣpadanta, and others—
all of whom possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants— slaughtered that Asura army.
Bali, however, held back the Daityas, the foremost among the Dānavas.
"Do not fight; turn back! Time is not a bestower of benefit for us, he who was once the god who brought about our prosperity, yet has now turned against us, O dwellers of heaven.
"That very same Blessed One has today come to oppose us."
Therefore, having suffered defeat, we must now remain under his command;
but when the time arrives again, we shall conquer through the power of Hari.
Having heard these words of Bali, the Daityas entered the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
Then, there Garuḍa bound Bali with the nooses of Varuṇa.
A great cry of lamentation arose throughout the entire universe, in place after place.
Vāmana spoke to him as he was bound, deprived of his kingdom and abandoned by prosperity.
Three steps were granted; one remains there.
Your kingdom has been traversed by two; provide the third.
For one who does not give what has been promised, residence in hell is certain.
"Enjoy for some years the fruit of your deception: hell.
Thus treated with hostility, the devotee spoke to the Lord, seeking to please him:
"May my word not prove false, for the sake of your grace. (19)
My own body has been offered for the sake of the third step.
Indeed, let both your noose and your foot belong to me for the sake of liberation;
for you are a praiseworthy teacher, whose condition remains beyond the reach of the nature of the asuras.
O Lord, my grandfather was indeed protected by you;
likewise, Prahlāda here too has been well-guarded from the noose of worldly existence.
A noose fashioned by your hand is not a bond, but rather a means for liberation.
Kingdom, heaven, happiness, kinsman, life, death, teacher, liberation, and even bondage—whatever exists, You alone abide as that for me.
I know no other who bestows happiness, or who grants both bondage and liberation. (23–24)
Then, rising from his seat, Prahlāda said to Keśava:
"The delusion regarding this state granted by you has been destroyed by you; that itself is the grace bestowed. Without you, who could have liberated him?"
Sandhyāvalī, the wife of Bali, spoke with palms joined in reverence to Mādhava:
"By you it was given, by you it was enjoyed, and likewise by you it was offered back.
All of this is merely your play; O fool, what is the grandeur of ownership?"
Brahmā said: "O Lord, release this Sāttvata Bali, who has offered himself as a devotee and who rejoices even while in bondage.
All his possessions have been taken away, and his imprisonment has been fully established."
"And since his body has been offered by him, he does not deserve punishment.

Vāmana said: "If, through the power of Māyā, there is 'I-ness' and 'mine-ness' toward my devotee, yet he is harmful to the kingdom and so forth, then what favor indeed would that be for me? (1.147.30)

If one is not utterly deluded by birth, occupation, age, form, learning, power, wealth, and the like, that indeed is my grace toward him. If he should be deluded, I shall surely destroy that delusion by force.
Even then, if my mind were so inclined, he would indeed have conquered the unconquerable.
"What kind of devotee is this of mine, who has now been tested by me?
