Although forbidden by my guru, he did not abandon the truth for my sake;
yet, when asked for his all by means of a pretext, I took it from him by force.
Nevertheless, that man of noble mind does not relinquish his state of servitude to me.
Therefore, I shall not abandon him who is so intent on propitiating me.
I shall grant him the auspicious and prosperous realm of Rasātala,
[the domain] of all the Dānavas, Nāgas, and aquatic beings as well.
"I shall make you king until the dissolution of all beings;
and during the Sāvarṇi Manvantara, you shall again become Indra.
O Bali, whatever I bestow as a favor upon you, I shall later withdraw it all."
"Having utterly destroyed his pride and delusion, I shall restore him to prosperity once more.
Then Bali said to the Lord:
"O Master, such a boon as I have obtained cannot be acquired by anyone else; what further words of my great good fortune need I speak?"
"Only my head remains here for the sake of Your third step;
place Your foot there, and everything shall be obtained by me.
Moved by compassion, Hari placed His own foot upon his head.
Having attained the third stage and having his desires completely fulfilled,
he forcibly brought Bali down to the netherworld (rasātala) with his weight;
there, he installed him in the kingdom, surrounded by his kinsmen.
Bali said to Vāmana: "O Blessed One, upon your lotus-soft sole, my hair-thorns are indeed pierced and cause me great pain.
Where is the adamantine body of the Daitya, and where is the lotus-foot of Hari?"
"O Lord of the Kurus, since pain has arisen in my foot, please grant me forgiveness.
Having said this, Bali licked his foot there with his tongue;
out of love, he repeatedly kissed the soft, lotus-like sole that bestows liberation.
Since all this that has been obtained is already established within That which is the object of attainment, how could there not be a tasting of That, which grants the drinking of the nectar of bliss?
Hari said: "Enough of those [prayers], O Bala; I am pleased by your devotion. Your desire is granted."
"Listen; if there were anything at all that I possessed, there would be nothing I could not give to you.
Bali replied: "Let this auspicious foot of yours always dwell in my house for the sake of its perpetual worship—this foot which washes away the sins of the Daityas."
"O Lord of Śrī, dig a well for me; always grant me protection.
May I never again fall into the state of a demon; O Master, make me Your attendant.
Hari then said, "Standing at the gateway, I shall provide you protection."
And my Sudarśana discus shall provide protection for the kingdom.
I do not remain without Bali, nor does Bali remain without me;
I stand here at your city gate to grant you my vision.
My discus shall destroy those wicked ones who transgress your command;
I shall always protect you, along with your family and attendants.
You shall see me ever present within your own home.
By the power of my grace, that asuric nature of yours shall indeed perish.
Rule the kingdom of Rāsātala; in Sutala your grandfather [Virocana] is present, and in Pātāla there is Prahlāda, my devotee, as well as Hāṭakeśvara.
Śambhu is my devotee; I dwell here and there.
Taking up my mace, Govinda dwells in the palace of Bali.
Then the Lord Vāmana, having assumed another form, [resides there].
Vāmana,
having assumed the guise of a young brahmin, accepted the worlds from Bali for the sake of his protection and gave them back to Mahendra,
who was adorned with a crown, necklaces, and forehead marks. 56–57.
Having performed the auspicious rites of consecration, he bestowed upon him the sovereignty over the three worlds.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas and the sages of great luster who dwell in the fourteen levels of existence, honored the infallible Indra.
Then the final oblation of the sacrifice was performed, augmented by *śrīphala* fruits.
There, Viṣṇu, acting through the hand of Indra, completed the work of merit. Then Hari spoke to Śukra regarding the flaw in the ritual as well as its proper sequence.
Since you, as the preceptor, must indeed avoid partiality,
Śukra said to Hari: "Wherever you are considered the witness of the action,
how can there be any partiality in that action, since the Lord of Sacrifice is worshipped therein?"
Through mantra and tantra, and regarding place, time, and the appropriate materials,
everything that has occurred is rendered flawless by your direct presence.
Having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the concluding purificatory bath (avabhṛthasnāna) in the ocean, [the rite is complete].
In the great sacred field of Somanātha,
all the sacrificial priests sent by Viṣṇu returned each to his own abode.
O Lord of the Gods, you have attained the great sovereignty over the three worlds.
Then Prajāpati Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Śaṅkara, along with Dakṣa,
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and other leading celestial sages, ancestors, and kings,
[assembled] for the pleasure of Kaśyapa and Aditi, and for the peace of all the worlds.
The guardians of the quarters and the protectors of the worlds indeed made Vāmana their lord—
likewise the sages, the ascetics, the gods, and the mountains;
[the lords] of the worlds, the protectors of the worlds, of dharma, of fame, and of prosperity.
For the sake of all prosperity— of vows, of the duty of giving, of sacrifices, of meritorious deeds,
of auspicious rites, of sovereign powers, as well as of heaven and liberation—
they appointed Upendra as their lord.
Then everyone rejoiced after bowing down to Vāmana;
they returned each to their own capital, while Indra, having led his younger brother Vāmana to his own palace by means of the celestial vehicle, worshipped the Imperishable One.
Having obtained sovereignty over the three worlds and being protected by the arms of Upendra, Mahendra rejoiced;
the gods, too, were happy, having taken refuge in Vāmana.
Thus, in ancient times, the gods including Indra were well protected by Śrī Viṣṇu.
Supreme joy arose among the gods, centered upon Vāmana; Vāmana set his mind on making Vāmanasthalī his dwelling. It was there that in former times Vāmana had repeatedly requested alms.
Indeed, because of the suppression of Bali, that city was destroyed by the Daityas;
thus, the Daityas led the entire city and its prosperity to Rasātala.
Then the blessed Lord questioned the brahmin Garga.
"In which place should I perform the Vaiṣṇava rite? Tell me of that city where there is both happiness and liberation for men from the bondage of worldly existence.
[76] "In Vastrāpatha, to the west of Raivata, is Vāmanasthalī."

The city was built by Viśvakarman and bestowed upon the brahmins. In ancient times, its sovereignty was held by a brahmin devoted to his wife; though it had passed through a succession of dynasties, at the end of the age it fell into the hands of another.
On Mount Raivata, three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) also reside.
Bhadrā, Madhumatī, Urjasvatī, and Svarṇasurakṣikā—all these wives of the Blessed One abide there in the form of rivers. (79)

By the mere remembrance of whose name, by bathing where, and by giving gifts there, one is delivered. (1.147.80) In every kalpa, great sacrifices were performed by Bali in some places on the slopes of the Himālaya mountains and in others upon the earth at Puṣkara. (1.147.81)
In one instance, on Mount Raivata; in another, on the bank of the Narmadā;
and in another kalpa, this Vāmana, having gone to the sacrifice of Bali on the bank of the Narmadā, will bind Bali and seize the three worlds.
In this way, there are indeed thousands of dwarf-forms;
in every kalpa and in every set of four ages, these dwarfs are known to appear in various forms.
There is no end to my incarnations; I have described only a mere indication of them.
"All this majesty of Vāmana has been recounted to you, O beloved.
Speak, Lakṣmī! What further meritorious and heart-pleasing account do you wish to hear? (85).

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh [chapter] of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, titled "The Description of Bali’s Binding with Nooses, the Granting of the Kingdom of Rasātala, Vāmana’s Residence in Bali’s House, the Giving of the Three Worlds to Indra, the Concluding Bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*), and the Founding of the City named Vāmanasthalī," and so forth.
Chapter 147:
[The Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga] from the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Part 1.
Chapter 148.
[The Author: Chapter 149.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Of what nature is the milk-vow (payovrata) and the vow for non-widowhood (avaidhavyavrata), and how are they performed?
"That by which the attainment of sons and constant union with one's husband may occur.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "This was first proclaimed by Brahmā to the high-souled Kaśyapa."
He then related this to his wife named Aditi.
Consequently, Aditi became the mother of sons such as Hiraṇyākṣa.
That vow, which gratifies Keśava, must be observed for twelve days.
This vow is proclaimed for the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
beginning from the first day (pratipad) until the thirteenth day of the bright half.
One should observe celibacy, sleep on the ground, and perform ablutions three times a day.
One should speak the truth and renounce all diverse enjoyments born of passion (rājasa).
One should always abandon malice and violence, and perform the worship of Hari with dance,
instrumental music, song, hymns of praise, and recitations of auspicious blessings.
One should always worship with the sixteen types of offerings, with sacred discourses, and likewise with acts of devotion; furthermore, one should feed five Brahmins according to one's capacity.
At the commencement, on the new moon day, [one should perform this] at midday at home.
Having smeared herself with cow-dung and earth, she should bring about purification.
(8) Having washed her own clothes and other items, a woman should perform the rite of purification.
At evening time, the woman observing the vow should bathe after smearing herself with pure earth. (9)
She should bring earth from a field or from the very source of a stream. At the time of taking the earth, the bride should recite the mantra in her own language:
"O Goddess, you were lifted up by Śrī Varāha in the form of the Earth."
"Uddharāmi namastubhyaṃ pāpmānaṃ me vināśaya" (I lift you up; salutations to you; destroy my sin).
Having recited this, one should then collect the clay and bring it home.
Having bathed, one should worship Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa at the beginning of the night.
At the beginning of the night, one should worship Hari with the sixteen types of offerings.
One should then make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "Tomorrow I shall observe the milk-vow (payovrata) for the sake of obtaining a son;
may that vow of mine be fulfilled through Your grace."
During this twelve-day vow, I shall observe the restraints such as celibacy and the like;
I shall always feed at least two Brahmins,
and for twelve days I shall perform your worship with sixteen types of offerings.
One should daily worship Śrī Hari with a spirit of devotion in an image, on a sacrificial mound, in the sun, in water, in fire, in the guru, or in the Lord of the universe;
and one should offer auspicious praise composed of meaningful words in the vernacular tongue.
Homage to you, O Blessed One; salutations again and again to the Supreme Person. Homage to Vāsudeva, who dwells within all, the Witness;
homage to the Unmanifest, the Subtle, and the Manifested Person; salutations again and again. (17–18)
Salutations to the twenty-four principles, the cause of transformation.
Salutations to the two-headed one, the three-footed, the four-horned, the bearer of the thread.
Salutations to the seven-handed one, the sacrifice, whose self is the three Vedas.
Salutations again and again to Mahādeva, to Rudra, to the Bull;
salutations to him who is established in all knowledge, the Lord of living beings.
Salutations to the one whose treasury is gold, to the soul of the vital breath of the universe.
Salutations to you who possess the sovereignty of perfected yoga, and salutations to you, the performer of yoga.
Salutations to the primordial god of all; salutations to you who abide within the self.
Salutations to you, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the seer Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
Homage to the one whose body is dark as a blue lotus, to the glorious one; homage!
(23) Homage to you, O Keśava, O Ananta! Homage to the one clad in yellow garments!
You are the giver of boons, the most excellent, the Lord who grants the desires of all people. (24)
The dust of your feet, when worshipped, truly bestows liberation;
the gods follow after you, and Śrī abides at your feet.
O Blessed One, I long for the fragrance of your compassion; may you be gracious toward me.
Having thus praised Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world, one should invoke him.
One should offer Harim water for the feet (pādya), the guest-offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and a seat (āsana).
Then, having rubbed [the image] with excellent oil, arka-plant, and so forth, one should present the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should offer a bath with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar;
one should also perform a bath with pure water and a consecratory sprinkling (abhiṣeka).
Having performed the wiping with a cloth, one should present auspicious garments.
One should worship the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) and the Kaustubha gem with the essence of oil and the Arka flower.
One should worship the Lord with saffron, barley, clay, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should offer sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (naivedya).
One should wear ornaments, weapons, a crown, and so forth, as well as forehead marks and the like;
one should offer water, incense, and the arati lamp, and likewise place betel leaf in the mouth.
One should offer fruit, offer water, and perform prostrations with the body fully extended like a staff.
One should perform circumambulation, give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and present the guest-offering (arghya).
"I shall perform your worship for twelve days; grant me a son," [he should say]. He should mutter the mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*. ||32-33||
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should offer oblations of milk-preparation (*dugdhapāka*) or some other food,
completely filled with ghee and sugar, using the *japa-vidyā*.
One should then present the offered milk-preparation or another sweet dish.
One should give very little, indeed very little, to the devotees out of a spirit of grace.
One should eat oneself for the sake of one's sons, and praise the Lord with hymns of praise. Having placed that water upon one's head, one should then bid farewell to the deity.
There, he should feed the most excellent Brahmins with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Then, permitted by them, the observer of the vow and the performer of the rite should eat.
At the beginning of the night, having performed the purificatory rites, the observer of the vow should sleep upon the ground.
He should sleep at night observing celibacy, and when the first day has dawned,
having bathed according to the rule during the Brāhma-muhūrta in the manner prescribed,
and having likewise bathed [the deity] according to the rule, he should always perform worship every morning.

Until the completion of the vow, one should eat only a single meal dedicated to the Lord Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, consisting of milk-preparations and nothing else. One should spend the day with devotion and the night in prayer and sleep.
One should constantly offer oblations into the fire and also feed Brāhmaṇas.
Thus one should perform this daily for twelve days while observing the milk-vow.
Accompanied by the worship of Hari, one should observe this vow of subsisting solely on milk.

Beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) until the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, both the husband and the wife, being devoted to Kṛṣṇa, should perform the worship of Hari, the fire sacrifice (homa), ritual adoration, and the feeding of the virtuous.

On the morning of the thirteenth day, one should have the bathing and other rites for Śrī Hari performed entirely according to the prescribed rules by Brāhmaṇas who are experts in the ritual procedures. One should perform the great worship (mahāpūjā) and should not practice stinginess regarding the expenditure of wealth.
Having cooked the *caru* in the fire of the milk-boiling (*dugdhapāka*) for the sake of the oblation,
he should worship Kṛṣṇa with that boiled offering at the mouth of the fire.
He should present the food offering (*naivedya*) to Nārāyaṇa, which bestows great satisfaction.
One should greatly satisfy the preceptor, who is learned in the Vedas and endowed with knowledge, with cows,
ornaments, clothing, and other gifts. One should also satisfy the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and feed them with many kinds of delicious foods, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and so forth.
He should joyfully feed other brahmins, as well as virtuous men and virtuous women;
and he should give excellent sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the brahmin, the preceptor, the teacher, and the virtuous man and woman, according to their merit, as well as to others who have arrived.
One should satisfy guests who have arrived, even those as low as the dog-cookers (outcastes),
by giving food, water, and other necessities; likewise, one should satisfy the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others, reflecting that when they are satisfied, Viṣṇu is satisfied.
Having given gifts such as cows, horses, and even ants, one should eat together with one's kinsmen;

one should spend the remainder of the day in the supreme service of the Supreme Person through the chanting of His names, narrations of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, hymns of praise, and the recitation of mantras. (52)
This milk-vow (payovrata) has been proclaimed and fully described by me to you.
In the preparation of the milk, either rice grains or wild millet (nivāra) are considered auspicious.
One must not consume leafy vegetables; for one who eats vegetables becomes dark-complexioned.

He should consume the milk-preparation (dugdhapāka), by which he will obtain offspring radiant with strength. After the final oblation of the vow, on even nights, the wife herself should lie with him; by this means, a powerful son shall be born.
One should approach one's wife on the odd-numbered lunar days; thus a daughter shall be born, who bestows success.
O Lakṣmī! This auspicious vow, which has austerity as its essence, grants sons;
it should be performed by both husband and wife together to yield its fruit.
Otherwise, it would not indeed yield fruit; rather, its result would be uncertain.
O beloved, listen as I also describe the vow of lifelong chastity (*avaidhavyavrata*).
Raivatī was the daughter of Mount Raivata on Mount Raivataka.
It stands eternally in the western direction from Dāmodara.
There indeed exists the Raivatī-kuṇḍa, which destroys sins; it ensures that women do not become widows and likewise serves as a cause for progeny. (1.148.60)
That water bestows good fortune upon all women;
by bathing there, a woman shall be endowed with many sons and wealth.
She shall never suffer widowhood, and her good fortune shall be incomparable.
Having bathed, fruits should be offered, as well as saffron with kajjala;
a thread for Gaurī should be given, along with betel, flowers,
and also a yellow garment, a bodice, and a staff.
Having placed fruits in bamboo vessels, as well as sweet foods,
one should offer them along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā) to virtuous and chaste women.
Then, having bathed in the morning, the vision of Raivatī should be performed.
And worship must indeed be performed with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
One should offer praise for the sake of obtaining a son and also for the sake of avoiding widowhood:
"O ever-compassionate Goddess Raivati, show me your grace! (65–66)
"May I never suffer widowhood, may I likewise possess sons and grandsons, and may I be endowed with wealth and grain; O auspicious one, grant me my desire.
Having thus offered praise and prostrated, she beheld Dāmodara.
Having established the limit of fifteen days during the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
one should always go to one's own home; furthermore, the food to be eaten should consist of milk-rice,
sweet dishes, side-dishes, and likewise items cooked in ghee.
She should dwell together with her husband, and not be prohibited from doing so;
likewise, she should not observe fasts, nor does she require any other form of worship.
When the observer of the vow beholds the praise of Raivata, he should perform the ritual bathing of the sacrificial pit.
The giving of the aforementioned fruits and other gifts, and the sight of Dāmodara performed on the morning of the fifteenth day, increase one's good fortune.
Thus has this vow, which ensures freedom from widowhood, been shown to you.
"Then, O Mahālakṣmī, what else do you wish to hear from me? Lakṣmī said: "O Ocean of Mercy, tell me of the holy fords on Mount Raivata and whatever other [sacred sites] dwell in its vicinity."
"O Keśava, I wish to hear how much power these [vows] truly possess.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Milk-Vow that Grants Sons and the Vow of Non-Widowhood," in the first section, "The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga," of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
[Chapter 148: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 1 (*Kṛta-Yuga-Santāna*)]
Chapter 149 [Author:
Chapter 150 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe the holy places situated on Mount Raivata, which are endowed with the fruit of pilgrimage and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. I shall also tell you of the holy places of Vastrāpatha and by whom they were established.
I shall also relate those [accounts] to you, which bestow both heaven and liberation.
In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Bhoja in Kānyakubja.
A forest-guard came to him from the forest and spoke this to him.
"O King, a marvel has now been seen by me as I wandered in the forest:
I beheld a woman with the face of a deer, moving among a herd of deer.
Thereupon, that king of the Bhojas spoke to his commander-in-chief.
We must go this very moment to where that young woman is staying.
Let the horses and foot-soldiers go and surround the forest and the mountain;
for that woman wearing female attire is like a doe who must be brought under control.
The Bhoja king surrounded the mountain with his army foot-soldiers.
But the deer-faced woman, though being carried away by the army, was rescued by Hari;
the king then brought that doe, who possessed the body of a woman, to Kānyakubja.
Upon seeing her, a sense of wonder arose among everyone in the king’s palace.
The king bathed her with divine perfumes and ointments;
then, in a secluded and private place, he spoke to her as she was beautifully adorned.
"Who are you? Whose daughter are you? And for what reason, O deer-faced one, do you not speak even when questioned? Thus asked, she neither ate nor drank.
Then Bhoja summoned astrologers, experts in mantras, and physicians.
Having paid due homage to the Tantrikas, he spoke: "Behold, O twice-born ones!
How indeed can she have the body of a woman? And how is it that her face is like that of a deer? How will she come to have the speech and countenance of a human? || 11-12 ||
The Brahmins said: "In Kurukṣetra, there is a Brahmin named Sārasvata;
he knows the matter exactly as it is and will tell it.
Bhoja went to that Brahmin, who was performing such penance.
Having paid his respects, that Brahmin spoke to Bhoja as he sat there:
"Let us go where that woman is; she herself will tell us.
Thus, the twice-born Sārasvata arrived at the place where the woman was.
Having smeared the ground and arranged a svastika,
having placed a water-filled pitcher and established the fire-rite,
and having seated Indra and the gods who are the guardians of the directions within the pitcher— (16)
Having offered oblations into the fire and prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru), he performed the worship of the planets.
He himself performed the consecration and had that woman consecrated as well.
Then, by means of divine vision, she spoke of her many previous births.
O Bhoja! In your seventh previous birth, you were a king of the Kaliṅga country, and I was your wife, born in Vaṅga.
You were wicked-minded, ill-behaved, and devoid of compassion and righteousness. || 19 ||
"You were one who destroyed cows, land, Brahmins, teachers, the Vedas, gods, and the scriptures;
having conspired with the subjects, you, the opponent of the world, were slain.
Taking my deceased husband, I entered the fire and died along with him."
If a wife, taking her deceased husband with her, enters the fire,
both shall indeed be honored in heaven until the dissolution of all beings.
Thereafter, in the land of Mālava, you became a brahmin who was an atheist.
I, however, was your devoted Brahmin wife.
When you attained death after abandoning the gold and wealth acquired by you, I did not die with you out of greed; rather, I died at a later time.
"You were indeed a white serpent, and I was a Brahmin maiden.
You married another Brahmin, and you bit that Brahmin.
I, however, became a widow, while you, the serpent, were killed by people. (25)
"Having inflicted widowhood upon me, both the brahmin and the serpent have died.
Having died yourself, you were then born as a crocodile in the Godāvarī; even then, I came together with people to visit the Bhīmeśvara holy site."
Just as I had entered the water to bathe, I was indeed seized by a crocodile;
the crocodile was struck down by the people with blows from spears and other weapons,
and at that moment, I too met my death by the fangs of the crocodile.
From that [karma], you were born as a hunter and I became a Śabara woman in the forest.
(29) Those for whom death comes from fire, water, snakes, elephants, lions, or even horses; or from anger, boils, or [other causes]—they go to hell. (1.149.30)
One who destroys himself, a killer of an embryo, a killer of a woman, a killer of a Brahmin, a false witness, one who sells a maiden, one who utters false accusations,
one who sells a sacrifice, and a twice-born man who drinks liquor— [these are all equal]. (31)
The traitor to the king, the thief of gold, the one who destroys the livelihood of a Brahmin,
the killer of a cow, the one who misappropriates a deposit, and he who seizes the boundary of a village—
all these go to hell, as does the woman who deceives her husband. (32–33)

I, Śabarī, having died from disease, was then born as a female curlew in the forest. Once, while I was intent on sporting with a male curlew out of desire, that curlew was struck down by a hunter with an arrow. (34)
Then, cursed by Krauñca, you became cruel in the great forest;
deprived of women, you became a tiger-like creature, suffering again and again.
Thereafter, you took the form of a tiger on Mount Raivata.
Having died by the power of fate, the female curlew was reborn as a doe on Mount Raivata.
While I had come to drink the water of the Svarṇarakṣā river to the west of Bhaveshvara,
I was then seen by a lion.
Out of fear of him, I leaped up and fell upon the opposite bank;
just then, the lion sprang forward and landed forcefully before me,
as I turned back and prepared to leap once more.
My head was caught between two hollow bamboos standing in the water at my side;
while swimming between the two bamboos, it became as if bound by a noose.
My body remained in the midst of the water, while my head was lodged within the bamboo.
Held by the lion at the neck and deprived of his fangs,
as the lion was still dragging my body out from the midst of the water, I slipped away on my feet through the presence of the śaivala plants and fell back into the water.
From the bottomless water, which was thick with moss on all sides, that lion was unable to emerge; he met his death.
The lion died in the waters of Svarṇarākṣa and became King Bhoja.
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), he attained the status of a king.
This is indeed his seventh birth, well-known as King Bhoja.
My head remains suspended on my lineage, while my body stays within the water.
There, my body was scattered in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā, but my face did not fall; skin and flesh remained fixed upon my head.
Thereafter, I was born from the womb of a doe, possessing a human form.
"Since my face was born from that of a doe and has not fallen into the water, I am not a daughter of a deer;
rather, I am the daughter of the noble sage Uddālaka.
Once, while he had come to bathe for the protection of his gold... (47–48)
At that time, the yoginīs came to that very place to bathe.
Then, the sage was tested repeatedly by the yoginīs:
"What kind of person is this celibate student—is he firm or is he weak? (49)

Having seized him with neck-ropes and embraced him again and again, they sported with him in many ways; yet the sage did not undergo any transformation. Then, at that time, there was one yoginī named Kāmadāhā.
By the power of yoga, she entered within the body of Uddālaka;
at that moment, Kama became terrified and fled from the body of the sage.
Otherwise, that Yoginī, remaining inside him, would have reduced him to ashes.
Due to the flight of Kāmadeva, the heat of the Yoginī,
the force of the onset of youth, and from playing with her and other such activities,
the element (the semen), though then obstructed, fell into the water by the force of its momentum. (53–54)
Along with the current, the mineral element entered the Nārāyaṇa lake.
There, a certain doe drank water mixed with that mineral.
By the force of her past karma, my dwelling was within her womb.

I am the daughter of the sage Uddālaka, born with the face of a deer (Mṛgānanā). Since I was raised by yoginīs and am thus the daughter of yoginīs, I am a yoginī with the face of a deer; though divine, I am likewise human.
"O King, my seventh birth likewise exists in the same manner as yours.
This sage Sārasvata knows it indeed through the power of yoga.
Having entered the fire in a previous life, she died together with you in the seventh."
"May my husband not be without you even in death"—this was what I requested.
Then, O Indra among kings, an incorporeal voice spoke from the sky:
"This king is a man of evil deeds; he is violent, cruel, and exceedingly greedy. (1.149.60)
One who is not skilled in the Vedas and Shastras, devoid of compassion and righteousness,
lustful, arrogant, greatly wrathful, and bereft of truthfulness and right conduct—
such a person of evil intent knows neither God, nor the Guru, nor the Brahmins. (61)
He does not honor the virtuous nor the virtuous women, being excessively arrogant;
he is a speaker of untruth, evil-minded, and a destroyer of sacrifices and dharma.
He is indeed a meat-eater, a reviler of Viṣṇu, and a robber of livelihoods.
He who visits a prostitute is devoid of bathing, giving, and righteous deeds;
having attained the state of a Caṇḍāla, how great is his sin?
It would be impossible to calculate it—such is this sinful man.
Although you, a virtuous woman, have indeed been burned by him,
you shall nevertheless be united with him for seven lifetimes;
however, due to his great sins, heaven shall not be his lot.
Having first experienced the fruit of your sin, you shall later possess a kingdom.
Your eighth birth shall be a birth among the gods.
Then, having become human once more, you will afterwards go to heaven.
Having spoken thus, she ceased; "I remember everything through my yogic power.
Even the skull of my head remains fixed upon a bamboo pole.
If someone goes to Vastrāpatha and offers his own head [in exchange], [I shall give it back]."
"O King, in the waters of Svarṇarakṣā, my face would become human;
I am one with a human face, yet I appear to others with the face of a deer. This face of mine, shaped like a deer's, is shrouded by the shadow of sin."

Having heard this, King Bhoja dispatched a doorkeeper to that place. He saw that in the great forest, the constellation Mṛgaśiras was suspended upon a bamboo pole above the waters of the Svarṇarekhā river.
As soon as it was seized and cast into the waters of the Svarṇarekhā,
her auspicious face, which resembled the moon, became divine within the palace of King Bhoja;
its human eyes, like lotus petals, became celestial.
She was most beautiful, with long hair, long ears, and auspicious teeth;
she had a neck like a conch shell, the fragrance of a lotus, and was endowed with all the marks of excellence.
She was neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva maiden, nor an Asura woman, nor a Kinnara nymph.
At that time, that beautiful woman was born with the nature of a sacred ford (tīrtha). She was married by Bhojarāja;
that queen, the beauty of Bhoja, became renowned as Mṛgānanā.
Why was she made the chief queen by the wise King Bhoja?

[It was because] it is the best of countries among countries, the best of mountains among mountains, the most excellent of sacred fields among fields, and the most excellent of forests among forests. (77–78)
The Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Revā, and Svarṇarekhā reside within its waters.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, all the Rudras and other gods,
as well as the Nāgas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas, are established in this sacred field.
Having bathed in the Svarṇa, Rakṣā, Nandī, and Vārī rivers, and in the Nārāyaṇa lake;
likewise, having bathed in the Mṛgī-tīrtha and in the pool named Dāmodara,
as well as in the Revatī-kuṇḍa, one shall attain heaven and liberation.
The holy Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and Yamunā in the form of gold have arrived at the river and remain there; golden leaves are seen.
Sarasvatī is in the form of gold, while the Gaṅgā has silver leaves.
The Yamunā, with its copper-colored leaves, shines within the waters of that river.
Thus, the river known as Suvarṇarakṣā, endowed with golden streaks,
flows on Mount Raivata, bestowing liberation.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the slayer of a fetus, and the violator of the guru’s bed—
by bathing in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā, one is liberated from all sins.
And those insects, moths, and other creatures that die in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā [attain liberation].
Even trees, creepers, shrubs, and bushes attain the supreme goal.
Having praised the Brahmin Sārasvata, Bhoja spoke these words:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, Sūrya, Indra, Agni, and the hosts of Maruts—"
O Lord, you have been propitiated by me through my celibacy and austerity; therefore,
if you have compassion, you should come with me to Mount Raivata for the sake of our journey,
so that I too may achieve my purpose.
What is to be grasped, and what is to be consumed? What is to be given, and what is not to be given?
Tell me briefly everything regarding fasting at sacred sites, bathing, the sequence of rituals for twilight ablutions, worship, sleep, and recitation during the night.
Thus questioned by the king, Sārasvata explained that procedure;
the brahmin recounted the entire fruit of the gift and other rites exactly as they are.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Svarṇarakṣā River through the Account of Seven Births of King Bhoja and His Wife Mṛgānanā," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Then the great sage, the brāhmaṇa Sārasvata, spoke to him regarding the power of the pilgrimage to Raivata Mountain in Saurāṣṭra. || 1 ||
When one is to go to the Raivataka mountain in the land of Saurāṣṭra, then,
having observed the strength of Jupiter and performed the libation to the Sun,
and having placed [the Sun] on the left or behind, one should examine the other purifications of the day.
Having observed that the moon, the ascendant, and the planets are strong from the perspective of the birth sign,
and having perceived an auspicious omen, people should indeed set out.
[The asterisms] Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are well-adorned for this purpose.
Mṛgaśīrṣa, Citrā, Puṣya, Mūla, and Hasta are always auspicious for the giving away of a daughter,
for journeys, and for rites such as consecrations.
Venus and the Moon, when situated in the birth asterism or the second house, bestow auspicious results.
The Moon, Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter are [situated] in the third house;
Mars, Saturn, the Moon, and the Sun are [in the fourth]; Mercury is excellent in the fourth house;
and Venus and Jupiter, joined with the Moon and Ketu, are in the fifth house.

Mars is auspicious in the sixth house along with Saturn and the Sun; Jupiter and the Moon are excellent in the seventh; Mercury and Venus are best in the eighth; Jupiter situated in the ninth is auspicious;
the Sun, Rāhu, and the Moon are favorable in the tenth; and all the planets are beneficial in the eleventh.
Then Mercury, as well as Venus in the twelfth house, will be a bestower of happiness.
Capricorn is excellent with Leo; Aries is supreme with Virgo; Pisces with Libra, and Cancer with Aquarius. (1.150.10)
The Bull is best with the Bow, and the Scorpion with the Gemini;
this is the "Six-Eight" configuration which leads to affection, of this there is no doubt.
The Moon and Mercury are movable (cara), Jupiter is quick (kṣipra), Venus is soft (mṛdu), and the Sun is fixed (dhruva).
Saturn is to be known as cruel, Mars as fierce, and the Moon as mild.
One should march with the *cara* (movable) and *kṣipra* (swift) nakṣatras, and enter [the city] with the *mṛdu* (soft) and *dhruva* (fixed) ones.
Warriors desiring victory should engage in battle with the *dāruṇa* (cruel) and *ugra* (fierce) nakṣatras. (12–13)
The coronation of a king and fire rituals are recommended on a Monday. On a Monday, one should also undertake the construction of houses and similar projects when the moon is in Libra or Libra-Aries.
Commanding an army, heroic combat, and the practice of weapons are prescribed for Tuesday.
The accomplishment of rites, mantras, and journeys are prescribed for Mercury (Budha).
Recitation, worship of the gods, clothing, ornaments, and so forth belong to Jupiter (Guru).
The giving away of a daughter, mounting an elephant, and the marriageable age of a woman occur during Venus (Śukra). (15–16)

Establishing a foundation, entering a house, and tethering an elephant are auspicious when Saturn is present; likewise, the Moon situated in the seventh house or in any of the *upacaya* (beneficial) houses is auspicious in all matters.
Furthermore, during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), the second, fifth, and ninth lunar days are likewise favorable.
Honored by the people, the Moon is regarded like a preceptor.
In the first house, it produces contentment; in the second, there is no peace.
In the third, there is honor from kings; in the fourth, the arrival of quarrels. (18–19)
By the fifth, marked by the deer, there shall indeed be the acquisition of a wife;
in the sixth, the arrival of wealth and grain; in the seventh, pleasure and honor;
in the eighth, danger to life; and in the ninth, the accumulation of a treasury.
In the tenth [tithi], the accomplishment of the task is certain; in the eleventh, victory.
With the twelfth moon, there is indeed death, without a doubt. The first tithi when not bright (the dark fortnight) is excellent, as is the second joined with the son of the Moon (Mercury).
The third [lunar day] is auspicious with the son of the Earth (Mars), the fourth with Saturn;
the fifth is auspicious with Jupiter, and the sixth with Mars and Venus.
The seventh is auspicious with the son of the Moon (Mercury), and the eighth with Mars and the Sun.
The ninth [tithi] with Monday, and the tenth with Jupiter, are auspicious.
On the eleventh, Jupiter is pure; on the twelfth, Mercury likewise.
On the thirteenth, Venus and Mars [are favorable]; the fourteenth is excellent with Saturday. (24–25)

The full moon day (Paurṇamāsī) and the new moon day (Amāvāsyā) occurring on a Thursday are most auspicious; likewise, the Sun in Mūla, the Moon in Śravaṇa, Mars in Uttaraproṣṭhapadā, Mercury in Kṛttikā, Jupiter in Punarvasu, and [Venus] in [Puṣya]. (26)
Pūrvaphalgunī with Venus, and Svāti with Saturn—
these are the Amṛta yogas, which accomplish all undertakings.
The Sun in Hasta, Jupiter in Puṣya, and Anurādhā with Mercury are auspicious.
Rohiṇī is excellent on Saturday; Mṛgaśīrṣa is indeed auspicious with the Moon;
Revatī is excellent on Friday; and Aśvinī is auspicious on Tuesday.
In these [combinations], the Siddhi-yogas indeed destroy all defects.
One should undertake an enterprise there when these [constellations] grant the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Aśvinī, Anurādhā, Revatī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Mūla, Punarvasu,
Puṣya, Hasta, and likewise Jyeṣṭhā are said to be excellent for setting out on a journey.
The Yoginīs must also be awakened; they cause extreme suffering when encountered face-to-face.
Brahmāṇī is stationed in the east on the first and ninth lunar days (tithis);
Māheśvarī is in the north on the second and tenth lunar days.
On the fifth and the thirteenth [tithis], Vārāhī is situated in the south;
on the sixth and the fourteenth, Indrāṇī is situated in the west;
and on the seventh and the full moon, Cāmuṇḍā is in the direction of the wind (the northwest).
On the eighth lunar day conjoined with the new moon, Mahālakṣmī resides in the northeast;
on the eleventh and third days, Vaiṣṇavī is in the southeast;
and on the twelfth and fourth days, Kaumārī is likewise in the southwest.
One should never engage in going or other such activities in the presence of the Yoginīs.
The fourth, the sixth, the eighth, the ninth, as well as the new moon, the full moon, the twelfth, and the fourteenth [lunar days] are inauspicious. (36–37)
The Sun burns the twelfth lunar day, and the Moon burns the eleventh;
Mars burns the tenth, and Mercury burns the ninth.
Jupiter burns the eighth, and Venus burns the seventh.

The son of the Sun (Saturn) burns the sixth lunar day; indeed, there is no [auspicious] departure on these days. One should avoid setting out from afar on the first, ninth, and fourteenth days, as well as on the eighth, and on Wednesday. (1.150.40)
The sixth lunar day [is auspicious] in Aries and Cancer; the eighth in Virgo and Gemini;
the fourth in Taurus and Aquarius; the twelfth in Capricorn and Libra;
the tenth in Scorpio and Leo; and the fourteenth in Sagittarius and Pisces. (41)
These [nakṣatras] are burnt; indeed, living human beings must not travel during them.
When the Sun is in the three Viśākhās, the Moon in the three Pūrvāṣāḍhās, Mars in the third Dhaniṣṭhā, and Mercury in the three Revatīs—[these are the burnt nakṣatras]. (42–43)
When Jupiter is in the three asterisms beginning with Rohiṇī, and Venus is likewise in the three beginning with Puṣya,
one should avoid the three Uttarāphalgunīs on Saturday;
this is an accidental (inauspicious) conjunction that brings about death, disease, and other calamities.
In Viṣkambha, five ghaṭikās are proclaimed; in Śūla, seven;
six in Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa; nine in Vyāghāta and Vajra;
and [nine] in Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vaidhṛti—day after day.
These are indeed joined with death; one should avoid all undertakings during them.
Viśākhā, the three Uttarās, Maghā, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, as well as Āśleṣā and Kṛttikā—these, when setting out on a journey, bring about death.
Therefore, this very departure will indeed become a source of happiness only after due deliberation.
[One should see] a full pitcher, a brahmin, a courtesan, white grains, a mirror,
curd, clarified butter, honey, parched grain, flowers, dūrvā grass, and white unbroken rice.
A bull, a lordly elephant, a horse, a blazing fire, gold,
wool, various ripe fruits,
a woman with a husband and sons, a lamp, and a supreme jewel.

A pearl necklace, a garland of flowers, fresh meat, and sandalwood—these auspicious objects are indeed seen before one. A Brahmin, a maiden, a corpse, a cow, a conch shell, a kettle-drum, and the earth [are likewise auspicious]. (5.1–5.2)
A bamboo flute, a woman, and a full water-jar are auspicious when seen during a journey.
On the left side, Śiva, a camel, a donkey, a mongoose, a water-jar, and a corpse are auspicious.
So too are the royal swan, the peacock, the wagtail, the parrot, and the cuckoo.
The pigeon, the *śaṅkhacilla* bird, the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), and the *māṅgalya*;
the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*), the fragrant cow, the yak, and the white chowrie; and a cow accompanied by her calf—these are auspicious when positioned on the right as banners. (54–55)
Cotton, medicinal herbs, oils, cooked food, charcoal, and serpents;
a woman with disheveled hair, red garlands, and a naked person—these are seen as inauspicious at dawn.
Hiccups occurring in the southeast cause grief, while those in the south are considered to bring loss.
In the southwest, it causes agitation; in the west, it bestows sweet food;
in the northwest, it is said to grant wealth; in the north, it creates strife;
and in the northeast, it brings death—thus should the auspicious and inauspicious results be known.
One should always go to a sacred ford (tīrtha); all months are auspicious for it, and all lunar days (tithis) are excellent for bathing, giving gifts, worship, and other rites.
Departure on a pilgrimage to a sacred ford during the spring season is said to be the most excellent.
Having restrained their senses, become disciplined, pure, bathed, and conquered their faculties—
those people who, having abandoned elephants, horses, and chariots, travel on foot,
go to the abode of Kṛṣṇa by means of a celestial vehicle drawn by swans.
Whether by eating once a day, or by eating only at night, or likewise by eating only what is unasked for;
or by subsisting on alms-food, or water, or fruit;
or by fasting, or by the *kṛcchra* penance, or by subsisting on vegetables—[if people [practice this]... 62.
For those who undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), their worlds are eternal.
Or rather, O Goddess, being fanned and honored by hosts of deities, he goes to heaven;
the pilgrim, with feet bare of shoes, ascends to the solar orb.
Having abandoned mother, father, country, brothers, kinsmen, and relatives, as well as village, land, and home, and having practiced restraint of the senses,
that person who, having received Vaiṣṇava initiation, goes to Raivata— ||65||
"Through the power of Dāmodara, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation for him.

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Auspicious and Inauspicious Planets, Constellations, Days, Yoginīs, Omens, and so forth, at the Beginning of the Pilgrimage Journey," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 152 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Sārasvata spoke to the king, the bull among the Bhojas:
"There is delicious food, delightful meals, and various auspicious drinks;
there are vessels worthy of honor, flowers, and all necessary utensils."
That person who, placing upon his shoulder garments worthy of being given, fragrant sandalwood,
various lotuses, and ornaments of gold, silver, and so forth,
undertakes a journey on foot; || 2-3 ||
And having offered these at the front of the horse, one shall obtain imperishable merit.
One should likewise offer water from the Gaṅgā, honey, clarified butter, saffron, agallochum,
sandalwood, guggulu resin, bilva leaves, and dhattūra flowers.
Walking on foot, one should carry the Lord himself upon one's shoulder and worship him;
whoever goes to the Lord of the Abode (Bhavanātha) should likewise report [his arrival] after seeing him.
Having bathed in the Golden River (Svarṇanadī), one should worship Dāmodara.
Completely liberated from all bonds, he shall indeed attain Kailāsa;
he becomes a liberated Gaṇa for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
[This occurs] through wives, friends, sons, brothers, or virtuous people.
He who goes while remembering the Lord, accompanied by friends, relatives, and others,
goes to heaven along with that circle [of companions] as far as the sun.
Having fashioned an auspicious divine form, well-established and seated upon a chariot, he proceeds.
Worshiping her with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron,
as well as with various flowers, incense, lamps, and the like;
and with songs, dances accompanied by musical instruments, laughter, and many kinds of graceful movements.
Bestowing land, gold, cows, water, food, clothing,
grass, fuel, and pleasing speech, he goes to Raivata;
then, having gone to Dāmodara and likewise to Bhava-Īśvara, he worships them.
In the lake at Svarṇavatī or in the pool fashioned by Raivatī,
he bathes, chants the name of Govinda, and gives food in abundance.
There, whatever person bestows gifts and even his entire possessions, [attains the highest goal].

Having performed the rites of bathing, twilight worship, and so forth at a sacred ford (tīrtha) according to the words of a Brahmin, he goes to the Nandana grove and, grasped by the hands of celestial nymphs, enjoys auspicious pleasures as long as the moon and stars endure. (14–15)
Then, with faith, one should offer darbha grass, sesame seeds, and sacrificial food (haviṣya);
as well as agastya, bhṛṅgarāja, and auspicious śatadala flowers;
camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, saffron, and tulasī leaves. (16)
Whatever is resolved upon by mortals at a sacred ford (tīrtha) becomes infinite.
One should indeed offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) the size of bilva fruits at the sites of sacred fords,
along with betel leaves, fruits, offerings, sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water.
Within the month, during the bright fortnight, on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father,
under the Gajacchāyā yoga on the thirteenth lunar day, or when wealth has been acquired, O best of the twice-born,
one should perform a Śrāddha at home for the sake of liberating the ancestors from their debt.

A hundred times more than at home is the merit at a river; and that which flows to the ocean is even greater. From that, it is infinitely greater in a temple in the presence of a deity, and at the sacred sites of Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Gayā, and Piṇḍatāraka.
One should perform the śrāddha at Prayāga, at the Gomatī, at Bhāva, at Dāmodara, at the Narmadā, at Tapatī, and at Trivikrama;
likewise at Svarṇarakṣā, at the Āpagā, and at the Nārāyaṇa-hrada.
If a person performs a *śrāddha* at Ojasvatī, Bhadrā, Śatrujita-taṭa,
Vāmanasthala, and the edge of Kuṇḍa,
his ancestors, liberated from all sins, attain the supreme goal.
Having attained the highest lineage and enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures,
the performer of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) ascends a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and proceeds to liberation.
[This applies] during sacrifices such as the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), at weddings, and in domestic rituals.
At the commencement of the installation of a deity, and in works such as the digging of wells and tanks,
all the deities are satisfied and the ancestors of men rejoice.
When the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is performed in the home, every auspiciousness arises.
Lust, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication, pride, and the like;
deceit, envy, malice, lack of discernment, and lack of reflection;
egoism, caprice, restlessness, and fickleness—these too [are obstacles]. (28)
Exertion toward unjust means, negligence, malice, and violence;
laziness, procrastination, and consorting with another's wife—these faults must always be abandoned by a person traveling to a sacred pilgrimage site. (1.151.30)
He shall indeed be an ornament to the land, the region, and the city;
he shall be illustrious, learned, and of noble birth, and he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords (tīrtha).
Bathing, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), Vedic study (svādhyāya), and libations to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa)—[these are his duties].
The ancestral rite (śrāddha) and the worship of the Divine arise for one who has abandoned all faults.
Rising again and again, one should bathe; likewise, Hari and Hara are to be worshipped.
Truth should be spoken, what is beneficial should be done, and gifts should be given according to one's capacity.
Fear of slandering others, avoidance of the wives of others,
not adopting the faults of heretics, and the joyful service of the virtuous;
one should not even mentally harbor what is displeasing toward one's father, mother, or gurus.

A householder should give medicine and vegetables to those in need. On the eleventh, fifteenth, fourteenth, and eighth lunar days, on the new moon day, during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, at the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), and during eclipses— [on these occasions, one should observe the fast].
On the day of Vaidhṛti, on the anniversary of the death of one's father or mother, on an auspicious day,
or on the first day of a Yuga or Manvantara, a great festival should be celebrated at home;
or one should go to a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha), whereby the merit becomes a hundredfold.
One must achieve mastery over the senses and avoid intoxicants and gambling.

(38) Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, worship of the gods, honoring the twice-born, and the veneration of virtuous men and women should be performed, for they bestow imperishable merit. (39)
Even a single cow, adorned with clothes and ornaments, yielding milk, accompanied by its calf, and provided with clothing, should be given to a virtuous twice-born man.
To a holy man, well-prepared food should be given, and to a virtuous woman, adornments such as garments and the like.
Food and goods should be given so that there may indeed be satisfaction.
Even one who is most sinful throughout seven lifetimes and base in this present birth is liberated from all sins if he gives a single cow. 41–42.
When he is led bound along the path of Yama by the servants,
then the cow approaches and protects him like her own son;
having conquered those messengers with a mere "hum" sound, she drives them far away.
A cow, having taken its donor with it, indeed goes to the abode of Hari.
The bull is declared to be Dharma; therefore, the gift of a bull should be made at a sacred ford.
Dharma shall protect [the gift], and it leads the donor to heaven.
Even a mere morsel of alms should be given by householders at a sacred place of pilgrimage. By giving cooked food prepared in jars, leaves, and so forth, as well as an umbrella, sandals, a water-pot,
a finger-ring, and garments, a person goes to heaven.
Drink should be given to one afflicted by thirst from fatigue, and food indeed to one afflicted by hunger;
clothing should be given to the naked. O Goddesses, they lead such a person to heaven. Food soaked in ghee should be given constantly according to one's ability.
There is great suffering from hunger in the world; food is considered its medicine. Through that, it attains peace, and the gift of food is the most excellent.
Food, clothing, fruit, water, buttermilk, vegetables, ghee, and honey—

A leaf, a flower, as well as sandals, a patched garment, a staff, and a water-pot; an umbrella, a bowl, as well as knowledge, a book, and the worship of the gods; a maiden, items brought by a *kuśa*-grass mat, and houses containing seeds and medicinal herbs. (1.151.5–51)
A jewel, a sacred field, sacrificial vessels, a meditation belt, and sandals;

a black antelope skin, the gift of wisdom, and the narration of discourses on Dharma—having gone to a holy ford (tīrtha), much should be given by him, for through that great spiritual merit shall arise. 52.
Having brought about the destruction of all sins, the donor goes to the abode of Hari.
Whatever fruit may accrue to men from sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, or from the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā, that same fruit shall be obtained upon seeing Dāmodara on this earth.
On the eleventh day, having performed his ablutions, he should be intent upon the worship of the deity.
Having bathed with water from a sacred ford and having consecrated the image with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
he should bathe it with water mixed with saffron, agallochum, sandalwood, and camphor.
Then, having worshipped with fragrant lotuses,
many white *mālatī* flowers, and *tulasī* leaves,
one should offer a garment, a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and burn incense.
One should offer a lamp with ghee, or even with oil in the absence of ghee.
One should also present various kinds of food offerings (naivedya), as well as fruit and betel leaf.
Furthermore, one should perform the worship of the temple through the offering of a banner and other such acts.
Then one should give a cow with its calf, which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Thereafter, having performed a circumambulation accompanied by the sounds of singing and musical instruments,
as well as the recitation of the Vedas and Purāṇas, and with commentaries and divine narratives.
One should perform a vigil before the deity on grounds illuminated by lamps,
arranging seven mountains made of the seven grains and provided with lamps,
honoring them with fruits, betel leaves, and cooked food.
The narrative of Viṣṇu should indeed be heard by learned men, Vedic scholars, peaceful brāhmaṇas, and likewise by virtuous people, as well as by chaste women and householders;
in this manner, a vigil should be observed by those who are free from passion, hatred, and other such afflictions.
Having kept a vigil at night, when the solar orb has risen,
and having performed the morning twilight rites (pūrva-sandhyā) after bathing, one should perform the midday rites.
Having offered libations to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings according to the prescribed rules, [one should proceed].
Having performed the ritual bath for the ancestors, one should give gifts according to one's capacity.
Then, having worshipped Lord Dāmodara with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
one should again perform a bath in the waters of the Raivatī-kuṇḍa.
One should indeed behold Rādhā and the others in the waters of the Golden River (Svarṇadī).
Then one should proceed to the Arohaṇa step-well and behold Hanumān; there, one should indeed drink the water. After that, once again—
One should undertake the ascent of a mountain, or else return toward the city;
having arranged for the sight of the strides of Trivikrama,
one should by all means provide various gifts, such as food and other offerings.
"Having given and performed [the rite], the builder of the sacred site (tīrthakāraka) should depart for his own abode.
Thus has this supreme, liberation-bestowing construction of a sacred site been described to you.
Having heard this, King Bhoja also went to Mount Raivata.
Having performed auspicious rites, he visited the principal holy fords (tīrthas):
Bhava, Dāmodara, Svarṇarakṣā, Mṛgānanāsthalī, Ambā, Dattātreyarūpa, and likewise Nārāyaṇahrada. || 71–72 ||
Having beheld Raivatācala, Gaṅgā, and likewise Gomukhikā;
Trivikrama-raṇacchoḍa-mandira and Vāmanasthalī;
Baler-makhasthalī, Bhadrā, and likewise Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Having likewise visited Ojasvatī, Somanātha, and Suvarṇadvārikā—
these and various other sacred fords (tīrthas)— and having given land, cows,
gold, silver, and other gems as well as jeweled ornaments; || 74–75 ||
Having given garments and food in abundance to the Brahmins, to virtuous men and women, and to the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others,
the lord of men returned to his kingdom of Kanyakubja.
He caused a great festival to be held for the journey together with Svarājñī.
At that time, by the power of his merit, Bhoja’s vision indeed became divine;
he beheld Vaikuṇṭha and Kailāsa, as well as Hari and Hara along with their attendants.
Then he beheld a magnificent, divine celestial chariot that grants liberation.
Established there by the attendants, he, possessing a divine form along with his wife,
went to Vaikuṇṭha itself, having become liberated through the power of Hari.
"Thus, O beloved Ramā, Camatkāra was told [the glory] of Raivata.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Rules for Holy Places, Rituals, Gifts, and so forth," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Chapter 152 [Author:
Chapter 153 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lotus-born One! I shall now declare the observances (*niyamas*) and restraints (*yamas*) to be maintained at the sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
The observance of these *niyamas* and *yamas* shall be fruitful.
He who is a conqueror of lust and anger, and who is free from greed, delusion, and the like—
One who is faithful, a believer in the hereafter, and pure shall partake in the fruit of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Indeed, he whose hands, feet, belly, tongue, mind,
and genitals are restrained truly attains the fruit of the sacred ford.
Truthful in speech, firm in his vows, tranquil, and regarding all beings as equal to himself,
one who has attained purity through austerity and sacred knowledge enjoys the fruit of visiting holy places (tīrtha).
Indeed, at a holy place, one should observe a fast, undergo a shave, and perform the Śrāddha rite along with the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka).
5. Alms should be given with sincere devotion to virtuous monks and nuns.
6. Shaving is never prescribed for women whose husbands are living;
no one should ever perform an examination of those who are to receive alms.
And there, one should perform the primary worship of the deities residing therein with ornaments,
garments, substances, vessels, fruits, food offerings, and other articles.
However, one who is unable to do so should offer salutations and likewise perform tasks such as sweeping.
Service to the feet of the virtuous bestows grace.
(8) For him by whom the virtuous are served with body, mind, and material things, there shall be the fruit of all great worship and the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites. (9)
For one by whom the virtuous have been gratified through the means of surrendering all one's possessions,
the fruit of every gift belongs to them, because the virtuous are indeed Nārāyaṇa himself.
Whatever merit is performed at holy pilgrimage sites along with their confluences, [that too is attained].
Even that which is performed a thousandfold shall yield infinite fruit.
Whatever is done at a sacred site (tīrtha), even if it be very little, increases through the power of the sacred site.
Merit increases eternally, while sin is always dissolved.
Among living beings who have made a sacred ford (tīrtha), not even a trace of sin exists;
because it enables people to cross over [saṃsāra], it is therefore called a tīrtha.
Whatever one performs at a true tīrtha, all that becomes a bestower of merit.
Those who possess a body must certainly abide at a sacred ford (tīrtha) according to the rule.
A seeker of the ford should cultivate purity of mind as well as service to the virtuous.
[This applies] even to one who is greedy, malicious, cruel, or deceitful.
For one who is impure, a thief, an atheist, a rogue, a slanderer, or a traitor,
there shall never be the fruit of pilgrimage.
Even when physical impurity is abandoned, the mind does not become pure.
Upon abandoning the perception of faults, the mind becomes stainless.
Passion and hatred are the forms of impurity; by abandoning them, one becomes pure.
Whether by women or by men, divine nature is to be beheld at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Through a divine state, one's own inner divinity increases day by day.
The Lord should be held within the divine internal organ at a sacred pilgrimage site;
He indeed delivers the pure devotee who is a vessel of merit.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and lack of possessiveness;
(1.152.20) purity, austerity, contentment, self-study, and devotion to Hari;
chanting, worship, beholding the Deity, hearing [His glories], and prostration. (1.152.21)
These duties must be performed especially so that the full fruit of the sacred ford may be attained.
Anger should not be harbored at a sacred ford, for it indeed consumes one's merit.
At a sacred ford, one must never eat the food of another, nor ever drink the water belonging to another.
And one must not accept gifts, for they rob the power of one's austerity (tapas).
[One should offer] sweetmeat balls, pearls, delightful kasāras, fried cakes filled with ghee,
saṃyāvas, milk-puddings, apūpas, śaṣkulis, khājakas, and so forth.
With side dishes such as *parpikā* and *piṇḍaka*, along with split pulses (*dvidala*) and the like; with curds, milk, and buttermilk; with the excellent juices of sandalwood and milk;
with well-cooked ghee and sugar, and other various foods fit for eating and licking.
The virtuous, brahmins, and virtuous women, as well as the poor and children, should be gratified.
By that, his ancestors shall be satisfied, and his merit becomes infinite.
One who desires the fruit of the sacred ford (tīrtha) must eat and cause others to eat.
One who desires happiness should never make a pilgrimage site (tīrtha) barren;
for a conscious pilgrimage site is considered superior to a site that is merely inert.
The virtuous, chaste women, yogis, ascetics, and celibate students [constitute such sites].
All those [pilgrimages] are conscious holy places (tīrtha), and the merit gained from attaining them is great.
During the Cāturmāsya period, in particular, the service of holy places is enjoined;
at that auspicious time for austerity and restraint, the fruit shall indeed be infinite.
For those who perform these excellent Cāturmāsya vows— which require little effort, yield abundant fruit, and bestow the fortune of sons— their reward is inexhaustible.
Having touched a cow, bowed to a Brāhmaṇa, and fully honored virtuous deities, [one attains this merit].
An ascetic, a renunciant, one who is tranquil, a learned Vedic scholar, and a celibate student;
one's mother and father, one's sister, her husband, the husband of one's daughter, one's nephew, one's grandson, and friends, relations, and kinsmen. (32–33)
Virtuous women, chaste wives, and maidens; the poor, the blind, and the wretched;
children, the elderly, and the sick; cows, guests, and the helpless;
beggars, the hungry, the weary travelers, and those dwelling at sacred pilgrimage sites—[he protected them all].
Having fed them, householders are liberated from their sins.
A king, an elephant, a horse, a mongoose, a virtuous woman, a bull, a mountain, a mirror, a milk-tree, one who gives food, and likewise virtuous people—[these are auspicious omens]. (35–36)
For one established in the Cāturmāsya vow, these holy places consisting of water and land, as well as temples and divine images, purify merely by being seen.
Having heard discourses on the Vedic Dharma and having beheld men intent on liberation, [one attains purification].
Having recollected Lakṣmī, Hari, Śambhu, Śivā, and Gaṅgā, the celestial river;
having kept a vigil for Viṣṇu and given gifts according to one's ability—
betel, flowers, lamps, food offerings, and *tulasī* leaves.
By performing song, dance, and instrumental music in the temple of the gods,
one attains great prosperity as well as the fruit of heaven and the granting of liberation.
One-pointed concentration of the senses and the mind is the highest austerity.
Therefore, people should achieve one-pointed concentration upon Vāsudeva through meditation and other means.
During the four-month rainy season retreat (cāturmāsya), sages and ascetics, having quickly conquered the taste for the tongue,
perform austerities in order to obtain the fruit of pilgrimage.
Subsisting on fruits, drinking milk, or eating only once a day;
or the renunciation of vegetables, or subsisting on vegetables alone, or eating sesame seeds;
consuming curd, the renunciation of ghee, or likewise eating only one meal a day.
Eating only a measure of black gram, mung beans, and so forth, or even the mere observance of a vow;
sleeping on the ground, bathing in water, and the avoidance of oil massages and the like;
devotion, worship, wearing garlands, chanting, and the glorification of Śrī Hari. (44–45)
Constantly hearing the sacred narrative, beholding one’s chosen deity, serving holy men at a sacred ford, and observing many merit-bestowing vows;
Brahmins and holy men are to be honored and fed with excellent flavors.
The vow of worshiping Kṛṣṇa daily with the sixteen excellent services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) is a supreme observance;
likewise, the constant honoring of saintly persons, or the performance of fire-offerings (homa), is a supreme vow.
Furthermore, the avoidance of ghee, sugarcane products, salt, and so forth is considered a vow. (47–48)
One’s vow consists of eating and consuming only that which is offered daily to the Blessed One.
That vow is the most excellent because it is through such action that both the virtuous and the Blessed One are pleased; therefore, one should perform that vow which bestows liberation.
Service to one's mother, father, and teacher is the highest of vows. (1.152.5) Service to her husband is the vow of a wife; pleasing her husband is the vow of a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
Service to the teacher is the vow of a disciple; pleasing the teacher is the vow of a disciple. (1.152.51)
On Mount Raivata, the Kārttika-vrata must especially be performed at Vaṭatāla,
in the sacred field of Hari-Hara, and at Kapilāśrama.
Alternatively, one may observe the vow known as Māsopavāsa or the Cāndrāyaṇa.
The auspicious Cāndrāyaṇa vow should be performed starting from the full moon.
On the full moon of Āśvina, there are indeed fifteen morsels;
on the first day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika, there are fourteen mouthfuls.
There is indeed a reduction of one morsel for each successive lunar day (*tithi*). On the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), there should be a fast; on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), there is only one morsel.
There are two morsels on the second lunar day, and so on, until the full moon (*pūrṇimā*).
The increase in mouthfuls should be performed according to the increase in guests, and that is the rule for the vow.
Such a mouthful as passes down the throat with a single effort—neither less nor more—is always approved for the purpose of the vow. (56–57)
Alternatively, another austerity and vow proclaimed by the founders of other sects is as follows:
from sunrise until sunset, one remains in water during the day; this is the *jalakṛcchra*.
On the tenth day, one takes cow urine, cow dung, ghee, milk, and curd.
Fasting on the eleventh day is indeed the *harikṛcchra* vow.
From the seventh day onwards, one should sequentially consume water, milk, curd, and ghee;
fasting on the eleventh day is the *paitāmaha-kṛcchra*.
From the sixth day, one should drink milk for three days and fast for three days;
this is called the Māhendrakṛcchra, which should especially be performed at a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
From the third day, one should eat food such as wild rice (nīvāra) for three days, and then [fast] for three days.
Fasting for three days on barley and other such grains is indeed the Vaiṣṇava Kṛcchra.
(6.2) Drinking milk for five days, eating curd for five days, and fasting on the eleventh day is called the Bhāskara Kṛcchra. (6.3)
From the fifth day onwards, one should eat in sequence: beans, barley, vegetables, curd, milk, ghee, and water on the eleventh day; this is called the *ṛṣikṛcchra*.
Water well-boiled with leaves of the *palāśa*, *bilva*, *darbha*, lotus, and *udumbara* [trees]...
One should drink milk on the first lunar day and observe a fast on the sixth;
this very vow is proclaimed as the *Āgneya-kṛcchra*.
From the seventh day onwards, one should subsist on bilva, lotus, and lotus-stalks along with milk.
Fasting on the eleventh day is declared to be the Lakṣmī-kṛcchra.
Eating only from leaves for eleven days constitutes the Parṇa-kṛcchra.
One should eat in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, and eat food obtained unasked for three days.
Fasting for three days is declared to be the *prājāpatya* *kṛcchra*.
Fasting for twelve days is called the *pārāka* *kṛcchra*.
By consuming only fruit, it is proclaimed as the *phala-kṛcchra*.
By the consumption of water alone, that is called the *jalakṛcchra*;
likewise, by the consumption of leaves alone, it is called the *dalakṛcchra*.
By the consumption of flowers alone, it is proclaimed as the *puṣpakṛcchra*.
By taking only a seed, that is called a *bījakṛcchra* penance.
By taking a sesame seed, by taking a chickpea, or by taking fried rice grains, each respective *kṛcchra* is said to be performed. (7.1–7.2)
The cooked *kṛcchra*, the uncooked *kṛcchra*, and the *kṛcchra* of barley meal and rice-vows—
these *kṛcchras* should be performed according to the rules during the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
accompanied in every way by devotion to the Blessed One. (73)
These [observances] grant the fruits of enjoyment and liberation; otherwise, they are considered to bestow heaven.
If fainting occurs in the midst of a *kṛcchra* penance, one should then have the person drink cow’s milk.
Water, roots, fruit, milk, leaves, flowers, ghee, and curd [are also recommended]. 75.
Buttermilk, oil, sugar and the like, forest grains, vegetables, and sea-products;
camphor, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, neem, black pepper, and medicinal herbs;
substances for cleansing the mouth, ginger, and decoctions as well. 76.
Indeed, twenty-four such principles constitute the non-violation of a vow.
Alternatively, there are: eating only what is unasked for, subsisting on alms, or eating only uncooked food;
the renunciation of vegetables, the renunciation of fruits, the renunciation of savory juices, and the renunciation of cooked grain. (77–78)
The renunciation of salt, the renunciation of dairy products, and the renunciation of sugarcane juice—
these vows are indeed well-spoken, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
These should be performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), during the rainy season, or in the month of Kārttika.
The gift of food, the gift of water, the gift of clothing, and providing assistance;
the gift of vehicles, the gift of land, the gift of a daughter, and the offering of cows;
the gift of gold, the gift of sesame seeds, the gift of lamps, and the offering of a house.
Thus, one who desires [the fruit] again must give everything that is required for oneself.
The worship of Rāmā and Āmodara is called a vow (vrata).
[It is performed] with the flowers of the *ketakī*, *jāti*, and *agasti*, as well as with lotuses.
One should worship Hari with a hundred thousand lotuses and tulasī leaves (8.3).
For every leaf and every flower, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One whose body is anointed with the juice of dhātrī fruits and who subsists on a meal of dhātrī fruits [attains the same] (8.4).
With his body adorned with *dhātrī* fruits and taking refuge in the shade of a *dhātrī* tree,
one should worship Dāmodara and proceed to the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
At the onset of night, a sky-lamp (*ākāśadīpa*) should be offered in the temple.
The wealthy should always offer cooked foods to the Lord.
In the month of Kārtika, people should take up the initiation of the Great Bhāgavata and wear around their necks a garland made of tulasī placed at the feet of Hari.
That individual is surely liberated from the bondage of birth and *saṃsāra*.
By even a single vow during the month of *ūrja*, one obtains the fruit of the *cāturmāsya* observance.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Yamas, Niyamas, Dānas, Kṛcchras, Vratas, and so forth to be Observed," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 152.
