Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: To the northwest of Vastrāpatha is a divine lake;
to its western side is a forest of dense trees.
There, in the center, was a linga made of clay within a bilva tree.
At that time, a certain hunter arrived in the spring seeking water;
having approached, he remained seated beneath a pippala tree.
Having rested for a moment at the foot [of the tree], he went to drink water.
At that time, he then saw two men, one dark and one pale,
wearing yellow garments and skins, and possessing beautiful hair and fine matted locks.
Wearing the Kaustubha gem and a crown, holding a discus and a trident in their hands, they possess garlands of Vṛndā and Rudrākṣa beads, and have four eyes and three eyes respectively. || 5 ||
Their foreheads were adorned with the crescent moon as a tilaka, and they were served by the virtuous Padmā;
they were joined by Garuḍa and Vāsuki, and their necks possessed the beautiful luster of a conch and a sapphire.
Divine, they possessed forms that bring an end to worldly existence and exerted themselves toward the cessation of rebirth.
Possessed of supreme valor and traversing the path of the sky,
the two went toward a grove of *bilva* trees; just as the hunter saw them,
they both vanished from sight, having entered into a linga and a stone slab respectively.
The white one vanished into the *liṅga*, while the black one entered the stone slab.
Then the hunter, filled with wonder, went to that spot;
there he saw a *liṅga* made of clay and the form of Viṣṇu made of stone.
But having seen him there, the hunter abandoned his drinking of water.
Remaining well-established right there, the two gods meditated upon that with devotion;
hungry and thirsty, they remained in this very state at evening.
This was what occurred at evening on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
In that secluded place, those two gods remembered [him] again and again. ||12||
The hunter, repeatedly worshipping these two— Liṅga and Viṣṇu— takes bilva leaves and lotuses from the lake and offers them;
thereafter, taking water, he bathes and honors them with flowers.
At that time, in the middle of the night, those two, Nīla and Pāṇḍura, were saluted.
From that very [lotus], two men of divine form emerged;
they spoke to that hunter because, in this forest, today you had come and offered bilva and lotuses. (15)
By the power of this worship, your sins have likewise been burnt away. ||16||
"O god, possessing a divine body, you shall remain in heaven until the dissolution of all beings;
yet, by virtue of worshipping Śivarātri, you shall become a hunter.
Through the performance of the Śivarātri vow and through keeping vigil on Śivarātri—"
And because you dwell beneath the Pippala tree, you shall become a devotee of Viṣṇu. ||18||
Having thus granted the boon, Hari and Hara vanished;
at that moment, a celestial chariot, brilliantly golden-hued and radiant as the moon,
adorned with Apsarases, descended from the path of the sky.
Endowed with every prosperity and inhabited by male and female servants, the goddesses then spoke to that virtuous hunter:
"Come, my beloved, to a beautiful heaven; we women have been prepared for you."
"You are a prosperous deity because of your worship of Śiva and Viṣṇu;
since you performed a vigil on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight during a Monday in the month of Māgha, all this has been obtained. Ascend it and take hold of it."
In this way, those celestial women regarded even that hunter as their beloved.
Having fashioned this celestial chariot and placed him upon it, they departed for heaven, the city of Indra.
And Indra, beholding him, was then utterly amazed. (24)
And when the hunter was then asked by whom he had obtained that merit, he replied that it was through the Śivarātri [vow] that he had seen them both. (25)
The one possessing a divine form [related] all of that— the vow, the worship, and how it had occurred—
and then, when the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha arrived once again, ||26||
On that day, O Lakṣmī! O Goddess! Indra arrived upon the surface of the earth, having bowed to Bhava and Mādhava along with countless gods and goddesses. (27)
He worshipped according to the prescribed rite and brought his vow to completion.
What is the use of many gifts given? What is the use of vows? What is the use of the worship of gods? (28)
What is the use of sacrifices, what use of austerities, and likewise what use of celibacy?
What use is the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā, or dying at Prayāga? (29)
What is the use of going to Someśvara, to Sarasvatī, or to the lunar festival;
what would be gained by going to Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu? (1.153.30)
What would be gained by the gift of gold equal to a tulā-weight or by the recitation of the Vedas?
What need is there for the ritual release of a bull, by which all sins are destroyed? (31)

What indeed does the gift of a cow accomplish? What does the gift of sesame seeds accomplish? And what kind of fruit is obtained during the solstices, the equinoxes, and the transits of the sun? ||32||
Whatever fruit is obtained when a vigil is performed on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, that same imperishable fruit Mahendra attained. ||33||
Having worshipped Vāmana, Trivikrama, Dāmodara, and Bhaveśvara according to the scriptures, and having likewise performed the vow, Hari [attains his goal]. //34//
Having bathed in the Nārāyaṇa lake and sipped water from the mouth of a cow, Vāsava paid homage to Ambā, Nātha, and Dattātreya. (35)
Having gone toward the north, he indeed found rest for a moment;
there, the Linga known as Indreśvara was installed by the mountain-dwelling god. (36)
Worshipped by Vāsava and likewise bathed by the goddesses, Bhava, the Lord of Devas, came directly within the range of Indra's vision. ||37||
Likewise, the four-armed god Viṣṇu was seen there;
Viṣṇu, having four arms, was thus established on that spot by Indra. (38)
Having been honored, fed, consecrated with the *nīrājana* rite, and saluted, Viṣṇu said to Indra: "In another birth, may you become Brahmā. (39)
"Having indeed ruled over another Brahmāṇḍa, attain Vaikuṇṭha.
Having received this boon from Indra and having thus established Hara and Hari, [he departed].
The Lord of the Gods went to heaven; he goes there every year for the sake of one who observes the Śivarātri vow while residing at Vastrāpatha. ||41||
He was bathing in the lake of Nārāyaṇa, serving Dāmodara, a true devotee of Bhaveśvara, and a worshiper of Trivikrama. ||42||
To lead away the bridegroom and to perform the rites accordingly, the beautiful women arrive;
desiring to see the bridegroom, they choose one another from the abode of Indra. (43)
"May this divine husband of mine, equal to Śambhu and Nārāyaṇa, be yours;
for he, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), is indeed my husband, not yours. (44)
Trees, insects, moths, as well as beasts and birds—having become equal to Viṣṇu, they indeed die and go to heaven. 45.
Then, in Vastrāpatha, those goddesses take various men as their husbands;
having obtained a husband who is like the god Śambhu and possesses the form of Viṣṇu,
they laugh, sing, dance, and offer praise.
They proclaim his victory and lead that god to a bed of bliss.
Even in the Nandana grove, the goddesses question that god:
"Tell us, by what power has the divine lord become such as you? (47-48)
Then that deity indeed speaks by the power of Vastrāpatha:
"O gods, you shall become divine; furthermore, that holy place bestows liberation. (49)
When Maheśvara arrived, having mounted Airāvata, that king of elephants stood upon the summit of Mount Ūrjayanta. (1.153.50)
For a specific reason, that elephant placed its foot upon the head of the mountain;
pressed down by it, the great mountain discharged pure water. (51)
"The water produced from the elephant's footprints shall indeed always remain stable.
Thus did the Lord of the Gods act for the benefit of those seeking sacred sites. (52)
Furthermore, in the northern quarter, there is a Liṅga established by Dhanada, known as Dhanadeśvara, a sacred site that bestows happiness. (53)
Likewise, the goddess Pārvatī, the wielder of the trident, shines there;
and in the southwest corner of Bhava is the host known as Hāiramba.
Yameśvara was established by Yama, and Bāṇa likewise exists there; Citragupteśvara was established by Citragupta,
and Prajāpati erected Kedāreśa to the west.
Likewise, on the Raivata mountain peak, there is Neminātha-Śiva. ||56||
On the southern side of Bhava, Nṛsiṃha and Śrī Hari were likewise installed by the venerable Vāmana; they are especially worthy of worship. //57//
Having attained a human birth and having recognized Hara as well as Hari, those seeking liberation must observe Śivarātri and Vāmanadvādaśī. (58)
It is declared to be the giver of merit, the giver of happiness, and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
this annual vow is to be performed by people for twelve years. (59)
The life of men is fickle; therefore, one should perform monthly duties.
Every month, one should observe the vow of Śivarātri or the vow of the fourteenth day (Caturdaśī). || 1.153.60 ||
If an obstacle arises in the middle, or even by the turn of fate, there shall be no violation of the vow; that which was undertaken is considered completed.
On the fourteenth and twelfth days of the dark fortnight, having performed his daily rites,
he should undertake the vow and its observances and bathe in a river or an auspicious lake.
One should not perform an oil massage, nor should one engage in royal activities;
one should practice visiting sacred fords and serving holy men, which brings happiness.
Devotion to the deity should be practiced by those dedicated to celibacy;
having gone before the deity at night, the seven mountain offerings should be performed. //64//
Honored with cooked food, fruit, betel, flowers, incense, and so forth, a ghee lamp should be offered for the purpose of destroying sins. 65.
Whether by day, at night, or during the twilight, a lamp should be offered according to one's capacity;
a divine lamp should be prepared, for its fruit is considered great. (66)
The gods are satisfied in every way by even a slight manifestation [of light];
one should keep vigil at night accompanied by song and instrumental music.
The narrative of Śivarātri and the vow of Vāmanadvādaśī should be heard, and songs of devotion (bhajanas) should be performed by the circles (maṇḍalas).
Likewise, gifts should be given at night during the vow and the ritual vigil (jāgaraṇa).
Furthermore, having bathed again at dawn, both Hari and Hara should be worshipped.
The virtuous are to be honored with food, clothing, and other necessities;
householders should provide meals for ascetics.
Specifically, twelve, eight, four, or six [such persons] should be fed.

Even a single knower of Brahman, or a celibate student (brahmacārī), when honored, becomes equal to thousands [of others] if he is worshipped in the house with devotion. On the preceding day, one should personally eat food that is free from pungent spices and salt. ||71-72||
Likewise, food must be given to one's sons, friends, and wife;
in this manner, the Śivarātri fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed. //73//
Vāmana himself shall be pleased, and Śiva shall be repeatedly gratified.
At the conclusion of the vow, an auspicious black cow together with her calf should be given as a gift.
Divine [images], adorned with garments and ornaments and beautified by bells, horns, and other such items,
should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and to the Brahmins according to one’s capacity.
Having distributed food to the ascetics, one should likewise ask for their forgiveness.
Thus, for that devotee who acts in this way, no sin exists.
Having become a meritorious soul and purified, and having enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures,
he shall obtain an excellent lineage as well as peace in this world.
Mounted upon a celestial chariot and surrounded by divine women, he is led to the world of the Lord amidst the sounds of singing and instrumental music. //78//
In the month of Bhādra, during the bright fortnight, on the twelfth lunar day under the asterism called Śravaṇā, at the time of midday on a Wednesday, Vāmana was born to Aditi. (79)
On the eleventh and twelfth days, subsisting on fruit is prescribed;
one may observe a fast on the eleventh day, or likewise take only a single meal at night on the twelfth.
At that time, for the purpose of worship, one should fashion an image of Vāmana out of gold.
Short, with matted hair, and provided with a parasol, a staff, and a water-pot. ||81||

Then, one should worship Vāmana— who is richly adorned with yellow garments and ornaments— with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth, using the sixteen excellent modes of service (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
One should worship Him at midday within the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
And with whatever offerings are available, such as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth, one should worship with devotion. (83)
One should worship Aditi, Kaśyapa, and Indra along with their families;
one should offer auspicious food offerings consisting of sweets such as ghee and sugar-candy. ||84||
One should cause the deeds of the Vāmana incarnation to be sung;
and on the thirteenth day, one should satisfy many hungry people with sweet foods.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, at the dead of night, Mahādeva appeared between Viṣṇu and Brahmā as the radiant form of Śrī Hari. ||86||
He became the very essence of the Śiva-liṅga, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns;
indeed, Mahādeva, the third, was invisible within that liṅga.
For at the time of creation, this [manifestation] arose from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
On the fourteenth day, one should worship Mahādeva and wear variegated garments.
One should wear a fine, variegated garment and golden ornaments, and with affection, one should worship Maheśvara along with his family. (89)
One should cause the Rudra-sūkta to be recited, preceded by an ablution;
at midnight, one should worship Śambhu with the leaves and fruits of the *bhaṅgā* plant,
along with jasmine, *kunda* flowers, *kanaka*, and *karavīraka*.
One should worship with sixteen kinds of substances and other materials as well. ||91||
One should offer various kinds of food offerings according to the place and time; and then, one should have the hymns of the Hara-Rudra recited as a single unified work. 92.
One should bestow various kinds of gifts and abundant precious gems according to the prescribed rites;
on the second day, one should perform a most magnificent festival of feasting. (93)
Likewise, one should observe the vow of Hari and Hara on Mount Raivata;
and in the months of Kārttika and Māgha, one should perform the pilgrimage that bestows liberation.
For such a person, residence in Kailāsa, the world of Viṣṇu, and final emancipation are certain.
Whether a man or even a woman, one may attain liberation through this vow.
A woman who possesses desire becomes, by means of it, Ramā or Pārvatī;
a woman who is free from desire surely attains liberation in the divine abode.

In the month of Māgha, all people should perform circumambulation of Raivataka mountain clockwise, observing their vows; likewise, worship, charity, and the observance of vows should be performed on Mount Raivata. (97)
By him, the circumambulation of the earth must be performed;
it shall be equivalent to the worship of thirty-three crores of gods. ||98||
Those seeking liberation should not let the two barren months of Kārttika and Māgha pass in vain;
for if these are barren, one should understand that the human birth itself has become utterly barren. (99)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Hunter’s Vision of Hari and Hara, the Installation of Indreśvara and Viṣṇu, Gajapada, the Tīrthas of Dhaneśvara, Triśūlinī, Yameśvara, Citragupteśvara, and Nṛsiṃha, and the Greatness of the Vows of Vāmana-dvādaśī and Śivarātri," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 154 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (Continuity of the Kṛta-yuga) Chapter 154: The Greatness of the Vow of the Ekādaśī of the Moonless Night (Amāvāsyā-ekādaśī) and the Installation of the Lord of the World. Sūta said: O sages, I shall now describe the greatness of the vow of the Ekādaśī of the Amāvāsyā, which destroys all sins, as well as the installation of the Lord of the World. Listen with devotion. Formerly, in the city of Avantī, there was a king named Mahīpāla. He was a devotee of Viṣṇu, truthful, and a protector of his subjects. Once, while he was seated upon his throne, a messenger arrived from the city of Ayodhyā. Having approached the king, he spoke these words: "O King, know me to be the messenger of Rāma, who has come here from Ayodhyā. The king asked: "What message does the descendant of Raghu send? What command does he give? The messenger replied: "O King, the son of Daśaratha, having conquered the earth, is now residing in Ayodhyā. He sends this message to you: 'I have conquered the entire world; therefore, you must come to me quickly. Hearing these words, the king became distressed. He thought, "If I do not go, I will incur the sin of failing to obey my master's command. Reflecting thus, he consulted his ministers and, having made preparations for the journey, set out for Ayodhyā with his army. Upon reaching Ayodhyā, he met Rāma. Having bowed down, he offered obeisance. Rāma, seeing him, embraced him and honored him with great respect. The king then related everything that had occurred in his kingdom. Rāma, being pleased, granted him many boons. Then, taking leave of Rāma, the king returned to his own city. While returning, he reached a forest. There, he saw a hunter who was extremely emaciated and suffering from hunger and thirst. Seeing him, the king felt compassion and gave him food and drink. The hunter, having eaten and drunk, was restored to health. Then, the king asked him: "Who are you? Why are you in such a miserable state? The hunter replied: "O King, I am a hunter by caste. I live in this forest, killing deer and other animals for my livelihood. Because of my sinful deeds, I am suffering greatly. The king said: "Do not fear. I am a protector of all beings. Tell me your story in detail. The hunter said: "O King, in my youth I was very wicked. I killed many animals. Once, while wandering in the forest, I encountered a sage. Seeing me, the sage spoke: 'O hunter, you are committing terrible sins. You will surely fall into hell. Hearing these words, I was terrified and sought refuge at his feet. The sage, being compassionate, taught me the mantra of the Lord of the World and instructed me in the vow of the Ekādaśī of the Amāvāsyā. I performed that vow with great faith. By the power of that vow, I have been liberated from my sins. Now, O King, please grant me permission to go to the holy place where the Lord of the World resides. Hearing this, the king was filled with wonder. He said: "Excellent! By the grace of the Lord, you have attained liberation. Go now to the holy place and perform penance. Having taken leave of the king, the hunter went to the holy place. There, he installed the Lord of the World and performed severe penance. By the power of that penance, he attained the supreme goal. The king, having heard this account, was amazed. He understood the greatness of the vow of the Ekādaśī of the Amāvāsyā. He then installed the Lord of the World in his own city and ruled the kingdom righteously. Thus, O sages, I have described the greatness of the vow of the Ekādaśī of the Amāvāsyā and the installation of the Lord of the World. This destroys all sins and grants liberation. One should always listen to it with devotion. Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Vow of the Ekādaśī of the Amāvāsyā and the Installation of the Lord of the World," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 155: The Greatness of the Vow of the Ekādaśī of the Full Moon (Pūrṇimā-ekādaśī). Sūta said: O sages, I shall now describe the greatness of the vow of the Ekādaśī of the Pūrṇimā, which is the most excellent of all vows and destroys all sins. In ancient times, there was a king named Sudharmā in the city of Dharmapura. He was a devotee of Viṣṇu and a performer of sacrifices. Once, a great sage named Jaimini came to his city. The king, having welcomed him, sat at his feet and asked: "O Sage, what is the best vow for the destruction of all sins? Please tell me. The sage replied: "O King, the vow of the Ekādaśī of the Pūrṇimā is the most excellent. It is superior even to the Cāturmāsya-vrata. It grants all desires and leads to liberation. One should observe this vow with fasting and devotion. By its power, one attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Hearing this, the king was delighted. He observed the vow of the Pūrṇimā-ekādaśī with great faith. By the power of that vow, he attained the eternal realm of Viṣṇu. Therefore, O sages, one should always observe the vow of the Pūrṇimā-ekādaśī. It is the destroyer of all sins and the giver of all auspiciousness. Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Vow of the Ekādaśī of the Full Moon," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 156: The Greatness of the Vow of the Ekādaśī of the New Moon (Amāvāsyā-ekādaśī) and the Story of King Bali. Sūta said: O sages, I shall now relate the greatness of the vow of the Ekādaśī of the Amāvāsyā and the ancient history of King Bali. In the city of Pratisthāna, there was a king named Bali. He was a devotee of Viṣṇu and a performer of great sacrifices. Once, the sage Śukra came to his city. The king, having bowed down, asked: "O Sage, how can I attain the supreme goal? Please instruct me. Śukra replied: "O King, the vow of the Ekādaśī of the Amāvāsyā is the most difficult to perform. It is the destroyer of all sins. By observing it, you will attain the eternal realm of Viṣṇu. Following the instructions of the sage, King Bali observed the vow of the Amāvāsyā-ekādaśī. By the power of that vow, he conquered the three worlds and established his sovereignty. Therefore, O sages, one should always observe the vow of the Amāvāsyā-ekādaśī with devotion. It is the giver of all prosperity and the path to liberation. Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Vow of the Ekādaśī of the New Moon and the Story of King Bali," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Sa
[The Author: Chapter 155.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! On the Raivata mountain, which is composed of a multitude of jewels and possesses divine luster.
Mount Mandara arrived, mixed with golden stones.
Having entered there into that divine, radiant [ocean], it remained joined with it in a gross state; because of that, the luster of the jewel was not seen. (1–2)
Likewise, Kumudādri arrived there at Mount Raivataka;
he too, having entered within, exists in a massive form upon the Raivata mountain.
Listen now to that divine narrative which originated in the former Kṛta Yuga.
In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, all the mountains were made winged.
Those great-bodied ones flew about and fell at will.
Then Brahmā restrained Meru, Mandara, and Kailāsa, making them stable.
But when others, though restrained, did not remain stationary,
their wings were then lopped off by Indra with his own thunderbolt.
On the southern peak of Mount Meru, however, there is a mountain named Kumuda.
Divine, golden, and winged, it was enriched with celestial gardens. (7) The entire landscape was prosperous and most beautiful, resembling Vaikuṇṭha.
Above that, the divine city of Viṣṇu was established by Viṣṇu himself. (8)
And in the midst of that, O Viṣṇu, is a great palace accompanied by Ramā.
On the peak of Meru known as Mandara is the beautiful city of Śiva.
There, in a golden assembly hall, Bhavānī always rejoices.
The city and palace of Brahmā are filled with excellent citizens;
rich with jewels, diamonds, and gems, it stands upon the peak of that Aruṇācala mountain,
where those three gods hold their council.
In the Vaiṣṇava abode of Kumuda, there were golden creepers;
the flowers were also tawny and golden, as was their fragrance.
A sweet scent from the flowers is constantly wafted through the city by a gentle breeze.
The trees, too, were endowed with fragrant leaves and clusters of blossoms;
and the winds carried sweet scents from every palace.
Once, the Lord Rudra arrived at Kumuda.
Seeing Hara arrived at their home, he was worshipped by Viṣṇu;
and Gaurī, having been honored by Lakṣmī, was greatly delighted and highly esteemed.
Seated together on a single seat, the two conversed with one another.
At that time, indeed, Kumuda and the mountain Mandara assumed human forms and arrived there for the sake of service. There, Śambhu said to Hari: "Since Bali is powerful... (16–17).
O Hari, you must by all means lead [him] from the earth to Sutala;
having assumed the form of Vāmana on Mount Raivataka,
I too shall go there to Mount Raivataka.
"Having caused Bali to dwell in Sutala by means of a stratagem,
we shall return here once our purpose for the sake of the gods has been accomplished.
Mādhava said to him, "So be it," and those two mountains were filled with joy.
"Kumuda and Mandara, we two shall go together before Hari and Hara to that place where Hari and Hara dwell.
Having received this boon with the words "So be it," those two mountains vanished from sight.
Hari and Hara, accompanied by their consorts, went toward the Creator.
There, on the peak of Aruṇācala, was the city of Prajāpati;
having then held a consultation for the purpose of providing a residence in Sutala for Bali, [they proceeded].
The two of them returned again to their respective cities and their respective mountains.
When the appointed time arrived, Viṣṇu indeed became Vāmana;
he went to the sacrifice of Bali, and Śaṅkara also went.
Then, in the region of Raivata in Saurāṣṭra, Kumuda and Mandara,
those two who travel through the sky, flew up with their wings and arrived.
With great speed, they dragged many other hosts of stars along with them.

Then they both went to Mount Raivata, situated on the river Svarṇarekhā. At that time, having personally learned of their misconduct, the Lord of Gods took up his own thunderbolt for the purpose of destroying their wings.
Having ascended his excellent celestial chariot, he went to where those two mountains were.
Just as he was about to hurl his thunderbolt, those two mountains repeatedly spoke with palms joined in reverence to the gods Hara and Acyuta for their protection. (28–29)
Then Indra, with the thunderbolt in his hand, was instantly paralyzed;
Harā and Acyuta said to him, "Do not kill these two mountains.
Indra then entreated them for release from that paralysis.
He chose as his boon the cessation of the upheaval of Mount Mandara and Kumuda.
Having granted that boon, saying "So be it," Mahendra then restrained the upheaval and settled Mount Kumuda upon Mount Raivata, while Mount Mandara remained fixed.
Hari and Hara have eternally established themselves upon the Taijasa mountain;
this very Mandara is Ambā’s [throne], while Kumuda surrounds it on all sides.
Having attained the form of a lotus through its division into twelve petals, it stands as such.
These two mountains are seen within the fiery jewel;
those two earthly [mountains] were established within the fiery principle of Raivata.
There, Viṣṇu as Dāmodara and Śambhu as Bhava were established.
Having brought Aruṇācala there, Brahmā indeed arrived at that place;
he established Aruṇācala on the eastern side of Mandara.
Having made his own dwelling there, Brahmā resided in his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).

Where that reservoir of water was held in the Mandara lake, there arose the Kamaṇḍalukuṇḍa, a sacred ford (tīrtha) that bestows imperishable merit. On the first peak of Aruṇādri, Brahmā indeed resided. || 37-38 ||
That place became the holy site known as Brahmakuṭī, which bestows liberation.
And on the second Aruṇādri, the great lord Dattātreya performed severe penance;
that holy site, too, grants liberation.
Thus, O beloved, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva remain supported by Revatī on Mandara, Kumuda, and Aruṇādri, respectively. When the dissolution arrives, those three mountains will go to Meru.
They will indeed go to Sapakṣa and remain there;
in those three [regions] dwell the three gods and thirty-three crores [of deities]. O beloved, this secret has been told to you.
By circumambulating Raivata, one has performed the circumambulation of Meru;
by worshipping Raivata, one has performed the worship of Meru;
and by beholding Raivata, one has beheld Meru. (43–44)
Those who perform a circumambulation of Mount Raivata, which extends for thirty *krośas*,
have thereby performed a circumambulation of Meru and the entire earth in this world.
Those by whom a circumambulation of Mandara and Aruṇa has been performed [have likewise done so].
By performing a circumambulation of the two worlds named Satya and Kailāsa,
and by performing a circumambulation of Kumuda and the twelve mountains,
one has performed a circumambulation of Vaikuṇṭha.
When the three gods had assembled there for the purpose of dwelling,
Nara and Nārāyaṇa went to that forest known as Boriyā.
From the Brahmakamaṇḍalukuṇḍa, the Gaṅgā became hidden as Jāmbavī.
He fell down to the earth at the hermitage of Badarikāśrama, located in the region called Boriya.
There, the two ascetics Nara and Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by all the ṛṣis, remain invisible to ordinary people and are seen only by those possessed of great merit. (1.154.50)
To the south of Mount Mandara, at the source of the Gaṅgā, those two always dwell;
to the north of Mandara there are indeed mango groves.
[This place] has come from the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, situated within the enclosure of water.
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and the Lord of Sītā [reside] together with mango groves;
the Self and the liberated ones are indeed eternal and always abounding in fruit.
With well-formed vessels, leaves, and branches, it is the abode of those from Sāketa.
There is the Sughaṭṭa forest, which is called Sītāvana;
likewise the forest of Lakṣmaṇa, the forest of Rāma, and the forest of the monkeys. That divine forest-ground is like a celestial abode.
Where the sun indeed does not shine, nor does the moon or the stars;
where even the lightning does not gleam, how then could fire shine?
Such was that great, divine place, endowed with flowing springs of water.
There is a vast, divine forest that provides comfort in all seasons and is filled with mines of earth containing minerals such as gold, silver, and red ochre.
In that eternal forest of Sāketa, there is a spring.
Even as the Sarayū flows with its waters broken by cascading torrents,
Hanumān remains there in the forest for the purpose of protection.
This great sacred site (tīrtha) is said to be supreme, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And in the eastern Raivata region, near Aruṇācala,
the Indradyumna lake is situated there; having arrived there,
he installs Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, as well as Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Having heard that Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Sītā-Rāma had arrived,
the Lord Jagannātha himself, from the city of Puruṣottama,
brought the mountain named Nīla as well as the banyan tree born from the ocean.
Having arrived here to dwell, they surely spent the night in the eastern direction;
there were trees bearing ṭīmburu fruits, as well as *jambu*, *āmalaka*, and *karmada* trees, and mangoes, *rāvaṇa* trees, jujubes, and *amṛta* trees. (53)
In that place, there are indeed forests with abundant *sītā* fruits;
where the water is like milk and the fruits have the taste of nectar;
and where the happiness is equal to that of heaven, on the mountain Eraivata in the eastern region. (64–65)
Where there is black earth mixed with the essence of gold, and where various minerals exist over an area of twenty *krośas*;
to the east of that is the auspicious field of Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara.
The delightful Ciñcāṅgūdīvana, the auspicious Kuṅkumavāpikā,
the gentle Śatrūñjitā river, and the field of Kambharā are proclaimed; there,
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is known by the name Kambharā-Gopāla.
It is worshipped and saluted by gods, Brahmins, and likewise by humans;
even there, the lineage of that Brahmin devoted to his wife remains.
It is situated two *krośas* further to the north of Kuṅkumavāpikā.

There exists a meritorious field, delightful and endowed with forests and other such features. (1.154.70) There is the Laṅkācatuṣṭakī field, where the Sarasvatī flows both hidden and manifest, filled with most divine waters. (71)
When the goddess Sarasvatī, the great river, departed for the western ocean from the Himācala mountain taking the Vāḍava fire with her,
then likewise from Arbuda mountain [she took] Siddhakṣetra and Śrīnagara.
Having gone to the city of Virāṭa and reached the fortress of Sāraṅga,
and then having indeed reached Unmattagaṅgā, Bhogā, and Bhadrā,
she arrived at Jayanta after reaching the field of Laṅkācatuṣṭakī.
Having gone to the Ghaṭṭa known as Bhadreśvara-Nṛsiṃha, she proceeded north from there to Skandapura and then to the city of Kālīvaṭa. Reaching Ājyāprakāśa, she went to Suvarṣādvārikā.
Then, on the southern side, having reached Bilveśa, the bestower of joy, on the mountain named Barāṭaka, she arrived at Navanītādri; having reached Vāmanasthala,
she came to Umā at Vastrāpatha.
Having circumambulated Mount Raivataka and Mount Kṛtasmara,
and having ignited the sacrificial pit and gone to the Pippala tree situated in the east,
she reached Ekatarṣisthala and arrived at Somanātha.
Then, having reached the auspicious and secret Prayāga in the tiger-forest,
she went to the divine land of the lion-forest and entered the salt ocean;
having cast off the Vāḍava fire, she [reappeared] again on Mount Raivata.
The goddess Sarasvatī is eternally established in every location;
the goddess resides in every pool for the sake of the welfare of all people.
On Mount Raivata, there are monkeys renowned by the name of Hanumān.
Sītāmaḍhī, Hanumanmaḍhī, and Santamaḍhī;
the great goddess Vyāghreśvarī resides on the mountain named Māhiṣa.
[There are also] the Śrīrāmapādukā-tīrtha, Bilveśa, and Hāṭakeśvara.
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, there are other sacred fords on Mount Raivata which are indeed like stars for living beings, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
[One may visit them] by any means whatsoever— through faith and the like, even for one's own sake, or even with indifference.
For those by whom sacred fords have been visited or likewise seen,
or whose waters, dust, and mud have been bathed in or worn,
there shall certainly be enjoyment and liberation through the destruction of their sins. (85–86)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Mountains Kumuda, Mandara, Aruṇa, Nīla, and Others, as well as the Holy Places Badrikā, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Sītā-Rāma, Jagannātha, Sarasvatī, and so forth, upon the Taijasa Raivata Mountain during the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga.
