Chapter 156 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Mahālakṣmī, who dwells in the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, arrived at Raivata together with Nārāyaṇa himself. At that time, when Bali was indeed bound by Hari on this Raivata mountain— || 1 ||
In the pavilion, Bali’s wife then remembered the Supreme Goddess Mahālakṣmī—
who resides in the abode of Great Vaikuṇṭha and dwells within the heart— with devotion through hymns of praise, for the sake of ending Bali’s bondage. (2–3)
Sandhyāvalī, with palms joined in reverence, bowed to her and spoke from her heart:
"Obeisance to the Mother, Mahālakṣmī; protect my husband, who is devoted to you.
Obeisance to you, known as Prakṛti, the Root; obeisance again and again to you."

Salutations again and again to you, the destroyer and the supreme Brahman, who creates from your own womb. Salutations to you whose mouth contains both the dwarfs and the long ones, as well as the Nārāyaṇas;
salutations to you whose morsels include Mahākāla and the others.
The Saṃkarṣaṇas, the Rudras, and the Yamas are all within your mouth, being chewed by your single fangs; O Great One, salutations again and again!
Likewise, Vāsudeva, Bhūman, and the Nārāyaṇa-Puruṣas [are there].
Struck by the blow of your palm, salutations again and again to the Great Power (Mahāśakti)!
From you Lakṣmī was born; Mahāviṣṇu is born from your lap;
and the cosmic eggs reside within your pores—protect us! Salutations again and again to Lakṣmī! 8–9.
The great fires and the submarine fires (Vāḍava) are hidden within your sweat;
O Blessed One, may salutation protect you in your womb, O Caṇḍalakṣmī!
The dissolutions (Pralayas) exist in your yawn, O Caṇḍā, and Time trembles.
The great eggs are being pulverized upon the back of your nest; salutations be to you!
O Great Illusion, Supreme Goddess, protect, protect my husband!
Caṇḍī, Taṇḍī, Mahāmuṇḍī, Ghaṇḍī, Ḍiṇḍikā, and the others— [1–2]
Kālī, Karālī, Prajvālī, Lihālī, Raktilā, and the others—these are your powers (śaktis). [Give] me a drop of blood; protect my beloved and act quickly!
Protect me swiftly, otherwise I shall sever your throat and worship [with it].
If I am to become a widow, may you first become a widow.
If I am to be deprived of my kingdom, may you be deprived of Vaikuṇṭha. If the king is to be humiliated, may your husband likewise be humiliated. (14–15)
"If there should be an obstacle to my sacrifice, let it likewise be so for your sacrifice!
Thus spoke Caṇḍavegā, even as she was rushing toward the members of the assembly.
Then the gods restrained that woman, crying out, "Do not! Do not!"
Just then, Mahālakṣmī, the wife of the Great Lord, arrived there.
Having consoled the queen, she fell at her husband's feet and said:
"O Lord, do not do this! O Master, do not utterly destroy one who is devoted to you."
Then Vāmana said: "I shall certainly not kill him, nor shall I deprive him of his kingdom;
rather, I will make him my devoted servant.
O beloved, let Sandhyāvalī remain possessed of great good fortune along with her son."
"O beloved, let this Daitya rule the kingdom of the Daityas in Sutala.
If I were to abandon Vaikuṇṭha, I would dwell in the house of Bali;
O Mahālakṣmī, you shall be my queen and perform service for me."

Having bestowed the sovereignty of the gods upon the gods and the sovereignty of the Daityas upon those two powerful ones, and having established [them], she should depart; thus there will be welfare for Sandhyāvalī.
Then, that Mahālakṣmī was worshipped by the foremost of the Daityas.

The Mother, who protects all prosperity, was honored by the gods. Together with Vāmana, she—Mahālakṣmī herself—was also requested by them on Mount Raivata and dwelt there for the sake of bestowing all auspicious fortune. (23–24)
To the west of Raivata, on that height, Mahāmāyā Mahālakṣmī is eternally established, the protector of life;
she is saluted and worshipped with flowers, saffron, unbroken rice, and sandalwood. (25)
With vermilion, wood-apples, cloth, fine garments, oil, and fragrances;
likewise with auspicious articles of good fortune, various kinds of wholesome food, and ornaments such as bracelets, armlets, earrings, and nose-rings. (26–27)
With various kinds of garments such as bodices and shawls,
and with auspicious threads, earrings, and other ornaments,
she who is Mahālakṣmī is always pleased on the day of the festival of lights when worshipped with devotion.

That [image] bestows misfortune, inauspiciousness, and calamity. For the purpose of worshipping Mahālakṣmī, an image with four arms should be fashioned; it grants welfare, sovereignty, a beloved son, and likewise wealth. (1.155.30)
She is made of gold, of beautiful form, lovely, and sixteen years of age;
she holds a lotus and a jar of nectar in her [right] hands, and likewise a vessel for worship in her [left] hands;
and she grants the gesture of fearlessness with her right and left hands respectively.
One should worship her with the sixteen types of secondary offerings (upaparicāra-vastu).
Having presented food offerings (naivedya), fruit, and betel, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Various kinds of meals and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should also be given.
Through the power of Mahālakṣmī, his merit shall become inexhaustible from gifts consisting of jewels, diamonds, gems, and gold, as well as fine silk garments, woolen blankets, and cows.
After having enjoyed manifold pleasures, one shall dwell in Vaikuṇṭha.
Maidens twelve years of age or younger, who are embodiments of Lakṣmī, should be worshipped like Lakṣmī herself with gifts of clothing, food, and wealth. (35–36)

Likewise, virtuous women who are detached and established in Sāṃkhya and Yoga should be fed, adorned with ornaments and articles of beauty, and served various delicious cooked foods, milk-rice, and other savory delicacies. (37)
And those worthy of worship should be given various gifts that bring about desired results.
When there is indeed wealth available, women who have children and husbands, as well as widows, the destitute, those seeking refuge, and the helpless, [should be supported]. (38–39)

Those who are worthy of food, worthy of worship, and worthy of receiving sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā) should always be honored; for when they are satisfied, Śrī herself is satisfied. When Mahālakṣmī is pleased, all prosperity increases.
There shall be no deficiency whatsoever; whatever it requires, that shall be united [with it]. (41) When fully worshipped, she drives away all misfortune from the home.
Listen, O Lakṣmī! To the story concerning you here, regarding the churning of the ocean. (42)
I shall now relate, in this context, that story which bestows happiness:
how Indra cast upon the head of his elephant the garland of *pārijāta* flowers given by Durvāsas, and how the elephant trampled it under its foot.
Seeing her in such a state, the sage cursed the Lord of the Day (the Sun):
"May the fortune of you who have insulted my garland be destroyed!
In an instant, Lakṣmī vanished and the jewels fell into the ocean.
To recover that [nectar], the ocean was milked and churned by the gods and demons;
at that time, Mount Mandara was held upon his back by Hari in the form of a tortoise.
From the churning, the terrible and great poison Kālakūṭa arose.
The Lord drank all of that, and they churned it once again.
O Lotus-born One, while that was being churned by me and the gods,
the goddess Jyeṣṭhā emerged, clothed in red garlands and garments.
That elder sister of yours is Alakṣmī herself; she is unsightly even in her body.
She resembles a Kirāta woman in form and a fisherwoman in her face;
she is like a lizard at her ear and like a reed-pipe at her nose.
Her eyes were like those of a buffalo, but her head was like that of a rākṣasī;
her forehead resembled a bird’s beak, while her cheeks were like smears of soot;
her teeth were like the points of pikes, and her lips were like those of a camel. (1.155.50–51)
She resembles an elephant in her neck, a she-ass in her voice,
a *varbura* tree in her hand, and an anthill in her two breasts;
she is like a granary in her belly and like a stone in her back.
Her waist resembles an oil-press; her feet are like the trunks of date-palm trees;
her fingers resemble leeches; her nails are like the backs of crabs;
her tongue has the appearance of a frog; yet by nature she is like a bitch. (53–54)
In the case of a favor, she is like a poor woman; in laughter, she is like a skeleton.
In clothing, she resembles a leather-worker's wife; in her dwelling, she is like a Caṇḍāla woman.
In yawning, she is like a pit dug in dry water; in stretching, she is like a mine.
In her dwelling, she resembled Bhāṇḍī; at her wedding, she resembled the saline earth (kṣārabhū).
In conversation, she was like the battlefield; in her despondency, she possessed the luster of prosperity.
Having seen her, the gods, dānavas, and humans were distressed there and comforted there.
They deliberated: "Who is this, adorned with every inauspicious thing?
Is she the Night of Doom, the Great Plague, or perhaps the Hunger at the End of Time?
Holding a garland of chains in her hand, she seeks a husband. (58)
When she went here and there searching for her husband, all the gods and asuras saw her and fled far away, unwilling [to help];
they cried out, "She is not to be led; go away! Do not let her go to another! (1.155.60)
When the garland of choice was not accepted by anyone, she, becoming despondent, said: "Give me a dwelling somewhere where I may stay;
for I have been born in vain, and what is to be done by me? (61)
Then the hosts of gods and asuras quickly said to that goddess:
"We shall grant you that place where quarrels constantly break out within the home; dwell there, filled with inauspiciousness. (62–63)

In whose house there is the worship of skulls and bones for the purpose of malevolent magic (abhicāra), where harsh speech is uttered, and where there is the destruction [of others] through mantras and tantras;
where there is falsehood, violence, gambling, drinking, hunting, and intoxication—[in such a place... (64)
Neglecting one’s mother and father, as well as showing disrespect toward the guru;
the sighs of women and children, the distress caused by householders and kinsmen; where there is infidelity, and where there is a breach of the dining row (paṅkti-bheda). //65-66//
Dwell in the houses of those who bring suffering and poverty, where indeed the breaths of their own dependent living beings— such as cattle and others— are constantly exhausted,
and where the protection of those who have sought refuge does not occur according to the principles of righteous conduct.
Where there is mutual discord between mother-in-law and father-in-law, husband and wife, two sons,
father and son, two brothers, mother and daughter, or two sisters,
stay away from that place, for there is loss.
When a housewife within the household acts with a proclivity for expenditure through theft among her circle of kinsmen, and each member asserts their own proprietary rights,
then even one's own home is regarded as belonging to another by those very relatives. (1.155.70)
Laziness in performing one's duties, a livelihood dependent on others,
where the words of the elders are not respected at all,
and where bathing, the worship of the deity, and the recitation of mantras do not exist. (71–72)
Stay where there are no festivals—neither human nor divine—nor those held annually;
stay where there is no greed and no expenditure for unrighteousness; stay there and be happy.
For wherever there is the harming of living beings and the censuring of the virtuous, [stay not there].
O you who delight in strife, dwell there where there is treachery toward the Dharma and atheism;
where there is no hospitality for guests, where purity does not exist, where filth prevails, and where there is a lack of effort. (74–75)
In which moment after moment there is anger, where there is thirst for sense objects, where there is gluttony as well as lust, and where there is addiction beyond all bounds;
where there is the oppression of male and female slaves and laborers, conducted outside the bounds of justice. (76)
One should dwell in a place where there is no harassment of cattle, birds, cows, buffaloes, elephants, horses, and so forth;
where there is no lack of trust among the household members; and where neither the *śrāddha* rite nor the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) takes place. (77–78)

Where the ritual utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* are not found; where indeed there is no sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtayajña*), no sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), and no sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*);
and where there is falsehood regarding one's wife, children, home, property, ministers, and servants.
Where there is the eating of impure food, where there is malice toward others,

where there is failure to protect those who ought to be protected, likewise where there is failure to nourish those who ought to be nourished, and where there is failure to punish those who deserve punishment— there one should not dwell. (1.155.80–81)
Always dwell in the house of those who seize the livelihood of gods, brahmins, and cows;
in the house of those who cause suffering to the helpless, the wretched, and the blind;
and in the house of those who harbor malice toward holy men, virtuous women, ascetics, yogis, and the dispassionate.
Dwell in the house of those who prohibit the practice of giving;
dwell in the house of one who steals the body, who steals the breath, and who steals the heart.
Dwell in the house of one who acquires wealth through unjust means and who uses false scales.
Let it be ordained that you always dwell in the house of one who gives false testimony;
dwell forever in the house of one who insults the learned.
In whichever of the fourteen worlds there is injustice and lack of discernment— 85.
Let residence be ordained there where the order of worshiping those worthy of worship is transgressed;
let residence always be ordained in trade mixed with fraud, in business accompanied by deceit, and in conduct prescribed by hypocrisy. (86–87)
Where the king sides with righteousness but the subjects consume through violence,
and where the kingdom devours its own heart— there you should always dwell.
Where the wealth [obtained] from the sale of a maiden is digested within one's belly...
There, you shall always have your dwelling among those whose livelihood is the sale of women;
there, where neither virtuous conduct nor vows exist, and where the heart is not pure,
even the recitation of sacred verses proceeds from deceit— there, indeed, shall your constant abode be in hypocrisy.
One whose day passes driven by passion and hatred,
and where there exists a lineage of unrighteousness— dwell always in such a place.
[Dwell not] with the ungrateful, the deceiver, the gambler, or the assassin.

Residence must be permanently assigned in the house of one who sets fire to dwellings, one who administers poison, a murderer, or likewise one who acts unjustly; or in the house of one who stands outside the law,
or in the house of one who reveals secrets guarded by others, or similarly in the house of a wicked person.
Dwell always in the house of one who does not give food, clothing, or land;
dwell in the house of a slanderer, a sower of discord, and a causer of suffering.
[Dwell] in a kingdom, a realm, a forest, in gardens, and in groves.
In a garden, in a field, on a mountain, on land, or in water;
in a tree, in grain, as well as in seed, in a gem, in gold, in mercury, or in battle;
in combat, in a festival, in a divine matter, or in a human one—whether on land or in water. (95–96)
At a sacred ford, in eating, in legal proceedings, in buying and likewise in selling;
in learning, in the arts, in craftsmanship, and in the seasonal rains—wherever the ruler is deceitful, fraudulent, a gambler, a thief, or tyrannical. (97)
May the wicked, the unjust, and the great sinner dwell forever in those places.
What need is there for much that you have said? For wherever there is violence, falsehood, as well as theft, sexual misconduct, greed, impurity, thirst, and reviling— [98–99]
"May you always have your dwelling there, where Lakṣmī has no dwelling.
Having spoken thus, the gods gave her to the sage Uddālaka.
Then he sent Alakṣmī away along with her husband.
They all, with great concentration, performed the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Then the goddess Vāruṇī, with a beautiful countenance, emerged;
thereafter, Ananta, the king of serpents, took hold of that fair-eyed lady.
Then the goddess Gāruḍī was born, endowed with auspicious marks;
she became the wife of Vainateya, adorned with every excellent characteristic.
Then the divine hosts of Apsarases and the Gandharvas of great power [appeared].
They were born endowed with beauty and devoted to singing songs of sweetness.
Then Airāvata was born, as well as the horse Uccaiḥśravas;
Dhanvantari, the Pārijāta tree, and Surabhi, the cow who grants all desires.
The thousand-eyed Indra, honored by all, took hold of all these;
then, at the time of dawn on the twelfth day when the sun had risen,
as the great ocean was being churned, Śrī Mahālakṣmī emerged.
From that [moon] was born Tulasī, who is dear to Hari.
Together with Tulasī, Lakṣmī chose Keśava as her husband.
Then the Blessed One spoke to all the great sages: (107–108)
The Ekādaśī is immensely meritorious and the destroyer of all calamities;
therefore, the Dvādaśī is always meritorious and dear to me.
From this day forward, those people who fast on the Ekādaśī—
On the twelfth lunar day, when the sun has risen, those who, endowed with supreme faith and devotion,
worship me along with Śrī using tulasī,
are all liberated from bondage and attain my abode.
And those who do not worship me, the Supreme Person, on the twelfth day—
those sinners, bound by sense objects, my Maya, which is difficult to overcome,
casts them incessantly into the cycle of worldly existence, for they are atheists who have turned their backs on me.
When that Lakṣmī emerged from the ocean on the twelfth day,
from that time forward the ṛṣis, the gods led by Brahmā,
the Siddhas, humans, yogins, and the best of sages [worshipped her].
Placing the command of Viṣṇu before them and endowed with supreme devotion,
they fasted on the eleventh day; then, with devotion,
they worshipped me as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa on the twelfth day.
The twelfth day is your day, for it is indeed my day as well.
It is called Hari’s day and also Lakṣmī’s day;
because the couple are always one, what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Mahālakṣmī’s Arrival at Raivatācala in the Kṛtayuga Lineage, Her Worship and Offerings, the Emergence of Alakṣmī during the Churning of the Ocean, Her Nature and Dwelling Places, and the Glory of the Dvādaśī Festival upon the Manifestation of Lakṣmī and Tulasī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (Kṛtayuga Lineage), Chapter 155.
Chapter 156 [Author: Chapter 157 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the procedure for the twelfth day (dvādaśī), O Lord; tell me, my dear one, how all the worship of Viṣṇu and other rites are to be performed,
as well as the power of its merit.
"But the power of my vow must be heard by me in every way.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you the vow for your birthday."
I shall always be satisfied by the resolve of your vow.
Ekādaśī was born from my own limbs as my wife;
likewise, you are my wife, born from my left side.
Furthermore, as you were born from the ocean, you are called "Abdhijā" (Born of the Sea);
on Mount Aruṇa, you are named Padmā; and as the daughter of Bhṛgu, you are Bhārgavī.
You are Kaṃbharā, born of love, and Suvarṇikā, born of the earth.
Although Ramā, who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, has given birth again and again, my divine wife is eternal; wherever I am, you are indeed there. You abide in every house, yet you never remain without me.
When, in the supreme abode, I— whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman—
willed a second form from myself for the sake of delight,
then you stood upon my left side, invisible by my will.
She was born as a female servant who was not inferior in six respects—namely, her own nature and so forth—to me.
(9) In beauty, in virtue, likewise in sovereignty, in happiness, in enjoyment, and in elegance, she was no less; yet, in the state of being a woman, there was the deficiency of being male. (1.156.10)
That alone is the deficiency in a woman; indeed, there is no other deficiency for me. Those powers which belong to my eleven sense organs have come together and become you, my twelfth.
Therefore, you alone are to be understood as Dvādaśī in the form of my wife;
for the twelfth manifestation of your appearance came into being.
For that reason, you are called Dvādaśī, my wife, my consort.
Because you dwell within me and protect me, O Hari-vāsara, you are the Dvādaśī; you are my wife, appearing as my very day.
My form, my dwelling, and my delight are always in you.
Therefore, you yourself are considered the day of Hari, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
This secret has indeed been told by me to you in confidence.
Furthermore, at the time of the churning of the ocean on that twelfth day, [it occurred]. 15–16.
In the morning you were indeed born, and from that [time] onwards, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) became yours;
thus your birth-festival (janmajayantī) became renowned everywhere.
And at whatever time and wherever there is [a festival] for me, Hari Nārāyaṇa—
Moreover, the manifestation of your splendor shall become powerful at that time;
even Time itself becomes powerful through the power of Hari and bestows merit.
Indeed, when my birth and your birth truly take place here— || 18–19 ||
In each such instance, great festivals should be celebrated with gifts and feasts,
with songs, instrumental music, and dances, and with worship, hymns of praise, and devotion.
Having observed a fast here on every Ekādaśī that arrives, men [attain their goal].
Freed from all sins, they go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
(21) Then, the full merit of the Ekādaśī vow shall be attained;
on the Dvādaśī day, one should perform the worship of us two and then break the fast. (22)
Sin accumulated over seven lifetimes, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly,
dissolves in an instant through the worship of the boat on the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī).
[This is equal to] thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of the fast on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī).
The twelfth day (Dvādaśī) bestows merit, grants wealth, fulfills all desires, and grants liberation to all people, wherein both you and I are worshipped. (24–25)
And that goddess Ekādaśī is the great power of my senses;
she indeed requested this vow, which is entirely without food. In this matter, no food at all should be consumed, for sin is established in food.
There exists nothing that provides protection from sin equal to Ekādaśī.
O beloved, whatever sin has been committed by means of the eleven senses,
all of that shall go to destruction through the fast of Ekādaśī.
The eleventh day is also my wife, and it is called my own day;
by fasting on that day, I shall be pleased with you again and again.
Having offered my food-offering (naivedya) on the twelfth day, one should then break the fast.
Therefore, I am always satisfied and indeed remain joyful.
When I am satisfied, the entire world is satisfied; this is the fruit of universal satisfaction.
My beloved, the Saṃhitās proclaim this again and again.
When the day of Hari has arrived, one must not eat on the eleventh day (ekādaśī).
O beloved, for all castes and stages of life, as well as for women and children,
fasting on the eleventh day must always be observed in every way.
If the Śrāddha for one's mother or father falls on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), which is the anniversary of their death,
it should be offered on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) and never on the day of the fast.
Vaiṣṇava ancestors do not eat the Śrāddha offering on the day of Ekādaśī.
One should avoid with great effort that [Ekādaśī] which is mixed with the tenth day.
If it is mixed with the twelfth day at the time of dawn (aruṇodaya),
one should discard that [tenth-day-tainted Ekādaśī] and observe the pure twelfth day without hesitation.
Then, having quickly performed his bath and other rites on the morning of the thirteenth day,
if even a fraction of the thirteenth day persists at sunrise,
then indeed [the fast] occurs in the portion of the twelfth day prior to sunrise.
The breaking of the fast must indeed be performed, but not during the "defect" (pala) of the thirteenth day.
Fasting is on the twelfth day, and the breaking of the fast is likewise on the twelfth day alone.
That vow consists of staying awake throughout the night while situated in the middle of the night.
The day of Hari is said to be the most excellent of all and dear to me.
He who, having abandoned this vow, performs another vow, is like one who, having cast away a great kingdom held in his own hand, begs for alms. (1.156.40)
If even a single *kalā* of the eleventh day exists when the sun has risen on the twelfth day,
the observer of the vow should abandon that entire eleventh day and fast on that [twelfth] day alone.
If the rising of the sun should occur during even a *kalā* of the thirteenth day, [the same applies].
On that previous day, the twelfth lunar day alone, being pure, is considered the time for the vow.
On the tenth day, one should eat only once, abstaining from sexual intercourse at night;
sleeping on the ground in the morning, one should be anointed with the fruit of the dhātrī tree. 42.
One should bathe, perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and offer worship to me.
Fasting on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) in the evening, one should worship me with perfumes,
flowers, incense, lamps, garments, ornaments, and food.
One should worship with devotion at night through recitations, hymns of praise, and prostrations.
One should also worship Lakṣmī at night with articles and substances that bring good fortune.
There, one should have one's hair dressed and wear a garland of flowers.
Then one should braid the hair and fashion it into a *kabarī* (topknot).
One should apply vermilion, scented oil, and other substances to the hair and the head.
On the forehead, one should apply sandalwood paste, saffron, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, as well as a beautiful chain.
One should provide a golden necklace and fashion a beautiful crescent ornament;
one should also wear earrings and fine nose-ornaments.
One should apply collyrium to the eyes and perform the coloring of the lips.
One should apply decorative leaf-patterns on the cheeks and fine tilaka-marks on the temples;
one should wear golden ornaments on the neck and well-bear floral garlands.
One should place bracelets on the arms and jeweled rings on the forearms.
She should wear rings upon her fingers and wear a saffron-colored bodice (51).
She should wear a garment with a border of golden thread, a sacred thread, and a Kaustubha gem;
she should wear a long necklace of full-blown leaves and a golden fillet around her neck (52).
One should wear a golden girdle at the waist and a saffron-colored *ghargharī* (a type of belt).
On the feet, one should place golden anklets joined with small bells and silver ornaments,
and one should apply lac-dye to the soles of the feet.
One should wear rings on the fingers and indeed sandals on the feet;
these sandals, made of gold or silver, should be soft like *makhammālī* cloth and should be perfumed with great respect using fragrant sandalwood oil.
One should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony for Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa with five wicks, circumambulate them, prostrate like a staff, and offer salutations, hymns of praise, and recitations.
One should also present as an offering food consisting of sugar, ghee, fruits, and other such items.
Then one should offer water for rinsing the mouth, betel-leaf, and purification; thereafter,
one should provide a comfortable bed with soft pillows and the like, as well as a white cotton sheet, a variegated rug, a royal mattress, and a pillow of peacock feathers.
One should indeed scatter flower petals upon the bed;
one should provide a breeze with a fan and perform a massage of the feet.
By the command of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, one should perform a full-body massage.

Having put those two deities to sleep, one should awaken them in the morning with fragrant waters and bathe them with devotion, preceded by the cleaning of their teeth. One should wipe the two deities with a cloth and dress them in new garments.
Having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods with water mixed with *tulasī*,
one should worship Janārdana, the Lord of the worlds, together with Lakṣmī,
using tender *tulasī* leaves, lotuses, and land-lotuses (*sthalapadmaka*).
Then, with fragrant unbroken grains and flowers that bring about good fortune and auspiciousness,
with water, ritual implements, ornaments, and jewels,
one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony there one hundred and eight times.
One should properly present a garland made of *śatapatra* flowers to those two;
one should also offer incense, a lamp, food offerings (*naivedya*), and betel leaf.
[65] One should also offer divine milk-rice (*pāyasa*) together with sugar and saffron.
Along with well-prepared nutmeg, scented with cloth-powder (celācūrṇa),
there were many kinds of *pūrikās*, *polikās*, vegetables, and cooked foods;
likewise, buttermilk, curd, milk, soup, broth, and boiled rice.
One should offer parpaṭas, cakes, and numerous vessels of sour gruel (āranāla),
as well as fruits, water, a small gift for cleansing the mouth, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Furthermore, one should perform a circumambulation, a prostration, and a request for forgiveness.
After the worship, one should indeed choose a boon that is desired by oneself and bestows happiness:
wealth, grain, constant health, clothing, and even a vehicle; as well as a carriage, vessels, ornaments, a field, and likewise a fine garden. (1.156.70)
Cows, buffaloes, bulls, and the like; likewise, the happiness of husband and wife;
offspring; long life; the absence of obstacles to one's undertakings; prosperity; great power; sovereignty; and a home and kingdom. (71)
Choose your family, the attainment of happiness, heaven, or whatever else you desire;
choose all the wealth of happiness and good fortune from these two deities.
Liberate us from affliction, calamity, suffering, distress, and anxiety.
"May widowhood and childlessness never befall me at any time;
may my family, consisting of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and others, be happy.
One should likewise offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter into the fire."
With devotion, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) into the fire verse by verse with the Puruṣasūkta and the Śrīsūkta. With devotion, one should feed the Brahmins and the virtuous,
and having personally fed one's own dependents, one should then eat oneself.
One should spend the auspicious day listening to the *Saṃhitā* and other scriptures;
remaining celibate and sleeping on the ground, one should likewise avoid censure and the like.
One should keep a vigil at night; such is the *Dvādaśikā-vrata*.

The Lord, being pleased, will certainly grant all desired boons. (78) In the house of one who observes the vow of Hari’s day, the eight Vasus indeed dwell in heaven by virtue of the boon granted by Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī. (79)
Āma, Bhava, Soma, Dhara, Nala, Anila,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa— these eight Vasus indeed dwell there.
At whatever sacred ford (tīrtha) your worship is performed, or in whatever house your adoration takes place, [there they reside].

Wherever you have memory in the forest, wherever there is mention of your name in the ocean, wherever your fame exists in the world—dwell everywhere there. Wherever, during the hour sacred to Brahmā, your meditation and my own mental contemplation take place. || 81-82 ||
Remembrance of my name and devotion— dwell there with me where the assembly of children remains serene and happy in the morning;
where they neither cry nor shout, dwell there with me.

Dwell where there is no hardship for husband and wife in the morning. Dwell in that state of purity where the body is cleansed by bathing and washing, and where the bedding and clothing are pure. 84–85.
Dwell there where the house is brightened by water, by sweeping, and by smearing;
where there is auspiciousness through colored lines and the *svastika* symbol;
and where the lamp and the fire on the hearth are kindled at dawn. (86)
Dwell there where there is curd, milk, ghee, sweets, and cooked food;
where there is flour-based food, barley meal, well-ripened rice and the like, and in the morning, wheat cakes and such—always dwell wherever these are found. (87–88)
In the morning, the water from wells, ponds, and other sources that has been brought into the house and placed in two water-jars—
reside always there in that water as the water for worship.
It is there that my morning bath is always taken, as well as my meditation and the worship of the deities and others.

Dwell there where the worshipful are honored and the elders are respected. O Lakṣmī, dwell always in that place where the courtyards, cow-pens, and other areas are swept clean at dawn, and where purification from stale food and the like is maintained.
Dwell where there is the sight of Brahmins in the morning, as well as of the virtuous,
of chaste women who are devotees of Hari, and of one's parents;
and where there are learned men, gurus, and meritorious, faithful wives.
Dwell there where you may behold the gods and cows at dawn;
dwell upon that forehead which possesses the merit of the moon-mark and collyrium upon the eyes;
and dwell within that mouth where there is flower and fragrant substance. (93–94)
The Agnihotra fire-sacrifice, the Gāyatrī mantra, the worship of Viṣṇu, the adoration of Śiva,
the worship of the gods at dawn, and the offering of oblations— dwell there [in that state] regarding these.
The cleaning of the teeth with wood and purification with earth, water, and so forth.
Dwell always wherever there is bathing, auspicious ornaments, and the like;
dwell always where there is the nursing of infants at the breast, the tending of calves and the like, and the provision of grass and water for animals. (96–97)
Where there is always the protection of birds such as parrots and dogs such as dogs, where one may dwell anywhere provided for food and water,
and where there is indeed no fear while driving oxen, horses, elephants, or camels— [there you should live]. (98)
Likewise, do not dwell where there is terror from other animals.
Dwell always in that place where the various types of plants—such as houses, gardens, trees, and creepers—as well as water and food, obtain their sustenance. (1.156.100)
Dwell always in that house where grains of flour and the like are obtained from householders for the sake of insects, ants, and other small creatures;
and where the cattle of the village are not needlessly beaten by people. (101)
O my beloved, may you dwell there in the house of the compassionate.
Dwell where guests, visitors, mendicants, and travelers are satisfied with food, water, and kind words. (10.2–10.3)
Live where food is not for one's own sake, but is for others as the remains of offerings to the gods; where there is no division in the row of diners, and where there is no pursuit of self-interest.
Live where there are ancestral rites, vows, festivals, and righteous dancing and singing.
Dwell there where there are social gatherings and feasts for kinsmen, yet which are for the sake of others;
where there is devotion to the virtuous, contentment, and the habit of giving; and where there is honor for the great and compassion for the wretched—there you should dwell. (105–106)
The virtuous should provide food, clothing, water, and shelter to those destitute beings;
one should dwell where the livelihood of many is provided in accordance with justice.
[107] That which is found in the homes of holy men, celibate students, and the helpless—
Dwell there where there is great satisfaction through service and where all one's possessions are shared.
(108) Dwell in that place where there is no deceit, no suffering, no deception, no dishonesty, and no cruelty, but only perfect peace. (109)
Greed, anger, great agitation, envy, unrighteous conduct,
jealousy, malice, hypocrisy— dwell where these do not exist.
Greediness, censure, backbiting, treachery, intoxication, and pride [are likewise absent there].
Dwell there where the exposure of others' faults does not exist.
(111) The food of the unjust, the food of beggars, the food of others, the food of sinners, and the food of the wicked—dwell there in whose stomach such food is never digested. (112)
Dwell always where business is conducted according to justice, where buying and selling are fair, where there is no deceit in weights and measures, in acquiring wealth, or in giving it away;
and where there is no deceit regarding old and new goods, nor in mixing them.

Do not dwell there where there is deceit in the giving of one's word or in the giving of the heart. Dwell where there is expenditure of wealth for the sake of helping others, for the merit of sacrifice, for the welfare of the kingdom, and for the benefit of others.
O Lakṣmī, dwell happily where there is no killing of animals, birds, or living beings that depend on others, and where no fear exists;
likewise, where there is no harm to children, maidens, virtuous women, or the righteous. (116)
Always dwell in a food-distribution hall for the wretched, the helpless, and the poor.
Always dwell in a step-well, a well, a pond, and the like; in a river, a lake, on the ground, in a dug-out pit, in a natural spring, or at a water-station.
Dwell there among those who have generous masters— the mountains, forests, and fields that abound with grain, gardens, and groves—
wherein the sacrifices of giving, the sacrifices of ritual action, and the sacrifices of yoga are performed in their homes. (119)

Dwell always wherever there are sacrifices of devotion, sacrifices of knowledge, sacrifices for beings, sacrifices to Brahman, sacrifices to the gods, sacrifices of Vedic study, and where there is devotion and service. 1.156.120–121.
Dwell where there is no addiction to liquor, meat, theft, unrighteousness, or the pursuit of women and the like, and where there is no useless vice.
One who is wicked in life, wicked in heart, wicked in speech, and wicked in action— [dwell not with such].
Dwell not where there is no one who abides there for their own sake or for the sake of others.
Dwell always where there is the virtue of devotion to one’s husband, where there is the vow of a wife and good character, and where there is trustworthiness and gratitude.
Through policy alone comes the performance of duty; through policy alone comes the distribution of wealth.
Through policy alone comes the protection of the subjects—dwell forever among those who possess such policy.
Where there is the exhaustion of the subjects and likewise the wailing of women, [that is not a kingdom].

Dwell happily where there is no oppression of the distressed (1.26). Always dwell in the home of those who honor women, who assist others, and who have made their efforts fruitful— this is what should be meditated upon (1.27).
Dwell forever in the kingdom of those kings who protect their subjects like their own children, who sacrifice even their own lives, and who are righteous and devoted.
[But avoid] enemies, the violent, thieves, the arrogant, the greedy, and deceivers.
Dwell always in that kingdom where there are no rogues, scoundrels, or heretics.
Dwell there where the sovereign, ministers, princes, queens, counselors, domestic priests, army commanders, and forest guards are not corrupt.
The jailer, the superintendent of religious affairs, the wall-guards,
the inner-apartment attendants, and the doorkeepers— do not dwell there with those who are wicked.
The guild-leaders, the jewelers, the goldsmiths, the artisans, and the laborers— [131] — [should likewise avoid such company].
Those who follow the scriptures and those who act according to justice are not wicked; dwell there among them.
Among the stages of life (*āśramas*), among the social classes (*varṇas*), among women and men, and among those in villages or forests—dwell there, for there is no wickedness at all.
Among servants, spies, disciples, and dependents, as well as among teachers and kings— do not dwell there with a wicked disposition.
[1.34] Whether in the netherworld, on the surface of the earth, in the ground, in a mine, in heaven, or in the atmosphere;
Do not dwell there with wickedness regarding truth, ritual propriety, or the womb;

nor do you dwell there with wickedness in what is to be eaten, what is to be consumed, as well as in what is to be drunk, in ornament, in cooking, in fire, in wind, in form, in taste, or in smell. (135–136)
Dwell where there is no wickedness of mind, no wickedness of leaders, no deception of the people, no wickedness of kings, no wickedness of teachers, and no wickedness of women;
where there is no wickedness toward you, no wickedness toward me, and no deceit of impostors.
Do not dwell here or there among those who are nihilists and whose conduct is wicked.
(1.38) May you always reside wherever the fruit of offerings made to the deity, and whatever profit gained from service to the deity, may be utilized by all. (1.39)
What is the use of many details? I shall speak in brief:
wherever there is righteousness, devotion, and likewise I myself as Nārāyaṇa;
wherever there are the virtuous and the lineage of Dharma—there let your dwelling always be.
Thus have I described to you the abundance of places for the sake of finding a dwelling. I must reside there for the benefit of others, just as it is in my heart.
Yet, wherever there is the eating of what is not to be eaten and the drinking of what is not to be drunk— || 142 ||
Where there is no performance of improper acts and no deviation from right conduct, where the Age of Truth (Satyayuga) exists— there dwell with me.
Among both lords and common beings, the lineage of Dharma is dear to me.
There you should always make your dwelling, as on Mount Raivataka, where there is evening worship of the deity, discourses, and festivals of kīrtana;
where living beings find their rest—there should always be your residence. (144–145)
O Lakṣmī, by my command, you should always reside in that place where there is great honor for the virtuous who belong to the lineage of Acyuta,
and where the dharma of the Vedas, Śāstras, and other scriptures is always observed. (146)
Let there be no atheism regarding divine rites, nor let you ever dwell there.
O beloved, you must by all means reside wherever people exert themselves from dawn until evening. 147–148.
Wherein not even the slightest sense of "another's ownership" exists regarding one's own property—therein one should always remain; what need is there for much speaking, O fair-faced one?
Your devotees are humans, gods, demons, serpents, and likewise lords.
The ṛṣis, the munis, and all those who dwell in the creation, though not gods,
are constantly intent upon your worship and ever desirous of your sacred teachings;
they have exerted themselves for your sake and would even offer up their lives for you.
Through devotion to you, people abroad endure hardships;
for your sake, they abandon their own kin and go elsewhere to desolate places.
Whether or not you are attained, death itself is certain to occur.
Having seen their asceticism there, dwell with them if it pleases you.
Always dwell in each respective house according to their efforts; O beloved, dwell as required in the hands of those who perform those various tasks.
"Go wherever you wish, O blessed lady, but return again to my home. Indeed, there is no other eternal house for you to dwell in except with me.
O sinless one, a lovely home has been prepared for you by me, always within my heart. (155)
"O beloved, take my heart with you and dwell wherever you please. Dwell everywhere as you wish, but do not touch that lord of the planet [Mars].
O beloved, my devotion to my husband must be protected by all means."
Wherever you may dwell, there is my state as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin). O my beloved, I am all-pervading and I abide everywhere;
therefore, out of devotion as a faithful wife (pātivratya), worship me alone in every place.
Not even the slightest portion of your dharma as a devoted wife is lost.
Wherever you dwell in a home, there I also reside upon the forehead of its master;
you exist there in the form of garments and ornaments, while I am the radiance upon the forehead.
Wherever your eldest sister Alakṣmī dwells in a house, both of you should join her there and make your home even in that half of the house.
Indeed, not all are possessed of Lakṣmī, nor likewise are all devoid of Lakṣmī.
In one half of the house there is prosperity, and in the other half there is misfortune.
One part is slightly deficient and brings suffering, while another is excellent and bestows happiness.
Within a single dwelling, everything exists; nothing belongs exclusively to everyone as something supreme.

O sinless one, you must live with such a person in the house, enduring everything peacefully even in the presence of misfortune. You should stay in one corner, while your elder sister stays in another corner.
One should dwell with misfortune as one's elder sister and never engage in quarreling.
Strength and weakness must be observed according to the lines of destiny;
the instruction is that one who is weak should yield ground to the powerful.
"The principle that 'it exists' is everywhere ordained for the sake of happiness alone.
However, I shall now describe to you other sacred sites on Mount Raivata.
Thus ends [the section] in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter One Hundred and Fifty-Six, titled "The Explanation of the Reasons for the Twelfth Day Being Hari’s Day, the Ritual Worship of Lakṣmī and its Fruit, and the Abodes of Lakṣmī."

Chapter 158 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said: It has been mentioned as "Revatīkuṇḍa"; who indeed was that Revatī?
Let my curiosity regarding her be appeased first, and thereafter speak to me of the holy places.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! That narrative belonging to the Satya Yuga is now being told—how Revatī was born and how the Kuṇḍa Tīrtha came to be named after her. 2.
She who was the daughter of Dakṣa and the wife of the Moon exists indeed as Revatī in the form of a lunar mansion, shining in the sky.
From Sūrya, through Saṃjñā’s nose, the son Raivata was born.
O Goddess, that fifth Manu is renowned by the name Raivata.
For he who dwells within the Raivata mountain as its very life-force is called Kṛtavāk, the son of the Manu named Raivata. (4–5)
When the birth of a son occurred in the house of Kṛtavāk, O King, the lunar mansion at that time was named Revatī; it became his birth-star (janmarkṣa).
He celebrated the festival of the son's birth and performed the postnatal rites (jātakarma) and other ceremonies.
He bestowed various kinds of gifts upon the Brahmins alone.
(7) Likewise, the king performed the other sacraments as they reached their proper time.
At the moment of his son's birth, however, the king suffered from a great fever. (8)
Even in his dream, he saw himself performing the act of pulling a cart;
his left limb throbbed, and a crow cawed upon his head.
From the treasury, golden coins were departing, while scorpions emerged from the gods.
A female jackal howls facing him; a dog barks directly at his face.
His crown has fallen from his head, and his staff has fallen from his hand.
Having spoken, he fell from the stairs of the palace, rolling upon the ground.
Thus, when the son was born, there were these ill omens;
from the moment he was born,
that king was afflicted by a chronic illness, and his mother became a leper.
The king fell into deep thought, distressed by the question, "What is this? (13). For a son who is foolish and unfortunate brings sorrow to his father;
especially one who has strayed from the right path will cause suffering upon suffering. (14)
For human beings, childlessness is better than having a bad son;
for it does not bring benefit to friends, nor does it lead to the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Indeed, day by day, a bad son leads to the ruin of his mother and father.
In the end, however, the wicked son perishes right here along with his own self.
Better is it not to take a wife at all; better is it not to approach one’s wife during her fertile season; better for a woman is barrenness; and better is the destruction of the embryo. (16–17)
Better is a child who dies at birth, or better still is the death of an infant;
indeed, exile is better—surely a wicked son is not considered better.
For those who have died, there is grief only for as long as they are remembered.
But for foolish and wicked sons, there is grief and torment at every step.
Such a son makes his parents' hearts heavy—devoid of fulfillment, joyless, and overwhelmed by suffering and sorrow—while he always brings delight to their enemies. (1.157.20)
An evil son brings about premature old age for his father;
it leads neither to heaven nor to hell, and is not even for his own benefit.
A good son, however, knows the heart of his mother and father day by day.

Blessed are those sons who are esteemed by the whole world, who act for the benefit of others, who are peaceful, and who are devoted to virtuous deeds. But fie on the birth of those with wicked sons! Fie on their kingdom and fie on their wealth!
Thus, by the conduct of his exceedingly wicked son, he—
whose speech was faltering and whose mind was consumed with grief— questioned the aged Garga:
"In former times, the Vedas were studied by me according to the prescribed rules through the observance of excellent vows."
Having completed his studies according to the prescribed rules, he then took a wife;
he maintained every duty perfectly and never set his mind upon unrighteousness.
For the sake of obtaining a son, this one was begotten—how can such a son as this be so?
Is this wicked, evil, and greedy hunter born thus as a bringer of sorrow to us through his own fault or through my mother's fault? He is a violent man,
a drunkard, a thief, and one who always causes misery and poverty.
One who always treats his parents with contempt and is devoid of the duty of service—
his fortune indeed departs from the house after his birth;
for upon seeing his face in the morning, strife inevitably arises.
My food became spoiled, and the day turned into a foul day;
at that time, my wife became afflicted with leprosy,
and I too was constantly afflicted by the disease of fever.
Those others whom I am to support will surely suffer loss as well.
Whatever task I perform here will not bear fruit;
and if it were to succeed, a twofold loss would instead befall me.
"Therefore, O brahmin-sage, having reflected, tell me what the cause here might be;
I shall effect a rite for his pacification if I may obtain happiness.
Garga replied: "This son of yours was born under the constellation Revatī."
He was born during an evil period; therefore, indeed, he suffers.
Revatī has almost passed, for it is said that the time is indeed evil. Whatever birth occurs at the end of Revatī, all of that becomes a giver of suffering.
There is no fault for the son, nor indeed for the mother, nor is there any corruption on your part;
rather, it is because of the cause of misconduct that birth occurs at the end of Revatī.
When [the moon] is between Revatī and Aśvinī, as well as between Āśleṣā and Maghā—
It is also said that the *gaṇḍānta* occurring between Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla brings fear.
Men, women, and horses born during the three *gaṇḍas* do not remain in their home for long; even if they do remain, they bring danger. (37–38)
Thus addressed by Garga, Kṛtavāk then became enraged and said:
"The birth of my son occurred at the end of Revatī;
does Revatī not know this? Will the brahmin curse me? (39)
"Let Revatī, blazing, fall from that very sky! (1.157.40).
When these words were thus spoken, while all the world looked on with minds filled with wonder, she fell down right at the edge of Revatī. (41)
By the power of the Lord’s will, an exceedingly radiant fragment fell everywhere upon Mount Kumuda as far as Revatī;
indeed, that mountain-fragment is proclaimed by the name Ūrjayanta.
Having fallen upon the head of Kumuda and being thus pacified by Kumuda,
he suddenly illuminated the forest, the caves, and the mountain torrents.
Strengthening himself, the mountain established a friendship with Kumuda.
The Revatī-khaṇḍa, indeed, always resided in Kumuda while bestowing strength;
therefore, Raivataka is called Kumuda as well.
Until the dissolution of all beings, those two remain established in mutual dependence.
And from that same region, Mount Kumuda became known as Raivataka.
Ūrjayanta is fire-colored, while Kumuda has the hue of the moon;
through the blending of these two, Mount Raivata is the color of red chalk.
Moreover, the Revatī-khaṇḍa is indeed situated within Kumuda;
at some point, Jvālāmukhī will surely become Raivata.
For both Mandara and Aruṇa, too, are so designated through their connection with the Revatī-khaṇḍa.
Jvālāmukha will indeed become Layagrāha at some point.
Ūrjayanta, Kumuda, Mandara, Aruṇācala, Kṛtasmara, and Raivatācala—these five shall unite. (1.157.50)
There stands the very great, divine Mount Raivata, shining with the luster of gold.
That mountain Raivataka later begot a daughter who was equal to Revatī in splendor and possessed a face like that of Revatī.
The auspicious Revatī, the sister of the one named Khaṭvāṅga Suvarṇāṅgada, was there addressed by name by a bull among the twice-born who was performing austerities on that mountain;
he was known as Pramucu and behaved toward her like a father. || 52-53 ||
The sage Pramucasa gave her the name Revatī after his own father; Raivata also called that daughter by the name Revatī.
Having taken up residence there, she dwells in a mountain cave.
And that place is composed of splendor and is the refuge for the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha).
Furthermore, the flow of the Gaṅgā’s water, the water of the Yamunā,
and the water of the Sarasvatī— these three are present there in those hollows.
That pit situated at the mouth of the cave is called Revatī-kuṇḍa.
It was there in that cave that the young girl was raised by the great ṛṣi;
she attained her youth there on Mount Raivataka.
And seeing her endowed with youth, that sage Pramuca reflected in solitude:
"Who will become her husband?
Having offered oblation after oblation, that best of the twice-born questioned the fire, his spiritual preceptor.
"Be gracious to me and tell me: who will become her husband?
Is there a suitor worthy of her, or is there no one at all?
Then, rising from the sacrificial fire-pit, the eater of oblations himself appeared in bodily form.
She said, "Listen to my words: who will become her husband?
He shall be born in the lineage of Priyavrata, possessed of great strength and prowess, the son of Vikramaśīla, born from the womb of Kālindī."
"A lord of the earth named Durdama shall indeed become her husband. In the meantime, that king Durdama arrived there under the pretext of hunting and beheld that cave.
Having seen the maiden, Durdama said by the turn of fate:
"O beloved, where is your father? May I have an audience with him, or not?
Standing there in the fire-sanctuary, the sage heard those words.
Reflecting on who might be the one addressing him as "dear one," he went outside and beheld the king.
Seeing Durdama, who was to become his son-in-law, he rejoiced.
And he said to his disciple Gautama: "Offer him auspicious water for the feet (arghya) and other honors;
by the turn of fate, he shall be my son-in-law and my daughter’s husband.
When that great sage had taken the arghya and was seated upon a throne, the brahmin [spoke].
Pramuca said: "O Indra among kings, is all well in your city?
Is there welfare in your treasury, your army, your friends, and among your servants and ministers?
Welcome to you here, who have returned by the turn of fate after living abroad."
"O King, tell me everything as it truly is: is there well-being for you, in whom all things are established? Are your wives well?
Durmada replied, "O Pramuca! By your grace, may it always be so for me. (1.157.70–71)
The kingdom and the wives, being skilled, look especially toward you;
likewise Subhadrā, Śāntapāpā, the daughter of the Kāverī,
Surāmā born of Jānu, and Kadambā of excellent progeny.
"Vipāṭhā and Nandinī are my other wives, who are always skillful.
[73] Pramuca said, "O Durdama! You have called her 'Priyā' (the Beloved);
that Revatī, indeed, was called 'Priyā' by me as well—she is your beloved. [74]
"That which you have spoken will not be otherwise; it is not a word uttered at random.
Accept this auspicious maiden as your wife by my command.
With these and other such words, the king was persuaded by his wife.
The Brahmin was thus prepared to perform the marriage according to the prescribed rites.
At that moment, Revatī said, "O Sage, listen to something from me:
let my marriage with Durmada indeed take place under the asterism of Revatī."
"Without the constellation Revatī, my auspicious moment will be fruitless.
The sage then said to his disciple, "There is no moon joined with Revatī;
another constellation is currently present. Therefore, I shall do as you say. (78)
The maiden said, "By means of ascetic power, make the moon joined with Revatī.
"So be it; may you be blessed," Pramuñca said to his daughter, "I shall place both of you upon the path of the moon for the sake of the constellation Revatī."
Then, by the power of his asceticism, the great sage joined the constellation Revatī with the moon, and subsequently performed the marriage ceremony.
Then the Ṛṣi said to his son-in-law: "What wedding gift shall I give?"
"I shall grant even that which is difficult to obtain, for I possess great ascetic power.
Then the king said to the brahmin, "Listen indeed to these words that are difficult to accomplish:
Saṃjñā, the wife of the Sun, became a mare by her own form."
Then, through the conjunction of her horse-form with the Sun,
Raivata was born from her nose; he exists there as the Adhyātma on Mount Kumuda, remaining invisible when the constellation Revatī arrives.
"May this maiden Revatī, born to me, become my wife;
and through her may that son Raivata be born again by means of my yoga.
O sage, I have now been born into the lineage of Svāyambhuva Manu. (85–86)
"By your grace, I choose as my son one who shall be the lord of a Manvantara;
having indeed obtained birth through him, he shall become the Manu of that Manvantara.
I choose that he alone shall be the fifth Manu."
"So be it," the sage replied; "it shall be so, O Manu.
Having bathed in the Revatī-kuṇḍa, Revatī will grant you a son.
That son, being a portion of Manu himself, shall indeed become Manu."
"Born from a portion of Revatī, he shall be known as Raivata;
and he who is called Parvata shall always remain as two distinct Manus.
Having thus obtained the boon, the king bathed in the waters of the Revatī.
Revatī also, having bathed in that same manner, gave birth to a son through her union.
He was given the name Raivata, and he indeed became a Manu.
Thus, in whosever house one shall bathe in the Revatī-kuṇḍa, a son [shall be born].
Indeed, he shall become fortunate, a possessor of a kingdom, wise, and renowned for his fame.
Those women who bathe there shall be freed from suffering and poverty;
they shall obtain a son of radiant splendor, honored by all the world.
Thus has this sacred site associated with Revatīkuṇḍa been described to you.
Then Revatī propitiated Vāmana Hari through her ascetic penance;
Dāmodara, being pleased, spoke thus to Revatī.
"Let your union with Śaśin be as it was before.
Choose another boon that resides in your mind; I am pleased.
Revatī said: 'O Lord, here at the mouth of this cave indeed...'"
In this pool joined by the river Svarṇarekhā where I have bathed—may the mountains of sins of those who bathe there be destroyed;
may they go to heaven, may they attain happiness, and may they obtain sons. (97–98)
Furthermore, when the churning of the ocean took place,
the Pārijāta and other trees emerged from that which was being churned; at that time,
the Āmardaka tree also appeared there.
She was born during the crushing of all the gods, and thus she is known as Āmardakī.
She was presented by Hari to Candra as he was departing for heaven;
out of great affection, Candra then gave her to me in the celestial realm.
The tree situated in that Raivataka region fell while remaining within that very region;
when it fell due to the curse of Kṛtavāk,
that tree indeed came together with me to Mount Raivata.
It is divine, rich with fragrant flowers, and is the abode of Lakṣmī.
(103) Lakṣmī resides in this tree and is served by the best of the gods;
this Vaiṣṇava tree is worshipped by all the deities, beginning with Brahmā. (104)
O beloved, those who shall perform the procession of this tree on the day of Hari— on the eleventh or the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna—
their sons and grandsons shall become preeminent in virtue.
There is no doubt that one’s residence will be in Viṣṇu’s city;
this occurs for one who has fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, having bathed before an image of the goddess Ekādaśī on a mountain or in a forest. (106–107)
She should be worshipped with auspicious flowers at night, and people should observe a vigil.
She should be circumambulated one hundred and eight times with fruits.
One should subsist on her fruit, and two water-pots filled with water should be offered.
A lamp filled with ghee should be placed at the mouth [of the image] together with a bilva fruit (śrīphala).
Likewise, sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), betel leaf, fruits, and so forth should be offered.
Furthermore, a vigil (jāgaraṇa) should be observed by those intent on listening to sacred narratives.
Human beings are liberated from the grave sins arising from their actions;
at the end of their bodies, all those men are honored in the abode of Hari. Then, the goddess Revatī spoke to the one who had arrived and addressed her.
He spoke with supreme affection: "May your fever and leprosy be destroyed.
May your son be endowed with excellent qualities. I am indeed returning to heaven; however, by a portion of myself, I shall remain here at Revatī-tīrtha until the end of the kalpa."
Having spoken thus, she ascended to heaven and united with the Moon;
that sacred bathing place became known as Revatīkuṇḍa.
Now, the son of Brahmā was Marīci, and his son was Kaśyapa.

His son was Vivasvān, and his son is called Śaryāti. His son, however, was known as Ānarta, by whom, after performing austerities at the western ocean, a portion [of land] was brought from Goloka from Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
This very fragment of the jewel was brought forth and called Saurāṣṭra;
that divine and foremost mountain attained the status of being the excellent son of Ānarta. Because he was a portion of him, he was then given the name Raivata.
Raivata arrived at the Svarṇanadī for the purpose of a pilgrimage.
Having been bathed in the waters of the Revatī for the sake of obtaining a son by Kṛtavāk, Raivata said: "O brahmin-sage, may I indeed have a son equal to you."
"So be it," the brahmin-sage replied; and then, having made his preparations for departure,
Raivata went to Kuśasthalī, the city of his father Ānarta,
which had been built by Ānarta, and arrived at his father's house.
The brahmin-sage Kṛtavāk became incarnate as a portion [of himself] in the form of a son.
And in heaven, Revatī heard that her guru had met his end;
she was the excellent daughter of Raivata, the noble son of Ānarta. (121–122)
Then, out of affection, Revatī also arrived;
she became the daughter of the noble son of Revata, named Kakudmin.
And in the house of Kakudmin, Revatī was born as a partial incarnation.
And having observed that she was endowed with beauty, virtue, and youth, and was thus fit for selection,
