both gods accepted the hospitality and worship offered by the inhabitants of that place and departed from there for Goloka, the supreme abode filled with Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs.
In the midst of millions of cowherds and cowherdesses, the pilgrim brahmin was seen by Patnīvrata to be Kṛṣṇa himself in his true form.
Honored there by the locals, Kṛṣṇa listened to the chanting of the nectarine glories.

By the power of bathing in the Nārāyaṇa lake, many who have attained liberation come to the temple of Kṛṣṇa; they are satisfied by the contact with the particles [of the water]. Through the festivals of bathing and other rites performed there, Kṛṣṇa becomes pleased. (34–35)
When Kṛṣṇa is pleased, all of Goloka is eternally satisfied;
having heard this, the two gods went to the great abode of Vaikuṇṭha. There they were likewise honored by the residents and seated upon their own thrones.
There, those two divine brahmins became Nārāyaṇas.
There was not even an atom's worth of deficiency in those two, who were of the nature of Nārāyaṇa; they were born with four arms and were attended by many Lakṣmīs.
Having honored and served those two, they beheld each other’s forms and heard the auspicious, divine hymns of praise uttered by Lakṣmī and the others.
They likewise performed ablutions, drinking, and libations in the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Whatever has been done by whomsoever for their sake, they shall indeed become residents of Vaikuṇṭha. Hari himself accepts the great worship performed by them;
Nārāyaṇa, the ever-glorious one, certainly becomes pleased.
"Upon attaining his favor, we are forever satisfied—Om!
Having heard these words filled with bliss, they attained nectar. Indeed, in that immortal abode, upon the excellent seat provided by its resident, [they sat]. 42.
Those two, having been honored and repeatedly respected, stood nearby;
they heard the account related by Lakṣmī concerning the waters of the great and divine river Svarṇarekhā at the place called Raivata. (43–44)
From bathing in the Nārāyaṇa lake, as well as from drinking its water and offering libations,
the Lord of the Earth, Nārāyaṇa, certainly becomes satisfied and gracious.
Through His grace, satisfaction, and fulfillment, we are always considered to be satisfied.
Having heard of those two Nārāyaṇas in the world of Prakṛta-puruṣa,
they then went to the world of Pradhāna-puruṣa; from there,
they proceeded to the world called Hairaṇyakośa and likewise to the Vairāja world.
In Śvetadvīpa, at Badarī, in the Vaiṣṇava abode of Kṣīra,
likewise in the realm of Sadāśiva, in Māyāloka, and in the various enclosures (āvaraṇas),
they were honored by the inhabitants upon their arrival in the worlds of Īśvara.
Having been saluted and honored there, they heard the auspicious discourse.
By bathing in the Nārāyaṇa lake, by giving gifts, by drinking [the water], and by performing libations,
Nārāyaṇa indeed becomes pleased through the power of His grace.
We are always satisfied here with that very divine nectar;
the Lake of Nārāyaṇa is the abode of Brahman and is indeed the Imperishable (Akṣara).
That water is that very abode, and that satisfaction is the liquid of bliss itself.
"That which is indeed the bliss and joy of the form of Nārāyaṇa—
by that we are always satisfied here through the grace of Hari.
Thus spoke those two Brāhmaṇas, who were Nārāyaṇas themselves, acting in the role of lords.
Then, having seen that they had arrived at the world of truth (satyaloka) on the level known as Vairāja,
many of the sages, ancestors, and munis residing there,
as well as Sarasvatī and others in the assembly of Brahmā, [beheld them]. (54)
And likewise with Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Asiknī, and Sandhyā;
with Paliknī and Viriṇī, as well as Śatarūpā and the others;
with Rati, Sṛṣṭi, Mohinī, Kadrū, and the women of the ascetics.
The two gods were saluted, worshipped, honored, and seated upon mats;
having heard the divine narrative, [he declared] "Blessed is the lake of Nārāyaṇa, wherein indeed the brahmins nourish us through this libation. (57)
For one who has performed the libation there even once on the full moon day of Kārttika,
our satisfaction shall be eternal for ten billion ages of Brahmā.
Furthermore, those twice-born men who abide upon this earth renowned for their devotion to their wives—
"There they will perform the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), worship, and likewise the libations (*tarpaṇa*);
by that, there shall indeed be inexhaustible satisfaction, leading to happiness upon happiness.
Having heard this, the two then arrived on Kailāsa in the presence of Śiva.
There, having been honored by the hosts of Śambhu’s attendants,
the two were seated upon excellent thrones and listened to his story at the divine Nārāyaṇa lake in the immediate presence of Bhava-Īśvara.
"In a former age, during the Satya Yuga, we were gratified by the Brahmins in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā;
indeed, we remain satisfied here until this very day.
Now, these two Brahmins, having gone there, will perform the libation."
"Then we shall surely attain great satisfaction once more.
(64) Now, above Dhruva, in the world of Viṣṇu, in the solar orb, in the orb of Agni, and in the regions of Mahas, Janas, and Tapas; (65)
Having traveled both to the world of the guardians of the quarters in heaven and to the realm of Bhuvarloka,
they there heard of the excellent libation performed at the Nārāyaṇahrada in the past.
"Until now we have been satisfied, yet these two will act again.
Through that act of propitiation, we shall indeed attain eternal satisfaction for many years.
Having heard this, those two abodes of compassion proceeded along the southern path.
The Śrāvaṇa ancestors were seen, and the ancestors who are hungry ghosts (pretas) were seen;
the ancestors of Yama were seen, and the realms of Yama were seen.
And there, in each of those places, those living beings [attained liberation] through contact with the body of Nārāyaṇa.

By the touch of the wind, they indeed became happy in an instant. Being greatly distressed, they said to those two: "O Lords, perform our deliverance! You two are meritorious brahmins, givers of merit, who have come within the range of our sight. (1.159.70–71)

"O auspicious ones, perform for our sake the *śrāddha*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the bath at this Nārāyaṇa-hrada; thus we shall attain divine satisfaction. Then the two of them arrived on the ground there at all four pits.
Those two abodes of compassion were requested by the living beings dwelling there for the sake of their gratification.
Thus, everything down to the subterranean realm (pātāla) was shown in its entirety to Pativratā by Nārāyaṇa through his perfect meditative absorption (susamādhi). || 73–74 ||
The inhabitants there requested the destruction of their suffering:
"In the divine Nārāyaṇahrada, within the waters of the Svarṇarekhā, you two gods shall perform the libation for our sake. (75)

"By that, eternal satisfaction shall indeed be ours, as well as liberation. Having heard this request, they arrived a moment later at the place where the Nārāyaṇa lake was located; there stood a twice-born man devoted to his wife.
Emerging from his meditative absorption, he was struck with wonder:
"Aha! What have I seen? Where am I, and where indeed have they gone?
Who is this traveling Brahmin, and what is this dream that has come upon me? (78)
Then, the four-armed Lord Hari, Nārāyaṇa, was born there;
the God seated upon the shoulder of Garuḍa, with Lakṣmī established in His lap, was honored by His attendants with auspicious verses beginning with "Victory! (jaya).
Having then beheld the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, he was filled with joy;
having offered salutations and performed worship, the god prostrated at his feet. With a heart bowed in humility, the brahmin spoke in a faltering voice.
"What is this that has been shown, O Lord? How is it that a brahmin is a heretic?
What is the reason for this, O Kṛṣṇa? I have been delivered by the compassionate one!
Oh, what great fortune and merit is mine, that I have come into the sight of Hari!"
What do I consider to be a greater fruit of pilgrimage than this? You, the Lord Nārāyaṇa Dāmodara himself, have assumed the guise of a pilgrim for the sake of my deliverance. (84)
I am born [in purpose], I am graced, I am fulfilled, and I am highly esteemed.
There is nothing lacking for my liberation, since you, who are considered the goal, have appeared before me.
Nārāyaṇa himself has met with me on this Raivata plateau.
And indeed, within that meditative absorption, the creation of Brahmā was shown, as well as another—
the creation of Īśa; likewise the creations of the luminous realms and the worlds,
the creation of Yama, the creation of the Nāgas, and whatever else remains to be seen.
"Everything has indeed been shown to me; instruct me, what may I do for you?
Nārāyaṇa then spoke to that twice-born man who was devoted to his wife:
"Listen, O Brāhmaṇa, to this verse as I describe who you are. (88–89)
He who is Kṛṣṇa himself in Goloka, and his beloved Rukmiṇī—
those two deities manifested themselves in Kuṅkumavāpī as the mental forms known as Kambharā and Gopāla for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Rukmiṇī was born as Kambharā, and Kṛṣṇa was known as Gopāla.
During the Kṛta Yuga, they both resided there at the great holy site of Aśvapaṭṭa.
You indeed are Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord and Sovereign of Vaikuṇṭha.
Having brought that Lakṣmī, known as the devoted wife, to that place,
you indeed manifested here on the surface of the earth as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Previously, I indeed made both of you into Brāhmaṇas.
When you alone, O Bhava, the source of creation, manifested from the mind upon the earth,
then indeed there was the expansion of your lineage and progeny;
likewise in the imperishable world of cows (Goloka), in Vaikuṇṭha, and in the unmanifest (Avyākṛta).
In the nectar, in the white-splendid [Kailāsa], in the milk, and in the radiant ocean—indeed, throughout the fourteen worlds, those belonging to your lineage exist.
They have been shown to you by me; but you yourself are Nārāyaṇa.
The eternal Lord is the bestower of satisfaction through the gratification of the souls of creation. (97) Thus has the primary truth been shown to you—that which you and your parents are.
Now, having come here, perform my worship, libations, and other rites. (98)
Because he performed [austerities] at Dāmodara, I, Hari myself, was pleased;
I desired to grant him a vision, and therefore I have brought him here from that place to my beautiful and most auspicious holy site, the Nārāyaṇahrada.
"I was seen by you in a secluded place; indeed, this is an ocean of grace.
O Brahmin, you must awaken me, for you are none other than I myself.
I am Kṛṣṇa and you are Viṣṇu; we are both the nourishers of the world."
Therefore, since this Nārāyaṇa lake grants satisfaction to the worlds,
one should perform *śrāddha* and libations (*tarpaṇa*) here for the sake of the satisfaction of all.
You shall be the preceptor (*guru*), and I shall indeed be the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) here.
I have cows by my side in Goloka that yield milk;
likewise, there are fruit-bearing trees and creepers, and the earth is considered a giver of grain.
Every kind of sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is present in great abundance before me.
"Perform here a great *śrāddha* and a universal libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having thus commanded those two gods, they bathed there in that auspicious lake.
At that moment, the gods and goddesses also arrived there.
The world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, the rivers, and likewise the mountains;
countless wish-fulfilling cows arrived from Goloka;
and all the Ramas from Vaikuṇṭha, as well as all other holy beings. (106–107)
The great sages, the ascetics, the trees, the creepers,
and the aged all arrived here, bringing the requisites for the *śrāddha*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, Dāmodara, was indeed the patron of the sacrifice.
Nārāyaṇa himself, observing the vow of a devoted husband, became the performer of the śrāddha.
Whatever is given with faith is indeed considered a śrāddha, which is regarded as an act of worship;
that [worship] should indeed be performed for all [ancestors], beginning with Nārāyaṇa.

Devotion consisting of the total surrender of everything is considered *śrāddha* toward Nārāyaṇa and others; devotion consisting of the offering of satisfaction is considered *śrāddha* toward the departed ancestors (*preta*) and others. (11.1)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Brahmin named Patnīvrata’s Pilgrimage to Raivatācala, His Direct Vision [of the Lord] through the Worship of Dāmodara and other rites, the Vision of All Abodes and All Worlds in Samādhi, the Manifestation of Himself as an Incarnation of Nārāyaṇa, and His Arrival at Nārāyaṇahrada for the Purpose of Performing Śrāddha," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 160 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* – Section 1 (Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga)
— Chapter 160.
[Author: Chapter 161.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then Nārāyaṇa [addressed] both of those twice-born ones.
They stayed at the Nārāyaṇaghaṭṭa in the grove of Tulasī.

Having made a formal resolve for the sake of performing the Śrāddha rites, they were provided with all necessary implements, as well as Darbha grass, funeral cakes (piṇḍas), fruits, flowers, milk-rice (pāyasa), cooked food, and other offerings. || 1–2 ||
Wherever a śrāddha is offered from the two hands of Nārāyaṇa,
it shall uplift one hundred and seven generations of the families of the seven gotras:
the father, the mother, the wife, the sister, and likewise the daughter.
The father’s sister and the mother’s sister— these indeed constitute the seven lineages.
Twenty-four [generations] are prescribed for the father's side, twenty for the mother's side,
sixteen for the wife's side, and twelve are recorded for the sister's side.
"Eleven daughters [of his own], ten daughters of his father's sisters, and eight daughters of his mother's sisters are to be understood; thus there are one hundred and one families.
Having bathed in the Nārāyaṇa lake, those two best of the twice-born..."
There they performed a libation for the sake of attaining happiness in the three worlds:

"May all conscious beings in the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśvara, and the creation of the individual soul—the classes beginning with the Lord (Bhagavān), Brahmā, Īśvara, and the individual souls—be satisfied. (7–8)
I gratify with water Hari, the Lord of All, who resides in the abode of the imperishable Supreme Brahman; may He be satisfied for eternal years.
May the Supreme Self, who transcends the imperishable, the Puruṣottama who dwells within the self, be pleased.
To Him by whom all this is pervaded, to Him I offer this morsel.
Whatever food there is—whether solid, soft, lickable, or drinkable, the fourfold kind—to that Śrī Hari it is given; may Hari indeed attain satisfaction.
May this water offered to that abode which is called the Imperishable (akṣara), which is all-pervading and the object of service, attain eternal satisfaction.
May this fourfold food— milk-rice, plantains, and so forth— be offered.
May this [offering] consisting of a ball of food, which has been given, indeed attend upon Brahmā.

Indeed, those who are liberated and those who are bound from time immemorial, those who have gone there and those who will go, those who abide within the physical form and those who are situated outside— [may it reach them all].
Just as the pearls [were offered], so may the goddesses and those others who reside therein attain eternal satisfaction with this water. May they be satisfied by their food,
foremost of which is milk-rice, along with plantains and other fruits.
Food that is chewed, food that is eaten, food that is licked, and food that is sucked—these are the four kinds of food. O best of the imperishable! This ball of rice is given by me into your hand;
give it to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.
All sovereign powers, virtues, and manifestations;
the divine emblems of the Form, as well as the ornaments;
all weapons indeed, and various splendors.
I offer water with faith to those powers of Hari, which exist in manifold forms within His manifest body; possessing both embodied and unembodied natures,
may I satisfy them with this water so that they remain gratified for eternal ages.
Along with milk-rice and other primary foods, together with plantains and other fruits—
whatever fourfold food there is, consisting of that which is chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked—
this ball of rice (piṇḍa) is offered by me into your hand, O Janārdana!
Grant [these offerings] to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.
May they, too, attain eternal satisfaction through this *śrāddha* offering.
Through the satisfaction of Hari, may there be eternal satisfaction for those who abide in Hari.
In the imperishable abode and among those who are liberated, there are the manifestations of sovereignty,
powers of capability, other qualities,
and prosperities; as well as that which is to be enjoyed, the instruments of enjoyment, and the means of enjoyment.

Whatever exists—the palace, the wall, cattle, living beings, gardens, fields, and pleasant places—every single thing is of the nature of the abode of Brahman and is of the nature of liberation. Furthermore, whatever fourfold food there is—whether it be that which is chewed, eaten, licked, or sucked—is likewise so. (25–26)
Whatever divine and sentient beings are always present there,
may they all attain eternal satisfaction through this water.
To them, [I offer] milk-rice and other primary foods, together with plantains and other fruits.
Food for chewing, food for eating, food for licking, and food for sucking—these four kinds of auspicious food, O Janārdana, this ball of rice is given by me into your hand;
give it to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction. (28–29)
Nārāyaṇa is the imperishable abode; those who are liberated are His manifestations.
May they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha.
Therein are the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as well as devotion and worship.

Muktirājñī, Mumukṣā, Kathā, Vārtā, Dīkṣaṇā, Parāvidyā, Ramā, Sevā, Jayā, and the other female attendants; there also are the forests, rivers, mountains, and ten million liberated souls (muktakoṭayaḥ). || 3.1–3.2 ||
Gardens, monasteries, and grounds designated by letters;
the elements, mines, excavations, elevations, and peaks;
and all celestial palaces as well as the various classes of their respective attendants.
There were Gandharvas, dancers, storytellers, and flute-players;
servants, performers of sacrifices, chanters of Sāmans, panegyrists, and industrious men; artisans, craftsmen, and circles of both those who had renounced and those who had not. (34–35)
Thus, in this divine, imperishable abode, whatever beings and whatever things exist there, I gratify them with water; may they be satisfied for eternal years.
To them, [I offer] food headed by milk-rice, together with plantains and other fruits.
Whatever food there is— whether solid, soft, lickable, or drinkable, comprising the fourfold types of sustenance—
this ball of rice is offered by me into your hand, O Janārdana.
Give it to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.
Now, for the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa— who is entreated by Rādhā, Virajā, and others,
as well as by Rukmiṇī, and who makes his abode in Goloka—
may this water offered by me stand present for the sake of His satisfaction.
"O Janārdana, this fourfold food— milk-rice, fruit, and so forth— is the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered by me into your hand. May they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha."
Vasudeva and Devakī, Nanda and Yaśodā, as well as Uddhava, Sātyaki, Garga, Akrūra, and other Sātvatas;
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and likewise his beloved Jāmbavatī.
Kālindī, Mitravindā, Satyabhāmā, and another,
Bhadrā, and Lakṣmaṇā— these were the queens who were there;
as well as the circle of sixteen thousand wives, numbering one hundred and sixteen thousand.
Sarasvatī, the divine attendants, the cowherds and cowherdesses,
the cows, the Surabhis, the wish-fulfilling cows, and the dark-blue bulls;
the four-tusked elephants, the horses, and likewise the Garuḍas.
The trees, the creepers, the swans, the parrots, the cranes, and the peacocks;
the instrumentalists, the dancers, the singers, and those who are attendants; as well as the friends of Rādhā and those who are considered the friends of the queens. (46–47)
In the sixteenth gate are the thirty-three Gopikās;
in the other gates are these hundreds of beloveds of Hari.
And the gatekeepers are Śrīdāmā, Sudāmā, and likewise Subala.
Supārśva, Ratnabhānu, and likewise Śakrabhānu;
Devabhānu, Vasubhānu, Sūryabhānu, and Candrabha; Vīrabhānu, and others—these were the cowherd women, their female companions, and the cowherds. (1.160.49–50)
Suśīlā, Candrakalā, Yamunā, Mādhavī, Rati, Kadambamālā, Sukuntī, Jāhnavī, Svayaṃprabhā,
Padmamukhī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Sumukhī, and Sudhā. ||51||
Padmālayā, Pārijātā, Sugaurī, Sarvamaṅgalā;
Kālikā, Kamalā, Durgā, Bhāratī, and Sarasvatī;
Gaṅgā, Ambikā, Madhumatī, Campā, Aparṇā, and Sundarī.
Kṛṣṇapriyā, Brahmasatī, Nandinī, and likewise Nandanā;
the attendants (pārṣadas), the Kumāras, and those who are considered the handmaidens (kiṃkarīs);
the Pārijāta trees, the Vṛndā trees, and the imperishable Bhāṇḍīraka banyan tree.
May the wish-fulfilling trees, the forests, and whatever other insentient things there may be;
and those sentient beings residing in Goloka, such as Śataśṛṅga and others—may they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha offering. ||55–56||
I satisfy these with water; may they be satiated for eternal years.
Whatever food there is—edible, chewable, lickable, and suckable, the fourfold food—these balls of rice have been placed by me in your hand, O Janārdana.
Grant these to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.
(58) Furthermore, I satisfy with water the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who resides in the abode of Mahāvaikuṇṭha, together with Lakṣmī and Ramā. (59)
May this water offered by me attend upon Śrī Hari.
This fourfold food— milk-rice, other grains, fruits,
and so forth— and this *piṇḍa* offered by me into your hand, O Supporter of the Universe!
"Accept this and attain eternal satisfaction through this *śrāddha*.
[Therein are] Mahālakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, and those who are the beloveds of Hari; there also are Dharaṇī, Līlā, Vimalā, and Utkarṣiṇī. (61–62)
Jñānā, Kriyā, Yogā, Prahvī, Satyeśanī,
as well as Padmā, Jayā, Pāñcālī, Bhārgavī, Lalitā, Ramā,
Pārvatī, Prabhā, Māṇikyā, Lakṣmī, and Īśvarī. (63)
Amṛtā, Pradīpā, Kṛṣṇā, and likewise Kumbhastanī;
Amūlyā, Takṣiṇī, Premā, Caturā, Maṇidhanyakā; Ujjayinī, Nandanā, Ojasvatī, and Kurujāminī. (64–65)
Navavratā, Manovārā, Ratnā, Jāhnavikā, Laḍḍumānā, Muktā, Amṛtā, Mauktikamānadā,
Kastūrī, Śāntidā, Haṃsā, Kāntā, Revā, and Savitṛjā.
Mūlajā, Rūṭikā, Mañjulikā, and Queen Nirmalā;
Godāvarī, Rallayātā, Jaṭilā, Dayā, and Ramā;
Pānapātrī, Pracampā, Miṣṭagopikā, who is born of my love. 67–68.
Manujā, Vañjulīpuṣpā, Mahiṣī, Hemajā, Rājatī, Padmā, Nalinī, and Mādhavī are the beloved consorts of the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Likewise, Dharmadeva, Nanda, and Sunanda are his devoted followers.
Śrutadeva, Jayanta, Vijaya, and Jaya; Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Puṣpadanta, and Sātvata;
Viṣvaksena, Garuḍa, Prabala, and Bala as well.
Kumuda and Kumudākṣa, those who are the attendants there,
as well as Kūrma, Śeṣa, Garuḍa, Haṃsa, the Vedas, and the formulators of mantras—
may they all attain satisfaction through this water of the sacred ford.

I offer into the hand of Hari food to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked, as well as milk-rice, fruits, and the like; may these morsels satisfy you. May the musicians, singers, devotees, chroniclers, panegyrists, and heralds [be satisfied].
The female dancers, the male dancers, the doorkeepers, and those who are attendants;
likewise the Nārāyaṇīs and others, as well as the Nārāyaṇas equal to them;
and Ramā, Rukmiṇī, Sītā, Padmā, Padmālayā, and Śivā.
Sudakṣiṇā and Suśīlā, who were attendants of the Blessed One;
Bhadra, Subhadra, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and likewise Śubha;
Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, and others as well. (76–77)
The high-souled and illustrious Vaiṣṇavas and Sātvatas,
the Siddhas, the Kalpavṛkṣas, the forests, and the sentient gardens;
Sāketa, the two Panasa trees, and those maidens who are devotees of Viṣṇu.
The gatekeepers are the weapons, and the Vedas take the form of his attendants.
Prahlāda, Nārada, Puṇḍarīka, Parāśara,
Ambarīṣa, and Dhruva— these indeed are the dwellers of Vaikuṇṭha.
May all those who are the attendants of Hari, as well as his female and male servants,
attain eternal satisfaction through this water.
May they be satisfied with the four kinds of food to be eaten, such as milk-rice, fruits, and the like.
"O Supporter of the World, these rice-balls have been given by me into your hand.
Give them to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.
Then, in the second Vaikuṇṭha, beyond the covering of water—
Divya and Nārāyaṇa; his beloveds were Kamalalocanā, Vimalā, Sumatī, Śyāmā, Suśīlā, as well as Kuśalā, Dīpāvalī, Jayantī, Ramā, and Bhāgīrathī. ||84||
Sukhā, Kanakā, Vidyullatā, and Candrakalā;
likewise, the hundreds of thousands of women who were his divine-bodied attendants;
and those who were Bharata, Śatrughna, Lakṣmaṇa, Śeṣa, and Śarada. (85–86)
May the city Devavatī, the divine beings residing there, the millions of lords,
the celestial birds, the divine trees, and likewise the weapons—
all of them attain satisfaction through this food and water offered at the sacred ford.
Food is of four kinds: milk, cooked food, ripe fruit, and so forth.
(88) These *piṇḍas* have been offered by me into your hand, O Supporter of the World.
Grant satisfaction to all of them, and may they attain eternal contentment. (89)

Now, I offer libations with these excellent waters from the sacred fords to Śrī Hari Nārāyaṇa, who resides there in the third Vaikuṇṭha, the abode known as Śvetadvīpa, together with Lakṣmī; may He be satisfied.
I offer four kinds of sweet food, milk-rice, fruits, and so forth.
May this *piṇḍa* offered by me be accepted.
May the supreme sages and yogins, such as Sanaka and others who reside there, [be pleased].
Voḍhu, Pacaśikha, and he known as Sanatsujāta;
other sages also dwell there, as do Tanu and the others;
and virtuous women, holy men, and other ascetics who reside there.
Ananta, Vainateya, Haṃsa, Karī, and the excellent Vaiṣṇavas;
Īśāvāsya, Mahādevī, Jāhnavī, Kamalā, Ramā, Sāvitrī, Śāntā, Kāntā, Brāhmī, and Sarojanī. (94–95)
Likewise, there were female servants there: Wisdom, Intelligence, Fortitude, Forbearance, Faith, Retention, Peace, Learning, Discernment, and Memory;
as well as Rain, Intellect, Thought, and Forest-Prosperity—all of whom were indeed handmaidens.
May all those there— the male and female servants, and the conscious ascetics who have attained liberation—
attain eternal satisfaction through this water. May they also receive the four kinds of delicious food, including milk-rice, fruits, and the like.
"O Janārdana, these rice-balls have been given by me into your hand;
give them to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.
Then [he addressed] Nārāyaṇa, the dweller in the Ocean of Milk, the teacher of the world.

Accompanied by Lakṣmī and Śeṣa, and attended by Garuḍa and the others—I satisfy you with this water; may Janārdana be satisfied for me. O Lord, I offer this milk and the fruit-filled rice-ball into your hand.
I gratify you along with your devotees; may you be satisfied for eternal years.
Mārkaṇḍeya, Bali, Bāṇa, Aśvatthāman, Hanumān, and Varāha; Nimi, Vibhīṣaṇa, Paraśurāma, Vyāsa, and likewise Manu.
Satyavrata, Nanda, Gaya, and other attendants were there,
as well as other female servants: Narmadā,
Tapatī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Kāverī, Gaṅgā, and Godāvarī.
The Sindhu, the Phalgu, the Gaṇḍakī, the Tāmraparṇī, the Sarasvatī, the Karatoyā, the Karmanāśā, the Sābhramatī, and the Gomatī;
the Ojasvatī, the Bhadrāvatī, the Sarayū, and the Svarṇarakṣikā.
Indradyumna, Puṣkara, and likewise Nārāyaṇasara;
Aśvapaṭṭasara and the Mānasa lake—
thus [are] the rivers, streams, lakes, and oceans.

O Sustainer of the World, I offer into your hand long-lived, embodied devotees who dwell there, as well as water for Nārāyaṇa, a śrāddha with milk-rice, and likewise the funeral cakes (piṇḍas). || 108 ||
Grant these to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.

(1.09) Now, [he offered oblations] to Vāsudeva, who dwells in the unmanifest realm, who is the Infinite (Bhūman), who is worshipped by Rāmā, and likewise to Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is served by his devotees. (1.160.110)
Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Mahākāla, and Puruṣa; likewise here Mahāpuruṣa, as well as Prakṛtipuruṣa,
Pradhānapuruṣa, Mahāviṣṇu, and Mahāramā.
I truly gratify them, together with their male and female servants, with water;
may they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha, consisting of the four kinds of food, such as milk-rice, grains, fruits, and the like.
Indeed, [I bow to] the Lord Ramā-Nārāyaṇa, who resides in the abode of nectar;
to Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the ascetics dwelling at Badarikāśrama;
and to the Fish, Tortoise, and Boar incarnations, each residing in their respective abodes.
Dattātreya, Kapila, Pṛthu, Haṃsa, and Vāmana;
Ṛṣabha, Nṛhari, Paraśurāma, Yajña, and the Kumāras;
Hayagrīva, Nārada, Hari, Buddha, and likewise Manu.
I satisfy Vyāsa, those residing in their respective abodes, the liberated souls, the attendants, the male and female servants, and the devotees with water,
as well as with the four kinds of food, such as milk-rice, cooked rice, fruits, and so forth.
May they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha.
These rice-balls (piṇḍas) have been offered by me; having descended into your hand, bestow them upon all of them so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.
Hiraṇyagarbha, Vairāja, and the eight lords of the enclosures (āvaraṇa);
Viṣṇu, Sadāśiva, Mūla-prakṛti, and Māyā; whatever principles (tattvas) there may be;
their respective deities, as well as their qualities and conscious beings.
I indeed satiate with water those who have gone to various other non-sovereign realms of consciousness,
as well as the conscious beings of the Vairāja world, the conscious beings of the Saura world, the conscious beings of the Āgneya world,
and all the worlds of Īśa.
May they all attain satisfaction through these fourfold offerings of food, such as milk-rice, cooked rice, fruits, and the like, by being offered into the hands of Nārāyaṇa.
May these funeral cakes (piṇḍas) offered by me satisfy them for eternal years.
May those others who have a thousand faces, and those Viṣṇus with hundreds and so forth of mouths; likewise the Brahmās with their mouths, and the Śambhus with their faces— may they all,
by the tens of millions, together with their Śaktis, be satisfied with the waters of this sacred ford.
O Janārdana, these rice-balls (piṇḍas) offered by me with milk-rice, four kinds of cooked food, and likewise fruits and other offerings, are placed in your hand;
grant them to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.
May the three qualities, the four internal organs, the ten external organs,
the ten elements, the ten vital breaths, and the conscious principles—
these constituent elements— attain satisfaction through the fruits and water offered as food. (1.27–1.28)
Liṅga, Bāṇa, Sthālā, Śambhu, Satī, and Kārtika;
Gaṇeśa, Kṣema, Lābha, Ṛddhi, Siddhi, and the Śivayogins;
the Yoginīs, Hanumān, Durgā, and the goddesses Kumārikās. (129)
There are eleven crores of Rudras, a hundred Jyotis, and twelve [others].
Gaṅgā, Vīrabhadra, Jalandhara, Tāraka, Tārakākṣa, Gaja, Mahiṣa, and Caṇḍa as well. (1.160.130–131)
Pracaṇḍa, Nanda, Upananda, Śṛṅgī, Bhṛṅgirīṭika, Kirīṭin, Candramas, Vahni, and Maṅgala;
Durvāsas, Kālabhīru, Viṣa, Muṇḍa, and other excellent attendants.
The trident, the serpent, the rudrākṣa, and likewise the bull;
the peacock, the mouse, the lion, and Kailāsa—these are his manifestations.
There are also the ear-bells, Meghanāda, and other hosts of attendants by the millions. (133–134)
May Mahākālī and the others, as well as the Śaktis of Pārvatī,
and all those sentient beings belonging to Śiva who reside on Kailāsa—
may all those male servants and female attendants be satiated by the waters of this sacred ford.
The fourfold food— fruits, drinks, and whatever milk-rice (pāyasa) is suitable—
these balls of rice (piṇḍas) have been placed by me in your hand, O Janārdana;
give them to all those [ancestors], and let them attain eternal satisfaction.
May all those who are devotees of Śiva be satisfied for eternal ages.
May Brahmā, the sons of Brahmā, and likewise the wives of Brahmā;
Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Viriṇī—[all be satisfied].
Asiknī, Paliknī, Śatarūpā, and Kadrukī; Rati, Sandhyā, Sṛṣṭi, Vidyā, Avidyā, and Mohinī;
and likewise the eighty-eight thousand Bālakhilyas.
Likewise, there were sixty thousand others known as the Bālakhilyas;
five thousand Haryaśvas and five thousand Śabalāśvas;
and one thousand five hundred sons who were born of the lineage of Brahmā.
The celestial sage Nārada and others, the great sages Sanaka and others,
the seven sages, Dakṣa and the rest, as well as Dharma and Adharma together with their lineages, and likewise the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, Ājyapa, and Somapa [ancestral manes]. (142–143)
Likewise, the Pitṛs, the four Meghas, Madana, Rati,
the five arrows, the flowers, and the Brahmachārins—
those who have gone to Satyaloka are likewise of the Ūrdhvasrotas class.
May those possessed of knowledge, ascetics, the renouncers, and likewise those who have abandoned worldly ties;
those who have made their dwelling in the world of Brahmā, the Sādhyas, and the virtuous— all of them may attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha offering.
I gratify [the ancestors] with the waters of the Svarṇarekhā, with excellent milk-rice and other offerings, with the four kinds of food, fruits, and drinks; may they be satisfied for eternal years.
May these rice-balls, offered into the hand of Hari, satisfy them.
Now, those who were the sages and others, as well as the various Manvantaras;
the Vyāsas and the disciples of Vyāsa, the sages endowed with the splendor of Brahman;
the Brāhmaṇas such as Patnīvrata and others, and likewise the social classes and the stages of life.
The Vedas, the Śāstras, the Ākhyānas, and even the Upavyākhyānas; the ancient and modern Itihāsas, as well as Caritras, Kathās, meters, musical notes, Rāgas, Rāgiṇīs, and musical compositions.

May those who possess form and consciousness— whether they be functions, mental states, hunger, thirst, fire, or the bodily constituents— attain satisfaction through these waters. May they be satiated for eternal years with milk-rice, cooked rice, and the four kinds of food.
The great sages who dwell in the penance groves of the people, and the ancestors;
the year, the months, the fortnights, the days, and the nights;
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, Pāṅkteya, and Paktipāvana.
The Gārhapatya, the Dākṣiṇātya, the Āvasathya, the Agnihotraja,
the Ārārtrika, the Nāciketa, the Bārhaspatya, the Cūllija, the Vānaprasthya, the Sānyasya, the Bhauma, and also the Udarya. (154–155)
The celestial, the mine-born, the corpse-dweller, the cemetery-dweller, the forest-fire, the wild-fire, the sacrifice-born, the flame-mouthed, and likewise the submarine fire—
these are the ancestors who have been described, as well as Vaiśravaṇa and the others.
The pretas, the pitṛs of Yama, the hell-beings, and likewise those belonging to Śravaṇa;

other messengers who are pitṛs, as well as the pitṛs of torment; those born in one’s own lineage and those born in other lineages, including those among the stationary beings (sthāvara). || 157–158 ||
May those ancestors who are born of wind among mobile beings, as well as those who are born of water, and those such as the Munis, Ṛṣis, Āryas, and others who appear in every Kalpa—
may they, as ancestors, be satisfied by these waters for eternal years.

I offer into the hand of Hari four kinds of food: milk-rice, fruits and the like, as well as the food of sages and suitable food. O Janārdana, these funeral cakes (piṇḍas) have been given by me into your hand.
Grant these to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction:
the guardians of the quarters, the guardians of the worlds, and likewise those who are the guardians of heaven;
Indra and the other eight, as well as the eight supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
The eight Vasus beginning with Āpa, the eight directions, the nine planets,
the nine treasures, the Vidyādharas, the six Mothers,
the stars, the comets, the minor stars, and the smoke-colored comets (dhūmraketavaḥ). || 163–164 ||
The twelve Suns, the twelve Ādityas, the three Moons, and their digits;
the twenty-seven lunar mansions and the thirty-three deities;
the Maruts, the lightnings, the Sādhyas, and the Viśvedevas. (165)
May the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Sūtas, Māgadhas, Bandins,
Kiṃpuruṣas, and Kinnaras attain satisfaction through the water offered to them. May they partake of food, nectar-like milk-rice, cooked grains, ripe fruits, and the like.
All four kinds of food, as well as many varieties of drinks—
these morsels have been placed by me in your hand, O Janārdana.
Give them to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.

May they all attain eternal satisfaction through this *śrāddha*. And those who have gone to the *bhuvarloka*, as well as those situated in the intermediate space (*antarīkṣa*), the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas whose support is the wind and whose bodies are composed of air— may they too be satisfied.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and vināyakas; vetālas, bhairavas, and others who are killers and progenitors;
as well as maternal uncles, rāhavas, and others who are dark-colored and black.
The Ḍākinī, the Śākinī, the Yoginī, and likewise the Bhakṣiṇī;
the Vetālinī, the Khañjinī, the Śītalā, and likewise the Mātṛkā; the Mārikā, the Bālikī, the Kṛtyā, the Hikkā, and also the Tānikā. (172–173)
The attractor, the great pestilence, fevers— both cold and hot— as well as diseases, royal maladies, intense torments, old age and the like,
the various stages [of life], powers, specific incapacities, and likewise the sick one.
Mantras, tantras, and yantras; oaths and fetters;
nooses, missiles, and weapons; lightning, as well as foul weather; the confusion of the directions, firebrands whirled into circles, clouds, mists, and blinding darkness. (175–176)
May Tṛṇāvarta, portents, earthquakes, wind and rain, calamities, assailants, and whatever there may be such as showers of dust—
all these shall forever find satisfaction through the waters of the sacred fords.
I satisfy them with water and offerings so that they may be satiated for eternal years.
Beans and rice, rice mixed with sesame (kṛśara), and the food of sky-dwellers are of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Various kinds of food are of the nature of passion (rājasa), as is the fourfold milk-rice (pāyasa).
"I give you appropriate food, fruit, and drink;
with those various foods, I have offered rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) into the hands of Hari.
Give these to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction."
May they all be forever satisfied by this *śrāddha*:
those dwelling on the earth, whether born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, or as sprouts; all sentient beings, as well as Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. (18.1–18.2)

Vaiśyas, Śūdras, those of mixed castes, Cāṇḍālas, and likewise those who have fallen from their status; those born in the natural order (anuloma), those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), the hairless, and the half-men;
lifelong students, householders, forest-dwellers, and likewise renunciants.
The Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Śāktas, Vaidikas, and those others besides them;
those born from cow-hair, those born from water, those born from land, and likewise those born from the sky;
small living beings and great ones, as well as insects, winged insects, and birds. (184–185)
Likewise, the household deities extending as far as a blade of grass,
the village deities, the forest deities, and the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas);
the deities of the six wheels within the body, and the gurus and deities in the skull.
Forests, mountains, wildernesses, and likewise rivers;
streams, ponds, groves, and lakes; excavated pools as well as natural hollows, oceans, and highlands—187–188.
Battlefields, desert regions, and all places of the gods;
sacred trees, sacred shrines, sanctuaries, and riverbanks;
dilapidated temples of the goddesses, as well as villages, hamlets, and market towns. (189)
May the towns, royal capitals, ancient cities, and likewise great metropolises—
whatever sentient beings dwell therein and whatever sentient beings preside over them—
all attain perpetual satisfaction through these waters that have been offered.
And for them, there were various kinds of food— those of the nature of fire, wind, water, and earth, as well as those produced by rain and transformed [substances]—
consisting of the four types of food fit for consumption, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like.
With tears, with droplets from clouds, with the resins of trees, and with mud; with the coolness of moonbeams, with the heat of sunbeams, with poisons, and with other fruits and such;
and even with froth—here I perform this śrāddha; may you all be satisfied.
May they be pleased with these waters; may they remain satisfied for eternal years.
These rice-balls (*piṇḍas*), which bestow satisfaction upon them, have been offered by me into the hand of Hari.
Grant satisfaction to all of them, and may they attain eternal contentment.
One's mothers, maternal grandmothers, and likewise maternal great-grandmothers;
one's fathers, paternal grandfathers, and likewise paternal great-grandfathers;
brothers, sisters, brothers' wives, sons-in-law, maternal uncles, and so forth.

I gratify with water and other offerings my brothers, sons, and so forth; my wives; the family members of my father-in-law; my father’s sisters and mother’s sisters; my daughters and excellent female ascetic companions (suyoginīs); as well as their sons, daughters, grandsons, and others.

Likewise, with foods such as milk-rice, with the four kinds of food, and with fruits—O Janārdana, I perform the *śrāddha* for them; may they attain eternal satisfaction. These rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) have been offered by me into your hand.
Grant these to all of them; may they attain eternal satisfaction.
I gratify them with water and food; may they be satisfied for eternal years.
[To] the Prācetasas, the Nāciketasas, the Mārutas, and the Kālakeyas.
[He summoned] the Yāmyas, the Saṃśaptakas, the Vārkṣas, the Bhūjātas, the Śalabhas, and others;
likewise, the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas residing in the worlds of Atala and below,
as well as the serpents, reptiles, Nāgas, and whoever else dwells there.
I gratify them with cool, desired water, food, fruits, and milk-rice; I offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to them, so that they may be satisfied for eternal years.
Likewise, [I honor] the chosen deity, as well as Brahmā, the supreme preceptor, and the teacher.
I gratify [the ancestors] with the waters of sacred fords, with milk-rice, and likewise with fruits.
May they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha.
O Janārdana, this rice-ball (piṇḍa) is offered by me into your hand.
Grant these to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction!
"All this is pervaded by the Lord; may the Supreme Lord be satisfied!
(207) Those who belong to the past, the future, and the present, and those who have gone through the paths of coming and going—

I gratify them with food and water; may they be satisfied for eternal years. Likewise, those dwelling on Mount Meru and those residing upon the Lokāloka mountain—may they attain satisfaction through milk preparations, fruits, water, and the like. (208–209)

I also satisfy all those vital breaths (*asavaḥ*) that have not been remembered, those that have not been attended to, and those that have not yet arrived, with fruits, food, and water. O Janārdana, these *piṇḍas* have been offered by me into your hand.
Grant them to all of them, so that they may attain eternal satisfaction.
This Śrāddha performed by Nārāyaṇa and caused to be performed by Nārāyaṇa has indeed fully satisfied the three worlds, and they have attained eternal bliss.

And all those who had gathered there, having attained eternal satisfaction, returned each to their own world; that śrāddha was thus made complete. Through the constant offering of libations (tarpaṇa), their satisfaction becomes perpetual.
Nourishment, sovereignty, longevity, and progeny for the performer of the śrāddha—varied prosperity attends him, and liberation follows in due course.
[This applies] to the deities, the ancestors, and the great yogis as well. (214–215)
Salutations always be offered to Svāhā and to Svadhā;
this mantra should be recited during the Śrāddha ceremony, for it increases prosperity, longevity, and strength.
By means of this recitation and through its observance, the ancestors are gratified. (216)

I shall proclaim the auspicious *Saptārcis*, which grants all desires. I always pay homage to those ancestors— both formless and embodied— who possess radiant splendor, who are absorbed in meditation, and who possess the eye of yoga.
I bow to those who grant all desires—the progenitors of Indra and the other gods, as well as of Bhṛgu and Mārīci, of the Seven Sages, and of the Pitṛs;
likewise, the progenitors of Manu and the other lords of the gods, and of the sun and the moon. (219)
Having paid homage to all those ancestors who bestow well-being—
namely the ancestors of the stars, the planets, and so forth, as well as the grandfathers—
and likewise to Heaven and Earth, I bow with palms joined in reverence.
With palms joined in reverence, I bow to those who are the progenitors of the celestial sages, who are honored by all the worlds, and who are the constant bestowers of fearlessness—
to Prajāpati Kaśyapa, to Soma, and to Varuṇa. (222)
With palms joined in reverence, I bow to the masters of yoga;
I pay homage to the seven groups of ancestors throughout the seven worlds;
and I offer salutations to the Self-Existent Brahmā, whose eye is yoga.
Endowed with this method, a person obtains three boons;
the ancestors bestow food, long life, and sons upon those on earth who are possessed of supreme devotion, full of faith, and have conquered their senses. (225)
Whoever recites the Saptarṣi hymn shall become the sole sovereign of the earth. What more need be said? This sacred site grants liberation to all.
[Therein], one is not harmed by horned animals, fanged beasts, serpents, poison, fire, women, or water.
One who dies while playing and has no other refuge is born in the womb of a preta;
likewise, one who dies having done something displeasing to the nāgas, or is struck by lightning,
or is executed by the king himself on account of the crime of theft.
Delighting in the wives of others, they were slain by their husbands out of hatred;
having engaged in conflict with those of unequal status, with mixed castes, and with Cāṇḍālas and the like,
they were killed by them, and they in turn took refuge among the Cāṇḍālas and others.
Those who give cows, fire, or poison, as well as heretics of cruel intellect, generally commit suicide out of anger by means of poison, fire, weapons, hanging, or water;
or, being deeply distressed, they throw themselves from a mountain or a tree. (231)
Those who live by ignoble crafts, those who preside over the five slaughterhouses,
those who are like serpents at a sacrifice, those who are mostly wretched, those who are eunuchs,
those struck down by the punishment of the righteous, and those who have been killed by Brahmins— [these are the ones excluded]. (232–233)
Those who are perpetrators of great sins, those who have fallen, and those who cause social confusion—
whether dead or living, whether by their own action or through the act of another—
they indeed attain purification by bathing in the waters of the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you this supreme majesty of the lake,
which pacifies all sins and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the ancestors.
Any man who listens to it with devotion during a Śrāddha ceremony, on a festival day, or daily, [attains these rewards].
Or, O lady of beautiful hips, he who causes it to be heard shall also become a partaker of the world of Brahmā.
This [text] is auspicious, meritorious, and brings wealth; for men, it grants heaven, fame, and long life, and increases sons and grandsons.
The divine rite consisting of worship and *śrāddha* is offered to the two Hari-lakes.
Having bathed in the Dāmodara-kuṇḍa and likewise in the Mṛgī-kuṇḍa, and having bathed in the Nārāyaṇa-hrada, one should perform the *śrāddha*; such is the established rule. (238–239)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of Universal Śrāddha and Tarpaṇa for the Two Nārāyaṇas in the Waters of the Nārāyaṇa Lake, as well as the Praise of the Seven-Flamed Fire and its Fruits," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 161 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga)
— Chapter 161.
[Author: Chapter 162.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Then the two gods, Dāmodara and Narāyaṇa...
Then, having fed all the assembled Brahmins and gods,
they both partook of that prasāda and the milk-rice (pāyasa) offered to Hari.
Thereafter, Dāmodara spoke of the greatness of Nārāyaṇa.

This is the most secret sacred field (kṣetra), which brings happiness to all living beings and grants liberation to all creatures, whether they be Vaiṣṇavas or Śaivas. Even those who have killed a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, their mother, their teacher, or an infant [are purified here].
Those who have killed women, having bathed here in this lake, are liberated; of this there is no doubt. (4) Having bathed here and become virtuous, one who dies shall go to the supreme state.
Those devotees who dwell in this sacred field and are virtuous toward Hari—(5)
Indeed, those capable of extracting others are considered equal to Nārāyaṇa;
having pierced the web of the bonds of birth, they cause one to reach the abode of Hari.
Iḍā is known as Ojasvatī, Bodhyā, and Piṅgalā is considered Bhadrā.
The Suṣumṇā is the Svarṇarekhā; by means of it, one may attain liberation.
(7) Indeed, where the attainment of liberation occurs without effort—even for those of various castes, those who perform forbidden acts, and the outcaste Cāṇḍālas who are held in contempt—(8)
For those whose bodies are filled with sins and likewise with the most heinous crimes,
Vastrāpatha is considered the supreme medicine;
it is for the wicked, the blind, the wretched, the miserable, the sinful, and those who have committed evil deeds.
Out of compassion, I lead all of them to the supreme goal.
Those men who have gone to Vastrāpatha and performed great meritorious deeds indeed become free from decay, free from old age, and bodiless (liberated).
Whatever unwholesome karma has been committed— whether out of ignorance or knowledge, by a woman or by a man, or even by one of wicked intellect—
all that shall be reduced to ashes upon entering Vastrāpatha.

A man established on the Raivata mountain always performs sacrifice with ritual offerings, always bestows gifts, and is always an ascetic. On the Raivata mountain, austerity and truth are practiced by all living beings with their whole being.
That destination which is ordained for men who dwell on Mount Raivata is not attained at Kurukṣetra, nor at Gaṅgādvāra, nor at Puṣkara.
On Mount Raivata they remain eternally, [covered] by dust driven by the wind.
Even those who have committed evil deeds, once they have touched [this mountain], surely attain the supreme goal.
He who dwells on Mount Revata with a self-controlled mind and concentrated focus is considered equal to one who subsists only on air, even if he were to enjoy the three worlds.
Dwelling on Mount Raivata, eating sparingly, and having conquered his senses,
he indeed fulfills the vows of the four-month period;
having overcome the fear of birth and death, he attains the supreme goal.
One shall attain the meritorious state of supreme beatitude as well as the state of yoga.
Indeed, the goal of Brahman is not obtainable even in hundreds of other births;
it is attained through the strength of Raivata and likewise through the power of Śrī Hari.

He who remains on Mount Raivata for a month, eating but a single meal a day, destroys in that one month the sins committed throughout his entire life. Even if he is struck down by obstacles, he who does not abandon Mount Raivata—
He abandons old age and death, for this birth is indeed perishable.
(22) But those who serve Mount Raivata until the fall of their bodies, they, upon death, travel by means of a swan-vehicle to the divine worlds. (23)
Even a person whose mind is pervaded by the cycle of existence and who has abandoned the practice for liberation,
if they die on Mount Raivata, shall not enter saṃsāra again.
This supreme tīrtha on earth is the cause of both heaven and liberation.

Whoever meets their death there attains liberation; of this there is no doubt. (25) The state that a yogi might attain after a thousand lifetimes, one reaches as supreme liberation upon dying on the Raivata mountain. (26)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of mixed castes;
even worms, Mlecchas, and those of mixed and sinful births;
as well as insects, ants, and whatever other beasts and birds there may be—
Even those lords of the gods are recorded as having met their death in due time.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, even one born in the animal realm who gives up his life on Mount Raivata becomes a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt. (28–29)
Those who have made their dwelling on Mount Raivata, who bathe in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā,
and whose hearts and lives are centered on Dāmodara, are undoubtedly liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
At the time of death on Mount Raivata, Hari himself appears as Dāmodara.

With a heart exceedingly gracious, he himself imparts the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa mantra as an ear-whispered prayer to anyone at all— whether it be one who is about to die or another— who dwells upon the Raivata mountain.
I shall impart my mantra to you; he will certainly become liberated.
No one who dies at Dāmodara ever goes to hell.
Favored by Vāmana, they all attain the supreme goal.
Having abandoned their vital breaths here, people do not enjoy [existence] anywhere again.
34. First is Revatī-kuṇḍa, then the one called Dāmodara;
the third is named Nārāyaṇa, and Mṛgī-kuṇḍa is the fourth. 35.
The fifth is Bhavakuṇḍa, and the sixth is Gaṅgā Gomukhī;
the seventh is Kamaṇḍalu, and the eighth is named Bhairava.
Mārkaṇḍeya is the tenth, and Dattakṛt is the eleventh.

These [waters], when bathed in, drunk, seen, sipped, or even touched, indeed purify people and lead them to liberation. That goal which is considered the goal of yogis is the infinite goal for those [who partake of these waters]. (37–38)
Among them, liberation is proclaimed as the purifier for those who have fallen;
even there, the lake of Nārāyaṇa is the most excellent of all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
As is the lake of Nārāyaṇa, so is the lake of Dāmodara.
Where there is the constant presence of Śrī Hari and Vāmana, a righteous soul who bathes there obtains the fruit remembered for ten horse-sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. (1.161.40–41)
But he who, having observed a fast, gratifies Brahmins and virtuous men,
certainly obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
By offering a lamp there, his sensory faculty flashes forth like wisdom.
By the offering of the *ārārtrika* lamp, health is always produced.
What is the use of much speaking here? For one who performs acts such as dharma while dedicating them to Śrī Hari, there shall be infinite fruit.
The merit of performing ten horse-sacrifices is proclaimed for the offering of flowers;
the fruit of the *agnihotra* sacrifice for incense; and the fruit of gifting land for fragrance. Here, the fruit of gifting a cow is proclaimed for the act of sweeping.
Anointing with ointments is said to yield tenfold merit, and offering garlands is remembered as yielding tenfold;
singing is considered to yield a thousandfold, and instrumental music is held to yield a hundred-thousandfold for those who worship and praise Dāmodara on Mount Raivata.
Freed from all sins, they go to the eternal Vaikuṇṭha;
even after hundreds of millions of kalpas, there is no rebirth for them.
But those who, having attained meditation, are liberated in soul and composed in mind—
With their senses restrained, they perform the recitation of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Dwelling eternally on Mount Raivata, those best of men have achieved their life's purpose;
having delivered infinite living beings, they depart for the world of Viṣṇu.
On the full moon day of Māgha as well as Kārttika, virtuous women and virtuous men were seen,
touched, bowed to, honored, and fed; likewise,
they were served, massaged, attended upon, and carried.
By whatever means and by whichever people they have been propitiated,
by them Ramā has been propitiated, and by them Nārāyaṇa has been propitiated.
For in that place, Lakṣmī and likewise Nārāyaṇa always reside.
In the form of a virtuous woman and a virtuous man, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa himself wanders through Vastrāpatha for the sake of the welfare of the people. By their grace, every mental desire is accomplished.
Whatever is performed here with the body, mind, speech, service, food, and offerings— at Vastrāpatha on Mount Raivata— will certainly and surely bear fruit both in this world and the next. (55–56)
When saintly persons are properly served, all the deities are effectively served;
indeed, Lord Hari himself, when served, grants liberation to his devotee.
At the great pilgrimage site of Vastrāpatha, there dwell saintly men, saintly women, and deities.
Those people who revile you will certainly go to hell.
The Blessed One Nṛsiṃha, having come to Mount Raivata,
took up residence in a cave on the bank of the golden river.
That place is meritorious, bestowing liberation; even a particle of dust there destroys sin.
What need is there for more? At this great holy site, even every single particle of dust [is sacred].
On Mount Raivata at Vastrāpatha, even a leaf, a flower, or a blade of grass [is likewise pure].
Everything there is divine, destructive of sins, and bestows liberation; of this there is no doubt.
By King Ānarta, that region known as Saurāṣṭra was established from Goloka in the central sanctuary, and furthermore, from the throat of Hari, [the sacred site] was established there.
The mountain Raivata, consisting of fire, was brought there by fragments of the Kaustubha gem;
furthermore, a fragment of the constellation Revatī is also situated there.
Moreover, the peaks of Meru—Mandara and Kumuda as well—are present.
Aruṇa, Divya, and likewise Ūrjayanta;
there the lords Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa dwell eternally.
There also flows the divine river Svarṇarekhā, as well as the Ojasvatī, which is auspicious.
Kṛṣṇā, Bhadrā, and other wives of Hari exist in the form of rivers;
likewise, the Sarasvatī and the Ākāśagaṅgā flow among the peaks.
Who indeed can reach the limit of the majesty of this King Raivata?

All the divine beings have gathered there; therefore, that is indeed the place of liberation (mokṣasthala). Extending ten times further than the distance from the surface of the earth, the Raivata mountain has entered into the interior of the earth.
Those scattered mountains that are seen in Vastrāpatha are actually only peaks that appear; the mountain itself is not seen.
For when Raivataka Mountain came and fell into the chasm, it was only its peaks that were visible.
That Raivata mountain was indeed ten yojanas in height.
When it descended to the earth with great force,
it whirled in the sky for a hundred yojanas before finally alighting.
When he repeatedly caused the mountain to rotate from the northeastern direction with diminished speed, then, by virtue of that momentum,
a thousand peaks [were cast] toward the southern direction from its summit. (72)
Having been shattered, separated, and torn apart, they fell in great abundance;
indeed, those peaks of Raivata fell into the tiger-infested forest and shall remain there just so, as long as the moon and stars endure. (73–74)
Beginning from Somanātha and extending as far as Bhīmanātha on this earth,
the peaks have fallen within the region of the tiger-infested forest.
Therefore, here in this Raivata region, there is Bhava as well as Dāmodara.
"Remembering death, they shall go [to heaven], and they shall indeed attain liberation.
Having thus taught this greatness, Hari Dāmodara himself then embraced that brahmin repeatedly, praising his devotion to his wife's vow again and again.
He spoke thus regarding his departure for the sacred ford and then vanished of his own accord.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you that former life-story which,
whether read, taught, or heard, always bestows liberation.
There is nothing else like this; what more do you wish to hear? (79).

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Raivata Mountain, Vastrapatha, Kṣetra, and Tīrtha," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 161. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*).
Chapter 162 [Author:
Chapter 163 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord, you have previously mentioned Satī, the goddess Pārvatī, the mother of Gaṇeśa; how and when did Satī indeed come into being?
Furthermore, that which is the all-pervading existence within the form of Nārāyaṇa— [how is she related to that? || 1 ||
"Is she Satī reborn, or is she someone else? Who is this Satī?
(1) Is she that very Satī, Pārvatī, or is there another Pārvatī who is the beloved of Śiva?
O Kṛṣṇa, O Nārāyaṇa, O Acyuta, sever this doubt of mine. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: You have asked a most excellent question concerning a secret matter from beginningless time;
even though they know it, others do not understand such an account.

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall relate that story exactly as it is, hearing which you too will gain understanding: what indeed is the nature of a virtuous woman? Śrī Puruṣottama is endowed with all sovereignty and all power.
At the time of the great dissolution, he alone shines forth in the imperishable abode,
having withdrawn everything else into himself.
The Lord, the king of kings, does not delight in being alone.
Then, from the left side of his form, he longed for a second [form] that would possess many liberated abodes,
virtues, sovereign powers, and attendants;
as well as divine incarnations, male lords, and goddesses of celestial form.

The Blessed Lord Hari, the sovereign of all beings, manifested numerous male and female servants, as well as the three eternal qualities (guṇas). He is the universal ruler who governs everything, and that sovereignty which resides in Hari is the source of all existence.
She existed from time immemorial and then manifested;
she is that Being whose nature consists of the three *guṇas*, the mother of all creation, and indeed,
she became the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
That state of equilibrium is Māyā, whose form is Brahman and who is dear to Hari;
she is Rādhā by form, Mahālakṣmī by form, and the very essence of Ramā.
Indeed, she repeatedly manifests as Lakṣmī and as Sāvitrī. (12–13)
When I become Rudra from the forehead of Vairāja,
then Māyā indeed becomes my wife, Rudrāṇī;
as such, I manifest there in the form of Śiva.
In each of those places, she was born as my companion.
She alone is my beloved wife, my mother, Śivā, in the form of Satī.
O dear one, listen to me as I tell you everything about how she came to be born with a physical body.
Just as the wife of Vairāja gave birth to Brahmā and the others,
so indeed that goddess Mānā became the mother of Brahmā and the rest.
And from the forehead of Brahmā, Rudra Śambhu was born.
At that time, she was the wife of Śambhu and indeed the daughter-in-law of Brahmā.
When she was born as the daughter of Dakṣa, she then truly became the granddaughter of Brahmā’s son; for that Satī was the very embodiment of existence (sattā).
When Śambhu became the son of Virāṭ, the brother of Brahmā,
then she was indeed proclaimed to be the sister-in-law of Brahmā.
Thus indeed is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), whose nature is that of Mahālakṣmī.
Having herself become whatever is required for her task, she exists as the sustainer of creation.
When Brahmā was born from the lotus at the navel of Vairāja,
Viṣṇu, his brother, was born upon seeing his ascetic penance.
When a quarrel arose between the two due to their mutual greatness, a ray of Śrī Hari’s splendor appeared in the middle to bring it to an end.
Then, within that ray, the Lord Śiva was seen.
Then that auspicious Māyā was indeed seen together with him.
At that time, those two were requested by Brahmā as his assistants;
thus, Sadāśiva himself was requested from the forehead of Vairāja.
Then Śambhu arose in his [manifest] form, and Śivā too appeared as his consort;
born together with Śiva, she was established on Śiva’s left side.
At that time, Śiva indeed existed in the form of half-woman and half-man.
Then, by the force of necessity, Śivā herself became a woman in a separate form.
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you how she, the destroyer of the Daityas, came to be.
Whenever she manifests for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods— ||| 58 ||

At that time, she was called "the born" (utpannā) in the world, even though she is eternal. Then, once upon a time in the first Kṛta Yuga, Brahmā himself remained engaged in austerity within a lotus, and Śiva likewise remained there.
Absorbed in samādhi, he became immersed in meditation, free from all thought of creation.
Viṣṇu, however, remained like a yogi upon his bed of Śeṣa during the period of rest. Then, when the time for the commencement of creation had nearly arrived at dawn, [he arose].
Then, O Lotus-born One, as Viṣṇu was in the state of waking, an itch arose repeatedly in his ears due to the application of the collyrium.
And then, by Viṣṇu’s application of the tip of a golden probe, [the collyrium was removed].
The itching was removed from the earwax, and two pills were extracted;
having drawn those two pills out, they were cast into the water.
Then there arose two terrible demons, renowned as Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Born from the wax of his ears, those two of great strength and prowess suddenly approached the surface of the water after bowing to Viṣṇu. There, they beheld a lotus accompanied by Brahmā.
Beholding that wondrous sight, these two prepared to slay Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, overcome with fear, praised Janārdana;
becoming single-minded, he lauded him again and again.
Then, repeatedly seeking his own protection,
the Lord Hari rose up once more and fought with those two for five thousand years, using only his arms as weapons.
Then, in order to delude those two demons,
the Blessed Lord Hari called to mind Mahāmāyā, who resides as half of Śiva’s body;
she immediately emerged from Śiva’s form, assuming the distinct appearance of a woman.
Having become like a maidservant, the Queen of the Gods approached and stood before him;
then the Blessed One indeed accepted her into his own eyes.
He said to her: "O Mahāmāyā! May you pervade me in every way."
Quickly [enter] my eyes, face, nose, arms, heart, thighs, and feet, so that those two may behold me as a beautiful woman who causes delusion;
just as the auspicious Māyā herself, consisting of delusion, accepted the command of Śiva. (42–43)
Then, just as a curtain was drawn over the form of Viṣṇu by me,
Viṣṇu was seen within and Māyā without, like a mother containing her child within her womb.
At that moment, she was seen, and both of them beheld her.
Seeing her who was composed of radiant energy, the two Daityas were bewildered.
Then, intoxicated by their great strength and deluded by the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), they said:
"O lady of auspicious appearance, choose a boon from us! (45–46)
The Blessed One, concealed there behind a curtain of illusion,
spoke to them with great love, captivating their minds:
"May both of you, who were to be slain by me, be satisfied with me today."
"What need is there for any other boon here? For me, this much alone has been accomplished:

we have been deluded by desires and intentions, deprived of the path of knowledge, rendered devoid of luster, and become incapable of discerning between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. (48–49)
Seeing the water on all sides residing within the lotus-abode of Brahmā,
they said, "Destroy it where there is a portion of the earth devoid of water for us.
At that time, in the first Kṛta Yuga, the water indeed entered a state of dissolution.
The earth, devoid of water, appeared as a mere sphere.
Then, by the Blessed One, who bears the conch, discus, and mace,
their two heads were severed at the neck with his discus.
This deluding illusion (māyā) became known by the name Mohanī.
Pleased with her, the Lord Brahmā, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise:
"Obeisance to the Mother! Obeisance to the Sister! Obeisance, repeated obeisance, to the Daughter! (53)
Salutations be to the brother’s wife; salutations again and again to you, Śivā. Salutations to the wife; salutations to the power that accomplishes all tasks.
Salutations indeed to the goddess Vaiṣṇavī; salutations again and again to her who is the left half of [the Lord’s] body.
You are Lakṣmī and she is Sāvitrī; you are the supreme Goddess, the Mother.
By you alone is everything sustained, and by you this world is created.
O Goddess, it is by you that this is protected, and you always consume it at the end.
You are the Great Knowledge, the Great Illusion, the Great Wisdom, and the Great Memory;
you are the Great Delusion, the Great Goddess, and the Great Goddess of the Asuras.
You are Śrī, you are Īśvarī, you are Brahmāṇī, the helper of the gods. (57–58)
They hold as weapons the sword, the trident, the mace, the discus, the conch, and the bow;
they bear the *bhuśuṇḍī*, the iron club, the *prāśa*, the arrow, the excellent *tomara*, and other arms.
Whatever object exists anywhere, whether real or unreal, consisting of all things—[they possess it].
You are the power of all that exists, the one who accomplishes this task.
You are the slender Śambhu’s half-body, the lovely Ramā, Viṣṇu’s half-body, and Brāhmī, the half-body of the Creator; dwell among the gods who are to be created.
Thus being sought after by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the wielder of the Pināka (Śiva), that enchanting goddess,
who herself causes delusion, made her dwelling there;
having attained invisibility, Viṣṇu departed for the ocean.
Brahmā, seeing the creation within the body of Viṣṇu as before, brought it forth.
He created the sages, the munis, the ancestors, the gods, the demigods, and human beings;
as well as the Daityas, serpents, and immobile beings—and among them, that Mohinī dwelt.
Indeed, that Mahāmāyā, the accomplisher of all tasks, dwelt within the senses in the form of brilliance, strength, grace,
and beauty; she assumed various forms according to each respective species, O beautiful-bodied one.
By her alone was that beauty produced among men and women.
Then, after some time, she— the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura,
the fulfiller of the gods' purpose, the Sovereign of the Universe— manifested herself.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Forms of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Sāvitrī, Śivā, and Others as the Great Māyā Constituting the Half-Body of the Supreme Brahman, and the Description of the Assumed Form of Mohinī for the Purpose of Destroying Madhu and Kaiṭabha," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 162. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna).
Chapter 163 [Author:
Chapter 164 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
When and how did the asura named Mahiṣa come into being?
I wish to hear about his destruction by the Goddess; please tell me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen: who was this Mahiṣa, how did he attain the state of an asura, and by what means was his destruction brought about by the Goddess? Understand this from me. Long ago, there were two exceedingly fierce Daityas who caused agitation throughout the world.
Raṃbha and Karaṃbha also performed austerities for the sake of obtaining sons.
For many groups of years, one of them, Karaṃbha, remained submerged in water;
having become a crocodile, Mahendra struck him in the water with his tusk.
When his brother was lost, Rambha became overwhelmed with extreme rage;
that great asura desired to offer his own head into the fire after having severed it.
Just as he took up his sword and was indeed preparing to cut it off—
"For now, fire has been forbidden; do not act rashly!
Do not die. I shall grant you whatever you desire—speak without delay.
Rambhā replied, "May there be a son for me who shall conquer the three worlds."
"He shall be invincible by all the gods, and likewise superior to you in splendor;
he shall be able to assume any form at will, skilled in the use of weapons, and possessed of great strength and prowess.
Vahni replied to him, "So be it; it shall be as you desire."
"Death shall come to you through her upon whom your mind is fixed.
Having been addressed thus, O Ramba, he then went to see the yakṣa named Mālavaṭa in the cattle-pen of Mālavaṭa.
Elephants, buffaloes, horses, cows, goats, and sheep were there in great numbers; she set her heart upon a buffalo.
Desiring him, that three-year-old cow approached the lord of the Daityas.
And he too, having become a powerful buffalo, engaged in sexual intercourse. Taking that pregnant buffalo-cow, he went to his own home;
there in Pātāla, he, a doer of forbidden acts, was abandoned by the Dānavas.
Taking the buffalo-cow again, he returned to his dwelling with the yakṣa named Mālavaṭa; the buffalo-cow gave birth to a son,
a brilliant buffalo capable of changing form at will and possessed of great strength.
Having obtained his son, Raṃbha rejoiced indeed again and again. (15) Then another buffalo, seeing that very same buffalo-cow in her season, desired her; she, in turn, spoke of this to Raṃbha. (16)
Then a most terrible battle took place between Rambha and the buffalo. Struck in the heart by its two sharp horns, Rambha’s heart was pierced; he fell down and died.
Then the queen went for refuge to the Yakṣas.
Protected by the Yakṣas and having warded off another buffalo,
the Yakṣas, such as Mālavaṭa and others, then [beheld] that dead Raṃbha.
They placed her upon the funeral pyre, and she indeed ascended it there.
Then, from the midst of the fire, a man fierce and terrifying arose;
with sword in hand, he then drove the yakṣas away from that place.
He caused buffaloes to be slaughtered and nourished his son with affection.
This very person became the son of Raṃbha, known by the name Raktabīja;
he was indeed possessed of great strength, invincible, and always able to assume any form at will.
That youth fought with the gods as well as with the other guardians of the world;
the guardians of the quarters, the protectors of the worlds, and the planets were all conquered by him in battle.
Then, having brought Aja and Śaṅkara, the gods went to Janārdana.
They reported the activities of Mahiṣa and Raktabīja:
"O Lord, the kingdoms of the Aśvins, Sūrya, Candra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Agni, Brahmā,
Kubera, Indra, and the other gods have indeed been assailed."
"O Lord, we gods have been cast out from our abode and now dwell upon the earth.
Whether it be Viṣṇu or Śambhu, if you do not provide us protection,
then being driven away by him, we shall surely go to the subterranean realm (rasātala)."
Upon hearing this, the Blessed One felt unbearable anger;
at that moment, a great splendor issued forth from the mouths of the Lord Śambhu, as well as from Brahmā and the gods led by Indra.
That goddess who, having slain Madhu and Kaiṭabha, was indeed the embodiment of the strength of all their senses— that very energy emerged [from them].
All of that, when gathered together, was like a mountain, supreme and unbearable.
And in the hermitage of the great seer Kātyāyana, she was endowed with his splendor. From him was born the large-eyed Maheśvarī Kātyāyanī.
Śambhu’s splendor became her face, and the splendor of the fire became her three eyes.
His hair was born from the splendor of Yama, and his arms were born from the splendor of Hari;
eighteen arms came forth in total.
His pair of breasts and his chest were formed by the splendor of Soma and Indra, respectively.
The thighs, shanks, hips, and waist were formed by the splendor of the moon (33).
The pair of feet became the brilliance of Brahmā, soft and reddish;
the fingers [were formed] by the splendor of the sun, and the teeth by the splendor of Prajāpati (34).
Her nose was formed from the splendor of the Yakṣas, her ears from the splendor of Vāyu,
and her eyebrows from the splendor of the Sādhyas— were they perhaps the very bows of the arrows of Kāma?
Thus, having gathered the splendors of the gods there, the beautiful maiden [came into being].
She was born by the name Kātyāyanī for the purpose of destroying Mahiṣa. Then Śambhu gave her a trident, Hari gave her a discus,
the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) gave her a conch, and the Consumer of Oblations (Agni) gave her a spear.
Vāyu gave him a bow and arrows that were swift and inexhaustible;
the Sun-god gave him a thunderbolt and a bell; likewise, Yama gave him a staff;
Kubera presented him with a mace; and Brahmā gave him a water-pot.
Kāla gave her a rosary, and he gave her a sword and a shield. Soma gave her a necklace and two chowries, and the Ocean gave her a brilliant garland.
Himālaya gave the goddess Śrī a lion as her vehicle.
Viśvakarman gave him an axe, a crescent moon, and two earrings;
Citraratha gave him a crest-jewel and a drinking vessel;
Śeṣa gave him a serpent-necklace, and the Seasons gave him a garland of unfading flowers.
The gods presented her with all kinds of weapons and ornaments.
Then the Goddess was exceedingly pleased and let out a great laugh;
honored with blessings by all the gods, she went to the Vindhya mountain.
Making her home upon a high peak, she remained there, captivating the heart.
The two messengers of Mahiṣāsura, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, beheld her;
having gone to Mahiṣa, they spoke of that maiden who was beautiful in every limb.
How can you, being so healthy, lie down? Go and enjoy the maiden who has arrived.
What is the luster of her moon-like face? Her hair resembles dark clouds. Does she have three fires and three eyes? And does she have a conch-shell mark situated on her neck? 45–46.
Her breasts were well-rounded with depressed nipples, resembling jars;
her eighteen arms were plump, auspicious, and equipped with weapons. Her abdomen was marked by three folds, and her waist was devoid of hair.
Her shanks, the vessels of beauty, and her thighs possess the splendor of gold.

"Furthermore, due to the death of your husband and being distressed by childlessness, you shall burn in the fire of time; become dull-witted and miserable. Thus was the curse then pronounced upon the queen, the consort.
