And at that time, you shall become a human king from the very beginning—
the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of the Pracetasas.

Thus was Dakṣa, the son of Aṅgiras, born as the son of Pracetas.
At the very moment Mahāmāyā took birth in his house,
during that same interval, two exceedingly powerful Daityas appeared.
Niśumbha and Śumbha were born as the bringers of misery to the worlds.
To Kaśyapa, who had a wife named Danu—the daughter of Dakṣa—three sons of great strength and prowess were born. (1.165.70)
The eldest was known as Śumbha, another asura was Niśumbha,
and the third was named Namuci, who constantly caused suffering to the gods.
Indra took up his thunderbolt to slay that Namuci, the giver of misery.
Out of fear, Namuci indeed entered the chariot of the Sun;
even though struck, he did not emerge from the Sun's chariot.
Repeatedly cast out by the Sun and beaten with his foot-lash, [he remained within]. (72–73)
Nevertheless, he did not go outside at that time out of fear of Indra’s thunderbolt;
perceiving him to have sought refuge, the Sun protected him from Vāsava.
Then he made a compact with both the Sun and Vāsava.
"I shall certainly not remain on earth, nor ever in heaven;
I will dwell in the netherworld (pātāla). Let me be released by this gift of life.
Thereupon, he was released by the Lord of the Gods, and then he chose a boon as follows.
"O Lord of the Gods, grant me the boon of invincibility against weapons and missiles," [he said].
"So be it," Indra replied, as the Dānava accepted the boon.
Having secured the boon of invincibility against his own weapons and missiles, that Dānava [acted accordingly].
Abandoning the chariot of Bhāskara, he quickly entered the ocean.
Even as he was sinking into the waters, the lord of the Dānavas saw the excellent foam of the sea; seizing it, he remained within the water.
Having filled his mouth, nose, ears, and other orifices, he remained within the water;
yet Śakra hurled a concealed thunderbolt at him. Struck by that thunderbolt which was of the nature of foam, he fell down and died.
With his nose and mouth blocked by the foam-bodied vajra, he indeed died.
Then his two heroic brothers, Śumbha and Niśumbha, filled with rage,
made a supreme effort and arrived for the purpose of destroying the goddess.
The gods also set out for battle, relying upon Indra;
a most tumultuous war ensued, and the deities were conquered after being overwhelmed.
Even the vanguard, along with their forces and mounts, was defeated by the two Daityas.
The elephant of Śakra was seized by you, and the buffalo was taken from Yama.
The jeweled parasol of Varuṇa was taken, and the mace of Hari was seized.
The treasures, such as Śaṅkha, Padma, and the rest, were forcibly taken from Kubera.
The three worlds have been brought under his control, and sovereign kingship has been mastered.
The guardians of the quarters and the world-protectors have for the most part been subdued;
having come to the earth, kings too have for the most part been brought under his sway.
Having reached him as he was ruling his kingdom on the bank of the Revā, those two spoke to the one named Raktabīja: "Who are you? He replied:
"I am a Daitya, the minister of Mahiṣa, known as Raktabīja."
Out of fear of the Goddess, I rule here in secret.
The two ministers of Mahiṣa, named Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa,
remain submerged in the water out of dread of the Goddess, O mighty-armed one.
"Thus our situation has been described; you two should also understand it.
When they had thus questioned him, Śumbha and Niśumbha said to him:
"I am Śumbha, the elder; this one is Niśumbha, the younger."
"The two sons of Danu, born of Kaśyapa, conquered the gods and others,
as well as the great protectors who dwell upon the earth.
While they were speaking thus on the bank of the Narmadā at that time—
Emerging from their dwelling in the waters, the two Dānavas Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa joined with one another;
those five Dānavas met together to avenge themselves upon Mahiṣa and Namuci. (93–94)
Having deliberated for the sake of her defeat, those truthful ones said,
"We shall marry that virtuous woman who is like a jewel.
Having thus addressed one another, they went to the Vindhya mountain to seek out Satī.
Though invisible, she was seen; she did not go to the Himalayas from there.
Seeing the virtuous Pārvatī going there to bathe, they said, "Choose us! and Pārvatī then spoke to them.
"I am the goddess Vindhyācalī, and I have come here for the sake of the holy ford (tīrtha).
You must not speak thus; let those who go to a true tīrtha depart from here just as they came.
My residence is on the Vindhya mountain; there, what is held in my heart shall be spoken."
"Having performed my rites at the sacred ford, I shall depart; you indeed go there.
Having thus dispatched the Daityas, Śumbha and the others, Pārvatī proceeded forward to the celestial Gaṅgā for the purpose of bathing.
Then, having assembled and gathered there, the lords of the gods first praised the Goddess for the sake of dispelling their own suffering:
"Indeed, a boon was granted to us by you, that when we are remembered in times of calamity, you shall become manifest. (101)

"I shall indeed destroy suffering, for the time of calamity has arrived. (102) Thus ends the chapter titled "The Description of the Birth of the Eight Sages through the Sacrifice of His Own Vital Energy by Brahmā in the First Section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga; the Cause of the Goddess Satī’s Birth in the House of Dakṣa Āṅgirasa; the Cause of the Birth of Dakṣa Prācetasa; the Cause of the Birth of Kaśyapa and Nārada from Brahmā and Nārada; the Sons and Daughters of Dakṣa; the Birth of the Sons of Danu, such as Śumbha and Niśumbha; the Defeat of the Gods; and the Prayer of the Goddess," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, having meditated upon Maheśvarī, the gods offered her praise.

Having gathered on the banks of the Gaṅgā, listen as I tell you [this story]. (1) Salutations again and again to you, the Mother, the Great Mother, the Progenitress; salutations to Māyā, the Great Māyā—to you, the Māyā, repeated salutations. (2)
Salutations again and again to you, O Brahmāṇī, O Akṣarāṇī, and to you, O Muktānī;
salutations again and again to Vāsudevī, to Prakṛti, and to Pradhānā.
Salutations again and again to Bhūmā, to Kālī, to Mahākālī, and to Mahālakṣmī.
Salutations again and again to you, Hiraṇyā, the mother of noble offspring, the daughter of Virāja.
Salutations again and again to you, Vaireṇyā, possessed of excellent form, the mistress of Goloka.
Salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇī, Kṛṣṇā, and Vaikuṇṭhā.
Salutations again and again to Śvetā, Badarī, and Mārtaṇḍā;
salutations again and again to Pāvanī, Pavamānā, and Avyākṛtī.
Salutations again and again to you, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and Raudrī.
Salutations again and again to you who are Dhātrī, Gaurī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Jyotsnā.
(7) Salutations again and again to you who are the foremost among those practicing celibacy and who are Vīryā.
Salutations again and again to you who are Mahatī, Abhimānā, and Ākūtī. (8)
Salutations again and again to Citti, Vṛtti, Pravṛtti, and Pralaya;
salutations again and again to Svargā, Satyaloka, and Lokapā.
Salutations again and again to Ramā, Jayā, and Vijayā.
Salutations again and again to you, Rādhā, the accomplisher of all, Lakṣmī! Salutations again and again to you, Nairṛtī, the perfection of happiness, and Saumyā!
Salutations again and again to you, Vārkṣī, whose nature is the seed-syllable, the goddess Rati! 1.166.10–11.
Salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, repeated salutations to her— the Goddess who is established as Viṣṇu’s Māyā among all beings;
she who exists in the form of consciousness and intellect, and who abides in the form of sleep.

She who exists as shadow-form, as the form of hunger, and as the form of power—she is called thirst, patience, and compassion; salutations again and again to her! She is likewise said to be modesty, peace, faith, splendor, conduct, and memory. (13–14)
Salutations again and again to you who are called Tuṣṭi and Puṣṭi;
salutations again and again to you, the Goddess Mātṛ, the Sustainer and the Ordainer.
O great river of the Asuras, a great calamity is occurring.
"Salutations again and again to you who remain within [all things] as the observer!
16. While being praised in this manner, Pārvatī, the Supreme Goddess, arrived there by way of her bathing path at the very place where the gods were offering praise. 17.
Then, being pleased, she spoke to those gods as they bowed before her:
"Having extracted from my body this beautiful one in the form of a sheath, I give her for the protection of the gods; O gods, take me."
"May they assume my form, beautiful and endowed with divine splendor.
(19) Then the gods, having taken the maiden Kauśikī, went to the Vindhya mountain.
And Kauśikī then became established within the goddess on the Vindhya mountain. (20)
Then the gods made an effort for the sake of destroying the asuras.
That body of Pārvatī, which was the form of a treasury and consisted of the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, became black in color;
she is known by the name Kālī, the Dark One.
Following the words of the Goddess, the Daityas went to the Vindhya mountain.
There, they held a consultation with messengers regarding a wife;
they dispatched Sugrīva as a messenger toward the Vindhya range.
The messenger said: "O Great Goddess! I have been sent by Śumbha.
Śumbha is a great king, the sole sovereign and lord of the three worlds.
Listen to what that king, whose mind is enamored of you, has said. (24)
By me, indeed, the fourteen worlds together with their guardians have been conquered.
Whatever kingdoms exist in the three worlds have been brought under my control;
whatever jewels are in the three worlds are now in my house. (25–26)
Airāvata and other elephants dwell in my palace; Uccaiḥśravas and other horses are present in my palace;
and the Kalpavṛkṣa and Pārijāta trees perfume my home.
The celestial chariots yoked with swans belonging to the gods, gandharvas, and nāgas;
indeed, the great treasures such as Mahāpadma and others exist in my house; and the jewels of the ocean, including parasols, chowries, and garlands.
There were various wonderful chariots made of the finest jewels,
as well as diverse and excellent elixirs that bestow eternal youth and nourishment.
Likewise, there were male and female servants, and manifold ornaments for the sake of desire.
Everything is subject to my will, and all supernatural powers reside in my home.
Mountains, rivers, the seven oceans, forests, and deities—
the abundant suns themselves— are my servants in my abode.
The queens have thousands of handmaidens according to their desire;
I shall indeed make them all your servants if you become mine.
For you are a jewel among women of renowned beauty, while we are the enjoyers of jewels.
"O Goddess, accept either me or my younger brother, for you are the most excellent jewel!
Make me your chief queen and come under my protection.
O Goddess, why do you not accept me, a jewel among men?"
Thus addressed, she, with a deep inner smile, spoke to him:
"What has been said by Śumbha, the conqueror of the three worlds, is indeed true;
however, there is a family tradition passed down through our lineage of goddesses."
"He who conquers a maiden in battle, she shall become his beloved.
Therefore, let such a renowned and auspicious man come;
or let Niśumbha himself come to the field of battle and conquer me."
"Why does he not take the hand of such a maiden in marriage here so soon?
The messenger then said to the queen: "Do not be disdainful in this matter;
by that arrogant man, the kings of the fourteen worlds have been conquered."
"Go with me, preceded by a grand welcome;
let there be no humiliation for you arising from the pulling of your hair.
The Goddess said: "You speak of my dignity exactly as it is."
"But the ancestral tradition of the Goddess's family can never be altered;
therefore, explain that to Śumbha so that he may act as is appropriate.
Having bowed, the messenger went to Śumbha and related it to him in detail.
Hearing this, the highly arrogant one became enraged and spoke to Dhūmrākṣa with respect:
"Go quickly with your army and bring that wicked woman here after first pulling her by the hair; meanwhile, slaughter her protectors."
Having heard those words, Dhūmrākṣa, accompanied by sixty thousand dānavas,
went quickly to the one dwelling on the Vindhya mountain.
He said, "Come, accept this auspicious husband in a straightforward manner."
"If you do not [consent], I shall simply take her by force; do as you wish.
Then the Goddess said to the Daitya: "Without a battle, I have no wager.
You are powerful and endowed with strength; do as you wish."
Having heard this, he, unable to endure it, arrived with the intent to seize [her] by force;
however, right there, he was reduced to ashes by the Goddess’s fire of the syllable *hūṃ*.
Then, a highly enraged army arrived for the purpose of destroying the Goddess.
They covered the Goddess with arrows, weapons, missiles, spears, and axes;
they shrouded her with a rain of arrow-bundles.
Then, by the command of the Goddess, the lion let out a roar.
Then, from the thundering spray and droplets of foam, thousands of other lions were born, possessing manes and tufts of hair, with claws and fangs as their weapons;
they were powerful, endowed with youth, and capable of leaping into the sky.
Sixty thousand [demons] fell upon the army of Dhūmranetra.
Then, some [of the gods] struck the asuras with blows from their trunks, some with their tusks,
some with their tails, some with their claws, and others by trampling them.
They tore open the bellies and heads of some,
drank their blood, and devoured their entrails in great quantities.
The entire army was destroyed by them, and the earth shone red with blood.

Upon hearing this, Śumbha became enraged; with his lower lip quivering from anger, he spoke fiercely to Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa: "Go at once and, having seized her by the hair and bound her, bring that doe here!"
"If you have any doubt regarding the vital matter, let that gentle doe be killed;
let the lions also be slain, and provide me with information.
Thus commanded, the Daityas, Caṇḍa and the others, took up their weapons and assembled.
Endowed with the fourfold army, they proceeded toward the Vindhya mountain.
From afar, they cried out to her: "O Goddess, come quickly!
Come, O Kauśikī, desire Śumbha as your auspicious husband!"
"If we do not carry her away by force while she is overwhelmed by the pulling of her hair," Kauśikī then directed a fierce wrath toward those enemies;
looking at Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, she knit her brows into a triple-furrowed frown.
Then, overflowing with extreme rage, she became one with a terrifying countenance.
From the knitting of her brows, which was dark as the black night and infused with wrath, Mahākālī emerged—a yoginī bearing weapons. (61–62)
Holding a sword in her hand, she is beautified by a khaṭvāṅga in her grasp;
she is adorned with a sword, noose, goad, mace, bell, and mallet.
Clad in a lion’s skin, she is decorated with a garland of severed heads.
With wide-open eyes, a lolling tongue, protruding fangs, and a cavernous mouth, that Mahākālī, armed with weapons, struck down the enemies of the gods;
she cut some asuras with her sword and others with her *khaṭvāṅga* staff. (64–65)
In battle, she destroyed horses, elephants, chariots, maces,
and men; then Kauśikī, assuming a form as massive as a mountain, held back those who had come to the fray— camels, elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers.
Mahākālī threw the army into her own mouth and devoured them;
she seized some by the heads and others by the waists and feet,
depriving the warriors of the entire host of their lives on all sides.
Ruru fled from the army toward the caves of the Vindhya mountains;
Kālī pursued that great asura in order to overpower him.
With great force, the Goddess struck him violently on the head with her khaṭvāṅga staff.
His head became matted; at that very moment, he met his death.
Having cut off the hair from the corpse of the Ruru king, the goddess Kālī bound her own hair with it and shone exceedingly like a *kiṃśuka* tree.
Having separated one matted lock and plucked it out, Kālī cast it upon the ground. It then became a girl, half of whose body was black and half white.
Kālī said to that girl, "Bring Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa here."
"I myself shall kill them both," she said, and rushed toward them.
Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa also fled toward the south out of fear.
Caṇḍamārī mounted a very swift donkey.
When those two Daityas had departed, she followed after them in a rage;
on the way, she saw a buffalo named Pauṇḍra belonging to Yama.
Having uprooted its horn, she pursued the Dānavas with speed.
Then Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, having abandoned the earth, took to the sky.
At that time, the nāga Karkoṭaka, while passing by, came within the sight of the Goddess;
likewise, Garuḍa was seen, and she seized his feathers.
Having thus seized Karkoṭaka, they rushed at the two [Nāgas] with great speed;
they were overpowered, crushed, and bound by the cords of Karkoṭaka’s own body.
Brought into the presence of Kālī, he presented them to her.
Then both Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa were rendered headless by the Goddess. There, upon the strap of Ruru’s hide, the heads of the Asuras were indeed fastened like variegated feathers of Garuḍa by Kṛṣṇā.
Having fashioned an incomparable garland, he offered it to Caṇḍikā;
then he also offered her that *ghargharī* lute made from the skin of a *ruru* deer.
Furthermore, having fashioned another garland from the feathers of Tārkṣya, he presented it.
Then Kālī placed [the heads] upon her own head in her braided hair and was satisfied;
she drank the abundant blood of the Dānavas until she was satiated.
The two, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, having been slain by the Goddess, were made into ornaments for her head.
Because the heads of Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and others were placed upon her crest,
she thereafter became known by the name Cāmuṇḍā due to that association with those [heads].
At that time, they were thus Cāmuṇḍā, Kālī, and Kauśikī.
Together, the three of them wrought great destruction upon the Daityas.

(85) Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Praise of Pārvatī by the Gods on Kailāsa; Kauśikī, born from the body of Pārvatī, goes to Vindhyācala; the arrival of the messenger Sugrīva sent by Śumbha; the destruction of Dhūmrākṣa; the manifestation of Kālī; and the account of her name Cāmuṇḍā due to the destruction of Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and others," in the first section, the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī, Śumbha himself, desiring to fight, approached and said to the Daitya Raktabīja: "Kill these women who are like she-asses!"
Then the heroic great asura Raktabīja, accompanied by an army of three hundred million and joined by Kātyāyanī, Kauśikī, Kālī, and Cāmuṇḍā,
arrived to do battle.
And then the sounds of war-instruments pervaded all directions.
At that time, those four goddesses produced great roars;
from the regions of their mouths, millions of Brahmāṇīs emerged.
The Māheśvarīs were three-eyed and bore tridents;
they were fierce, encircled by great serpents, and possessed of earrings. There, the Kaumārīs appeared by the millions, adorned with peacock feathers.
There, crores of Śaktis appeared with peacocks as their vehicles;
crores of Vaiṣṇavīs appeared mounted upon Garuḍas with their two arms;
and crores of Vārāhīs were born with Śeṣa as their vehicle at their backs.
Indeed, millions of Nakhinīs and Nārasiṃhīs were born from the heart;
their great roars caused the destruction of the universe.
Upon hearing them, Śaṅkara indeed arrived.
Śivā also arrived together with him and saw the effort made by the Daityas.
Then Śivā said to Śambhu: "O Śaṅkara, go to the Daitya;
speak to Śumbha and Niśumbha if you wish to live."
"Therefore, go and take her to the seventh subterranean realm (rasātala);
let Vāsava obtain heaven, and let the gods be free from affliction.
From that time on, the goddess was known by the name Śivadūtī.
Having heard the words of the messenger, they all, filled with pride,
rushed to where Kātyāyanī, Kālī, and Kauśikī were;
[armed] with goads, spears, arrows, javelins, and *bhūśuṇḍi* weapons.
They rained down upon Kātyāyanī spears, iron clubs, barbed missiles, tridents, and battle-axes; she, however, swiftly cut them all apart with her sharp-edged,
feathered arrows.
And with great arrows she struck down the great asuras who were intoxicated with battle (15).
But Raṇacaṇḍī Cāmuṇḍā slew ten thousand dānavas;
Kātyāyanī Mahāmārī struck them down with tridents (16).
Kauśikī, Brāhmī, Kumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī likewise—
stationed for heroic deeds— slew tens of millions of Dānavas with skull-topped staffs, water-nooses, spears, and thunderbolts.
Caṇḍī struck them with thunderbolts, Vārāhī with her snouts and discuses, Nārasiṃhī with her fangs and claws, and Śivadūtī with fire;
likewise, Kālī struck the demon soldiers with swords. (18–19)
Thus, being struck there by the hosts of goddesses,
those Dānavas and Asuras fell down, having indeed abandoned their lives.
Others, out of fear, then went for refuge to Raktabīja.
Then Raktabīja approached and, out of anger, struck the circle of Mothers in many ways with excellent weapons; he entered the central area,
and all the Mothers then struck him back with sharp missiles.
As many drops of blood as fell from the red-bodied Raktabīja upon the earth, so many Raktabījas were born;
indeed, from the body of Raktabīja, armies then arose.
Then Kātyāyanī said to Kālī, "Devour the Dānava Raktabīja, so that the production of the army may be quickly halted. Mahākālī immediately cast that Raktabīja into her mouth.
Then Carmamuṇḍā, having become as large as a mountain at the mouth of the cave, cast down and devoured the armies born of Raktabīja.
At that time, the other Dānavas cried out, "Alas, brother! Alas, father! (296).
With their bodies and limbs severed, they went to Niśumbha for refuge.
(27) Niśumbha suddenly took up a sword and desired to kill [her], but he was momentarily bewildered and paralyzed by her true form. (28)
The Goddess said: "O Niśumbha, you wish to conquer me through delusion.
Go, O Daitya; you have already been conquered by me. Being deluded, you shall not defeat me.
Then the Daitya said to the Goddess: "O Goddess, you possess a very delicate body!"
"How can she be slain by me? Therefore, I shall not kill Sundarī. Furthermore, I am unable to conquer you in battle without the discharge of a weapon;
yet if a weapon were discharged, your destruction would occur and my purpose would not be achieved. (1.167.30–31)
Thus, out of a sense of what ought to be done, I have maintained this state of bewilderment:
"If the weapon falls upon me, there is no gain for me; nor is there any gain if the weapon does not fall.
Therefore, O beautiful one, what benefit is there in your death?
"Turn your mind away from battle; become my wife and grant me pleasure.
Having heard this, the goddess laughed and said to the Dānava Niśumbha:
"O hero, I am not conquered in battle; I shall not become the wife of anyone."
Whether it be your death or my own death,
even fleeing from battle is worse than death itself. Furthermore,
He is considered by women to be worthless and a eunuch;
indeed, those lowest of men who seek to conquer a woman through battle are fools.
Women are never to be conquered by war, nor has it ever been heard anywhere that wives are so won.

Whichever woman does not wish to become the wife of a man, she alone desires a destructive battle with that man. In such a battle, there is the destruction of only one; she shall not fall into the hands of the weak. (38)
If she should come into one’s hands by force, she certainly destroys that man.
She has no friend who does not abide in her mind, nor is there any enemy who truly abides in her mind.
Therefore, O Viśālākṣī, act quickly so that you may come to abide in my mind. 1.167.40.
"Since you desire me as your wife, then conquer me in combat!
I shall never become the wife of a eunuch or a fool.
Having been addressed thus, the Dānava, his eyes copper-red with rage, brandished his sword.
She hurled it with great force, but he cut it apart with his sword. Just as the Daitya was about to hurl his mace, Kālikā severed both his arms right at the shoulders with a razor-edged arrow.
Like a branch severed from its trunk, the Daitya was split apart even at the head.
Upon the destruction of Niśumbha, Caṇḍa and the others raised a tumultuous shout of joy;
"Victory, O Goddess! the gods exclaimed, and they released a rain of flowers.
And the sound of musical instruments proclaimed his victory. (45) Then, ill omens befell his brother Śumbha: at night, a jackal entered the camp and howled with a harsh voice. (46)
Crows remain in the camp, shrieking day and night;
black, fierce, and terrifying serpents slither through the dwellings.
Crows, vultures, and cranes, wandering about, fly over the camp.
The fetuses conceived in women, cows, and does were all miscarried;
there was no ghee in the milk, nor was oil found in the sesame seeds.
There, the people fought one another within their own camps.
Dark-complexioned, quarrelsome, with long hair and blind eyes,
she went weeping toward the abode of the lord of the Dānavas, unrecognized.
At that time, a certain ascetic, covered in ashes, was filled with anger.
A certain silent, naked ascetic was seen wandering about in the camp.
(5.1) Bare-chested, he sounded his hand-drum and uttered the syllable "Hūṃ";
he caused unseasonable clouds to release rain and produced the glare of lightning. (5.2)
Hailstones fell from the clouds and thunder roared repeatedly;
an earthquake occurred, and a conflagration of the quarters also arose.
At night, packs of dogs stood before [the city] and howled with their mouths upturned.
Owls shrieked during the day, and a comet appeared in the sky.
There, the solar disc was seen surrounded and encircled by a wheel.
Headless trunks were visible in the heavens, and the moon did not shine.

Then the stars were seen in the sky during the day by the Dānavas; likewise, the various classes of beings were seen as embryos within the Dānava women. The horses neighed and the elephants, though excellent, fell upon their backs.
At that time, the ministers were seen to be devoid of mental composure within the camp. The fire did not burn in the hearth, nor did the wind blow fiercely;
the banners in the armies seemed to blaze, and the sky became greyish.
In his dream, Śumbha’s heart became agitated;
on the battlefield, he saw his own head severed from his trunk.
Seated upon a ram, he was heading toward the southern direction.
A certain naked female demon performs an oil massage;
she, wearing red garments, strives to embrace him, offers wine for drinking, and likewise gives a kiss. (1.167.60–61)
Having shaved his head, he then cries out and goes toward the south;
he sees the camp fallen and destroyed by tigers;
he sees his own body being torn apart by naked women with disheveled hair.
Śumbha likewise tasted the drinking of his own blood;
he saw his own body cast upon the funeral pyre by Śumbha’s wife.
Thus, while awake, the Daitya Śumbha experienced all these things in a dream.
The signs of his destruction were visible, and for that reason he indeed fell into a state of dejection; having heard of the death of Niśumbha and the crushing of the army,
he wept there in many ways and fainted again and again.
Nevertheless, due to a state of darkness and passion rooted in desire,
he regained his mindfulness and, seeking to avenge his enmity,
mounted a great elephant and approached with a spear in hand.
Meanwhile, the guest arrived, intent on slaying Kauśikī in battle;
indeed, the war-drums and *ḍiṇḍima* kettledrums were sounded again and again.
Then, eighty-four armies of the Kambūyas marched forth from there.
Then fifty clans of Asuras emerged;
then another hundred clans of Dhūmras emerged;
and there were millions of clans of Kālakas, Daurhṛtas, and Mauryas.
Beholding Karīṣṭha, who was adorned with splendor, approaching the field of battle with eight arms and great weapons, the gods sounded their conchs;
they made their bows twang and rang their bells.
Then Ambikā filled the quarters with the sounds of battle.
But the lion let out a roar as he was made to release the great rutting elephant;
and thousands of lions there filled the vault of heaven with their roars.
They filled the battlefield with an exceedingly fierce resonance;
thousands of goddesses arrived there on the field of battle.
By the command of Mahādevī, all the queens also became fierce warriors in combat.
Those goddesses who are the female servants of Brahmā, and those who are the female servants of Indra and Bala;
likewise, the female servants of Varuṇa and the female servants of Yama by the millions;
and the female servants of Kubera’s servants, as well as the female servants of the servants of Īśāna. (76)
Ten thousand female servants of Agni, as many female servants of Nirṛti,
ten million female servants of Vāyu, and female servants of the world-protectors;
all these foremost female servants of the guardians of the world were exhausted by their service to the army.
Skilled in the arts of war, weapons, and missiles, they numbered in the hundreds of millions and tens of millions;
they were resplendent with infinite divine vehicles such as chariots and weapons, were renowned throughout the fourteen worlds, and were like jewels among beings. (78–79)
The wives of the army, who were well-acquainted with the nature of war, assembled together and said:
"The destruction of all the asuras must certainly be brought about;
otherwise, happiness for the millions of gods will never be possible."
Happiness is attained by staking one's head as a wager.
(8.1) Clad in armor and helmets, beautifully arrayed in military attire, these women—possessing the full strength of youth—move with power like mighty forces. (8.2)
With all the components of war fully prepared, they arrived at the field of battle;
on that battlefield, Mahendra caused them all to drink the nectar (*amṛta*),
as well as the *sandhinī*, the *jīvanī*, and the *viśalyakaraṇī*.
Then the Aśvinī Kumāras brought various medicinal herbs that bestow rest, remove fainting, and stop bleeding;
they are the means for joining together the severed fragments of bodies split in two. (84–85)
Then, by means of the swift movement of their vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the sages brought forth juices there—
foods that were nectar-like and drinks that were like ambrosia—
which had been preserved in the camps during the battle by the gods and others.
A ninth [weapon] was prepared by the gods for the protection of the army of women:
"In victory in battle, there shall certainly be no destruction even of a single hair;
nor shall there be death or injury to anyone on the side of the Goddess. (87–88)
Thus, all this was gathered together by those skilled in action;
furthermore, a protection was arranged by Śumbha himself in his presence so that he might be guarded.
Then, there arose a great sound signaling the commencement of battle.
The asuras produced the sounds of battle-trumpets and drums in the path of the sky.
(1.167.90) Then a great battle took place between the armies of the Goddess and Śumbha;
at that time, goddesses numbering in the hundreds of millions struck down the asuras. (91)
Tens of millions, billions, and trillions of asuras destroyed that forest filled with goddesses;
and the kettledrums of the tens of millions of asuras cried out: "Listen, O asuras!
This army of women is for the sake of destroying the lineages of the Daityas and Dānavas! || 92 ||
"He has arrived in the fray; wage battle that takes life!
Let them not look back, nor let them seek refuge in heaven during the fight.
Thinking 'this is a woman,' let them not abandon her on the field of battle. (93-94)
Today the earth shall surely become either filled with asuras or filled with gods;
let there be the existence of only one of these two, not both sides together.
Let the gods live, or else let only the asuras live.
"Let there now be no further creation mixed with gods and asuras.
Let the gods be widowers, or let the daughters of the Danavas be widows;
whatever may happen, let it be so—do not flee! (96–97)
"Let them kill, let them destroy, and let them slaughter!
Let the impetuous ones assault, crush, and grind to powder!"—
thus do the drums of the Dānavas proclaim on the field of battle.
Then Śaṅkha proclaimed among the goddesses on the field of battle:
"Devour! Feast upon! Destroy the Dānavas!
Tear them apart! Finish them off! Slay those who cause delusion!"
The Asuras terrify the gods at every moment in every way.
Let them terrify, let them diminish, let them devour [the enemies] before me!
All the gods have arrived for the sake of assisting you.
"Let them not make [the world] five-footed; let them perish and let them cause others to perish!"—thus did the thundering of the sky arise at that time, bestowing awakening.
The sounds produced by kettledrums and conchs were heard, impelled by Time.
"For those who die in battle there is heaven; for those who survive, lordship over the earth;
but for those who retreat, there is nothing at all. Therefore, one must indeed die here.
In this way, the tips of the spears instruct the great warriors in the fray.
For that long, blows were dealt and weapons were struck down.
With sharp arrows, shafts, and iron bolts, they struck the foremost warriors;
with razor-edged arrows, crescent-headed shafts, and spears, they struck one another.
The army of the Dānavas was covered by arrows in the sky by Kātyāyanī, Kauśikī, Kālī, and likewise Cāmuṇḍā;
[and by the weapons] of the Kambukas, Kālakas, Dhauṃmas, Kālakeyas, and Daurhṛtas.
The army and the goddesses were covered by arrows in the sky. They cut down the volleys of arrows with their own arrows and struck others with yet more;
though their quivers contained inexhaustible shafts, they reached a state of depletion there.
When the arrows of the Daityas and goddesses were destroyed, set ablaze, shattered, and broken by the blows of their tridents,
hundreds of thousands of slain Daityas lay crushed upon the surface of the earth.
With their feet severed, their hands severed, and their necks and chests cut open, hundreds of thousands of goddesses fainted there upon the field of battle;
their mounts were destroyed, and elephants and other beasts were broken or dead. (111–112)
Lions, buffaloes, peacocks, and camels died there in the battle;
they were restored to life again by the gods and the daityas through vital essences and mantras.
Then, with weapons, arrows, tridents, and bhūśuṇḍis—
With iron clubs, maces, spears,
and lances, as well as with swords, javelins, sharp scimitars, and battle-axes,
there then occurred a mutual combat that caused mutual destruction.
There they are cut from their bodies, likewise split asunder from the chest;
they are severed from the waist and likewise hacked from the hands.
There they die from the throat and are likewise cast down from the thighs.
Dragging them again and again, they were slain; embracing them repeatedly, they were crushed.
(1.17) Grasping foot by foot, they were split in two on the battlefield. A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; no one could discern who this was or what this was. (1.18)
At that very moment, the body of whoever arrived there was split in two;
thus did that battle of blinding speed, burdened with tumultuous confusion,
arise, wherein millions upon millions of soldiers were then destroyed.
The earth was rich with the color of blood, filled with the corpses of gods and demons;
it was pervaded by hundreds of rivers of blood, a forest of bodies where people came and went;
it was strewn with the corpses of those whose teeth were like mountains, along with the dead bodies of donkeys, camels, and other creatures.

Covered with countless dead bodies visible even in the season of frost, there were headless trunks (kabandhas) that had fallen there, half-killed and naked; rising up again and again upon the ground, they cried out, "Drink! Drink! (122).
They fled even while bearing weapons and fell again upon the earth.
At that time, no one there offered assistance to anyone else.
There were tens of millions of delicate goddesses and Daityas in the prime of their youth.
In battle, those who possess the form of gold, having died, shine like the moon;
though they are crushed and destroyed in the fray, that is indeed the work of Mahākāla.
A great terror arose even in the hearts of the onlookers.
Then indeed, Brahmā informed Vibhāvarī there:
"O beloved, employ the weapon of sleep at the proper time; that is appropriate for you.
At that time, Vibhāvarī [was addressed] regarding the deity presiding over the mantra of sleep.
Then, having joined the missile to the tip of his arrow and released it,
the armies of both the goddess and the dānavas were overcome by sleep;
they fell into a deep slumber and rested completely.
Then the Daityas rained down nectar and life-giving medicinal herbs upon the army of the goddesses;
indeed, the goddesses, the lions, the mounts, and all those who were conscious beings [were thus revived].
All of them were indeed restored to life by a rain of nectar;
and then the Daityas also brought the Daityas back to life with mantras,
using the *saṃjīvanī*, the *sandhinī*, the *viśalyā*, and the *virāmā*.

By means of the *mūrchānāśikā* [mantra], the *raktarodhinī*, and life-bestowing juices, the army was treated medically; it was restored to life and made free from disease. Then everyone became healthy, as if having arisen from sleep. (132–133)
In that manner, the great army of the goddess once again became ready; likewise, the army of the Daityas also became ready once more.
Then, at the command of Brahmā, Vibhāvarī [was stationed] within her own forces.
She brought forth the weapon of sleep, and there was comfort for both armies.
Then Brahmā spoke to Śambhu regarding the destruction of the Dānavas:
"The battle must be waged with weapons alone; let Caṇḍikā and the others fight."
Having brandished the weapon with wrath and visualized the enemies, one should employ it.
"O Kālakavala, may this mantra be given by you to the goddesses:
Om! From death, from the death of death, O Great Death, remain firm together with death! (137)
"O Death, O Great Death, O Death of Death, become extinguished!
(138) Having thus uttered this preceded by the *phuṭ* sound, whatever weapon—such as an arrow or the like—one hurls at the body of the enemy, having died, he does not live again. (139)
Despite many medicines, mantras, and medical treatments,
he did not return to life due to the power of Mahākāla, by whom he was slain at that time by the command of Brahmā. (1.167.140)
And he was instructed by the goddesses in the mantra for devouring Time (Kāla).
By the power of Mahākāla, this [mantra] was perfected in a mere moment.
And by the will of Brahmā, he remained there in embodied form.
Terror-inspiring, the death of Death itself, armed and devouring the asuras,
he was seen by the goddesses as he rose up, consuming living beings.
In that very instant, before the goddesses, he assumed manifold forms.
And he became firmly established upon their tongues, facing toward their task.
This activity of Brahmā and Rudra was not understood by the Daityas;
they rose up, considering themselves immortal, and engaged in battle.

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, [is described] the origin of the goddess Anantā from the demon Raktabīja during the battle with him; the destruction of the original Raktabīja and the slaying of Niśumbha; the ill omens of Śumbha; the mounting of the Dānavas; the arrival of the army of the Goddesses from the fourteen worlds; the appearance of Sañjīvanī and others; and the awakening of the Goddesses by the sleep-inducing weapon (*nidrāstra*) released by Vibhāvarī during the great destruction caused by the tumultuous battle involving musical instruments, weapons, and the like, which restored life to the army of the Goddesses.
The one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Kālakavala Mantra," etc., [ends].
Chapter 167 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga.
Chapter 168.
[The Author: Chapter 169.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen again, O Mahālakṣmī, to that which is fearless regarding death.
And a battle between the two armies commenced, from which there was no return.
Brahmā knows it, Śambhu knows it, and the goddesses know it— that the destruction of tens of millions of Daityas has indeed arrived through the power of Time.
Then, by the command of Śumbha, eighty-four crores of Kambus fought with missiles and weapons, as well as with mountains and forest trees;
the Asuras fought with showers of stones, showers of fire, and arrows.
Then those goddesses, the Vārāhīs, engaged them in battle with missiles,
weapons, showers of stones, mountains, tusks, trees,
showers of fire, arrows, and mantras joined with the *kālakavala* [death-swallowing] spell. (4–5)
Then the Nārasiṃhas fought for their assistance;
with fierce claws, fangs, tails, hands, and feet,
as well as with froth from their mouths and enchanted weapons, they fought repeatedly.
Marked by weapons, missiles, rocks, trees, arrows, foam, and the like,
the Daityas, slain by Time and Mantra, do not rise again once dead.
Then, fifty crores of the Asura clans stood in battle.
Likewise, the guardians of the directions and the consorts of Indra, by the hundreds of millions,
fought with weapons empowered by mantras known as Kāla;
those Asuras were destroyed and slain, and did not rise again in that battle.
Then hundreds of millions of families of the Dhaumras arrived;
they fought with the goddesses Mahāmārī, Caṇḍikā, and others,
and those who met their death by weapons empowered by the mantras of Time were [consumed].
Furthermore, they did not even breathe; they were as good as dead, having departed in every way.
The Kālakeyas and the Kālakas—daityas numbering in the tens of millions and billions—rose up there with their armies for the purpose of destroying the goddesses.
And thirty million women, adorned with earrings and bearing tridents, fought against them.
Overcome by the mantra of Time (Kāla), they did not wake up from their vital breath.
The Mauryas and the Daurhratas waged an exceedingly fierce battle. (13–14)
At that time, tens of millions of their clans were destroyed by lions in their hundreds of thousands;
though they were raised back to life by medicinal herbs, they were slain again by young maidens.
Rendered powerless by weapons consecrated with mantras that swallow up Time (Kāla), they could not even breathe.
Then other Śambaras and Daityas— those of the sea, those of the mountains,
others from the netherworld (pātāla), those dwelling on the earth, as well as Nāgas, tree-dwellers, and those enveloped by old age—
were utterly bewildered upon merely beholding the forms of the goddesses, yet they engaged in battle.
The Śaktis, the messengers of Śiva, struck them with weapons empowered by mantras;
once dead, they do not return, for having gone, they have attained ultimate life.
There were crores and arbudas of asuras and kharvas of crores of Daityas.

The lotuses of the Dānavas, as well as their scattered spears, were destroyed; they had gone, died, perished, and vanished, deprived of both name and form. A sea of blood arose from them, swelling with rivers of gore.
Even now it does not dry up, nor does it appear discolored;
this great battle occurring in the northwestern direction will proclaim itself through the sky, the earth becoming a crimson ocean and the ground a sea of blood. (21)
Then the demon Śumbha, standing on the Vindhya mountain— expanded by the sky,
its peaks touched by Rāhu and Ketu— beheld the slaughter.
The great earth was covered in every direction by his slain armies.
"Such a universal war between the goddesses and the dānavas, who fight intensely in the paths of the sky, shall never happen again.
And that Śumbha, on the peak of the Vindhya mountains, possesses a vision extending for a hundred thousand yojanas."
He then desired to burn Kailāsa and Badarikāśrama with that weapon.
A lightning bolt was hurled from the peak of the Vindhya mountains upon Hara and Hara;
from it, millions of fires and thunderclaps were produced. (25–26)
Desiring to consume both Meru and Mandara, they descended to the earth;
blazing from the path of the sky, they reached Kailāsa and the abode of Badrikā.
Then, the Tāmra weapon was released there by Maheśānī.
Having drawn that [weapon] away from the lightning, it entered the netherworld (atalaloka).
Then, the armies of the goddesses in the sky to the north of the Vindhya mountains took a moment's rest; at that time, the fire-weapon (agnyāstra) was discharged against them.
He set ablaze the planets, the gods, and the piśācas who have the wind as their support;
he caused the two worlds, heaven and earth, to roar, and he fell upon the domain of Śambhu.
He also set many fires ablaze on Kailāsa and at Badarī.
Then, seeing that the weapon of fire had been neutralized by the goddess Vāruṇī,
she discharged the Śītaśaila (Cold-Mountain) weapon, consisting of stones that rained down cold. By means of that shower of snow and cold rain, masses of rocks fell.
The fire-weapon was also pacified by showers of snow and masses of ice;
from that time on, the Golden Mountain became the great Himālaya.
Then, for the sake of destroying them, he discharged the weapon of obstruction (nirodhāstra).
Then the goddess Vāyavyā, who effects the destruction of the obstruction of breath,
swiftly discharged the Vāyu-missile, and the Nirodha-missile was indeed destroyed.
Thereupon, the king of the Daityas performed a fire-oblation with the mantras of the Rākṣasas.
Rākṣasas, resembling mountains, arose by the millions;
with weapons and missiles in their hands, they fell from the sky upon the army of the Goddess.
The space was completely covered by them, as if by masses of clouds during the rainy season.
The forest was thus crushed by the rain of the goddesses' weapons.
Seeing this, the goddesses unleashed the *nairṛta* weapon;
from that, the *nairṛtas* arose and began devouring the *rākṣasas*.
Just as the *timiṅgila* fish devour the *timi* fish, so did [the demons] devour them.
Then Śumbha discharged another weapon, the hungry *preta* weapon;
at that very moment, armies of *pretas* arose by the millions.
The goddesses of Yama created the weapon of Yama, and the messengers of Yama were formed.
At that time, the terrifying messengers of Yama devoured the *pretas*.
Thereafter, a place named Avīci was prepared for the messengers of Yama.
Śumbha produced tens of millions of hellish fevers,
and then the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī created Vaiṣṇava fevers;
by those Vaiṣṇava fevers, the torments of the hells were indeed dissolved, and they went to the Avīci hell.
The Brahmāstra, which had been hurled by the Dānava against the armies of the goddesses,
discharged great splendors, sounds, arrows, and thunderbolts;
from that [weapon], great fires of the universal dissolution arose, destined to reduce all creation to ashes.
Terrified by those [weapons] throughout the three worlds, the goddesses were scorched and fled;
there was a great cry of "Alas! and the goddesses then fell unconscious.
Brahmāṇī quickly deployed the Brahmā-weapon there.
A battle between the two took place in the great sky along the path of the sun.
Then, the Kaumudī, which removes fainting, was joined with those [other powers] as the nectar of immortality by means of the great mantra of Candrakāntā, the goddess of the moon.
The fainting caused by excessive heat was dispelled by showers of nectar;
meanwhile, the Creator drew back two Brahma-missiles from the sky. At that moment, Śumbha became empty, utterly deprived of his weapons and missiles.
Then, empowered by Kālī and Mahākālī and consecrated with the Yamadaṇḍa mantra,
Śumbha was dispatched for her destruction; indeed, he then employed his illusory power (māyā),
and millions of Śumbhas appeared within the darkness.
In the dense darkness of Māyā, Śumbha seized Caṇḍikā;
but as soon as the sword was struck at Śumbha by Caṇḍī,
Śumbha no longer existed, for he had become a false Śumbha.
The blow of the weapon proved futile; Śumbha seized Kālikā.
Then Kālī brought her great sword down upon the head of the Daitya;
at that moment the Daitya was no more, for the blow of the sword had been in vain.
Just as he, having assumed the form of Kauśikī, was fleeing,
he was struck on the head with a *khaṭvāṅga* by Cāmuṇḍā.
Kauśikī remained visible there, but Śumbha, as he fell, could no longer be seen.
Indeed, he committed an assault upon the goddesses with false forms.
Out of lust, he touched the breast of Kātyāyanī in order to violate her;
a sharp trident was then hurled by Raudrī at his head and throat.
Just then, even there, this Śumbha remained hidden at a distance.
Laughing, Rudrāṇī spoke to Śarvāṇī and Śivadūtī:
"In a deceptive form, he touched my breast without having conquered me, Kātyāyanī."
"Therefore, this one who has perished through unrighteousness shall surely meet his destruction before long.
(568) When the curse had been thus pronounced, its power became latent;
he fell there upon the surface of the earth like a eunuch. (19)
Those who had been engaged in battle in the form of ten million illusions fell to the earth as false Śumbhas, like eunuchs.
[They were] unconscious, fainted, exhausted, and crying out, "I am yours!"
One should not slay in battle one who is drinking, urinating, or unarmed.
Therefore, even when the opportune moment had arrived, Śumbha was not slain by the Goddess.
Consequently, the false Śumbhas dissolved away, and that illusory darkness also vanished.
Then Śumbha was seen fallen upon the ground, unconscious;
at that time, Kātyāyanī caused all those goddesses she had created herself—
except for the wives of the gods— to dissolve back into her own breast.
Having regained consciousness, Śumbha roared at her;
he then created another illusory night accompanied by wind and rain,
and advanced to assault the great goddess Kātyāyanī.
That Daitya made contact with her heart and the region of her breasts;
at that moment, the goddess struck him across the chest with her palm.
Enraged, he leapt up, seized the goddess, and ascended into the sky.
Mounting his own elephant, he became intent on flight.
Just then, leaping into the sky, he was seized by the goddess by the hair;
she lifted him up, whirled him around, and hurled him to the ground.
Just as he was about to fall, that goddess seized a trident at that very moment;
she tore open his chest and split his throat.
Then the lord of the Daityas repeatedly cast his hands and feet upon the ground.
He became like one whose life was nearly spent, shaking the entire earth;
falling upon his back on the ground with his hands and feet outstretched,
tossing about in the dust in many ways, he ceased and died.
The sky became stainless and the wind and rain subsided. Then the gods and goddesses, their minds filled with joy,
honored Kātyāyanī with blessings of victory and offered worship with delight.
They performed [the rites] with many offerings, and the Gandharvas sang charmingly;
the throngs of Apsarases danced and played musical instruments.
Pleasant breezes blew, and the sun shone, endowed with its brilliance.

The fires blazed peacefully, and the three worlds became partakers of happiness. Then, the portions of the kingdom were duly offered by Aja to the gods, as well as the sacrificial gifts that were presented there to them at that time.
To the goddesses who had fought, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and likewise Śambhu presented necklaces, long pendants, and sealed ornaments;
as well as decorations called *vijaya*, small strings of beads, and beautiful rings.
Diadems, bracelets, armlets, anklets, girdles, as well as necklaces,
crests, earrings, ear-ornaments, and bodices;
water-pots, silken garments, golden and jeweled cushions.
There were parchments known as the *Ratna*, *Hīraka*, *Sauvarṇa*, and *Vijaya*;
as well as foods, drinks, vehicles, and mounts,
and various other jewels situated within the house of the Daitya.
In that assembly, much heartfelt wealth known as a reward was bestowed appropriately according to their respective services.
The queens, enriched with pearl necklaces and wearing crowns adorned with all manner of gems, [were present].
Then, being pleased, they spoke words that were pleasing to the heart:
"Whether they be gods, humans, animals, or even gods and asuras;
whether they be household deities, the wives of householders, sisters, daughters, or daughters-in-law. (82–83)
They will treat their mothers, wives, and female slaves with sincere affection;
they will delight them with things desired by them and honor them with objects such as food, drink, clothing, ornaments, cosmetics, and perfumes. (84)
With a disposition of heartfelt affection, they will always seek to please us.
We, the goddesses, shall indeed dwell in their houses among the women;
we shall delight them with our sovereign powers and with the abundance of wealth, sons, and prosperity.
We shall protect all those people as if they were our own gods, and we shall surely provide them with objects of enjoyment, pleasures, pastimes, and the like.
May they all be happy, wherever the womenfolk are happy.
"May all those places where women are unhappy become unhappy for you.
Thus were blessings pronounced by all the foremost goddesses and the gods;
thereafter, the great goddess Kātyāyanī was worshipped in many ways.
Then the gods offered praise in that assembly for the sake of victory:
"O Kātyāyanī! Salutations to you! O Kauśikī! Salutations, salutations to you! O Kālikā! O Kālī! Salutations to you eternally! O Cāmuṇḍā! Salutations, salutations to you! (1.168.90)
O Mahāmārī, homage to you; O Brahmāṇī, salutations again and again.
O Cāndrī, Vāruṇī, Kuṇḍalinī, salutations again and again to you.
O Triśūlinī, homage to you; O Kaumāri Śaktinī, salutations!
O Nārasiṃhī, O Śivadūtī, O Vaiṣṇavī, salutations again and again to you!
O Vārāhī, O Caṇḍikā, O Caṇḍā, O Carmamuṇḍā, salutations to you!
O Raudrī, O Siṃhī, O Yamadāsī, O Yāmyā, O Goddess, salutations to you!
O Sovereign, O Guardian of the Direction, O Goddess of the South-West, homage be to you!
O Aindrī, O Vāyavī, O Auspicious One, O Blessed Lady, let there be homage to you!
Homage be to you of infinite forms; homage to you, the Bestower of Sovereignty! 94–95.
Salutations to you, O destroyer of the pride of the Daityas; salutations to you who possess eighteen arms.
Salutations to you, O Nārāyaṇī, O Brāhmī, O wielder of the discus. Salutations again and again to you, the bearer of the thunderbolt, whose banner bears the elephant.
O you who are borne by peacocks, let there be salutation to you; O you who are borne by swans, salutation to you!
(97) O you who wear a garland of skulls, salutation to you; O you with beautiful hair, salutation to you!
O three-eyed goddess, granter of boons, salutation to you; be gracious! (98)

O Goddess, remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge, O Mother, be gracious and protect me! O you who are the earth, the eternal support; you who are water, the source of satisfaction; you who are the seed, the form of delusion, and the form of liberation—salutations be to you!
Salutations again and again to you, whose form is knowledge and who embodies the nature of all women.
O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, bestower of heaven and liberation, salutations be to you!
You are the form of Time, the form of the ultimate principles, and the embodiment of both cause and effect.

(103) In the form of the Mothers, endowed with breast-milk; in the form of a wife, bearing a child;

In age after age, perform the destruction of the great afflictions caused by the asuras;

O Goddess, may the trident always protect me from fear; salutations be unto you!

"In the act of creation, you must always perform protection in this very manner.

I shall slay the Asuras Gṛdhra, Garja, Harja, Jaṭhra,

There is no end to my actions throughout time and creation;

On the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth [lunar days], for one of single-minded focus, there shall be poverty, the occurrence of evil karma, and fear of undesirable weapons and the like;

To him, I shall grant valor, auspiciousness, and freedom from fear.
Wealth, grain, gold, and so forth, as well as the prosperity of wife, sons, and grandsons;

In disease, in suffering born of demons and the like, in battle, against an enemy, in the wilderness;

One should also recite my various deeds with devotion;

Listen, Lakṣmī! She herself, when pleased, brings an increase of prosperity to the home.

Śrī Lakṣmī said:

her birth in the house of Dakṣa, her marriage with Śambhu, and likewise the fire-bath of Satī at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, along with its cause. (1–2)
The birth of Satī from Menakā on the Himālaya mountain, her fierce penance,
the falling of Śambhu’s liṅga upon his chest, and another great feat of prowess—

"O Goddess, a son shall be born with limbs made of the essence of adamant.

Having bound the thousand-eyed one, he led him before his own mother.

When the moon was clearly visible and honored by the God of Love,

From that time forward, Dakṣa’s wife was excessively disfigured by her pregnancy-longings; even the purificatory rites beginning with the *ādhāna* were performed for her by Dakṣa himself. When the time for delivery arrived, she illuminated the palace.

Seeing [the hand] with upward lines, the *nāgavallī* leaf, the fish, and other auspicious marks;

As she was being born, all living beings— both stationary and moving— became happy and prosperous, having found their home in that which is the abode of all worlds. Even for those in hell, there arose at that time a happiness equal to that of heaven.

That power of the Supreme Brahman is established in four forms;

The peaceful, the cruel, the industrious, and the servile—these indeed are their respective modes of livelihood.

I am Satī, Śivā, and Raudrī, made manifest in your home.
(1.37) I am the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, and I have come forth for the sake of Śiva.
And Śiva himself, the Blessed One, is likewise the very nature of the Supreme Brahman. (1.38)
The Lord shines upon Kailāsa, while I, the Goddess, am situated in your home.
Therefore, in every way, you who are my devotee and devoted to me—
having gone to me alone for refuge— should worship me everywhere with your mind.
"O dear one, whatever is my true nature that has become the object of your mind, remain established in that,
be devoted to that, and be intent upon its worship. Furthermore,
O dear one, you must petition Śiva on my behalf."
And this eternal daughter Śivā must indeed be given by you to Śiva,
for the sake of establishing righteousness and by the command of Brahmā.
Born from Asiknī, she has come to rely upon you alone as her father.
"You shall offer it to Mahendra; that Śaṅkara will be pleased with you.
Because of that, all the gods and others will bow to you with devotion.
Entrust it to me and go for refuge to Śaṅkara. (143–144)
Having thus instructed Dakṣa, Satī was indeed born as a young girl.
Dakṣa was supremely pleased, recognizing his daughter as the Supreme Goddess.

(145) Thus, in the first section, "The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga," within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [described are]: the birth of Satī from Vibhāvarī, the auspicious great festival, the vision of the divine Satī by Dakṣa, the hymn of praise, the meditation upon the daughter, and the oneness of Śivā and Śiva with the Supreme Brahman.
