Śrī Lakṣmī said: "Indeed, who is this Vibhāvarī, she who is the virtuous daughter of Dakṣa?"
Born as the goddess whose essence is Brahman, [she said: "O Hari, sever my doubt.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī, how Satī became the night, Vibhāvarī."
In the abode of Goloka, the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa shines resplendent.
He is the Supreme Brahman, the sovereign Lord and master of Goloka.
And she who is the root primordial nature (Mūla-prakṛti), the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), dwells upon the left side of Brahman.
Standing to the left of Kṛṣṇa, she shone forth in a form that was both manifest and yet merged with him.
Kṛṣṇa did not delight in being alone; he then desired a second companion.
At that moment, a beautiful maiden emerged from the left side of Kṛṣṇa’s body.
Having run and brought a flower born from a royal campaka tree,
she placed it at Kṛṣṇa’s feet and herself wore it during the rāsa dance.
Because of that, Rādhā was then addressed as "Kāryasiddhikarī" (the one who accomplishes the task).
Having led her beloved Kṛṣṇa with her, she entered a bower of trees;
he gave her the bliss of passion, and she, in turn, bestowed upon him the intoxication of love. And as that great pleasure proceeded, he even fell into a deep sleep.
Then Rādhā said to Kṛṣṇa: "Why do you not move, O Kṛṣṇa?
Kṛṣṇa replied: "My dear, sleep has come upon me for a moment due to fatigue.
Then Rādhā became angry; even sleep itself was like a young girl.
Having stood by his side, bowing down and casting her dark eyes away, Rādhā then looked at him and said: "O Sleep, you who destroy delight!
May you have no residence in Goloka; go instead to the Vairāja Puruṣa! (1.170.10)

The destroyer of all joy, characterized by darkness (*tāmasī*), she is united with Rudra. O Goddess, may you always be *bhava*, the one of dark nature and the one who effects withdrawal (*saṃhāriṇī*).
You are the state of sleep (*nidrā*), the support for the cognition of non-existence (*abhāvapratyayādhārā*), and the destroyer [of worldly activity]. (11–12)
Be always sufficient for the destruction of the terrible asuras;
remain eternally prepared within the armies of the Daityas as the dark power (tāmasī).
In the creation of all living beings, you are the bringer of rest to their senses.
Rudrāṇī, united with Rudra, established the duration of existence.
Indeed, you shall become Night (Rātri), because you are the sister of Bhāna, whose purpose is radiance;
and since radiance has departed from you, you shall be known as Vibhāvarī.
Brahmā himself will take you, the daughter of Vairāja, for his own creation;
he, in turn, will give the goddess Vibhāvarī as a daughter to Dakṣa.
Dakṣa, however, will give that most excellent maiden, Satī, to Śambhu.
That goddess Kālī Caṇḍikā will indeed destroy the asuras.
As such, you shall become Kālī, Night, the Dark One, and Sleep; having become the companion of Rudra, you will sport in the quality of darkness (tamas).
By the command of Hari, out of desire, and likewise due to the necessity of future events,
she, who was the night (Vibhāvarī), became the daughter of Dakṣa.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Now, when Śambhu was born from the Vairāja Puruṣa, it is heard that the Śāmbhavī Śakti was born simultaneously with him; is there,
then, any difference between this Śivā and that Night?
"Śivā is indeed my wife forever; what else could the night be but my consort?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Goddess, you have asked a fitting question regarding my profound conduct."
This is not known by others as to what occurred or when it happened.
Listen to how it previously took place, that which must be understood;
I shall relate the remainder of the story concerning the primordial nature of Śiva.
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all, the cause of all causes,
shines in the imperishable and supreme abode, served by the liberated.
Whenever He desires and whenever He wills creation, He unfailingly brings it forth.
I shall tell you what he did on that occasion by way of context:
when Rādhā was born from the very limb of the Supreme Brahman, he created for her the abode of Goloka and assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa. (25–26)
And she was the wife of Kṛṣṇa, dearer to him than his own life;
a goddess sixteen years of age, with blossoming youth, wearing garments as pure as fire, her limbs tender and radiant. (27)
The beautiful and most enchanting woman was oppressed by the weight of her full hips;
her lips were red, soft, and lovely, and her broad buttocks and breasts were full.
She was captivating with a row of teeth that gleamed like a string of pearls. (28–29)
Her face possessed a mass of splendor exceeding that of ten million full moons;
her eyes were as expansive as lotus petals; she was adorned with fine hair, garments, and other ornaments;
her nose was as beautiful as a sesame flower or the beak of a parrot; and she was exceedingly lovely.
The radiance of her pair of cheeks, possessing a golden hue, was intensely brilliant;
she was exquisitely adorned with earrings set with gold, gems, and jewels, and decorated with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, vermilion, saffron, and other such substances. (3.1–3.2)
With her two skull-cups serving as ear-ornaments, her hair-knot woven with flowers, and the parting of her hair marked by a streak of vermilion;
with her moving feet possessing the lovely luster of the petals of a land-lotus. (33)
With a gait like that of a swan or an elephant, her chest was broad and her movements were slow and graceful.
[She wore] necklaces of gems and jewels, a captivating garland of forest flowers, necklaces fashioned from diamonds, as well as jeweled armlets and bracelets. (34–35)
Wearing bracelets fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems and jeweled armlets, she,
being virtuous, bore a girdle of tinkling golden bells;
she was further delighted by the resonant sound of anklets made of priceless jewels.
Bearing a lotus enriched with various kinds of jewels,
her hands and feet lovely with nails and lips touched by red lac,
she sat with a smile upon half of her husband’s jeweled lion-throne. (37–38)
Then, from her pores, there immediately emerged a multitude of cowherd women,
equal to her in dress, form, and appearance, possessed of perpetual youth,
numbering in the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions, a host of gopīs in Goloka.
Indeed, one named Kṛṣṇadāsī constantly manifested;
then, from the pores of Kṛṣṇa's body, a multitude of cowherds also instantly appeared, identical in form, dress, and other attributes.
Indeed, that host of Kṛṣṇa’s servants numbered thirty crores;
they manifested instantly from the pores of Kṛṣṇa’s skin.
There was also a multitude of cows of many colors, eternally possessed of perfect youth.
The bulls were fragrant, as were the heifers and the calves;
indeed, at that time, auspicious and beautiful signs appeared.
Among them was one bull, equal in strength to ten million lions.
For the sake of obtaining a vehicle for Śambhu, Kṛṣṇa protected the captivating [swan];
from the hollows of the nails of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, a row of swans,
exceedingly white and eternally beautiful with the marks of male and female, manifested.

Among them, Kṛṣṇa protected one royal swan, which was exceedingly white and possessed great strength and prowess, for the sake of obtaining a vehicle for Veda. From the cavity of Kṛṣṇa’s left ear, that most enchanting [bird emerged].
A permanent host of white horses appeared;
among them, the Lord Kṛṣṇa himself personally protected one that was the whitest for the sake of obtaining the vehicle of Dharma, and gave the others to the gods.
From the cavity of Kṛṣṇa’s right ear,
a row of lions of beautiful form and great strength and prowess emerged.
Kṛṣṇa gave one of those mighty ones to Vibhāvarī.
Considering whatever was required for enjoyment at that time, the yogi Kṛṣṇa fashioned five divine chariots that were all-pervading,
studded with various jewels, capable of moving as fast as thought, and exceedingly great.
It is one hundred thousand yojanas in length and rises a hundred yojanas upward;
it possesses wheels of a hundred thousand [yojanas], is filled with the wind, and contains sporting-pavilions of a hundred thousand [yojanas].
It is adorned with pleasure gardens and sporting parks, featuring couches and other articles for enjoyment and adornment. (52–53)
In every house there was the illumination of hundreds of thousands of jewel-lamps;
it was augmented by divine archways, water-pots, banners, and various paintings,
as well as by jeweled mirrors, yak-tail fans, parasols, and pearl-encrusted windows.
It was beautifully adorned with necklaces of sapphire, pearl, ruby, and diamond;
it was graced by blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses.
Among them, one was offered to the one whose nature is the resident of Vaikuṇṭha.
Another was offered to the one who dwells in the unmanifest and possesses a divine form; the third, however, was for the one who possesses a divine form in the nature of Mahāviṣṇu;
the fourth was for Rādhikā, and the fifth was protected for himself.
The Guhyakas appeared from the secret parts of Kṛṣṇa’s body:
Kubera, the lord of the Guhyakas, and Sundarī, the Guhyakī.
Then, the Pārṣadas emerged from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa.
Clad in yellow garments, wearing forest garlands, dark-complexioned, and four-armed;
adorned with conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses, and bearing crowns and jeweled earrings— many such four-armed beings he gave to Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha.
The attendants were made two-armed, dark-complexioned, and resembling Kṛṣṇa;
they were made Vaiṣṇavas, servants of servants, and devoted solely to Kṛṣṇa.
Protected in their own service, they meditated upon his lotus feet.
From the left eye of Kṛṣṇa there appeared a bearer of the trident,
white in color and characterized by tamas; he had three eyes, the crescent moon upon his forehead,
wore a tiger skin, carried a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in his hand, and possessed matted hair.
He became the lord Īśāna, the highly fortunate sovereign of the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas).
Likewise, other Gaṇas came into being—bearers of the trident and the Paṭṭiśa weapon, with the moon as their crest-jewel, three-eyed, and of massive form. || 64–65 ||
From every location of Kṛṣṇa’s form, thirty million goddesses appeared;
they all remained stationed in their respective places:
Rati, Mūrti, Sāvitrī, Manoramā, and Sarasvatī.
From the lotus of his heart, Mahālakṣmī, Satī, and Lakṣmī came forth.
He respectfully gave Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī to Nārāyaṇa, Sāvitrī to Brahmā, and his own form to Dharma. (67–68)
He gave Rati, rich in beauty, to Kāma; the delightful [Rambhā] to Kubera;
Lakṣmī to Viṣṇu; and he offered Satī to Śiva.
Then the yogi Śiva, having bowed, spoke to the infallible Kṛṣṇa.
Now I do not accept material nature as an ordinary person does—nature which is opposed to yoga, knowledge, celibacy, servitude, and devotion;
which binds one who desires liberation; and which is full of desire and increases worldly longing. (1.170.70–71)
[One should abandon] hunger, which destroys austerity, devours the satisfaction of the mind,
acts as a firm shackle within the terrible prison of worldly existence,
perpetually generates delusion, and cuts away right understanding.

[One should abandon] this creeper that clings to the tree of the body, which always has enjoyments and wealth as its essence, which increases the desire for sense objects, which consists of excrement and urine,
which casts one further into the pursuit of pleasure, and which is entirely absorbed in self-interest. (73–74)

"O Lord, I do not desire a wife who destroys my independence, who is composed of grief, delusion, and worldly existence, who is firmly bound by the limbs of concentration and meditation, and who is an obstacle to the meditation on Brahman. Grant me my desired boon."
Love for devotion to you and for the state of servitude increases incessantly [in me].
[This occurs] in the chanting of your name, in service at your feet, in the act of worship,
in hearing, in proclaiming, in praising, in remembering, and in cultivating the feeling of friendship.
Whether awake or dreaming, I wander only within you;
no satisfaction arises for me even in meditation, yoga, or asceticism.
[I find fulfillment] only in your invocation, offering of a seat, the ritual sipping of water, bathing, and service.
In the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, garments, lamps, sandalwood paste,
food offerings, water, betel nut, the waving of lights, hymns of praise,
prostrations, circumambulations, ornaments, and the presentation of excellent fruits; (79–80)
O Ocean of Compassion, grant me such satisfaction that no longing remains for the offering of myself, nor for the enjoyment of Your eternal grace—
whether it be *sārṣṭi*, *sālokya*, *sārūpya*, *sāmīpya*, *sāyujya*, or *līnatā*.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of a fraction of the bliss of devotion to you.
(82) Aṇimā, laghimā, prāpti, prākāmya, mahimā, as well as īśitva, vaśitva, and sarvakāmāvasāyitā. (83)
Omniscience, far-sightedness, as well as hearing from afar;
entering the bodies of others, perfection of speech, and the power of the wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpavallī);
the great power over birth and destruction, and likewise immortality—these [are attained]. (84)
The sixteen supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are not worth even a sixteenth part of devotion.
Yoga, austerities, gifts, vows, and fasting;
fame, renown, truthful speech, righteousness, pilgrimage sites, and the worship of the gods—[all these do not equal devotion]. (85–86)
Beholding the image of the Deity, traversing the entire circle of the earth, the enjoyment of all the pleasures of heaven, bathing in all the oceans,
performing all the ritual purificatory baths (avabhṛtha), and attaining the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. (87)
Furthermore, the sovereignty of Vairāja and whatever other prosperities there may be,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of a fraction of a portion of Your devotion.
Therefore, O Lord, nothing other than devotion should be sought by me.
"Neither Satī nor Śaṭhī is required by me, for both are my innate natures.
The kind of happiness found in detachment is not the same as that found in passion.
Having heard these words of Śaṅkara, the Blessed One spoke with a smile.
O Śambhu, if you do not now accept the virtuous Prakṛti,
let that auspicious one, consisting of yogic sleep, dwell within my eyes;
when you have need of her, then I shall give her to you.
"For that long, she shall provide service to my eyes," having said this, the Blessed One took Śivā into his eyes;
and he protected his Vaiṣṇava son for the sake of service to Śambhu.

Then Kṛṣṇa said to Śambhu: "Perform service to me in every way, as long as your necessary duty regarding creation does not arise. He who is worshipped by ascetics, perfected ones, yogis, knowers, gods, and Vaiṣṇavas— ॥94-95॥
"Obtain immortality here and become a conqueror of death;
by my boon, attain the perfection of omniscience in the Vedas, Shastras, and all else.
Indeed, behold here itself, as if in play, the destruction of countless Brahmas."

By knowledge, by splendor, by power, by age, by fame, by fortune, by valor, by austerity, and by majesty, become my equal, O Śiva. You are dearer to me than my own life-breaths, the best of devotees. (97–98)
"You ought to make my meaningful words come true at this time.
I shall honor your word, my son; stay in my house.
You will thus fulfill both my word and your own."
Having taken up the state of a householder at the proper time, you shall practice the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
You are not merely an ascetic; you are a great lord equal to me.
Therefore, be a householder at the proper time, and later become an ascetic according to your desire.
Now listen to what you have said regarding the suffering in union with a wife:
She makes her beloved happy through service known as the offering of herself.
(103) For women of noble family, the husband alone is the kinsman, the supporter, the master, the supreme deity, the Supreme Brahman, and their very own self. (104)
Whether fallen or unfallen, whether wretched or powerful,
firm or even weak— the husband is indeed the everything for women of noble family.
But she who is born of an ignoble lineage and is tainted by the bad character of her parents [is otherwise].
Surely she would become the object of another's enjoyment, for there is always nothing more censurable than a husband. Kṛṣṇa is my husband, Viṣṇu is my husband, and Śambhu is always my husband;
for noble women, all the gods are seen within the god who is their husband.
Such indeed is your auspicious, great, and virtuous consort;
O Śiva, she shall become the auspicious Śivā, the Prakṛti of both Śiva and Viṣṇu.
O Lord of Gods, dwell in Goloka as long as your creative activity does not extend toward the creation of the world.
"Always immersed in my samādhi or intent upon my service"—
having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa ensured his protection in his own service;
for one day in Goloka is equal to a thousand cycles of the Vairāja Brahmās.
What count can there be of those minor Brahmāṇḍa-creators who perish therein?
When Brahmā and Viṣṇu shall emerge from the body of Vairāja,
then Sadāśiva will indeed appear within the flow of that radiance.
The fiery linga shall become Śiva’s manifest form and attain renown in the world.
That virtuous woman shall remain by Śiva’s side as Śivā;
thereafter, in the course of time, she will become Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa.
Then the Blessed One spoke to Śivā, the resident of his eye:
"Now remain, my child, within my eyes in Goloka.
In due time, you shall worship Śambhu, the son of Virāṭ and the abode of auspiciousness."
Then, having manifested within the splendors of all the gods and subsequently withdrawn them,
you shall become Vindhyavāsinī after destroying all the Daityas.
You shall become the daughter of Dakṣa, Suśīlā, the wife of Śambhu.
Then, having abandoned her body due to the censure of her husband at the sacrifice,
she will become Pārvatī in Menā, the wife of the mountain king;
and you shall become Caṇḍikā, performing many deeds and being fierce.
"You shall become one who possesses many names and many forms, and you shall be characterized by *tamas*.
By my boon, among all the deities of the five-fold shrines (*pañcāyatana*), Śivā and her son Śiva shall indeed be the foremost among all the worlds. (1.18–1.19)
In villages and indeed in cities, you shall be worshipped as a village deity; there, you will bear various names and other such designations. And there, great attendants shall serve you.
Those who, desiring the attainment of the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
shall worship you there at that holy pilgrimage site on earth,
their fame, renown, and sovereignty will increase greatly. (1.21–22)
With these blessings, Mādhava gratified Śiva and Śivā;
he protected Śiva through his service and protected Śivā within his eyes.
Because she resided in his eyes, Śivā became sleep, which is always a source of happiness.
Sleep and the dark night are one and the same; they are not different.
She was born from the heart of Kṛṣṇa and resided within the two eyes of Śiva. By the word of Rādhikā, Sleep departed from the eyes of Vairāja.
And there, together with Śambhu, Śivā is eternally manifested;
she alone resides within the senses of Nārāyaṇa in the Ocean of Milk.
She alone is established within the multitude of senses of all the foremost gods.

That very Śakti, who is Śivā, Yoganidrā, Rātri, Vibhāvarī, Satī, Kātyāyanī, Kauśikī, Caṇḍikā, Kālī, and Pārvatī, [arises] from the senses and other faculties of the glorious Nārāyaṇa as he lies upon the serpent Śeṣa. (127–128)
It has been revealed according to the sequential method, as required, and according to its function.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the form of Satī, which is of the nature of the Real (Sat). 1.29

Thus, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga and the life-story of Satī: the curse upon Kṛṣṇa’s eyes for falling asleep while Rādhā was sporting in Goloka; the manifestation from the limbs of Śrī Kṛṣṇa of the forms of Rādhā, the cowherds, the cowherd girls, the herds of cows, the swans, the white horse, the five lions, the chariot, Śiva, Śivā, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Sāvitrī, and others; Satī’s offering of herself to Śiva and Śiva’s resulting detachment; and the birth of the one residing in Kṛṣṇa’s eye as the daughter of Vairāja, and subsequently as Kātyāyanī born from the senses of the Lord of Devas.

Chapter 172 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, from the Vairāja Puruṣa, the Unborn (Brahmā) arose from the lotus at his navel, and Viṣṇu was born from his heart; thus, indeed, were Viṣṇu and Padmajā (Brahmā).
They disputed over preeminence, each saying, "I am the great sacrifice" and "I am the Great One."
Then, between those two, a great radiance of light appeared.
There, the third deity, Śambhu himself, manifested;
he had been sent from Goloka for the protection of this cosmic egg.
Śaṅkara himself was joyfully sent here by Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
he arose by the will of Hari as a Vaiṣṇava and the best of devotees. At that very moment, a ray from the form of Hari [emerged] from the eyes of Vairāja.
Having arrived, it became exceedingly firm through his power.
From his forehead emerged Maheśvara, rich in rays;
that ray was indeed a divine arrow, the very emblem of Brahmā.
There, Maheśa was born as the son of Vairāja, and Śivā was born as his daughter, Asā. By Kṛṣṇa’s command, she entered his body on the left side, yet at that time Śiva did not perceive her.
And Śiva alone knew his own self as the God there, apart from Śivā.
However, Śivā, who was the invisible power (śakti) in the form of Śambhu’s left [eye],
she who had resided in Kṛṣṇa’s eye, became present in the two eyes of Śiva.

Impelled by Brahmā, that night became the daughter of Dakṣa; by his command, Dakṣa gave her the name Satī. Then her mother, having performed the appropriate purificatory rites for her daughter, [prepared her].
By the ritual procedure for suckling infants, he gave her breast milk and other nourishment.
Then, protected by Vīriṇī and Asiknī, she grew up under Dakṣa’s care;
indeed, all excellent virtues entered into her even during her childhood.
Even while engaged in play among her friends, she would, by her very nature,
occasionally draw images of Lord Śambhu;
and amidst songs appropriate for childhood, she repeatedly sang of Rudra, Hara.
Thus, the devoted Hare repeatedly remembered the Destroyer of Remembrance (Śiva).
Toward her, her parents’ great compassion increased constantly; though she was but a child, she was mature in virtue and pleased those who had given her birth.
Once, Nārada and Brahmā went to the palace of Dakṣa. There they saw the auspicious Satī seated at the side of Dakṣa.
Both were saluted by her father, and she too saluted them both.
At the conclusion of their salutations, seeing Satī seated upon an auspicious throne provided by Dakṣa, they honored her according to the rites of hospitality and spoke with joy.
Brahmā said to the sage: "Behold, O Nārada, the Goddess Maheśvarī."
"Whose wife would you be most suitable? Look at my lines and tell me.
Thereupon Nārada, having bowed to the Queen of the Gods, said to Sukanyā:
"Come, let me examine the lines on your hand to see who you are destined to be."
Then, smiling, as the hand-palms were displayed by the maiden,
there appeared a bow, a fish, a banner, a svastika, a trident,
a lamp, a lotus, two arrows, a goad, a conch, and a discus.
An axe, an arrow, and a spear—these six are in the left hands and six in the right hands;
these were seen by Nārada through a line [of marks].
On the forehead is a third eye, and a digit of the moon is curved upon the face.
In the heart, there is an auspicious form of Śiva made of golden lines.
Above the navel is the mark of a shield, and below it is a sword; likewise, there is a bow joined with an arrow, and at the feet, a lion and a bull. 23–24.
The pinnacle, the creeper, the elephant-leaf, and likewise the lion-throne—
these are seen with lines above as serpent-hoods by means of the line. This was indeed told by Nārada to Brahmā and also to Dakṣa.
She is indeed neither the daughter of Manu, nor divine, nor any other;
she is the Mother of the World, the Guru of gurus, the Supreme Vaiṣṇavī,
the consort of Kṛṣṇa, the left-hand [beloved] of Nārāyaṇa, and the Supreme Sovereign.
Whether she be the consort of Brahmā, the supreme goddess who is the consort of Viṣṇu,
or the consort of Śiva— there can be no other Mother of the World.
I believe that Śarva resides within her heart, and the two moons of his eyes are upon her forehead.
There is a trident mark on his hand and a bull on his foot;
therefore, he is certainly the jewel of Śiva and not anyone else’s.
Hearing this, she quickly became bashful, cast her face downward, and smiled. || 1.171.30 ||
Then he went inside the house and informed his mother of that; and at that time, Asiknī, having come out from the house,
paid homage to them both and honored them with water, food, fruits, and other offerings.
Having saluted her elders with reverence, Satī then emerged from the house once more;
taking the wonderful painting of Bharga she had herself drawn, she came outside and, smiling, showed it to the great seer, who responded with the word "Om."
She bowed to Nārada and she prostrated before Brahmā;
then Brahmā, placing his joined palms to his head, said:
"O virtuous lady, he who desires you and whom you likewise desire—"
Obtain him as your husband—the omniscient God, the Lord of the universe.
O auspicious lady, may he who has never taken another wife, nor does he take one now, nor will he ever take one, become your husband; for he is peerless and without equal.

Having spoken thus and remained for a very long time in the house of Dakṣa, they were both dismissed by him and returned to their own abode, O daughter of the ocean. Then Dakṣa became delighted, considering himself to be blessed.
And Satī, growing up, attained a certain stage of youth. Dakṣa then reflected upon Śiva as a bridegroom worthy of Satī:
"The childhood of my daughter has passed away, and likewise her maidenhood has gone."
"I shall by all means give Satī— who has reached the bloom of youth within, who is a maiden worthy of marriage,
and who is enriched with a golden form through her austerities— to Bharga. Within her heart, Satī likewise desired to attain Bharga herself.
Having understood her father’s decision, that virtuous woman said to her mother:
"O Mother, for the sake of Śaṅkara, show me the penances, vows, and so forth;
by your command, I shall indeed perform the vow to please Śiva."
Having received her mother’s permission, that virtuous woman of firm resolve, desiring to attain Śiva,
worshipped him in her home with various vows.
On the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, she honored Śaṅkara.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika, Satī worshipped Śaṅkara with offerings of rice mixed with jaggery and salt, as well as cakes and milk-rice,
along with the sixteen primary services and other rites. || 44–45 ||
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, Satī worshipped Śaṅkara with rice mixed with sesame and barley, along with the sixteen primary offerings.
Then, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, she performed a vigil at night.
In the morning, that virtuous woman worshipped Śaṅkara with kṛśara rice.
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Māgha, having kept a vigil through the night,
she performed the worship of Śaṅkara on the riverbank while still wearing her wet clothes.
On the night of Śivarātri in the month of Phālguna, she performed the vow of keeping vigil at night;
with actors and sixteen kinds of offerings, she worshipped Him day and night.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, she worshipped Śiva with *palāśa* and *damana* leaves.

She worshipped [him] day and night with the sixteen and other ritual offerings. On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, Satī worshipped Śaṅkara with meals of sesame and barley, and with the sixteen new offerings.
On the full moon night of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the virtuous Satī, fasting and observing her vow, worshipped Śaṅkara with garments and bṛhatī flowers.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, she worshipped him with dark-colored cloth.
During her vow, the virtuous Satī worshipped Śambhu with *bṛhatī* flowers.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
she also worshipped Śiva with sacred threads, garments, and purifying offerings.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the virtuous woman, having worshipped with many flowers and fruits,
took only water as her food on the fourteenth day;
the virtuous woman [offered] various kinds of leaves, flowers, and fruits produced in that season.
In the month of Āśvina, she observed the Śiva-vow with strictly regulated diet (56).
And in all months, being solely devoted to the worship of Śiva, she became firm in her vow; she remembered no other god at all except him (57).
Having thus completed the entire Nandā-vrata, the virtuous female ascetic meditated upon Śiva with the same devotion as a yoginī established in her spiritual states;
though her limbs were emaciated by penance, she was a radiant embodiment of splendor and possessed of beautiful form.
Born as the gentle one consisting of Śiva, she attained the state of being worthy of worship upon the lap of Śiva.
On her twelfth birthday, during the great festival of Janmajayantī, Dakṣa summoned the gods, the Manus, and other great sages. (1.171.59–60)
Then, O beloved, all the gods and sages without exception— I, Brahmā, the guardians of the quarters, the protectors of the worlds, and the deities—
went to Dakṣa’s house to bestow their blessings.
All the gods, having been honored in that great assembly, bestowed their blessings upon Satī;
and Satī bowed down to them.
Previously she had been seen nourished by her asceticism, yet now not even half of that remained.

Having seen her performing such intense penance and realizing it was solely for the sake of Śiva, all the gods and others became delighted and repeatedly offered salutations to the Goddess. They said: "O Satī! Do not perform this penance, which is so exceedingly painful."
"Your husband will certainly be Śarva, the Great God (Mahādeva).
Having thus bestowed these blessings and accepted her offering,
they then praised her asceticism as she had attained the state of perfection.
Having received the words of Dakṣa and the desire of Satī, the sages and gods,
having performed worship and bowed to Satī, departed for Mount Kailāsa.
Brahmā, urged by Sāvitrī, as well as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, likewise [departed].
Viṣṇu accompanied by Ramā, the gods together with their goddesses,
the seven sages with their wives, and likewise the Manus,
went to the peak of Kailāsa where the god Maheśvara resides.
Having gone there, they bowed to Śambhu, and having beheld the peaceful yogi, they joyfully praised him with various hymns with their palms joined in reverence:
"Salutations to the one whose nature is the imperishable syllable; salutations to the soul of Kṛṣṇa’s eyes."

Salutations to you who are named Sadāśiva; salutations to you, the object of worship as radiant energy. Salutations to you in the form of the son of Vairāja; salutations to you, the embodiment of celibacy. Salutations to you whose nature is Brahman; salutations to you who are eternally peaceful.
Salutations again and again to the one devoid of qualities, yet rich in virtues, the devotee of Viṣṇu;
salutations to you, the unmanifest, whose body is night, and who is changeless.
Salutations to the Great Lord, the Supreme Lord, the sovereign of Śiva.
Salutations to you who occasionally bring about peace and occasional withdrawal;
salutations to you, Śeṣa, whose very nature is Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Salutations to you who are clothed in dispassion, yet possess true passion.
Salutations to that Śiva, whose station and true nature are not known even by the gods, the ṛṣis, the siddhas, the virtuous women, and the virtuous men.
Yogins always strive, desiring to behold His station.
Salutation to that Supreme Lord; salutations again and again to You who abide in Yoga.
Salutation to You who are endowed with infinite perfections and are beyond the reach of words.
Salutation to You who are self-luminous; salutation to You who abide in Nirvāṇa.
Salutations to You, the Knower, who are free from action and the perceiver of the Self;
salutations to You, who are swiftly pleased by austerity and the giver of all.
Salutations to You, the three-eyed one, accompanied by the moon, and the sovereign overseer of all.
Salutations to You, who grant the desired objects sought by those who have come for refuge;
salutations to You, the bestower of sovereign powers and the giver of liberation.
Salutations to You, the fulfiller of the desires of Your devotees and the ocean of the Vedas.
Salutations to You, the self-luminous, the eternal, and the inner witness.
Whether with desires or free from desires, Your devotees have come to You for refuge;
salutations to You, by whom they do not turn back until they have attained perfection.
A certain maiden is indeed performing intense penance for your sake.
Why are you so merciless? Be gracious; salutations to you!
O Śaṅkara, consider this for the sake of the continuous flow of the world’s affairs.
We bow to you and praise you, who are accessible through internal yoga.
You are neither a god, nor an asura, nor a mortal; you are not an animal, nor a bird, nor a beast.
You are neither female, nor neuter, nor male; whatever you are, that you are—salutations to you!
We bow down to the creator of the universe and the sustainer of the universe.

To Him whom the followers of Sāṃkhya perceive through knowledge and the yogis perceive in meditative absorption (samādhi), and whom the devotees perceive through grace—Him who consists of the three Vedas, we offer our salutations. (86–87)
Salutations to the one who uplifts his devotees; salutations to you of hidden splendor.
Salutations to the manifest deity and to the direct experience [of the Absolute]. Salutations to the play of the Night of Time (Kālarātri) and to the one entreated by the daughter of Dakṣa.
"Salutations to you who have entered into manifestation, and salutations to you who have withdrawn from it.
O Lord, fulfiller of the desires of your devotees, please fulfill the desire of the Creator.
Having praised him thus and remaining silent, Śambhu heard this and indeed laughed.
Having seen the god, the sages, and the others together with their wives, he offered them a welcome and hospitality as was appropriate, and then asked the reason for their visit:
"O Viṣṇu! O Brahmā! O gods! O preeminent sages and ṛṣis!"
"Tell me truly the reason for your own arrival.
All of you have come with your wives; what business do you have with me?
Thus was Brahmā questioned, being urged by Viṣṇu at that time. (92–93)
He spoke to Śambhu with sweet words: "O Lord, nothing is unknown to you.
Nevertheless, O Master, because it is the way of the world, I must speak; listen.
In particular, we—gods, humans, and others—are seekers of common goals."
Asuras are created in many ways and are born again and again.
Among them, some are to be slain by me, and some are to be slain by Hari;
others, being exceedingly cruel, are to be slain by you, O Goddess, while yet others are to be slain by you.
Moreover, others indeed become fit to be slain by a son of your prowess;
for without destroying those wicked ones,
the world cannot attain its fearless stability while you remain established on the path of yoga, free from passion and hatred.
If they were of the nature of mere compassion, they would never perish.
(98) If the nourishment of those performing austerities by means of boons were certain, then how could the Sāttvika creation remain stable? (99)
Therefore, it is indeed fitting that among us— who are elevated and joined with the unjoined—
the tasks of creation, maintenance, and dissolution shall be performed by us alone.
For we are of one single nature, yet distinct due to the diversity of our functions.
If the difference in function is not established, then the difference in form is irrelevant.
(101) "I and Viṣṇu, together with our wives, were well-born due to the necessity of our respective functions;
likewise, you too should indeed become possessed of a wife for the welfare of the world. (102)
Accept this one beautiful woman as your wife;
having married her, accomplish the most important task for the world.
Just as Padmālayā belongs to Viṣṇu, and Sāvitrī belongs to me.
"Likewise, O Śambhu, accept this beloved companion as your wife.
Śambhu, smiling, spoke to Brahmā and Viṣṇu regarding the ultimate truth:
"O Brahmā, O Hari, you two have always been most dear to me."
From seeing you both today, great joy arises within me. However,
that worldly arrangement which has been decided by you for my sake,
though it may be appropriate, does not please my heart.
For one who is ascetic, dispassionate, and has transcended the path of yoga;

for the man of knowledge, free from desire, who delights in his own self in every way; and for the seer of the Self who has completely withdrawn from worldly life—what need has he for a woman? (107–108)

For me, whose self is fixed in yoga, there is indeed constant bliss; I do not become a remnant of the pleasure obtained through association with another. Marriage is a terrible bondage for both parties to one another.
"O Yogin, why indeed would you forcibly take her from one who is free of desire?
Therefore, I tell you truly: it is not my pleasure that she become your wife.
Having heard this, Viṣṇu, as shown by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, then spoke to Śambhu.
"Whatever task was promised in Goloka shall come to pass during creation;
whenever you have need, I will give you Vibhāvarī (Night).
At the proper time, having taken hold of Prakṛti, you will perform the act of love."
At the proper time one should be a householder, and at the proper time, one should become an ascetic according to one's desire.
A widower is never prescribed for any auspicious rite here;
even the residence of a widower among those with wives would bring fear.
Having become impartial, one should be honored among equals alone, not among those who are unequal.
Among equals, the partial shall perish; among the partial, the impartial shall perish. (1.15) There is equality among householders who are the executors of the laws of creation.
Therefore, you must now always be accompanied by a wife;
for a brother who is without a wife is not a ground for trust regarding women,
nor is he fit for rites such as sacrifices or ancestral offerings without his wife.
One who is industrious but devoid of women is always inauspicious;
likewise, one who is not industrious but joined with women would also be inauspicious.
O Śambhu, you are the presiding authority over the work of creation; therefore, do not dwell as one who is inauspicious.
"Having reflected, remain among us always being well-disposed.
O Śaṅkara, become one who has a wife, remembering the words of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu and then having recalled the speech uttered by Kṛṣṇa...
Having reflected upon the dharma that consists in attaining Śiva, who is eternally perfected, Śaṅkara said:
"O Viṣṇu, I shall always perform what you have spoken for our benefit.
Thus considering your most weighty words as well as the command of Śrī Hari, [he acted].
"I shall indeed perform the marriage, for I am always under the sway of Kṛṣṇa.
However, listen to the kind of bride I shall take—
one who will be firm enough to receive and sustain my splendor."
"May she become like me—a yogi and one possessed of knowledge—equal to me in battle, in yoga, in realized wisdom, in virtue, in sovereignty, and in devotion.
If it is not so, then we shall remain together in happiness forever, without marriage. (124)
"Therefore, point out a wife for me if she conducts herself like me.
Even in that case, let there be one condition: she must behave toward me exactly as I do;
if there is no trust in my word, she shall be abandoned by me. || 125-126 ||
Having heard these words of Śambhu, Viṣṇu and Brahmā laughed and said to him:
"We have searched thoroughly for her who is so dear to you;
she is Śivā, who resides in the heart of Kṛṣṇa in Goloka and is situated within his eyes. (127)
Abiding in the eyes of Vairāja, she is the radiant power within the senses of the Lord of Gods (Indra).
She who resides within the circle of the senses of Śrī Hari as he reclines upon Śeṣa is Night, O Śambhu; she is the dark night, and she is the auspicious Śivā who dwells on your left side.
Inseparably connected and existing as his daughter of Dakṣa,
she would become a wife like you, endowed with even greater luster and strength.
O Lord of Gods, she performs penance for your sake, firm in her vows.
That maiden, desiring to obtain you as her husband, is currently in the house of Dakṣa. O Maheśvara, go to grant her a boon; have mercy on her.
Bestow upon her a boon that grants all desires, and marry her with great affection.
"Fulfill the desire of the gods who have come here.
May there be supreme auspiciousness, and let us behold that festival.
Having heard this, Śaṅkara said, "Om; it is accepted by me."
"I go to bestow the fruit of my asceticism; O gods, you may depart.
You shall see me again at the time of the marriage festival.
Thus commanded and honored, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the gods, and the others departed. (134–135)
Having bestowed the words of blessing, "May your desire be fulfilled," they, together with their wives, went to their respective abodes, exceedingly joyful.

(1.36) Thus, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, [is described] the birth of Śambhu from the forehead of Vairāja; the arrival of Brahmā and Nārada after Śivā’s manifestation in the house of Dakṣa; and [the recognition of] Śiva’s wife by means of the lines and signs described by Nārada.

Chapter One Hundred and Seventy-One: Description of Satī’s performance of the annual penance and vow due to her lack of certainty; the arrival of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods with their wives at the festival of the twelfth anniversary of Satī’s birth; the departure of Brahmā and the others for Kailāsa upon witnessing Satī’s austerity; and the instruction given to Śaṅkara regarding the granting of a boon for Satī’s marriage.
Chapter 171. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 172.
[The Author: Chapter 173.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen to me, my dear Lakṣmī; for your sake, Śambhu is eager.
Having awakened his meditative absorption, he reflected on going to the house of Dakṣa.
(1) Then, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, Satī, having observed a fast, worshipped Śaṅkara with sixteen offerings. (2)
Thus, when the Nandā-vrata was completed on the ninth day,
the god Śiva, beautiful in all his limbs, became manifest before her eyes.
He was fair-complexioned, five-faced, three-eyed, and bore the moon upon his crest.
With a serene soul, blue-throated, four-armed, and accompanied by Vāsuki;
adorned with a trident, rudrākṣa beads, a choice lotus, and sacred ash; his matted hair graced by the Gaṅgā; and his entire body resembling the color of gold. (4–5)
His body possessed great loveliness, beauty, and delicacy;
he was more enchanting than ten million Cupids, and his face was equal to ten million moons.
Overcome by blossoming youth, he was in every way captivating to women.
Having seen Śaṅkara directly before her eyes and considering him her own wealth,
Satī was exceedingly thrilled in her heart; with her face bowed down in great modesty,
she paid homage at the feet of Śambhu and drank in his face with her eyes.
Having mentally surrendered all her possessions, she considered herself most fortunate.
Then Hara, although desiring a wife who was dear to his heart,
[remained] in order to perceive Satī’s eternal love arising from the depths of her own being.

Desiring to hear pleasant words, he spoke to his virtuous wife who was firm in her vows; beholding for a moment his own devoted wife— beautiful, fortunate, golden-hued, and having reached the bloom of youth— he was utterly infatuated.
"O girl of virtuous vows, daughter of Dakṣa! I am pleased with this Nandā-vrata; I shall grant you a boon—choose whatever you desire.
Then Satī became filled with bashfulness and overwhelmed with love.
Holding his sacred thread, he was unable to speak what was in his heart.
Knowing the state of his heart, Śaṅkara, who is eternally compassionate, became exceedingly pleased and said:
"Choose a boon! Choose a boon! Choose a boon again and again! (13–14)
Desiring friendship here, he spoke those seven steps to her.
The virtuous woman said: "Having observed your vow, having observed your austerity, and having beheld your heart;
having seen your state, and having seen the wonderful picture of Bharga painted by me. (15)
Having learned of the taking up of the sacred thread and of your arrival from afar, [I have come]. Bestow that friendship which is formed by walking seven steps together, whatever boon you desire.
Then, having clearly grasped the inner meaning of those words, Hara—
To complete the sentence: "Give me half of your body as a wife.
"O beloved, why do you not quickly let me know the meaning of the remainder of the sentence?
[He replied: "I have granted the boon that she shall be my wife."
Having received the sweet words of Śambhu, Satī became immersed in love;
she stood silent and joyful, having obtained the boon desired by her heart, her mind filled with longing and her face graced with a beautiful smile.
They performed natural gestures that increase the intensity of love;
and by resorting to those gestures, emotions, and playful charms within their hearts,
the essence of erotic love quickly entered the hearts of the two of them at that time.
An indescribable splendor appeared in those two who were emulating the divine play of the world. Satī shone having attained Hara, just as the night shines having attained the moon;
she embraced him upon his chest, remaining there for a long time and experiencing his touch.
Satī said: With hands joined in devotion and face bowed low out of love, she said, "O God of gods, O Lord of my husband, O Sovereign!
Having brought me before my father and having accepted me according to the rite of marriage, go with me, O All-pervading One."
Having heard those words with such insistence, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of all,
replied, "So be it," and gazing at her with love,
he reflected for a moment, thinking, "She shall become [my wife] gradually."
Then Satī, having bowed to Hara and received his command,
went in haste to announce Śaṅkara’s arrival to her mother. Asiknī, learning from her daughter what had been said, quickly went outside.
Just as she was proceeding to behold the form of her future son-in-law,
Śivā beheld Śambhu for a moment, his body radiant like crystal;
she rejoiced exceedingly, [thinking], "Śambhu has become invisible to you."
Seeing that his son-in-law was worthy of his daughter and destined for the highest excellence,
he meditated upon him alone within his heart and considered him his supreme fortune.
Hara, too, having gone to his own Kailāsa and entered his hermitage, [remained there].
He meditated upon Brahmā in accordance with worldly custom. (31) Brahmā quickly arrived there together with Sarasvatī.
Upon seeing the Creator, Śambhu, bound by love, spoke to him. (32)
O Satī, I have been propitiated by Dakṣa’s daughter with supreme devotion;
a boon consisting of the fruit of the Nandā-vrata was granted to her by me.
O Lord, she requested a husband as her deity according to the rites of marriage.
"Having made my father your object of pursuit, take me with you.
"So be it," I said slowly upon making that firm resolve. And while my mother remained before me, I have come here to you.
Therefore, go to the abode of Dakṣa on my behalf;
act in such a way that Dakṣa will give his own daughter to me.
Brahmā said: O Śambhu, Hara, [this is the request] of the gods, of me, and of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
That persistence of yours is entirely for the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods.
Your marriage shall take place with haste; we shall act quickly accordingly.
Dakṣa himself will bestow his own daughter upon you. (37–38)
"I shall relate that matter to you quickly; please grant me peace.
Such is the news concerning Śambhu that has been circulating on Kailāsa with Brahmā.
In the meantime, Asiknī spoke to Dakṣa, who was firm in his vow as a satī.
Having performed penance and obtained the boon desired by her mind, Satī, upon gaining the sight of Śaṅkara, became truly fulfilled. Hearing this, Dakṣa said to Satī: "Daughter, may you be happy."
When Dakṣa desired to know everything, he related her devotion to truth (*satīvrata*),
the obtaining of boons from Maheśvara, and her marriage.
Having heard the entire account from the mouth of Satī, both mother and father—

She attained supreme bliss and celebrated a great festival. (43) At the conclusion of the Nandāvrata, Satī obtained a vision of Śambhu; for that reason, upon the completion of the vow, she caused a grand festival to be held. (44)
She gave gifts of wealth, jewels, and garments to the brahmins;
she also gave riches to others who were blind and destitute, as well as to Vīriṇī.
And Satī gave food to her female companions and to the young girls.
And she joyfully gave her wealth, garments, ointments, and other articles.
Embracing her daughter Siddhabhāvanā, Vīriṇī,
filled with delight, smelled the crown of her head and praised her again and again.
Then Dakṣa thought: "Even though Śaṅkara himself has arrived, how is it that he has turned back and departed without taking my daughter?
Although Mahādeva came, he went away even while being well-disposed."
Furthermore, how will he come here for the sake of his daughter?
By what means can this daughter of mine now be given to Śambhu?
Therefore, I must immediately dispatch someone to the presence of Śambhu.
If he does not accept my words, everything of mine will be in vain;
or else, let my daughter Nandā perform the vow once again,
so that she may obtain Śambhu as her husband once more.

While Dakṣa was thus occupied with his thoughts, the Unborn (Aja) then appeared before him together with Sarasvatī, out of compassion. Seeing his father, Dakṣa bowed down and prostrated himself before him.
He offered him the foremost seat and performed the rites of hospitality with great devotion;
he then asked the reason for his arrival, as well as the nature of their affection or any other purpose.
Brahmā said: "Listen, Dakṣa, to the purpose for which I have come."

"Having performed penance and propitiated Mahādeva, your daughter obtained a boon; the time for that boon has now arrived. It was for this very purpose that I was sent by Śambhu after he had made his decision."
Therefore, in this matter, determine what action would be most beneficial.
After granting the boon, Rudra meditated upon and remembered your daughter as she remained within his heart;
yet even so, he did not immediately attain peace.
"O God, that deity who has conquered desire is indeed pierced by desire;
he remains distracted, contemplating Satī, like an ordinary man.
Having abandoned his natural and meaningful speech, he wanders among the Gaṇas here and there. (58–59)
"Where is Satī? he asked, speaking in the midst of the people while praising your daughter:
"That which was previously desired by me, by you, by Kāma, by Kṛṣṇa, and likewise by the ṛṣis, has now certainly been accomplished. (1.172.60)

Śambhu was propitiated by your daughter, and Satī is now being propitiated by Śambhu. Therefore, give your own daughter, who has been prepared for the sake of Śambhu, to him without delay; thus you shall have fulfilled your purpose.
"I shall bring Śambhu to your abode with Nārada;
O son, bestow Satī upon him according to the rites of marriage.
Having heard his father's words, Dakṣa, filled with joy, replied, "So be it."
Brahmā, having accepted the honor, went to the abode of Śaṅkara.
Upon seeing the creator of the worlds with a gracious mind, Hara,
having resolved that his purpose would be accomplished, bowed down to the Grandfather.
He asked, "What indeed did Dakṣa do regarding Satī?
Brahmā said: "At that time, O Śambhu, your purpose was already accomplished;
it was the firm resolve of Dakṣa that his daughter must be given to Śambhu."
Because my word must be honored, by the power of truth and austerity,
and through the granting of this boon by you, Satī must be given to Śambhu.
Let Śaṅkara arrive at an auspicious lunar mansion and a favorable moment.
"Then I shall give my virtuous daughter Satī as alms to Śambhu.
Thus Dakṣa spoke to me; therefore, you must go to his house.
Then Rudra, following worldly custom, said to the Creator (Brahmā):
"I shall go to that house together with you and Nārada.
Therefore, remember me, Nārada, and the great sages such as Marīci; accompanied by them, I will go to Dakṣa’s abode in splendor."
Thus commanded, Parameṣṭhin called to mind Nārada and the others.
Thereupon all the supreme ṛṣis born of his mind arrived,
as did the gods, the ancestors, along with their wives and kinsmen.

Viṣṇu arrived there along with Lakṣmī and his attendants. Śrī Kṛṣṇa came from the abode of Goloka accompanied by Rādhikā, joined by hosts of gopas and gopīs, and attended by hundreds of thousands of maidservants.
From Vaikuṇṭha, Nārāyaṇa arrived accompanied by Ramā,
attended by ten million Vaiṣṇava associates, male servants, and female servants.
Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Agni, and Kubera— these [also came].
Yama, Sūrya, and Candra, as well as other household deities;
the Ṛṣis, Munis, and Brahmins; the Sādhyas and virtuous people;
and the goddesses, Apsarases, as well as other dancers and singers. (76–77)

Having performed the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony (*kautuka*), they assembled in the army of Śaṅkara. Then, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, under the constellation presided over by Bhaga and with the Sun in the ascendant, Maheśvara set forth.
Accompanied by the gods led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
along with sages and seers, Maheśvara shone as he departed from Kailāsa.
And millions of his attendants set forth, celebrating the great festival for the side of the bridegroom.
Then, as the army marched along the road, a great festival arose among the hosts of gods and others whose minds were filled with joy.
The adornment of Mahālakṣmī and Śaṅkara was performed at their respective stations.
Then his matted locks were graced by Gaṅgā in her embodied form;
a digit of the moon became an ornament upon his forehead,
and Vāsuki, for the purpose of serving as a sacred thread, rested comfortably upon his left shoulder.
A garland of rudrākṣa beads and skulls was worn around his neck, which was smeared with poison;
a trident was held in his hand, and an elephant hide was draped over his back.
A tiger skin was fastened at the edge of his waist, and his body was covered in ashes.
On his feet were hidden sandals, and a loincloth made of deer-skin.
Around his waist was a serpent, Kuhaka, serving as a girdle ornament.
Thus adorned, Śambhu stood mounted upon a bull. (85–86)
And others, by the will of Śiva, remained standing upon their respective broken vehicles.
Then Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī went forth with joy, seated upon Garuḍa;
and then Brahmā and Sāvitrī went forth with joy, seated upon a swan.
The sun, the moon, and other luminaries were stationed upon chariots; the deities headed by Indra were mounted on elephants.
At that time, the ṛṣis and munis were seated in celestial vehicles (vimānas).
The women were situated within the vimānas, traveling through the sky in excellent conveyances.
Then, standing in the midst of the chariot-guard, they sang songs;
musical instruments were played, and bards offered hymns of praise. Blessings were likewise bestowed by sages and brahmins.
Thus that army of Śambhu, resounding with the tinkling of networks of small bells,
graced by divine women and wondrous with the forms of the gods,
reached the vicinity of King Dakṣa’s capital, presided over by Śambhu.
Then Dakṣa, self-controlled and with his hair standing on end from joy,
went forward to meet Śambhu, accompanied by all his own followers;
as did all the gods, the sages, the seers, and the women.
There, honored by Dakṣa himself with water for their feet and other offerings,
the sages reached Dakṣa’s residence and took their places upon the seats;
likewise, the elder gods and ṛṣis were established according to their rank.
Dakṣa honored Śiva from within his home;
he worshipped him according to the prescribed rites after offering an unsurpassed seat.
Then [he honored] Viṣṇu, the gods, Brahmā, and all the celestial beings.
He worshipped the Gaṇas with true devotion and joy by means of various articles;
he fed them with delicious foods, gratified them with drinks, delighted them with ornaments, and sprinkled them with fragrant perfumes. (97–98)
He honored them with offerings of betel and other gifts, as well as with seats;
having performed the appropriate worship, he entered into consultation with the gods and the sages,
for Brahmā had been impelled toward this ritual procedure.
Instructed by Dakṣa regarding the marriage rites that were to be performed,
he carried them out according to the rules with a joyful heart.
Then, at an auspicious moment and under a favorable planetary conjunction, he proceeded.
Dakṣa joyfully gave his daughter Satī to Śambhu; and according to the rites of marriage, Śambhu took Satī’s hand. At the time of Satī’s wedding, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the gods, and others—
They all bowed down and gratified the two lords with hymns of praise.
There was a great festival preceded by dancing and singing;
they attained supreme bliss through food, clothing, and other such provisions.
Dakṣa also became fulfilled after giving his daughter to Śambhu;
both Śivā and Śiva were pleased, and indeed everything became auspicious. Having performed the giving away of his daughter, Dakṣa bestowed various kinds of wedding gifts (yautaka).
She offered various kinds of wealth to the twice-born for the sake of Hara, and she presented the multitude of people [to him].
(106) That true garland of choice was then placed by Satyā upon the throat of Hara;
at that time, she indeed whirled the pestle and other implements over the head of Śambhu. (107)
The husband and wife gave each other delicious and sweet food from their mouths;
they even played with a golden ring in the vessel of milk. (108) Then Viṣṇu spoke auspicious words to Hara and Satī.
O Śambhu, you are the father of the worlds; Satī is the mother, the progenitor of the universe.
You two are playful incarnations, always existing for the welfare of the virtuous. Indeed, you have been born as a divine couple for the purpose of subduing the wicked.
Adopting the duties of a householder, you two shall move about performing your shared dharma; having assumed these forms for the purpose of destruction, you shall proceed with the act of withdrawal.
And for the sake of protecting righteous people, cows, and the virtuous—
Exert yourselves in sacrifices, in the service of the Brahmins, and in the study of the Vedas.
You must protect the truth and likewise bring auspiciousness to your devotees.
Indeed, whoever, having seen or heard of this, should feel a longing for it—
"O Lord, Master of Time, it is my firm conviction that you must slay him;
for the Asuras are powerful, with hands itching for combat. Their itching must be scratched away by you, Satya, and by your son."
"And likewise, he should be remembered at the proper time if assistance is requested.
Having heard these words of Hari, Śaṅkara then smiled and,
saying "So be it," honored the Lord of Kamalā and bowed before him.
Then Dakṣa caused a festive celebration to be held according to the established conventions;
and Brahmā performed the entire ritual for the fire-offering in that pavilion, following the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras in full detail.
And he caused the *homa* sacrifice to be performed according to the rules in the fire-pit (118).
Then Śivā and Śiva, with great joy and in accordance with the prescribed rites,
[invoked] Agni as the witness, by the command of the Brahmin preceptor (119).
Having performed four circumambulations, Śiva and Śivā then stood there;
they bowed to the Gārhapatya fire and subsequently sat down.
At that time, a wonderful and great festival took place there in the palace of Dakṣa.
The spectators gathered at the pavilion listen to the music, which brings joy to all and is preceded by song and dance;
and they gaze again and again upon the beauty of the bride and the noble groom.
O Lotus-born One! Many men and women there were deluded; indeed, not even a single woman was as beautiful as Satī. Nor was there anyone there whose complexion was as white as that of Śambhu.
The union of the jewel and gold is like that of moonlight and the moon;
the union of lightning and white copper is likewise the union of Satī and Śaṅkara.
[It is the union] of the cakora-birds of women’s eyes with the sparks of men’s eyes.
Like the moon and like a flame of fire, he became the bestower of the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Indeed, the men present there in the pavilion were not bewildered upon seeing Satī;
nor were the women bewildered upon seeing Hara there in the pavilion.

The union of Satī and Śaṅkara was likewise a cause of delusion. This marriage, rooted in delusion, was for the purpose of instructing the world; at that time, the entire manifestation of the God of Love was of a passionate (rājasa) nature.
In the case of a marriage, people generally become anxious to see the face of the bride due to worldly custom;
likewise, even there, Satī herself was indeed eager to see his face.
For the most part, they were all then covered with garments out of shame.
From her very nails up to the crest of her hair,
Satī, who possessed a golden complexion, was indeed completely enveloped by her shawl and other clothes.
From her body, which was like a flash of lightning, radiance broke away from her garments and went outside;
and upon seeing it, the eyes of the spectators there indeed closed due to that excessive brilliance, even the pavilion itself. (132)
He shone, having become brilliantly radiant, as if the sky itself had descended there.
"Listen, Lakṣmī! Then another marvel occurred for Brahmā.
Having assumed a passionate (rājasa) disposition, the Creator [assumed] a form in order to behold [it]. (133–134)
He deliberated in many ways, yet he was unable to find [the way] to look;
know that this task had indeed become the duty of Śaṅkara alone.
Brahmā first gave the impulse to delude me.
"May they all be deluded in the presence of me at my wedding.
Having thought thus, that form was manifested there through yoga; and having seen it, everyone was utterly bewildered, deluded by the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā). || 136-137 ||
Then, however, Brahmā devised an auspicious means there:
by casting abundant moist fuel into that fire,
he caused the production of smoke from the moist substances through the offering of only a small amount of clarified butter.
A great smoke appeared there, pervading everything on all sides.
By that [smoke], the pavilion there then became filled with darkness.
Śambhu playfully covered his eyes, which were obscured by the smoky haze.
At that moment, Brahmā lifted his garment and gazed repeatedly at the face of Satī with love; he was likewise watched by many others. Then, Brahmā’s semen fell upon the edge of the cloth.
It was covered and crushed so that no one could perceive it.
From that crushing, however, there arose particles resembling a mass of snow;
those which became clouds were four in number, each consisting of four particles. (142–143)
Then the clouds— namely Saṃvartaka, Āvarta, Puṣkara, and Droṇa—
along with others of harsh sound, thundered and burst forth in the sky;
other droplets numbering eighty-eight thousand then appeared.
From them were born the Bālakhilyas, resembling the joints of a thumb.
Those sages were then gathered together in the worlds of Virāja;
indeed, they remain there forever, for they are ever devoted to the vow of Brahman.
Then, other particles that had become stuck to his garment likewise became sixty thousand Bālakhilyas;
they were indeed the size of a thumb-joint, like the rays of the sun.
Drinking [the water] while facing the sun, they run from behind with their feet foremost.
Day after day, they destroy the Mandeha Rākṣasas.
By virtue of the eternal boon granted by Brahmā, they live on and destroy them.
Then the Blessed Lord Śambhu, having perceived this with his divine eye, said in anger: "O Brahmā, what is this that has been done? Why has this been performed?
Thus spoke Śaṅkara as he raised his trident to slay Brahmā.
Though he was prepared for battle, forbidden, and restrained by the great seers, they all then instructed him in the unity of the three:
"Brahmā is not distinct from Bhava; nor does Bhava possess any difference from Brahmā. (151–152)

Viṣṇu is not divided from the other two, for there is indeed a unity among the three; just as there is no division in a single body despite the distinctions of head, neck, and so forth, so too the gods are the limbs of the Supreme Self and are non-different from it. (153)
"O Śambhu, your anger toward Brahman, who is your own true nature, is not appropriate.
Having heard this, Śaṅkara became tranquil and spoke again to the Creator:
"Touch your own head with your hand; carry out my command without hesitation."
As soon as Brahmā touched his own head with his hand, he immediately became a bull, the supreme vehicle;
and upon its back, Śambhu himself sat down as the rider.
"By this very form, presided over by me, perform penance;
your fame shall spread, and you will become Rudraśiras.
Therein, the bull shall be a portion of Brahmā, and Śaṅkara’s portion shall be the restrainer. (157–158)
Having become so, the two remained forever at the wedding altar.
Then, by the command of Śambhu, Brahmā assumed his original form and swiftly brought the remaining wedding rites to completion.
A rain of flowers fell upon the heads of both Śiva and Śivā,
while musical instruments were being played, they were singing,
and groups of brahmins, filled with devotion, were reciting the Vedas.
O Lotus-born One, while Rambhā and other celestial women were dancing with devotion, a great festival took place among the wives of the gods.
Śambhu said: "O Brahmā, that which was performed by you regarding the marriage..."
"Accept ten million as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), for you are my own preceptor who has secured this auspicious conjunction.
(163) Then, having accepted the fee, Brahmā requested at that time:
"Everyone must go to their own homes; it remains no longer necessary to stay here. (164)
Then, having taken leave of Dakṣa, the Lord, together with his wife Satī,
was indeed intent on departing; at that moment, Dakṣa praised Śaṅkara,
as did the gods, sages, brahmins, and the ṛṣis who serve Viṣṇu.

Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Sūrya, Candra, Indra, and the others likewise went to the Lord, accompanied by their respective families and retinues. By the command of Dakṣa, Śambhu joyfully placed Satī upon his bull. (166–167)
He caused his bull to move toward Kailāsa, his own abode. Some played musical instruments while others sang with beautiful voices;
they joyfully followed Śiva, whose fame is auspicious and pure.
Then, dismissed from the Middle Path by Śambhu with affection,
Dakṣa departed for his own abode along with his attendants. Śambhu, overwhelmed with love,
went there and [confronted] all the gods, the sages, and the supreme beings as well.
Having honored him greatly and respectfully, he joyfully dismissed him.
Addressing Śambhu, the deities headed by Kṛṣṇa, as well as Viṣṇu and all the other sages, took their food and other offerings and departed for their respective abodes with delight. (171)
Śiva too, exceedingly delighted, sported repeatedly with his new bride on Mount Kailāsa according to his pleasure. Thus,
O Lakṣmī, has the marriage festival of Śaṅkara been narrated.
Whoever hears this at the time of a wedding, during a sacrifice, or at the commencement [of a rite],
all his auspicious marriage-related ceremonies shall proceed without obstacle;
and the bride shall be endowed with happiness, good fortune, virtuous conduct, and excellent qualities.
"A virtuous woman, blessed with sons, and endowed with all prosperity in her home would be fortunate.
Then this yogi Śaṅkara entered a mountain cave;
he sent Nandin and the other attendants away and spoke to them at that time.
"O my Gaṇas, when I remember you here with minds full of respect for that remembrance, you shall then quickly come to my side.
All those Gaṇas then departed from Kailāsa and went to various places. (177)
Then Śambhu took delight with his bride, even without the pleasure of desire.
At times he would grasp a garland of flowers and offer it to Satī;
at other times, together with Satī, he gazed at his own face in a mirror.
Sometimes Hara even placed Satī’s earrings upon his own ears;
sometimes he dyed her feet with red lac;
and sometimes, seating her upon his own lap, he fashioned her hair into a beautiful arrangement.
At times, Śambhu applied a leaf-design with sandalwood paste upon his forehead.
Having gathered lotus flowers and other beautiful blossoms, Śaṅkara respectfully fashioned floral ornaments for all his limbs.
Thus, in many ways, he took delight in diverting Satī;
without her, he did not go about, he did not sit, and he did not move.
Without her, Śaṅkara found no happiness even for a moment.
He went to the slopes of the Himalayas and, by his own will, called Smara to mind.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [is described]: Satī’s vision of Śaṅkara, the granting of the boon "Become my wife," Śambhu’s departure for Kailāsa, Brahmā’s dispatching to the house of Dakṣa, and his return to Kailāsa; Śaṅkara’s journey to the house of Dakṣa with Janavāhinī, the marriage of Satī, the falling of the seed of Brahmā—who was infatuated by Satī’s beauty—upon her, and from that, the birth of the clouds and the Vālakhilyas, and [the account] of Janavāhinī.
Chapter One Hundred and Seventy-Two: The Return to Kailāsa, the Dismissal of the Host of Attendants, and the Sporting of Satī and Śaṅkara in a Cave of Kailāsa.
Chapter One Hundred and Seventy-Three: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga (Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Book 1).
[The Author: Chapter 174.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, as they were then sporting on the Himālaya mountain.
Through the recollection of desire, the god of love entered into his presence.
When Śambhu had entered there and the auspicious desire was present, he then fully understood Śambhu’s state of being in every respect. (1–2)
Spring began its own duty in the presence of Hara,
and the Malaya breeze blew, rich with mild fragrance and coolness.
Then all the trees and the creepers were in full bloom.
The *palāśa* trees shone with their tender red *kiṃśuka* blossoms;
(4) and lotuses of many colors also gleamed within the lakes.
There, in the presence of Hara, a breeze blew, rich with the fragrance of lotus flowers. (5)
There, the *nāgakeśara* flowers of the high-souled Śaṅkara became delightful, possessing a golden hue and a sweet fragrance;
and the wind was permeated with the scent of that fragrant aroma, as was the betel vine.
While Satī was in the presence of Śaṅkara, she sent forth that which causes delusion.
At that time, cuckoos sang with sweet and enchanting voices;
the mango trees were in full bloom and shone with their leaves and flower-clusters.
The waters shone with stainless clarity, and the kāśa flowers were in full bloom;
the circles of stars gleamed with the splendors of springtime.
Even the nights, though red with moonlight, became dear once more.
The grassy meadows and excellent regions became providers of sensual pleasure.
In the rivers, groves, caves, and open lands,
Śambhu took delight with Satī, and Satī shone resplendently with Śambhu.
He delighted the Lord of the Gods with various pastimes;
and Hara, moreover, adorned his beloved with flower garlands,
by arranging her hair, by laying her on his lap, and likewise by kissing her.
She gratified him with gentle words, smiles, glances, and caresses. Intoxicated by drinking the nectar flowing from the moon of his face,
she then directed her beloved toward various kinds of postures and amorous positions.
Bound by the fragrance of Satī’s mouth, by her beauty, her wit,
her love, and her passion, Śaṅkara was truly delighted.
Thus, having caused Satī to rejoice upon the peak of Himavat, Śiva—
He went to Kailāsa and found peace in his own abode. (16) When the time of heat had passed and the arrival of the clouds occurred, Satī then said to Śambhu: "Listen to my words, O beloved. (17)
This is the season of dense gathering; the clouds rain constantly. The winds blow pleasantly, yet with extreme force they cause trembling.
Everywhere the ground is saturated, rich with mud, and offers no refuge. (18)
The trees and creepers have blossomed, becoming moist and laden with water;
the roaring of clouds and the play of lightning arise,
and both the sun and the moon are no longer visible in the sky, being shrouded by clouds.
Great trees, struck by the wind, fall to the ground causing terror;
tigers, lions, and extremely cruel venomous creatures roam the desolate forest, along with cold, heat, wind, and fire. (21)
These and other obstacles, which always cause suffering, arise [for you].
Therefore, you must now build a house for the purpose of dwelling somewhere, where there is shade, comfortable beds, and the abundance of food and drink. (22–23)
Furthermore, those who observe conventional agreements (*sāmayika*) would always be able to protect [the forest] if there were no building for people to obtain rest.
Otherwise, what benefit is there for a forest-dweller in carrying wood? (24)

Even birds such as the ruddy goose and the pigeon, though lacking a fixed dwelling, construct nests in tree hollows when the time arrives; ants and mice likewise build their subterranean dwellings. (25–26)
Therefore, the protection of offspring is an integral part of the duties of the householder;
it should indeed take place at home, which is secure, firm, and provides comfort in all seasons.
As for my other sisters, their dwellings are indeed large.
Innumerable divine prosperities exist [for them], yet I have no home.
(28) In this ocean of saṃsāra, the first suffering is the emptiness of one's home;
the second is the lack of grain; the third is the absence of wealth. (29)
The fourth is childlessness, and the fifth is considered to be impurity.
The sixth is friendship with the diseased, and the seventh is [the presence of] cows and the like. The eighth is distress in the home caused by lions, bulls, and serpents.
"This eightfold suffering belongs to me; what use has a yogin for the life of a householder?
One may be a yogin and not a seeker of enjoyment, or one may be a seeker of enjoyment but possess the state of a yogin.
Therefore, let the fruit of yoga be applied toward the destruction of this eightfold suffering. (31-32)
Behold, in this forest a forest fire indeed breaks out in many ways;
yet, in this very dwelling place, the crops grow thick and lush.
There are varieties of grass that are dark green, silvery, red, and white.
Indeed, on the ground where one sits, even slight patches of mud may sprout. An uneven, crooked, and marshy place is difficult to inhabit and brings great suffering;
during sleep or sexual union, such places are terrifying at midnight.
Fierce sounds are heard, causing extreme suffering through the destruction of one's purpose;
at midday there is intense heat, and the showers of rain are painful.
Behold the constant presence of sharp thorns upon my feet.
The hut is situated there; what kind of thorns are present?
(37) Behold the misfortune of the raindrops upon my body:
having fallen, they cover the body, causing the suffering of cold. (38)
In this difficult time, the crows and the cakora birds are building nests as their homes; without you, how will they find peace?
A great fear, as if arising from a cloud, has today been born within my heart.
"Therefore, strive for the sake of wealth; do not delay at my word.
A wife must be protected, one must dwell in the forest, and pleasure—not food—must be enjoyed.
All of this leads to our destruction, not to our happiness."
O Śaṅkara, construct a dwelling fit for habitation on Kailāsa, or on the Himālaya, or on the banks of the Gaṅgā, or anywhere else upon the earth,
where guests may arrive and find peace in this hermitage.
"In this abundance of wealth and grain, act according to your desire.
Having heard what Satī had spoken and considering it meaningful in his mind,
Śambhu then spoke to the Goddess, repeatedly delighting her heart.
"Speak, O Goddess, for clouds never go anywhere at all;
there, O Śivā, I would have a palace built, if it pleases you.
The clouds move as far as the slopes of this mountain."
Or, if it pleases you, I shall build it on a peak of mine similar to that;
or likewise, O Goddess, on the slope of Kailāsa, where clouds generally move even during the rainy season—if that pleases you, I shall build it there. (46–47)
On the peaks and slopes of Aruṇācala, clouds generally move about,
but they never go beyond that point.
On Mount Raivata in Saurāṣṭra, on Svargaśṛṅga, and on Sutaijasa—
Where clouds resting on the slopes do not ascend upward;
where, upon the Śiva-peak of Himālaya, clouds never go;
where there is the coolness born of the moon—I wish to build a palace there, for it pleases me. (1.173.50)
"Since these lords of mountains were seen by you in a previous birth,
tell me quickly which among them is pleasing to your heart. Indeed,
on the lofty golden peaks of which do the wives of the Siddhas dwell?"
If you have a desire for that place, I shall construct a great temple there;
where the goddesses dwell with joyful curiosity upon the Golden Peak,
if you should have a wish for that spot, I shall build a palace made of gold.
On Mount Āruṇa, Maṇikuṭṭa, Lokāloka, or Raivata,
the daughters of the Nāgas, the daughters of the mountains, the Kinnarīs, the daughters of the Phaṇis,
the Gandharvīs, the Apsarases, and the Vidyādharīs dwell.
"Wherever you have a desire, I shall build a home for you like heaven. O beloved, they shall all constantly perform service for you;
may you always rejoice in them with shared vehicles, shared play, and so forth. (56) [61]
Beholding this incomparable form of yours and your lovely face,
they will cast aside their own bodies and become your handmaidens;
or else, on the Himalayas, Menā, endowed with many forms and qualities, [will do so].

There, that daughter of the mountains will bring you joy through her constant service. If it pleases you, there is indeed a beautiful peak named Śiva, where those seeking instruction go daily. (58–59)
O beloved, do you wish to dwell here, which is always filled with the power of spring, surrounded by flocks of cuckoos warbling with various delightful notes,
and abounding in numerous lakes crowded with countless lotuses? 1.173.60.
It was endowed with wish-fulfilling trees, the nectar-creeper, and the celestial cow;
its herds of wild beasts were pacified, and it was well-frequented by ascetics and holy men;
it was adorned with crystal, celestial diamonds, and silver. (61–62)
