It was frequented by mind-born swans, horses, and celestial elephants;
it was beautifully adorned with golden lotuses—both buds and full-blown flowers—as well as clusters of jewels and lovely blossoms such as blue water-lilies. 63.
It was beautifully adorned with saffron, all kinds of perfumes, and shimmering scented waters; with young grassy meadows and tall bamboo trees;
and with aged peacocks dancing and bees and other insects humming.
It was filled with cranes and cuckoos uttering sweet cries,
and it resounded daily with the constant singing of those [birds]. It was always attended by playful women and served as an inflamer of passion.
"O beloved, do you wish to dwell accompanied by ever-new companions?
Or rather, do you wish to sport, together with your friends and adorned by a host of celestial nymphs (apsaras), upon the most excellent and greatly auspicious peak of Mount Meru?"
"If you desire to take pleasure there, I shall construct a supreme palace;
Śacī will always perform service and assistance for you.
[69] [She spoke thus regarding the lords of the waters, Kubera, Īśāna, and Yama.]

On the peaks of Meru, the lofty abode of the gods, adorned with cities belonging to Agni, the deity Nairṛta, the Maruts, or others, and frequented by hosts of women with thighs like those of Rambhā, such as Śacī, Rambhā, Menakā, and the rest; (1.173.70–71).
If you wish to dwell there, I shall construct a great abode for you;
or else, on Kailāsa, the king of mountains and my eternal refuge,
you may choose a beautiful place in the vicinity of Kubera’s city.
Moistened by droplets of Ganges water, radiant like the full moon,
adorned by the daughters of Brahmā in its caves, ridges, and valleys,
it was a dwelling place for various deer and surrounded by hundreds of lotus ponds.

Furthermore, please quickly tell me that place which is superior even to Mount Meru, adorned with the jewels of excellent qualities, favorable to both of us, and where we have a desire to dwell for a long time. 75.

"I shall indeed make my home filled with the wealth of gold, gems, and jewels. Satī then said to Śambhu: "I desire to dwell forever on the Himālaya; therefore, O granter of desires, establish your residence there without delay."
Having heard this, Śambhu always took Satī and went to a lofty peak,
which was graced by groves and lakes, frequented by hosts of Siddha women,
covered with diverse flowers, and variegated in many ways with jewels. (78)
It was indeed inaccessible even to birds, composed of crystal and clouds,
endowed with clusters of various flowers, verdant grassy plots, and young shoots,
and resounded with the humming of bees on the tips of the branches of blossoming trees.
It was filled with blossoming lotuses and clusters of blue water-lilies, frequented by celestial cranes, swans, parrots, and peacocks,
and served by horse-faced Siddhas and Apsarases.
It was frequented by Vidyādharīs, goddesses, and Kinnarīs;
it was filled with matrons, mountain-dwelling women, and maidens;
and it resounded with the sounds of lutes, harps, three-stringed instruments, clay drums, and kettledrums.
It was beautified by the festive performances of dancing apsarases,
and was completely surrounded by fragrant ponds named Devikā;
it was further adorned with beautiful groves of flowering creeper-vines.

Having gone joyfully with the daughter of Dakṣa to the delightful Śivaśṛṅga— a mountain with vast peaks, as enchanting as heaven— near the city of Himālaya and in the vicinity of Kubera’s city, Hara [remained there]. (85–86)
Having constructed a new city named Kailāsa, complete with walls and great palaces, he took his pleasure for a long time there;
having summoned Viśvakarman, he had that excellent city built. (87)
There, the city named Kailāsa shone with palaces (88) that were firm,
with walls inlaid with gold, jewels, and gems;
they possessed delightful bedchambers and bathing areas (89).
There were pools of cool water and warm water, as well as ponds of sweet water;
there were delightful kitchens and auspicious fire-sanctuaries;
and there were stores for provisions such as hard and soft foods, as well as guard stations.
There are pavilions for amusement and laughter, well-suited for the performance of amorous pastimes (91). There are also private palaces for the sake of amorous gestures, emotions, and dalliance,
as well as very large houses for the residence of guests (92).

There are sleeping quarters rich with couches for the end of slumber, and excellent upper floors and galleries resplendent with swings, hammocks, and the like; as well as arenas for gambling and other games, and pavilions for social assemblies. (93)
There were watchtowers with four corners and water-pitchers on all sides.
(94) There were gardens, house-gardens, and electric vehicles;
there were lamps, sound-machines, and sight-machines as well. (95)
Indeed, garments of many varieties were made by the hundreds of thousands;
vessels of gold and silver, ornaments of gems and refined gold;
likewise, dwellings and chambers with doors secured for protection. (96)
There were wind-fans and mechanical devices, houses for amorous music and song,
paths for mental delight, and marketplaces with many sights; likewise, there were excellent and noble residences numbering in the millions, hundreds of thousands, and tens of thousands.
Gardens, monasteries, and auspicious royal capitals were established there,
wherein exist divine nectars of immortality as well as the essence of Brahman (brahmarasa). Indeed, in those places are found excellent flavors, such as drinks that stimulate desire.
There were grounds for medicinal creepers that bestow the vigor of fresh youth,
as well as auspicious abodes of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) and laboratories of elixirs (rasa).
There were also vehicles in the form of bulls, lions, Garuḍas, elephants, and horses.
Schools for the education of girls were indeed established and commissioned there;
such was that new Kailāsa, the best of cities, built by Śambhu through Viśvakarman as a most excellent work. (102)
In her presence, the palaces of the world-protectors then became insignificant.
Beholding, gazing upon, and repeatedly surveying her own city, which possessed a hundredfold greater prosperity than the home of Dakṣa, Satī rejoiced again and again. (103–104)
Whatever object is conceived, that very thing appears there;
nothing is lacking, from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods downwards.
Even the supreme lord of kings and the auspicious Śiva are served by excellent prosperity.
They shine with the splendor of the Lord of the Kings of Kings through parasols and chowries.
Having ascended a supreme celestial chariot, they travel at times to another region;
and having sported in the sky over Mount Meru and in the heavens and other realms, they proceed. (106–107)
Having gone again and again to the ever-new Kailāsa and returned, the two, Sati and Śiva, took delight; thus did they emulate the bliss of the householder’s life.
In this way, Satī constantly beheld the happiness of the illustrious Śaṅkara.
The illustrious Śambhu also perceived everywhere the happiness of Satī.
(10.9) Thus, through their mutual association, Satī and Śiva caused the tree of passion to grow by watering it with the moisture of their affection. (1.173.110)
Once, while staying there, Satī, her face filled with wonder, having attained a state of dispassion yet remaining contented with the enjoyment of happiness, questioned Śambhu:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, show mercy toward me."
You have attained identity with the Supreme Brahman; you are the supreme one, devoid of qualities.
Blessed am I, having become your beloved; you have become my husband and lord.
O Lord of Gods, I desire to know that reality by which one may cross over worldly existence.
Having heard that by performing which the embodied soul necessarily goes to the supreme state— that which Śiva spoke here for the sake of Satī’s knowledge— he said:
"Listen, O beloved, I shall declare the reality by which one becomes liberated."
Know Hari Nārāyaṇa to be the supreme reality at all times.
O beloved, his realization is difficult to attain, and those who know him are rare.
I am a servant of Nārāyaṇa, the Brahman, the Supreme Self.
Devotion to Nārāyaṇa bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess, you were remembered in a previous birth in the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
having gone there, you became a Vaiṣṇava, and thus you were made a Vaiṣṇavī.
I am indeed a Vaiṣṇava from Goloka, and I shall become a Vaiṣṇava once again.
You too must remain a Vaiṣṇavī through devotion to Brahman in my house,
for this Nārāyaṇa who dwells in the abode of Brahman is [the goal] in every way.
Mindfulness, consciousness itself, propitiation, and worship at all times;
reflection, as well as devotion and the service of love—these constitute oneness.
By that alone, indeed, is Nārāyaṇa attained, and not by anything else whatsoever.
The nature of grace from Him is easily attained; it is proclaimed here as being ninefold:
hearing, chanting, remembering, and constant service, as well as servitude, worship, salutation, and likewise devotion to Śrī Hari, O Goddess. (121–122)
Friendship, self-surrender, and those nine limbs—constantly honoring Hare with one's body and so forth, drinking that which is for His sake with steadfastness;
this is called *śravaṇa*. (123)
Having heard it, one must reflect upon its meaning, for that indeed yields fruit.
(1.24) Constantly contemplating in one's heart the births and deeds of Śrī Hari, and reciting them with great affection—this is called kīrtana. (1.25)

Having realized that the glorious Hari is all-pervading, he indeed remembers Him everywhere and at all times with his mind; that is declared to be "remembrance" (smaraṇa). In every way, whether in the waking state or in dreams, [he remains mindful] through objects that are very dear to himself.
Service (paricaryā) is declared to be the act of attending upon Him.
(127) Always acting with a favorable disposition, through the enjoyment of the nectar of the heart, and behaving in a manner pleasing to Hari—that indeed is declared to be servitude (dāsya). (128)

The worship of the Supreme Self consists of the offering of the sixteen articles, beginning with water for the feet, performed at all times according to the prescribed rule in accordance with prosperity;
likewise, it is accomplished through the recitation of His names and meditation, both mentally and verbally. 129.
When one prostrates like a staff, touching the ground with eight limbs, that indeed is *daṇḍavat-vandana*.
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious thing Śrī Hari does for me,
the conviction that "all of that is for my welfare" is called friendship (*sakhya*).

Having made everything, including one's own body and so forth, an offering to Him for His pleasure, and having surrendered one's own emptiness to Hari for the sake of sustenance, this is the offering of the self to Hari.
The nine limbs of devotion to Hari bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 132.
O my beloved, there are many ancillary practices (*upāṅga*) of devotion to Him that are dear to me and which produce supreme discernment:
such as the service of *tulasī*, the sweeping of the temple, and so forth. (133–134)
"Considering all matters such as the protection of temples and so forth, O beloved, this devotion to Hari, complete with its primary and secondary limbs, is the most excellent of all;
it shines forth as the mother of knowledge and dispassion, and the handmaid of liberation. (135)
In the three worlds, there is no path that brings such happiness as devotion.
For a person possessed of devotion, Śrī Hari is the helper.
The essence of devotion is that very reality which leads to the attainment of the Supreme Reality. (136–137)
Furthermore, that devotion is twofold: with attributes (saguṇā) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇā).
All that which is performed with a desire for a fruit is described as saguṇā;
that very same devotion, when devoid of the desire for a fruit, is called nirguṇā.
Furthermore, that devotion is of two kinds: the ritual (vaidhī) and the natural (svābhāvikī).
That which is performed by means of an injunction through compulsion is the ritual;
however, that which is performed by one's very nature is considered the natural. (1.173.139–140)

Furthermore, that devotion (bhakti) is twofold: the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā). The higher has the form of the goal, Lord Hari; the lower has the form of the means. It is also twofold: steadfast (naiṣṭhikī) and non-steadfast (anaiṣṭhikī). The steadfast devotion is considered to be of six kinds.
Faith, choosing [the Lord], entrusting oneself, humility, and firm resolve;
(142) avoidance of opposition accompanied by conformity—this is the sixfold *naiṣṭhikī* devotion, while the *anaiṣṭhikī* is considered to be of one kind. (143)

Devotion performed solely for one's own sake is proclaimed as non-consummated (*anaiṣṭhikī*). It is further considered twofold: prescribed (*vihitā*) and unprescribed (*avihitā*). Among these, the prescribed is regarded as "Command" (*ājñā*), while the unprescribed is called "Non-command" (*anājñā*). Furthermore, each of these is divided into three types: middling, superior, and inferior.
There, through various states of being that range from inferior to superior, it manifests in many ways.
Nowhere else does equality with the chanting of Hari’s name exist;
for one who utters the word "Hari"—which signifies Brahman—while remembering Lord Hari. (145–146)
He who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal.
The world is pleased by devotion, and indeed Hari is pleased by devotion.
Listen, O Goddess, to what occurred in a former kalpa regarding Nārāyaṇa.
Sixty thousand ages of extremely difficult penance were performed by me.
Then Nārāyaṇa himself became visible to my sight—a youth with exceedingly beautiful limbs, dark and handsome. (148–149)
With limbs proportionate to his form and exceedingly serene and charming,
upon seeing Hari in such a state, my eyes truly found no satisfaction;
beholding him, I became devoid of blinking and was not satiated for a long time.
Then the Blessed One said to me: "O Śambhu, why are you not at all satisfied?
I am going to my own abode; choose a boon as you desire.
I am pleased by your devotion and your penance; do not delay. (151–152)
Then, O beloved, listen to what I requested of Nārāyaṇa:
"Whatever may be for your enjoyment, let that not be for my enjoyment beforehand.
O Lord, I consider the entirety of your grace to be my own enjoyment."
May I always have service unto you, as well as the offering of my very self.
May I also possess various other forms of devotion that grant me liberation.
Indeed, may matted hair remain forever upon my head, serving as a reminder of my ascetic practice.
May the ashes from the funeral pyre upon my body indeed awaken dispassion;
may there be equanimity toward sandalwood paste and mud, and toward a clod of earth and a sovereign jewel.
O Lord, may I never wear ornaments such as crowns and the like.
In that regard, O Hari, serpents who hate Garuḍa must be maintained by me.
Furthermore, the bull, which was offered to Kṛṣṇa from Goloka, is my very vehicle.
Also, fragrant flowers such as the Pārijāta and scented substances such as sandalwood [are mine]. (157–158)
May that which is suitable for you be mine; may I have no share whatsoever in anything else.
May my love always be for the *dhattūra* flower, and for the avoidance of *bilva* leaves. Through detachment, may my affection be for flowers devoid of fragrance.
Let there be no passion for clothing; let it be for the skins of elephants and tigers. (1.173.160) Let there never be delight in celestial beds or divine enjoyments;
let my dwelling always be in the cremation ground, and never among the crowds of people. (161)
In a cremation ground free from obstacles, may your meditation always be mine;
O Śrī Hari, may your knowledge be eternally mine, destroying the three qualities (guṇas).
May my trident-form be yours, and your ash-form be mine—this is dispassion (vairāgya). || 162 ||
"May Dharma appear to me in the form of a bull; may I possess devotion and the state of a yogi toward you.
Your necklace for the neck has been fashioned from the heads of those opposed to devotion; and your ornamental garlands are composed of unsuitable rudrākṣa fruits. (163–164)
May there be no enjoyment for you from trees such as the *vṛnda* and others, nor may there be anything for me on their account;
may Goddess Lakṣmī never belong to me, but rather may misfortune (*alakṣmī*) truly be mine.
May whatever sweet drink belongs to Hari never belong to me at any time.
"May I always possess the power to destroy poison, dhatūra, elephants, and the like.
Thus was everything requested by me at the time of my penance;
and Hari granted that boon for my welfare.
For the sake of instructing the devotees and to manifest the devotion of a servant,
and for the purpose of deluding the asuras, it was protected by His command.
Therefore, O Satī, you must maintain the conduct of a servant toward Hari and not otherwise.
Listen to another excellent narrative, filled with the grace of Hari:
Once Sanatkumāra went to Vaikuṇṭha, and there the sage beheld Nārāyaṇa, Hari, having finished his meal. (1.173.170)
Having prostrated with devotion, he praised him with secret hymns.
Being pleased, the Lord who is kind to his devotees gave him the remainder.
There, he ate a little of that very food himself, while the rest was kept as a remnant. 171.

He indeed guarded that [food], which was difficult to obtain, for the sake of feeding his kinsmen. Furthermore, he gave a small portion of it to me while I was staying at Siddhāśrama; and all of that was eaten by me with reverence.
Having partaken of the rare grace of Hari, I performed a dance;
with all my limbs covered in horripilation and eyes filled with tears, I became filled with joy.
I sang the praises of Śrī Hari’s qualities in a beautiful voice, keeping perfect rhythm and measure. 174.
Then, with my mind entirely focused on the distinction between passion [and devotion], and through my devotion, the hand-drum (ḍamaru), the horn, and the tiger-skin fell from my hands.
Afterward, I myself collapsed, weeping and even falling into a swoon. (175–176)

The form of Śrī Hari is exceedingly desirable and captivating; being overwhelmed by it in my heart, I meditate upon it alone. Then, in that very interval, you, O beautiful lady Durgā, arrived there with joy. 177.
O beautiful lady, as soon as I rose from my fainting spell and stood up, I was asked about the cause of that fainting;
however, I told you only what I had obtained through your grace. (178–179)
O Goddess, having perceived that you were angry, you then said to me:
"You are the nourisher and protector of the worlds, and especially my own;
you are the speaker of the four Vedas and the bestower of all prosperity. (1.173.180)
If you practice such wicked policy, who will protect the Dharma?
I am always to be protected by you, nourished, devoted, and a servant;
yet, due to the fault of my past actions, I have been deprived of partaking in the grace of Hari.

Some things are purified by gold, some are purified by air, and some by washing alone; but everything is purified by offering it to Viṣṇu. All the deities should be worshipped with food that has been offered to Viṣṇu.
It is established in the Vedas that the ancestors and guests are likewise [to be honored].
(184) That which is not offered is unfit for consumption, whereas what is offered as *naivedya* is indeed fit for consumption.
He who eats thus with devotion shall become a foremost attendant (*pārṣada*). (185)

The nectar of the food offered to Viṣṇu is the most desired essence of all things and is exceedingly difficult to obtain; it does not equal even a sixteenth part of that [other] nectar which merely deludes the foolish and destroys untimely death. (186)
Indeed, the food offering (naivedya) of Hari alone makes one equal to Hari—oh, how marvelous!
Whoever, through the company of the virtuous, eats that food offering by chance, obtains the fruit of sixty thousand years of austerity. (187–188)
He who, being a devotee, constantly eats after having offered food to Hari with devotion—he should be known as a sanctifier of the assembly, for he is equal to the splendor of Hari himself.
(189) "I am not the author of the Vedas; how could I be the mistress capable of speaking [on such matters]?"
"O Lord, after performing austerities for a very long time, you were obtained by me as my master.
O Lord, how have I been deceived by you through the grace of Viṣṇu?
Having spoken thus, you, Durgā, began to weep.
Then, out of supreme love, I respectfully placed you upon my chest and, wiping the tears from your eyes with my hand, repeatedly tried to awaken you.
At that time, being fully satisfied, you spoke to me, your husband: [192]
"I shall cast off this body if it is without an offering to Hari.
I constantly sustain this body which increases your good fortune;
how then can I carry a body devoid of such good fortune?"
"The unprecedented food offering to Hari, which removes birth, death, and old age, was not given to me;
therefore, behold, I shall cast off my body.
Having spoken thus, O Great Goddess, you prepared to abandon your body.
Then you were indeed praised by me: "O Great Goddess! Be firm.
O Beautiful One, you ought to forgive all my transgressions;
show mercy toward me, your servant, who has been won over by my penance. (196–197)
"It is the will of Śrī Hari himself; I am not even capable of granting it.
Upon hearing this desire of Śrī Hari, Durgā became pleased.
Then she quickly went to the celestial river (Gaṅgā) for the purpose of bathing. 198.
Having bathed and worshipped with devotion, she then prepared cooked food and offered it as a *naivedya* to me; then I, Nārāyaṇa,
went there, ate everything myself, and granted her whatever she desired.
And she went to Vaikuṇṭha, O Lakṣmī, having given that very grace to her husband; and Śeṣa ate what Durgā had left over.
Thus, Śivā and Śiva were indeed Vaiṣṇavas in their previous birth.
Those two supreme yogis, whose forms are eternally immersed [in meditation], remain ever thus.
(202) I do not dwell in Goloka, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor upon your chest; I am forever bound to the heart of Sadāśiva by the noose of devotion. (203)
By this son of mine, the five-faced Śaṅkara spontaneously sings my song forever; therefore, I am established within his heart.
[I grant] devotion to me, service, liberation, and all perfections.
Śaṅkara bestows all perfections upon me alone.
(2.05) Indeed, he who chants my name day and night at the five-faced [Lord], and who constantly meditates on my form—there is no devotee superior to Śaṅkara. (2.06)

Thus, in the first book, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*: the recreation of Satī and Śiva on Himācala; Satī’s request for the construction of a home and the names of suitable mountains and other sites; the building of the city of Kailāsa on the Himalayas; Satī’s inquiry regarding the means of crossing the ocean of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*); the ninefold devotion to Hari as taught by Śiva; Śiva’s vision of Hari through the penance performed in a previous kalpa; and that which is to be enjoyed by Hari but not by Śiva—[ends here].
Chapter One Hundred and Seventy-Three: Description of the Wearing of Datura Ashes and Other Substances, and the Greatness of the Food Offered to Hari as Spoken by Pārvatī.
[The *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga] Chapter One Hundred and Seventy-Four.
[The Author: Chapter 175.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī, how Dakṣa Prajāpati himself [acted] out of affection for his daughter.
He indeed came to the abode of Śaṅkara for the purpose of obtaining a daughter. Seeing Dakṣa approaching, Mahādeva offered him worship and hospitality as was appropriate.
Dakṣa was a man of honor, while Śambhu was a lord of sages devoid of worldly pride.
When the two met, Dakṣa desired that he be accorded greater honor;
however, Śambhu accorded him only honor equal to that of a sage.
But when he rose, he did not proceed toward him there.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the great and beneficial reason for that:
he had attained preeminence through austerity, righteousness, and yoga. || 5 ||
One should not rise to greet someone who is inferior to oneself according to the scriptures;
when a superior person rises for the sake of one who is lowly, all of one's merit is destroyed.
Having reflected thus, Hara did not rise there toward Dakṣa.
But Dakṣa, having fallen into a state of darkness, became angry within himself.
Thinking, "This is but a child, Śaṅkara," he said nothing at all. Thus enraged, he went home in silence.
Then, when Satī had arrived home, Dakṣa, deeply distressed in mind, said:
"Your other husbands, the wielders of the Pināka bow, are superior;
for they all rise up and show me honor with great respect."
"Śambhu has risen and does not show honor toward my daughter.
Śambhu seems to me to be unworldly and childish. Let it be; I shall certainly not grieve. O girl, what indeed is this insult?"
Having spoken thus, he bestowed great honor upon his own daughter.
Satī, having received that hospitality, went to her own home on Kailāsa;
then indeed, the beloved spoke all those things to Śambhu. (12)
"May Dakṣa’s good deed not perish, now that it has been clearly revealed.
Having understood his heart's intent, Satī said nothing at all there;
she considered that what had been done by Śarva for her father’s benefit was indeed conducive to his welfare.
Moreover, the twice-born Dakṣa, son of Aṅgiras, has been cursed by Śambhu;
yet he desires honor from me that is excessive and impossible.
Therefore, let him enter the womb of a Kṣatriya woman in the house of Prācetas.
"Let that Kṣatriya, from whom my desire for guidance arises, be the son of Pracetas. "May there never be greater honor for me than from one like me"—
thus did the minor curse of Śambhu fall upon Dakṣa Prajāpati.
Since Nārada also received a curse regarding his rebirth, Dakṣa obtained this second birth in the house of the Pracetases;
nevertheless, the impressions of his former life persist within Dakṣa’s mind. (18)

Thinking "I am the father from my previous birth" and "I am real," the conceited person continues to exist in every way; for a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is never destroyed. Furthermore, in another birth, who is whose father-in-law, mother, or father? (1.174.20)
In this world, Śambhu does not even count his own father-in-law as a kṣatriya who is conceited about his status, though he is a guardian of the world;
nevertheless, Satī remains one who remembers her previous births. (21)
This Dakṣa was indeed his father in a previous birth, yet he has been born again;
nevertheless, thinking, "What remains here for me? Everything from my former birth has passed away," Śambhu does not regard him as his own father-in-law.
Then, O beloved, on another occasion, a similar situation arose;
Śambhu himself, while in his own Kailāsa, reflected upon building a city and summoned Viśvakarmā to construct a beautiful and highly prosperous capital. (24)
In his own fragrant hall, he had a beautiful,
spacious, and well-constructed mansion built; therein was an excellent throne,
and there also a great, divine umbrella, most wonderful and supreme in every respect.
Indeed, for the purpose of preparing that site, he held a truly great festival;
he quickly summoned all the hosts of deities, beginning with Śakra, as well as the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Nāgas, and all the instructors in their entirety. (27)
He [honored] the gods, the sages, and the Āgamas, as well as the ritual procedures along with their disciples and the seers;
likewise, all the goddesses accompanied by Apsarases and various objects.
And [he honored] those of the gods, the seers, the Siddhas, and even the hooded serpents.
Bringing sixteen maidens each with auspicious offerings in their hands,
as well as various musical instruments headed by the lute (*vīṇā*) and the drum (*mṛdaṅga*),
he caused a festival to be celebrated, having them played by excellent singers.

Then, with his own attendants, he brought materials suitable for the royal consecration along with all medicinal herbs, five water-pots filled with the waters of manifest sacred fords, and other divine preparations. (31–32)
There, the Brahmins raised a great roar like the sound of the Vedas;
having seated Hari with much affection upon an excellent new throne at an auspicious moment, Hara adorned him in every way.
Having tied on his beautiful crown and performed the auspicious rites of consecration,
Śambhu praised Viṣṇu— the independent one who is kind to his devotees—
and having bowed to him and the entire assembly, Hara stood there. (34–35)
Then Dakṣa arrived there with the human beings accompanied by the Prajāpatis;
all were honored by Śambhu, and Dakṣa likewise was honored along with them.
They were provided with food, clothing, drink, vehicles, carriages, and places for recreation.

Everyone was honored in every way, yet Dakṣa desired to show him special distinction. However, due to the insistence of his daughter-in-law, Dakṣa went into the middle of Śambhu’s house to see the face of his own daughter.
At that time, Śambhu did not rise to see, question, or offer comfort and peace;
then Dakṣa, being exceedingly proud in his heart, became truly enraged once more.
Having inquired after Satī’s welfare, happiness, and health, [he spoke].
Dakṣa went to his own palace, and the others also departed for their respective homes.
This was a manifest insult to Prajāpati;
for it is most excellent not to come when uninvited and unknown.
Keeping this in mind, even then the capable Dakṣa protected his own dignity and did not manifest it outwardly at all.
Then, after some time, in the Naimiṣa forest, those whose wealth was their austerity—
While the great sages, Bhṛgu and others, were performing a long-duration sacrifice (dīrghasattra),
Hara and the other gods arrived there and sat down together.
Having arrived, those gods beheld the sages engaged in the long sacrifice.
All rose up simultaneously, joyful and eager;
having offered water for the feet and respectful oblations, the sages, freed from all taint, paid their respects.
They beheld Hara, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Pulaha, and the others.
The Mānavas arrived there, and Dakṣa also arrived;
having come by chance, he was honored by the great ṛṣis with hymns of praise and prostrations, as well as by all the gods and asuras.
Having been thus honored, he sat down within the assembly;
yet Rudra did not offer him the customary rising or marks of special respect.
Consequently, no particular sense of honor arose in him from being treated with such courtesy by Rudra.
Then Dakṣa, the Prajāpati, quickly became enraged at Rudra;
he indeed spoke harsh words directed toward Rudra there:
"All these brahmins, as well as the gods, asuras, and others, bow down to me. (1.174.50)
"Everyone honors me greatly with rising from their seats and other marks of respect;
why is it that this Lord of Beings does not rise at all, like a wicked man?
He dwells in cremation grounds, is shameless, and is accompanied by ghosts and piśācas. (5.1)
My peerless friend does not show me any partiality.
(52) He is inferior by birth and in his actions; he is a heretic, fond of wicked people, evil-natured, arrogant, a reviler, and indeed impure. (53)
This king of fools must always be avoided by the virtuous and excluded in every way;
for whenever I went to his house,
this supreme fool would not rise even in my presence and would indeed treat me with contempt.
Therefore, from this day forward, let him always remain outside the sacrifice.
And those who are followers of Rudra— let them also be excluded from the Vedas, joined with heretical doctrines, and devoid of the conduct of the learned.
"May the skull-bearers become addicted to drink and have blackened faces!
Having heard those words, Nandin was filled with rage toward Dakṣa;
he cursed Dakṣa, as well as the Brahmins on his side and those of other castes.
Devoted to the recitation of the Vedas, you shall proclaim that there is nothing else;
possessed by desire, intent upon heaven, and filled with anger and greed, O Brahmins, you shall become priests for Śūdras according to Vedic rites. (58–59)
"Let them become poor here, likewise addicted to receiving gifts;
let them all follow the path of the unrighteous and become *brahmarākṣasas*.
Then Śambhu, being pacified, spoke to his own attendant, Nandin.
"You ought never to harbor anger toward the Brahmins.
Who is this? Who are you? And who indeed am I? Why have the twice-born been cursed by you?
Abandoning the construction of this phenomenal world, become awakened, O servant! (61-62)
All were brought to peace by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the gods, and others;
Dakṣa went to his own home, repeatedly remembering his humiliation.
Then, in due time, a great sacrifice was indeed commenced by him.
There, at that extensive sacrifice performed by the consecrated Dakṣa,
the sages were invited; Vasiṣṭha and other ascetics arrived,
as did Kaśyapa, Atri, Vāmadeva, Agastya, and Bhṛgu.
Parāśara, Dadhīca, Vyāsa, Gautama, Śita,
Garga, Paila, Bharadvāja, Bhārgava, Kakupa, and Kṛti;
likewise other sages, gods, world-protectors, and lords of the directions.
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Vidyādharas, and hosts of Apsarases;
the Unborn One (Aja), accompanied by Sāvitrī, was brought from Satyaloka;
and then Viṣṇu, together with Lakṣmī, Ramā, and others, arrived from Vaikuṇṭha.
Indra was brought there from heaven along with Indrāṇī;
likewise Candra with Rohiṇī, and Varuṇa with Vāruṇī.
Kubera was mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot, and Māruta had a deer for his vehicle.
Pāvaka has a goat for his vehicle, and Nairṛta has a ghost for his vehicle.
Their wives, sons, disciples, attendants, ministers,
as well as their retinues and the Vedas, all assembled there.
Thus others arrived at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, showing great respect;
they were all honored by Dakṣa with many articles. There were costly, magnificent, and splendid palaces of vast dimensions.
These divine [weapons] were fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ and indeed bestowed upon them by him.
They all took their positions as was appropriate within those respective stations; honored by Viṣṇu and by me, they all remained without a king.
Then Asiknī, the mother of Satī, who had been previously married to Dakṣa,
having learned that Dakṣa had been reborn, came there and resided permanently.
And it was for the sake of Śambhu that Asiknī performed penance there while she was Satī.

She did not see him arrive; then, having bowed to Prajāpati Dakṣa with her inner self humbled and her body bent low, she spoke: "How is it that Satī and Śambhu are not seen here at this festival? (76-77)
Then Dakṣa said to Asiknī, "There is no purpose for those two [children].
But Satī was always affectionate toward her parents and desired their honor.
[She thought: "Śarva is deceitful; he is not at all affectionate toward me, but rather a source of humiliation."
Having obtained my virtuous daughter, he has become exceedingly arrogant.
He is likely dear to no one, nor is anyone dear to him. Of what lineage is he, of what clan, from what country, and of what nature? (1.174.80)
What is his conduct, what is his behavior—this one who rides a bull and is full of dejection?
He does not generally appear to be an ascetic; where is his penance, and where is his bearing of weapons?
He is not to be counted among householders, for he always dwells in the cremation ground.
He cannot be a religious student (brahmacārī), since he has been wedded in truth;
nor can there be the stage of forest-dwelling (vānaprastha) for him, as he is deluded by the intoxication of power.
I know not whether he is even a Brahmin, since the Veda does not recognize him.

I do not know if there is any longer a Kṣatriya, for generally there is no protection from injury (*kṣatāt-trāṇam*) in this world which delights in universal destruction, due to the mere accumulation of weapons and missiles.
Even a Vaiśya who is destitute and finds delight in the forest does not shine at all in my eyes.
How can there be the inclusion of a Śūdra who wears the sacred thread of a Nāga?
Thus, who could possibly understand one who has transcended the castes and stages of life?
Everyone would perceive him as Sthāṇu (Śiva), for he is devoid of material nature.
Generally speaking, this person is not a man, since he consists half of a woman;
nor is he a woman alone, since his face is bearded;
nor is he a eunuch, yet his gender is highly honored.
Nor is he of the form of a child, since he has existed for many years.
Marīci and the others consider him to be old, because he is not a youth.
Furthermore, how can he be regarded as old when he is devoid of both aging and death?
Even though he destroys everyone, he is not a sinner;
how could there be even a trace of merit here in one who destroys the head of Brahmā? Wherein lies his purity while wearing a garland of skulls and being clothed only by the directions?
He possesses neither wealth, nor offspring, nor a family;
he has no mother, no lineage, no clan, and no physical body. He dwells eternally in the cremation ground, yet he is not perceived as a dog-eater (outcaste). || 91-92 ||
O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking? His conduct is not understood by me.
Oh, what audacity! This matted-haired one has shown me, his father-in-law and preceptor, such contempt that he did not rise from his seat upon seeing me. (93)
Such indeed are those who are bereft of mother and father:
devoid of virtue, lacking noble lineage, fallen from their duties, unrestrained, acting according to their own whims, full of self-conceit, and deprived of a driver. (94–95)
Even those who possess nothing may become arrogant and imagine themselves to be lords;
a son-in-law equal to a jackal treats his father-in-law like a deer.
O Asiknī, your son-in-law is the one who destroyed my head.
"Since one who despises me has been born, therefore I did not invite him.
I shall undoubtedly take away the entirety of his pride; just as I have been insulted, so too shall I insult him. (97-98)
"Therefore, you must not remember him, lest he become a sharer in the fruit of the sacrifice.
Thus addressed by Dakṣa, the foremost wife observed a vow of silence;
then, sighing deeply, she cursed her daughter in his absence.
One does not see one’s own sons, daughters, sons-in-law, and so forth [in that place].
That is called a "blazing festival" (prajvalad-utsava), wherein the sight of one's own daughters and others is not obtained. (1.174.100–101)
Thus, the sacrifice, already consumed by the mind of Asiknī and reduced to ashes,
will certainly be further incinerated when scorched by the curse of the Mother of the King.
And Dakṣa, having arrived, shall likewise address me, Viṣṇu, as the "Person of Sacrifice" (Yajñapuruṣa).
Having offered his own head as an oblation, he made [the Lord] the witness of his great sacrifice.
He spoke to the gods, the sages, the brahmins, the protectors of creatures, and likewise to the Manus:
"I am desirous of performing a sacrifice; you shall be my assistants in the rite."
"Prepare the materials for the sacrifice; bring them here with haste!
Listen, Lakṣmī! While the sacrifice at the Kanakhala Tīrtha was underway, all the ṛṣis who were exponents of the Veda became his officiating priests."
Bhṛgu and the others were knowers of the three periods of time and were indeed embodiments of the Vedas.
I myself was the presiding deity Viṣṇu, together with all the hosts of Maruts;
and Brahmā was there as Brahmā, the instructor of the ritual according to the three Vedas.
In the same way, all the guardians of the quarters, the gatekeepers, and the protectors—
equipped with weapons, accompanied by their retinues, and ever full of curiosity—
approached him in person at his sacrifice, appearing in embodied form.

The great sages themselves became the upholders of the Vedas at the sacrifice. Then, during that great festival of the sacrifice, Agni himself instantly assumed his own form in a thousand ways in order to receive the oblations.
Eighty-eight thousand officiating priests offered oblations;
sixty-four thousand celestial sages were the Udgātṛs;
and as many again—Nārada and others—were the Adhvaryus and Hotṛs. (111)
The seven Ṛṣis performed their respective duties as chanters of the Sāman hymns (112).
At that great sacrifice, Dakṣa chose many hosts of Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Ādityas, as well as all the Nāgas and serpents (113).

Then Dakṣa, accompanied by the twice-born sages, the royal sages, the Vasus, the hosts of celestial treasures, and kings enriched by friends, ministers, and armies— surrounded by those who were to assist at the sacrifice and himself engaged in the initiatory rites (dīkṣā)— performed the auspicious marriage ceremonies. 114.
Accompanied by his wife and having had the rites for success performed, he shone intensely. At that sacrifice, everyone was invited except Hara alone;
they excluded him, having decided, "He is a skull-bearer," and thus he was not worthy of that sacrifice.
Thinking, "Let there be no share for me even in the sacrifice," Satī—
his elder sister and his own daughter— was not invited by Dakṣa, who perceived only faults, regarding her as the wife of a Kapālin. (11.7)

While this great festival of Dakṣa’s sacrifice was thus proceeding, all those who were esteemed for the ritual were intent upon their own duties. Yet, in that celebration, Śaṅkara and Satī were not seen there.
With an agitated mind, Dadhīca, a devotee of Śiva, spoke these words:
"O Dakṣa Prajāpati, O Dakṣa who directly bears the very form of the Creator!
Neither splendor nor capability for performing a sacrifice is seen in you."
Such a sacrifice as has been commenced is truly not capable of being completed.
Indeed, a sacrifice must never be undertaken; there is no enemy equal to a sacrifice.
However, a sacrifice may be performed only if one possesses such wealth as this.
Agni himself, manifest in bodily form, shines here within this sacrificial pit;
likewise, Indra and the other gods are present in person, having assembled here.
Furthermore, all the mantras are present in person throughout the sacrificial rites.
The Lord Yajña himself shines here in embodied form;
Bṛhaspati himself is resplendent here in the position of preceptor;
Brahmā himself is in the position of Brahmā, and Bhṛgu himself is the performer of the ritual rites.
He is Pūṣan and Bhaga; he is the goddess Sarasvatī herself, as well as Śāradā;
he is Lakṣmī herself, and Nārāyaṇa himself.
He is the guardians of the quarters and the protectors of the worlds, who personally provide protection.
This son-in-law of yours has arrived with his wives; this is your duty.
And you yourself have entered the initiation for the sacrifice together with your wife;
let that moon-like one, accompanied by twenty-seven wives, perform the ritual task.
This Mārīca Kaśyapa, the performer of the Rājasūya sacrifice,
has arrived at your sacrifice after bestowing the three worlds as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Your thirteen daughters have come as his wives.
Your other excellent daughters and their husbands have also gone there. Indeed, the wish-fulfilling cows (Kāmadhenu) offer you clarified butter and other sacrificial oblations,
while the wish-granting trees (Kalpavṛkṣa) themselves bring the sacrificial fuel and Kuśa grass.

Wooden vessels, vehicles, pavilions, and whatever else is required are offered by the trees themselves as they approach. Viśvakarman also provides the ornaments for the invited priests and guests. (132)
The eight Vasus are providing garments here at your sacrifice.
Lakṣmī herself is adorning the married women at your sacrifice.
O Dakṣa, everything seen here at your sacrifice brings about happiness.
Just as a body devoid of life does not shine at all anywhere,
even if it is adorned, so too a sacrifice does not shine without Śambhu.
This ground here is painful and like a cremation ground.
"Without Śambhu, your sacrifice appears like a funeral pyre.
O all you foremost among the gods and sages, listen indeed to my words here:
why is Śambhu not present at this great festival of sacrifice? (1.36–37)
Since all auspicious things depend upon him,
why is that very Prāṇa not seen here as Hara,
by whose presiding presence even inauspicious things become auspicious? (138)
"How is it that Śaṅkara, the auspicious one, has not come here?
Therefore, Dakṣa must issue an invitation to the Supreme Lord,
or else to Brahmā, or Viṣṇu, together with the sages."
"Now, you all—the twice-born, the lions, and the world-protectors headed by Indra—must go to the mountain where Śaṅkara resides.
Bring Śambhu together with the daughter of Dakṣa; thus it shall be auspicious."
If Śaṅkara is brought here, the sacrifice will be completed with its final purificatory bath;
otherwise, there will be an obstacle. I speak the truth regarding what is destined to happen.
That which ought to be reported by me has already been reported right here.
Having heard these words spoken by Dadhīci, Dakṣa, the performer of the sacrifice, blazed up intensely.
His soul overwhelmed with rage, he spoke these words full of contention:
"O Dadhīci, you are a Brāhmaṇa; maintain silence and go outside! (144)
"Standing as I am initiated for sacrifice, I am unable to commit such a slaughter.
By whom were you asked, that you have come here and boast?
Viṣṇu is the root of the gods, wherein the eternal dharmas reside. (145–146)
I have brought here that which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things;
where the Vedas, the sacrifices, and various rituals reside—
where the Lord of Sacrifice himself is present, what could possibly be lacking in this sacrificial rite?
This Viṣṇu, the foundation of all ritual acts, is present at my sacrifice,
where this Śatakratu, the lord of the three worlds and the sovereign of thirty-three crores of immortals, has assembled for the rite.
Brahmā, accompanied by Sāvitrī, arrived from Satyaloka along with all the Vedas, Upaniṣads, Āgamas, and Brāhmaṇas;
Dharmarāja also arrived together with his wives, sons, and grandsons.
Likewise, you sages and others who know dharma and adharma [are present];
Kubera, the giver of wealth, and Pāvaka (Agni) together with his wives;
and Bṛhaspati himself has taken his place as the presiding priest of the sacrifice. || 151–152 ||
"These great sages are worthy of sacrifice, peaceful, and purifying;
they are the performers of rites at my sacrifice. Oh, you call that place a cremation ground! Yet it is a cremation ground where spirits, ghosts, and piśācas always dwell. (153)
The hosts of Śaṅkara dwell right there in that house, where all the servants and the leaders have gathered together. What is lacking for us here, such that we even need Rudra? (154–155)
That very place where these great sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, perform their priestly duties—you compare that auspicious refuge here to a cremation ground!
Indeed, urged by Brahmā, I have given my daughter to him. (156)
This brahmin is of low birth and devoid of mother and father;
he is the lord of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, arrogant, stubborn, and always impure.
He is unfit for this task, which is why I did not bring him.
"Therefore, you must never again speak such words that cause obstacles to a sacrifice.
Sacrifices may be performed without Hari; let him not be a partaker of the sacrificial offerings.
Having heard this, Dadhīci spoke once more with reasoned words.
Hari is in every way the most auspicious among all that is auspicious.
Nevertheless, in the Veda, Viṣṇu is regarded as Nārāyaṇa;
Durvāsas is a portion of Śaṅkara, and indeed, Indra [Śatakratu] is in his hand.
Having fallen, he attained a state devoid of splendor for a moment;
yet, by propitiating Bharga, he regained his own Amarāvatī in the midst of the ocean.
Dharma remains here for the sake of protecting the sacrifice; let it endure forever.

But the King of Dharma was conquered by the white-clad sage Śveta, a devotee of Śiva; I know his power in every respect. Even Kubera, the friend of Tryambaka, will not remain [in his position] without Śiva.
Fire was always his eye situated on the forehead.
When the Moon assailed Tārā, Tryambaka then became a protector for the Preceptor of the Gods, having been propitiated by Bṛhaspati. 165.
When all these people know Śiva as auspicious happiness,
and when that which is yet to come is inauspicious, then this Rudra is indeed Śiva—
if my word as a Brahmin is held in your heart. (166–167)
"Summon Śambhu so that this great sacrifice may proceed;
for without him, even if this rite is performed, it would be as if it were not performed at all.
When Śambhu is present, your desires will surely bear fruit. (168)
As speech is when devoid of meaning, as a body is when devoid of dharma;
as a woman is when devoid of a husband, as a home is when devoid of sons;
as lands are when devoid of the Gaṅgā, as twice-born men are when devoid of sacred learning. (1.174.169–170)
Just as prosperity devoid of charity, or a libation lacking sesame seeds;
just as a kingdom lacking counsel, or happiness without a wife;
just as the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) lacking darbha grass, or an oblation lacking clarified butter. (171)
"Likewise, sacrifices performed without Hara are declared to be fruitless.
Thus it was declared by Dadhīci, yet Dakṣa did not accept it at all;
and being exceedingly enraged, he said: "What concern is this of yours regarding my sacrifice?"
In this world, ritual acts succeed when performed according to their true purpose;
even the act of the Lord would not succeed if performed contrary to that purpose.
Then Dadhīci also said: "Even from performing [the rite] according to its true purpose..."
Moreover, due to the hostility of the Lord, even one's success perishes.
(175) Whether it be inauspicious or auspicious, when he comes to the sacrifice, then the sacrifice will have achieved its purpose; otherwise, there will be ruin. (176)
When Dadhīci spoke thus, Dakṣa became enraged and dispatched his own servants to expel that outcaste of a Brahmin. Seeing Dakṣa utterly deluded by pride, Dadhīci indeed addressed him.
"Why do you drive me away, O fool? May you indeed go far away!
May you always be devoid of all auspicious things along with these [others].
The fire born of your anger shall fall upon your head in a place where it does not belong. (178–179)
Having spoken thus, Dadhīca, the knower of truth, departed from the sacrificial ground;
Cyavana, Agastya, Durvāsas, and likewise Ṛcīka departed;
as did Uddālaka, Upamanyu, Uttaṅka, Garga, and Gautama.
Māṇḍavya, Vāmadeva, Gālava, and the others,
as well as other Śaivas who knew the three periods of time, departed from the sacrifice.
Then Dakṣa, the enemy of Śiva, laughing, spoke to them all.
"Indeed, all thorns have been removed; my assembly has become large.
These wicked men, who are outside the Veda, must certainly be excluded from the sacrificial rites.
The Vedic gods and Brahmins, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu,"
"May you all make my sacrifice fruitful and complete without delay.
(184) When the partisans of Śiva had departed, the great sacrifice proceeded; to those Brāhmaṇas who remained there, he gave double the sacrificial fee. (185)
He bestowed abundant sacrificial fees and gave even more wealth to others;
all his sons-in-law were greatly gratified by him with vast riches.
All the daughters were adorned with ornaments and provided with gifts of great opulence.
The wives of the sages were honored many times over, as were the wives of the gods in great numbers;
likewise, the women of the cities and the women of the provinces were also worshipped.
While the sacrifice was thus being conducted, Dakṣa remained constantly engaged in it.
He fed them, satisfied them, and offered wealth and other gifts;
by that, Agni gradually attained a state of weak digestion day after day.
Through the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*, the gods and others [were likewise satisfied].
The people there are eternally satisfied by means of excellent food, drink, and other provisions.
Mountains of cooked foods have been prepared there in every place;
there are thousands of streams of ghee, streams of honey, and streams of milk.
Heaped up were piles of jaggery, sugar, and fruits;
there were also peaks of fine silk, jewels, and objects of enjoyment.
A sacrificial enclosure was constructed, fashioned from gold and silver.
The sound of auspicious songs pervaded every direction.
The hosts of apsarases rejoiced, the gandharvas were exceedingly delighted, the vidyādharas exulted, and the earth increased greatly in joy. (193–194)
Every day, living beings there are satisfied with their desired objects;
thus does the sacrifice proceed. But Nārada, rising from the sacrificial ground, looked everywhere and saw the sprout of a beautiful quarrel being watered.
Creating doubt in the minds of all during the closing of Rudra’s eyes, he soared into the sky and went to Mount Kailāsa;
at that time, the very intentions of cowards turned toward flight. (196–197)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Dakṣa’s Three Visits to Śambhu’s House in the Kṛta-yuga Lineage of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," including his repeated humiliations, the mutual cursing of Bhṛgu and others in the Naimiṣa forest, Dakṣa’s reviling of Śambhu, the arrival of the gods and others at Dakṣa’s sacrifice in Kanakhala, and the cursing of Dakṣa by Dadhīca due to Śambhu’s non-arrival.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! The house of strife has gone to the house of Rudra. When two houses are united as one, what misfortune does not arise? || 1 ||
Having reached the abode of Śiva by way of the sky, Nārada descended to the ground there in the great garden of Kailāsa for a moment; meanwhile,
Satī rested outside, meditating upon Hari.
She sported with her friends in that very same excellent garden.
There she saw the celestial chariots of her sisters, accompanied by male and female servants, descending from heaven to earth through the sky itself. (3–4)
Indeed, seeing the great splendor of those who had been adorned by their husbands, the virtuous Satī looked at her friend Vijayā and said to Rohiṇī:
"O best of friends, look! This is my sister Rohiṇī."
"Ask her quickly: 'Where is she going, seated in her celestial chariot and joined with the Moon?
(6) Vijayā, having been questioned, quickly ascertained that he was engaged in a sacrificial festival and so forth;
she told her, "She is going there because she is currently at the house of Dakṣa. (7)
Meanwhile, other celestial chariots were traveling along the path of the sky;
beholding them in many ways, Satī reflected in her mind:
"My father is Dakṣa, and my mothers are indeed Asiknī and Vīriṇī."
“They do not summon me; have they forgotten their virtuous daughter?
Thinking thus, Satī quickly went with Śaṅkara to ask him respectfully about the reason for everything. (1.175.10)
Then, having been honored by Śaṅkara, Satī spoke to the Lord:
"I have heard that my father is performing a great sacrifice.
There is a grand festival there, and the great ṛṣis have assembled."
"In that regard, tell me why your going does not please you.
"We two must go there so that many may see us.
Śambhu said: "Dakṣa is particularly hostile toward me. (12–13)
"O virtuous lady, those who have arrived at your father’s sacrifice are proud and devoid of knowledge.
Since there is no place for me in that ritual, how shall we proceed?
For those people who go to another's house uninvited [are ill-fated]."
They undergo such humiliation that it exceeds even death.
Since even Indra becomes insignificant when he has gone to another's house, therefore neither you nor I should go to that home. (15–16)
Even when pierced by the arrows of an enemy,
a person does not suffer as much as they are tormented by the harsh words of their own kin that pierce the vital organs.
Because she performed austerities directed toward me, she was wedded by me.
If one like me had not practiced austerities, how could he have fallen into this snare?
When pride arises from learning, power, and the like, the wicked indeed take no account of the virtues of the virtuous; they pay no heed to great men.
Having heard this, the Goddess immediately spoke to her own protector:
"Why were we not invited by Dakṣa? I wish to know the truth of this.
O Lord, grant me permission to go today to Dakṣa’s sacrifice."
Śambhu said to Satī: "O virtuous lady, your desire to go is powerful.
If it is so, then mount the bull, which is ready and adorned;
having performed the rites befitting a great queen and having led many attendants, depart. (21–22)
"O Subhūṣitā, go to the sacrifice, distinguished by the parasol and the chowries. In the meantime, Nārada also arrived there before Hara.
Having seen the two Śivas and having prostrated, he was then honored with great respect by Śambhu.
The great sage sat down upon the beautiful seat provided by him.
Śambhu said: "O sage, how was this audience granted by you?
If there is anything wonderful, tell it quickly and do not delay."
Having received this command, the celestial sage related that event to Śaṅkara:
"Today, having seen what seemed like a void near Haridvāra on the Blue Mountain (Nīlagiri),
I have arrived in your presence."
Whatever collection of men exists in the three worlds, along with their wives, sons,
and so forth— adorned, equal [to one another], and with lotus-faces full of joy—
I have seen all this at Dakṣa’s sacrifice; yet your pair has not been beheld.
Generally, not seeing you there caused great distress;
indeed, Dakṣa’s words, which pierced the very vitals, were heard.
Having heard those words censuring you, it is truly impossible to recount them.
But I closed my ears and did not respond to what was said by Dadhīci.
(1.175.30) Dakṣa, having been cursed, abandoned the sacrifice; and many of the twice-born, headed by Durvāsas, departed upon hearing the censure of Śambhu. (3.1)
The great sacrifice proceeded with those who had transgressed against Dakṣa’s faction;
as for those sisters there who were the attendants of their own masters,
they received honor from Dakṣa himself, of which I am not able to speak.
"In this matter, that which is to be done should be performed; I am now departing.
When Nārada had gone, the Goddess, with palms joined in reverence, said to Śaṅkara:
"Be victorious, O destroyer of Andhaka! Grant me permission, O Lord."
"Having gone, I shall see the wickedness; how have we two been rejected?
Śambhu said to his beloved: "The sacrifice must be attended; it does not appear to me that there is any purpose in going.
What is incomplete for you here? Do not go even for the sake of an investigation. (35)
"Why do you wish to abandon me? No good is seen in going.
Satī said: "My mind will certainly remain fixed upon your feet;
I am going to see my father's sacrifice, for I have never before witnessed a sacrifice."

Śambhu said: "If you look down [at me], then I shall take back the sacrifice—the ritual, as well as the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa) and the world-protectors. Quickly appoint other sages to the office of officiating priest."
Satī said, "The sacrificial rite of my father must not be witnessed by me.
Then Śambhu spoke to the Goddess, who had forcibly mounted the bull:
"O Goddess, today in the western direction the day is inauspicious and marked by a spike of ill omen. (1.175.40)
"The lunar days, constellations, and astrological conjunctions have indeed become adverse.
O Goddess, do not go; having departed today, you shall not see me again.
Then Satī spoke: "If by name I am truly Satī..."
"Then, even by means of another body, I shall perform service for you.
To this, Bhava spoke again: "Who is capable of restraining either a woman or a man whose mental disposition is possessed by such obstinacy?"
"Do not go, O Goddess; having left me, you will not meet me again.
Furthermore, O Goddess, those who desire the wealth of great honor must not go [elsewhere], even to the homes of their mother and father, without being invited, O Beloved. (44)
"O Goddess, I tell you the truth: there shall be no further sight of me.
The Goddess said: "If [my heart] is attached to your two lotus-feet, then you alone shall be my lord in another birth."
Having spoken thus, the goddess departed with her mind forcibly blinded;
she did not then bow to Śambhu, nor did she perform a circumambulation.
For that very reason, the goddess went away and never returned.
Seeing that Satī departing, even the god was pained in his heart.
He said to the Gaṇas: "Let them go with the goddess, accompanied by their armies;
let Satī indeed depart, having ascended the celestial chariot bearing the insignia of Śaṅkara."

The Goddess, having ascended her celestial chariot, proceeded to the courtyard of the sacrificial ground; indeed, Śaṅkara provided for her all the services due to a Great Queen, including excellent parasols, chowries, fine garments, and ornaments.
Sixty thousand fierce hosts went forth by the command of Śiva.
Equipped with weapons, mounted on vehicles, and filled with curiosity and festive joy,
she descended with speed from her celestial chariot into the courtyard of the sky.
Upon entering the sacrificial enclosure, her joy increased;
the beloved of Śiva was honored by Vāmadeva and the other sages.
The Gaṇas were filled with wonder and sang the praises of the two Śivas.
The leaders of the Gaṇas leaped and performed acrobatic jumps in the sky.
The world was filled with cries of "Victory, O Ambikā! Victory, O Śambhu!
Dakṣāyaṇī then went to that sacrificial ground of great splendor.
Having paid homage to the god Agni and to the assembly gathered in the pavilion— which was filled with the curiosity of gods, asuras, great sages,
and others— he then went to his father’s palace to drink water.
He beheld that beautiful and radiant place, filled with various wonders,
inhabited by his mother’s sisters, daughters, their sons, grandsons, and others.
And he saw Satī, as well as Asiknī and Vīriṇī, who had arrived there.
Her sisters also showed her due respect as was fitting;
they gave her water for drinking and other refreshments, as well as a seat that granted comfort and peace.
Having rested for a moment and then bowed to her mother and her sisters, [she sat down].
Quickly descending from her seat, she went alone to the sacrificial arena.
There, having bowed to her father as well as other eminent elders,
she was joined by her mother and the other women wearing crowns, all of whom were adorned with auspicious ornaments and attire.
And the sisters with their husbands, both elder and younger, adorned with new ornaments— housewives filled with wonder and joy,
gazing on her with amazement, exclaiming, "Oh, Satī has arrived! (62).

Having bowed down to all those who were like her elder mothers and beloved of Hara, Satī went before Dakṣa in the assembly gathered in the pavilion. Questioned by her father and mother, she was told: "Is it well that you have come? (63–64)
"Come, stay, dear daughter! Is your son-in-law free from illness? And do they too indeed possess that heavenly happiness which is eternal and free from all affliction?
Satyuvāca said: "If my parents are happy, then I am happy."
Moreover, your son-in-law Śiva is indeed always happy.
The only sorrow in this situation is that he is not seen;
for he, by whose presence the sacrifice would have been made complete, is not present here.
"If my welfare were to arise from this union, why have neither Śambhu nor I been invited to this great festival? Other sons-in-law and daughters-in-law have been invited as a matter of course. (68)
"Having abandoned Satī and Śambhu, how can there be well-being or auspiciousness for you?
Indeed, I perceive misfortune and inauspiciousness here within a mere moment.
Having spoken thus, she shed teardrops in the presence of her father.
Dakṣa said: "O daughter, O most fortunate one, O most auspicious one!
There is not even the slightest fault in you; do not let your mind be filled with grief.
Cast off your agitation and remain at ease; the fault lies entirely with me."
O Śarva, since I, lacking in wisdom, have bestowed this jewel of a maiden upon you;
had I known that you, though the Lord, were devoid of mastery over the inner self,
then how could I have given her to you, O auspicious one, who are the master of illusion?
I have been deceived by one named Śiva into performing inauspicious deeds;
yet this very person has been praised by Brahmā in many ways before me:
"This is Śaṅkara, this is Śambhu, Śiva is one whose name is truly meaningful. (74)
Give him your virtuous daughter; she is in every way worthy of him.
He is Śrīkaṇṭha, he is Maheśa, he is the omniscient one whose banner bears the bull;
he is the archer whose name is truly meaningful—give him your daughter Satī.
Thus, having instilled confidence in you, the Creator indeed caused you to be given away;
yet that Virūpākṣa—the bull-rider, the consumer of poison, the dweller in the cremation ground, the bearer of the trident, and the bearer of the skull—was not recognized. (77)
He is charming through association with the double-tongued [serpents], a reservoir of water, and possesses matted locks (kaparda).
His head is marked by a stain, and he is smeared with dust and grime.
At times he wears a loincloth, and at times he is naked like one driven mad by the wind.
In some places he was clothed in skins, in others he delighted in wandering for alms;
accompanied by hideous beings, he was as motionless as a pillar and possessed of fierce tamas-guṇa.
Rudra, with his fierce retinue, assumed the body of Mahākāla.
Surrounded by a circle of human skulls and devoid of caste or lineage, he was described as virtuous by Brahmā; yet, knowing this, I have been deceived.
What more need be said, O daughter who possesses every excellence? (8.1–8.2)
Where [is he] who is clothed in a tattered garment of dust, adorned with a great conch shell, wearing armlets of coiled serpents, and possessing a mass of matted hair that is grey with ash;
whose fingertips are occupied with a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), and who bears the crescent moon? (8.3)
One who delights in the ostentation of the *tāṇḍava* dance and whose every action is inauspicious—
where is such a Hara, and where is this sacrifice, the abode of all auspiciousness?
For this very reason, you two were not invited to this auspicious sacrifice.
"Suitable silk garments and jeweled ornaments, as well as the finest necklaces and decorations, were already set aside by me for your sake.
Look at them all, my daughter; they have been preserved, so take them! || 86 ||
"O daughter, O virtuous lady, whatever you desire to bring for the sake of Śaṅkara must all be taken along with you after the completion of the sacrifice,
so that these friends and sisters of yours may dwell together at the sacrificial rite. (87–88)
"Stay here for even longer than that, if it pleases you.
Hearing this, Satī, her heart deeply pained, began to speak.
She beheld the portions [of the sacrifice] belonging to the gods, Viṣṇu and the others, at that sacrificial rite.
Seeing Śambhu’s arrival, he began to speak of his distress:
"I heard nothing at all while you were speaking, father;
having now heard those two words of yours, I shall relate them to you."
This very Lord of Māyā, though knowing all, was himself deceived;
this which you have declared is true: he is indeed the Lord of Māyā, the Supreme Brahman and the Supreme Self, existing in the form of Śiva. (92)
Śiva is indeed possessed of *māyā*, yet he is distinct from *māyā*.
You were deceived previously, and you are deceived even now; having given away your daughter without understanding [the truth], you are speaking incoherently after the gift has been made. (93–94)
Śambhu thought thus: "Why did he not give me [the fruit] then?
Your mind was not the cause there; rather, the cause was the weight of my own merit, by which this entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, has been purified. (95)
He is the sacrifice, the best among those who know sacrifice, the limb of sacrifice, and the sacrificial fee.
Śambhu himself is the performer of the sacrifice; without him, how can there be a rite?
Behold, O Dakṣa, in this very moment, how my body itself becomes the sacrifice.
Oh, by the mere remembrance of whom everything becomes purified—
without that Śambhu, everything performed is as if unperformed.
All substances, mantras, and so forth, which are considered as offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya), [are likewise rendered fruitless].

"Indeed, everything performed without Śambhu will become impure. Did you show such disregard because you considered Śiva to be no different from the common gods? Or has your intellect entirely failed, as if you were in old age? (1.175.100)
"Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and all others know him as the Supreme Lord;
you do not know that Śambhu—do not think otherwise.
"How have these, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the rest, come to this sacrifice?"
Even though they know [the truth], their eyes do not feel shame in the presence of Śambhu.
O Viṣṇu, you are seen here at this sacrifice having abandoned Mahādeva;
you do not feel shame, for you proceed here having forgotten your eternal friend.
O Brahmā, you became five-faced out of pride toward Hara;
he made you four-faced, and yet you have forgotten that miracle.
If Mahādeva were angry, he would destroy even all four [faces].
O Sūrya, Candra, Indra, and others, you do not know Śaṅkara.
Nor indeed do the sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and the rest, know Śaṅkara—he by whom the blazing thunderbolt was [mastered] and likewise Kāma was consumed. 105–106.
By him, at the collapse of the Liṅga in the Dāru forest, the world was set ablaze;
do you perhaps forget his wonders from former births?
If he were to fall into a rage, what would become of you? (107)
"Everyone has fallen into some kind of folly, except for Śambhu;
depart!"—thus did the Great Goddess speak these words at the sacrifice, Satī, who was there accompanied by Kauśikī and whose heart was tormented with grief. || 108-109 ||
Having heard this, the assembly became silent and overwhelmed with fear.

Listen, Lakṣmī, then the enraged Dakṣa spoke these words that bring about destruction: "What is the use of saying much more to you? Indeed, there is no further business for you at present. (1.175.110)
"Go, or stay, daughter; why have you come here?
Having arrived at this sacrifice, you treat one worthy of all honor with contempt.
Go, or dwell here in silence; you were not invited, O shameless woman! || 111–112 ||
Your husband is inauspicious—he is the king of ghosts, spirits, and piśācas; he is of low birth and outside the Vedic fold. He was not invited by me there at that time.
Yet, urged by Brahmā, I offered you to him in the assembly of celestial rishis.
"What could happen to one of such little fortune who has not understood the purpose of Rudra?
O Rudrāṇī, do not give way to anger; be composed, O lady of pure smiles!
Since you have come to my sacrifice, accept for yourself the gift."
Then, having heard the censure of Śambhu, that virtuous woman reflected in her heart:
"Even if I take this gift, what would become of me? How indeed shall I go to Śaṅkara?
If questioned there by Śaṅkara, what answer shall I give?"
"Therefore, I must die right here; I shall attain Hara in another body.
Having thus resolved, she sighed and spoke to her father:
"O father, what is the use of my life while I hear such reproach against my husband?"
He who reviles Mahādeva, or hears him being reviled—
both of them go to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
If one is able, one should indeed forcibly cut out the tongue of the reviler.
"If I am unable [to endure it], I shall go to another place, covering my ears.
"Though forbidden by Śambhu, I have come here by force;
I have obtained the fruit of that [action] here. Where should I go now?"
She felt remorse for having spoken those words against Śiva;
having become enraged, she spoke fearlessly to Dakṣa regarding the sages and the gods:
"O father, you are a reviler of Śambhu, and you shall come to repentance."
"Let this smoke not become the cause of rain here for your sacrifice;
rather, let it surely be the cause of tears for those who have come to enjoy the sacrifice. Clearly, you all have indeed encountered those who are hostile to Śambhu. (123–124)
I shall perform a counter-sacrifice against those who oppose me, a purification of the sacrifice;
without Śambhu, no sacrifice can exist, so I shall satisfy the sacrificial fire. Dakṣa offers his own [oblation] into his own fire, yet he is counted among my own followers.
"I shall offer my own self and all that belongs to me into the fire; I will perform my sacrifice for myself.
What is the use of many words? O Hari, the foolish Dakṣa is always wicked; I have no need whatsoever for a body produced from him."
Fie on that birth which brings about the contempt of the great! Indeed, the very connection with such a birth must be specifically abandoned.
When dejected, Śambhu always says to me, "O Daughter of Dakṣa."
Therefore, this loathsome corpse born from the body of Dakṣa must certainly be cast away;
it must surely be abandoned here and offered into the fire.
One must not listen to the reproaches of the lord of one's life as long as one lives.
He spoke these final truthful words: "May those who revile Śiva perish!
But I, in the fire blazing with wrath that has the form of Mahādeva, shall offer the fuel of my body by means of the practice of breath-restraint."

Having spoken thus, Satī then slowly performed breath control (prāṇāyāma). As soon as Satī had firmly restrained her breath, the breath of all the gods and others was likewise restrained at that moment.
The fire did not blaze as it had before with offerings of clarified butter;
at that very moment, the mantras became blunted in their efficacy.
A great whirlwind arrived, capable of shaking the mountains.
In an instant, the ground of the sacrificial pavilion was made uneven by him.
Suddenly, there occurred a fall of lightning that caused the earth to tremble;
meteors fell from the sky, and *piśāca* demons broke into dance. (135–136)
In the sky above, the swooping vultures formed circles;
there, jackals howled fiercely and inauspiciously at the enemies of the gods.
And there, clouds signaled an extreme ill omen by raining down blood.
A thunderous roar arose from the earth, making the heart tremble;
divine weapons fought one another most terrifyingly;
and the great sacrificial materials were defiled by jackals and dogs.
At that time, through the restraint of all [senses], the true suppressions of the vital breaths occurred;
the sacrificial ground became motionless like a cemetery grove.
Whatever was placed there remained fixed in that very spot.
And likewise, by the power of restraining their breath, they became as if fixed in a painting;
at that time, Cakradhara and the others became utterly motionless.
Then the Goddess, having drawn her breath outward, quelled the terror.

Although this miracle was displayed by the Goddess, the King of the Dakṣas, his intellect destroyed by pride, did not utter a word calling for Śaṅkara. Satī, having become silent, remembered her husband Śambhu with reverence.
Then, with her mind completely stilled, she suddenly sat down upon the ground.
Having sipped water according to the rules and purified herself by covering her body with her garment, she closed her eyes, remembered her husband, and adopted the practice of yoga. (144–145)
Having again equalized the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, she then raises the *udāna* and *samāna* from the navel-center (*nābhicakra*) and leads them upward;
having reached the heart and then the chest, she proceeds from the throat to the space between the eyebrows.
Bringing [the fire] through the middle channel, she went with great haste to the aperture of the day (dyurandhra).
Abiding in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), she produced fire;
indeed, her body was set ablaze by the fire from the aperture of Brahmā. || 147–148 ||
Rising from the sky through the air, he descended into the fire-pit;
Satī, coming within the range of sight, was reduced to ashes in the pit.
As they watched her in the sky and on the ground, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
"The entire world cried out 'Alas! Alas!', and Viṣṇu, the gods, and others were struck with fear.

(1.175.150) Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Satī’s Observation of Her Sisters’ Palaces from the Sky; Śambhu’s Command to Go to Dakṣa’s Sacrifice; Nārada’s Arrival at Kailāsa; Dadhīci’s Departure from the Sacrifice; Satī’s Presence at the Sacrifice; the Disappearance of Śaṅkara’s Throne; Satī’s Words to Dakṣa; and Satī’s Abandonment of Her Body," in the first section, the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (Chapter 175)
