Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī! For what kind of terror-inducing thing was that?
Indeed, no one other than her father could have done such a thing to one who has no protector.
When Satī’s body had been reduced to ashes, the visible assembly was then filled with compassion, and a piteous exchange of words arose among them:
"Alas! Śambhu’s supreme beloved has today cast off her life out of anger!"
Behold with your own eyes the wickedness of this Prajāpati!
Even the heart of him whose subjects consist of both the moving and the unmoving is always agitated, enraged, harsh, and parched—alas, such is the misery of saṃsāra! (3–4)

Always the beloved of Śaṅkara and ever worthy of honor by the virtuous, she became dejected even during that great festival because of Dakṣa. Therefore, his heart was filled with unbearable resentment; he reviled Brahmā and held his daughter in contempt.
He shall incur great infamy throughout all the worlds—
he who, hating Śambhu, rejected his own daughter when she approached him.
By abandoning his daughter through such an offense, he shall experience the torments of the great hells.
While the people were speaking thus upon seeing Satī’s separation from her life,
the cruel attendants suddenly rose up with weapons raised;
all sixty thousand of them surrounded the sacrificial ground.
"Let no one go outside; let them slay [him] on the sacrificial ground!
Crying out with cries of 'Alas!', saying 'Fie, fie upon Dakṣa!', let them kill, destroy, and crush him in the precinct of the sacrifice! || 9-10 ||
Then, O beloved, the sky was filled with cries of "Alas! Alas!
All the gods, as well as the sages and others who were present, were seized by fear, thinking, "An unprovoked battle has begun; surely the dissolution of the world is at hand. (11)
They indeed carried out a great slaughter of those who had come to Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
With extremely sharp, life-destroying weapons, they struck down the vital organs [of their enemies].
Thus, twenty thousand were slain there by the faction of Dakṣa at that time.
Others, raising their weapons, set out to destroy Dakṣa.

Seeing the force of those as they rushed forward, the venerable Bhṛgu then offered oblations into the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni) with a sacrificial formula (yajuṣ) that slays the destroyers of sacrifice.
As the oblation was being offered, thousands of Ṛbhus rose up;
all of them, equipped with firebrands as weapons and endowed with the power of Bhṛgu’s fire,
fought there against the Pramathas with the intent of offering their very lives.
There, being struck down by the powerful Ṛbhus, twenty thousand of the virtuous women were killed;
the remainder fled.
Of the armies on Dakṣa’s side, one hundred thousand went to the abode of Yama.
At that time, thinking "those venerable persons— the pure Viṣṇus and Brahman-sages—
must not be slain," the earth-dwellers (Brahmins) were likewise not killed.
Then those sages, the gods led by Śakra, together with the hosts of Maruts, [acted].
The Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the world-protectors (Lokapālas), and the planets and other celestial bodies remained silent,
stationed in their respective aerial chariots upon the path of the sky;
anxious, they repeatedly prayed for the absence of obstacles.
The sons-in-law of Dakṣa, the daughters of Dakṣa, and the householders of Dakṣa—
[all these] were protected with great effort by the hosts of Viṣṇu and the Brahman-sages.
Then the sacrificial ground was purified by the removal of the corpses.
Then, on the sacrificial ground, all were stationed once more due to Dakṣa’s taking hold [of them];
thereafter, with the desire for the completion of the sacrifice, the rite of oblation (homa) quickly took place.
In the meantime, a voice from the sky spoke there:
"O Dakṣa, O you of wicked conduct, O hypocrite, O great villain!
What is this that you have done, O fool? You have brought about your own ruin;
Dadhīci has departed after casting a curse upon your sacrifice, and you did not realize it."
O ignorant one! You did not honor your worthy eldest daughter who had come to your home; out of pride, you did not worship Śiva and Śivā;
and regarding Satī as merely a daughter, you did not propitiate her who bestows the fruit [of liberation]. || 26 ||
You have not propitiated the virtuous goddess who bestows all auspicious fortune;
you have not worshipped the Goddess who grants the welfare of her devotees;
and you have not delighted the Power (Śakti) who removes all fears by bowing down before her.

He did not propitiate with love the Goddess who is bowed down by her devotees and who grants their heart's desires; he did not worship the Sovereign who bestows fame and prosperity after meditating upon her;
nor did he feed the Mother who grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He did not hold in his heart her who is the protector, the nourisher, and the destroyer; he did not lead her, the progenitor of all creation, to peace;
nor did he offer a portion of Śambhu to the consort of Śambhu at the sacrifice.
For the perfected ones perform austerities, and virtuous women desire a vision of them;
likewise, yogis engage in yogic practices out of a longing to behold them.
Yet he did not show due honor to those two, who are the parents of the entire world.
Therefore, the destruction of this sacrifice will certainly come to pass.
Since you have not honored those who deserved honor, how can there be any prosperity?
Misfortune has been transferred to you, and calamities have likewise been transferred to you.
"Thinking, 'May I attain prosperity without having worshipped Śivā and Śambhu'—what has come over you that you have become so arrogant? Your pride shall perish today.
Having turned your back on Śaṅkara, who among these gods is there for you?"
I do not see anyone here who can provide assistance—
not the gods nor any others who are currently your allies; they will surely meet their destruction by fire, like moths.
Let your head blaze up, and let the sacrificial offerings also burn!
Let your companions enter into this inauspicious state and be consumed by flames!
Let the gods depart from this sacrificial ground along with their own followers.
"Today, at this very spot, there shall be destruction for those who remain here in another moment.
Let the children, the elders, the women, and others depart from the sacrificial ground;
O Viṣṇu, O Brahmā, let the two luminaries [the sun and moon] also depart from the site of the sacrifice."
"Otherwise, your destruction will surely occur in the next moment.
Having thus addressed them all, the celestial voice indeed ceased;
yet those who had gone to the sacrificial ground did not depart, as they were destined for destruction by fate.
Even though he was filled with grief, that time of sacrifice was for the sake of completing the sacrifice alone;
they quickly performed the oblation, and the sacrificial rite proceeded.
Then, immediately after the burning of Satī, the divine Lord Nārada [arrived] swiftly. 42–43.
He went to Kailāsa to relate the entire account of Satī to Hara; having approached Śambhu and bowed to Hara, the Wind-god displayed his distress, sorrow, and dejection. (44)
Generating excessive compassion and manifesting fear, shedding tears from his eyes and trembling, he said to Śaṅkara:
"It is observed that there can be no subversion of Māyā by one who is free from Māyā. (49–50)
Even if everything were to perish, what concern could there be for a yogi in this matter?
Nothing of yours would diminish, nor would anything of yours increase. Because of your imperishability and your perfection, whence could there be loss or gain for you?
Today, Dakṣa has indeed encroached upon your sovereignty with his foot.
For one to whom honor and dishonor, as well as blame and praise, are equal,
and for whom loss and gain are not reckoned— what indeed can Ravi do before such a person?
Even when his own destruction was imminent, he did not tremble at all;
why then did he vainly accumulate that burden born of power and treasury? He possessed no wealth of pride, nor any sorrow born of contempt.
He related everything before him, just as the story had been told before the queen.
Before one who is free from pride, a woman full of pride is excellent;
she is blessed who belongs to one without pride, for she is truly a virtuous wife.
"O Sage, is she heard, or is she sleeping, or do you even have ears, or not?
For, upon hearing your censure, that virtuous woman has treated her own life as a blade of grass.
Having heard this, Śambhu then became like another Mahākāla.
Rudra became exceedingly fierce, inflamed by the fire of his great wrath.
With a terrifying countenance, he then spoke quickly to Nārada:
"Huṃ! Huṃ! Huṃ! What has happened there? He has treated his own life as if it were a blade of grass!"
"O Nārada! What do you say? Satī has abandoned her life?
"Ḍūṃh ḍūṃh ḍūṃh ḍūṃh ḍūṃh ḍamāk ḍaṃ ḍūṃh! Having sounded his *ḍamaru* drum, Śaṅkara, with fury, violently shook his matted locks and struck them against the surface of the earth. 56.
From the violent collision, a great smoky vapor arose, digging into the earth.
From the midst of that, a mountain with a towering mass of flames emerged;
from that mountain was born Girideva, who causes even Death at the end of time to tremble.
Manifest in the form of an image, he was as terrifying as Rudra;
Vīrabhadra was another Rudra, possessing the prowess of the hundred Rudras.
At that time, there was a mace in his hand equal in size to Mount Mandara.
His Bhūśuṇḍī was as long as the Vindhya mountain, and his iron club like Mount Raivata.
His two eyes were wide open like the sun and the moon;
his lolling tongue resembled the flaming crest of the goddess Jvālāmukhī.
His chest shone like Mount Arbuda.
Grasping the peak of the Himalaya quickly between his big toe and his toes,
he held it against his belly like Śiva holds the crescent moon.
Having bowed to Śambhu, he then said: "What service may I perform for you?
At your command, I shall swallow the entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, as a single morsel;
I shall drink all the oceans with a single handful."
Having exchanged the netherworlds, I shall lead them downward and even upward;
here I shall bring the world-protectors, including Indra, seizing them by their hair.
Likewise, having bound Time and Death, I shall bring them into your presence.
"In the battle against the Daityas and Dānavas, I shall slay the powerful ones.
Behold, from my falling upon the ground, the circle of the earth trembles;
and with my two arms, I shall crush all the mountains by my might."
"What is the use of much speaking? Grant me your command; there is nothing that is impossible for me.
Know that today, having relied upon the power of your feet, my thought has been accomplished.
Having spoken thus, Vīrabhadra, possessing a thousand uplifted arms, [stood ready].
As long as he held the dust of Śambhu’s feet upon his head in his presence, so long did the Gaṇas arrive there from the sacrifice weeping and said:
"O God, Mahādeva! Protect us who have come to you for refuge!"
O Lord, listen with respectful interest to the detailed account of Satī.
Out of pride, Dakṣa showed Satī disrespect;
he did not give her a share for you, yet he offered portions to the gods.
Hearing these harsh words, Satī became enraged at the sacrifice and spoke aloud.
Having reproached her father many times, she consumed her own body in the sacrificial fire.
At that time, forty thousand Gaṇas perished in the rite.
Out of shame, they engaged in a fierce battle and were slain at the sacrifice;
likewise, our own factions and the Gaṇas who had brought about the destruction of the sacrifice were then killed at the sacrifice by the Ṛbhus produced through the oblation of Bhṛgu.
Others, who were originally intended to be a hundred thousand, were indeed slain by the hosts of Dakṣa.
Nevertheless, having purified the sacrificial ground,
Dakṣa and the celestial sages who support his side continue to perform the sacrifice.
They do not grieve for Satī, nor do they even remember Śambhu;
laughing at the destruction of Satī, they point their teeth at you.
Your dishonor toward Satī was especially manifest at that sacrifice.
All those wicked ones, Dakṣa and the others, became exceedingly arrogant. [They said:
"For the sake of reviving our lost hosts, please grant us the mantra that turns ashes into gold; grant us the nectar-like shower! || 78-79 ||
In that regard, grant me the great power of absorption (*mahālayā-śakti*) so that I may destroy and obstruct those others, Bhṛgu and the rest, whom they are about to produce.
This [power], known as *Kālakavala*, was bestowed upon Śambhu by Brahmā.
That mantra was bestowed by Śambhu upon the wise Vīrabhadra.
Having brandished his weapon in wrath, he should employ it upon seeing his enemies;
for that is the "Mantra of the Mouth of Time," let it be granted to others as well.
"Oṃ mṛte-mṛtyo mahāmṛtyo, be firm together with Mṛtyā!
Oṃ mṛti-mṛtyo mahāmṛtyau, be hidden along with your own Mṛtyā!"—
thus, preceded by the *phuṭkāra* sound, [he should cast] whatever weapon there may be, such as arrows and the like.
One should hurl it into the body of the enemy; having died, he does not live again.
At that time, Vīrabhadra was instructed by Lord Śaṅkara himself, and he was likewise empowered there by the command of Śaṅkara.
Then, having smeared his body with ashes and performed ten thousand oblations (*homa*) into the fire,
and having performed one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) right there with bodies as vast as ten thousand [yojanas],
he mastered the Kāla-mantra and caused his bodies to dissolve.

Then, becoming once again a solitary being, the great destroyer Vīrabhadra prepared himself for departure and requested permission from the Earth. Hara, moreover, [learned] from Nārada that the body of Satī had been reduced to ashes.
Having heard his own censure from the assemblies and the extreme arrogance of Dakṣa,
he struck his own matted locks upon the ground in anger and violently dashed them against it for the sake of destroying Dakṣa and everyone else.

Out of intense anger, he shook [them] from all sides and rubbed them away. From the power known as Mahālaya, through the expansion of his matted locks and their striking, fevers were produced; those called Kālikā arose from the rubbing.
By his shaking, hosts were born in numbers of arbudas and arbuda-koṭis; by the clapping of his hands, millions of spirits (*bhūta*) who cause great terror appeared.
There were goddesses of the *mahālaya* class, numbering in the tens of millions and even arbudas.
Armed with weapons, possessing eight excellent hands, and proud of their fresh youth;
having forms that inspire extreme terror, they have exerted themselves in the acts of war—these thirteen crores of cruel fevers, personified in bodily form. (93–94)
Armed with weapons, they bring about the end of destruction; never returning to their enemies, these great Caṇḍīs, such as Kālikā and others, dance upon the field of battle.
Abounding in the power of mantras and weapons, these Mahākālīs are terrifying.
All the hosts, numbering in the millions and even tens of millions,
equipped with weapons and armor, experts in missiles and the like, and skilled in warfare,
rushed toward Hara, blazing through the ten directions. || 96-97 ||
Beholding the gateway of Śambhu’s command, they indeed made haste to prepare.
An entirely new and innumerable army appeared there on Kailāsa.
Vīrabhadra said to Hara: "O Lord, give your orders quickly."
"O Śambhu, I could dry up the oceans in half a moment;
I could grind the mountains there in half a moment;
and in a single instant, I could reduce the universe or even the gods to ashes. (1.176.100)
All the worlds have fallen into ruin; tell me, what should I do?
I bow to you, O Mahādeva; again and yet again, I prostrate myself before you.
Even the throbbing of your left limbs brings about victory.
"An unprecedented surge of joy and enthusiasm has arisen within me.
O Śambhu, send me quickly; tell me at once what task must be done.
Then Śambhu, his eyes copper-red, spoke to Vīrabhadra.
Out of pride, Dakṣa is quickly performing a sacrifice in opposition to me;
therefore, having reduced that sacrifice along with its assembly and attendants to ashes,
return once more to Kailāsa— go quickly and make haste!
Whether they be gods opposed to me, or Gandharvas, or other sages;
whether they be seers, or Brahmins, or whoever else has assembled there—
reduce even them to ashes instantly and with haste this very day.
If Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Mahendra, or even Yama should take the side of Dakṣa, reduce them all to ashes! Those who,
transgressing the opinion of Dadhīci, have become partisans of Dakṣa—
"O Bhadraka, reduce those who remain at the sacrifice to ashes!
(108) Even though they have been warned by a voice from the sky, they still do not go outside;
O Bhadraka, reduce those enemies of my sacrifice to ashes! (109)
O Bhadraka, reduce to ashes those who obtained wealth at Dakṣa’s sacrifice and who proclaim the superiority of Dakṣa— those who were consumed by the nose of Śambhu along with Satī;
and even those belonging to Dakṣa’s faction who, upon seeing the fear of death, [fled].
Let them be yours for a moment; reduce even them to ashes!
Whether they be gods or sons of gods, Manus or sons of Manu, Brahmās or sons of Brahmā, or even their grandsons—whosoever they may be, if they are wicked. (111–112)
"Reduce to ashes all those who oppose Satī and Śambhu— those with their wives and those with their sons— and afterwards drink the water.
Thus addressed, Vīrabhadra became repeatedly possessed by a fit of blood-red fury.
Likewise, there arose the fierce possession by Rudra and the possession by Kāla;
it was invisible and unassailable even by Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā.
There occurred the possession of dissolution and the terrifying possession of fear.
Then, from his head, oceans of the fire of time emerged;
having bowed to Śaṅkara while setting the cosmic egg ablaze, he set forth.
Nārada also, having clearly perceived Kali, went before the sacrifice.
He spoke to Viṣṇu, Śakra, Brahmā, and likewise to the gods:
"Vīrabhadra is approaching; he is a terrifying destruction.
Therefore, depart from here; do not let them see the abode of Yama."
This time is not merely the destroyer of family and kinship;
therefore, those of sound intellect must flee from the onsets of dissolution.
Having heard this, Viṣṇu, Yama, Brahmā, Indra, the gods, and others—
Those who despised Dakṣa’s faction departed from that sacrifice.
Accompanied by their wives and retinues, seated within their respective celestial chariots,
they traveled along the path of the sky, proceeding further and further away.

Then, having discerned through the rites of oblation that the armies of the hosts beginning with Ṛbhu, Śambhu, Dhara, and Ambhu numbered nine hundred million (*arbudas*) and nine *parārdhas*, Bhṛgu brought them under control by means of the wrath of Dakṣa.
Armed with weapons and accompanied by fires, assuming forms at will both beautiful and hideous,
those Yakṣas and Rākṣasas— skilled solely in combat, devoid of mantras, and lacking life-force— became ready upon the earth and in the sky. (123–124)
The sacrificial rite proceeds; only its completion remains.
Since the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is to take place at midday, the officiating priests then perform the sacrificial duties with great haste. (125)
However, due to the curse of Satī and the words of Dadhīci,
the sacrifice was not to be completed; indeed, before even midday had passed,
Vīrabhadra arrived with an army numbering in the hundreds of millions.
From a distance of a hundred yojanas, the roar of the army was heard approaching;
from ten yojanas behind, a mountain of dust was seen rising.
Within a short interval, those followers of Śaṅkara were seen resembling mountains.
Terrifying and fierce hosts of warriors, clad in armor,
descended and alighted from the sky upon the armies of the Ṛbhus;
they also descended upon the armies of the Śṛṅbhus on the earth and upon the forces of the Dharāmbhus.
Then Śambhu dispatched another hundred crores of great hosts of attendants following Vīrabhadra, who had arisen from his own breath;
by them the sky was overspread, and they moved at his sides and behind him.
Indeed, the peaks of the mountains were torn away by some;
by others, the mountains were uprooted from their very crests to their foundations. Some, having uprooted *śāla* trees, departed taking them with them.
All the attendants of the Destroyer of Time (Kāla) were in the form of Rudra;
ten thousand times ten thousand lions, tigers, crocodiles, and elephants,
holding millions and hundreds of thousands of vehicles and mounts, [followed].
The armies went there, and as they departed, a rain of flowers fell.
Kālī, Kātyāyanī, Īśānī, Cāmuṇḍā, Muṇḍamardinī,
Bhadrakālī, as well as Bhadrā, Kauśikī, and Vaiṣṇavī likewise [departed].
Accompanied by these nine Durgās, Mahākālī, assuming a terrible form, went forth with great haste for the destruction of Dakṣa.
She was joined by Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, hosts of Bhūtas, Pramathas, and Guhyakas.
The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Parpaṭas, Caṭakas, and Brahmarākṣasas;
the Bhairavas, Kṣetrapālas, Vetālas, and Vināyakas—all these heroes, destroyers of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, went forth with haste. (138–139)
In the same way, the circle of Yoginīs, accompanied by sixty-four hosts and joined by ten million Vetālinīs, suddenly set forth in a state of wrath.
And Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas, advanced with ten million [attendants].
Kekarākṣa with ten, Vikṛta with eight,
Viśākha with four, Pāriyātrika with nine, Sarvāṅka with six, and likewise Vīra and Vikṛtānana with six. (141–142)
Jvālakeśa went with twelve crores, while Jīma went with seven;
Dudrubha went with eight crores, and Kapālīśa with five. Saṃdāraka went with six, and Kokuṇḍa went with a crore of crores.
Viṣṭambha, the best of the Gaṇas, would go with sixty-four crores;
Śaṅkhānada and Pippala likewise would go with a thousand crores; Āveśāna and Candratāpana would each go with eight crores. (144–145)
Mahāveśa went with a thousand [attendants], and Gaṇapa likewise with ten million;
Kuṇḍī went with twelve crores, as did Parvataka. Kāla, Kālaka, and the Gaṇa Mahākāla also departed.

By a hundred times ten million [offerings], they each met with the destruction of their sacrifices. By a hundred times ten million [offerings] to Agni, there was one named Agnimukha; by ten million, Ādityamūrdhā; and likewise by ten million, Ghanāvaha. (147–148)
Sannāha with a hundred koṭis, and Kumuda with a koṭi; Amogha and Kokila, the lords of the hosts, each with ten million koṭis (koṭikoṭi).
Kāṣṭhāgūḍha with sixty-four [koṭis], as well as Sukeśī and Vṛṣabha.
Sumantra, Gaṇādhīśa, Kākapādodara, Santānaka, Mahābala, and Puṅgava likewise departed for the sacrifice, accompanied by sixty crores,
nine crores, and so forth.
Madhupiṅga and Pūrṇabhadra went forth with ninety crores [of followers].
So too did Virūpākṣa, Tālaketu, Ṣaḍāsya, Pañcavaktraka,
Saṃvartaka, Kulīśa, Daityānta, and Lokāntaka.
Bhṛṅgīriṭi, Śṛṅgiriṭi, Aśani, and Bhālaka—
these, together with sixty-four [attendants], each went to the sacrifice.
There were thousands of crores of spirits (bhūtas), and a pack of dogs numbering three crores.
It fell through the path of the sky onto the sacrificial grounds of Dakṣa.
And because of it, kettledrums, conchs, drums, and even gomukhas,
as well as various kinds of horns, resounded during the festival of battle.
A throbbing occurred in his right and left eyes, arms, and thighs.
At midday, an earthquake took place; Dakṣa saw stars [by day], the quarters were filled with robbers, and the sun became devoid of luster.
Surrounded by seven halos, he was terrifying;
the stars fell, and there were untimely peals of thunder.
At that time, the motion of the stars became crooked and downward-facing.
The vulture, having touched the head of Dakṣa, departed, carrying away the head-cloth.
At that time, jackals howled, harsh winds blew,
and there was a rain of meteors, a rain of dust, and a shower of white scorpions.
Tumultuous clouds, like swarms of locusts, were seen in the sky above the sacrifice;
the sacrificial pavilion of Dakṣa was carried upward by the winds.
Then those officiating priests vomited blood and became trembling with fear.

A rain of blood, the burning of the quarters, and the directions shrouded in darkness—those present at Dakṣa’s sacrifice beheld such portents of ill omen. They fell to the ground in a swoon, crying out, "Alas! We are slain! (162–163).
In the meantime, a voice from the sky spoke to them:
"Fie on you, Dakṣa! Fie on you, gods and others! Irresistible suffering has come upon you.
At that moment, Śambhu’s armies entered the sacrificial courtyard.
Then, overcome by fear, Dakṣa indeed went for refuge to Hari.

(165) Thus ends the section titled "The Description of the Battle of Satī’s Attendants, the Celestial Voice to Dakṣa, Nārada’s Return to Kailāsa, the Birth of Vīrabhadra from Śambhu’s Matted Hair, the Arrival of the Remaining Gaṇas at Kailāsa, the Creation of the Armies of Kālī, Jvara, the Gaṇas, Bhūtas, Siṃhas, and Others, their Dispatch to the Sacrifice, Nārada’s Return to the Sacrifice, and the Inauspicious Omens for Dakṣa and the Others" in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter One Hundred and Seventy-Six.
Chapter 176 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (*Kṛtayuga-Santāna*).
Chapter 177.
[The Author: Chapter 178.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Dakṣa, agitated by fear, remembered Viṣṇu, O Lotus-born One.
O God of gods, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Teacher of the World!
(1) Protection must be afforded by you to me, to the sacrifice, and to the people;
let there be no destruction of the sacrifice, for you, O Acyuta, are the very soul of the sacrifice. (2)
Then his prayer was heard by Brahmā and Viṣṇu; mounting their respective vehicles, the swan and Garuḍa, they returned from their own abodes. With a mind agitated by fear, he fell at their feet.
Then Viṣṇu, having raised up Dakṣa whose mind was overwhelmed with grief, said:
"O Dakṣa, listen to this truth, my speech which is beneficial in every way.
For you, O Dakṣa, being ignorant of the truth, have indeed shown contempt."
Everything done with disregard for the Lord becomes fruitless;
it is not merely useless, but brings misfortune at every step.
Where those unworthy of worship are honored and the one worthy of worship is not honored... [6]
In that situation, three things indeed occurred: poverty, death, and fear.
A great danger arose from Mahādeva, who had been treated with disrespect.
Śaṅkara is indeed a Vaiṣṇava deity, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, an offense has been committed by you against a devotee of Nārāyaṇa;
for a master is truly not capable of providing protection to one who offends his devotee.
(9) Go for refuge to Śiva; he indeed will provide protection.
"I am dependent on my devotees; I am pained by the destruction of the virtuous.
What fruit shall you obtain from this cruel deed you have committed?
Hearing those words, Dakṣa became pale-faced.
And he said to Śrī Hari: "O Kṛṣṇa, this commencement of the sacrifice has been performed by Your power.
It was done as a witness to all deeds for the perfection of the Vedic dharma.
Therefore, O Lord, protection must be provided for this sacrifice of mine!"
"Without you, there is no one capable of protecting the sacrifice and us.
Viṣṇu said: "The protection of the sacrifice must certainly be performed by me;
for my entire vow is well known to be the preservation of dharma. (13–14)
The boundary of the Vedic dharma must always be protected by me;
likewise, there is a share for the three deities in the sacrifice, as well as for other great-souled ones and the gods—so the Veda declares, and not otherwise. (15)
"An offense against him was committed by you through pride during the sacrifice.
Speak, O Dakṣa: how could I have abandoned the stake of dharma?
Why were Satī and Śiva not previously invited to the sacrifice by you?"
How indeed has the boundary of the sacrifice been transgressed by one who knows?
O evil-minded one, do you not see what is action and what is inaction?
This sacrifice, devoid of the one God, will certainly yield no fruit.
Relying solely on knowledge and relying on ritual authority, those priests,
having abandoned God, remain fixed in mere action;
they are indeed bound by the fetters consisting of action throughout many births.
Those who have shown contempt for the Lord are being cooked in the hells;
yet on one side, the army of the brother named Śiva has arrived,
and on the other, the host of Dakṣa and others, including their sons and grandsons.
All the gods are indeed kinsmen, yet the family is truly one.
Tell me now: where should the Sudarśana discus be released?
[It must be spared] from the family members, the servants, and all those who are great-souled.
"Your destruction is imminent here due to the fault of insulting Śiva;
destruction has been summoned by your intellect, and the ruin of your home is at hand.
This is Vīrabhadra, the lord of Rudra’s hosts and the crusher of enemies. || 24 ||
"He has indeed come for the purpose of destroying everything; of this there is no doubt.
While Govinda was speaking thus, the army then arrived.
The gods and others beheld it on all sides around the sacrificial ground.
Then Indra, laughing at Rudra and the attendant Vīrabhadra,
took the thunderbolt in his hand and prepared for battle along with the host of gods.
Indra mounted his own elephant, and Anala himself mounted a goat.
Yama, mounted upon a buffalo, and Nirṛti, whose vehicle is a ghost;
Varuṇa, mounted upon a crocodile, and likewise Anila, mounted upon a deer;
and Kubera, mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot—these fought together with the attendants of Śaṅkara.
Likewise, other valiant warriors— the gods, yakṣas, cāraṇas, and guhyakas—
mounted their respective vehicles and fought;
at that time, there was a great battle between the gods and the hosts.
Conchs, kettledrums, and great drums resounded;
likewise, ḍiṇḍimas, paṭahas, war-trumpets, and gomukhas blared.
With sharp *tomaras* and *nārācas*, the gods struck down many of the *gaṇas*.
The hosts of Śambhu, including Indra and the other world-protectors, were utterly defeated by the armies born from Bhṛgu’s mantras; they were vanquished and fled.
Then, the sacrificer Bhṛgu performed their eradication.
And the armies of the Caṇḍikas also rushed upon that sacrifice.
The armies of the Mahālayas fought in the battle with the Ṛbhus.
There were also the Kālas and Bhairavas, archers accompanied by bhūtas, pretas, and other spirits.
The armies fought a battle with the hosts of the gods and the hosts of the Ṛbhus; all were struck down by the Ṛbhus, Śṛṅbhus, Dharāmbhus, and Ambhus,
and were sent to the abode of Yama in numbers reaching into the hundreds of millions, billions, and beyond.
And a forest of corpses arose from those who had fallen in battle.
Seeing his own [forces] defeated, Vīrabhadra, who resembled a mountain,
placed those very *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas* behind him.
Placing his great hosts at the forefront, he rushed onto the field of battle;
seizing a great trident,
he struck down the gods, the Sādhyas, the Yakṣas, the Cāraṇas, and even the Guhyakas.
They struck them with spears, javelins, and excellent pikes.
Some were cut in two by swords, others were crushed by mallets;
likewise, the gods were pierced by other weapons and missiles by the great hosts.
By means of the *kālakavala* mantras, his own soldiers were restored to life;
the soldiers of Dakṣa perished, for there was no one to revive them.
All the gods were defeated and intent on flight.
Having abandoned the battlefield, they all departed for heaven (triviṣṭapa).
Only those world-protectors, Śakra and the others, remained there full of anxiety.
Vīrabhadra spoke to all those who had fallen on the side of Dakṣa: 43–44.
"All of you have come for the sake of a virtuous deed because of your childishness.
I shall grant you a virtuous deed; come into my presence!
O Śakra, O Guru, O Bhānu, O Śaśin, O Yama, O Dhaneśvara!"
"O Vāyu, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, Śeṣa, Sūrya, and the other gods, assemble here;
I offer this oblation for your presence.
Having spoken thus, [he struck them] with sharp arrows, weapons, missiles, and mountains.
He struck down all the gods— the guardians of the quarters, Indra, and the lords of the asuras—
and they, intent on flight, fled in the ten directions.
Then, seeing them fleeing, Yajñanārāyaṇa himself [advanced].
Nārāyaṇa, having become Nara, blew his conch of great sound.
Hearing that blast of the conch, those gods returned once more;
Śakra fought with Nandin, and Vahni there with Aśman.
The Lord of Wealth (Kubera) fought with Kuṣmāṇḍa by giving up his life;
Mahāloka fought with Yama, while Muṇḍa indeed fought with Varuṇa.
Caṇḍa fought with Nairṛta, and Vāyu likewise with Bhṛṅgin.
The great leader of the Bhairavas, joined by the circle of Yoginīs,
tore apart the other gods and drank their warm blood;
the Kṣetrapālas devoured them, and Kālī drank the blood.
Then the remaining gods fled;
Viṣṇu and Brahmā departed for their respective worlds before that sacrifice.
At that time, the destruction of billions upon billions occurred at the site of the sacrifice.
Having entered the sacrifice, the Gaṇas indeed began their destruction:
some uprooted the sacrificial posts, some filled the fire-pits,
some demolished the pavilions, and others dug up the altars.
By some the sacrificial offerings were eaten, and by others clarified butter was drunk;
by some the cooked foods were devoured, and by others milk-rice was consumed.
Cooked meals were partaken of, and milks were tasted.
The sacrificial vessels were completely pulverized and broken;
some carts were shattered, and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles were crushed. Some devoured the sacrificial animals, and the fires in the ritual pits were extinguished. (58–59)
Some held fine silken garments and jewels at that spot;
beholding that calamity, the sacrifice, assuming the form of a deer,
fled through the sky in fear and was seized by Vīrabhadra.
Then, by means of a whirling firebrand,
Nandin was rendered headless; he then plucked out both eyes of Bhaga,
who had repeatedly signaled toward Dakṣa with his two eyes while he was cursing him.
And Caṇḍa, with great force, tore out the teeth of Pūṣan—
he who had previously laughed while showing his teeth as Hara was pronouncing a curse.
Furthermore, Vīrabhadra cut off the tip of Sarasvatī’s nose.
Another, Bhadraka, cut off Aditi’s lips;
the exceedingly powerful Maṇibhadra dashed Bhṛgu against the earth. Having trampled him upon the chest with his foot, he tore out his beard.
Then another tore out the pair of arms of Aryaman;
another group then tore out the tongue of Agni;
and another group, increasing his strength, cut off the testicles of Vāyu.
A certain member of the Gaṇas named Yamaśiras bound Yama with ropes;
and Śṛṅgin then bound Nairṛta to a tree with his matted hair,
weighing him down on a branch and striking him below the waist.
Having seized Kubera by the feet and bound him face-down with a rope,
the Gaṇa named Dharābhu lifted him up onto the top of a sacrificial post.
Meanwhile, the Rudras warded off the devourers who sought the oblations of the sacrifice.
Pressing upon Varuṇa’s belly, they vomited up clarified butter.
Indra, taking the form of a peacock, flew away and hid himself on the mountain.
The first [of the priests] began to drive away the other sacrificers as well.
Seizing Ariṣṭanemi, Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa,
Datta, and Kṛśāśva, Bhadraka struck them on the head with his foot.
Then, having torn apart other gods and others as well upon the surface of the earth, [he continued].
Vīrabhadra and the others did not find peace among the sages and ṛṣis.
Svadhā, Svāhā, Dakṣiṇā, and other women were mocked; likewise, the mantras, the tantras, and all other remaining objects were destroyed. (73–74)
In their rage, the hosts showered various kinds of filth upon the fire.
That sacrificial ground was made by the Pramathas to resemble a cremation ground.
Seeing them fallen into a most piteous state, Vīrabhadra spoke to the Gaṇas:
"Where is that wicked Dakṣa, and where are the gods who partake in the sacrifice?
Seize them all and bring them here; go, O Gaṇas, with the utmost speed!
Seeing them rushing off at his command, Janārdana became enraged.
Because he had caused the diminution of their power, such that the Gaṇas were reduced to mere dry grass, the enraged Vīrabhadra beheld Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Summoning Dakṣa, he said: "Give him up, or fight with me!"
Hari said, "I too am here, my intellect skilled in protecting Dakṣa.
I shall observe your capability; how will you carry him off?
Thinking thus, he released the discus he had been wielding at Vīrabhadra.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when it was stuck on Bhadragala's throat;
but as soon as he cut the throat, Śambhu established himself within that throat.
Having left the throat, it indeed came into the hand of Viṣṇu.
Then Garuḍa, enraged, tore each individual Pramatha with his claws;
they reached the number of hundreds of thousands and acquired the splendor of *kiṃśuka* flowers.
Thereupon, Viṣṇu paralyzed all the Gaṇas in that place.
Just as Hari was about to hurl his Sudarśana discus for the destruction of Vīrabhadra, a voice from the sky spoke to him:
"O Hari, do not act with such rashness; Hara is present within Vīrabhadra."
"Your effort to destroy Hari brings shame; desist!
Let Dakṣa alone receive the fruit of his action; let no one else act in such a manner.
Having heard this, Hari did not release the discus again at that time.
Having reached Dakṣa, who was hidden and concealed within the sacrificial altar, Vīrabhadra roared loudly and said: "Fie upon this reviler of Śambhu!
He whose wealth is such as this, and in whose assembly the gods themselves sit! (87)
How could he, possessing such wisdom, not perform the sacrifice with the Lord? Since Śiva has been reviled by you through this impure mouth,
I shall swiftly cut off that mouth of yours with a sharp-edged sword.

Having spoken thus, he struck his head there with a sword; yet it did not become severed from the trunk, for it was indeed indestructible due to its yogic power. Perceiving that head to be impenetrable by any means, even by all manner of weapons and missiles, [he reflected].
Saying, "I shall grind you to powder," he crushed him with slaps.
Having seized him by the chest with both hands and feet,
Vīrabhadra threw him into the fire-pit and offered him as an oblation.
Then, having seized and crushed others who were supporting the sacrifice,

Śrī Lakṣmī said: What kinds of wonders did Śaṅkara indeed perform at that time?

Then Mohinī, who deludes the minds of the three worlds, began to speak.
"Understand my words, O virtuous one, which shall bring happiness to you who desire a woman.
Abandoning your hardness, accept me, who am hidden and bestow happiness;
for you are the most excellent among the chosen in creation, and I am worthy of being chosen as a bride."
A new union between a clever woman and a clever man is difficult to find.
Who would not rejoice in happiness upon seeing my pair of breasts, my thighs, and my beautiful lotus-face, accompanied by smiles and the play of my eyebrows? (92)
The essence of women is the very core of pleasure, desired even by sages.
The enjoyment of pleasure with those who relish it is sufficient and exceedingly rare.
O best of gods, abandon your meditation and enjoy her as the fruit of your asceticism.
He who, though having conquered his senses, does not accept a beloved woman who has come to him of her own accord,
perishes, consumed by the fire of her sighs.
Having heard these words, Śambhu spoke to her what was both beneficial and true.
Listen, O beloved, I shall declare that which brings happiness in its ultimate fruition:
the truth appropriate to the family dharma of ascetic Brahmins. Sexual union with one's own wife at the proper time is praised as dharma. (96–97)

Whosoever, having taken birth anywhere at all, finds pleasure in another's wife, from his home Fortune indeed departs in anger. Furthermore, a woman who has come to him should be accepted by householders, but not by ascetics.

For householders, there is a fault in renunciation; such a householder becomes a recipient of curses and a partaker of sin. Brahmā, the creator of the universe, possesses a wife and is not one who has attained dispassion.
There would be a fault in his renunciation, but never for us who have renounced.

He who abandons his own wife and takes another’s woman suffers the loss of fame, wealth, and longevity, and finds no higher state either in this world or the next. What is the use of great prosperity or even imperial sovereignty to an ascetic? "What use have you for me, who am intoxicated and free from desire?
(10.2) "O beautiful one, go to someone else who is well-dressed, handsome, robust, and young. Having heard this rejection, she replied with great humility: (10.3)
Possessing the lovely hue of the campaka flower and as beautiful as Kandarpa himself, he is endowed with a wife through the power of his asceticism; he is well-formed and highly esteemed by women.
Without you, whom else shall I go to? Or what man is there who is more devoted than you?
Where else could one like me go, afflicted by love, after abandoning you?
O Lord of Yogis, accept me quickly, for I am utterly consumed by the fire of passion. If not, I shall cast a curse; otherwise, take me at once.
The vital breaths are burnt, the mind is burnt, and now one's own self is being consumed. Attain the state of bliss through drinking the nectar of fresh love.
She who is afflicted by the suffering within her heart surely curses him.
Neither the Creator nor Śaṅkara is able to annul this curse.
Behold me, who am most excellent, yet consumed by the fires of passion—my fresh blood now welling forth, yet remaining uninjured and unassailed by anyone. (108–109)
Wearing a dot of vermilion along with a dot of musk,
possessing the beautiful hue of a campaka flower, eternally fixed in the bloom of youth,
with broad hips and full buttocks and breasts.
Her face was like a handful of the brilliant light of the full moon in autumn;
she was clad in fine garments and adorned with jewel ornaments.
She was capable of enchanting everyone at will by her mere side-long glances.

"Take me quickly—me, who desires one such as you, who moves with the gait of a lordly elephant in rut, whose every limb is covered in horripilation, and who is on the verge of fainting; take me, whose throat, lips, and palate are parched. (113)
Thus, Māhinī sought to delude Śarva with her words;
yet Śiva did not fall into delusion, nor did he ever abandon his meditation. Just then, the Apsaras Rambhā arrived there and spoke.
Listen, O friend! To this mantra for attracting young yogis, if your heart desires to sport with a young man.
Accomplish your own desired aim with the assistance of Kāmadeva.
"Brahmā will grant you whatever you desire along with the necessary means upon your request.
If you have no passion for him, seek out another youth;
either by assuming an unprecedented guise or by first employing the god of love. || 117-118 ||

Go there yourself with him and delude him, O enchantress! For who, without the aid of Kama, is capable of conquering this Lord, the foremost among those who have mastered their senses, who is the very embodiment of Narayana? (119)
"O deluder, go as you wish to that place where Kāma has made his dwelling on this side;
the compassionate lord of women will immediately become your companion.
Having been addressed thus, Mohinī went there to the abode of Smara.
Kāma, too, being deluded upon seeing Mohinī, fell into agitation; Kāma suddenly stumbled and for a moment became as if inert. From that essence, two sons were born: Śṛṅgāraka and Vasantaka.
Richly endowed with forms as enchanting as those of the Goddess Mohinī and being the vessels of all beauty,
their two sons were born with the sudden blossoming of youth, providing assistance to the God of Love.
Indeed, for the sake of Mohinī, even Kāma himself accompanied them at their birth.
Requested for the sake of companionship, he arrived where Śaṅkara was;
there he beheld Hara, the yogi, established in self-restraint, yet being deluded by Mohinī. Standing before him, she began to bewitch him as well.
For a moment she danced beautifully with graceful limbs, and for a moment she sang;
[she sang] that music concerning Satī, which deludes the minds of devotees.
Having heard her desired music, the Teacher of the worlds [responded]. (126–127)
With all her limbs covered in horripilation, she opened her eyes and gazed;
overcome by desire, Hara became infatuated with her, his eyes filled with tears. Seeing the five-faced one thus bewildered, the enchantress was delighted at heart.
There, by way of sport, he displayed his true nature and the measure of his artistic skill (kalā).
He revealed his own limbs, preceded by a smile and the play of his eyebrows.
What shame can there be for one in this world whose consciousness is struck down by desire?
Nevertheless, the steadfast Śaṅkara, closing his eyes there,
desisted from the path of yoga and did not look at Mohinī;
yet indeed, that Mohinī ascended into the heart of Śambhu.
Even while he was in meditation, that deluding power appeared within his inner organ;
for a moment, that enchantress incited his desire, which dwells outside, as well as his mind—the foremost of all the senses and a portion of Viṣṇu. (1.32–1.33)
The seed-syllable of passion (*ratibīja*), the five arrows, eternally presided over by women,
accompanied by fragrant breezes, and impelled by the intoxication of amorous grace—
then this God of Love (*Kāmadeva*) also prepared himself at the will of Hari.
Standing himself in the intermediate space, he fixed an arrow;
he discharged a great weapon purified by mantras at Śaṅkara.
And Śambhu became agitated, for he was a lover stirred by the weapon of Kāma.

He gazed again and again for a moment at the face of Mohinī, which was smiling, possessed of curved eyes, and raining down the sentiment of love. In that interval, Kāma, who knew the proper time and was skilled in yoga, [appeared].
Having manifested, he hurled the five arrows at Śaṅkara:
first Sammohana (the Enchanter), second Sampravega (the Impeller),
third Unmattavīrya (the Intoxicator), and fourth Jvalajvara (the Blazing Fever).
Having dispatched the fifth, Cetanahara, along the path of the sky,
he sent forth the servants Kiṅkara, Kokila, and Vasantaka,
as well as the bees and the fragrant breeze; and he himself also went to Hari.
Near him, the male cuckoo uttered its sweet cry; standing before him, the bee hummed a beautiful, subtle song. O beloved, a fragrant breeze blew constantly—gentle and exceedingly cool. (141–142)
There, Madhu himself wandered about constantly in a state of joy;
and Kāma, taking his place in the mind, brought about a transformation within him.
Śaṅkara, the lord of yogis, became one whose entire body was covered with horripilation.
Seeing his state of infatuation, she laughed again and again.
With her eyes askance, her consciousness struck by the arrows of Kama, she spoke:
"By a mere gesture from women, the mind becomes instantly intoxicated. (144-145)
He who, having drawn her in, brings about sexual enjoyment, is considered the best;
whereas that man who, having clearly understood the woman's intention, performs the amorous act only after being summoned by her, is considered mediocre. (146)

He who is repeatedly solicited by a woman afflicted by desire, and having been seized, consents to her touch, is considered a *kaniṣṭha* man. But he who is not touched by her in private is a *klība*; alas, he is no man at all. (147–148)

Arise, O Lord of the worlds! O helmsman, bring me to the further shore of this terrible and impassable ocean of passion, in which I am submerged in fear. In birth after birth, I am your servant, my mind ever fixed upon you.
"Purchase me quickly with the price of pleasure— that jewel which is beyond value.
Having spoken thus, Mohinī, overwhelmed by desire and smiling, approached Śambhu there and drew his hand toward her.
And as Śambhu also rose up, desiring to embrace her, Satī then said to Kṛṣṇa: "Lead him to the region of the Himalayas;
let the Lord of Mohinī take her hand in marriage in a secluded place."
Desiring to depart, he moved forward, yet Śaṅkara followed behind him.
In another moment, Mohinī led him to the plateau of the Himalayas.
Hari then took hold of Hara—who was paralyzed by desire and thus slightly defiled, though otherwise untainted.
In the vicinity of Kailāsa, which was endowed with various trees and creepers, pervaded by a breeze rich in coolness and gentle fragrance, and pleasantly cool;
in a charming bower where the branches were adorned with beautiful flowers. (155)
In a secluded place near a cascade of flowing water, Mohinī said to Śambhu: "O beloved, lie down like the God of Love;
come here and let us enjoy ourselves through many varieties of amorous delights. (1517) / 156 //
Standing within the hollow of a tree, she spoke to Satī under the guise of her eyes:
"O friend, behold the incomparable play of these two divine beings.
Having said this, the enchanting woman prepared a soft bed of flowers.
Holding Śambhu to her breast, the woman beautiful as she desired slept; meanwhile,
Smara then dispatched well-prepared means to incite desire in Śambhu in every direction.
Struck by the arrows of Kāma, Śambhu— agitated and deprived of his composure— embraced that most beautiful enchantress who possessed the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Just as he desired to unite with her, at that moment, she went outside.
All his vigor indeed surged forth, yet he was unable to restrain it.
He caused everything to fall upon that spot consisting of a bed of flowers;
then Mohinī, rising suddenly, vanished from that place.
Having embraced Satī as he desired and commanded her to go to his own abode,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa reached Goloka, accompanied by the hosts of gopīs.
Śaṅkara, becoming startled, realized Kṛṣṇa’s deed.
He did not consider it a humiliation; indeed, he went to Kailāsa itself.
At that time, the Seven Sages had gathered there from Satyaloka to witness that conduct; having seen everything, they remained hidden in seclusion.
Having placed this vigor within a leaf for the sake of Rāma’s body,
they guarded it within the fold of the leaf so that there might be no obstacle.
In the meantime, the auspicious Añjanī, daughter of Keśarin—
There, in a lonely forest, she performed difficult austerities.
To her who was performing penance out of a desire for a son, a voice from the sky proclaimed:
"The fruit of your austerity shall be a son endowed with the strength of the wind. (168–169)
The Wind-god himself will come here and bestow the seed;
O lady of auspicious countenance, accept it without hesitation, even though you are an ascetic.
There shall be no fault in that for you, since it is for the sake of Rāma’s mission.
"Even though you are unhurt, your son shall be possessed of great strength.
"So be it," she said, and quickly bowed in that direction.
The voice from the sky ceased, while she remained waiting for the seed.
Then Vāyu, seeing her, was exceedingly agitated by her beauty;
having seen the maiden in that solitary place, he approached her assuming a divine form.
By the turn of fate, the Seven Sages also arrived at that very spot.

Vāyu, having become bashful upon beholding those sages there, was addressed by the great seers: "Indeed, for the sake of the task of the gods, you must perform a great deed here, specifically for the sake of Rāma's mission. (174–175)
"Take the seed of Śaṅkara and go to Kaiśarī, the daughter of Añjanā.
Then, having become composed, Vāyu took up the seed of Śaṅkara.
When Vāyu opened the fold of leaves and looked at it, [he saw...]
Then, blazing like fire and becoming a mass of flames, it quickly turned into heat and entered the body of the wind;
at that time, the wind was no longer able to sustain it. (177–178)
He blazed within his belly and ran from place to place in that body.
On his path, there was a spot where the female ascetic Añjanī remained,
having always stayed there after digging a hole in the earth as deep as her neck.
Above, cool grass and the surface of the earth were visible;
yet her body was not seen, only her headless trunk appeared.
Then Vāyu, becoming a lion, rushed about restlessly. (1.184.180–181)
While running on that ground, Vāyu fell due to tripping over his feet;
perceiving the cool, grassy surface, he embraced it, and by the power of fate, his head entered the ear of Añjanī—that very *liṅga* of Vāyu. (182)

And that Śāmbhava *vīrya*, which was situated in the wind, fell entirely into the space between Añjanī’s ears; it descended from her throat down below and entered the womb-cavity, where it remained firm. (183–184)
By the will of fate, Kaisarī indeed conceived that embryo;
and Añjanī’s body blazed up with particular intensity.
Emerging from the earth, she remained upon a grassy bank in the water.
In another moment, a son endowed with divine power was born.
On the fourteenth lunar day, when the sun was in Aries and in conjunction with the Citrā asterism,
the son of the Wind-god appeared in the waters of the Suvarṇamukharī.
He was equal to Vāyu in strength, equal to Śambhu in sovereign powers and accomplishments,
equal to Kṛṣṇa in celibacy, and likewise an ṛṣi in his devotion.
In appearance he was like a monkey, and in asceticism he was equal to Añjanī.
In his indifference toward forms he was like a beggar, and in his dwelling he was like the rainy season;
he was like a monkey in his knowledge of all medicinal herbs in particular;
and he was like a female ascetic—tranquil and self-restrained in freedom from the pairs of opposites.
In his army he was like the forest; in his deluding power, like Cirajīvin;
in his hair, resembling spring; and in his nails, like a wood.
In his frown he was like Rudra; in his chest, like the Himālaya mountain.
He was one who, according to his will, brought about the destruction of the pride of the Rākṣasas. In his heart he was like a lush meadow; in his steadfastness, he was always like the earth;
in his protection, he was like a protective shield; and in his heroism, he possessed the true luster of valor. (192–193)
At that time, he became like fire for the incineration of the elements and other things;
then, seeing his mother’s jaw hanging down,
she called that infant by the very name "Hanumān."
In that very instant, he grew until he was like a mountain.
Seeing his strength and prowess, his mother rejoiced exceedingly.
Then, in the form of a child, with palms joined in reverence, he spoke to his own mother in the morning.
"O Mother, hunger oppresses me; give me that which brings peace to my stomach.
Placing the infant upon her lap, she suckled him with her breast-milk.
Nevertheless, her hunger was not appeased, and she beheld a fruit in the sky.
Then, at dawn, he endeavored to take the solar orb into the sky.
But having recognized the Sun as a god, he desisted from that act at the request of the deity.
Having obtained divine boons mixed with devotion granted by the celestial sages, [he remained]. (198–199)
Then Hanumān, exceedingly joyful, went into the presence of his own mother and related that entire event to her with great respect. Thereupon,
by her command, the steadfast one [set out] from that treasury of all sciences and so forth.
That monkey, having gone daily to his presence, recited [the scriptures] from the Sun;
and with palms joined in reverence, he repeatedly requested service [from him].
His mother, however, said: "Tell me how my residence may be in Vaikuṇṭha."
"O son, perform service in this manner; nothing else indeed pleases me here.
The son then said, "O mother, sit right upon my shoulder;
I shall carry you to eternal Vaikuṇṭha with this very body."
The monkey climbed onto his mother’s shoulder as if it were a celestial chariot.
Having flown forcefully into the sky with his first leap,
he surpassed the sun, pressing down upon that orb with his hind foot.
In the second leap, having certainly ascended and pressed upon that *dhruva*,
he went to the assembly hall of Brahmā in Satyaloka during the third leap.
In the fourth leap, [he reached] Gaṅgādvāra and the shell of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍakaṭāhaka*).
Having pierced the earth and pressed down upon it with his foot, he of great strength swiftly reached the second abode, Vaikuṇṭha, which lies between the waters and the fire; there,
with devotion, he placed his mother at the feet of Rāma.
Having obtained from Rāma both the mantra and the Vaiṣṇava rosary, and having become a Vaiṣṇava and received boons that made known his service as an attendant of Rāma’s incarnation,
he returned once more to the earth and struck Śani with his foot.
At the time of his birth, Saturn, beholding him with a malevolent gaze, became the source of suffering for him.
Then, from the blow of that [monkey's] tail, Saturn fell to the surface of the earth.
He thought, "This monkey is a celibate student; he shall not touch a woman. (1.184.210–211)
Śani, having assumed the form of a woman, fled through the sky;
meanwhile, Hanumān seized him by the hair on his head and cast him down.
He did this constantly, thinking, "May this Śani be forcibly brought under my control."
Having been thoroughly ground upon a copper plate for as long as the moon and sun endure, he prostrated at the feet of the son of Vāyu and made this request:
for his own release and for the restoration of his home. (213–214)
Then the Lord of Monkeys, assuming a second form, said to him:
"Go back to your own home, having made a firm promise here in every respect, to wherever the *Hanumat-stotra* and the worship of Hanuman and so forth are found. (215)
In every such place, no suffering caused by the gaze of Saturn shall befall him.
May you always take the form of a woman, trodden upon by the soles of my feet;
wherever the footprint of Hanumān exists, there Saturn is rendered powerless.
May you receive the fruit of this deceit in the form of a woman, and may there be your restraint. I shall give you the name Pannati; always remain within my domain.
Go now in your second form and become a householder, O son of the Sun.
"Having recognized you as the son of the Sun, I shall not bind you while you live.
Depart from my shadow and exert your prowess elsewhere.
Having made this vow, Śanaiścara went to his own planet.
"Oṃ, salutation to Hanumān, the destroyer of suffering, kṣaḥ phaṭ svāhā.
Thus, he who constantly triumphs with this sixteen-syllable mantra never experiences affliction born of malevolent planets anywhere. (221)
In the Himalayas, where his birth took place, there in a grove of plantain trees (222),
that Hanumān dwells eternally as a long-lived and steadfast being.
Performing the service of Rāma, he also resides in the presence of Rāma (223).
Thus, O Goddess, I have related to you the birth of Hanumān from Śaṅkara;
it bestows longevity and happiness, destroys sins, and grants strength and devotion.
It originates from the enchantment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and removes all suffering through its recitation and hearing.
"What more do you wish to hear regarding that which purifies through its glorification? (225).

Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the first part, the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga: the remembrance of Satī by the distressed Śaṅkara on the Himalayas; his journey to Goloka via a celestial voice and his wandering in the form of a bull; Kṛṣṇa’s prayer to bring Satī from the Himālayas to Śambhu; Śambhu’s arrival at Satyaloka with Kṛṣṇa in the form of Mohinī; and how, from the seed of Brahmā who faltered upon seeing Mohinī, the cities of the hundred-thousand Brahmās were born, while as for the seed of the faltering Kāmadeva...

Śṛṅgāra and Vasantaka were born. Mohinī came with Śaṅkara to the Himālaya mountains and embraced Śambhu; from the emission of Śambhu, which was diverted by the wind and entered the ear of Añjanī through the wind in the form of a monkey, Hanumān was born. Knowing the sun to be his fruit, he bore it; he led Añjanī to Vaikuṇṭha. Having become a Vaiṣṇava there, while returning, he struck Śani with his foot and cast him down, and he protected the female serpent in the form of a woman on the path. This is the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of These and Other Matters. 184.
