Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Hari, when Himālaya had been reached by Pārvatī for the sake of obtaining Śambhu, what was done by Śambhu as well? Tell that to me."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Satī performed penance for the sake of Hara, and Hara performed penance for the sake of Satī;
O Mahālakṣmī, understand from me how the efforts of both proceeded with great intensity.
Having taken with him certain peaceful leaders of the Gaṇas, such as Nandin and others,
the Lord went to the descent of the Gaṅgā on the plateau of the Himavat.
There, the Gaṅgā first fell from the world of Brahmā onto the mountain.
Having established himself there, the self-controlled Hara commenced his ascetic practice.
With one-pointed focus, he meditated upon his own self, which is the supreme Brahman. At that time, some of his attendants remained absorbed in meditation, while others were intent on service.
Some were intent on silence, while others became gatekeepers. In the meantime, the Lord of the Snowy Mountains arrived there;
he prostrated before the Lord Rudra and praised him with palms joined in reverence.
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O you who possess the form of a yogin, salutations be to you!
(7) Salutations to you who are without attributes and yet possessed of attributes, who manifest through divine play;
salutations to you who are perfectly complete and free from transformation. (8)
Salutations again and again to You, the tranquil Brahman whose nature is bliss; salutations again and again to You, the bestower of the fruits of austerity, who abide in austerity.
Salutations to You, the Supreme Self, who creates enjoyments that do not exist externally.
Salutations to You, the embodiment of the Supreme Self, the husband of Satī.
(1.185.10) The fruit of the rise of my good fortune is that You have come here to my home; O Lord, bestower of happiness upon the virtuous, You have made me truly possessed of a protector. (11)
Today my birth has become fruitful, today my life has become fruitful;
today everything of mine has become fruitful because you have arrived here.
O Lord, if you know me to be your exclusive servant, then grant me your command.
"I shall always perform service to you with affection, according to the rules of servitude.
(13) Having heard this, Hara opened his eyes and, seeing Himālaya standing before him, spoke with affection to the lord of mountains while remaining established in the yoga of meditation. (14)
I have come to your back to perform secret penance;
act in such a way that no one indeed approaches nearby.
You are likewise the refuge of sages, yogis, ascetics, and renunciants.
You are the abode of asceticism and a great soul among the gods, sages, yakṣas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, brahmins, and nāgas;
you are eternally purified by the Gaṅgā, always devoted to the welfare of others, and the great lord of mountains. (16–17)
"I am performing penance here at the place where the Gaṅgā descends;
may my penance be free from obstacles—grant me your assistance and service.
Having heard this, the Mountain then spoke these words to Śambhu out of affection:
"I shall provide protection in every way so that no obstacle may arise for your asceticism.
O Lord of Gods, perform this supreme penance free from hindrance;
I, remaining steadfast, shall serve you like a servant."
I consider myself a recipient of your grace even greater than that of the Lord of the Gods; for he who is unattainable even through fierce asceticism has appeared before me of his own accord.
There is no one more meritorious than I, since you have established yourself upon my back for the sake of penance.
"I go for the sake of obeying your command; be forever gracious.
Having spoken thus and returned to his own place, he said to the ministers and others in every way:
"Let them indeed go to the descent of the Gaṅgā for the purpose of guarding it on all sides."
"The Lord of Gods is performing penance on my mountain peak, established in meditation.
From this day forward, let no one go there, whether they be one's own kin or even an enemy.
If any person should go there, that great villain—"
"I shall punish him especially, even for the sake of Śaṅkara.
(25) Then, having been thus commanded, the Mountain himself took a collection of excellent flowers and fruits and went into the presence of Śiva together with his daughter. (26)
Having bowed and placed fruits and other offerings before him, he said to Śaṅkara:
"O Blessed One! My daughter Pārvatī, being virtuous, has been brought here by her two companions;
she is eager to serve you."
"O Lord, grant her [permission], if you have any favor toward me.
(28) Then Śaṅkara beheld her, whose youth had first begun to bloom, who possessed the luster of a full-blown blue lotus flower, and whose face was like the full moon. (29)
She was beautiful, large-eyed, and radiant with a golden luster;
her full, firm breasts were like thick lotus buds.
She had a slender waist, broad hips, and a thin belly marked by the three folds.
Seeing her, who was resplendent with the beauty of feet resembling land-lotuses,
capable of causing one's asceticism to fail, tender, and increasing desire,
he closed his eyes and quickly meditated upon his own true nature.
Then the Mountain said to Śambhu: "Behold me, who have come to you for refuge;
the scriptures do not know you, for you are eternally beyond speech and mind.
Yet the sovereign Śruti designates you through the exclusion of what you are not."
Those upon whom you have cast your compassion know you as Hara.
I am fortunate through your grace; considering me your servant, show me mercy.
O Lord, with this daughter, I shall serve you daily with devotion.
Having heard this, the God of gods opened his eyes and then said:
"O Mountain, leave the maiden in her home and perform service for me.
The mountain replied: "Tell me, O Lord, why should I not bring my daughter here?"
Śambhu said: "A woman is always the illusion that creates obstacles for ascetics.
An ascetic certainly falls from his austerity through association with a young woman;
therefore, O Mountain, an ascetic must never engage in sexual union with a woman. (37–38)
Having heard this and bowed, Bhavānī then spoke these words:
"O Rudra, that power by which you now perform penance is the primordial Prakṛti; that Satī resides within you."

"But without you, how shall I be worthy of worship, salutation, and meditation? (1.185.40) Then Śambhu said: "Having destroyed that Prakṛti through austerity, I shall remain as the immutable and blissful Supreme Brahman. (41)
Kālī said: "Then Śambhu is established in the destruction of *prakṛti*.
Let it be considered whether she is that *prakṛti* or something else. [Śiva replied:
"Even at that time, that state of Brahmā is called *prakṛti*."
Now, that state of Śāmbhavī is called Prakṛti (Nature).
If you are beyond Prakṛti, for what purpose do you perform penance?
If you are within Prakṛti, how can you forbid Satī?
O Lord of Yogis, what is the use of much speaking? That for which you perform penance is directly perceived here as more powerful than all means of valid cognition;
and that [Self] am I, and you are that Person, for by me alone do you possess qualities.
"Without me, you are inactive; therefore, you ought not to do anything at all.
This being the case, O Nirguṇa, you must not harbor ill will even in my presence.
Then Śambhu said to the Goddess: "If I am indeed the attributeless Brahman..."
"The Self is indeed stainless, non-doing, non-enjoying, and untainted.
Therefore, O gentle one, perform service; what else will you do for me?
Even without her father, that Kālī constantly [performed service] together with her two friends.
She remains constantly engaged in service to Śambhu, never departing from him.
This indeed is the great fortitude of the steadfast and the truly ascetic:
that they are not struck down even by obstacles created by her who is the very embodiment of impediment. (1.185.50)
Kālī washed her feet and drank that water from his feet;
she performed the cleaning of that night with a cloth purified by fire.
Having worshipped Hara according to the rules with the sixteen types of offerings, [she remained there].

Having bowed down again and again, she went somewhere to her father’s house. When a long period of time had passed, she, accompanied by her friend, performed beautiful singing with excellent rhythm in the hermitage of Śaṅkara, which increased the god of love.
Gazing at Lord Śaṅkara with desire, she was filled with wonder;
and Śaṅkara, too, constantly reflected upon her in every way—
her who was a mass of great beauty and always remained by his side.

She constantly meditated upon Śambhu with the thought that he was her husband, [he who is] the infallible one. In the meantime, the gods led by Śakra, as well as the sages and those headed by Brahmā, were being tormented by the extremely wicked Tāraka.
Although Hara repeatedly sent Kāma to bring about the union of those two and made many efforts in various ways, he did not succeed;
for Tāraka could not be overcome without a son born from the seed of Śiva.
Indra reflected again and again that the great asura would surely be destroyed;
he then intensely called to mind Smara, who is accompanied by Vasanta and is dear to Rati.
At that very moment, Kāma arrived, together with Vasanta and Rati.
With palms joined in reverence, he said to Śakra, "I have arrived as your servant.
Indra replied, "Be victorious! You are my great and true friend.
For the sake of my victory, I always have two weapons: the thunderbolt and desire."

The vajra, however, would indeed be fruitless; you, on the other hand, shall never be so. The test of a donor occurs in a famine; that of a hero, in battle; that of a friend, in a time of calamity; and that of women and of lineage, in times of incapacity.
When a crisis of forbearance has arisen, when truth is hidden from view, and when there is a great task involving deep affection—otherwise, there is no testing of these.
And what can he accomplish who speaks much in vain? (63)
"O Smara, perform this task which is requested by all the gods and others! Smara replied to Indra: 'If anyone performs penance in order to seize your position, I shall cast him down in an instant.'"
With the side-glances of women, I shall cause the celestial sages and the Dānavas to fall in an instant.
Let your thunderbolt, weapons, and missiles remain far away when I am present.
I could topple Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Viṣṇu within a mere moment.
There is no counting others; they are illusory forms under my control.
My arrows are only five, and they are made of flowers;
my bow is likewise threefold and made of flowers, and its string is formed by bees.
A beautiful young woman is my strength; Spring is my constant minister.
I am the god who possesses the five powers, and the Moon is my friend. Śṛṅgāra (the erotic sentiment) is my commander-in-chief, and the *hāva* and *bhāva* gestures are my soldiers. (69)
"These weapons of mine are mild, and I myself am indeed mild. A wise man should accomplish whatever task is fulfilled by whichever means;
therefore, employ me in that task which is appropriate for me."
Having heard that which was previously declared by Brahmā—
that the death of the great Daitya named Tāraka would come from a son of Śambhu— Mahendra spoke; and Pārvatī, being virtuous, remained in the service of Śambhu.
And you must act in such a way that his desire for her arises just as it did for Śarva;
by doing so, all suffering will perish.
Having said "Om" and bowed down, Smara departed together with his retinue.
Having reached that point, he reflected upon the means for accomplishing his task:
"For the high-souled ones are unshakable, and their minds are very difficult to overcome.
Therefore, by first agitating them, their victory [over me] might be achieved."
"From her attachment to anger, which is more cruel [than any other], she is the terrifying great companion of envy;
through her fickleness, she has utterly destroyed the great strength that supports my fortitude.
I shall employ this corruption of the mind before him. (76–77)
"Having closed the doors of fortitude and drawn away my contentment,
I shall arouse the thirst of passion and then enter [Hara], O Hari. Having thought thus, Madana went to the abode of Hara.
Kāma, having gradually approached his presence, slowly beheld Śaṅkara.
He, the deluder of Madhu, stood there spreading forth religious duties;
at that time, the influence of spring extended everywhere.
The forests were in full bloom, and the flowers of the mango trees shone;
the buds of the aśoka trees gleamed, laden with fragrance.
And there were white water-lilies, frequented by wandering bees.
They became especially provocative of passion;
the warbling of the cuckoos, which kindles desire, was exceedingly beautiful, charming, and most dear. (82–83)
At that time, the sounds of the bees became stimulators of passion;
the bright luster of the moon was scattered everywhere, and it became a cool lamp for both lovers and their beloveds. (84)
Then a pleasant breeze, created by their union, blew forth.
Thus did the expansion of spring occur, awakening the god of love;
at that time, even inanimate things were overcome by the power of passion for their beloved.
O Lakṣmī, what description can be given of those sentient beings—
foresters, sages, and ascetics— for whom even that which was unbearable became endurable?
Then, assuming the humming of bees as his disguise, he remained with an invisible form.
Madana entered the mind of Bhava through the cavity of his ear.
Then Śaṅkara, having heard that sweet sound concerning Madana,
remembered his beloved Satī there, his mind intent on dalliance.
Then she, being exceedingly pure, gradually vanished;
and Madana immediately entered her and brought about a transformation.
Dhūrjaṭi, seized by a slight anger, then summoned his fortitude.
Having cast aside Madana by the power of yoga, he remained steadfast.
Then Smara blazed forth, having emerged from his heart;
drawing back his mango-blossom arrow, he stood at his left side.
Seeing a beautiful cluster of blossoms on a mango tree trembling in a gentle breeze,
Madana, whose banner is the sea-monster, quickly discharged an arrow named Mohana at the chest of Hara. (93)
The enchanting flower-arrowed god fell upon Hara’s heart;
his heart pierced, he became unsteady and turned toward passion.
Thus, as the act of love proceeded, even Śṛṅgāra joined with the Gaṇas. ||94-95||
Accompanied by gestures of amorous allure (*hāva*) and emotional expressions (*bhāva*), he entered into the presence of Hara.
Yet, due to the power of his yoga, Hara remained motionless within his own self;
he did not perceive even the slightest opening through which [the god of love] might enter. (96)
In the meantime, Śivā, accompanied by her two friends,
having clearly brought many flowers for the purpose of worshipping Śaṅkara,
stood near Śiva, intoxicated with the pride of her beauty and youth. (97–98)
At that very moment, Śaṅkara, having abandoned his meditation, remained still for an instant.
Seizing that opportunity, Madana gladdened Śambhu with the arrow called Harṣaṇa;
and seeing him thus delighted, Satī was filled with joy.
With various amorous gestures and emotional expressions, she provided assistance to Kāma.
At that very moment, Kāma again urged forth his arrow named Ruci;
seeing Hara filled with passion (rucimant), Smara released that flower-arrow.
Indeed, she was seen by Śambhu, who, out of her feminine nature, was deeply bashful;
yet, revealing her own limbs, she approached for the sake of an embrace. And under the pretext of performing worship, she touched his two feet.
Taking hold of the offering of the necklace, the cheeks and temples are touched;
taking hold of the tilaka-mark on the forehead, the brow, the eyes, and the beautiful eyebrows are touched;
and taking hold of the flower-ornament on the wrist, the palms of the hands and so forth are touched. (103–104)
Holding onto her flower-girdle, Śiva touched her waist, thighs, and navel;
holding onto the liquid sandalwood paste, he touched all her limbs.
Greatly infatuated by these touches, Śiva described Pārvatī.
What is her face, and what is the moon? What are her eyes, and what are the blue lotuses?
Oh! Her two eyebrows are bows worthy of worship for the abode of Kandarpa.
What is her lower lip, and what is the bimba fruit? What is her nose, and what is the beak of a parrot? 106–107.
Is her voice the warbling of a cuckoo? What is her waist like, and what is her altar-like [posture]?
What is her form, what is her gait, and what is her fitness for garments and ornaments? What is her grace, and what is her loveliness in every limb?
"Aho! This form is truly wonderful, a treasure-house of beauty and loveliness.
She was surely created for my sake; I shall certainly take her, there is no doubt.
Having thought thus, Hara began to strip away her garment.
Because she was still a young girl, she felt bashful and moved away to a distance;
yet, repeatedly looking back while exposing her own limbs, she stood there with a beautiful smile, gazing intently out of great delight. (111)
Upon seeing that beautiful woman worthy of being enjoyed, Śambhu reflected:
"Aha! By the mere sight of her, great bliss arises. What great happiness would there not be if I were to embrace her? (112–113)
Having reflected thus, he rose and approached Pārvatī;
yet, in that very manner, the goddess retreated further and further behind him.
Then, realizing himself to be under her control and likewise realizing her to be beyond his control, [he remained there].
Śambhu reflected: "Who is this woman who mocks me?
If I, the Lord who has mastery over myself, should desire the touch of another's body, then who else would be incapable [of it]? What base thing indeed would he not do? (1.15–1.16)
"Have obstacles arisen while I am performing this supreme austerity?
By what assailant has my mind been disturbed here?
The violation of a woman who is not one's own wife is a contradiction of dharma and a transgression of the Vedas."
"This is not fitting for those such as me; how has he come to such a state?"—
having reflected thus, he looked around apprehensively and saw Kāma standing on his left side, with his arrow drawn.
At that very moment, O beloved, a great wrath arose within Śambhu;
Kāma, too, having flown up and stationed himself in the sky, discharged his unfailing arrows.
Even though they were unfailing, they became futile before the enraged Maheśvara.
Manmatha was instantly seized by fear and trembled, overwhelmed by dread.
He called to mind all the gods; they arrived and offered praise.
Yet, even so, his mouth remained pervaded by the fire of great wrath. (121–122)
The three eyes and the forehead, unrestrained and filled with fire,
became fierce, formidable, and terrifying;
by force, the third eye was awakened by the fire.
From the forehead of Rudra, whose form was fierce and who was terrifying in his destruction of the world,
a great fire issued forth from the third eye situated in the middle of his brow with a sudden force, possessing a radiance equal to the fire of universal dissolution.
Blazing with upward-pointing flames, appearing as a torrent of fire, it blazed intensely.
In whichever direction Śambhu looked, there the great fire would leap up and fall down;
whirling again and again, the great conflagration rushed forward wherever his gaze fell.
In the meantime, Śambhu beheld Smara standing at his side.
Thinking, "This is Kāma, the one who has caused the agitation of my mind," Śaṅkara opened wide the eye on his forehead and directed it toward him.
Hara reduced Kama to ashes at will with the fire arising from that [third eye].
"Be appeased! Be appeased! were the words of the gods.
But he, having reduced him to ashes, began to expand in order to burn the world.
Then Bhava, for the sake of the world, divided the fire of Jātavedas into its various parts:
into the mango tree, the spring season, the moon, flowers, and others;
and into bees, the mouths of cuckoos, and the fire of Smara. (1.185.13–131)
When that heroic Smara was consumed by fire, the gods were overcome with grief.
Accompanied by her friends, Pārvatī, looking withered, went to the palace of her father. And Rati fell there, unconscious, as if she were dead.
Then, when her consciousness had returned, she lamented with cries of distress:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? What has been done here by the gods?
Having summoned my husband, they have destroyed him before the Lord."
"Alas, alas! O Lord, remember me, O Master, O beloved of my life, O bestower of happiness!
What has happened here? Alas, my fortune has been torn asunder!
Thus lamenting, she stretched out her hands and feet upon the ground.
There he tore out his hair and repeatedly struck his own head.
Hearing her lamentation, everyone became deeply distressed; the gods arrived, reflected thoroughly, and offered words of consolation. (136–137)
"Take some of this ash and preserve it with care; cast away your fear.
Śambhu will restore you to life, and you shall regain your husband.
Then the gods, having propitiated him again and again, spoke to Śiva.
"This was done there by Kāma; he has no self-interest therein.
It was indeed caused to be done by all the gods who were oppressed by Tāraka.
By you, through the burning of Kāma, they have been rendered fruitless along with their wives. (1.185.140)
"How might the flow of the world continue when this has been done?
O Śarva, comfort Rati; bring about the removal of her grief.
Then Rati also went to Śambhu for refuge.
With her body smeared with the beautiful and heart-pleasing ashes of Smara, she knelt upon the ground and, from the ocean of her sorrow, spoke:
"Homage be to Śambhu, who by name and by his very deeds is the giver of suffering! (142–143)
Salutations to you, the husband of Pārvatī; salutations to the one who causes Rati to lament;
salutations to the deer of Satī; salutations to the occasional yogin.
Salutations to you, the substratum of Māyā and the like; salutations to you who are free from Māyā.
Salutations to you whose nature is that of Brahmā; salutations to you in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Salutations to you in the form of Vairāja; salutations to you, Sadāśiva.
Salutations to Śiva, to Rudra; salutations to you in the form of the Liṅga. 145–146.

Homage to you who are the embodiment of light, to you, the hundred Rudras; homage to you, the ten million Rudras; homage to the dweller of Kailāsa. Homage to you of dual form; homage to the one free from suffering.
Salutations again and again to you, the tranquil yogin who has Sati as his lord.
Salutations to you in the form of a bull, and salutations to you as Śarabha.
Salutations to you in the form of a Kirāta, and salutations to you who are naked.
Homage to you, the mendicant who finds delight in brahmin women;
homage to you, the bodiless one, the great-bodied one, and the life-force itself. Homage be to you, the one possessed of desire, and homage to you, the one whose desires have been destroyed.
Salutations to you, the refuge; salutations to you, the bestower of the desires of your devotees.
(151) Salutations to you, whose anger is irresistible; salutations to you, the giver of union with the beloved.
Grant me the substance of my desire: how can I live without my husband? (152)
Having praised him thus, Rati again lamented there.
Śambhu said, "I am pleased; I shall restore you to life within my own being. O Rati, do not grieve, always in your mind and heart."

The desire of all living beings shall dwell eternally in an invisible form. May you dwell among the assembly of women, and may the bodiless god of love dwell among men; and when two young women are together, may there always be an inner union between them.
Whatever has occurred through my wrath shall be exactly so and not otherwise;
for as long as he remains bodiless, there can be no other outcome for the Lord of Rati.
At the end of the first Dvāpara age, Kṛṣṇa shall become the Lord of Gold (Hiraṇyeśa).
He shall procreate Hiraṇyā and the one named Pradyumna, who is Kāma. Śambara shall indeed seize Pradyumna, the incarnation of Kāma;
having cast him into the ocean, he will return to his own city. || 157–158 ||
"O Rati, dwell happily for that long in the city of Śambara!
Then Kāma, together with his body, will reunite with you there.
And Kāma, having slain Śambara and taken the wealth, [will come] with you. || 159 ||
"He will go back to his own eternal city born of the realm of truth (Satyaloka). There, until the dissolution of all beings, you two shall exist in happiness.
Having been addressed thus, the beloved of Kāma bowed her head to Śaṅkara.
And Rati went to another grove on the Snowy Mountain;
distressed, she wept many times in various delightful spots.
Thus Rati wandered through the forests for many years.
Then, having gone to the city ruled by the asura Śambara,
she lived there as a servant, always desiring the birth of a husband;
she awaited that time of a yuga’s duration ordained by Rudra.
Then, O beloved, Brahmā, taking that submarine fire which was composed of wrath and desirous of burning the three worlds,
assumed a gentle-flamed form and went to the ocean along with Vāḍava for the welfare of the world.
Brahmā said to the salt ocean: "I shall point it out; take it!
This is the wrath of Maheśa, which has assumed the form of the Vāḍava fire;
you must hold this Jvālāmukha until the dissolution of all beings."
"Food and water shall be yours eternally," he said;
thus addressed, the Ocean accepted the Vāḍava fire.
Then, having entered the ocean, he became pure, assuming the form of the Vāḍava fire.
Blazing intensely with garlands of flames, he consumed the torrents of water poured upon him.
Then, having drunk that desired water, the clouds rained down upon the surface of the earth;
the entire world regained its composure, being liberated from the fear of the submarine fire (Vāḍava).

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Śambhu’s Penance, Pārvatī’s Service, the Discharge of Arrows by Kāma Sent by Indra, the Burning of Kāma by the Fire from the Third Eye, Ratī’s Lamentation, the Granting of a Boon to Anaṅga— who was to later possess a body as Pradyumna— and the Residence of Ratī in the House of Śambara, as well as the Residence of the Vāḍava Fire, which is the Fire of Wrath, in the Ocean," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
