Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; after burning Kāma, Mahādeva went to his own abode, Kailāsa, while Pārvatī remained with a distressed mind. (1)
Then, having gone to her father’s house and met her mother herself, she,
being greatly distressed, considered herself as if born again;
she censured her own form and found no peace anywhere.
During sleep, drinking, walking, bathing, traveling, and wandering, as well as when moving among her companions, Śivā indeed found no happiness at all.
"Fie upon my own nature, and likewise upon my birth and my actions! (3–4)
She grieved constantly and was bewildered again and again;
she found no happiness at all, and she cried out, "O Śiva! O Śiva!
Even so, when his efforts had proven fruitless, Nārada was addressed by Mahendra.
Then, reminded of the purpose of the gods' task, he went to Indra.
At that time, the king of the gods sent Nārada to the lord of mountains.
Nārada arrived at the mountain and accepted his worship and other honors.
He heard that the burner of Kama was also suffering because of Parvati.
Then Narada, the destroyer of sorrow, said to Kali:
"Listen, Kali; he has been served by you here through penance, even without [further] effort."
And that lord of yours, having become dispassionate after burning away the god of love, has sent you forth.
Therefore, endowed with great asceticism, worship the Lord for a long time; he too is performing penance for a true purpose, and the union of the two shall come to pass.
No rite whatsoever is accomplished without the grace of a true guru.
"I give you this mantra: *Namaḥ Śivāya*. Recite it always.
By hearing this king of mantras, Śaṅkara becomes well-pleased.
By this, Śambhu will be propitiated and will become manifest before you.
Contemplating His form, perform penance while reciting the mantra.
Indeed, the fruit of all things is obtained through penance alone, and never otherwise.
Having thus given his command, the divine sage departed for another place;
Satī, meanwhile, taking her two friends Jayā and Vijayā with her,
then questioned her mother and father through those two companions.

O Himavat! This daughter of yours desires to attain Hara—who is to be won through asceticism—and thereby bring fulfillment to her body and her lineage. O Lord, let Girijā go to the forest and perform great penance at your command. (15–16)
The Mountain said, "It pleases me; let it also please Menā.
Then, having gone to Menā and bowed, they both said: "O Goddess, salutations to you!
For the sake of Śiva, this daughter has come here after obtaining her father’s permission. (17)
“If your permission could be obtained, O Mother,” she asked her mother.
Menā did not grant it, but rather became distressed in mind. Then Pārvatī, joining her palms, spoke to her own mother: (18–19)
"What benefit is there for me from this unfortunate body without a husband?
How might that Śambhu, who grants happiness, be obtained as my husband forever?
Through austerities, one’s desired goal is attained; indeed, nothing is impossible for one who practices penance. (1.186.20)
People carry around misfortune in vain when the means [to remedy it] exist.
O Mother, tomorrow morning I shall go to perform austerities to attain Maheśvara;
grant me permission today to depart for the penance grove.
Menā said: "O Śivā, what have you gained by your previous penance?
On the contrary, having become sorrowful, you have obtained birth here in my house.
O Pārvatī, perform penance now within the home; do not go outside!"
"All the gods and all the sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell constantly in our home.
O daughter, you must not be obstinate; you must not go anywhere outside.
Your body is delicate, whereas asceticism is great and harsh."
"Daughter, you must not go; that is not at all fitting for women.
Having been thus forbidden by her mother, she was thereafter known by the name Umā.
"I shall either win Śambhu as my husband or I shall cast down his body."
"Grant me permission for asceticism; otherwise, Pārvatī will not remain here.
Seeing such intense persistence, she then gave her command.
Having bowed to her mother and father, she departed together with her two friends.
Having abandoned all objects of enjoyment and various garments,
and having quickly donned bark-cloths and tied on a girdle of muñja grass;
having likewise cast aside his necklace and put on the beautiful skin of a deer.
Śailajā set out toward the plateau where the descent of the Gaṅgā occurs—
the very place where, in former times, Śambhu remained and performed austerities for the sake of a worthy goal.
And she beheld that plateau of the Himavat mountain, which had been rendered empty by Hara.
Crying out "Alas, Hari!", she was momentarily overwhelmed with grief upon remembering that this very peak had attained the fame of Gaurīśikhara,
the holy descent of the Gaṅgā, adorned with various minerals. (32)
It was covered with celestial flowering creepers, its trees resounded with the humming of bees;
it possessed divine cool waterfalls and was inhabited by beasts and birds, made fragrant by the blossoming lotuses of both the water and the land. (33–34)
Containing deep caverns within its interior, it was endowed with abodes for divine dwellers;
it possessed the green luster of *kalpa*-tree creepers, vines, grasses, and shrubs, and was richly filled with the filaments of flower buds and fruits from every season. (35)
There, the virtuous Pārvatī became initiated for the sake of her religious observance (niyama).
By her, excellent trees were planted there and nourished with water.
Having consecrated the ground and personally constructed an altar, Pārvatī [proceeded].
Having bathed three times a day and subsisting on dry leaves, she began a great penance;
restraining all her senses along with the internal mind,
she remained established in her own self, which is of the nature of Śiva, having withdrawn her very mode of existence into it.
And in the summer, having placed a blazing fire all around her day and night,
she stood in their midst and performed the penance of the five fires; meanwhile,
she was constantly chanting the five-syllable mantra of Hara within herself.
During the rains, she maintained a firm posture upon stone slabs amidst the downpour;
in the cold, she remained constantly in the midst of water, devoted to the fire of Śiva.
Even during gale-force winds, intense heat, and frosty nights, she persisted.
She meditated, keeping Śiva—the future husband—within her heart while performing austerities.
She spent the first thousand years subsisting on fruits, the second on leaves, and the third on a single leaf at a time. ||42–43||
Then, having even abandoned leaves, Aparṇā remained fixed in austerity;
standing on one foot and subsisting on air alone,
she meditated upon Śaṅkara for three thousand years in the forest of penance.

Where Hara performed austerities for sixty thousand years, Satī calculated that the threefold suffering had neither come nor gone. Having stayed for a moment in the presence of Hara, that virtuous woman reflected thus: (45–46).
O Mahādeva, do you not know me now, even though I abide by my vows?
O Lord, if I am devoted to you with my whole being, then be gracious to me!
O Lord, if this mantra has been performed with devotion, then be gracious to me!
"If I am yours, then know me as such; be gracious to me, O Lord.
If I am to be accepted by you, O Protector, then be gracious to me, O Lord.
Having thus prayed every day, the virtuous woman remained devoted to her ascetic penance.
By the power of Pārvatī’s asceticism there,
even naturally antagonistic creatures did not harm one another.
All the trees, as well as the grasses and the meadows, [flourished] there.
Variegated flowers and tender leaves were always produced;
thus the forest became like Mount Kailāsa.
Through the power of her asceticism, it was born as a manifestation of spiritual perfection and remained so forever.
While Pārvatī was thus performing her austerities for five thousand years,
the Mountain approached and said to her:
"By him, Kāma— who left you, his devoted servant— was reduced to ashes."
"O daughter, the angry Hara has departed; being devoid of virtue, he will not return.
O daughter, you have fallen into vain delusion; the Lord does not desire you. Therefore arise, O Pārvatī, and come quickly to your own home."
In this very manner, she was addressed by Menā as well as by Meru,
Sahya, Mandara, Maināka, and the mountain Krauñca; yet,
despite her brothers, sisters, and others, she did not abandon her ascetic penance.
Either I shall win over Hara, or I shall cast away my own body.
This is my sole vow: how is it that the Lord does not come?
It is fortunate that Smara was burnt by him; having abandoned me, he departed as one devoid of merit.
"If I am truly devoted to him, I shall bring him here by the power of my asceticism.
All of you may go; I will not go to his house.
Only after having brought my lord Śambhu back will I return to that home."
Having spoken thus, the sweet-spoken daughter of the mountain became silent. Perceiving the firm resolve of that great and truthful woman, they all departed for their own abodes,
bestowing blessings while filled with great wonder.
Accompanied by her friends, Satī performed severe penance;
by that, the entire triple world, including all things mobile and immobile, became scorched.
Then the gods, asuras, siddhas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and cāraṇas—
The Guhyakas, Munis, Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, and Mahoragas;
the Asuras, Mānavas, Prajāpatis, and likewise the Lokapālas—having encountered this most painful heat, they did not know its cause. (63–64)
Then, having gone there, they questioned the Creator regarding the cause of the asceticism.
Brahmā, too, having understood that the heat was produced by Pārvatī’s penance,
went accompanied by the hosts of gods to relate it to Hari.
Having praised and bowed down to Him who was shining in the Ocean of Milk, he spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"Save us, save us, who have come to You for refuge!
We are scorched by the heat of our wife's devotion; O Teacher of the World, grant us peace."
Having heard this, Hari said to them all, "Let us go to Śaṅkara;
let us pray for the sake of Satī’s marriage, so that thereafter there may be happiness.
Having thus deliberated, the gods and others went to behold Satī’s ascetic penance.
They bowed to her, the Mother of the World, and then went toward Hara.
They beheld him seated at ease, gracious, and affectionate toward his devotees;
having prostrated before Śaṅkara, who sat upon his yogic mat, they offered him praise.

Salutations be to the destroyer of heat; salutations again and again to the bestower of peace. Salutations again and again to the one who perfectly grants the fruit of Pārvatī’s austerities. (7.1) If you, being devoid of passion, do not accept Pārvatī, [then...]
"In that case, she will consume this entire world of moving and non-moving beings with her ascetic power.
Furthermore, upon her taking a husband, the work of the gods will be accomplished.
Therefore, having granted her a boon, quickly restrain her asceticism."
Having heard this, Śambhu said to them: "A great task has been accomplished by me;
Kāma has been burnt. Remain free from desire and as celibate students (brahmacārins).
Indeed, be endowed with supreme bliss and remain free from all transformations."
If Satī is captured, she will surely bring him back to life again.
From desire arise anger, delusion, the loss of memory, and so forth;
all these are givers of suffering and torment—may the gods always abandon them.
If a woman is married, she is known as a great fetter;
there are many evil associations, but association with women is greater than those.
One is released from all bonds, yet one is not released from the bond of women.
Indeed, even for a yogi, desires increase due to association with women.
If one wishes for the liberation of Brahman, one should abandon the snare of women from afar. For a man, a woman is like a white-washed gourd-fruit filled with poison. (78–79)
For the sake of women, even a man is like a white-powdered *indravāruṇī* gourd;
thus, one should understand that each is poison to the other. Nevertheless, I shall uphold your word in order to avert the calamity of the gods.
"Go to your respective abodes and remain there forever without fear.
"I shall go for the sake of the peace resulting from the penance of Satī and for the welfare [of all].
Having heard this, all the gods then bowed and departed for their own homes.
Then Śaṅkara remembered the seven sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others;
with serene countenances, the seven sages arrived swiftly.
Having bowed down, they all sat down, highly honored by Śambhu.
And it has been said that she practices unbroken penance at Pārśva,
having abandoned all desires and longing only to obtain me as her husband.
Go there and test the firmness of her love.
Thus commanded, they all went to where that virtuous lady was performing her penance.
Having bowed to the daughter of the mountain, they said: "For what purpose do you perform this austerity?
Tell us, O Goddess; we shall carry out whatever you desire exactly as it is."
Having bowed to the sages, Satī spoke according to the procedure prescribed by Nārada:
"May Rudra be my husband," she resolved, and remained steadfast in austerity.
May Lord Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, fulfill her hope. (87–88)
Having heard this, the sages laughed and spoke these deceptive and false words:
"How can Nārada—who is fond of strife, a creator of distress, and full of guile—be trusted? In every way, he is a deceiver who incites others to suffering. (89)
You know the sons of Dakṣa, and for that reason they were cast out by you.
You know Citraketu; that wicked man caused him to lose his kingdom. You know Prahlāda; he caused Hiraṇyakaśipu to be alienated from him.
Indeed, as soon as Nārada’s art of wickedness fell even slightly upon his ear,
he abandoned his own home and became miserable, just like you.
Nārada is foul-souled, though his body appears radiant on the outside.
As his neighbors, we know him especially well:
they describe Baka as a virtuous man who never eats fish at all.
A co-resident should understand the character of one who lives with them. (93–94)
Moreover, you who have remained steadfast in austerity, having placed your trust in his words, have been deceived, O Great Goddess! Return home and abandon your penance.
He for whose sake you undergo this suffering has become indifferent toward you.
Ever servile, shameless, inauspicious, homeless, and of low birth;
having ghosts, spirits, and demons for his kin, naked and wearing wretched raiment—by that spear-bearer, the foremost of rogues, have you been deceived. (96–97)
Having granted the boon, he departed; after five thousand years, he does not return.
O Goddess of Gods, consider this: how can one who was so affectionate toward Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, now be nothing but a deceiver? 98.
Having married her, he did not provide for her protection; what will he do now?
He remains just as angry as before and will not support you.
That deceiver will simply find fault with you once more and abandon you.
He who has no compassion in his heart does not truly see a maiden;
since he has burnt Kāma, the giver of pleasure, how will you live with him?
O maiden, honor our words and go home.
For one whose mind is unsettled, the desire for tranquility is like a flower in the sky. (102) A beautiful woman such as you would shine in every way in the house of Viṣṇu.
All virtues reside in you; great virtues reside in Viṣṇu. (103)
His home is a great, prosperous, and divine Vaikuṇṭha, the most excellent,
inhabited by millions of male and female servants and adorned with celestial chariots and gardens.
O beautiful one, worship Him— the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of Ramā, or the Lord of Rādhā.
"Therefore, we shall arrange your marriage; abandon Śaṅkara.
It is said that a maiden's marriage is appropriate in her fourteenth year.
You have performed service during that suitable time and made such a request."
Nevertheless, he did not take your hand in marriage;
five thousand years have passed since then.
Even so, that fool still does not accept you, for you are even more [beautiful] than she.
Therefore, abandoning all forceful exertion, be happy through Viṣṇu.
(108) Just as there can be no satisfaction for the thirsty from the water of a mirage in the desert, O daughter, there are two kinds of happiness for embodied beings in this world. (109)
If there were union of body with body, there would be supreme bliss in the mind;
for just as the body of a maiden is indeed tender, beautiful, and auspicious,
so too would the body of a youth be, should there be pleasure born of the body.
Indeed, physical pleasure can arise only between a husband and wife, and not otherwise.
By nature, however, he [Śiva] is naked as the sky-clad one, terrible, adorned with bellows and bones, a bearer of a skull, a mendicant, nude, three-eyed, and of unstable conduct. (111–112)

He has the appearance of one intoxicated or insane, and he is possessed by the loathsome; he is this very misfortune personified, attended by a host of spirits. Carrying human fat and bones, he is terrifying with the hissing of serpents.
How is it that one dwelling in a cremation ground like a dog-cooker (śvapaca) is desired by you as a son?
Hari exists as the sustainer of the world, the enjoyer of sacrifice, and the subduer of Pāka;
he is the god of gods, the blazing fire, and the vital breath of embodied beings.
Kubera, the Moon, the Sun, Varuṇa, and other gods—
those who enjoy their desires at will, who assume forms at will, and whose prosperity is according to their desire—
why do you not wish to obtain even one of these?
The hardship endured for the sake of attaining Śiva is likewise a fruitless tree.
Therefore, come, daughter; remaining at home, be happy.
Choose another husband, O auspicious one; [this effort] will bear fruit somewhere else.
Having heard this and more in detail, Pārvatī smiled and said:
"Although what you have said is logical according to my own understanding,
it is indeed for the sake of one who is weak, lacking faith, and unsteady."
By birth I am a daughter of the mountains—hard, powerful, and firm;
steadfast, invincible, and resolute. Whether Hara unites with me or not, O gentle one, I shall not abandon this penance which is innate to our nature.
"I shall obtain him or I shall choose him; otherwise, I shall remain without fuel.
Suffering, asceticism, the forest, and austerity are natural to one born of the mountain race.
All of these are indeed as I desire; you ought not to restrain me."
"Nārada’s words are wholesome and indeed suited to my birth.
They will surely come to pass for one dwelling in the forest with one who dwells on the mountain.
Victory is ever with those whose steadfastness lies in the words of their gurus. (123–124)
For those who pursue what is undesirable, there is only suffering here and in the hereafter, and never any happiness.
Know this: to whom does space belong? To whom does fire belong? To whom does the wind belong?
To whom does Indra belong? To whom does Varuṇa belong? And to whom do the sun and moon belong as eyes? (125)

For just as the intellect of those afflicted by insanity and the like becomes such that they perceive even desired objects as contrary; just as they perceive what is small and insignificant as superior, and what is superior as small and insignificant. (126–127)
I dwell in the void or do not resort to anything else,
for Viṣṇu— the abode of all virtues, the wanderer, and the ever-prosperous— is eternally present there.
He indeed displays worldly sovereignty to human beings.
Śambhu, however, is devoid of qualities, changeless, and free from pride and the like;
he is the Avadhūta, the supreme Haṃsa, the highest bliss, the supreme Lord.
To those smeared by Māyā, he appears as having a fondness for ornaments and such, but for Brahman, there is none.
O Brahmins, if that Śiva does not perform my marriage,
then even though I am auspicious, I shall remain forever unmarried and shunned.
I have no thirst for sensual desire, nor do I practice austerity for the sake of desire.
I am performing penance for the very same purpose for which you are performing penance.
(1.32) If Śarva accepts my hand, both of us will find happiness;
if he does not accept her hand, then her happiness as a virtuous wife will be even greater. (1.33)
Now I shall accomplish that which is pure; thereafter, I will achieve even more.
Whether it succeeds here or not, it will certainly succeed in liberation.
Whatever I do, having reflected upon it, there will be neither loss nor gain.
"Why should I desire another husband? For I have no longing for sensual pleasure. I beg you for forgiveness regarding my excessive speech; may you accept my hospitality.
May the swans unite the swan with auspicious blessings, so that they may be joined together. (1.36)
By your words of blessing, Mārkaṇḍeya became long-lived;
by your grace, the outcaste became the sage Arundhatī;
and by your favor, Viśvāmitra attained the status of a Brahmin-sage.
"Likewise, by a mere fragment of your grace, may Śarvāṇikā become a mountain stream.
Having spoken thus, she prostrated before them and honored them with divine objects; then, remembering Śiva, she who was devoted to the unwavering dharma of Śiva fell silent. (138–139)
"May it be auspicious for the sages as well; may their heart's desire be fulfilled.
May the fruit of their asceticism be realized swiftly, and may they attain union with Śambhu.
May their marriage take place soon, and may there be our honoring."
"May we be carriers of people; may all be most auspicious!
(141) Having thus properly honored Śivā with these blessings, they departed for Hara—those who were pleased, intent on the task of the gods, ever hopeful, and discerning. (142)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Pārvatī’s Grief, Nārada’s Instruction, and the Prohibition of Her Austerities, as well as Gaurī’s Five Thousand Years of Penance on Gaurīśṛṅga and Her Examination and Bestowal of Blessings by the Seven Sages, Despite the Austerities Having Been Forbidden," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
[Chapter 187] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna)
— Chapter 187.
[The Author: Chapter 188.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O beloved, the sages, composed and undisturbed, spoke to Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods.
For the sake of Śaṅkara, Pārvatī indeed made her life the wager;
fearless, without support, without hope, and without possessions,
devoid of qualities and free from desire, she performed penance until the dissolution of all beings.
If Śambhu’s asceticism, born of the nature of the mountain, were to meet with [worldly] pleasure, both might meet;
yet from that, the bliss born of liberation would not meet.
Indeed, happiness increases through austerity; there is no such thing as useless penance.
I shall either accomplish auspiciousness or cast off this body;
I shall either marry Śambhu or remain forever a maiden;
I shall lead a life of celibacy or I shall take up the life of a wandering ascetic.
"I shall die and go to the state of a perpetual celibate (naiṣṭhika) to reach Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
Having made this resolution, that virtuous woman (Satī) performed penance.
Then, whatever was to be done there and whatever was to be performed by the Lord indeed occurred.
Having thus reported the event and received permission, they went to their own homes.
Śaṅkara, desiring then to test the Goddess’s asceticism,
assumed an excellent matted-hair form, eager for the trial.
Having become an elderly brahmin, richly adorned with various marks and carrying a staff and an umbrella,
he went to that peak, blazing on all sides with splendor.
He wore a deerskin, a girdle of muñja grass, and carried a water-pot.

Seeing that great elder approaching her hermitage— a mendicant with a sacred thread, aged, covered in wrinkles, and his body smeared with ashes— she rose up and bowed to him as he arrived. (1.187.10–11)
Approaching him with affection, the virtuous woman fell at his feet;
she then honored him with all the articles used for hospitable reception, as he was worthy of hospitality from all.
She then inquired after the welfare of him who was in the form of a religious student.
"O Brahmin, from where have you come, and in what place is your hermitage?
To which direction will you go? Please rest here for a while.
The mendicant said: "O female ascetic, I am coming here from the sacred fords (tīrthas)."
My residence was in Vārāṇasī; I shall go to the region of Pṛthūdaka.
I have bathed at Prayāga, at Kubjāmra, and at Caṇḍikeśvara;
[I have also bathed] in the assembly of kinsmen, at Kurukṣetra, at Haridvāra, and at Kanakhala.
From Kedāra and Badarīkuṇḍa, I then came to your hermitage.
Having performed the rites for this sacred ford, I shall go to Pṛthūdaka.
I am an ascetic who travels according to my own will and bestows happiness upon others.
Skilled in the journey of renunciation, I am the destroyer of the suffering of ascetics; free from the pairs of opposites and desirous of liberation, I am a worshiper of the gods.
I am old, and I emaciate my body through penance as is fitting.
I ask you this, and you ought to tell me the reason for it:
O auspicious lady, why do you, established in the first stage of life, perform such fierce asceticism that causes one to experience suffering? (1.187.20)
Who are you? Whose daughter are you? For what purpose do you perform this formidable penance, so difficult even for sages, in this lonely forest?
You are neither a child nor an old woman; you appear as a beautiful young woman.
"O mature woman, why indeed do you perform such severe penance without your husband?
For women in their middle age, there is enjoyment with their husbands; when youth is stable, periods of time spent in excellent pleasures pass away. (22-23)
"O auspicious one, are you the companion of some ascetic?
O Goddess, that ascetic does not support you; he has gone elsewhere.
Tell me, in whose family were you born, who is your father, and what is your status?"
You are a vessel of great good fortune; how is it that you take delight in asceticism?
Are you Lakṣmī, born from the Vedas, or are you Ramā, or perhaps Sarasvatī? I believe that even you are endowed with beauty, people, sovereignty, and prosperity.
Therefore, for what purpose have you cast aside these ornaments and taken up matted locks?
Having abandoned fine Chinese silk, why indeed have you donned bark garments?
To whom do they belong, for what purpose, and who are you? Tell me, for I am worthy to hear it.
Having heard this, Pārvatī, the daughter of Himavat, spoke to the lord of sages:
"For the sake of Śaṅkara, I perform penance; I shall find Śaṅkara as my husband. Formerly, I was Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, composed of yoga."
With my body consumed by fire, I have now become a daughter of the mountain;
I remained here engaged in service to Śambhu as he performed his austerities.
Having reduced Manmatha to ashes, he departed, leaving me behind.

But I, having come here for the sake of penance and yet not having attained Śaṅkara, was about to enter the fire at the conclusion of my austerities when I saw you and paused for a moment. Go now; I shall enter the fire, seeking Śiva in another birth.
Having spoken thus, Pārvatī indeed entered the fire before him;
at that very moment, the fire became cool like sandalwood paste.
Then, after a short while, rising from the fire by way of the path of the sky—
As she was rising up into the sky, the twice-born one asked her with a smile:
"Aho! Great indeed is the power of your supreme austerity, by the force of which even the fire did not burn you, remaining quite cool. (34-35)
"Speak, O Goddess, according to the truth; I shall fulfill your heart's desire.
What boon do you wish for, O fair-browed one? You must not conceal even the slightest thing.
For you possess all power; what need have you for ascetic penance?"
Having obtained a jewel in your hand, why do you seek worthless glass?
(37) How has such beauty of form been rendered useless?
Having abandoned ornaments, garments, flowers, and precious substances, you have donned bark-cloth. (38)

"Having abandoned my home, I have obtained the forest for my dwelling, which is always a source of suffering. Tell me, O Goddess, how there may be happiness for me; I shall do what is beneficial for you.
Having heard this, Ambikā urged her friend Vijayā to speak.

Vijayā said: "O aged Brahmin, this daughter of the Mountain King is named Pārvatī, also known as Kālī; she desires Śaṅkara as her husband. This friend of mine is still a maiden, for she has not been wedded by anyone. (1.187.40–41)
Five thousand years have indeed passed while she was performing penance;
nevertheless, because she is the daughter of a god, she appears as though only sixteen years old.
For among those of noble divine lineage, there is no diminution of their physical forms due to years.
The form of those whose lifespan is ten million years is indeed like that of sixteen-year-olds;
it remains forever perfectly stable, with neither old age nor graying hair.
This [earth], having abandoned Mahendra and the others, and having abandoned Viṣṇu and Brahmā, [remains].
Pārvatī desires to obtain Śaṅkara as her husband.
By her, trees have been planted that are rich in fruits and flowers;
they have always been held in her heart as being worthy for the worship of Śaṅkara.
Having performed every act of self-surrender, she remains constantly engaged in austerity.
Whether she comes or does not come, she is indeed dedicated to Śarva.
Thus I have declared to you the mental resolve of Pārvatī.
The matted-haired ascetic also spoke with a laugh: "I do not trust what has been said by a friend.
If it is the truth, there would be no laughter; let him speak for himself.
Pārvatī, knowing in her mind that he was a person connected to Śambhu—
With a serene mind, she said: "O friend, what you have said is exactly so.
In thought, word, and deed, Śaṅkara has indeed been chosen by me.
I knew that Śambhu was difficult to attain, yet I considered him as if he were easily won. (1.187.50)
I shall perform penance until the end of my life, for such is my conviction.
Even if he does not meet me outwardly, he has indeed met me within.
Oh, how great is my fortune to behold the Seven Sages!
The vision of the venerable Brahmadeva, which is pregnant with Śiva,
has been obtained by me here in this terrible forest, even upon that mountain peak; thus,
the tree of my desire has reached its seasonal bloom.
Whether that indifferent Lord knows or does not know, I know this: impelled by a trace of the Compassionate One’s grace, the Brahmin speaks; therefore, he is called the "mouth" of this [Lord]. (54)
"I know only this much: Śaṅkara is hidden within you.
Therefore, let my salutation be offered to him, joining my head to his feet, just as I have bowed with my head joined to your feet.
Having heard that, the Brahmin said: "Listen, O maiden beloved of Hara!
O fair-browed one, O lady of excellent vows, you speak everything appropriately and as is fitting.
I know Mahādeva; listen with attention."
In some places Hara is naked; in others he wears the skins of tigers and elephants.
He has the bull as his emblem, is smeared with ashes, and is disfigured by his mass of matted locks.
Skulls and bones are at his hands and neck, and his limbs are entwined with serpents. (58–59)

He is one who eats poison, one who eats what is unfit to be eaten, and one with deformed eyes; he is entirely devoid of knowledge regarding his home, birth, and origins, and is cheated of the enjoyments of domestic life. With ten arms, served by hosts of spirits, he is filthy and miserable.
He is declared to be cruel, the performer of destruction, and the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and other rites.
(61) In whose house there is indeed no happiness, but rather affliction upon affliction—how can you desire such a man as he, O beautiful lady? (62)
You are a jewel among women, and your father is the king of all monarchs;
why do you seek such a husband through such severe asceticism?
Having given away gold coins, you wish to receive only glass.
Having abandoned the finest sandalwood, you wish to smear yourself with mud.
Having cast aside the splendor of the sun, you desire the light of a firefly.
Having discarded fine Chinese silk, you desire skins and bark garments.
Abandoning a residence in a palace, you desire a wretched dwelling;
casting aside a treasure of jewels, you desire black charcoal.
Having utterly abandoned kings, you desire a cowherd.
"Having abandoned the world-protectors, why do you desire the protector of spirits?
This does not seem appropriate to me; it appears contrary to what is right.
Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, and where is that fire-eyed one?"
Who are you with a face like the moon, and where is he with a face of five fires?
Who are you with a braid upon your head, and where is he with matted locks upon his crown?
Where are you, whose limbs are fit for sandalwood paste, and where is he smeared with the ashes of the funeral pyre?
Where is she who wears soft, smooth, and excellent garments, and where is he whose clothing is tiger skin and elephant hide?
Where is she who is worthy of golden ornaments, and where is he who has cruel serpents for his crest-ornament?
Where is the goddess who delights in the food of sages, and where is he who is very fond of offerings to the spirits?
Where is the lute and the sweet chanting, and where is this drum-beating with its harsh *ḍḍaṃhaḍḍaṃha* sounds?
Where is the sweetness of your throat, and where is this harsh, bull-like bray?
Where is the softness of the land-lotus, and where is this touch that is rough and coarse?
He possesses not even the slightest wealth, nor does he obtain even a bit of clothing.
He has not even the slightest prosperity, save for his two oxen and his serpents;
he has no true servants, save for the naked spirits and the like.
He has no gentle people, except for Bhairavas and Vīrakas;
he has no sweet food, except for the poison of hemp and *gṛñjana* garlic; and there is no betel-leaf in his mouth, except for the venom of the *dhattūra*.
He has no garland made of flowers except for the skull of a corpse;
he has nothing soft in his hand except for the stone trident;
and there is no essence of love upon his lips except for the cruelty of destruction.
Its side is not tender-limbed without a wooden frame;
its image does not possess a golden luster without black ash and the like.
Nor can it remain hidden, for it was fashioned by Brahmins in the past.
Or perhaps this third person is a man who merely appears in the form of a woman;
he has no wife with whom he is pleased, and thus he must be of the third gender. Indeed, it was for the concealment of his third nature that Kama was reduced to ashes by him.
At that time, you indeed showed him disregard and, having left him, went elsewhere.
Great eggs have formed in his belly like the feathers of a crow;
he has the disease of egg-enlargement, yet you did not recognize it.
Even during the dead of night, he does not allow her to sleep;
he enjoys himself even more with his wife and causes her great distress.
He possesses such ill-omened characteristics that he will surely cause you suffering as well.
O Sati! Abandon even his name; though Śiva, he is forever inauspicious to you.
He has no caste, no lineage, no mother—how then could there be a father?
Indeed, in Śaṅkara there is no knowledge, no goodness, and no faith whatsoever.
Protection is seen on his body, yet poison is visible upon his neck (85).
Anger is seen within him, and indeed not even a trace of passion remains;
he maintains only hatred, by which he destroys all creatures (86).
Where is your chest, worthy of being adorned with necklaces, and where is its contact with that shaven head?
Where is your body-unguent and beauty, and where is the dust of the funeral pyre?
That indeed does not please me; do as you wish.
Whatever is an unreal thing, all of that is pleasing to you.
I think you have been utterly deluded by some malevolent spell or mantra; or else, you have been thus thrown into confusion by the power of previously accumulated unseen karma (*adṛṣṭa*). (88–89)
"Otherwise, why do you wish to fall into this pit after seeing me?
I am going, O Great Goddess; do as you wish.
Pārvatī spoke thus to that brahmin, considering him to be a reviler of Śiva.
"Go! If you go, O Brahmin, why did your foot touch this place?
Even the foot of one who reviles and is impure destroys merit.
Whether he be Śiva or Bhīma, whether he be wealthy or poor," || 91-92 ||
Whether unadorned or adorned, as he is or whatever he may be;
whether inauspicious or auspicious, gentle, harsh, or even dull-witted; whether lacking prosperity or lacking a vehicle, or even poisoned or poisonless— (93)
Whether he possesses bad qualities or is devoid of qualities, whether he has virtues or is lacking them;
whether he is foul-smelling or fragrant, odorless or carrying a skull;
whether he is naked or clothed, wearing garments of dust, ashes, and the like. (94–95)
Whether possessing marks or devoid of marks, whether of the third gender,
an enemy of desire, possessed of great desire, or free from desire and inactive;
whether richly smeared with ashes, richly clad in skins, rich in spirits, or accompanied by a hand-drum (ḍamaru).
One born with [the Sun in] Aśleṣā is either wealthy yet has a rough body, or is destitute of wealth;
||97|| or he may be addicted to hemp, leeks, datura, poison, and the like; or he suffers from a trident-like pain (tuberculosis), or bears the marks of a woman, or has large testicles. ||98||
Whether he be confused, fatherless, a destroyer, or even a protector;
whether he be inert, conscious, a mere stump, or even a stone—
he alone is my husband, both in this creation and in every other creation.
In age after age, in another interval of time, or even in this very life in another birth,
he alone has been my husband, he remains so now, and he shall be so in the future.
Many times have I been born both as one without a husband and as one with a husband.
"In Mahālaya I am indeed a widow, but in creation I am always a wife with her husband.
What concern do you have for my unhappiness? Go, O Brahmin, as you please.
You have no share in my happiness, nor indeed any share in my sorrow."
"You vainly revile me, Śambhu, becoming a venomous serpent through your asceticism.
Indeed, this much was known by me: that you had come desiring a journey;
but that you were an ascetic who acts for the welfare of others, and not one who acts contrarily, was not known. (103–104)
Without knowing him, you revile Śambhu, the vessel of all sovereignty.
One who roams at will may indeed sometimes assume an appearance such as yours:
a deceiver, powerful, sporting, a celibate student, and a fraud. (1.05)
He, possessing many forms, dwells in the forest as one who is independent of others.

Though devoid of qualities, he may by his own sport assume the state of having qualities in some instances. Indeed, birth belongs to that which has a companion; there is no such thing as birth in a solitary entity.
Indeed, the non-difference of the individual manifestation from the universal class is in every way a sublation [of that claim].

For one whose very nature is knowledge and bliss, what indeed is the purpose of acquiring further knowledge and so forth? Since a quality cannot reside in another quality, why is knowledge sought within knowledge itself? (108)
He possesses knowledge and is the possessor of knowledge; He is the eternal substratum of knowledge.

(10.9) How can the stages of life produced by the activity of the sun be attributed to the Sun? How can the marks of the body and so forth, which are produced by karma, belong to Brahman, who is beyond karma? (1.187.11)
Knowledge, action, and volition are the three powers born from that [Brahman];
however, these do not operate intensely within that Brahman, for it is devoid of power [in its own nature].
Through its grace, there arise prosperities, and otherwise, misfortunes.
What need has he for prosperity or its lack, since his every resolve is ever true?
(112) Indeed, it is by a mere fragment of his grace that the gods have attained their godhood;
whether in divinity or in impurity, what purpose does he have therein? (113)
For one whose servants— the guardians of the world— stand ever at his door,
what desire could he have for the state of a king or even for that of a cowherd?
His eye is the sun, and his trident is complete within the Great Abode.
What use has that eternal host of noble lineages for a progenitor?
What use has that which is ever pure for external impurities, or what use for external purities?
[For it is] free from old age, free from death, free from thirst, and free from hunger.

What need has Satyakāma, whose resolve is truth, for houses? What need for garments or material possessions? For he who abounds in auspicious virtues possesses the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) rolling about in the dust within his home. (1.17)

What need is there for me to calculate the number of those gathered there in that throng of millions of yoginīs? (1.18) Since even inauspicious things become auspicious by taking refuge at her feet, what need is there to mention those who contemplate the meaning of inauspiciousness? (1.19)
One who becomes wealthy through service to him is already pervaded by the lines of poverty; what calculation can there be for one whose very nature is possessionless?
For the fruit of honoring him would be the prosperity of sovereignty over the three worlds.
How could there be any effort on the part of that great-souled one who is devoid of all exertion?
(121) Since conscious beings become purified by the chanting of the name "Śiva," what will this [deity], who is sought after by the gods, do with inauspicious ashes and the like? (122)
For one who, performing ritual acts, reviles Śiva without knowing the truth, the merit accumulated from birth is indeed reduced to ashes.
Whether Rudra exists in such a manner or whether he does not exist at all as a stone—[it matters not]. (123)
“Rudra is most dear to me; I shall perform penance for that [offense]. Depart quickly from our place and do not commit blasphemy against Śiva.
Having heard this, the Brahmin desired to say something in reply. (124–125)
Pārvatī said to Vijayā: "Restrain this reviler!
Sin arises from malice both for the speaker and likewise for the listener.
We must by no means listen to any calumny against the Lord."
"This wicked man will not leave this place; he will surely utter insults.
Let us abandon this spot this very day and go elsewhere without delay, lest there be further conversation with this reviler. (1.27–1.28)
Having spoken thus, as soon as Pārvatī rose and began to take steps toward another place, the mendicant became Śiva—
handsome, beautiful, gentle, and a youth sixteen years of age.
He is well-nourished, with matted locks possessing the luster of tawny gold, and bears the crescent moon upon his brow.
He carries the trident and the serpent Vāsuki, is clothed in an elephant hide, and is exceedingly enchanting.
His beauty surpasses that of ten million Cupids, and his body is encircled by a halo of splendor.
Having shown this form of his own— which serves as a cause for Satī’s recognition,
which she had previously served and experienced in another birth—
Śiva spoke to Pārvatī, who stood with her face cast downward.
"Do not go elsewhere, O auspicious lady; behold my sovereign form.
This peak of ours is named Gaurīśaṅkara;
and because you sought Rudra here, the Lord was fashioned out of clay."
"He shall become famous in the world as Gaurī-Bhadreśvara.
O Goddess, you do not abandon me, nor am I to be abandoned by you again.
I am pleased; choose a boon, for there is nothing that should not be granted to you."
"From this day forward, I am your wealth; I have been purchased by you through your asceticism.
Now, O beautiful one, you are considered my wife; cast aside your reserve!
O dear ascetic woman, you have been thoroughly tested by me; please forgive me."
"I have never seen a woman as firm as you, an ascetic who has no self-interest.
I am your very self and subject to you; let my own desire be fulfilled, my dear.
Come to my side, my beloved, and stay for a moment in my embrace. (138)
"We shall go to your father’s palace for the sake of obtaining the marriage rites. Thus addressed with respect, Satī quickly sat upon the lap of Hara;
delighted by her husband, she abandoned the hardships of her ascetic penance.
"When the fruit is obtained, the former effort perishes, along with that which is most ancient.
Thus replied the great virtuous lady, who is an ocean of bliss upon the lap of Hara;
Śivā was exceedingly happy, her face blossoming with extreme affection.
With your limbs thrilled by intense joy and overflowing with fresh bliss, you said:
"O Lord of Gods, you are my protector; have you forgotten what was done before? Having encountered the miseries of domestic life, why have you now embraced renunciation? (142–143)
Or was it after reflecting upon the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and Satī’s resolve,
and considering the life of a householder to be a source of suffering, that you adopted this state of renunciation? For in the grasp of women, a man’s life becomes dependent upon them.
Knowing that [the world] is dependent on others, why have you maintained detachment?
(145) Since the yoga of Brahman is shattered by union with women, O ascetic, knowing that because of this there is no liberation, why have you maintained detachment? (146)
The expansion of offspring and so forth arises from a wife for the householder;
considering the maintenance of those to be a hardship, have you adopted dispassion?
Through union with a wife, worldly connection always increases.
Knowing that it was a gale-force wind, why did you maintain such detachment?
(148) At the time of meditation, during tranquility, while sleeping, and when reflecting upon the Self—did you perhaps not remember me because you perceived a woman as an obstacle? (149)
I do not know how a period of a hundred thousand years becomes like a single moment for one in the form of Brahman;
yet I know that for a mind intent on its own interests, even a single moment becomes like an eon.
How was this time of five thousand years passed by me?

"Without my husband, my dear life," she said, and shed tears. Having regained her composure, he spoke again: "In the past, you were Satī and I was Menā’s son; today I am your husband—fulfill my word. (15.1–15.2)
Upon hearing this, Śambhu became momentarily dejected, but then his distress vanished;
wiping Satī’s head with both hands and embracing her face,
he kissed it for the sake of remembrance and to forget that sorrow.
The Lord said to the Goddess, "O beloved, go to your own father's abode.
For your sake, I shall dispatch great sages to the home of Himavat.
Accepting the command with "Om," Pārvatī spoke at the conclusion [of the conversation].
"Having become a monk, come to me and beg from the Himalayas;
make my father's entire household life fruitful.
My father will quickly carry out what has been spoken by the sage.
O Lord, when the daughter of Dakṣa was married by you,
she was reduced to ashes due to the fault of transgressing the rules regarding the lunar mansion (vidhi) and the fault of the planetary positions (graha).
Therefore, you ought to perform the marriage according to the prescribed injunctions.
O Śaṅkara, perform the marriage ceremony preceded by many kinds of festivals!
Let every rite of the wedding be carried out in its entirety.
Indeed, let the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds become the bearers of the bride.
"May Himavat know this correctly; may the lords of the world know it.
May all that is moving and unmoving understand that Pārvatī has performed penance.
Whatever effort must be made for her attainment, let there be a great festival commensurate with it."
In one creation after another, people sing this verse:
"He who was obtained by Pārvatī through her ascetic penance, but was not obtained even by the great seers;
he who was purchased by Pārvatī through her resolve, but was not purchased by the exponents of the Vedas."
That which was obtained directly by Pārvatī, but was not obtained even by the virtuous;
that which was obtained by Pārvatī in her own courtyard, but was not obtained by those wandering to sacred fords;
that which was obtained by Pārvatī through love, but was not obtained even by yogis. (163–164)
Obtained by Pārvatī through ritual means, yet not obtained even by the performers of sacrifice;
found by Pārvatī upon the mountain, yet not found by the means for attaining heaven; reached by Pārvatī upon her breast, yet not reached by those who practice mental concentration on the heart.
He was obtained by Pārvatī in an instant, yet he was not obtained by the Creator even in an aeon.
Though he has been obtained again by Pārvatī, he is characterized by the state of no-return [to rebirth]. Thus shall they sing of the white glory of Śiva, the bestower of liberation.
"Thus they shall proceed toward the supreme means that grants liberation;
the rite for marriage shall be established in the world just as it was between us two.
Having heard this, the one who does what is dear to his beloved spoke these kind words in return.
"Go, O Goddess, and quickly perform what is appropriate for the sake of great auspiciousness.
I myself will certainly not go first, like a mendicant;
for even a high-souled one, though most venerable due to his great virtues, is considered a mendicant [if he goes first]."
By the mere word "give," a man immediately incurs insignificance;
therefore, having become a beggar, I would never ask anything of you.
However, previously, for your sake, I dispatched the Seven Sages.
"Let them make a decision regarding the giving of my word; thereafter I shall go to your home.
By the power of your asceticism, I shall ask your father for you.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara embraced the face of Pārvatī. (172–173)
Having placed his hands upon the heads of Vijayā and Jayā,
and having received their prostration, he vanished on the spot;
he then departed for Kailāsa and related what had occurred to Nandin and the others.
Having heard this, the hosts led by Bhairava celebrated a great festival there.
Having brought her asceticism to completion and paid homage to the presiding deities of the forest,
Pārvatī, joyful and accompanied by her friends, went to her father’s abode.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*: the seven sages report Pārvatī’s life-risking penance to Śaṅkara; Śaṅkara’s return toward Pārvatī in the guise of an old matted-haired brahmin; the description of Śambhu as being beyond qualities (*aguṇa*) and devoid of qualities (*viguṇa*); Pārvatī’s realization that Śambhu is the supreme possessor of all virtues and the one to be accepted; the manifestation of Śambhu in his own true form; their pleasant conversation with one another; and the declaration of the decision for their marriage.
The one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Completion of Austerities," etc.,
from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga),
Chapter 188.
[The Author: Chapter 189.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen with great pleasure, O Lakṣmī, to what occurred immediately thereafter.

Upon hearing of Pārvatī’s arrival, Himācala, accompanied by Menā, prepared excellent vehicles and set forth, overwhelmed with joy. The family priest, the citizens, the friends, and the young maidens also departed. (1–2)
Likewise, other relatives and brothers, overwhelmed with joy,
went toward that female ascetic while uttering cries of victory.
Having set down jars of auspicious substances on the leveled royal highway, [they proceeded].
Adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, fruits, branches, and other such things;
crowded with priests, brahmins, sages, and celestial rishis;
and resounded with the voices of women, dancers, and singers.
It was filled with vehicles and mounts such as lordly elephants, horses, and great swans;
it was beautifully adorned with archways made of *aśoka* and mango leaves;
and it shone with pavilions and other structures fashioned from pillars of plantain trees.
Resounding with the voices of groups of women accompanied by their sons,
whitened by the radiance of hundreds of thousands of lamps, and made festive by throngs of brahmins uttering auspicious sounds. (7–8)
Amidst the pervading sounds of various musical instruments, marked by the signs of welcome,
the groups of people from various regions indeed proceeded toward Pārvatī.
In the meantime, Durgā arrived near the city gate.

Entering the city, she first beheld her parents in her heart—exceedingly serene, with eyes full of tears and minds overwhelmed with joy. Seeing their daughter, they ran toward her; the virtuous lady, accompanied by her companions, bowed down to them.
Placing their daughter upon their chests, the two of them bestowed auspicious blessings;
the women, headed by the brothers’ wives, gave her firm embraces.
"The one who saves the lineage has been accomplished through asceticism; we have been purified."
Having thus praised her, they bowed and honored her with flowers and sandalwood paste.
(13) The gods from the sky rained down a shower of flowers, bowed, and offered hymns of praise;
they then escorted her into the city amidst great festivals and the sounding of many musical instruments. (14)
Then the Brahmins, the family priests, her friends, and other women ushered Satī into the house with great respect.
Her friends performed the ritual cleansing, and the elderly women offered their blessings.
They considered their birth fruitful, for a daughter is better than a bad son.
Himācala gave gifts of wealth to virtuous brahmins and bards,
and with great celebration, he had various auspicious songs sung.
When the singing of excellent songs had commenced, O beloved, the elders, sisters, brothers, kinsmen, and citizens gathered together in the pavilion.
There were women— both old and young— as well as maidens and other children.
They heard auspicious singing and beheld the dancing. In the meantime, Śaṅkara himself, having become a skilled dancer-actor by his own will, entered the pavilion.
Holding a horn in his left hand and likewise a *ḍamaru* drum in his right,
and wearing behind him a variegated and beautiful curtain along with a bodice,
he— clad in red garments and skilled in dance and song— performed a dance.
She performed a captivating song, overflowing with the essence of divine love.
There, she played the *ḍamaru* drum with its deep *ghurghura* sounds;
she tinkled the small bells and caused her necklace to dance.
She drew the women toward her and meditated upon Pārvatī;
she showed the men her singular mastery in dancing.
Menakā informed the female ascetic that his mind was fixed on the wedding.
He awakened the citizens, for he was a worthy recipient of the great festival.
Other citizens came to see that extraordinary sight;
the men and women were struck with wonder, and Pārvatī attained supreme joy.
With his heart filled with joy, he beheld Śambhu, equipped with the trident and other weapons;
adorned with sacred ash, wearing a garland of bones, the three-eyed Hara,
who possessed the moon, wore a serpent as a sacred thread, and was clothed in the skins of tigers and elephants.

Seeing him with matted hair, white-complexioned, well-nourished, and sixteen years of age, who said, "Choose a boon," she bowed down to him. She chose this mental boon: "May you become my husband. || 28-29 ||
Having granted the boon, the mendicant vanished and danced outside;
Menā, however, offered jewels under the pretext of a reward. He did not accept them, but instead requested Pārvatī as alms.
Menā became exceedingly enraged and rebuked the mendicant.
Then he displayed a miracle to Himavat;
the Mountain beheld him wearing a forest garland and bearing the form of Viṣṇu.
He beheld everything— that crown and earrings, the yellow garment, and the four arms—
as well as whatever flowers and other offerings had been given to the wielder of the mace at the time of worship,
all upon the body and head of the mendicant.
Then, right there, he beheld the four-armed Brahmā,
reciting the Vedic hymns along with the Vedas, carrying a water-pot;
and then [he saw] the one whose nature is like the sun, whose form is the eye of the universe.
Then he beheld that Lord Śambhu together with Pārvatī; he was of the nature of splendor and in the form of a *jyotirliṅga*. Again, contracting his forms, he danced in many ways and sang.
Although many jewels were offered, he did not accept anything except for Satī.
He begged Pārvatī as alms, but Himavat did not give her to him.
Then, glancing briefly at Śivā, Hara vanished right there.
Then Indra and the others reflected at length:
"Śaṅkara has begged for alms, yet Parvata did not give it; nor was it given by Menā. Alas! What a loss! Truly, there is a violation of the agreement. (39)
Menakā knows it, and Himācala also knows it:
"This daughter must be given to Śambhu; indeed, that has been entirely forgotten.
That which was not given to Rudra, the worthy recipient, is a truly great loss.
"Oh, how great is the illusion of Śaṅkara! By her, delusion is spread abroad:
'Having promised, "I shall give," she thinks, "I will not give.
"Indeed, we must wait for further time due to the deficiency of our merit.
Having reflected thus, those gods spent a month and then departed;
having bowed to Śambhu on Kailāsa, they went there and praised him with eager devotion.
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, we have come to you for refuge.
O Ocean of Compassion, O Rescuer of the Wretched, show us mercy; salutations be unto you!
(45) If Śaila, through his exclusive devotion, shall bestow his daughter upon you...
"By virtue of his merit, Śaila will abandon the earth and attain liberation.
The earth will become empty, devoid of the mountain rich in infinite jewels.
O lords, where shall we go to sport and dwell? (46–47)
"O Śambhu! Even for you, Kailāsa would become a peak leading to liberation.
Therefore, one should not act in this manner; rather, one should do that which bestows benefit. The mountain shall remain forever upon the earth, and Pārvatī and Hara shall attain their goal."

O Three-eyed One, act in such a way that there may be constant gain for me. O Maheśvara, by hearing the censure of the gods, all merit is destroyed; therefore, go there and subject yourself to censure.
Censuring others destroys merit, while censuring oneself leads to fame.
Having heard your censure, he will be unwilling to surrender his daughter;
consequently, the girl herself will choose you by force.
"Abandoning you, Satī Durgā will not choose any other as her husband.
All this is certain; therefore, go, O Maheśvara.
Furthermore, no merit shall accrue from giving away a daughter to one who is unwilling. || 52-53 ||
"May it be such that Himācala shall surely attain Nirvāṇa,
and may he also obtain the status of a lord of the earth, longevity, fame, and honor.
Having said, "So be it," Hara departed for the snowy mountain.
Carrying a staff, wearing a parasol and golden garments, and bearing the vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* mark;
holding a fine garland of *tulasī* in his hand and a *śālagrāma* stone around his neck;
chanting with devotion the names of Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Hari. (55–56)
Seeing him wearing the garb of a holy man, Śaila rose quickly and prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground with devotion, honoring the guest as one never before seen.
Pārvatī, however, recognized through the power of her asceticism that he was Śaṅkara and bowed down.

The Vaiṣṇava accepted the honey-mixture and other offerings presented by the mountain. The Brahmin bestowed his blessings, and the mountain inquired after his welfare, his well-being, his purpose for being there, and whether he had suffered any illness. || 58–59 ||
Then the brahmin replied: "I am a Vaiṣṇava wandering among patrons for my livelihood;
by the power of my guru, I am all-knowing.
I have learned that you wish to give your own daughter to Hara."

To one who is devoid of a house door, to one destitute of wealth, to one prone to anger, to one whose occupation is the cremation ground, to one who has serpents for friends, and to one who is greedy— to him [I give] this divine hand, like a lotus, with fingers as tender as lotus filaments. (6.1–62)
To one who is naked, whose limbs are deformed, who is of bad conduct, and smeared with ashes;

to one whose family, lineage, purpose, age, and name are unknown, and who wears matted hair; to one who follows an evil path, who is addicted to vices, and who wanders about begging for alms. || 63 ||
Why indeed would a wise man give his daughter to such a person?
Where is your family, renowned for its wealth and fame, and where is he, who wallows in the cremation ground?
If any respectable person hears of this, they will surely laugh.
"Ask your elders, your kinsmen, and Menakā themselves regarding Pārvatī:
the father seeks noble lineage, the mother desires a prosperous home;
the daughter wishes for a handsome husband, while other people desire sweet food. (66)
"O Śaila! You consider yourself the lineage of Śambhu, yet there is no prosperity for Śambhu.
O Satī! Śambhu is ugly; how can I have a desire for sweet food?
Abandon such a person who is as hard as a stone and utterly wicked. (67–68)
"Even though medicine is wholesome for a patient, it does not please him if it is unpalatable.
Having said this and received his meal, the brahmin Hara departed.
Menā said to her husband, "O Lord, you have heard the conduct of Śambhu."
Such a person should not be given [in marriage] by me, nor should a daughter be cast into a pit.
(1.188.70) If you do not heed my words, I shall die—of this there is no doubt.
I shall either immediately abandon my home or consume poison. (1.188.71)
"Having bound my daughter around my neck, I shall go to the dense forest;
I shall drown in the great ocean—I will not give my daughter to him.
Śaila considered this appropriate, thinking, "My daughter must not be given to one devoid of virtue."
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? My daughter is indeed making a firm insistence:
'I am to be married to Śaṅkara alone, and not to anyone else;
otherwise, I shall either die or live as a forest-dweller. || 73-74 ||
"Let that which is destined to be happen; I have no desire for it.
Let her go according to her fortune to be given to Śaṅkara.
Thus Menā and the Mountain attained a state of indifference toward Hara.
Thinking that what was desired had come to pass, the gods and others were indeed filled with joy.

(76) Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Pārvatī’s Welcome upon the Cessation of Her Austerities, Śambhu’s Dancing in the Pavilion in the Guise of a Performer, Pārvatī’s Request, its Rejection by Menā and the Mountain King, Śambhu’s Return in the Guise of a Vaiṣṇava, the Censure for Not Giving Him to Śiva, and the Manifestation of Menā and the Mountain King," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 188.
← Chapter 188: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 189 [Author:
Chapter 190 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O lotus-eyed one, Rudra, established on Kailāsa, remembered the seven sages, who are oceans of knowledge, together with Arundhatī. 1.
And they all gathered together at Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara.
Seeing that they had arrived, Śaṅkara rose up, honored them,
and said, "Please be seated," upon soft, golden-colored cushions.
"O Kaśyapa, O Atri, O son of Varuṇa, O son of Gādhi, listen, O Gautama!
(3) O Bharadvāja, do you listen; and you, O Aṅgiras, listen as well!
You, O most excellent ones, go toward the king of mountains, the Himālaya. (4)
"Let the Lord of Mountains, Himavat, be entreated for Pārvatī on my behalf;
according to the principles of the Vedas, those two are surely desirous of giving their daughter.
Indeed, at the instigation of the gods, I have indeed performed this censure."
Having heard that, the two of them became utterly despondent and exceedingly dejected.
"The seven sages do not wish to give their daughter to me now," they thought; and having offered their salutations, they quickly departed for the Himalayas. (6–7)
Śambhu said to Arundhatī, "O beautiful one, go to the mountain;
for housewives indeed know the way to accomplish the good works of other housewives.
Thus commanded, Arundhatī departed together with the Seven Sages.
Having gone to the city of the Himavat mountain situated on the Oṣadhī peak,
they entered it along with Sunābha and the host of mountain women,
preceded by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and others.
The world of Himālaya is delightful, vast, and radiant with gold.
Rising up and taking excellent offerings, Himācala himself came to the gate and worshipped the Supreme Lords.
Having brought them to the assembly hall where they had taken their seats,
and perceiving that his birth was now fruitful, he, beautiful with a smile, spoke:
"Is this a rain without clouds, or rather a fruit without flowers?"

The arrival of your auspicious self is beyond reasoning and inconceivable. I am blessed and purified, since you, O compassionate ones, have made my courtyard pure by removing the contact with the wicked. (14)

With all their desires fulfilled, they wander upon the surface of the earth for the sake of others. I believe you have come here for the accomplishment of some task of mine; I am commanded by you, so let that which is worthy of a servant be told. (15–16)
Aṅgiras spoke to the lord of mountains: "Indeed, we have been sent here by the three-eyed Śiva; hear what we must request of you.
This daughter of yours, Kālī, who is the most beautiful among all women—"
"Pinākin himself seeks that daughter of yours in person.
Therefore, quickly purify yourself and offer the maiden to Śaṅkara;
for this task of the gods has been pending for a very long time. (18–19)
This endeavor must be undertaken for the sake of uplifting the world;
indeed, he alone is a blessed father whose daughter obtains Hara as her husband,
attaining the Lord of the God of Gods through the power of asceticism.
"May all the lords of the gods bow down to Pārvatī and Hara.
We are the supplicants, Śarva is the giver of the boon, and you are Umā.
You are the bride and the mother of the entire world; do that which is for your own welfare."
Having heard those words of Ānanda, Himādri summoned his own kinsmen—
the preeminent mountains such as Meru and others— from all directions.
They arrived and took their seats upon golden thrones.
Udaya, Hemakūṭa, Ramyaka, and Mandara;
Uddālaka, Vāruṇa, Varāha, Garuḍāsana, Śuktimān, Vegasānu, Dṛḍhaśṛṅga, and Raivata. (24–25)
Citrakūṭa, Trikūṭa, Śṛṅgavān, and other mountains were there;
then Girīśa himself summoned his wife Menā.
Then Himālaya, having addressed them all, spoke in a melodious voice.
"These Sārṣṛtayas have come today as suitors for my daughter.
Regarding the maiden's marriage to Maheśvara, this must indeed be reported to you.
Therefore, speak according to what is right; you alone are my kinsmen. (27–28)
Having heard this, Meru and the others said, "In every respect, you are worthy;
for the sages are petitioners and Śaṅkara himself is the bridegroom.
O Mountain, let this Kālī be given away, for he is indeed our desired son-in-law. (29)
Having heard these words of his kinsmen, Himavat,
the king of mountains, bowed to the sages, joined his palms, and spoke this:
"O highly fortunate Seven Sages, that which has been uttered by you— " (1.189.31).
For that has been accepted by me in every way, as well as by my wife.
Now, a certain brahmin, a follower of the Vaiṣṇava dharma, arrived and spoke these words: "Śiva is a pit of misery; he is not a goddess. (32)
Neither she nor I desires the marriage of our daughter with Rudra.
Indeed, a daughter should not be given to one who is miserable and a mendicant for the sake of happiness.
I beg your forbearance so that my daughter may not fall into suffering.
Having spoken thus, that king of mountains became entirely silent.
Menakā, however, having gone into the interior of the house, slept motionless.
The sages then sent Arundhatī back to Menakā.
Upon seeing Arundhatī, Menakā bowed and said:
"Oh! What a merit is this today for us, whose births are blessed, that the devoted wife of Vasiṣṭha has arrived here! (36–37)
"For what purpose have you come, O Goddess? Please inform me, your servant.
Having heard this, Arundhatī said: "O beloved, listen to the reason for which you have come;
O Menā, may you attain the complete fulfillment of your birth, my friend! (38)
"Give Pārvatī to Śiva; Śiva is indeed Brahman itself.
There is no end to his prosperity; by whom have you been deluded in vain?
She who is the wife of one devoid of fortune shall be bound to a wild ox. || 1.189.40 ||
She who is the wife of one possessing all fortune shall be honored by all.
Śaṅkara is a man of great renunciation as long as there is no daughter-in-law in his home;
once he has a daughter-in-law, he will fashion a supreme city from Vaikuṇṭha.

Wherever your daughter’s feet have trodden, whether on land or in the forest, there great prosperity shall abide; even Śiva himself will become prosperous. By whom have you been discouraged, O lady? Do not grieve; remain steadfast.
"You are worthy of worship by one who is worshipped by the world; become his eternal mother-in-law.
Having spoken thus and taking her with him, he departed toward the Seven Sages.
Then the Seven Sages spoke these beneficial words to the Lord of Mountains:
"Give Pārvatī to Śiva; become the father-in-law of the Destroyer.
At the request of Brahmā, Śambhu will accept your daughter.
The Mountain replied, "I do not perceive the royal majesty of Śambhu. (45–46)
If a father gives his daughter to an unsuitable suitor— whether for the sake of some power, wealth, or relatives and kin—
he is ruined by desire, delusion, fear, or greed, and shall go to hell.
Then the maiden, also distressed, uttered a curse that would last as long as her life.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O Lord of Mountains, speech is considered to be of three kinds:
the first is harmful in every respect, while the second ends in happiness. (48–49)
Having carefully deliberated, one should indeed grasp that which is pleasant in the beginning, the middle, and the end;
whereas that which is untrue, harmful in the future, though currently pleasing to the ear,
is spoken by an enemy of one's own intelligence and is never at all beneficial.
That which produces displeasure at first but brings happiness in the end—
such is the teaching of a compassionate and virtuous kinsman, which,
upon merely hearing it, is like nectar and brings happiness at all times. (51–52)
The supreme speech uttered by the Benefactor is that truth is the essential core.
A householder gives his own daughter to one who possesses royal wealth;
yet, by giving a maiden to one who is miserable, the father becomes a slayer of his daughter.
Who knows that Śaṅkara is suffering, he whose servant is Kubera? Indeed, he is capable of creating and destroying the universe by the mere play of a movement of his eyebrows.
He who is called the Supreme Brahman is indeed Śaṅkara himself.

And his threefold form consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. Brahmā is the creator in Satyaloka; Viṣṇu is the nourisher in Vaikuṇṭha; and Hara is the destroyer on Kailāsa—these are the manifested powers of Brahman.
The Prakṛti of Brahmā is threefold: Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī.
O Mountain! This Pārvatī, the wife of Hara, was Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa; having been consumed by fire in birth after birth, Śaṅkara wears her ashes.

Therefore, by your own will, give the maiden to Nityavara; or else, having gone to the place of your daughter's asceticism and having consoled Pārvatī, she herself will go to the abode of her beloved. 59. Your daughter, having gone to the site of her penance, shall comfort Pārvatī.
Having become a mendicant here, he begged you, Pārvatī.
We were sent by him, having even taken Arundhatī with us;
we are indeed instructing you: "Give Pārvatī to Rudra."
Indeed, that marriage shall take place here by the power of destiny;
Śaṅkara himself granted this boon to Pārvatī while she was performing penance. For that which has been promised by the Lord does not turn out otherwise.
O Lord of Mountains, by giving away even one [daughter], all prosperity must indeed be protected.
But if you do not give away even one, O Lord of Mountains, all your prosperities will be destroyed.
If Pārvatī is not given away, he, the Destroyer, will reduce everything to ashes.
What need is there for much? Give your daughter to Śaṅkara; happiness will ensue.
Whether today or at the end of the year, the girl must be given—either to him who is the worthy recipient of the boon, or to some other distinguished person.
"Having understood this, O daughter of Brahmā, give Pārvatī to Īśvara.
O Lord of Mountains, abandon your anger along with your wife Menā.
Then Menā spoke to them all regarding that which had occurred between Pārvatī and Śaṅkara.
"A son named Sena shall be born, and he will slay Tāraka.
She, being worthy, must be given to Śambhu, who is likewise worthy, for the sake of attaining happiness.
Then the father, the Mountain, spoke to his daughter, who was distressed by what she had heard.
"Daughter, you have been given by me and likewise by Menā to Śarva.
Kālī, the wife of Śambhu, then joyfully praised the sages.
Then Arundhatī, having consoled Kālī, bestowed blessings upon her.
Then the Seven Sages said: "O King of Mountains, listen!
This is a meritorious and most auspicious lunar day, endowed with the quality of *jāmitra*.
When seven days have passed, it is a moment exceedingly difficult to find and highly propitious."
When the lord of the ascendant is situated in the ascendant, and the Moon is joined with its own son (Mercury),
is joyful, conjoined with Rohiṇī, and when the moon and stars are pure;
in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on a Monday, free from all defects.

O Parvata, having given your daughter to Śarva— who is free from all false attachments, who has abandoned the view of grasping at the unreal, and who bestows virtuous offspring— be one who has fulfilled his duty.
"On that lunar day, Hara shall take her hand with the recitation of mantras.
Other mountains also said, "O Mountain, act accordingly.
Then Menā, out of affection, addressed Pārvatī as "Śivānī."
Having fed the sages, Arundhatī, and the mountain, he himself ate;
and having adorned Pārvatī, he seated her upon the lap of the Ṛṣi.
"This portion must be given to Śaṅkara"—this was firmly resolved.
Śaṅkara was the mendicant, Brahmā himself was the donor, and Himālaya was the host;
Pārvatī was the alms-food—what could be more excellent than this?
Then the great sages bestowed auspicious blessings upon her.
"By touching her with your hand there, prosperity shall be yours;
may you always possess auspiciousness that is unbroken and radiant.
Having spoken thus and given [the daughter] to Himācala, all the sages—
Then flowers laden with fruit served as a sign [of success].
Arundhatī tempted Menakā with the virtues of Śambhu;
she wiped away the mountain’s beard with turmeric and saffron.
Having performed the worldly customs, which are the supreme auspicious rites,
and having then fixed an excellent moment for the fourth day,
they met one another with mutual satisfaction and went into the presence of Śiva.
And they said, "All that has been promised by him shall indeed bear fruit;
therefore, O Hara, go to the auspicious abode of Himācala for the sake of marriage and wed Pārvatī according to the prescribed rites. ||84-85||
Śiva said: "Marriage has never been practiced nor even seen before;
the ritual must be performed by the great sages from beginning to end.
The sages replied to Viṣṇu, along with Brahmā and the assembly.
Bring Indra, the hosts of *muni*s, *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, *siddhas*, and *kinnaras*;
the *vidyādharas*, the gods, the *sādhyas*, and others, along with the hosts of Maruts; and the hosts of *apsarases* and the hosts of the Brahma-lake. (87–88)
"All are well-versed in worldly affairs, possessed of wives, and followers of the householder's dharma;
they will successfully accomplish your task in its entirety, just as it is fitting.
Having spoken thus, the sages bowed, accepted the honors, and departed.
"Śambhu said: 'You must come to my wedding with due respect.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Departure of the Seven Sages Sent by Śiva to the House of Himālaya, the Summoning of the Mountains, the Consultation for the Giving of Pārvatī’s Hand in Marriage, the Bestowal of Her Hand, and the Determination of the Auspicious Day," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
