Chapter 191 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Lakṣmī, having consulted with her own family priest Garga,
had a marriage horoscope prepared for Meru and the others;
she sent it along with the necessary materials and a formal letter to Śiva.

Having performed the *tilaka* rite, the Brahmin gave her to Śaṅkara. Then, having been greatly honored, the twice-born returned to the mountain. The Mountain [Himavat] invited his kinsmen and others residing in all directions.
He caused a collection of various excellent foods and other provisions to be prepared—
materials of diverse kinds suitable for the performance of the wedding ceremony—
including abundant quantities of rice, chickpeas, and flattened grains (pṛthuka).
Mountains of wheat, barley, and split pulses;
(5) excellent mountains of jaggery, sugar, and salts;
and mountains of *laḍḍukas*, *śaṣkulis*, and *khājās*. (6)
Mountains of garments steamed in ghee with hundreds of holes and the like,
mountains of pearl clusters and also of *parpīs*,
vast heaps of *pūrīs*, *polikās*, and *bharjikās*.
Various kinds of *phullavaṭī* pancakes and *parpaṭa* wafers;
peaks of *svastika* cakes and grains sprinkled with sugar; and [offerings] of milk, ghee, curd, and sweet water. (8–9)
He likewise constructed long ponds of nectar, sugarcane juice,
and fermented liquors, as well as reservoirs for various liquid drinks; and he built lofty towers of the finest fresh butter, the essence of milk.
He caused anthills to be constructed that were like mountains of various cooked foods (11).
There were many items for various preparations, such as leafy vegetables and the like, as well as mustard oil, curd, sour gruel, and so forth (12).
Priceless golden garments, grass mats, and lion-thrones; large canopies made of fine cotton, silk, and other materials;
and various kinds of gems and jewels, as well as gold and silver. (13)
He collected many kinds of vessels, vehicles,
and mounts; having gathered these and other such fragrant items,
the Mountain began to perform auspicious rites on that day of auspiciousness.
Then the wives of the mountain caused Pārvatī to undergo the purificatory rites according to the prescribed rules; they adorned her and sang songs.
They performed the ceremonies with auspicious ornaments and auspicious substances.
The women of the city, filled with joy, performed the customary rites.
Delighted by the arrival of his kinsmen, even the Mountain performed the auspicious ceremonies with every aspect of his being, celebrating that most auspicious of festivals. (17–18)
Then indeed, the divine mountain, the abode of the gods, arrived there in embodied form,
bringing great jewels and priceless implements,
accompanied by an assembly resplendent with many excellent diamonds, gems, and precious stones.
Mount Mandara arrived with its kinsmen and its offerings;
Mount Asta arrived adorned with its family and bringing gifts, carrying gold ornaments and jewels of precious gems along with its relatives. (1.190.20–21)
Filled with great joy upon the arrival of Udayādri,
Malayādri came forth, accompanied by a retinue of jewels.
Possessing divine splendor and accompanied by his wife and others, Dardura also arrived.
Niṣadha arrived with his attendants and retinue;
Gandhamādana came accompanied by his wives, sons, gold, and other wealth; and the immensely prosperous Karavīra and Mahendra also arrived. || 23-24 ||
Accompanied by his sons, wife, male and female servants, and kinsmen,
Pāriyātra arrived there, bringing a mine of jewels and gems;
likewise, Krauñca came, bringing offerings for the assembly along with his servants and retinue.
And Puruṣottamaśaila arrived, bringing offerings and the like;
Nīlādri came with his retinue and various gifts;
and Raivatādri arrived there accompanied by his wives, sons, and others. (26–27)
Urala arrived there accompanied by his army, and Vindhya likewise came with many jewels, utensils, and other articles.
Also present were Trikūṭa, Citrakūṭa, Veṅkaṭa, and the auspicious Śrīgiri.

Gokāmukha came from Mount Nārada along with his own dependents and others; Kālañjara arrived with his retinue, as did Kailāsa in its divine form. Other mountains as well, those situated on the earth and those located upon the islands, [all came]. (1.190.29–30)
Those who dwell in the oceans, in the atmosphere, and even among the planets and mountains,
were invited by Himavat together with their wives, sons, grandsons, and so forth,
along with their male and female slaves, servants, armies, retinues, and household members.
With excellent gems, jewels, diamonds, gold, silver, and other such objects,
with ornaments, garments, celestial chariots, and many priceless gifts,
they arrived with great joy for the wedding of Śiva and [Pārvatī]. || 32–33 ||
Gharghara, Śoṇabhadra, and the great river Brahmaputra—
other rivers arrived as well, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Pārvatī.
The Godāvarī, Yamunā, Triveṇī, and Sarasvatī also came.
Adorned with divine ornaments, they arrived, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Śivā.
With great joy, Narmadā, Gaṅgā, and the daughters of Rudra also arrived divinely, out of great affection, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Śivā."
The Sindhutapati, the Kāverī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, and the river Mahī;
the Ojasvatī, the Svarṇarekhā, the Bhadrā, and likewise the Sābhramatī;
the Śatrujitā, the Gomatī, the Bhogavatī, and the Gaṇḍakī. (37)
The Tāmraparṇī, the celestial rivers, and other auspicious streams,
crowded with sons, daughters, retinues, and kinsmen, were accompanied by all the necessary materials for offering ornaments, jewels, and precious gifts. (38–39)
Divine women, possessing the forms of goddesses, beautiful and radiant as gold,
all of them embodiments of loveliness, not yet sixteen years of age,
arrived with great joy, thinking it was the wedding of Śiva and Pārvatī. (1.190.40)
They respectfully visited Mahākālavana, the forest called Sundara, Madhuvana,
Vṛndāvana, and other forests,
as well as Siṃhāraṇya, Dharmāraṇya, and Naimiṣa.
Out of reverence, they proceeded to other prosperous forests as well—
Kurukṣetra, Bhṛgukṣetra, Brahmakṣetra, and others—
and out of love for the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī, they went joyfully to those most flourishing regions.

The cities of Svarṇapūrī and others, as well as divine cities, arrived, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Śivā. Divine ornaments of gold and silver, and celestial garments, also came. (4.4–45)
All fragrant substances and the like that are fit for rubbing,
as well as unfading fruits and flowers, excellent gems, jewels, and diamonds;
various and abundant vessels, and likewise many seats.
Vehicles, excellent carriages, and great celestial mansions;
divine pearl necklaces, divine utensils, various ornaments, and garments of exquisite appearance. (47–48)
Then, having arrived from all directions with wedding gifts consisting of divine ornaments blazing like the sun and possessing boundless beauty,
all of them gathered around the Lord of Snows.
At that time, the divine city was crowded and endowed with great splendor.
Its gate-towers were beautified with banners, flags, canopies, and arches;
and with water-jars, cloths, garlands of *kalī* flowers, auspicious plantain trees, and *svastika* symbols.
The royal highways, crossroads, streets, palaces, pleasure gardens, and the grounds of the parks were adorned with colorful garlands, decorated with lamps and musical instruments,
and rendered magnificent through the splendor of sweeping and watering.
The pavilions were well-constructed, perfumed, and adorned, truly resembling heaven;
they provided excellent shade and protected against the heat of the sun. Dining halls and resting areas had also been prepared.
Assemblies of actors, dancers, musicians, wrestlers, and wandering performers were provided,
along with expositions, entertainments, games, displays, and storytelling—
all of which produced manifold delights for the sake of the guests. (55)
What could possibly be lacking where the Mountain-Dweller himself is one's father-in-law?
(56) Where the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara will come to the house as one's son-in-law, and where the Mother of the World, Mahāmāyā, becomes one's daughter-in-law. (57)
Just as heaven is divine, or Vaikuṇṭha,
or even the world of Brahmā, so indeed does that city shine.
Himālaya, with great love, devotion, faith, and respect—
He paid due honor to all those who had assembled, according to their respective rank,
in beautiful palaces provided with swings, gardens, and water features, and shining with excellent swings, couches, pavilions, seats, and furnishings. (1.190.59–60)
He assigned separate dwellings within the forms of his own celestial palaces,
and at that time, he appointed hundreds of thousands of male and female servants for their service.
And the King of Mountains provided them with many kinds of desirable articles.
The mountain satisfied [the guests] entirely with gifts and objects of enjoyment.
In his own city, in his own courtyard, he had an auspicious arrangement made;
indeed, at every gate, auspicious items such as plantain trees were set up.
Rambhā fashioned a courtyard provided with pillars of cloth,
adorned with arches made of *rasāla* leaves fastened to pillars of fine silk,
and furnished with armlets fashioned from strings of jasmine garlands.

Placing Garga at the forefront, who was adorned with highly auspicious articles and other items on all four sides, the Mountain (Himavat) then joyfully performed every most excellent rite suitable for the occasion for the sake of his daughter. (65–66)
The goddess Pṛthivī, having arrived, gave the ground for the purpose of the pavilion;
that earth, situated in the intermediate space, then shone like the sky.
Having summoned Viśvakarman, he caused the pavilion to be constructed.
It was made of gold, exceedingly vast, and beautiful with its railings and other features (68).
Extending for many yojanas in the foothills of the Himalayas,
it was endowed with manifold wonders and stood in the sky like heaven itself (69).
All things, both stationary and moving, were mutually similar to one another,
creating an illusion for the observer as they mingled with the retinue of Haṃsa.
At that time, the moving beings were surpassed in beauty by the stationary ones.
The immobile was conquered by the mobile through its superior beauty.
(7.1) The earth was conquered by water, and water was conquered by dry land; there, one could not truly distinguish what was land and what was water. (7.2)
At the gate, on the side of the Karmānikā tree, there were in some places artificial lions;
in some places cranes and swans, and in others there were elephants.
In some places there were peacocks, parrots, pheasants, and mainas.

And in some places there, artificial cuckoos seemed as if they were conscious beings. In other places, women—artificial as well—were made to dance upon pillars by men; they captivated the spectators with their glances. (74–75)
In some uppermost parts, divine and artificial apsarases stand, adorned with flower garlands and endowed with wings;
at the tops of the staircases and gate-towers, door-keepers stand equipped with bows.
Armed with weapons, accompanied by shouts of "dhūs-kṛta," and likewise provided with *bhū-śuṇḍīs*, they stand there;
the immovable [images] appear like moving beings, including the inexhaustible ghee.
At the door stands Mahālakṣmī, beautiful and artificial, positioned above.
On both sides of the elephant, artificial Sarasvatī is consecrated with jars and lotuses;
meanwhile, a slender woman sings from a lute.
In the quadrangle, artificial elephants adorned with ornaments stand together with Ambalikā.
Horses adorned with ornaments, horsemen, elephant-riders, and so forth;
chariots, beautifully adorned at their front by riders pulling the vehicles;
and numerous mounts such as Garuḍas and swans serving as conveyances.
There were palanquins and celestial mansions, both artificial and beyond comparison with anything man-made;
in his assembly hall was an artificial garden possessing rows of trees.
There were also artificial actors, actresses, and dancers who could assume many forms.
And circles were drawn for the Apsarases, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras.
Thus, much was prepared within the pavilion for the purpose of enchantment, as well as for the sages, seers, gods, rivers, and likewise for the mountains. (83–84)
Furthermore, artificial rows of forms were created by Viśvakarman for both the rivers and the forests;
all of them were made to produce the illusion of being animate.
Whosoever else has come there, and those who will arrive at that place—
Viśvakarmā indeed fashioned artificial [images] upon the ground in the pavilion.
For the gratification of Śambhu, Viśvakarmā created an artificial Śaṅkara, mounted upon his bull, dressed as a bridegroom, and carrying people [as his retinue]. (86–87)
Likewise, at the great gate, O Bho, a large crystal Nandi was fashioned;
and above the Nandi, in the sky,
a great artificial celestial chariot named Puṣpaka, rich with jewels, was constructed as a support for the hump.
It was adorned with yak-tail fans, mirrors, leaves, and archways;
it was perfumed by celestial lamps and stars and was as radiant as the moon;
it was further embellished with garlands of plantain sprouts, flowers, and fruits. (89–90)
On the left side, two golden-colored elephants were fashioned, accompanied by their female mates;
they had four tusks, were sixty years of age, were in rut, and possessed the luster of mountains.
Likewise, there were two artificial horses, sun-colored and well-adorned.
Other attendants were fashioned as doorkeepers, men bearing golden staffs;
and auspicious, artificial guardians of the world (lokapālas) were made, laughing.
All the gods, together with their goddesses, were fashioned along with their families.
The secondary gods, the Guhyakas, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras,
as well as the Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, and even the Manavas who are created—
though their self-nature is unjoined [to consciousness], they appear as if possessed of sentience.
Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī, and Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Ramā;
likewise Brahmā accompanied by Vāṇī, as well as Garuḍa and Haṃsa, along with their respective attendants and families in every respect. (95–96)
The Vedas, Sanaka and the others, and the reciters holding books in their hands—
all these were fashioned as artificial creations by the pleased Viśvakarman.
Indra, seated upon Airāvata, was likewise provided with his wife, sons, and other attendants.

And others, such as Dhanada and the rest, the guardians of the quarters and protectors of the worlds, were indeed fashioned there by Viśvakarmā, the lord of craftsmen. O Lakṣmī, what is the use of much speaking? For whoever belongs to either of the two sides—
The assembly has arrived, and the great multitude will yet come;
all of them and all those women were fashioned by Viśvakarman as artificial beings,
appearing as if they were real, created for the sake of the wonder of those two.

In this pavilion, there were couches and grass mats, and above them, beautiful panels with the luster of milk, crystal, and mirrors; and delightful grounds resembling the moon, green and consisting of lush meadows. (10.1–102)

There, those of deluded minds might be confused by artificial and painted things. For the purpose of providing a dwelling for the Self-born (Brahmā), an artificial palace born of Satyaloka was constructed— a marvelous, man-made mansion with the excellent assembly hall known as Sudharmā.
For the purpose of providing a dwelling for Viṣṇu, the divine city of Vaikuṇṭha, filled with manifold opulence,
wonderful, and celestial, shone forth, fashioned by Viśvakarman;
it was like the artificial city of Indra situated in heaven.
Likewise, for the residence of the guardians of the other directions and of the Lokapālas who were not inferior to them,
Viśvakarman constructed artificial cities there in the sky for their respective dwellings.
And for their residence, Viśvakarman, with his great intelligence, fashioned in an instant magnificent and wondrous divine palaces;
rows of mansions and artificial royal ramparts were constructed. (107–108)
Likewise, he fashioned the divine Kailāsa, brilliantly radiant,
a dwelling for the high-souled Śaṅkara that abounds in every prosperity.
Therein are Badarikāśrama and the white Ocean of Milk.
There, Goloka was painted, and it was fashioned as an artificial representation using liquid pigments.
Such auspicious structures were created by Viśvakarman with the desire that Śiva,
Hari, and all the others might be pleased.
The Lord of the Snowy Mountains joyfully prepared and caused to be prepared everything that was necessary and beautiful, in order to increase the splendor of his daughter’s wedding.
Having thus made all arrangements and enhanced the worldly custom, [he waited].
Himācala gazed with joy at the arrival of Śambhu.

(11.3) Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of Himālaya’s Preparation of Mountains of Exquisite Cooked Foods and Utensils, the Performance of Auspicious Rites, the Arrival of the Invited Mountains, Rivers, Tīrthas, Forests, Gods, and Goddesses, and the Beauty of the City and Pavilions Created by Viśvakarman," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 190:
The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga — Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Part 1,
Chapter 191.
[Author: Chapter 192.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall tell you what and what Śambhu did.
The Lord, residing on Kailāsa, received the auspicious letter;
having read it, he showed honor and accepted it according to the prescribed rites. Having treated the messenger of the letter with hospitality, he sent him away with due respect.
Śaṅkara invited the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu:
"Let all of them come with enthusiasm, together with their wives, sons, grandsons, and so forth.
But those who do not come here to this festival of my marriage—" || 3 ||
"One should not consider as one's own kin anyone at all, even those who are great men.
(4) He dispatched Nārada to the fourteen worlds;
having invited everyone with honor, the sage returned to Śaṅkara. (5)
Then, for the sake of honoring his guests, Śambhu created another new, divine city, Kailāsa.
Therein were hundreds of thousands of palaces and likewise tens of millions of houses.
There were thousands of gardens and hundreds of groves; likewise, there were ponds, oblong lakes, celestial mansions, and pavilions;
as well as kitchens for various flavors, cooking halls, dance halls, and pleasure-parks.
Dining halls, pleasure halls, incomparable exhibition halls, drinking saloons, bathing halls, sacrificial pits, and assembly houses for discourse;
divine pavilions were constructed, and everything was established as if in heaven. (9)
Neither from the world of Brahmā, nor from Vaikuṇṭha, nor even from heaven did anyone come short;
for all the inhabitants of the universe who were invited arrived, accompanied by their families, retinues, male and female servants, and friends. (1.191.10–11)
He arrived, adorned on all sides by groups of male and female servants;
likewise, the Vairājas, the Brahma-sages, Vāsudeva and others, the incarnations of Hari, and crores of Rudras were present. (13–14)
Yama and the other ancestors, the hosts of the Sun and the Moon,
the world-protectors, the sages, and the guardians of the directions— each with distinct forms,
adorned with ornaments, full of grace, and endowed with all their attendants. (15)
Accompanied by their wives, sons, daughters, kinsmen, and retinues, they arrived at Śiva’s Kailāsa for the wedding of Śiva and Śivā.
Their parents, the heavens, all the yakṣas, and even the rākṣasas came as well. (16–17)
The Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas, and hosts numbering in the hundreds of millions;
the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Bhairavas, Vaitālas, and likewise the fires;
the lightning-flashes, Mahākāla, and the great abodes of old age and death.
The smoky nights, the goddesses beginning with Caṇḍikā, and the Mothers;
likewise the fevers, the diseases, the comets, and the planets; as well as the portents—all these arrived because of the wedding of Śiva and Pārvatī.
The Kimpuruṣas, the Māgadhas, the Sūtas, and the Bandins; likewise the Cāraṇas dwelling on earth, those of divine and human origin;
the stationary and the moving, as well as the oceans, rivers, streams, and so forth. (21)
The Asuras, Dānavas, Daityas, and those born of Kadru who were devotees of Śiva;
the Nāgas, Sarpas, Garuḍas, and others belonging to the faction of Śiva;
and the gods and goddesses, numbering in the hundreds of millions, at that time—|| 22–23 ||
Wives, sons, and family members, as well as the earth and other elements, are all forms of Śiva—
full of vigor, accompanied by their retinues, adorned with ornaments, and mounted upon their vehicles.
So too are the great yogis such as Durvāsas and others, as well as the yoginīs.
Then virtuous women, excellent Avadhūtas, and Avadhūtīs arrived;
celibate women came, and likewise the goddesses Durgās arrived; all the Śaktis also came for the wedding of Śiva and Śivā.
Śambhu himself performed various honors for those who had arrived;
during the great festival, a troupe of female dancers performed beautiful dances.
To carry out the bridal procession on Kailāsa, the dignitaries [prepared].
Considering their own duty to have been fulfilled, they rendered excellent assistance.
(28) All the Mothers fashioned the bricks for Śambhu’s temple;
and they performed the supreme rite of adorning Śiva in a manner that was most appropriate. (29)
Then, beautiful musical instruments were played during the rite of Śiva’s adornment;
the dignitaries feasted, and the celestial women danced.
The porters individually decorated the vehicles with ornaments. (1.191.30)
The goddesses anointed their limbs with fragrant unguents.
At that time, the Gaṇeśas and Kārtikas, who had arisen in the previous creation, were proceeding with great enthusiasm from pavilion to pavilion. (31–32)
Hundreds of thousands arrived from the Vairāja realm for the sake of auspiciousness,
acting as assistants for the army in the service of their eternal father.
Now listen, my dear, to what Śiva’s attire was like at that time.
At that time, his natural appearance became his mode of adornment.
Amidst his mass of naturally matted hair, the flashes of lightning and the thunders remained as cool, yet they appeared like brilliantly glowing tufts of hair. || 34-35 ||

Then the Gaṅgā herself, in the form of water, mingled with the rays of Brahmā and created a halo of light all around that abode consisting of pure radiance. From Goloka, the divine Svarṇamukuṭa appeared, acting as an assistant for [the Lord’s] matted locks.
Offered by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, a garland of Pārijāta flowers together with a kalpa-tree shines upon her head (37). A string of Pārijāta blossoms hangs there;
on the forehead of the second [goddess], the full moon serves as a tilaka mark (38).
The third eye on the forehead, tranquil and with wide-open pupils,
then becomes manifest upon the forehead as the design of the *tripuṇḍra*.
At that time, the two serpents Vāsuki and Kāmarūpadhara [serve as] earrings at the ears.
The two earrings of Śambhu became radiant, inlaid with precious gems; upon his neck appeared the auspicious golden necklace Vāsuki;
and then the two golden bracelets on his arms became the serpents Vāsuki and Takṣaka.
Then the rudrākṣas on Śambhu’s forearm became like chains, made of gold,
set with gems, and capable of assuming any form at will.
His crystal rosary became auspicious rings made of fire-born [coral].
Then the funeral pyre ashes became collyrium for his eyes;
that ash on Śambhu’s face indeed turned into a liquid born of milk,
while the white powder for anointing became ash upon his body.
Then the bark became an excellent golden tunic;
then the elephant hide became a well-woven upper garment for the sovereign;
and then the girdle became a divine golden waist-band.
Then the drops of snow from Śambhu became worthy of being honored as sandalwood paste, enriched with twenty-seven strings of fine gems and diamonds;
and the poison residing in his throat then indeed became the Kaustubha gem. (46–47)
A tiger skin was upon his waist, and he wore a yellow silk garment.
He held a trident and a brilliantly shining golden sword. His staff was a beautiful, auspicious rod made of gold.

My wooden sandals became as soft as gold, like delicate wrestlers, exceedingly smooth, protective for the feet, and divinely beautiful. At that time, his betel, though naturally very fragrant, became stale. (1.191.50)
Then his upper garment became a supreme stimulating pill;
his golden ornaments then became armlets and anklets.
His garland of skulls became a great necklace of priceless jewels. (51)
Then his skull became an excellent and beautiful crest-ornament.
There, the bull turned into a white celestial chariot,
equipped with a thousand white elephants, horses, bulls, and other mounts.
Mounted upon his elephant, the thousand-eyed Indra, together with Indrāṇī, held up a wide, dry cloth as a parasol for the Lord.
At that time, Yamunā, the best of rivers, was situated upon a tortoise.
Holding a white yak-tail fan, Sarasvatī shone at his side; she, mounted upon a second elephant, attended him. The six seasons offered handfuls of flowers to Hari.
The fires stood on all sides holding lamps,
and the ocean remained present taking a vessel of ointment;
such a beautiful form, capable of assuming any shape at will, was then assumed.
If everything were subject to transformation, then [it would not exist] in the Supreme Self, who is beyond transformation.
By the will of the Lord, they then assumed cruel forms;
by the will of Śrī Śaṅkara, they became suitable for choosing [a bride] and adorned with appropriate ornaments.
When the traveling party had been thus prepared, those belonging to Śaṅkara’s faction approached and said, "O Lord, proceed with us.
Then Viṣṇu spoke to Śambhu: "Today, indeed, according to the ritual prescribed for domestic rites..."
"You ought to perform here the rites for your own marriage with Pārvatī.
Have the erection of the pavilion and the *nāndīmukha* ceremony performed;
for Brahmā is the authorized officiant there for the rites appropriate to such an auspicious occasion."
Urged by Brahmā, the sages performed the ritual according to the prescribed rules:
Kaśyapa, Atri, Gautama, Kaṇva, Bṛhaspati the preceptor, Vasiṣṭha, Bhāguri, Śakti, Agastya, and likewise Cyavana. (63)
Garga, Śilāda, Akṛtaśrama, Aruṇa, and Parāśara;
Jamadagni, Śilāpāka, Mārkaṇḍeya, Akṛtavraṇa, Bharadvāja, Dadhīci, Upamanyu, and likewise Kuśika. (64–65)
Pippalāda, Kautsa, Śvetavyāsa with his disciples—

all of whom performed rites according to the injunctions of the Vedas and had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences— along with hundreds of thousands of sages known as Maṅgala, arrived there. (66)
And they performed the protection of Śambhu after performing the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony (kautuka-maṅgala).
According to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas, they performed various auspicious rites with the hymns of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas,
as well as the worship of the planets by Śambhu.
They performed worship of the deities stationed in the mandala for the pacification of obstacles.
Then Śiva, being pleased, bowed to the best of the twice-born;
placing the brahmins and the gods before him, he indeed departed.
Having prepared himself outside Kailāsa, Hara went there and stood;
then the festival of song, instrumental music, and beautiful dancing took place.
And the other Gaṇas also departed, with the exception of those who protect Kailāsa.
Śaṅkhakarṇa approached with a very prosperous retinue of ten million;
Kekarākṣa with ten crores, and Vikṛta with eight crores.
Viśākha came with four crores, and Pārijāta with nine crores.
Sarvāntaka and Vikṛtānana [are accompanied] by sixty crores;
Dundubha by eight crores; and Kapāla by five crores.
Both Kanduka and Kundaka are joined by groups of ten billion (koṭikoṭi).
Sandāraka is joined with six [koṭis], and Viṣṭambhaka is endowed with eight koṭis;
Pippala and Sanāda are each joined with a thousand koṭis;
Āveśana is with eight koṭis, and likewise Candratāpana.
The host of Mahākeśa went forth, joined by ten billion [attendants].
Kuṇḍa and Parvata likewise went, accompanied by twelve crores;
as did Kāla, Kālaka, Agni, and Mahākāla—these lords of the Gaṇas.
Śatakoṭi is joined by a multitude of hundreds of millions; Agnimukha likewise leads a crore.
Ādityamūrdhā leads a crore, and Ghanāvaha also leads a crore.
Sannāha, Kumuda, Amogha, and Kokila are the leaders of the hosts (gaṇanāyakas).
Then Śatakoṭi departed with a hundred crores, and Sumantra with ten million crores;
Kākapādodara with sixty crores, and Santānaka likewise;
Mahābala, who was honey-tawny in hue, was joined by nine crores.
Nīla and Pūrṇabhadra are accompanied by ninety crores;
Caturvaktra with seven crores; Karaṇa with twenty crores;
Yajvākṣa, Śatamanyu, and another, Meghamanyu.
Ahiromaka went accompanied by ninety crores [of followers]. Kāṣṭhāgūṣṭa, the leader of the hosts, went with sixty-four [crores], as did Virūpākṣa, Sukeśa, Vṛṣabha, and Sanātana. (82–83)
Saṃvartaka, Lakulīśa, Cañcvāsya, and Ṣaḍānana;
Saṃvartaka, Tālaketu, Nakulīśa, and Caitraka;
Lokāntaka, Dīptātman, and likewise Bhṛṅgidaityāntaka.
Riṭi, Devapriya, Aśani, and Bhānuka—these were the Gaṇas.
With sixty-four crores of Gaṇas, they went forth for the festival of the wedding.
Adorned with ornaments and dressed in auspicious attire, [they attended] the marriage of Śiva and Śivā.
A thousand *bhūtakotis* went forth with Pramatha, and Vīrabhadra with sixty-four; the hair-born ones (*romaja*) went with three *koṭis*,
and Nandī and the others with two thousand, along with thousands of millions of *koṭis*.
Then Bhairava also went forth, accompanied by hosts of many millions.
They had many arms, were handsome in form, and wore crowns of matted hair;
they bore the moon upon their foreheads, possessed three eyes, had blue throats, and carried tridents. || 88-89 ||
Adorned with the splendor of rudrākṣa beads and sacred ash, these great lords possess divine forms;
they are decorated with necklaces, armlets, earrings, crowns, and other ornaments.
Attended by the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, they move through the sky, the earth, and the heavens.
And who were those who traveled through the seven heavens and the seven netherworlds?
All of them, with serene minds and assuming forms at will,
having become gentle deities, then proceeded to that great festival.
Not everyone rejoiced at the wedding of Śiva and Pārvatī.
Caṇḍī, the sister of Rudra, was adorned with ornaments of serpents;
she was mounted upon a corpse-bearer and bore a golden pitcher upon her head. (93)
Carrying a jar filled with water, she, beautiful and overwhelmed with joy,
arrived there at that great festival accompanied by curiosity.
Surrounded by millions of hosts of spirits, she came proclaiming victory.
Followed by eleven crores of Rudras who had gone to her rear,
the great roar of their *ḍamaru* drums then pervaded the three worlds;
the universe was filled with the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, and large drums.
Behind the hosts were the gods, followed by the Siddhas and the great seers (maharṣis).
Then followed the guardians of the world, and in their midst was Hari, together with Garuḍa,
accompanied by Lakṣmī and his auspicious attendants adorned with their own ornaments.
Accompanied by crores and billions of Vaiṣṇava servants belonging to the classes of the lotus-born,
as well as by Lakṣmīs, Ramās, and Kamalās, he departed.
Then Brahmā [departed] with the knowledge of the Vedas, Śāstras, Saṃhitās, and Āgamas.
Adorned by the Vairājas, those established in celibacy, the Siddhas headed by Sanaka,
the Prajāpatis with their sons such as Sāvitrī and Pramada,
and likewise by the Ṛṣis and Munis, he proceeded along.
Adorned with vehicles such as palanquins drawn by swans and other well-embellished mounts,
Indra then appeared, seated upon Airāvata and accompanied by his army.
Surrounded by numerous hosts of gods, the virtuous one shone forth, magnificently adorned.
Then the sages, the brahmins, the Sādhyas, and likewise the virtuous ones,
the renunciants, the forest-dwellers, and the Vaiṣṇavas all went forth with joy,
having been invited and delighted by the thought that it was the wedding of Śiva and Śivā.

Then the yogins, the ascetics, those free from passion, and the renunciants who follow the path to Śiva, as well as crores upon crores of attendants and courtesans following the path to Śiva, went forth for the marriage of Śiva and [Umā]. (105)
Innumerable crores of Gaṇas’ female servants and wives went forth,
all resplendent with ornaments, dress, and the like, beautified by every kind of decoration.
Thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Śivā," they all proceeded toward Kailāsa.
Then they went joyfully to crores of maṇḍalas of yoginīs and to hundreds of millions of groups of female renunciants—
for whose sake all hermitages exist and for whose sake the castes are so highly esteemed. (108)
"For which purpose there are these traditions— that is the marriage of Śiva and Śivā.
Then the Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, Vetālinīs, Mātṛs, Bhairavīs, Yātudhānīs, and Kinnarīs also departed.
Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, Hūhū, Parvata, and others—
the Gandharvas and Kinnaras— went forth joyfully, blowing their musical instruments.
Surrounded by ten million maidens, the bridegroom was adorned with the splendor of love.
Then Śaṅkara, honored by songs from the goddesses, departed;
mounted upon a celestial chariot drawn by a bull as radiant as pure crystal,
he was reverently worshipped by the Brahma-lakes in the sky.
Strengthened by a rain of flowers and shouts of victory, Śaṅkara proceeded;
Hara went forth for the purpose of taking the hand of the daughter of the Snowy Mountain.
Nārada was sent ahead toward the abode of Himavat.
He departed swiftly to announce the arrival of the bridegroom’s procession.

(115) Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of Śaṅkara Receiving the Marriage Proposal, the Invitation and Arrival of the Dwellers of the Fourteen Worlds, Śiva’s Auspicious Preparations such as the Bridegroom’s Attire, the Erection of the Pavilion and the Nāndī Ceremony, the Organization of the Procession for the Bridegroom, and the First Dispatching of Nārada," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Listen, Lakṣmī; having gone there, Nārada was struck with wonder upon seeing that marvelous creation fashioned by Viśvakarman. Deluded by the artificiality, Nārada spoke to the mountain king: 1. Listen, Lakṣmī; having gone there, Nārada was struck with wonder upon seeing that marvelous creation fashioned by Viśvakarman.
Deluded by the artificiality, Nārada spoke to the mountain king.
"Varavāhinī has already arrived here; what else could there be?
The mountain replied, "O divine sage, cast aside this artificial astonishment.
This visible circle of gods and others was fashioned by Viśvakarman."
Having been fed, honored, and requested to come to Śambhu, Nārada went quickly and spoke to Śambhu and the gods:
"Himādri awaits you; indeed, the bridegroom’s procession is about to arrive."
Therein, for the purpose of delusion and also for the sake of a great wonder, an illusory artifice consisting of a painting was created, wherein the three worlds were depicted;
all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahendra, were beautifully painted there. (5–6)
"Artificial things have been left with nothing remaining because of their variegated forms;
for that which is seen as inert is indeed perceived as active only when it possesses consciousness.
Having heard this, Varā and the others became distressed at the sight.
By the command of Śiva, the procession of the army set forth.
The host of Hara arrived at the city of Hemādri;
having heard this, Hemādri dispatched other mountains.

Having gathered the necessary provisions, Śaila himself went forth with his army to hold a discourse with the Lord, as well as with the Brahmins. Then he [approached] the great army of the lords of mountains and those even more numerous belonging to Śiva.
Having seen them belonging to both sides, they were struck with supreme wonder.
The eastern and western oceans, having met together, became free from passion; and the golden mountains, the brahmins, and others bowed down repeatedly to Śaṅkara.
Seated upon his bull-vehicle, with a most gracious countenance and beautifully adorned,
he illuminates the quarters of the sky with the sublime luster of his divine limbs.
Served by the lords of the gods with parasols and chowries, he is borne upon a vehicle filled with jewels.
With Hari (Viṣṇu) stationed on his left and Brahmā stationed on his right,
and likewise with Mahendra stationed at his back, surrounded by hosts of gods; then,
having honored the excellent one with necklaces and other ornaments, as well as with water for drinking and so forth.

Having established the groom’s party in rest-houses by the command of Śiva, the Himālaya mountain proceeded to the sacrificial altar according to the prescribed rites. Then, those invited along with their lords arrived to perform the customary wedding ceremonies for the bridegroom.
The lords, headed by Īśa, made their way to the abode of the King of Mountains as the vanguard.
At that moment, Menā, longing for the sight of Śiva,
approached the upper chamber, having placed Nārada at her side.
Śiva also, desiring to display his own creative power (*camatkāra*),
spoke to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who had gone separately to the sacrificial post:
"Having made our army devoid of its essence, let us go to Sudarśana."
Menā rejoiced upon seeing the beautiful army stationed there.
First, at the mountain gate, were the radiant Gandharvas, handsome, adorned with divine ornaments and garments, fortunate, and accompanied by their mounts. (1.192.20–21)
Playing musical instruments and accompanied by apsarases who sang melodiously, they entered then, adorned with banners and victory scrolls.
Then, seeing the Lord of Wealth, she said, "This is Śiva."
Nārada said: "This is not he; these are indeed the servants of Śiva.
Then, seeing the lord of the Yakṣa army named Maṇigrīva, who was enriched with double the splendor, she said, "This is Rudra."

Nārada said, "This is not he; for these too are servants of Śiva. Then, seeing Anala entering the midst of the army, which was enriched with double the splendor, she said, "This one who has arrived is indeed the master of Śivā."
Nārada said: "This is not he; this is indeed the fire from Śiva’s eye.
Then Yama arrived, possessing twice the splendor of that [fire].
Seeing him accompanied by his own army, Menā said, "This is Śiva."
Nārada said, "This is not he; this is Yama, the son of the Sun.
Then, seeing Nirṛti approaching accompanied by his own army—the great lord of the Puṇyajanas, endowed with twice the splendor of Yama—she [spoke].
"This one is Śiva," Menā said; Nārada replied, "No.
Then, seeing Varuṇa approaching, endowed with double the splendor and situated in the midst of his army, she asked, "Is this indeed Rudra?"
Nārada said, "This is not he; Vāyu has arrived.
Then, seeing him in the midst of the army with twice the splendor [of Vāyu], Menā said, "This is Rudra," but Nārada replied, "It is certainly not he."
Then the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) arrived, endowed with twice the splendor of that [previous host].
Seeing him standing in the midst of his army, Menā said, "This is indeed Śiva.
Nārada replied, "This is not he; this is the lord of the Guhyakas."
Then Īśāna arrived, surrounded by his own army.
Seeing him endowed with twice the splendor, Menakā said:
"This is Rudra. To her, Nārada replied: "This is not Śaṅkara."
Then Indra, rich in the splendor of his army and possessing double the wealth [of Śiva], arrived.
Seeing him, Menā was delighted and said, "This is my Śiva’s husband.
Nārada said, "This is not he; rather, this is Indra, the lord of the gods. (35–36)
Then Candra arrived, appearing twice as beautiful as before;
seeing him in the midst of his own army, Menā said, "This is indeed Śiva.
Nārada replied, "This is not he, but rather that moon who is his crest-ornament."
Then the self-ruling Sun arrived, situated in the midst of his own army.
Seeing him with twice the splendor, she said, "This is Śiva.
Nārada said, "This is not he; rather, this is the Sun, his very body."
Then the sages, headed by Bhṛgu and others, preeminent in their spiritual luster and accompanied by the armies of their own disciples, arrived; seeing Bṛhaspati standing in their midst,
she, beholding him with double the splendor, said, "This is Śiva."
Nārada said: "This is not he; rather, this is the Preceptor of the Gods.
(41) Indeed, the Unborn One was then honored by the circles of sages with their masses of splendor;
even more richly endowed with beauty than that, the Grandfather arrived. (42)
Then, seeing that great splendor, Menā became filled with joy;
she thought, "This must be Śaṅkara," but Nārada said, "It is not he.
Instead, it was Brahmā, the creator of the universe, and Menā was struck with wonder.
Then Viṣṇu appeared in many forms, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Umā;
endowed with all splendor, dark as a rain cloud yet radiant as gold, possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, he wore yellow garments and had four arms. (44–45)
Bearing the marks of the discus and other symbols, with the Kaustubha gem shining upon his chest,
adorned with a crown, bracelets, and other ornaments, his eyes resembling lotus petals;
he was a treasury of grace and beauty, radiant with immeasurable splendor.
Amidst an army of infinite male and female servants, he who was adorned by the king of birds (Garuḍa) entered.
Seeing him approaching, Menā became overwhelmed with extreme joy; her eyes grew wide with wonder, and she said, "This is indeed he! || 47-48 ||
Nārada said: "O Menakā, this is indeed not the husband of your daughter;
for this is Viṣṇu, the brother of Śiva, who is authorized to carry out the work of Śiva.
He is the great minister at the wedding, the chief attendant, standing by the side of the bridegroom. (49)
"Śiva is indeed superior to him in the splendor of his form, wealth, and other such majesties.
(1.192.50) Then eleven crores of Rudras entered;
all were identical in appearance to Śambhu and possessed ornaments equal to those of Viṣṇu. (1.192.51)
Then twelve crores of Ādityas entered [the body];
all were identical in form to Viṣṇu, possessing the excellent forms of Nārāyaṇa.
Seeing them, who were beyond the reach of thought, Menā considered her own fortune to be exceedingly great.
They questioned Nārada again and again, "Where is Śaṅkara?
Just then, the Vairājas, who were perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas) and endowed with forms and splendors even greater than those of Nārāyaṇa, entered there.
Within that interval, there were twenty-four crores of those [beings]; there Mahāviṣṇu shone, preeminent in every respect through the splendor of the sovereign of kings.
Following him were all the virtuous ones and yogins, numbering in the hundreds of millions.
And those who had assumed the form of Mahāviṣṇu arrived at the city gate.
Seeing Mahāviṣṇu there, Menā was overwhelmed with joy; filled with great enthusiasm, she said: "This is Śiva who has arrived!"
"Oh, what great fortune for my daughter! She has performed the penance worthy of her.
Since such a husband has been won, may my daughter be happy.
Menā said to Nārada: "This is not Śiva; he is your Śiva-pati (husband of Pārvatī)."
But Śiva, the Sadāśiva, shines resplendent among the creations of the Lord.
His brother is indeed this Great Emperor, Mahāviṣṇu;
therefore, the Lord of Pārvatī is exceedingly handsome and prosperous. (1.192.60)
Indeed, it is not possible for me to describe its splendor.
O Menā, do not be in such haste; behold who this is that has arrived!
At that moment, Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, the self-effulgent Lord Śrī Rādhākṛṣṇa, appeared.
Accompanied by hundreds of millions, billions, and trillions of servants and attendants, Nārada arrived; he prostrated before him, and Menā also bowed down.
Upon seeing his form as Kṛṣṇa, she fainted for a moment.
Then, flooded with the bliss of beholding his form and drawn inward, she attained the joy of meditative absorption; yet in another moment, having arisen, she said:
"O Nārada! This is undoubtedly the husband of Pārvatī. (64)
Nārada said: "She indeed considered him to be the father of Śiva’s consort;
for Śiva was born from her and is always her heir.
This Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman, the Lord and Sovereign of Goloka. (65–66)
And from that form was born a mind-born son, Śiva, whose embodiment is great dispassion; he cannot be fully described.
Behold, immediately thereafter arrives one who is a great mine of beauty and virtue.
Then Menā, having seen her father-in-law, became free from doubt;
she was repeatedly filled with great joy and became eager to see him. Just then, Śambhu arrived.
Now, the entire display of amorous grace had become equal to that of Kṛṣṇa;
there was nothing lacking in splendor, yet the bridegroom’s splendor was even greater.
In the flowing stream of the bridegroom’s procession, the bridegroom’s splendor excelled all others.
Beholding that form resembling Śrī Kṛṣṇa, radiant with the splendor, beauty, and loveliness of ten million Cupids, Menā was exceedingly delighted;
through her devotion of self-surrender, she became pure, as did the King of Mountains.
He thought, "Aha! I have seen all the leaders of the gods;
he who is their lord shall be the husband of my daughter here.
He considered his own fortune to be great, and even greater than that, the fortune of his daughter.
"Having obtained him as her husband, my daughter shall become the mother of the world;
even my entire family shall partake in his glory.
As they were thus extolling their own good fortune, she beheld Kṛṣṇa and Śambhu.
In this very way, Śambhu became [as he was], yet Menā and Himālaya—
if they had beheld Śambhu so beautifully adorned with devotion—
would have considered themselves to have fulfilled their purpose through the heartfelt gift of their daughter.
Through devotion to meditation in every way, they both shall attain purity.
(77) Through the knowledge of Śambhu’s majesty and the certainty of ultimate reality, they shall both immediately go to liberation, and the mountain shall attain dissolution. (78)
If that were so, there would be great suffering arising from the destruction of my father-in-law,
and the grief over the death of my mother-in-law would be even more excessive.
Furthermore, there would be a collapse on the stage, and the destruction of Kailāsa itself would occur.
And when the snow has melted, there would be the destruction of the abodes of millions of gods.
With the destruction of the Himālaya, the earth would then become empty;
likewise, all the innumerable medicinal herbs would perish at that time.
Thus, with the desire that all these [objections] should not apply to you, [the author] wrote for the purpose of establishing the devotion born of affection among Menā, Himācala, and the others;
for the purpose of perceiving [only] virtues and not faults; and for the sake of securing residence on the mountain for the Goddess. (82)
Then Śaṅkara indeed transformed his own form;
having revealed his Rudra-form, a shape identical to that of Kṛṣṇa, he assumed the form of Śambhu and granted himself a vision to Menā. (83–84)
Likewise, he granted his own vision to Himālaya and similarly to the mountains and other such beings; he appeared smeared with ashes, wearing a garland of skulls,
adorned with matted locks, serpents, rudrākṣa beads, a trident, and a hide.
He was of dwarfish form, with a past half-life span, and a coarse physique;
he held a *pināka* bow, had five faces, and wore a well-washed tiger skin;
he had ten arms, carried a *ḍamaru* drum, possessed a fierce appearance, and was Dhūrjaṭi. (86–87)
He showed him one with a coarse beard and hair over his entire body, frequented by spirits, ghosts, and the like;
wearing matted locks and carrying a skull-cup, it was a great source of terror to the beholder.
He also showed him one addicted to drinking from wine-vats, with eyes rolling in intoxication.

"Then Menā said: 'Who is this? Where has he gone who bore the form of Kṛṣṇa? That handsome one has vanished; who indeed is this one here of such fierce appearance—swollen, excessively fat, dark-complexioned, and dwarfed? (89-90)"
"Behold, Nārada! Where is my son-in-law? Show him to me here!
Nārada then spoke to Menakā as she gazed upon his ugly form:
"He who approaches here, standing upon a bull in the midst of the army of the Rudras—"
The great lord sat surrounded by hosts of pretas, bhūtas, and other spirits.
In his army were banners in the form of winds, possessing rustling forms;
they were crooked-faced, deformed, formidable, and likewise bearded. (92–93)
Indeed, some were lame and blind, holding staffs, nooses, and maces in their hands;
others blew conchs, *ḍamaru* drums, and cow-horns like dancers, mounted facing the tails upon mounts that were at odds with one another. (94)
Some were turned away, some faced backward, and others had many faces;
some were handless, some had deformed hands, and some had many hands;
likewise, there were those without heads, those with severed heads, those with misshapen heads, and those who were headless.

Some were without eyes while others had many eyes; some were without ears while others had many ears; some were without noses while others had severed noses; some were mangled, and others had squinting eyes.
Some were tawny, some were smoke-colored, and others even had hair growing upwards.

Indeed, all these disciples of the Trident-bearer are possessed of great heroism. Behold, O Menā! They are serving your son-in-law with devotion. All of them are free from fear, devoid of possessions and conflict. (98–99)
"Free from dualities, free from worldly desires, powerful, auspicious ascetics—
behold these groups of your sons-in-law, as well as your son-in-law himself.
Having pointed this out with his finger, Nārada showed them to him.
Beholding that fierce form, which the mind could not conceive, Śivā’s mother became terrified;
she grew sorrowful and, saying "I have been deceived," she fell into a swoon.
"I have been deceived even by my daughter, and now I have been deceived by you as well, O Nārada. (101–102)
Deceived by the Seven Sages, the daughter was indeed cast away among non-humans in Vigarta—
a land of short lifespans, ill-fated, bearded, and devoid of virtue;
a place generally bringing misery, unpleasant to the eye, and unattractive.
"The meritorious creeper has been abandoned by me upon a harsh tree thick with thorns.
Thus Menā grieved and suffered repeatedly in her mind;
then, with eyes full of tears, she was attended by her female friends.
In an instant, summoning her fortitude, she spoke to Kālika out of agitation;
her throat faltered from the onset of misfortune, for she was indeed tormented by grief.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Splendor of the Chariots Carrying the Bridesmaids in the Procession of Suitors, Menā’s Waiting for the Suitor’s Arrival, and Menā’s Grief upon Seeing Śaṅkara," in the first section, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! At that time, in the theater, a collapse occurred on account of Menakā.
Upon seeing the fierce vision of Śiva, an ocean of sorrow became easily accessible. || 1 ||
Placing his hands upon his two skull-bowls and wiping his eyes from exhaustion,
he spoke repeatedly with a broken heart words devoid of emotion:
"By whom and by which [women] was it said that the daughter should be given to Śarva?"
Whether it was proposed, made known, or accepted;
whether it was understood, attempted, or likewise approved—
I indeed utterly repudiate all those deceitful ones who were so deeply agitated.
O Nārada, in the end you have been a source of suffering and you are deceitful;
by you, my daughter, who was like gold, has been cast into the mire.
And this fruit, contrary and harmful, has been witnessed by me.
"Though you have been forcibly incited, you have nonetheless deceived me in every way.
Yet, the fruit of this shall be yours as well; I adjure you again and again:
even though the auspicious moment has arrived, do not take the girl for yourself, O foul-faced one! (6–7)

"O daughter, having performed such penance, how did you propitiate this monkey—who is the king of ghosts, spirits, and piśācas and whose wrath is unbearable? What business do you have today, now that the assembly has gathered and come to our home? (8)
Nevertheless, I am her mother and am capable of warding [this off].
(9) If my daughter should say, "This man is not a suitable husband for me," then even though I have made every effort, if my daughter does not agree, (1.193.10)
"Everything I have done has been in vain; what shall I do, O wicked daughter? My lineage and all else are ruined, and my life has been rendered useless.
Where have those sages gone? I shall surely pluck out their beards! (11)
"Where is that rogue Arundhatī, by whom everything has been turned into poison?
Such people, deceitful for their own ends, do not speak of the destruction of others.
Therefore, she who gave birth to the girl should go there herself and investigate."
A house, prosperity, and even virtuous conduct are better than ever giving away a daughter by relying on the trust of another.
O daughter, lotus-faced one, you have indeed worshipped a mere stone.
Having given gold for glass, have you now sought after a gayal?
O daughter, having abandoned sandalwood, you have indeed sought out mire and mud.
Not seeing swans or cranes, the crow is considered the best of all.
Having abandoned the taste of the Ocean of Milk, you have craved the taste of the salt ocean;
and having abandoned the sun, a firefly has been sought by you at the end of your penance.
O virtuous daughter, having abandoned the seeds, why have you begun eating the husks?
Having first rejected clarified butter and choice food, you have consumed dried cow-dung from the very beginning.
Disregarding the shade of a mango tree, you have taken shelter in the shade of a jackal.
Having abandoned the knowledge consisting of Brahman, you have sought after the knowledge of base vessels.
Without resorting to Yajñabhūti, you have instead taken hold of funeral ashes. O! Having abandoned the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), why indeed have you grasped a mere pebble?
Having discarded the milk-boiled rice, why have you drunk the bitter neem juice?
"Alas, daughter! Your intellect is misguided; for five thousand years you have performed austerities to obtain this one who dwells in the cremation ground.
This is not the intellect of a woman, nor is it true intellect; the intellect of a woman is dependent on another."
Whether he possesses qualities or is devoid of them, whoever she is attached to is her husband;
therefore, a maiden should never choose a husband by her own intellect.
Her father or mother should marry her off after observing a suitable groom according to the age.

Fie upon your asceticism, intellect, conduct, beauty, and character! Fie upon Nārada, the sages, the Grandfather [Brahmā], and likewise the gods! My lineage, my skill in ritual action, and my fame have all been disgraced by you. (24–25)
"My family has been ruined by you; I shall marry [him], for I will certainly not die here.
Let no one—be it the seven sages, Nārada, the Himālaya mountain, or even the Grandfather (Brahmā)—come near me or show their faces. (26)
What excellent thing has been accomplished here? On the contrary, the family has been destroyed.
Having gathered together, my daughter has been cast into the jaws of Death.
Better indeed than this is barrenness, or better still is the miscarriage of the fetus.
Better death from birth, or better being devoured by a *rākṣasa*;
even maidenhood is better than being given away to a base husband.
For the army of the naked ascetic has arrived at the house.
"Should I burn myself here, or die here, or go elsewhere—what is to be done?
She must not be given away, she must not be given away; let the groom go to his own home.
Let the wedding procession depart, and let the guests also proceed."
I, however, shall take my daughter and go to my father’s domain;
let everyone depart, let them scatter, and let them leave my house empty!
Let the Himalaya go to the forest; Pārvatī must not be given to him.
Having lamented thus, she went to her daughter and embraced her repeatedly against her heart;
drawing her close to her chest and holding her firmly with both hands, she remained there in the house.
At that time, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the guests indeed.
Having heard this first, the Grandfather (Brahmā) went there;
but upon suddenly hearing the cries of "Holi! and "Kā," Menakā said to Brahmā:
"Go, you wicked one of intoxicated intellect! A fire has been ignited by you, O Puṣpa."
Becoming shameless and arrogant, he strove for the destruction of the maidens.
"Who here calls you, O Jarā, you betrayer of trust?
Brahmā became paralyzed with shock upon hearing this, and Caṇḍikā, the mother of Caṇḍī, likewise.
Having reflected thus, he became silent; meanwhile, the Seven Sages departed, and the gods, who are foremost in receiving worship, arrived to pacify Menā.
They said to Menā, "It is the truth that Rudra has no form like that of Śambhu."
This has been sustained by him as a mere play; it is momentary and not eternal.
Look! Arise, abandon your obstinacy, and give your daughter to Śiva.
This indeed is the supreme gain: Sadāśiva is the Supreme Brahman.
"Kṛṣṇa’s son, possessing Kṛṣṇa’s own form, has come to your palace;
he is the worthy recipient for your daughter, the fruit of the penances she has earned.
Hearing this, Menakā said, "All [these people] are deceitful and full of guile."
I am prepared to render her beauty and life useless.
I shall kill her with weapons and other means; I will not give her to that man of terrible deeds.
All of you, go far away from here; none of you must come near me.
The groom was deceitful and multiformed, and likewise the groomsmen were deceitful;
joined together by these deceivers, they were indeed life-takers for the other.
Upon hearing this, everyone placed their fingers in their mouths and stood stunned, with their faces drooping.
Then the Himalaya set out for the sake of awakening his daughter;
yet, in the midst of many excellent people, she said nothing at all to her father.
She heard the gentle and timely words spoken by the King of Mountains.
Listen, my dear: if the bridegroom should be exactly as you have seen him, then your beloved daughter must not be given away; otherwise, she must be given—consider this well.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, Candra, Sūrya, Indra, and the other deities...
The Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, the Sādhyas, and likewise the preceptors of the gods;
crores of goddesses, such as Mahālakṣmī and others, virtuous women with devotion;
the world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, and the sovereign lords of kings. || 48–49 ||
"O wife, consider this: whose vehicle these two have entered? They would not go to Menakā’s house on the river of Śambhu that flows downward.
O beautiful one, observe well within your heart: what kind of supreme being could he be?"

Śivā knows that Śarva was her companion in a previous birth. (51) If their affection is eternal, what cause for distress is there for you? Even if one’s wife is very prosperous, if the mind does not find delight in a husband, (52) [what is the use?]
Even though her virtues and beauty are abundant, what is the use of her life, which is like poison?
My daughter has been seen by me; may she always be happy.
O beloved, do not be hesitant regarding her being given to him to whom she belongs.
"See who has come to the house; do not reproach them, my dear!
O beloved, look at this Śambhu standing at the door, bearing a divine form and equal to Kṛṣṇa in beauty; arise, O increaser of fame! || 54-55 ||
Then the Lord of Mountains ceased speaking, and at that moment Menā said to him:
"If he were exactly like Rudra as I have seen him,
I would seize him by the neck with a firm grip and cast him down."
But you, having taken my daughter and me and cast aside compassion, might become happy by drowning us in the ocean. I will not give my daughter to Hara;
if you force her upon him, I shall today abandon this body.
Then Pārvatī, seeing her mother’s boundless sorrow—
which she reflected upon as being causeless and born of ignorance— sat slowly upon her lap,
wiped away the tears from her eyes, and said with affection, "Do not weep."
Having spoken thus, he attained peace; he said that it would become as sweet as desired.
"O Mother, there is a boon: he is well-formed, the Lord of all, and superior even to Hari.
All his riches are a thousandfold greater than those of the Supreme. (1.193.60-61)
Just as Kṛṣṇa was seen by you yourself, and as Mahāviṣṇu was beheld;
just as Viṣṇu, the Sun, the Moon, and the Lord of the Gods were seen by you—
so too there exists one even superior to him in beauty, military strength, and prosperity.
Indeed, even the formidable Kailāsa is surpassed by Vaikuṇṭha;
my youth of sixteen years surpasses [even] the beauty of Kṛṣṇa.
But that which has been seen by you here has never been seen by me anywhere.
I do not know why you have displayed this many distorted forms;
for even this Mahākāla becomes a bearer of manifold forms.
Having withdrawn the leaders of the universe, the auspicious one sports and delights.
"Having become one who takes refuge in the Dharma, do not abandon the Dharma of speech.
For those gods who have arrived here are indeed the servants of Śiva; they stand at your door for my sake, full of celebration—what more could there be than this? (66–67)
"Give me to this Śiva; make my life fruitful.
O Mother, Hara has been chosen by me again and again through thought, word, and deed.
A lion’s portion goes to a lion; I do not choose any other boon. (68)
"I shall die if you do not grant me [this], or do as you wish.
Having heard these contrary words spoken by her daughter in the presence of everyone, Menā cried out, "Dhabāk!
Dhabāk! and struck her daughter with her fists and elbows.
Then, filled with great rage, she struck that divine maiden.
The sages, having restrained her, led Pārvatī far away.
Menā, moreover, spread out her feet, her hands, and her hair.
Having uprooted the earth, he struck his own head like one intoxicated.
He spoke at length, saying, "I shall kill my daughter;
I shall give her poison, or throw her into a well, or cut her into pieces."
"I shall even die rather than give my daughter to one of such hideous form!
What kind of suitor has this wicked woman sought as a husband?
A terrible mockery has been spread throughout the families of both her mother and father."
He has no mother and no father, nor a younger brother nor an elder;
he has no family, no lineage, no home, no beauty, and no straightforwardness.
He has no ornaments, no clothes, and no vehicle—his bull is his only equal.
Neither wealth, nor suitable age, nor learning, nor purity—
seeing what [of these] should I give my daughter to this miserable-bodied man?
Brahmā, the Siddhas, Sanaka and the others, the gods, and the lords of progeny—
They are rendering my daughter’s life in the cave of Rudra utterly futile.
Let the daughter be slain with your own hands; through this, peace shall be established.
She must not be given, nor indeed should she be given; she is never to be given away.
It is not offered to one who carries corpses, to the terrible, to the destitute, to the defeated, to one who dwells in cremation grounds, to the naked, or to the impure.
All these [who were sent] were intent on killing the daughter, being full of deceitful schemes.
To the bull, to the buffalo, and to the one who assumes many forms;
[food] should certainly not be given to a heretic, nor should it be given to one who destroys everything.
May they depart from the door of my house; for why look upon those who are truly helpless?
Having spoken thus, she became silent and wept aloud in distress;
Pārvatī also, like a mother toward her child, shed tears at that time.
Then Brahmā and all the others were startled and filled with wonder.
All of them became hopeless when Viṣṇu arrived.
He said, "O Mother, abandon your grief; we shall do what is agreeable to you.
Śambhu shall indeed become exactly as he was seen by you. (84–85)
"In that case, my daughter must certainly not be given away; such is my resolve.
O Mother, listen to how Śarva displayed such a form—first, a divine one, as radiant as Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (86)
If you have seen such a form— exceedingly opulent and bestowing a mass of supreme bliss— and can show it to me again in that same way,
then both you and your husband will be filled with love and devotion. (87–88)
Having offered yourselves as a surrender, you two shall perform the dedication of your sons;
by the power of that offering, having become purified,
you two shall leave this earthly realm and come to the abode of Brahman, O excellent liberated ones.
At that time, the earth would be stripped of its mountains, causing the destruction of the abodes of the gods;
likewise, it would destroy medicinal herbs and cause the ruin of Kailāsa.
Having reflected upon this and considering the underlying cause, he thought, "Let this not happen. (1.193.90–91)
In such a way that it would indeed be an offense against his son-in-law Śaṅkara,
Śambhu assumed a form that was entirely and supremely terrifying.
Because he was devoid of mental intention (*amanaska*) regarding the giving of his daughter, liberation (*mokṣa*) was certainly not the fruit [of his action].
But that other fruit would be the merit gained from marrying ten sons;
O Menā, that fruit might indeed be yours, but it would certainly not be the fruit of liberation.
It was thus arranged by Śambhu in order to make you perceive your own faults and defects.
The formidable form has been shown, yet such a thing is not eternal.
Come, behold Mahādeva and likewise the hosts of Mahādeva;
all of them are entirely like Viṣṇu in appearance and are perfectly prosperous in every way.
Thus enlightened, Menā somehow became somewhat softened.
Nevertheless, she was further awakened by Viṣṇu with illustrative examples:
"And who indeed are you, standing here as mere leaves, assuming the form of stones?"
Nevertheless, what kind of gentle beings are they here who assume divine forms?
In some places they take the form of emperors, and likewise in others they become birds.
Thus, I am Viṣṇu, assuming the forms of the Fish, the Boar, and the Man-lion.
Just as Dharma may sometimes become a bull or even Yama;
just as rivers, though consisting of water, take the form of women; and just as Menā, though being a mountain, is born in the form of a bird. (1.193.100)
Now you are a young woman, and so indeed do all beings become; we are all of divine origin, capable of assuming any form at will.
No delusion should be felt therein, and likewise, let sorrow be abandoned.
Behold the forms of Śaṅkara’s army and the form of Śaṅkara himself!
For the sake of his purpose, the Lord of All assumes such a form;
and I too have assumed the form of Mohinī for the sake of deluding Śiva.
"Even a man assumes the state of a woman for the sake of accomplishing a purpose; know this, O Mother, and bring about my welfare by abandoning your obstinacy.
That penance which was performed by Pārvatī was indeed rendered appropriate by her."

Śaṅkara, being gratified, granted a suitable boon; likewise, the formal betrothal of his daughter was performed. Thinking, "This too is appropriate," Śaṅkara accepted your daughter; that indeed was fitting.
Śaṅkara indeed became fierce, yet he acted appropriately;
you likewise tormented yourself for the sake of your daughter, and that too was entirely appropriate.
If a mother does not act appropriately for the sake of her own daughter, [she would be a mother in name only].
"Then who else would have acted thus? You have performed what was appropriate.
Moreover, although all the deities were insulted by you, even that was entirely fitting during the rite of marriage. (108–109)
Moreover, O Lord of Gods, behold Śaṅkara again, who is of beautiful form;
if he should be considered by you to be both prosperous and handsome,
then your daughter must be given to him, and never otherwise.
"If you do not wish to give her to Śaṅkara alone, then I shall take your daughter's hand myself; abandon your grief.
Thus was Menakā exhorted in many ways, and thereafter—
Having regained her composure, she rose and went outside to see Śambhu;
and Menā said to Hari: "If Hara, whose form is so beautiful, is in every way according to my wish along with his retinue..."
"Then my daughter must be given by me; not otherwise, even through millions of efforts.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu quickly sent Nārada;
having gone there to conciliate Śambhu, he enlightened Hara.
Having received the message, Śambhubhū assumed an extraordinary form;
a form superior even to Viṣṇu’s, sixteen years of age and in the prime of youth.
In its softness it equaled Pārvatī, and its slenderness was auspiciously well-proportioned. (116)
In terms of fullness, it is superior to the fiery [element], depending on what is appropriate;
in charm and beauty, it is superior to ten million gods of love;
and in ornaments, garments, and attire, it is the supreme, exceeding all others. (1.17–1.18)
Then, having concealed all his attendants and even the armies— which were more numerous than those— along with the entire multitude of living beings, he assumed ever-new forms,
such as the form residing in Goloka and the supreme form of Vaikuṇṭha. (119)
Śaṅkara then displayed all that— even surpassing it— the supreme majesty of Vairāja, Sūrya, Candra, and Indra; and at that time,
he did so before both wings of the two armies.
At that time, there was nothing by which Śaṅkara could be compared,
nor indeed were there any people by whom he might be compared.
Then Menā, together with Viṣṇu, came to the moon-chamber.
He beheld that form of Śiva, filled with supreme bliss;
it resembled ten million suns, was a vessel of great beauty, enriched with divine garments and ornaments, and showered forth smiles and loveliness. (122–124)
A source of agitation arose for the goddesses, causing even Mohinī to be deluded.
Deprived of their composure, the goddesses stumbled there, deceived by Māyā.
The sun held a parasol over him, and the moon fanned him with chowries upon his head.
It was then adorned by Kubera and impelled by Dharma;
it was fanned by Gaṅgā and Yamunā, and made to dance by the Siddhas.
It was likewise energized by the gods, while the Gaṇas cried out, "Victory!"
It was sung by hosts of Viśvāvasus and Apsarases before Śiva;
it was likewise praised as the Supreme Brahman by sages and seers;
and at that time, it was treated as Nārāyaṇa by all the Gaṇas and soldiers.
They acted as if they had four arms, and likewise, they acted as if they were wearing crowns.
Then, by the hosts of spirits, ghosts, and piśācas, it was made to appear as if they had vanished;
meanwhile, by the armies of Śaṅkara, it was made to appear as if they were the people of Viṣṇu.
By as many women as there were, Lakṣmī was then treated as Amā;
by all the mounts as well, she was then treated as Garuḍa.
O Lakṣmī! What can I describe? Everything was then treated as "Madā" (intoxication).
Upon seeing [the child], Menakā, being exceedingly joyful, forgot her grief. Hari said: "O Menā, you have grieved in vain without cause;
behold Śarva, the bestower of boons! Should your daughter be given to him, or not?"

Menā said, "I am pleased; [the bride] must certainly be given, yes, she must certainly be given. Then she quickly approached Śaṅkara at the mountain gate, and having addressed him with "May you prosper" and praised Śaṅkara, she spoke.
Having offered salutations with joined palms for the removal of suffering and having uttered blessings,
and having entreated him, saying "Forgive us," Menā became overcome with shame.
Then the women of the city, upon seeing him, attained the very fruit of their eyes.

And they said: "Aha! What kind of husband has Tapatī obtained, such that if Brahmā had not united this pair of Śiva and Śivā, then even his labor, though performed and fruitful, would have become fruitless? (1.37)

Having spoken thus, the women then worshipped Śiva with sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice; they respectfully showered parched grain upon him. Then Śambhu entered the abode of the mountain together with the gods.
Menā also quickly went inside her own house;
the virtuous lady, holding a lamp-vessel in her hand for the purpose of performing the *nīrājana* rite for Śambhu,
went respectfully to the doorway together with other women.
Having seen him, who has the luster of the color of a campaka flower, wearing a single garment and a crown;
whose face is bright with a slight smile; adorned with jewels, gold, and other ornaments;
graced with a garland of mālatī flowers; and decorated with bracelets and armlets. (141–142)
Exceedingly radiant with divine garments of wondrous golden hue, adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and beautiful saffron;
exceedingly youthful, manifest like Viṣṇu himself, and four-armed. (143)
Beholding again and again that face, which was like the moon beloved by amorous women and capable of enchanting ten million gods of love, Menā considered herself to have achieved her life's purpose;
she praised her own good fortune, her daughter’s fortune, and the lineage of the mountain.
She first performed the lustration rite (*nīrājana*) and rejoiced again and again;
overcome with supreme wonder, she entered her own home once more.
The young maidens desired, "May our husband be like this."
The foremost of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced;
the lords among musicians played many musical instruments.
Then the affectionate Himācala performed the rites of hospitality at the gateway.
Having made her inquiries, Menā went to her own home filled with joy;
Śarva went to the place where he had been informed, traveling by means of human carriers. Then the women, maidens, and wives went to see the Lord.
With steady eyes, they stood respectfully by the side of the royal road.
Having reached his place, Hara rested after drinking, chewing betel, and eating;
he then assumed yogic sleep for a moment.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of Menakā’s Lamentations Driven by Extreme Agitation, Viṣṇu’s Instruction on Assuming Many Forms with Examples for the Destruction of Menā’s Grief, the Transformation of Hara into the Form of Viṣṇu and the Gaṇas into the Form of Vaiṣṇavas, and the Ritual Conduct Performed by Menā and Śaila through Vardhana and Others," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Listen, Lakṣmī! Then the attendants of Durgā’s inner apartments went outside to worship her family deity, taking it with them along the royal road leading to the palace where Śambhu resides. Pārvatī [followed].

she was anointed with the fragrance of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
Her forearms were adorned with rows of tinkling small bells that produced a jingling sound.
Her shanks and lower ankles were resplendent with golden anklets;
she was adorned with golden garlands and decorated with lotuses for playing in colored powders.
Her gait was slow, captivating the lotus-eyes of the entire assembly.
With her pair of breasts slightly budding and youth just beginning to emerge,

In meditation, she is rich with a downward gaze; in the heart, she moves upward toward Hara.

Then the excellent mountain,

accompanied by mountain-dwellers and Brahmins who held beautiful auspicious objects in their hands, who were accompanied by the great sound of musical instruments, and who were producing the sacred sound of the Vedas (brahmaghoṣa). || 3.2–3.3 ||

And Śaṅkara ascended the altar together with the consumer of oblations (Agni). Then Sunābha, his brother, led Kālī, who was adorned by women and decorated with all ornaments, into the presence of Śambhu.

he showered them upon Pārvatī and showered them upon Śiva as well.
Thus honored by her with curd, unbroken rice, kuśa grass, and water, Rudra [accepted the worship].
Devoted to worldly custom, Śambhu honored Śivā;
thus, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, honoring one another and gazing at each other, shone with splendor. (53–54)
Then, having been consecrated with the lustration rite by Lakṣmī and other women, as well as by the Goddess and others,

Then Himavat, commanded by Garga, together with Menā,
took a golden pitcher filled with water and containing unbroken rice and other auspicious items.
According to the procedure prescribed by the family priest, he chose the bridegroom with devotion, offering garments, sandalwood paste, ornaments,

"Proclaim in every way the Veda named Pravara and its branch.

O Śambhu, O Kṛṣṇa, O Mahāviṣṇu, O Viṣṇu, O Brahmā, O Lord of the Gods! (143) O Sun, O Moon, O gods, O goddesses, O ancestors, and other sages; O seers, O world-protectors, O guardians of the quarters, and O lords of the worlds! (144)

They caused the vehicles carrying the people of the groom’s party to hear the auspicious sounds.
Laughing with gentle words, they uttered many insults.
(158) Having eaten and performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth according to rule, those devotees of Śiva took leave of the mountain and dwelt comfortably on the second and third days. (159)
When the fourth day arrived, the fourth-day rite was performed according to the rules for the sake of purification,
by which the festival had been interrupted;

Having heard that, the Mountain said: "O gods, show me mercy!
Let you all remain for some days; everything here is yours. Having spoken thus, he respectfully caused them to dwell there for many days.

Every day there were dances, songs, musical instruments, and festivities.
Every day he causes many gifts and songs to be performed;

and daily the performance of divine dramas and sacrificial rites.

"Out of compassion for your daughter-in-law, you shall forgive her even for a hundred faults.
