For your sake, through mind, speech, action, and much austerity, I have endured great hardship; now that you have attained the fruit, protect this servant who has come to you.
If she should remember me, or if she should wish to see me, bring her here. 172.
"Then, from seeing you both, I too shall experience great happiness.
News of your conduct and circumstances should be sent by messengers frequently. May you two be happy and well; I shall always remember you both. (173–174)
Listen, daughter, to these beneficial words that grant you purpose regarding your status as a wife:
in this world, a woman devoted to her husband is always honored after attaining victory.
There is no dharma equal to devotion to one's husband that bestows all goals upon a woman.
She serves her husband with her whole being, in every way and at all times.
Having enjoyed all pleasures here with her husband, she attains a blessed state in the end;
she becomes a purifier of all worlds, worthy of worship, and especially fortunate. (176–177)
She should eat when her beloved husband has eaten, remain standing when he stands,
sleep when he sleeps, and always wake up first. In every way, she should act for his welfare, conducting herself with sincerity and without guile.
She should certainly not present herself to her husband without being adorned.
When her husband has gone away on business, she should remain devoid of ornaments.
Even when reviled, she should not revile in return; even when struck, she should remain composed.
If he should say, "I shall strike you," she should say, "My lord, have mercy.
When summoned, she should leave her household duties and go to his side.
She should not stand for long at the door, nor should she ever remain in another's house.

(182) One should prepare the articles for worship and perform service even if it has not been specifically mentioned; one should remain waiting for an opportunity to serve. (183)
She should not utter her husband’s name, nor should she reveal the household’s secrets.
She should never, under any circumstances, go on a pilgrimage to sacred sites without her husband’s permission. She should never attend social gatherings or similar events without her husband.
The water from washing the husband’s feet is considered a sacred ford, the most excellent of all sacred fords (185).
One should eat food through the husband’s grace, regarding it as a great favor;
and one should not eat without having shared it with the gods, the ancestors, and guests (186).
Among the circles of attendants, the cattle, and the community of mendicants, she should be restrained in her household utensils, skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure.
By the command of her husband, she should observe her vows; otherwise, they would be fruitless.

When her husband is comfortably seated, resting at ease, or enjoying himself according to his whim, she should never rouse him even for matters concerning her own internal affairs. While her husband is asleep, she should never disturb his sleep under any circumstances.

She must not disregard her husband alone, even if he is impotent, in a difficult situation, diseased, old, destitute, or even suffering. During the three nights of her menstrual period, she must not show her face at all.
She should not even utter her own words until she has become pure through bathing.
Having bathed, she should look upon the face of her husband and never that of another.
If her husband is far away, she should look at the sun while remembering him. (191–192)

vermilion, collyrium, lac-dye, fragrant oil,

A necklace, a breast-ornament, a neck-chain, ear-flower ornaments, and earrings;

She should propitiate her husband, who bestows no small amount [of benefit].

Without her husband, even if she eats sweets or speaks eloquently, she becomes like a sow; but if she speaks harshly to her husband, she is born among people as one who is mute.

If she does not look upon her husband out of desire, she shall become one-eyed and deformed.
(215) Furthermore, she is the very root of domestic happiness and dharma;

In every house there are women proud of their beauty and charm;

They are of four kinds: superior, middling, inferior, and most inferior.

yet you are Maheśī, the Mother of the World, and Śiva is your manifest husband.

O beloved, this divine marriage of Brahmā and Brāhmī has thus been described.

"O Lakṣmī! Thus has been told this auspicious account of the wedding, which bestows great fame, leads to heaven, grants progeny and lineage, fulfills all desires, and is supreme; it should especially be recited everywhere during the festivals of Śiva. (241)

Thus ends the first section, "The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga," in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the worship of the family deity, Pārvatī’s investiture with the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), the ornaments and other gifts sent by Śiva, her arrival at the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and other sites, the offering of *madhuparka* and other rites, and the declaration of names and lineages (*gotra*).

by seeing and worshipping him, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are obtained."
Having said "one another," they took hold of roots, fruits, and other offerings; likewise, some embraced one another, while others held each other's hands.
Through that mutual touch, the wives of the sages became completely absorbed in one another.

"Accept alms," those wives of the sages said to that god. He too, extending his begging bowl toward the women, said: "Give me alms; may it be well with you; may you be possessed of wealth and sons. (18–19)
Having given alms, those fickle women laughed much and asked: "What is this naked vow you have undertaken?
You are indeed a charming ascetic; tell us, if you please. (1.196.20)
Śaṅkara, however, laughing, said: "I have a secret vow;
thinking that there would be no fruit in its disclosure, do not ask.
Thus addressed, those wives of Brahmā replied: "Come to our home."
Having uttered this, they then indeed seized him with their sprout-like hands:
some at his neck, some on his back, and some on the region of his belly;
some on his knees and hips, as well as on his matted locks and sides.
Some [seized] his feet, others his nose and ears;
thus surrounding the Lord of the Bhikṣukas on all sides,
those wives of the twice-born drew him toward each of themselves and delighted him.

In the meantime, O brahmins, the other brahmins took their sacrificial fuel and went to their own homes; there they witnessed this marvel. Seeing that which was contrary to what they expected, they became filled with rage in an instant.
"Who is this? Of what sort is he, this intoxicated man who causes such agitation among women?
"Who are you? From where have you come? Why do you not wear clothes?
Though questioned thus, that Avadhūta, naked as the directions, did not say anything at all. (27-28)
On the contrary, by not listening to him, she brought about restlessness in the Linga;
like a negligent yogi, she displayed the power of her desire there.
Seeing that agitation, the gods realized that he was indeed negligent.
Seeing the phallus (*liṅga*) had undergone a transformation, they struck it with a blade of *darbha* grass.
They beat it excessively with wood, stones, and planks;
indeed, with that blade of *darbha* grass accompanied by mantras, they struck it right down to its base.
The *liṅga* fell to the earth, its testicles severed and struck;
when it was struck with the probe, it broke into twelve fragments.
Once the *liṅga* had been cast down, the Lord vanished from sight.
Then, grief arose among those sages of purified souls.
They all became agitated and said, "We do not know Śaṅkara;
who is this yogi, how has he arrived, and for what purpose has this ascetic come himself? (33–34)
As they all spoke thus, they considered what they had done to be a sinful act; then all the fragments of the *liṅga* flew up into the sky,
and wherever each fragment went, there it blazed like fire.
It burns whatever it encounters in front of it, and then, leaping up again, it moves forward. Wherever and whomever it goes, there it burns in every way.
Fragments have gone to the netherworld (pātāla), and likewise they have reached the heavens (svarga).
They moved everywhere upon the earth, flying up and falling down;
they scorched the entire universe and never remained still in any place.
The worlds became agitated, and those sages were deeply distressed. (38)
Neither gods, nor asuras, nor sages, nor humans found any peace.
Deprived of any means for pacification, they went to Brahmā for refuge.
Having gone there, they all then bowed to and praised the Creator.
At the time of dissolution, they remained with their faces cast down out of shame;
they related all that had occurred to Brahmā, the creator.
Having understood that deed of Śaṅkara, Brahmā spoke these words:
Alas! These Brahmins are always angry and do not know the ultimate reality (tāttvika).
With deluded intellects, they know neither dharma nor any sacred rite.
Those who truly understand the reality of Brahman (brahmatattva) are proclaimed as true Brāhmaṇas.
In Brahman there is no desire, nor is there any transformation or anger from any source.
The attributes of the body do not truly exist in the presiding self, according to the reality of things.
The gods on earth know that the attributes of the Self do not reside in the body.
For those who are devoid of this knowledge and possessed by the notions of "I" and "mine" regarding the body,
they become angry by relying upon the body; they cause others to be slain, and they even act with malice, based on the distinction between what belongs to others and what belongs to themselves.
Thereupon, by the power of karma, they indeed experience the states of heaven and hell;
therefore, the wise man should purify that mind through the cultivation of knowledge, yoga, and the self.
For when that [mind] is purified, the inner self becomes spontaneously free from modification.
The body is not afflicted by the afflictions (kleśas) nor by the bodily qualities (dharmas) that are pure or impure.
This being so, there is no obsession rooted in desire, anger, and the like;
and when that is absent, such misfortune as this would not arise.
"Sirs, you who dwell in this hermitage are overcome by anger and desire;
yet in the hermitage of the wise, the mastery over anger and desire is futile.
In reality, there is no body of women that truly bears the name 'woman'. (1.196.50)
Nor is even the body of a man designated by the name "man.
However, in both cases, there is always the embodied self (śārīrātman) that bears the designation "man.
That body which is to be enjoyed by a man is proclaimed as "woman" (nārī). ||51-52||
A body, whether possessing a beard or hairless, is called a "woman.
There is enjoyment only of the body itself, not of any other body.
The pleasure and pain of another's body are not experienced by one's own self. (53)
For one's own pleasure and pain are experienced by one's own self alone.

Therefore, who is this woman, and to whom does she belong? Likewise, who is this man, and to whom does he belong? Where has all desire been laid to rest, and where is this delusion consisting of women? 54–55.

Where is such terrible anger by which you do not even know yourselves? Whatever one who is full of anger sacrifices, gives, or even mutters prayers, and whatever he offers in the fire—he does not obtain the fruit thereof; his actions are in vain.
O twice-born ones, those who know [the truth] indeed perform what is censurable.
If, however, they were ignorant, then what wonder would there be in that?
Who could ever attain well-being or prosperity by opposing Śiva? (57–58)

One should not disregard a guest who has arrived at the time of midday; for by taking away that person's merit and giving one’s own demerit, one departs from the abode of the Guest—how much more so from where Śaṅkara resides? (59)
"As long as the Liṅga is not stable, there will surely be no well-being for the worlds. You must act in such a way that stability may be achieved here.
Having heard this, the sages said, "O Brahman, instruct us regarding the truth."
Brahmā said: "Having propitiated Hara, we shall obtain happiness;
let us go for refuge to the god on Kailāsa, the abode of Śiva.
And having gone there together, they beheld Śaṅkara standing there.
Then the gods began to praise the Formless One (aliṅga):
"Salutations to you who are without form, whose nature is the great flame of fire;
salutations to the sky-clad one, the unchanging, who possesses the supreme form. (63–64)

Salutations to you, whose divine play is manifold; salutations to you, who are of a forgiving nature. Salutations to you whose true form is peaceful; salutations to you, who possess a formidable manifestation.
O Mahādeva, forgive our offenses here; let there be salutations to you.
O Lord, O God, withdraw your own fallen linga!
It is ablaze with fire, assuming twelve forms, and consumes the three worlds.
Have mercy, O Mahādeva; the universe is composed of your divine play.
Thus praised and gratified, Śaṅkara then spoke with joy:
"O twice-born ones, perform worship for him against whom the offense was committed.
Then there will be peace, and the liṅga shall remain fixed in its place."
"O Brahmins, I shall indeed become such that my supreme pleasure may be attained;
from that, you shall obtain the happiness you desire—whether you be gods, sages, seers, brahmins, or even asuras. (1.196.70)
Having gathered together, let them perform the worship of my *liṅga* with the sixteen services (*upacāras*). Then those twelve shall indeed become pacified;
this is the nature of my *liṅga*, and never otherwise.
"Wherever they fall—be it at Kurukṣetra or elsewhere—O twice-born ones, establish them upon the seats of their respective wombs. First, you all must go together to Kurukṣetra. (72–73)
Having bathed there in that lake, perform the worship of one [liṅga];
upon its pacification, the others will become pacified fires.
Wherever fragments of the liṅga have fallen, there the worship should be performed.

"Let the illustrious ones act; let them go without delay, for [they must] propitiate my wife of a former birth, Satī Sthirāyanā, having transformed her into the form of a womb, and establish that [sacrificial fire] therein. (75–76)
Having established a single water-pot and fashioned an excellent eight-petaled lotus [diagram] within it,
let them fill it with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and with sprouts of dūrvā grass.
Then, let them consecrate that pot with Vedic mantras.
Having worshipped that pitcher, let them perform an ablution with its water,
as well as a sprinkling with the Śatarudrīya mantras for the sake of peace;
when this is done upon her who has the form of a womb, Bāṇa will attain peace.
Having thus established a fragment of a *liṅga* before the *liṅga*, let them invoke me;
likewise, let them gratify the Supreme Lord with fragrant sandalwood, flowers, incense, and other offerings,
as well as with worship including food offerings (*naivedya*).
With prostrations, hymns of praise, dances, songs, and circumambulations, (8.1) and then having performed a rite for well-being, let them proclaim, "Victory!
"O God, grant total peace; be gracious in every way. (8.2)
"Be peaceful, O Mahādeva, and always grant us protection.
O brahmins, act accordingly; let them depart without delay.
Having been addressed thus, those gods, brahmins, and others bowed to Maheśvara.
Having reached the shore of the lake at Kurukṣetra with serene minds, the goddess Satī was propitiated there by the brahmins;
remembering her purpose, she, the divine one, immediately appeared for the sake of Śaṅkara. (84–85)
Then that divine source, having been worshipped by the Brahmins, assumed a physical form.
Thereupon, the tip of the *liṅga* was established by the Brahmins with mantras;
all the blood and other [impurities] were washed away and made level through rubbing and other means.
There, the tip of the *liṅga* was worshipped with devotion by the gods and others using the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) and Vedic mantras, as well as various articles of worship;
and Mahādeva, being well-pleased, appeared there in embodied form.
Then Hara, golden-hued, exceedingly radiant, encircled by rays of light,
with a gracious countenance and tranquil, spoke to them all:
"O Brahmins, that act of yours known as malice has been pacified."
Wherever all these [deities] are peaceful, they shall remain there likewise. But this [liṅga], which Satī has honored and placed within my womb,
that tip of the liṅga shall attain fame by the name Hāṭakeśa.
And let that [Liṅga] dwell in Pātāla under the name Hāṭakeśvara; meanwhile,
Brahmā, the creator of the universe, having then installed that first Liṅga made of stone here,
personally worshipped it thereafter.
Brahmā established its renown by the name Sthāṇvīśvara.
Know, therefore, that in a future time, it shall indeed attain the fame of the name Nāgeśvara, having taken refuge in Dārukāvana. (93–94)
Then, wherever the fragments had fallen, the gods went there and purified them, establishing them as *yonipīṭhas*.
And in each of those places, those fragments received worship with devotion.
Having become invisible, they were joined together in due order.
And the tip of the *liṅga*, having risen from the netherworld (*pātāla*), arrived;
it too then attained union with its proper place.
Thus, having attained fullness, that conscious *liṅga* then reached the testicles of Śiva and remained in its proper place;
it was joined there correctly by Śiva, whose deeds are miraculous.
Neither Brahmā, nor Śaṅkara, nor Viṣṇu would be able to do so;
indeed, no one else possesses such power for killing, joining, or moving it.
This miracle was performed for the purpose of honoring all of them. (1.196.100)
Then, indeed, on the dark fortnight of Caitra, the descent of the Liṅga occurred.
On that day, twelve Liṅgas worthy of worship appeared,
due to the conjunction with a divine asterism on the thirteenth lunar day of the month of Caitra.
On an auspicious day of supreme merit, during the conjunction of Venus, the Sun, and the Moon,
the Sthāṇu-liṅga was installed by Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds;
it has been worshipped by sages and hosts of gods for eternal years.
Thus, these twelve *liṅgas* are indeed the *jyotirliṅgas*;
for they are the great *liṅgas* consisting of light belonging to Śaṅkara. Indeed, it is there that the fragments of his conscious nature reside.

He who performs worship and consecration is indeed Śaṅkara himself; he exists visibly as those very [images]. Mahat-Brahman, in the form of light, shines eternally as Śaṅkara himself in embodied form.
I shall now describe those very jyotirliṅgas; listen, O beloved:
Somanātha in Saurāṣṭra, Mallikārjuna on Śrīśaila, Mahākāla in Ujjayinī, and Amareśvara at Oṃkāra. (107)
Kedāra on the back of the Himavat, Bhīmaśaṅkara at Ḍākinī;
Viśveśa in Vārāṇasī, Tryambaka on the bank of the Gomatī;
Vaidyanātha on the cremation ground, and Nāgeśa in the Dāruka forest.
At Setubandha, one should diligently partake of the *naivedya* (sacrificial food) offered to Rāmeśa, and at Śivālaya, that of Ghuśmeśa; furthermore,
these [offerings] should be taken repeatedly as they are established in those respective locations during times of decline.
O beloved, listen as I describe those liṅgas here for the sake of devotees:
In Saurāṣṭra is Somanātha, who brings an end to the suffering of the Moon;
that god, installed by Candra, became manifest and then entered into a state of latent absorption. || 111–112 ||
O Dear One, through worship, he is the destroyer of diseases such as consumption and leprosy;
Someśa, an incarnation of Śiva, is established in the form of a *liṅga*.
Furthermore, there is indeed the incarnation of Śaṅkara known by the name Mallikārjuna.
The second [manifestation] is said to be on Śrīgiri, existing in the form of a *liṅga*.
When Kārttikeya, out of anger at Gaṇeśa’s marriage, departed after making a vow of lifelong celibacy (*brahmacāri-vrata*), [the Lord remained there]. || 1.14–1.15 ||
There, overcome with grief due to the separation from his son, Śaṅkara departed;
that second Hara himself remained there in the form of a *liṅga*.
In the city of Ujjayinī, however, Hara is known by the name Mahākāla.

For the protection of the Brahmin learned in the Vedas, Śaṅkara went there in embodied form. Then Hara, by a mere "hum" sound, quickly reduced to ashes the demon named Dūṣaṇa, who was a destroyer of the Vedic dharma.
This very one, known as Mahākāla, is established in the form of a *liṅga*.
Śambhu, having been entreated by the gods, assumed the nature of a *jyotirliṅga*.
Then, meditated upon by the Vindhya mountain, Śaṅkara himself appeared in embodied form.
Established there by Brahmā as the fourth *jyotirliṅga*,
Śambhu resides there under the name Oṃkāreśvara;
Hara himself is personally present on Mount Kedāra, the snowy mountain.
By the will of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the fifth divine [manifestation] named Kedāreśvara remains there in embodied form as Bāṇa.
Now follows the sixth, the supreme incarnation of Śiva’s jyotir-liṅga.
Having slain the terrible asura Bhīma, Hara protected the king named Sudakṣiṇa, the lord of Kāmarūpa; for he is indeed Bhīmeśvara.
Abiding personally within the Ḍākinī in the form of a jyotirliṅga. || 123–124 ||
He who came from Mount Mandara and established himself personally in Kāśī,
that Jyotiḥsvarūpa (the Embodiment of Light), Viśveśvara of Kāśī, is the seventh.
Then, through the praise of Gautama, Hara himself manifested.
Likewise, the eighth is the one named Tryambakeśvara on the bank of the Godāvarī.
Then, through the praise of Rāvaṇa, Hara himself appeared upon the cremation ground at Vaidyanātheśvara, established as a mass of light.
Then Hara killed the rākṣasa known as Dāruka;
thereafter, Śambhu himself, accompanied by Ambikā and assuming the form of a jyotirliṅga, protected his devotee, the vaiśya named Supriya, and remained there.
Now, the eleventh [linga], established by Rāmāditya, is Śambhu himself in the form of Rāmeśvara, consisting of a *jyotirliṅga*;
he shines forth for his devotees, bestowing the boon of victory. (1.196.130)

Propitiated by the devotee Ghuṣma, Hara himself went there for the protection of Ghuṣma’s son, who had indeed been slain by Sudehya. Thereafter, he shines forth in the form of the Ghuṣmeśvara jyotirliṅga.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the twelve forms of Hara have been described to you.
By seeing them, worshipping them, meditating upon them, or even hearing of them, a human being is liberated from all sins and attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having thus taken hold of these signs, they became jyotirliṅgas.
Then, in the course of time, due to the decline of the sites and the distinction between the yugas,
others will establish [new ones] through the work of restoring what has decayed.
"What else do you wish to hear regarding the further divisions of the ages?

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Falling of the Liṅga with a Blade of Darbha Grass and the Twelve Jyotir-liṅgas for the Naked Śaṅkara Who Went to Dāruvana for Alms," within the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 196: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Age)*
Chapter 197 [Author:
Chapter 198 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
The worship of the Ācārya, the worship of Vyāsa, and the worship of the Guru—
O Blessed Lord, O God, tell me that which constitutes the nature of daily worship.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
One should worship the preceptor Vyāsa and likewise the Guru with devotion according to the prescribed rites.
Having brought the vessel of worship along with the ritual offerings and having gone before the Guru,
one should first prostrate and touch his feet with one's head.
Then, one should perform the consecration of the right big toe with water (3).
Thereafter, one should place flowers, saffron, and unbroken rice grains into the vessel;
one should offer sandalwood paste and smear it there with a drop [of liquid] (4).
Afterwards, one should smear that sandalwood paste on the forehead in the form of an upright line.
One should fashion an auspicious crescent moon made of saffron in the center, together with unbroken grains of rice.
On the head, one should place a highly valuable and radiant turban.
One should likewise provide a long, excellent, and richly colored neck-cloth (*galapaṭṭa*) set with gold threads,
as well as a fine woolen bodice (*kañcuka*), an upper garment (*uttarīya*) with gold threads, and two pairs of washed garments (*dhautra*) of the same kind. (6–7)
One should give a lower garment, a bathing cloth, and likewise a new upper robe;
and one should give a beautiful, soft ball with a concealed cord.
One should also give a couch, a mattress, pieces of cloth, and a coverlet.
One should also give a soft leaf-cloth and a sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
Likewise, one should provide a shoulder-strap and an excellent seat.
Furthermore, one should give two cotton side-cloths as well as a cotton quilt.
Likewise, there should be two small bowls and two small vats;
also the vessel for sipping water, the vessel for the fire-oblation, the vessel for worship, and the three-mouthed vessel;
as well as a circular vessel, a drinking vessel, and an excellent pitcher.
One should give a betel-box along with an umbrella and two very soft sandals;
likewise, one should give wooden shoes, a staff, and an excellent waist-belt,
all fashioned from various metals and materials.
Golden ornaments for the ears and auspicious ornaments for the neck;
ornaments for the hands, ornaments for the waist, and ornaments for the feet in their entirety;
chains, bracelets, garlands, rings, and excellent necklaces.
One should offer a golden girdle and the finest fragrant substances—
musk, camphor, various oils with diverse scents, as well as unguents for the body— offering these indeed with great devotion. (15–16)
One should give vehicles, celestial chariots, carts, mounts, and milch cows;
likewise, male and female servants, as well as wealth— specifically gold and silver—
and various kinds of fine food, grain, and pulses.

One should offer to the venerable Guru—who is Nārāyaṇa himself, the realized yogi—the articles for preparation such as bowls and the like, as well as cumin and sour liquids; sugar-cane products, fresh butter, ghee, and various kinds of food. (18–19)
To the Brahmin, the giver of knowledge and the giver of mantras, who is compassionate;
whatever is dear to one's own heart, that one should offer to the venerable Guru.
Having performed everything in this manner, one should then [place him] again near one's side.
Whoever indeed gives various fruits, whether dry or fresh,
as a gift to the venerable Guru— thereby bestowing the gift of liberation— and then bows at his feet, saying "Abīra Gulāla," [attains the highest state].
One should offer the sacred tulasī leaf and various kinds of flowers,
and perform the washing of the two holy feet with milk.
Furthermore, one should perform the ceremonial bathing of the guru with milk according to the prescribed rite.
Having thus bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and pure water,
and having bathed it again and again with substances that remove impurities,
one should massage the major limbs of the Guru in order to dispel fatigue.
One should cleanse the body with cloths and then offer fragrant substances.
One should put on garments, ornaments, and finery;
[one should adorn oneself] with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, garlands, collyrium, and fragrant powders for the head.
One should worship with devotion using golden necklaces, gems, diamonds, and the like,
as well as incense, lamps, and various auspicious food offerings (*naivedya*).
One should worship and feed [the deity] comfortably with sweet, heart-pleasing, and most delicious foods.
One should offer fragrant water for drinking and excellent betel leaf;
likewise, one should offer pleasant fruit and perform the *ārātrika* ceremony.
Then, one should prostrate like a staff, offer beautiful hymns of praise, perform obeisances, and subsequently request forgiveness.

One should circumambulate [the preceptor] with palms joined in reverence and offer a handful of flowers. Having received the blessings spoken by the guru and having accepted the gift of grace (*prasādaka*), one should take leave of him and return home, carrying that gift of grace along.
Having bestowed that very grace upon his own kinsmen,
he should always meditate on the Guru in the morning and worship him in due order.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara.
The Guru is the manifest Supreme Brahman; he is indeed the purifier who bestows liberation.
There is no substance equal to the Guru; there is no deity higher than the Guru.
There is no liberation other than through the Guru; there is no merit greater than the Guru.
Within the body of the Guru, Hari, the Supreme Brahman, shines eternally;
Vāsudeva, the imperishable Brahman, is in the head, and on the forehead is [the syllable] "Vā.
In the two eyes are the Sun and the Moon, and in the nose are the two Aśvinīkumāras.
Nārāyaṇa is in the mouth as the sacrifice; the circle of the Vedas is on the tongue.
Sarasvatī resides in the speech of the guru, and Viṣṇu himself is stationed in the heart.
In the stomach, the Lord Vaiśvānara dwells at all times.
In her hand is the lotus, and Kamalā, the Great Lakṣmī, resides in her mind;
the Vasus dwell in her feet, as do the purifying holy fords (tīrthas).
The fundamental principles (tattvas) and the deities reside in all her sense organs, and they are present within the pores of her skin.
The form of the Guru is a form of merit; the Great Goddess is the form of the mantra.
Heaven, Satyaloka, and Vaikuṇṭha are all established within the form of the Guru.
In the Guru resides the eternal, unconditioned bliss of Brahman.
One who knows Brahman as bliss is indeed a guru, and no other;
the syllable *ga* signifies light or knowledge, while the syllable *ra* signifies substance or giving.
Because he bestows knowledge and substance, he is called a guru; he himself possesses both illumination and material wealth. (41)
The syllable *ga* is the knowledge of the mantra, and likewise, the syllable *ra* is the act of giving.
Hari himself is the Guru, the locus of the power to bestow the mantra.
A meal given to the Guru shall produce the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. (42–43)
Giving garments and other gifts to the guru bestows the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Worship of the guru is worship of Hari; the guru is considered the fruit of yoga.
The guru is the vow, the guru is the sacrifice, and the guru alone is meditative absorption (samādhi).
Tradition is declared to be the Guru; direct realization is considered the Guru.
When the Guru is pleased, the restraints (yamas), the observances (niyamas), tranquility (śama), and all means of accomplishment (sādhanas) are truly fulfilled. 45–46.
At birth, the parents are declared to be the gurus; the one who performs the naming ceremony is the guru;
the mother is the teacher of speech, and the sister is the instructor in duties and such.
The Brahmin who bestows the sacred thread and likewise the teacher of the scriptures [is also a guru].
The supreme guru is the bestower of mantras and knowledge, as well as the giver of liberation.
This self, submerged in beginningless ignorance, wanders through the various wombs;
by destroying that ignorance through the constant granting of knowledge, [the guru acts]. 48–49.
Having brought about the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanās*) and karmas,
he certainly shows the path of enjoyment through the propitiation of Hari;
he leads one to the state of liberation— this is the Guru who bestows everything.
Who else is a greater teacher than He who removes suffering and bestows happiness?
(5.1) Having entered the disciple’s soul through the power of the Guru, which is of the nature of knowledge, the Guru brings about liberation by means of his own direct realization. (5.2)
Initiation, possessing the power of knowledge, enters the body of the disciple and,
through its bestowal and purification by the strength of the Guru, leads him to liberation.
According to the instructions of initiation, the disciple becomes worthy of grace.
But in the absence of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and instruction (*śikṣā*), there is no attainment of knowledge, perfection, or liberation.
(54) Therefore, through the purificatory rite known as initiation and the acquisition of knowledge known as instruction, the disciple shall always attain purity gradually by means of the Guru. (55)
Because he is to be instructed and because he is the cause of reverence for the teacher, and following the conduct of the cultured, the disciple should practice respect toward the teacher.
He who is the teacher is declared to be Hari; he who is Hari is remembered as the teacher.
The Guru is Lord Hari himself; Kṛṣṇa abides as the very essence of knowledge and instruction. (57) As is Kṛṣṇa, so is knowledge; as is knowledge, so is the Guru.
The fruit obtained through the worship of Kṛṣṇa, knowledge, and the Guru is identical. (58)
This Guru is the essence of all gods and consists of all mantras;
the disciple, with every effort, should bear the Guru’s command upon his head.
If one seeks the highest good, one should not transgress the Guru’s command even in thought.
The disciple who obeys the command of the guru attains the perfection of knowledge. Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, he should carry out the word of the guru;
by the guru’s command, he should perform all other duties as one who has offered himself to the teacher.
One should perform all actions in the presence of the guru and with his permission.
In the guru’s house or in his presence, one should not sit as one pleases;
for the guru is the manifest God himself, and his house is a temple of the Divine.
Just as gold here sheds its impurity through contact with fire;
just as clarified butter placed near a fire melts quickly;
and just as dry wood is consumed when the fire blazes. (63–64)
In the same way, through contact with the Guru, a human being sheds impurity;
all sin dissolves and latent tendencies are consumed by fire.
One should not provoke the anger of the Guru through thought, deed, or speech.
By his anger, indeed, longevity, prosperity, knowledge, and virtuous deeds are consumed.
For those who provoke his anger, their sacrifices become fruitless;
even their restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) truly become fruitless.
One should never speak anything contrary that pierces the vital points of the guru;
for if a disciple speaks so out of great arrogance, he indeed goes to a downward state.
In thought, deed, or word, one should not practice false conduct.
One should always do what is beneficial and pleasing to the guru, whether commanded or not.
Whether in the guru’s presence or out of sight, one should act for his pleasure.
Setting aside all of one's own affairs, one should attend to the guru's business. (1.197.70)
The reality that generates consciousness, infused with supreme bliss—
he who has realized this here in the world is the very one who bestows liberation. Does a boat carry what it carries across, or would a stone carry a stone?
In one devoid of Brahman, whence can there be awakening? And whence indeed can there be the realization of the Self?
(72) One who is united with the reality of Brahman is liberated here and liberates all beings;
his intellect, satisfied by direct experience, has reached the pinnacle of bliss. (73)
By the mere sight of him, supreme bliss arises;
by the act of serving him, liberation from karma is certainly attained.
Through the desire to serve him, everything is accomplished for the embodied soul.
That very one, full of bliss, is indeed to be served by those seeking liberation.
For knowledge, which is the realization of the Self and the attainment of Brahman, does not constitute liberation;
nor is bliss attained [merely] through that, for it cannot be realized while remaining in the state of a guru. //75-76//

One should always serve with devotion the Guru’s brothers and sons, who bestow awakening and gather [disciples] through devotion; one should constantly propitiate the Guru, the giver of fearlessness to all, whose mind is overcome with compassion. (77)
One should propitiate [the guru] in many ways with devotion and with worship consisting of the offering of one’s entire being.
The disciple should continue to serve him until he becomes pleased;
when the guru is pleased, the disciple’s sins are instantly destroyed. (78–79)
Therefore, one should devotedly give to the preceptor, according to one's means, these things: wealth, jewels, fields, houses, ornaments, garments, vehicles, beds, and seats. (1.197.80)
One should not practice stinginess with wealth if one desires one's own welfare.
(81) He alone is the father, the mother, the husband, the kinsman, the wealth, the happiness, the companion, and the friend; therefore, one should report everything to him. (82)
Those who do not fall into despondency even when reviled or beaten;
who are non-violent and compassionate, with minds intent upon liberation;
who are free from pride, wise, devoid of rivalry, and speak kindly—[they are the steadfast]. (83)
Upright, gentle, clear-sighted, disciplined, and steady-minded—
such auspicious women and men, as well as female and male disciples, who are eternally composed of pure being, should take refuge in a true guru. (84–85)

Those disciples who, being fully committed, perform service for their teacher, incur no fault due to a lack of independence, because their actions are for the sake of another. What need is there for much speaking on this point? Even anyone at all who has taken refuge in a teacher [is free from blame].
"Having entered the path of Brahman, he shall become a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt.
(87) Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 199 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
It has been heard that in ancient times Kāma was born from the form of Nārāyaṇa;
at that time, his residence among the lords was purely mental.
Furthermore, when was he manifested during a creation by Brahmā?
Therefore, O Purāṇa-Puruṣottama, tell me that according to the truth.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having propitiated Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds...
He created all those subjects, beginning with the gods, asuras, and humans.
Having created the foremost of the gods, the lords of creatures headed by Dakṣa,
he then created from his mind Sandhyā, who was of beautiful form and engaged in silent recitation.
Having seen her— who was exceedingly beautiful, possessed of lovely eyebrows, capable of deluding the minds of sages, worthy of a man, and endowed with every perfection—
the mental states of all were then filled with passion for that woman. (5)

May such women as these be fortunate, being the very locus of the qualities of passion. And may there always be for those couples a power that increases their affection and takes the form of mutual attraction.
Having thus understood their intentions, the Creator himself mentally resolved, "So be it," and fashioned such a man. Meanwhile, a beautiful man born from the mind of Brahmā appeared there.
He appeared, golden-hued, with a broad chest and a fine nose;
his thighs, hips, and shanks were well-rounded, and the tips of his hair were dark and curled;
his pair of eyebrows met, he was graceful, and his face possessed the exceeding splendor of the full moon.
Possessing a very firm and broad, beautiful chest, adorned with a swarm of hair like bees; handsome, cloud-colored, stout, and wearing fine blue garments;
with his hands, eyes, face, feet, and palms appearing slightly reddish.
Slender-waisted, with beautiful teeth, possessing the scent of an elephant in rut;
with eyes like the petals of a full-blown lotus, his mouth perfumed by betel; with a neck like a conch shell, bearing the fish-banner, tall in stature, and having the makara as his vehicle.
Arrogant, bearing five flower-weapons and adorned with a bow of blossoms,
he was handsome as he moved his two eyes with side-long glances;
flickering with his beautiful eyes, he was steeped in the aesthetic sentiment of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
Upon seeing him, all the men— the sons of Brahmā beginning with Dakṣa—
were seized by the utmost eagerness, their minds drawn away by wonder;
and the hearts of them all were suddenly transformed.
There was no fortitude at all among those whose minds were agitated by desire.
Then Kāma himself, having bowed to Brahmā, spoke in haste:
"What shall I do? I am your servant; O Brahmā, employ me in some task."
A wise man should employ a servant according to his qualities and appearance.
Having heard this, Brahmā spoke to his son Kāma, the bestower of happiness:
"With this form of yours and with your five flower-arrows..."
Deluding both men and women, create the eternal creation;
all beings, including those with vital breath and consciousness— myself, Viṣṇu, and others as well—
shall remain under your control and shall act as your providers of sustenance.
Having entered into the minds of people while remaining invisible in form,
and having become a great bestower of happiness, perform the eternal creation.
For the mind of living beings, longing for pleasure, is the target of your arrow.
"Let it be so; your place has been established, yet the vital essence (sattva) born of the body remains.
Let your sense organ be the garden, and may you there become the source of intoxication.
Thus has your great function, which sets creation in motion, been described.
Just as our minds were churned by you,
so too was he called Manmatha (the Churner) because of the mutual longing between you two.
Furthermore, because he is born from the mind (*manas*), he is renowned as Manobhava (Born of the Mind).
Because you cause intoxication, you shall be Madana; because you inspire pride, you shall be Kandarpa. Your fame will be as "the one with flower-arrows" and "the lord of Rati.
Among the gods, there shall indeed be no one equal to you in pervasive power.
Therefore, may all places belong to you, the omnipresent one.
O sinless one, your weapons have always been declared to be those that cause exhilaration, attraction, delusion, as well as withering and even death.
"Accompanied by them, you shall indeed achieve victory over all created beings.
Having received this benediction from Sandhyā,
he discharged arrows at Brahmā in order to test their efficacy.
In this manner, he repeatedly fitted his bow with arrows.
Having assumed the *ālīḍha* stance and drawing the bow with great effort, he formed it into a circle; fragrant winds began to blow. (1.198.30–31)
The Enchanter deluded all the mental sages;
gazing at Sandhyā, they were filled with the impulse of transformation. Their passion increased and their senses became agitated. (32)
Seeing the twilight, forty-nine states were born from the body.
It was contemplated that what had been indicated by Brahmā through desire could now be accomplished.
Then, the element of water fell from the body of Brahmā at that time.
The groups of Pitṛs known as the Agniṣvāttas are remembered as those Pitṛs who are blue-complexioned ascetics, emptying the house of worldly existence.
Indeed, sixty-four thousand of these Agniṣvāttas are purifiers.
Likewise, there were eighty-six thousand others known as the Barhiṣads.
(3.6) Then, from the body of Dakṣa, the bodily fluids fell upon the earth;
from that, a woman endowed with every excellence was born. (3.7)
Her limbs were gentle, her waist slender, and her hair was fine like gold;
her body was soft, her teeth were beautiful, and she blazed with a halo of splendor.
Her lovely limbs possessed a golden luster, and that woman was filled with the radiance of the moon.
Twelve years of age, named Rati, she was most enchanting;
she was filled with the essence of passion and a true mine of all beauty.
Then [she appeared] before Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, and Aṅgiras. (1.198.40)
The seed of those who had not restrained their senses fell upon the ground;
from it were born the classes of Pitṛs known as the Somapas and the Ājyapas,
as well as the Sukālins, the Haviṣmants, and the Kavyavāhakas.
The Vāsiṣṭhas, born later in time, were born from Kratu as Soma-drinkers (Somapās).
From Pulastya were born the Ājyapas, and the sons of Aṅgiras were the Haviṣmats.
This entire group of ancestors became, in every respect, the Kavyavāṭs.
Sandhyā, having become the mother of the ancestors (Pitṛs), became intent upon that purpose. Then Dakṣa said to Kāma:
"Take this daughter of mine as your wife; she is worthy of you and endowed with similar virtues."
Having spoken thus, he gave her— who was born from the sweat of his body—
to Kandarpa as a wife, together with Rati, who sought him as her husband.
Having married her, Smara too rejoiced exceedingly with that noble Rati.
Beholding her pair of eyebrows, he forgot his own bow;
seeing the movement of her side-long glances, he forgot the discharge of his arrows;
and smelling her fragrant breath, he forgot the wind carrying the scent of flowers.
Beholding her face, which was as lovely as the moon’s orb, she forgot the moon itself.
Seeing her two breasts, which resembled golden lotus buds and were adorned with a pair of nipples, she remembered a pair of stars. (48–49)
Seeing the garland hanging down between her two firm, plump, and elevated breasts as far as her navel— its surface broad like a moonlight night— he remembered the *kaumudī* festival;
he forgot even the string of his own bow, which resounded with the humming of bees.
Beholding her pair of eyes, O lotus-petal-eyed one, he forgot [his own].
Beholding her slender belly, he remembered the golden altar;
beholding her two thighs, he remembered a pair of plantain trees. (51–52)
And beholding the reddened portions at the heels, the soles, and the tips of her feet,
he recalled his friend named Anurāga, who resided upon those very feet.
Her pair of hands was red with nails resembling *kiṃśuka* flowers.

Beholding her pair of arms, which were as long as a pair of lotus stalks and captivating with their rounded fingers that tapered to delicate tips, he recalled the coils of the excellent jewels upon the serpent-arms of Hari. (54–55)
Seeing her soft, glossy, and coral-hued [hair], Kāma indeed rejoiced;
that enchanting mass of hair resembled dark blue clouds.
Resembling the tail of a yak, it shone forth as the very life of Smara.
Such was she, possessing a lotus-like face with a circle of teeth and adorned with fragments of lotus stalks;
the abode of all beauty, charming in every limb,
endowed with twelve ornaments, and possessed of the sixteen amorous graces.
Seeing that enchanting Rati, Kāma seized her with eager longing;
there, Brahmā duly performed their marriage ceremony.
At that time, a great festival took place there, proceeding with happiness.
Dakṣa was exceedingly pleased, and his daughter Rati rejoiced; Kāma attained supreme happiness and shone brilliantly with her. Beholding her again and again, he held her close upon his heart.
She who was formerly Sandhyā, the daughter of Brahmā born from his mind,
having performed austerities and cast off her body, was born as Arundhatī.
Having become the daughter of Medhātithi, she chose Vasiṣṭha as her husband.
She performed austerities for four yugas on the bank of the Candrabhāgā river.
Then, a request was made: "Let Smara not enter [her] as soon as she is born.
Brahmā also granted this boon, saying, "So be it."
From that day forward, Smara entered into twelve [years] of the subjects;
she too, having thus withdrawn her asceticism,
went into the sky and dwelt in the constellation of the Seven Sages as a companion to Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this story of Kāmaka has been told to you once more.
At the beginning of the Kalpa, she was born as the daughter of a Caṇḍāla and was exceedingly virtuous. During a twelve-year drought, the sages, desiring food, [approached her]. (66–67)
Then, sent by her father, they came together for the sake of alms;
along with that alms-food, she was offered to the purifying Vasiṣṭha.
She was drawn from the midst of the cows, purified, and wedded.
She herself is the goddess Arundhatī, devoted solely to her husband.
Thus everything has been told to you exactly as it is.
Regarding the different creations in the various Kalpas, what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Birth of Sandhyā, Pitṛ, Kāma, Rati, and Arundhatī within the Creation of Living Beings," in the first section, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord, during the churning of the ocean, you became [the goddess Māyā] for the purpose of deluding the Daityas.

"O Lord, having seen you then in the form of Mohinī, how did Śaṅkara—even though he is the master of Māyā and devoid of qualities—fall under the delusion of Māyā? Cut through this doubt of mine; relate that story."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī! Hear everything exactly as it is, without any doubt.
I am Nārāyaṇa himself, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest. (3)
Although I am eternally devoid of qualities, I also become the source of divine qualities.
From my quality-less body, the entire world—
endowed with qualities and intermingled with the *guṇas* such as *sattva* and the rest— has arisen through my will.
I am the impeller and the instigator of both primordial nature and its qualities.
(5) Whatever effect arises—wherever it occurs and in whatever manner—I myself accomplish all of that by assuming a corresponding form. (6)
Resorting to the entry into another [state], I accomplish my purpose as one who seeks virtue.
Śaṅkara is my devotee; he is eternally untainted by *māyā*.
Unperturbed by the qualities of *māyā*, he is not defiled by *māyā*.
Nevertheless, for the sake of instructing others, I have displayed delusion.
Both virtuous women and virtuous men who have taken refuge in the vow of renunciation indeed become divine beings only after they have conquered delusion.
Nevertheless, when yoga is occasionally interrupted by the force of the senses,
those who perform vulgar acts may fall into delusion.
Even Śaṅkara, the king of yogis and a devotee, fell under the power of Māyā’s delusion.
Therefore, those desiring liberation must break free from the senses and so forth.
(11) Heedfulness must always be maintained; heedlessness is said to be death.
Heedlessness is indeed delusion, born from the union of men and women. (12)
"Those devoted to Him must never at any time partake of intoxicants produced from the body.
This was shown by me to Śaṅkara for the purpose of providing this counter-instruction.
Furthermore, [this was done] so that gold might be obtained from the womb of this Earth.
This was performed by me for the purpose of bestowing the *śivadhātu*, together with its underlying cause.
Listen to that very narrative of mine exactly as it occurred;
this story is considered to grant liberation through hearing because of the identity of the two.
Having heard that Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a woman, had deluded the Dānavas and caused the gods to drink the Soma,
Śaṅkara himself desired to see that form and arrived there with great haste.
Then Hari, the Deluder, having understood the intention of Śaṅkara,
caused the gods to drink the nectar and withdrew from where Hara was;
he became a sixteen-year-old woman, filled with the fullness of desire.
Adorned with a braid of hair and richly decorated with shimmering leaf-patterns,
her face was as captivating as the full moon of autumn;
she held the two eyebrows upon her forehead, which were like the arrows of Kāma reaching the heart.
Adorned with ear-ornaments of red, yellow, and pure white flowers;
her exquisite braided hair-knot was fashioned from clusters of land-lotuses;
and she was provided with leaf-patterns made of saffron mixed with fragrant sandalwood.
Her beautiful eyes, with outer corners moistened by dark, shimmering collyrium, reminded one of the secret cave of the God of Love through the bindus of light in their centers;
she wore earrings adorned with fine gems, jewels, gold, and diamonds. (22)
Adorned with hanging tassels of fine, shimmering pearls;
possessing golden moon-shaped cheek-plates set with brilliant diamonds;
and featuring a jeweled nose-peg made of gold in the form of a slender star.
Her pair of lips, like ripe bimba fruits, recalled the act of kissing;
her chin was adorned with a shimmering golden mark set between two jewels;
and she was graced by the excellent Kaustubha gem, whose luster equaled the rising sun and the moon. (25)

Her two breasts adorned her chest, which was beautified by a series of golden necklaces; she possessed a neck like a conch shell and wore a jeweled necklace. Her beautiful arms were like the core of a plantain tree, and the luster of her fingernails—shining like the moon—possessed the splendor of red young shoots.
Adorned with golden rings, armlets, beautiful bracelets, and *vaṅgīḍīs*,
her two feet shone with anklets, girdles, waist-bands, and toe-rings;
she was further graced by golden *mañjīras* joined with tinkling little bells.

Adorned with golden bells of variegated and wondrous red color, she was clothed in a shimmering garment whose borders were beautified by golden stars; she wore a bodice that resembled a fresh panel of many-colored cloth. (1.199.29–30)
Holding in her hand a garment possessing the luster of the moon and lightning, she repeatedly played with an excellent leaping ball;
moving through a tree-thicket richly adorned with flowers and tender shoots. (31)
Her breasts and hips were slightly trembling and possessed a restless movement;
her face became visible as she turned back the veil of her garment; and her long eyes flickered with amorous gestures, emotions, and graceful charms.
Placing her hand upon her breasts, she pressed them exceedingly;
at times, grasping her braid of hair, she adjusted her garment. Delighting in playing with a ball, she was one who caused extreme infatuation of the mind.
Frequently smiling, she goes along repeatedly lifting up her garment;
having tucked away her water-flask, she creeps toward where Śaṅkara is with some pretext, revealing her uncovered thighs.
Beholding her thus entirely absorbed in single-minded devotion with his own single-minded focus, Śambhu became motionless, his soul overwhelmed and his inner being struck down;
deprived of consciousness and memory, he was rendered devoid of luster. (37)
Absorbed in that state, her resolve was mounted solely upon the radiance of sensual existence.
At that moment, she became deprived of her fine silken garment, which was tossed by the waves of the wind;
with her waist-knot loosening, she fell to the ground, crying out in distress amidst the interval.
Having beheld within her a drop of lightning situated in the space of consciousness— like a flash amidst the clouds,
radiant with great light, and possessing the luster of gold, campaka flowers, and the sun—
Śaṅkara set his mind upon becoming intensely attached to her.
The wind carried away her garments, and she, in turn, carried away Śaṅkara.
Then, overcome with modesty, she moved from tree to tree;
meanwhile, his senses had become harshened by the force of passion, and he was filled with virility.
Having pursued him with great persistence, he seized his hair and body;
drawing him close and lifting him up, he embraced him with both arms.
Thus forcibly embraced, she was kissed again and again.
And she, being unwilling, freed herself from his embrace and fled into the thicket of trees; Hara pursued her,
and due to the intensity of the force of his semen, there was an emission as he ran.
Wherever she fled, they pursued her;
the semen that fell upon the earth became mines of gold.
Mohinī, moving ahead, proceeded swiftly along the path of the sky.
Deluded by the force of desire, Maheśvara pursued her. Wherever Mahādeva ran— on the earth, in forests, on mountains, along rivers, and in groves— the seed fell accordingly.
And in various places, through contact with that [semen], the earth indeed became composed of silver.
Following the discharge of the entire essence of Śaṅkara,
a state of exhaustion arose, and from that, awakening occurred once again.
"Who indeed is this one in the form of Mohinī? Who am I, and where am I going?
How have I incurred this stain, for I have remained unchanged?
Such a form could not exist except through the Creator of the world."
What illusion can there be for one who is free from illusion, by whom illusion has been brought under control?
"Come to me"—this is surely the Māyā of Viṣṇu, despite his efforts;
by His very Māyā, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded.
If I am drawn by him, then there is indeed nothing wonderful for me;
for joined by him alone, I always delight with Śivā, and impelled by him alone, I sport according to his will. (53–54)
Having reflected thus, his lower lip rejoiced and did not wither;
and the Blessed One, too, considering that devotee to be a true knower (*pramātṛ*), assumed the form of the *mohinī* and said: "Who are you, and why have you been rendered insentient?"
Where has your noble courage gone, like one lacking in spirit, without your yoga?
By what means has such a state been brought upon you, even though you are capable?
Come, come; let us enjoy ourselves in the secluded bowers of the lonely forest.
"Never again shall you obtain such a woman with an intact womb"—
thinking thus, Kṛṣṇa himself, Nārāyaṇa, kissed him.
But Hara, his member pierced by the instrument and overcome by flaccidity, [remained there].
He had no desire to take pleasure with her there.
He said to Mohinī: "Nowhere else is anyone capable of stealing the mental composure of yogis except for Nārāyaṇa. (1.199.60)
Salutation to that Blessed One who assumes illusory forms;
salutation to the divine Kṛṣṇa, to Nārāyaṇa, to Viṣṇu.
Salutation to You, whose essential nature is Mohinī and who takes the form of delusion.
I have no grief here regarding you, O Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme (62).
Nevertheless, O Lord of the gods of gods, protect me from the delusion of Māyā;
for this delusion, which arises from latent impressions (vāsanā), is the cause of bondage for the worlds (63).
Your yoga is considered to be both delusive in nature and liberating, yet devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). This supreme form of yours, which possesses the most worthy beauty,
does not lead to bondage for me or others, for it bestows liberation alone.
Therefore, that which has indeed been done by you is truly my supreme gain.
Even while living together with Pārvatī, I shall always remember you, the Enchantress, and I will become obsessed;
I shall surely attain a state devoid of all qualities.
Having heard this, the Lord, the husband of Kamalā, who knows the heart of Śambhu,
withdrew his female form and in an instant became four-armed; then,
the Soul of All embraced Hara within his heart and spoke with a smile.
"O Śaṅkara, you, my devotee, have conquered the illusion created by me through knowledge,
fortitude, and likewise through supreme devotion;
indeed, no one other than you could cross over this illusion in the form of a woman."
This delusive manifestation, which creates these states of existence like a deceptive illusion, is in essence a rope known as bondage; yet it does not touch those who have taken refuge in Me.
It deludes the non-devotees, but for the devotees, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
She alone, having entered into my yoga, is eternally beyond the gunas for my devotees.
She is Mahāmāyā, Mahālakṣmī, Kamalā, Rādhikā, Ramā, Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, and Pārvatī; she never bestows bondage.
Rukmiṇī, Kambharā, Brāhmī, the devoted Jānakī,
Mohinī, and Tulasī— these grant liberation and do not cause bondage. Prabhā, Māṇikī, Jayā, and Lalitā likewise do not cause bondage.
All of them are black in form, yet they are remembered as bestowers of liberation through yoga.
They are Haṃsā, Mañjulā, Campā, Haimī, Dayā,
Ramā, Puṣpā, Muktā, the goddess Śāntā, Godāvarī, and Manu.
Ojasvatī, Jīvā, and Maṅgalā—these were their excellent companions;
they were divine embodiments, virtuous and indeed yoginīs.
Dwelling within the very lap of Kṛṣṇa, they were therefore purifying and bestowers of liberation.
In this world, those who are Sāṃkhya-yoginīs as well as those who are renunciants (saṃnyāsinīs),
those who are dispassionate, those who possess my form, and even the female ascetics (yatinyas) who bestow liberation—
all of them are indeed my powers (mama śaktayaḥ), and being of my very nature, they are beyond all qualities (nirguṇāḥ).
Whosoever has attained union with them, those living beings are always devoid of qualities;
they are pure while living here and are indeed liberated, without a doubt.
Just as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara possess union with them.
Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others are eternally liberated and are forever the supreme lords.
Furthermore, those living beings who are the objects of their compassion are always lords of liberation.
Thus, O Śambhu, I have told you my unsurpassed majesty.
Those whose vision is clouded by an attachment to defects do not correctly understand this; nor do those who are attached to my own nature, nor those who grasp at awakening from me.
Those who know that all this is of my very self, and that it is indeed non-different from me, [attain true knowledge]. 82.
"Such are they, possessing such wisdom; they are indeed persistent in every way. Having said this to Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu vanished in an instant.
Then Mahādeva also went to the Gaṅgā for the purpose of bathing.
"Thus, O Lakṣmī! I have related everything regarding the power of Mohinī that was displayed to Śaṅkara. What more do you wish to hear?

[The Author: Chapter 201 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Furthermore, the rebirth of Nārada as the son of a maidservant—"
"Tell me, O Mādhava, when was he born? I wish to hear it.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! To this divine narrative which destroys all sins in every way."
Having created the universe according to the domestic dharma within Sāvitrī, Brahmā performed the act of impregnation;
and after more than a hundred years,
she gave birth to the four Vedas and all their auxiliary limbs in every respect.
The thirty-six passionate ones (Rāgiṇīs) and the six passions (Rāgas) conjoined with rhythmic measures (Tālas);
the four ages (Yugas), Time (Kāla), the Yogas, and the six auspicious Kṛttikās;
and the divine army Mahāṣaṣṭhī, the virtuous beloved of Kārttikeya.
Among the Mātṛkās, he [visualizes] her as the foremost, the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) of children;
(5) the fourfold dissolution, the Daughter of Death, and likewise the hosts of diseases;
Adharma from his back, and Alakṣmī from his left side. (6)
From his navel [he created] Viśvakarman and the eight Vasus of great strength;
from his mind, the four sons known as Sanaka and the others, who were like Kumāras;
and from his mouth, the son Svāyambhuva together with Śatarūpā.
Brahmā, the creator, spoke to all of them, commanding them to perform the act of creation.
They departed, saying "No," as they were solely devoted to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of performing austerities.
Because of that reason, Brahmā became enraged, and from his forehead [a being emerged].
The eleven Rudras were born; among them, one was the cause of destruction.
Pulastya arose from the right ear, and Pulaha from the left ear.
Likewise, Atri came from the right eye, and Kratu himself from the left eye.
Araṇi was born from the nostrils, and Aṅgiras from the mouth;
Bhṛgu from the left side, and Dakṣa from the right side.
From his shadow (chāyā) Kardama was born, and likewise Pañcaśikha from his navel.
From his chest came Voḍhu, from the region of his throat Nārada, from the region of his shoulders Marīci, and from his neck Apāntaratamas;
from the region of his tongue came Vasiṣṭha, and from his lower lip Pracetās.

Hamsa from the left side and Yati likewise from the right side—thus the Creator of the Universe gave the command to produce all his sons. Then Nārada spoke these auspicious words, full of reason: || 15 ||
O Grandfather, O Lord of the World, first bring our elder brothers Sanaka and the others; having united us with wives, speak to us.
If they have been engaged in austerities, how can we remain for the sake of worldly existence?
How can it be that nectar is given to one person while poison is given to another?
For one who has fallen into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, there is no deliverance even in ten million kalpas; therefore, [one must strive] within this ocean of saṃsāra. (17–18)
O Father, do not cast us down like one who is ignorant, though you are our benefactor;
for Nārāyaṇa himself is said here to be the seed of liberation. He alone is indeed the giver of all, the giver of devotion, and the giver of liberation.
He who has devotion as his sole refuge, who is affectionate toward his devotees, and who is a treasure-house of compassion;
who is dear to his devotees, the lord of his devotees, and the one who bestows grace upon his devotees;
who is to be propitiated by his devotees and is attainable through his devotees—he alone is himself the savior. (1.200.20–21)
Having abandoned that Supreme Brahman, what fool would wander among sense objects?
What ignorant person, having rejected the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s service, would consume poison?
All sense objects are perishable, trivial, and causes of death.
Like dreams, they are not stable; like the flickering of a lamp’s flame, they are transient.
Like fish caught on a hook or ground upon a fisherman’s stone, these afflictions cause suffering and bring death. What person of sound mind would indulge in them? (23–24)
"Therefore, O Father, we who partake of Brahman and manifest the lineage of Brahman, contemplate only Brahman; we do not perform creation.
Having spoken thus, Nārada became silent, desiring a reply.
Then Brahmā became enraged and, with his lips quivering, spoke:
"O Nārada! Disregarding your father's word, you are full of pride; though claiming to be a man of knowledge, you are instructing me and forbidding my act of creation. (16–17)
Therefore, become devoid of knowledge and a libertine among women;
be a creator of dalliance with those who possess enduring youth and beautiful forms.
Become the husband of fifty passionate women and one who knows the arts of love.

"Be a knower of the science of love (*śṛṅgāra-śāstra*) and a creator of great passion. Be the teacher of teachers who possess various specialized knowledges of love. Be the foremost among the *gandharvas*, a singer with a beautiful voice. (1.200.30)
"Skilled in playing the lute and forever possessed of stable youth,
you shall live for two hundred thousand years without a doubt;
yet, by my curse, you shall again become the son of a maidservant."
Then, through association with Vaiṣṇavas, by eating the remnants of the food of Vaiṣṇavas,
and by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you shall become my son;
I shall bestow upon you again that divine, primordial knowledge.
"Now you have become ruined; fall down as my son, certainly!
Nārada said to his father, "O Creator of the Universe, restrain your anger!
A wise man should curse or even abandon a son who walks upon a wrong path."
"O Father, how can you deserve to curse your ascetic son?
Grant me this boon: wherever my birth may be, may I always possess devotion to Viṣṇu; may the Veda never abandon my devotion to Hari."
Even if one’s birth were among those possessing great fortune and abundant wealth,
yet if it is devoid of devotion, all of that is base and leads to a miserable rebirth.
Even if one’s birth were as a pig, provided that it possessed the memory of past lives (jātismara), [it would be superior].
But that which is joined with devotion is indeed supreme, for it bestows the abode of Goloka.
Devotion to the feet of Śrī Hari is proclaimed as divine honey;
for the Vaiṣṇavas who consume it, the earth becomes purified by their footsteps.
The sacred sites of the Vaiṣṇavas always desire to be touched,
indeed for the washing away of the sins of sinners who have been cleansed through bathing there.
By receiving the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, men truly become liberated.
Those named Koṭimuktā have been liberated by the mere utterance of their names, and they continue to be so born.
Likewise, millions will be liberated through devotion to the Name;
the masses of sins accumulated over ten million births are destroyed by the mantra.
They indeed become pure and liberated through mere actionlessness (naiṣkarmya);
they also uproot all previously performed karma by its very name.
[They renounce] their home, male servants, female servants, children, and kinsmen.

He who shows the right path to his sons, wives, disciples, servants, and family members also attains the state of the righteous. Is he not the true guru? Is he not the true father? Is he not the true master? Is he not the true son? (44–45)
He who shows the wrong path to people whom he has gained the confidence of through various means,
and who is incapable of bestowing devotion at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa—
you do not grant me devotion, but rather you obstruct me.
"Therefore, you too shall become as venerable as the Vedas throughout the three worlds.
Having spoken thus, Nārada ceased for a moment,
because by the curse of the Creator of the Universe, he had indeed become a Gandharva.
I shall relate in great detail that account concerning the wife of the Gandharva king, who bore the name Upabarhaṇa; listen to it.
The Gandharva king was the supreme lord of all the Gandharvas.
Though endowed with supreme sovereignty, he was indeed childless.
By the command of his guru, he performed severe penance at Puṣkara;
and Vasiṣṭha gave him a twelve-syllable hymn.
He chanted the protective mantra (*kavaca*) of Śiva for a hundred years,
performing austerities while abstaining from food; then he beheld Śiva before him,
whose nature is great splendor and who bestows grace upon his devotees.
With a gentle smile and a serene countenance, bestowing the fruits of ascetic practice;
the giver of all prosperity to those who have sought refuge in him with devotion;
bearing the trident and the sharp-edged spear, seated upon the bull, and adorned with the crescent moon upon his crest. (53–54)
Seeing him with a mass of matted hair like molten gold, blue-throated, three-eyed,
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread and clad in animal skin— the bestower of supreme devotion—
the king of the Gandharvas prostrated himself upon the ground like a staff.
He praised the gracious, white-complexioned Hara with the supreme mantra.
"Choose a boon," Hara said to that ascetic.
He requested devotion to Hara and a son who was a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Śambhu said: "You have achieved your purpose; everything is established in devotion.
By choosing one boon, you have chosen everything else; all other things are merely chewing what has already been chewed.
For he who possesses devotion to Hari truly possesses all sovereignty. (58)
All perfections belong to him; not even the slightest thing remains unattained.
He is capable here of protecting all the worlds and of creating them;
he likewise protects a hundred million of his own kinsmen and a hundred of his maternal grandfather’s lineage.
Having uplifted men, he goes to his abode, Goloka;
having destroyed the sins accumulated over ten million births, he attains the service of Hari.
Until then, one has a husband, a wife, sons, daughters, wealth, and so forth.
Human beings experience happiness and suffering only so long as they lack devotion to Hari.
Devotion to Hari is indeed a wish-fulfilling tree that grants every desired object;
devotion is a great, sharp sword that cuts through the very roots of the tree of karma.
But when the mind is fixed upon Hari, everything indeed becomes accomplished.
For those whose merit is supreme, their sons become Vaiṣṇavas;
through such service, they surely deliver ten million members of their lineage.
Whether it be sensual pleasure, or even the sovereignty of Brahmā, or any kind of auspicious attainment whatsoever, he is not at all satisfied;
for him, the single desired goal is that there be devotion and a devoted son. (65–66)
A person whose purpose has been fulfilled by such a supreme boon as this—what need is there for a second boon, since it does not bring eternal satisfaction?
For the wealth of Vaiṣṇavas is the highest: namely, eternal devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever devotion and service has been accumulated, all of that has indeed been gathered by him.
(68) Although you have requested the most excellent boon, the very best of all, nevertheless we are not capable of granting such a favor. (69)
Choose another boon, O King, whatever dwells in your mind:
obtain the status of Mahendra, immortality, the state of Brahmā, or lordship; likewise, attain the perfections, yoga, higher knowledge, and the power of conquering death.
"I shall give you everything; therefore, obtain it and certainly renounce the service of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard this, the king of the Gandharvas then spoke to Śrī Śaṅkara: "By the mere movement of whose eyelashes the fall of Brahmā and the other gods occurs... (71-72)
Neither that state of Brahmanhood, nor the status of Great Indra, nor immortality is dear to me; nor are the supernatural powers, great sovereignty, yoga, or even the conquest of death—O Lord!
none of these is exceedingly dear to me without devotion and knowledge.
The Vaiṣṇavas never desire even *sālokya*, *sārṣṭi*, *sāmīpya*, *sāyujya*, or oneness [with the Lord] without His service;
rather, they desire eternal *dāsya-bhakti* (devotion as a servant) both in sleep and while awake. || 74–75 ||
Therefore, I choose from you—the giver of boons who are satisfied—only the service of a slave and devotion, as well as the status of being your devoted son; having renounced everything else.
O Śambhu, if you do not grant this, it is certain that my past actions have been wicked.
"Having cut off my head, I shall offer it before you in the sacrificial fire.
Hearing this, Śaṅkara—the ocean of compassion and merciful toward his devotees—said:
"May you obtain the devotion of service to Śrī Hari and a son who is a true Vaiṣṇava."
Having granted him a boon— [one who was] skilled in the Gandharva arts, long-lived, with senses conquered,
wise, devoted to his guru, and eternally possessed of stable youth—
Śambhu departed, and the Gandharva went to his own abode.
In due time, Nārada was born from his wife;
on Mount Gandhamādana, Vasiṣṭha gave him that name,
and he became renowned as the Gandharva named Upabarhaṇa.
The prefix *upa-* should be understood as having the sense of "excessive" (*adhika*) and "worthy of worship" (*pūjya*), with the meaning of "strengthening" (*barhaṇa*).
Thus, in the sense of "excessively worthy of worship," that name is *upabarhaṇa*.
Filled with joy, he celebrated the great festival of his son's birth.
He gave jewels, grains, wealth, and diamonds;
riches, fields, garments, and cattle as abundant gifts.
Then Upabarhaṇa, the Gandharva, [received] the supreme mantra from Vasiṣṭha.
Having arrived, he performed difficult penance for the sake of propitiating Kṛṣṇa on the bank of the river Gaṇḍakī, which was covered with a thicket of trees—
[the Lord who is] blazing, having attained youth, and most enchanting, as he performed his austerities. (85)

Upon seeing him, those women who had gathered there for the sake of bathing and obtaining water repeatedly fainted from passion; all those wives of the Gandharvas swooned due to the influence of desire. (86–87)
Having performed intense austerities and having renounced their lives through yoga,
those fifty became the daughters of Citraratha;
they chose that Gandharva Upabarhaṇa as their husband.
The amorous maidens gave garlands to that ascetic.
They became his wives, and with them he went home;
for two hundred thousand divine years, he, full of desire, took delight with them.
Then, at another time, in the assembly of the gods in Satyaloka,
he went there to the court of Brahmā and sang a song. There, when the sequence of the dance of the Apsaras Rambhā had commenced—
Seeing the beauty of her thighs and breasts, he fell into a swoon. Overwhelmed by the force of passion, his composure failed him;
abandoning the musical performance, he sat down upon the floor of the assembly hall.
The gods laughed aloud, and Brahmā cursed him out of anger:
"Upabarhaṇa! Though you know yourself to be the husband of fifty women, you have fallen into delusion upon seeing Rambhā, acting like one who lacks self-control. (94)
Therefore, casting off this Gandharva body, quickly become a Śūdra.
There, having attained devotion to Hari and association with the Sātvatas, when the time arrives once more, you shall become my son again. (95–96)
"Without adversity, greatness cannot exist for happiness or peace; therefore,
since happiness and suffering must inevitably occur to everyone in turn," having spoken thus,
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, ceased speaking.
The Gandharva Upabarhaṇa departed for his own home.
Having summoned all his wives and related the events to them,
he took recourse to yoga upon his seat and, with great care, abandoned that body.
Having pierced the six chakras— the Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā—
he [pierced] the Iḍā, Suṣumṇā, Medhā, and Piṅgalā, which carries away the vital breath.
And also [the mudrās] that bestow all-knowledge, as well as the restrainer of the mind;
the pure and the restrained, and likewise the mover of the vital breath (vāyu); the drier of fire (tejas) and the nourisher of strength. 101–102.
Having pierced these sixteen channels— which move through the intellect and cause the expansion of knowledge— he brought the *haṃsa*, joined with the mind,
to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and united his self with Keśava.

The lord of yogis abandoned his body and attained the eternal Brahman. (104) Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of how the mind-born sons were produced by Brahmā through Sāvitrī in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the first book of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the birth of Nārada; Nārada’s refusal of the command for the sake of creation; his dwelling as a Gandharva named Upabarhaṇa due to a curse from Brahmā; and his abandonment of the body due to a curse while singing in the assembly of Brahmā," and so forth. (200)
