Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: When the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa, having resorted to yoga and mentally resolved upon his seat, remained there for the sake of death, at that very moment he [Mṛtyu] appeared.
Placing the three-stringed vīṇā, so difficult to obtain, upon his left shoulder,
and holding a rosary of pure crystal in his right hand,
he was uttering the imperishable Brahman, the two syllables "Kṛ-ṣ-ṇ-a."
Placing his head toward the east and his two feet toward the west,
he lay upon a bed of *darbha* grass, meditating in his mind on Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
through yoga, he attained Brahman, while his wife and others wept bitterly.
Then Mālāvatī, the chief queen among the fifty women, wept loudly and intensely, placing her beloved upon her breast. She said:
"Even contact with the form of the Blessed One brings about liberation."
Indeed, for women, union with a god arises only through great good fortune. (6) Association with a virtuous person is more difficult to attain than Vaikuṇṭha;
separation from a virtuous person is more unbearable than death. (7)

Even more than that, the separation from kinsmen is considered a giver of great sorrow; even more than that, the loss of one's offspring exceeds death itself. And greater even than all of that is the great grief born from the separation from a husband.
Truly, there is suffering, distress, and horror, yet there is no suffering greater than that.
Whether lying down, eating, bathing, traveling, sleeping, or waking,
the fresh sorrow born of separation from her husband arises indeed day after day.
By the mere union with her husband, she may forget all sorrows;
I see nothing else that could cause her to forget her lord so completely.
For virtuous women born of noble families, there is no kinsman other than their husband.
What indeed will be the sorrow-inducing fate of these sisters of mine, and of me as well, without my lord? What will it be without a husband?
O lords of the quarters, O guardians of the directions, O Dharma, O Prajāpati! (12–13)
"O Śambhu! O beloved of Ramā! Grant me the gift of a husband!
Having spoken thus, that daughter of Citraratha fell into a swoon;
then, regaining consciousness, she lamented repeatedly and most bitterly.
Others, lamenting most bitterly, awakened Hari and wept:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the worlds, Protector of the universe, Sovereign!
Having rendered this woman weak and powerless, why do you kill her in vain?"
Your husband is your own body; why is he not protected by you?
It is through karma that a husband is obtained, and through karma that he is separated.
In union there is supreme bliss; in separation there is great distress.
Husband, son, wife, and kinsmen are always [bound] by one's own karma;
when renounced by oneself, they lead to happiness, but when caused to be renounced by others, they lead to suffering.
Therefore, the virtuous, having renounced them themselves, are always happy. (18–19)
"We women are indeed not truthful, nor even possessed of wisdom;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, grant us our beloved husband back and restore him to life.
A handsome lover such as this, who knows the Self, has never been found by anyone."
In beauty, virtue, splendor, and prowess;
in knowledge, tranquility, and contentment, our lord is indeed equal to Hari.
Devoted to Hari, he is like Hari himself; in profundity, he is comparable to the ocean. (21–22)
In brilliance he is equal to the sun; in purity he is like fire, the purifier;
in appearance he is equal to the moon; and in passion he is like Kandarpa.
In intellect he is equal to Bṛhaspati; likewise, in poetry he is equal to a poet.
In speech he was equal to Sarasvatī; in genius, he was as renowned as Bhṛgu.
In wealth he resembled Kubera; in generosity, he was like another Manu. In righteousness he was a virtuous man equal to Dharma himself; in truthfulness, he was like another Satyavrata.
Equal to Skanda in asceticism, like a Brahmin in virtuous conduct,
equal to Śakra in sovereignty, and like the earth in forbearance—
how is it that our life-breaths do not depart when such a beloved husband has died? (26)
How can these Suras, who partake in the sacrifice, be capable of consuming clarified butter?
O Nārāyaṇa, beloved of the world, revive our husband quickly!
O Prajāpati, Mahādeva, God of Dharma, Lord of Yama! (27–28)
"Bring our master back to life; how can you truly be so merciless? Otherwise, we shall curse you all without delay.
Then Brahmā and all the others indeed fell into a state of exhaustion out of fear.
"These goddesses shall curse the gods; the deities will go to their destruction.
"Alas! The power of a devoted wife is the supreme among all powers!
The gods deliberated thus as to what should be done in this matter. (1.201.30–31)
In the meantime, suddenly an incorporeal voice arose:
"Go for the sake of peace to where the virtuous Mālāvatī is, performing a yogic posture while holding a corpse against her chest. (32)
The gods went to the bank of the Kauśikī where the devoted wife Mālāvatī was; seeing the gods, she prostrated herself before them again and again,
and placing her beloved husband down, she wept profusely while the gods listened.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu himself arrived there in the guise of a young brahmin, wearing a brilliant tilaka.
He said to Mālavatī, "O goddesses, how have you come here?"
"Brahmā, Śambhu, Dharma, Ravi, Candra, Hutāśana, Kāla, and Yama—these are the lords of the gods; who is this woman, Satī, who is like a corpse?
Having heard this, Mālāvatī bowed to that wise man and spoke.
"I am Mālāvatī by name, the wife of Upabarhaṇa;
these others are my sisters, and this corpse is our husband.
For two hundred thousand divine years, we have sported with our lord. (38)
"O beloved, the affection of virtuous women for their husbands is indeed immeasurable.
Our husband has suddenly abandoned his life-breaths due to the curse of Brahmā;
therefore, let us lament before the gods so that our husband may indeed return to life. (1.201.40)
Happiness, suffering, fear, grief, torment, prosperity, festival,
sovereignty, supreme bliss, birth, death, and liberation—
of these, the gods are the progenitors and the bestowers of the fruits of karma.
They are the destroyers of the root, yet they are also the givers of roots and sprouts.
Indeed, there is no kinsman higher than the God; there is no protector other than the God.
There is no one superior to the God as a compassionate remover of suffering.
I entreat all the gods for the gift of a husband that I desire;
if they grant me a lover, every kind of prosperity shall be mine.
Otherwise, I shall curse them with a terrible and unavoidable curse.
Having heard this, Viṣṇu, remaining unperturbed, then said to Mālāvatī:
"O garland-maker, it is indeed true that the gods are the dispensers of the fruits of actions;
like a farmer with his grain, they do not bestow results upon men immediately, but only after a long time."
When a householder sows grain in a field through the agency of a farmer,
its sprout will emerge in due time, and in due time it will even bear fruit as a tree.
In due time it becomes fully ripe, and in due time the householder receives it.
In this way, it should be inferred that the fruit of action appears only after a long time.
Neither strength, nor beauty, nor sovereignty, nor wealth, nor a son, nor even a wife, nor a beloved husband—what can exist without austerity? (48–49)
By serving Prakṛti, a person obtains a beloved wife endowed with excellent qualities,
as well as stable fortune, sons, grandsons, land, wealth, and splendor.
By serving Śiva, one attains learning, wisdom, sons, and supreme prosperity.

Through the service of Brahmā, one obtains strength, wealth, a virtuous wife, and a noble husband; through the service of the Sun, one obtains knowledge, sovereignty, prosperity, bliss, and excellent progeny;
and through the service of Sūrya, one obtains learning, health, wealth, sons, and so forth.
Through the service of Gaṇeśa, one attains the destruction of obstacles, sons, wealth, and so forth;
and through the service of the Lord of Lakṣmī, one obtains liberation, worldly enjoyment, and constant prosperity.
A person likewise gains austerity, righteousness, glory, fame, and happiness. (53)
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes at the end to the abode of Śrī Hari.
He who indeed worships Śrī Hari, who is beyond even the imperishable (akṣara), is truly liberated while living; he does not desire any boon whatsoever. || 54-55 ||
He considers the fourfold states, beginning with residence in the same world as the deity (sālokya), to be utterly trivial;
for even the status of Brahmā, immortality, or liberation, when compared to the Reality, are like something worthless.
Furthermore, he regards sovereign power as equal to a clod of earth and as perishable.
He considers even the status of Indra, the status of Manu, and long life itself to be utterly trivial, like bubbles on the water;
yet, whether in dream or in waking, he constantly desires service [to others]. (57–58)
One should not seek the supreme abode of Śrī Hari without servitude;
having attained firm devotion at His lotus feet, one becomes perfected.
He [delivers] ten million ancestors of his own lineage and a hundred of his maternal grandfather’s.

He who rescues his father-in-law, a hundred sons and so forth, as well as a hundred others, along with a male slave, a female slave, his mother, and his wife, goes to that abode. He into whose ear the Viṣṇu-mantra enters from the mouth of a guru [attains the same]. (1.201.60–61)
Yama, out of fear, distances himself at that very moment from whatever is being written;
Brahmā, however, should beforehand offer him the madhuparka and other honors. Even the worshippers residing in the world of Brahmā stand along the path.
"Aha! Having bypassed our world, he shall go by this path.
Whatever ancient karma he has performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, Kṛṣṇa continually cuts it away with his sharp-edged discus. (63–64)
Free from fear, he departs for Goloka, casting off his human body;
having gone there and assumed a divine (brāhmī) form, he serves Śrī Hari forever.
As long as Kṛṣṇa remains in Goloka, so long shall the devotee dwell there eternally.
A servant considers even a moment to be as fleeting as the lifespan of Brahmā.
O virtuous lady, tell me, by what disease has your husband met his death? Or rather, was he dead already, being like one already deceased, within the span of seven days?
With great medicinal herbs, I shall indeed restore that dead man to life while he is still alive.
Having brought here before you Yama, the Time of Death, and the King of Mortality, as well as Disease itself,
I shall bind them and show them to you, so that they may never move about again.

I know the seeds of disease and the binding mantras in their true essence. (69) Whosoever has died after casting off the body through yoga, I shall restore him to life; and whosoever has died by poison or exhaustion, I shall restore him to life. (1.201.70)
Hearing this, Mālāvatī was delighted; with a tender heart, she said to him:
"O Śrī Hari, if it be so, quickly restore my husband to life here!
You are the master, the creator, the destroyer, the ruler, the nourisher, and the protector. (71)
The chosen deity is to be worshipped, but the preceptor is not superior to the master.
(72) I am a maiden born of a noble family, protected by the watchfulness of my beloved;
I am the wife of Upabarhaṇa and the daughter of Citraratha. (73)
O Hari, the bride of the Gandharva king is ever devoted to her beloved;
yet you, O Mādhava, are capable of bringing everything under your control.
Bring Kāla, Yama, and Mṛtyu into my presence.
Having heard Mālāvatī’s words, the Blessed One, the mine of compassion,
summoned them into the assembly and showed them [the truth] directly.
There, the Daughter of Death was seen by Mālāvatī as she arrived.
Dark-complexioned, of terrible form, clad in red garments, and inspiring great fear,
she has six arms and stands thus on the left side of her husband named Kāla;
she is smiling, has a fierce brow, and is accompanied by sixty-four sons.
And Mālatī beheld the six-faced, hideous, and roaring Kāla;
he had twenty-four eyes, sixteen arms, and was fierce; he had six feet, was black in color, wore red garments, and was terrifying. (78–79)
Thus were terrifying hosts of diseases seen by Mālāvatī;
children, the aged, the very old, and youths, all exceedingly deformed.
There she beheld Yama, dark-complexioned and of cruel appearance.
Having seen him previously, Mālāvatī questioned the teacher of Dharma:
"O Dharmarāja, how is it that you take away my beloved at an improper time?
Yama replied: "No one on earth dies before their time has come."
O virtuous lady, without the command of the Lord, I do not move even a falsehood.
I am Time, the Daughter of Death, and the Diseases—all servants of the Lord.
Just as by the rite of conception, we lead away the embodied soul according to its destiny.
The Daughter of Death also spoke: "O Mālikā, listen with respect!
Though I was created long ago by the Creator of the Universe for this very task, I am not able to abandon a living being whose death has arrived. (84–85)
And if Satī were capable of reducing everything to ashes in this world,
then I would certainly not have been turned to ash, nor would I have killed embodied beings.
Impelled by Time, I and my sons, the diseases, [acted thus].
"We shall perform the task as commanded; there is no fault in this for us.
Then Mālāvatī spoke to him, who was born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa:
"O Lord, how can you carry away my beloved while I am still alive? (87-88)
Kāla said: "Listen, Mālāvatī, to everything done by Hari.
Who am I? Who is Yama? And who is the daughter of Death, as well as the mental agonies?
We wander constantly as the executors of Kṛṣṇa’s commands. (8-9)
We who are all to be created by Him— Brahmā and the others,
the Vairājas, the ṛṣis, the gods, human beings, and all living creatures—
as well as the wind that blows out of fear of Him and the sun that shines out of fear of Him; (1.201.90–91)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—the creator, the protector, and the destroyer—exist out of fear of him; likewise, Yama, the witness of actions, and Dharma function out of fear of him.
Even the zodiac signs and the planets revolve in their proper order out of fear of him.
The lords of the quarters and the guardians of the directions carry out his command;
out of fear of him, the seasons bestow flowers upon the trees and other plants,
the clouds pour down rain, and the earth likewise yields its treasures.
The support of all, endowed with patience, she protects everyone like a mother;
Māyā is considered the progenitor of all, who fulfills [desires] out of fear of Him.
He whose limit no one knows, who is omniscient, and who dwells within the heart.
"I am a sixteenth part of Him; He is Time, the maker of the end of time. Therefore, meditate with devotion upon that Acyuta, who is the death of Death and the granter of desires.
This very Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of mercy, will grant you a husband. (96–97)
"He who has impelled us all is the giver of all prosperity.
Having said this, Kāla ceased speaking; then Hari spoke to her:
"Kāla has been seen, Yama has been seen, as well as the Daughter of Death and the mental afflictions. || 98 ||
"If you have seen him quickly, ask what is in his mind. Mālāvatī said: "Just as an incurable disease does not persist, you ought to tell me here the entire means by which that might be achieved."

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Mālāvatī, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings, [spoke].
He said to Mālāvatī: "O Mālā, listen; I shall speak to you exactly as it is.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, is the pacifier of all diseases.
That Lord created the four Vedas, which are the source of all auspiciousness."
Having examined the Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan, and having reflected upon their meaning, Prajāpati composed Āyurveda.
Having made it the fifth Veda, the Lord gave it to Bhāskara.
Then Bhāskara himself composed the Bhāskarasaṃhitā. He gave it to his own disciples,
and thereafter they composed other saṃhitās concerning the practice of treating diseases.
Dhanvantari indeed composed the *Cikitsātattvavijñāna*.
[His disciples were] Divodāsa, the King of Kāśī; the two sons of the Aśvins;
Nakula, Sahadeva, Arkī, Cyavana, Janaka, and Budha.
Jābāla, Jājali, Paila, Karatha, and Agastya—
these sixteen are all physicians who destroy disease.
In the medical treatment of one's own body, however, one's very self shall be the teacher.

Then diseases do not arrive, and those already present perish. Listen, O virtuous one: health must be protected with vigilance by means of [proper] vision, water, exercise, and massaging the feet with oil. (9)
Oil applied to the ears and the head destroys old age and disease.
(1.202.10) Old age does not approach that man who wanders about in the spring, who maintains a small fire, and who enjoys the company of young women at the proper time. (11)

He who practices bathing in cold water in the morning and uses sandalwood paste during the summer heat, and who does not seek the breeze in the midst of the sweltering season—old age does not approach him.
Furthermore, he who bathes in warm water during the rainy season and does not resort to dense clouds [for shelter]... [12] ...does not suffer from old age.
When one eats wholesome food at the proper time, old age does not approach him.
(13) In winter, he does not endure excessive cold; he bathes after digging [a pond] for water.
He eats fresh and warm food; old age does not approach him. (14)
Fresh meat, new grain, young women, a diet of milk,
and ghee— he who partakes of these does not encounter old age.
One should eat wholesome food when hungry and drink water when thirsty.
He who constantly consumes betel leaf, fresh butter, and jaggery;
who eats curd and *haiyaṅgavīna* (fresh butter from a cow’s first milk)—old age does not approach him.
For those who practice exercise daily, old age flees far away.

Old age, along with its brothers, approaches with great joy one who indulges in an elderly woman, dried meat, the morning sun, and fresh curd. Old age has sixty-four daughters, the daughters of the maiden Death, and disease is her son.
Old age wanders perpetually upon the earth together with its brothers.
Those who consume curd at night, those who consort with an aged woman or one in her menses, and those who engage in excessive sexual intercourse—old age swiftly devours them. (1.202.20)
When hunger is burning intensely and no food is obtained, bile arises in the *maṇipūraka* cakra of living beings.
Having eaten the fruit of the *tāla* or *bilva* tree, one should drink water at that very moment. (21)
That very [pitta] becomes the supreme destroyer of life instantly.
He who consumes bitter food on his head with heated water in the month of Bhādra,
and further eats unwholesome food, in him pitta is produced.
Coriander ground with sugar and mixed with cold water;
chickpeas and all products of the cow except curd and buttermilk;
ripe wood-apple and palmyra fruit—and likewise all alms-food. (24)
Fresh ginger, mung bean soup, and sesame paste with sugar (25) immediately alleviate pitta and cause its depletion; they are supreme for bestowing strength and nourishment.
Bathing after a meal [is forbidden], as is drinking water except when one is thirsty. (26)
Stale food, buttermilk, cooked plantain, curd, rainwater, water with sugar, and the watering of turbid water;
coconut water, radish, and likewise the karkaṭī fruit. (27)
Bathing after eating during the rainy season causes all of that to become phlegm-inducing.
Birth [of semen] at the *brahmarandhra* results in the destruction of great virility.
[One should avoid] black pepper, long pepper, dried ginger, fresh ginger, *jīvaka*, and honey. (28–29)

Indeed, the consumption of fire [as medicine] immediately removes phlegm; it bestows strength and nourishment, and is a destroyer of disease. O beautiful one, tell me, by what fault has your beloved died?
Having heard this, Mālāvatī said: "My husband has died by means of yoga.
Now, O Janārdana, give me back my beloved life; give him back!
Having bowed before you, we women shall go to our own home together with our lord."
Having heard this, Janārdana quickly went to the assembly of the gods. There,
the daughter of Citraratha, the wife of Upabarhaṇa,
together with her sisters, requested the gift of life for her husband.

Desiring to curse all the gods, she was dissuaded by me for the sake of peace. Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Nārada, and Upabarhaṇa spoke to him regarding what should now be determined as the performance of this task.
He gave up his life-breaths through yoga, yet due to my very curse,
his stay upon the earth shall extend for a period of a hundred thousand yugas.
Then, having entered a Śūdra womb, he shall become my son once again.
O Supreme Lord, there remains a small portion of his allotted time;
however, by the grace of Viṣṇu himself, I shall grant him the gift of life, for his lifespan at present is indeed a thousand years. (37–38)
"I shall certainly act so that this curse does not come to pass upon them.
The word *viṣi* signifies pervasion (*vyāpti*), and the particle *nu* denotes 'everywhere' (*sarvatra*).
Thus, Viṣṇu, who indeed pervades all, shall grant life."
Having spoken thus, they departed for where the bride Mālāvatī was.
Brahmā poured the water from his *kamaṇḍalu* upon the body of the corpse; he restored the movement of its mind and made its form beautiful once more.
Śiva gave him knowledge; then Dharma gave him righteousness.
The digestive fire gave him the internal heat, and then the wind-god gave him the vital breath.
The sun gave him sight, and then Speech gave him the power of speech.

Lakṣmī gave him beauty, and the husband of Śacī (Indra) gave him the power of action; yet even so, the corpse did not rise. Then Viṣṇu gave him life, but he attained only a distinguished consciousness and did not rise without a witness.
Then Mālāvatī, overcome with grief, bowed to Mādhava:
"Apart from you, I have no husband; you alone are my husband in form.
You are the very life-breath of all living beings; restore my husband to life! (45)
Hari indeed established his presence there by means of his own powers.
At that moment, the Gandharva rose up, taking up his lute and two garments,
and bowed down before the host of gods and Viṣṇu, who stood before them.
Then the kettledrums resounded and a rain of flowers fell;
all the gods bestowed supreme blessings upon the couple.
Then he, named Upabarhaṇa, danced and sang.
By the grace of the gods, he indeed regained his life;
he then returned once more to the city of the Gandharvas along with his wives.
At that time, the queens received ten million jewels and hundreds of thousands of cattle as wealth.
They gave [gifts] to the Brahmins and fed many of them;
they respectfully celebrated various great festivals,
and they conducted various searches for their own husbands.
They performed service and offered worship to their husband according to the proper custom;
together with him, those beautiful women enjoyed themselves for a very long time.
By that same mantra, they all obtained a Gandharva as their husband.
O Mistress of Kamala, listen to that sixteen-syllable mantra, the hymn, and the armor (kavaca) bestowed by Vasiṣṭha:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate rāsamaṇḍaleśāya svāhā*.
Know this sixteen-syllable mantra to be a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
After that, Kṛṣṇa gave it to the Lord in Goloka;
likewise, in former times, Kṛṣṇa gave it to Brahmā at Puṣkara.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, gave this armor to Kumāra; Hari himself is the purifier of this armor of the universe.
Hari is its seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is its meter (chandas), and I, the Lord Hari, am its deity.
Its application is always considered to be for the sake of virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), desire (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*).
By reciting it three hundred thousand times, it becomes the bestower of all perfections (*siddhi*).
May the *praṇava* protect my head, and may "namo rāmeśvarāya" [protect] me.
May the forehead protect me; salutations to the Lord of Rādhā for the pair of eyes.
May Kṛṣṇa protect the pair of ears, and may Śrī Hari protect the sense of smell.
May the consort of Agni protect the tongue; salutations everywhere to Kṛṣṇa.
May the six-syllable mantra protect the wood [of the body]: "Śrīkṛṣṇāya svāhā.
" Hrīṃ kṛṣṇāya namaḥ" protects the face; "klīṃ" and that which precedes it [namely, "kṛṣṇāya"] protect the two arms.
"Namogopāṅganeśāya" protects the shoulders; may the eight-syllable mantra protect them. (6.1–6.2)
Salutations to the Lord of the Gopīs for the row of teeth and the pair of lips.
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Sovereign of the Rāsa-maṇḍala; svāhā!
May Hari, the sixteen-syllable mantra-essence, protect the region of the chest.
"Oṃ *śrīkṛṣṇāya svāhā*—may this always protect the pair of ears. Oṃ *viṣṇave svāhā*—may this protect the cheeks on all sides.
Oṃ *haraye namaḥ*—may this always protect the back and the feet. (64–65)
Oṃ, svāhā to the upholder of Govardhana; may my entire body be protected.
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa protect me in the east, and Mādhava protect me in the southeast.
May the Lord of the Gopīs protect me in the south, and the Son of Nanda protect me in the southwest.
May Govinda protect [me] in the west; may the Lord of Rādhikā protect [me] in the northwest.
May the Lord of the Rāsa dance protect [me] in the north; may Acyuta himself protect [me] in the northeast.
May Hari Nārāyaṇa himself protect [me] constantly from all sides.
Having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste,
and having bathed and prostrated before him, the wise man should wear the armor (*kavaca*).
By the grace of this armor, a person becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
If one should possess this perfected armor, O beloved, he would indeed become Viṣṇu himself.
From the recitation of this, there arises great merit, equal to the fruit of all sacred fords.
One who is childless obtains a son; one who lacks a wife obtains a virtuous woman.
One seeking knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one seeking wealth shall attain wealth.
One who has lost his kingdom shall regain his kingdom, and one desiring supernatural powers (siddhi) shall attain sovereignty.
One afflicted by disease shall be freed from disease, and one who is bound shall be released from bondage.
Having attained devotion to Hari, one obtains the imperishable abode at the end.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world and achieved extremely rare fame, one becomes a preeminent attendant and goes to the abode of Goloka. (73–74)
Thus the eminent Gandharva named Upabarhaṇa enjoyed himself with those wives with devotion for the remainder of his lifespan,
and he performed various kinds of excellent sacrifices together with his sons.
Then, in due course, having cast off his life-breaths due to the curse of a Brahmin,
Upabarhaṇa was born from the womb of a Śūdra woman by means of a Brahmin’s seed as a result of that curse.
The virtuous Mālāvatī likewise gave up her life in the sacrificial fire-pit.
Moreover, there were others who remained always established in the dharma of widowhood;
among them was she, the wife of King Sañjaya born of the lineage of Manu, who was born with the memory of her past lives, [knowing]: "He shall be my husband. (78)
"I was formerly the wife of the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa.
In the region of Kānyakubja, there was a king named Drumila;
his wife was Kalāvatī, who was both barren and devoted to her husband."
Due to her husband’s fault, she was barren; nevertheless, at her husband’s command during her fertile season, she approached the sage Kāśyapa Nārada in a terrible forest.
He was indeed the son of Kaśyapa who had been born through the curse of Dakṣa.
She went to that second son of Kaśyapa, Nārada,
who was meditating upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa and blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
Having dressed herself elegantly, she stood before the sage at the conclusion of his meditation.
And Nārada saw before him Sundarī, possessed of perpetual youth;
golden-hued, adorned with golden ornaments, moon-faced, and lotus-eyed;
she had arrived there out of a desire for a son, and was radiant with the beauty of love and passion. (84)
The sage questioned that queen: "Who are you? To whom do you belong? Tell me.
Then Kalāvatī, having remembered Hari, spoke to Nārada:
"I am the wife of Drumila; by my husband's command, I am a cowherd woman."
"Desiring a son, I have come into your presence; show me mercy.
Bestow your seed upon my womb, for a woman who has approached you must not be neglected.
Indeed, it is no fault for those of great power, just as fire consumes everything."
The righteous-souled Brāhmaṇa Nārada, practicing dharma, said:
"That Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, takes a Śūdra woman as his wife, falls to a lower status by birth and is no longer eligible for the rites of the twice-born. (88–89)
In the ancestral *śrāddha* rite, in a sacrifice, in touching a sacred stone, or in the worship of the gods,
a twice-born man who has sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman becomes devoid of qualification.
His chosen deity does not accept his food offering, nor does He accept his water.
That brahmin takes birth from a *śūdra* womb; that is the fruit thereof.
You have said that for those of great luster, even such a thing is not a fault, and it is like nectar.
I shall give you the seed from afar; take it, if you have the power.
"By virtue of holding [the seed] within her womb, no fault exists at that time;
I shall not engage in sexual union, for a fault would arise from such union.
Having been addressed thus, that wife of a Śūdra remained devoted to her husband's vow.
Then, remembering her own husband, she became absorbed in meditation.
Having dissolved her gross body, she entered [Nārada] entirely through yoga by means of her subtle body; and Nārada, too, for a moment at that time, [did the same].
Through the process of her entry, she did not perceive her own body— endowed with desire and composed of the elements— as being separate from the gross body, as if it were a dream.
There, upon a bed of *sarja* leaves, the sage’s semen fell.
Immediately, the Śūdra woman swallowed it and protected the embryo within her womb.
Having bowed to the sage, she was delighted; though devoid of physical union, she accomplished her purpose.
And the sage too was filled with joy; though devoid of the fault of contact, he had fulfilled his aim.
Having gone into the presence of her husband, she related the entire account.
Drumila also became pleased and spoke these comforting words to his beloved:
"That which was indeed the seed of the Vaiṣṇava Nārada has entered your womb."
That child shall indeed be a Vaiṣṇava; he is none other than a portion of Nārada.
In whose womb a Vaiṣṇava is born, or by whose seed such a one exists—hundreds upon hundreds of generations of men from both [the father and mother] go to Vaikuṇṭha.
And those two, traveling by means of a divine Viṣṇu-chariot resplendent with jewels,
went to the city of Vaikuṇṭha, which removes birth, death, and old age.
Having spoken thus, that king of cowherds bathed and performed the libation ceremony (tarpaṇa).
Having worshipped his chosen deity, he gave wealth to the Brāhmaṇas.
(103) With joy, he gave to the Brāhmaṇas thousands of elephants, horses, chariots, cows, swans, male and female servants, as well as vessels, ornaments, garments, and jewels. (104)
Seeing his wife pregnant with a son and remembering Lord Hari in his heart,
he perceived the auspicious thread of his lineage and thereafter attained detachment.
He went to the sacred field of Badarī and, through yoga, gave up his life-breaths.
By means of a celestial chariot sent by the messengers of Hari, he went to Vaikuṇṭha.
There he attained the service of Hari and became a servant of Hari. Within that same year, the goddess Kalāvatī was protected by the brāhmaṇas.
She gave birth to an auspicious son, radiant with the luster of molten gold,
surpassing Kāmadeva in beauty and blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
His feet were marked with the signs of the lotus and the wheel, and his lotus-like hands held a bow and a banner.
Seeing that her chest bore a vertical tilaka of gold and was adorned with the mark of a garland,
and recognizing her as having the form of Viṣṇu, all the people rejoiced;
the Brāhmaṇas nourished the queen along with her son, just as they would their own daughter.
Accompanied by her son, she served the twice-born like a maidservant of the brahmins.
There that boy grew like the moon in the bright fortnight;

The offering of the arati lamp and so forth should be given, followed by the worship consisting of the sixteen-fold self-offering (ṣoḍaśātmaprapūjana).

Then there is the bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), as well as the consecratory bath (abhiṣeka-snāna). Furthermore, garments, sandalwood paste and the like, flowers, and ornaments [should be offered]. (35–36)
The seat, the lamp, incense, and the food offering; water for drinking, betel leaf, the waving of lights (ārārtika), and circumambulation;
along with hymns of praise, prostration, and the handful of flowers—these also constitute the sixteen [services].
38. Offerings for the worship of Hari should always be presented with devotion.

39. First, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), then the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), followed by the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the limbs and sub-limbs, and thereafter the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa).
Then, having performed the placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa), one should designate the arghya vessel.
Having drawn a triangular maṇḍala, one should worship Kūrma there.
Then, having filled a conch with water, one should likewise place it upon Kūrma.
Having performed the invocation of the sacred waters (*tīrthāvāhana*) in the water, one should cleanse the ritual objects.
One should worship the bell, worship the conch, and likewise worship the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
One should worship the *śālagrāma* stone, and thereafter indeed worship Hari.
Having worshipped with the sixteen types of offerings, one should dismiss the deities.
One should likewise perform the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*) and the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) according to one's means.
In honoring guests, one should perform the sacrifice to all beings (*bhūtayajña*) according to one's capacity.
One should always salute the elders and pay homage to the sun and other deities.
Having first fed those who are to be supported, the householder should eat daily;
for sacrificial food (haviṣya) is always recommended for Brāhmaṇas and householders.
The remains of Nārāyaṇa’s meal are desirable; that which has not been offered is unfit to be eaten.
He who constantly eats the food offering (naivedya) of Śrī Viṣṇu is indeed a Vaiṣṇava.
Food, water, fruit, flowers, and leaves offered to Śrī Hari [are likewise fit].
Now, that which is fit to be eaten and that which is fit to be drunk are distinct from those things which are unfit to be drunk and unfit to be eaten.

Whatever is corrupted by its species (*jāti-duṣṭa*), corrupted by its appearance (*rūpa-duṣṭa*), corrupted by its form (*ākṛti-duṣṭa*), corrupted by its quality (*guṇa-duṣṭa*), or corrupted by its transformation (*pariṇāma-duṣṭa*)—that indeed must not be eaten. (47–48)
During vows, food must certainly not be eaten; it must not be eaten prior to the performance of worship.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—these are the *yamas*, which should be guarded, for they bestow happiness and even liberation.

Purity, contentment, austerity, study, and the worship of Kṛṣṇa grant liberation. (1.204.50) One should never, under any circumstances, revile anyone at all. Even if it is true, one must not speak words that cause pain to others, for such speech brings suffering. (1.204.51)
For dharma is that purpose characterized by being impelling, and not that which is purposeless;
one should never practice ingratitude, nor should one ever act with deceit. Furthermore, wealth should be acquired through lawful means and used for worldly transactions according to justice.
One should exert effort according to one's strength toward wealth, grain, and livelihood.
One must not falsely accuse another, nor should one ever take what belongs to another.
During the day, effort should be applied; in the evening, one should perform the twilight prayers, recitations, and so forth.
Having performed the visit to the temple of Hari, as well as hymns of praise, congregational chanting, and so forth,
householders should sleep after reciting the mantra concerning income and expenditure.
Women must be protected in every way and satisfied with material objects.
One should not be possessed by agitation, nor should one ever give way to affliction.
Those seeking liberation must indeed engage in the investigation of the self and the non-self and so forth.
The Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, resides within all embodied beings.

The five vital breaths (*pañcaprāṇāḥ*) are both witnesses and the givers of fruit for the actions of the body; they are Viṣṇu himself and should be gratified with excellent food. The mind (*manas*) is Brahmā and should be gratified by means of bliss, delight, and so forth.
Indra and Rudra, who are the presiding deities of the senses, are to be gratified with the true objects of experience;

Māyā, whose form is knowledge, is to be gratified through hearing [the scriptures] and other such means; and the Self, the witness who is Brahman itself, is to be satisfied by the offerings of whatever arises. (1.204.59–60)
The Supreme Brahman, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, eternally resides within all conscious beings;
indeed, those conscious selves are dependent upon Him, yet they possess distinct karmic functions.
Endowed with the fruits of their actions, these individual souls subsist through various activities among insentient objects.
Inert things, being for the sake of another, are joined with that other in order to attain the state of being an object of enjoyment;
and sentient beings are indeed joined with real objects for the attainment of experience.
Māyā, consisting of the three guṇas, is inert; from that, the principle of Mahat (the Great Principle) arose.
From that, ego (ahaṃkāra) was born; from it, the deities of the senses [arose].
From the subtle elements, the gross elements emerged.
Their physical body was obtained by consciousness through its own past actions.
Through knowledge comes the destruction of karma, and through detachment comes freedom from bondage.
Through dharma comes progress upward, and through merit and devotion comes travel to the abode of Hari.
One should not consider oneself the doer; indeed, it is the Blessed Lord who acts.
The self is the embodied soul, yet it is not the agent; Hari himself is the agent and the sustainer.
By their very nature, Prakṛti is bound and liberated, but the conscious spirit is not.
The body is produced from the aggregates of the elements, but there is no birth of the self.
The body decays through its constituent states, but there is no disintegration of the self.
A similar [self] is always experienced by means of a similar body;
for the body is experienced by means of the body, since it is indeed an object of experience.
The gross [body] is the locus of enjoyment, while the subtle assumes various forms; within [the mind], there arises the thought, "I am happy," regarding that which has been obtained and experienced,
but this occurs in the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) produced by egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), not in the Self (*ātman*).
"Otherwise, this [self] knows within itself; surely, this is an error. (7.1) Even "error" is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), accompanied by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by it.
In the absence of error, there is the absence of the house; indeed, that is the very absence of transmigratory existence. (7.2)
When there is the reality of delusion, there is the reality of the house and likewise the perception of a wife.
Where is the house? Where is the wife? All of this is said to be mere mental impression (*vāsanā*).
In the absence of that [delusion], where is the house, where is the wife, and where are the sons and the rest?
The body itself does not even exist; what then can be said of those who are well-yoked to it?
Therefore, the self is a devotee of the Supreme Brahman, a ray of Hari;
it is devoid of the qualities of *māyā* and is not tainted by time.
There is no stain from action, nor is there any inherent nature therein.
For the consciousness that is devoid of qualities and whose very form is bliss, what indeed could constitute bondage?
The Lord indeed performs everything; this alone must be understood as such.
The farmer sows the seed; the farmer waters [it] with water.
(77) The farmer guards the food; the farmer also gives [it away].
The cultivator reaps the grain; the cultivator also eats [it]. (78)
The ordinary farmer produces the entire crop, yet he does not produce it at all;
for Kṛṣṇa is the great farmer who brings forth the seed.
Mādhava protects that seed within the womb and grants it birth.
In childhood, youth, or old age, Keśava indeed protects him. Kṛṣṇa alone provides food, water, and clothing;
Kṛṣṇa impels death, and Mādhava leads one to dissolution.

"Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is the witness who performs everything; indeed, I do nothing at all. Thus, having surrendered everything to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of liberation from bondage, one should always practice worship and perform service to Mādhava. (82)
Whatever devotion and service there may be, all of it should indeed be offered in every way to the Lord of Kamalā;
for that is the liberation of one while living here.
The Lord of Śrī is the Sovereign who pervades everywhere as the inner controller.
Endowed with all divine qualities, he resides in Goloka, the supreme imperishable realm,
as well as in Vaikuṇṭha, Śvetadvīpa, Badarī, Amṛta, and the ethereal sky.
He is Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Naravāsa, Nārāyaṇa, and the Lord of Śrī.
He is indeed the Lord of Rādhā, the Radiant Master, the Sovereign of Māṇikya;
he is the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Beloved of Kambharā, and Śrī Hari himself.
He is the Lord of Sītā, the Master of Satī, and the Lord of Pārvatī.
Lord Hari exists in six forms: He is the Lord of all, Kṛṣṇa Himself, Śrī Kṛṣṇa who is eternally manifest in form, the Supreme Vyūha, the Vibhava, the Antaryāmin, and the Mūrti;
thus the Blessed One exists as these six forms.
Though formless, He possesses form; though the Infinite, He has a beautiful embodiment.
Though invisible, He is clearly visible to those endowed with such vision.
He is the object of meditation for yogis and the bond of love for devotees. (1.204.90)
To women, He is the object of their husbands; to the distressed, He is the very essence of their wretchedness.
Though invisible to the physical eye, He is indeed visible through the divine eye.
Yogis constantly meditate upon that Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest.
It is of the nature of supreme bliss and the cause of all causes.
Just as a potter indeed fashions a jar from clay, so too does the Supreme Brahman fashion the creation in every way through primordial nature (prakṛti). ||92-93||
That supreme Brahman is eternal, and Prakṛti is indeed considered eternal.
That Prakṛti is the power of Brahman, the body in the form of a seed.
Brahman, endowed with the power of Prakṛti and possessed of splendor, truly exists eternally.
He in whom that splendor resides is indeed the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa).
How or from what cause could an effect exist without a cause?
That great effect, which is his splendor, would certainly not exist without the Puruṣa.
The Vaiṣṇavas meditate in every way upon that Supreme Soul’s beautiful, enchanting, and divine form, which is adorned with pearls and other ornaments; they meditate on the Lord,
who is dark as a fresh rain-cloud and possesses the age of a youth.
His beautiful eyes were illuminated by the splendor of the midday sun in autumn;
his face possessed a radiance exceeding that of ten million full moons of the autumnal new-moon day;
and he delighted the god of love with the playful charm of ten million Cupids. (98–99)
I bow to Hari, whose every limb is full and adorned with the sweetness of all-encompassing beauty; who smiles, holds a flute in his hand, and wears yellow garments;
whose entire body is anointed with sandalwood paste and who shines with the Kaustubha gem.
Adorned with a garland of jasmine and a forest garland reaching down to his knees;
standing in the triple-bend posture (*tribhaṅga*); decorated with jewels, gems, and the like;
with a crest of peacock feathers and radiant with a crown of diamonds. (101–102)
Adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and gem-studded anklets;
beautifully graced on the cheeks by a pair of jeweled earrings;
possessing teeth as white as pearls, lips like ripe bimba fruit, and a nose like that of a parrot.
He was gazed upon with respect by the Gopīs, who possessed eternal youth and were smiling, as well as by Ramā, Rādhā, Jayā, and the others;
he is the beloved of his devotees, the Lord of devotees, and the one who bestows grace upon his devotees. || 104-105 ||
The Lord of the rāsa dance, full of divine relish, well-served by the great liberated souls,
the imperishable, supreme Brahman, the eternal Blessed One—
O Lakṣmī, the Vaiṣṇavas indeed meditate here upon Hari in such a form.
That very same Lord, the two-armed Master, in Ādigoloka,
is served by his attendants who are cowherds dressed as cowherds;
he is the most perfect, glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Rādhikā.
The Inner Self of all is directly perceptible everywhere through the state of devotion.
The word *kṛṣi* signifies "all," and the syllable *na* denotes the "Self.
Thus, Kṛṣṇa is proclaimed to be the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all. (10.9)
The syllable *kṛṣ* signifies "all," and the letter *na* signifies "the beginning.
(1.204.110) The all-pervading Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa himself, is thus proclaimed.
The word *kṛṣ* denotes the earth (*bhū*), and the letter *ṇa* denotes fulfillment (*nirvṛtti*). (111)
The ground of bliss, the Supreme Brahman, exists in every way as Kṛṣṇa.
*Kṛṣi* means the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and *na* means leading [the soul] to its own abode.
Because He bestows liberation upon the pure [soul], He is therefore proclaimed as Kṛṣṇa Himself. 112.
*Kṛṣi* means drawing forth (*karṣaṇa*), and *na* means leading (*nayana*) to the divine, imperishable state. Having led them to His own abode, He Himself becomes manifest as Kṛṣṇa.
That very Lord, by His partial expansion (*aṃśena*), is the four-armed one in Vaikuṇṭha.
The Lord of Kamalā, served by four-armed attendants, is that very Viṣṇu who, as the Protector and Lord of Ramā, is himself four-armed.
He alone, as the four-armed Lord of the Daughter of the Ocean, resides in the White World (Śvetadvīpa).
He himself is Hari, reclining upon the remnants within the ocean of milk;
he alone is the cause of all forms, abiding in the imperishable.
Śrī Hari is indeed the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, and the Supreme Lord. (116–117)
"All this has been told to you; indeed, he must be meditated upon by you.
Having spoken thus, Nārada praised Śambhu as he ceased speaking.
O Nārada, having attained knowledge and having mastered all mantras and the like—
Having bowed to the divine Śaṅkara, he went to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Daily Duties, the Worship of Nārāyaṇa, the Knowledge of Reality, the Permissible and Forbidden Foods, the Supreme Brahman, and so forth were told to Nārada by Śaṅkara," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 204: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 205 [Author: Chapter 206 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! Śrī Nārada went to that most excellent hermitage, which was joined with the exceedingly beautiful Badarī forest, and he beheld it. 1.
It was adorned with celestial trees, lovely creepers, and great forest giants;
it resounded with the calls of the cātaka, the menā bird, the kīra, and the puṃskokila;
and it was frequented by śarabhas, lions, tigers, elephants, and cows.
Indeed, due to the union of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, it was free from the fear of violence;

it was adorned with thirty million hermitages belonging to perfected beings, sages, and celestial musicians, and was endowed with groves of *kalpa* trees, sandalwood, *tulasī*, and *pārijāta* flowers. (3–4)
It was a divine great forest, endowed with all classes of divine sentient and insentient beings, bestowing peace, and inaccessible to those with earthly bodies;
there, Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the two ascetics and protectors of the world, resided. (5)
The two Blessed Ones, the excellent kings, were there along with countless other sages.
Beneath a banyan tree, in a place fragrant with the breeze,
beautiful and delightful, they sat in the midst of the sages within the assembly hall at the foot of the banyan tree.
He beheld those two blessed ones seated upon a jeweled lion-throne,
chanting the supreme Brahman, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
And seeing them, the supreme teachers of yogis, he prostrated before them.
Rising up, they embraced him and exchanged auspicious blessings. They both inquired after his welfare and performed the rites of honoring a guest;
then, with great respect, they seated him upon a jeweled throne.
Seated upon a delightful seat, free from the fatigue of the journey,
he spoke to those two most excellent and eternal blessed ṛṣis:
"Having indeed studied all the Vedas from my father so that they might become meaningful..."
Having received both knowledge and the mantra from Śaṅkara on Kailāsa,
I have come here to obtain further specialized knowledge and the supreme grace of the Lord; O Blessed Ones, I bow to you, the deliverers from saṃsāra.
Having spoken thus, Nārada sang a hymn of praise with his own lute, in beautiful meter, with a melodious voice, and accompanied by fine dancing and rhythmic cymbals:
"Victory, victory to you, Hari-Kṛṣṇa! O Lord Nārāyaṇa, the hand-protector of Rādhā!"
Victory to you, O Sati! O Lord of the Siddhas! O you who stride through the three worlds! O liberator from battle! O small one!
We praise you, the supreme Brahman, the destroyer of the graspers, the liberator from battle, the small one!
Victory to you, O Sati! O Lord of the Siddhas! O you who stride through the three worlds! O liberator from battle, the small one! 15.
Victory, victory to You, who transcend the conceptualizations of existence, non-existence, and that which is other than both! You are the movement of the Vedic revelation "That Thou Art.
You are the tree named Aśvattha, with its roots turned upward, the support for both consciousness and unconsciousness.
We praise You, the support for both consciousness and unconsciousness, the frictionless ground of both the individual and the universal.
The tree named Aśvattha has its roots turned upward and supports both the conscious and the unconscious.

Victory, victory to you, O Sustainer of the Universe! O Soul of the Universe! You are the excellent exposition of the world within your own self. The Vedas declare that you abide as the transformation and the middle state, and you are the substratum of the universe.
The Vedas declare that you, whose feet crush all misfortunes, who possess the nature of the Supreme Reality,

and who abide in the midst of transformation, are the substratum of the universe. Victory, victory to you, O Lord of the three worlds, O possessor of attributes, O Lord of the three, O son of Vṛṣa, O sustainer of the three principles!

We choose the one whose service is performed by the Goddess stationed at his side, his heart, and his lap; he who bestows the knowledge of the Veda and removes ignorance, whose service is performed by the Goddess stationed at his side, his heart, and his lap. 18.
Victory, victory to You, who are to be known through the Vedas, meters, and limbs [of the Veda], and who are the fruit of the fruits of the sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*)!
Victory to You, the enjoyer! Victory to You, the offerer! Victory to You, the sacrificial oblation, whose nature is delighting in Your own Self!
We worship that delighting in Your own Self, which is the hand of the sages and the people.
Victory to You, O Enjoyer, O Invoker; victory to You, O Oblation! Victory to the one whose nature is delighting in the Self!
Victory, victory to You, the nourisher of the qualities of lifelong asceticism! Victory to You, O Ascetic, the refuge of the mine of compassion!
Victory to You, the Right-hand One! Victory to You, the Left-hand One! Victory to the dual-natured one who removes the intellect of the worldly-minded!
We bow to the remover of the vulgar mind, who grants a good state to his own feet;
victory to the right-hand one, victory to the left-hand one, O you of dual nature, the remover of the vulgar mind!
Having thus praised him and prostrated like a staff, his body bristling with horripilation—
With eyes clouded by tears, he bowed down again and again.
Having heard this, Nārāyaṇa was exceedingly pleased and said to Nārada:
"O best of Gandharvas, having today heard this song accompanied by dance," || 22 ||
With rhythm, with melody, with a moistened heart, and filled with inner emotion—O master of the supreme Gandharva art, I am pleased; become here the bridge between the further and near shores.
May you be the promoter of devotion for me; remain one who performs constant worship.
May you become an ocean of all the qualities of knowledge, possessing eternal and stable youth.
Indeed, with this very body, may you be liberated from the body and become imperishable.
For you there shall be no death, no disease, no old age, and no transformation.
"O Nara, just as I am, so are you; O Mānasa, always remain in my own form and, though a devotee, become the Lord himself.
Having received this blessing, the incarnation of Brahmā himself [departed].
Indeed, by the grace of Nārāyaṇa, he became a portion of a fraction (kalāṃśa).
Then Nārāyaṇa, having touched his head with his hand, spoke again:
"O great sage, you have truly been accepted today as dear to my heart."
May that same perfect omniscience which resides in me be established in you as well, never to be revoked.
Compose for me the *Pañcarātra* scripture, which bestows devotion.
Viṣṇu, Śiva, the Creator of the Universe, Śeṣa, Gaṇapati, and the gods—
Worship him whom the Manus and the Munis worship as their lords;
worship him whom Lakṣmī, Śivā, Sāvitrī, Ramā, Ṛddhi, Siddhi, Devikā,
Mānavī, and the Īśvarīs worship.
Worship him whom the Gaṅgā, Gomatī, Revā, Gaṇḍakī, Sarasvatī,
Yamunā, and Svarṇarekhā worship.
Pārvatī, Prabhā, Amṛtā, Lakṣmī, and Māṇikī likewise worship him.
Worship Him whom the festival of lights (Dīpotsava) and Rādhā worship. To cross the ocean of worldly existence, to leap over the forest fire of rebirth,
and to protect oneself from the serpent of the world, indeed take up the service of Hari.
Having crossed the forest of birth and seeking to cross the mountain of death,
as you set out toward the realm of light, take refuge in the celestial chariot of Kṛṣṇa—
in that chariot upon whose hairs the entire universe resides and on the tip of whose tooth the whole earth rests.
Worship that Kṛṣṇa who, while standing on the ground, held Govardhana on the tip of his finger.
O Nārada, worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who moves through all the scriptures, from whose mouth the Vedas have emerged and in whose mouth they reside. (36-37)
Time, Māyā, evil karma, and the Yama-servants are all of the nature of His power; since these lords exist by a mere fraction of His potency, worship that Kṛṣṇa at all times.
Bhūḥ, Sītā, Bhārgavī, Padmā, the Gopīs, Vṛndā, and Kubjikā—[are likewise His powers].
Worship Him whom Śabarī and the goddess Piṅgalā worship.
Worship that Hari, of whom the Virāṭ is a mere fraction (kalā), and of whom the liberated souls, the Manus, and the sages are but fractions and sub-fractions of fractions. 1.205.40.
The earth rests upon the thousand-headed Śeṣa, he upon the tortoise, and he upon the waters;
those waters rest upon his splendor, that splendor upon his great splendor, and that great splendor rests upon Hari—worship Hari, the support of all.
(41) Those who abide in the abode, those who abide in the celestial spheres of the worlds, those established in yoga, and those established in Brahman—all abide in Him.
Those who remain established in their own nature do not indeed reach the further shore; worship Hari, who is shoreless.
Worship that infinite Hari, whose liberated ones are beyond counting, whose servants are infinite in number, and whose Vedas and creations are endless.
Worship that Nārāyaṇa, of whom Śrī, Lakṣmī, Dhī, Brāhmī, Sādhyā, and Māyā are but single portions of his form, acting as his powers (śaktis).
Nārāyaṇī is the power of Hari; women have been made from her portions.
"O child, having married, take as your wife Nārāyaṇī;
accept her as your bride, who is my command and your father’s command incarnate.
Thus, a protector of dharma, you shall be honored and victorious."
He who indeed delights his own wife with garments, ornaments, and articles—Nārāyaṇī, being pleased with him, delivers him just as Kṛṣṇa does.
Lakṣmī is the power (śakti) of Nārāyaṇa; she indeed exists in the form of a woman.
By insulting women, she becomes defeated;
and by her being insulted, the man becomes insulted.
Being insulted by her, that unfortunate man finds no happiness anywhere. (48–49)
By him who worships that divine woman, who bestows all desired objects,
she becomes a virtuous wife with sons, the giver of all auspiciousness.
She is the one primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), whose very form is the perfect Brahman.
And she indeed exists in six forms, to be worshipped by those seeking auspiciousness.
For she is Rādhikā, the beloved who is the very life-breath of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
and the second is Lakṣmī, the bestower of prosperity, who is the life-breath of Nārāyaṇa. (51–52)
The third is Sarasvatī, the goddess presiding over speech;
the fourth is Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, who is the life-breath of Brahmā;
and the fifth is Satī Pārvatī, whose form is the life-breath of Śaṅkara. 53.
That maiden has been wedded as the bride of every embodied being.
She is to be understood as the sixth [tattva], whose form is the root-prakṛti, and who bestows progeny.
Serving her, become a lord of yogis like another Kṛṣṇa.
"Let there be no bondage for you therein; I have fashioned myself in my own form.
Thus was knowledge granted by me; always retain this, O Nārada.
And Nārada, having received the command of Hari, bowed down.
Having prostrated like a staff out of love and performed circumambulation,
and having meditated upon that Nārāyaṇa, he went there with Nara to perform the holy rites, even though he himself was already liberated. ||57-58||
Previously, he bathed in the cold waters of the Cālakanandā;
at that moment, his body became divine like that of Nārāyaṇa,
and it then became invulnerable in terms of place, time, and substance.
"Pure consciousness alone, the substratum of all capacities, is like the body of Kṛṣṇa.

(1.205.60) Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Journey to Badarikāśrama, His Vision of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, His Praise through Song, His Attainment of Divinity, the Instruction on Devotion, and the Command to Perform the Marriage," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 206 [Author: Chapter 207 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
And in that hermitage, O Blessed One, tell me briefly which holy fords (tīrthas) were indeed established by the sage, and how they are purifying. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Having bathed in the Gaṅgā and assumed a divine form, Nārada went first to Badarī, which is the descent of the imperishable Brahman. Having bowed down, praised, worshipped, and likewise performed a circumambulation [of it], he departed.
And having eaten its leaf and jujube fruit, which were the very form of her grace—
glossy, thornless, divine, green, endowed with sprouts,
possessed of flowers and fruit, and beautiful— one should meditate upon that form within.
