having slain the two asuras and recovered the Vedas,
the blessed Lord Hayaśīrṣa returned to the presence of Brahmā and restored them to him.
At that spot where the Creator of the Universe gave the Vedas and became composed, the Blessed One merged [into the earth];
that is called the most excellent of tīrthas.
It is renowned as Brahmakuṇḍa—divine, auspicious, and bestowing knowledge. (52–53)
From the mere sight [of it], there is the destruction of sin and one attains the world of Brahmā;
for by bathing in Viṣṇu’s [lake], living beings go to Vaikuṇṭha.
There, the Vedas were praised by the Siddhas as they assumed pairs of forms.
"Let one of your forms remain here in liquid form in a secluded place;
let the second go again to the world of Brahmā along with Brahmā himself.
Then, the four Vedas shall have their own forms divided into two."
Together with Brahmā, they went to the world of Brahmā, filled with great joy;
yet, remaining in their liquid form at Badarī, they continued to dwell there eternally.
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas remained by the side of the Blessed Lord.
They exist there in the form of sacred fords (tīrthas), and bathing and other rites were performed there. Then Nārada [performed] the rising of the Vedas;
there, in the waters of the auspicious Sārasvata ford, he performed his ablutions.
Through seeing, touching, bathing in, worshipping, praising,
and saluting Sarasvatī, there shall never be an interruption of [the lineage] in his family;
moreover, the perfection of mantras arises, and Vāṇī bestows the power of speech.
Indeed, there arises a stream of liquid belonging to the Tīrthaṅkaras.
Having performed the rite of pilgrimage there, slightly to the south of that point,
there is a flow of liquid where Indra performed penance in former times.
That name "Indrapada" was also renowned as his second;
having performed most formidable austerities and having gratified Nārāyaṇa,
he obtained the station of Indra, which is saluted by all gods and demons.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight every month, for the propitiation of Hari,
one who observes two fasts and worships Janārdana is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śakra.
In that very place, there is indeed a sacred ford named Mānasodbheda,
where it is held that the great sages have their residence eternally;
and there they completely untie the knot of the conscious and the unconscious within the mind.
They break the knots of the heart and sever many doubts;
they exhaust our karmas—thus it became known as Mānasodbheda.
Sages and ascetics always dwell there on all sides.
In mountain caves, subsisting on fruits, roots, water, and air,
they bathed at the three sessions of the day, always having their inner senses fully conquered.
When a meritorious person obtains even a single drop of water there, [he attains great merit].
He becomes like Vyāsa and, in due course, equal to Yama and his father [Dharma].
Whether possessing desire or free from desire, and whether seeking worldly enjoyment or liberation, he performs various kinds of virtuous deeds at Mānasodbhedaka.
Having enjoyed the fruit [of his actions], he indeed attains liberation again; of this there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed the fruits in heaven and other realms, a person shall attain the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha).
Now, to the west of that place, there is a site known as Vasudhārā.

Accompanied by Nara, this very Nārada went to that sacred ford (tīrtha). Having heard from the foremost Nārada that Badarikāśrama is the most excellent of all sacred fords in the three worlds, the eight Vasus departed first.
For thirty thousand years they performed austerities subsisting on water and leaves;
they attained perfection and beheld Nārāyaṇa.
Delighted by that vision, they obtained supreme bliss.
Having received the Vaiṣṇava initiation, they departed each to his own abode.
Here, the light of the meritorious is seen from within the water;
having bathed there and worshipped Nārāyaṇa as well as Nara, [one attains the goal].
Having enjoyed every happiness here, they go at the end to the imperishable state (akṣara-pada). Having fasted for three days, virtuous practitioners behold the Siddhas:
Āma, Bhava, Soma, Dhara, Nala, and Anila.
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa— those who dwell there as the eight Vasus—
the pilgrims see them there as well, possessed of divine forms; even those who are impure become purified and partake in liberation.
Having bathed at the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Vasudhārā, Nārada then proceeded to the sacred ford consisting of five streams located in the south-western direction;
[namely] Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, Gayā, and Naimiṣa.

These five sacred fords (tīrthas), though defiled by the taint of sin, went to the Creator of the Universe to become pure once more. Having heard the reason for their arrival and remembering Badarikāśrama, Brahmā— 82–83.
He said, "Depart quickly for Hari’s Badarikāśrama,
where by the mere act of entering, merit is gained that destroys all sin.
Then, having bowed down, they all went from the various holy places to Badarikāśrama.
By merely entering there, their sins were purified.
Then, assuming a twofold form, they remain in a liquid state;
even when returned to their own places, they abide in their respective forms.
Having bathed in those [tirthas] and bowed to Hari, a person who observes five fasts shall enjoy abundant pleasures here and attain the same world as Hari (sālokya).

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Vainateya-śilā, Gāruḍī-śilā, Pañcamukhī-gaṅgā, Nārasiṃhī-śilā, Brahma-tīrtha, Sarasvatī-tīrtha, Dravadhārendrapada-tīrtha, Mānasodbheda, Vasudhārā, Pañcadhārā-tīrtha, and others," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
← Chapter 207: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 208 [Author: Chapter 209 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Then Nārada went to Somakuṇḍaka, the place where in ancient times the blessed Soma performed penance. (1)

But Soma, the son of Atri, having repeatedly heard from the Gandharvas about the great celestial happiness of heaven, asked his father the means of attaining it; and when the father spoke again, he said: "O Father, how may I become [that]?"
"He is the supreme lord of the planets, constellations, stars, and medicinal herbs.
Having heard this, Atri said to him: "Tell me the means for my success;
likewise, everything is attained through austerity by propitiating Hari."
Indeed, for the virtuous, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain in either world;
for there exists such a supreme sacred site as Badarikāśrama.
Having heard this, Soma went to Badarī to worship Viṣṇu.

Preceded by the recitation of the eight-syllable mantra, he indeed performed [austerities]. For eighty-eight thousand years, devoted solely to the Blessed One and bathing daily at the three sessions of the day, he practiced most rigorous penance.
Śrī Hari, being pleased by that austerity,
arrived and said to Soma again and again, "Choose a boon.
Then Soma, having bowed to Hari there in the manner of a staff while laughing, [spoke].

"By your grace, may I become the lord of the planets, constellations, stars, and medicinal herbs, as well as of all the twice-born. Hari said, "You do not possess such ascetic power; choose something else. (1.208.10)
Soma did not indeed ask for any other boon, but performed penance once more for thirty thousand years; thereafter, the Blessed One appeared and said to Soma,
"Choose a boon," and Soma likewise requested such a one.
Having heard this, Hari chose [the boon] and then vanished;
Soma then performed most terrible penance for forty thousand years.
Thereupon, Hari—bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus—was pleased with him.
He appeared and said, "Choose a boon as a gift.
Soma replied, "If you are pleased with me, grant me this boon:
bestow upon me the sovereignty over the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars."
"O Lord of the World, regarding the herbs, the brahmins, and the night, the Blessed One said:
'Soma has indeed been requested by you, though it is difficult to obtain; nevertheless, I grant it today. Become a king of such a kind. (15–16)
Then all the inhabitants of heaven assembled in the Badarī forest and, with great respect, duly consecrated Soma as king.
Thereupon, having ascended his celestial chariot, he became the Moon, the maker of night.
And having gone to heaven, that sacred ford became renowned as Somakuṇḍa. By the mere sight of it, people become free from defects and proceed to the world of Soma;
by touching it or bathing there, they likewise proceed to the world of Viṣṇu.
For them there is no returning again, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
By remaining for three nights reciting the mantra, one attains perfection easily.
Having thus visited Somatīrtha, the sage Śrī Nārada departed.
At the Āditya-tīrtha, he performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites.
(21) Having performed most rigorous penance, Kaśyapa’s sons, the Ādityas, attained the status of the Sun; indeed, that tīrtha is the destroyer of sins. (22)
Indeed, on Sundays, on the seventh lunar day, and during a solar transit (saṃkrānti),
a person who bathes according to the prescribed rite effects the destruction of the sins acquired over seven lifetimes.
Furthermore, he who performs the Pārāka and Kṛcchra penances according to the rules [attains the same].

Having enjoyed happiness in the world of the Sun, he proceeds to the world of Viṣṇu. (24) By bathing and drinking [there], one is liberated from great diseases; there is no doubt about this. Having performed his ablutions at that holy place, he then went to Catuḥsrotas, the most excellent of sacred sites. (25)
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa exist here in their substantial forms;
they abide in the directions starting from the east in sequence, serving as the means for the liberation of beings.
These others also exist here in this supreme field, in accordance with the command of Hari.
These do not meet in any other field; they are difficult to attain even for the gods.
Those sattvic persons who have acquired merits through the service of Nārāyaṇa behold these personified goals of human endeavor here. (27–28)
At the Pumarthas tirtha, Brahma and the other gods, as well as sages and seers,
come purified on festival days to bathe for the sake of its renown.
Having performed his rites at that tirtha, the venerable Narada went away.
There is a sacred ford named Satyapada, adorned with a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, stationed within that triangle and composed in meditation,
perform austerities along with the sages for the gratification of the worlds.
On the eleventh day, Hari himself, the purifier, comes there;
likewise, the sages, the ascetics, the gods, and others whose wealth is their austerity,
devoted to the worship of Hari, come to this pool to bathe.
For those who perform chanting, austerity, praise, meditation, salutation, and worship of Hari,
even Brahmā is unable to describe the mass of their merit.
Having bathed, observed a fast, and worshipped the Lord Hari—
Having become liberated while living (jīvanmukta) here, one thereafter becomes liberated into Brahman;
having bathed and reached Satyaloka, one then proceeds to the state of final liberation.
There, at midday on the day of Hari, [one beholds] the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Divine songs were indeed heard from those devoted to the vow of truth.
By the majesty of that place, sins and other evils dissolved upon the mere sight of it.
Having performed the rites for the sacred ford, he proceeded to the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
There is seen a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the foremost of all holy sites, containing supremely pure water;
therein it appears in two forms, namely white and non-white.
Having bathed there and having worshipped Hari, one is liberated from sin.
Having performed the ritual at that sacred ford, he went to the supreme Urvaśī-tīrtha,
where on the peak of Nārāyaṇāvāsa there is pure water abounding in coolness; it is there that Nārada, the king of sages, resides.
And he questioned the man regarding his history, and the man indeed spoke:
"Mūrti was the wife of Dharma; from them were born two sons, Nara and Nārāyaṇa. Of these, the Blessed Lord Hari is the possessor of the imperishable abode."
Nara is proclaimed as the Imperishable (Akṣara), and Nārāyaṇa is Hari himself.
Those two, indeed, remained on two mountains to perform penance;
by the command of their parents, they constantly practiced severe austerity.
"Indeed, these two are for the sake of protecting the subjects and for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
Indra, terrified by their ascetic power and apprehensive of the loss of his kingdom,
dispatched Kāma along with his retinue, accompanied by Vasanta.
Joy, love, as well as arrows and bows, and likewise the Apsarases;
the wind, rich with fragrance, cool, and gladdening;
and the auspicious time of night mingled with droplets from the clouds. (45–46)
The moonlight is white, as are the cuckoos and the cātaka birds;
likewise, there are peacocks, singers, dancers, and musicians.
Thus, when all have assembled, the means [for success] will not be deficient.
Then, by the command of Indra, they all joined with Kāma and went to where the two great sages,
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, were performing austerities; there,
first of all, the moon remained, spreading its moonlight.
The entire surface became tranquil, as if washed by whiteness;
even the night spread its passionate impetus there through the radiance of clear darkness, and the season, too,
was characterized by passion.
Arising from the thought of passion, they repeatedly became intensely excited.
(5.1) The cuckoos dwelling in the world of the gods, as well as peacocks and pheasants, began to utter their sweet-sounding cries and gentle *kekā* notes. (5.2)
The mango trees, awakening desire, shine with flowers and blossoms;
spring has assumed the form of fragrant flowers upon the trees and creepers.
At that time, a gentle and cool breeze arose, rich with sweet fragrance.
All the singers, dancers, and instrumentalists performed accordingly;
indeed, they engaged in singing, dancing, and playing music infused with passion.
At that time, joy and love entered Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
With his bow, the Mind-born [god] discharged arrows such as Mohanā (the Enchanting), and a divine host of Apsarases who displayed gestures, expressions, and amorous charms;
they bewildered him by demonstrating various movements of their limbs. (56)
Then Cakrāyudha, assuming the form of a fifteen-year-old boy, devoutly massaged the feet of Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
going to their sides again and again, he kissed them many times. (57–58)

Likewise, Kāma discharged his arrows at the cheeks, hands, and thighs [of Nara and Nārāyaṇa]; thereafter, he indeed became exhausted. Even though all such transformations were employed, Nara and Nārāyaṇa remained as they were.
With their eyes motionless, they remained fixed as if in ascetic penance;
not wavering even slightly, they stood thus absorbed in meditation.
At that time, the assembly of Kāmadeva became fruitless.
When they were unable to bring about the destruction of their ascetic power, they all departed dejected; being unsettled, they spoke to Mahendra:
"Indeed, our strength exerts no effect there at all; it is fruitless. (62)
Whatever has been born or created, all that is according to the command of Hari, like the tortoise [supporting the world].
Having heard this from them all, Indra went to that place and once again caused them to perform acts of desire.
They became fruitless while remaining in perfect meditative absorption before Hari.
Then Nārāyaṇa himself, rising from his meditation, spoke to those who had arrived:
"For what purpose have you come? Please accept my hospitality."
Having spoken thus, he gave them fruits and roots in great abundance.
Then Nārāyaṇa said to Nara: "Behold the circle of Indra;
this Mahendra is conceiving pride in his mind because of the celestial nymphs."
Nowhere else do there exist such deluding celestial nymphs;
yet he, utterly infatuated, does not recognize even a fraction of my sovereignty.
All of them were created by me alone, and they merge back into me.
"He does not even know that these beautiful women were nourished by me alone.
Therefore, go without delay and bring clusters of mango blossoms;
once there, crush them with your left thigh right here in his presence."
When Nara had thus performed [the sacrifice], a most radiant woman was born there;
she was Urvaśī, born from his thigh, and even at twelve years of age she was full of desire.
Her limbs were proportionate to her beauty, and before her, the other Apsarases appeared dark.
Then they became lusterless, and even Kama’s pride was shattered.
Seeing Urvaśī restored to youth, Indra’s face grew pale—
she whose touch had indeed made him more beautiful than the finest flower in the three worlds.
"A jewel among women has appeared; who is capable of deluding her?
Thinking thus, he went to Nārāyaṇa to beg for forgiveness, quickly falling at his feet and saying, "Save me from my transgression!"
Becoming agitated, like a man who has committed an offense, he spoke.
Then Nārāyaṇa said: "Your task has been accomplished by you;
I do not take your transgression into account. Go to heaven and be happy."
I practice austerity for the sake of the happiness of the worlds, not out of craving;
nor for the sake of your kingdom, nor of another's, nor even for the sake of supreme sovereignty.
I have no craving for a kingdom, nor do I have any desire for your kingdom.
Vaikuṇṭha, comprising all that is conscious and unconscious, is indeed my eternal kingdom.
This entire universe was created by me; I am certainly not deluded therein.
Yet you, considering it to be material, have sought to delude me, an ascetic.

"All my exertion regarding me, Nārāyaṇa, has indeed been in vain. Indra, deluded by the power of Urvaśī, bowed to Nārāyaṇa and again requested her from Hari for the sake of his illusory work and her beautiful form.
"O Blessed One, such a jewel as this is an obstacle for ascetics.
It appears to me to be worthy of heaven; you have no need for it.
Therefore, O Lord, give it to me; I am your servant and I beg of you. (8.1–8.2)
"I shall certainly never commit an offense against you again regarding the performance of your penance.
Having heard this from Nārāyaṇa, he gave the beautiful Urvaśī to Indra;
and he, being delighted, went to heaven along with his celestial retinue.
The place where Urvaśī was born from the crushing of Nara’s thigh is the Urvaśīkuṇḍa Tīrtha, which abounds in water.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and having fasted for two nights, [one attains the fruit]. ॥84–85॥
Having worshipped Hari there, a man shall become Nārāyaṇa;
for one who possesses desire, a goddess resembling Urvaśī shall appear in heaven.
Having reached the Urvaśī-kuṇḍa, a person whose desires are powerful [attains this].
One shall attain the world of Urvaśī merely by bathing there with devotion. The Lord himself, the embodiment of austerity, always remains there in the vicinity of the Urvaśī-kuṇḍa,
inspiring the welfare of all living beings.
"Insects, moths, and birds laugh at the gods in heaven;
we are endowed with both enjoyment and liberation, while you grant only liberation.
Having reached the Urvaśī-kuṇḍa, a man should dwell there for one day.
On the southern side of Urvaśī, the weapons of the Lord of the World are indeed present;
by the sight of them, one shall not suffer from the fear of weapons.
There are many sacred fords (*tīrtha*) on the mountain inhabited by Nārāyaṇa.
I know all of them, and no other ordinary person indeed knows them.
Whoever hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard while composed in mind,
or reads it, or causes it to be read— let there be for him the fruit of each respective sacred ford (tīrtha).
"Having shaken off all sins, one shall attain the same realm as Hari (sālokya).

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Soma-kuṇḍa Tīrtha, Āditya-tīrtha, the Tīrtha of the Four Puruṣārthas, the Origin of Urvaśī, and Other Tīrthas," in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, Nārada then went to the auspicious place known as Meru,
a sacred site situated to the south of Brahmakuṇḍa.
That mountain Meru, the abode of men, was established here by Hari;
when the Blessed One made his auspicious residence in Viśālā,
then the Vidyādharas and Cāraṇas abandoned Meru itself.
The gods, great seers, and perfected beings, longing for a vision of Hari,
arrived at Viśālā, full of eager anticipation to dwell there forever; they had set aside their own abodes because they found greater satisfaction in beholding the Blessed One.
Meru, deprived of the gods and others, became filled with grief;
distressed, he went to Nārāyaṇa for the purpose of making a request.
He said: "O Blessed One, all are longing for a vision of you."
"Having come here leaving me behind, you dwell in this auspicious abode without me.
Therefore, I do not shine there; indeed, I must not dwell there at all.
I too wish to dwell here at your feet."
Then the Blessed One said: "This will certainly not lead to your welfare. It is held that the stability of the fourteen worlds depends upon your staying [there].
Therefore, by my command, you must indeed remain there along with the gods and others."
And you must remain right here with your second form;
for you too, O second one, must always stay here in my hermitage, because the attainment of service to me is possible only here.
Having thus received this command, the peaks of Mount Meru,
assuming a second form, arrived in a subtle state from all sides.
Hari indeed [received] those golden forms with his own hand.
Having taken them up and established them there for the sake of all dwellings,
they all beheld the peaks which were like gold; filled with joy, serene,
and satisfied, they praised the compassionate Lord Nārāyaṇa.
The compassionate Lord, the God of the gods, brought the peaks of Mount Meru for the sake of the happiness of the denizens of heaven; to Him we offer our salutations.
He who, out of compassion for His devotees, bestows manifold fruits even upon those with meager devotion.
May this Lord Narayana, the abode of compassion, be pleased.
Always compassionate like a father, he bestows instruction upon us;
may Krishna, the ocean of mercy, protect us even from calamities.
"May the Blessed One, the protector of his devotees, who grants the desires of the minds of the Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Ṛṣis, always protect us here.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, said to them, "Choose a boon."
The gods said: "And for those people who behold the peaks of Meru, let their residence on Meru come to pass through your grace.
This place must not be abandoned by you, nor indeed should Meru be abandoned."
"May those who obtain residence with me have their dissolution in you at the end of their enjoyment.
Having spoken thus, "So be it," Hari vanished right there.
From that time forward, the gods and others [resided] in the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
In some places on Meru, in some places in heaven, and in some places on Mount Raivata,
they dwell without fear wherever Nārāyaṇa, the Man, resides.
Thus, having established the sacred site of Meru, Nārada departed from there.

Hari himself went to Meru, that gentle sacred site presided over by the world-protectors and endowed with lakes; there he beheld the deities, as well as the seers, sages, world-protectors, gods, and others. (23)
Having seen them, he said to the world-protectors: "You are indeed kings;
dwelling in the hermitage of sages and such is not suitable for you.
Come, therefore, to places prepared by me that are fitting for you."
"And let them dwell right there, relying upon my presence.
Thus the world-protectors were brought from the central region of Mount Meru and established;
and for their comfort, a great reservoir was constructed.
Having struck the earth with his staff, he created a pleasure-pool.
There, the world-protectors, Gandharvas, and gods, accompanied by their consorts, wander about, rejoice, and sing at all times. (27–28)
Indeed, he created forests delightful with the fragrance of flowers;
and the Blessed One himself, bringing supreme joy to everyone,
would personally come for his bath on the twelfth and the full-moon day.
At midday, a supreme radiance is seen in the water;
there itself the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas) is obtained.
The Daṇḍapuṣkariṇī Tīrtha bestows rewards both in this world and the next.
From the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the fruit born here at Puṣkara on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha shall be eightfold that of Gayā.
By performing sacrifice, charity, and austerity here, a person becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
One enjoys inexhaustible fruit and thereafter attains liberation.
This [place] indeed exists hidden in the midst of the Badarī-tīrtha;
those who have produced abundant merit behold it, and no others.
Having thus performed the *daṇḍodaka* rite at that sacred ford, Nārada departed for the supreme holy site at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Mānasodbheda. There,
for thirty thousand years, he enjoyed the fruit of his ascetic penance at Prayāga.
The fruit of that [merit] shall be obtained by performing a ritual bath at the Mānasodbheda tīrtha.
To the south of the confluence is the auspicious abode of Dharma,
where the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa took birth in embodied form.
Wherein Dharma exists with its four feet— truth, sacrifice, austerity,
and likewise charity— the fruit of what is performed there becomes inexhaustible.
Then, in the southern region, [is the place] named Urvaśīsaṃgama.
Then there is the Kūrmoddhāra Tīrtha, which brings purity to a being through bathing.
Then there is the Brahmāvarta Tīrtha, for it indeed bestows the world of Brahmā. In this way, there are many sacred fords within the Badarī forest.
By sight, remembrance, bathing, drinking, sipping water, and likewise by sprinkling,
these [waters] destroy sins and grant liberation through yoga.
Having visited all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), Nārada returned once again.
Then, staying at the sun-like hermitage of Nara, he heard from the mouth of Nara the majesty of the sacred field that removes all suffering with its peace-bestowing and one-pointed wisdom.
[He heard of] the field of Hari known as Badarī, which is difficult to attain within the three worlds. (42–43)
By remembering it, even his most terrible sins are destroyed.
The merit acquired at another sacred site becomes equal to that of Badarī through its remembrance.
Whatever fruit belongs to a thousand horse-sacrifices for one who subsists on air alone—
In another sacred field, at Badarī, that same fruit is obtained in a mere moment.
Known by the name Muktipradā in the Kṛta age, it grants the perfection of yoga in the Tretā;
known as Viśālā in the Dvāpara, it is indeed called Badaryāśrama in the Kali age.
Just as she is the bestower of liberation and the grantor of success in yoga in every way, so too,
because of the destruction of the body composed of the *śāla* tree,
and due to its connection with the *badarī* tree, that hermitage is indeed called Badarikāśrama.
One may abandon all sacred fords at the end of time or even during the transition between Yugas;
however, Hari Nārāyaṇa never abandons Badarī.
Indeed, the fruit that is obtained through yoga in Kāśī for sixty thousand years [is attained here].
Indeed, at Badarī, that fruit is obtained in a single day,
for there stand the distinguished halls of the gods, the sacred fords, and the ṛṣis. Viśālā is considered significant, and Śālā is likewise known as the abode of knowledge.
That Viśālā is beginninglessly established, just as the Vedas are the body of Hari.
(51) Except through death resulting from the performance of one's own duties, liberation is held in the very hands of men simply by the sight of Badarī. (52)
Having conquered both merit and demerit, and having beheld Narāyaṇa, the Lord of Badarī,
a person here indeed attains liberation without effort.
In all ages, the Blessed One [resides there], auspicious and like Vaikuṇṭha itself.
Having reached Badarī, one dwells in the very presence [of the Lord].
Without knowledge, without yoga, and without the exhaustion of wandering to various holy fords, a living being attains the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya) in a single lifetime. || 54-55 ||
He by whom Hari has been worshipped throughout thousands of previous births may go to see Badarī, where having gone, one does not grieve.
By uttering "Badarī, Badarī," even incidentally, one becomes a partaker of liberation.

Having beheld the vast Badarī, how can a person have fear of death? (57) The entire earth, including its mountains and forests, is circumambulated tenfold when one performs a single circumambulation of Hari on the ground at Badarī; indeed, it is accomplished at every step. (58)
The merit gained at every step in this place is indeed equal to that of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, and the circumambulation of Hari.
Whatever food, having attained divine nature, the Blessed One eats at Badarī—
For the purification of their being, that [food] should be consumed by all without hesitation.
(1.209.60) The immortals become intent on consuming the *naivedya* offered to Hari.
Even if one has committed a mortal sin in childhood, youth, or old age... (61)
Having eaten what was offered to Viṣṇu at Badarī, one returns there;

The form of Hari is in the heart, His name is in the mouth, and His *naivedya* is in the stomach.
He upon whose head is the water from the feet along with the remains of the floral offering (nirmālya) is [indeed] Acyuta himself.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed by the nectar of the feet.
What is the use of gifts, austerities, pilgrimages, religious observances, or arduous efforts? (63–64)
If even a mere drop from Viṣṇu’s feet and other [limbs] at Badarī should touch one,
it yields a fruit greater than that of a great gift made at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse;
indeed, by a single mouthful at Badarī, one obtains more than the fruit of the Cāturmāsya vow.
The merit gained from hearing the Vedānta is [surpassed] by the nectar of the feet at Badarī.
Even those who are dull-witted, if they receive Vaiṣṇava initiation at Badarī,
liberation is in the palm of their hands even from merely seeing the sacred ground.
Whoever constantly hears this, causes it to be heard, or causes it to be recited,
or recites it himself— freed from sin, he attains the abode of Viṣṇu.
A king obtains victory, and one who desires a son obtains a son.
One seeking a daughter obtains a daughter; a daughter finds a virtuous husband.
One seeking wealth attains wealth; it destroys disease, sorrow, and poverty.
It is the destroyer of misfortune, untimely death, malefic planetary influences, evil dreams, and the like.
Having heard [their words], having bowed to Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and having partaken of the *prasāda*,
that Nārada departed for the true world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) for the sake of his marriage.

Thus ends the section on the Meru-tīrtha, Daṇḍa-puṣkariṇī, the manifestation of Mānasa, the birthplace of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the union with Urvaśī, the lifting of the tortoise, Brahmāvarta, and other sacred sites, within the first book, the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
The fires are indeed the mouths of Brahmā; they are portions of Brahmā and the deities of sacrifice.
O Lord, tell me the story of when and from what they were born.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The cause of fire, which possesses the quality of heat and is of the nature of an effect,
is that conscious deity Vahni, the mind-born son of Brahmā.
From that Agni, the deity presiding over fire, Svāhā was born;
she gave birth to three sons: Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci.
Śuci is indeed the solar [fire], while Pāvaka is considered to be the lightning [fire].
In the Śrāddha rite, Vahni is Pavamāna, and his son is Kavyavāhana.
Likewise, Pāvaka’s excellent son was named Saharakṣas.
The son of Śuci was Havyavāha, who provides food for the gods.
Kavyavāha was the son of the Pitṛs, and Saharakṣas was the son of the Asuras;
their sons and grandsons numbered forty-nine.
Vaidyuta’s son was Brahmaudana, whose son was named Bharata.
His fire is Vaiśvānara, and his essence is indeed the sap of the waters (Kāvya).
From the churning of the Puṣkara ocean, Atharvan Agni was born;
his son was Dadhyañca Bodhya, who resides within the circle of fire.

Atharvan is said to be Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras is the son of Atharvaṇa; therefore, the fire of the world is proclaimed as both Bhārgava and Āṅgirasa. Pavamāna is the fire produced by friction (nirmathya), and it is also known by the name Gārhapatya.
He had two sons, Śaṃsya and Śukra by name.
Śaṃsya was the Āhavanīya fire, which carries the oblations and is the essence of ritual action;
likewise, Sabhya and Āvasathya are considered the two sons of the fire Śaṃsya.
The praiseworthy [king] desired sixteen excellent women from the rivers:
the Kāverī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, the Narmadā, and likewise the Yamunā;
the Godāvarī, the Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, and the Irāvatī.
The Vipāśā, the Kauśikī, the Śatadrū, and likewise the Sarayū;
the Sītā, the Sarasvatī, the Hrādinī, and the Pāvanī—
those fires which were produced from these rivers are indeed celebrated as the Dhiṣṇyas.
Ṛtu, Pravāhaṇa, Agnīdhra, Samrāḍagni, and Kṛśānuka;
the eight Samrāḍagnis, and likewise Nabhas by name, Parṣan, Vasu, Havyasūrya, and Viśvāyu as the fifth. (15)
Ṛtudhāman, Ajaikapād, and Ahirbudhnya are recorded as such.
They are the sons of Śaṃsyā; they are to be honored and their sons are to be distributed.
There are eight to be distributed: Śānti, Pracetas, and Satyaka.
Viśvadeva, Avakṣu, Acchāvāka, Uśīraka,
and Vyaratni— these are to be known [as the priests] according to their transition through the pressings (savana) in the sacrifice.
Apām Garbha, Pāvaka, Avabhṛtha, and Hṛcchraya belong to that [Avabhṛtha rite].
The son of Jāṭhara was Manyu, and his son was Ghorasaṃvartaka.
In the ocean he became known as Vaḍava; his son was Saharakṣaka. His son was Kṣāma, and his son was Kravyāda; these are the fires born of the lineage of Pāvaka.
The fire of Śuci, born from the Araṇi wood, is called Āyu;
his son was Mahimā, and his son is considered to be Śava.
His son was Savana, and his son is said to be Adbhuta.
The son of Adbhuta is said to be Vivici, and his son is Arka.
The sons of Arka are Anīkavat, Vāsṛja, Rakṣohā, Pitṛkṛt, Surabhi, and Rukmavān; these are the Vahnis (fires). ||22–23||
"In all Manvantaras, there arise Jātavedas fires;
they are all remembered as the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) and are endowed with light.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the fires have been described to you according to their principal names."
All of them always bestow fruits through fire-offerings and other rites, and they grant the perfection of mantras.
Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Vahni," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

he is said to be the very son of Brahmā.
Svārociṣa was indeed the second Manu; he was the son of Agni.
Auttama was the third Manu, the son of Priyavrata.
Tāmasa was the fourth Manu, and he was indeed the brother of Uttama.
The fifth Manu is said to be Raivata, the uterine brother of Tāmasa;
and the sixth Manu is indeed named Cākṣuṣa, the son of Cakṣus.
These are Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, and likewise Raivata.
These four are considered to belong to the lineage of Priyavrata.
In the dynasty of Uttānapāda, Cākṣuṣa is called a Manu.
Kaśyapa’s sons by Aditi are known as the twelve Ādityas. (54–55)
Therein, the son of Vivasvat is known as Śrāddhadeva;
he is this Vaivasvata Manu, who is called the seventh Manu.
And Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun from Chāyā, is the eighth Manu.
The ninth Manu is Dakṣasāvarṇi, born from Varuṇa.
The tenth Manu is Brahmasāvarṇi, the son of Upaśloka.
The eleventh is declared to be Dharmasāvarṇi Manu. (57–58)
Rudrasāvarṇi will be the twelfth Manu by name;
the thirteenth Manu will be Devasāvarṇi, the son of Sunṛtā;
and he who is the heir of Satyasahas will indeed be Vedasāvarṇi.
And Manu Indrasāvarṇi is called the fourteenth.
O beloved, these fourteen indeed occur in every kalpa.
A kalpa, as measured by these [Manus], consists of a cycle of a thousand yugas.
And his night is of equal duration, consisting of a thousand cycles of yugas;
here, the word "yuga" should indeed be understood as referring to the four yugas [of a mahāyuga].
In this same manner, there are other kalpas and fourteen other Manus.
In this manner, fourteen other Indras indeed come into being;
likewise, there are other groups of seven sages of that same kind.
Furthermore, there are other guardians of the quarters and protectors of the worlds who perform similar functions.
Other Vedavyāsas appear in every cycle of four yugas;
there are twenty-four incarnations of Hari for each such cycle.
Furthermore, there are infinite partial manifestations, infusions of power, and portions of portions, corresponding to every virtuous soul.
Indeed, incarnations occur for the sake of the welfare of the world.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Many Kalpas and Fourteen Manus," in the first section, the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 214.
Chapter 215 [Author:
Chapter 216 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To the characteristics of the Kali age and all those at the end of the Dvāpara age.
When the first Dvāpara arrived, creation arose from pairs;
that [creation] was produced by the dharma of union, born from the association of man and woman.
When the evil qualities born of desire began to prevail there—
namely, the acts of cowherds, theft, anger, selfishness,
violence, falsehood, as well as stealing, the loss of virility, and possessiveness. (2–3)
Impurity, thirst, enjoyment, exertion, excessive greed,
and the sense of "I" and "mine" regarding the body, the physical world, the conscious, and the unconscious—
these arise in every individual, increasing through the flow of self-interest. (4)
Consequently, embodied beings are born with little merit or no merit at all.
(5) Their minds become turbid, their intellects become perverted, evil intentions arise, and they proceed upon the path of the unrighteous. (6)
Gambling, drinking, women, and slaughter—these are indeed the seats of unrighteousness;
likewise, gold, falsehood, lust, intoxication, enmity, and passion (rajas).
These five are the very sources of affliction created by the dwelling of the Kali age.
All people will be mostly barbarians, likewise devoted to unrighteousness and falsehood;
they will be slayers of women, children, cows, and brahmins, and they will have no regard for the wives or wealth of others;
they will rise and set as if devoid of purpose, giving only trifling gifts and possessing intense anger.
They will be unrefined, devoid of ritual action, possessing little strength and short lifespans;
pervaded by passion and ignorance, they will be mostly barbarians who are masters of wealth.
Their lords and the people of their lands will be devoted to those very same character traits and customs.

Dharma, truth, compassion, forbearance, purity, longevity, mindfulness, and strength—all these daily undergo decay as the power of the Kali age increases. Regarding every kind of excellence, wealth alone brings about prosperity. (11–12)
In the establishment of justice and law, wealth is the cause and becomes the power;

in marriage, mutual desire is the cause, or else wealth or even the object of affection. In the state of a Brahmin, the sacred thread is the mark; in the act of shaving the head, victory is considered the goal.
In scholarship there is only cavil; in the practice of generosity, poverty.
(14) A hypocrite should be considered a great saint; at a wedding, the consent of both parties is required.
Bathing is merely for outward show, and the display of splendor is a deception. (15)
The sacred ford may be far away; the wearing of matted hair is merely an ornament.
Fulfilling one's own belly is true merit, while truthfulness is invincible.
Skill in accomplishing one’s own purpose is proficiency, and the practice of giving is for the sake of fame.

Two hundred, one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, and finally fifteen years—this is the lifespan when beings have reached their end. Those who indulge in theft, falsehood, senseless violence, sexual misconduct, and so forth [attain these lifespans]. (1.7–18)
In the Kali age, young women will remain unmarried and wear very little clothing; men and women will touch one another indiscriminately, and likewise, they will seize all that belongs to others.
All social orders will consist mostly of barbarians, and cows will consist mostly of goats.
Hermitages consist of wives; kinsmen consist primarily of wealth;
medicinal herbs are like mere blades of grass; trees are those reachable only from great heights;
clouds bring rain for but a moment; and houses are devoid of substance.
In the Kṛta age there was truth, compassion, charity, and austerity, but those do not exist in the Kali age. In the Kṛta age,
all people were contented, compassionate, friendly, peaceful, self-controlled, patient,
delighting in the Self, and possessed of equal vision.
In the Tretā age, those portions of Dharma consisting of three quarters indeed diminish;
unrighteousness enters, along with falsehood, violence, greed,
and strife, as people there proceed according to their own nature.
However, in the *tretā* age, people are devoted to austerity, are neither excessively violent nor licentious,
and are primarily intent upon virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and desire (*kāma*).
Even the social classes (*varṇas*) have Brahmins as their foremost, yet they are corrupted by their livelihoods.
In the Dvāpara age, austerity, truth, compassion, and charity lose half their power.
In the Kali age, even a quarter of the Bull of Dharma perishes through violence, craving, falsehood, hatred, censure, envy, and threats— through unrighteousness and evil qualities.
Cruel, hostile, greedy, full of craving, and devouring all things;
of wicked conduct and eager for the vices of drinking and sensual enjoyment—all subjects indeed become thus, driven solely by the purposes of the tongue and the genitals. (28)

Deceit, falsehood, sleep, laziness, hatred, despondency, grief, delusion, fear, and wretchedness prevail daily among the people in the Kali age. They are destitute of wealth, lacking the capacity for expenditure, addicted to drinking liquor, and possessed of false views. (1.215.30)
Men and women will be intent on their own self-interest, and everything will have desire as its root.
The lands will be filled with bandits, the Vedas will be destroyed by heretics, and kings will devour their subjects; people will be satisfied only with their genitals and stomachs.
Then there will be mendicants wearing saffron robes who are devoid of vows and accompanied by their wives;
they will practice penance for the sake of gain through hypocrisy, and even deposit trusts for the purpose of seizing wealth.
They will be dwarfish, gluttonous, have many children, and keep many women.
Even women— speaking sweetly like female cranes, naked and wearing only rags, deceitful in their dealings and wagers, mean-spirited, and stained by love for the path of the unrighteous—
abandon a husband who is destitute, even leaving behind their own families. (34)
Abandoning their fathers, brothers, and friends, they go instead to those who gratify their lusts.
All accept gifts, and all indeed act as officiating priests;
all assume authority over the mantras, even the barbarians who pride themselves on being Brahmins. (35–36)
Deceitful people instruct their deceitful disciples;
indeed, deceitful disciples resort to a deceitful teacher according to their own nature.
Furthermore, those who lack righteousness speak of righteousness among the unrighteous.
Those who always harbor hatred, censure, and envy toward their own kin;
those deprived of food, wealth, clothing, and home, and even lacking sustenance—these indeed die prematurely when the terrible Kali age has arrived. (38–39)

In the Kali age, people will suffer from drought, excessive enemies, and severe illness; they will become destroyers for the sake of achieving their own meager interests. In that age, wicked sons will not protect their aged parents.
In the Kali age, wicked men do not protect their virtuous wives;
instead, they protect women for the sake of sensual pleasures as they desire.
Women, however, seek out a man who provides wealth and gives them sexual gratification.
In the Kali age, people undergo suffering like cats for the sake of a single cowrie shell; they even sacrifice their very lives for the sake of falsehood.
Destroying their own welfare for the sake of a trifle, they strike down even their own kin.
In the Kali age, teachers and gurus whose minds are pervaded by heresy do not attain happiness, nor nirvāṇa, nor peace.
Seized by time, their subjects quickly go to destruction, being constantly agitated.
Men will be born with little faith, untruthful, prone to great anger, and unrighteous, being thoroughly intermingled with Yavanas;
they will kill women and children and even slay one another.
In the Kali age, men enjoy the fruits of their conduct corrupted by the defects of the age.
Indeed, all kings and Brahmins— whether belonging to highly exalted lineages or those who have risen only to fall— become fit to be fed by outcasts, like dog-cookers.

Then, in the Kali age, when the population consists mostly of women and only a few men remain, people will be devoid of virtue, desire, and wealth; they will follow the conduct of barbarians in every respect, be possessed by nihilism, and meet with destruction.
Falling away bit by bit from their lifespan, physical form, strength, and sacred knowledge,
and being oppressed by barbarians, those barbarians indeed repeatedly go to their destruction.
Deprived of their wealth, afflicted by many diseases, and ruined by drought and other calamities, they perish.
The forest-dwellers will become destitute and deprived of their livelihoods;
cities, villages, and the like will be destroyed, and people will lose their mutual affection.
Taking refuge in rivers and mountains, they will resort to intermixture of castes and become hunchbacked.
Like fishermen, those dwelling in the forest become eaters of fish.
At that time, they subsist on deer, fish, birds, beasts of prey, tigers, honey, vegetables, fruits, roots, and small creatures. (53–54)
They wear rags, various leaves, bark garments, and skins;
they wear loincloths and have taken up a life dependent on animals.
Dwelling by rivers, they tend goats, sheep, donkeys, and camels.
Having many children, lacking food, and devoid of purity and proper conduct,
they will then adopt increasingly base and unrighteous ways, resorting to the status of beasts.
The Brahmins will become like Śūdras, performing rites such as the employment of mantras for malevolent purposes.
In the home, women will be the chief counselors and brothers-in-law will be the primary authorities;
the marital bond will be subject to sale, and there will be a state of mindlessness leading to separation.
Holy places will be afflicted by Yavanas, and the gods will be insulted by Cāṇḍālas. (58)
In the Kali age, righteous practices have been destroyed by barbarians and reduced to a single uniformity.
There is no yogi, no perfected one, no man of knowledge, nor anyone who meditates upon Brahman; everything is empty due to impotence. Behold, O Lakṣmī, the power of the Kali age! (1.215.60)
In the Kali age, countries will always be destitute of food, Brahmins will be sellers of stories, and women will always be sellers of their charms. Indeed,
all people— deceitful and wicked, devoid of substance— will act like demons of sin.
The subjects are indeed like mere husks—devoid of grain and lacking sprouts.
(62) This story is heard by all, yet it is maintained by no one.
In the Kali age, during the auspicious month of Śrāvaṇa, the very essence of the narrative shall have departed. (63)
In the Kali age, when the welfare of those following external paths has declined, people may bathe at sacred fords, dwell there, and observe vows,
yet the essence of their discourse will have vanished for those whose minds are agitated by desire, anger, fear, greed, and thirst. (64)

In the Kali age, when the merit of asceticism has vanished due to the lack of self-control of the mind, greed, hypocrisy, and reliance on heretical doctrines, the essence of austerity shall be lost. In the Kali age, when the merit born of meditation has vanished, the essence of meditation shall be lost. (65–66)
Thus, in every place, the very essence of things goes to dissolution;
indeed, by the power of the Yuga, all that [degeneration] occurs, yet there is no fault attributable to anyone.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Observation of the Arising of the Nature, Qualities, and Defects of the Kali Age," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (215)
