Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: When five thousand years of the Kali age have passed, the foremost of sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others, shall depart from the surface of the earth for the abode of Śrī Hari. (1)
The Śālagrāma is the form of Hari, and Jagannātha is a deity;
after a short time has passed, they shall belong to the side of Hari.
Initiations, divine mantras, ritual injunctions, ancestral rites, and water libations [shall likewise follow].
And virtuous deeds shall go to the abode of Hari.
Worship of Hari, as well as that of Hara, and the chanting of His names and qualities—all forms of knowledge of reality shall go to the abode of Hari. (3–4)

Vows, asceticism, fasting, and welcoming the village deities—these do not exist in the Kali age; nor do those who observe periods of ritual impurity and the like. Men of high standing are indeed cruel, full of ego, and murderers.
In the Kali age, there is no mutual distinction among men, nor indeed among women.

(6) Throughout the entire earth, both in the home and in the forest, women are masters over men; they are unchaste and constantly strike their paramours as well as their husbands with threats and reproaches. (7)
In the Kali age, the mistress of the house becomes the wife, and the husband becomes a servant even more wretched than his servants; daughters-in-law become equal to maidservants and slaves;
and those related by birth or kinship become the powerful masters within the home. (8)
In the Kali age, the mother-in-law and the father-in-law alone are the primary authorities in the household.
Even conversation with one's own kinsmen and relatives does not take place; they are regarded as strangers, just like others. (1.216.10)

In the Kali age, those who preach the doctrine of the body and its worldly concerns study the sciences of the barbarians; they are considered superior though devoid of essence, serving as attendants to Śūdras.
Deprived of the sacred thread and lacking any protection, they become cultivators of the soil.
In the Kali age, the twice-born will be devoid of dharma and will perform the work of barbarians;
trees will be devoid of fruit, women will be devoid of offspring,
cows will be devoid of milk, and milk will be devoid of clarified butter.
Husbands and wives will be devoid of affection, and local residents will be bereft of happiness; kings will be lacking in virtue, and the subjects will be oppressed by taxes.
Rivers, streams, ponds, wells, and lakes will be devoid of water.
Among hundreds of thousands, some rare person of merit may perhaps be found, or they may not be found at all.
In the Kali age, men, women, and children are born base and deformed; evil news and wicked paths prevail. (16, 19)
In the Kali age, cities and villages will surely no longer exist; people will dwell among trees and in pits, subsisting on leaves like rabbits for a long time.
Forests will arise upon the lands of villages and cities.
In the Kali age, rivers, ponds, crops, fields, and forests [will perish];
wealth is seen nowhere for one who has resorted to the livelihood of a beast.
There is trust in truth placed in a rogue, and the status of merit is attributed to a sinner.
In the Kali age, those who are unrefined are considered refined; the lecherous are counted as those who have conquered their senses; prostitutes are reckoned as venerable chaste women;
paramours there are regarded as observers of the vow of Brahman; and those who consort with all women are considered lifelong celibates.
In the Kali age, those who conceal their sins while appearing as ascetics, those who revile others yet consider themselves truthful,
those who are killers yet appear compassionate, those who are thieves yet wear the ornaments of the virtuous,
and those who are beggars yet are deceivers— they indeed come into being.

In the Kali age, those who serve the lowly, those who serve the great, those who delight others with tales of hatred, those who provide laughter, the dull-witted, and hunters— these indeed are to be honored.
Even in childhood, they are afflicted by disease and old age, becoming grey-haired in a very short time.
In the Kali age, even at fifteen years of age, women become very old.
A five-year-old girl may have her menses and bear children;
a woman who gives birth within six months becomes aged by twelve.
For the most part, they were frequently barren, those who caused miscarriages,
gamblers, sellers of daughters, and sellers of sons in every respect;
they were intent on procuring paramours for their mothers, wives, and daughters-in-law.
Those who live by violating the modesty of maidens and sisters,
those who sell the names of Hari, those who perform acts of charity for the sake of fame, and those who steal the livelihoods of gods, brahmins, and gurus. (27–28)
In the Kali age, men who engage in sexual intercourse with their daughters-in-law, mothers-in-law, daughters, co-wives, sisters, and female snakes,
as well as those who consort with the wives of their brothers,
abandon their birth-status and wander about.
In the Kali age, there is no certainty regarding wives or husbands;
likewise, those who hold authority over subjects, property,
or villages are all speakers of falsehood, and thieves prevail by force in the Kali age.
In the Kali age, people are indeed destroyers of men, as well as destroyers of women; they are destroyers of their elders and destroyers of the Dharma.
They engage in the trade of lac, metals, poisons, and salt.
In the Kali age, they act as masters over their sons and even their wives.
Indeed, unchaste women, usurers, those without husbands, procuresses, menstruating women,
widows, and beggars prevail within the kitchen.
There is no certainty regarding the types of food, nor is there any certainty regarding the origins [of beings].

There is no certainty regarding the marks [of gender], and for children, there is none at all. Trees are measured by the span of a hand, and human beings are measured by the *vitasti* (the distance between the extended thumb and little finger).
At that time, at the end of the age, animals will be only half a span in size.
There will be the slaughter of the virtuous, the elders, and the ascetics;
there will be constant fear of drought as well as the ruin of countries.
In the Kali age, men and women alike will die from the heat of poison, perish by firebrands, and meet their destruction all at once; this will occur through ill-performed sacrifices,
poorly studied texts, evil deeds, and false scriptures.
In the Kali age, there is the downfall of both the brahmins due to the defects of their actions and of the subjects.
Among men in the Tiṣya age, there arise violence, deceit, envy, anger, malice, and intolerance; O Rāma, there is also cruelty and greed among people.
In that Kali age, there are disturbances, conflicts, and afflictions among every person;
there are all kinds of relations—even with those of the lowest birth—through sleeping and eating together.
Lifespan, intelligence, strength, beauty, and noble lineage all perish.
In the Kali age, there will also be ḍākinīs, Māriṇīs, and female practitioners of mantras.
There will be an increase in beasts of prey and a decline in cattle;
and when the terrible Kali age has set in, the sacred traditions will perish.
At that time, the gods will rain down variegated things, and people will have variegated offspring;
merchants will use false measures, and those of evil character will take on the appearance of hunters.
The world will be full of beggars and devoid of gratitude.

In the Kali age, people become mentally deranged and reckless; they have disheveled hair and dress as women. There will be thieves of grain and thieves of clothing, even thieves of thieves, and indeed, plunderers of those who themselves plunder. ||45-46||
In the Kali age, insects, mice, and snakes even assault human beings;
having committed the slaughter of women, children, and cattle, or having killed one another,
they destroy their own lineage while seeking personal comfort.
In the Kali age, due to suffering, fear, and unrighteousness, people will indeed turn away from dharma and become dominated by tamas.
In the Tretā age, dharma lasted for four months; in the Dvāpara, it lasted for one month; but in the Kali age, for those who are atheists and powerless, it lasts for only a single day.

In the Kali age, there is always the neglect of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the neglect of Vedic study (*brahman*), and the neglect of purificatory rites and sacrifices; as well as the neglect of rules regarding menstruation, birth-impurity, and untouchability.
There is also the neglect of purification for cooked and uncooked food, and the cleansing of the mouth by rinsing with water. (1.216.50)
In the Kali age, the purification of corpses, cremation grounds, and so forth will perish.
Temples and images, as well as the worship of the great ones, will then [decline];
and in the Kali age, acts of benevolence toward others and charitable almshouses will perish.

In the Kali age, the distinctions between virtuous and widowed women, those residing in households and those who are householders, as well as the distinctions between those worthy of honor and those bound by social restraints, perish.
Furthermore, the discernment between those deserving of punishment and those not, and the channels for determining who is to be protected and who is not, fall away.
In the Kali age, the discernment between those who should be served and those who should not will perish.
At that time in the Kali age, women, cows, and virgins shall become as strong as oxen; even in the court of justice, women and outcastes shall occupy the royal throne.
In that Kali age, there will indeed arise the empire of the outcaste (śvapaca);
the rule of the shaveling, the rule of the youth, and the rule of self-interest will prevail forever in the Kali age.
In the Kali age, there shall be the rule of the powerful, the rule of the rogue, and the rule of the naked.
In the Kali age, that which is seen as truth and whatever else is considered invalid;
in the Kali age, there is quickly an equality of wealth, an equality of palaces, and an equality of inheritance;
in the Kali age, there is an equality of people, an equality of actions, and an equality of nakedness.
In the Kali age, O Guhyaka, there is equality with women, equality with men, and equality with the aged; there is equality in action, equality in armor, and equality in suffering.
There is equality in the face, equality in the hair, and equality in the breasts and the head.
In that Kali age, there will be equality with the naked, equality of thighs, and equality of the womb.
There will be an equality between oil, ghee, fat, clarified butter, water, and poverty;
and an equality between milk, curd, *haiyaṅgavīna* (fresh butter), and so forth, during that Kali age.

In the Kali age, sugarcane, tubers, fruits, roots, sugar, molasses, and other such granular sweets; as well as sweet, salty, pungent, and bitter tastes—all these will become equal [in quality]. Likewise, equality of speech, equality of action, equality of form, and uniformity of dress [will prevail]. (62)
In the Kali age, there will be equality among gods, humans, yakṣas, and nāgas (63).
There will then be an equality of festivals, grief, erotic passion, vehicles, and seats,
as well as an equality of mind among children, youths, the elderly, and heroes (64).

In the Kali age, there is equality in the loss of one's own interests and those of others, as well as in the loss of friends and enemies; there is equality in decline, equality in expenditure, and equality in hunger.
There is equality in the seasons, equality in the rains, and equality between night and day.

In that Kali age, there will be a similarity between the states of sleep and waking; then, beds, couches, grass mats, granaries, and water-jars will be considered equal [in value]. Furthermore, forts, walls, gate-towers, and courtyards will be regarded as equivalent. (66–67)

In the Kali age, there is an equality between living in forests, gardens, wildernesses, hamlets, and villages; humans, cattle, birds, and the like are equal to insects. Instructions, teachings, and injunctions are treated as mere idle chatter and sophistry.
In the Kali age, there is an equality in the failure of the certainty of true causes;
Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī share the same fate as widows in the Kali age;
and in the Kali yuga, the learned who subsist on their own efforts are equal to eunuchs.
In the Kali age, indeed, there is a similarity between rains and the sky, a similarity between agricultural labors and time,
and a similarity between the earth and the back of a tortoise; likewise,
there is a similarity between faces and eclipses, and a similarity between hearts and the sound of a bursting bubble.
In the Kali age, there is indeed a similarity between love and war.
In the Tiṣya age, there is a similarity between virtuous deeds and the restraint of the senses.
In the Kali age, there is no similarity in the signs of either [of these] regarding theistic conviction.
Furthermore, when the Kṛta Yuga arrives, the world will once again become animated;
through the yoga of Hari, it will likewise become blissful, endowed with the power of Brahman, filled with all prosperity, and possessed of all dharma, action, and qualities. (74)
Thus has this *kalpa* been described to you; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Specific Description of the Dharmas of the Kali Age," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 216. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*).
Chapter 217 [Author: Chapter 218 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear about that ground which was brought here by King Ānarta through his own austerity during the first Dvāpara age,
where the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa has eternally established His residence.
"O Lord, tell me the great majesty of that sacred ford (tīrtha), along with its history.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"In the most terrible Kali age, which is frequented by many heretics..."
I shall describe for the sake of crossing over at this great holy ford; listen to me.
Situated along the shore of the western ocean is that which was established by King Kuśa as Kuśasthalī. 3–4.
Even before that, the region of the earth brought by the King of Ānarta was indeed the city of Ānarta; it existed prior to all others,
where the Gomatī flows and joins with the ocean.
And that city of Dvāravatī is celebrated by the name Ānarta.
There dwells Hari, the soul of the universe, who eternally bestows liberation;
he is endowed with sixteen digits (kalās) and joined with twelve forms.
That Dvārakā is indeed blessed, for there the four-armed Kṛṣṇa resides;
having gone there, people shall attain liberation in age after age.
Ānarta was indeed a great devotee; he was the son of Śaryāti.
And when the kingdom was being divided by his father, he did not accept his own share. Likewise, the devoted Arthaka instructed his father:
"This human body of mine is intended solely for liberation."
"This king must not be allowed to perish; he is a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpabhūruha) difficult to find.
For by me alone can liberation be achieved here, through this [king] who is equal to a thought-gem (cintāmaṇi).
Having heard what was thus spoken by his father, [he replied: "What you consider improper..."
"In my lineage, no son who fails to rule the kingdom is pleasing to me.
Either accept a share of the kingdom, or else go to another land.
Having heard this from his father, Ānarta bowed and departed for the western region.
On the shore of the salt ocean, where the ground was covered with sand,
he performed austerities for a long time, worshipping Hari by the name of Kṛṣṇa.
Then Kṛṣṇa, being pleased, approached the presence of that devotee.
He said to Ānarta, "O my devotee! What dwells in your mind?
Choose a boon—blessings upon you—I shall grant whatever you desire.
Having prostrated himself like a staff, he replied, "O Lord, lead me to Goloka! (15–16)
"I have no thirst for anything whatsoever, nor do I have any attachment to the body;
I have no regard for the purpose of asceticism other than service at your feet.
Laughing, the Blessed One said, "Listen, O devotee, to that which is for your benefit!"
Exiled by your father, you perform penance for my sake.
A great kingdom, which has come under the absolute control of your father, must be given to you by me;
come with me, and I shall grant you a divine realm upon earth.

Having done this, Śrī Kṛṣṇa took him along and departed for his abode in Goloka. Having divided a divine portion from his own Goloka, he bestowed it upon Ānarta, saying, "Accept this auspicious jewel."
"Go to the divine world and then to the earthly realm where you performed your austerities.
There, indeed, install this fragment of a jewel on a beautiful seashore.
This shall become a sovereign kingdom under your independent rule."
Having thus fulfilled their hopes and led them to a portion of Goloka,
Anarta returned to the land on the shore of the western ocean.
As soon as the jewel was released there, it attained a vast expansion.
A hundred yojanas in extent, it was a supreme and divine ground.
That new earthly realm became a divine kingdom.
Then, because Kṛṣṇa was remembered by Ānarta, it thereafter became the city of Ānartapura.
The royal capital was constructed exactly as Kṛṣṇa had directed.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa arrived there at the time of worship and said to him:
"Therefore, I must dwell here at the conclusion of the Dvāpara age."
"Establish a most excellent and delightful city that abides in me.
Following the path instructed by Kṛṣṇa, Ānarta also established that auspicious and divine city as the foremost one, possessing the splendor of the abode of Goloka. (27–28)
Thus, this region of Ānarta, characterized by its serene beauty, is frequented [by the virtuous].
This very territory of Surāṣṭra, composed of sacred fords (tīrthas), is the bestower of liberation.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Thereafter, after some time, by the waters of the ocean...
Many times this city had been submerged by floods of water.
When, at the end of the Dvāpara age, Kṛṣṇa set his mind on coming there,
not even a village or a very well-situated city could be found.
Afterwards, Kṛṣṇa himself, joined by his brother Saṃkarṣaṇa, bowed to his parents; then Hari called Garuḍa to mind.
Standing at the foot of a banyan tree in Madhupurī, he called the ocean to mind.
He remembered Viśvakarman and assumed the guise of a king;
then, casting off the attire of a cowherd, he called to mind his eternal discus,
Sudarśana, which arrived with a splendor equal to ten million suns.
He bore that Sudarśana, the most effective of all weapons, which was equal to Kṛṣṇa in brilliance and the destroyer of all enemies;
and Garuḍa also appeared, bringing forward his jewel-adorned vehicle.
Viśvakarmā and the artisans went to the vicinity of the ocean.
Seeing them, the Ocean trembled; having bowed down, he presented himself before them.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to the Ocean: "A space of ten yojanas shall be yours as dry land."
"Give me a portion of Goloka for the sake of my city.
Immediately, the ocean rendered that much of the earth waterless;
that divine region of Goloka shone forth as if it were another [world].
He spoke to Viśvakarman himself: "Level the ground!
O artisan, build for me a city that is beautiful in the three worlds, delightful, most divine, and desirable to women. (1.217.40)
And it shall be the desired abode for my devotees, supreme and like Goloka,
the crown of all heavens and my own dwelling place.
O Garuḍa, day and night you shall remain in the presence of Viśvakarman.
"Remain for the sake of the city until he builds my city.
And, O Sudarśana, remain by my side day and night.
Having thus commanded him, Kṛṣṇa himself departed for Madhupurī.
Every evening, Viśvakarmā would indeed approach Kṛṣṇa;
he reported what work had been completed and also considered what was yet to be done.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for his part, explained the sequence of construction to Viśvakarmā.
The city, extending for ten yojanas, was exceedingly beautiful.
It was adorned with rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and deep blue stones,
as well as with rucakas, pāribhadrakas, palaṅkas, and syamantakas.
With fragrant substances, as well as with gālima and sūryakānta stones;
with moonstones (candrakānta), with gold-precipitating suhīraka gems;
and with yellow, green, dark, and white-colored crystals.
With yellow substances like *gorocanā* and the forms of pomegranate seeds;
with lotus seeds possessing their own juices and blue lotus pigments;
and with dark, clear, and radiant gems resembling collyrium.
With white [garments] having the luster of campaka flowers, resembling molten gold, of great value and many virtues, beautiful with reddish-yellow hues,
and with the most precious, excellent, and noble gems, jewels, and diamonds.
"According to the prescribed rule and as is appropriate, wherever and whatever is desired—
perform now for me the divine [rite] for sixteen thousand women,
and also for the one hundred and eight other wives."
The camp, surrounded by excellent moats and high walls, was provided with twelve halls and beautifully adorned with lion-gates;
its doors and other features were well-decorated with paintings of the three colors and other designs. (53)
It was beautifully adorned with groves of *nākiya* trees, gardens, circular pavilions, and the like;
it possessed auspicious characteristics, a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*), a moon-piercing device (*candravedha*), and a sun-house (*ravigṛha*).
It contained the knowledge of the circle of constellations (*nakṣatracakra*), the knowledge of the elements (*bhūtajñāna*), and the wheel of the seasons (*ṛtucakra*). (54–55)
It possessed an assembly hall, a slaughterhouse, a subterranean chamber, and an aerial pavilion;
it contained a lecture hall equipped with sound-amplifying machines, a hall for hearing from afar,
a hall for seeing from afar, and was provided with lightning chambers and other such facilities.
There shall be knowledge of the seasons, knowledge of the earth, and likewise knowledge of the winds;
there shall be knowledge of the ground and knowledge of portents.
Arrange all of that in that city on a suitable site.
Have beautiful hermitages for the Yadus and houses for the servants built,
as well as residences, gardens, and pleasure-grounds for the laborers. And for King Ugrasena, build a palace that surpasses all others and is worthy of heaven.
"Build a beautiful hermitage, a mansion auspicious in every way;
likewise, construct for my father Vasudeva a divine, vast, and preeminent hermitage endowed with all perfections and renown."
Viśvakarman spoke to Hari with the desire to inquire about the excellence of trees:
"Which trees are commendable, and which likewise are forbidden? Which ones bestow auspiciousness and which bring misfortune? O Teacher of the World, please tell me of them. (62)
To whom does the army belong, and where is the camp, whether it be comfortable or uncomfortable?
O Lord, tell me in which direction the water is auspicious and in which it is inauspicious;
and in which direction does a planted tree indeed bestow prosperity?
O Lord, tell me the dimensions of the houses and the courtyards;
O benefactor, in which direction are the groves of trees and the flower gardens?
Also, what are the measurements of the ramparts, the moats, and the gates?
O Lord, tell me the dimensions of the various types of dwellings and palaces.
O Lord, tell me also which wood from which specific tree is auspicious for a house, and which woods would be inauspicious; tell me that as well, O Lord. (66–67)
Then Kṛṣṇa said to the carpenter: "Listen, having performed meditation:
a coconut tree in a hermitage bestows wealth upon householders;
if it is in the northeast or the east of the camp, that tree bestows sons. (68)
The charming king of trees, the *rasāla* (mango), brings auspiciousness everywhere;
in the east, it bestows prosperity upon men.
The *bilva*, *panasa* (jackfruit), and *badarī* (jujube) are considered to grant happiness at all times. (1.217.70)
In the east they bestow progeny, and in the south they bestow wealth;
everywhere they bestow prosperity, and from them the householder prospers.
The Jambū tree, the pomegranate, the plantain, and likewise the Āmrātaka—
In the east, it bestows kinsmen; in the south, it bestows friends.
Likewise, in the south it grants eloquence, and in the west, it bestows happiness and joy.
A tree situated at the side of a house bestows wealth and sons everywhere.
A *campaka* tree near the house, however, bestows auspiciousness everywhere;
in the northeast (*īśāna*), it likewise grants happiness and brings about gold and other riches.
An *alābu*, a large *kuṣmāṇḍa*, an *āyāmbu*, and a *kiṃśuka* [should also be planted there].
The date palm and the karkaṭī gourd are auspicious when grown within the camp;
the vāstūka, the kārabilva, and the eggplant (vārtāka) bestow happiness.
Furthermore, climbing plants and their fruits, when cultivated beside the house, grant well-being.
Likewise, fruit-bearing trees and flowering trees always bestow auspiciousness;
similarly, fruit-bearing creepers and flowering creepers likewise bestow auspiciousness.
In every way, trees, creepers, grasses, along with their fragrances, flowers, and fruits [are auspicious].
Indeed, only auspicious things arise, bestowing sons, wealth, and prosperity.
Whatever [trees] have leaves of various colors and wonderful flowers,
even their trunks become gentle and grant happiness.
Listen now to those that are praised, as well as those that are prohibited.
Wild trees are forbidden, as are those devoid of fruit and flowers.
[This applies] in the house, the palace, the garden, the city, and likewise at the city gate.
The trees of the forest are not considered auspicious when they are barren or prohibited;
where vultures, herons, and crows dwell, and where those spirits and piśācas reside,
they are indeed forbidden and devoid of fragrance.
The banyan tree (*vaṭa*) is forbidden within a camp, as it constantly inspires fear of thieves;
however, when seen in cities or on vast stretches of land, it bestows merit.
The silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*) is not recommended in a camp, a city, or a village.
It is considered to be constantly a source of suffering for kings;
it is not prohibited in a village or a city, nor on the outskirts, but it is strictly forbidden in a place of learning, because it is always a bringer of misery. (84–85)
The tamarind tree causes the destruction of wealth and the ruin of the subjects;
it is strictly forbidden in a military camp, while in a city its presence is merely slight.
It is not forbidden anywhere; it is established both in villages and in cities.
A wise man should always avoid that which is forbidden in a place of learning (a school).
Both the date palm (*kharjūra*) and the *gahu* tree are forbidden within a camp;
they are also forbidden in a village or a city, but not in an area outside [of these]. || 87–88 ||
Indeed, trees of chickpeas and other grains are truly auspicious;
whether in a village, a city, a camp, or a house, they should be placed on all sides.
Sugarcane stalks are always bringers of good fortune and constant increasers of prosperity.
The Aśoka, the Śirīṣa, and the Kadamba bestow auspiciousness.
Haridrā should be understood as a giver of auspiciousness, and likewise Ārdrakas are givers of auspiciousness.
Harītakīs are givers of auspiciousness, and Āmalakīs bestow auspiciousness.
The bone of elephants brings auspiciousness; the bone of horses brings happiness;
[the bones] of monkeys, humans, donkeys, and even cows [are likewise beneficial].
However, the bones of cocks, jackals, and cats are inauspicious.
The bone of a wild boar found in the bladder [region] bestows auspiciousness.
(93) Furthermore, water to the northeast, east, west, and north of the camp is auspicious; elsewhere, it is indeed inauspicious. (94)
One should not construct a temple on ground that is low-lying, uneven, or irregular.
A square house or palace built on such ground causes the destruction of wealth for its inhabitants.
Furthermore, [the length] should be free from zero and likewise free from three.

An auspicious house and city become empty and bring emptiness to men. For houses, a doorway that is two cubits wide and three cubits long before the threshold brings good fortune to both the enclosure wall and the house. (96–97)
In the central region (Madhyadeśa), nothing should be done that is deficient or excessive;

it is auspicious [to build] a square camp with a "moon-piercing" (candravedha) layout, which bestows well-being. A camp with a "sun-piercing" (sūryabheda) layout is inauspicious and does not grant prosperity.
The courtyard that brings inauspiciousness and causes the piercing of the sun does not bestow welfare.
But when the auspicious Tulasī is always planted within the camp, it bestows wealth and progeny, as well as dharma and liberation. (1.217.100)
Mālatī, Yūthikā, Kunda, Mādhava, as well as Ketakī, Nāgacampaka, Mallikā, Dhattūra, Bakula,
and the auspicious Aparājitā— these bring good fortune; their garden bestows wealth.
In the east and the south, it likewise bestows auspiciousness and happiness.
A householder should not construct a house higher than sixteen cubits;
a wall higher than twenty cubits does not bring good fortune.
One should not allow an oil-presser, a goldsmith seeking to purchase diamonds and such, or a carpenter to reside within the garden or in the middle of the village.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, virtuous Śūdras, and astrologers are auspicious [to have nearby].

One should station a skilled physician and a florist near the camp. A moat for the rampart measuring one hundred cubits is recommended; however, for the camps themselves, a width of ten cubits all around is recommended.
A secret gate protected by a moat is highly recommended, provided it has a prearranged signal.
There should also be *tintiḍī*, *śālmali*, *hintāla*, and *sindhuvāraka* trees;
likewise, *nimba*, *udumbara*, *dhattūra*, *eraṇḍa*, and *vaṭa* trees.
Since inauspicious trees bestow suffering, one should not plant them within the camp. Furthermore, the king should always avoid the *vajrahasta* tree;
for it destroys sons, wives, and wealth, and therefore he must not establish it there.

Having received this command from Hari, Viśvakarmā slept at the foot of a banyan tree on the shore of the ocean; there, in a dream, he beheld Dvārakā. Seeing Viśvakarmā, the gods, who were intent on performing their task well, [spoke].
Those by whom Dvārakā was constructed laughed at him as he slept;
for it had been perfectly completed during the night, just as it was seen in his dream.
Upon waking in the morning, the artisan beheld the auspicious Dvārakā.
Buddha beheld that city of Pūrṇā, which Viśvakarmā had built with modesty,
extending for ten *yojanas* exactly as Śrī Kṛṣṇa had described,
and shining with excellence as it surpassed the cities of Brahmā and the other gods.
And with their splendors, they adorned the second heaven with heaps of jewels. In the meantime, O Lakṣmī, the lords of the fourteen worlds arrived at dawn itself to behold Dvārāvatī.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Construction of Dvārakā, Complete with Auspicious and Inauspicious Trees, Creepers, and Other Features, in Saurāṣṭra— which consists of the portion of Goloka brought by Ānarta, the son of Śaryāti"— within the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 217 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*)
Chapter 218 [Author:
Chapter 219 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Brahmā arrived with his consort to behold the city,
as did Bhava accompanied by Bhavānī, Ananta, Dharma, and Bhāskara;
and Hutāśa, Kubera, Varuṇa, Pavana, and Yama.
Then the eleven Rudras, Candra, Mahendra, and likewise the Vasus,
the Ādityas, Kinnaras, Daityas, and Gandharvas arrived.
Seated in their celestial chariots at the foot of the banyan tree, they paid homage to Kṛṣṇa, who was standing there.
Praised by them, they beheld Dvārakā— delightful and exceedingly enchanting,
resplendent with rows of pearls, rubies, diamonds, and various gems;
it was square on all sides and ten yojanas in extent.
It was well-encircled by seven deep moats,
provided with nine ramparts, and adorned with lakes for water-sports,
as well as various aquatic flowers such as white lilies, blue lotuses, and red lotuses.
It was adorned on all sides with *sarvatobhadra* trees and flowering gardens,
beautified by blossoming flowers and made fragrant by the breeze;
it was graced with slow-growing sandalwood trees and *tulasī* shrubs.
It was made fragrant by gentle, cool breezes carrying sweet scents;
it was exceedingly beautiful with groves of coconut trees and areca palms,
and it was further adorned with hundreds of thousands of betel-nut trees.
Furthermore, it was beautifully adorned with mango trees possessing fourfold qualities,
and illuminated on all sides by as many breadfruit trees;
likewise, it was filled with palmyra trees, as well as *aśvattha*, *badarī*, and other such trees.
With *vaṭa*, *āmratika*, *bilva*, *jambu*, *kadamba*, and *vaṃśaka* trees;
with *śālmali*, *tintiḍī*, *nāraṅga*, *jambīra*, and *dāḍima*;
and with *campaka*, *bakula*, *nāgeśvara*, *arjuna*, and *kharjūra* trees. (11–12)
It was completely covered on all sides by canes, golden *kāñcana* trees, *harītakī* and *dhātrī* trees,
moon-like [white] blossoms, *śāla*, *priyāla*, *hintāla*, cool *saptaparṇa* trees, and creepers,
and it was adorned with golden pitchers.
It was endowed with nine hundred thousand beautiful palaces and lovely, lofty mansions;
it was adorned with pearls and rubies fashioned from the finest essence of gems,
and its temples featured golden domes set with rubies, diamonds, and precious stones.
It possessed stairs, door-panels, and walls fashioned from jewels;
its pillars were made of emeralds and its floors of white crystal;
it was adorned with mirrors and chowries of variegated, wondrous, and extremely fine fabrics.
Its courtyards were fashioned with rubies, its noble mansions were white, and it was provided with streets and lanes filled with sapphires;
it was beautified by royal highways whose centers and other parts were inlaid with jewels. (17–18)
Blazing with the brilliance of jewels like the midday sun in summer,
it possessed rows of great palaces and other structures endowed with hundreds of thousands of windows;
it had elephant stables, horse stables, and lattices of swans and *garuḍa*s.
Having thus beheld the beautiful Dvārakā, all the assembled gods marveled.
The region of Ānarta shone upon its hundred-yojana expanse of earth;
joined by Dvārakā, it appeared as if doubled in splendor.
Then Kṛṣṇa remembered Vasudeva and Devakī,
Ugrasena and the Yādavas, and the Pāṇḍavas along with their mother;
he remembered Nanda, Yaśodā, the cowherds, the Gandharvas, the Kinnaras, and the sages.
All of them, being thus remembered, arrived while crying out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!
By the power of Kṛṣṇa, those divine beings—Vidyādharīs, Kinnarīs, dancers, and singers—possessing the splendor of divine movement through the sky, [came there]. (23–24)
Singers, musicians, bards, astrologers, and mendicants;
kings residing in many lands, physicians, and Brahmins;
renunciants, ascetics, forest-dwellers, and celibate students.
Likewise, the Avadhūtas, the Siddhas, and the Munis arrived;
namely Sananda, Sanaka, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra,
Sanatsujāta, Voḍha, Pañcaśikha, and Āsuri.
Hundreds of thousands of people came there, observers of the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*); Durvāsas also arrived there, accompanied by ten thousand disciples.
The Lord himself, whose nature is that of the Great Brahman, was present, devoted to his wife.
Accompanied by a hundred thousand disciples, he came to the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
Kaśyapa arrived with a hundred thousand disciples, Vālmīki with a thousand,
Gautama with a hundred thousand disciples, and Bṛhaspati with ten million gods.
Śukra also had ten million disciples, Bharadvāja one hundred thousand, Aṅgiras ten thousand, Vasiṣṭha ten thousand,
Pracetas a hundred, and Pulastya was joined by a thousand.
Agastya arrived with ten thousand disciples, and Pulaha with a thousand;
Kratu came with a hundred disciples, as did Atri and Bhṛgu with their followers;
likewise, Marīci arrived there with a thousand disciples.
Śatānanda followed with five hundred attendants, as did Pāṇini; and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and Vibhāṇḍaka went accompanied by a thousand disciples;
likewise Kātyāyana and Yājñavalkya went with a thousand followers.
Vyāsa [was accompanied] by a thousand disciples, Garga by more than a hundred disciples,
Gālava by a hundred, Saubhari by twenty people,
Lomaśa by ten lakhs, and Mārkaṇḍeya by three lakhs. (35–36)
Sāndīpani and Devala were each with hundreds of their own disciples;
Boḍu and Pañcaśikha were both accompanied by sixty disciples and their disciples’ disciples;
and Nara and Nārāyaṇa were with ascetics in great numbers.
Viśvāmitra and Vatsa likewise departed with thousands of disciples;
Jaratkāru and Āstīka, Paraśurāma and Dakṣaka, Saṃvarta, Jaimini, and Paila also went with their own followers.
Upamanyu, Śukadeva, Kaca, Gauramukha, as well as Lālāyana and others, Aśvatthāman and Droṇa,
Kṛpa, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and likewise other deities of the ages (yugadevatās).
Sudivya, Kambha, and the one named Gopāla arrived together with their disciples.
In the rite for the consecration of the site (vāstukarman), there were the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Yakṣas,
the Cāraṇas, the Pitṛs, the Rudras, the Mātṛkās, and the guardians of the directions.
The four classes of beings beginning with those born from the soil, as well as those dwelling in the netherworlds and below,
the planets, lunar mansions, and stars— all arrived at the abode of Kṛṣṇa;
likewise the Vasus, the treasures (Nidhis), and the other Seven Sages.
The Prajāpatis, the Manus, and the Vālakhilyas were present in their entirety;
as were the six seasons beginning with spring, born from the families of Dharma and Adharma;
the Apsarases headed by Kāma, the Parya goddesses, and the female servants.
Virtuous ascetics, female ascetics, renunciants free from passion, and indeed female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga—these alone may enter; or Kṛṣṇa himself may indeed construct the dwelling.
Likewise, the Avadhūtīs, Caṇḍīs, Durgās, Māyās, Ramās, and so forth [may do so].
The goddesses Lakṣmī, Jayā, Vijayā, and others; the friends who are daughters of Maṇikya;
Prabhā, Pārvatī, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī; the gopīs and gopas residing in Goloka, as well as those dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha. 47–48.
Then maidens and youths, as well as female and male celibate students (brahmacārin), arrived;
likewise, the Śaktis, the Smṛddhis, and the personified Siddhis came forth.
The principles (tattvas), the Vedic scriptures, and various auspicious branches of knowledge also appeared.
The qualities, the power of sovereignty, those who were liberated and those who were not,
the four stages of life, the social classes, the wretched, embodied beings without protectors, and even the worlds and the non-worlds all came when Kṛṣṇa was building his dwelling. (1.218.50–51)
Listen, Lakṣmī! What need is there for me to describe that land where all the holy places and the lords of the lords of holy places have assembled?
Dvārakā is the supreme among all holy places, the most excellent, and the bestower of abundant merit.
By merely entering it, birth and death are destroyed;
charity, ancestral rites, and worship of the gods yield infinite fruits. Among all sacred fords, what sacred ford is superior to Dvārakā, which is the very embodiment of all holy places? (53–54)
The great king Ugrasena always resided within Dvārakā at his own abode, which surpassed even the palace of Mahendra, by the command of Kṛṣṇa.
He beheld the gate guarded by thousands of doorkeepers.
And within the inner camp, from the six very gates,
there were hundreds of palaces resplendent with jeweled fruit;
likewise, ten thousand rutting lordly elephants and ten thousand horses.
The bull among kings beheld ten thousand camels and likewise ten thousand chariots, as well as fifty thousand charioteers.
Within that delightful interior, he saw a multitude of gods and sages gathered together.
He entered the divine assembly hall named Sudharmā, which was furnished with golden lion-thrones,
adorned with pure silken cloths, and radiant with the luster of jewels;
he entered that beautiful hall and heard the resonant sound of conch shells.
Hearing the sound of kettledrums and the chanting of the sages,
Hari and Balarāma entered the assembly hall where Ugrasena was present;
likewise, Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Śeṣa— the preeminent among the gods— were there.
All the gods, sages, and likewise human beings rose up.
By the command of Hari, Garga, and the gods, Ugrasena, the lord of kings, sat upon a beautiful jeweled throne. (62–63)
There, Nārada performed the royal consecration for the king with a pitcher filled with water from the seven sacred fords (tīrtha) and Vedic mantras.
A pair of garments was given to him by the high-souled Varuṇa.

Baladeva gave him separately garlands of *pārijāta* flowers, sandalwood paste, jewel ornaments, and such things as a jeweled parasol. Brahmā gave him a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and Maheśvara gave him a trident.

Pārvatī gave a necklace of jewels and a crown; Kṛṣṇa himself [gave gifts]; the lords of kings gave golden ornaments, as did the subjects with their offerings. Others, the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds, gave wedding gifts.
Vasudeva gave him two white chowries;
Nanda gave the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), and Yaśodā gave a garland of jewels.
At the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Akrūra held the umbrella out of devotion.
On a beautiful jeweled throne, the king beheld a mirror;
he heard the auspicious words of the bhaṭṭas, mendicants, and learned brahmins.
Gods, sages, and twice-born priests bestowed auspicious blessings upon him.
Mādhava gave jewels by the millions to the brahmins who were mendicants;
he bestowed garments, food, drink, and golden vessels in great abundance upon all those worthy recipients of charity.
Hari Kṛṣṇa, the source of all auspiciousness, performed the Vāstuyajña sacrifice;
he indeed fed everyone with foods that were pleasing to their taste.
In the assembly hall, the inhabitants of the world bowed down before the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
And they said: "O Blessed One, Dvārakā is delightful and exceedingly enchanting;
protected by Your arms, it is purifying and the destroyer of sins.
Indeed, no other city such as this exists here within the entire universe. (74–75)
"Those earthly realms of ours have indeed been forgotten through the mere sight of this;
nowhere else is such a supreme, divine place to be seen.
Thus was the city of Dvārakā praised by the gods.
Then Kṛṣṇa began to bestow gifts upon them:
at that time, the gods headed by Brahmā, the lords, the guardians of the world,
the sages, the ascetics, the goddesses, and all those born of the divine race.
The oceans, divine rivers, mountains, and fertile lands;
forests, sacred abodes, cities, groves, and streams;
lakes, ponds, peaks, and caves. (79)
Likewise, temples—both those that were excavated and those that were not—are most purifying.
Having bowed to Hari in embodied form, they earnestly prayed:
"O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, may your auspicious blessings be upon us. (1.218.80–81)
All gifts that bestow the highest good and liberation do not surpass this one;
therefore, O Lord, if it pleases you, we shall request this as our gift:
that we may always remain here in your presence in divine forms.
"By your yoga, great bliss shall indeed be ours forever.
And we shall become purifiers for any assembly of holy places that touches you.
O Lord Śrī Hari, protect us always in Dvārakā. (83–84)
"Have mercy, O Lord of Mercy! We shall dwell here in your abode;
for elsewhere, even the most sinful among us must indeed wash away their sins.
After giving [their merit] to us, they all depart, while we remain shrouded in sin. (85)
We shall fall at your feet and indeed wash them;
we shall become purifiers at your feet.
Therefore, O Lord, grant us a permanent dwelling here in this city of yours.
Wherever we may dwell— here in this forest, on the shore, or outside, and even all around or at its sides— we shall always live happily.
We shall behold you and indeed drink your nectar.
"Having purified ourselves by washing your feet, we shall carry them upon our heads;
thus we shall make our births meaningful here at your two feet.
Hearing this request, Hari then spoke to all those lords:
"May all of you dwell happily in Dvārakā, each according to your station.
This Nārada, my devotee, will show you the sacred sites;
those holy places shall bear your names."
"‘I must remain with you continuously at every single place,’—
having received this command from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self,
all the deities and sacred fords dwelt upon the soil of Ānarta."
To the east, as far as the city boundary; to the south, as far as Mount Raivata;
and to the north, up to the lake named Nārāyaṇa—this entire region, dear to the Earth, became filled with sacred fords and deities at every step. (94)
Then Kṛṣṇa, having invited them all once they had made their quarters,
honored them with sincere devotion and fed them excellent flavors:
fine foods, the most sublime food of sages, and drinking water.
He performed worship for all the sages according to their respective ranks. With joy,
he gave pearls, rubies, coral, gold, supreme wealth, and diamonds,
emeralds, and other gems to those who had arrived.
He gave the jewel of an elephant, the jewel of a cow, and charming horses;
he likewise gave seats, vessels, ornaments, and gems;
and he also gave many grains, crops, and garments.
Mādhava Keśava caused vehicles, draft animals, celestial chariots, and all the requisites suitable for a household to be provided;
he had drums beaten and had auspicious rites performed.
He fed them all and provided lodging for everyone.
Then, having summoned the sacred fords (tīrthas), the Blessed One spoke to them according to the truth: "When the Kali age has arrived, human beings will become sinful."

Dvārakā, the divine city, has been established by me upon this earth as the abode of all sacred fords (tīrthas) for the sake of their deliverance. Those people who are blackened by the impurities of the Kali age, whether they be in the water or on the land here—
Those who perform the rites at the sacred ford shall go to my abode—[that place] which removes birth, death, old age, and disease; which brings supreme joy;
which takes away grief and torment; and which cuts through the very root of karma.

Constantly meditating upon me, Hari, the Supreme Brahman residing in Dvārakā, may they attain devotion and go to the supreme state. When Kali arrives, the destroyer of the very root of dharma, [may they attain it].

There will be no restriction regarding women or men, nor will there be any restriction regarding castes. (107) For the Brahmin, the twilight prayers and so forth will not exist; the mark of the sacred thread will be gone. The sacrificial thread and the sectarian mark (tilaka)—the rest will have vanished. (108)
Devoted to sexual intercourse by day and abstaining from righteous deeds,
men and women will become thieves in every household.
Furthermore, there will be a total disappearance of sacrifices, vows, and ascetic practices.
A husband shall always remain under the control of a woman who acts according to her own will. A woman may strike or revile her husband; in the Kali age, all women are intent upon serving paramours.
Her affection for her lover will be equal to that she has for a hundred sons;
she will give food to her husband as if to a servant out of anger.
Smiling, she looks upon her lover with a glance full of nectar out of desire.

With a poisonous gaze and a cruel look, she regards her husband with anger. She constantly displays such respect and affection toward her paramour as she does not toward her husband; indeed, she perpetually strikes her husband with the palm of her hand. (113–114)
She gives sweet food with faith and devotion to her paramour;
she is constantly dressed in finery and intent upon serving her paramour.
In the Kali age, for women, the paramour is their life-breath, their kinsman, their refuge, and their very self.
The service of guests will be abandoned, and the worship of Viṣṇu will be utterly lost;
in the Kali age, the worship of the ancestors and the gods will cease.
In the Kali age, men will become haters of Viṣṇu and his devotees.
At that time, there will be people who embrace perverse doctrines;
such deceitful men, devoted to the conduct of barbarians, will not even touch a *śālagrāma*, *tulasī*, *kuśa* grass, or the water of the Gaṅgā.
After five thousand years of the Kali age, my worship shall indeed perish.
After four thousand years of the Kali age, the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī,
the sacred fords, and the devotees of Viṣṇu will vanish from the surface of the earth.
At the end of this [age], in the Kali Yuga, all will be intermingled with one another;
they will become a single caste—outcastes (cāṇḍālas)—powerful yet deceitful.
Service to parents, service to the guru, and service to gods and brahmins [will cease].
It is shunned by all people, and likewise by guests.
The earth becomes devoid of crops, the world becomes devoid of rain;
likewise, the trees become devoid of fruit, and the rivers become devoid of water. (122–1223)
A Brāhmaṇa devoid of the Vedas, a king devoid of power,
all people devoid of their caste, and likewise kings who are Mlecchas— these,
O dear one, a son may strike like a servant, as may a disciple strike his teacher. 124.
A householder shall beat his beloved wife like a greedy cock. (125) When dharma has gone to its destruction, then in the Kali age, people will become false toward those who are dear to them. (126)
The connection will be ever new, existing solely for one's own sake.
Those who thrive on the Kali age will become supreme gurus;
they will be even lower than the lowly, performing only base deeds. (127)
In the Kali age, the wicked will not cross over [the ocean of worldly existence] at all without devotion to Hari.
For the sake of their upliftment, Dvārakā—the ground that embodies all sacred fords (tīrthas), which purifies all and is capable of delivering those of the Kali age—is [manifested]. (128–129)
Where not even a trace of the Kali age exists, such a place has been established upon the earth.
Therein, bathing, beholding, vows, worship, and offering prayers;
devotion, drinking the water, bathing in the dust, and chanting [the name]—[all these are accomplished].
"Out of devotion, people will perform [these rites], and they shall go to the supreme state.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of Divine Dvārikā, the Arrival of Innumerable Gods, Sages, and Others, Their Worship, Their Residence, and the Majesty of the Forest Endowed with the Greatness of that Tīrtha," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 218: Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā — Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga)*
Chapter 219 [Author:
Chapter 220 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, O Mahālakṣmī! For that Dvārakā, the abode of the Blessed Lord, is composed of all sacred fords (tīrthas); what more need be said of its excellence? Nevertheless, I shall describe some of the sacred fords as they are.
There, one should indeed go to the principal Gomatī, which takes refuge in Kṛṣṇa.
By the mere sight of her, one is liberated from all sins;
by the mere touch of her, she destroys inauspiciousness and evils.
One should bow to the merit-bestowing water of the Gomatī, which fulfills all desires;
indeed, the water of the Gomatī bestows both spiritual welfare and a favorable rebirth.
Long ago, when the single ocean had arisen and all moving and stationary beings had perished...

Brahmā was born from the navel-lotus; by him indeed were Sanaka and the others produced and commanded for the very purpose of the work of creation. But they, disregarding his word, then departed for the sake of ascetic penance.
Taking up the western direction on the shore of the lord of rivers and streams,
they then desired to behold Hari, whose very nature consists of light.
Having fixed their minds upon Hari, they performed severe penance.
After many thousands of years, the Blessed One himself became pleased.
He set his own discus, Sudarśana, into motion;
Sudarśana, consisting of pure light, pierced the earth and brought forth water. (8–9)
Seeing the discus, which was like the sun, possessed of a thousand spokes, difficult to approach,
the slayer of Daityas and Dānavas, and the eternal protector of devotees,
the sons of Brahmā were struck with wonder at one another.
Then a voice from the sky spoke to those youths:
"O Brahmins, O perfected yogis! Nārāyaṇa himself, Hari, being pleased by your austerity, will manifest directly and swiftly."
At his request, this water appeared before the Arhat.
"Quickly offer the *arghya* with this pure water!
This weapon, pervaded by splendor, is the Sudarśana. (13)
"Therefore, offer this arghya to Śrī Hari, the Lord of the World.
Having heard that, Sanaka and the others praised Sudarśana:
"Obeisance to you whose nature is light; obeisance to you, the weapon of Brahmā!"
"Salutations to you who protect your devotees; salutations to you, the weapon of Viṣṇu!
Salutations again and again to you, the thousand-rayed sun, the unerring one!
Having thus praised him and bowed down, they worshipped him with unblemished offerings.
They prostrated again and again with flowers, leaves, water, and hymns of praise.
Then Hari, Brahmā, and Vasiṣṭha arrived at that place;
delighted by the sons' ascetic penance, they then granted them their vision.
Gangā, though residing in Satyaloka, arrived there in bodily form.
Then Brahmā said to Gangā: "Follow my son Vasiṣṭha to the edge of the ocean; becoming water, dwell within the waters."
Where the gateway of Sudarśana stands and where merit has arisen,
there let your abode always be— a sacred ford that destroys all sins.
O daughter, by the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet, may you forever be auspicious.
"Because you shall always abide in the waters produced by the Sudarśana [discus] of the rays of the cows, let your auspicious name indeed be Gomatī.
Having become a follower of Vasiṣṭha, O daughter, become a river."

"Be like a daughter to me, as a father is to his son"— as Vasiṣṭha’s daughters said this, she replied, "So be it," and set out with them. Because of her watery nature, Gaṅgā followed behind Vasiṣṭha as he went on ahead.
Seeing her, all men, gods, and millions of holy places paid homage to that most meritorious river as she proceeded toward the western ocean;
following Vasiṣṭha, she set out for the abode of Varuṇa.
The highly fortunate ones strewed that river with *sumana* flowers;
the gods and others, filled with wonder, worshipped it with divine garlands, fragrant scents, perfumes, incense, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). || 26-27 ||
"By the mere sight of her, human beings shall attain liberation;
how much more so by performing ablutions, giving gifts, and other rites—such people go to the abode of Hari!
Having spoken thus and offered the *arghya* water, they praised Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Hari.
Clad in yellow silk garments and adorned with a forest garland;
richly perfumed with divine fragrances and endowed with divine golden armlets;
possessing divine ornaments and weapons, and wearing earrings shaped like sea-monsters.
He wears a blazing crown and tiara, his chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa,
and his four long arms grant fearlessness to his devotees;
he is dark as a rain cloud, possesses a gracious countenance, and his lotus feet are served by Lakṣmī.
They bowed down and bowed again, and they praised him repeatedly.
Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, with a gracious mind and supreme affection, spoke to the twice-born,
the gods, and the youths.
"All of you remain here, untouched by my *māyā*;
being wise, liberated, and indeed purifiers, dwell here indeed.
This Gomatī Gaṅgā has been brought by me for your sake."
I have established my preeminence over all of you holy places (tīrthas).
Furthermore, I was propitiated here by the Kumāras who were seeking liberation;
therefore, this supreme tīrtha named Gomati is the bestower of liberation.
O brahmins, for the sake of favoring you, I first displayed the Sudarśana discus; having pierced through the earth and likewise the waters,
it emerged before me, divine and composed of radiant energy.
It shall become renowned as Cakratīrtha on the Gomatī river.
My residence there shall be constant, and yours as well;
indeed, your eternal dwelling shall always be at Cakratīrtha.
For those people and others who bathe at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean,
and for those who have bathed at Cakratīrtha, liberation is held in the palm of their hand. Indeed, all sacred fords (tīrthas) reside within the Gomatī and the sea.
Indeed, all the gods and sages dwell at the confluence.
Then Sanaka and the others, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), bathed, and drunk the water,
washed the feet of Hari and then placed that water upon their heads.
There, Gomatī was worshipped by all the gods as well as by the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds; likewise, her meritorious water was drunk,
and her water was held upon their heads while the feet of Hari were washed.
Gomatī, having become a maiden and taking water in a jar,
worshipped the feet of Hari and held the water to her head.
Having prepared an *arghya* for Śrī Hari, she offered it as a handful of water.
Having scattered flowers there, the great sages headed by Sanaka, as well as the gods and the munis, entered the abode of Varuṇa;
and whatever sacred fords, cities, and forests existed there, they all arrived.
Each of them established themselves there, situated together in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha).
Thus, through the power of Śrī Hari, that auspicious Gomatī became composed of all sacred fords, highly prosperous, purifying, and the bestower of liberation.
And Hari vanished from the sight of all the holy fords (*tīrtha*s).
All the gods and others, having bowed toward that direction, returned to their own abodes.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, did that Gomatī come to flow toward the ocean.
"Through union with Kṛṣṇa, Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, removes all sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the History and Greatness of Gomatī-tīrtha and Cakra-tīrtha," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 219. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*).
Chapter 220 [Author:
Chapter 221 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having gone to the bank of the Gomatī and prostrating before her like a staff,
and having purified his hands and feet with water while holding *kuśa* grass, he should,
facing the east, offer unbroken rice grains, fruit, and curd, as well as the *arghya* offering.
"O Gomatī, for the sake of purifying all sins, I offer this *argha*.
O Goddess Gomatī, worshipped by the three worlds, take away my sin.
Having recited this, one should obtain earth, remember Viṣṇu, and then utter [the following]. (2–3)
O Earth, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, traversed by Viṣṇu!
You were lifted up by the boar, by Kṛṣṇa of the hundred arms.
O Clay, take away my sin that has been accumulated by me in the past.
"By slaying you, this sinful one shall be liberated from all sins.
(5) Having thus applied the clay, one should perform a bath in river water;
the merit that is obtained at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse is thereby acquired. (6)
By the mere act of bathing according to the prescribed rite in the Gomatī in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, one should, endowed with devotion, offer libations to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings.
By the gift of the waters of the Gomatī, they attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having invited Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas, one should perform the Śrāddha for the ancestors (8).
And one should give a sacrificial fee consisting of gold, silver, garments, and so forth;
[one should also give] a cow equipped with horns of gold and adorned with silver hooves (9).

Having worshipped it with garments, ornaments, and decorations, one should give away that cow— which has a tail of jewels, is filled with milk, has a copper-colored back, and is accompanied by its calf—
while also giving seven kinds of grain, saying: "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me."
Bathing in the dust raised by cows, the gift of a cow, gopi-candana,
and the sight of the Lord of the Gopīs— these five things beginning with the letter ‘ga’ are difficult to obtain.
By performing the ancestral rites (śrāddha) at the Gomatī, the deceased indeed become liberated.
Even those in the hells, the immobile beings, and the winds that have attained the state of insects—
all of them attain liberation through the performance of *śrāddha* and the giving of gifts at the Gomatī. [This is equal to] the merit of the horse sacrifice (*hayamedha*) and bathing at Prayāga.
The fruit of that [merit] from the water of the Gomatī is equal to that of one who offers oblations daily into the fire.
Indeed, the ancestors born of three lineages go to the world of Viṣṇu;
[they are freed from] whatever was committed through speech, mind, and action over many thousands of births.
Indeed, sin goes to dissolution by the sight of the Gomatī;
Hari, being pleased and endowed with prosperity, belongs to one who bathes in the Gomatī during the month of Kārtika.
When the full month of Kārtika has arrived on a Wednesday, ||| 16 ||
One should bathe Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with water from sacred fords (tīrtha).
One should anoint him with sandalwood paste mixed with musk and saffron.
One should worship Hari with flower garlands, fruits, lamps, and incense.
One should offer a pleasing food offering (naivedya), saying, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me.
One should keep a vigil with songs, instrumental music, sacred narratives, hymns of praise, and dance.
At the end of the month of Kārttika, one should perform a ritual bath at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean.
Only by worshipping the Lord of Ramā does the vow reach completion.
Hari, accompanied by Śrī, becomes pleased with the performer of the Māgha bath in the Gomatī river, and He grants even liberation.
Sesame seeds, gold, silver, and sweetmeats mixed with jaggery,
as well as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), should be given to a Brāhmaṇa on the bank of a river.
An oblation (homa) performed with sesame seeds, clarified butter, grains, and fruits is also highly esteemed.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should also give a red garment, a bodice, and a turban;
likewise, one should give sandals and a meal of sweet food, both fried in oil and fried in ghee, saying: "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me."

By performing the Māgha bath here at the Gomatī, a person indeed attains the fruit of all gifts as well as the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas); he obtains all his desires and reaches the eternal world of Viṣṇu. || 25 ||
One should complete the month of Māgha at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean on the full moon day of Māgha.
By the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, everything deficient shall reach perfection. Through bathing there, the sin of those who have stolen the property of Brahmins or the gods is destroyed.
The sin of betraying a friend or killing a teacher is destroyed by touching [this];
by seeing it, one attains a station higher than the realms of Brahmā and Rudra.
Whatever fruit a person obtains by granting fearlessness to those who are afraid—
One attains that fruit through contact with the waters of the Gomatī. A person who drinks the water of the Gomatī becomes one who has fulfilled their purpose;
and he who drinks even a mouthful [of its water] is indeed liberated from the three debts.
Devotees who serve the Gomatī dwell in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
they are four-armed, adorned with forest garlands and divine fragrant unguents.
The men possess the very form of Viṣṇu, and the women possess the very form of Lakṣmī. (31)
Having done so, they go to the station of Viṣṇu, which is characterized by the absence of rebirth.
After visiting the Gomatī-tīrtha, one should indeed proceed to Cakratīrtha,
where stones marked with the discus are seen everywhere.
Even a stone held around the neck sends the person who holds it to Goloka by the power of the Lord marked with the discus;
and wherever one's bone falls, even that person attains the supreme goal.
This Cakratīrtha, which bestows liberation, is superior even to Prayāga.
Wherever the branding with the discus is obtained, by staying there for six months and shaking off all sins, a person goes to the abode of Hari.
Having gone to Cakratīrtha and washed his hands and feet,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should then prostrate himself like a staff before Kṛṣṇa.
Then, taking the five jewels, as well as leaves, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), [he should offer them].
Having gazed upon the ocean, one should indeed offer perfume, fruit, gold, sandalwood, and even the arghya water to Viṣṇu in the form of the Discus (Cakra), [reciting]:
"Obeisance to you who are the very form of Viṣṇu; obeisance to you, the Discus of Viṣṇu."
Accept this *arghya* offered by me; be the granter of all desires.
You are born from fire, the body of sacrifice, the strength of Viṣṇu, and the bestower of liberation.
You bear the discus of Viṣṇu, you are the ocean, and you are eternally endowed with the sacred site of Cakratīrtha.
"I perform my bath here at this sacred ford; O Wielder of the Discus, grant me liberation!
(41) Then, having placed earth upon his head and bathed while worshipping Hari, he offered libations to the gods, the ancestors, men, and to Hari along with his attendants. (42)
O Kṛṣṇa, by honoring [the deity] in this manner at Cakratīrtha according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices merely by bathing there.
By the gift of gold, the Viśvedevas are pleased; by the gift of silver, the ancestors.
At Cakratīrthaka, they become fully satiated even with food.
One should give clothing and ornaments to the poor and the wretched;
the gift of a chariot is declared to be preeminent, along with wealth consisting of draft animals and equipment.
Horses, bulls, and especially carriages should be given as gifts;
furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be offered for the sake of pleasing the Lord of the World.
The ancestors born within the three lineages—whether as departed spirits, insects, or those in hell—[are satisfied thereby].

All of them attain liberation through the power of Cakratīrtha. (47) It should be understood that the merit of performing a Śrāddha at Gayā is obtained here; bathing is considered equal to the attainment of the sacrificer’s goal;
offering libations yields the fruit arising from a lunar eclipse; and giving gifts is superior even to that of a solar eclipse. (48)
The fruit shall be obtained; men should take up the mark of the disc upon their arms.
The sin born of thought, word, and deed is destroyed by bathing.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the Cakratīrtha has certainly been described to you.
"Pure people who perform the rites at these sacred sites (*tīrtha*) shall attain union with Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals and Fruits of Gomatī-tīrtha and Cakra-tīrtha," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*), Chapter 220.
Chapter 221 [Author:
Chapter 222 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Mahālakṣmī, one should go to the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean;
that is declared to be the gateway to liberation in the Kali age, without a doubt.
[1] At the junction of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean.
Whatever fruit is obtained here at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean,
that sin is destroyed by bathing; indeed, one should offer the arghya according to the prescribed rite,
holding kuśa grass in both hands as well as a coconut fruit.
Having offered salutations, one should present the *argha* to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul:
"O King of Holy Places (*tīrtharāja*), obeisance to you; protect me from the ocean of worldly existence!
O Mine of Jewels (*ratnākara*), accept this *argha*; together with the Gomatī, obeisance to you! (4)

Having offered the *argha* water, tied his topknot, and meditated upon the Lord reclining upon the waters, he should perform his bath while facing the east; thereafter, he should offer libations to the ancestors.
Having likewise performed the ancestral *śrāddha*, he should give an auspicious sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
One should give gold, two garments, as well as a tunic and a turban;
and one should give great gifts if one desires one's own welfare.
[Saying] "May Hari himself, Viṣṇu, be pleased with me along with Lakṣmī."
Having spoken thus, one should bestow various gifts and foods.
(8) One should also perform the Tulāpuruṣa gift at the confluence of the ocean;
having become a king of the seven continents, that person goes to Vaikuṇṭha. (9)
He who weighs himself against gold, silver, and the like,
or against garments, saffron, camphor, sugar, fruits, and flavorful juices—
having enjoyed pleasant pleasures here, he goes to liberation, honored by the gods.
The gift of gold, the Vājapeya sacrifice, bathing in the waters of the Gomatī,
the gift of a daughter, the gift of land, and the gift of knowledge performed according to the prescribed rules—
at the confluence of the Gomatī, one who performs these indeed goes to the abode of Brahmā. (11–12)
Having indeed bestowed a cow made of gold, a cow made of ghee, and a cow made of sesame seeds,
and having given a cow made of cloth and sugar, one goes to the supreme state.
On the principal lunar days marking the beginning of the Yugas, during the Pañcaka periods, and on the Aṣṭakā days, [one attains this].
Likewise during the *vaidhṛti* and *vyatīpāta* yogas, as well as on the occasion called *gajacchāyā*;
and having bathed in the ocean, or similarly at the *gomatī* and *cakratīrtha*, on the sixth, ninth, eleventh, eighth, or twelfth lunar day, or during a *śrāddha* or a virtuous vow. (14–15)
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean, one attains the state of Brahmā. On the day of the new moon, a śrāddha ceremony should be performed at the junction of the Gomatī;
by doing so, a person obtains in a single day the merit that results from performing the fortnightly śrāddha.
Even if it lacks faith, lacks mantras, or lacks a worthy recipient;

even if it lacks ritual materials, lacks the proper time, or is devoid of one-pointed concentration—if it is performed with complete devotion, it becomes for the ancestors as vast as the ocean. (17–18)
One shall dwell in the ocean at Gomatī, Kamalā, and Candrabhāgā;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā and by casting bones at Prayāga, and by giving śrāddha on the new moon day (amā), eternal merit is attained. (19)
If a man observing vows should desire to bathe in all sacred fords,
he should indeed perform his bath with devotion at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean.
So too should a woman who is childless, whose children have died, who has given birth only to stillborn infants, or whose children perish in infancy.
At the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean, a woman is liberated from her defects.
There, performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), giving gifts, as well as libations to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), beholding the waters,
observing vows, bathing, merit, recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and glorification [of the deity]— all these are efficacious.
At the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean, there is merit that produces eternal satisfaction.
[Therein dwell] those on the mother’s side, those on the father’s side, as well as those on the sister’s side;
those on the daughter’s side, those on the mother-in-law’s side, and likewise those on the father-in-law’s side. (23–24)
Those belonging to the side of the father’s sister, as well as people on the side of the daughter-in-law;
those on the side of the co-wife, and also those on the side of the female guardian;
those on the side of the brother’s wife, and those on the side of the sister’s daughter and so forth.
Even those who were fathers, brothers, sons, wives, and so forth;

even those who maintained relationships as friends, kinsmen, or servants; and those who have gone to other births, whether in hellish realms or within the womb of a womb—[all these are remembered]. (26–27)

When all of them are remembered during a *śrāddha* ceremony at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean, and when they are remembered while bathing and giving gifts, they attain eternal satisfaction.
They are liberated from all sins and attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gomatī and worshipped Vāmana on the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one attains the supreme world;
becoming clad in yellow garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
Bearing four arms and adorned with a forest garland,
served by celestial women and traveling in a celestial chariot as his vehicle,
that person who worships Śrī Hari is praised by the sages.
Purified at the confluence of the Gomatī, one goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having bathed at the meeting of the Gomatī and the ocean, one should go to the Seven Kuṇḍas;
there, Kṛṣṇa Hari, being propitiated by all, manifested himself.
Having seen Hari together with Lakṣmī, the great sages headed by Sanaka dug seven wells of beloved water and sprinkled Indirā [with it].
Therefore, these are known as the Lakṣmī-wells; in the Kali age, they are the Rukmiṇī-wells.
These were frequented by Bhṛgu, and thus it is remembered as Bhṛgutīrtha.
Having washed one's feet there and likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then take up kuśa grass,
face the east, and receive the arghya offering with unbroken rice grains (akṣata) and other ingredients.
Raising both hands above his head, he should offer an *argha* with fruits and other offerings here in the pool named Rukmiṇī.
Then, having meditated upon the sacred fords (*tīrtha*s) and the ancestors and deities, he should perform his bath.
Having gratified the gods, humans, and ancestors with devotion to Hari,
one should invite Brahmins and perform the śrāddha ceremony with devotion.
[One should offer] sacrificial fees, silver, gold, fruit, sweet food, and clothing.
One should also give food to the couple, as well as ornaments and the like;
an excellent lower garment, a bodice, a girdle, rags, and so forth.
Having honored the rows of ancestors, one should honor other women and young maidens.
Having performed worship, one should give gifts with the thought, "May Rukmiṇī be pleased.
There is no doubt that Lakṣmī always dwells in his house;
he attains all prosperity, and Lakṣmī is gracious toward him.
One should offer gifts separately at each of these seven lakes;
all that becomes inexhaustible, bestowing happiness in the world of Lakṣmī.
Misfortune perishes for him in whom Lakṣmī is pleased.
Livestock, sons, houses, gardens, fields, mansions, and granaries—these always become excellent for one toward whom Lakṣmī is pleased;
indeed, when Lakṣmī is satisfied with someone, there is an increase in gold and other riches for them. (44–45)
One obtains all desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
At the Seven Lakes (Saptahradas), it is excellent to provide food for women in the name of Lakṣmī,
as well as gifts, worship, honor, ornaments, and the like.
One should indeed offer separately the erotic arts, vehicles, conveyances, the body, utensils, and so forth, saying, "May Lakṣmī be pleased with me.
For him, Lakṣmī dwells always in his home; of this there is no doubt. (47–48)
He shall not be of low fortune, nor shall he be a beggar of others;
he who bathes in the Rukmiṇī-hrada becomes the foremost among all.
There shall be no returning for that man; he goes to Vaikuṇṭha.
Accompanied by his wife, he, possessing four arms, enjoys eternal happiness.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals for the Gomatī-Sāgara Confluence Tīrtha and the Lakṣmī-Saptahrada Tīrtha," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
