Chapter 223 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Thence one should go to the great tīrtha that grants liberation to Kṛkalāsa,
renowned as Nṛga-tīrtha,
where Nṛga was a sovereign lord under whose rule there were many hundreds of thousands of kings.
He was constantly devoted to his guru and intent upon the worship of the gods.
(2) He gave great gifts perpetually by the thousands; indeed, he constantly bestowed thousands of cows upon the brahmins. (3)
Having devoutly washed their feet and likewise offered them a pair of linen garments,
and having worshipped each brahmin with sandalwood paste and flowers, he gave a cow to every one of them.
He also gave monetary gifts and indeed grass for the sake of the cows.
Having offered betel, he said, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me.
(5) As he was giving gifts, performing sacrifices,
enjoying pleasures, and likewise worshipping Śrī Hari, (6)
As he protected the earth according to dharma, time passed filled with happiness. Once, having summoned the brahmin Gautama— who was always free from possessions—
the king honored him and gave him a cow.
Having led the cow— adorned with golden horns, beautified by silver hooves and other ornaments,
accompanied by her calf, well-fed, and lovely— to his own home, Gautama bound her with a rope and led her to the watering place.
Taking water to give it to drink, the brahmin went out from his house;
seeing a camel on the road, she became terrified and snatched it from his hand. Running away, the cow went toward a vast herd of royal cattle.
Searching for that cow, Gautama did not find it and went to his own home.
On the second day, King Nṛga again summoned the Brahmins and,
according to the prescribed rites, gave away many gifts, including numerous cows.
Having honored her with devotion and treated her well with garments, ornaments, and food,
that King Nṛga gave that cow to Somaśarman according to the prescribed rites.
Having accepted it, he too departed from the royal palace taking that cow with him.
Gautama, too, while searching, saw that very cow;
as she was walking behind Somaśarman, he spoke to him:
"Having carried off this cow of mine like a bandit, where will you go? (14–15)
Upon hearing that he himself was a thief, Somaka was struck with amazement and said to him:
"Having obtained this from the king for the purpose of giving it away, I am not a thief today.
My ownership extends to the cow; I shall lead the cow to my own home. (16)
Gautama said: "O King, this cow was indeed brought by me yesterday.
Ownership of the cow rests with me alone in this gift; it does not belong to you. O Soma, how can you take her away while Gautama is still alive?"
Thus, while disputing, the two brahmins arrived at the king’s gate, engaging in a fierce quarrel with affectionate gestures toward the gatekeepers.
Seeing the two twice-born men at his door, King Nṛga bowed to them and honored them in return.
The best of kings requested that the quarrel be pacified:
"For each single cow, I shall give a hundred thousand gold coins as a price,
and I also provide a thousand cows as collateral security."
"O two brahmins, let one of you accept this single cow given by me;
the other shall receive a thousand cows and a thousand gold rings.
Thus did Gautama and Soma both speak with great pride.
"Out of a sudden impulse, we both claim this single cow; we do not accept a thousand.
Gautama said, "I indeed take this cow as my own. Soma said, "And I indeed take this cow as being under my control. (13–24)
"I do not accept a thousand cows nor a thousand pieces of gold; I have no need for wealth, even for a thousand of my own cows.
Though they were entreated by the king, instructed, and honored, [they remained steadfast].
With their minds agitated by anger, the two of them fasted for three nights.
Then, having been treated with contempt by the king as unworthy recipients, the two foolish Brahmins were told:
"Go to your own homes, O Brahmins; you are fools, devoid of luster. (26–27)

When an unfavorable time has arrived, a wise person should indeed take the path [of diplomacy]. When one [party] must be conciliatory and the other is hostile, pride should be abandoned and obstinacy should be relinquished; when there is no other way, that is the course to follow.
"But that is not being done, O Brahmins; what can I do when the situation is equal?
In this matter, both of you will suffer over the same object.
Therefore, go to him, O fierce ones, and do as you wish, O twice-born ones. (1.222.30)
Thus addressed,
the two Brahmins, being capable of dealing with the king, then spoke these words in anger to the monarch:
"Since you treat us with contempt and do not act with justice..."
"Because of this, you shall undoubtedly become a lizard.
Having thus cursed him, the two brahmins then abandoned the cow;
and at that time, O King, they both prepared to go to their own homes in sorrow.
Nṛga, having approached the gate and prostrated himself like a staff, made this petition: "O twice-born ones, your words are unfailing;
out of compassion for me, please quickly grant an end to the curse."
Then Somaśarman said: "At the end of the Dvāpara age, Hari himself will come to Dvārakā and grant you liberation. That Vāsudeva, Kṛṣṇa, will indeed lead you to Goloka."
Having spoken thus, those two brahmins then departed for their own abodes.
King Nṛga, too, having met the law of time due to that curse,
reached the abode of Dharmarāja and was questioned regarding his karma to be experienced.
"First you shall experience the fruit of merit or sin; speak quickly!
[The sage replied: "You possess infinite merit, but there is a sin born from the mistreatment of cows.
Having heard this, Nṛga said: "I shall indeed experience only a small amount of that evil deed."
By the permission of Yama, this great lizard came into being.
For thousands of years he remained in a well and a pond;
remembering his former births, he subsisted on grains of food and forest herbs.
Once, being pulled here and there by the Yadu boys,
he took delight with them while remembering Hari and considering that to be the time of his own liberation;
however, when his body became heavy and he was overcome with fatigue, [he grew weary].
Having fallen upon the earth in a swoon, he did not move;
indeed, by means of yoga, he remained there having made his body exceedingly grosser than the gross.
Even though he was being pulled by many boys, he did not stir.
Having reached an extreme state of bulkiness, it grew larger moment by moment.
Seeing him, some children were startled and filled with fear;
they reported [the matter] to Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa, too, recognized that animal.
Having arrived, he then touched Nṛga with his hand;
released from the bond of the curse, King Nṛga became divine.
With a body equal to that of a god, he then stood with palms joined in devotion.
He praised the Supreme Lord, the bestower of liberation, the most excellent Kṛṣṇa:
"O Blessed One, my karma is complete; nothing else remains.
My auspiciousness has been placed in Your refuge; grant me liberation, O Acyuta! || 47-48 ||
Then Kṛṣṇa said to him: "O King, by my yoga, go to the worlds of the merit-makers and enjoy unsurpassed pleasures;
thereafter, you shall attain my abode, which is characterized by no return."

And Nṛga said to Kṛṣṇa: "O Hari, if you are pleased with me, let this pit become a merit-bestowing holy site (tīrtha) by my name. Whoever bathes here and performs the libation (tarpaṇa) for the ancestors," [51]
"By your grace, may the ancestors go to your abode;
and those who perform the pilgrimage here shall indeed be partakers of liberation.
Having said "So be it" to the king, Kṛṣṇa then departed.
The king traveled by means of a divine celestial chariot to the abode of those who perform sacrifices—
Vaikuṇṭha, which is indeed called the second station of Vairāja.
From that time forth, Nṛgakūpa became the most excellent sacred site (tīrtha) on earth.
One should offer the *argha* water to Nṛga-Kṛṣṇa, bathe, and drink the water;
one should satiate the ancestors, the gods, and human beings, and perform the *śrāddha* rite.
One should also give gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and various other gifts.
One obtains inexhaustible fruit and, at the end, indeed the supreme goal.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of King Nṛga’s Birth as a Chameleon Due to the Mismatch in the Gift of Cows, His Liberation by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the Nṛga-well Tīrtha," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 232.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Thereafter, O Mahālakṣmī, one should go to the holy site originating from Viṣṇu’s foot,
where the Gaṅgā arose, she who takes refuge in the foot of Viṣṇu.
Once, Durvāsas arrived for the purpose of pilgrimage.
Hearing of this, the Lord, together with Ramā, rose up suddenly;
the Master went toward Durvāsas in order to perform the rites of hospitality.
"The gods do not accept the offerings of one who has no housewife in his home and whose wealth does not go to worthy recipients;
likewise, the ancestors do not accept the water libations.
Thinking thus, Śrī and Kṛṣṇa departed together, filled with joy.
Having mounted his chariot, Śrī Kṛṣṇa went together with Rukmiṇī.
On the shore of the ocean, he approached Agni, who was weary and had bathed, blazing with splendor.
Bowing with devotion, the Blessed One likewise inquired after his well-being.
The sage said: "O Kṛṣṇa, is all well? Where is your dwelling now?
How many wives and riches do you have? Is everything always well with you?
Kṛṣṇa replied: "By your blessings alone, O sage, all is well with me."
By your very sight, my lineage has been especially purified.
Ten yojanas of land were granted to me by the Ocean;
upon that ten-yojana stretch of ground, a city made of gold was built by me.
There, nine hundred thousand palaces were constructed.
Dwelling therein, I live joyfully and without fear through your grace.
Having heard that, Durvāsas said: "Tell me the number of yours."
"O Blessed One, please have mercy upon me; Śrī Kṛṣṇa said that in my home there are as many queens, sons, and attendants as there are,
along with sixteen thousand wives and one hundred and eight more."
In each [wife] there were ten sons and one daughter as my offspring.
I have fifty-six kinsmen and attendants;
this Rukmiṇī, who is known as Ramā, was my principal wife.
"You are worthy of worship by sages; please come to my home.
By placing your feet upon my head, I shall thereafter attain purity.
Durvāsas replied, "O Kṛṣṇa, I am always intolerant."
"I become angry in an instant; why do you lead me away, Keśava?
Lead me [only] if you will do my bidding along with your wife. If you truly desire to take me, then carry the chariot together with your wife. (15–16)
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa, together with Rukmiṇī, then became delighted;
saying, "I am purified," he quickly became the driver of the chariot.
And then that best of sages, having joined Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī together—
Standing on the chariot and grasping the reins, he said, "Go! Go! (18).
Being honored by the gods with flowers, O Kṛṣṇa, he proceeded.
As the chariot was being driven by those two, Rukmiṇī became thirsty. (19)
She said to her beloved, "Give me water; thirst afflicts me now.
Hearing that, Kṛṣṇa struck the earth with his foot-lace.
Then the ground was split, and the cool Gaṅgā issued forth.
Fragrant, white, and beautiful in its watery form, it shone forth.
Without asking the sage for permission, Rukmiṇī drank the water of the Ganges;
seeing this, the rishi quickly became enraged and cursed the supreme lady.
"Because you drank the water without asking me, you shall therefore experience the fruit of that act— separation from Kṛṣṇa. Speaking thus, he descended from the chariot and,
with eyes exceedingly red, stood upon the very ground.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Ramā, praised him with humility:
"O best of sages, may your words come true in every way.
Let Rukmiṇī, separated from me, become water in this forest. (24–25)
May she remain eternally with Gaṅgā in the form of Gaṅgā,
where the water, having burst through the earth, became manifest.
May that water be the eternal holy site (tīrtha) in the form of Rukmiṇī.

"Let Rukmiṇī’s residence always remain right here in the forest, and let there also be liberation for those visiting the holy ford through the grace of Ramā. Then, at the end of the night, Durvāsas spoke to Kṛṣṇa in the morning: [27–28]
"May there be eternal union with you, O Rukmiṇī; I grant you my grace.
Having spoken thus, the sage, the son of Atri, departed from that place.
Rukmiṇī remained there in that preeminent palace within the garden.
In her second form as water, she is also established;
that form of water is indeed the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as the water from Viṣṇu’s feet.
In her primary form, she is always engaged in the service of Kṛṣṇa as his queen.

He also bestowed this favor, saying, "May you always remain in this palace. Having received that boon and having obtained worship, Durvāsas departed for Kailāsa from that place; Kṛṣṇa, for his part, went home.
And Rukmiṇī became threefold: one form was the water in the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet;
the second form was she [Rukmiṇī] herself in the palace situated in that garden;
and the third was the Great Queen, eternally united with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, this Rukmiṇī-tīrtha, which is indeed the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet,
became the auspicious Gaṅgā herself; it bestows liberation upon those who bathe therein,
and likewise grants inexhaustible merit to the ancestors of one who performs ancestral rites (śrāddha).
It bestows inexhaustible satisfaction and likewise grants the abode of Goloka.
Whatever gift, fire-oblation, recitation, meditation, worship,
or water-offering one performs in that place, all of it becomes the source of imperishable merit.
Where Kṛṣṇa himself, endowed with splendor, dwells at all times,
what indeed could be lacking for those residing at that holy site compared to Goloka?
Even for those who perform pilgrimages, no fruit inferior to that of Goloka is obtained.
One should offer various kinds of food and a sacrificial fee consisting of gold and silver. (39) Alms should be given according to the prescribed rules to the poor, the blind, and the wretched.
Sandals should be presented, as well as a water-jar together with a cloth. (40)
Curd-rice and various grains should be offered,
as well as red cloth, a skirt, a bodice, and a waist-belt.
Ornaments and articles of adornment should be presented to Rukmiṇī.
One should worship a pair of Brahmins with the thought, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me.
When this is performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), the ancestors born of the three lineages go to the world of Hari, satisfied; and Hari, being gracious, is accompanied by Śrī.
"Having constantly enjoyed desires here and the splendors of heaven and other realms,
those purified by the Rukmiṇī-tīrtha go at last to the abode of Hari.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Rukmiṇī-tīrtha— Water from the Ganges Issuing from the Striking of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s Foot to Quench the Thirst of Rukmiṇī While She Was Occupied with Driving Durvāsas’s Chariot— and the Threefold Nature of Rukmiṇī," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
From there, one should go to the most divine Gopītaḍāga-tīrtha, where indeed the first meeting between Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs took place. (1)
By giving gifts, by bathing, by chanting prayers, by performing ancestral rites (śrāddha), and by worshiping there during the month of Śrāvaṇa, a human being indeed attains liberation.
While residing in Dvārakā, Śrī Kṛṣṇa [spoke] to Uddhava, the foremost among devotees.
He sent Uddhava to Gokula to bring joy to the gopīs, their friends,
and the cowherds, and to speak of his own welfare.
Seeing that Uddhava had arrived, the residents of Gokula were filled with longing.
They honored Uddhava with garments, ornaments, and food.
Once he had eaten and rested, Yaśodā, who was deeply affectionate toward her son,
inquired after his well-being, and Nanda inquired after the welfare of Hari.
"Is Kṛṣṇa dwelling in happiness? Is Rāma prospering in comfort?
Does Kṛṣṇa remember the dear people here? Will Śrī Kṛṣṇa come and deliver us from our misery? (6–7)
"O Uddhava, is the family of Kṛṣṇa also living in great happiness?
Having asked this, their eyes became filled with tears of affection. At that time, Uddhava [inquired] about them and those other people residing in Gokula.
With sweet messages from Kṛṣṇa, drenched in affection, he brought [joy] forth.
(9) Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and the women of the household offer salutations to their parents;
they inquire after their well-being and remain in good health. (1.224.10)
"Kṛṣṇa will soon come to Gokula along with Rāma;
he will provide all happiness and will bring about your welfare.
Having thus consoled them with these messages from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Uddhava—
And he slept happily in a secluded spot to dispel his fatigue.
Meanwhile, seeing the chariot shining like the sun, the gopīs were struck with wonder and approached, asking, "Whose is this, and who has come here? (12–13).
Having gathered together, all those women of Vraja, emaciated by grief, asked him in private about Kṛṣṇa’s message:
"Is Kṛṣṇa well? Why has he not come here? (14)
"Having taken our very lives with him, how has he gone and not returned?
Remembering this, the gopīs then wept, overwhelmed by grief and delusion;
they gazed upon the servant of Kṛṣṇa, being themselves completely captivated by love for Kṛṣṇa.
Uddhava comforted them with words that brought solace;
and Kṛṣṇa too, remembering you again and again day and night, was pained by love and became sorrowful as he thought of you. (17)
Meanwhile, the gopīs became distraught and spoke many kinds of words:
"Having seized us mercilessly and then abandoned us, he has gone and does not return; who is the beloved of that slayer of Pūtanā? (18–19)
"Wherever one goes, there a new beloved is found;
for one surrounded by city women, we have no further need.
What should be done? Where should one go? How will the Lord be reunited?"
Lamenting with these words and remembering Hari, they wept.
Seeing their exclusive devotion, Uddhava then said:
"The birth, life, youth, and wealth of all of you have become fruitful."
"Those who possess unswerving devotion for Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to us, 'Lead us to where He, our beloved as dear as life, resides.
Having understood their firm resolve, Uddhava replied to them, 'So be it.'"
Together with Uddhava, they all departed with the desire to behold Kṛṣṇa.
Singing the songs of Kṛṣṇa, they went toward Dvārakā;
indeed, the fatigue of the journey did not touch them because their minds were united with Kṛṣṇa.
Having reached the bank of the lake dug by Maya, Uddhava prostrated himself and said, "O Gopīs, please remain here;
I shall go to inform Kṛṣṇa, who will provide for your welfare. (26)
Having spoken thus, Uddhava departed for Kṛṣṇa and said to him:
"The gopīs are standing on the bank of the lake; do as you wish.
Kṛṣṇa then quickly went to the pond by means of a human vehicle.
He saw him approaching, in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), radiant and adorned;
wearing a flaming crown, diadem, necklace, and shark-shaped earrings;
marked with the *śrīvatsa* sign, long-armed, and beautifully clothed in yellow garments. 29.
Seeing their beloved adorned with a sunshade, beautiful whisks, golden handles, and exquisite garments, they embraced him from all sides—
on his hands, back, breasts, cheeks, neck, head, and face.
Touching his face, eyes, chin, shoulders, chest, thighs, sides,
hips, legs, feet, forearms, garments, waist-cloth, and belly,
they— overwhelmed with love— embraced Kṛṣṇa and kissed him again and again.
Having gazed upon their beloved for a long time, they fainted and wept most bitterly.
"Alas, O Lord! O Beloved! Alas, O Master! Alas, O Enchanting Lord of Vraja!
We have all been abandoned by you; why are you angry, O one whose heart is parched? (33-34)

O Janārdana, O Kṛṣṇa, you who abandoned your father and mother and abandoned your devotees—we have been forsaken by you and have not been looked upon by you again. How can your separation be endured? How shall we survive, O Remover of Suffering?
"Do with these days, deprived of their lord, as you wish.
(36) Having heard them, the Blessed One, who understood their inner state, instructed them thus:
"Indeed, there is never any separation from you for me. (37)
"I am the inner self of all, especially yours; know that my union with you is always through the form of your husband. Desire, happiness, and eternal bliss—everything proceeds from me. (38)
"Knowing this, O great saintly women, do not grieve in vain.
(3.9) Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, they embraced him again and again; their distress born of long separation vanished, and they were exceedingly comforted. (1.224.40)
"Today our birth has become fruitful; today our eyes have become fruitful, for we behold you, O Hari Kṛṣṇa," they said repeatedly.
And Kṛṣṇa said to them all, "I shall have a pond constructed here."
"It shall certainly become famous by the name Gopītaḍāga.
Since my vision has occurred here and I have fulfilled their desires,
let the cowherd girls bathe together with me today."
Having done this, Hari then bathed together with the gopīs;
there the gopīs were fed with sweet foods, such as *piṇḍakas* and other delicacies.
Having thus sported in the water, Kṛṣṇa would regularly return to his palace.
And Hari, the bestower of happiness, gladdened them all according to their desire.
Having bathed in the lake on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, he will satisfy his ancestors; for them, there shall be eternal satisfaction.
Whoever offers a gift while meditating upon me with the ancestors in mind,
attains the eternal realm of Viṣṇu together with those ancestors.
Likewise, the water-offering (argha) should be presented, the śrāddha rite performed, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) bestowed.
Milk-rice, ghee, and auspicious food with sugar should be served as a meal;
garments, umbrellas, woolen blankets, shawls, bodices,
and waist-bands should be given as gifts here at the pond, while you all likewise remember me.

"Endowed with sons and grandsons, and possessed of wealth and grain, having enjoyed many pleasures here, they shall at the end attain the imperishable state. Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Tīrtha through the Meeting of the Gopīs of Gokula with Kṛṣṇa at Gopītaḍāka in the Presence of Uddhava," in the first section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (224)
← Chapter 224: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 225 [Author: Chapter 226 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In the vicinity of Lake Māyā, he created another lake;
O Lotus-born One, that great sacred ford is indeed known as Gopī-saras.
That which was enjoyed by the women of the Yadu clan as well as by the Yadu youths,
and that auspicious [pastime] which Kṛṣṇa caused to be performed for the sake of the cowherd girls—
[the word] "go" is a term denoting speech; [therefore], with me, it shall be [used] by you.
Its name shall indeed be Gopracāra, and it will first be known as Gopīsarai. It will become famous in the world as Gopītaḍāga.
Having offered the *argha* according to the prescribed rite, a wise man should perform his bath.
One should give a cow along with its calf, adorned with garments and ornaments,
accompanied by the prescribed sacrificial fee, to a Brahmin who maintains a family.
Indeed, the fruit obtained here from the gift of the earth is attained through the gift of a cow.
By merely bathing [there], a person indeed obtains the fruit of giving a cow. As many steps as a human being takes toward the Gopikāsaras lake,
for that many generations their family rejoices in heaven in the abode of Hari.
Those who go to the lake while chanting the glories of Kṛṣṇa shall have no further residence here within a mother’s womb.
Furthermore, that person who performs the pilgrimage at the holy site on the shore of Gopī-sarovara—
One obtains all desires and shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, one should perform the Śrāddha rite and especially offer libations to the ancestors;
furthermore, one should give betel, collyrium, gold, and clothing as gifts.
One should give garments, ornaments, and wealth to the husband and wife;
one should provide food, clothing, ornaments, wealth, and so forth for the maidens.
By this, the Gopīs shall be pleased and will always bestow good fortune and prosperity.
Cows, bulls, elephants, horses, and maidens should be given as gifts;
whatever the world desires, that one should give, and it shall be obtained again.
As long as the worlds shall exist, so long indeed shall this lake endure.
And the gopīs, dwelling in the city of Dvārakā while constantly meditating upon the supreme Kṛṣṇa with the feeling of him being their husband or else with the feeling of him being Brahman,
and serving him eternally, thereby became truly fulfilled.
Having offered obeisances at the command of Kṛṣṇa and having served Kṛṣṇa with full satisfaction,
she went together with Uddhava to Gokula, her own auspicious home.
By Kṛṣṇa, that holy place was made the most excellent on earth for the sake of the gopīs.
The dust from the bodies of the gopīs is divine, as is the divine soil and the Piṅgalā river;
likewise, the water is divine, and the trees and creepers standing upon its banks are divine.
Divine are his dwellings, and divine are the sentient beings there, such as the beasts and birds.
Indeed, those who are authorized for the divine realm of Goloka are truly [the ones who attain it].

A human being whose limbs are smeared with gopīcandana, who bears the vertical sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) made from the dust of the gopīs, and whose mouth contains particles of the earth of the gopīs, becomes liberated. (18–19)
O Lotus-born One, upon seeing one whose forehead is marked with a dot of *gopīcandana*, even the messengers of Yama flee far away. Indeed,
the deities always [revere] the Vaiṣṇava who bears the *tilaka* of *gopīcandana*.
Those who behold it daily at dawn, their sins are destroyed.
Indeed, for him by whom a mark of Gopīcandana is placed on the neck, the forehead, or the arms, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt. (21–22)

A woman—whether she be a married wife, a widow, a maiden, a young girl, or even one who is distressed; whether a courtesan, a servant, a slave, a refugee, or one who has sought shelter—who has turned the moon into dust by her gaze [upon the Gopīs]. 23.
She may be without support or distracted, mindless or wandering far;
she may be wealthy or a pauper, wise or a fool, and likewise deceitful.
She may be of any such nature—thievish, lustful, or full of latent desires. (24–25)
She is instantly purified of sins and becomes endowed with millions of merits;
she becomes divine like Gopī and attains fitness for the lap of Kṛṣṇa.
Having enjoyed inexhaustible pleasures in heaven for ten million yugas, she [attains liberation].
Worshipped by the gods, she shall go at the end to the abode of Goloka.
There, having become a gopī equal to Rādhā, she rejoices with Kṛṣṇa. And as for any insect, moth, or fly that [dies] in the Gopī-sarovara lake... || 27-28 ||
All beings— beasts, birds, reptiles, ants, wild animals, and so forth—
who shall meet their death [there], will certainly go to Goloka.
Having bathed with the clay of Kṛṣṇa and washed with the clay of the Gopīs, [they shall attain that state].
He is immersed in the lake of divine love and is the sovereign of Goloka.
(1.225.30) Such a station is not attained through sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by prayers, nor by Vedic study or austerities, as it is attained even by the dust of the cowherd girls. (1.225.31)
Gomatī, Gopikātāla, Gopālakṛṣṇa,
Gopīdhūlī, and the gift of cows— these five words beginning with the letter *ga* bestow liberation. By those who have attained these five *ga*-words, everything indeed has been attained.
What remains for one by whom Kṛṣṇa Hari has been attained?
(33) Even if a mere speck of the dust from a gopī should fall upon the face of anyone at the time of death, even he attains liberation; of this there is no doubt. (34)
For one who dies in the presence of the Gomatī river, at Gopikā-tāla, or nearby,
Goloka-dhāma is certainly secured for them by the attendants of Viṣṇu.
Even birds that travel through the path of the sky have gone to heaven.
How much more so, then, when offered at the Gopikā-tālavana or during a ritual immersion?
Even water,
if it has been used for the offering to Hari and is mixed with gopīcandana, shall indeed become his very grace.
If, due to irregularities in place, time, or other factors, one does not obtain the prasāda of Hari, then one should add a small grain of it to the food or the drink.
Then one may eat and drink; for that indeed becomes prasāda.
Indeed, there shall certainly be no transgression for one who eats food that has not been offered.
(3.9) A person afflicted by the pain of possession by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, or *piśācas*, should wear an auspicious pill of *gopīcandana* around his neck. (1.225.40)
One should consume the dust from the feet of a cowherd girl and bathe in her water;
with a concentrated mind, one should always place a mark like a moon upon the middle of the forehead.
When this is done, possession by piśācas and other spirits is certainly destroyed.
The meritorious soul becomes healthy and is purified in every respect (42).
Even for the poor, fortune indeed increases, bestowing prosperity;
likewise, there shall be the destruction of disease and the destruction of suffering (43).
Through their connection with the divine form of Kṛṣṇa, even the clods of earth attained divinity; for they are considered to be free from all qualities (nirguṇa) and bestowers of liberation.
Through union with Kṛṣṇa, the cows, the Gomatī river, and the cowherd girls assumed the very form of Kṛṣṇa.
They lead the living beings who come to them by chance to the state of the attributeless Self (nirguṇātmatā).
Those who are connected with Kṛṣṇa, whether insentient or sentient, become free from the material qualities (nirguṇa);
likewise, those whose minds are fixed on Kṛṣṇa liberate others just as Kṛṣṇa does.
Desire, greed, anger, pride, delusion, and envy— these,
O Kṛṣṇaka, abandon their own nature as defects and attain the state of virtues.
Women, men, animals, demons, weapons, and vehicles [all follow suit].
Clothing, food, as well as drink—everything becomes devoid of qualities.
Even divine illusion (māyā) becomes qualityless through association with Him.
What more need be said regarding that which is united with the qualityless Kṛṣṇa?
"Blessed indeed is the cowherd caste, blessed likewise is the lineage of cows;
blessed is the lineage of Goloka, which is filled with the bliss of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Gopīcandana," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 225.
← Chapter 225: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 226 [[Author: → Chapter 227
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
From there, one should go to the Brahmakuṇḍa, a sacred site that destroys all sins,
which was indeed visited by the gods for the purpose of beholding Kṛṣṇa.
And Brahmā arrived at the city of Dvāravatī during the festival;
likewise Pāśī (Varuṇa), Indra, Yama, and Vittīśa (Kubera), as well as Sūrya and Candramas (the Sun and Moon).
Other guardians of the quarters and others also assembled there for the purpose of seeing [the Lord].
And at that time, in the place where the assembly was arranged by Brahmā, there is indeed a great sacred site (tīrtha) and the Brahmakuṇḍa on its bank;
there the Sun-god was installed by Brahmā, and he remains there forever. (3–4)
And that is declared to be Sūryatīrtha, which destroys all sins.
Having seen both Brahmatīrtha and Sūryatīrtha, the Moon created a lake;
it became renowned by the name of the Candra-taḍāga.
The site of the Sun is the primary sacred place, bestowing the merit of a thousand *śrāddha* rites.
It is delightful, satisfying the ancestors, and destroying ten million sins.
Having bathed on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha and having smeared the ground of the Sun [with unguents]... (6–7)
The person who shall worship the Sun with offerings of flowers, incense,
water, leaves, fruits, and ritual fees,
having enjoyed all desires here, will go to the world of Brahmā.
Then, having had a temple for Sāvitrī constructed near the temple of the Sun by Brahmā,
he himself installed her in that sanctuary within the chariot of the Sun under the name Sāvitrī.

The lotus-born Brahmā worshipped the image of the Goddess according to the prescribed rites. Furthermore, that supreme creator, the Parameṣṭhin, established the Candra-saras lake as well as the excellent temple site for Sāvitrī; thus was that most excellent sacred ford (tīrtha) created by him.
Brahmā himself likewise took up residence within his own form.
By means of the ritual of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), the Unborn One performed his own consecration;
and that became the Brahma-tīrtha, which destroys the power of diseases and mental afflictions.
Those who, having seen [it], worship Brahmā, Sāvitrī, Sūrya, and likewise Candramas, shall go to the supreme goal.
Then, the auspicious Gāyatrī was established there by Brahmā.
And there, he performed an auspicious rite for the consecration by his own hand.
This supreme Gāyatrī-tīrtha bestows the world of Brahmā.
[He worshipped] those gods and goddesses with flowers, water-offerings, water, and saffron.
One should bathe and worship [the deity] with devotion through garments, food offerings, and meals;
likewise with ornaments, vessels, camphor, cardamom, and the like,
as well as with betel leaves and saffron, one should worship with great sincerity.
One should meditate upon Him, bow down, and with eager devotion prostrate like a staff.
One should worship with a lamp, a sacred thread, *tulasī*, *karavīra* flowers, other fragrant blossoms, offerings of light (*ārātrika*), and likewise with hymns of praise. (18–19)
One should worship those gods together with Viṣṇu by performing circumambulations;
one should worship Kṛṣṇa there, and one should worship the Śālagrāma.
Then, one should worship Śaṅkara along with Pārvatī and his attendants.
Having worshipped her, one should bathe Sāvitrī; thus the fruit of the pilgrimage shall be attained.
Thereafter, there will be no widowhood, no misfortune, and no barrenness.
Furthermore, there shall never be the state of having children who die, nor the state of being childless in any way.

For one who worships the Sun and the other [deities] day after day, there arise abundance of wealth, grain, and land, as well as the attainment of sons, grandsons, and so forth. Kṛṣṇa becomes thoroughly pleased, and the pilgrimage becomes fruitful.
Then one should worship Kṛṣṇa together with Rukmiṇī there.
Furthermore, Brahmā created the Brahmaliṅga lake there,
and Indra likewise made a most beautiful lake there.
He established Brahmā and Mahendra together with Śacī;
by bathing there at the station of Indra, they attain both heaven and truth.
Likewise [he established] Brahmeśvara, Indreśvara, and Vṛddhīśvara.
Having bathed, worshipped, and beheld [the deity], one is liberated from worldly existence.
Whatever is performed on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days yields inexhaustible merit;
through the performance of a śrāddha ceremony there, eternal satisfaction is produced for the ancestors.
In particular, one should perform worship when the sun is situated in Capricorn;
at dawn on the day of the winter solstice (*uttarāyaṇa-saṃkrānti*), on Śivarātri, and other such occasions,
having bathed in those respective lakes, one should visit those specific sacred sites (*tīrthas*).
Having worshipped those gods, one becomes a partaker of liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
And likewise, Śaṅkara, together with Satī, performed his rites there;
having bathed in that water as well, one should worship Śaṅkara and Satī.

Having bathed there together with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the wielder of the Pināka bow became known on the surface of the earth as Mahādevasaras. The offering of libations and the performance of Śrāddha there bestows inexhaustible happiness upon the ancestors.
By the mere sight of Mahādeva’s lake, one is liberated from sin.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and the worship of the gods—all these, when performed there, bestow inexhaustible fruit upon the practitioner. (33–34)

There is no misfortune for a man, nor is there childlessness for a woman, who bathes here in the Gaurī-saras; they shall attain all their desires. And Varuṇa, too, having indeed seen all those very places, [attained his goal].
And there he caused a divine lake to be made after his own name;
and upon its bank, he installed the goddess Vāruṇī as well as his own image as a water-deity, and worshipped them with devotion.
On the full moon day of Bhādrapada, having performed the viewing of Varuṇa, one should perform the Śrāddha and the libation (tarpaṇa); there, the fruit is inexhaustible.
One should also give water-pots, curd-rice, and excellent food.

Having said, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me," one should likewise give cows, garments, jewels, cooked food, and flavors, as well as umbrellas and other such items; by giving them to a virtuous Brahmin or a virtuous woman, the fruit is inexhaustible.
The donor attains the state of Brahmā, reaching which he no longer grieves;
and having seen the lake of Varuṇa, Kubera created a lake.
Consequently, it became renowned by the name "Kubera-saras. (41)
Having bathed at Kubera-darśana and performed the rites on the bank, one should feed brahmins,
virtuous men, and virtuous women, and likewise offer sacrificial fees and incense;
one should also give a gift of gold, for the Lord of Wealth (Dhanesha) is quickly pleased.
This increases prosperity and shall bear fruit a thousandfold.
Whether it be silver, gold, copper, brass, tin,
diamond, or a gem, a jewel, or clothing and the like—
Wealth, grain, as well as cows, buffaloes, and maidens;
clothing, beds, balls, and so forth; a water-pot, a vessel, as well as flowers, fruit, sweet food, oil, or even fragrant substances. (45–46)
Camphor and other articles of adornment such as sandalwood paste,
as well as sandals, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and a vehicle; likewise,
a carriage, a woman, a son, a servant, livestock, one's own property, and a cart.
A chest, ornaments, and other things, as well as food, drink, and meals—
whatever one might give, even a broom, a mortar, a grinding stone, a hearth, a water-pot, or a cooking vessel— one becomes a giver of all these a thousandfold. (48–49)
Having remembered Kṛṣṇa and Kubera, and having meditated upon Sūrya and Śiva,
and having remembered the great goddesses beginning with Rukmiṇī, one should give [this gift], which bestows infinity,
great merit, and the great heaven, as well as the abode of Hari at the end.
And indeed, a human being who performs a pilgrimage to Kubera-tīrtha attains the imperishable state.
Thereafter, one should go to the supreme purifying tīrtha of Pañcanada,
as well as to Gomatī, Lakṣmīgaṅgā, and Dvārāvatī.
Having likewise beheld Gopītāla and other lakes,
the lords of creatures established a sacred ford consisting of five rivers.
The five rivers were summoned there and arrived with great haste.
Marīci summoned the Gomatī and Trilakṣmaṇā;
Aṅgiras summoned the Candrabhāgā, and Pulaha, the Kuśāvatī.
There, Kratu also summoned the river Jāmbavatī.
In those rivers bathe the sons of Brahmā and all the gods;
that sacred ford is known as Pañcanada and is the supreme bestower of liberation.
One should bathe there according to the prescribed rites, and one should also offer the respectful water-offering (arghya).
"May the rivers accept this water-offering; may they become bestowers of heaven and liberation.
(57) One should perform the ritual bath, drink the water, and likewise offer libations to the ancestors.
One should give five jewels and seven grains to a twice-born man. (58)
One should give whatever object one desires to the poor, the blind, and the miserable;
such a person attains all their wishes and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Accompanied by sons and grandsons, he shall obtain supreme happiness.
And all the ancestors who are hungry ghosts shall attain liberation at that spot.
Thereafter, one should certainly go to the great tirtha known as Siddheśvara;
that very linga was established by the four Siddhas, beginning with Sanaka.
And nearby, they dug a well of sweet water which became famous as Ṛṣitīrtha; by drinking its water, one is liberated.
Merely by bathing there with devotion, one attains the world of Brahmā.

Even those who are wicked, slanderers, deceivers, and dishonest people are purified by merely bathing at Ṛṣitīrtha; of this there is no doubt. This is true on the equinoxes, on the lunar days of the Manus, and on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Yugas.
Whoever, residing at Ṛṣitīrtha on the night of Śivarātri during the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, worships Siddheśa while chanting the eternal Supreme Brahman;
having bathed, worshipped the Lord, and bowed down, should also perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
One should perform the *śrāddha* rite and likewise bestow various kinds of gifts;
for him, liberation will surely come into his grasp—of this there is no doubt.
In this matter, juicy fruits should especially be given.
He gave śyāmāka and nīvāra grains, coral, and sesame seeds;
seven kinds of rice, the seven types of grain, and parched flour mixed with sugar;
clarified butter, garlands, betel, perfumes, garments, and cow’s milk.
In this manner, dinars should indeed be given to Brahmins, virtuous men, and the poor.
By bathing Siddheśvara with milk, one shall become a partaker of liberation.
When humans behold Siddheśvara Mahādeva, [they attain the highest goal]. (1.226.70)
Those without sons shall have sons and grandsons;
those without wealth shall become wealthy and experience happiness.
Maidens shall obtain virtuous husbands and be endowed with good fortune.
Evil deeds go to destruction and merit also increases.
(72) Thereafter, O Mahālakṣmī, one should go to the unsurpassed Gadātīrtha, where by bathing a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. (73)
There, having bowed to the Blessed One in the form of the Boar,
and having saluted, praised, and worshipped him, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
There, at the junction of the first age, the Blessed One himself appeared as the Boar.
Having arrived, he rested for a moment and set down his mace.
Then one should go to Nāgatīrtha with the desire to behold Kṛṣṇa;
there the serpents emerged from Pātāla and stayed for a moment in Dvārakā.
Having bathed there, one shall attain the Supreme Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
Thence one should go to the great and supreme holy site named Candrabhāgā.
Having bathed there with devotion, a person shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Candrabhāgā, holding a spear in her hand and bearing a sword and shield, is the sister of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa who bestows fearlessness upon Kaṃsa and other demons;
by the mere sight of her, one shall attain all desires. (78–79)
From there, one should go to the holy site named Muktidvāra,
where the Gomatī river was brought by Vasiṣṭha and remains established. By placing that water upon one's head, one shall attain the heavenly world.
From there, one should go to the unsurpassed Kālindī-saras tīrtha.
The daughter of the Sun, Yamī, always resides here;
by bathing there, one who is constantly devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa shall attain liberation.
From there, one should go to Sāmbatīrtha, a most purifying sacred site.
In ancient times, Śambhu, accompanied by Ambā, became the son of Kṛṣṇa.
His great place is a sacred site that grants excellent liberation; it is known as Sāmbatīrtha.

Having bathed there with devotion, a person shall obtain a golden form. Thereafter, one should go to the Lakṣmī-nadī, which is situated at Nāyaṇa; for there Lakṣmī herself, longing for Kṛṣṇa, dwelt in the form of water. (84–85)
By the mere touch of which one is liberated from all sins;
from there one should go to Kambusaras and drink its pure water,
where indeed the water of the conch was held by Nārāyaṇa.
There, that very lake was formed and Śaṅkha was established.
That is declared to be the Śarava Tīrtha; having bathed there, one attains liberation.
Then one should go to the Jāleśvara Tīrtha, which purifies the world.
In ancient times, the sons of Yadu were cursed there by the sage Kaṇva,
that the lineage of Yadu would meet its destruction through the snare of that curse.
Consequently, the great god Jāleśvara was installed there by the boys.
For the sake of pacifying that curse, that sacred ford (tīrtha) is supremely bestowing happiness.
Having fully worshipped Jāleśa, one shall attain the world of Śiva.
Thence, one should go to the most purifying Jaratkāru-tīrtha.
In that place indeed dwells a certain Naga maiden named Jaratkarvi,
who was married by the sage Jaratkaru for the sake of rescuing her ancestors;
by obtaining a son, her ancestors were entirely delivered by him.
And that sacred ford (tīrtha) indeed delivers the ancestors through bathing and giving gifts.
[There are] the Ānakadundubhi-tīrtha, the Akrūra-tīrtha,
the Bala-tīrtha, the Ugrasena-tīrtha, and the Arjuna-tīrtha.
The Devakī-tīrtha is the foremost, as is the Rohiṇī-tīrtha;
also the Subhadrā-tīrtha and the Kardama-tīrtha. Indeed, there are the tīrthas of Kṛṣṇa’s attendants and the tīrthas of his wives.
In this place there are also holy sites of devotees and those that produce wonders;
there are famous and even lost holy sites existing by the millions.
Since Goloka itself exists here visibly, what is there that does not exist? (96-97)
There is no doubt that holy fords exist at every step,
repeatedly washed by the waters of the ocean and covered with dust;
even the dust of this place bestows liberation, and its breeze destroys all sins.
The water given by the body of Diti [Kṛṣṇa] through his union with Kṛṣṇa is beyond doubt.
O Lakṣmī! Dvārakā is the gateway to liberation, the gateway to heaven, and the gateway to happiness; indeed, that sacred ford named Dvārakā should always be resorted to. (1.226.100)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Thirty-Six Holy Places, including the Brahma-kuṇḍa, the Sun, Varuṇa, Kubera, Prabhati, the Deva-sarovara, and the Five Rivers at Dvārakā," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 226. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (Kṛta-yuga Lineage).
Chapter 227 [Author:
Chapter 228 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear of those gatekeepers who dwell in every direction;
stationed all around Dvārakā, they protect the realm of Kṛṣṇa. In the east, Jayanta, the son of Indra, is ever present.
His disciples and the Danujas likewise remain as obedient executors of his commands.
Vajranābha, Sunābha, Vajrabāhu, Mahāhanu,
Vajradaṃṣṭra, Vajradhārī, Vajrahā, and Vajralocana— [these are they].
Śvetamūrdhan, Śvetamālin, Naranātha, Vināyaka, Sūrya, the seven Mothers, Śambhu, Takṣaka,
Kārttikeya, Rājasa, and the Dānava named Dīrgharoman.
The Gandharva Viśvāvasu and the Apsaras Menakā;
Sanatkumāra, Vasiṣṭha, and Nyagrodha, the great banyan tree;
furthermore, in the direction of Agni stand Jvālāmukha and Aruṇākṣaka.
Kuśa, who dwells in cremation grounds, eats flesh, and drinks blood;
Kṛṣṇa, who wears black matted hair, as well as Trāsana and Bhañjana;
Agnisthālī, Apsarā, Gandharva, and likewise Amāvāsu. (7)
Then, in the southern direction, there were Daṇḍapāṇi, Mahāsvara,
Pāśahasta, Trinetra, Ativarta, Māraṇa,
Dundubhisvaraka, Kharasvara, and Ghargharava.
Maunapriya, Mallika, Durdarśa, Vināyaka,
Mahiṣīka, Sūrya, Bhūṣaṇa, Catura,
Citrāṅgada, Sugandha, and the one named after the Apsaras Urvaśī. (1.227.10)
Goraja, Dānava, Śāla, Mahādruma,
and the eternal seer Agastya are the guardians of the southern gate.
Now, in the southwestern quarter (the direction of Nirṛti), there are Gomukha and Muṇḍana.
Nagna, Kambalī, Rodana, and Hasana;
Lambagrīva, Bhrūvikāra, Dvijambhaka, Sūryaka, Muśalī, and Menakā—these indeed protect the southwestern direction (nairṛtī). || 12–13 ||
Then, in the western direction, there is Svastika, who has a conch for a head, a beautiful face, and blue garments; he has feet and hands, and his source is the root.
He is one-footed, one-eyed, with thick calves and a large head.
Puṣpadanta, Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Satrājiteśvara;
Tumburu, Ghṛtācī, Mahodara, Sarīsṛpa; Ghaṭotkaca, Pañcajana, Kāśyapa, and Kapālinī. (15–16)
The Aśvattha tree and Kapila protect the western direction; then, in the northwestern quarter, there are Bhañjana and Bhairava,
as well as Ghaṭodara, Kālika, Daṇḍaka, Mardana, and Ruru.
Ṣaṅga, Sarvabhuja, Ghṛṇī, and Supārśva are those born in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest).
Then, in the north, there are Mūlasthāna, Sūrya, Indreśvara Śiva,
Kaṇṭheśvarī, Khañjana, Vāsuki, and the Dānava Kūrma.
Sanaka, the Rākṣasa named Golaka, Nārada,
the Apsaras Rambhā, and the Plakṣa tree protect the northern direction. Now, in the northeast, there are Kilika, Durdhara, and Bhairavānana.
Dīrghāsya, Meghavaktra, Karāla, and likewise Vikaca;
Mūka, Balibhuk, Balipriya, and Māṃsabhuk—
O Lotus-born One, all these are the guardians of the quarters residing there.
Jayanta, the foremost of all, protects the *pattala* [enclosure].
Having worshipped these, the great worship of Kṛṣṇa’s task is indeed accomplished. Then follows the worship and the vision of Rukmi-Gaṇeśa.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, the arrangements for the gate were to be carried out according to the prescribed rite.
Bhīṣmaka had prepared a festival to give Rukmiṇī to Kṛṣṇa, but Rukmin,
holding a contrary view, did not agree with those words.
And when the Blessed Lord Hari Kṛṣṇa carried away Rukmiṇī from Ambikāsthala, Rukmin then made this vow:
"I shall certainly not withdraw from the battlefield until I have slain Kṛṣṇa. (26)
Thus, out of impetuosity, Rukmaka went to do battle with Kṛṣṇa.
Having been bound by Kṛṣṇa, he too had half of his beard shaved off. Due to this humiliation, he became determined to die.

Protected by the Blessed Lord for the sake of pleasing Rukmiṇī, he was indeed honored and appointed as the leader of the Gaṇas. Therefore, his worship should always be performed for the satisfaction of Kṛṣṇa.
Then one should worship Durvāsas and Baladeva.
One should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa in his temple, which resembles a celestial abode.
This yields the fruit of all sacrifices as well as the fruit of all sacrificial fees.
Through worship, one obtains the fruit of all yogas, the fruit of knowledge, the fruit of the Gaṅgā, as well as the fruit of all gifts and the fruit of liberation. Thereafter,
one should joyfully worship the Lord Trivikrama as Vāmana.
Once, while King Bali was ruling the kingdom upon the surface of the earth,
Durvāsas arrived at Cakratīrtha to bathe;
there he was struck excessively with knees and fists by the gods.
And the great asura named Ruru warded them off;
meanwhile, Durvāsas, having been protected, then departed for Kailāsa.
In this interval, O King, the Blessed Lord Vāmana himself appeared.
Standing at the gate of Bali, he conquered the earth with three steps. Then Durvāsas felt a comforting anxiety and sought refuge in Vāmana, who was being served by Bali.

Then, beholding the sage approaching, Bali, the lord of the Daityas, rose to meet him, offered him due honors, and seated him upon a throne. Bowing low, he said, "Tell me the reason for your visit here."

And Durvāsas, seeing the four-armed Viṣṇu at the gate of Bali, weeping and sighing repeatedly with great intensity, cried out, "Save me! Save me! Seeing the distressed brahmin, the compassionate Mādhava spoke.

"O Sage, tell me quickly why you have fallen into distress. Durvāsas replied, "O Blessed One, knowing that this sacred ford grants liberation, I went to Cakratīrtha to bathe; however, I did not complete my bath."
Seized by the neck and struck violently with fists by the Daityas,
he was forcibly stripped of his garments, as well as his *kuśa* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
and driven out while they shouted, "We shall kill him if he returns! (42–43).
"Having bathed at Cakratīrtha, I shall then take my meal;
therefore, O Govinda, bathe me and protect me who have come to you for refuge.
Having spoken thus, the wrathful sage Durvāsas ceased.
The Lord, whose divinity is the Brahman, spoke to that Brāhmaṇa:
"Having slain the Daityas, I shall perform my ablutions; come with me.
And the Lord Trivikrama arrived together with the sage.
And Kṛṣṇa said, "O sage, perform your bath for the sake of peace.
Hearing those words, Durvāsas quickly performed his bath;
the twice-born one then began to perform his daily rites, such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*).
Thereupon the Dānava Durmukha, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
arrived and indeed sought to kill Durvāsas.
Kṛṣṇa effortlessly severed Durmukha’s head with his discus.
Then the Daityas, skilled in weapons, assembled for the sake of battle.
Viṣṇu, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Vāmana—
these [heroes] completely struck down the Daityas in the fray with arrows, missiles, and weapons.
They slew Duḥsaha, Kūrmapṛṣṭha, Golaka, Vedadūṣaka,
Yajñaghna, Yajñahantṛ, and Dharmānta.
Then Kuśa arrived, having resolved to engage in battle.
There was an army of ten thousand elephants and likewise ten thousand more;
two tens of thousands of chariots and one hundred thousand horses.
Vakrago, Dīrghanakha, Nighasa, and Prasava were there as well.
With arms raised, head bent, clad in armor, and with mouths like stone slabs;
likewise Yajñaghna, Rāhu, Babaraka, Mahāhanu, Sunāman, and Vasunāman—these Daityas went forth for battle. (54–55)
Then Kuśa, desiring victory, worshipped Mahādeva;
taking a sword in his hand, he rushed with speed toward Keśava.
He said: "If I conquer him, my fame shall indeed be incomparable."
"Whether I have fallen by your hand or shall go to the supreme goal," he said;
having spoken thus, [the sage] effortlessly severed the head of the fleeing [demon].
Having fallen into the presence of Śiva, he was restored to life and rose up again.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, he said: "What harm has been done to you by the Daityas?
Having bathed Durvāsas, do as you wish.
Kṛṣṇa replied: "Indeed, the holy ford has been obstructed by you in every way."
"Therefore, I shall slay all the Dānavas; of this there is no doubt. Then Kuśa fought with Kṛṣṇa with great speed, and the Blessed One, filled with wrath, struck off his head with his discus.
Then, by the grace of Śaṅkara, his body and head were cast into the temple of Śiva by the Daityas; at that very moment,
he suddenly appeared, grasping a mace and ready to fight.
Since he was made immortal by the gratified Mahādeva,
[he was spared]; yet later, his head was split by Hari with his own mace,
and Kuśa was then cast into a pit and filled up with earth and stones.
Then Viṣṇu installed a Śiva-liṅga upon him;
although he was restored to life, he did not rise again, and he said:
"O Viṣṇu, since you have placed a Śiva-liṅga upon me," || 65 ||
"Let this place become renowned by my name as Kuśeśa. Thus, for the sake of favoring Kuśa, Kṛṣṇa said, "So be it," and likewise established the great holy site of Kuśeśa in Kuśasthalī.
Then, on another occasion, Mādhava destroyed all the other Dānavas;
some went to the subterranean realm (rasātala), while others remained as his servants.
Vāmana, Viṣṇu, Ananta, and the sage Krodhana were likewise [his attendants].
These and others, having established their abodes in Dvāravatī, remain there forever. Indeed, those holy fords exist in a second form as Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Vāmana, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Durvāsas.
The Tīrthaṅkara should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, and ornaments;
with garments, fruits, betel, unbroken grains, sandalwood, and saffron;
and with the waving of lights, incense, lamps, musical instruments, and hymns of praise.
Having worshipped them with circumambulations, sacrificial fees, hymns of praise,
prostrations, and offerings of everything one possesses, one should keep a vigil at night.
On the eighth and twelfth days of the month of Bhādrapada, one should likewise worship those deities.
One attains the abode of Goloka, reaching which one does not grieve;
having bathed Hari-Kṛṣṇa and worshipped Him according to the prescribed rite,
and having worshipped Tulasī, one should then honor Durvāsas.
Thereafter, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Vainateya.
Then, one should worship Rukmiṇī according to one's ability with the sixteen secondary offerings (upacāras).
Thus, affliction from the planets will not arise, nor shall diseases occur.
Afflictions caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and other spirits shall perish through the worship of Rukmiṇī.
One should bathe Rukmiṇī with curd, milk, and likewise with honey, sugar, ghee, fragrant scents, and sweet-smelling sandalwood. (77)
Then, with excellent oils from the North and waters prepared for consecration,
one should, with great devotion, anoint Mahālakṣmī and Rukmiṇī with sandalwood, saffron, musk, and saffron filaments.
The sonless shall obtain a son, and the destitute shall obtain wealth;
he shall acquire servants, attendants, cattle, and cows, as well as enjoyments and prosperity.
He should worship with *mālatī* flowers, *śatapatra* lilies, and fragrant blossoms.
With *karavīra*, *mallikā*, *tulasī*, and *rājacampaka* flowers;
with *karavīra* and *ketaka* flowers, with incense, garments, and wealth;
and with ornaments, gems, jewels, and decorations—one should adorn the Goddess. (8.1–8.2)
For one who worships in this manner, there shall never be anyone in the family who is destitute,
nor childless, nor unfortunate, nor a servant of the lowly.
Then, one should offer as a food-offering (naivedya) various kinds of delicious foods, both hard and soft, that are pleasing.
One should offer betel-leaf with camphor with a devout disposition.
Then one should present fruit, water, and the arghya offering, followed by the ārātrika ceremony.
Having performed the lustration (nīrājana) with camphor, one should then [offer] water from a conch shell.
One should brandish it in all directions as a means of protection and wear it upon one's head.
One should prostrate on the ground like a staff, saying, "Obeisance to the beloved of Kṛṣṇa!
Then, one should give various kinds of gifts to the wife of a Brahmin.
Sindūra, necklaces, garments, perfumes, flowers, saffron,
collyrium, betel-leaf, and ever-new foods and delicacies—
then [he gave these] to Queen Satyabhāmā as well as Jāmbavatī. (87–88)
Having worshipped Mitravindā, Kālindī, Bhadrā, and likewise Agnijitī,
and having gratified them with sixteen offerings of milk-rice (pāyasa),
the worshipper attains all desires both in this world and in the hereafter.

Therefore, with every effort, the queens who are beloved by Kṛṣṇa should be gratified with supreme devotion; they are the bestowers of heaven and liberation. Their life becomes fruitful, and their desires are fulfilled.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, on the twelfth day of Caitra,
as well as on the eighth day of Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Bhādrapada, and Kārttika—
on these twelfth days of the bright fortnights, she is worshipped together with Kṛṣṇa.
He shall indeed bestow long life and an inexhaustible lineage of sons.
And he who causes a very firm temple of Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa to be built,
his residence shall be in the abode of Goloka, within the palace of Kṛṣṇa.
Whoever establishes a complete system for the perpetual offering of food (nityanaivedya),
in his abode there shall be the constant bestowal of the Lord’s grace.
[This includes] clothing, fans, an excellent umbrella, chowries, water-pots, and so forth.
For one who offers this to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there shall be infinite [merit] in His abode.
For the servant of the feet of Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī, there are always abundant and divine riches, as well as women who are the objects of Kṛṣṇa’s enjoyment. || 96–97 ||

He who bathes in all sacred fords and gives gifts according to his capacity does not obtain the fruit of all sacrifices in the Kali age as he does from the worship of the glory of Kṛṣṇa. Indeed, except in the meritorious Dvāravatī, there is no liberation anywhere else in the Kali age.
"And Mahālakṣmī is obtained; that divine field is mine.
(9.9) Thus has the supreme greatness of this principal sacred site been told to you.
By hearing and by reciting it, a person shall obtain the fruit of that sacred site. (1.227.100)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Names of the Protectors of the Dwārakā Region, the Destruction of the Kuśāda Daityas for the Purpose of Durvāsas’s Bath, and the Tīrthas such as Kuśeśvara, Vāmana, and Paṭṭarājñī," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
[Chapter 228] *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (Continuity of the Kṛta Yuga),
Chapter 228.
[Author: Chapter 229.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Those who hear and read the greatness of Kṛṣṇa in the Kali age,
Their residence is considered to be eternally in the abodes of Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka.
(1) For one for whom the eternal discourse of Kṛṣṇa is dearer than life itself, nothing desired is difficult to attain, both in this world and in the next. (2)
Whatever fruit is obtained from residing in Kāśī for a thousand *manvantaras*,
that same fruit is attained by residing in Dvāravatī for five days.
Even a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*) dwelling here shall attain the goal of the ascetics (*yatis*).

"For one who has set out toward Dvārakā, there shall be merit at every step," so said the Lotus-born One (Brahmā). "The fruit that comes from bathing during a solar eclipse at Kurukṣetra is obtained here by the mere sight [of the deity] during a lunar eclipse."
Whatever fruit is obtained at Puṣkara by bathing during the month of Kārttika through ten million years,
that same fruit accrues to an embodied being by dwelling constantly in Dvārakā.
O beloved, whatever fruit is obtained in Avantī by a hundred men [in a year], [that is attained here].
The fruit of that may be obtained by staying for even a single day in Dvārakā.
(7) The merit of beholding Kṛṣṇa is considered superior to ten million vows.
The fruit of serving Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa is liberation in Goloka. (8)
Blessed are they and fulfilled are they who have beheld the orb of Kṛṣṇa; and he who,
with true devotion, performs the worship of Kṛṣṇa on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) and causes him to be bathed with milk, attains the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Water from *darbha* grass is ten times more effective than milk; clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is ten times more effective than that;
honey is ten times more effective than clarified butter, according to Śaṅkha;
and water infused with flowers and water from *darbha* grass increase tenfold beyond that.
Bathing with water consecrated by mantras and with scented water is ten times more meritorious than that;
bathing even with sugarcane juice is equal to a hundred horse-sacrifices (aśvamedhas).
Bathing in the waters of a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha) is remembered as being ten times more meritorious than that.
One with desires shall attain heaven; one free from desire shall attain liberation.
(13) That person who wipes dry with a cloth the body of Kṛṣṇa, still moist from his bath, has the sins of a hundred thousand lifetimes wiped away. (14)
Whoever bathes Hari and offers him a garland of flowers,
his merit shall be equal to the fruit of giving ten million gold coins (*niṣka*).
At the time of bathing, one should utter a thousand names of Kṛṣṇa.
For every syllable, one gains the merit of giving a hundred tawny cows.
(16) Furthermore, he who performs dancing or singing before Kṛṣṇa at the time of his bath becomes a beloved of Kṛṣṇa in Goloka. (17)
At the time of bathing, those who cry out "Victory to Hari! Victory to Kṛṣṇa!
while clapping their hands, do not experience the emergence from the womb.
Those who worship Him with garments, incense, and golden ornaments— [do not experience the emergence from the womb]. (18)
Thereafter, there is a residence in Vaikuṇṭha for a hundred manvantaras;
by serving Kṛṣṇa with ketakī, tulasī blossoms, or other flowers, one attains eternal residence in Goloka.
Those women who worship the Lord of Rukmiṇī with *mālatī* flowers sport together with their husbands in the seven celestial realms for a full hundred *manvantaras*,
after which they attain Goloka.
For yogins and sacrificers, for donors and those who frequent sacred fords,
for those devoted to their fathers and mothers, as well as for those observing the vow of Dvādaśī,
and for those keeping a vigil on Ekādaśī while dancing; ||| 22–23 ||
Whatever fruit is obtained by those who sing, remember, proclaim the Vedas, and likewise recite the thousand names of Viṣṇu—
that same fruit is attained through the worship of Kṛṣṇa by the offering of Tulasī.
And the fruit of the worship of Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa is even greater than that. Just as Lakṣmī is dear to Viṣṇu, Tulasī is even more so;
indeed, wherever Hari is worshipped with Tulasī, he is truly honored.

There, he shall obtain the fruit of a pilgrimage to Dvārakā. By worshipping Kṛṣṇa even with a single *ketakī* flower, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice for every blossom; indeed, at the end, the attainment of Goloka is reached.
One should worship Kṛṣṇa with *mālatī* flowers, and thus one attains the abode of Hari.
Or, if one worships Hari, the Lord of Śrī, even with flowers whose petals have fallen, having enjoyed divine and human pleasures, one goes to the abode of Hari. (28–29)
This eight-syllable mantra is: "Śrīkṛṣṇaḥ śaraṇaṃ mama.
Reciting it, one should worship Kṛṣṇa with fragrant sandalwood paste, camphor, and musk; such a person shall attain equality with Kṛṣṇa.

He who offers incense of guggulu with clarified butter to Hari shakes off all sin and becomes beautiful in the imperishable realm. He who causes a row of lamps to be lit day after day during the month of Kṛṣṇāyana [attains the same].
Indeed, he shall become the sovereign of the seven islands; for such is the fruit for every single island.
He who offers various kinds of food offerings to Kṛṣṇa—his ancestors, being fully satisfied, shall attain eternal liberation.

For one who offers betel leaf combined with camphor and mixed with the powder of areca nut and other ingredients to Kṛṣṇa, there is no rebirth here in this world of illusion. Cool water, rich with fragrance, should be offered to Kṛṣṇa for his satisfaction.

There shall be eternal satisfaction for him from the constant drinking of nectar and other such draughts; likewise, from offering fruits that are beautiful, sweet, and ripe, as well as from giving other things for the sake of cleansing the mouth. (36)
One shall attain eternal satisfaction in Goloka and possess fragrant breath.
He who causes a flower garden to be constructed around the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which is the abode of the King of Gods for the Lord who performs his strides, [attains these rewards]. (37–38)
She sports in the Puṣpaka chariot with millions of celestial beings;
and for her who offers a breeze to Kṛṣṇa with chowries and fans,
Kṛṣṇa himself kisses the lotus-face in her abode.

And Keśava sleeps upon the bed made by the maker of the bed. (1.228.40) Whoever causes a pavilion for Śrī Kṛṣṇa to be built with plantain pillars, for him the Apsarases, who resemble plantains, perform service. (41)
The person who adorns the abode of Kṛṣṇa with banners shall always dwell in the world of the Sun like the Sun himself.
One should perfume the temple of Hari with incense, sandalwood, and superior fragrances.
His temple shall indeed become a celestial abode.
She who always mentally serves as the foot-massager for Kṛṣṇa rejoices in Goloka with Kṛṣṇa, having become Rāmā.
Having prepared fresh food, she should feed Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
she indeed becomes Lakṣmī forever and shall worship Śrī Hari in Vaikuṇṭha.
Those people on earth who always perform service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
Surrounded by celestial maidens in heaven, he is served by hosts of apsarases.
And whoever raises a beautiful banner on the peak of Śrīkṛṣṇa,
for him there shall be a mansion with a banner in the supreme, imperishable abode.
Whoever causes a painting to be made in the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa will certainly attain a celestial chariot made of pictures in his abode.
And he who offers a mirror before Kṛṣṇa goes to the world of Soma.
Having enjoyed pleasures for the duration of a kalpa, he shall go to the eternal Goloka.

(49) Furthermore, one who gives an umbrella with many ribs and lined with fine linen to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow shall become a sovereign emperor over the worlds of Virāja and then go to Hari. (50)
One should give a vehicle, a celestial chariot, a draft animal, a couch, a grass mat, or a straw mat;
having become Kubera until the end of the kalpa, they attain liberation at the conclusion.
One should perform the waving of lights (ārātrika) for Hari with many wicks, ghee, and other offerings.
The *ārātrika* (luminous waving) rite is performed for him every day by millions of gods.
Whoever waves a water-filled conch over Keśava shall become a dweller in the Milk Ocean in the presence of Kṛṣṇa. (52–53)
One should perform circumambulation of Kṛṣṇa; at every step, one obtains the fruit of gifting the entire earth.
One should perform prostrations like a staff; the fruit shall be that of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
One should perform the chanting of Śrī Hari’s names; one shall obtain the fruit of the Sāmaveda.
One should perform dance before Hari, which destroys ten million sins.
For those dwelling in Dvārakā, there is the fruit arising from residing in the abode of Goloka. And for one who drinks the water of the Gomatī, there is liberation.
At Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, on the Gaṅgā, in Kurujāṅgala,
at Puṣkara, Prabhāsa, Śrīsthala, and Śuklatīrtha—
indeed, here on a single day, one obtains the fruit of a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
Those who resort to Dvārakā, the Gomatī river, Kṛṣṇa, Gopī, and Tāla [trees]...

58. Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness and Fruits of Worshipping Kṛṣṇa while Residing in Dvārakā," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 228. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*).
Chapter 229 [Author:
Chapter 230 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Mahālakṣmī! Dvārakā and likewise Gomatī were created by Kṛṣṇa in the Kali age as a ladder to heaven;
Gomatī bestows constant happiness upon those who serve her and grants liberation through the mere act of bathing.
Where there are stones marked with the discus, originating from the Gomatī and the ocean,
which grant supreme liberation even when merely seen by those who behold them—
who would not serve that city, whose very clay grants liberation? (2–3)
A certain Brāhmaṇa from Avanti named Somaśarman was a devotee of Śiva; he did not know the vows dedicated to any other deity.
He observed the fourteenth-day fast (Caturdaśī) alone, yet he did not even think of Viṣṇu.
Every year he used to visit Somanātha.
Seventy thousand years passed for him, and he indeed became worn out.
Indeed, there were tens of millions of people on the pilgrimage to Somanātha.

Having visited that great holy site and traveled to Raivata, they all then departed for a pilgrimage to Dvārakā; the twice-born Somaśarman, however, did not go. He returned to his own home and slept there alone.
And in his dream, his fathers and grandfathers arrived,
together with his great-grandfathers and the kinsmen of his extended lineage;
they were in the form of *preta*s, overwhelmed by hunger, fierce, and filled with grief.
Seeing them, he was seized with fear and, trembling, said:
"Who are you, possessed of such fierce forms; from where and for what reason have you come?
The *pretas* replied to that son: "We are your grandfathers."
"Afflicted by suffering and hunger, we have come here into your presence.
The son said: "I have given, performed penance, offered oblations, and fed others for the sake of attaining your satisfaction; and you likewise have done so."
"How do you remain in the state of a preta? Tell me the reason for this.
The pretas said: "Listen, my son; the day of Hari has indeed been neglected by us, and the day of Hari is not observed by you either. (13)
Because of that fault, this miserable state of being a preta was chosen by us.
Furthermore, there is no deliverance for you from such great sin;
you do not observe the vows of the Blessed One, nor do you perform pilgrimages.
"O son, you do not honor Kṛṣṇa, nor do you go to Dvārakā;
you worship only the god Śaṅkara and you revile the Lord.
Because of that fault, you have attained the state of a ghost, and you shall attain it once again."

Śambhu will certainly not grant a good rebirth to those who hate Viṣṇu. Śaṅkara is a devotee of Viṣṇu; he is the foremost among Vaiṣṇavas, and he does not accept worship from one who reviles Kṛṣṇa. (17–18)
For those devoid of devotion to Hari and who have abandoned the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī),
sin does not perish and the state of being a preta does not cease.
Even if Śaṅkara is worshipped, [the goal is not attained] without the worship of Keśava.
The killing of a cow is a sinful act that results in the painful and miserable suffering of hell.
First Keśava is to be worshipped; afterwards Śrī Śaṅkara deserves worship.
After that, the gods are to be worshipped, and then others—such is the established order.
Out of a nihilistic disposition, you do not worship Hari himself;
neither the worship of Śiva, nor that of the Sun, nor that of Pitāmaha (Brahmā) can protect you. Indeed, the state of being a ghost caused by the day of the eclipse does not spare you.
If one observes the third lunar day (tithi) of Vaiśākha when it is pierced [by the second],
the gods do not accept his offerings to the gods (havya), nor do the ancestors accept his offerings to the ancestors (kavya).
If he performs it out of delusion, his state as a preta is indeed certain.
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) and the full moon (pūrṇamāsī) are like a single day for one's parents throughout the year; he who observes them as joined with the preceding day falls into hell.
Having bowed to Somanātha, you do not go to Dvārakā at all.
"You perform service to Kṛṣṇa, yet you do not obtain the fruit of pilgrimage.
Therefore, after seeing Someśvara, one must go to the city of Dvārakā.
He who goes to Dvārakā without having seen the god Someśvara [does not attain the full merit]."
"O son, he has fallen into a terrible hell along with our ancestors;
thus we have all fallen, and you have caused us to fall further.
We see no way for us to emerge from the realm of Yama."

O son, through contact with the waters of the Gomatī, by beholding the face of Kṛṣṇa, and by offering śrāddha at the Gopī-saras lake, the ancestors cross over [to the higher realms]. Having gone to Dvārakā, behold the face of the Lord Hari, of Kṛṣṇa. (1.229.30)
Perform the *śrāddha* rite and give gifts at the confluence of the Gomati with the ocean;
perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) at Gopikātāla and offer yourself to Kṛṣṇa.
Thus your merit shall become pure, and our own destination shall be secured.
When Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the gods of gods and served by Rukmiṇī, is worshipped,
we too shall be honored; we shall bestow prosperity consisting of sons and grandsons,
and, liberated from the state of being a ghost, we shall attain the supreme goal.
Indeed, for one who dies at the confluence of the Gomatī and the Niradha, there is no state of being a preta.
By the offering of śrāddha there, the ancestors attain satisfaction and liberation.
Whatever fruit is obtained through thousands of crores of other holy places is attained there by means of śrāddhas.
All that fruit is obtained by offering water at Dvārakā.
Whatever fruit is gained from feeding ascetics and from the meal of Kṛṣṇa, that auspicious fruit—providing satisfaction for ten million kalpas—is attained [by this]. (35–36)
The liberation of the inhabitants of Dvārakā is considered eternal in every respect;
for them there is no return, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Any woman who is widowed and constantly takes refuge in Dvārakā [attains the same].
She indeed becomes the fortune that brings about what is dear to Kṛṣṇa.
Whoever goes to Kṛṣṇa’s city and worships Kṛṣṇa with *tulasī* leaves has obtained the fruit of his birth, and his ancestors have been delivered. (38–39)
Whoever wears a garland of Tulasī leaves that has been worn by Kṛṣṇa obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices for every single leaf.
One who is adorned with a Tulasī garland should perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) and acts of charity.
Even a very small offering made to the ancestors and the deities becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
Seeing a garland of Tulasī wood, the Yāmas (messengers of death) flee;
for in whatever house there is Tulasī wood—whether its leaves be dry or fresh—[the messengers of death flee].
In your house, there shall never be any transference of sin.
Therefore, my son, having become a Vaiṣṇava by wearing a garland of Tulasī,
go to the auspicious Dvārakā of Hari and perform the Śrāddha ceremony.
Perform libations with the waters of sacred fords and thereby liberate them. O son, you must observe the Unmolanī, Śayanī, Triḥspṛśā, Pakṣavardhinī, Jayantī, Vijayā, and Jayā festivals.
"The Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī should be observed; it destroys all sins, bestows all prosperity, and grants liberation. Go and perform [the rites] with happiness.
Having heard this from the ancestors who had become *pretas*, the twice-born [man] went to Dvārakā.
Candraśarmā went to that place which is like the eternal abode of Goloka,
where Śrī Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa reside, where holy fords are ever-present,
and where sacrifices, deities, and stainless sages dwell. (47–48)
Dvārakā is served by Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Gandharvas;
there, the Gomatī flows like a ladder for ascending to heaven.
Upon entering its boundaries, the mountains of one's sins are destroyed.

That city was beheld by the best of the twice-born with his clear vision. Having attained joy there, the brahmin bowed with devotion to the Gomatī, the temple of Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa himself, the ocean, and Dvārāvatī.
And he considered himself to have accomplished his purpose, blessed, and endowed with the dawning of good fortune,
thinking: "Now there is no need for me for thousands of crores of sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas),
for the auspicious month of Vaiśākha has arrived, bringing the goddess Madhusūdanī."
The twelfth day [of the lunar fortnight] known as Triḥspṛśā destroys ten million sins.
Thinking, "O, what a rise of merit has occurred! Today I have beheld Dvārakā," one should touch water, bathe, and offer libations to the deities. (53–54)
Having reached Cakratīrtha, he worshipped the stone marked with the discus. With a heart full of devotion, he performed the vision of Kṛṣṇa, the worship with the sixteen services,
and likewise the worship of Śiva.
Having offered the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the ancestors and water according to the prescribed rite,
[he should perform] the bathing of Hari with milk, anointing him with sandalwood paste,
and offering incense, a lamp, food offerings, fresh grain, and tubers and roots.
