Betel, camphor, clothing, fruit, and likewise the ārārtika offering;
circumambulation, prostration, hymn of praise, and the handful of flowers (kusumāñjali);
performing obeisance like a staff and requesting forgiveness, as well as keeping a vigil.
When three watches of the night had passed, he indeed offered this prayer:
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto You!
You alone are the refuge and the happiness for those who are wretched, blind, and submerged in suffering. (1.229.60)
The fruit of service at your feet is eternal great bliss;
indeed, all suffering shall perish for those who observe your Dvādaśī.
Whatever sin born of the overlap with the tenth day (Daśamī-vedha) was committed by my ancestors—

May all that go to dissolution, and may my ancestors attain liberation. O Lord of Gods, O Master of the World, act in such a way that my forefathers may be freed from the state of being a *preta* and attain release. (62–63)
By me, a devotee of Śivaprabha, even your slight was committed;
since neither worship, nor salutation, nor pilgrimage, nor even a sight of you was performed by me,
may the great sin born thereof always go to dissolution for me.
I have not made a pilgrimage to Dvārakā, nor have I served Kṛṣṇa here; nor have I bathed in the Gomatī. O Hari, wipe away that fault! From this day forward, O Keśava, I am your Vaiṣṇava servant.
I shall perform your worship, your vow, your recitation, and your service;
I shall perform your anointing, glorification, hymn of praise, and salutation to you.
I shall listen to your stories and wear the water from your feet.
"O Hari, I shall always partake of your food offerings (naivedya).
Be gracious, O Blessed One; burn away my sins.
Grant liberation to my ancestors and accept this prayer, O Lord. (68–69)
Having heard these words, Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa indeed appeared before them:
"O Candra, I am pleased with your devotion, as are your ancestors;
and you, having shaken off all sins, shall go to my own abode."
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa vanished, and the ancestors appeared before him.
They said: "O son, by your effort, we have attained liberation without a doubt—through the gift of water from the Gomatī, through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), and through your vision."

Released from the womb of a preta, we go to the supreme goal. Blessed are those ancestors in this world whose son, having gone to Dvārakā, always delivers his forefathers through service to Kṛṣṇa and other such means. (73)
Blessed is that widow who performs the pilgrimage to Kṛṣṇa;
she surely delivers her father, her husband, and a hundred of her lineage.
Even if an outcaste performs the pilgrimage with his mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa, [he attains the same]. (74–75)
Surrounded by his ancestors, he attains supreme liberation;
for all sacred fords, all gods,
and likewise all sacrifices come to Dvārakā three times a day in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
There, a person obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
But he who, having seen Someśvara, does not behold Dvārakā—fie upon his son and his lineage; his ancestors remain in hell. (77–78)
Brahmā, Rudra, as well as Sūrya, Mahendra, and the other deities;
human beings, kings, Brahmins, serpents, Nāgas, and foot-soldiers;
rivers, streams, mountains, forests, and groves.
Cities, villages, towns, oceans, and lakes; yakṣas, gaṇas, gandharvas, siddhas, and likewise vidyādharas; apsarases, cities, Kubera, and the daityas and rākṣasas. (1.229.80–81)
The sages, the seers, the yogis, Sanaka and the other holy men,
the virtuous women, the circle of yoginīs, and also the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs;
the houses, the lunar mansions, the yogas, Dhruva, and the guardians of the world.
Whatever exists within the three worlds, whether stationary or moving,
remains eternally in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa every single day;
indeed, he never leaves the meritorious city of Dvārakā, which is adorned by Kṛṣṇa.
"O son, by your service and by the sight of Kṛṣṇa, we have been liberated from the womb of ghosts; we are going to the supreme goal.
May it be well with you; we shall not go to that divine abode, Goloka."
"O son, you have attained the state of Kṛṣṇa, and you shall go to that very abode.
In the Kali age, the Vedas do not yield fruit, nor do gifts or sacrifices;
the Gomatī alone is considered to grant fruit, heaven, and liberation in every way. (86–87)
In the Kali age, Kāśī, Mathurā, Avantī, Revatācala,
Ayodhyā, Kuṅkumavāpī, Kāñcī, Puruṣottama,
Śālagrāma, the Māyā river, Badarī, and likewise Gayā [are the sacred sites]. 88.
Kurukṣetra, Bhṛgukṣetra, Puṣkara, Śuklatīrtha,
Prayāga, Prabhāsa, and also Hāṭakeśvara; Gaṅgādvāra, Vārāha, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
O son, [visit] Naimiṣa, the Daṇḍaka forest, as well as Vṛndāvana,
the region of Sindhukṣetra, Arbuda, and all other forests;
likewise, visit the groves and sacred abodes, and whatever others there may be.
The mountains, the *śaileya* minerals, the sacred fords, the snows, and the forests;
all the rivers and oceans were eager to serve Kṛṣṇa, desiring the destruction of their sins and longing for divine bliss. (92–93)
In the Kali Yuga, they shall dwell in Dvārakā on the banks of the Gomatī.
Indeed, there is no city equal to Dvārakā in the three worlds.
When your full lifespan has been reached, your death will be divine.
"Because you touched [the water] three times on a Wednesday during the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha,
your departure for the abode of Hari shall be through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra)," said his ancestors, who appeared in their four-armed forms. || 95–96 ||
Residing in a divine celestial chariot, they departed for that abode of Goloka;
Somaśarman, having become a Vaiṣṇava, went to his own home,
and when the end of his life arrived, he went to the city of Dvāravatī.
Having cast off his life-breaths through the instruction of Kṛṣṇa, he attained liberation.
For those who hear or read this account of the greatness arising from Dvārakā, the entire fruit indeed arises, and at the end, liberation shall certainly be theirs. (98–99)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Ancestors of the Devotee of Śiva, Somaśarman, by Means of a Pilgrimage to Dvārakā," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Chapter 229. [Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Part 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna), Chapter 230]
[The Author: Chapter 231.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Śaṅkhoddhāra is a great sacred ford (tīrtha); here, the demon Śaṅkha [was slain] by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
It has been uplifted by Kṛṣṇa; one should go there for the sake of liberation.

Likewise, the holy places beginning with Prabhāsa, the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, the mountains, the oceans, the sacred fields, and the divine shrines and trees [are all contained therein]. || 2 ||
Sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha and others, deities such as Mahendra and others, sages such as Bhṛgu and others, Gandharvas foremost among whom is Tumburu,
and lords of wealth such as Kubera, along with attendants such as Viṣvaksena and others. (3)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the Siddhas and Apsarases—
what more need be said? The three worlds, both insentient and sentient,
abide at Śaṅkhoddhāra, having entered into union with the supreme self.
Those who constantly remember the great lake Śaṅkhoddhāra in their homes shall not return [to this world] until the dissolution of all beings.
And those who remember in their minds both Śaṅkhoddhāra and the Lord who holds the conch (Śaṅkhin) [shall likewise not return].
Accompanied by hundreds of millions of their kin, they dwell in the world of Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever fruit is obtained at the Sarasvatī during ten million solar eclipses,
that same fruit a man gains who, with devotion, feeds ascetics constantly for a hundred years.
At Śaṅkhoddhāra, O beloved of mine, three and a half crores of holy places exist; therefore, for one who bathes there, all other holy places do not equal even a sixteenth part of its merit,
for it is the abode where the fruit of all holy places resides.
Thousands of killings of Brahmins and acts of approaching women who should not be approached—
all such sins go to destruction for one who touches the water of Śaṅkhoddhāra.
He who gives a cow or a house, or gold, obtains the fruit of ten million such gifts.
The fruit obtained by residing at Kurukṣetra and by dying in the Gaṅgā is attained merely by bathing in the Gomatī and by beholding [the deity] situated within the conch.
Dvārakā, situated in the midst of the ocean's waters, is exceedingly difficult to conquer.
In its center stands the Lord, the bearer of the conch, the destroyer of sins.
From there, one should go to the Piṇḍāraka Tīrtha, which destroys all evil,
where Kṛṣṇa himself, four-armed, eternally resides.
By bathing wherever the river Rukmavatī flows, one is liberated. There is the world-renowned pond of the sage Agastya;
by bathing there and likewise performing a *śrāddha*, a son truly liberates his ancestors.

Likewise, there is the sacrificial enclosure and the sacred ford where, in former times, the first Prajāpati performed a sacrifice according to the prescribed rites for the welfare of all the worlds; and there, too,
the hands of the Daitya who destroyed sacrifices were severed.
Having seen that [place], one is indeed released from sin by Viṣṇu, the God of gods.
There, the ancestors truly desire rice-balls for the sake of complete satisfaction.
When the Śrāddha is performed in Vaiśākha, one is released from the three types of transgressions.
One should perform acts of charity, faith, vows, recitation, and libations.
Indeed, for a person traveling to Dvārakā, the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices shall accrue at every step. (1.230.20)
And for one who remembers Piṇḍāraka, that fruit is certain to arise:
having seen Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the temple at Śaṅkhoddhāra, and the Holder of the Conch (Śaṅkhin) there,
and having beheld the Four-Armed One at Piṇḍāraka, one shall attain liberation.
Śrī, Kṛṣṇa, Cakratīrtha, Piṇḍāraka, the Gomatī,
and even gopīcandana and tulasī are difficult to find in the Kali age;
yet they all come together in Dvāravatī through association with Kṛṣṇa.
Vardhinī, Dvārakā, Gaṅgā, Lakṣmī, Govinda,
Gomatī, Gopikā, Tāla, and Mṛttikā— these are difficult to obtain.
For one who has observed the vigil on the day of Vardhinī-Dvādaśī, [the fruit is attained].
By that devotee who has performed the vigil for Keśava on the day of Trispṛśā, O beloved, rebirth is entirely burnt away;
he certainly becomes absorbed into the body of Keśava. (25–26)
A swing should be given to Kṛṣṇa; its merit is infinite. Whether it be made of gold, silver, wood, or cloth, it should indeed be offered to Viṣṇu; the fruit of that is residence in Vaikuṇṭha.
One should slowly and repeatedly swing Hari Kṛṣṇa on a swing (28).
One should also perform a vigil here, which bestows liberation and is meritorious;
likewise, the gift of a maiden, the Śrāddha rite at Gayā, and the planting of an Aśvattha tree [yield great merit] (29).
Even keeping a vigil on the twelfth day is equal to ten thousand horse-sacrifices;
O Lakṣmī, at every moment one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
All the gods, all the sacred fords, and likewise the liberated sages [are present there].
Indeed, O Lord, they come on the night of the eleventh day for the vigil.
Truly, the dust from the feet of Kṛṣṇa as he goes from his home toward the temple for the sake of the vigil [is sacred]. (3.1–3.2)

For as many [times] as they touch [the feet], for that many thousands of years one shall enjoy divine pleasures in heaven and thereafter attain the abode of Goloka. Once, during a vigil, the goddess Pārvatī spoke to Śaṅkara:

"How is it, O Śambhu, that you dance at night while playing the hand-drum (ḍamaru)? Śambhu replied: "I, the Goddess, perform the vigil on the day of Hari for the sake of pleasing Kṛṣṇa, wherein no laziness may occur."
By any means whatsoever, one must certainly remain awake—
through song, beautiful dance, and the chanting of the praises of the Lord,
and through play consisting of festivals celebrated by assemblies of men and women.
A devotee who remembers Kṛṣṇa should remain awake by means of storytelling, conversation, playing cymbals,
and service; he should act in such a way that neither laziness nor negligence occurs.
Thus, for the sake of pleasing Kṛṣṇa, I perform this dance vigil;
you, moreover, must remember the Lord of Kamalā and perform this same task:
on the eleventh day one must not eat, and likewise a vigil must be observed. (39)

Even he who has gathered there in the assembly hall attains the supreme goal. (1.230.40) Even heaps of sin as large as Mount Meru and Mandara, when [encountered] during the vigil for Kṛṣṇa, are all carried away like a pile of cotton. (41)
The vigil (jāgara) dear to Kṛṣṇa is superior even to all sacred fords and sacrifices;
all the gods arrive at the vigil dear to Kṛṣṇa. During the vigil dear to Kṛṣṇa, women become truly charming.
Having spoken thus, even Hara ceased, O beloved of Kṛṣṇa!

(43) Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Extraction of the Conch in Dvārakā, the Piṇḍāraka Tīrtha, the River Rukmavatī, the Tank of Agastya, the Sacrificial Tīrtha, and the Observances of the Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī Fast and the Vigil," in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (230)
← Chapter 230: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 231 [[Author:
→ Chapter 232
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! When Jupiter had entered the zodiac sign of Leo, the sage Nārada went to the hermitage of Gautama on the banks of the Godāvarī. (1)
Having seen that all the purifying holy places had arrived from every direction and were indeed staying for the duration of the rainy season, he resided there for one year.
These included Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Madhupurī, and Avantikā.
Māyā, Kāñcī, Sāketa, Gayā, and Kuṅkumavāpikā;
the three Gayās, the field of Hari-Hara, and Puruṣottama; Prabhāsa and other sacred forests, hermitages, the Gaṅgā, and the Sarasvatī. || 3–4 ||
The Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Sarayū, Bhīmarathī, Gaṇḍakī,
Kṛṣṇā, Svarṇā, Kāverī, the lakes, the springs, and the Yamī—
whatever rivers there are in the fourteen worlds, they are indeed these. (5)
The mountains, the vast lands, and the elephants stood upon the banks of the Godāvarī.
While the lion was there under the influence of Jupiter, they remained for one year filled with great joy.
Likewise, the rivers beginning with the Puṣkara, as well as the boundary-mountains, [remained there].
The Vedas and Shastras, the Siddhas, Rishis, and deities, the ancestors, the gods, the Brahmins, the yogis, the holy men,
the virtuous women, the goddesses, and the gods all rained down with great joy at Prayaga.
Gautama and Nārada, along with those great sages, beheld them;
having washed away their own sins by means of the waters offered by the pilgrims,
they indeed prepared to go to the Gautamī river.
At that time, the Godāvarī spoke to Nārada:
"O Nārada, by my grace all these holy fords have become free from sin,
and they have bestowed their sins upon me."
"Where indeed must I go to cast off that burden of sin?
O Lord, now being scorched by the fires of those various sins, where shall I go, O Sage? I am exceedingly distressed; what should I do next? (12-13)
Having heard that, Nārada reflected for a moment and remained silent;
at that very time, the lord of sages, the yogi Gautama, arrived there.
He said to the sage, "By your grace, O Gautama, [the river] Gautamī is called a holy site (tīrtha)."

Just as we were indeed purified by her arrival upon the surface of the earth, so too, O Gautama, reflect upon this: she becomes liberated from sin through the merits acquired at our water-stations along the Godāvarī. (15–16)
Gautama thought: "Such a holy place exists that destroys sin;
nevertheless, at that time, it did not manifest clearly within his intellect.
Adopting a vow of silence, Gautama meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then the goddess of the ethereal voice, gladdening her, spoke:
"Listen, O sages of the sacred fords and others; out of compassion I shall relate it. She dwells having taken refuge on the shore of the western ocean. (18–19)
And there is the most excellent sacred field of Dvārakā, where the auspicious Gomatī flows;
there Mahāviṣṇu eternally resides, facing the west. All of that is the burner even of the most formidable heaps of sins.
"Therefore, O deities, go to Gautamī in order to burn away our sins.
Having heard that it was the most excellent sacred field, the deities of the tīrtha cried out: "Victory! Victory! We have triumphed! We are blessed, most blessed! (21–22)
Having spoken thus, they all departed for Dvārakā, which was protected by Kṛṣṇa.
Residence in Dvārakā is difficult to attain; the sight of Kṛṣṇa is likewise difficult to attain;
the bath in the Gomatī is difficult to attain, as is the sight of Rukmiṇī.
"The sight of Dvārakā will bring us merit.
Then Nārada, Gautama, the Godāvarī, sacred fords, and deities—
all approached the boundary of Dvārāvatī with great reverence.

Having questioned Nārada with joy regarding the ritual for the sacred ford, he spoke to them; for Nārada indeed knows the ritual exactly as it is. Having performed his bath in the Gomatī, he then worshipped the Gomatī.
One should behold Kṛṣṇa and feed virtuous brāhmaṇas.
Having partaken of the prasāda of Kṛṣṇa, the pilgrim should sleep upon the ground.
And at dawn, having bathed again and worshipped the Supreme Lord, [he should proceed].
Having circumambulated and paid obeisance to the true guru, and having prostrated before him,
one should perform singing, chanting, and likewise the worship of Śrī Hari.
One should strictly preserve celibacy and restrain the senses.
One should perform the massaging of the feet of the gods and the virtuous;
one should offer them vision and worship, and give gifts according to one's ability.
Even a very small gift, when given according to one's capacity, becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
The fruit arising from the gift of the entire earth is equal to the fruit of giving even a single morsel of food;
when one virtuous person is fed, the fruit is equal to ten thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
[32] One should give shoes, food, drink, sandals, umbrellas, and woolen blankets.
One should offer garments and vessels of water to Kṛṣṇa for his satisfaction.
For one whose hands, feet, mind, tongue,
and organ of generation are restrained, the merit of sacred pilgrimage sites becomes infinite.
One should avoid the food of others, the cooking of others, and the possessions of others. One should listen to the sacred stories of Viṣṇu and chant the names of Hari.
Festivals should be celebrated with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
Likewise, one should offer the fruit of the *ārārtrika* rite and the *naivedya* offering.
One should likewise perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa with the sixteen articles;
indeed, it is impossible to describe the fruit of that [worship] even by means of the number of eons.
Thus addressed by Nārada, those holy places, deities, and great sages performed everything exactly as instructed at the sacred site, endowed with devotion.
Some listen to their stories, while others describe their various virtues.
Some sing His glory, while others remember Śrī Hari;
some chant His name, and some behold Him. Others proceed with festivals, and still others dance at that time. (1.231.39–40)
Some repeatedly shout the cry of victory for Hari all at once;
some sweep the house of Hari and chant the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Immersed in love, they laugh and touch the lotus feet of the saintly.
Gathering together on the path, they sing songs of praise to his virtues in every way.
Forming a circle, the holy pilgrimage sites perform their ritual duties for him.
Seeing them, even those who have slain a Brahmin seek purification; I tell you this as the truth, the absolute truth.
All these Vaiṣṇavas indeed, appearing in the forms of men and women, and all the holy fords such as Prayāga, the sacred fields, mountains, and oceans—
all assuming human form— truly proceed together in a group.
Then the goddesses who are rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, went there in the forms of women.
Kuṃkumavāpikā also departed, taking her own sacred bathing places with her;
for at that time, a divine assembly of those situated on the fourteenth step had indeed come together.
At that time, everyone indeed performed instrumental music and chanting within the Saṅgha;
then the great pilgrimage of Dvārakā was undertaken by the Saṅgha. They performed their ablutions in the Gomatī river and beheld Kṛṣṇa.
The entire procedure for the pilgrimage was performed, and all sin was destroyed.
At that time, the Godāvarī became exceedingly pure, joined by the assembly [of sages]. Whatever dust there was from them as they were traveling on the road at that moment—
What need is there for me to describe the merit-bestowing power of touching [the dust of] horse-sacrifices?
For those traveling on the path to Dvārakā, with every step taken,
the merit of thousands of sacrifices arises from each individual particle of dust.
Nārada spoke to all those divine members of the assembly of pilgrims:
"Indeed, there are thousands of heaps of your masses of merit, for you have beheld the Gomatī-tīrtha as well as the glorious Lord Hari. (51)
O you all, all the holy fords (tīrthas) and sacred fields (kṣetras) in their entirety are blessed here, because the city of Kṛṣṇa has been seen by you! O holy fords!
O you all, best of rivers! Behold this [city]. || 52–53 ||
Dvārakā is the destroyer of the sins of men and the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Dvārakā, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, brings glory to the entire universe.
Therein lie the Gomatī river, Lord Kṛṣṇa himself, and Rukmiṇī, the beloved of Hari.
This earth shines everywhere as being superior even to Goloka;
it should be understood as Vaikuṇṭha itself, for it is like a reflection of Vaikuṇṭha.
At that time, when Nārada had offered his praise, [the Lord] himself [spoke]. || 55-56 ||
Then Dvārakā and the personified Gomatī arrived, desiring to offer a welcome;
they were saluted by the gods and the sacred fords as well.
At that time, Nārada spoke to Dvārakā and likewise to the Gomatī.
Gautamī and Prayāgarāja bow at your feet;
so too do Gaṅgā, Narmadā, Sūryaputrī, Prācī, Sarasvatī, Candrabhāgā, Sarayū, Kṣiprā, and Kuṅkumavāpikā. (59)
The Sindhu, Śoṇā, Gaṇḍakī, Vipāśā, and Tapatī,
as well as the Kṛṣṇā, Bhīmarathī, Svarṇā, and Payoṣṇī, indeed bow down to you.
This Vārāṇasī also certainly bows at your feet.
Kurukṣetra, Mathurā, and Avantikā indeed bow down to you;
Māyā, Ayodhyā, Gayā, Kāñcī, and Viśālā also bow down to you.
Śālagrāma, the great sacred field, Prabhāsa, and Puruṣottama likewise pay homage to you.
Saptārṇava, Dhenuka, Daśāraṇya, Daṇḍaka, Arbuda, Kurukṣetra, Dharmāraṇya, Kālaka,
Nārāyaṇasaras, Puṣkara, and likewise Gokula.
"O Dvārakā, served by Kṛṣṇa! Mānasa, Meru, Kailāsa, Mandara, Himavat, and Vindhya—all these bow at your feet. As Nārada spoke thus, the people of Dvārakā were filled with joy in their hearts. (64–65)
Remembering Gomatī with his hands, he spoke these charming words:
"You are blessed to have arrived; this is a great gain for me.
I offer a welcome to all of you; please partake of the food of Kṛṣṇa."
"Drink the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s feet and remain here indeed!
By the yoga of Kṛṣṇa and by my touch,
all your sins have been utterly consumed through the grace of Śrī Hari."
Thus, at that time, he gladdened everyone with words of welcome.
And indeed, the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā were seen in the sky, along with Śiva and Śivā accompanied by their Gaṇas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras. (69)
The Maruts, the guardians of the worlds, the Siddhas, and likewise the Vidyādharas;
all the Viśvedevas, the Ādityas, and the planets; as well as the sages beginning with Bhṛgu, the great sages beginning with Sanaka, and the Vairājas who are supreme lords.
Devoted to their wives, they danced and descended [from the mountain] filled with great joy;
having bathed on the earth at the Gomatī, they beheld Kṛṣṇa. Having drunk the gracious water and seen the assembly of pilgrims, [they were satisfied].
Overcome with supreme wonder,
they repeatedly made proclamations from within their joyful hearts, saying, "Victory to the Tīrthas! And Dvārakā indeed offered them a welcome and due honor.
And by Gomatī as well, the washing away of the sins of all was accomplished.
All the gods and all the sacred fords (tīrthas) bowed down simultaneously with devotion.
The host of gods and the host of sacred fords bowed to one another.
Then they all bowed down simultaneously and became filled with joy;
having recognized the preeminence of Dvārakā as well as the preeminence of the Gomatī, they cried out, "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Victory to Kṛṣṇa! ||76-77||
Then, with devotion, they performed the worship of Gomatī, Dvārakā, Śrī, and Kṛṣṇa with divine garments, divine fragrant ointments,
and excellent divine ornaments made of precious gems, diamonds, and the like.
With divine garlands and ornaments, with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood;
with tulasī, saffron, incense, the waving of lamps, and circumambulations;
with various divine food offerings, sweet foods, and delicious drinks. (79–80)
Having honored him with betel leaves, sweet powders, beloved offerings,
highly auspicious substances, and fans and whisks, they,
having fulfilled their purpose, danced before Hari.
Then Kṛṣṇa himself appeared and spoke to them with a smile:
"O holy fords, O gods, goddesses, mountains, and great sages! I am pleased with you because of your performance of the rite of pilgrimage; may there be peace for you."
Then the holy places and others said: "O All-pervading Lord, we have been delivered by the Supreme Self;
through your grace, O Lord, we have obtained our heart's desire.
May there be for us unfailing devotion to your lotus feet."
"Thus may this Dvārakā always be worthy of worship by all.
Having spoken thus, both of them then consecrated Dvārakā and the Gomatī as sovereigns over all sacred fords (tīrthas).
With palms joined in reverence, they repeatedly performed worship with divine offerings.
Then, the great divine attendants of Hari arrived and said,
"This auspicious lady is indeed the Great Queen of the Kings of Tīrthas."
"Indeed, Dvārakā is to be served; may you all remain here always according to your own will.
Then, having circumambulated Dvārakā and prostrated before it, the deities of the sacred fields and holy fords took up their residence there.
O beloved, fifty crores of holy fords (tīrthas) are situated in the north;
in the eastern direction are rivers with sixty crores of holy fords;
and in the south are sacred mountains, forests, and lakes.
They remained together with their own kinsmen, numbering nine hundred and ninety million.
The seven oceans and other such bodies of water are situated in the western direction;
and in all the intermediate directions, the number of sacred fords (tīrthas) is beyond reckoning.
A hundred crore of holy fords dwell at the confluence of the ocean;
Vārāṇasī is in the northeast, while Avantī is situated in the east;
Kuṅkumavāpī is in the southeast, Kāñcī is in the south, and Mathurā is in the southwest.
Māyā is situated in the southwest, and Ayodhyā is situated in the west;
Kurukṣetra is in the northwest, and likewise Harikṣetra is in the north. Thus, the first enclosure is protected by sacred fords, fields, and other such sites. (94–95)
The second [enclosure] was by the lords of creatures (Prajeśvaras), the third by the leaders of the gods;
the fourth by the multitudes of sages and Siddhas, and the fifth by the Gaṅgā and other rivers. The sixth enclosure was by the sacred fords (Tīrthas), and the seventh by Kāśī and other such places.
The eighth [field] is with the foremost of fields and so forth; the ninth is with the hermitages and so forth;
and the tenth is with Meru and so forth—those of divine vision indeed behold these.
Thus, O attendants, the gods and the holy fords (tīrthas) purify others.
They established their own residence with their second forms;
having received leave from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of the Gomatī,
all the holy places, deities, and attendants performed their ritual ablutions and departed.
And they arrive every year when Jupiter is situated in the zodiac sign of Leo.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Mass Gathering and Residence at the Dvārakā Tīrtha by All the Tīrthas, Devas, and Pārṣadas, along with the Godāvarī, when Jupiter is in the Sign of Leo," within the *Dvārakā-māhātmya* of the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 231.
Chapter 232 [[Author:
Chapter 233 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Especially, O Mahālakṣmī! when Jupiter is situated in the zodiac sign of Leo, the heaps of sins of those who perform pilgrimage to the holy site of Dvārakā are consumed by fire.
Those who undertake the journey to Dvārakā every year—
By touching the dust of their feet, human beings attain liberation.
I shall first relate that which was asked by Dilīpa of Vasiṣṭha:
"The sin committed in another field perishes through the service of sacred fords (tīrthas)."
It is said that the sins committed at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and sacred fields (*kṣetra*) possess the quality of being "adamantine glue" (*vajralepa*).
Since such sin is like adamantine glue, is there anywhere any liberation from it, or not?
O Sage, tell me: where is that field said to exist where sin does not take root?
Having heard that, Vasiṣṭha, who possessed divine vision, said to the king:
"A certain ascetic named Māyānanda, a bearer of the triple staff (tridaṇḍin) residing in Kāśī,
has indeed become infatuated with a beautiful young woman of the Mātaṅga caste."
Drawn by a passionate nature toward liquor and meat,
his mind deluded by the pride of desire, he indulged in such food;
bearing the state of a *caṇḍāla*, he committed theft at night out of greed.
His sins increased repeatedly through his association with this Mātaṅgī.
By the power of time, he died in Kāśī and became a wild wolf;
thereafter, he became a tiger, a monkey, a dog, a jackal, and a boar.

That sin had not perished even after thousands of births; then, on a saline wasteland in a desolate place, by the power of Kāśikā, he became a Rākṣasa endowed with the memory of his former lives. Wandering through forests and mountains, the Rākṣasa reached the Vindhya mountain.
There, his liberation from that sinful birth was truly marvelous.
Having performed the great pilgrimage at Dvārāvatī and beheld Kṛṣṇa,
he bathed in the waters of the Gomatī and drank the nectar-like water of Kṛṣṇa.
A certain Brahmin residing in Gayā, while traveling home,
stood for a moment on the road by a sturdy tree on the Vindhya mountain to rest.
He was a devoted Brahmin with a vertical *tilaka* and wearing a garland of *tulasī*.
There the Rākṣasa saw [him] purified by the water of the Gomatī.
Merely by the sight of him, the mass of his sins—which was as hard as adamant and destined to bring future suffering—was reduced to ashes in an instant. (14–15)
By the manifestation of his merit, he recognized Kṛṣṇa as a traveler;
then, having approached him face-to-face, that traveler from Dvārakā who was Kṛṣṇa, he bowed to and praised him, and said: "By the sight of you today, for me..."
"The adamantine ointment and the accumulation of sins have been burnt; I am liberated in every way.
(17) Thereupon the traveler went to his own home, and then the Rākṣasa arrived at Dvārakā, having realized there the great power of the sacred ford. (18)
Having cast off his own body in the Gomatī, he attained the station of Viṣṇu;
sins do not sprout again from the sight of her who is intent on pilgrimage.
What then need be said regarding the fruit of actually being present at Dvāravatī during a conjunction [of planets]? || 19 ||
It is the great burner of sins that are as thick as adamantine paste;
it is the supreme field born of Goloka, the foremost among all sacred fields.
Dvārakā-kṣetra alone exists on earth, established by Kṛṣṇa himself.
Having heard this, Dilīpa also went to Dvārakā for the sake of visiting the sacred sites;
and having seen Kṛṣṇa and the Gomatī river, he attained supreme perfection.
In Dvārakā, both men and women remained four-armed.
Those who reside in Goloka are indeed beheld by the denizens of heaven (divaukasas).
Even insects, moths, and the like, as well as the dull-witted and immobile beings,
having reached their dwellings in Dvārakā, become divine embodiments of Goloka.

For those whose goal is Dvāravatī and for those of perpetual celibacy, such a destination is difficult to attain. O Lakṣmī! Whatever is offered in sacrifice, recited as prayer, given as charity, used for bathing, or performed as austerity in Dvārakā—all that becomes ten-million-fold and indeed infinite in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
All the men and women residing in Dvārakā possess four arms.
Indeed, by the power of Hari, no sin takes root in Dvārakā;
even its most meritorious dust effects the liberation of sinners.
Beginning from Kuśāvarta up to where it meets the ocean, the Gomatī flows; when Jupiter is situated in the zodiac sign of Leo,
bathing there yields a fruit greater than sixty-two baths in the Godāvarī.

Those who remember Dvārakā, the Gomatī river, the Gopīs’ lake, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself every day— even if they reside a thousand yojanas away— partake in the full fruit of the sacred pilgrimage site of Dvāravatī.
The betrayer of friends, the killer of a brother, the slayer of a cow, and he who is devoted to another’s wife;
the murderer of a mother, the murderer of a father, the destroyer of an embryo, the killer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
all these are liberated from all sins by the sight of Kṛṣṇa at Dvārakā.
Especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, on the Jayantī, and on the day of Viṣṇu;
and particularly in the months of Māgha, Phālguna, and Caitra—on the full moon, the new moon, the eleventh day (ekādaśī), and likewise at a confluence of rivers. ||32-33||
On the twelfth lunar day, at the beginning of each fortnight, as well as under the asterisms of Rohiṇī and Śravaṇa,
and likewise under Puṣya and Punarvasu, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the day of the destruction of the day (dinakṣaya),
when the lunar day and asterism are auspicious, and during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
Beholding Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Dvārāvatī bestows infinite merit.
In that city, one should establish a sacrificial session, a water-station, a mansion, a temple, or even a monastery;
likewise, a residence for ascetics and holy men, a hall for virtuous women, and a shrine. (35–36)
Having caused a step-well, a well, a pond, the restoration of ruins, a means of livelihood,
the consecration of an image of Viṣṇu, and likewise royal enjoyments and the like to be made,
a man or a woman, having experienced divine pleasures, remains in heaven.

One shall attain the enjoyments of Vaikuṇṭha belonging to the Vairāja class and achieve equality with Kṛṣṇa. (38) He who installs an image made of wood or stone in Dvāravatī, having attained the status of a sovereign ruler, shall reach equality with Śrī Viṣṇu. (39)
Having traveled to the sacred ford of Dvārakā, they surely deliver one hundred and one generations of their lineage,
along with seven ancestral clans, through the power of Kṛṣṇa,
for every single step taken toward the city of Dvārāvatī.
In the Kali age, the merit of thousands of sacrifices accrues to embodied beings.
Even a stone marked with the discus, when seen by someone, becomes a source of liberation.
Both Sudarśana, the single-discus [Viṣṇu], and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa [are likewise liberating].
With three he is Acyuta, with four he is Janārdana-Indra;
with five he is Vāsudeva, and with six he is indeed Pradyumna.
With seven he is Baladeva, and with eight he is Puruṣottama.
The soul of all, possessing nine wheels and ten wheels, the lord of ten;
with eleven he is Mahāviṣṇu, while as the twelvefold self, he is the bestower of liberation.
Beyond that, he is Ananta, the granter of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Those who perform the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) on the full moon days of Vaiśākha and Kārtika,
having abandoned their state as ghosts in Dvārakā, their ancestors are liberated—
thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of their kin.

By beholding Kṛṣṇa during the Trispṛśā festival, those who abide in good deeds as well as those who abide in forbidden acts dwell in that abode of Viṣṇu. O my beloved, what indeed is the need for bathing in the sixty-seven sacred pilgrimage sites? 47–48.
"If one has attained a human body but does not go to Dvārakā,
the divine people residing in Dvārakā grieve for that person as having lived a life in vain.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you everything concerning my sacred field.
"By hearing whose greatness, liberation is considered to be within one's grasp.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Pilgrimage to Dvārakā, Which Destroys Sins as Indestructible as Vajra-Lepa, Belonging to Māyānandayati Residing in Kāśī," in the section on the Greatness of Dvārakā within the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*). Chapter 232.
Chapter 233 [Author: Chapter 234 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Mahāviṣṇu, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī Kamalā!
From hearing the clay of Dvārakā, great joy arises within me.
O Lord, I have been made one who has fulfilled her purpose by you, the Primordial Compassionate One.
"Tell me the greatness or even the essential nature of Trispṛśā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you the greatness of Trispṛśā."
There is no other vow equal to this, which bestows both fruit and liberation.
Having fully understood its fruit, one is released from the bondage of karma;
through the instruction of this vow, one attains liberation, and Mādhava rejoices because of the vow.
Therefore, I shall declare to you that which fulfills all intentions:
the vow by which Kṛṣṇa was directly worshipped.
One who utters the name of Trispṛśā partakes in the merit of the *puraścaraṇa* rite.

O Lotus-born One, liberation cannot be attained by him through the Vedas, nor through ancient narratives, nor through sacrifices, nor through multitudes of sacred fords (tīrthas), nor through other innumerable austerities, nor even by worshipping the deities and others, if the Trispṛśā has not been performed.
Thus questioned by Brahmā, I then spoke:
"The Trispṛśā vow alone is the great path for crossing over the multitude of people afflicted by the objects of the senses; there is no other path that grants liberation. (8)
For those whose horses are the senses, there is no stability without austerity.

Indeed, I have declared that the Ekādaśī which involves the "three touches" is austerity; for if they should observe the vow while immersed in the forest of sense-objects, [it will be in vain]. (1.233.10)
Then, for those who observe the Trispṛśā vow, their liberation shall be eternal.
This bestower of liberation should be performed by the most excellent of the virtuous;
it occurs when it falls through astrological conjunction during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
It bestows the merit of ten thousand Soma sacrifices and grants liberation in the northern region.
It is the destroyer of the great sin of ten million killings and possesses great power.
By taking refuge in the Trispṛśā vow, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed.
They go to immediate dissolution; what need is there to mention other sins?
This does not happen at Prayāga, nor at Puṣkara, nor at Badarī, nor in the region of Kāśī; nor indeed at the Gomatī, nor at the Revā, nor at Raivata, nor at Indradyumna.
O Mahālakṣmī! Liberation shall not occur at Kuṅkumavāpī, Kedāra, Rāmeśvara, or Mathurā, if the Trispṛśā vow has not been performed;
nor does it come through the abandonment of life at Prayāga, Kāśī, or likewise at Kuśapura.

The eternal liberation that is considered to result from bathing in the Gomatī is attained at home through fasting on the Trispṛśā day. It is said to grant liberation even to the ignorant, and especially to women and Śūdras. (17)
The knowledge of this [Vidyā] is always meritorious, purifying, and bestows the ultimate truth;
it immediately generates auspiciousness and grants dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
It is the life-force for those devoted to Viṣṇu, and especially so for women. (18–19)
She is the purifier and the meritorious mother of all, like the Mother of the Vedas;
she is as purifying as Kamalā, a protector equal to Ramā,
and the bestower of fruits that encompass even the superior fruits of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Accompanied by hundreds of millions of sacred fords (tīrthas), she goes to the Ganges with the desire to bathe;
she goes to the vicinity of Kṛṣṇa at the Gomatī for the sake of purification.
Thousands of millions of sacred fords reside on the banks of the Gomatī.
She too performs the Trispṛśā vow for the purification of her sins:
[the sin of] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, killing a cow, killing a woman;
stealing the property of a Brahmin or a deity, and beating one's mother or father. (23)
Betrayal of the guru, hostility toward Hari, and the eating of forbidden food; indeed, approaching those who should not be approached, violence, and the constant disparagement of the virtuous;
as well as other cruel deeds and whatever other sins there may be—[these are all destroyed]. (24–25)

That Trispṛśā, the most excellent purifier, truly dispels all misfortune; it is indeed superior to Sarasvatī and is highly honored even by Arbuda. It surpasses ten million sacrifices and excels in the merit of burnt offerings and gifts.
It is meritorious beyond ten million recitations, and likewise it excels the goals of human endeavor;
it surpasses Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and is honored as the pinnacle of self-knowledge.
Indeed, this Trispṛśā vow, which bestows liberation, must be performed.
If the Ekādaśī is conjoined with the Sun, followed by Dvādaśī,
and Trayodaśī remains at the end of the night, that is indeed the Trispṛśā Ekādaśī;
provided it occurs at the time of dawn, prior to the rising of the Sun.
If the tenth day persists, that is called the "piercing" (vedha) of the tenth day.
O my beloved, I cannot tolerate the defect born of the piercing of the tenth day;
for indeed, when accompanied by the piercing of the tenth day, it must never be observed.
Just as a husband is also defiled by the fault of his wife’s menstruation,
so too does the Ekādaśī overlapping with the tenth day (Daśamī) bestow a fault.
When the auspicious Daśamī and Ekādaśī occur on the same day, [it is defective].
Even then, that Trispṛśā day must be avoided with great effort;
for he by whom the Ekādaśī vow is performed when it is mixed with the tenth day has consumed Hālāhala poison, and not performed that vow.
The merit accumulated over ten million births is exhausted within one’s own continuum;
one’s family falls from heaven, and thereafter one indeed goes to the Raurava hell.
Therefore, that day of mine joined with the tenth lunar day must certainly be avoided.
When [the Ekādaśī] is increasing, it should be abandoned if it is pierced by the Daśamī, and one should observe the Ekādaśī joined with the Dvādaśī.
By the Creator, a dwelling was granted to Mohinī in the case of a Daśamī-piercing;
therefore, a great sin is to be understood for one who observes the vow when it is conjoined with a Daśamī-piercing.
Likewise, whether there is an increase or a decrease [in lunar days], or when a doubt has arisen, the Dvādaśī most dear to me must always be observed by my command.
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the correct procedure for the Trispṛśā vow.
O Lotus-born One, a golden image of me should be fashioned according to one's wealth—using a *pala*, half a *pala*, or even half of that.
A copper vessel filled with sesame seeds, along with a jar containing gems, water, and other offerings, [should also be provided]. (1.233.40)
Likewise, provided with leaves, flowers, white cloth, camphor, and other offerings,
it should be placed upon a *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala made of grain.
O my beloved, that golden image of mine should be placed in a jar or a vessel.
One should establish Lakṣmī by my side and then perform the worship.
One should offer the invocation, the seat, water for the feet, and the respectful offering (arghya). Then one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) and a bath with water.
One should perform a bath with milk, a bath with curds, and thereafter a bath with ghee;
one should then cause a bath with sugar to be performed and offer a bath with honey.
One should perform a consecration with waters from sacred fords and wipe [the image] with cloths.
One should offer a lower garment, a fine cloth, an arm-guard, and likewise a bodice;
as well as an upper garment, a sash, and even a sacred thread.
One should also give an auspicious thread, a kaustubha gem, and a small string of beads.
She should attend to her hair, wear oils, flowers, and the like;
she should arrange her braid, style her topknot, and likewise apply perfumes and tie it in a knot.
She should apply collyrium to her eyes and a sectarian mark with a crescent moon upon her forehead.
One should worship with sandalwood paste mixed with musk and enriched with camphor. One should place the Nāsānasthī on the nose, the Cibuka on the chin, and the Ṭibakī on the cheeks;
likewise, one should offer the Kuṇḍalas as ear-ornaments for the ears and the Śṛṅkhalas as well.
One should apply vermilion and saffron as a coloring for the lips;
one should offer garlands of *tulasī* with beautiful clusters of flowers,
as well as necklaces of gold, gems, and jewels, along with chains and bracelets.
One should give rings, a girdle, and beautiful anklets enriched with small bells;
one should give sandals, two sticks, and garments with silk fringes;
likewise, one should provide a crown, flower-crests, and ear-ornaments.
One should offer a fan and sandals, well-adorned and fit for a king;
one should offer garlands of *tulasī* to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa for me.
One should also offer *gulāl*, blood from a *bīra*, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers.
A person should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings to Śrī Viṣṇu.
One should indeed present pleasing food offerings, many kinds of sweet dishes, very sweet fruits, and cool water. (54–55)
One should offer fragrant, desirable drinking water that bestows peace;
one should give betel-leaf enriched with many ingredients for the purification of the mouth.
And one should indeed offer a golden ring as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Keśava.
Therefore, one should offer whatever is required for that worship.
(57) One should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) with nine or five wicks;
then, one should wipe [the image] with a white cloth three times, again and again. (58)
Then, one should perform the whirling of the conch at the tip of the face;
thereafter, with sincere devotion, one should pour water from the head while wearing wet clothes.
One should offer praise like a staff and perform circumambulations again and again.
One should perform many prostrations and also offer a request for forgiveness. (1.233.60) Having scattered a handful of flowers, one should pray to the Supreme Lord;
closing the eyes, one should meditate upon His form while standing before Him. (1.233.61)
To Dāmodara, indeed, [he offered] the feet; to Mādhava, the knees; to Kāmasvarūpa, the private parts; to Vāmanamūrti, the waist;
to Padmanābha, the navel; and to Viśvahetu, the belly.
The heart to the embodiment of knowledge, the throat to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha;
the arms to the thousand-armed one, and the eyes to the one whose form is yoga;
the head to the thousand-headed one, and likewise all the limbs to the Lord.
I meditate indeed upon Your form both as divided and as unified within me.
O Great King, You who are attainable through meditation, You swiftly destroy my sin.
When remembered, You take away sins, evil dreams, and ill-considered thoughts.
[Protect me] from ill omens, from fear of Yama, and from the suffering born of miserable rebirths;
and from whatever else may be bodily, pertaining to this world, or pertaining to the next world—
protect me from all that and from every offense that brings about suffering.
O Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, may there always be devotion unto You!
Grant me service at Your feet and lead me indeed to Vaikuṇṭha.
For the Trispṛśā [Ekādaśī], Nārāyaṇa Himself is the Creator, the Master, and the Lord.
"May you alone, Hari Mādhava, grant me liberation.
Having thus offered praise, he should then perform a dance before the presence of the God, accompanied by song and instrumental music, with beautiful tones and a pleasing appearance.
Thus, having worshipped the Lord Kṛṣṇa in the morning according to the prescribed rite— having fashioned an image made of gold in the form of Ekādaśī and the form of Lakṣmī—
one should then pay obeisances and proceed to the assembly of the virtuous for the sacred narrative.
One should spend the day in every possible way—through chanting, as well as through devotion, worship, and recitation;
through hearing, remembering, and service;
or through ritual honoring or by means of perfect salutation. (72–73)

Whether capable or incapable, one should observe the vow that bestows the fruit of one’s desired prosperity— whether by abstaining from food, subsisting on water, eating only at night, or eating but once a day—
at the time of midday, one should offer betel, food, and fruit.
One should likewise offer water, a bed, a couch, a pillow, and a bolster.
In the evening, one should again offer water and perform the *ārātrika* ceremony according to the prescribed rite.
One should also perform worship with devotion using the sixteen excellent articles of offering.
Having thus worshipped the Guru, one should keep a vigil during the night,
accompanied by singing, dancing, ritual performance, and hymns of praise.
Then, at the end of the night, having offered the *argha* to Hari according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
Having performed the rites such as bathing, one should feed virtuous Brahmins;
one should also feed virtuous women and children, and give gifts and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
Thus, on the portion of the twelfth day, or even on the thirteenth day.
For the sake of breaking the fast, one should indeed eat with devotion after showing grace;
then, according to the prescribed rite, one should dismiss the *sarvatobhadra* mandala, the water-pot, and likewise Lord Hari. By doing so, one shall attain the fruit of liberation.
Upon hearing this narration of the Trispṛśā vow, one shall obtain its fruit.
By him who has performed the fast of Trispṛśā, thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices have indeed been accomplished.
One who performs the Trispṛśā vow certainly delivers one hundred and eight generations of their lineage,
including both maternal and paternal ancestors, in every way.
Joined by all of them, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
One who observes the Trispṛśā vow obtains the fruit of ten million sacred fords and ten million holy fields.
Men and women of all castes attain liberation by means of that vow.
It was first established by Brahmā and later by the great sages.
This [vow] should always be performed by devotees, both those with desires and those free from desire.
Whatever fruit may arise from bathing in the Gaṅgā for ten million years,
even greater than that shall be the true merit of one who observes the Trispṛśā vow.
Whatever fruit might be obtained at Kurukṣetra during ten million solar eclipses,
or whatever fruit is gained there by the daily gift of hundreds of loads of gold—
that merit born of giving ten million cows shall belong to one who observes the Trispṛśā vow.
Thousands of millions of sins and hundreds of millions of killings are destroyed by the fast of the Ekādaśī, specifically the Trispṛśā vow.
Furthermore, whoever proclaims this vow shall also obtain its fruit.

The *Trispṛśā* is difficult to obtain in this world; it is not attained by men at all. Even those ancestors who, having their deeds unknown, have fallen into the state of *preta*s, a man born of noble lineage may rescue them from their downward descent by performing the *Trispṛśā*.
What more need be said here? This Trispṛśā [Ekādaśī] bestows liberation; it grants prosperity in this world and indeed bestows salvation in the next.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits and Worship of the Trispṛśā Ekādaśī Vow," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 233: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 234 [[Author: Chapter 235 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! to the narrative that explains the origin of Ekādaśī, which arose in the former Kṛta Yuga and was manifested by Nārāyaṇa.
In that Satya Yuga, there was born in the Tālajaṅgha clan a great and most wonderful asura named Nāḍījaṅgha, who was exceedingly fierce. His son was Murajaṅgha, who struck fear into the gods.
Having performed austerities for a thousand years, he attained supreme power.
By him even Indra was conquered, and all the gods were likewise defeated;
driven out from heaven, the gods wandered across the surface of the earth.
Terrified and deprived of their composure, they went where Purandara was;
Purandara, too, filled with grief, went where Janārdana was.
Śaṅkara, as well as Brahmā and the other lords of the gods, likewise departed.
They offered praise to Śrī Nārāyaṇa as he lay within the waters:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge;
you are the crusher of the Dānavas, Daityas, and Asuras. (6–7)
You are always the refuge for the afflicted and the destroyer of the suffering of those seeking shelter.
O ocean of compassion, protect us from the Daitya who has increased his strength!
You are the goal, you are supreme bliss, and you are the ultimate resort for your devotees.
You are the mother, the protector, the master; you are the father, the guardian, and the Lord.
You are that which is rightly spoken of as the cause, as well as the origin and the creation.
You alone are the fulfiller therein; you alone are the embodied Hara.
You alone are the deity who effects withdrawal; you are the giver of food.
You are *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*; you alone are the fire and the syllable *oṃ*.
Indeed, you are Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṃkarṣaṇa.
You alone are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna; you alone are the millions of gods.
You alone are the sun and the moon, as well as space, wind, fire, water, and earth.
Therefore, O Puruṣottama, you alone are the intermediate creation as well.
You are the giver of boons, the protector, and the withdrawer of boons;
everything, both the stationary and the moving, is established in you alone.
The foremost of the gods have been defeated by the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
When they become unhappy, they then go to you for refuge. (15) We have all fallen from heaven and are oppressed by the Dānavas and others;
we wander through the forest regions, O Lord, desiring protection. (16)
"O Lord, protect us in every way from the Dānava named Mura.
Having heard them, Nārāyaṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, asked them:
"What is that Dānava like? What is his name, what is his strength, and what is his status?"
"Tell me everything, O lords of the gods, so that having heard it, I may contemplate his destruction.
Then Indra spoke to the god Viṣṇu, the Lord Nārāyaṇa:
"He is born of the lineage of Brahmā; he is a Danuja born from Kaśyapa."
Tālajaṅgha was exceedingly cruel, and his son was Nāḍīprajaṅghaka. That son was a great sinner;
he had a son who, by the name of Murajaṅgha, performed severe penance.
Indeed, for a thousand years he remained without food;
then, standing on the big toe of his foot, he performed penance for a hundred years.
For another hundred years, lying in water, he practiced formidable austerities.
For a hundred years he subsisted on air, gazing at the sun for a hundred years;
having performed most rigorous penance, he subsisted on vapors for a hundred years and practiced austerity in meditative absorption for five hundred years.
Upon his body there was an anthill covered with glass shards,
overrun by trees and creepers, resembling a mountain peak.
From it, a most terrible smoke emerged and ascended to heaven.
From his head arose a great fire by which the sky then blazed, as did the earth and the worlds beginning with Satya; the gods and humans trembled,
and they all went for refuge to Brahmā, the Great-Grandfather.
They did not say that they themselves had failed to fall [into the fire], but rather that [the world] was an ocean of suffering:
"What is this fire? How has it arisen? Alas, it consumes everything!
Protect, protect us, O Lord of Creatures; bring peace, O Master of the World! (27–28)
Having heard these words, Brahmā, together with the gods, set out to search for him;
following the trail of smoke from the fire, he reached his source situated upon the earth.
Seeing the trees and other things there, the Creator then became bewildered.
"Aha! Indeed, no ascetic person is seen here at all.
How and why should he be sought by me here?
Having reflected thus, Brahmā sat down upon the surface of the earth.
Then Viṣṇu indeed blew the great conch shell repeatedly;
yet even so, O gods, Mura did not wake there at that time.
All the deities stood with their hopes destroyed, their inner desires withered away.
Then Viṣṇu established his meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and self-restraint (*saṃyama*) there;
he entered the body of the demon Mura, which was like dry wood, a mere mass of dried channels, flesh, and bones. (33–34)
Having made the body of the unborn one possessed of form and endowed with activity, he drenched it;
and when he again sprinkled the head with water from his water-pot,
the body of the demon Muradānava then attained the state of a sprout.
When his eyes were opened and he saw the gods, that Dānava bowed and said:
"How have you come with the desire to destroy my penance?
Go far away; I have no business at all with the gods."
Then Brahmā said to the Daitya: "We have been pleased by your asceticism; we have arrived to grant you a boon. Speak your desire, my son.
Mura replied: "Let there be no death for me at the hands of anyone created by you, under any circumstances."
"Let it be granted by Viṣṇu or even by Hara; grant this to me.
Having given the boon, saying "So be it," Brahmā and the others then departed.
Mura also, rising up delighted, went to his own abode.
Mera protected the beautiful ancestral capital, Candrāvatī, according to the prescribed rites, though it was inhabited by dānavas.
By him the gods were utterly defeated and even expelled from heaven.
Having seized the position of Indra, the Dānava was made into Indra;
having taken his own place as Agni, another was created as Agni;
and two others were made as the Sun and Moon, accompanied by the planets and constellations. (42–43)
Other Dānavas born of his own lineage were appointed as the guardians of the directions;
indeed, having defeated the gods, Mura made others the guardians of the worlds (lokapālas).
The hosts of gods were cast into prison and bound in fetters.
Another world of the gods has been created and adorned by the Dānavas.
Indeed, everything else was previously made and then overturned by him;
therefore, O Lord, abandon him before he arrives for the sake of seizing Lakṣmī.
"For as long as the Lord delays, there is loss at every passing moment.
Therefore, rising quickly, set your mind upon his destruction.
Having heard these words of Indra, Hari himself, who reclines upon Śeṣa, [acted accordingly].
Having risen up, he resolved to destroy Mura.
Hari, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, as well as the gods and great sages,
went to that city where the great asura was located— Candrāvatī.
Then Hari, standing outside near the vicinity, blew his conch shell.
Hearing that sound which signaled the call to battle,
he came out from the city with his army and waged a fierce war for the sake of combat.
Assuming many forms, the heroic Mura, with millions of missiles and weapons,
with mantras, powers of illusion, sorcery, and millions of shapes,
waged a terrible battle that caused the destruction of the gods. (51–52)
The gods, whose very nature consists of various forms, were wounded, slain, and destroyed;
they were broken, fainted, perished, and deprived of consciousness by the foremost of the Asuras with thousands of countless weapons. (53)
Being struck down, all the gods fled in the ten directions.
Seeing Viṣṇu, Mura said to him, "Stay! Stay!
Mukunda hurled a heavy mace, but Mura shattered it.
With his own mace, he swiftly hurled the formidable discus;
yet by the power of the boon, the discus was shattered against Mura.
Viṣṇu, filled with wonder, his eyes bloodshot with rage, [was struck].
Taking up a second discus, he hurled it at the millions of soldiers.
Those foremost Dānavas and Daityas had their heads severed; others fell dead, while some fainted and became lifeless. (57–58)
There, having attained its true purpose by becoming the ground for the distinction between Daityas and others,
that battlefield became like a forest of Dānavas lying asleep;
indeed, there was no spot on the surface of the earth anywhere that was not occupied by a headless torso (kabandha).
Then Mura suffered great distress due to the destruction of his army.
He wandered alone and fought with weapons against Viṣṇu;
at that time, the foremost of Viṣṇu’s weapons were destroyed by that enemy.
Then all the weapons were seized once more;
when Viṣṇu became deprived of his missiles and weapons,
the hosts of Daityas rejoiced and the great Dānavas exulted.
The Suras indeed fell into despondency, while the Asuras were intent on survival.
Then, realizing that Viṣṇu was disarmed, Mura engaged in a fierce hand-to-hand combat with Viṣṇu through his strategic skill.
By means of his illusory power (*māyā*), the demon Mura assailed the arm of Viṣṇu;
he bound that arm, and indeed the [other] arms became paralyzed.
All four of them were there, and the gods truly became distressed.
Crying out "Alas! Alas! with piteous lamentations, they were terrified and their hopes were shattered.
(66) At that time, Muru’s victory was complete in the crushing of the gods;
having conquered Satyaloka, he ruled over a splendid kingdom. (67)
Then Muru became the sovereign of the fourteen worlds;
terrified, Viṣṇu went to Badarikāśrama on the snowy mountain.
On the Himalaya, there is a great cave named Siṃhavatī.

It extends for four yojanas in both length and breadth. Having gone to it, which has but a single gate, the Great Lord, desiring the welfare of the worlds, showed fear to those who were asleep. (1.234.70)
Searching for his son Dānava there in that cave, he discovered Viṣṇu fast asleep; having recognized him, he entered the interior of the cavern.
Seeing Śrī Hari asleep, the lord of the Dānavas spoke to him:
"Aha! O you who are worshiped by the three worlds, why do you take refuge in a cave?
Why do you not provide protection for those who have sought shelter with you in this time of calamity?
Arise, Viṣṇu, may it be well with you; arise and engage in battle! (72–73)
Is the sleeping of jackals like you natural?
Either I shall lead you to the abode of Yama, or you may take refuge with me.
Always perform service for me, and grant me Vaikuṇṭha itself.
"Or else, O Viṣṇu, engage in battle; do not practice deceit at this time.
While Muru was speaking thus for his own destruction, Hari, while still asleep, reflected within himself.
He indeed called upon Mahālakṣmī for the sake of the destroyer of the Dānavas;
having remembered the boon granted by Brahmā to the ancestor of Mura,
and reflecting that there must be no destruction of those created by the Creator, [he did so].
Hari indeed manifested that divine power, which consists of a portion of Lakṣmī and is composed of his own eleven senses;
it took on a physical form there as a most beautiful maiden. (78–79)
That maiden was intensely radiant with great splendor, resembling gold; she was cooled by a mass of light pervaded by the brilliance of the moon;
she possessed a form suited to every excellence, and was as exceedingly beautiful as the form of Hari.
Equipped with divine weapons, her fresh breasts were fully developed;
she was slightly surpassed in beauty by the God of Love, captivating to the sight, and adorned with garments and hair that served as ornaments of auspicious fortune. (8.1–8.2)
Overwhelmed by the brilliance of lightning, her long eyes reaching to her ears,
she was possessed of great power, like an enchanting woman incarnate;
rich with the splendor of golden ornaments, her breath was fragrant.
She possessed a melodious voice, and her lotus-face was serene with all-encompassing loveliness.
(84) Her hands, feet, and soles were the hue of the *campaka* flower, and she was radiant with the luster of her fingers;
tender and soft-limbed, she was the abode of every beauty. (85)
Captivating the eyes, enchanting the mind, and stealing the very soul, she was exceedingly alluring;
having manifested in a most beautiful form, she broke into laughter.
Shining there in the midst of that splendor, she was beheld by Mura.
And Mura, having fallen into delusion, proceeded to embrace her.
The maiden said: "O great Daitya, you are wise and you are righteous;
yet, without the performance of a marriage ceremony, I cannot consent to be yours. (87–88)
"O Dānava, having defeated me, take her today; this is my stake.
Having conquered her in battle, take this high-minded woman as your slave.
Hearing these words from her, Mura forgot even Viṣṇu.
He became ready for the course of battle, equipped with weapons, missiles, and other gear.
When the maiden engaged the great Asura in the heat of combat,
his head was indeed severed from the region of his neck, and it was then reduced to ashes.
His body was crushed to powder by the mace and the blows of his feet;
Mura was slain, and his warriors were likewise killed by it.
Hearing a great clamor, Viṣṇu abandoned his sleep.
Seeing Mura dead, he was struck with amazement and realized:
"Aha! By this maiden, indeed, the mighty asura has been slain—he whom I myself could not previously conquer; he has been defeated and killed by her."
This Mahālakṣmī is indeed the Great Power (Mahāśakti) and the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā);
she is capable of destroying the suffering of the gods and acts for their welfare.
Every benefit has been rendered both to the gods and to me.
"The wicked Dānava, who struck terror into gods and asuras, has been slain.
Having attained such joy, he then questioned the maiden:
"Who are you? How was the Daitya killed? What is it that dwells in your mind?"
The maiden said to Hari: "I am considered the Ekādaśī of Viṣṇu;
I am the destroyer of all enemies and the annihilator of all sins. I consist of all splendor and bestow all the goals of human existence. (98)
"I am born from your body; I have arisen from the power of your senses.
O Lord, I am your daughter, joined with your consciousness. A Daitya has arrived here to kill my father while he sleeps. (1.234.100)
And the power of consciousness (cicchakti), beholding the Asura, emerged with the sense organs and so forth; thus, O Hari, I become for you composed of the splendor of the eleven organs.
Therefore, O Hari, I am known by the name Ekādaśī, the bestower of all merit.
"I have arisen for the destruction of the Asura, O Mādhava.
"The great Daitya, who caused suffering to the gods, has been destroyed by me.
Having heard these words of her daughter, Hari spoke to that daughter.
"Choose a boon, O auspicious lady; a great task has been accomplished for me.
I am pleased, and may prosperity be yours; I shall grant you everything that is in your heart.
O Goddess, there is nothing that should not be given to you, for the gods have been well protected by you. (104)
Dharma has been firmly established and the divine vow has been observed.
You have constantly provided the path of well-being for all people;
therefore, indeed, everything belonging to yourself must be given for your sake.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, Ekādaśī said:
"I am indeed Ekādaśī by name, the presiding deity whose essence is the vow.
I am the day of Ekādaśī; that day is considered mine."
My divine day is both white and black; it is indeed a sacred vow. This day is of great merit and purity, the most meritorious among all meritorious acts.
Therefore, my day should be observed through vows, fasting, and keeping vigil. (108–109)
On that day, the objects of the senses must be avoided with great effort.
That man who observes a fast here on my day certainly attains merit equal to an Ashvamedha sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.

Whether by eating once a day, by eating only at night, by fasting, or even with fruit, or even with water alone, one should perform the vow; such a person shall go to the abode of Mādhava. One should keep a vigil at night and perform the worship of Hari.
With flowers, incense, lamps, and various excellent articles, you should cause my worship to be performed; indeed, you should carry out the concluding rite (*udyāpana*).
Thus, O performer of the vow, you shall go to my imperishable abode.
May he never again enter a womb and may he be entirely free from sin.
On my day, may purity always arise for my devotees;
may their devotion to the Lord increase, as well as their faith in my vow.
"O Lord, if boons are to be granted to me, let them be such that hunger does not afflict my devotees, those observing vows, or women.
O Hari, these should be granted to me; furthermore, O Lord, hear from me another [request]."
Hari is the father, Hari is the mother, and Hari is always my kinsman.
Hari is the sustainer, Hari is the creator, Hari himself is the nourisher and the destroyer;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, become my husband forever through all your various forms.
"May I become your wife in twenty-six forms; act accordingly so that the defect of my lack of sacramental rites may be destroyed through marriage.
Devoted eternally to my husband, I shall serve you, my beloved lord."
"O Lord, grant me a boon; likewise, increase my good fortune.
Having heard this, Hari said, "O blessed lady, let that which you desire be fulfilled.
Let your vow be meritorious, and may you possess beautiful forms."
May I become your husband through various forms; be the bestower of the highest good.
May you be the granter, in every way, of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
May those purified by the vow of Ekādaśī attain my Vaiṣṇava abode.
"Having obtained good fruit in this world, they shall attain liberation at the end.
"Thus, O my beloved, I bestow these boons upon you.
Having said "Om," Ekādaśī herself became manifold.
Then Hari, through twenty-six forms of his own body,
duly took for himself the eleventh wife-form;
having dissolved her daughter-form, she exists together with the other wife-forms.
In a year of twelve months, there are indeed two [intercalary] months as well.
When combined, they are considered to be twenty-six in number.
An Ekādaśī is [valid] for a full day and night, even if there is a single Ghaṭikā of Daśamī [present].
That lunar day (tithi) must be avoided; rather, the auspicious twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast.

When the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is complete and the twelfth day is increasing in duration, one should break the fast on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī), for the merit gained by fasting on that [eleventh] day is multiplied a hundredfold when the breaking of the fast occurs on the thirteenth.
In this way, a person who observes the vow shall partake of its fruit and become a partaker of liberation.
Neither the Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor even Puṣkara,
nor indeed any Vaiṣṇava sacred field is equal to the day of Hari (Ekādaśī).
Having thus offered praise and taking his wife with him, Hari departed for the royal capital of Candrāvatī, which was indeed built by Mura. There, Hari liberated the gods who were bound in fetters.
Having made heaven his own through the grace of the Lord, the Master departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
(1.32) Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the supreme majesty of this vow;
what else do you wish to hear concerning the Ekādaśī known as Trispṛśā? (1.33)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Ekādaśī on Account of the Battle with the Dānava Mura, the Vow, and the Granting of Boons," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 235: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna).
Chapter 235.
[The Author: Chapter 236.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Hari, tell me about the vows of the twenty-six Ekādaśīs.
How should the rites be performed and how is the worship to be conducted?
What are the names, the lords, the fruits, the actions, and the rules for each of all the Ekādaśīs? Describe them individually.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! To that purifying story of theirs which bestows liberation, which is endowed with yoga, divine, and grants Vaikuṇṭha and other realms. (3)
Listen now to me regarding Unmīlanī and Pakṣavardhinī as well;
with a focused mind, understand from me the fruit of keeping vigil.
Indeed, Ekādaśī lasts for a full day and night, and there may be a ghaṭikā remaining at dawn.
That [river] is to be known as Unmīlanī, and she is exceedingly dear to Hari.
Whatever holy fords (tīrthas) and sacred places exist in the three worlds, as well as penance, the Vedas, and sacrifices—all these are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of her. (5–6)
They are indeed never equal to Unmīlanī anywhere;
nothing has been, nor will there ever be, anything equal to Unmīlanī.
Neither Kāśī, nor Gayā, nor Prayāga, nor the land of the Kurus [is its equal].
Neither the Puṣkara lake, nor Nārāyaṇa, nor the Himavat mountain;
neither Raivata, nor the Vindhya range, nor Malaya, nor even Meru;
neither Kuṅkumavāpī, nor Naimiṣa, nor Kālakṣetra, nor the forest. (8–9)
Neither the Candrabhāgā nor the Kāverī, nor the Sarayū nor the Gomatī;
neither the Godāvarī nor the Narmadā, nor the Svarṇalekhā nor the Vedikā; neither the Tāpī nor the Bhadrā, nor the Sindhu nor the Candanā.
Neither Śatruñjitā nor Ojasvatī, nor Vipāśā nor Gaṇḍakī;
neither Śoṇa nor Tuṅgabhadrā, nor even Sarasvatī; indeed, no other sacred fords (tīrthas) whatsoever are equal to Unmīlanī.
There is no merit equal to that of the Non-closing Day (Amāvāsyā), nor is there a deity higher than Śrī Hari.
Those who, having reached the day of Un-closing (Pūrṇimā), perform the worship of Hari,
cast off their mass of sins and go to the imperishable abode.
In whichever month the auspicious lunar day Ekādaśī occurs,
one should fashion an image of Hari made of gold according to the name of that month and worship it with supreme faith, devotion, and many excellent offerings. (14–15)
One should place a water-pot in the central mandala, filled with purifying water and endowed with the five jewels;
it should be provided with fragrances, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and adorned with garlands and cloth,
along with coconuts and other fruits.
In this [mandala] known as Sarvatobhadra, one should install the image and worship it.
There should be a vessel filled with wheat, endowed with various jewels,
mixed with various fragrances, and scented with the aroma of jasmine.
One should place a vessel filled with white-eyed rice and jasmine flowers near a banyan tree;
one should also place it by the side of the jar and worship Hari repeatedly.
One should give a pair of garments along with an upper cloth and a sacred thread;
one should also give sandals, an umbrella, a cooking pot, a water-pot,
vessels filled with the seven types of grain, and sesame seeds in abundance.
One should give silver, gold, cotton, and likewise milk-rice; as well as signet rings, finger-rings, and beautiful cows.
One should also present ornaments and various kinds of vessels.
Then he should give to the preceptor a cow with golden horns, silver hooves, a copper back, and a bell; one that yields milk from a bronze vessel and has a tail adorned with jewels.
He should also give a bed accompanied by a couch and provided with a ball and other furnishings.
One should offer incense, lamps, food offerings, fruits, leaves, and so forth;
likewise, various *tulasī* leaves and lotus flowers.
Then, during the worship of Hari, one should present various sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
One should meditate upon the form of Śrī Hari, especially limb by limb:
one should remember the feet by the name of the month, the knees by the name Viṣṇu, the private parts by the name Śrīśa, and the hips by the name Kṛṣṇa. (26–27)

One should remember the navel with the name "Brahman," the belly with the name "Viśva," the heart with the name "Jñātṛ," the throat with the word denoting "Vaikuṇṭhavāsin," the forehead with the name of one's Guru,
and the head with the Supreme Brahman.
The wise man should likewise meditate upon all the limbs [of the deity] under the name "Antaryāmin.
Having performed meditation, he should indeed worship the weapons, ornaments, garments, and decorations with devotion, and offer the arghya and other articles. (1.235.30)
Having placed a fruit upon a conch shell, accompanied by fragrant flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata),
and having wrapped it with a thread, one should offer the arghya with devotion.
In this manner, one should worship Hari with the sixteen excellent articles of offering.
And having bowed to Hari, one should pray: "Lift me up from the great ocean!
Although not even a small amount of merit has been performed by me for my own deliverance, nevertheless, you are my master; lift me up from the great ocean!"
By means of the Unmilini vow, deliver my ancestors here—
those who have fallen into base births, those who are sinful, and likewise those who have met with death.
Deliver others as well, both those of the past and those yet to come, from the great ocean of existence.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Mādhava, grant great liberation to all the pretas. Grant eternal devotion to Your form for me, who am afflicted.
Thus, with incense, lamps, food offerings, and water-offerings, [worship Him].
One should fully satisfy Śrī Hari with hymns of praise, lustration rites, and dances;
likewise, with gifts of clothing, gifts of cows, meals, and service.
The devotee should satisfy the Guru so that the Guru attains complete satisfaction.
In whatever way it may be, one should act so that when the guru is pleased, there is great fruit;
for since the guru was created by the Creator for the sake of delivering the worlds,
one should always please the guru with the service of all one's possessions and other such means.
One must perform worship of the guru, for the guru is Lord Hari, the bestower of liberation.
He who indeed releases one from what is harmful and always shows what is beneficial, who destroys ignorance through the gift of knowledge, shall become the giver of happiness. (1.235.40)
One should sever the beginningless bondage and bestow eternal happiness.
One should always take refuge in that Guru, who is Hari himself and skilled in the knowledge of Dharma and Artha;
