one should serve him at all times with devotion and never practice deceit regarding wealth. 41–42.
The grace of the Guru must be obtained so that the vow may become complete.
Having bathed on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), the devotee should worship Hari.
Afterwards, he should feed the Guru and feed many Brahmins.
Having fed virtuous men and women, one should perform one's own breaking of the fast.
The time of one who observes the vow should be spent with narrations of Kṛṣṇa’s deeds;
indeed, there is no gift equal to the gift of knowledge.
Knowledge should always be imparted constantly through the recitation of scriptures and other means;
Viṣṇu should be offered within that knowledge, and the donor shall attain liberation.
He who thus performs the Unmīlana-ekādaśī vow [attains the same].
He dwells eternally in Vaikuṇṭha for an infinite duration of kalpas.
O Lakṣmī, this Vaiṣṇava vow has been proclaimed to you;
by hearing it, all sinners attain liberation at that very moment.
The performer of the Unmīlanī vow is honored in the heavenly world;
both the gods and the ancestors shall attain a divine state.
A seeker of knowledge obtains auspicious knowledge that brings about all prosperity.
The vow of Ekādaśī, the worship of Viṣṇu, the adoration of Vaiṣṇavas, and the excellent service of saintly men and women—these four are difficult to attain.
By hearing this, one may be liberated from the bondage of birth and death throughout one's life. (1.235.50–51)
Neither Viṣṇu nor Vaiṣṇavas should ever be treated with hostility;
rather, after honoring and feeding them, one should then partake of one's own meal.
The Śālagrāma stone should be worshipped, and the Vaiṣṇava especially so.
One should offer incense, the ārātrika lamp, and scented water to Viṣṇu;
one should also present food offerings (naivedya) to Viṣṇu and likewise to the Vaiṣṇavas.
Then, the observer of the Ekādaśī vow should partake of a meal.
One should offer a lamp, likewise perform singing, and daily offer salutations;
one should perform worship with *śyāmā* sprouts, overflowing with love.
When worship is performed with *dūrvā* grass, the merit is equal to the gift of the entire earth.
Worship with the sprouts of *dūrvā* grass is exceedingly dear [to the Lord].
(56) There is nothing in this world as auspicious as the sprouts of *dūrvā*;
one who desires union (*sāyujya*) with Viṣṇu should perform worship with them. (57)
One should worship Hari with *dūrvā* grass, barley, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
On every twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), one should perform the worship according to the rules at dawn;
this is auspicious, bestowing liberation, happiness, and long life.
This is declared to be the Viṣṇu-vow, which bestows prosperity upon Vaiṣṇavas;
it grants happiness to householders and bestows liberation upon ascetics.
It pacifies all diseases and the like, and purifies the three bodies. (1.235.59–60)
The great *unmīlanī* vow, free from the overlap of the tenth lunar day, should be observed with a night vigil; it is supreme, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with one hundred thousand *tulasī* leaves.

One should wear the moon-like mark of Gopīcandana as an upward-pointing tilaka or puṇḍra for the purpose of worship, for its mere sight bestows liberation. One should also wear the Vaiṣṇava Astra-mantra and Varma-mantra, which destroy all suffering.
The killer of a Brahmin, the stealer of gold, the drinker of intoxicants, the eater of meat, the committer of forbidden sexual acts, the great sinner, and the speaker of insults and falsehoods—
these attain liberation from their sins by wearing the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
A Vaiṣṇava devotee should wear around his neck a garland of *dhātrī* fruits as well as a garland of *tulasī*, which constitutes a form of initiation for worship; likewise,
he should carry a stone from Dvārakā, a stone from the Gaṇḍakī, or even [an image of] Viṣṇu.
One should worship Tulasī daily; it yields the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
A day marked by an astrological conjunction (vedha) of Viṣṇu must certainly not be observed as a fast. Indeed, that king in whose kingdom such a day occurs [is at fault].

And the king is tainted by that sin and shall become a denizen of hell. (68) Having abandoned all kinds of piercing rituals and observed the fast on the day of Hari, there shall be the deliverance of ten million ancestors and the attainment of the abode of Viṣṇu. (69)
If fifty-five *ghaṭikās* remain from the sunrise of the tenth day, that eleventh day belongs to the following day; it is called a "pierced" (*viddha*) eleventh day.
However, if even a single *ghaṭikā* of the tenth day exists within the full twenty-four-hour period of the eleventh day, [it is pierced].
That lunar day (tithi) is certainly not to be observed as a fast; rather, the Dvādaśī vow is intended [to be observed].
When two Ekādaśīs occur, the later one is to be fasted upon, not the earlier one.
But when two Dvādaśīs occur, the earlier Dvādaśī is indeed to be fasted upon.
When the Ekādaśī is diminished, one should observe the fast on the Dvādaśī for the sake of the vow;
when the Daśamī is diminished, one should observe the fast on the Dvādaśī for the sake of the vow;
but when the Daśamī overlaps [the Ekādaśī], then one should observe the fast on the Ekādaśī.
When the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is reached at its conclusion, one should observe the fast on the eleventh day (ekādaśī).
Knowing this, one should perform the vow; Hari becomes pleased.
The performer of the vow goes to the abode of Hari by the will of Śrī Hari.
And on the twelfth day, that single *ghaṭikā* of the *ekādaśī* which occurs after the dawn (*aruṇodaya*) and at the time when the day begins to unfold,
serves as the time for the awakening of men for the purpose of their spiritual unfolding.

Therefore, O beloved, it has been declared by me that its name is Unmīlanī. Because it joins together (melayet) the upper realms— Brahmavaikuṇṭha, the supreme abode, the imperishable, and likewise Goloka—
it is described by me as Unmīlanī.
She who, through the practice of her vows, unites with the Supreme Brahman, the dark Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Hari, rising upwards, is called Unmīlanī.
She who tears asunder ignorance— which is of the nature of sin— and fear, which is death.
"For it truly brings together the higher world and light; thus it is meaningful.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual Worship and Observance of the Ekādaśī Vrata named Unmīlanī," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
(Chapter 235, Book 1: *Kṛtayuga-santāna*)
Chapter 236 [Author:
Chapter 237 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe to you the Ekādaśī known as Pakṣavardhinikā, which is exceedingly dear to me; by means of it, one may attain liberation.
An Ekādaśī that is full yet joined with the taint of Daśamī [is not to be observed].
When the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is joined with the piercing [of the twelfth], and the twelfth day exists at the rising of the sun;
likewise, in this sequence, when the new moon (amāvāsyā) or the full moon (pūrṇimā) exists at the moment prior to the sun’s rise,
it is a complete sixty-minute period, and the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) is of the same nature.
When, beginning from Ekādaśī and ending on the day of Pratipad,
the duration of the day measures a full sixty nāḍīs,
then that Ekādaśī is to be known by the name Pakṣavardhinī.
That twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast, and the vow should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
That fortnight-increasing (pakṣavardhinī) [twelfth] shall be equal to ten thousand horse-sacrifices;
by performing it, O Mahālakṣmī, one attains infinite fruit.
When Viṣṇu is worshipped and honored, the fruit of Vaikuṇṭha is attained.
I shall now describe that worship by which Keśava is pleased.
One should construct a *maṇḍala* called Sarvatobhadra using seven kinds of grain.
In the center, one should place a new golden jar filled with water (8).
Or else, a copper jar here, adorned with the five types of sprouts,
joined with the five jewels, and wrapped in a white cloth (9).

One should properly arrange upon that vessel a large copper bowl containing wheat, accompanied by fruit, a coconut, and delicious food; this [bowl] should be anointed with sandalwood paste and encircled by garlands of flowers.
One should have an image of Kṛṣṇa made of gold, bearing the name corresponding to the month [in question].
One should then bathe Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, one should perform the consecration with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha) and apply [fragrant] unguents.
Saffron, unbroken grains of rice, musk, sandalwood, attar, and camphor;
a pair of garments, a sacred thread, the Kaustubha gem, and ornaments—these, as well as flower garlands and the like, should be offered. (13)
Bracelets, armlets, crowns, chains, girdles, and rings;
a lion-throne should be offered together with an umbrella and sandals. And very potent fragrant substances should be offered with devotion. (14–15)
And there, Lakṣmī should be established, adorned with all ornaments;
she should be decorated with all the substances of auspiciousness and every kind of finery. Ekādaśī herself, in her own form, should be worshipped by the side of Hari.
One should worship Śrī Hari there, seated upon a vessel atop a water-pot (kumbha).
One should meditate upon Padmanābha; indeed, one should contemplate His feet there.
Having contemplated Him as the Universal Form (viśvamūrti), one should then remember His knees.
Recalling Him who is attainable through knowledge, one should meditate upon the thighs there;
recalling Hari, the bestower of knowledge, one should also meditate upon the hips.
Recalling Hari, the Lord of the Universe, one should thoroughly meditate upon the abdomen.
Having remembered Śrīdhara, one should contemplate the heart of Hari;
having remembered Hari with the Kaustubha gem, one should properly contemplate the throat;
having remembered the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, one should properly contemplate the arms.
Having recollected Hari as the sky of consciousness, one should then contemplate the forehead;
having meditated upon Hari in all His forms, one should properly contemplate the head.
One should contemplate all the weapons and all the limbs by means of the name "Kṛṣṇa."
Having meditated thus, one should then offer the *arghya* with a coconut:
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Keśava, lift me up from the ocean of *saṃsāra*.
O Lord, accept this worship and the *arghya*; O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, salutations be unto You. (24)
The sixteen varieties of offerings should be presented to the Supreme Self.
One should offer various kinds of food oblations and give cool water.
With devotion, one should also offer betel leaf that is highly fragrant and of excellent quality.
Then, with devotion, one should offer a lamp fed with either ghee or oil.
One should perform the waving of lights (ārātrika), prostrations, circumambulation, and hymns of praise;
one should request forgiveness and offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
Having performed the auspicious worship of Hari, one should likewise carry out the worship of the Guru by offering sandalwood paste and the like, as well as garments, ornaments, and other gifts;
one should also present him with a bodice, a turban, necklaces, and fragrant substances.
One should offer a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of food, grain, and so forth, as well as ritual hand-gestures (*mudrā*) and other items.

Having given food and betel-leaf, one should satisfy the preceptor (*ācārya*). The festival should be celebrated in the best possible manner, according to one's wealth and according to one's capacity. (1.236.29–30)
In the evening as well, worship should be performed with a spirit of devotion;
thereafter, one should keep a vigil accompanied by song and dance,
joined with ancient narrative tales and filled with laughter and joy.
One should worship her named Pakṣavardhinī in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
One should listen to her majesty and obtain the fruit of the vow. Whatever merit there may be in the practice of the five fires or in ten million sacred fords, [one obtains that by this].
A person attains that fruit by keeping a vigil for Viṣṇu;
when a fast is observed there, the destruction of ten million killings occurs.
This should especially be performed by Vaiṣṇavas who are practitioners of the yoga of knowledge.
Neither sacred fords, nor forest retreats, nor principal mountains rescue people in the same way that the *pakṣavardhinī* [lunar day] rescues them;
just as there is an increase of digits in the bright fortnight of the moon, so too is there an increase of merit on this [day]. (35–36)
Just as darkness is destroyed at sunrise, so too does she destroy ignorance;
she is the one who increases the fortnight, and she is the one who increases the side of liberation.
She bestows the digit of liberation and nourishes the sixteen digits and beyond.
It is always equal to Kāśī in bestowing liberation and likewise similar to Dvārakā;
it is equal to Kuṅkumavāpikā and grants whatever is desired.
Indeed, it ever increases the side of liberation for its devotees.
It increases knowledge, righteousness, and likewise devotion in every way;
one should not make any distinction between it being white or black.
It delivers the performer [of the rite], as well as ten ancestors and ten descendants.
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) observed on both sides saves the practitioner of vows.
It is equivalent to residing in Vārāṇasī for sixty thousand years,
performing sacrifices and giving gifts at Kurukṣetra, or observing a thousand lunar eclipses.
During the excellent yogas such as Vidhṛti and others, the most supreme gift of a hundred thousand [gold pieces] was performed;
at Kurukṣetra, a hundred gifts of the sun and moon were made,
or else a gift was made at Prabhāsa equal to a thousand Soma sacrifices.

Whatever fruit one obtains by constantly eating at the house of a *yati* (ascetic), that fruit is attained simply by drinking the water of Kedāra, which results in not being seen again in this world. [The fruits of other acts] do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*). 44–45.
The fruit of giving a thousand cows is said to be a thousandfold;
the fruit of honoring the virtuous is ten times that.
Furthermore, in the worship of one established in Brahman, the fruit is again ten times greater than that.
The merit for one who gives land for the sake of the gods, and likewise for one who gives a daughter in marriage, is tenfold greater than that;
the merit for one who purifies himself at the final ablution (avabhṛtha) of a sacrifice is ten times greater still;
and the fruit for one who observes the Ekādaśī vow is indeed infinite.
Whatever merit is found in fasting, half of that is obtained by eating only at night;
half of the merit of eating at night is obtained by eating a single meal, or by eating only fruit.
[By means of] eating a single meal, eating at night, fasting, and eating fruit—
Whatever merit one obtains by keeping a vigil at night, the measure of the merit of fasting on the Ekādaśī is not known. Listen as I proclaim the greatness of each individual day. || 51 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual Worship and Observance of the Pakṣavardhinī Ekādaśī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 236. [Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna), Chapter 237]
[The Author: Chapter 238.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the Great Sleep (Mahānidrā), which brings about the exhaustion of merit.

It must be avoided in every way, both during the night of the vow and even by day. (1) The tendency toward sleep is most terrible; it is characterized by darkness (*tamas*), it clouds the mind, it consists in taking the absence of objects as its support, and it produces laziness. (2)
She is the cause of defects such as those occurring in dreams and the obstructer of devotion and service;
sometimes, when the *rajas* quality has increased due to an abundance of faults,
she brings about the breaking of the vow of celibacy and causes seminal discharge.
She would cause the destruction of the vow by means of [the consumption of] the strength and speed of the wind.
Therefore, one must by all means keep a vigil at night for the sake of the vow;
for when there is an abundance of food and many meals, the bodily constituents generally [increase]. || 4-5 ||
They become nourished through that [practice], though occasionally, due to the inevitable depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), there may be weakness.
However, if the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is broken, fasting is useless.
Therefore, in such cases, a diet of fruits and the like is briefly prescribed.
On the day of the vow, people must always avoid taking food (7).
Sleep, however, must be avoided by all means, for it destroys the conduct of the virtuous;
it causes the depletion of merit, is the repository of all faults, and is characterized by extreme darkness (tamas) (8).
Indeed, the devotee observing the vow must strive with effort to conquer [the senses].
One should diligently perform a vigil that nourishes the observance.
On the eleventh day, having worshipped Kṛṣṇa with love at night, the person [should remain awake].
Having gathered together with Vaiṣṇavas, one should observe the vigil during the vow by means of singing, instrumental music, dancing, and so forth; by reciting the Saṃhitās and the like;
through conversation consisting of the glory of the Blessed Lord; and by service. (1.237.10–11)
A devotee should keep a vigil for the sake of the success of the vow,
offering incense, lamps, food offerings, flowers, fragrant unguents,
fruits, water for honor, as well as faith, ornaments, and a spirit of love.
One should faithfully offer and perform every vow without negligence;
thus, completely purified of all sins, one becomes an attendant of Hari.
When the time for the vow and the night vigil arrives, the Vaiṣṇavas are indeed filled with enthusiasm.
Fasting, they should observe the vow and keep a vigil accompanied by the *tāṇḍava* dance;
indeed, they should perform that vow known as Viṣṇu’s and chant his names.
Having meditated upon Śrī Hari with their minds, they should repeatedly utter His name.
But those are most blessed in the world, my attendants and saviors.
Chanting the name of Hari during exhalation and inhalation yields fourfold merit;
chanting the name for one watch (three hours) yields a fruit ten million times greater.

Devotion to the Name during the four watches of the night is considered to yield immeasurable fruit; likewise, keeping vigil for even half a moment in the presence of the Image yields a most unsurpassed fruit multiplied by ten million times ten million times a hundred billion. (18)
One should perform a dance before Kṛṣṇa that is full of wonder and filled with love;
it should be performed with enthusiasm and entirely free from negligence, laziness, and the like.
Likewise, one should perform circumambulations and offer salutations again and again. (1.237.20)
One should likewise perform the *ārārtrika* rite again and again during every watch of the night, beholding the image moment by moment with a heart full of moist devotion.
One should strike the hand-clappers; in this way, the vigil shall be accomplished. (11)
He who performs the vigil during this vow, endowed with such manifold virtues, should not practice stinginess regarding his wealth, nor should he harbor greed in his worship.
He who acts thus with devotion is not born again upon this earth. (22–23)
Indeed, the observer of the vow who performs the vigil becomes absorbed in Viṣṇu;
one should never deceive oneself by being an atheist regarding the vow.
For one who mocks the vigil during the Nārāyaṇa-vrata [incurs great sin].
For sixty thousand years, he is born as a worm in excrement.
Furthermore, that Brahmin who knows the Vedas but makes himself an object of ridicule through dancing becomes tainted with fault in this world; indeed, he is even lower than a Caṇḍāla. (25–26)

Whether for a moment or even for a watch of the night, he who remains awake engaged in dancing and imbued with devotion shall attain the fruit of the fourfold aims of life. Even a Vedic priest who reviles another during the vigil [incurs sin].
One who possesses twenty-one families falls into hell.
Those bitten by the serpent of atheism indeed sleep during their vow;
deluded by illusion, they certainly do not keep watch. || 28-29 ||
They are lost, there is no doubt; for they have fallen away from liberation.
Indeed, they are blind and devoid of knowledge, having strayed from the goals of human life.
When the wakeful narrator has arrived, one should cause the story of Hari to be told.
One should repeatedly cause the various divine wonders of Hari to be heard.
In the absence of a reciter, one should have them recited among themselves;
one should perform singing and dancing, as well as laughter and other such expressions born of union with Hari.

During the festival, one should cause the *rāsamaṇa*—the divine play of Kṛṣṇa—to be sung. When the vow of keeping a vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) is performed, the merit shall be ten million times that of a thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*) and ten thousand *vājapeya* sacrifices. (33)
Without keeping a vigil during the vow, there would be a loss of the merit of that vow.
When the vigil is performed during the vow, those on the father’s side, the mother’s side, and likewise the wife’s side—each by the hundreds—are surely uplifted. (34–35)
If the night or day of the fast is pierced by sleep, that vow is pierced; it is indeed an Asura-vow. Its fruit, however, will consist of an Asura nature and take the form of a curse.
Viṣṇu does not come there, and even having arrived, he departs.
Hari, having given a curse at a place intended for sleep, departs;
but when a vigil is performed at that place, Hari indeed remains even while Lakṣmī is obstructed.
When seen, He approaches and dances Himself among His devotees;
having entered into those most beloved and pure devotees, He rejoices exceedingly.
As long as one performs vows and keeps a vigil in the presence of Hari...
For that many ages, the observer of the vow is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
(40) In the house of one who constantly sleeps on the day of the Ekādaśī and other such observances, the Asuras, Rākṣasas, and the servants of Yama—the doers of evil—dance with joy. (41)
On the day of Hari’s vow, one should perform singing, recitation, and chanting.
If one departs [from the assembly] like a mute, one will suffer from muteness for seven births.
He who does not perform dancing before Hari out of excessive shame—
Lameness should be understood as his lot both in this life and in the next birth.
But for one who performs song, dance, recitation, and vigil,
my supreme Vaiṣṇava abode has been fashioned by me for their residence.
He who causes other devotees to keep vigil on the day of Hari shall dwell in my abode as one of my foremost attendants, remaining ever-watchful.
He who, while others are sleeping, engages them in a state of wakefulness on the day of Hari [attains the same].
He shall dwell for a long time in Vaikuṇṭha, accompanied by ten million ancestors.
He who gives his mind to the vow of Kṛṣṇa regarding the vigil (jāgaraṇa) shall indeed reside in Śvetadvīpa for sixty thousand years.
Whatever sin has been committed by you through the fault of desire, whether in this life or in another,
all of it goes to destruction during the night vigil for Śrī Hari.
Likewise, one should keep a vigil before Hari and before a Śālagrāma.
Indeed, the fruit they produce becomes equal to that performed at ten million sacred fords (tīrtha).
Otherwise, all merit perishes through sleep;
even through censure, the vow perishes—how then could its fruit be realized? (1.237.50)
The goals of human life, prosperities, sons, fame, wealth, and so forth,
as well as eternal worlds in heaven, are obtained through the vow of the vigil (*jāgara*).
Without the vigil, there can be no favor from Viṣṇu.
The eternal world is certainly not attained anywhere even through ten thousand sacrifices.
(52) But when the vow and the vigil are accomplished, the eternal abode is attained.
For one who goes for the sake of the vigil, there shall be at every step the fruit born of a horse-sacrifice. (53)
For as many thousands of divine years as there are grains of dust clinging to his feet,
he remains awake in Vaikuṇṭha, in the highest heaven.
On the night of the vow, one must go to the temple of Hari for the sake of keeping vigil.
One shall dwell in the house of Hari for as many ages as there are particles of dust clinging to one's feet.
Likewise, on the nights of the eleventh and twelfth lunar days,
one should diligently perform the ritual vigil (prajāgara) in order to shake off the ignorance of the living soul.
It is indeed considered to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Among these, the superior form should certainly be practiced;
it consists specifically of being engaged in sacred narratives, singing, and dancing.
A vigil endowed with a state of pure sattva is considered the best.

A vigil accompanied by the singing of the *Gāndharva*, the praises of Hari, and so forth; joined with rhythmic beats (*tāla*) and the like; and enriched by the splendor of lamps, incense, and other offerings, is also considered the best vigil. (58–59)
Accompanied by a spirit of devotion and endowed with the chanting of the Name,
the vigil that generates purity and contentment is considered supreme. It is further characterized by delighting the world, enthusiasm, and festive celebrations.
An excellent vigil (jāgara) is one accompanied by offerings of food, fruits, drinks,
and the like; where there is the waving of lights (ārātrika) for Hari, where there is the circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa) of Hari,
and where there is a gathering of people before Hari— that indeed is the most excellent vigil.
That place where there is knowledge of the scriptures, service to the guru, and service to the Lord;

where there is remembrance [of Him], service at His feet, and keeping vigil—that indeed is supreme. Where all states of being are centered on Hari, and where there are the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas—[that is the best]. (63)
Indeed, one should observe a vigil during both the bright and dark fortnights through vows, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and so forth;
for what other meritorious acts would there be if one does not keep vigil during the vow? (64–65)
Whether in travel, in a forest, in a field, in a wilderness, or even in another village;
in a garden, in an assembly, by a river, on a mountain, or in a great battle;
in a state of exhaustion, at an improper time, or while dependent on others on the great highway— (66)
One who performs the vigil for my vow is exceedingly dear to me.
Whether he be a devotee of anyone else or a devotee of mine, if he completely abandons sleep on the day of the vow, he shall attain the fruit. (67–68)
Whether one is a devotee of Śiva, Sūrya, Śakti, or Gaṇeśa, or even a devotee of my own manifestations, one should observe the vigil during the vow.
However, one who is prone to sleep should be known as a beast; such a person is merely one who delights in the objects of the senses.
He has done what is displeasing to me; he did not keep the vigil for our vow.
He who indulges in sleep and food—which are the nourishment of the senses—during my vow shall repeatedly become an animal in a subhuman womb at every moment.
By him his ancestors were slain and the slaughter of the gods was committed;
by him the line of merit was destroyed and her good fortune ruined.
By that excessively proud man, prosperity was made a vessel for calamities.
And by whomsoever the vigil and vow have not been performed on the day of Hari,
they should perform the vigil while playing cymbals and percussion instruments, playing wind instruments, dancing, singing, and displaying festive enthusiasm. (73–74)
Delighting the Vaiṣṇava people by reminding them of the Lord’s deeds,
displaying his hair standing on end with joy and full of love,
generating charming conversations, and manifesting sweet sentiments. (75)
Discerning the gestures (*hāva*), the implied meanings (*vyaṅgya*), the powerful indications (*śaktilakṣya*), and the purposes of the recitations;
performing the vigil (*jāgara*) in this manner during the vow while manifesting love—moment by moment, his merit shall be equal to that of Naimiṣa. (76–77)
For him, there is the fruit of ten million sacred fords and the great fruit of ten million sacrifices;
indeed, there is the fruit of ten million heavens and the great fruit of ten million acts of charity.
(78) Likewise, with a tranquil mind, one should offer incense, a lamp, and the *nīrājana* ceremony.
One should also keep a vigil during the night; such a person shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Indeed, great sins and heinous crimes, even those equal to ten million killings, completely dissolve into pieces when this vow is properly observed with a vigil.
On one side are all merits, and on the other side is the vigil kept during a vow;
the great merit of the vigil is distinguished as superior to all other merits.
Kāśī, Dvārāvatī, Raivatācala, and Somapāṭṭaṇa—
Arbuda, Aruṇa, Mandara, the Himavat mountain, Sahyādri, Navala-kṣa, Vindhya, and Droṇācala;
likewise Mahākālavana, Vṛndāvana, and Avantikā. (82–83)
Puṣkara, Prayāga, the Revā, the Svarṇā, and Yamunā (the sister of Yama);
Gayā, Gokula, the Godāvarī, and the Bhadrikā;
the Gaṇḍakī, the Tāmraparṇī, the Brahmaputrā, and other rivers.
Kukūmavāpikā, Māyā, Kāñcī, and Śrīpuruṣottamā—
though all these have been established according to the rules for sacred sites (tīrtha), they do not bestow such fruit as that which is obtained from the vow of the day of Hari. || 85–86 ||
Since the merit derived from being awake [in this practice] surpasses all other merit, therefore:
sacred fords, mountains, rivers, oceans, forests,
wildernesses, shrines, islands, and likewise the entire earth—
The principles (tattvas), the gods, the seers, the sages, the ancestors, and the fires;
the gandharvas, kinnaras, nāgas, cāraṇas, and those born of Brahmā’s creation; the inhabitants of celestial chariots, the Vairājas, and the lords who preside over time—[all these abide there]. 88–89.
Whosoever are called the Tārakas, they are all the sustainers of the world;
indeed, on the night of vigil for Ekādaśī, they all assemble from every direction.
Therefore, those who perform the vigil are truly gods; of this there is no doubt.
There, one should satisfy the assembled gods with offerings of prasāda. (91) The prasāda and the excellent naivedya must be guarded with great care;
on the twelfth day, at the time of breaking the fast, they should be consumed by the seeker of the vow. (92)
Having bathed at dawn during the Brāhma-muhūrta and having worshipped Hari,
one should offer up the fast, the vigil, and the vow itself.
One should dedicate everything— the vow and its fruit— to Hari.
"Be gracious to me, O Śrī Hari, through this vow in every way.
Having uttered this, one should offer water upon the ground in the presence of Hari:
"Be the giver of knowledge, the giver of liberation, and the giver of happiness to devotees in every way. (94–95)
Having spoken thus and bowed down, the observer of the vow should indeed feed the Vaiṣṇavas;
thereafter, he should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) before them as far as possible,
and he should also give a gift known as the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala.
One should give to the preceptor a vessel containing grain, along with a water-pot and other items, together with an image.

(97) When the twelfth day (dvādaśī) occurs at dawn, even if it is very short, one should by all means perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) during the night, while it is still the twelfth day. (98)
In that regard, there is no fault regarding the night, nor is there a prohibition against breaking the fast.
Bathing at night and breaking the fast therein do not bring about any defect.
One should perform the ritual actions during the first and last watches of the night just as one would during the day.
When even a very small portion of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) remains on the day of breaking the fast,
one should then perform both the morning and midday rites at dawn;
he by whom the twelfth day is thus accomplished gains indeed infinite fruit.
Thus, by whoever this vow is performed, everything shall be accomplished.
Having observed the vow on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) and having perfected the day of Hari,
many divine Vaiṣṇavas have indeed gone to the abode of Viṣṇu.
There is no god equal to Hari, and no lunar day equal to the twelfth (dvādaśī).
There is no vow equal to Ekādaśī, because this triad bestows liberation.
Furthermore, through union with Hari, all of that becomes complete and eternal. (103–104)

Hari makes himself dear to his devotees, and he who performs vows, vigils, and worship becomes dear to Hari. (1.237.105) Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ekādaśī Vow, the Vigil, and Other Rites," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. (237)
← Chapter 237: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 238 [[Author: Chapter 239 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Once Mahādeva approached me and inquired about the greatness arising from each Ekādaśī.
I have also recounted to him the majesty of the twelfth day (Dvādaśī),
hearing which all the sages attained their fruit and went to heaven;
that I shall now declare to you, which bestows the fruit of ten million heavens.
The Ekādaśī is always considered most excellent when conjoined with a [specific] lunar mansion (ṛkṣa).
Jayā, Vijayā, and Jayantī are likewise regarded as most excellent.
When the Punarvasu mansion occurs on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, [it is Jayantī].
She should be known by the name Jayā as the most excellent lunar day for the purpose of the vow.
And when the Śravaṇa asterism occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, it is celebrated as Vijayā; its fruit is multiplied a thousandfold.
And when the Prājāpatya [nakṣatra] occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
then that lunar day is named Jayantī; it destroys all sins and shall annihilate the dry and wet sins committed during seven lifetimes.
Whenever the Puṣya constellation occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
that lunar day is to be known as most meritorious and the most excellent of all.
Indeed, he who makes an offering of a prastha of sesame seeds for the duration of a year [attains great merit].
And whoever should observe a fast on that day, his reward shall be even greater.
By the performance of this vow, Hari himself becomes pleased;
he grants a direct vision of himself, and the fruit shall be the bestowal of liberation.

By fasting on the day conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, one obtains liberation as well as the supreme state, [freed] from sins committed through speech, mind, and body over seven lifetimes; furthermore,
one gains the fruit of a thousand Ekādaśī vows from this observance.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and worship of the deities—
whatever is performed on this [day] yields inexhaustible fruit and bestows liberation.
Indeed, by King Svarṇāṅgada, [these were offered] to a brahmin devoted to his wife.

In the former Kṛta Yuga, [the sages] asked about the back [of the wheel]: "What is the fruit of fasting, eating at night, and eating only once a day, when performed with the desire to attain liberation?
Or what is the fruit of dwelling in the Lord for those whose senses have turned away from sense-objects? (14)
In this world, that fast is indeed fruitful when performed before an image;
whether it be without water or with water, it is called a fast.
It is declared to be successful even when accompanied by the drinking of milk. (15–16)
On the tenth day, having observed a single meal, one should perform the vow;
or likewise on the tenth day, having eaten only at night, one should indeed perform the vow.
During the eighth part of the day, when the sun has grown dim—
"Eating at night" is what is meant by *nakta*, not eating during the night.
For a person engaged in spiritual practice, *nakta* indeed occurs when the stars are visible;
for one who is industrious, eating at night on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) constitutes *nakta*. (18–19)
Since there is no one among his attendants to prevent him,
he may observe the vow even by eating only once at midday;
this regard for food is intended for one who is weak or infirm.
Then, at the time of dawn on the eleventh day,
the person observing the vow should undertake the discipline of turning away from the objects of the senses;
and in the morning, he should worship Hari with the sixteen types of ritual offerings.
And one should pray to Hari: "May my vow be fulfilled;
may there be no obstacle for me therein, nor any loss of faith.
Furthermore, during that vow, one should not engage in worldly activities.
One should perform the necessary duties that do not contravene the rules of the vow.
Milk, water, fruit, roots, leaves, vegetables, juices, as well as medicinal herbs, the word of the guru, the word of the Veda, and submission [to the teacher] [are permitted]. 24–25.

Indeed, these eleven [acts] do not destroy one's religious vows; furthermore, it should be understood that even for one who is unable [to fast], taking food does not destroy the vow. At midday, one should also perform a bath in water and worship Hari.
Bathing in a well is the lowest; bathing in a large oblong pond is indeed middling.
Bathing in a tank or a river is considered the highest.
Furthermore, bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a great river, or in the ocean is the most excellent of all.
Indeed, for one who is unable [to bathe in a river], bathing at home is certainly prescribed even for a wealthy person.
O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, trodden by Viṣṇu!
O Clay, I smear you upon my body; grant me forgiveness.

"Take away all sins; perform meritorious deeds now! Having spoken thus, a person, observing silence and remembering the name of Kṛṣṇa, should apply clay to his body for the sake of purification while standing in auspicious water.

Likewise, the observer of the vow should bathe and have an offering of food (naivedya) presented there to Hari; he should offer water and pass the time with sacred narrations. With devotion to the Blessed One, the observer of the vow should spend the entire day.

Likewise, at night, one should respectfully perform the worship of the God of gods with objects possessing great significance, and observe a vigil during the night. Just as it is prescribed for the bright fortnight, so too for the dark fortnight; one should perform it according to this very rule.
One should not spend the day of Ekādaśī fruitlessly, devoid of the observance of the vow.
For one who thus performs the vow, the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari himself becomes pleased and leads that person to His own abode.

And he bestows the eternal fruit, whose nature is perfect bliss. (36) Indeed, the gift bestowed by one who observes the fast on Ekādaśī is not equal to even a single fraction of the merit of giving four hundred thousand gifts on the days of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti). (37)
Whatever fruit is obtained at Prabhāsa, in the land of the Kurus, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, that fruit is surpassed by one who fasts on the eleventh day (ekādaśī).
Furthermore, having drunk the water at Kedāra, there is no rebirth.

And thus, for one who possesses the merit of Ekādaśī, rebirth does not exist. (39) The merit in this vow would be greater than that of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha; it is equivalent to the merit of a thousand ascetics residing in one's house every day for a year. (1.238.40)
And he enjoys the most excellent fruit of that person who observes the fast on Ekādaśī;
a merit greater than a thousand cows, exceeding even a hundredfold, arises for him.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa dwell together with one who has observed Ekādaśī.
In this body, Keśava, who is of the nature of a god, becomes the observer of the vow.
There is no end to the merit of serving the Lord of Rukmiṇī;
nor is there any measure of the merit of the Ekādaśī vow.
By means of fasting, one indeed attains the full merit; by eating only at night, half of that;
and by eating only once a day, half of that again arises as merit in this vow.
So long do sacred fords, gifts, and religious observances roar [with pride].
As long as a person does not fast for the day beloved by Hari,
there is no thousand great sacrifices equal to Ekādaśī,
nor a thousand great gifts, nor even a hundred great heavens.
Indeed, she is considered to be for the sake of liberation through the merit of Ekādaśī;
moreover, because she was born in the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, she is dear to me.
And because she was born [on that day], she is known by the name Utpattikādaśī.
The observer of the vow should perform its origin, the ritual procedure, and the worship.
She is also declared to be Abhayā (Fearlessness), and he who possesses auspicious marks is to be worshipped.
Kṛṣṇa [is worshipped] with sesame flowers, and jaggery-rice is offered as the food offering.
In the case of a worthy recipient, the gift of a fruit from a *skandha* tree is prescribed, as is the gift of a bull;
likewise, a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given to Kṛṣṇa in the form of golden rings.
Furthermore, at the festival of the vow, the ritual of origin (*utpatti*) must be performed there according to the prescribed rule.
In the morning, Nārāyaṇa is under the influence of sleep within a cave,
like a lion on a mountain in the Himalayas.
A cave in the Himālayas must be constructed, and Śrī Hari himself should be placed therein.
One should first ascertain that he is asleep; then Muradānava must be made.
Likewise, the divine Ekādaśī, born of gold and in the form of a maiden, should be fashioned equipped with weapons, and she should then display the battle.
Likewise, the destruction of Mura and the waking nature of Nārāyaṇa should be brought about;
and there, in that cave, one should perform the worship of Hari on the eleventh lunar day with the sixteen articles of offering. ||54–55||
In this case, a mandala named Sarvatobhadra should be constructed using the seven types of grain; and in its center, a vessel made of gold or copper should be placed,
adorned with five precious gems, cloth, and sprouts.
It should be placed there together with its fruit; a vessel containing sesame seeds should also be placed there.
Indeed, two images should be installed there with the recitation of mantras.
The auspicious worship should be performed according to the rules, following the previously mentioned procedure.
A comfortable bed, provided with a couch and granting ease, should be prepared;
a vow must be observed, and a vigil should be kept day and night.
Furthermore, the worship of Hari must be performed there directly during the night.
The morning bath, worship, the gift of a cow, and the gift of land;
the gift of gold according to one's capacity to a guru or a Brahmin should be performed.
Afterwards, the formal dismissal [of the deity] should be done, and one should undertake the breaking of the fast.
One should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, children, Brahmins, and the poor;
and one should perform the gift of the image to the preceptor with devotion.
Furthermore, an extensive ceremony should be carried out according to one's wealth and according to one's capacity.
The gift of a kingdom, the gift of a village, the gift of a field, and the offering of a house;
the gift of a daughter, the gift of livestock, and the bestowing of jewels and gems; the gift of an elephant, the gift of a horse, and the gift of vehicles and mounts. (63–64)
The gift of food, the gift of clothing, and the bestowing of knowledge and learning—
whatever capacity a donor may possess, such is always considered the true nature of giving.
Neither a wealthy man nor a king should practice stinginess regarding their wealth.
The giving of fruit, the giving of wood, or even the giving of sesame seeds and so forth—
these should be performed even by one who is destitute; or else, service arising from the body,
or likewise service through speech, mind, or both hands.
Sweeping, smearing, fetching water, and massaging the feet—
these should be performed in the temple like a servant for the sake of attaining infinite fruits;
the Blessed One is pleased by service rendered with devotion.
Listen to that auspicious narrative which can deliver one even by being heard alone.
Long ago, in the third kalpa of Brahmā, there was a king born in the Maru country named Maruddhanvan, who was devoted solely to his own self-interest.
At the end of the eon, in the Kali age, the king became excessively addicted to sensual objects; and through the defects arising from desire and greed, the subjects likewise became so.
When there is an abundance of defects among the subjects, the king is tainted by that defect.
Indeed, due to the king's sin, rain does not fall at its proper season.
When the rain is thus obstructed, all subjects are severely afflicted;
they seize from one another their own clothes, food, and all other necessities in every way.
Everything is taken away by force, and no justice is found therein;
in this manner, the time passes without rain.
That king, having oppressed his subjects, drags away their wealth and food.
The king forcibly carries off all those women and cattle.
(75) In a land defiled by sins such as violence, falsehood, theft, and coercion, the destruction of the subjects occurs, and the king himself faces his own ruin. (76)
He repeatedly committed many kinds of great sins;
consequently, for as long as seven years, no rain fell at all.
Due to the lack of food and the intense onset of disease, the king’s wife [was overcome].
When his son likewise stood facing death, that king cried out:
"O Supreme Self, deliver me!
I have committed only great sins; no merit has been earned by me. (78–79)
I have obtained great suffering as my fruit, and destruction itself has been placed upon my head.
O Mādhava, from this point on, I am truly unable to do anything more.
Lift me up from this great misery, for my life is being destroyed by hunger.

Thus reviling Hari, he cried out with lamentation while meditating upon Him. At that moment, a voice from the sky said: "O King, do not weep; by repentance and likewise by the remembrance of Me, your sins have been burnt away. (8.1–8.2)
"Take this rainwater and likewise these leaves and other provisions;
eat them, for your lives will be preserved, and may you be happy.
Furthermore, on the third day from now, it shall be my Ekādaśī."
The beloved lunar day is approaching; perform the vow for it.
Rain will fall everywhere throughout your kingdom, bringing happiness, and your subjects will once again turn toward the pursuit of well-being within your realm.
"And as the fruit of that, the land shall abound in wealth and grain;
moreover, those subjects shall obtain [these benefits] if they observe the Ekādaśī vow.
Having spoken thus, the king, the queen, and the son ceased.
They observed a waterless vow (vrata), and from that great merit arose;
when the vow was completed, a great rain fell and the land became rich with crops. Consequently, a settlement for the people was established, and the queen attained freedom from disease.
The son was born happy, and he entrusted his own burden to him.
In that year, indeed, the Ekādaśīs were observed by everyone throughout the entire year.
At that moment, two celestial chariots arrived through the path of the sky.
"O King, for your sake and for the sake of the monarch, the denizens of the celestial chariots have taken up residence here. The messengers of heaven said to the two of them:
'Come here, for the merit born of your vows shall indeed grant you a thousand celestial realms.'"
It exists for a duration spanning a thousand yugas, indeed as something to be experienced.
By that merit, O Lord of the Earth, you shall become a god named Marut in the fourth kalpa, together with your wife; take this [merit] for yourself in heaven.
Thus addressed, that lord of the earth, together with his wife, abandoned his body and went to the heaven-bestowing realm;
in another kalpa, he became a god again and again,
and having become a god, he enjoyed pleasures over and over with great devotion.
Having become a great devotee of the Lord, Svarṇāṅgada served Hari like an exceedingly humble servant and attained the abode that is free from rebirth.
Then [he performed] the vow of Ekādaśī on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
One should strive with diligence for liberation from heaven to heaven;
by means of this Ekādaśikā vow known as Utpatti, there shall always be the attainment of kingdom, sons, and wealth, as well as perpetual health. (96–97)
"Every desired object shall meet [the devotee], and from that, even liberation (mokṣa) shall arise.
That great vow must be performed by both those with desires and those free from desires.

(98) Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Ekādaśī Vow in the Dark Fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, its Ritual Procedure, and the Attainment of its Fruits," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 238:
[The Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga] — Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Part 1,
Chapter 239.
[The Author: Chapter 240.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
I bow to the Lord of the gods, who bestows happiness upon all living beings.
Having propitiated the Inner Controller, the one to be worshipped who bestows the fruits of all desires—
O Blessed Viṣṇu, I ask [you] out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
for the destruction of the sins of the sinful, and for the prosperity of those with desires. (1–2)
In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, what is the name of the auspicious Ekādaśī?
What is its fruit, what is its ritual procedure, who is its presiding deity, and who is its sovereign Lord?
O Lord, explain all that to me in detail and according to the truth.
Having heard this, Lord Śrī Hari, the benefactor of his devotees, spoke:
"Listen, Lakṣmī, to the vow of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa.
By merely hearing of it, the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice shall be obtained."
On the tenth day, one should eat only at night, sleep on the ground during the night,
remain celibate, and abandon faults such as anger.
On the eleventh day, one should maintain vigilance during the muhūrta known as Brāhma.
One should remember Dāmodara Kṛṣṇa, the Lord and Master who bestows liberation.
(7) Known by the name Mokṣadā, she removes all sins, grants liberation, and is designated as "Liberation" itself; she was proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa according to his own desire. (8)
On Mount Raivata, she was accepted by him in the form of Dāmodara;
therefore, the Lord Dāmodara, together with her, is to be worshipped.
One should remember Hari Dāmodara and his beloved, who grants liberation, at dawn.

A householder should resolve: "Today I shall perform this vow for the sake of liberation, or for prosperity, or indeed for all desires. Then, having performed purification such as cleansing and having bathed at a sacred bathing place (sutīrtha), [he should proceed].
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should prepare the materials for the worship of Hari.
One should have a Sarvatobhadra mandala constructed using the seven kinds of grain.
Then, one should place a vessel made of gold or copper in the center.
One should place the vessel— filled with five sprouts, cloth, and so forth, along with the five jewels, fruit,
and water— or a pot containing sesame seeds and clarified butter, there with the *saddhara* mantra. One should also install the golden image of Dāmodara and Mokṣaprada.
One should install and worship [the deity] according to the prescribed rite with the sixteen types of offerings,
with auspicious jasmine blossoms, incense, lamps, and so forth,
and with garlands of *mālatī* flowers, together with Śrī and Keśava.
The *arghya* offering should consist of a fruit, specifically a pomegranate, and likewise, sweetmeats (*modaka*) should be offered as the food offering (*naivedya*).
For the attainment of special fruits, the seven grains should be given:
barley, wheat, rice, sesame seeds, and likewise *kaṅgu*. (16–17)
Śyāmāka and cīnaka—these indeed are the seven grains;
they should be given according to one's capacity, for they are in every way excellent for the act of giving.
At that time, she should pray to Keśava, the Lord, together with Śrī.
This vow for the sake of attaining you has been performed by me for the Goddess who bestows liberation.
O Keśava, worship has indeed been offered to you by me according to my ability;
be gracious, O Lord of Gods, and become the granter of all prosperity.
"O Lord, be the giver of liberation to me, the one who carries me across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having praised him thus, and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), fruit, and water,
he should then give betel-leaf with fragrance and perform prostration.
One should perform the circumambulation at night and offer salutations, hymns of praise, prostrations, and full-length obeisances;
one should also present a handful of flowers.
Whatever sins there may be, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly— [one should confess them]. (22–23)
"O Lord of Gods, may [all obstacles] go to dissolution through this worship, vow, and other rites of Yours.
Having uttered this and bowed once more, one should then perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
At midday, one should cause sweet food to be offered to the God.
In the evening, at the onset of night, one should perform worship with the sixteen excellent articles;
thereafter, one should cause a vigil to be conducted by the devotees.
And likewise on the twelfth day, having bathed in the morning and worshipped Keśava, [one should continue the rites].
One should distribute gifts and cause various offerings to be bestowed;
one should give abundant wealth and food, and so forth, to the preceptor.
Thus, the performer of the vow shall possess the power of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He shall be the savior of his ancestors, who are afflicted by the suffering of hundreds of lineages.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this ancient narrative which grants liberation through the bestowal of its fruit:
all the ancestors who had entered lower wombs attained final release.
In the city of Campā, there was a great king named Vaiśvānara;
later, he attained the state of a great Vaiṣṇava and became the savior of his ancestors.
That monarch protected all his subjects as if they were his own sons.
Many Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas lived in that city;
they were learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, devoted to virtuous deeds and other duties, prosperous with great wealth, and their subjects were likewise endowed with abundance and prosperity.
Indeed, King Vaiśvānara’s years were filled with happiness; yet, although he had obtained a prosperous and vast kingdom through his previously accumulated mass of merit and asceticism,
he was always possessed by the intoxication of sovereignty.
Due to his nihilism, the king performed no vows nor gave gifts;
he did not perform the *śrāddha* rites, nor did he give food, water, or other offerings;
nor did he ever cause any meritorious deed to be done.
No new merit is produced; therefore, the ancestors are distressed.
Deprived of food and water, they have descended from the world of the ancestors.
[They curse] their own kinsman who is a king, yet one who is devoid of rites such as the *śrāddha*.
Having seen [this], they became extremely distressed, with hot sighs and very weak;
due to the king's sins, such as his atheism, they fell into hell.
But at night, having come together, they appeared before him in a dream.
Weeping and gasping, afflicted and likewise emaciated;
with throats excessively parched by thirst, powerless and likewise deprived of strength;
devoid of luster, with shriveled veins and darkened faces.
Crying out like destitute beggars, they were indeed miserable;
speaking among themselves of their unbearable sorrows, they said:
"Alas! Even though he was born of our own lineage, that atheist remains established in the kingdom!"
He does not perform the ancestral rites, nor does even Vaiśvānara give him water;
indeed, he does not offer anything at all during the fortnight of the ancestors, not even for a moment.
He offers no funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and gives no water whatsoever.
He does not perform libations at all, nor does he ever cause them to be performed.
Tormented by that suffering, we have always been miserable;
we have all gone to a downward path and likewise fallen into hell.
"This king has become an atheist; what is the use of such a bad son?
Better indeed is childlessness, or better still is having a son who is a believer.
Even the state of liberation is better than having a wicked son. (45)
Others will certainly not give, and our son does not give either.
How, why, and from where could even a little food or water be obtained?
If he were to offer water and funeral cakes (piṇḍas), we would be filled with happiness.
Having spoken thus, they all vanished; the king was filled with wonder.
In the morning, he related that account born of his dream to the brahmins:
"In a dream, I saw my ancestors fallen into hell."
And they said, "O son, deliver us who have fallen into this downward state.
As they spoke thus, sighing and weeping with loud lamentation, I beheld them; and even now, remembering them, I find no peace.
Today my kingdom is prosperous, as are my queen, elephants, and horses;
yet nothing appears to grant me happiness, and even food does not please me.
The sin of having killed my son burns within me constantly; it brings me no pleasure at all.
"What shall I do? My heart is tormented by the fire born of my ancestors.
O best of the twice-born, where shall I go for their deliverance?
Let that austerity or vow be declared by which my ancestors may be liberated. (52–53)
Whether it be yoga, sacrifice, or some other great festival such as giving charity, or whatever else—be it great or small—that is said to be a means of deliverance;
provided that both parents are alive, capable, and fit for their son. (54)
When they suffer in the terrible hell, what then will be the fruit of my son?
In this matter, their deliverance must by all means be desired by me.
Let the twice-born not hesitate; I speak the truth. (55–56)
Having heard the king’s excellent words, the twice-born were then greatly delighted. Those brahmins spoke to him regarding that effort for his father's welfare which relied upon a brahmin:
"O King, among us, this great sage is indeed capable. (57)
Jaigīṣavya, who possesses supreme yoga, discerns both the past and the future.
Having understood everything through his divine vision in meditative absorption, he will quickly inform you how your virtuous fathers have gone to the lower realms. (58–59)
Then, having meditated for a moment upon his ancestors after being entreated, the great sage Jaigīṣavya spoke there to that king:
"O King, it is not merely atheism alone that is the cause."
"But the cause is your father's atheism.
Listen, I shall tell you the truth; do not be angry, but seek peace.
I know all the past deeds of your ancestors. (6.1–6.2)

I shall tell you of your father; listen and be attentive. When he was ruling the kingdom, out of a nihilistic disposition, he seized the means of subsistence that had been granted to your deity by his ancestors.
Furthermore, he did not take the dharma of the scriptures into account at all.
Having succumbed to the intoxication of sovereignty, he gave himself over to unchaste women.
Having gone to another village, he was detained by an unchaste courtesan.
Even during her fertile season, you did not come to your mother’s own home;
nor was the righteous *ṛtudāna* given to your mother.
Having behaved thus repeatedly, you became heavily defiled by sin.

Likewise, at the time for the *śrāddha*, the *śrāddha* was not performed by that violator of dharma. By the power of that sin, having caused his own ancestors to fall and having made them dwell in hell, he became filled with a state of atheism (*nāstikya*).
Having performed the final seasonal sacrifice for you and for your mother,
he met his death in due time and fell into hell;
together with his ancestors, he fell into hell on account of his own sin.
Bestowing one's own wife upon another during her fertile season, as well as approaching an unchaste woman;
atheism toward the ancestors, and likewise the failure to perform śrāddha and other rites—
these are the causes for the fall of the ancestors from the world of heaven and its great happiness.
These very people, having fallen, long here for deliverance through a son;
yet you, though born as a son, were indeed begotten from one who was an atheist. For whatever the disposition was during the *niṣeka* (conception rite), such it remains toward the son.
Since you were born of an atheist and an unrighteous man, you yourself have become an atheist and do not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) at all.
O father, you have become a usurper of the gods' sustenance; this is the retribution for that.
There is no atonement even for hundreds of millions of eons.
The livelihood of a deity, once granted by kings of old, must never be taken away.
Because of that sin, there is no end to suffering in hell.
"Even the dust from the feet of one who subsists on the remnants of offerings to the gods—
if that falls upon someone— it shall cause them to dwell in hell for seven kalpas.
Thus was it said in the past by a Caṇḍālī woman to Mahendra as he was passing before her.
Once, a certain low-caste woman was in the cremation ground; there,
upon a hearth made from the breast-bone of a village pig,
she held a human skull as a cooking vessel and placed dog-flesh within it.
Having thrown it into the wine-like water, he cooked it with the fire of the funeral pyre.
Just as Mahendra emerged from his side,
the cooking vessel was quickly covered with a sandalwood shoe.
Then Indra, being suspicious, questioned that eloquent woman:
"O Nṛmuṇḍā, how is it that all this dog-meat cooked in wine over the funeral pyre's fire is entirely impure, yet covered with skin? (8.1)
Then that Cāṇḍālī replied: "Listen, O King of the Gods!
This [leather] is indeed covered with hide out of fear of the dust from the feet of those who seize or cause others to seize the livelihood of gods, brahmins, and cows. (82–83)
"If you were such a person, my cooked food would become impure;
it would not be fit for me to eat, as it has been defiled by the sin that destroys one's livelihood.
Indra said, "How can a woman commit such a great sin?"
The Cāṇḍālī said: "Understand my words according to their true meaning.
The gods are indeed called the fathers, and likewise the deities are the mothers.
The gods are the givers of rain, and the gods are always the protectors. (85–86)
All the deities are the providers of security and well-being for the worlds;
indeed, one who destroys another's livelihood is called a slayer of life itself.
Without a livelihood there is no living, and without a livelihood one is as good as dead.
Therefore, one who lives off the livelihood of the gods is a slayer of his father and likewise a slayer of his mother;
he is a slayer of the gods, a slayer of dharma, and indeed a slayer of himself and a slayer of heaven.
He is a slayer of rain, a slayer of the world, a killer of cows, and a killer of Brahmins.
He would indeed be a destroyer of gods, a destroyer of rain, and a destroyer of all;
even the dust of his feet is a stain that causes great sin.
If that [dust] should fall upon dog-meat, it is not to be eaten by me, for it is indeed a defilement.
Therefore, that vessel which was indeed covered by me with leather—
if you are the giver and the performer for those who live like gods,
then let the flesh here be purified by the dust of your feet.
"I have no fear regarding my clothing; go, O venerable one, as you please.
Even Indra, in his own assembly hall adorned by celestial rishis, ancestors, and humans, spoke these words:
"May they not become obstacles to your livelihood."
No atonement has ever been declared anywhere for one who seizes another's livelihood.
From that time forward, the gift of a livelihood has been praised throughout the three worlds.
Therefore, O King, there is indeed no deed that can deliver your father from this state.
By means of which their upliftment occurs even without a connection to Hari,
and a true connection with Hari arises through the vow alone—
this vow is the giver of liberation, bestowing liberation by the power of Hari.
It is declared that this is the refuge for those who have no refuge, and the atonement for those sinners who have committed acts as grave as the murder of a Vajra-holder.
All rites must be performed without water; let the fruit be offered to the ancestors.
Through the merits of the vow born of the Ekādaśī that grants liberation, there shall be final release.
Thinking, "It will come to pass," he took all of that, honored it,
and having treated the virtuous brāhmaṇas with respect, announced his intention to depart for home.
Then, when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa had arrived, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight—
The king performed the worship of Hari according to the prescribed rites after fasting;
having prepared the *sarvatobhadra* diagram, he worshipped Ekādaśī and Hari according to the rules and gave away abundant gifts.
He remained awake throughout the night, and likewise performed his morning ablutions and other rites;
having thus completed this meritorious act and offered it to the ancestors,
King Vaiśvānara broke his fast according to the prescribed injunctions.
Then, by the merit of the gift of the Mokṣada Ekādaśī, all his ancestors,
together with his own father, quickly attained liberation. When the merit was bestowed upon the ancestors and they were liberated, the gods [appeared] in celestial chariots.
They rained down a shower of flowers and spoke these holy words:
"Hail, hail! O son, we gods have assembled here;
by your gift of merit on the eleventh day, your ancestors have been delivered."
Having attained liberation, all those ancestors said to him:
"O son, we have attained liberation; may it be well with you.
Be happy always, and be a bestower of happiness upon all embodied beings."
Be a performer of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), a performer of sacrifices, and a worshiper of the gods.
O sinless one, always be a servant to your mother and father.
May you be long-lived and a believer; be devoted to the vow of fidelity toward your wife.
A bestower of livelihoods upon the gods and a worshiper of the Brāhmaṇas;
a performer of service for the virtuous and a protector of the vows of chaste women; a constant guardian of cows and land—may you always be prosperous, O son. (10.9–110)
Thus, having joined with such benedictions, the ancestors and the gods,
praising the power of the merit of the vow that bestows liberation,
departed for their respective abodes as they pleased, repeatedly uttering "svasti."
By the power of Pāpanāśā, who bestows liberation, the king,
together with his family, became a great devotee of the Lord, endowed with equanimity and faith; he performed sacrifices and offerings constantly, and was a worshiper of Brahmins and the virtuous.
He was a performer of divine worship, righteous, and free from faults.
He had a son named Hutabhuk, who was a great devotee of Viṣṇu and highly virtuous.
Having bestowed the kingdom upon his son, he attained supreme liberation.
And the consumer of oblations (Agni), being of divine nature, resides within the bellies of living beings.
Having become the great Vaiṣṇava fire, he remains in the form of fire.
The sovereignty of the vow that bestows liberation should be understood as that which grants the state of divinity.
O Lakṣmī, for one who thus observes the auspicious Mokṣā Ekādaśī, their sins are destroyed; upon death, they shall attain liberation.
There is nothing superior to this for the destruction of adamantine sins.
It became a bestower of liberation, possessing the power of Nārāyaṇa himself.
There is no counting its merit; indeed, this vow is dear to me.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), it grants liberation and is very dear to me.

"By reading or even by hearing it, this [Vrata] bestows a fruit equal to that of the vow itself; it grants sons and prosperity, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is dear to me. Thus ends the section on the ritual procedure for the Mokṣada-Ekādaśī Vrata in the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, within the first book, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning Vaiśvānara—
Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-Nine: Description of the Account of the King, the Liberation of His Father, and Other Matters.
Chapter Two Hundred and Forty: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga. (Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Part 1) Chapter 240.
[The Author: Chapter 241.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
What is the name of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, and what is its ritual procedure?
"What is the fruit, what is the glory, and which deity is worshipped? Tell me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "O Lakṣmī, listen; I shall describe the vow of the Ekādaśī of the month of Pauṣa."

I am pleased in every way by the vow of Ekādaśī. Indeed, that which occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa is called Saphalā; on that day, one should worship the Lord and Master Nārāyaṇa, known as Saṃkarṣaṇa.
One should worship the consort of Sunanda while endowed with meditative visualization.
For the worship, sage-like flowers are used; for the food offering, jaggery-laddus;
and here, for the water-offering (arghya), the amṛtaphala fruit is recommended, as is the gift of gold.
The tenth and eleventh lunar days should be observed according to the previously mentioned procedure;
likewise, the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day should be performed according to the stated method.
On the morning of the day of the vow, within the Sarvatobhadra mandala, [the ritual should be performed].
Having placed the jar before Hari, the observer of the vow should offer various fruits:
coconut fruits, betel nuts,
citrons, jambīras, pomegranates, and likewise auspicious myrobalan fruits.
One should worship specifically with *lavaṅga*, *badara*, and especially with *āmra* fruits;
wherever a particular fruit may be obtained, one should worship with those very fruits.
One should perform the great worship with the sixteen secondary articles (*upacāra*) and so forth.
One should especially perform the offering of lamps during the Saphalā festival.
One should also give gifts of grain, gifts of clothing, gifts of gold, and the donation of cows.
At night, one should keep a vigil together with assembled Vaiṣṇavas.
If one should remain awake for even a mere moment of the night,
the fruit thereof shall exceed that of a sacrifice; it shall be the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords,
and it shall be a fruit superior to the fruit of a thousand years of ascetic penance.
Listen, Lakṣmī! In ancient times, during the Satya Yuga, there arose the story of King Māhiṣmata, which became fruitful through his recourse to a vow.
It took place in a forest on the bank of the Narmadā, on ground consisting mostly of mountains.
In the southern part of Bhārata, in the middle region, there was the auspicious city of Māhiṣmatī.
That kingdom belonged to King Māhiṣmata, and it was exceedingly great. He had five gentle sons, all of whom were young princes. (14–15)
The wise one, the glorious one, the steadfast one, the famous one, and the powerful one—
among them, the wise one indeed became the eldest, yet he was devoted to sin.
Having attained youth, he drank wine and the like, and devoured meat.
He consorted with courtesans, violated the wives of others, and committed thefts in foreign kingdoms by force through his own men;
he was a sinner, exceedingly wicked, corrupt, and possessed of most base conduct. (17–18)
Cultivating these vices— gambling, drinking, hunting, women, and meat—
he indeed squandered his father’s wealth;
through his sinful deeds, he exhausted the jewels, gems, gold, and other riches.
Thereupon he was born hungry, filthy, and a reviler of the Vedas;
he became one who held false views regarding the Brahmins, a censurer of the dharma of the virtuous, and especially a reviler of the Vaiṣṇavas and the gods. (1.240.20–21)
For he constantly causes affliction among the subjects in every way, like a *piśāca*; therefore, having been summoned by the king,
the man named Lumbhaka was indeed abandoned by his father and all his kinsmen.
He was indeed expelled from the kingdom by the subjects with beatings and other such punishments.
Wherever that rogue went, he met with contempt; he obtained no happiness, and no one honored him. (23–24)
Bereft of wealth and deprived of his vitality, even rejected by a courtesan,
he wandered among the trees of the forest, himself afflicted by hunger and thirst. Indeed,
he endured a most terrible and exceedingly harsh austerity that was of the very nature of suffering.
He repeatedly felt remorse for the actions he had himself committed:
"I have been abandoned by my kinsmen, my father, and my subjects, as well as by my courtesan; I have been expelled from the kingdom and despised by everyone. (26–27)
"Better to dwell here in this forest than for our supreme enmity to remain unappeased.
Indeed, I shall slay my enemies solely to bring an end to that hostility;
furthermore, I will utterly destroy my father's entire city."
"I shall cause the palaces to crumble and seize the wealth and other possessions.
This task must be carried out gradually; that supreme wealth must be taken away so that I may dwell hidden in the forest and not fall into their hands. (1.240.30)
Having formed such an evil intent, dwelling in a dreadful, dense forest,
constantly delighting in the slaughter of living beings and devoted to theft, violence, and other cruelties,
he would go to the city at night and [kill] many people with weapons.

Having caused [people] to be killed, he took away abundant wealth, grain, and clothing; he carried them off to the great forest and ate and rejoiced there repeatedly. By that man of sinful conduct, the entire city was plundered.
Great terror reigned continuously among the people;
suddenly, he forcibly robbed the wealthy merchants of their wealth.
In some places he made them crooked, and in others he even killed them while they were still alive.
Once he entered the house of the king’s minister.
He stole much wealth, ate food, enjoyed women, and likewise beat the children. (35–36)
His house was set ablaze and a great calamity was wrought;
meanwhile, the king’s soldiers, who were like night-stalkers, arrived there,
seized him, bound him with fetters, and held him by his hands with ropes.
He said to them, "I am indeed the son of King Māhiṣmata.
I alone must be released here; otherwise, there will be no happiness for you.
I shall take away your lives and destroy you with my weapons."
I shall bring about the very destruction of you who desire wealth, wives, and homes.
A king’s son must never be seized by those who seek their own happiness.
Indeed, a serpent, a brahmin, and a kṣatriya are not to be provoked.
"Indeed, they grant the fruit of destruction, yet when bowed down to, they are always protectors.
Having heard this, he was released by them and went back into the forest;
there he constantly ate meat and the fruits of trees.
He sustained his life by means of roots and other forest produce;
even through theft, he maintained his livelihood while dwelling in the forest.
In that forest, there was an ancient and deserted shrine of Viṣṇu.
At the base of an Aśvattha tree, there was a place where the walls had crumbled,
the door was lost, the courtyard was ruined, the shade had vanished, and it was utterly desolate.
There, indeed, stood the broken altar of Viṣṇu by means of this [image].
Rest was accepted here for the sake of a dwelling, and here rest is indeed obtained;
even this pipal tree, though its branches are withered and it is many years old,
exists as a deity through its union with Viṣṇu.
Because of his residence there, O Goddess, and by the power of that sacred site, a *sāttvika* intellect arose within him and he reflected:
"Alas! I have committed many sins for which there is no atonement. (47–48)
Moreover, I must not commit violence that takes life;
instead, taking refuge at a *pippala* tree, I shall sustain myself by eating roots and the like.
For Viṣṇu himself dwells here within this *pippala* tree as its very form.
"It will bring me spiritual welfare; it will burn away my sin.
Having thus resolved, even in the season of cold, he spent the night on the ground by the base of a tree trunk with great hardship.
Just then, other forest-dwelling thieves arrived there and plundered Lumbhaka’s clothes and belongings during the dark fortnight of Pauṣa.
Indeed, on the morning of the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, he—
Having gathered fruits, he ate them with great difficulty; thus the day passed.
But at night, an unexpected cold set in and it rained intensely with snow, such that there was no protection even by means of warming oneself with fire.
Thus, he indeed became an object of enjoyment for the flow of cold;
stripped of clothing, with rolling eyes and a closed mouth, he became senseless.
His pleasure in sleep was destroyed, and he became like one whose life had departed. (55)
With his teeth and tongue protruding from his mouth, and his hands and feet rendered motionless,
he was then born like a corpse, tormented by cold;
yet his vital breaths had not departed, for he remained devoid of movement.
Internally, he repeatedly remembered Viṣṇu as his protector;
yet even though it was the morning of the fruitful Ekādaśī,
he did not regain consciousness at sunrise, for he remained chilled and drenched with cold.
When the sun had reached the meridian, that Lumbhaka indeed regained consciousness;
looking here and there, he then rose up.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, the tree, and the sun, he went into the forest, stumbling with his feet.
Moving slowly like one who is lame, emaciated by hunger and devoid of strength,
with his limbs trembling, he gathered excellent fruits;
for those were to be offered to Viṣṇu and subsequently taken by me.

Thus, having arrived unthinkingly and set down [the child] at the foot of the tree—(62)—while the extremely weak Lumbinīka remained beneath the tree, the sun went to its setting; he then indeed lamented his misfortune. (63)
Shedding tears, what state will be mine?
The cold afflicts me intensely, and there will be no protection from leaves.
There are no thick garments such as bark-cloths to ward off the cold.
"There is no cave here, nor even a grass mat;
nevertheless, I shall take refuge in this heap of grass and sleep.
Having reflected thus, he was eager to gather grass nearby. (65–66)
Having placed the fruits near the form of Viṣṇu, he recited:
