"May Hari, the Lord of Śrī, be pleased with these fruits.
Then he went very close for the purpose of gathering grass.
But, his strength having failed, he fell into a swoon once more near the altar, remembering Nārāyaṇa; then,
rising after a moment, he took some grass from a *pippala* tree.
As soon as he himself arrived and sat upon the base of the pillar,
fainting occurred once again, yet he regained consciousness.
Recalling Viṣṇu, that Lumbhaka found no restful sleep.
"I shall eat fruits in the morning"— with this thought he passed the night.
Thus, though he was helpless and did not even know that it was the day of his vow,
he observed the fast and kept the vigil, afflicted by the cold.

Keśava considered the worship with those fruits to be his own offering of food (naivedya); Viṣṇu likewise considered the night vigil of that evil-minded one to be the fruit of his vow and the austerity arising from his own refuge.

Viṣṇu, the compassionate one who is affectionate toward the distressed, attained a state of grace; he made the fortune of the Lumbhaka eternally auspicious and rich in merit. Indeed, that Lumbhaka had performed this very vow quite spontaneously. (74–75)
Then, on the morning of the twelfth day, having eaten fruits before Hari,
he offered praise to the Lord for protection from the cycle of worldly existence.
Until the rising of the sun, Viṣṇu remained there with four arms.
He manifested before him in the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
richly endowed with the beauty of divine limbs, adorned with divine ornaments,
and graced by the splendor of a divine, gentle, and serene countenance, with its smiles and graceful movements. (77–78)
Touching that *lumbha* with his right hand, he said at the head [of the boy]:
"O devotee, you shall obtain the kingdom through the power of Saphalā.
Go to your own city; there your father has met his end."
Other sons opposed one another regarding the consecration.
Mutually contending, they were deprived of the crown of sovereignty;
unauthorized by the ministers and the subjects, they did not obtain the kingdom.
Your subjects await your arrival for the increase of their fortune;
this time has come again for you, indeed, for the arising of the fruit of Ekādaśī. By those who were previously struck down and humiliated by the force of time—
Indeed, they further maintain that the power of time is truly great.
There is great suffering from the loss of fortune, whereas happiness arises from the dawning of fortune.
This dawn of fortune is produced by means of rituals and the like; therefore, that very [ritual] must be performed.
"Therefore, go to your own kingdom and take it; do not delay.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu vanished right there.
Lumbhaka, having bowed to Viṣṇu at the Pippala tree, indeed obtained his splendor.
Having assumed a divine form and nature, he went to his own city.
Honored by the foremost among ministers and subjects, welcomed with cries of "Victory!", and adorned with the splendor of divine ornaments, the devotee of Viṣṇu [entered]. || 86-87 ||
Having become [the king], he obtained the royal consecration passed down through his ancestral lineage by the grace of Hari and by the fruitfulness of his vow;
through the dawning of his fortune, that king attained a kingdom free from thorns.
His reign was auspicious due to his performance of duties such as protecting and governing the subjects.
Having ruled that kingdom for a hundred years and likewise having worshipped Hari,
he received the benedictions of his subjects and [appointed] his son named Mānajit.
Having consecrated [his son] in the kingdom, he departed for the forest where [the Lord] had formerly appeared;
there, having propitiated Viṣṇu and constructed a temple for Viṣṇu,
he installed an image of Hari and worshipped it daily.
Having exhausted the latent impressions within his heart through austerity and the equilibrium of yoga,
he went to the presence of Kṛṣṇa by means of a brilliantly effulgent celestial chariot;
and there, the attendants of Hari, having taken hold of him on that chariot, [honored him].
They went to the divine abode of Hari, reaching which one no longer grieves.
In that very realm known as Goloka,
King Lumbhaka eternally serves Śrī Kṛṣṇa, honored by the personal attendants (pārṣadas).
Thus, whoever in this world performs this supreme vow that yields fruit,
having attained happiness in this world, shall obtain liberation upon death.
Blessed are those men in the world who perform the fruitful vow.
But for those by whom this vow has been performed with true devotion, their birth is fruitful, and their wealth and other possessions are fruitful;
indeed, this Ekādaśī is fruitful, bestowing the fruit of the form of royal fortune.
And because it bestows liberation, it should be performed by those who desire both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By reading it, by hearing it, and likewise by performing the vow, a person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. (98–99)

The observer of the vow obtains sons, grandsons, wealth, prosperity, fortune, even sovereignty, as well as knowledge, nourishment, health, and liberation. (1.240.10) Thus ends [the section on] the ritual procedure for the fruitful Ekādaśī of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the first book of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, concerning the prince of King Pāpilumbhaka.
The two hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Narration of the Attainment of Sovereignty," etc., [Chapter 240].

Chapter 241.
[Author: Chapter 242.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, salutations to you, the ancient Supreme Person (Purāṇapuruṣottama).

You cause to be heard this auspicious vow, which brings liberation to living beings and bestows fruit— by means of which the heaps of sins are indeed set ablaze. And that auspicious Ekādaśī which occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa— || 1–2 ||
"Please tell me out of grace: what is its name, and what is the ritual procedure?
Which deity is worshipped there, and what is considered the extent of the fruit?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O beloved, for the sake of the welfare and benefit of the worlds, I shall describe that [vow]:
the Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa is named Putradā (Bestower of Sons).
It removes all sins; this should be observed with great effort by devotees.
She is called Sānandā because she bestows the joy of having sons.
Here, Nārāyaṇa, together with Padmā, is the presiding deity to be worshipped;
he is the god who grants all perfections and fulfills the desire for a son.
He should be worshipped with *guggulu* flowers, as well as other seasonal blossoms;
and one should offer powdered sweets and *laḍḍukas* as a food offering (*naivedya*) to the Supreme Self.
One should also present an *arghya* of pomegranate fruit and other fruits as well.
Likewise, a jar filled with ghee should be offered to the Lord of Śrī Padmā.
Furthermore, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given, especially in the form of gold.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should eat only at night and sleep upon the ground.
On the eleventh lunar day, having risen during the hour sacred to Brahmā, one should remember Hari.
Having bathed and gathered the materials for worship, one should worship Hari.
Having placed [the deity] in a worthy vessel, one should [bathe Him] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and water.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods of gods and clothe him in garments and ornaments (11).
One should anoint him with fragrant substances and the like, and beautify him with garlands of flowers.
One should worship him with the full array of incense, lamps, unbroken grains, and flowers (12).
One should offer food offerings such as sweet delicacies, as well as water for drinking and so forth;
one should propitiate [the deity] with the waving of lights, hymns of praise, circumambulations, and other rites.
One should pray again and again to the Lord Nārāyaṇa for the sake of the vow.
"I shall perform the Putradāyī vow; may it reach completion.
Having thus prayed, one should then fashion an auspicious *sarvatobhadra* mandala with the seven grains, and a water-pot (*ghaṭa*) should indeed be placed there.
On a level spot, one should place a vessel filled with sesame seeds, auspicious and provided with sprouts and other offerings; upon that, the image of Hari should likewise be established.
Having installed it, one should worship the Lord with the sixteen articles of offering.
Then one should offer the nightly lamp (ārātrika) and a handful of flowers;
thereafter, one should pray for the attainment of fruits and likewise cause gifts to be given.
At midday as well, one should likewise offer worship, food offerings (naivedya), and so forth.

Furthermore, after evening, one should perform a distinguished worship; likewise, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), one should observe a vigil in that same manner. Then, the observer of the vow should perform worship and the giving of material gifts to the people.
One should feed the twice-born, the virtuous, and virtuous women, and perform the breaking of the fast oneself.
By doing so, the vow becomes complete, and its fruit—liberation and other such goals—shall come to pass.
Indeed, that person who performs this very vow with devotion shall obtain sons and wealth. (1.241.20–21)
By the grace of Śrī Hari, the observer of this vow shall obtain auspicious sons, daughters, elephants, cattle, horses, grain, fields, and so forth, as well as liberation.
In this regard, listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate a narrative to you.
It bestows sons, wives, fruits, and gains, grants self-wealth, and is the supreme giver of happiness.
23. Formerly, in a [past] age, in the city named Bhadrāvatī in Saurāṣṭra, there was a king named Ketumān; his queen was named Cumpā. 24.
Although the king had reached extreme old age, no son was born to him; consequently, being childless, the monarch grieved day after day.
Time passed, yet there was no hope even from his own wife for the sake of a son.
The two of them reflected upon the giving of gifts and worship that brings about the attainment of a son.
And they performed various kinds [of rites], exactly as they had been shown by the Brahmins;
whatever was proclaimed by many in many ways, all that auspicious variety was performed. (26–27)
Then the king obtained no son at all to continue his lineage.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Old age is seen before me.
Somehow, even at this final hour, may the attainment of a son come to pass. (28)
Having thus resolved, the king again employed various means;
he went to virtuous people renowned in many places who were rich in capability, and he received their blessings, yet those efforts proved fruitless. (1.241.30)
Suketumān found no happiness in his kingdom nor in his realm;
he remained perpetually and intensely distressed, as if with a virtuous wife who was always night.
And by those two, who were overcome by anxiety and grief, water and other such things were offered [to him].
At the *śrāddha* ceremony, however, all the ancestors partake of food that is merely lukewarm.
(32) Now that Ketumatī has died, we do not see anyone born into our lineage who can offer us libations. What can we do? Who will satisfy our thirst? (33)
Thus, all the ancestors go forth in suffering, devoid of happiness;
nor do their kinsmen, friends, ministers, counselors,
well-wishers, subjects, male servants, female servants, riches, or elephants [accompany them].
Indeed, even in dreams, things occur that cause suffering for this king.
His mind is perpetually unsettled and tormented by despair;
this is true for any person without a son, and it is especially so for a monarch.
For a prosperous ruler of a kingdom, there is truly no fruit of birth.
For one without a son, the house, the wife, and prosperity appear as mere emptiness.
Without a son, one is not released from the debt owed to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages.
Having obtained a legitimate son, one attains freedom from debt toward the ancestors and the gods;
in this world, fame is gained, and in the next world, an auspicious state is reached.
Since it is through a son that these things arise, a person should procreate a son.
A son is born as a constant bestower of happiness to those who perform meritorious deeds;
he increases longevity, health, prosperity, wealth, and grain. Indeed, the birth of a son does not occur without the grace of Hari and merit.
Moreover, even for those who have performed meritorious deeds, there is no attainment of the higher worlds without a son.
A son is declared to be great wealth; a son indeed is called prosperity. A son is said to be one's home, and a son is also celebrated as one's kin among the worlds. (41–42)
Without a daughter there is no alliance, and without that no status as a householder;
without her there is no fame in the world, and without that no expenditure of wealth.
Thinking of this day and night himself, the king finds no peace.
"If I bring about my own destruction, there will be a most miserable state resulting from self-slaughter.
Even in this world, fasting leads to cries of 'Alas! and a miserable state.
Therefore, having reflected thus day and night, what should be done by me? (44-45)
With his mind set on spiritual practice, he considered it better to emaciate his body through austerity;
mounting his horse at night, he went alone into the forest.
Neither his subjects nor his wife and household knew of this.
"Where has this great king gone?"—thus they reflected. Overcome with anxiety and extreme sorrow, they set out indeed to search for him;
seeing the tracks of the horse's hooves again and again, they proceeded into the forest.
When they saw no marks of the horses' hooves upon the ground in that place of extremely thick grass, they returned toward their own city;
filled with grief and anxiety, they sent word to those who were dependent on them.
Though they searched for him in the forest among the wild animals, they did not find the king.
From one forest to another, and from that to a forest even more dense,
the king entered further and further into the distance, a place frequented by lions and elephants.
By the power of fortune, the king was indeed not slain by any of the hunters;
nor did even the horse meet its death, for it lived on through the turn of fate.
[They saw] forest trees—*vaṭas*, *bilvas*, *kadambas*, *panasas*, and *dhavas*.
Beholding date palms, long peppers, and golden campakas;
likewise beholding palmyra trees, sarja trees, tamālas, uḍumbaras, plakṣas, bakulas, saptaparṇas, and tamarinds. (193–194)
Beholding *iṅgudī*, *badarī*, *jambū*, and *karamardaka* trees;
*vaṃśa*, *aśoka*, *kadalī*, *nāryaṅga*, and *nārikela* trees—
he went through the formidable forest, observing lions, deer, and birds.
He saw flamingos, swans, ducks, and cranes;
yaks, cows, and hares; tigers, bears, and rhinoceroses; horned deer and porcupines; as well as elephants, gayals, wild buffaloes, and serpents. (56–57)
Beholding embodied beings such as he had never seen before, filled with wonder,
and hearing the cries of owls, jackals, bears, deer, and other wild animals,
the king proceeded on, eating forest flowers and fruits.
Thirsty and with his throat and gullet parched, he reflected;
following the cries of birds, he searched for a reservoir of water.
There he beheld a beautiful lake of divine water, naturally formed.
Known as Aśvapaṭṭa, it flows from the Raivata mountain;
it is adorned with fish such as the Mīna, Makara, and Matsya, and filled with lotuses,
as well as with swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, cakravāka birds, and fire-colored fowls.
Upon seeing it adorned, he experienced supreme bliss.
Then the king, eager to drink water, went there in haste;
at that moment, his auspicious right eye, hand, and chest throbbed.
In the water, he beheld the divine gods who were performing their ablutions;
having gone there and dismounted from his horse, he stood before them and bowed.
He paid homage individually to each of the gods, who were in the form of sages.
To Śrī Hari and his attendants, who were chanting their prayers and whose bodies were emaciated by their vows,
he spoke with folded hands and a faltering voice, and prostrated himself like a staff.
Flooded with their blessings, the king then questioned those gods.
"Who are you, sirs, who have come here to bathe in this waterless, desolate forest thicket where no human dwells?
Tell me the truth of the matter, so that it may be well for me as well. (67)
"The sight of the virtuous is indeed considered [beneficial] for those who suffer, for the destruction of their suffering.
(68) Thus questioned, those gods spoke to him whose fortune was now favorable:
"O King, we are the Viśvedevas, gods who dwell in heaven. (69)
We have come in the form of sages for the purpose of bathing during the Putradā vow;
today is indeed the Ekādaśī known by the name Putradā.
We have come from Mount Raivata to this sacred ford (tīrtha) to bathe there.
"Having bathed, we shall go to heaven, for today there is indeed a great vow [to be observed].
How have you come to this desolate and dense forest?
Hearing this, the king was exceedingly delighted, even though he was suffering from hunger and thirst.
Considering the water to be pleasant to him, he did not drink it at that time;
rather, thinking that the vow had naturally become one that would grant the fruit of a son, the king said to those sages: "I am indeed childless, and I desire a son."
"Even though I have performed many meritorious deeds, I did not obtain a son.
Therefore, with my limbs overwhelmed by grief, I have come here for the sake of penance.
Out of compassion for you, I shall perform penance here for the sake of a son. (74-75)
Then the sages said, "O King, by virtue of your vow to grant a son, this merit which brings about the attainment of a son has arisen for you; do not perform further austerity.
You should keep a vigil at night and, having worshipped Keśava in the morning," ||| 76 ||
"Having performed the breaking of the fast with water and likewise with leaves, flowers, and so forth, go home;
you shall have a son who will be a lord of men.
Thus, through the conjunction of fate and by the performance of that vow, [it came to pass].
Having received the blessings of the gods, he returned home;
in due time the queen conceived, and a son of great fortune was born.
That lord of men became a long-lived protector of his subjects.
Because of his name, Saurāṣṭra became famous as the kingdom known by the name Kaṅka; indeed, his lineage also became devoted to Viṣṇu. Therefore, O Lakṣmī, the Putrada Ekādaśī vow must be observed.
And for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, this has been told by me to you.
Those people here who shall perform this auspicious vow regarding sons and daughters will obtain sons in this world, and having died, they will indeed go to heaven.
Wealth, grain, cattle, sons, and even long life;
a beautiful wife, a gentle husband, a fertile field, and supreme prosperity—by performing this vow, people will certainly obtain all these things. (83–84)
"O Lakṣmī! From reading this, as well as from hearing and remembering it, one shall obtain the fruit of attaining a son, and likewise the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of a Son for the Royal Sage Ketumān through the Greatness of the Pauṣa Śukla Putraikādaśī Vrata," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 242.
[The Author: Chapter 243.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Mahāviṣṇu, O Hari, O Vāsudeva, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Master!
Having bestowed your supreme favor, please speak concerning the dark fortnight of Māgha:
what is the name of the Ekādaśī, who is the presiding lord, the prescribed ritual, the fruit, and whatever special gifts (dāna) there may be? (1–2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved, to the Ekādaśī of the dark fortnight of Māgha, known by the name Ṣaṭtilā. Its presiding deity is Vāsudeva, together with his consort Śrī.
He should be worshipped with land-lotuses and likewise with tender *gulābja* flowers.
For the food offering (*naivedya*), there should be *ghṛtapūra* cakes, and for the respectful oblation (*arghya*), grapes.
Woolen garments, blankets, and the like should be offered with devotion.
Foods prepared with fenugreek, snacks made of black gram, and meals consisting of black gram sweets (māṣalaḍḍuka);
other substances that promote nourishment and cooling garments—such as these should be offered during rites of worship, giving, and so forth. (5–6)
The *tiladeyā* has been fully described as the destroyer of all sins.
Pulastya formerly told Dālbhya of this vow which bestows happiness.
Men endowed with youth who are emaciated by the suffering of poverty [should observe it].

And those who, being helpless, commit sins for the sake of a livelihood—such as the killing of a Brahmin, the killing of a child, the killing of a woman, the slaughter of cows, and so forth; as well as violence, the theft of another's property, and vices. (8–9)
Lack of attachment to one's own wife, the destruction of another's prosperity,
forcibly inflicting suffering, reviling teachers, falsehoods,
living by means of evil deeds, and likewise the sale of daughters. (1.242.1)
The mixing of flavors with what is undesirable, treachery, and deception—
whatever such sins as these arise among men through passion, this vow brings about their destruction. (11–12)
The form of the Tiladaikādaśī vow, which burns away all sins,
is most powerful when performed during the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha;
it purifies the inner self of a living being and likewise washes away their sins.
There is no other such vow that so quickly purifies living beings.
(14) The observer of the Māgha vow, bathing in the month of Māgha, should eat only one meal on the tenth day of the dark fortnight; thereafter, he should sleep upon the ground at night. (15)
On the eleventh day known as Brāhma, one should remain a celibate student;
having risen during that hour, one should remember Nārāyaṇa within the heart.
And likewise, one should accept [the teachings] from the most excellent, virtuous, and devoted Sātvatas.
One should perform the worship of Hari’s names for even a moment.
Having struck the rhythm on the hand-clap and repeatedly remembered the Form, one should chant:
"O Hare, O Rāma, O Dark as a Rain-cloud, O Lord, O Nārāyaṇa, O Master! (17–18).
"I am yours forever; remain with me, O Giver of Liberation.
Having praised him thus, one should then go outside for the sake of purification.
Having performed the cleansing with earth and water, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa).
Then the observer of the vow should thoroughly rub *tila* (sesame) powder upon his body.
Next, he should bathe with water mixed with sesame while chanting the names of Hari.
He should also perform an oblation (*homa*) of sesame seeds and likewise drink sesame-water.

One should perform the gift of sesame seeds and practice the consumption of sesame. One who bathes with sesame, rubs oneself with sesame, offers oblations of sesame, and drinks water infused with sesame—being both a giver and an eater of sesame—is one for whom the "six sesame seeds" destroy all evil. (22)
As many seeds as grow from the sprout of a sesame plant— including branches and further sesame seeds—
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world.
Black sesame seeds are considered the most excellent for bathing, giving, and worship.

Having bathed, the observer of the vow should worship Vāsudeva, joined by Śrī, at the very dawn with sixteen new articles, including the gift of sesame seeds. And during the offering of handfuls of flowers, he should pray for the fulfillment of the *ṣaṭtilā* vow.
"O Lord, I shall perform [this]; may it be free from obstacles for me and grant its fruit.
By even a single drop of your grace, may there be the complete fulfillment of my vow.
May desire, anger, greed, delusion, and malice indeed not exist in me. (26–27)
Having thus entreated the preceptor, bowed to him, and remembered Śrī Hari alone,
the observer of the vow should cause the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala to be prepared in the morning. In its center, he should place an excellent vessel made of gold or copper.
Filled with the five sprouts, excellent jewels, water, and other substances,
one should place it and wrap it with cloth and thread;
then one should worship it, and upon it, [place] black sesame seeds.
One should place a vessel for the cooked oblation (sthālīpātra) there, and upon it, an image of Vāsudeva made of gold, accompanied by the six tilas dear to Śrī.
One should bathe that image with ablutions consisting of the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should wear garments and the like, as well as ornaments such as decorations.
[One should worship] with vermilion, saffron, *abīra*, sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and garlands;
with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel leaf, and fine fruits. (32–33)
With *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruits, coconuts, *amṛta* fruits, and *bījapūraka* fruits,
and with circumambulations, prostrations like a staff, hymns of praise,
and so forth, one should worship Śrī Vāsudeva and ask for forgiveness again and again.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) and provide sweet water for drinking.
One should give betel leaf (tāmbūla) prepared with camphor, fragrance, cardamom, and cinnamon.
Likewise, one should offer a couch with its furnishings, as well as a mirror and a fan.
One should devoutly offer a yak-tail whisk and clusters of flowers;
then, having performed the lustration ceremony nine times and bowed to Keśava,
one should carry out one's ordinary daily affairs so that no obstacle indeed arises for the vow.
At midday, one should offer to Hari sweet and auspicious food.
One should offer water, fruit, and a betel-roll for cleansing the mouth, as well as fragrant essence, richly scented land-lotus, and arka-water. (38–39)
In the evening as well, the observer of the vow should properly perform the worship of Hari;
he should conduct all the rites such as the *ārārtika* offering and also partake of his meal. Prior to the ten days, the person observing the vow should himself bathe.
There, the practitioner, having collected cow dung that has not fallen to the ground,
should add sesame seeds and cotton, and fashion small cakes until they have become dry, numbering one hundred and eight.
Then, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, under the asterism of Mūla or Ārdrā,
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) at night, reciting the names of Hari three times.
One should keep a vigil at night and cause the verses sacred to Viṣṇu (viṣṇupadī) to be sung.
Having risen early on the twelfth day and bathed, one should perform worship.
One should offer gifts of sixteen kinds to the venerable Guru:
a water-pot, a golden image, gold coins, and silver coins. (44–45)
One should give me a vessel of sesame seeds, a bed, garments, grains, and fine juices; an umbrella, sandals, and bowls—may Hari be pleased with me.
A black cow should be given, along with a vessel filled with sesame seeds.
The offering is said here to be made to the guru or to a brahmin who has a family.
From the gift of sesame seeds, food, drink, and so forth are obtained in heaven and other realms;
even in liberation, eternal satisfaction arises for one who partakes in emancipation.
If all that was to be done—namely, the gift of food and the offering of sesame seeds—is not performed, then in the hereafter one will encounter nothing at all;
no food whatsoever will be found there. Therefore, sesame, food, and so forth must be given; indeed, everything must be given.
Whatever is required here—women, sons, houses, and gardens;
pleasure groves, cows, buffaloes, elephants, horses, goats, and so forth;
as well as vehicles, celestial chariots, and household utensils. (1.242.50–51)
In this world, there are great means for attainment, such as the pursuit of dharma, wealth, and pleasure;
likewise, golden ornaments, various foods, and drinks;
as well as sights to be enjoyed, sounds to be heard, and objects of delight. (52)
Upon the attainment of Ekādaśī, various kinds of gifts should be given;
through that merit, one will obtain those very gifts multiplied a hundred thousandfold in the hereafter.
Therefore, the performer of Ekādaśī should especially bestow gifts.
Listen now to a hair-raising story concerning this matter from the east:
in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a virtuous Brāhmaṇī named Kapilā,
who was learned, a maiden, and devoted to the practice of celibacy.
Possessing self-knowledge, always delighted by the worship of the gods, and though free from possessions, she lived filled with the desire for the fruits of heaven and other realms;
indeed, her body was emaciated by fasts and virtuous vows. (56–57)
Whatever household goods and the like are acquired through learning, wisdom, and other means,
all that is offered as a gift to a worthy recipient at an auspicious time.
[58] Likewise, [gifts are made] to the gods, to Brahmins, to virgins, and to the virtuous.
Bestowing houses upon virtuous women established in Brahman,
that great chaste lady, providing various other articles of utility,
always remains engaged in the worship of the gods with a desire for their happiness.
Pervaded by excessive craving and great delusion due to her very nature as a woman,
she practices self-knowledge yet does not abandon her desire for pleasure.
Knowing that food is easily obtained, she does not give it to a mendicant.
The virtuous were not satiated, nor were the children fed.
(62) Indeed, everything else was given away, but not even a grain of food was given;
out of a mere trace of ignorance, no alms were offered to the mendicants. (63)
Once, a profound thought arose within me regarding that devotee of mine;
for there is no doubt that the body of that pure-minded woman had been purified by arduous vows.
And Lord Hari was repeatedly worshipped by her with many offerings.
The world of Viṣṇu is indeed honored through the physical austerity of reality.
Every auspicious act performed with this desire-driven motivation is done with a longing for reward;
heaven exists for her sake, but here [in this world], there is nothing at all for her by means of this [desire].
Indeed, no gift of food was made by her, having disregarded its priceless value;
consequently, no food will be available for her in the heavenly worlds.
For through the gift of food, one attains edible ambrosia (*amṛta*) in heaven.
"Indeed, that which is given there is surely obtained by the one through whom supreme satisfaction arises.
Therefore, for the sake of the happiness of my devotee, I must by all means beg for food there in the form of a mendicant. (68–69)
"She will give food to me; she shall obtain the fruit of that in heaven.
O Lakṣmī, having reflected thus, I came to the world of mortals. Assuming the form of the master Kapila, I went to her house for the sake of alms.
"Madam, give alms," I said, having requested alms.
She was occupied with the midday worship of my image;
perceiving this obstacle to the worship, she abandoned the fruit of her alms-giving. (71–72)
Due to the force of his anger, he did not say anything at all at that time.
Again I said to him, "O beautiful one, give me alms!
as well as the earth from the Tulasī plant there, which had been offered in worship with devotion.
It was taken up, moistened with water, and by its very nature formed into a lump.
Then, out of great anger, she threw that lump of clay into my copper vessel; not even a tiny bit of food was given to me. (74–75)
Although I begged for food in her name, she did not give it to me;
instead, she drove me out with insults and the like.
I departed for my own Vaikuṇṭha, and in time, that female ascetic died.
By the power of her celibate life and by the gift of a house and other offerings,
she became a goddess and went to heaven, where she was honored by the goddesses in the celestial realm.
She obtained a beautiful house as the fruit of giving a small lump of clay.
She beheld a divine house, filled with every prosperity yet devoid of heaps of grain; no food was to be seen.
Having departed from that house, she arrived at my palace.

That second Vaikuṇṭha of mine which exists above the waters—there, indeed, by the power of her celibacy, that Kapilā, radiant like the sun, being overcome with anger, said to me: "Why is there no food for me in your house? (81)
I have obtained a magnificent palace in the divine Triviṣṭapa that is devoid of food;
there is no nectar whatsoever, and neither solid food nor drink exists there.
How am I to live in this place of enjoyment, this great heaven?
Therefore, O Great Viṣṇu, O Lord, give food to your devotee.
Otherwise, I shall not remain in this house which is like a cremation ground.
And I said to her then: "Food was never given by you to her at any time."

"O virtuous lady! Was this not given by me to Brahmins or to the righteous, nor was it offered as alms to virtuous women? Yet you have offered this lump of clay to me. Do you remember this, or not, O virtuous one? Its fruit is that no food is obtained."
What is performed and given in the land of action (karmabhūmi) yields its fruit in heaven.
Since you did not indeed bestow food, how could it reach you in the celestial realm?
Nevertheless, you are my devotee and must always be favored by me.
From the gift of this clay, may alms-food be your fruit;
indeed, may even this clay always become food in the form of grain, so that you may eat the fruit of nectar.
Through your vows, penances, and numerous fasts, [may this be granted].
I have been honored by your offerings; may the fruit of that be nectar within your home.
O beloved, let my house never be empty for you.
Go to heaven, for those filled with curiosity long to see you anew.
The goddesses who perform the Ṣaṭtilā vow will arrive;
you must not open the door, but remain out of their sight.
If they insist on seeing you, [then you may show yourself].
Then those goddesses should be addressed: "If you desire a vision, give me the merit of the six sesame seeds previously performed by you;
I shall open the door so that you may behold me, the beloved of Hari. (92–93)
The merit arising from that Ṣaṭtilaikādaśī, which had been bestowed by them, was then revealed;
consequently, the door was opened and they beheld the beloved of Hari.
Neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura woman, nor a Pannaga woman [was she].
Nor was there any other such divine cow in heaven as Kapilā;
O Mahālakṣmī, through her union with Hari, she became equal to you in the celestial realm—endowed with beauty of form, belonging to Viṣṇu, and dear to me. ||95-96||
By the acquisition of the merit of those six sesame seeds, a mansion filled with the nectar of food appeared instantly; indeed, nothing greater than this occurred elsewhere.
Through the attainment of the merit of those six sesame seeds, that dwelling became abundantly prosperous.
Filled with wealth, grain, fine garments, gold, silver, and other riches,
it was enjoyed until the end of the kalpa; thereafter, that Kapilā entered into the eternal dissolution, and Kapilā came to my abode.
There, my beloved, in the form of Ramā, became four-armed;
through her intense devotion in serving me, she became your friend and attends upon me.
Therefore, those by whom this supreme Ṣaṭtilā-vrata has been performed in person—
What is it that he does not obtain? Everything shall be attained by him in every way.
By my yoga, one who observes the *tiladā* vow shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One must not practice stinginess regarding wealth, nor should greed ever be indulged in.
O noble lady, every kind of gift that ought to be given shall be obtained once it has been bestowed.
According to one's own wealth, one should cause sesame seeds and grains to be given,
as well as clothing, food, vehicles, carriages, houses, water, and household utensils.
He who gives [this] in this life obtains freedom from disease in the hereafter.
(1.04) Through fasting on the day of the six sesame seeds, the devotee shall not fall into poverty, nor suffering, nor misfortune, nor emptiness, nor shall he suffer division. (1.05)
Therefore, one should undertake the vow and perform the gift of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rite;
thus one is liberated from sins and attains both worldly enjoyment and supreme liberation.
Whoever hears this, or causes it to be heard, or recites it [shall likewise attain these fruits].
O beloved, the merit arising from the vow of the six sesame seeds belongs to him;
no inauspiciousness remains that could cause obstruction either here or in the hereafter.
A Brahmin shall attain spiritual merit, and a Kṣatriya shall attain victory.
A Vaiśya shall attain abundance of wealth, and another shall enjoy supreme happiness;
one who seeks dharma attains dharma, and one who seeks desire obtains a woman.
One who seeks wealth acquires wealth, and one who seeks a son shall enjoy a virtuous son.
He attains vast fame and becomes the preeminent among his kinsmen.
Having obtained unshakable prosperity, he shall attain the highest good.
Fear shall perish for him, and he gains splendor and heroism.
A woman who has fulfilled the vow of the six sesame seeds shall delight in a beloved husband;
she shall obtain sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, and unbroken conjugal felicity.
Having obtained sensual pleasure here on earth, she rejoices as a goddess in heaven.

And having become Ramā, the consort of Viṣṇu, she rejoices upon the couches of Hari. Furthermore, in Vaikuṇṭha and in Goloka, she eternally enjoys the pleasures of youth and love together with her own husband, Kṛṣṇa-Hari.
"There is no other vow equal to the Ṣaṭtilā-vow that bestows such happiness.
It was performed by Padmā in the past; indeed, you are that Lakṣmī of mine.

Thus ends the description of the greatness of the Ṣaṭtilā Ekādaśī vow in the dark fortnight of Māgha, within the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning how Kapilā Nārī attained the status of a goddess and the state of being Ramā through the merit of that vow.
Chapter Two Hundred and Forty-Two: Paṇanāma.

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Hari! O Kṛṣṇa! O ocean of mercy! O bringer of liberation to the world!
Out of your grace, tell me about the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha. What is the procedure, who is the presiding deity here, and what is the fruit of this vow?
Also, tell me of its concluding rite (*udyāpana*), which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the observer of the vow.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; on the bright fortnight of Māgha, there is the day named Jayā, which bestows great merit.
It destroys sins, grants liberation, fulfills desires, and bestows happiness. (3)
The auspicious Ekādaśī is declared to be observed by one who has taken a vow;
it destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and eliminates states such as being a *piśāca*.
It bestows all prosperity upon kings and grants victory in battle.
It bestows victory in heaven and victory in worldly affairs.
(5) In whatever undertaking it is performed, it is considered to yield the fruit of victory;
that fruit is declared to grant victory to those who travel through the three worlds. (6)
For this reason, O Lakṣmī, she should be worshipped with great effort by oneself on the tenth day, either by eating only one meal or by eating only at night;
while maintaining the sustenance of the body, one should sleep upon the ground at night.
Having risen in the morning during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should remember Śrī Hari.
(8) Having performed purification, bathing, and other rites, one should perform the Sandhyā-vandana;
then, having recited the Gāyatrī, one should perform the worship of Hari. (9)
The Lord Mādhava, her husband, should be fully worshipped together with Nityā.
First, one should bathe him with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with consecrated waters;
then one should bathe Kṛṣṇa with pure water from sacred fords and anoint him with fragrant paste.
One should anoint [the deity] with excellent oils such as sandalwood and the finest fragrant essences.
(11) Furthermore, one should bathe [the deity] with waters from sacred fords and clothe [him] in garments.
[One should also offer] a crown, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and finger-rings. (12)
One should likewise wear all divine ornaments made of chains, girdles, jewels, diamonds, and so forth.
One should worship the Lord with *gulāla*, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and *bīra*.
One should worship with incense, lamps, and flowers of the bakula tree;
with other blossoms produced at that time, such as lotuses and land-lotuses (sthalapadmaka);
and with ornaments, necklaces, excellent leaves, and clusters of tulasī.
Then one should worship Śrī Hari with sandalwood and fragrant substances;
as for the food offerings (naivedya), there should be sweetmeats and citron fruits,
as well as *maṇḍakas*, *laḍḍukas*, and auspicious pearl-like sweets made from mung beans.
Milk-puddings mixed with fragrant substances should be offered to Hari.
Likewise, pomegranates, fresh mangoes, coconut fruits, as well as grapes and plantains, should be offered. (17–18)
Then the nightly lamp-offering (ārātrika) should be performed, followed by circumambulations and so forth;
having offered a handful of flowers and requested forgiveness, one should then formally undertake the vow:
"Today, on this auspicious Ekādaśī named Jayā, I shall indeed observe the vow."
"O Kṛṣṇa, I perform this so that there may be extreme favor toward you.
May that vow of mine be fully accomplished; here, show me your grace.
Having thus prayed and then bowed to Mādhava, the God of gods, [he continued].
The observer of the vow should have a mandala prepared, adorned with the seven types of grain;
in its center, he should place a golden pitcher or a copper one, beautified with five kinds of sprouts, gems, water, cloth, and other offerings. (22)
One should place a sesame-filled vessel there, together with fruit, inside the jar.
One should worship the jar there and likewise invoke the holy fords (tīrthas).
[One should also install] a golden image of Mādhava, fashioned together with Jayā.
One should likewise establish her together with her eternal consort;
one should worship her through the sequence beginning with invocation, and likewise bathe her.
One should adorn her and offer flowers, food, and other such gifts.
One should worship [the Lord] with great devotion using the sixteen types of offerings, beginning with water for the feet.
Then, having offered a drink of water, one should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for Mādhava.
There, one should offer betel-leaf and ask for forgiveness for any transgressions.
For the sake of the vow, one should pray, "May my vow be fulfilled.
One should perform the worship of a cow and also cause the gift of a cow to be made.
One should cause the gift of land, the gift of clothing, and the gift of gold to be performed.
Having thus completed the worship in the afternoon, one should perform one's own daily duties for that day.
Likewise at midday, one should offer to the god Mādhava the four kinds of food— eatables, chewables, lickables, and drinkables— which are pure and essential.

In the evening and at night, for the sake of worshipping Kṛṣṇa, one should have a large and auspicious pavilion constructed and arrange a canopy there. Having performed the worship of Śrī Hari, one should conduct the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) according to the prescribed rules.
Having offered the food oblation (naivedya) and the request for forgiveness (kṣamā-dāna) before Lord Hari,
one should then have the verses of Śrī Hari sung in the pavilion according to the style of the Rāsa dance.
One should keep a vigil at night and delight Kṛṣṇa exceedingly.
Devotees should perform dancing, chanting, instrumental music, and a vigil; then, having bathed in the morning, the Lord Mādhava should be worshipped.
Various kinds of gifts should also be given according to one's capacity.
One should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, and Brahmins with the offered food.
Then one should personally perform the breaking of the fast; when the vow is performed in this manner, the fruit becomes complete and victory shall surely be attained in every respect.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to an ancient tale regarding this vow which I shall tell you.
While Mahendra was indeed ruling over the world of heaven,
all the hosts of deities dwelt there happily, nourished by the drinking of nectar.
Honored by Apsarases, goddesses, and celestial nymphs, the gods,
worshipped and happy, sport in the Nandana grove;
they delight their goddesses, dance, and sing praises.
In the divine forest named Nandana, near the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā,
in that garden rich with the beauty of flowers and served by fragrant breezes,
a dance was performed by the Apsarases for the pleasure of Indra.
There the Gandharvas sang and the Apsarases danced;
the Gandharvas played instruments and the women kept the rhythm.
Thus, as the singing and dancing proceeded with great joy, (41–42)
Mahendra, the spectator, also arrived at the stage of his own accord;
that Indra, the leader of fifty million [ganas], danced with joy.
The Gandharvas sang along, and Puṣpadanta sang with a beautiful voice.
Likewise, Citrasena and his wife Puṣpavatī were there;
and the son of Puṣpadanta was named Mālyavān.
At that time, Mālyavān was infatuated with the beauty of Puṣpavatī.
By the side-long glances of Puṣpavatī, Mālyavān was brought under her control.
Both Puṣpavatī and Mālyavān came together for the sake of a dance to please Indra,
and their limbs became overwhelmed with desire.
Possessed by mental delusion and fallen under the power of the arrows of desire,
they sang pure songs with unblinking eyes out of passion;
and Indra himself danced perfectly, following the singing with his dance.
He encountered the ruin of those two, the destruction of *tāla* and *māna*.
Having reflected upon their union,
Maghavan perceived a simultaneous deficiency in both the *tāla* and the *māna* within the song.
Seeing their supreme transgression of the proper order and considering it an insult to himself,
he became enraged and, speaking thus, cursed them both there:
"Fie upon you two, fallen fools who have destroyed the majesty of my greatness!"
Even though an abundance of sensory objects is constantly being enjoyed in heaven, there is no satisfaction; nor do I possess the resolve to maintain the bounds of propriety.
For, even when I am encouraged in my skill during the time of dancing, you two [stand in the way].
"Having considered this in the midst of the assembly, were you two indeed deluded by the dance?
Therefore, become a pair of *piśācas* assuming the forms of a husband and wife; you are no longer worthy of the status of *gandharvas*, as you have caused a breach of dignity."
Having reached the world of mortals, experiencing the fruit of their karma and indeed enduring suffering,
they remained there for many long years.
Thus, due to the curse of Mahendra, they were on the Himavat mountain, which was exceedingly dreadful.
Having become Piśācas, they were tormented by sufferings and found no peace.
Forgetting their former states as Gandharvas and Apsarases, they wandered in the forest, being repeatedly afflicted by an intense, piercing cold. (56–57)
Grinding their teeth and speaking to one another, the Piśāca said to his dear wife, the Piśācī:
"Alas! For such a minor offense, the fruit is this great and most painful suffering."
This is indeed a terrible hell in the form of a *piśāca*.
When will it come to an end? When will peace be found?
Because of the extreme cold here, suffering arises intensely. (1.243.60)
Thus, lost in thought and emaciated by the pain of hunger,
the two of them took up residence in the trunk of a tree known as the Pippala.
On the night of the tenth day, due to a fall of snow, on the eleventh day—

And likewise on the night of the eleventh day, trembling with a cold and stormy wind, they did not go out from their own dwelling for the sake of food. By the turn of fate, that day was the *jayā* eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) of the month of Māgha. ||62–63||
The night was spent by the two of them keeping a vigil;
there they both remained, abstaining from food, water, and drink.
Deprived of all nourishment, they endured the piercing cold wind with great hardship.
No living being was killed, nor was any fruit consumed;
there was not even the drinking of water, nor any gratification of the senses.
Not even sleep came upon them, and they found no happiness.
While those two were thus suffering, the night passed away.
When morning arrived and the sun rose on the twelfth day,
I manifested in the form of a Pippala tree, and devotion was placed within their hearts.
"For I am indeed the Aśvattha tree among trees, existing in embodied form;
therefore, I am the provider of shelter for those two. Calculating the fruit of their vow, which was rich in vigils, I gave it to Jayāti and his guest. (68–69)
By the power of that fruit, their state as piśācas came to an end;
they became two gandharvas of divine form, possessing their former appearances,
endowed with their ancient affection, and adorned with their previous ornaments.

Seated upon their excellent celestial chariot, Puṣpāvatī and Mālyavān went to heaven and joyfully paid homage to the Lord of the Gods. Seeing those two gods, the Gandharvas, Indra was amazed and said: ||| 71-72 ||
"By what merit was your state as *piśācas* destroyed?
And by which sage were you two indeed released from my curse?
Then, by the turn of fate, the King of the Gods spoke to them both.
"By the grace of Vāsudeva and by this vow, may there be victory!
Through the power of devotion to you, our state as *piśācas* has been destroyed.
Having heard this, Maghavat was delighted and spoke to them again with respect: (74–75)
"By virtue of your vows, you two have become the foremost recipients of Hari's grace;
therefore, by the power of the merit of those vows, you have become worthy of my worship.
Out of great joy, always drink the nectar of my words."
And may you two, my beloveds, always enjoy yourselves in heaven with happiness.
Those who perform the vow of Hari and are devoted to the worship of Hari—
whether they be mortals or immortals— they are always worthy of our honor.
Thus, O Lakṣmī! those two Piśācas, a Gandharva and a Gandharvī, were born again as inhabitants of heaven through the power of Jayā’s vow.
For this reason, O Lakṣmī! the Jayā-vow must be performed.
Jayā is the remover of sins, the bestower of merit, and likewise the giver of heaven;
she is the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and the granter of liberation.
By him who has performed the Jayā-vrata, all gifts have been given. (1.243.80–81)
All sacrificial rites were performed by him when the excellent Jayāvrata was observed;
and acts of service to others were performed when the excellent Jayāvrata was observed.
[He attained] wealth, grain, sons, wife, house, cattle, horses, and a virtuous husband.
Indeed, by means of the Jayā-vow on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one attains [all things].
For the observer of this vow, nothing whatsoever shall be difficult to obtain either in this world or the next.
Through union with Hari, all becomes easily attainable; indeed, nothing remains difficult to find.
Therefore, one must by all means observe this vow on the Jayā-suvāsara day;
the performer shall dwell in Vaikuṇṭha for ten million kalpas and will certainly rejoice there.
By hearing the account of this vow, or even by reciting it, [one attains the same reward].

One shall indeed obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (86) Thus ends the two hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Jayā Ekādaśī Vow in the Bright Fortnight of Māgha, and How the Gandharvas named Mālyavat and Mālyavan, who had attained the state of Piśācas, were liberated through that vow," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
