Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Beloved of devotees, Lord of devotees, Beloved of Ramā, my husband!
O Gopāla, protector of Lakṣmī, ocean of compassion, you who are my everything! (1)
O Dharmapāla, promoter of righteous conduct, honored by the gods!
Tell me, what is the name of the lunar day in the dark fortnight of Phālguna?
And likewise, O Lord, who is to be worshipped on the eleventh day, and what is the nature of that vow?
"O Hari, tell me all that which should especially be given as a gift.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "In the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, there is a day known by the name Vijayā."
O beloved, Ekādaśī is considered the destroyer of all sins. On that day, Pradyumna should be worshipped by those observing the vow with devotion.
In the worship, *tulasī* should be offered, and a citron fruit (*jambīra*) should be presented as an offering.
As for the food offering (naivedya), meals such as *sohālikā* and other delicacies should be presented;
for gifts, sandals are primary, along with wealth and other items according to one's faith.
With reverence, a festival should be celebrated and offerings made to the devotees of Viṣṇu.
Devotees endowed with faith and devoted to the Lord of Śrī should diligently observe the fast that bestows victory.
Just as the bright fortnight, so too the dark fortnight should be observed for the sake of attaining one's meditative goal.
By repeatedly drinking water, milk, and other such liquids; by engaging in sexual intercourse;
by being prone to anger and shedding tears; likewise, by causing distress and the like, and even by the slightest trace of faults such as theft, the fruit of fasting shall not be attained.

Charity, self-reflection, meditation, burnt offerings, recitation, and worship—these must be performed with diligence by one observing vows who desires their fruit. On the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), one should perform that recitation and listen to its stories; thus, victory shall be attained. (1.244.10–11)
O Dear One! If there is contact with the sight or touch of food that violates the fast, that contact must be avoided by all means on the day of the fast.
However, one who is unable to observe the fast may perform a vow consisting of fruit offerings.
O auspicious lady, roots, fruits, milk, and water shall be the objects of enjoyment for one who is unable [to fast].
Likewise, for such a person, eating only at night, food fit for sacrifice (haviṣyānna), boiled rice,
or consuming fruits and sesame seeds, as well as drinking ghee, milk, and water, are permitted.
One should avoid the enjoyment of perfumes and betel-leaf for the successful completion of the vow;
otherwise, without the vigil and the worship of Viṣṇu, the vow yields only half its fruit.
For the practitioner, however, the vigil and the worship shall yield the full fruit of the vow.
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall relate the account that bestows victory.
(16) In the time following the Satya Yuga, the great sage Jamadagni, who was indeed righteous, dwelt in the forest by the river Kauśikī. (17)
Always devoted to the sixfold duties such as ritual bathing and the twilight prayers, he is inwardly pure;
adorned with virtues such as compassion, courtesy, silence, and forbearance;
skilled in sacrifices, offerings, and the like, he is dedicated to the service of the gods. (18)
In whose hut the fire-god Jamadagni dwells in embodied form, consuming the food offered to him—
he is indeed known as Jamadagni. Residing on the bank of the Narmadā and performing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, he worships Mādhava.
Reṇukā was his wife, and she too was devoted to dharma and faithful to her husband.
That virtuous woman, dedicated to the duty toward her husband, served him daily.
Even as time passed, they remained peaceful, content with whatever came to them by chance.
Although they were worshipping Brahmā, the two of them did not obtain offspring.
Once, after bathing, Reṇukā performed the worship of Hari and then the worship of her husband; at that time, she fell into reflection.
"The husband is born in the form of a son"—such indeed is the Vedic revelation.
"May my husband be handsome, and likewise may he be a son to me. [She prays:
"May my husband [be capable] in the creation and the nourishment of a new creation. (24)
He is capable of both the creation and the dissolution [of the world], like the three gods.
May my son also be one by whom the gods are summoned and come daily to his sacrifice, and who fulfills everything according to his will. //25-26//
May my son become a lord equal to a god, a true master who possesses wish-fulfilling trees and the cows of plenty within his mind;
may he possess palaces like heaven and the prosperity of Vaikuṇṭha. (27)
Indeed, the very essences of Goloka reside within his resolve;
his established status is equal to that of Brahmā, his dispassion is equal to that of Śambhu, and his supernatural powers are equal to those of Śeṣa—all of which abide in his resolve. (28–29)
Liberation rests in his palm, and prosperity dwells in his nectar-like words of blessing;
enjoyments such as the fulfillment of true desires abide in his presence.
The Vedas, the sciences, the arts, and skillfulness all reside within his form.
May all virtues such as celibacy and the like reside within his heart;
may the son of that sage Jamadagni be equal to him.
May the gods grant me blessings for the attainment of a son.
Thinking thus, she worshipped her own husband and,
with Viṣṇu in her mind, drank the water from the big toe of his right foot.
At that moment, a most enchanting voice arose there, coming from the sky.
"I am pleased with you, O Goddess, because of your constant service to your husband.
Viṣṇu dwells within you always in the form of your husband, accepting your service. I grant you this word, O Goddess Reṇukā: he who is born from your womb shall be [my son]."
"I shall become your son, a lord equal to your husband;
there is no other for you who resembles or matches the form of a husband. Therefore, while your husband is like the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), I shall indeed grant your desires. (36)
"O Mother, listen to the vow that must be performed by you there, for it is truly effective for those devoted wives who remain steadfast in their vows;
it yields fruit, grants sons in this world, brings renown, and is a means to liberation. (37–38)
"The vow of the eleventh day, Vijayā, fulfills all intentions.
In every age, victory shall be yours in the attainment of a son.
Having spoken thus, this voice ceased, and Reṇukā likewise [became silent].
She observed the vow on the eleventh lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna (40).
Indeed, she gave various gifts for the satisfaction of Viṣṇu;
and by the grace of Hari and through that vow, she obtained a son (41).
This great lord known as Paraśurāma was a portion (aṃśa) of Viṣṇu;
after his birth, Hari assumed his own four-armed form. Śrī Kamalāpati granted his divine vision to his mother.
Having performed this, that Reṇukā became possessed of a son,
Vijayā. Listen, my dear, thereafter this boy Viṣṇu, a young brahmin,
became the son of Jamadagni and devoted to the dharma of sages.
Protecting the duties of the Brahmins, honoring the sages and the gods,
and constantly worshipping the Lord of Śrī, he obtained the sacred thread.
Instructed by his father, he mastered the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences.
By virtue of his knowledge and splendor, he became like another sun;
even from childhood, his prowess was no less than his father's,
and his movement through the paths of the three worlds was as unimpeded as that of the Lord of Kamalā.
The prince Vipra was most devoted to Brahman and dedicated to the life of celibacy;
by the mere sight of him, men on earth indeed attain liberation,
and by his service, the gods attain divinity and the riches of heaven.
And others who were living beings attained the supreme status of world-protectors.
This very person now dwells in the forest lands within the huts of mendicants;
this is indeed the divine play of Nārāyaṇa, which brings liberation to the wretched.
Now listen, O Lakṣmī! Once, the Kṣatriya race became arrogant;
they no longer took any account of their own venerable forest-dwelling twice-born ones.
And there was a king in Māhiṣmatī named Sahasrārjuna.
The descendant of the Lunar dynasty, Kṛtavīrya’s son, who possessed the prowess of his arms,
gratified the ascetic Dattātreya— an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa— through his services, thereby obtaining a thousand arms for battle. (52–53)
Likewise, he obtained the perfection of the power of yoga from Śrīdatta.
While wandering at will for the hunt in the dense forest, accompanied by his great army through the wilderness regions, [he encountered him]. (54)
While wandering about, he arrived at the hermitage of the great sage Jamadagni.
By the power of yoga, the ṛṣi bestowed upon that king, along with his army, ministers, and mounts, abundant hospitality, honor, and respect.
By the grace of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), he manifested at that very moment a splendor even greater than that of heaven and worshipped her there;
the king, beholding the sage’s power, was struck with great wonder.
He perceived that [the cow] surpassed his own sovereignty and was never before seen or heard of anywhere (58).
Having recognized that she possessed the power to produce all manifestations, such as palaces and other structures, he indeed seized that Kāmadhenu by force (59).
He led her, who was crying out along with her calf, to his own city;
at that time, Paraśurāma had gone outside the house.
Having returned home, he saw his mother weeping.
Then, having heard of the king’s wickedness, he was filled with anger.
He said to his mother: "Tell me, what must I, your son, do?
Tell me how victory may be mine and how that [debt] may be discharged."
"O Mother, show me how; tell me now what I should do.
I shall discipline the Kṣatriya who has gone astray, for I am invincible.
Instruct me thus, O Mother; I am your son and your servant."
The mother said, "O son! May you be completely victorious; act accordingly.
Previously, when I was childless, I observed the vow for the sake of desiring a son on the lunar day of Vijaya-ekādaśī, as Hari had commanded. (64–65)
He became gracious within my womb and attained birth in your form;
you are indeed Hari himself. Behold the auspicious bow in your hand, and look at the axe and the banner in the form of lines.
And you, O son, perform the auspicious vow of the Vijaya-Ekādaśī;
victory will always be yours in battle against Kṣatriya warriors.
Perform this vow for the instruction of the Kṣatriyas, my good son. (67–68)
"Then go forth to bestow the staff; may victory indeed be yours!
Thus addressed, Paraśurāma performed the *vijayātitheḥ* vow without water during the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, in accordance with his mother’s word.

On the tenth day, he ate only at night and likewise slept on the ground. After his morning bath, he worshipped with devoted piety the god Pradyumna, as well as Kṛṣṇa together with Vijayā, with a focused mind.
Having prepared a *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala there, one should place an auspicious jar filled with sesame seeds, endowed with jewels, sprouts, cloth, water, perfumes, and so forth;
and then, upon that [jar], [place another] auspicious one filled with sesame seeds.
Having set aside the vessel and established the image made of gold,
he worshipped the daughter of Pradyumna— who was stationed at his side within his mind— with many offerings.
Having bathed her with the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), he offered her a sacred thread (upavītaka).
Having adorned [the deity] with ornaments such as garments and jewelry,
and having worshipped [him] with sandalwood and other fragrant substances, with unbroken grains (akṣata) and beautiful flowers,
and having fully honored [him] with fruits and the like, as well as with sprouts and leaves of tulasī.
With offerings of incense, lamps, and the like, as well as circumambulations, hymns of praise, and so forth;
likewise with nightly illuminations and requests for forgiveness for his offenses, he worshipped him.
Having worshipped him in the same manner at midday as well, he offered him food and water.
In the evening, he worshipped him with sixteen excellent offerings;
he kept a vigil with the chanting of the Vedas and sacred narratives.
When the hour of Brahma arrived, he himself once again—
Having bathed, he performed the worship of the Lord with great affection.
He offered this prayer: "O Lord, through my vow of Vijayā, may there be victory for me—a brahmin who is not overly powerful and whose nature is gentle. (1.244.80)
O Kṛṣṇa, let there be victory in battle against that kṣatriya host who follows such a cruel and evil path; indeed, may we remain unharmed and invincible.
This very time has arrived for us to discipline the kṣatriyas who stand upon such a wrong path.
"Under my pretext, may you yourself achieve victory, O Blessed One.
While he was thus entreating him, the four-armed Viṣṇu appeared and said to him, "May victory be yours in every way."
"O best of the twice-born, I am pleased by your vow of Vijayā;
O lord of brahmins, you are my very form, for you are indeed a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
By the fruit of the Vijaya-ekādaśī, victory is yours."
"Let this instruction for the protectors of the earth be on your account.
If indeed the course of the teachers, the rulers of the land, should become corrupt, then I have made the Brāhmaṇas their correctors. (85–86)
The strength of Kṣatriyas arises from dharma, while the strength of Brahmins is born of the Veda. The punishment of unrighteous Kṣatriyas has been entrusted to the Brahmins.
Therefore, O lord of Brahmins, fight and subdue the prideless Kṣatriya.
"By this vow of Vijayā, may there be victory for you here in the world of mortals;
even without me, may you have victory throughout the three worlds in every direction.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished from that place.
Parśurāma also, taking up his sharp-edged axe as well as his bow, arrows, sword, shield, spear, and discus,
went alone to where King Kārtavīrya, the lord of Māhiṣmatī, was located.
Named Sahasrārjuna, adorned with a thousand arms, he shines resplendent in his own palace there, having seized the king.
Rāma said: "O great villain! O slayer of Kāmadhenu! 91–92.
Go forth for the purpose of seizing my life; experience the fruit of your own karma!
Give me my life, give me battle, and grant me the wish-fulfilling cow.
Or else, grant me defeat—for the word of Rāma is eternal.
Upon hearing this, the exceedingly powerful Arjuna became enraged and fought;
however, his thousand arms were indeed severed at the roots in battle by the sharp, divine edge of Rāma’s axe.
Indeed, many akṣauhiṇī divisions were torn asunder by that twice-born one;
his sons were destroyed, and Arjuna himself was slain at that time.
Having recovered the Kāmadhenu, he then departed for heaven himself.
He wandered upon the earth for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas;
twenty-one times he became the end-maker of the Kṣatriyas,
victorious on earth through the power of the Vijaya-ekādaśī vow.
That lotus-eyed Rāma became the most excellent of brahmins;
the cow was obtained, the kṣatriyas were conquered, and Arjuna was slain in battle.
In this world, victory was attained by Rāma through his vow of victory.
Arjuna was indeed an incarnation of Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus;
nevertheless, he who followed a false path was slain by Paraśurāma.
By reading or even hearing this, one shall obtain the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Victory of Paraśurāma through Austerity for the Purpose of Destroying Sahasrārjuna," within the section on the Greatness of the Phālguna-Kṛṣṇa Vijayā Ekādaśī Vrata, in the first part, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 245. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (Kṛtayuga-Santāna).
Chapter 245.
[The Author: Chapter 246.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Kṛṣṇa himself is the Supreme Brahman, for the sake of protecting the world.
Having assumed an incarnation, he even performs his own specific vow.
For the sake of gathering and sustaining the world, he indeed practices it himself; and he teaches people how to act as true teachers, being himself composed of pure goodness.
Speak, O Kṛṣṇa! A virtuous vow must also be observed here by me, just as it was by you, through the power of which liberation shall come into one's grasp.
May even ordinary people, having performed this vow, attain the supreme fruit.

"O son of Dharma, tell me that Ekādaśī which is known by the name of Arjuna in the bright fortnight of Phālguna, O Lord Nārāyaṇa, for my sake. Thus questioned, Hari Viṣṇu spoke of the vow to his beloved.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O auspicious goddess, O beloved who bestows all prosperity!
By means of which vow the great riches of people attain nourishment. (6)
Prosperities and riches indeed always increase for him;
liberation in abundance and great liberation abide according to his will.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, there occurs the auspicious Ekādaśī.
Known by the name Āmalakī, she bestows the fruit of the world of Viṣṇu.
(8) In Vaikuṇṭha, Śrī Hari asked Lakṣmī: "What is required?
What do you desire, O Lakṣmī? Tell me that, and I shall grant it to you. (9)
O you whose form is Brahman, there is nothing yet unattained that remains to be attained through your grace.
Whatever is mine is yours, and is of your very essence.
Therefore, choose a boon—blessings upon you—I shall fulfill your desire.
"Do not feel any hesitation, Lakṣmī! Whatever you possess, that is mine.
Having heard this from Hari, Lakṣmī replied: "O Blessed One, I have a beloved forehead ornament, a *tantikā*; O Lord, give that to me."
Then Hari, having resolved to provide an ornament, [placed] upon his forehead a fresh and auspicious mark— golden-hued, full of vitality, cooling to the touch,
clear, divine, resembling a gem, like the moon, and endowed with all excellent qualities.
He manifested upon his forehead an ornament consisting of a *bindu*.
That *bindu* became a fruit-like jewel, excellent and radiant; it was unblemished, circular, gentle, and resembled a golden gem. (14–15)
From that [source], many other divine jewels were also produced;
from them, a beautiful necklace was fashioned, consisting of strings of beads.
It appeared like a sun-gem (sūryakānta) in its brilliance, yet was equal to a moon-gem (candrakānta) in its quality.

In its heart-pleasing quality, it is equal to the Kaustubha gem; in its nature as an ornament for the neck, it is like a necklace. (17) When worn, it is like a crest-jewel; when touched, it is soft and delicate.
When applied to the body, it is as meritorious as the Viṣṇu-stone, and when worn, it is as cooling as sandalwood. (18)
In Sugandha, he is rich with divine fragrance; in Puṣṭi, he is like breast-milk;
and in Śāśvata, he is the great divine being born from the drop on the forehead of Hari.
In Tantikā, he is known as the ornament called the necklace (hāra), stainless and new.
The refined [garland] consists of forty-one fruits as given by Hari:
seven fruits in the middle, twenty-eight gems enriched on both sides by two threads, and six fruits at the two ends. (1.245.20–21)
And having received from Hari, the Supreme Self, a necklace that was offered to Mahālakṣmī—
a necklace that was radiant like the sun,
yet cool, full of flavor, and eternal— she rejoiced and exulted greatly.
He smelled it, touched it, and gazed upon it with reverence;
again and again he held it to his forehead and beheld it—this fresh [flower], resembling gold and filled with fragrant essence. (23–24)
Seeing on her forehead that which grants peace, smooth to the touch, and adorned with lines—
created by Hari himself for her sake—
she rejoiced; she praised it, extolled it, and took hold of it again and again.
She became joyful and showed [the fruit] to her friends. The Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, too, having observed the purity of the fruit on all sides, gave it a name according to its qualities.
And Lakṣmī tied to his forehead a string made of *āmalaka* fruits;
she shone with supreme splendor on all sides, just as the sky shines with rows of many moons. (28)
Mahālakṣmī shone brightly upon reaching Sutantikā.
Thus, when great joy had arisen even here at the creation of the Creator, and when the elemental creation of moving and non-moving beings had occurred at the beginning of the Kalpa. (1.245.30)
Accompanied by Lakṣmī, Hari himself— the Supreme Soul, higher than the highest— the beloved of Lakṣmī,
arrived upon the earth with great respect.
And from the forehead of Lakṣmī, the auspicious fruit of the *tantikā* [appeared].
Śrī Hari caused it to fall upon the earth for the sake of attaining its essence.
From that fruit was born a great *dhātrī* tree, bent down by the weight of its fruit and possessing many branches and twigs. (32–33)
He is proclaimed as the most excellent of all trees;
endowed with fruits resembling gold, this auspicious tree is dear to Lakṣmī.
Just as the forehead of Nārāyaṇa is beloved, so too is this tree beloved.
This [liṅga] has the nature of Nārāyaṇa and was created by Nārāyaṇa.
For the sake of Nārāyaṇī, it bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
It was first manifested here at Badarikāśrama. (35–36)
And from that Raivata mountain, that great tree arrived;
all these trees called *āmalaka* are givers of liberation.
On the day this tree was manifested by Hari—
That very day was also known as Ekādaśī. Because the Āmalakī tree originated on that day, the lunar day (tithi) of Ekādaśī was indeed designated by the name "Āmalakī" by the best of the divine sages.
Gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas;
Kinnaras, humans, Nāgas, Ṛṣis, and other Munis;
Vidyādharas, Kiṃpuruṣas, Yogins, and likewise the Brahmins who dwell on earth.
Ascetics, renunciants, virtuous women, yoginīs, and those observing celibacy—
(41) as well as others endowed with divine vision whom the Creator had fashioned—
all of them went to the *āmalaka* tree upon hearing of your wondrous deed. (42)
Filled with wonder, they proceeded while contemplating the *āmalakī* tree and praising its *āmalaka* fruits, which are worthy of the highest adornment.
Then the gods and others arrived at that place where the *dhātrī*, beloved by Hari, was located.
Seeing it, his wives were filled with great wonder.
Viṣṇu himself said to them, "This is indeed a preeminent Vaiṣṇava;
even the mere remembrance of this *āmalakī* tree yields the fruit of gifting a cow."
The merit from touching [the *āmalaka* fruit] is twofold, and likewise, that from eating it is threefold.
For those by whom *āmalaka* fruits are worn on the forehead, the ears, the neck, or the hands,
their residence in Vaikuṇṭha is indeed certain.
The āmalaka fruit, born from me, is dear and removes all sins;
it belongs to Viṣṇu, leads one to Viṣṇu, and purifies sin through its consumption.
Therefore, people should serve the āmalakī tree with every effort. (87–88)
When Śrī Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, the goddesses then said to Hari:
"O Lord of gods, O All-pervading One, give us fruits for the purpose of our ornaments.
Then, indeed, countless fruits were [offered] there by Śrī Hari.
Having conceived them and manifested them, they were also offered to those [goddesses].
Then, many ornaments fashioned by them were worn right there upon their foreheads,
necks, hands, ears, and other parts.
They rejoiced exceedingly and accepted [the offering] as they desired.
Then the gods and others also spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world:
"O Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Lord, hear our request."
"This tree is pleasing to us;
let the consecration be granted to us, by whose dwelling there shall always be the highest spiritual welfare for us.
Hari then said to the gods, "What you have requested is appropriate."
"Whichever place pleases you for residence, enter it.
Having heard these words of Hari, the gods entered according to their preference;
they entered the Āmalakī tree and have dwelt there eternally.
Viṣṇu stands at its root, and above him is the Grandfather (Brahmā).
On the trunk is the Lord Rudra, and the sages are stationed on the branches.
The other gods are on the twigs, and the Vasus are stationed on the leaves.
All the Maruts were in the flowers, and the Lords of Creatures (Prajeśvaras) were in the fruits;
the Ṛṣis were in the petals and stalks, while Brahmā himself was situated in the bark.
The essence of Brahman resided in the sap, and contentment was established in the form.
Through fragrance, there is union with Brahman; through touch, liberation is established.
Pearls reside within fruits, and the Lord of Śrī is situated in the seed of the thread and so forth.
Indeed, this Dhātrī, the mother of the world, should be understood as being composed of all the gods. (1.245.60)
Bestowing fortune, Ramā is to be served; bestowing prosperity, she is exceedingly dear.
Therefore, she is indeed most worthy of worship by all who are devoted to bhakti.
In the month of Phālguna, those men who observe the vow of Amalaka [attain these fruits].
They should go into the shade of an *āmalakī* tree for my worship.
There, they should observe a vow and keep a vigil preceded by devotion;
on the twelfth day as well, having gone to that very place, they should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*).
O lords of the gods, that fruit is declared to be eternal due to its connection with me.
Furthermore, if one performs acts such as eating beneath an *āmalakī* tree during the months of Kārttika or Phālguna, the fruit thereof is indeed eternal.

One whose limbs are smeared with *dhātrī* fruit, one adorned with *dhātrī* fruit ornaments, and one whose food consists of *dhātrī* fruit—such a person attains liberation. Whoever, having taken refuge in the shade of a *dhātrī* tree, worships the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), [attains the same]. (65–66)
O beloved, for every flower offered by him while worshipping Hari Kṛṣṇa at the foot of a dhātrī tree, there shall be the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice;
and by feeding virtuous brāhmaṇas, he will certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha.
By giving a gift at the foot of a dhātrī tree, one shall attain heaven.
By consuming the juice of the dhātrī fruit, one shall reach a state beyond qualities (nirguṇatā).
Indeed, by eating the dhātrī fruit, the observer of the vow shall attain divine liberation.
If one dies while chanting the name "Dhātrī,
Dhātrī," then Lakṣmī, like a nurse (dhātrī), comes together with Nārāyaṇa and leads him to the divine,
imperishable abode of Hari, Vaikuṇṭha.
On the day one is born from the womb, a person desiring liberation should observe the vow in the form of Ekādaśī;
it bestows wealth and grain, is meritorious, and brings satisfaction to the self. (71–72)
This vow is the most excellent among vows, requiring little effort yet yielding great fruit;
by performing it, a person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
If, during the bright fortnight of Phālguna, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) coincides with the Puṣya asterism—

This Ekādaśī shall be meritorious and the destroyer of great sins (mahāpātaka). It must be observed by one who has taken vows, for it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. On the tenth day, however, one should eat only once and likewise sleep on the ground at night.
Even the state of celibacy must be protected by one who seeks the vows.
Having risen at the Brahma-hour on the eleventh day, within his own inner self,
he should remember and meditate upon Hari, and then perform his bath in a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Then, having approached before Hari, one should make the formal vow (saṃkalpa):
"O Lord, by the grace of the gods, I shall today perform the waterless vow (nirjala-vrata).
May it indeed reach completion; O Master, may no obstacle befall me. (77–78)
Having thus offered this prayer, one should indeed perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and carry out the twilight devotions (sandhyā) and so forth.
One should perform the daily worship of Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa.
Then, indeed, within a mandala called Sarvatobhadra fashioned from food—
In the center, one should place a vessel made of gold, copper, or the five precious gems;
it should be arranged with cloth, sprouts, water, thread, fruit, and so forth.
One should set it down and place there a very beautiful vessel of sesame seeds.
One should place there an image of Govinda, the presiding deity of Āmalakī, fashioned from gold, together with his wife Candravatī, and worship him.
Then, beginning from the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), [the ritual should be performed]. || 82 ||
There, the practitioner observing the vow should perform worship with divine articles:
with the sixteen types of offerings as well as other services,
including the waving of lights, hymns of praise, food, water, betel, and various ritual substances.

One should worship the God with flowers such as *guladāvadikā* and *kamala*, as well as with rice, saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood. In particular, one should offer *kaṃsāra-pūrikā* and other such foods as an offering.
One should offer an akṣoḍa fruit with great devotion during worship.
Likewise, one should give a vessel of sesame seeds as a gift, along with wealth such as gold and other riches.
Having thus performed the morning worship, one should practice devotion.
On the day of the Dhātrī tree, worship is considered especially significant at midday.
Self-controlled, whether by a river, a pond, a well, or in one's home,
one should apply clay to the body and then perform the ritual bath.
"May all sacred fords (tīrthas) come there; I shall perform my ablutions.
Having bathed thus and put on clean garments, he should then apply the *puṇḍra* mark, fashion the *tilaka* and *candraka*, and proceed to the *āmalakī* tree. (1.245.90)
Equipped with all necessary utensils and provided with the implements for worship, and having taken recourse to the shade of an *dhātrī* tree after purifying the area on all sides,
one should construct the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala made from the seven grains.
In the center, one should place a water-pot made of gold or copper (92),
endowed with the five jewels, perfumed with divine fragrances,
provided with an umbrella, sandals, and cloth, and smeared with white sandalwood paste (93).
With a garland of flowers suspended from its neck, perfumed by all kinds of incense, filled with rows of lamps, beautiful, and enchanting on all sides— (94)—
one should place it upon a vessel, and above that, one filled with divine parched grain (lāja).
In a vessel of sesame seeds, one should place parched grain in a pot together with Candrāvatī;
likewise, one should install the golden image of Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni, along with his axe, as well as the auspicious golden image of Dhātrī. || 95–96 ||
One should offer the invocation, a seat, water for the feet, and the arghya-water;

one should give water for sipping and bathe the Lord with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). Then, one should bathe the deity with waters from sacred pilgrimage sites and perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana).
One should wear the sacred thread upon the garment and cause a jewel to be given.
One should offer all ornaments, such as the crown and so forth;
one should also offer fragrant sandalwood and the like, as well as attara oil and other such substances.
With *gulāla*, saffron, *abīra*, *aguru* paste, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
as well as with various kinds of flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings;
with the ritual of waving lights (*nīrājana*), water, betel-leaf, and excellent fruits— [one should worship] the Lord.

With prostrations like a staff, with praises and obeisances, with requests for forgiveness for one's offenses, with circumambulations and ritual fees (dakṣiṇās), and likewise with handfuls of excellent flowers,
one should worship the Lord of Devas at the auspicious foot of a Dhātrī tree.

One should meditate upon the form of the Blessed One as having a gentle luster at the feet; at the knees, one should meditate on the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa), and at the thighs, on the one whose nature is splendor (Tejaḥsvarūpaka).
One should meditate on Dāmodara at the waist, and likewise on Padmanābha at the abdomen.

One should meditate on the Śrīvatsa mark upon the chest, the Discus-bearer on the left arm, the Mace-bearer on the right arm, and Vaikuṇṭha on the neck; Yajñamukha on the face, and Sukhasāgara on the nose. (104–105)
One should meditate on Vāsudeva in the two eyes, and likewise on Vāmana in the forehead;
having meditated on the Soul of All in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should contemplate the limbs [of the mantra].
Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; homage be to you, O son of Jamadagni.

"Accept with supreme affection this great worship performed by me, accompanied by the offering of *dhātrī* fruits; be the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Having thus worshipped and completed the rite, one should then indeed proceed with the meal and other activities.

One should give [the remains] to the cows, and likewise cause them to be given even to minute creatures. At the root of the *dhātrī* tree, the remnant (*prasāda*) should be offered with a sense of divinity.
Water should be poured at the root of the *dhātrī* tree as an offering to satisfy the ancestors.

One should offer a respectful salutation with joined palms to the Sun, and with devotion, for the sake of the ancestors. One should give a portion of the consecrated food to the spirits and to children;
then one should take the remainder of the consecrated food to one's own home and preserve it.
On the twelfth day, one should consume fruit and water;
if these are to be accepted by the observer of the vow on that day, it shall not indeed be a violation of the vow.
Having thus performed the acts of giving, such as gifts consisting of jewels and gold—
Ornaments, garments, various foods,
lands, cows, buffaloes, houses, gardens, vehicles, and mounts,
as well as most excellent jewels and many kinds of sweetmeats. (113–114)
He shall obtain the eternal fruit of that [merit] in Brahman at the foot of the dhātrī tree;
his heaven shall likewise be imperishable and unsurpassed.
Such is the vow and the gift that bestows the fruits of both heaven and liberation.
Having satisfied everyone with gifts of water, food, and clothing,
and having bowed to Hari and prostrated before him, one should give whatever else remains to a twice-born man;
then, with supreme devotion, one should go home at all times, even during the afternoon.
One should pass the night likewise with devotion through the chanting of hymns;
having performed the worship according to the rules and having offered the waving of lights (ārātrika) and so forth,
one should present the food offering, water, fragrance, and betel leaf.

One should swing the Lord on swings, hammocks, and the like, and likewise observe a vigil with dances, songs, musical instruments, and the nectar of sacred stories; as well as with religious discourses and the singing of verses concerning Kṛṣṇa’s amorous pastimes. (1.245.119–120)
Whether in his home, in a temple, or at the foot of a dhātrī tree,
the observer of the vow should install an image of Paraśurāma and perform worship, the observance of the vow, and a vigil day and night at the site of the tree.
They should pass this night with Vaiṣṇava narratives known as "Bestowers of Liberation.
Then, one should perform circumambulations of the Dhātrī and the tree of Viṣṇu while reciting the names of Viṣṇu,
numbering either one hundred and eight or twenty-eight.
Having recognized the Dhātrī tree as Hari, one should perform worship in the morning;
having bathed and performed the lustration rite (nīrājana), and having worshipped the Brahmin,
one should honor the Guru and offer everything worthy of gift to him.
Then he should offer a water-pot, gold, a pair of garments,
and sandals to the preceptor, who is the very embodiment of Paraśurāma (the son of Jamadagni).
Having performed a circumambulation and touched an *āmalaka* fruit, he should speak as follows.
O Keśava, may you be pleased with me in your form as the son of Jamadagni;
may you bestow the supreme grace of Viṣṇu upon your devotees. Having duly given food and water to those who have taken refuge in you, [may you grant this].
One should feed the Brahmins, children, virtuous men, and virtuous women as well as young girls.
Then, surrounded by one's family, one should eat oneself.
By performing it in this manner, the merit shall be eternal and bestow liberation.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit in all acts of giving,
and whatever merit in all sacrifices— that fruit the observer of the vow obtains.
Freed from all sins, he attains supreme liberation.
For one who observes the Āmalakī vow, residence in the world of Viṣṇu is considered certain.
(131) All this has been told to you—the supreme among vows, which bestows sons, victory, splendor, and likewise liberation. (132)
It bestows unimpeded progress and the attainment of heaven, swiftly grants spiritual perfections (*siddhi*), fulfills the fruits of all intentions, and grants the favor of Lakṣmī;
it is auspicious, granting vehicles, mounts, fine ornaments, and various articles of utility. (133)
This vow is invincible and liberates one from all sins;
it bestows upon a woman the nature of Lakṣmī and grants her the state of Ramā, while for a man it confers the form of the four-armed Viṣṇu. (134–135)

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Ekādaśī Vow Named Āmalakī in the Bright Fortnight of Phālguna within the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning the manifestation of the Āmalakī tree for the purpose of adorning the forehead of Lakṣmī, as well as the greatness of worshipping the tree-form on earth during the Ekādaśī vow.

In vehicles and utensils, in foods that are chewed, eaten, and licked;

"For when this vow of Ekādaśī is performed according to the prescribed rules, the heap of sins shall perish, and at the end, the observer of the vow shall attain liberation. Having heard these words of his father, he performed that most excellent vow. (134–135)

Enjoyment, liberation, and great liberation—indeed, everything is attained through this single vow.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Caitra-Kṛṣṇa Pāpamocanī Ekādaśī Vow, wherein the Apsaras named Majjughoṣā—who had been a Piśācī due to the curse of a sage after having enjoyed [the fruits of her merit] for a thousand years through the austerity of the ascetic Medhāvin—obtained liberation by performing the vow," in the first section on the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"In this world, there is no other savior besides the Blessed One;

And for living beings, there is no destroyer of sin other than the virtuous;
likewise, in this world, there is nothing other than a vow that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
There is nothing other than Ekādaśī that destroys curses and sins.
It bestows heaven, it bestows perfection, it bestows wealth and sons, and likewise it bestows liberation.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear; please tell me:
what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the bright fortnight of Caitra?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the bright fortnight of Caitra, there is the most meritorious Ekādaśī known by the name Kāmadā, which is a forest fire to the fuel of sins.
She is also called Vimalā, the bestower of all desires;
for Viṣṇu, accompanied by Ramā, is worshipped as her husband with the sixteen types of offerings, according to one's wealth and according to the prescribed rules. (6)
For the water-offering (*arghya*), fruits such as *cirbhaṭa* and others; for worship (*pūjana*), mango blossoms;

On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should either eat a single meal or observe the *nakta* fast;

One should meditate upon the form of Śrī Hari and, having bathed, worship the Lord.
One should bathe Him with the five nectars and with waters originating from sacred fords (tīrthas),
and offer garments and ornaments of great value.
One should adorn [the deity] with erotic articles and fragrant substances,
with flowers, necklaces, as well as incense, lamps, food offerings, and excellent fruits;
with drinking water, mouth-perfumes, betel, cardamom, and cloves.
One should propitiate [the deity] with nightly recitations, hymns of praise, circumambulations, and so forth.

On the cheeks and at the sides of the *puṇḍra* marks, one should fashion decorations with sparse leaf-patterns (25).
In the center, these should be filled with extremely fine dots;
thus one should fashion and adorn the forehead as if it were another abode of Lakṣmī (26).
One should apply collyrium to the eyes using a golden probe;
one should apply a powder rich in white and red fragrances upon the face—this entire rite being for the purpose of fully manifesting beauty and charm. (27)
One should apply a very beautiful red tilaka on the cheeks;
likewise, one should apply a small, deep-red bindu on the chin as well, for the purpose of manifesting the beauty of the two lips like land-lotuses. 28–29.
One should apply appropriate color to the nose, including the nasal septum;
one should offer earrings and such ornaments for the ears, and provide bracelets and anklets.
One should likewise present those made of gold or silver, enriched with excellent gems.
One should wear necklaces of gold and flowers, as well as excellent diamonds such as the Kaustubha, around the neck;
on the two arms, one should wear bracelets set with jewels;
and on the two forearms, one should wear golden chains and bangles.
One should place gold rings set with gems and other jewels upon the fingers,
and one should color the nails on the palms of the hands with a substance suitable for staining.
Furthermore, one should apply divine sandalwood paste to the chest and to the breasts as well.
One should offer golden necklaces, flower garlands, and a bodice for binding the breasts;
a beautiful girdle made of gold to be placed upon the waist,
and a highly valuable silken garment with golden threads at its borders.
Likewise, one should wear a triple-stranded girdle that is pleasing to the eyes,
pleasant to the touch, made of fine cloth, dyed with various colors, and beautifully decorated;
it should be lovely to behold, with its beautiful strands pervading both the outer and inner edges.
One should indeed give a fine leather hand-cover for the purpose of support;
likewise, a golden vessel in the shape of a lotus, a beautiful fan,
two auspicious chowries, an umbrella, and a pair of sandals.
Having given ornaments for the feet and ankles, chains equipped with small bells, bracelets, armlets, finger-rings, and likewise finger-protectors (karaṭas),
one should worship Lakṣmī, Hari, Ekādaśī, and Ramā.
Likewise, one should give to Ekādaśī ornaments just as one gives to Ramā;
for just as Ramā is so, Ekādaśī is the beloved wife of Hari.
One should provide every utensil, every household article, and every excellent object.
One should also give all kinds of ornaments to her for the attainment of the fruit.
Having thus performed the worship with sandalwood and other fragrant substances,
as well as incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel-leaf, and drinks;
One should offer [the oblation] to the God and the Goddess, and then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Then, one should perform circumambulation, ask for forgiveness, offer praise, and prostrate;
thereafter, the observer of the vow should offer a handful of flowers. Thus is the morning ritual. ||43-44||
Having established the form of Hari situated in the center of the *sarvatobhadra* [mandala],
one should then go to one's own home and perform recitation (*japa*) for the sake of worship.
Likewise, at midday, having performed worship, one should offer the food offering (*naivedya*).
One should offer water, betel leaf, and everything else as before.
In the evening as well, one should perform worship, including the waving of lamps (ārātrika) and so forth.
One should observe this entire, preeminent, and festive vow, which bestows great merit.
At night, one should construct a pavilion adorned with plantain pillars;
one should fashion an archway of sprouts and indeed fasten a swing to a tree.
One should swing Lord Hari Viṣṇu, who is accompanied by Vimalā and Kāmadā.
The observer of the vow should offer food offerings, water for drinking, and other gifts to the God;
at night, he should keep a vigil with great festivities of dance and song.
By offering everything in accordance with the prescribed rite, the observer of the vow should propitiate Hari.
Having bathed in the morning, meditated upon Hari, and worshipped Janārdana; having given various gifts and performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for Mādhava;
and having whirled the wet garment and drawn out the water with a conch shell— || 51 ||
Having fed Hari, the Brahmins, holy men, virtuous women, and children with sweet foods, side dishes, and other delicacies accompanied by *tulasī* leaves,
the observer of the vow should then dismiss them and perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*). ||52-53||
By performing this rite in such a manner, eternal merit is attained;
whatever one desires, whether pertaining to this world or arising from the next, shall certainly come to pass.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this delightful narrative which grants liberation to two Gandharvas.

Formerly, in the beautiful and auspicious city of Nāgapura, which was filled with golden palaces, there lived the Gandharvas known as the Puṇḍarīkas. They were arrogant with pride, exceedingly cruel, and possessed of great power through intoxication. || 55-56 ||
Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and Kiñjanas, as well as Sarpis, Apsarases, goddesses, and maidens, all dwelt there.
In that city, King Puṇḍarīka indeed ruled his kingdom.
At that festival well-arranged by him who was known by the name Pauṇḍra,
there were Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Bandins, as well as Kiṃpuruṣas, singers, commentators, and Cāraṇas. (58–59)
Vedic scholars, Brahmins, those of passionate temperament (rājasa), and those of divine origin,
as well as experts in the Gāndharva Veda, gathered there for that festival. There, in the assembly hall upon the stage, the dance commenced.
The musicians sang with beautiful voices and played their instruments;
the dancers danced, while the other people watched. From Pātāla and from the world of the Nāgas, serpents capable of assuming any form at will [also came].
The Daityas and Dānavas also gathered for that festival;
they too, assuming forms equal to the gods in beauty, took their places at the celebration.
While other singers were engaged in dance and song, [the others remained].
Then, when the dancing of the female dancers and the singing had been concluded,
the Gandharva named Lalita— the lord of the Gandharvas and the foremost among those highly skilled in art— descended upon the stage before King Pauṇḍraka.
The Gandharva’s wife, named Lalitā, did not come there to the stage because of her household duties; at that time,
Lalita was alone and performed his singing and music without his beloved.
But because his beloved was not present then, Lalita—
deprived of her side and lacking assistance— sang, danced, and played musical instruments in rhythm, while remembering her in his mind. (67–68)
In her heart, the beautiful Lalitā dwells eternally; moreover, she becomes especially well-remembered during moments of intimacy.
In the heart of Lalitā, however, her husband dwells forever.
Both husband and wife, dyed with passion and bound by love, took their delight in the home just as Lalita had remembered;
his mind agitated by the recollection of his wife, he became like a dancer upon the stage. (1.247.70–71)
Remembering *lalitā*, his speech faltered and he stumbled over his foot-bindings;
his foot-bindings slipped away and his voice descended in pitch.
Thus, in the midst of the assembly of the Gandharvas, he became an object of ridicule.
Indeed, at that moment, Pauṇḍra’s reputation was ruined by that wound.
Then Pauṇḍra Puṇḍarīka, tormented by anger, cursed Lalita as he was singing on the stage, afflicted by love. (73–74)
"O evil-minded one, become a Rākṣasa, a flesh-eater who devours men!
Since, while remembering your wife and singing here at the great festival, you suffered a loss in the art of music due to your lack of attention in the assembly. (75)
"Both you and I have been made objects of ridicule by the assembly.
Therefore, having become a Rākṣasa, endure misery for many long years. At these words of Pauṇḍra, he assumed the form of a Rākṣasa. (76–77)
With a fierce countenance and distorted eyes, he was terrifying to behold;
his mouth, resembling a cavern, spanned many yojanas.
His two eyes were like two suns, and his neck was like a mountain.
His nose resembled a range of mountains, and his nostrils were like caves;
his lips were like a *gavyūti* in breadth and two *yojanas* in height.
Having become such a Rākṣasa, he was experiencing the fruit of his own actions. (1.247.79–80)
Lalitā went home, and seeing her husband’s deformed appearance, she, distressed by her husband's suffering, reflected:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? My husband is tormented by sin."
Having learned the entire account, Lalitā,
devoted solely to the service of her husband, wandered with him in the dense forest;
yet, repeatedly recollecting [the past] in her mind, she found no peace.
Though capable of assuming any form at will, she wandered through the difficult forest together with her husband, who likewise could assume any form at will;
though he was able to take any shape, he sported in the treacherous woods.
Cruel, devoted to evil, deformed, and a man-eater, he,
oppressed by his own sins, finds no happiness by night or by day.
Seeing her husband so deeply distressed, Lalitā became exceedingly sorrowful.
Afflicted by hunger, thirst, and other hardships, she wandered along with him;
he was indeed in the form of a Rākṣasa, while his wife was in the form of a Gandharva.
Seeing that extraordinary union of theirs, the forest-dwellers were truly amazed.
They were struck with supreme wonder and, terrified, fled from the spot. (88) Then the two of them reached the hermitage of the sage Śātātapa.
Lalitā went quickly and, having offered salutations, stood before him. (89)
That compassionate sage said, "Who are you, and for what reason have you arrived?
Lalitā replied, "I am a Gandharva maiden, the daughter of Vīradhanvan;
my name is Lalitā, and I have come here for the sake of a husband."
"My husband, known as Lalita, has become a Rākṣasa due to the curse of Pauṇḍra;
having become so, he wanders in this forest, and seeing him, I have no happiness.
By whatever merit my lord may be liberated from his state as a Rākṣasa," [she said].
"O Lord Śātātapa, instruct me in such a meritorious deed.
Having heard this, Śātātapa spoke these auspicious words that remove the sin of a curse:
"The Kāmada Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight of Caitra bestows merit and happiness."
"O beautiful lady, perform her vow according to the prescribed rite with certainty.
The resulting merit shall be bestowed upon your husband;
once that merit is given, the fault of his curse will vanish in an instant. (94–95)
Having heard the words of the sage Śātātapa, she became joyful;
she remained in that hermitage awaiting the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī).
Her husband lived there in the forest, dwelling near her at all times.
The Kāmada Ekādaśī has arrived; it was observed with a fast without water.
A vigil was kept during the night, and on the morning of the Dvādaśī, [the rites were performed] in the presence of Śātātapa and in the vicinity of the image of Hari. (97–98)
Lalitā spoke these words for the sake of her husband’s deliverance:
“Indeed, I have observed this vow, the fast of Kāmadā;
by the power of its merit, let his state as a piśāca perish. (99)
At that very moment, by the power of Lalitā’s words, his state as a *piśāca* vanished;
his demonic nature (*rākṣasatā*) departed, and he was born again as a *gandharva*.
Having cast off all sin, that Lalita became possessed of a divine body.
Adorned with gold and jewels, he took delight with Lalitā;
both of them, mounted upon a celestial chariot, were auspicious and possessed forms even more beautiful than their former ones. Thus the couple shone brilliantly as they both went to Nāgapura.
Thus, through the merit born of the vow that grants desires, her state as a *piśāca* was destroyed;
the curse was nullified, and she attained union with her own true form.
Knowing this, O Mahālakṣmī, this [vow] should be performed with the utmost devotion. (103–104)
It destroys sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, annihilates the state of being a Piśāca,
and bestows the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice through both recitation and hearing.

(105) Thus ends the two hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Caitra-Śukla-Kāmada-Ekādaśī Vrata in the First Section, the Kṛta-Yuga Cycle, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā," concerning how Lalita and Lalitā-Gandharva were liberated from the state of being Piśācas born from the curse of Pauṇḍra by means of this vow.
