Śrī Lakṣmī said: O Hare, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord who bestows liberation! O Master, the uplifter of people; O destroyer of the sins of sinners, those under a curse, and even those who cast curses! (1)
This divine vow, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been revealed by you.
Having heard it again and again, I rejoice; a desire to hear it arises within me.
O Lord, ocean of compassion, tell me [more] regarding the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha.
"What is the name of this Ekādaśī, who is its presiding deity, and what is its ritual procedure?
(3) Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "It is the bestower of good fortune, the giver of wealth consisting of sons and grandsons."
Bestowing happiness in this world and the next, granting prosperity, and destroying sin—this lunar day belonging to the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha is known by the name Varūthanī.
By means of her vow, the practitioner of the vow attains happiness in every respect. (4–5)
There is the destruction of sins and the attainment of good fortune as well;
even an unfortunate woman who performs this vow shall obtain all good fortune.
Indeed, for all those who observe the vow here, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It removes all sins, bestows merit, and is auspicious, taking away rebirth;
it destroys latent impressions (*vāsanā*), grants eternal bliss and liberation, and bestows everlasting stability. Indeed, that [practice] must be performed by one who observes vows.
Māndhātṛ, Dhundhumāra, and others who observed vows attained the heavenly realm.
Here, Puruṣottama is to be worshipped together with his Śakti, Nandā.
For worship, *jātiphala* and other fruits are used; for the food offering (*naivedya*), auspicious *vaṭaka* cakes are prescribed.
Flowers such as the *campaka*, as well as buds of the *kunda* flower,
land-lotuses (*sthalapadma*), and land itself should be given as gifts. Furthermore,
whatever else can be done according to one's capacity should be performed by the observer of the vow with a sense of fullness.
On the tenth day, having eaten either a single meal or only at night, one should sleep on the ground and observe celibacy; during the vow, one should remember Hari in the morning.
One should avoid bell-metal, meat, lentils, chickpeas, and likewise *kodrava* grain.

On the tenth day, a Vaiṣṇava who observes the vow should avoid ten things: leafy vegetables, honey, food from others, eating a second meal, sexual intercourse, gambling, sleep, betel nut, and cleaning the teeth. (13–14)
On the eleventh day, one should avoid speaking ill of others, slander, theft, violence, as well as delighting in them, anger, and false speech.
One should also avoid bell-metal, meat, liquor, honey, oil, and conversation with the fallen.
One should avoid physical exertion, travel, eating again, sexual intercourse,
and tamasic food such as lentils on the twelfth day.
On the eleventh day, the observer of the vow, having bathed in the morning, [should worship] Śrī Puruṣottama.
One should worship with new materials and the sixteen supreme offerings.
One should perform the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana), as well as the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the application of unguents.
[18] Thereafter, one should perform the bath with pure water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and the donning of garments and ornaments.
The gift of fragrant substances and liquids, as well as collyrium and eye-salve;
auspicious marks such as tilakas and crescent-shaped designs made with saffron and other powders;
clusters of flowers, as well as flower garlands and crests and the like. (1.248.20)
There, one should offer [the deity] to Hari and cause incense, lamps, and other offerings to be presented.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), bowed down, and completed the circumambulation,
one should praise Him, ask for forgiveness, and indeed offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
Having thus performed the worship in the morning, one should carry out the great worship (mahāpūjana).
Having fashioned an auspicious mandala called Sarvatobhadra with grains, either in a plantain pavilion or in the beautiful temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||22-23||

In the center of the mandala, one should place a new pitcher made of gold or copper, adorned with five precious gems and beautiful sprouts, and provided with water, sandalwood paste, rice, flowers, and fruit. (24)
There, upon that jar, one should place a new vessel filled with sesame seeds (25).
And likewise, one should place an image of Puruṣottama together with Nandā and together with Varūthinī within the mandala of sesame seeds (26).
One should worship her according to the prescribed rite and honor her with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should perform the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and the consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Likewise, one should offer bathing with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha), as well as the offering of ornaments and garments.
The offering of ornaments with erotic grace, the application of fragrant oil;
(28) the offering of sandalwood paste and the like, the offering of forehead marks, collyrium, and saffron;
the offering of garlands made of flowers, jewels, and so forth, and the offering of food oblations (naivedya). (29)
One should also offer water, betel, and the finest desirable fruits;
perform the lustration rite (nīrājana), prostrations, circumambulations, and requests for forgiveness.
Furthermore, for the fulfillment of the vow, one should make a prayer that destroys all obstacles.
One should give the supreme sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of objects such as beds, elephants, and moonstones;
and having completed the ritual of devotion, one should then perform [the concluding rites].
At midday as well, one should worship and feed Hari according to this very rule.
Having worshipped Hari in the evening, one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony;
one should offer food, water for drinking, and the like, and likewise observe a vigil (*jāgara*).
One should engage in dancing, singing, instrumental music, storytelling, and the chanting of His glories (*kīrtana*).
Having reflected upon the Lord of Lakṣmī at dawn, one should then perform worship.
[One should practice] the gift of horses, the gift of elephants, the gift of land,
the offering of sesame seeds, the gift of gold, the gift of food, the gift of a maiden, and the offering of cows.
One should likewise bestow the gift of knowledge and the gift known as fearlessness.
In this manner, one should construct the Varūthinī [chariot], which grants all desired objects.
Even a man who performs penance for ten thousand years [does not attain what this grants].
A man obtains a fruit equal to that by performing the Varūthinī vow.
By performing the Varūthinī, the observer of the vow attains the fruit of all possible gifts.
O Lakṣmī, in the former Kṛta Yuga, there occurred a most purifying narrative.

Having heard which, the great majesty of Varūthinī is known. There was a brahmin seer named Varūtha, the mind-born son of Brahmā, who was less than twenty years of age and devoted to the vow of studying the Vedas and other scriptures. (39)
Devoted to the service of his guru, pure, dwelling in the hermitage of Marīci,
free from pride and egoism, with the mirror of his mind made clear,
he was constantly engaged in meditation on Brahman, worshipping his guru as Brahman itself.
The word of the guru is the Vedic word; the Veda has issued from the mouth of the guru.
The guru is Viṣṇu, the guru is Brahmā, the guru is the Veda, and the guru is the Creator.
The guru is dharma, the guru is liberation, the guru is knowledge, and the guru is sacrifice.
The Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman; the command of the Guru is the Vedic revelation.
(43) By whatever means possible, the Guru must be satisfied, for when the Guru is pleased, Brahman is pleased; there is nothing higher than the Guru. (44)
The Guru is the reality of Brahman; there is no reality higher than the Guru.
The command of the Guru is the supreme dharma; indeed, the command of the Guru is heaven in this very world.
The command of the Guru is both worldly dharma and the dharma pertaining to the next world.
Thinking with supreme devotion that there is no other higher dharma,
he became the best of those devoted to the guru and performed service for the guru.
Whatever the guru might say, he did exactly as he was told.
He lives happily, engaged solely in the service of his guru;
constantly overflowing with bliss through his attendance upon Marīci,
he abides established in Brahman, free from identification with the body.
Living in the house of his guru, that twice-born man became one who delights in the Self.
He performed service to the guru and likewise attended upon the guru’s wife, Kalā, with undivided devotion, thinking, "She is indeed the guru himself. (1.248.49–50)
Kalā was the wife of Marīci; indeed, she was the half-body of Marīci.
Both Kalā and Marīca possess heaviness (*gurutva*).
The household service of the couple consisted of sweeping and likewise, plastering.
Fetching water as well as fetching the requisites for worship;
massaging the feet; wiping the bowl after the meal; making the canopy for the bed and likewise withdrawing the bed. (52–53)
Washing clothes, grooming the hair, applying collyrium as an ointment to the eyes, staining the palms of the hands with red lac,
massaging the body with oil, and likewise bathing with water— (54).
He also performs the wiping with a cloth and the offering of fragrances (55).
Day after day, through the state of being the qualified Brahman, he indeed carries out the adorning of the couple with garments, flowers, ornaments, and so forth (56).
He does not consider this body to be the self;

rather, he considers here that which is distinct from the body to be the self—indeed, the form of the self is changeless, stainless, devoid of both merit and demerit, and free from all affliction. (57)
The self is neither bound by sin nor smeared by sin.
Devotion to the guru is the supreme merit; there is no merit higher than this.
Apart from the guru, there is no other object for worship or meditation. (58–59)
Thinking always that he has satisfied his guru,
he never performs the worship of the form of Viṣṇu;
he does not offer food to Viṣṇu, nor does he even offer water.
He does not worship Acyuta Hari with the sixteen types of offerings and so forth;
he consumes what is not offered and drinks water that has not been offered.
He takes bark garments, roots, flowers, and the like for himself, without having first offered them.
Because she enjoyed things not offered to Hari, her intellect became defiled; pervaded by the quality of passion (*rajas*), it became intent upon worldly enjoyments.
(63) Furthermore, food and other offerings that have not been dedicated to Hari are said to be entirely unfit for consumption.
And from eating what is unfit to be eaten, the notion of identifying with the body arose in him. He became embodied in form, like one who delights in the objects of the senses;
and for this proponent of the doctrine that the self is the body, the sense-faculties became powerful. (64–65)
Even while youth brings about atheism and service to the teacher’s wife— both of which,
through constant association, cause the intense burning of the fever of passion—
he nonetheless protects his self-restraint by force of mind.
Thus, when a great deal of time had passed,
the Seven Sages were indeed summoned by Brahmā in the world of Satya, within the assembly of Brahmā, for the purpose of Śaṅkara’s marriage with the daughter of Dakṣa.
Then, as they were departing for the chariot, Marīci said to his son:
"Ensure that my word is properly observed and carried out;
the word of Kalā must also be honored, and you must do exactly as she says."
"O disciple, my home must be protected by you in every way, just as it is by me.
Having given this command, Marīci departed for the assembly of Brahmā.
Then the seven Ṛṣis, sent by Brahmā, set out for the house of Dakṣa.
While Śambhu was deliberating upon the granting of the gift of speech,
the Satyas remained fixed, yet they returned to their true state and departed again.
In this manner, a great deal of time passed there during that deliberation.
Kalā also became exceedingly delighted by the service of Varūtha—
through his companionship, her attendance, the massaging of his body,
the rubbing of his feet, and by sharing the same bed and seat. (73–74)
Attached by the power of passion to the body of Varūtha,
she— having obtained a firm youth and serving him in secluded dwellings—
bowed down and spoke with artful charm: "O Varūtha, accept me here."
"O sinless one, you who are consumed by the fever of love, grant me peace!
[76] Varūtha, honoring the words of his elder and considering Kalā’s speech, being possessed by a passionate disposition, served Kalā in secret. [77]
When their amorous act was completed and peace had arisen between them, she spoke words of blessing: "May heaven be yours, and it shall be imperishable.
Thus, by the power of desire, these two became enjoyers endowed with longing.
They remained with a mind full of desire, relying upon the words of Marīci.
(79) Having performed that service for the sake of Hara, the seven seers then returned home;
at that time, Marīci also went to his own auspicious hermitage. (80)
Marīci lived with Varūtha and Kalā,
and both of them conducted themselves according to the bounds of propriety, free from all carnal desire.
Nevertheless, [the seed] fell upon the foreheads of the preceptor’s wife and of Varūtha.
The line of longevity that was previously full has now come to an end;
it was seen to be broken by Marīci through direct perception.
There, Marīci asked the two of them: "How has your lifespan come to exhaustion? (82–83)
Marīci, overcome with wonder, spoke to them exactly as it was:
"Indeed, what was not done has been done by these two; for my word has truly been carried out.
That command of the Guru is always faultless when performed for the sake of his devotees."
By him my word was honored, yet this is a loss:
the seizing of a Brahmin’s property, violating the teacher’s bed, treachery toward trust, and ingratitude—these indeed are the destroyers of one's life. (85–86)
"Whatever was done by these two, that virtuous deed must be performed by me for them.
While he was thinking thus, the servants of Yama arrived,
surely to lead the two of them toward the city of Yama.
Marīci did not speak there; having led them away, the messengers of Yama departed swiftly.
Marīci, however, followed along in that very same body.
Then both of them were brought together before Dharmarāja by the messengers.
A rod of heated iron was joined with a red-hot metal spike;
Marīci said to the Lord of Dharma, "O All-pervading One, you have acted appropriately.
However, everything was done at my word; indeed, there is no fault in those two."
"If the word of my guru were wicked, I would become a vessel for fault.
As it is said in the *Yama-smṛti*: "The word of a guru does not cause fault;
if the word of Yama is true, then my word does not cause fault."
How could those two, being attached by my word, be possessed of fault? Therefore, they are not fit for punishment; do as you wish.
As long as you do not release them, so long shall there be no water or other [provisions].
"I accept your hospitality here; do as you wish.
But Dharma, having heard those words of his aged father Marīci, then reflected that his own lifespan had been lost through his improper deed.
By what powerful means might these two be reconciled,
so that both my word and the word of my guru may be equally authoritative?
Indeed, what must I do here in this truly contradictory situation?
"If my word is authoritative, then these two do not deserve punishment;
but if these two deserve punishment, then my word lacks authority.
Therefore, what should be done here regarding the act of joining our lives?"
Then, by means of that protective shield, he invoked there the power of his guru:
"If I am devoted to my guru and carry out my guru’s command,
then may Kṛṣṇa, who is identical with the guru, protect me according to the guru’s word."
While Varūtha was thus remembering Hari in the form of his guru, a voice from the sky then arose there:
"O Dharmarāja, listen; these two have neither drunk water nor received food."
Even Marīci now exists deprived of food and water;
for I am the Guru himself, since they both remember their Guru.
Because of these [reasons], I consider that the vow of Ekādaśī has been performed by them with me as its refuge.
May the line of life for both Kalāva and Varūtha be fulfilled today.
(103) By virtue of the removal of the *varūtha*, let this eleventh day also become renowned as "Varūthinī," the day that effects the removal of the *varūtha*. (104)
By reconnecting with a portion of his lifespan, he was restored to life by that *saṃjīvanī* [herb];
indeed, he was also gladdened by the bliss-bestowing celestial voice.
Accompanied by Nandā, Kṛṣṇa said, "I shall become the master of her birth."
Those men who worship me together with Nandā shall indeed become sanctified,
even if they are devoted to the wives of their gurus; and women who commit adultery with their disciples shall attain purity.
By my power, men and women who are observers of vows and free from sin shall become long-lived, even if their lifespans were previously exhausted. Likewise,
those who steal the property of others and those who are attached to the wives of others [shall be purified].
Purified by the Varūthinī vow, they shall become dwellers of heaven.
They shall have no fear of King Yama, nor shall there be any destruction of their lifespan.
There shall be neither widowhood, nor suffering, nor even separation from their husbands.
A person who is greatly afraid of the son of the Sun (Saturn) should perform the Varūthinī rite;
being liberated from all sins, he goes to the supreme goal.
Therefore, those who fear sin should perform it with every effort.
From hearing or reciting this, one shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Even if one performs the vow of Varūthinī out of ignorance or through sheer force,
I shall lead that person, liberated from all sins, to the world of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Yama, release these two:
Varūthaka and Kalā, the best of sages; and accept Marīci as your guest.
Perform the rites of hospitality by giving him your wife, and as his disciple, may you be happy.
Otherwise, this sage will cast a curse upon you on account of the merit of his vow.
Your entire region shall be reduced to ashes and become the domain of Yama.
Let your spies not go to the house of the performer of the vow, Varūthinī.
"Let not your messengers go to him who has fasted on the day of Varūthinī and is being sought; for he is one who observes a vow.
Having spoken thus, that celestial voice uttered by Hari ceased.
King Yama, seeing that they had completed their full lifespan, released them;
for they were faultless, abiding by the words of their guru, unstained by defects, and skilled in their arts.
Accompanied by Marīci, they departed from the abode of Yama and returned to their own residence.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the festival of the Varūthinī vow.
By performing, hearing, or reading it, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Vaiśākha-Kṛṣṇa Varūthinī Ekādaśī Vow, and How Kalā, the Wife of Marīci, was Rescued from the Fault of Association by the Vow through Her Disciple Varūtha, Who Was Devoted to the Words of His Preceptor’s Wife," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
← Chapter 248: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 249 [[Author: → Chapter 250
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, bestower of fearlessness upon devotees!
O All-pervading Lord, you have duly explained the vow that grants long life.
O Keśava, ocean of compassion, upon hearing this which destroys great sins, the mind becomes serene.
What is the name of the Ekādaśī that is observed during the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha?
"What is the fruit, what is the procedure there, and who is the deity? Tell me, O Mādhava.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Lotus-born One, I shall tell you out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds."
That which is the purifier of purifiers and the highest of vows—
O Lakṣmī, that Ekādaśī in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha known by the name Mohinī shall be the destroyer of all sins. (4–5)
The nets of evil are destroyed and delusion perishes through that vow;
great sufferings are destroyed and happiness arises through that vow.
Even by the mere performance of which evil is annihilated.
On the tenth day, one who seeks the vow should subsist on a single meal or even by eating only at night;
likewise, one should observe celibacy during the night.
Having risen in the morning, the practitioner of the vow should always remember Kṛṣṇa.
Having bathed, Hari should be well-worshipped by one seeking the vow; he is to be worshipped according to the daily ritual procedure. One should offer a prayer for the sake of the vow:
"O Acyuta, Lord of the gods of gods, today I shall perform the vow."
"By even a small fraction of your grace, may that become complete.
(1.249.10) Having thus concluded the worship which has been prescribed as a daily duty, one should have a *sarvatobhadra* mandala prepared with rice and other materials. (11)

In the center of that, one should place a well-fashioned vessel made of gold or a new one made of copper; it should be filled with water, joined with the five jewels, and provided with the five sprouts.
Its neck should be wrapped in cloth, and it should be honored with sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice.
One should place a coconut fruit at its side, filled with water;
upon its opening, one should place a beautiful vessel filled with sesame seeds,
and therein place gold, silver, copper, and sugar.
Having had an image of the Lord Madhusūdana, the master of Ekādaśī, fashioned out of gold— resplendent together with Mādhavī and joined there by Mohinī—
one should indeed place it within a vessel.
One should place and worship a ladder to heaven made of *kūpya* metal.
Having had a *svastika*, a *brahmasūtra*, a *candraka*, and likewise a *tilaka* fashioned from gold or silver, one should deposit them beside the jar.

One should cause to be given various fruits such as betel nuts (*pūgīphala*), along with cardamom (*elā*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), cinnamon bark (*tvaksāra*), nutmeg (*jātīphala*), powdered sugar, molasses, parched grain (*dhāna*), and so forth— these nine items. (18)
A couch, a ball, a secret fastening-cord, and likewise a side-pillow;
a mirror, a fan, an umbrella, a chowrie, and an auspicious staff; sandals, a hair-comb, and substances for perfumes. (1.249.20)
The performer of the vow should place a new earthen jar filled with water and ripe mango fruits,
and perform the worship according to the prescribed rite.
Among flowers, he should offer the *mallikā*, and the auspicious milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as the food offering (*naivedya*).
The *arghya* offering should consist of a jackfruit; the gift of a bed is most excellent.
(22) First, one should invoke Madhusūdana Acyuta into a vessel of sesame seeds, and then offer him a most superior seat. (23)
One should devoutly offer to the deity water for washing the feet, likewise auspicious water for worship,
and water for sipping (ācamana).
One should also offer a moist tooth-stick and fragrant powder.
One should cause his face to be washed with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
One should arrange for purification and so forth, and perform the cleansing of his hands and feet.
Then, one should bathe him with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and subsequently with pure water.
One should perform the wiping with cloths and offer fine garments;
likewise, one should offer a washed, subtle, auspicious, white, and new upper garment.
One should also offer sandalwood paste, oil, and highly fragrant substances.
One should offer sandalwood paste, jewels, a sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), collyrium and the like, saffron, *abīra*, *gulāla*, auspicious unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
flowers in the form of *kundakalikā* buds, and flower garlands. (28–29)
Then one should offer all ornaments, the finest articles of decoration,
and beautiful jewelry to Hari. One should indeed apply a *tilaka* and a crescent moon-mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste.
The observer of the vow should smear [the image] all around its body, beginning from the heart;
he should offer incense, a lamp, and food offerings consisting of excellent sweetmeats, sugar-cane products, the essence of curd, sandalwood, and *pūrikā* cakes. (31–32)
One should offer sugar-cane candy, cool water, mango fruit,
and a betel-roll prepared with betel leaves, as well as whatever else has been prepared. Likewise,
one should perform the waving of lights (ārātrika), prostration, hymns of praise, and circumambulation.

One should offer prostrations like a staff, a request for forgiveness, and a prayer for the fulfillment of the fruit [of the rite]. Then one should present a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and afterwards perform the dismissal (visarjana).
At that time, the observer of the vow should perform his necessary duties with a mind full of devotion.

At midday, one should worship Kṛṣṇa and provide him with abundant food. Then, being endowed with wealth, one should offer fifty-six articles of enjoyment, as well as drinking water and betel leaf for cleansing the mouth. (36)
Having paid obeisance to Him, the observer of the vow should offer that [gift] and perform acts of devotion and so forth.
(37) In the evening, he should perform the circumambulation with lamps, the offering of food, and the presentation of water.
He should have a pavilion constructed with plantain pillars and cause it to be bound together. (38)
The observer of the vow, having personally placed Hari upon a beautiful and splendid swing adorned with arches of fresh sprouts, should swing Him there;
the observer of the vow should perform the worship with the sixteen excellent articles.
During the night, he should spend the time filled with devotion together with the devotees.
In this manner, he should perform a vigil preceded by a great festival,
accompanied by dancing, singing, and vocal music, along with the proper rhythmic measures and tempos.
One should cause [others] to remember, recite, and perform narrations and stories. Men and women alike should, in every way, have the verses of Kṛṣṇa sung.
Furthermore, those engaged in the chanting of Hari’s praises should likewise keep a vigil.
Having bathed, one should remember Hari in the morning and perform worship again.
The observer of the vow should give gifts to the guru with great devotion;
he should feed the Brahmins and the virtuous, and honor the virtuous women and children.

One should feed the destitute, the wretched, young girls, and those who are dependent on others; likewise, one should feed dependents, laborers, women, and family members. One should also feed those worthy of honor with sweet food, as well as mothers and fathers.
One should feed the elderly and demonstrate a spirit of humility.
Then, the observer of the vow, remembering Lord Hari, should himself perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
[He should also give] gifts of beds, elephants, horses, and cows, as well as the offering of land and houses. (46–47)
One should indeed offer vehicles, draft animals, and wealth to a worthy recipient.
By performing the vow in this manner,
the practitioner attains the supreme state and eternal happiness in heaven according to his desire through the grace of Hari.
Listen, Lakṣmī! To this purifying story of a Vaiśya from a former birth.
[It took place] in Saurāṣṭra, not very far to the east of the Sarasvatī river, in the northern region indeed, to the south of the Bhadrāvatī. 1.249.50.
In the city named Bhāṇḍīra, there was indeed a king named Dhṛtisiṃha. He had a merchant named Dhanapāla, who was a treasury of wealth.
Dhanapāla was always renowned for his engagement in meritorious deeds.
He was a builder of kitchens, temples, monasteries, gardens, tanks, and houses;
a devotee of Viṣṇu, a servant of the virtuous, and one whose noble vow was to perform good deeds for others.
He possessed great faith in hearing the sacred narratives and was always intent upon devotion.
That merchant had five sons, all wealthy and distinguished:
Sumanas, Dyutimat, Medhāvin, and Sukṛti;
four of them were vessels of merit, while the fifth was a perpetrator of great evil.
Known as Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, he was addicted to the company of others' wives; he was devoted to vices such as gambling, took pleasure with courtesans,
neglected the worship of the gods, and was an atheist who disregarded the libations to the ancestors.
A reviler of the twice-born, a reviler of the Vedas, devoid of righteousness, evil-minded, a destroyer of his father’s wealth, a drinker of intoxicants,
a sinner who eats forbidden food, and one who causes the destruction of all prosperity.
Devoted to acts such as theft and associating with the wicked, he indeed performed no virtuous deeds.
His father saw him at a crossroads with his hand resting on the shoulder of a courtesan;
thus was he recognized by his kinsmen as one intent upon sinful conduct.
Expelled from his home by his father and banished by his kinsmen,
he squandered whatever wealth he had obtained as his share of the inheritance— just enough for his livelihood—
entirely through his constant association with courtesans.
Ornaments, vessels, garments,
and household utensils were all brought to ruin by him alone through his association with courtesans.
Consequently, being destitute of wealth, he was abandoned by those very courtesans.
Distressed by anxiety, deprived of clothing and wealth, and afflicted by hunger, he thought:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? I am destitute of any means of livelihood.
Therefore, he resolved: "I must practice thievery; I must commit robbery and even open violence."
"I live by means of plunder and robbery, and not otherwise.
Thus he commits forcible theft on forest paths,
and at night he practices thievery in his father's city.
He constantly drinks liquor and always eats meat;
he perpetually commits theft, having fallen into the company of unchaste women.
At that very moment, he committed the theft of gold during the night.
Though seized by the king’s messengers at night, he then gave them gold and wealth in the form of a wig;
having been released from bondage and attained freedom, he went into the forest and once again committed theft.
Again the royal messenger was seized for the failure to deliver the ransom;
having obtained release from bondage, he went once more to the forest.
Again he commenced theft, as well as the plundering of wealth.
He oppressed the people and likewise plundered the assemblies.
Then, he went out at night to commit theft in the city;
that man of wicked conduct was bound with strong ropes by the men.
Punished by the king with shackles and struck with lashes of the whip, he spent his time in prison according to the sentence; yet, having escaped,
he would again resort to the forest out of persistence and rush about for the sake of food.
Fierce as a lion, he slays deer, boars, and monkeys;
devoted to a diet of raw flesh, he roams everywhere in the forest.
Grasping a bow in his hand and carrying a quiver upon his back, he wanders thus.
Wandering on foot, he kills wild animals and birds:
ruddy geese, pigeons, doves, partridges,
chickens, cranes, peacocks, and even mice.
He kills boars, gayals, eagles, and swans;
indeed, this fierce and merciless man of arrogant intellect slays these and others.
Driven by former sins, he has entered upon a sinful path and is engaged in evil deeds. (76–77)

Overwhelmed by suffering and devoid of even a trace of happiness, he wandered day and night through trees, mountains, inaccessible places, and forest lands. Without a fixed seat, he roamed until, by chance, he reached the city named Kuṇḍina.
For there was a city rich with the beauty of gardens, situated near a forest region.
Not far from that forest, a great sage named Kauṇḍinya dwelt constantly in his hermitage, bestowing peace upon travelers. (1.249.80)
He honors guests with food, drink, seats, and other provisions.
Having heard that a sage whose wealth is austerity had arrived at the gate of his hermitage, [he went out to meet him].
In the month of Vaiśākha, he saw that ascetic who had performed his ablutions in a lake.
He of bold intellect approached, facing toward his own upliftment and prosperity.
Bowing low with a heart made tender by that very act, he fell at the feet [of the sage].
At that moment, drops from the wet garment of the seer fell upon him.
Upon the head, shoulders, and hands of Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, as the king of sages spoke, even the sound reached his ears: "We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva. (84)
Thus purified by the mantra, the sage, and the water,
he became one whose sins were destroyed by the mere touch of [the sage’s] feet.
And at that very moment, the sprouting of the seed of his desire for liberation arose within him.
Standing before Kauṇḍinya with palms joined in reverence, he spoke:
"O Brahmin, O bestower of liberation, having shown compassion toward me, [tell me] by what power of merit liberation comes even for a sinner. (87)
"Tell me of such a meritorious deed or a vow that bestows liberation.
Even those who have committed great sins cross over [the ocean of existence] through association with the great-souled; becoming purified themselves, they purify others as well. (88–89)

Therefore, having committed the evil practices of theft, drinking liquor, eating meat, and sexual intercourse, I have fallen completely. O Lord, purify me who am such as this and make me a partaker of liberation.
Having heard this, the sage Kauṇḍinya then said to him who had sought refuge:
"In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, there occurs the well-known Ekādaśī named Mohinī; perform the vow for it."
"By that vow, sins equal to Mount Meru will go to destruction;
for one who observes the vow, those accumulated over many lifetimes will surely perish quickly.
Having heard these virtuous words of Kauṇḍinya at that time, Dhṛṣṭasudhī—
He performed his vow according to the rules in the vicinity of Kauṇḍinya’s hermitage.
His sins were washed away, he became pure, and his latent impressions (vāsanās) dissolved.
His lifespan reached its end, and not even a trace of karma remained.
On the twelfth day, subsisting on fruits and leaves, he slept on the bank of the lake while remembering the sage and worshipping Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, chanting His name.
Having cast off his material body, he became possessed of a divine form.
Seated upon Garuḍa, he went indeed to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this auspicious vow of Mohinī bestows liberation;
there is nothing superior to it in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. (97–98)
Sacrifices, pilgrimages, and gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of this vow,
which removes sins and grants liberation through the power of Hari,
the deluder of those attached to *māyā* and the destroyer of delusion. (99)
She is the deluder of all except those who worship Brahman, bestowing infatuation upon them.
Since there is no delusion in her, she is called Mohinī for that reason. She is Mohī because by her one is led to a sinful abode or even to heaven. (1.249.100–101)

Mohinī, who bestows eternal happiness, is proclaimed to be connected with Kṛṣṇa; through this vow, she grants a fruit superior to the merit of ten million sacrifices. She, who bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, must be observed with diligent effort.
For the removal of the many sins of karma committed in previous births,

and specifically for the sake of a Vaiṣṇava, this [practice] should be performed to pacify delusion and to attain the state of being free from delusion regarding the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (103–104)
One who possesses desire shall obtain through the performance of this vow everything— sons, grandsons, wealth, wives, prosperity, vehicles, houses, and so forth— that may be attained. Indeed,
one destitute of wealth shall obtain wealth, and one lacking wisdom shall attain intelligence.
"Whatever the observer of the vow may resolve upon, he shall surely attain that.

(106) Thus ends the two hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Vaiśākha Śukla Mohinī Ekādaśī Vow, and how the liberation of the sinful Vaiśya named Dhṛṣṭabuddhi through the performance of the vow by the instruction of Kauṇḍinya," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga). Chapter 249.
Chapter 250 [Author:
Chapter 251 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Keśava, it is the natural way of living beings in this world regarding food,
drink, pleasure, ornaments, and beloved objects;
likewise, mortals in this world forget the law of Manu.
They travel along the path of beasts, their bodies and senses unsatisfied.
O gentle Lord Nārāyaṇa, there is no vow other than the vow of Ekādaśī that grants them liberation; indeed, it bestows immediate release.
O Lord, having heard this, my mind has become exceedingly serene.
O Keśava, please tell me the majesty [of that day], the ritual procedure, the mode of worship, and the vow for the guest who arrives on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.
"What is the name of this Ekādaśī? Who is its deity to be worshipped, and what is its fruit? (5) Nārāyaṇa said:
"This Ekādaśī is known as Aparā; it destroys even the greatest sins."
This [tithi] occurring on the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha indeed bestows sons and grandsons.
Its presiding deity is Lord Hari himself, Adhokṣaja, joined with his consort named Trayī; he is to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
He is to be worshipped with *ketaka* flowers as well as other auspicious blossoms.
In the water-offering (*arghya*), much fruit should be given, and in the food offering (*bhojana*), milk-rice and the like.
For the purpose of drinking, excellent cool water mixed with sugar should be offered.
In this context, the gift of a cow along with her calf to the preceptor is prescribed.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should subsist on a single meal or eat only at night;
he should sleep on the ground at night and maintain his celibacy.
Having risen on the eleventh day during the hour sacred to Brahmā, one should meditate upon Hari—
He with golden hair and lotus-eyes, with a nose as beautiful as a sesame flower,
adorned with earrings, a crown, armlets, and bracelets.
With red lips and a beautiful chin, adorned with a round face;
laughing, with teeth as radiant as rows of jasmine buds;
endowed with the bloom of fresh youth, and graced by a halo of splendor. (12–13)
Adorned with necklaces, gems, ornaments, and the like, and attended by people; his limbs were in perfect proportion to his form, and his lotus-face was serene;
he captivated the heart of the devotee, acting as an archer with side-long glances as his arrows. (14)

One should thus meditate upon Lord Hari Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul and Sovereign, who is filled with divine bliss and as beautiful as ten million Cupids. Then, having bathed, one should worship the Lord, the Master, according to the prescribed injunctions.
The observer of the vow should worship the Lord with the sixteenfold rites beginning with invocation,
up to the final offering of handfuls of flowers; having performed this daily worship,
he should at the conclusion pray for the pacification of obstacles to his observance.
"O Supreme Lord, today I shall perform the vow of Aparā;

may it be fulfilled for me without obstacle. Having thus spoken, the observer of the vow should have a *sarvatobhadra* mandala prepared with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and other materials. (18–19)
Then, having placed a golden jar filled with water— or one made of copper—
endowed with the five jewels and other such items, adorned with cloth and sprouts,
he should worship it and then invoke the sacred waters (tīrthas) into that water.
Having placed an image of Adhokṣaja fashioned from kunda flowers upon a vessel of sesame seeds atop a jar, one should worship it,
beginning with the invocation and ending with the ritual dismissal.
Having performed the bathing, adornment, perfuming, offering of food, water for the mouth, the waving of lights, hymns of praise, the offering of handfuls of flowers, and the request for forgiveness,
one should cause various kinds of gifts to be bestowed.
At midday as well, the observer of the vow should likewise perform worship and the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the three Vedas under the name of Adhokṣaja,
he should present sweet food offerings and offer betel leaves and other items.
In the evening, however, he beheld a beautiful green pavilion fashioned from plantain trees,
adorned with archways rich in fresh sprouts, flowers, and fruits;
it was provided with a canopy and rendered marvelous by the splendor of variegated, radiant paintings.
There, one should cause Mādhava to be placed upon a swing and rocked;
then the observer of the vow should perceive Adhokṣaja situated upon a throne in the midst of a cool garden sprinkled with the spray of water-lilies. ||27-28||
Having thus performed the great worship, one should conduct the rites for Hari at night; then, the waving of lamps (ārātrika) and so forth, as well as the food offering consisting of curd and sugar,
and auspicious items such as mangoes rich in delicious juices and fried cakes (pūrikā).
One should offer food for the night meal and present betel leaves and other such items.
One should also prepare a bed for the purpose of rest, a couch provided with a swing,
and a fine hammock suspended in the air from the branch of a neem tree.
One should also prepare a soft cushion, a ball, and a rug;
there, one should swing the Blessed One in the light of a ghee lamp.
Likewise, one should perform dance, song, chanting, remembrance, and worship.
Devotees should gather together in the presence of Hari and keep a vigil;
there they should listen to or recite the narrative of Ekādaśī, and proclaim the divine sports (*līlās*) of Hari through speech and other means. (33–34)
One should cause the worship with the name "Akhaṇḍa" to be performed loudly at night;
likewise, one should offer sweet water and fruits to the devotees.
One should give milk for the pacification of throat ailments, and provide whatever else is required.
One should serve the virtuous, the chaste, the noble women, and likewise the yogis;
one should perform the massaging of their feet to dispel their fatigue.
In this manner one should remain awake, avoiding all censure and contempt.
One should cultivate divine vision and meditate upon Adhokṣaja within the heart;
the observer of the Ekādaśī vigil vow should perform every auspicious deed and destroy idleness, physical ailments, and other such obstacles through the practice of Rāsa-dance.
A devotee should repeatedly engage in jumping, singing, dancing,
and laughing in order to destroy sleep and laziness; and he should perform running with circumambulation and playful sports among fellow devotees who are impartial toward all.
One should vividly contemplate Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes: the Rāsa-līlā, the pastime of giving gifts, the pastimes with the gopīs, his sporting with Rādhā, his wandering in the forest,
and his union with Padmā, Bhārgavī, and Ramā.

One should perform the marriage ceremony of Nārāyaṇa, which is characterized by great festivities. At night, one should celebrate a grand festival [depicting] Kṛṣṇa’s union with the Gopikā, or together with Pārvatī, Prabhā, Māṇikī, and Lakṣmī. || 42–43 ||
One should perform a wedding festival for Brahmā, the Supreme Self;
likewise, one should chant the birth-stanzas and the festivals of Śakti’s manifestation.
One should recite these during the vigil, and having bathed in the morning, one should worship [the deity].
One should worship Adhokṣaja with the sixteen types of offerings and so forth;
thereafter, one should fully honor the Trayī (the Vedas), the Ekādaśī, and the Guru.
For Kṛṣṇa is always present upon the head of the Guru.
The eyes of Kṛṣṇa are in the eyes of the guru; the face of Hari is in the mouth of the guru.
The ears of Kṛṣṇa are in the ears of the guru; the tongue of Hari is in the mouth of the guru.
The throat of Hari is in the throat of the guru; the lips of Mādhava are on the lips of the guru.
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa’s chest is one with the Guru’s chest; Hari’s belly is one with the Guru’s.
Hari’s hand is one with the Guru’s hand; Hari’s hip is one with the Guru’s hip.
Hari’s back is one with the Guru’s back; the heart of Hari is one with the heart of the Guru.
The intellect of the Guru is the intellect of Hari; the speech of the Guru is indeed the speech of Hari.

What is protected by the Guru is protected by Hari; the thighs of the Guru are the thighs of Hari. The skin of the Guru is indeed the skin of Hari; the strength of the body of the Guru is the strength of Hari.
The knees of the Guru are the knees of Hari, and the nails of the Guru are one with those of Hari.
On the feet of the Guru are the feet of Kṛṣṇa, and the nails of the Guru are one with those of Hari.
Kṛṣṇa himself resides within the Guru; there is no other Kṛṣṇa higher than the Guru.
"The Guru is Kṛṣṇa; Kṛṣṇa is the Guru. Salutation to that Śrī Guru.

Having meditated thus, one should properly worship the Guru with the realization that he is Kṛṣṇa. One should also offer to the Guru whatever is dear to him; for when the Guru is satisfied, [the Lord] is satisfied.
By serving the guru, the merit of serving Kṛṣṇa is certainly attained.
It should be understood that offering to the guru is offering to Kṛṣṇa; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Lakṣmī! I indeed appear in the form of the guru to my advanced disciples.
Abiding with the guru, I receive divine service performed with devotion and respect— by whatever means possible, whether through giving, worship, bowing, offering, service, or praise. (56)
The Guru should always be gratified by massaging his feet, by offering him beloved objects, or even by presenting him with a house and such;
therefore, one should offer the object of the Ekādaśī vow to the venerable Guru.
A Guru who is pleased can indeed deliver one's husband, wife, son, daughter, and even one's entire family; therefore, the Guru is identical with Kṛṣṇa.
Knowing this, one should indeed offer gifts to the Guru on the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī).
One should cause the Brahmins to break their fast and feed virtuous men and women;
one should also feed children and maidens and give abundant gifts.
Thus, the observer of the vow [attains success] on earth, in heaven, or even in the Vairāja realm.
One who serves the Supreme Lord, whether manifest or unmanifest, shall attain eternal bliss;
however, he who serves another [deity] attains renown in this world.
Even one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin, the murder of a cow, or the destruction of an embryo, [is purified].
One who has committed sins such as the killing of a woman or the killing of a Brahmin is liberated by this vow.
Likewise, a person devoted to slandering others or taking pleasure in the wives of others becomes free from sin through the attainment of another's vow. (63–64)
A false witness, a mother who deceives, one who practices fraud and guile, one who speaks falsely, and a slanderer—these are quickly liberated from sin.
Likewise, one who falsifies the Vedas, one who falsifies the scriptures, and one who falsifies the calculations of astrology; 65.
A physician who practices fraudulent Ayurveda is indeed liberated from this [sin] by means of this vow.
Brāhmaṇas fallen from Brahmanical status, Kṣatriyas who have failed in their duty of protection, and Vaiśyas who have turned away from giving—these are all liberated by this vow. (66–67)
Even Śūdras excluded from the Dharma, disciples who revile their teachers and others,
and even a son who has killed his mother or father, are indeed liberated by this vow.
Whatever fruit men obtain at Prayāga when the sun is situated in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, [that same fruit is obtained here].

Whatever merit is obtained at Kāśī by the vow of Śivarātri, whatever merit is considered to be bestowed upon the ancestors through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā, and whatever fruit is gained at the Godāvarī when Jupiter is situated in Leo; [all that is attained here]. 69–70.
The merit gained from beholding Kedāra is equal to the fruit born of the Badarī-tīrtha,
or from visiting all the holy fords at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse,
or from performing a sacrifice with sacrificial fees accompanied by the gift of elephants, horses, and gold.
The attainment of that fruit [which results from other vows] comes from the practice of this supreme vow.
It is an axe for the tree of sin, a forest fire for the jungle of faults, a sun for the darkness of evil, and a lioness for the deer of misfortune. (72–73)
The Aparā is considered to grant liberation, worldly enjoyment, and indeed whatever is desired;
for there remains no higher merit than that which arises from her vow.
Through union with Kṛṣṇa, she becomes meaningful for those who perform the rite.
For other women, however, only fragmented merit is obtained here through their vows.
For another woman, the fruit of universal sovereignty may be attained here through her vow;
for there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be obtained here by one who observes a vow.
O Lakṣmī! Both the listener and the reciter shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
The observer of the vow, having shaken off all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, other [scriptures] in its presence truly become insignificant in brilliance.

She is called "the other" (aparā) because there is no other supreme [reality] beyond her. (78) Only by fasting upon the Aparā and worshipping Adhokṣaja together with the Consort of the Three Vedas (Trayīpatnī), one is liberated from the adamantine bond (vajralepa). (79)
For those whose sins are devoid of atonement, this atonement is prescribed:
for a soul that has no other recourse, this very vow is its refuge.
Listen, Lakṣmī! To the narrative concerning Śalabhā in the Kṛta Yuga.
For the female ascetic, it became auspicious, wondrous, and a bestower of liberation. That virtuous woman, having received the Bhāgavata initiation from the female ascetic,
worshipped Lord Nārāyaṇa day and night.
In the forest on the mountain named Arbuda, near Puṣkara,
she wanders perpetually alone by the power of yoga.
From her childhood, she was an eminent yoginī who became the disciple of Sanaka.
When a hundred thousand years had passed and youth had reached its peak of power,
she repeatedly observed in the forest the mating of lions and lionesses— the wild beasts of the woods— as well as the various amorous unions of other forest-dwellers. (84–85)
Her mental disposition became fixed upon the pleasure of Kāmadeva;
having taken hold of that red-colored wild monkey dwelling in her own hermitage,
she delighted him constantly out of passionate desire.
Through the union with the monkey, the fetus was born and grew.
Having heard from the disciple of Vasiṣṭha, named Vedaśruta, that the mixture of species resulting from such an animal union is a sin that destroys liberation, she [then reflected]. || 87-88 ||
Having fallen into great remorse, she went to the hermitage of Sanaka.
Seeing that his female disciple was pregnant, Sanaka said to her:
"What is this that has happened to you, daughter? Your life of celibacy has been destroyed."

Nevertheless, everything has been described to the Guru without any deceit. Now, tell me that by which the destruction and purification of this sin—which causes loss of caste, degradation, and even downfall—may come to pass. (90–91)
Having thus entreated him, she, pregnant and distressed in mind, wept, thinking:
"The destruction of a fetus is a great sin, a transgression such as the killing of an embryo;
how might my fetus remain free from harm? (92)
To her who was thus reflecting, Sanaka said: "Listen!
Observe a waterless fast on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha;
your sin shall be destroyed and your *prārabdha* karma shall reach its completion."
"Moreover, liberation will be easily attained before the birth [of the child]; therefore, perform the vow.
Having heard this and bowed to the preceptor, she went to her own hermitage on Mount Arbuda and duly performed the auspicious vow of Aparā.

By that, she attained purity; her state of fallenness dissolved. Her life came to its end, and through steady devotion to Adhokṣaja, she then joined her self with him via the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 96–97 ||
Having led the consciousness situated in the *garbhādhāna* [stage] to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*),
she abandoned her body and attained supreme liberation through the practice of the *aparā*.
Indeed, the vow of the *aparā* is thus the destroyer of the mixture of sins.
O Lakṣmī! This must always be performed by a woman as well for the sake of purification.
It must certainly be done by an ascetic established in Brahman, by a yogi, and even by a renunciant, for the pacification of the sin of causing the mixture of castes. (1.250.99–100)

Thus ends the two hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Vow of the Eleventh Day of the Dark Half of Jyeṣṭha in the First Section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning how the pregnant woman Śalabhāyatī was freed from fault and attained liberation through the performance of this vow which destroys sins such as causing the mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*).
Chapter 251 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga)
— Chapter 251
[The Author: Chapter 252.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
In this essence-less cycle of existence, the Blessed Lord himself is the true essence.
By resorting to which men go to the imperishable state of Nirvāṇa.
(1) Through its association with Kṛṣṇa, the lunar day of Kṛṣṇa bestows fruits equal to those of Kṛṣṇa himself;
by performing its vow according to the rules, an embodied being attains the supreme goal. (2)
What is the name of the eleventh day (ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha?
O Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Mercy, Consort of Ramā, tell me: who is the presiding deity of that day, what is the procedure for its vow, what is the nature of the gift, and what is the fruit thereof?
And you are the one who bestows causeless grace upon your own devotees.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha is indeed known as Nirjalā (the Waterless).
The one named Trivikrama, accompanied by Padmākṣī, is desired as the object of worship.
He is to be worshipped with *yūthikā* flowers; for the *arghya*, a mango fruit is prescribed.
Curd, rice, and the like are intended as the food offering (*naivedya*), and the gift of an umbrella and so forth is also desired.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should subsist on a single meal or on food taken at night;
he should sleep on the ground at night and remain celibate as one observing the vow.
Having risen in the morning, he should meditate upon the Lord of Lakṣmī and contemplate his limbs.
Having bathed, the devotee should worship him with materials endowed with sincere devotion.
Beginning with the invocation, one should perform the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth;
then, having adorned him with garments, ornaments, and fragrant scents.
With betel leaves, saffron, musk, necklaces, ointments, and crest-ornaments; with lamps, excellent food offerings, drinks, betel nut, and ritual fees;
and with prostrations, hymns of praise, words of apology, and handfuls of flowers, [one worships] Hari.

Having performed worship, one should then have a *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala constructed with grains. One should place a pitcher made of gold— or likewise a pitcher made of copper— in the center, and similarly eight pitchers in the eight directions.
Having placed five jewels, fruits, sprouts, and rice,
as well as cloth, a vessel containing sesame seeds, and fragrant substances such as sandalwood,
one should install the image of Trivikrama within the jars.
A devotee should worship the golden image accompanied by Padmākṣī and Nirjalā according to the prescribed rite, and for the sake of the vow, he should resolve:
"O Kṛṣṇa, I perform this worship for the successful accomplishment of the Nirjalā vow."
"May you, who are filled with compassion, become the granter of all desires.
Having thus made this supplication, one should then worship the Leader of the Gaṇas in his Kṛṣṇa incarnation with *dūrvā* grass, vermilion, agallochum, sandalwood, and unbroken grains of rice.
Thereafter, one should offer sweetmeats (modakas) and worship Trivikrama.
Having performed the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), one should bathe Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) derived from a cow, and with pure water scented with fragrances. 17–18.
One should offer white garments, the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), and so forth;
as well as crowns, ornaments, necklaces, and armlets;
and also fragrant oils, substances for perfumes, collyrium, and lac-dye. (19)

Incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, and betel; the waving of lights, hymns of praise, circumambulations, and processions; the request for forgiveness, flowers, and the offering of joined palms—these are the rites. (1.251.20–21)
In this manner, the observer of the vow should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa with every prescribed rite;
thereafter, he should attend to his own duties, and likewise perform them at midday.
As for the food offering (naivedya), there should be the essence of sandalwood, fried cakes (pūrikā), and the excellent juice of mangoes.
One should then offer the deity water that is cool, sweetened with sugar, fragrant, and infused with pure intentions. Afterwards, in the evening,
one should have Śrī Hari mounted upon a swing in a flower garden or on the grounds of a grove of trees.
In the evening, one should cause Hari to sport upon a soft ground covered with green grass, moistened by water, cool and damp, and fanned by a gentle breeze.
At night, however, one should perform the waving of lights (ārātrika) and the offering of hymns of praise and so forth in their proper sequence.
One should offer buttermilk and a beautiful oblation of ghee mixed with curd;
one should offer excellent water of sweet essence for drinking,
as well as substances for cleansing the mouth and a beautiful bed.
The devotee, having gathered with many *sātvatas*, should perform the vigil; then, having bathed in the morning, bowed to Hari, and worshipped Him,
he should thereafter worship other venerable ones, feed them, and indeed perform the breaking of the fast with water.
Then the observer of the vow should take his meal, having offered it to Hari.
He should give various kinds of gifts for the attainment of excellent fruits.
A king should give elephants and the like, as well as jewels and cities.
A Brahmin should give books and the like; a Vaiśya, grains and wealth;
and a Śūdra should give new articles of artistry and food.
Everyone should give according to their capacity whatever is fit to be given before them.
One should perform the gift of cows, the gift of land, and other gifts as well.
Whatever one possesses oneself, that the observer of the vow should offer to a worthy recipient.
Thinking, "I offer this to Brahman," he should give it to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu).
One should give it to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and likewise to one's venerable Guru;
one should also give it to the destitute, the poor, and the helpless. One should give it to a woman and likewise offer it to a widow who is without a protector.
One should give sugar and other sweets to the boys and girls;
the observer of the vow should also give alms mixed with ghee to virtuous men and women,
and likewise present various other sweet foods and edibles.
Having thus performed this vow, the devotee goes to heaven and attains liberation.
This vow is an easy means, essential, and of great fruit;
it involves little hardship, requires only a few materials, and is accomplished through faith. (37)
Even those who are evil-doers, of wicked conduct, most sinful, and devoid of dharma— (38)—
if they do not eat in a waterless place nor drink water and the like,
and if they practice devotion to Hari, they do not go to the presence of Yama. (39)
Listen to the account of this vow which took place in the former Kṛta Yuga.
Just as at the beginning of the age, Brahmā created the world as before;
on that first day of the Satya Yuga, there was a sage named Kratu.
The sacrifice, whose mouth is Agni, became the son of the Creator and a source of food for many.
Whatever he consumed as it was offered turned to ashes at that very moment; even thousands and hundreds of thousands of meals were consumed simultaneously. (41–42)
He eats alone and immediately digests all those boundless foods within the span of a single ghaṭikā;
yet, he remains consumed by the forest fire of his internal digestive heat. //43//
When he no longer obtains the foods he desires to eat,
he then goes to the forest of the Himalayas, the forest of Meru, or some other vast wilderness; there he eats everything found in those places day and night.
For the sake of water, he falls into the desired ocean of milk;
he drinks the water until he is satisfied,
and so it is likewise with the sacrifice for the body while this journey is being undertaken.
Once, overcome by great hunger, he approached Brahmā and requested,
"May food that never fails to satisfy be granted to me eternally.
Brahmā said, "O son, I shall grant you satisfaction through a sacrifice."
Whatever conscious being, acting as a sacrificer for you,
offers food with incomparable devotion during the sacrifice—
to that same extent may hunger arise within you for the purpose of digestion.

But in the absence of meditation, even the destruction of your hunger would not occur; let there be satisfaction for you there only according to your meditation. From this moment on, my son, hunger shall no longer afflict you.
As he previously oppressed Hotr̥, so shall he oppress him now; for it is not otherwise.
However, they will offer even more sacrificial oblations to the very embodiment of the sacrifice.
Let it not be that, at the same time, this unwholesome act should be performed by many.
For this reason, your hunger shall indeed arise according to your own will:
"As much as someone may give you, let that be yours; then your hunger shall remain. When they do not give, then your hunger shall always be appeased. || 53–54 ||
"Be happy, O son Kratu; let there be no excessive greed for the tongue.
Thus addressed with blessings by Brahmā, Kratu departed from there.
With a tranquil heart, he dwelt in the permanent abodes of those who maintain the sacred fire.

He incessantly devours the various kinds of sacrificial offerings—daily oblations made in the morning, at midday, and in the evening—during the fire-sacrifices performed by the priests. Having eaten again and again, he is ever hungry and constantly desires food. (56–57)
Thus, by the power of practice, his eating three times [a day] becomes certain;
or even for a longer period than that, it must certainly be maintained.
In this way, through the habit of eating, he desires [food] at the proper times.
Various kinds of food, whether sacrificial offerings or otherwise, whether given or not given—through greed of the tongue, the desire for food arises again and again;
and by its own will, his hunger increases with great force. (1.251.60)
When Kratu had thus established himself, the great sages Dakṣa, Marīci, and the others went to the Badarikā forest to behold Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person.
Having bathed in the Mandākinī and beheld Hari, Nārāyaṇa, they [proceeded].

They sat there in the presence of Śrī Hari in the forest of Badarī. [62] They beheld the Supreme Lord, whose limbs were beautiful in form, who was as radiant as a mountain of snow, whose very nature was the vow of Brahman, and who was the embodiment of austerity. [63]
Having bowed and remembered Hari, Bhṛgu questioned the Supreme Lord:
"O Friend of the distressed, O Ocean of Mercy, O Lord who delivers the bound!
We bow to You, having sought refuge in You, who dwells within the heart and without."
Tell us of a simple vow that bestows merit and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
by which all faults arising from others' food, as well as those arising from food that is impure, may be destroyed in every respect. (61, 66)
O Lord, may those faults arising from food during a period of impurity (sūtaka),
from eating mixed food, from food obtained as alms, and from food that has turned stale—
whether committed knowingly or unknowingly— be destroyed.
"Tell me of such true austerity by which those faults—the faults arising from unconsecrated food and those arising from the breaking of the row for one's own sake—may be destroyed.
Having heard this, Śrī Hari said: "Listen, O best of Brahmins!"
The fast on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is considered the vow, the best of vows;
it is austerity, the foremost of austerities, and the destroyer of sins.
It is the supreme purifier of all defects rooted in food.
The vow that bestows all fruits is simple, easy to perform, subtle, and [yet] profound.
(7.1) One should not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights. O great sages! One should not eat even during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity. (7.2)
This vow must be observed for as long as one lives by one who desires the highest good;
even by one desiring heaven or liberation, that auspicious vow must be performed.
For one who observes the vow, there arise no innumerable faults dependent upon food.
For those who do not observe the vow of Ekādaśī, there is no liberation whatsoever, indeed, not at all.
(74) Even those of wicked conduct, the most sinful, and those devoid of dharma—who do not eat on Ekādaśī—do not go to the presence of Yama. (75)
"Those who eat food on the eleventh day go to the abode of Yama. Having heard those words, Kratu trembled within his lotus-heart and spoke to Nara and Nārāyaṇa regarding that great feast.
"O Blessed One, I am truly unable [to endure it]; my hunger is unbearable.
If I do not obtain food in the morning, death would occur at midday.
Indeed, I am not capable of withstanding hunger for five periods of time. (77–78)
In the morning I eat with the gods as my mouth; in the forenoon, with fire as my mouth; at midday and in the afternoon, with guests and mendicants facing me;
in the evening, I eat with all beings as my mouth; and at night, with all things mobile and immobile.
"Indeed, my food is thus prepared in every way.
Yet, even so, hunger afflicts me at the time of my daily practice;
therefore, I shall give gifts and I shall worship Keśava. (1.251.80–81)
"I shall perform another meritorious deed; I will not observe the fast.
Having said this, he ceased speaking. Then Nārāyaṇa said:
"If heaven is desired by you, and hell is not to be sought by you..."
"One should not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights.
[83] Kratu said to Hari, "O Lord, I speak the truth before you:
I am not able to take even a single meal, so how could I be capable of fasting? [84]
O Lord of Lakṣmī! I am truly named Kṛtu by name alone; yet the seven-tongued fire within my belly, which consumes, is called Kro.
That great fire is cruel (krūra), and my eating is excessive (ativela). 85.
When I eat very fatty food, then that [pain] is also pacified.
But if all of you were to fast, I would die without a doubt.
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, show me mercy so that I may be able to perform [the vow].
"By whatever means heaven is attained, that I shall perform at your command;
and tell me that one thing by which liberation may also be achieved for my sake—that which I may easily accomplish so that I might attain the highest good. (88)
Having heard him, the compassionate Nārāyaṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees,
reflected and spoke what was appropriate for those of such a nature:
"When the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) occurs while the sun is situated in Taurus or Gemini," || 1.251.90 ||
Having observed this fast with great effort during the month of Jyeṣṭha while abstaining from water—
avoiding even water for rinsing the mouth and sipping, and consuming nothing but [other] liquids— she has truly performed the "Waterless Fast" (Nirjalā). 91.

If water is swallowed during a waterless [Ekādaśī], the vow becomes deficient in its power. By avoiding water from sunrise until sunrise, the observer of the vow obtains the fruit arising from fasting on both the eleventh and twelfth lunar days. || 92-93 ||
Having observed a waterless vow accompanied by the worship of the deity and a night vigil,
and having performed a ritual bath and worship on the morning of the twelfth day,
one should give a water-pot filled with water and gold to a twice-born man.
Having given gifts of food, the observer of the vow should break his fast with his own people.
He should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, girls, and boys;
indeed, the observer of the vow shall obtain the fruit of eleven years of Ekādaśī observances.
Abandoning all other doctrines, one should take refuge in me alone;
by fasting on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), one is liberated from all sins.
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight.

Even there, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should remain without water. By fasting on even a single [such] day, one obtains the merit arising from fasting on all the Ekādaśīs of the year, whether they be bright or dark.

This auspicious [vow], when observed as a fast, bestows wealth and grain, grants sons, health, and other blessings, and yields the attainment of whatever one desires in the mind. (1.251.100) The messengers of Yama are massive-bodied, formidable, and have hideous faces.
Indeed, cruel men bearing staffs and nooses do not approach those who observe vows.
But the Vaiṣṇavas— wearing yellow garments, gentle, holding discs in their hands, and possessing the speed of thought— escort him at the end to the city of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Kratu, with every effort you must perform that rite;
my son, carry it out with faith, even though it is waterless and devoid of water.
By this, your intense digestive fire will become established in self-restraint.
It should be performed with enthusiasm and vigilance while abstaining from water.
(104) If, in a dream, the eating of food or the drinking of water occurs, then let there be no fault on my part; let there be no violation of my vow in this matter. (105)
O Lord, let there be no violation of my vow for me even through the fault of sleep;
let there be no violation of my vow for me even on account of drowsiness or laziness. O Lord of Gods, tomorrow I shall eat my meal after the day of Hari has passed.
Having thus entreated Hari-Kṛṣṇa, one should be intent upon fasting.
Whatever has been committed by a woman or a man— even if it were equal to the sins of Mount Meru or Lokāloka— all that goes to ashes through the power of Ekādaśī.
On the day of breaking the fast on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), a water-cow (jaladhenu) should be given as a gift;

Whatever small amount of bathing, giving, recitation, or fire-offering the observer of the vow performs,
all that yields eternal merit through the power of the word of Acyuta.
What other duty is there besides the Waterless Ekādaśī?
Whatever gold, food, or clothing is bestowed upon her,

Whatever merit has been performed by anyone shall all become inexhaustible. Those who, observing their vows, give gifts on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the day of breaking the fast, shall attain the supreme state.
The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, the hater of his guru, and the one who commits sexual misconduct—
these are liberated from their sins if they fast on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī).
O Kratu, listen now to the specific rule regarding the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) when it is observed without water.

Hari himself, who reclines upon the waters, should be worshipped by men and women endowed with faith; likewise, a cow made of water should then be given as a gift. Alternatively, a visible cow, either with her calf or without, should be given, for she shall grant liberation.

The virtuous twice-born, the saintly women, the boys, and the girls should be gratified with excellent sacrificial fees, and with various kinds of sweet foods. When they are satisfied, I, Kṛṣṇa— the giver of liberation— am also satisfied.
Those by whom no vow for her has been observed are undoubtedly slayers of their own souls.
Those who eat food on the day of Ekādaśī are indeed consumers of sin; they are evil-minded, of wicked conduct, and plundered—of this there is no doubt. (1.251.119–120)
By those who have observed this fast, remaining peaceful, self-controlled, devoted to charity, worshipping Hari, and keeping a vigil at night— by them, indeed,
a hundred future generations and likewise a hundred past generations of their lineage [are saved].
Together with them, they were led by himself to the palace of Vāsudeva.
There was food, cows, female buffaloes, clothing, beds, seats, water, a staff,
a water-pot, an umbrella, a bowl, gold, sesame seeds, and so forth.
He who gives a pair of sandals or anything else to a worthy recipient is honored in the heavenly world by means of a golden vehicle. Furthermore,
this vow must indeed be performed according to the rule as a fast without water.
On the twelfth day, Trivikrama, the Lord of the gods of gods, is to be worshipped.
Water-pots with sugar should be offered in the presence of Viṣṇu.
Then, having fed the Brahmins, one should personally partake of the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
Thus, he who observes the full Dvādaśī that destroys sins,
being liberated from all evils, goes to the state free from affliction.
Having heard this and having bowed down, Kratu returned to his own hermitage filled with joy.
On the day of the Nirjala Ekādaśī, he performed the vow according to the prescribed rules;
he obtained the full fruit thereof, and so shall anyone else who performs it.
He shall obtain the fruit resulting from the performance of twenty-four Ekādaśīs.
Whoever should hear this with devotion, and whoever should recite it—both of them shall attain heaven; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
