"Vices and sweet drinks must be abandoned"—this is the supreme austerity.
During the Cāturmāsya, the nectar of the feet of the holy ones must be prostrated to, their grace must be drunk, and their prasāda must be eaten; such is the vow. (1.253.90)
Likewise, the honoring of the virtuous, the true, and the noble,
as well as massaging their feet and carrying them on one’s own body, is a vow that grants liberation.
[This should be done] with body, mind, speech, wealth, food, and clothing.
To please the son together with his beloved wife is indeed a great vow.
Constantly seeing, touching, bowing to, serving at the feet of, honoring, and feeding the virtuous one—that is the great vow of pleasing him. (92–93)
One should always dwell in the proximity of the virtuous and perform service toward them in matters such as ritual bathing and the practice of knowledge, for holy men are purifiers.
Service to the gods, service to the ancestors, and service to the virtuous constitute the great vow.

The satisfaction of one's wife, service to one's husband, and the vow of pleasing the husband—whosoever gives these things, which are indeed desired, infused with love, their merit shall be inexhaustible; therefore, there is no vow superior to this. (95–96)

Satisfying those who depend on one, bestowing gold, food, and knowledge, granting villages, fields, jewels, gems, gardens, dwellings, and water; and serving constantly with one's own body—this shall be the vow of a sovereign ruler. 97.
Forgiveness, compassion, freedom from malice, absence of envy, and the avoidance of faults;
(98) appreciating the virtues of others, performing deeds that bring fame and renown—these constitute supreme austerity.
Humility, bestowing honor upon others, and perceiving the Self as equal [to all]—(99)
Neither heat when it is contrary, nor cold even when it is favorable;
the abandonment of joy, resentment, fear, and agitation is the supreme austerity.
Fruits, grain, leaves, petals, flowers, husks, grass, and so forth—
A great and perpetual vow is that which must be offered daily to Śrī Hari.
Wood, dried cow-dung, branches, twigs, stalks, and baskets—these auspicious items should be offered every day according to what is appropriate for the vow. (101–102)
Vegetables, well-prepared sweet foods, salt, ginger, and *dhānaka* (fried grain), as well as parched rice and other such items, should be offered daily; that indeed is the vow.
Edibles, drinks, chewables, meals, suckables, savory foods, and things to be licked [should likewise be provided].
Milk, curd, sweet juice, and long pepper should be offered; this is a great vow.
(10.4) Clothing, ornaments, collyrium, sandalwood, excellent and superior food, musk, saffron, powder, and red lac should be given; this is the vow. (10.5)
These vows indeed bestow heaven here and grant happiness;
they consist of the remembrance, devotion, worship, and offering to Śrī Hari.
Worship with the thirty-two modes of service is a vow that grants liberation.
Benefiting others with a pure mind is a vow that bestows merit;
performing various sacrifices, assisting the poor, digging wells, and planting trees—these too are that vow. (107–108)
The construction of roads, the establishment of hermitages and dwellings,
the building of shelters, sacrificial halls, and so forth, as well as the vow that grants heaven;
the instruction in the arts and crafts, and likewise the promotion of agriculture.
The operation of mechanical devices and similar acts constitute a vow that bestows heaven and happiness.
(1.253.110) The constant offering of flour to fish, ants, and other creatures; the watering of trees; and the giving of water to the thirsty—these are likewise vows. (1.253.111)

Giving food to the hungry, bestowing clothing upon the naked, and alleviating the various afflictions of those in distress— this is the vow. Giving medicine to the sick and providing the means of livelihood is the gift of sustenance.
Nourishing, protecting, and guarding [others] is the supreme vow.
(113) Constant practice of spiritual yoga, the study of the scriptures, and listening to the stories of Kṛṣṇa are the supreme vows that grant liberation. (114)
Prostrations like a staff and circumambulation are that vow;
the offering of lamps, the offering of water, and the presentation of food offerings and the like are the vow. 115.
Constantly offering fruits, offering grains, and also offering liquids [is the vow].
The offering of sugar-candies, molasses, honey, and so forth is a vow.
Cleansing, smearing, making bright, and bathing are vows;
as are the washing of vessels and garments, and the offering of the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*).
Drinking from the eyes of the embodied form, moving the water-stalls, pavilions, and so forth, and the construction of temples, excellent palaces, and the like, is the supreme vow.
Weaving [images] of paintings and other such works for the sake of the Blessed One by means of craftsmanship and the like [is also part of it]. (118)
Compilation is the composition of books and the description of meters, verses, and so forth.
Exposition is the narration of the vow that fulfills the desires of devotees;
it bestows happiness, grants heaven, and bestows liberation, for such service is itself a vow. (1.253.119–120)
I shall describe other vows; listen, Lakṣmī, to those very penances!
During the Cāturmāsya, sacred stories should be heard and virtuous people should be fed.
A great worship must be performed daily; these three vows grant excellent success.

The great vow is that the grand worship (mahāpūjā) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa must be performed daily. Reciting my name on a rosary one hundred times or more, the worship of devotees, the offering of oblations (havirhoma), and service to the deity—this vow bestows liberation. || 122–123 ||

The abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine," the strict observance of celibacy, and the avoidance of milk-rice, sugarcane products, salt, and oil-cakes constitute the vow. That which is the dharma associated with Kṛṣṇa is considered by me to be the supreme non-vow.

That vow by which the Blessed One and likewise the people would be pleased through its performance is declared to be a true vow; indeed, that alone should be performed. Now, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika, there is the worship of the Deity.
Having performed this offering before the Blessed One with a spirit of devotion:
"O Lord, O Master, this vow has been performed by me for your pleasure.
May whatever was deficient reach completion; through this, may you be pleased with me. (127)
Having thus completed the observances, one should then perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
Morning ablutions, worship of the deity, the daily salutation of elders, and the providing of food and other necessities after sharing with those who depend on one—these are the duties. (128–129)
Free from affliction, well-integrated, and possessing great affection for his family— he whose home is sweet and pleasant has heaven upon this very earth.
Among all vows, that which is most highly desired during the Cāturmāsya period is this vow.
That [service] must be performed in every way, beginning from the time of his lying down until dawn.
At midday, one should offer food and excellent water to Hari;
likewise, one should perform the same at evening, offering betel leaf and sweet drinks. (131–132)
One should perform the *ārārtrika* offering, hymns of praise, and the ritual of mounting the swing (*dolārohaṇa*).
There, one should cause Hari to sway on the swing and feed him milk-filled pastries (*pūrikā*).
At night, one should keep a vigil with the nectar of dance, song, and sacred narratives.
On the twelfth day, at the hour of Brahma, having bathed, one should perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
One should give gifts, primarily of gold, and break the fast. Being endowed with humility, one should feed the virtuous and satisfy them.
"In this manner, on the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, this auspicious vow, accompanied by its observances, should be performed;
it yields the fruit of all sacrifices and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(136) Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Āṣāḍha-Śukla-Śayanī-Ekādaśī Vow, the Sleeping of the Lord as Vāmana, and the Virtuous Vows of Restraint, Discipline, Self-Control, Subduing, Austerity, Emaciation, Renunciation, Service, Giving, and Beneficence during the Cāturmāsya," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-Santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 253: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 254 [Author: Chapter 255 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said: Through union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa Hari, everything becomes devoid of qualities (nirguṇa);
it bestows heaven, it bestows liberation, and it even grants the form of the four-armed Lord.
Whatever action is performed— whether it be for the sake of a desired fruit or free from the desire for results—
if it is done for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa, all of that indeed bestows Goloka. That alone is the true vow, that the beautiful ritual, that the true dharma, and that the true worship.
That by which the Lord Harikṛṣṇa, the master of the virtuous, may be pleased— namely,
that Cāturmāsya vow by which Mādhava is satisfied,
as well as those restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) by which Adhokṣaja is indeed gratified. (3–4)
"Tell me, O Lord: what is the name of the Ekādaśī considered to fall in the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa?
Who is its presiding deity, what is its ritual procedure, and what is its merit? Please tell me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I shall speak further to you:
the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa is known by the name Kāmikā.
On that day, Acyuta, joined with Vijayā, should be worshipped with devotion.
Among flowers, the *pārijāta* is considered best; for the *arghya*, the *bilva* fruit is prescribed.

For the food offering (*naivedya*), items such as the hundred-holed coconut are recommended. A practitioner of vows should give all these—both garments for men and women—as gifts that produce love for Acyuta.
Neither at the Gaṅgā, nor at Kāśī, nor at Naimiṣa, nor indeed at Puṣkara,
is that true fruit obtained which is truly gained from the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
[This is so] at the Godāvarī, when Jupiter is in Leo, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and at Daṇḍaka.
Whatever fruit is obtained from that, a superior fruit is said [to result from this].
(1.254.10) He who gives away the earth together with its oceans and forests, while observing the Kāmika vow, enjoys a fruit even greater than that. (11)
He who gives a cow with its accessories, specifically one that is "two-faced" (ubhayatomukhī),
obtains a fruit even greater than that of the Kāmikā vow.
The devotee who worships Śrīdhara-Kṛṣṇa during the month of Śrāvaṇa—
By him the gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Pannagas were fully honored.
For those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, there exists this supreme vow of Kāmika—
a boat fashioned by Hari that enables one to reach the further shore.
Indeed, the fruit obtainable through the science of the self is attained by means of the Kāmika vow.
Having performed this vow along with the night vigil, one never goes to an evil state of existence.
One does not behold the fierce Yama, nor does one ever find birth in a wretched womb.
By the merit of the Kāmika vow, yogins attained absolute liberation (kaivalya).
That person who worships Hari with leaves produced from the Tulasī plant is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
One bhāra of gold and four times that amount of silver are offered;
the attainment of the fruit thereof comes from worshipping with *tulasī* leaves.
When he is worshipped with red pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, and other such gems, [the merit is likewise attained].
Kṛṣṇa is not so pleased by anything else as he is by the leaves of the tulasī plant.
By whomsoever Mādhava is worshipped with the blossoms of the tulasī,
his sins accumulated over many lifetimes are indeed brought to complete destruction.
When seen, she pacifies evil; when touched, she purifies the body;
when praised, she dispels disease; when sprinkled with water, she wards off death;
and when planted, she brings about proximity to the feet of Kṛṣṇa. (21)
"Salutations again and again to that Tulasī, who, when offered, bestows the fruit of liberation.
Having spoken thus, one should offer the Tulasī to the Supreme Lord, the God.
He before whom a lamp burns on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) in the presence of Kṛṣṇa— [attains the highest state].
His ancestors, dwelling in heaven, are indeed satisfied by that nectar.
On the day of Hari, a lamp offering should indeed be made upon the peak;
even Viṣṇu himself does not fully know the measure of its merit.
Indeed, a lamp of ghee or sesame oil should be offered within the temple.
The donor goes to the celestial realm, blazing with hundreds of millions of lamps.
This act removes the sin of killing a Brahmin and bestows the fruit of great merit.
O beloved, the Ekādaśī that bestows the station of the third heaven, destroys sins such as the killing of a fetus, and fulfills all desires must be observed with faith; indeed,
the performer of the vow becomes sanctified when endowed with devotion.

He attains the world of Viṣṇu and enjoys eternal happiness. (28) On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should eat only once, sleep on the ground at night, remain celibate, and rise early in the morning. (29)
Having bathed and performed the daily worship, one should have an auspicious pavilion constructed;
thereafter, one should have the Sarvatobhadra mandala made with grains.
Then, [one should place] the golden image of Acyuta together with Vijayā.
One should worship there with devotion according to the prescribed rite, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth.
Then one should bathe the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and water, and subsequently purify it.
One should then adorn the deity with garments, ornaments, and the splendors of various decorations.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a sesame tray, one should set the tray atop a water-pot (ghaṭa),
provided with the five jewels, auspicious sprouts, fruits, and water.
One should feed [the recipient] with various kinds of food and offer betel leaves and other such items.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), offer hymns of praise, circumambulations, and salutations with joined palms.
One should pray to Hari, saying: "May my vow be free from obstacles.
At midday as well, the observer of the vow should gratify Acyuta with most delicious foods.
In the evening as well, the observer of the vow should likewise perform the great worship and other rites;
he should feed [the deity], worship, swing the limbs, and massage them.
And on the twelfth day, he should indeed keep a vigil in the very early morning.
Having bathed and performed worship, one should indeed give various gifts;
then, having fed virtuous women and children, one should break the fast.
Thus is the Sukāmikā-vrata, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
One desiring wealth obtains wealth; one desiring a son obtains a son;
one desiring a wife shall obtain a wife; and one who desires a husband shall obtain a husband.
One who desires the prosperity of house, field, cattle, and grain shall indeed obtain those.
One who desires fame, health, great honor, sovereignty, or power shall obtain those; 2.254.40.
One who desires dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa shall acquire them by performing this vow;
one who desires the destruction of enemies, calamities, obstacles, or diseases shall attain their destruction. 41.
Thus, this supreme Kāmika vow bestows everything;
it indeed grants heaven, it grants truth, and likewise grants the world of Virāja.
This vow grants Goloka and is the supreme bestower of the Imperishable.
Listen now to her ancient narrative, which bestows all accomplishments.
Formerly, the Śravaṇas were Pitṛs born into the lineage of Dharmarāja;
they were appointed by Dharma to bring back reports concerning the conduct of living beings.
Wherever they go to bring back news of living beings, they neither hear nor see anything; their action is subtler than the subtlest.
They do not even know the events—how then could they possibly bring them back?
"How could we report this to Yama if we were ignorant of it?"—
thinking thus, they all gathered together and spoke to Yama:
"Just as we know everything regarding those who have performed subtle deeds, so [should you inform him]."
O Dharmarāja, please ordain this: we know what the karma of living beings is.
We are twelve in number, yet there are countless millions of living beings.
How and where could our pervasion occur without [the attainment of] perfection?
"Therefore, grant us success, or else reveal that penance by which we may indeed possess all the powers of expression in your presence.
Having heard them, Yama said: "Practice the Kāmika vow."
In the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, that Ekādaśī is considered Kāmikā;
it brings about the complete fulfillment of all desires and bestows sovereign power.
Having heard the injunction for the vow of Kāmikā, [one should then observe] Śravaṇā.
They observed their vows for Kāmikā and gave abundant gifts.
On the twelfth day, at the time of breaking the fast, the pleased Dharmarāja himself arrived, having become a guest in the form of a brāhmaṇa. (52–53)
Having clearly uttered, "Give alms," he stood upon the ground of the courtyard;
with great devotion, he accepted the alms offered by the ears.
"O Kṣatriyas, choose a boon; I am pleased with your vow."
Thus spoke Dharmadeva himself, the progenitor of Acyuta, to them.
They said to him: "The Śravaṇas indeed declare that [the soul] possesses subtle karma among living beings;
grant us such omniscience as we may thereby understand this. (55–56)
Furthermore, there is the power of hearing from afar and the power of seeing from afar;
likewise, the knowledge of secret actions, the assumption of many forms, and pervasiveness among living beings situated in all places and so forth. (57)
"Grant to all of us, in every way, the supreme power of omniscience and that eternal memory which perceives things exactly as they are. Having heard this, Dharmarāja then spoke to them.

"The vow of the *Kāmikā* has been performed by you, and its fruit is great. Since I have been obtained— bestowing all desired things and consisting of all perfections— I shall grant you all perfections, so that you may become [as I am]."
"May all knowledge arising from the life-stories of all living beings at all times reside within you alone, just as it does in the Lord. Having thus granted this supreme boon, Dharmarāja vanished.
From that time on, twelve Śravaṇas always appeared;
assuming countless forms, they reported the deeds of living beings and stood perpetually before Citragupta as if they were omniscient.
They report the news of those who have died and gone before;
having attained the fruit of all desires through the Kāmikā vow,
that vow which bestows all perfections should therefore be performed by people.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another story concerning Rati as it occurred in the past:
when Kāmadeva was consumed by Śaṅkara on Mount Himālaya, Rati, the wife of Kāma, became a widow, deprived of her husband. (66)
Greatly afflicted and excessively emaciated by the pain of widowhood, she went to Śaṅkara and said: "O Lord, show mercy!
Without my husband, I have encountered this inauspiciousness that brings only suffering. (67-68)
"Therefore, O Śambhu, destroy my affliction and grant well-being to me, a woman.
Having heard her, Śambhu said: "Perform the vow of Kāmikā;
then misfortune will certainly depart far from you forever. (69)
"Though bodiless, your husband shall indeed meet you at the place of delight.
All your misfortune and ill-fortune shall come to an end.
Then your husband will be the son of Kṛṣṇa, named Pradyumna."
"You shall indeed obtain one with a beautiful body and great good fortune.
Having heard this, Rati joyfully undertook the vow of Kāmikā;
and according to the prescribed rites, she gave all manner of gifts with great devotion.
But at the time for breaking the fast, Śambhu, having indeed become a mendicant, arrived for the sake of alms; she offered him the alms-food.
Having eaten, Śambhu then said: "Ask for a boon; I shall grant it."
"By virtue of the vow of Kāmikā, I, Śaṅkara himself, am pleased.
Having heard this, Rati then said to her husband Kāma, "Grant it to me.
Having uttered the words, "So be it," Śaṅkara then became invisible.
Through his own passion (*rati*), he obtained a husband for her at the proper time and in the right place.
In every being, in every womb, he obtained a husband during sexual union.
Thereupon, the son of Kṛṣṇa, though embodied as the one named Pradyumna, was also obtained.
Thus, by the power of her vow, Rati attained auspicious fortune;
she pervaded all living beings in the universe and achieved eternal perfection.
Indeed, such is the vow of Kāmikā, which fulfills all desires.
It bestows the fulfillment of all intentions, grants all prosperity, destroys all suffering, is gentle, and bestows both heaven and liberation;
it is auspicious, the giver of the fruit of all sacrifices, and likewise the bringer of yogic perfections. (2.254.80)
It bestows lost objects and grants great, eternal sovereignty;
it bestows pleasure, fulfills desires, and likewise grants a wife and a husband.
It destroys suffering, pacifies affliction, and grants the happiness of sensual enjoyment.

O Lakṣmī! This [rite] must be performed in every way; it destroys obstacles, fulfills the desires of men and women, and is supreme in bestowing non-widowhood. It grants success in sexual power, the power of passion, and desire, and is thus called "Kāmya" (the desirable). 82–83.
"But for those free from desire, it is a vessel of merit that leads to Vaikuṇṭha;
even by hearing it, one receives the merit of a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Kāmika-Ekādaśī in the Dark Half of Śrāvaṇa, the Attainment of All Siddhis by the Pitṛs known as Śravaṇas, and the Attainment of Her Husband named Kāma by Ratī," in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 254: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 255 [Author: Chapter 256 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Nārāyaṇa himself, is the bestower of all desires;
he is indeed the giver of fruits, the giver of happiness, and the one who fulfills the vow.
Through faith merit is attained; he who is always established in faith, Viṣṇu, when accompanied by meditative cultivation and supported by vows, surely bears fruit.
Mādhava, the God who bestows liberation, dwells permanently within the means of accomplishment.
Indeed, without Him, those means of accomplishment never yield any fruit whatsoever.
That very Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Hari—the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of Ramā, the Lord of Śrī, whose hands bear the banner and the bow—is to be propitiated in every way. (3–4)
"Out of compassion, tell me, O Lord whose hands bear the marks of the fish and the svastika;
O Maṇikīśvara, Lord of Pārvatī, what is the name of the eleventh day (ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa? (5)
"What is the procedure for it, what is its fruit, and which deity is to be worshipped in this vow?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "The Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa is known as Putradā."
The Lord Śrīdhara, together with Kāntimatī, is to be worshipped here.
He is to be worshipped with lotuses and fed with cakes;
Kṛṣṇa is to be offered an *arghya* with *sītāphala* fruits, and a pair of sandals is to be presented.
The gift of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* is considered auspicious;
its divine narrative, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, should be heard.
On the tenth day, one should eat only once and likewise observe celibacy.
On the morning of the eleventh day, the observer of the vow should sleep on the ground at night.
Having bathed and performed his daily rites, he should perform a great worship within the pavilion,
where a golden jar has been placed upon a *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
Having placed a vessel of sesame seeds accompanied by the five jewels, garments, water, leaves, unbroken rice, and fruit, one should then install Śrīdhara.
One should worship him with total devotion using the sixteen auspicious articles.
One should perform the invocation and other rites, as well as the consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).

[One should worship] with garments, ornaments, cosmetics, collyrium, sandalwood paste, and unguents; with flower garlands, unbroken rice grains, aromatic powders, fruits, betel leaves, and food offerings.

Having worshipped Hari with the *ārārtika* offering, hymns of praise, prostrations like a staff, circumambulations, and the lighting of lamps, one should then pray for the vow to be free from obstacles.
At midday, one should offer food, betel leaf, and likewise water.
In the evening, one should offer milk-preparations, fried cakes (pūrikās), and vegetables.
At night, one should keep a vigil with storytelling, chanting the Lord’s glories, and dancing.
Then, on the twelfth day, having bathed at dawn and worshipped Mādhava, [one should proceed].
One should give all kinds of gifts according to one's capacity and according to one's wealth;
one should feed virtuous brāhmaṇas, virtuous women, boys, and girls.
Then, having fed one's own kinsmen, one should personally perform the breaking of the fast.
Thus performed, this merit shall grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation as desired.
Furthermore, the observer of the vow obtains auspicious wealth, grain, sons, wives, fields, gardens, houses, and so forth, as well as health, honor, and fame. (1.255.20)
Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear this divine story that occurred in the ancient Kṛta Yuga.
There was a king named Purūravas, the grandson of the Moon.
Purūravas, the son of Budha, ruled over his own kingdom.
He lived continuously in Śrīpurī on the banks of the Narmadā.
Having heard of his virtues from the mouth of the gods, the celestial nymph Urvaśī, a most excellent woman,
came there in person and presented herself as his wife.
Even after a long time had passed, no offspring was born to her.
For him who was thus deprived of a son, that kingdom did not bring happiness.
In this world and in the next, there is no happiness for one who has no son.
As he was thinking thus, a great deal of time passed.
Yet the king did not obtain a son, and so he lived in sorrow rather than happiness. He summoned the wise elders of his own kingdom and informed them of that matter. (25–26)
"O Brahmins, in this life no sin has been committed by me;
nor have I placed wealth acquired through unjust means into the treasury.
Furthermore, the property of Brahmins, the property of the gods, and the belongings of widows, the helpless, and the destitute [have not been misappropriated]. (27)

Furthermore, I have never taken what was not given; on the contrary, I have always protected the people like my own sons, and the subjects have been guarded according to the Dharma. The earth has been conquered through battle, and punishment has been inflicted upon the wicked. (28–29)
No injustice was committed toward them—toward your sons, kinsmen, and subjects;
those worthy of honor were always well-honored, and the elders were constantly saluted.
Those established on the path of justice were never hated, and the deities were always worshipped.
Brahmins, virtuous men, virtuous women, cows, and the distressed were honored;
sacrifices of material goods and sacrifices of knowledge were performed through association with the learned. Nevertheless, no son has been born in my house—let this be reflected upon.
Having heard these words, the twice-born, together with the elders and the family priests,
desiring the welfare of the king, went to the sage Lomaśa—
[the sage] of whom a single hair falls away at the passing of every kalpa.
Thus he became renowned by the name Lomaśa through common usage.
He was performing terrible austerities, fasting, and free from worldly effort;
he was peaceful, a knower of the truth of the excellent Dharma, and proficient in the scriptures and the Vedas.
Seeing that long-lived, great-souled sage— knower of the three times, beautifully adorned with matted hair and beard— the twice-born considered their own fortune to be most excellent.
Having bowed to the sage, whose self is Brahman, they stood before him filled with joy.
Seeing them thus with their elder brother, the sage Lomaśa spoke:
"O Brahmins who serve the elders, why have you come? Is there something to be accomplished—whether great, small, possible, or even impossible? (37–38)
"Whether it be obtainable or even unobtainable, I shall do it for the sake of the Brahmins. Tell me without hesitation; I will accomplish your welfare.
The word of the Brahmins is the Veda; it is the command of the Supreme Lord."
"By honoring your word, I shall indeed attain the fruit of my birth.
There is no doubt that the birth of ascetics is for the sake of benefiting others;
oh, today I shall make my birth fruitful by serving these brahmins."
Having thought thus, he performed hospitality, worship, and so forth;
he gave water, fruits, seats, and other offerings, for even the one worthy of worship acts as a guest to his guests.
Then the brahmins said to him, "Let our heart's desire be heard."

O Lord, we have come here into your presence for the sake of our own purpose, in order to dispel our doubts. By the mere sight of the virtuous, the hoard of sins accumulated in previous lives is destroyed. (43–44)
It is reduced to ashes instantly; how much more so through the service of your feet!
Apart from the Lotus-born Brahmā, no one else is found to be superior to you.
You are all-knowing, you have existed for many kalpas, you are a knower of much, and you possess meditative absorption.
O Sage, by the power of your asceticism, you know much of what has been, what is to be, and what is currently being born;
by the power of the identity of Brahman and the Self, you are capable of granting everything.
King Purūravas, however, is currently without a son.
We Brahmins have always been protected by him like his own children;
yet, seeing him bereft of a son, we are pained by his sorrow.
We [seek refuge] at the feet of you, who bring about deliverance from suffering.
"O Queen, we have come here into the shade; let what is appropriate be done.
For it is by his good fortune that you have been seen by us, O ascetic;
indeed, the accomplishment of men's purposes occurs simply through the sight of the great."
"Tell us, why is there no son, or by what means might one be obtained?
Having heard these words of theirs, Lomaśa entered into meditation for a moment and then replied to them regarding the king's previous birth.
In a previous birth, he was a wealthy Vaiśya named Vardhamāna.
Devoted to the business of trade, he caused the depletion of people through greed; desiring to deal in goods, he traveled from village to village. (52–53)
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
at midday while the heat was intense, he reached a reservoir of water on the outskirts of the village;
it was a single, dug-out pool, beautiful with its solitary descent into the water.
Having gone there to that landing-place, he sat down for a moment; then,
at the very instant he was washing his hands, feet, and face,
a cow accompanied by her calf arrived there, distressed by thirst.
Afflicted by the heat and filled with fear, she quickly descended into the landing-place;
but having stopped her after she had drunk only a mouthful, the dark one (Tāmasa) bathed himself,
drank the water, and performed the washing of his clothes.
Having stayed there for a long time, he did not give water to drink while searching for the path. That thirsty cow, along with her calf, waited for a long time on the path;
nevertheless, the wealthy man indeed did not leave that spot for eight *ghaṭikās*.
The thirsty calf said to its mother, "O Mother!
My life-breaths are departing from the pain of thirst; when will this [thirst] depart?
The cow-mother said to that calf, "This [thirst] will depart in a moment."
"Maintain your composure for now; we shall drink water in a moment.
But the wealthy man did not depart from there, and even the calf's throat became parched.
Then the cow said, "This wicked one will certainly not leave."
"The life-breaths are departing from my daughter; I shall surely drink the water by force.
Having thus resolved, the cow took her own calf and descended [into the water].
But Vardhamāna Dhanin struck her violently with a staff.
Then the cow cursed him: "O wicked merchant! You strike me in vain.
May you indeed remain childless throughout birth after birth;
may you live in the forest, separated from your wife, and suffer in many ways. (64–65)
Having cursed him and forcefully struck him with her two hooves and two horns, the cow drove the wealthy man far away; then, with composure, she drank the excellent water.
The calf drank the water peacefully, and the merchant then departed from that place.
Struck by a cow and overcome with pain, he reached the village and died.
Before his death, he had given all his wealth for the sake of a sacrifice;
the Brahmins performed the sacrifice, and by that merit, Vardhana [was restored].
This king born here is named Purūravas;
due to the curse of a cow, he is childless and devoid of the fortune of having sons.
Indeed, by virtue of that curse, he shall have no son throughout his successive births.
"In time, he shall also suffer separation from his wife.
Hearing this, the brahmins said: "The destruction of his sin shall come through merit, and the warding off of the curse as well, through the grace of one such as you."
"There is nothing whatsoever that is impossible for you; let there be a son for the king.
Instruct us in meritorious deeds, and the king will certainly perform them.
Lomaśa, having reflected upon their powerful vow, spoke to them all.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, there is the renowned Ekādaśī known as Putradā, which bestows one's desires; O twice-born ones, perform that vow!
Let the king, the queen, and you all likewise observe the vow with devotion. (73–74)
If Purūravas makes the gift of a hundred thousand cows on the morning of the day his son is born,
then a son will be born.
When the vow is completed and the gift of a hundred thousand cows is made, an incomparable son shall be born.
"By my word alone, the king shall surely do what you desire.
Having placed this command upon their heads, the twice-born went to Śrīnagara;
there, together with the king, they performed the vow according to the rules, including the ritual vigil.
Then she gave a gift of a hundred thousand cows to worthy recipients.
By that merit, the queen conceived a beautiful fetus.
However, previously, when she had returned from heaven for the sake of her husband—
At that time, she had made an agreement for her long-term stay:
"Upon seeing the king naked, I shall depart from this house.
Then, on this occasion during the night, having seen the king unclothed— || 1.255.80 ||

She departed for the forest, and Purūravas followed after her. While she was pregnant in the wilderness, she took the form of a fire-vessel and gave birth to a noble son, Vibhāvasu, who is indeed Jātavedas.
By means of this Ekādaśī vow alone, Vahni became his son.
Indeed, there were six other Ekādaśīs that likewise granted him sons;
for every vow, he performed the gift of a hundred thousand cows.
From him, through Urvaśī, there were six other sons born of her womb:
Āyu, Śrutāyu, Satyāyu, Raya, Vijaya, and Jaya.
Their sons and grandsons increased the lineage.

Through his fire and his progeny, the king attained the world of the Gandharvas. (85) Having enjoyed manifold pleasures and eventually cast off his body at the appointed time, he departed from heaven to Vaikuṇṭha himself, assuming a four-armed form. (86)
Listen, Lakṣmī! If one desires infinite golden ornaments and sovereignty, he must perform this supreme vow preceded by the gift of a cow.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun is situated in Cancer—
On the twelfth day, one should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) to Vāsudeva,
using threads made of linen, gold, silver, copper, silk, lotus fibers, *kuśa* grass, *kāśa* grass, fine cotton, hemp, or other such beautiful materials.

Having tripled that thread by means of three strands, one should purify it so that it appears like a beautiful jewel; for that indeed makes it sacred. One should then offer that purifying thread, which bestows the merit of gold, to Hari.
On the eleventh day, one should wear [the sacred thread] and perform a vigil at night.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, as well as Śūdras, men, and women—
all who are established in devotion to Hari should perform the auspicious *pavitraka* rite.
One should offer [the thread] to Hari and also dedicate it to the Guru.
Through the rite of *pavitrāropaṇa*, I become truly purified.
One should likewise acquire ornaments such as gold, silver, and silken garments.

Every year, people should perform the *pavitrāropaṇa* (the rite of offering the sacred thread) for their sons and heirs with the prescribed mantra; by this, one becomes wealthy. Furthermore, through the *pavitrāropaṇa*, one attains both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).
But for him who does not perform the Pavitrāropaṇa according to the prescribed rite,
the worship performed throughout the year becomes fruitless.
Having heard the greatness of the Putrapradā [rite], one is liberated from sin.
"Having attained the supreme heaven of bliss, one shall obtain the highest liberation.

(97) Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Śrāvaṇa-Śukla-Putradā-Ekādaśī Vow, the Acquisition of a Son by Purūravas—who was childless in a previous birth as a merchant guilty of offenses against cows—through the performance of this vow, the obtaining of a son from Urvaśī, the Pavitrāropaṇa ceremony, and so forth," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
