Chapter 257 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said: By the remembrance of Nārāyaṇa, the bondage of birth and worldly existence is surely destroyed for people; I indeed bow to that Nārāyaṇa. (1)

I bow to Lord Hari, the master, the all-pervading sovereign, the agent, the instrument, the effect, the impeller, the giver of happiness, the giver of sons, and the bestower of peace. O Nārāyaṇa, O Hare, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Consort of Ramā!
O Māṇikyeśa, O Prabhāsvāmin, O Pārvatīśvara, salutations to you!
(3) No satiety indeed arises for me from hearing stories from your mouth;
tell me, which Ekādaśī is recognized as occurring in the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada? (4)
"Who is the deity? What is the fruit of the gift? What flowers and other items are to be offered?
What is the procedure for that vow? O Lord, tell me this in detail.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen with a focused mind, O Lakṣmī! I shall describe it in detail:
the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada is called Ajā; it is the destroyer of sins. On that day, Lord Janārdana should be worshipped together with Sundarī.
Among flowers, the *pāṭalā* should be offered; for the *arghya*, the betel nut (*pūgīphala*) is considered appropriate.
For the gift (*dāna*), a buffalo should be given; for the food offering (*naivedya*), sweetmeats with molasses (*gūḍalaḍḍuka*).
One should act especially according to the season and according to what is available.
On the tenth day, one who seeks the vow should likewise eat but a single meal;
he should sleep upon the ground and must indeed preserve his Brahmanical conduct.
On the morning of the eleventh day, having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa and Janārdana, [he should proceed].
Having bathed, one should perform the daily worship with the sixteen articles.
The observer of the vow should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, adorned with many pillars,
and in its center, he should have a *sarvatobhadra* mandala prepared.
In the center of that [mandala], a golden pitcher filled with water containing the five jewels should be placed;
it should be provided with cloth, fruit, leaves, a sacred thread, sandalwood, and rice.
Beside it, one should also place a bell and a conch shell, and keep them protected.
One should worship according to the prescribed rites with mantras and place a vessel of sesame seeds in a jar.
Then, one should install an image of Janārdana together with Sundarī made of gold, or an eleven-faced image of Brahmā (Aja) made of silver, within that vessel. (13–14)

One should worship and massage the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), scented oils, and liquified sandalwood; one should bathe the deity with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha). Then, one should adorn the deity with garments, ornaments, cosmetics, jewelry, necklaces, and other royal regalia.
With the finest fragrant substances, with offerings of incense and lamps,
with the exquisite scents of liquid *kuṅkuma*, *aguru*, and musk, and with collyrium,
white and pale powders, crest-ornaments, and head-cloths. (16–17)

With staffs, sandals, umbrellas, chowries, vehicles, and mounts; with the waving of lamps, hymns of praise, prostrations, and gestures like a staff; with handfuls of flowers, water, betel, cardamom, and the chewing of cloves. (18–19)
One should worship the God with many dispositions through requests for forgiveness and other such acts.
(19) One should offer to the God a golden bed provided with excellent, soft coverings, and equipped with a mirror, a side-table, and a fan. (20)
Having thus worshipped Govinda, the observer of the vow should pray for the sake of the observance:
"O Kṛṣṇa, I perform this goat-vow; may it proceed without obstacle and reach completion.
(21) He should give various gifts consisting of excellent gems and refined gold.
One should also give auspicious gifts such as cows, buffaloes, and other animals that yield milk.
(22) Having worshipped Lord Hari-Kṛṣṇa even at midday, one should offer him the auspicious *mohana-sthāla* (the vessel of enchantment), pearls, and powdered sweetmeats (*cūrṇa-modaka*). (23)
Apūpas and likewise pūpas, polikās and sweet polikās, pūrikās, puṣpavaṭikās, and even rājikārāddha;
various kinds of vegetables and delicious āranālas. (24)
One should offer curds, milk, and the finest essences of all flavors;
likewise, one should give fruits, water, and mouth-fresheners.
In the evening, the observer of the vow should properly perform a grand worship.
Having tied Hari to a swing made from a tree or suspended in the air, one should swing Him.

At night, one should offer food consisting primarily of milk, which bestows strength. Likewise, one should perform the waving of lights (ārārtika), hymns of praise, a prayer for forgiveness, and the offering of handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
One should offer whatever is appropriate for another and whatever is required by Hari.
At night, one should keep vigil with dancing, singing, recitation, devotion to the glories and names of Hari, listening to sacred narratives, and playful pastimes.
Having bathed at dawn on the twelfth day and having worshipped Janārdana,
one should feed Hari and give various kinds of gifts. Having fed other virtuous twice-born brahmins who have taken refuge [in him] with sweet food, [one should likewise give gifts].
The observer of the vow should later perform the breaking of the fast with children at the conclusion of the superior vow.
When the vow has been performed in this manner, all the desires of the observer shall bear fruit;
whatever he may desire—whether heaven, liberation, or universal sovereignty—the observer of the vow shall attain it.
O Lakṣmī! Those human beings who perform such a vow as this, being liberated from all sins, go to the eternal heaven.
Listen to the auspicious narrative connected with the vow, which brings about the destruction of suffering.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there lived a king named Hariścandra, the lord of the city of Sāketa; he was endowed with the quality of truthfulness and possessed both wife and son. (34–35)

Ruling over the city of Sāketa, which extended five yojanas along the bank of the Sarayū river, the king protected his subjects. He was a universal monarch (cakravartin), true to his word, and the lord of the entire earth. (36)
He honored his guests and gave to them according to their desire. No seeker ever turned away from his house without being properly honored;
whatever a seeker desired, he always gave that very thing.
The Brahmins [were honored] with offerings of sweet food and alms; the Kṣatriyas with marks of great respect;
the Vaiśyas with the acquisition of assistance; and the Śūdras with the gathering at the hermitage.
The gods were honored with sacrificial oblations, and the sages with hospitality.

Sages are honored by him through devotion to Brahman and the like; those with desires, by the attainment of their wished-for objects; women, by the protection of their livelihood and so forth; children, by means of instruction and other forms of delight;
and others, by the fulfillment of whatever they desire—in every way, they are worshipped by him.
All are contented and go to their homes; his subjects live in happiness.
In his kingdom, there is no man lacking wealth or lacking devotion.
There is none who neglects service to the ancestors, nor anyone who shows cruelty toward women.
The sound of the Vedas, the offerings of the sacrifices, and the continuous flow of gifts to supplicants—
all these religious practices ceased not for a moment from the name of Hari.
As he lived in this manner, his fame spread throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions.
He became renowned throughout the three worlds as one who never deviates from the truth.
Then Brahmā, Hari, Śambhu, Viśvāmitra, and others indeed arrived for the purpose of testing him, wondering, "How much truth remains in him? || 45 ||
Hariścandra indeed showed great honor to those who had assumed the forms of brahmins;
he offered them hospitality and service, and announced his desired object. Viśvāmitra then said: "The entire kingdom is required."
"O Great King, let it be given to me; by this I shall be free from debt.
"So be it," the king replied, and having released the water, he then gave it.
Having accepted the kingdom, the sage separately requested a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

The king had no separate wealth for the sake of sacrificial fees; to fulfill that requirement, he was deprived of his kingdom and reduced to the service of others. Having sold his wife and son, he even proceeded to sell himself. (1.256.50)
Having attained the state of a slave to a Pulkasa, that king became a partaker of merit;
by adhering to truth in the cremation ground as a remover of the garments of the dead, he indeed became honored by kings, for he did not waver from the truth. || 5.1 ||
In this manner, many years passed for that king;
yet he continued to give Viśvāmitra his wages as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Nevertheless, the fee required to satisfy the sage was not fully completed.
Whatever clothing or alms-bowl may be obtained, he gives it all as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of fulfillment; yet he himself experiences suffering.
Thus is she fulfilled by the servant engaged in the performance of service.
Even though he received that much as a gift, he still performed service for the sake of his livelihood.
Yet, the end of his suffering did not arrive; consequently, he became consumed by anxiety:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can there be an end to this suffering? (55–56)
My wife is a maidservant in a merchant’s house, my son is a laborer elsewhere, and I am a frequenter of cremation grounds—alas, a servant to a Cāṇḍāla!
Where is the kingdom, and where is this servitude? Indeed, this entire wheel is composed of illusion.
"Nevertheless, I shall indeed exert myself so that there may be the destruction of suffering. While he was thinking thus, submerged in an ocean of sorrow,
the sage arrived there, having learned that the king was afflicted.
A Vaiṣṇava, a worthy recipient for blessings upon the subjects, and one who conducts himself according to justice—
this compassionate man named Gautama, who acts for the benefit of others,
bestowed blessings upon the king, saying, "May you be happy in every way."
Standing with palms joined in reverence, the king bowed to that brahmin.
He related his own story, which was filled with sorrow.
Having heard everything, Gautama became exceedingly astonished.
He taught that vow as the means for crossing over suffering:
"O King, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the dark fortnight, there occurs the exceedingly purifying Ekādaśī known as Ajā, which destroys all misery. (63)
O King, perform a vow for her; the destruction of her suffering will come to pass.
Let your wife also perform a vow that brings happiness for her;
or let your son perform the "one-meal" vow (ekabhukta) for the sake of attaining happiness.
Thus instructed, Hariścandra undertook the supreme vow of the goat;
the sage, having designated his son for that vow, departed for his wife.
The queen and the prince went to their own hermitage as directed.
And they both performed the goat-vow day and night according to their ability.
When that vow was completed, the king’s suffering came to an end in an instant;
and the queen’s and her servant’s suffering also came to an end in an instant.
There, although it was daytime, his son died;
however, by the power of that very vow, Rohita regained life.
That suffering, which would have had to be endured for many years, came to an end through the efficacy of the vow.
By the power of this vow, King Hariścandra was freed from his suffering;
indeed, he regained union with his wife, the life of his son, and union with that son as well. (1.256.70–71)
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Viśvāmitra, and the others, having assumed their own forms, appeared in person to dispel his sorrow.
They said, "Today the test of your truth has been completed."
All the gods and goddesses arrived at that festival for the purpose of bestowing blessings upon King Hariścandra. In heaven, the kettledrums resounded and a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
By the power of Ekādaśī, Hariścandra, together with his sons and his wife,
regained his entire kingdom free from all obstacles;
having enjoyed it for many years, he then performed devotion to Hari.

Having established his son in the kingdom, the dispassionate Hariścandra, together with his wife, his city, and his retinue, attained heaven. Having enjoyed that for an infinite time, he went to the abode of Sāketa.
O Lakṣmī! Those human beings who shall perform such a vow will be liberated from all sins and freed from all suffering;
they shall all go to heaven, to liberation, and to the supreme, highest state.
From reciting or even hearing it, the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice shall be obtained.
Therefore, this story should be heard and the vow should be performed with faith;
likewise, the giving of gifts, worship, and adoration that constitute its limbs should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
The performer of the vow becomes a washer-away of the sins of others;
he is a bringer of heaven and a warder-off of fears such as those from Yama.
How much more so, then, for his own sake, in the attainment of worldly enjoyment and liberation?
And it should be stated that [the practitioner] is capable, by virtue of the context of Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, one who observes this vow is never born again; therefore, she is considered "unborn" (ajā).
Liberation is "unborn," and because of this vow, she indeed becomes that unborn state.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Bhādrapada-Kṛṣṇa-Ajā-Ekādaśī Vow, Viśvāmitra’s Test of Hariścandra’s Truthful Vow, the Loss of Kingdom, Wife, and Son, and the Cessation of Suffering through the Ajā-Vow shown by Gautama," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 257 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) — Chapter 257.
[The Author: Chapter 258.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O remover of suffering, O creator of happiness, O granter of prosperity, O ocean of compassion!

Liberation for sinners certainly does not occur without you. But upon whomsoever you or your devotees bestow your grace, even one who is a great sinner or an extreme transgressor is surely purified; of this there is no doubt.
He who might resort to you out of desire, anger, fear, greed, or even for the sake of gain—
he shall be released from the snares of transmigratory existence and attain liberation.
Vows, sacrifice, compassion, charity, knowledge, meditation, recitation, and austerity—
O Ocean of Compassion, you alone are the one; through your grace, these [days] bestow liberation.
(4) Tell me, what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada?
Who is its presiding deity, what is its ritual procedure, what is its fruit, and how is it to be worshipped? (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada is named Padmā; it bestows liberation.
Here, Ṛṣikeśa is to be worshipped along with Aparājitā.
Kāśa flowers are for worship; *tilapāka* (sesame-cake) is for the offering;
a pumpkin (*kūṣmāṇḍa*) is indeed to be given as the respectful oblation (*arghya*); and for a gift, an auspicious house for a Brāhmaṇa [is recommended].
One should cause a temple, a mansion, or a palatial residence to be built, presided over by Hari.
One should indeed give a beautiful mansion to the preceptor who worships the deity.
(8) On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should subsist on a single meal at night; he should sleep upon the ground and must diligently maintain the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). (9)

This eleventh lunar day, occurring on the side [of the month], is considered sacred to Hari; for on this day, He who lies upon Śeṣa indeed turns over His side. During the Śayanī, Pārśvavartinī, and Prabodhinī days, men [should observe the appropriate rites].
The vow should be observed without food and without water, according to one's capacity.
(41) Here, those pitiless ones who eat food cause me pain in my side;
therefore, no food should be eaten, or if it must be eaten, only fruit should be consumed. (42)

One who possesses strength should drink milk; fasting without water must be observed by him, for by this the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Kamalā, is pleased. (13) Having risen at the hour of Brahmā on the eleventh day, the observer of the vow [should worship] Hari.
One should remember and meditate upon the names while reciting them, and then proceed to the bath. Having bathed and performed the daily worship of Kṛṣṇa,
the observer of the vow should have an auspicious *sarvatobhadra* mandala constructed with excellent grains.
In the center, one should place a golden jar or one made of copper, provided with the five jewels, unbroken rice, flowers, water, cloth, and fruit;
equipped with a conch, a bell, and other such items, one should worship it with sandalwood paste and other offerings. 16.
Having placed a vessel filled with sesame seeds upon that jar,
the observer of the vow should indeed install the image of Aparājitā from Ṛṣikeśa there;
he should also install and worship Padmā Ekādaśī.
By means of invocation and other rites, as well as the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and with garments, ornaments, cosmetics, water, sandalwood paste, and the like;
with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, crowns, crest-jewels, and so forth. (19)
With sandals, staffs, footwear, clusters of flowers, upper garments, and so forth;
with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel, and fine fruits; with the waving of lights (ārātrika), hymns of praise, prostrations like a staff, and circumambulations. (1.257.20–21)
Having worshipped the Blessed One with a handful of flowers requesting forgiveness, along with monetary gifts and other offerings, for the sake of the unimpeded accomplishment of the vow,
one should thereafter pray to Śrī Hari, bow down, and proceed with other duties.
At midday as well, the observer of the vow should offer sweet foods to the Blessed One;
he should offer betel leaf and drinking water, and cause the sacred narrative to be recited.
Then, in the afternoon and at evening, he should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) according to the prescribed rules.
One should offer hymns of praise and recitations, and provide milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other foods for the meal.
One should offer betel-leaf and water, and seat [the deity] upon the swing.
The devotee himself, along with other pure (*sāttvata*) devotees, should then swing [the deity].
Together with virtuous women, virtuous men, and even celibate students,
one should perform a vigil accompanied by festivities and songs.
There should be dancing and congregational chanting (kīrtana) joined with the names [of the Lord], as well as the nectar of sacred narratives.
Having bathed in the morning, one should worship Kṛṣṇa in his presence;
one should feed the Blessed Lord and the devotees with the sacred remnants (prasāda). Then, having caused others to break their fast, one should do so oneself.
One who observes the vow should indeed perform the ritual breaking of the fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) and practice charity.
[He should give] cows, buffaloes, elephants, horses, chariots, celestial vehicles (vimāna), and mounts;
houses, gardens, cities, villages, fields, clothing, food, and the means of livelihood. (1.257.30)
Jewels, diamonds, rubies, gems, gold, wealth, and so forth;
couches, carts, beds, chests, vessels, and door-panels;
mats, linen seats, lion-thrones, cushioned seats, and rugs. || 3.1 ||
A swing, a pestle, a ball, hidden ropes for the arms, knots, household implements, chains, a water-pot, and trees;
moving creepers, swaying pillars, and the skins of deer, tigers, and other beasts. (32–33)
On the twelfth day, whatever may be within one's capacity— such as tree bark, seats, bark garments, silk, wealth, and so forth— a king should give that,
as well as water-vehicles, land-vehicles, aerial vehicles, and the like.
One should likewise give various kinds of yantras to the preceptor and the teacher.
Whatever has been given by people to a worthy recipient is obtained in the next world.
[These include] the gift of knowledge, the gift of land, the gift of a maiden, and the offering of wealth. (35–36)
The gift of food, the gift of water, the gift of clothing, the offering of a house;
the gift of a cow, the gift of land, the gift of ritual implements, and the offering of a vow;
the gift of merit, as well as the offering of that which is most dear to oneself.
Whether in heaven or in another womb, that [gift] returns to its giver.
Therefore, when one has the capacity, one should give that which provides assistance in the next world;
one should practice the service of the virtuous, which bestows happiness both here and hereafter.
In whatever manner the virtuous may be pleased, in that very way they should be served; for the virtuous are indeed the very forms of Hari.
On this earth, the virtuous are the incarnations of Hari’s own essential nature.

If virtuous people, having practiced their vows, find satisfaction even within [the world], then for one who seeks the goal of the vow, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are attained; everything is accomplished.
Service to Hari, service to the virtuous, service to saintly women, and the offering of all to Acyuta—[these are the means]. 42.
Knowledge of the Self, the yoga of devotion, constant contemplation on the qualities of Hari, knowledge of Brahman, and the perfection of yoga—each of these is a means to liberation.
Vows, austerity, chanting, yoga, sacrifice, and self-surrender [are likewise means]. 43.
Possessing the path of surrender to Kṛṣṇa, this is the certain means to liberation.
Therefore, the observer of vows should practice the vow consisting of the excellent connection with Brahman.
For one who has desires, there shall be enjoyment; for one without desires, there is the supreme goal. 44–45.
The home of one who destroys another's dwelling certainly perishes;
indeed, the house of one who demolishes another's house collapses.
And for one who inflicts injury upon others, self-injury inevitably arises.
For one who inflicts suffering upon others, one's own suffering will certainly arise;
for one who bestows happiness upon others, one's own happiness will certainly arise.
For one who strikes down the prosperity of others, one's own prosperity will certainly perish.
In this case, the destruction of another inevitably results in one's own destruction;
for one who steals the property and other goods of another, the destruction of one's own property is certain;
and for one who brings about the ruin of another’s wife, the ruin of one's own wife will surely occur.

For one who gives fire or poison to others, there is certainly the burning of their own fire or poisoning by their own poison. For one who deceives others, there is certainly the deception of oneself. And for one who destroys the household life of another, there is certainly the dissolution of one's own household life.
For one who destroys the happiness of others, there is the destruction of one's own happiness;
for one whose nature is to benefit others, there is assistance in benefiting oneself. For one who bestows sensual pleasure, there is the arrival of sensual pleasure. (5.2)

For one who bestows happiness, there is the attainment of all means of accomplishment; for one who creates obstacles, there are indeed obstacles; and for one who bestows all things, all [attainments] certainly present themselves. (5.3–5.4)
Therefore, all gifts should be given for the sake of future attainment;
what is given here will certainly not be lost, nor will it fail to be obtained in the next world.
For those who have not given and are thus suffering, the vow of Ekādaśī is indeed the giver.
That [practice] should be performed with effort; it will certainly grant what is desired.
Suffering caused by the faults of an individual may occur for the community as a whole, while great merit produced by an individual arises for the assembly.
In the case of a king, merit or demerit is produced collectively;
likewise, the merit and demerit performed by the king touches the subjects as well.
Indeed, when the subjects are distressed by the violation of dharma by anyone whatsoever, [the king shares in that consequence]. (58)
The vow of Ekādaśī should be observed for the destruction of such suffering.
By that, indeed, sin is destroyed and incomparable happiness surely arises.
Listen to how such a thing occurred for King Māndhātṛ in the Kṛta Yuga. (1.257.60)
There was a royal sage named Māndhātṛ, born of the lineage of Vivasvat;
he became a universal monarch whose dominion extended from the land of sunrise to the land of sunset.
He protected his subjects with righteousness, as if they were his own children.
In his kingdom there was no famine, nor misfortune, nor diseases;
indeed, his realm, abounding in wealth and grain, was like heaven itself.
His treasury, too, filled with wealth acquired through righteous means, was like a treasure-store.
The castes and stages of life shine forth and flourish through his merits.
The earth is the bearer of wealth, cows grant all desires, and trees are like the wish-fulfilling kalpa-tree.
The Brahmins have attained perfection in speech; they are holy men who are the very ground of yoga.
The women were givers of joy, tranquil, and possessed of grace and auspiciousness.
The seasons acted according to one's desire, and the kingdom became like another heaven. Indeed, the subjects, immersed in happiness, attained a state of great well-being. (65–66)
The Brāhmaṇas remained established in their Vedic duties, the Kṣatriyas were devoted to protection,
the Vaiśyas were intent on the effort of acquiring wealth, and the Śūdras were servants;
as they all followed their own respective dharmas, the kingdom became happy.
As he ruled his kingdom in this manner, the planets were always auspicious;
the gods were gracious, and blessings abounded in every home. Now, there was a certain low-born man, a king among devotees, who desired the kingdom. 69.
Then, due to his abandonment of the duties of a Śūdra and his adoption of the duties of a Ṛṣi, he began severe penance in a desolate forest; meanwhile,
unrighteousness and lawlessness entered his kingdom.
For three years the clouds did not rain, and the subjects were distressed.
Some people were broken, some died, and others became afflicted by hunger.
[The traditional rites of] *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vaṣaṭkāra*, Vedic study, and worship [ceased].
Likewise, his religious observances, acts of assistance, honors, hospitality, gifts,
and all auspicious rites such as festivals were utterly destroyed.
Due to his misfortune, the entire region became afflicted by fate.
Then the subjects, having assembled, spoke thus to the lord of kings:
"Listen, O King, without rain this destruction of the kingdom will occur.
The Lord Viṣṇu, in the form of Parjanya, is established within the waters. (74–75)
He alone brings about rain; from rain comes food, and from that, the subjects.
In the absence of rain, O Great King, those people go to their destruction.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, provide for their security and prosperity so that it may be ensured.
Having heard this, the lord of the earth said:
"I shall strive so that there may be well-being for my subjects; for happiness has its root in the king.
Through the misconduct of kings, the suffering of the subjects occurs. (77–78)
"Even though I have never committed any sin anywhere since birth,
nevertheless, I shall strive for the welfare of my subjects.
Having spoken thus, the king, accompanied by his progeny and a limited retinue, [departed].
Prepared to seek out evil, he set out on a journey through the land.
He heard from the mouths of people that in the dense forest of the Himalayas,
a Śūdra was performing penance— a violation of dharma indeed within his kingdom.
For Brahmins, ascetics, and holy men, religious austerity is their duty;
for Śūdras, service is their duty, while austerity is indeed contrary to their dharma.
Because of the fault of austerity practiced by Śūdras, a drought has arisen today.
Thus, this dharma consisting of the obstruction of a Śūdra’s asceticism would result in rain.
Having heard this, the lord of the earth quickly went into the dense forest;
he visited the foremost sages and their hermitages inhabited by ascetics.
Then the king beheld the sage Aṅgiras, the son of Brahmā,
whose face was completely enveloped by a halo of splendor like that of the Lotus-born Lord himself.
With palms joined in reverence and bowed low, the king paid homage at his feet.
The sage asked after his welfare and whether the kingdom was free from affliction.
Having been offered a seat and sat down, Māndhātṛ replied to him:
"O Blessed One, as I am protecting the earth according to the ordinances of dharma..."
A drought has arisen and all the subjects are suffering;
three years have passed—what could be the cause of this?
I have heard from the mouths of people that a Śūdra is performing penance.
"Nevertheless, declare the final decision; what could be the cause here?
(89) Bring peace to the subjects by providing for their welfare and security.
Having meditated within himself for a moment, Aṅgiras said to the king: (90)
In this Kṛta Yuga, Dharma proceeds with four quarters.
Here, the people are devoted to Brahman and the Brāhmaṇas are devoted to austerity. Others are likewise authorized for austerity; indeed, there is no other path in the Kṛta Yuga.
Even though the object [of their desire] is present here, even that outcaste is intent on asceticism.
Due to the power of his unrighteousness, the clouds do not rain.
Make an effort to kill him; he is in a forest not far from here.
"O King, if this is done, there shall never again be a drought.
Having heard this, the highly fortunate king, who was devoted to compassion, said:
"I will not kill him as he performs penance and practices auspicious deeds."
"I shall gradually undertake the restraint of my ascetic heat under some pretext.
(95) If there should be some other means for bringing rain, then show it to me; indeed, I shall perform that which destroys the calamity. (96)
Aṅgiras said to the king: "If it is so, then it is excellent.
Perform the vow known as the Padma-ekādaśikā, which bestows well-being, grants all perfections, and destroys all calamities. (97)
The Padminī vow brings about all peace and bestows security and well-being.
O King, perform the Padminī vow together with your subjects and your retinue;
by the power of the Padminī vow, there will certainly be a bountiful rain.
Having accepted this command with his head and having honored that sage,
the king appointed an attendant to prevent the Śūdra from practicing austerities;
then, remembering Kṛṣṇa within his own heart, he returned to his palace.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, he performed the Padmā-vrata;
accompanied by all his subjects and joined by the four castes, having observed the vow, he made gifts and worshipped Hari. (101–102)
When this vow had been performed in this manner, O Lakṣmī, the clouds rained down.
The earth, fully satiated by the water, became abounding with crops;
for by the merit of the Ekādaśī vow, the drought was swiftly destroyed.
Therefore, the Padmā-vow should be observed for the sake of destroying the onset of suffering.
In that rite, there should be curd-rice, as well as a jar accompanied by garments and jewels,
a water-filled pitcher, and also an umbrella and sandals.
One should give [offerings] to a Brahmin who knows Brahman and is one's guru with the thought that he is Govinda;
likewise, that twice-born guru should be saluted, fed, and satisfied.
Having thus performed this supreme vow, a person shall obtain their desired goal.
"Indeed, by hearing and reciting this, the merit of the vow is obtained.

(107) Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-seventh chapter [257], titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Bhādrapada Śukla Padma-ekādaśī Vow, including the account of how there was a drought during the reign of King Māndhātṛ in the Satya Yuga when a Śūdra was performing penance, and how rain was brought about by the vow," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*) — Chapter 257.
Chapter 258 [Author: Chapter 259 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Salutations, salutations to you, O Govinda, O Lord of the Ṛṣikas, O Janārdana!
O Witness, O Impeller, O Master, O Nārāyaṇa, O Controller!
(1) You are the bestower of the object of sight, the giver of vision, established as the Seer.
O you who are the seed, existing in the form of the sprout, and abiding in the stalk, leaves, and so forth;
O you whose essence is the seed, dwelling in the stem, the stalk, and the beautiful flower—homage be to you!
O bestower of fruit, abiding in the fruit itself, you yourself bear fruit in its proper season.
O you who pervade the fruits of the seeds of karma, like rain upon seeds, homage be to you!
Tell me, O Āśvina, what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight?
What is its ritual procedure, what is its fruit, and what kind of vow is it considered to be?
"Which deity is worshipped here, and what are the offerings such as gifts and acts of worship?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, there is [a rite] known by the name Indirā."

Upendra, endowed with auspiciousness, is indeed to be worshipped here with *dūrvā* grass. An *āmalaka* fruit is for the water-offering (*arghya*), while a *śaṣkulī* cake is for the food offering (*naivedya*).
The gift of a maiden is preeminent, as is worship performed with all its constituent parts.
The primary libation for the ancestors must be performed, which is auspicious and provides satisfaction;
it is a vow accompanied by *śrāddha* and other rites that grants a way for those who have no way.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow, eating but one meal, shall remain celibate.
Sleeping on the ground and self-restrained, one should observe the vow on the eleventh day at dawn.
Having risen and remembered Śrī Hari, and then meditated upon the form of Hari,
one should bathe and, with a pure mind, perform the daily worship.
Having caused a pavilion to be constructed, one should place a new jar— either made of gold or copper— within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala;
it should be accompanied by the five jewels, auspicious sprouts, fruits, water, and fine garments.
One should indeed place a vessel filled with sesame seeds upon the jar.

Beside it, one should likewise place uncooked rice which provides satisfaction to the ancestors. Furthermore, one should place water brought from a sacred bathing site (tīrtha) in a vessel, as well as *kuśa* grass.
Then, one should place sugar, fruits, flour-cakes, and so forth at the sides; and there, the observer of the vow should install a golden image of Upendra, endowed with auspiciousness,
together with Indirā, within a vessel of sesame seeds.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, as well as the conch, the bell, and the water-pot (15), one should then worship Kṛṣṇa, remember him in the heart, and contemplate:
"May his head be upon my head, and may Hari’s eyes be in my eyes and other [senses]. (16)

May his heart be in my heart; may his hands and so forth be in my hands and so forth; may his waist and so forth be in my waist and so forth; and may Hari’s lotus feet be in my two feet. May the limbs of Hari be in my own limbs, and may Keśava reside within my very self.
Thus, having become a deity in every respect, one should worship Hari.
One should perform the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana), the ablution with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
the bathing with pure water, and the offering of garments.
The arranging of the hair and so forth, as well as worship with fragrant substances;
worship with gulāla, saffron, abīra, sandalwood, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
and the coloring with lac-dye, moist powder, and the like, as well as the application of kohl and cosmetic pigments.
Then one should apply ornaments and the like to all the limbs of the deity;
thereafter, one should greatly adorn the form, beautified with erotic grace, with flower garlands and other such items,
as well as with handsome bracelets, crowns, and so forth.
Incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel with lime, the waving of lights (*ārārtika*), hymns of praise, circumambulation, prostration like a staff, and so forth;
as well as the offering of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), unbroken grains, handfuls of flowers, and the request for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*). (23)
The observer of the vow, with a mind endowed with all aspects of ritual propriety,
should give and perform whatever is appropriate, and request the absence of obstacles for the vow.
Having remembered the ancestors, he should offer a handful of water enriched with grace.
One should indeed give gifts in the morning and perform worship at midday;
thereafter, one should feed Lord Nārāyaṇa with various kinds of food.
After the time following midday, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony for the ancestors.
One should offer water with the *pitṛtīrtha* [finger-portion] while pronouncing their respective names.
One should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍas*), fruits, and other things that provide satisfaction to the ancestors.
Having performed the evening *nīrājana* ceremony, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
One should feed [the devotees] milk-preparations and the like, and offer them water for drinking and so forth.
One should keep a vigil at night and cultivate the company of the virtuous. Likewise, one should engage in discourse, listen to the stories from the devotees, or recite them oneself.
One should perform dancing, singing, and a great festival of joyful enthusiasm. Having bathed in the morning, meditated upon Hari, and worshipped Him according to the prescribed rites,
one should offer food oblations to the Lord and then feed the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having fed the guests, the virtuous men, the virtuous women, and the twice-born,
the observer of the vow should then break his fast and bestow gifts upon worthy recipients;
he should also honor the teacher, his mother, the elders, his father, and his husband.
One should receive blessings and then perform one's own duties.
When the vow has been performed in this manner, O Lakṣmī, the desired goal is certainly accomplished.
One should cause food that satisfies the ancestors, as well as water, clothing, and other gifts, to be given.
One should cause other gifts to be made that effect the liberation of one's ancestors, such as cows, houses, gardens, livestock, fields, daughters, learning,
and excellent vehicles, along with gold, jewels, ornaments, and various kinds of household utensils.
The observer of the vow, with faith and with the sole intention of pleasing the ancestors, should cause [the gift] to be given.
He should give it to the Guru, who is Hari; this shall bring about the liberation of the ancestors.
Since that which grants worldly enjoyment is inferior to that which grants liberation, one should therefore practice that which grants liberation.
Since there may be an excessive longing for the sake of pacifying someone else's desire, one should act to pacify that very longing;
otherwise, a reversal will occur regarding the satisfaction of the ancestors for the descendant of the lineage. (38)
Therefore, whether it yields the fruit of desire or even the fruit of non-desire,
one born of the lineage should indeed perform [the rite] when the time has arrived for the satisfaction of the ancestors;
during the vow of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should perform it so as to bring about the specific fruit of complete satisfaction.
Whether it be very small or even vast, one should give [gifts] with their respective auspicious names;
that certainly becomes a source of happiness for those who have gone to the other world.
If the ancestors are established in liberation, then the fruit is considered to belong to the performer [of the rite].
Thinking that what has been done shall not go to waste, the wise person should act accordingly.

Just as a seed will surely yield a sprout, a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, so too the consecration performed by one endowed with faith does not go to waste in the field [of the recipient]. (42–43)
Seed sown in saline soil perishes, but it is not lost when sown in a worthy field;
cast into a sacred place, a worthy recipient, or a virtuous person, it certainly sprouts.
One should give to a person observing vows or to Hari as a worthy recipient; even what is cast therein is never fruitless.

Therefore, whether it be small or great, one should give a gift free from expectation of reward; by the grace of Hari, it surely bears fruit. Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this delightful story concerning a vow that grants satisfaction to the ancestors.
The Indira Ekādaśī is the best, bestowing a favorable destiny upon the ancestors who have fallen into lower wombs and granting the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. Indeed,
it was observed by King Indrasena as a means of delivering his ancestors.
In the great kingdom called Narmada,
during the previous Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Indrasena who was the lord of the city of Candrāvatī.
He protected his subjects with righteousness, as if they were his own biological sons.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, possessed of wealth and grain, provided with elephants, horses, and vehicles, and devoted solely to the worship of Viṣṇu,
he constantly chants the names of Śrī Hari, which grant liberation.
He spent his time solely in devotion, contemplating the meditation on the supreme self (adhyātma-dhyāna).
Once, while he was seated at home in a state of peace, the sage Nārada descended from the path of the sky and appeared before him.
Seeing that Nārada had arrived, he rose with palms joined in reverence;
having offered hospitality, he seated the sage upon a beautiful, comfortable seat.
He said, "Welcome to you, O best among the knowers of Brahman."
Today my kingdom, birth, deeds, lineage, and wealth have become fruitful.
My charity, sacrifices, recitations, oblations, and Vedic study have borne fruit for me through your grace, O best of sages; my fortune is most blessed.
Hundreds of sons, grandsons, wives, male servants, and female servants, as well as elephants, horses, and vehicles, have become fruitful for me through your arrival.
Indeed, the sight of a holy man is meritorious, and his touch destroys sin.
Service bestows heaven, while the surrender of one’s self grants divine liberation.
Those houses and dwellings in which the dust from the feet of holy men does not reside are equal to cremation grounds. (57–58)
"My entire family, my very own kin, has been delivered;
O divine sage, grant me your grace, for you have come here without any worldly desire.
Nārada replied, "O royal sage, listen to this which causes wonder."
"O Lord of the Earth, I have come from the world of Brahmā to the realm of Yama.
Honored with devotion according to dharma, I sat upon an excellent seat.
The virtuous, whose character is truth, attend upon Dharmarāja."
In their assembly, others— who were exceedingly proud of their great merit— laughed at your father as he stood behind them, devoid of luster.
In the hall of Śrāddhadeva, your father said to me:
O Lord of the Earth, listen to that message for the destruction of your sorrow.
O Brahmin, tell King Indrasena—the son of Candrāvatī—this message from your father, Candrasena. (6.3–6.4)
The mass of merit belonging to the King of Dharma remains in his city;
for although he performed much giving, he did not perform any vow.
By that merit, he is established in the city of Dharma.
Deprived of his splendor by the merit of the vow,
Vidura followed far behind and sat in the assembly hall, always overwhelmed by great sorrow.
Therefore, my son, you should perform the Ekādaśī vow dedicated to me.
"O my son, he shall grant me liberation through the merit-giving gift of Indirā.
Having been told this, O King, I have come into your presence.
O King, perform the Indirā-vrata for the sake of your father's liberation.
"By that merit, your father will certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha.
(69) Having heard his father's message, he asked Nārada about the vow:
"By what procedure should it be performed, and on which lunar fortnight and lunar day? (1.258.70)
Nārada said to the king:
"During the dark fortnight, on the tenth day, having risen in the morning and thereafter remembered Kṛṣṇa, one should bathe, worship the Lord, and then perform the midday bath. (71)
Having offered the food offering (naivedya) to Hari, one should observe a single meal.
Having bathed in the evening and meditated upon Hari, one should sleep on the ground at night.
On the morning of the eleventh day (ekādaśī), this observer of the vow should indeed abandon sleep.
Having remembered and meditated upon Hari, one should perform purification and other rites while chanting His name;
one should rinse the mouth repeatedly twelve times with water.
One should perform bathing with waters from sacred fords and carry out the worship of the Deity.
Having bowed to the form of Hari and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and other preliminary rites,
the observer of the vow should worship Kṛṣṇa Upendra with the sixteen types of offerings. Then, in His presence, he should undertake the rules for the fast.
"Having remained today without food and having renounced all enjoyments, O lotus-eyed Lord, I shall eat tomorrow; fulfill my vow, O Master.
Having thus undertaken this observance within the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala, [he should proceed].
Having placed Kṛṣṇa in the jar, one should perform the great worship (mahāpūjana).
Having completed the worship according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offer food.
At midday as well, having bathed oneself, one should likewise feed Śrī Hari.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), offer him rest, awaken him, and give him water to drink;
one should fan the Lord, massage him, and gladden him with desired offerings.
One should also perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) according to the rules before the Śālagrāma stone.

One should perform the *śrāddha* for the gratification of the ancestors, endowed with faith. (8.1) A *śrāddha* performed with wheat flour is considered mediocre. [A superior one is performed] with barley, rice, sesame, mung beans, wheat, and likewise chickpeas. (8.2)
The *śrāddha* performed by those observing vows should be most excellent;
however, having performed the *śrāddha*, one observing a vow must not eat what has been consumed by the ancestors.
For the sake of preserving the vow, one should indeed smell what has been offered.
Having smelled the ancestral food (paitryamanna), the wise man should give it to a cow.
At night, he should perform a great worship and likewise keep a vigil with festivities.
Then, on the morning of the twelfth day (dvādaśī), having bathed and worshipped Mādhava, he should proceed.

Then, having offered the sacrificial food (naivedya), fruit, and betel leaf, the observer of the vow should perform the waving of lights (ārātrika) and other rites, as well as the formal request for forgiveness (kṣamāyācanikā).
He should then bestow abundant gifts and feed the Brāhmaṇas and others.
One should feed virtuous men and women, as well as one's kinsmen, daughters' sons, and sons.
Having fed the poor and the blind, one should eat oneself while remaining silent.
O King, perform this vow with diligence according to this procedure.
"O King, your ancestors shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having spoken thus to the monarch, O Lakṣmī, Nārada vanished.
Then Indrasena performed that vow according to the prescribed injunctions.
Accompanied by his harem and attended by his sons and servants,
a rain of flowers fell from the sky when the vow was completed and the gift of cows was made.
And indeed, when the merit had been dedicated, Indrasena’s father— ||| 91 ||
Candrasena and his other fathers likewise remained there;
mounted upon Garuḍa and seated in celestial chariots, they indeed went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Indrasena also, having performed that vow protected by the Vaiṣṇavas, [attained the same].
Having enjoyed a kingdom free from all thorns and having bestowed it upon his eldest son,
Mahīsena, he thereafter departed for heaven himself.
Having fully exhausted his merit there, he indeed went to Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the greatness of this vow has been recounted by me to you.
By reading or even by hearing this, the merit of the vow shall also be attained.

(9.5) Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Āśvina-Kṛṣṇa Indira-Ekādaśī Vow," describing the liberation from the realm of Yama of King Indrasena’s ancestors, beginning with Candrasena, through the power of the merit of the vow, in the first section on the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 258: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 259 [Author: Chapter 260 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
You alone are the Lord, the embodiment of all merit; as an ocean of compassion, you yourself bestow the fruits of actions according to their nature.
Whatever humans perform and carry out while forgetting you,
they obtain the fruit of that here and in the hereafter, yet they remain beset by fear.
But those who remember you and carry out whatever actions they do—
O Blessed One, that fruit— which is devoid of qualities and consists of eternal bliss and liberation— is yours to grant to me, your beloved,
who has sought refuge in you.
For in this way you are the bestower of fruits, since you are composed of all actions.
O All-Knowing One, O Supreme Lord, show me compassion and tell me:
what is the name of the Ekādaśī in the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina?
Which deity is to be worshipped there, what is the ritual procedure, and likewise, what is the fruit [of its observance]?
"O Hari, tell me everything here: what gift should be given on that occasion?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "The eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Īṣa (Āśvina) is known by the name Pāśāṅkuśā."
It removes all sins, bestows merit, and likewise grants liberation.
(7) Here, Padmanābha, together with Padmavatī, should be worshipped with devotion.
Śamī leaves are intended for the worship, and the Kāmaphala fruit is prescribed for the arghya offering. (8)
Rice cooked with milk (*śālipāka*) should be offered as a food oblation (*naivedya*), and rice balls (*modaka*) made of grain should be given as a gift.
To attain all desired fruits, everything should be offered to Janārdana.
Even after performing most intense austerities for a long time, a sage whose senses are restrained—
Whatever fruit one attains by bowing to Padmanābha— having performed many sins, even a deluded man who bows to Hari Padmanābha during a vow does not go to hell.
All the holy fords and sacred shrines upon the earth were established by him through the worship of Padmanābha.
Those people who have taken refuge in Janārdana, the god of gods, Padmanābha—
For them, there is never any torment from the world of Yama.
Even if a person has committed terrible sins, by observing even a single Ekādaśī—even incidentally—they do not go to the torments of Yama. (13–14)

There exists nothing so purifying in the three worlds as this Ekādaśī of Padmanābha, which destroys all sins. Indeed, sins dwell openly and fearlessly only for as long as [this day has not arrived]. (15)
As long as a living being does not observe the fast on the day of Padmanābha’s festival, [they have not attained the fruit].
(16) Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the eleventh lunar day. (17)
In this world, there is nothing equal to Ekādaśī for washing away sins;
it bestows heaven and liberation here, grants wealth, friends, and so forth, provides bodily health, and gives wives, sons, daughters, and a lineage. (18)
Even that which is performed under a pretext, by him it is not gone to the abode of Yama.
O Lakṣmī! Neither the Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara, nor even the sacred field of the Kauravas is superior to the day of Hari.
One should keep a vigil at night and perform the great worship of Hari;
indeed, on the day of Hari, one should observe a fast even without water.
By that, O Lakṣmī, one surely attains my eternal abode.
Ten from the mother’s side, ten situated on the father’s side,
and ten belonging to the wife’s side certainly deliver one from the vow [of transmigration].
They are four-armed, of divine form, and seated upon the shoulders of Garuḍas.
Adorned with garlands and wearing yellow garments, they possess valor equal to that of Viṣṇu;
and the women, becoming like Lakṣmī herself, proceed to the abode of Hari.
Whether in childhood, youth, old age, or even in a state of helplessness—
Having observed the Ekādaśī fast, even an embodied being who is a sinner does not go to a miserable state. Indeed, by fasting on Pāśāṅkuśā alone, one goes to the world of Hari,
having given gold, sesame seeds, cows, water, food, and likewise clothing.
One who possesses shoes, an umbrella, or other such items does not see the world of Yama;
yet, for one devoid of merit and vows, life is considered fruitless.
For him whose days come and go devoid of merit, [life is in vain].
Though he breathes like a blacksmith’s bellows, he does not truly live.
(28) By performing bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, meditation, sacrificial sessions, and so forth, according to his ability, he should indeed pass his days fruitfully. (29)
In this world, men who perform meritorious deeds are seen to be long-lived, wealthy, of noble birth, and free from disease. Therefore,
one should undertake a vow consisting of the noose, the goad, and so forth.
On the tenth day, he should eat only once, observe celibacy, and likewise sleep on the ground. Having bathed in the morning,
he should perform his regular daily worship and seek the fulfillment of his vow through sixteen circumambulations.
One should have a Sarvatobhadra mandala prepared with seven kinds of grain.
In its center, one should place a water-filled jar endowed with the five jewels;
or, having filled it with wealth, one should set it down along with cloth and fruit.
One should place an auspicious golden vessel filled with sesame seeds upon the jar (34).
One should then install and worship the auspicious image of Śrī Padmanābha accompanied by Padmāvatī, and likewise provided with the noose and goad (35).

Having performed the invocation and other rites, one should then establish Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth, as well as with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha), and offer garments. One should also present sandalwood paste, fragrant scents, collyrium, and the like.
One should offer necklaces and ornaments made of flowers, jewels, gold, and so forth;
one should give various kinds of food and offer sweet water.
Having given mouth-perfume and fruit, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and bow down repeatedly.
Having offered praise, performed circumambulations, and prostrated like a staff, one should request forgiveness.
In a space provided with incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should suspend a swing in the air.
One should place Hari there and offer him a fine meal even at midday.
Having offered betel-leaf, water for drinking, and other such items, one should likewise perform the evening rites.

Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa with the sixteen types of offerings, one should perform the waving of lamps (ārātrika) and all other ceremonies according to the prescribed rule, and then offer food and drink.
Established among the devotees of the Lord, one should keep vigil at night, performing dancing,
singing, chanting, glorification, and likewise remembrance;
as well as bowing to His limbs, massaging them, serving Him, and so forth.

Having meditated upon Hari in the morning, bathed, and worshipped Keśava, one should feed the Blessed One and offer him betel-leaf and water. Thereafter, one should feed and honor virtuous men, virtuous women, and those who have taken refuge in oneself. (43–44)
Having bowed to the elders and remembered Hari, and having separately performed the five sacrifices,
one should then indeed break the fast and give gifts with devotion.
Having thus completed the vow, one should worship Hari on the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
The destruction of the bond of existence becomes certain for this observer of vows.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the divine story that releases one from the noose of Yama.
In former times, in the Kṛta age, there was a sage named Vāmadeva.
He had many disciples who were fully conversant with the knowers of Brahman;
there were other sages who had renounced the world, as well as householders who were the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman.
[They performed] ritual bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors.
When the sun had risen, they, being devoted to their respective duties, engaged in their tasks.
Among them, there was one sage named Vedaśiras who was a follower of the ritualistic path (karmakāṇḍin) and was indeed highly proficient in Vedic rites. (1.259.50)
Observing a vow for four months, he spent his time subsisting on a diet of tubers.
Indeed, a disease born from the transformation of those tubers arose in his stomach:
extreme weakness of the digestive fire and a burning inflammation of the intestines.
Whatever he might eat would remain undigested.
Thus, as his body grew emaciated, his incapacity increased;
he became indolent regarding bathing, the recitation of the *gāyatrī*, mantra-japa, worship, and other such duties.
Thus, having permanently abandoned bathing and worship due to the cessation of all worldly states,
the sage indeed maintains his bodily existence like a *śūdra*.
And by the renunciation of ritual action, he avoids the transgression prescribed for those who have reached the summit of the Vedas.
The merit that had arisen was indeed brought to exhaustion by that transgression.
When the end of his lifespan arrived and the messengers of Yama came,
Vedaśiras, being thoroughly distressed, then spoke to them.

"How may I avoid seeing the messengers of Yama, and by what action? The messengers of Yama replied to him: 'Having abandoned the experience of your own actions, you behave according to your own will; whatever fruit you have thus produced, that shall be your dwelling in the realm of Yama.'"
"For the Brahmin who has set out upon a wrong path, there is the abode of Yama.
Therefore, eat that which results from his transgression as a means of atonement.
Having spoken thus, they took Vedaśiras and went to the house of Yama.
King Yama, having truly observed his deed as it was,
then said to Citragupta: "Indeed, his transgression is great—
that great sin consisting of the forgetting of the Veda he had studied."
"It has been declared that this is equal to the murder of a Brahmin; therefore, bind him with nooses and lead him away!
Cast him into the Kālasūtra hell for those who slay Brahmins, and having led him to the Asipatravana forest, strike him down! || 61-62 ||
Having spoken thus, Yamarāja, the author of ethical codes, ceased.
Then the highly intelligent Vedaśiras spoke to the wise Yamarāja:
"In this time of bodily calamity, I have forgotten the Veda."
"Since I abandoned my duties only due to incapacity, how could hell befall me?
Indeed, the duties of a time of calamity do not count as unrighteousness;
therefore, there is no sin in me, nor anything for Yama to fill his realm with."
Then the King of Dharma said: "As long as passion still exists, dharma performed during a time of distress is considered by us to be like that of one who is ill;
however, when there is only a slight affliction, the abandonment of many [pleasures] is considered a great unrighteousness."
There is no such disease for you by which the Veda has not been recited.
Yet, through sheer indolence, you have indeed forgotten the entire Veda;
from that, transgression has arisen, and ritual action has been abandoned altogether. (67–68)
A wise Brāhmaṇa who understands should perform [his duties] according to his capacity.
When he has come to full understanding, how could it be possible for him to abandon everything?
Therefore, one who is devoid of the duty of action due to the fault of laziness—
"Having fallen from the path of the Brahma-observance, he deserves punishment in every respect.
(1.259.70) Then Vedaśiras reflected there upon his preceptor Mānasa;
that great Brahman incarnation, Vāmadeva, also arrived. (71)
Then Vāmadevaka, honored by the King of Dharma (Yama) and saluted even by his disciple, sat upon the seat offered to him.
Vāmadeva related all that deed which he had heard from the mouth of Yama.
"Truth that consists of transgression does not perish without punishment.
(73) The compassionate Vāmadeva reflected for his sake: "How might punishment not have to be endured, yet the karma also become fruitless? (74)
Having reflected thus, he spoke so that he might cross over;
looking all around there, he addressed his disciple Yama as well:
"Listen, both you disciples, O Yama and Vedaśiras!"
There is a great vow that destroys the Kālasūtra and Asipatra hells;
it is the powerful and esteemed Ekādaśī vow of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, which destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin and other sins equal to it. (76–77)
By performing this with faith, the expiation shall be accomplished;
likewise, through merely hearing the names of the Ekādaśīs and by the formal resolve for the vow,
one's lifespan is restored once again.
And by the power of his preceptor, he regained his life.
Having accepted the hospitality of their host, the two went to where the corpse was;
the preceptor caused his disciple to enter and then spoke the vow.
Having bathed and performed the worship of his guru, he remained in a state of well-being;
then, the observance of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha was undertaken.
Instantly, even the destruction of the sin arising from the forgetting of the Vedas occurred.
At that time, the sins such as the abandonment of one's duties were reduced to ashes.
Then, by the power of his preceptor and through the performance of the Ekādaśī vow, Vedaśiras indeed attained auspicious and long life.
Through the vow of service, the destruction of Yama’s noose occurred for him;
therefore, this Ekādaśī is considered the goad for nooses. Just as a goad is used for elephants, so too is the Pāśāṅkuśa-vrata.
Auspicious deeds should be performed by people for the destruction of Yama’s nooses—
deeds that bestow heaven and liberation, grant all prosperity, provide happiness, confer health, and are the supreme pacifier of the three kinds of suffering. (85–86)
It is the destroyer of the bonds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the eradicator of sin;
likewise, it is the destroyer of the fetters of the body and its worldly concerns, as well as of calamities.
It is the shatterer of the bonds of "I" and "mine," and of hatred and attachment.
It bestows tranquility, grants good fortune, and confers the status of husband and wife;
it extinguishes the forest fire of the afflictions and grants the eternal abode.
It bestows the yoga of Hari, as well as Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka. (88–89)
O Lakṣmī! The vow of the noose and the goad must be performed with great effort;
for by reading it or even by hearing it, one indeed obtains the merit of that vow. (1.259.90)

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter [counted as two hundred and fifty-nine] in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. This chapter is titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Āśvina Śukla Pāśāṅkuśa Ekādaśī Vrata," concerning how the sage Vedaśiras—a disciple of the seer Vāmadeva—fell into the world of Yama due to the power of his sin arising from laziness and the abandonment of righteous duties because of indigestion; and how, through the presence of his preceptor Vāmadeva whom he had remembered and by means of this vow, he was liberated from the noose of Yama. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 259.

Chapter 261 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Salutations to Mahākāla, Mahārudra, Yama, and the servants of Yama—
to those whose very selves govern the entire universe. Salutations to the noose,
the thunderbolt, the mace, the spear, the staff, the discus, and the trident.
Salutations to that sovereign power by which all beings are set in motion.
Salutations to that one whose essence is virtue, impelled by whom steadfastness, compassion, assistance, statesmanship, forbearance, and beneficence prevail.

Salutations to the one who is beyond attributes (nirguṇa), yet who has manifested as that which consists of the sense of "mine," otherness, selfhood, stability, nourishment, and liberation; salutations to the possessor of attributes (guṇin).
O Blessed One, your compassion for me is always like that between the near and far shores of an ocean.
Tell me, what is the name of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight of Kārttika?
Which deity is to be worshipped here? Tell me the gift, the merit, and the ritual procedure.
Also tell me, what kind of practice must be performed during this vow? || 5-6 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! This month of Kārtika indeed bestows liberation;
it is the concluding month of the Cāturmāsya, intended for vows, gifts, worship, and other such rites. (7)
This month is the most excellent for those observing vows;
therein, every auspicious and meritorious deed must indeed be performed.
Even within that, the Ekādaśī known as Ramā in the dark fortnight is the most excellent.
Lord Hari, the Supreme Sovereign, is to be worshipped together with Hiraṇyā; within her [the vessel], He is the presiding Lord.
Among flowers, the *baṭu-kunda* is preferred, and for the water offering (*arghya*), the plantain is considered best.
For the food offering (*naivedya*), there should be plantains soaked in sugar and ghee, as well as fried cakes (*polikā*).
Whatever one desires for oneself, such as gifts of jars of ghee and the like,
all that should be given away along with gold for the increase of prosperity.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should eat but once and sleep upon the ground.
One should be a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), free from the defects of anger, delusion, and the like.
(12) Having risen at dawn, one should meditate upon Govinda and, having bathed, worship Him.
Having performed the daily worship, one should cause seven kinds of grain to be prepared. (13)

One should prepare a *maṇḍala* known as Sarvatobhadra, beautifully adorned with various colored powders. In its center, one should place a vessel made of gold or copper, filled with water, unbroken rice grains, auspicious cloth, and the five precious gems.
The observer of the vow should place a silver vessel filled with sesame seeds at the front of that [image], combined with sugar, bilva fruit, betel nut, and sandalwood. Therein,
he should install the form of Hari, who possesses a golden complexion.
One should serve [the deity] with the rites of invocation and so forth, with the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and with massages using oil;
then one should offer garments, ornaments, cosmetics, and the like, as well as a garland of flowers, bracelets, a crown, and so on. (17)

One should offer incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel leaves, and so forth; one should perform the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) and other rites, recite hymns of praise, and request forgiveness.
At that time, one should give various kinds of gifts to the venerable Guru.
One should worship at midday as well, feed [the deity], and offer water.
Having bathed and worshipped in the evening, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite. After completing the hymns of praise and other rituals, one should feed and serve [the deity].
At night, adorned by a circle of devotees, one should keep a vigil;
one should engage in the delight of singing, dancing, conversation, storytelling, and discourse.
On the twelfth day, the observer of the vow, having bathed in the morning and worshipped Keśava, [should proceed].
Whether it be a king, a subject observing a vow,
a renunciant, a householder, a woman, or even a man, one should,
according to one's ability, feed virtuous and excellent Brahmins, as well as children. (23)
Then she should indeed perform the breaking of the fast and ensure the successful completion of the vow.
By performing the vow in this manner, a woman will certainly become equal to Lakṣmī;
and a man who performs the vow becomes a god and is truly liberated.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear the auspicious story of Candrabhāga and Śaśisena.
In ancient times, there was a king renowned as Mucukunda.
His city, named Indrakundana, was situated in the south. (26)
Dwelling in the capital, he ruled the earth as a sole sovereign.
He maintained a great friendship with Devendra,
and likewise with Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Agni.
Thus did he form a friendship with Vibhīṣaṇa;
by means of aerial chariots, he travels everywhere throughout the three worlds.
Devoted to Viṣṇu and true to his word, he rules a kingdom free from all thorns.
Indeed, all the people in his kingdom were Vaiṣṇavas;
when the day of Hari arrived, all his subjects, being devotees of Viṣṇu, did not eat food and observed a fast. (1.260.30–31)
The drum is beaten for him when the tenth day arrives:
"One must not eat, one must not eat, when the day of Hari has arrived.
[32] Even by means of elephants, horses, young elephants, and other animals as well...
On the day of Hari, one must not consume even grass, food, or water.
He caused all those established in his kingdom to observe this supreme vow.
The excellent river Candrabhāgā became his daughter.
Now, at the same time, on the bank of the Kāverī,
there was a meritorious king named Candrasena, the sovereign of the city called Kanaka.
To his son, named Śaśisena, who was endowed with excellent qualities—
The Candrabhāgā was indeed given [in marriage] by King Mucukunda.
She too was a great devotee of the Lord and observed the Vaiṣṇava vow.
Once, accompanied by her husband, she went to her father’s house.
Her husband became afflicted with fever and grew exceedingly weak;
meanwhile, the day of the Ekādaśī vow, which bestows great merit, arrived. When that vow had come, Candrabhāgā thought to herself:
"What will become of my husband, who is indeed utterly incapable of fulfilling his vow?
Suffering from illness, emaciated, and exceedingly weak, he cannot endure the pangs of hunger on this very day of his vow—my father, whose commands are stern. (1.260.40)
Whether capable or incapable, let one observe the vow of the teaching.
If it is transgressed by anyone, that person is undoubtedly subject to punishment. (41) Let that which is destined to happen, happen; what is to be done here by one who is helpless?
Thinking thus, she remained there even as the day of her vow arrived. When the tenth day had come, the drum was beaten:
"One must not eat, one must not eat, now that the day of Hari has arrived! (42–43)
"One who transgresses my command shall indeed be deserving of punishment.
Hearing the sound of the drum, Śaśisena said to his beloved:
"What must I do, O dear one? I shall die without food."
Then Candrabhāgā slowly spoke to her lover, who was distressed with anxiety:
"Today, in my father’s domain, no one—neither humans nor the beasts, birds, and reptiles dependent upon them—is permitted to eat. (45–46)
"Grass, food, water, or flour must not be consumed on the day of Hari. If you eat, my dear, you will then incur punishment and fall into reproach; therefore, make your mind firm. 47.
Having heard this, Śaśiṣeṇa said to her: "I shall observe the fast;
whatever is ordained by destiny for me will surely come to pass.
Having thus formed a firm resolve, he performed the vow without water.
Overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, he became greatly distressed;
at night, overcome by fainting, he took refuge in the *brahmarandhra*.
At the time of sunrise, Śaśisena met his death.
The king had him cremated with wood suitable for royalty.
Candrabhāgā, however, because she possessed an understanding of the greatness of devotion to Hari,
did not burn herself along with her husband, even though she was a devoted wife.
Having performed the funeral rites for her husband,
Śaśisena— possessing a divine body due to the great merit of the Rāmavrata— remained in the palace of Janaka;
meanwhile, having attained heaven, he obtained an independent sovereignty equal to that of Indra.
Abounding in great prosperity, invincible, and endowed with innumerable virtues;
[it was adorned] with palaces made of golden pillars, embellished with gems and lapis lazuli, and with various kinds of crystal structures, diverse and divinely radiant. 54–55.
He attained a heaven adorned with countless celestial mansions;
mounted upon an excellent aerial chariot and seated upon a lion-throne,
he was graced with a crown and earrings, and embellished by necklaces and armlets.
Being praised by hosts of Gandharvas, gods, and Apsarases,
and surrounded by those holding fans, umbrellas, and chowries in their hands,
Śaśisena shines and rejoices greatly in his own heaven.
Then once, a messenger of Mahendra arrived on earth;
he was sent by Indra to Mucukunda’s house for a specific purpose, as a great battle with the Daityas was about to take place against Indra. (59)
Then Mucukunda, having conquered the Daityas with the assistance of Indra,
became victorious indeed by virtue of a boon granted by Brahmā.
For this purpose, the messenger who had come was fed and likewise honored.
The king asked about the well-being of the gods in heaven;
then, after the messenger had reported everything for which he had come, he said to the king:
"I have beheld Śaśisena in heaven."

O Indra among kings, your son-in-law, a youth endowed with beauty and charm, shines forth like an ocean of power, prosperity, and majesty that is no less than Indra’s; he has come to this earth, and I have seen him approaching. (63–64)
He spoke thus on behalf of his father-in-law, King Candrasena, of his beloved wife Candrabhāgā, and likewise of the city:
"My welfare and well-being must be inquired after from my presence."
"You must convey my greetings and wish me well in all things pertaining to heaven as they truly are.
You must also tell my wife: 'Your husband awaits you.
For thus, O King, there is great happiness for your son-in-law in heaven."
All is well with him, and there exists a wonderful and marvelous marvel:
a city of diverse and beautiful splendor, never seen by anyone anywhere before;
divine, situated in the sky, moving through the air, radiant as the sun, and illuminated by its own light.

Abounding in the enjoyment of nectar, served by female celestial nymphs as its attendants—this city, filled with great wonders and eternal, has indeed been obtained by your son-in-law through the merit of his vows; I am unable to describe it fully. (1.260.69–70)
Having fasted on that day known as Ramā Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of Kārttika,
he died here and attained such a heaven.
Even one who performs a vow while lacking faith, having reached the highest heaven, [attains this].
From that celestial realm, he desired to go further upward from heaven.
Having heard this, Candrabhāgā, who was staying there, was delighted by the power of the Ramā-vrata performed by her own wife, and she spoke repeatedly: ||| 72-73 ||
"O messenger, lead me there where my beloved husband dwells, for I am filled with the intense longing to behold my lord.
Even though he resides in the abode of Brahmā, I shall bring him here by virtue of the merit of the Ramā-vrata."
"O messenger! Act in such a way that a union between us two may come to pass.
(75) Having heard this and received Mucukunda’s command, the messenger then assumed a divine body in the sky, took Candrabhāgā with him, and departed. (76)
She too, having attained a celestial form and youth worthy of heaven,
as well as divine flight, came into the presence of her husband.
Seeing and seeing her husband’s heaven and great kingdom, she rejoiced.
Indrasena rejoiced greatly upon seeing his beloved returned;
having summoned her, he seated her on his own left side.
The messenger, having received excellent hospitality, departed for Indra.
Then, out of joy, Candrabhāgā spoke these pleasing words to her beloved:
"Listen, my dear, to this beneficial speech regarding the merit that resides within me:
when I was more than eight years old, while living in my father's house..."
From that time forward, whatever Ekādaśī vow has been observed by me,
by the power of its merit we two shall go to the imperishable abode,
the eternal station of Śrī Hari, which is enriched with all desires.
Having enjoyed heaven for a long time through the power of their merit, those two went to the imperishable abode and became liberated, having attained the divine state.
Indeed, she is like a wish-fulfilling gem or even like a cow of plenty.
The Ekādaśī known as Ramā is like a wish-fulfilling tree for me.
(84) Regarding the vows of Ekādaśī on both fortnights, one should not make any distinction between the dark and the bright; as it is with the dark, so it is with the bright. (89)
Just as both a white and a black cow yield milk that is identical for both,
so too the two Ekādaśīs are remembered as yielding equal results.
The Ekādaśī observed by men bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"From hearing or even from reciting [this], one shall obtain a fruit equal to that of the vow itself.

(87) Thus ends the two hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Kārttika-Kṛṣṇa-Ramaikādaśī Vow, including the attainment of heaven by Indrasena, the husband of Candrabhāgā—the daughter of Mucukunda—due to his death on the day of the vow, followed by the wife's ascent to heaven, and subsequently the liberation of both," in the first section, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
