Śrī Lakṣmī said: Indeed,
for the sake of meritorious deeds during the four months of the rainy season, Kārtika enters [the body] and makes them exceedingly endowed with great majesty.
Indeed, the merit-bestowing vow performed during the Cāturmāsya period does not reach its fulfillment;

however, by performing it during the month of Kārttika, one obtains the fruit of the entire Cāturmāsya. It is the destroyer of sins and the bestower of the realms of heaven, truth, and the nectar of immortality.
For he is indeed the bestower of Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the imperishable world (Akṣara-loka). Whatever merit is performed during Kārtika becomes multiplied a thousandfold;
therefore, for one's own sake, the entire Kārtika vow should be observed.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, what is the name of the Ekādaśī that is recognized?
Who is the presiding deity, what is the procedure, what is the gift, what is the vow, and what is the fruit?
Furthermore, what is considered the specific excellence of the final month of the Cāturmāsya?
"Tell me also that by which those who observe vows attain liberation.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall explain [the rites] during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika."
The Ekādaśī known by the name Prabodhinī is declared to be the most excellent of the excellent. On this day, the righteous Lord of Lakṣmī, who usually reclines upon Śeṣa, awakens;
and by the power of its vow, the darkness born of ignorance is dissolved.
Because supreme self-realization arises from this, it is called *Prabodhinī* (the Awakener);
it bestows liberation, happiness, heaven, and enlightenment.
Having fasted there according to the prescribed rites, the Lord Dāmodara is to be worshipped.
Janārdana should be worshipped with many articles together with Rādhā and Prabhāvinī. He should be honored with lotuses and excellent flowers;
as an offering of food (naivedya), there should be mung-bean cakes (mudgalaḍḍukas), and for the water of respect (arghya), lotuses and fruits.
O Beloved Lakṣmī! In this vow of Prabodhinī, one should give a bed with its furnishings and other gifts as well; this vow destroys sins and increases merit.
Only so long do sacred fords, forests, and temples roar [with their fame]. (12)
Until the vow of Prabodhinī arrives in the month of Kārttika—
thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices, hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices,
and thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices are not equal to the merit of Prabodhinī.
On the day of Hari-bodhinī, she who has fasted indeed grants whatever was unobtainable, inaccessible, impossible to accomplish, or even impossible— be it knowledge,
wealth, royal power, the status of a subject, or stainless fame. (15)
When observed here as a fast, this Bodhinī bestows both spiritual perfection and prosperity.
By fasting on this day, one indeed burns away all great sins, heinous crimes, and acts that cause social confusion—whether they be dry or fresh. (16–17)
The night vigil performed during the Bodhinī vow burns away the mountain-like heaps of sins and misfortunes acquired over many lifetimes.
Whether observed knowingly or unknowingly, or even due to illness and such, this fast is meritorious.
Whether performed under the influence of another or while fasting, that [practice] bestows heaven and liberation.
Whatever is performed here according to the rules, with faith and devotion—even if it is very little—the fruit thereof becomes multiplied a hundred thousandfold. (1.261.20)

Whatever is done— even if it is vast as Mount Meru— if performed with ignorance, without following the prescribed rules, or without mental focus, and if accompanied by censure or malice, it is indeed fruitless.
One should certainly perform even a very small duty, but one must never practice censure or malice.
It is considered better not to perform [such acts] out of regard for censure or malice.
(22) Those men who, remembering their ancestors, perform meritorious deeds here, their ancestors, being satisfied, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (23)
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed by the vow of keeping vigil;
that which is difficult to attain even through sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice, and that which remains unobtainable through other supreme means—[all this is attained]. (24)
That [fruit] is attained with ease simply by keeping awake during the Prabodhinī [Ekādaśī].
Indeed, a fruit greater than the merit of bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) and the offering of gold to the Mahī river is obtained from keeping the vow and staying awake [in vigil]. (25–26)
He alone is truly virtuous and has sanctified a hundred lineages by whom the Prabodhinī vow was performed with devotion during the month of Kārttika.
The merit of that vow is declared to be eternal; everything else is impermanent.
Having reflected thus, one should properly perform the vow on the day of Hari.
In the home of the performer of the Prabodhinī vow, all sacred fords (tīrthas) from every quarter dwell;
that house is a king among sacred fords.
The Haribodhinī indeed bestows sons, grandsons, wealth, and prosperity;
for the sake of sons and other blessings, no other vow remains to be performed.
For one who observes the Prabodhinī vow, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are held within reach.
Established in the vow, fasting brings about knowledge, yoga, austerity, sacrifice, and self-restraint;
it nourishes righteousness, is dear to Viṣṇu, bestows liberation upon men,
and indeed destroys the sufferings of dwelling in the womb and other such miseries.
Through action, mind, and speech, Kṛṣṇa washes away both dry and moist sins during the vigil observed on the Prabodhinī vow.
Bathing, fire-offerings, recitation, and dedication performed on the Prabodhinī day directed toward Kṛṣṇa [bring this about].
This also becomes an inexhaustible libation for the ancestors.
This is declared to be the Great Vow; no other vow is like it.
It destroys the multitude of countless great sins accumulated over a hundred births.
Having gratified Janārdana here by means of the Prabodhinī vow,
he, honored by those residing in heaven, proceeds to the abode of Hari.
This is done with devotion by those seeking an abundance of beauty, loveliness, nourishment, and physical vigor.
By those desiring wives, sons, houses, fields, masters, and health;
by men and women desiring wealth, vehicles, conveyances, and the like, as well as prosperity, cattle, and riches—this Bodhinī must be diligently worshipped. (37–38)
Whatever sin has been committed during a hundred lifetimes through association with the stages of childhood, youth, and old age, is destroyed by this vow.
Whatever fruit is obtained on the Kaurava ground during a solar or lunar eclipse [is attained here].
Then, the merit of a vigil during the Prabodhinī [Ekādaśī] is a thousandfold greater.
For him whose month of Kārtika passes in vain,
his human birth is indeed fruitless both in this world and the next.
Even the fruit of meritorious deeds and other actions accumulated throughout one's life goes to waste during the month of Kārtika if it is spent in vain, and does not lead to happiness.
One should avoid food from others; by doing so, one obtains the merit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
In the month of Kārttika, the narrator of the story shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices.
Kṛṣṇa is not so pleased by sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by recitations and the like,
as he is pleased by scriptural discourses during the month of Kārttika.
Moreover, those who listen to or speak my discourse during the month of Kārttika obtain,
for every verse, the merit of gifting a thousand cows. In Kārttika, with a mind intent on the highest good and with great devotion before Keśava, [one should recite it].
O Lakṣmī! One who causes the story to be recited shall deliver a hundred families.
He who listens to the story here every day with regularity during the month of Kārttika obtains, through union with Hari, the fruit born of giving a thousand cows.
The practitioner who hears the life-story of Viṣṇu during the Prabodhinī vow obtains the fruit of gifting the earth with its seven islands.
Those who, having heard the narrative with the thought that it is Viṣṇu himself, worship the narrator of the story—
By providing them with wealth, grain, and clothing according to one's ability, their world is considered inexhaustible.
By chanting His names, worshipping Him, and listening to His life stories, one should pass the month of Kārtika; for such a person, there is indeed no returning to this world again.
He who performs storytelling, singing, instrumental music, dancing, and festivities before Lord Hari when the vow has arrived,
or does so regularly, shall indeed be a partaker of liberation. Furthermore, he who reads or listens to the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* [shall likewise attain that state].
For every single syllable of this [mantra], there shall be the fruit born from the gift of a tawny cow (kapilā).
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth when the day of Hari has arrived;
for by the giving of riches, immeasurable merit is produced.
On the tenth day, having eaten but one meal, the observer of the vow should sleep on the ground at night,
remaining self-controlled and celibate, while constantly remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa in his heart.
On the eleventh day, at dawn, he should indeed contemplate that "the Lord is awake."
Having meditated and bathed, and having made the sound of a bell, one should awaken Hari.
Having performed the daily worship of Hari, beginning with the invocation and ending with the dismissal, the observer of the vow should proceed to the excellent pavilion of Hari.
One should cause it to be adorned with plantain trunks, leaves, arches, and banners; one should have a beautiful canopy made and securely fasten it auspiciously.
In the four corners, one should place seven jars, one above the other.
One should have decorative borders fashioned all around it;
in the center, however, one should have a *sarvatobhadra* mandala made of the seven grains.
One should also have a jar made of copper or even of gold.
One should place a most excellent, new, and large jar in the center of the maṇḍala;
and there, around the maṇḍala, one should place twenty-four good jars made of gold or copper, filled with water and new.
[He should offer] rice grains adorned with the five jewels, the five leaves, and betel nuts (61);
beautified by cloth, thread, coconut fruits, and sweetmeats;
and honored with flowers, sandalwood, saffron, unbroken rice, and water (62).
Fresh vessels of sesame seeds, enriched with sugar, cardamom, and cloves, and accompanied by offerings of fruit, should be placed at their mouths.
In the central vessel, Rādhā-Dāmodara himself should be installed.
Lord Hari, in the form of the illustrious Mūrti, accompanied by Prabodhinī, should be seated on a couch at his side, adorned with the necessary implements for sleep:
a ball, a pillow, a secreted belt, and likewise a cloak. (64–65)
A fan, a chowrie, an umbrella, sandals, a mirror, as well as a tooth-stick, a water-pot, a cooking vessel, vegetable gardens, and flower gardens;
other things as well that are required, such as fruits and desired foods. || 66 ||
Those [images] should be placed right there on the couch for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa.
One should worship Śrī Gaṇeśa together with his family and offer [oblations].
One should also worship the bell, the water-pot, and the conch shell with the ritual services (upacāras).
Afterwards, the observer of the vow should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) and then invoke Hari;
he should then offer a seat, water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamana).
He should present a tooth-stick and perform the purification of cleanliness.
Thereafter, one should cause the rinsing of the mouth and the sprinkling with water from a sacred ford;
then, one should cause the bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and offer it.
Again, there is the bath with pure water, as well as the wiping with a cloth.
One should offer fine silk garments upon his limbs, worship him with fragrant substances,
and present the Kaustubha gem, the sacred thread, a tunic, a lower garment, and so forth;
one should also offer a washed tunic, a divine bodice, and a waist-belt.
A crown, an upper garment, earrings, and so forth; bracelets, anklets, and finger-rings; likewise gem-studded toe-rings, a girdle, jhanjhirās, a waist-string, a natthī, and garlands. (73–74)
One should offer necklaces made of gold and other ornaments;
as well as sandalwood paste, collyrium, powder, saffron, kesara, water, musk, white powder, vermilion, and lac-dye. (75)
One should offer other auspicious and excellent substances to the Lord of Rādhikā.
One should offer *abīra*, *gulāla*, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and flowers;
with many flowers, many fruits, camphor, agallochum (*aguru*), and saffron.
And one should perform the worship of Hari at dawn on the Bodhinī day in the month of Kārtika,
with various kinds of fruits, ritual substances, incense, lamps,
and food offerings, as well as with various sweet foods, leafy vegetables, and fermented gruel (āranālaka).
The observer of the vow should satisfy the Lord with food to be chewed, food to be eaten, food to be licked, food to be sucked, savory juices, sweet drinks,
and various kinds of fruits, doing so with devotion.
He should also satisfy Janārdana according to the prescribed rite with water from a conch shell.

The Lord whose banner is Garuḍa, the husband of Kamalā, when worshipped with a single petal of the Ketakī flower, becomes well-pleased for a thousand years. One should worship Kṛṣṇa with Agasti flowers according to the prescribed rite.
Upon merely seeing the worshiper, the fire of hell is extinguished.
Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, when worshipped with *munipuṣpa* flowers in the month of Kārttika, grants all desired objects—whether celestial, non-celestial, or even those beyond them. (82–83)
Having set aside all other flowers, he who worships Keśava with the flower of the sage (the *munipuṣpa*) with devotion in the month of Kārttika shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Likewise, [he should offer] leaves of Tulasī, flowers, and Śamī leaves.
One who offers Tulasī to Viṣṇu in the month of Kārttika shall burn away the sins accumulated over a hundred lifetimes.
Whether seen, touched, meditated upon, praised by name, lauded, planted, watered, or constantly worshipped and bowed to, Tulasī [yields this fruit]. (85–86)
O beloved, those who perform the ninefold devotion to Tulasī day after day extend their merit for thousands of millions of yugas,
as far as its branches, twigs, seeds, flowers, and fresh leaves.
The Tulasī planted by men flourishes upon the surface of the earth.
For those born in their lineage— those who have passed away, those who are yet to come, and those currently living—
their residence shall be in the abode of Hari for a thousand kalpas.

Whatever fruit is found in all flowers and whatever fruit is found in all leaves, that indeed is obtained by a single leaf of *tulasī* during the month of Kārtika. Furthermore, Viṣṇu is constantly [pleased] in Kārtika with *tulasī* leaves.
He is to be worshipped with lotuses, dhātrī leaves, and śamī leaves.
Whatever merit is gained by worshipping the gods with hundreds of sacrifices and by giving gifts many times over,
that same merit is obtained by worshipping Keśava with tulasī leaves during the month of Kārtika.
Having performed the nightly lamp-offering, prostrations, hymns of praise, circumambulations, as well as the ritual fee,
the prostration like a staff, the offering of handfuls of flowers, the request for forgiveness,
and the prayer for the completion of the vow, the practitioner should thereafter—
One should perform worship of the guru with food, clothing, and other such offerings;
(94) and with gifts of gold as dakṣiṇā for the sake of pleasing the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
Many gifts, beginning with cows, should also be bestowed. (95)
At midday, one should worship the Lord and feed Him according to the prescribed rules;
likewise in the evening, one should perform the great worship and feed Hari.
One should offer water for drinking and other necessities, and then place Him upon the swing.
One should swing [the image], gladden it, and perform a massage of its feet.
The observer of the vow should keep a vigil with singing, instrumental music, and dancing; with narrations of the Rāsa-līlā, imitations of the divine pastimes, and so forth. (97–98)
On the twelfth day at dawn, however, having bathed and worshipped Mādhava,
one should feed and satisfy [the deity] with the ārārtika offering and thus cause Hari to increase.
Having offered praise, one should dismiss all [the deities] and feed [the guests] with great devotion.
One should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, Sātvatas, Brahmins, and children well.
One should give various gifts and then perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
Having thus performed the concluding rite (udyāpana), one should present the water-pot and other items to the preceptor.
Having thus fulfilled the vow, one shall attain the Imperishable;
one obtains both worldly enjoyment and eternal, certain bliss.
Listen now regarding the performance of the Prabodhinī vow at the temple of Hari.

But Kīrtana alone, O beloved, was protected from the Rākṣasa by a single Cāṇḍāla. In the Raivata forest, at the site of Aśvapaṭṭasara, there was an unenclosed abode of Viṣṇu constructed by Brahmā. (103–104)

By the sight of whom forest-dwellers attain a happy rebirth—there was indeed a certain wretched man living on the banks of the Bhadrāvatī. He was a twice-born man who, though a *caṇḍāla* by his actions, was a wood-gatherer. 105.

For he, having lost his home, wife, and possessions due to the flooding of the river, took pleasure in dwelling in the forest by means of his work as a wood-gatherer. Endowed with auspicious latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), he was constantly devoted [to his practice] in the evening. || 106–107 ||

He goes to the abode of Viṣṇu and performs his glorification; having also brought about a vision [of the Lord], he returns once more to his own home. In the month of Kārttika, on the Prabodhinī day, he is eager to perform the ritual vigil (jāgara).
As he was traveling at night, a *rākṣasa* seized him on the road.
That *rākṣasa*, a wretch of karma, was filled with wonder and laughed; at the time of his death, he asked the fearless man the reason for his laughter. (1.261.110)
The outcaste laborer said to him: "I am blessed that death has come upon me;
today is the eleventh lunar day, the Prabhāvatī vow, which is my own fast.
I am going to the temple for chanting and worship."
"I go forth thus for the sake of awakening; even if death has arrived, then my destination is auspicious, for one who practices devotion does not go downward.
If you have hunger, then quickly devour me here."

"Or, having performed a vigil or other rites during your vow, eat me at dawn. The Rākṣasa said: "The person who is released from the very jaws of death does not return again to the place of death; therefore, my trust is placed in you."
The Cāṇḍāla said: "If it be so, come with me;
afterwards I shall perform kīrtana as you desire, then devour me.
Through kīrtana there shall be liberation, and through hearing it, too, there is deliverance."

The Rākṣasa said: "If it is so, I shall go with you; for previously, I indeed held office over the treasury of the gods' property. Within the city of Yaśodātrī, much of the gods' wealth was stolen. (117)
"By that sin, I was born as a Brahmin who is a Brahma-rākṣasa.
If indeed liberation occurs here through recitation or hearing [this], then my own liberation shall also occur; there is no need for the consumption of food. (118–119)
Having reflected thus, the two of them engaged in the vow at Viṣṇusthala during the night;
indeed, they performed a kīrtana accompanied by dancing and rhythmic clapping as sung by a Caṇḍāla,
and both observed a night vigil with great devotion.
In the morning, having become purified, the two of them met with the celestial vehicle (devayāna).
Having abandoned their bodies right there, they both went to heaven itself.
Having enjoyed pleasures for countless years, served by hosts of Apsarases, they [remained] there.
Subsequently, by the grace of Viṣṇu, those two attained liberation and went to Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, this Prabodhinī vow, which grants liberation even to those who have fallen into evil destinies, is the most excellent; it should be observed in every way by all people. 123.
Listen also to me regarding other vows that must be performed here:
when any one of these has occurred, Kārttika—the destroyer of sins—arrives;
one should bathe at the Brahma-hour and diligently perform the Kṛcchra penance.
Beginning from the month of Āśvayuja until the end of Kārttika,
one should devoutly perform the auspicious vow known as *māsopavāsa* (the month-long fast) or the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
In the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṬha*), when the lunar days decrease, the morsels of food should be the size of jujube fruits (*badara*).
Having abandoned one [mouthful] at a time, he should eat during the bright fortnight and increase [his intake].

(1.27) During the bright fortnight, as the lunar days increase, he should eat morsels the size of myrobalan fruits, increasing them by one each day; and during the other [dark] fortnight, he should decrease them. (1.28)
The first [type] is called *pipīlikā*, the second is named *yava*;
that which is diminished in the middle and increased [at the ends] is declared to be the auspicious *cāndrāyaṇa*.
Caru, alms-food, barley-meal, grain-particles, barley-gruel, and even vegetables [are its components].

Milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, or even water—these sacrificial offerings (havīṃṣi) are indeed increasingly meritorious during the vow. One should not eat on the new moon day; however, when the lunar day increases, one may eat sixteen times [during the course of the month].
When there is a loss of a lunar day (*tithi-kṣaya*), those [lost] morsels must indeed be taken as fourteen;
in any case, one should consume two hundred and forty morsels in a single month, and that too shall be the Moon-vow (*induvrata*).
If one eats eight morsels at each [meal], that is indeed the *cāndrāyaṇa* for ascetics;
if one eats four in the morning and four in the evening, that is the *śiśucāndrāyaṇa*.
Now I shall describe others; listen with a concentrated mind, O Lakṣmī! (133–134)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Kārttika Śukla Prabodhinī Vrata, the Liberation of the Outcaste-Karma Brāhmaṇa and the Rākṣasa through the Performance of the Vrata on Account of a Brāhmaṇa, and the Nature of the Cāndrāyaṇa," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 262 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 262.
[The Author: Chapter 263.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
What other vows indeed bestow merit during the month of Kārttika?
"And O Lord, tell me all those duties that must be performed by me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"A sky-lamp (ākāśadīpa) should be offered by one observing a vow in a temple of the deity."
Lamps should be offered at sacred fords by the hundreds or even by the thousands.
Lamps should be placed upon rivers, streams, ponds, lakes, oceans, wells, and tanks; these lamps are considered bestowers of heaven.
Eating only once a day and the offering of lamps during the month of Kārttika are also considered vows.
During Kārttika, it is held that one should give pulses and observe the vow of eating only at night.
One should eat three mouthfuls for a month; this is the Ṛṣiśaśi-vrata.
One should drink cow’s milk from four teats for seven nights;
from three teats for seven nights; from two teats for seven nights;
likewise from one teat for six nights; or one may subsist on air alone for three nights.
This is known as Somāyana, considered a great Cāndrāyaṇa; it consists of four days of eating a single meal, four days of eating only at night, four days of eating only what is unasked for,
and four days of fasting— thus completed in sixteen days.
That vow called *kṛcchra*, which destroys great sins, is now described.
One should drink milk, ghee, and warm water, each for one day, mixed together;
then one should fast for one day—that indeed is the *taptakṛcchra* vow. (8–9)
One should drink hot milk, ghee, and water, each separately, every day;
on the fourth day, one should fast. This is the *taptakṛcchra* penance. Furthermore, for three days at a time, one should consume hot water, milk, and ghee, followed by air [as the fourth substance].
Indeed, that is the *taptakṛcchra* vow, which one should perform by drinking [hot water] for twelve days.
And that is the *śītakṛcchra* vow, where one drinks cold [water] every three days;
the quantity for drinking is, respectively, three *palas*, two *palas*, and one *pala*.
For one day he should drink the five products of the cow mixed with darbha-water;
on the second day, by means of fasting, this is considered the Sāntapana vow.
Every day he should consume one of the products of the cow, and on the sixth day he should drink darbha-water.
On the seventh day, one should fast; this is the Madhyama-sāntapana vow.
By repeating the Sāntapana three times, it becomes the Mahāsāntapana over twenty-one days.
For each successive three-day period, one should consume cow urine, cow dung, and cow curd respectively.
Cow’s milk and cow’s ghee constitute a very great *sāntapana*;
mixed together for three days, they form the *pañcagavya*, which is the ascetic’s *sāntapana* vow.
[16] Separately, with the tender leaves of the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *padma*, and *bilva* trees...
The practitioner of the vow should drink water boiled with *kuśa* grass every day;
this is considered the *parṇakṛcchra* vow, which is to be accomplished in five days.
If one has fasted for three nights and drinks the fivefold decoction on the fourth day, [that is another form].
This vow of the leaf-bundle (*parṇakūrca*) is considered to last four days;
indeed, the month must be passed with fruits, for this is declared the *phalakṛcchra*.
With *śrīphala* fruits it is the *śrīphalakṛcchra*, and with lotuses it is the *padmakṛcchra*.
The *śrīkṛcchra* is performed with *āmalaka* fruits; the *patrakṛcchraka* with sprouts;
the *puṣpakṛcchra* with flowers; the *mūlakṛcchraka* with roots;
the *jalakṛcchra* with water; and the *dugdhakṛcchraka* with milk. (1.262.20–21)
That by which a month is passed is called the *kṛcchra* penance by that name.
By means of eating once a day, eating only at night, eating food received unasked, and fasting—
these four practices performed for four days constitute the vow known as the *pādakṛcchra*.
Three days of eating during the day, three days of eating at night, and three days of eating whatever is obtained spontaneously—then one should not eat for three days; that is the Prājāpatya vow.
Eating only as much food as fills the palm of the hand for twelve days is the Atikṛcchra.
Abstaining from food for three days is considered the Pādakṛcchra vow;
taking whatever is obtained by chance for three days is the second Pādakṛcchra;
likewise, eating only at night for three days is the third Pādakṛcchra. (25)
One should take [food] at midday for three days; this fourth part constitutes the *pādakṛcchra*.
Fifteen mouthfuls are prescribed for the middle [day], while twelve are prescribed for the night-meal (*nakta*).
For the meal taken at will (*yādṛcchika*), twenty-four mouthfuls are prescribed. (26–27)
One day [of eating] in the middle [of the day] should be observed, and the second day [should be] eating only at night (*naktaka*).
Then for two days there is eating as one pleases (*yādṛcchika*), and after that, fasting for two days.
Thus, this vow lasting six days is declared to be the *ardhakṛcchra*.
One should drink milk for twenty-one days; this is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance.
One should drink only water for twelve days; this is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance.
Fasting for twelve days is called the Pārāka Kṛcchra.
Daily consuming ground sesame and barley meal with buttermilk, followed by a fast for four days—this is declared to be the Saumya-kṛcchra vow.
Daily consuming ground sesame, buttermilk, water, and water infused with kuśa grass; ||| 31 ||

The *saumyakṛcchra* consists of fasting for five days; that is one variety of the *saumyakṛcchra*. (32) Eating sesame paste, boiled rice, liquid extract, buttermilk, water, and barley meal, followed by a six-day fast—that is considered another variety of the *saumyakṛcchra*. (33)
One should practice [the consumption of] sesame paste and so forth individually for three nights each;
that is to be understood as the *tulāpuruṣa-kṛcchra*, lasting fifteen days.
At the end of those fifteen days, one should then subsist on air for three days and again for three days.
The *tulānṛkṛcchra* consists of fasting for twenty-one days.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika, one should remain in water and subsist on air;
on the full moon day, one should fast—this is considered the *jalakṛcchra* vow.
On the tenth day, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and on the eleventh day, one should observe a fast;
one should perform the worship of Viṣṇu, for this is remembered as the Harikṛcchra vow.
From the seventh day onward, one should drink water, milk, curd, and ghee separately.
One should fast on the eleventh day; this is the Paitāmaha Kṛcchra vow.
(38) The practitioner should drink water for three days starting from the sixth lunar day and fast for another three days;
on the twelfth day he should perform the breaking of the fast; this is the Māhendraka Kṛcchra vow. (39)
For three days starting from the third day, one should consume rice mixed with water, and for three days, barley gruel (*yāvaka*).
Then, for three days, one should fast; that indeed is the Viṣṇu-kṛcchra vow.
Starting from the first lunar day (*pratipad*), one should consume milk for five days and curd for five days.
One should fast on the eleventh day; this is called the Bhāskara-kṛcchra.
From the fifth day of the bright fortnight, one should consume in sequence beans, barley, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, and water; this is the Saptarṣi-kṛcchra vow.
The practitioner should gradually drink either milk or boiled water,
using the leaves of *palāśa*, *bilva*, *darbha*, *abja*, *udumbara*, and *parṇaka* separately.
This fast on the sixth lunar day is known as the Agnikṛcchra vow.
From the seventh day onwards, one should respectively consume milk, a bilva fruit, and a lotus;
on the eleventh day, one should fast and eat lotus fibers.
This five-day rite is known as the Lakṣmī-kṛcchra vow.
The Brahmakūrca vow is the most excellent, the supreme among all vows;
by performing it, human beings are liberated from all sins.
This can be accomplished in three days; I shall now describe its procedure.
On the ninth day, however, one should fast and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with water infused with kuśa grass.
On the tenth day, one should consume cow urine, cow dung, milk, water from darbha grass, ghee, and curd; and on the eleventh day, one should fast.
That is declared to be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), which is purifying and cleanses the body:
the urine of a copper-colored cow, the dung of a white cow,
the milk of a golden-colored cow, and likewise the curd of a blue-colored cow.
Now, regarding the fivefold [offering] of ghee from either a black cow or a Kapila cow:
one is golden-hued, the second is tawny (apiṅgalā), the third has red eyes, and the fourth is deep tawny (gūḍapiṅgalā). || 51 ||
The fifth is Karburā; the sixth should be Śvetapiṅgalā;
the seventh is indeed Śvetapiṅgākṣī; the eighth is Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā;
the ninth should be Pāṭalā; and the tenth is Pucchapiṅgalā.
These ten types of *kapilā* cows, which provide the sacrificial oblation (*havya*), have been declared.
In the absence of any of these [cows], the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are considered auspicious.
Eight *māṣas* of cow urine and sixteen of cow dung;
Twelve *māṣakas* of milk are to be taken for the sake of awakening (*bodhi*); ten indeed for curd;
eight *māṣakas* of clarified butter; and four of *kuśa* water.
[This should be done] with the mantra bearing the name Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, or else with the *gāyatrī*.
Having taken that fivefold cow-product (pañcagavya) and having drawn it out, one should indeed offer it into the fire with a Ṛc verse, or with the Gāyatrī, or from the Puṃsūkta;
[using] Kuśa grass that is green, uncurved, and possessed of seven tips.
A fire sacrifice (homa) is prescribed with one hundred and eight recitations of the names of Hari.
The remainder of the oblation, consecrated with the Praṇava, is to be drunk.
It [the vessel] should be supported by the Praṇava and lifted up with the Praṇava. 58.
One should drink [the liquid] with a leaf from the middle of a *palāśa* tree, or with a lotus petal;
one may also drink from a golden vessel, a silver vessel, or by means of the *brahmatīrtha*.
This is called the *brahmakūrca*; it destroys sins and likewise bestows liberation. (1.262.60)
Having consumed sesame seeds for twelve days, that is the Agnikṛcchra vow.
One should complete the Yavakṛcchra by subsisting for a month on barley grains dropped by a cow;
indeed, one should eat only the flour of barley grains dropped by a cow for exactly one month.
That is declared to be the Yāmya-kṛcchra, which destroys the impurities of the body.
One should subsist daily on a handful of sesame paste for one month; that is declared to be the Kuberakṛcchra vow.
One should perform one's bath with cow urine, and one may even consume cow dung.
One should dwell in the midst of cows and likewise sleep upon cow-dung.
One should not drink until the cows have drunk, nor should one eat until they have eaten.
One should rise when they rise and sit down when they sit;
this vow is to be observed for exactly one month, and it should be understood as the "cow-vow" (gobrata).
It consists of dwelling among the virtuous, serving the virtuous, and conducting oneself like the virtuous.
The food and drink of a virtuous person are pleasing and constitute a righteous vow.
By means of *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), one may subsist for two months; by milk, for a fortnight;
by curd, for eight days; and by ghee, for three days.
One should remain without food for three days; this indeed is the Uddālaka vow.
A person desiring prosperity, desiring nourishment, likewise desiring heaven, and desiring to gratify the gods, should perform the Kṛcchra penance with devotion. (68–69)
Thus have these *kṛcchra* vows been described to you, O Lotus-born one; they destroy sin and grant liberation to all.
Performing all these *kṛcchras*, one should restrain speech, mind, and senses.
Wearing clean garments and remaining tranquil, one who has bathed should worship Hari.
(71) The observer of the vow should always consume all the ritual substances, such as milk and the like, only those things offered by Śrī Hari and nothing else. (72)
If, while performing difficult penances, he should become bewildered or fall into a swoon,
one should give that seeker of the vow to drink the nectar-like milk of cows.
Water, juice, fruit, flower, buttermilk, leaf, milk, and curd— [these are the permitted substances].
Cooked grain, curd-mixture, herbs, decoction, bulbous root, potherb, and the word of a guru;
the command of a Brahmin, an unknown morsel, the swallowing of calamity, mouth-freshening substances, fresh butter, and sugar. (74–75)
Concealed items include preparations of milk and the like, as well as sesame oil from sesame seeds and so forth;
likewise, *bhivārā* and other forest-hermit foods, *bhūphalī*, and the pulp of trees; cloves, cardamom, black pepper, cinnamon, ginger, *sūṃpha*, and *guṇḍraka*. (76)

Resin (śilārasa), musk (kastūrī), sandalwood (candana), salt (lavaṇa), honey (madhu), and Dhūmra—these forty indeed do not destroy a vow. At the conclusion of the vow, one should feed virtuous men; that shall become an eternal fruit.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Kṛcchra Vows to be Performed in Kārttika," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 262. [Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Part 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*), Chapter 263]
[The Author: Chapter 264.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
That which is called "kṛcchra" (hardship) is indeed suffering, yet that very suffering has been offered to you as happiness.
This difficult vow, which bestows happiness and merit, has been related to you incidentally.
(1) Indeed, you alone are the meritorious vow, as well as everything that is to be drunk and eaten;
for everything is fruitless without you, since that is certainly the case. (2)
Tell me, O Blessed One, regarding the month known as Puruṣottama:
what is the name of the Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight, and what is the fruit of its vow? What is the ritual procedure, what is the manner of worship, and which deity is worshipped therein?

What is the gift and what are the observances? Tell me all this in great detail. (4) What is the ritual bath, what is the mantra to be recited, and what food is considered most excellent? What is to be avoided during this month as well? Tell me that, O Janārdana. (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In the month exceeding eleven [days], she is known by the name Kamalā;
he is called Puruṣottama, and he, her husband, is to be worshipped.
The Lord Hari, the master, is accompanied by Lakṣmī and exists in the form of gold;
Śrī Lakṣmī and Puruṣottama, residing in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, are to be meditated upon.
By means of this vow dedicated to Kamalā, Kamalā herself shall become favorable here.
On the tenth day, one should eat but once; at night, one should sleep upon the ground.
One should remain celibate and abandon anger and the like.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and recollected Puruṣottama, [one should proceed]. (8–9)
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite on the first day of the month of Puruṣottama at dawn,
the observer of the vow should undertake the restraints that are indeed purifying for embodied beings and must be maintained.
There is a fixed rule for the recitation of the thousand or hundred-thousand names:

the recitation performed at home yields one-fold merit; it is remembered as two-fold by a river; it is a thousand-fold in a cow-pen; and that same merit becomes a hundred-thousand-fold in a fire-sanctuary. (11–12)
In sacred fields of the gods, at holy fords, and likewise in the presence of the virtuous, [the merit] is ten million-fold; in the presence of Tulasī, it is a hundred million-fold.
But in the presence of Viṣṇu, the recitation of prayers certainly becomes infinite.
The *mālikāvartana* is known as that which destroys the whirlpool of *saṃsāra*.
During the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*) dedicated to Puruṣottama, those observances (*niyamas*) must be undertaken in both months; they bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
These should be undertaken at the beginning of the month in the presence of the image of Hari.
One must avoid fermented foods, as well as the avoidance of oil.
There should be the avoidance of ghee and the renunciation of oils and the like, along with the avoidance of pungent substances.
The renunciation of fragrant oils, the avoidance of the enjoyment of flowers,
(17) the avoidance of pungent, sour, sweet, salty, bitter, and astringent [tastes],
the avoidance of betel-leaf, and also the avoidance of sweet fruits and the like. (18)
Eating from a *pālāśa* leaf, abstaining from oiling the feet,
renouncing the anointing of the head, and avoiding curd and milk;
(19) the renunciation of collyrium and the like, and abstaining from eating twice a day.
One should observe silence, engage in sacred discourse, and avoid vulgar conversation.
One should renounce the *sthālīpāka* offering, abstain from leafy vegetables, renounce all food,
and avoid at least one type of fruit.
Consuming food upon a stone slab, eating from a plantain leaf, performing ablutions at Puṣkara, and the avoidance of bathing at home;
touching the lotus feet of the Guru and bowing to the feet of Viṣṇu. 22.
Eating once a day, eating only at night, or fasting;
or performing the smearing, sweeping, and washing of Lord Hari’s temple;
and circumambulating Him one hundred and eight times, or even more. (23–24)
Singing, instrumental music, and dancing; or else consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
awakening through the discourse of the scriptures and the narration of the accounts of Vyāsa;
the worship with Tulasī leaves and the sprinkling of water in the temple of Viṣṇu.
Eating from leaves, the avoidance of split pulses and similar foods;
accepting only what is offered as a favor, not eating from copper vessels and the like;
not eating from bell-metal vessels, and not eating food that has been cooked by oneself. || 26–27 ||
Eating only grains cooked in water, eating only cooked grains,
eating from an earthen vessel, drinking water from one's cupped hands,
eating from the hollow of the palms, and sitting upon the bare ground. (28)

The gift of a tawny cow, food as radiant as a lotus petal, and alms-food which is like nectar—this auspicious vow brings about liberation. The gift of gold, the gift of silver, the gift of clothing, and the offering of a house. (1.263.30)

The constant giving of food and other gifts according to one's ability is a source of great merit. Viṣṇu and the virtuous man—these two are the supreme among men. One should perform their worship and likewise serve them every day.
Whether he be a Śūdra or even a Śūdra woman, one should perform service for the Guru, who is Hari.
The Guru is indeed the form of Viṣṇu; the Guru is the embodiment of the three deities.
Service should be performed with the body in such a way that the Guru may be pleased.
For this [practice], consisting of the five elements, has been declared to be purposeless;
yet by serving the Guru with it, one shall attain infinite fruit.
This dharma is difficult to find in the world, for it bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation.
The vow of "not asking" (ayācita) should be observed, avoiding malice, violence, and the like.
Generosity, compassion, and self-restraint must indeed be practiced even by the great.
Those who offer their bodies and worldly wealth to the Guru [attain this]. 35–36.
Indeed, by the power of their charity, they have attained the state of being beloved by Viṣṇu.
Honey should be abandoned, ghee should be abandoned, and likewise milk and other such items;
one should also avoid pomegranate, citron, and coconut.
The renunciation of rice, the renunciation of barley, and the avoidance of wheat;
[38] likewise, the recitation of a word, a verse, a hymn, a chapter, or a sacred narrative before Hari—this vow of Viṣṇu bestows his abode. [39]
The renunciation of sexual intercourse and the abandonment of ritual action constitute a great vow.
One should avoid curd, milk, buttermilk, molasses, and vegetables.
A bath should be performed with *āmalaka* fruits or indeed with sesame seeds.
The fruit of the *dhātrī* tree always removes sin, and sesame seeds are indeed purifying.
(41) The vow of silence during the twilight hours must be observed, as must the non-extinguishing of the sacred fire at night;
likewise, eating in silence is a virtuous vow that brings about purity. (42)
Eating in silence is known to yield fruit equal to a fast.
Falsehood, anger, and backbiting— whether characterized by passion (rājasa) or ignorance (tāmasa)—
must be abandoned in every way during the month of Puruṣottama.
One should perform meritorious deeds and auspicious actions, and abandon evil karma.
Puruṣottama is to be meditated upon, worshipped, propitiated, and remembered;
indeed, even difficult rites should be performed during the month of Puruṣottama.
For one who performs the vow of Kamalā, Kamalā is born in the home.
Likewise, for one who meditates at dawn on the eleventh day upon Kamalā, Lakṣmī, and Śrī Puruṣottama, and bathes according to the prescribed rite—
One should perform the daily worship within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala.
Then, one should worship twelve jars filled with water and precious petals, and provided with unbroken rice, fruits, garments, and other offerings. (47–48)
In the center, the observer of the vow should place a jar made of gold or copper;
he should then worship it together with pure water, fruits, jewels, and other such items.
Likewise, he should worship the bell, the conch, and the pitcher with these same materials.
Having placed the image of Puruṣottama upon a vessel of sesame seeds atop a water-pot,
the performer of the vow should worship Him according to the prescribed rite with all necessary materials.
He should perform the invocation and other rites, as well as the anointing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should cause the image to bathe with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and wipe its body clean.
One should offer garments, ornaments, decorations, sandalwood paste, and the like.
One should also offer collyrium, agallochum, musk, and fragrant oil.
One should offer necklaces, ornaments, beauty aids, incense, lamps, and so forth;
various kinds of food offerings, fruits, water, and aromatic powder; and having given auspicious betel leaf, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord. 53–54.
One should whirl the conch-water clockwise like a staff,
and having performed praise, salutation, and a request for forgiveness, one should prepare the bed and so forth;
then, by massaging the feet, one should cause bliss to blossom.
One should give abundant gifts; likewise, one should act similarly at midday.
One should feed various kinds of food and worship with extreme devotion.
In the evening, one should perform the ārārtika rite, and having offered hymns of praise, one should likewise feast [the deities].
At night, one should keep a vigil accompanied by dance and song;
then, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), having bathed at dawn and likewise worshipped Hari,
one should feed the preceptor, perform his worship, and feed many others.
Then, on the following day, one should break the fast and give gifts with devotion.
In this way, one should indeed perform the vow which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
likewise, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the observances, which yields fruit.
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, and a mandala made with the seven types of grain;
one should also have svastikas fashioned and gifts of beds distributed.
There, the observer of the vow should worship Śrī Hari and Ramā according to the prescribed rite.
One should give a cow, an image of a cow, and likewise food to virtuous people.
Then, after the great worship of the deity with sixteen articles, one should offer the teacher whatever is required, such as clothing, food, ornaments, and so forth. (62, 66)
Indeed, the observer of the vow himself should personally give various gifts;
at the conclusion of the rite, however, gifts must be given for the fulfillment of the vow.
When the concluding rite is performed, everything certainly becomes complete.

O Mahālakṣmī! Having undertaken a vow, if one does not perform its concluding rite (udyāpana), one will encounter a deficiency in the vow and shall not fully partake of its fruit. Whatever specific rule was personally observed during the vow, that which corresponds to it [must be fulfilled]. (65–66)
At the conclusion of the rite, the observer of the vow must personally bestow gifts.
It is traditionally taught that in the case of abstaining from oil, one should give ghee; in the case of abstaining from ghee, milk.
In the case of observing silence, sesame seeds and other such items, along with gold, should be given to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
During the meal, one should offer food accompanied by curd and rice (68).
One should indeed give sweet food enriched with gold in great abundance.
Furthermore, one who eats from a vessel made of *pālāśa* leaves should offer sweet items such as clarified butter and the like (69).
One who eats only at night should indeed give a meal endowed with the six flavors;
one who abstains from asking for alms should offer a bull along with its equipment;
and one who renounces black gram should give a well-characterized cow together with her calf.
One observing a vow should give a *māṣa* measure of gold during the ritual bath with *dhātrī* fruits.
Indeed, in the case of a restriction on fruits, one should give various kinds of fruits;
in the case of a restriction on grains, one should give grains such as rice and wheat.
One should give a bed with cotton and a pillow upon the ground;

indeed, for the sake of celibacy, one should provide meals for a married couple. Furthermore, when vegetables are renounced, one should give vegetables; and when beauty products are renounced, one should give liquids and the like.
In the vow of daily bathing, one should give ghee and roasted flour (saktu) to a person free from worldly attachment.
In the vow regarding nails and hair, one should give a mirror, a fan, and so forth.
Upon the renunciation of sandals, one should joyfully give a pair of sandals.
Upon the complete renunciation of milk and other such items, one should indeed give a tawny cow;
during the vow of the lamp, one should indeed give a golden lamp-vessel;
and upon the observance of the restraint from sexual intercourse, one should give silver, wealth, and so forth.
Thus, whatever vow has been performed according to one's desire, and whatever restraint has been observed,
one should effect the fulfillment of that restraint by giving those very things.
[One should perform] the gift of a cow, the gift of sugar, the gift of a house, and the offering of wealth.

The gift of land, the gift of a maiden, the gift of the sacred thread, the gift of knowledge, the gift of liberation, and even the offering of one’s own self—these indeed bestow heaven and liberation;
of this there is no doubt. (79)
What is the use of saying more here? Whatever may be most dear to one, for the sake of attaining that again, one should undoubtedly make a gift of it;
indeed, the supreme gift is the offering of all that is one’s own to Hari.
One should indeed give one’s entire possession to the Guru or to the giver of liberation.
A skillful person should achieve eternal liberation by means of that which is impermanent.
For one who performs the vow of Kamalā, Kamalā herself comes to his home.
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall relate the ancient narrative of what occurred in the past.
(83) At Haridvāra there was a certain Brahmin named Śākaṭāyana;
his cart was indeed small, serving as both his home and his place of rest. (84)
Subsisting on alms, using grass and cotton for bedding, and possessing only a mat and a ball for play, he lived near the celestial Gaṅgā with his hands as his only bowl.
Once, he went out toward the horizon to beg for alms.
"O beloved, his cart was indeed swept away by a sudden downpour of rain.
Seeing his cart taken away and himself without a vehicle, he then departed from there on foot,
alone for the sake of pilgrimage, toward the sacred site known as Prayāgarāja."
Emaciated by hunger, with a dejected face, he performed his ablutions in the Triveṇī;
afflicted by hunger, he searched there for the hermitages of the sages.
There, he beheld the divine and wonderful hermitage of Bhāradvāja.
Indeed, during the month of Puruṣottama, there was an assembly of people;
there, in that hermitage, he heard from the mouth of Bhāradvāja a delightful story concerning Kamalā, which is easily accessible and destroys all impurities.
Having heard the narrative of Ekādaśī— which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
is proclaimed in the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, and grants wealth—
that Brahmin Śākaṭāyana heard that story concerning Kamalā.
Having then performed the vow together with them while staying in the hermitage of the sage,
he kept a night vigil, remembering Kṛṣṇa within his heart.
At the hour of Brahmā on the twelfth day, Lakṣmī arrived there.
With divine limbs, divine luster, and adorned with divine ornaments, she said:
"I am pleased by my vow; I grant you a boon here.
The Brahmin Śākaṭāyana, filled with wonder, also questioned her.
"Who are you, and to whom do you belong, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks? And how have you become so gracious toward me?
Lakṣmī replied: "I have become gracious due to the power of your vow.
Urged by the God of gods, I have come here from Vaikuṇṭha."

"Because of your observance of the vow of Kamalā during the month of Puruṣottama, I have come here to bestow upon you abundant fortune and prosperity. Your vow was performed by you at Prayāga through the conjunction with a sage."
"Under the power of my vow, I grant you this blessing: 'May you become wealthy.
(98) Where the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) occurs at sunrise, the twelfth (Dvādaśī) at midday, and the thirteenth (Trayodaśī) at the end of the night—that is the most excellent of all vows. (99)
In that regard, there is great merit in breaking the fast on the thirteenth day;
you have observed this vow, O great sage, and I am well-pleased with you.
Accept this divine gem, from which gold is obtained.
Having spoken thus, Kamalā gave him the jewel and vanished.
The Brahmin Śākaṭāyana also took the jewel and went home.
This great jewel grants a hundred pieces of gold every morning.
The brahmin Śākaṭāyana also gave gifts day and night;
thus that excellent sage, the earthly deity Śākaṭāyana,
obtained prosperity even greater than Indra’s through the vow of Kamalā.
"Whatever a beggar desires from my house, that must be given to him.
Thus was it proclaimed by Śākaṭāyana upon the surface of the earth.
Then once, a certain Brahmin named Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, [arrived].
Having heard this account of Maṇi’s generosity, and having reflected upon it, the sage himself went to Śākaṭāyana’s house with the desire to beg for the jewel;
though the sage was free from worldly desire, he begged for that jewel, and Maṇi gave it to him.
Pulastya also, taking the jewel, went to the island of Siṃhala. There, he fashioned everything—cities, forests, and so forth—out of gold. He then presented that jewel to Kubera, the lord of wealth.
Then Rāvaṇa abducted her, and he made it his own golden Laṅkā.
Indeed, if the goddess Kamalā is pleased by this vow, she grants everything to the devotee for whom this vow is a source of satisfaction. (1.09)

Whether one hears or even reads [this], the fruit shall be that of Kamalā. (1.263.110) Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Majesty of the Kamala-Ekādaśī of the Dark Fortnight of the Month of Puruṣottama, the Observances, the Udyāpana Ceremony, the Attainment of Jewels and Lakṣmī through the Vow of Śākaṭāyana, and Subsequently the Acquisition of Gold by Pulastya, Kubera, and Rāvaṇa," in the first section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (Chapter 263)

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
This is most pleasant for listeners to hear, the unsurpassed among purifiers, divine, and a destroyer of bad dreams; it must be heard by me with great effort. (1)
Among months, the supreme month is known as Puruṣottama,
for in it the Lord himself is truly manifest as Puruṣottama.
All the immortal gods of heaven desire to take birth upon the surface of the earth [during this time].
They worship that supreme person, Nārāyaṇa.
(3) Those who always chant with devotion to the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa, are constantly worshipped by the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā. (4)
O Puruṣottama, tell me: what is the name of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of that month of the God of gods?
O Lord, tell me: what is the ritual procedure, what is the fruit, what is the gift, and who is the deity?
By performing which vow a person may attain the imperishable heaven.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the bright fortnight of the month of Puruṣottama, [there is] Dhāmadā.
It is called by the name Ekādaśī, which is the abode of Brahman.
Here, the ritual procedure consists of Brahman, and the fruit is traditionally held to consist of Brahman.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is considered the Lord of the abode of Brahman and its Master.
This Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is indeed beyond the syllable;
accompanied by his consort, the Imperishable, he bestows the divine abode.
He is to be worshipped with the flowers of the creeper of liberation and with the fruits of immortality.
Charity, sacred knowledge, and the Upanishads are indeed the givers of liberation.
The gift of initiation, the gift of Brahman, the gift of the Vedas, and the offering of one's own self— indeed,
the surrender of everything here is considered the highest among all gifts.
O beloved, any other gift is inferior compared to the foremost gift of the Bhagavān’s abode;
the gift that brings about the attainment of that abode is considered the most excellent gift.
On the tenth lunar day, one should eat but once, sleep on the ground, and observe celibacy.

Having risen in the morning, one should meditate upon the Imperishable Puruṣottama; and having recollected Him who bestows the [divine] abode, one should perform the ritual bath according to the rules. Having performed the daily worship, one should carry out the great worship (mahāpūjā).
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, featuring a *sarvatobhadra* mandala;
and one should have a flawless jar, filled with gems and containing gold, prepared.
Then, one should place it within the mandala, provided with cloth, water, and fruit.
One should place a large copper vessel upon a water-pot (kumbha).
There, one should display a twelve-petaled lotus made with saffron.
Therein, one should worship Puruṣottama together with the syllables (of the mantra). || 16–17 ||
Having thus installed [the deity] together with the lotus according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform the great worship (mahāpūjā) with the sixteen types of service (upacāra).
This [deity] is divine, served by the great liberated ones (mahāmukta) such as Prabhā and others.
I meditate upon the beautiful and supreme Lord, joined by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others.
With my mind, I invoke Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of grace upon His devotees.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Puruṣottama, please sit upon the golden throne.
Accept the Gaṅgā water for washing the feet along with the imperishable syllable (Oṃ).
Indeed, accept this water for the arghya offering, joined with fragrance, flowers, and other ingredients.
Accept this filtered water from the sacred ford as the water for sipping (ācamanīya).

O Janārdana, please graciously accept these five nectars— milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar— for the purpose of the ritual bath. Please accept the waters of the ocean and the rivers for the sake of the ablution.
Please accept this upper garment made of fine wool, as well as the bodice and other such items.
Indeed, take this cotton cloth, the waist-belt, the bodice, and so forth.
O Supreme Person, please accept this silk thread for the sacred thread.
Let armlets, bracelets, rings, crowns, and anklets;
let waist-bands, strings, and necklaces be taken; let gems, gold, flower-garlands, and ornaments be gathered. (25–26)
Apply anointment with musk, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood.
Take the kadamba, campaka, lotus, kunda, and jasmine flowers.
O Nārāyaṇa, accept this fragrant incense with devotion.
O Puruṣottama, accept this beautiful lamp made of ghee. O Puruṣottama, bring the highly radiant ārātrika, enriched with saffron, rice, gulāla, and collyrium; please accept it.
Take this food— milk-rice, cakes, and the like, along with cow-ghee polikās,
curd, milk, ghee, and sweets, O Lord of Kamalā! Drink this cool water, rich in fragrance, from sacred sites, O Mādhava!
Please accept this betel leaf, enriched with pūga-nuts and khadira-wood.
Please accept these plantains, mangoes, grapes, pomegranates, and bilva fruits.
O Kṛṣṇa, please accept this golden sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) along with diamonds and other gems.
"Please accept these flowers and unbroken grains held in my joined palms.
Salutations to you, O Beloved of Kamalā; salutations to the Sovereign Lord of the Imperishable. O Lord, Master of the Imperishable, I prostrate myself like a staff; please accept me."
There is no other refuge but you; you alone are my refuge.
(34) O Lord of Śrī, fulfill my vow; O Lord of the Imperishable, protect me!
[Grant] food, clothing, gold, vegetables, a bed, ghee, and so forth. (35)
"I offer this to the twice-born with the thought that it is for Hari; please accept it.
Having thus worshipped with true devotion, the observer of the vow should pass the remainder of the day, give gifts according to his capacity, and perform his necessary duties.
At midday as well, one should offer very sweet food, sacrificial offerings (naivedya), water, and so forth;
and in the evening, one should perform a great worship with many articles.
One should also perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) accompanied by five wicks of clarified butter.
Having offered food offerings, drinking water, betel-leaf, and a foot-massage,
and having performed recitations and songs, one should keep a vigil at night.
[One should go] toward the temple of Hari for the sake of the vigil, or toward the monastery of the virtuous.
For a man who goes [on this pilgrimage], there is the fruit of the horse-sacrifice at every step. (1.264.40) Having bathed in the morning, one should again perform the daily and occasional worship;
one should offer food to the Lord and then feed the devotees. (41)
Then the observer of the vow should present gifts of golden images to the preceptor;
furthermore, he should indeed give many other desired gifts.
He should feed virtuous Vaiṣṇavas and virtuous women with delicious food.
Then the observer of the vow should perform the breaking of the fast with sacrificial food (haviṣya).
On the twelfth day, he should avoid sleeping during the day, food from others, eating a second time, sexual intercourse, oil, and even tamasic food.
If even a very small portion of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be obtained on the day of breaking the fast,
the observer of the vow should perform the breaking of the fast on that very day and must not let it pass.
The first quarter of the twelfth day is said to be the day of Hari.
In that regard, one who desires imperishable merit must certainly not eat there.
Thus, the vow for the gift of a dwelling should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
And at the end, the Lord shall lead that devotee to His own abode by means of a celestial chariot.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear the account that occurred long ago during the Dhāmadā vow.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Puṇḍarīka, a devotee of Viṣṇu and a universal emperor who looked upon all things with equanimity. (48)
Like a virtuous person, he is entirely free from attachment to the body and all bodily things.
On the day of his vow, he spends half the day in worship and the remainder in administering justice;
indeed, on that specific day of observance, he performs only the act of worship.
His queen, named Kumudvatī, was devoted to her husband;
regarding her husband’s command as the very command of the scriptures, she served her husband.
Without having asked her own husband for permission, she did not form even the slightest mental resolve to do anything.
Once, while Puṇḍarīka was engaged in the worship of Dhāmadā,
the queen residing in the inner apartments was overcome by fever. In order to preserve her health, she went at evening without having asked her husband for permission.
Accompanied by her maidservants, she went to the garden in the grove.
Taking a fruit that was agreeable to her hunger and not aggravating her fever,
the devoted wife drank its juice, which possessed nine colors.
Since that devoted wife drank [the water] without having first offered it to her husband, a breach occurred in her wifely devotion and her fever increased greatly.
Having drunk the water out of thirst, she remained right there during the night. (55–56)
Today, in this day, my daily service to my husband was not performed in the morning;
likewise, the sight of my husband’s face in the morning did not occur at all.
Furthermore, I did not receive even a single drop of water from my husband’s thumb.
Fallen into a state of helplessness and afflicted by illness, her devotion to her husband was brought to ruin.
At that time, her fever became exceedingly intense and her body withered away;
through the power of her wifely devotion, the queen became a partaker of misfortune.
Facing death, she was tormented and utterly withered;
yet, despite her misfortune, the life-breaths of Kumudvatī did not depart.
Puṇḍarīka also heard of the queen’s illness.
When her vow was completed, he returned and performed service for her.
Her lifespan reached its full term, yet her life-breaths did not depart.
Then the king, having offered water, presented the fruit of Dhāmadā.
His life-breaths departed swiftly, and a divine celestial chariot arrived,
beautifully adorned by Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, and his attendants,
and graced by the glorious Puruṣottama together with the Imperishable One (Akṣara).
And the second celestial chariot arrived, which is the abode of the Imperishable.
First, she was led by Viṣṇu in that chariot accompanied by Ramā;
afterwards, she was brought to Vaikuṇṭha and ascended another celestial chariot.
She was led to the imperishable abode by the Lord of Śrī Puruṣottama;
thus, through the merit she gained, that giver of the abode herself entered the abode.
What then need be said of those who observe the vow of giving an abode? || 66 ||
Therefore, one should especially observe the vow of the month of Puruṣottama on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight;
for this vow bestows the supreme abode, as well as liberation and prosperity. (67–68)
By hearing and by reciting it, one shall obtain a fruit equal to that of the vow itself.
For those with desires, there shall arise great prosperity, the state of the supreme lord (Pārameṣṭhya), and so forth.
This should be performed according to one's capacity by one who desires auspiciousness.
"The Imperishable One, the Bestower of Abodes, shall grant him both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(1.264.7) Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Ekādaśī Vow of the White Abode in the Month of Puruṣottama within the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning how King Puṇḍarīka and his wife Kumudvatī—who, though deprived of even a slight share of service to her husband—attained the Abode of the Imperishable through this vow. 264.
