Chapter 266 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Blessed One, all the concluding rites (udyāpana) and the worship of all the gods have been described; O Lord, all of that has been understood by me. (1)
"If the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) for all Ekādaśīs were to be performed as a single act, then how extensive would it be? Tell me that.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the single characteristic of all [these rites], as well as the complete concluding ceremony (udyāpana) that bestows the full fruit. When a beautiful pavilion has been constructed, adorned with plantain pillars...
Having prepared a *sarvatobhadra* mandala, one should place a water-pot in its center (4).
It should be provided with the sprouts of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *cūta*, and *nyagrodha* trees, joined with gems, its neck wrapped in cloth, and likewise filled with water (5).
One should place a very large vessel filled with saffron before him.
Having fashioned a twelve-petaled lotus endowed with twelve petals,
one should place in its center a golden image of Vāsudeva, who is attended by Ramā.
One should install the twenty-four lords of the eleven [groups] all around.
One should also install them together with their respective consorts in order, starting from the east.
On the first [petal] are Śrī and Keśava; then on the lotus petals are Padmā and Nārāyaṇa.
Mādhava with Nityā, Govinda with Candrā,
Viṣṇu with Ramā, and Madhusūdana with Mādhavī;
Trivikrama with Padmākṣī, and Vāmana joined with Kamalā.
Śrīdhara with Kāntimatī, Hṛṣīkeśa with Aparājitā,
Padmanābha with Padmavatī, and then Rādhā and Dāmodara; furthermore,
on the eastern petal is Saṃkarṣaṇa together with Sunandā.
Then Vāsudeva was with Hariṇī, Pradyumna with Dhī, Aniruddha with Suśīlā, Puruṣottama with Nandā,
Adhokṣaja with Trayī, and Nṛkesarin with Kṣemaṃkarī.
Acyuta, joined with Vijayā, and Janārdana, with Sundarī;
Upendra, joined with Subhagā, and Hari, with Hiraṇyā;
Kṛṣṇa, joined with Sulakṣaṇā—these should be installed according to the prescribed rite. (13–14)

One should perform the bathing of the central deity with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), preceded by anointing with oil; then one should perform the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) and offer garments, ornaments, and the like.
One should worship with all types of perfumes, flowers, and *tulasī* leaves.

One should offer incense, a lamp, sandalwood, food offerings, and water. (16) Likewise, one should offer sweetmeats, fried cakes, flour preparations, butter-filled pastries, *sohilakas*, *kaṃsāras*, roasted barley flour, *sevās*, and *polikās*. (17)
Pūrikās, milk-rice (pāyasa), the essence of milk (dugdhasāra), as well as curd-rice (dadhyodana);
cakes (piṇḍakas), balls (vaṭakas), the hundred-holed (śatacchidrān), and śaṣkulīs;
sesame-preparations (tilapāka), rice-preparations (śālipāka), mung-bean flour (mudgacūrṇa), and jaggery-rice (guḍaudana).
Likewise, one should offer plantain fruit and other various kinds of sweet foods in abundance.
One should also offer diverse vegetables, various fruits, betel leaf with mouth-fresheners and the like, and water as well.
Having performed the great *nīrājana* ceremony, one should then offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
One should likewise perform praise, prostrations with the body like a staff (*namo-daṇḍavat*), and a request for forgiveness.
Having thus completed the worship, one should give gifts with sincere devotion.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, horses, elephants, vehicles,

and garments; then, in a temple or a cow-pen, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and boiled rice, accompanied by flower essences, while invoking each deity by their respective names.
One should give twenty-four cows, or even one cow accompanied by gold;
likewise, one should worship at midday and feed [the Brahmins] according to the prescribed rule.
In the evening, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and likewise worship and feed them.
Having kept a vigil at night, one should worship Hari at dawn.
The observer of the vow should give an image fashioned of gold to his own guru;
thereafter, the observer of the vow should also give ornaments, garments, and a bed.
One should feed twenty-four Brahmins, virtuous men, and chaste women;
one should offer water-pots to Viṣṇu and likewise bestow sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, after having fed one's own people, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
When this is done, the fruit of twenty-four Ekādaśīs shall be obtained. No stinginess regarding wealth should be practiced during the great festival of the concluding rite (udyāpana);
for Kṛṣṇa himself, the beloved of Lakṣmī, being the bestower of prosperity, is surely pleased.
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall speak of the cow-gift, the mountain-gift, and others; listen.
Having performed the worship, the observer of the vow should then give abundant wealth to the guru. In the event of great prosperity, the observer of the vow should give ten kinds of cows.
One should offer ten kinds of Merus; hear the procedure for that, O beloved.
There, having smeared the ground with cow dung and strewn it with Darbha grass, ten cows should be arranged with their feet toward the north and their faces toward the east.
The observer of the vow should fashion a cow of jaggery using exactly one hundred *prasthas* of jaggery and twenty-five *sīras* of the same;
or else, he may place jaggery in the place of the cow according to his faith.
Then, having fashioned those two according to his faith with molasses,
he wrapped them both in priceless, fine garments;
they were made with mother-of-pearl ears, sugarcane feet, and pure pearl eyes.
With copper-colored backs and tails of fine linen, with woolen blankets made of white wool,
with horns of gold and hooves of silver, and endowed with eyebrows like coral;
richly adorned with various ornaments and accompanied by bronze milking vessels.
Having thus prepared the two calf-figures, the observer of the vow should worship them according to the prescribed rite.
[37] He should likewise offer the excellent ghee-cow, milk-cow, sugar-cow, sesame-cow, honey-cow, and the excellent juice-cow. [38]
Having fashioned a curd-cow, a water-cow, and a gold-cow,
the observer of the vow should worship them after making their respective calves according to the first procedure.
Indeed, one should fashion the cows and calves according to one's capacity.
One should give all these to the preceptor for the satisfaction of Puruṣottama.
Likewise, having fashioned ten kinds of delightful mountains— complete with trees and ponds— and four corner-mountains, one should offer them.
One should worship according to the prescribed rite and offer it to the Guru for the satisfaction of Lord Hari.
Having smeared the ground of the pavilion with cow dung and spread *kuśa* grass upon the floor,
one should place in the center a Mount Meru made of rice, measuring one thousand *droṇas*.
One should prepare an excellent *droṇa* measure, amounting to twelve *prasthas*.
One should place pearls, diamonds, and rubies in the east;
yellow and dark gems in the south; and corals in the west and north.
One should fashion caves from stalks of sugarcane, and rocks and the like from pearl-shells;
one should fashion springs from clarified butter and clouds from cloths.
One should fashion peaks of gold and silver, and the sages and gods out of gold.
One should fashion the guardians of the quarters, beginning with Indra, out of silver, and the trees out of various metals.
Having fashioned the Mandāra, the Pārijāta, the Kalpadruma, and the Kadambaka,
one should adorn them with flowers and fruits made of gold and silver.
Mandarādri is to be made with barley in the east, Gandhamādana with wheat; Vipulādri with sesame seeds in the west, and Supārśva with black gram in the north.
These mountains should be fashioned beautifully, provided with their respective ornaments and appurtenances.
Having caused the recitation of the *svastyayana* and having invoked the divine mountains,
and having worshipped them, he should present the "wealthy mountains" to his preceptor;
likewise, he should give twenty-four cows as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins.

One should cause nine types of mountains to be fashioned according to one's capacity: a mountain of salt, a mountain of jaggery, a mountain of gold, a mountain of sesame seeds, a mountain of cotton, a mountain of ghee, a mountain of gems, a mountain of silver, and a mountain of sugar. (51)
Having likewise fashioned four mountains on each side,
as before, one should create manifold beauty;
one should worship them all according to the prescribed rite and present them to the preceptor.
One should cause the gift of a cow, the gift of land, the gift of a maiden, the offering of a house,
and the gift of vehicles, mounts, cities, and villages to be performed.
One should give one's entire property to the preceptor, and to the Brahmins according to their merit.
One should give food to the mendicants and whatever else is required to others.
Having thus performed the concluding rite (udyāpana), one should afterwards dismiss the deities.
One should give all that to the preceptor or offer it to the temple.
Whatever rules regarding things to be renounced have been undertaken during vows,
the gift of those very same things must likewise be performed at the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Everything given here indeed meets [the giver] in the hereafter, but certainly not otherwise.
Therefore, one should perform the fulfillment of the vow to the best of one's ability.
In former times, the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) was performed by Vaivasvata Manu;
likewise, the concluding rite was performed by Bhṛgu’s daughter and by Ramā.
Padmā, the daughter of the Earth, likewise performed the concluding rite (udyāpana),
and having attained Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha, she rejoices there forever. In ancient times, Pārvatī also performed the entire great concluding rite.
And Prabhā likewise performed the concluding rite (udyāpana) in the proper manner.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the vows have been described to you according to the rules.
Regarding all the Ekādaśīs, what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature and Procedure for the Great Concluding Ceremony (*udyāpana*) of All Ekādaśīs," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 265. [End of] Book 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*), Chapter 266.
[The Author: Chapter 267.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Describe in detail the nature of the vows that are observed annually.
Whatever humans perform by which they may attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation—
knowing that everything else, apart from the means of self-realization, is inevitably filled with suffering, tell me how a person should strive for the eternal goal. (1–2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall indeed proclaim all the purifying days, which consist of vows and grant the highest spiritual good.

Through the power of Hari’s manifestations and through association with the virtuous, time itself attains divinity in every way; one whose soul is devoted to vows shall become a bestower of liberation.
On whichever lunar day a particular vow is observed, whatever its fruit may be, and however its worship is performed—
I shall declare to you all that ritual procedure which is to be performed.

In the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight, at the beginning of the day on the first lunar day (pratipad), the Creator of the Universe brought forth this entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
In that regard, on the first lunar day (pratipad), one should perform a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) which bestows happiness,
pacifies all portents, grants wealth and good fortune,
provides longevity and nourishment, and bestows happiness in both worlds.
Having caused a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and a pavilion (maṇḍapa) to be constructed there on an auspicious spot,
the observer of the vow should indeed worship Brahmā, who bears the form of fire,
with water for the feet, respectful offerings (arghya), flowers, incense, garments, ornaments, and food. (8–9)

He should be worshipped especially with burnt offerings (homa), oblations (bali), and gifts (upahāra), as well as by the gratification of virtuous men and women, and with unbroken grains (akṣata), sandalwood, and excellent juices.
Having fashioned a golden image, one should worship Brahmā.
With sixteen supreme offerings and various kinds of food,
one should worship the god Brahmā, who has four faces, four arms, two feet, and the Vedas in his hands, and who holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in his hand. || 11–12 ||
After the ārātrika rite, the person performing the vow should pray to the Lord;
he may then eat fruit and such from the vow-offering, or even a single meal.
He should maintain celibacy and give gifts in abundance.
One should pray to the Creator for the continuation of one's lineage through sons and grandsons.
(14) One should give the gift of an image to the preceptor, who is the embodiment of the Imperishable;
likewise, the observer of the vow should give the gift of a daughter in marriage according to the formal resolve. (15)
This vow increases one’s lineage and bestows all happiness.
Having performed a salutation with the syllable *oṃ*, [one should offer] water from *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
along with clothing, gold, sweet food, cows, and other such gifts.

Furthermore, one should give as much wealth as one is able to a twice-born man who is learned in the Vedas as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of completing the vow. This is declared to be the Brāhma-vrata, which should be performed by those seeking their desires.
On this very lunar day, in the same manner, the auspicious Sarasvatī-vrata should be observed,
consisting of either a meal with fruit or even a single meal.
For Śāradā indeed emerged from the mouth of Brahmā in the morning.
She should be twelve years of age, accompanied by a lute and peacocks,
and endowed with blue and golden garments of great value;
her form should be made exceedingly radiant and worshipped according to the prescribed ritual.

Having worshipped that Goddess in the morning with the sixteen and other articles, the practitioner who observes the vow must then offer prayers for the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman. As for the food offering, milk-porridge and *pūrikā* cakes should be presented.
On that day, one who seeks the vow should partake of a meal of milk-porridge (kṣīrapāka).
On the second day, the commencement of the study of the Vidyā should be made; it shall be a bestower of wealth.
The observer of the vow should give various kinds of gifts to the venerable Guru.
Then one should offer an image of Svarṇasarasvatī to the venerable Guru;
one should pray, "May knowledge dance upon the tip of my tongue.
One should perform the ritual dismissal and give gifts according to one's capacity.
The observer of the vow should feed and honor Brahmins, virtuous men, and scholars.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, while the churning of the ocean was being performed by the gods and the Daityas, Hari appeared in the morning in the form of a tortoise. (26–27)
One should worship Vāsudeva in the form of a golden tortoise;
his upper body is human in form, while his lower body bears the shape of a tortoise.
One should place a conch and a mace in his two arms and offer him sweetmeats as food.
One should offer sugar, curd, tamarind and other fruits, and sweet water.
Indeed, one should perform a great festival for the narration of the *Kūrma* [Purāṇa].
Having thus performed the vow, the observer of the vow shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1.266.30)
Then, on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship in the morning the *karavīra* tree that has come from the celestial garden to the earth.
One should offer it red garments, incense, and unguents.
One should offer scents, unbroken rice grains, water, a nāraṅga fruit, and a bījapūraka fruit.
Having sprinkled sprouted grain and young shoots with water, one should perform a hymn of praise:
"O highly fortunate Karavīra, grant me fruits at all times."
"May the seven auspicious grains dwell within my granaries.
Having circumambulated [the grains] clockwise and given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the observer of the vow,
having offered salutations and water, should thereafter return to his own home.

Thus worshipped, the tree indeed bestows wealth and grain. On the first day of the bright fortnight, salutations! This great vow bestows fortune and intelligence, and is the means for accomplishing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the vow of silence is proclaimed.
One should perform the worship of Śiva according to the prescribed rite upon a water-pot (kumbha).
Furthermore, one should perform the worship of a golden image of Śiva with the sixteen articles of offering.
One should give sixteen sweet, ripe fruits to a Brahmin;
one should give sixteen offerings of cooked food to Śiva;
likewise, one should give a cow and other gifts, numbering sixteen.
Having performed this vow for the trident-bearing God of gods, O Lakṣmī,
one shall enjoy all pleasures until the end of the body for fourteen years and then attain Śiva.
The vow known as Aśoka, which begins on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, is likewise [efficacious].
The Aśoka, the best of trees, descended from heaven to the earth.
(4.1) One should perform the worship of the Aśoka there with sixteen articles;
by that, one becomes free from sorrow and filled with wealth and grain. (4.2)
At the conclusion of the vow, in the twelfth year, by devotedly offering an image of an *aśoka* tree to the preceptor, one shall become happy in the world of Viṣṇu.
His progeny shall be free from sorrow and endowed with the fruit of the *aśoka*.
Bestowing happiness and abundant wealth, they bear fruit on earth.
On this very first day (pratipad), one should observe the Navarātra;
during the Navarātra, one should subsist on a single meal or even live without soliciting food.
Alternatively, the observer of the vow should always fast or consume only fruit;
in the forenoon, he should worship Durgā after first performing the ritual installation of the water-pot (ghaṭasthāpana).
He should perform the sowing of sprouts using barley, wheat, and rice.
One should perform worship, recitation, and the chanting of the rosary every day.
One should daily recite the auspicious hymn composed by Mārkaṇḍeya.
Furthermore, one should always perform worship at night and likewise keep a vigil.
One should perform the worship of the maiden with excellent food and other offerings.
A person possessing great wealth should fashion an image of Durgā adorned with a thousand [ornaments].
On the final day, in the evening, one should release it into the water.
Having performed the vow in this manner, O Lakṣmī, one shall become an abode of all perfections.
Durgā bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon him; of this there is no doubt.
A practitioner of the vow must never practice stinginess regarding wealth nor weakness regarding strength.
On the first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should especially perform the vow known as the Annakūṭotsava, which increases the pleasure of Viṣṇu;
on this occasion, one should offer one hundred and one varieties of sweet foods.
And all kinds of vegetables, soups, side dishes, and leafy greens;
(5.3) meat-balls, tubers and roots, dairy products, and sugar-based sweets;
indeed, various types of foods to be chewed, swallowed, licked, and sucked. (5.4)
One should offer Govardhana to a Brāhmaṇa and likewise worship him;
then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the observer of the vow should partake of the food and obtain the sacred remains (prasāda).
The one who performs the festival of the mountain of grain (annakūṭa) shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On this very day, at dawn, one should worship the cows, calves, bulls, and heifers, as well as wealth, grain, liquids, garments, ornaments, vehicles, and other such riches,
with turmeric, saffron, and other substances.
Having worshipped them with flower garlands, erotic pastimes, fresh barley, and other offerings, one should play with them in the courtyard of Kṛṣṇa’s temple.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Dhanavrata is considered most excellent.
One should indeed perform the worship of Viṣṇu at night for the sake of attaining wealth.
The observer of the vow should have a golden image of [Viṣṇu] accompanied by Lakṣmī fashioned;
having worshipped that image in the presence of the fire-pit, || 1.266.60 ||
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations (homa) under the name of Lakṣmī;
one should worship her, covered with a pair of red garments and accompanied by Viṣṇu. One should give the image to the preceptor and cause other gifts to be bestowed.
By acting thus, one becomes filled with prosperity through wealth and grain;
having become affluent and cleansed of sin, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The observer of the vow should practice eating once a day, or at night, or subsist on fruit.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, one should perform the unsurpassed Bhānu-vrata;
with a spirit of devotion, one should worship the Sun with the sixteen articles of offering and others.
For in ancient times, on this very day, Sūrya became the twelve-fold soul.
One who observes the vow should present a golden image of the twelve-fold Āditya to his preceptor. Having become equal to the Sun, he is glorified in the heavenly world;
the man who performs this vow becomes like the Sun in both this world and the next.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, Fire was born from Maheśvara.
By worshipping Fire according to the prescribed rites, one shall attain the world of Fire.
Likewise, one should perform the offering of the form of Fire and the fire-oblation (*homa*) with sesame seeds and other materials.
A person observing the vow should perform all acts of worship and salutation.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, there is the "Dust-Gray" vow;
at dawn on that day, Śaṅkara [performed] the rite originating from the body of Satī.
His vow was to be smeared all over with ashes and greyed with dust;
therefore, there he fashioned Mahādeva, the God of gods, who is clothed in the directions,
his entire body grey with dust and sprinkled with water.
Hara, being pleased by that, grants him union with his own self (sāyujya).
Likewise, he should make his own body naked and smeared with mud;
Śambhu, satisfied by this rite, shall bestow the abode of bliss.
In the month of Phālguna, during the conjunction with the Phalgunī nakṣatra,
the man Hari became known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the deities of Dharma, in embodied form.
Having worshipped those two on a swing fixed within the hermitage of Dharma, [one should worship them].
The gods caused it to be shaken; therefore, a festival should be celebrated here.
In the morning, one should perform the worship of the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa with the sixteen types of offerings, including *tulasī*, garments, and sandalwood paste. (74–75)
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and jujube fruits (badara) as the food offering;
having likewise performed the festival of colors, the observer of the vow should partake of the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
The first day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is the supreme vow of Viṣṇu’s birth.

There, having worshipped Viṣṇu, the auspicious son of Vairāja, one should feed Brahmins and virtuous men and give abundant gifts. One should observe the vow of eating but once a day; thus one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the pure first day of the bright fortnight, Brahmā, the teacher of the world, was born.
On this day, his worship should be performed and gifts should be given like gold.
One should observe the vow of eating only one meal; it shall bestow all perfections.
In the end, it bestows the world of truth and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, the annual vows for each lunar day have been described here; among them, celibacy and the consumption of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) yield fruit.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Vows of the Creation of the World, the Birth of Sarasvatī, the Birth of Kūrma, the Arrival of Karavīra, the Lakṣmī-vrata, the Mauna-vrata, the Aśoka-vrata, the Navarātra, the Anna-kūṭa-dhana-vrata, the Dvādaśa-bhānu-vrata, the Origin of Fire, the Satī-bhasma-dhūlī-vrata, the Birth of Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the Birth of Viṣṇu, and the Brahma-janma-vrata," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga in the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 266.

Chapter 268 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! Indeed, regarding the annual vows of the second lunar day (Dvitīyā), human beings who perform them attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation in this world. 1.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Brahmā was married;
one should perform the festival of his wedding with Sāvitrī, as well as the vow.
Having constructed a great pavilion, two golden images of Sāvitrī and Agni should be fashioned.
Having performed worship with festive rites, one should feed [the recipients] food fit for sacrifice (haviṣyānna).
The observer of the vow should eat but once a day and shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
And when there is sufficient wealth, one should give the gift of a maiden and the gift of a cow.
Having obtained the fruit [of this vow], one shall attain all desires and ultimately go to the state of Brahman.
On this very day, O Lakṣmī, the Moon was born from the ocean;
therefore, the Candra-vrata should be performed, for it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having joyfully worshipped the risen young moon at the beginning of the night,
one should indeed offer a silver moon as a gift and feed a Brahmin.
The Brahmin, who is the very image of the moon, should be honored with white water-lilies.
Likewise, the Moon is to be sought after by me like a second mother;
[I seek] a hearth joined with a frying pan, two bulls, and a herd of cattle;
a home endowed with wealth and grain, and health among the people.
May you command me constantly; O Lord of the Second, salutations be unto you!
(9) You who grant me the medicine for worldly existence and the gift of food, bestow upon me an increase of splendor.
Be here always the nourisher of my youth and the giver of happiness. (1.267.10)
On this very day, from the Sun in the form of a horse, two boys were born to his wife named Saṃjñā, who was Aśvinī; they became the two Aśvins.
These two physicians, the sons of Aśvinī, are worthy of worship, for that is indeed their sacred vow.
One should observe the practice of eating only once a day, and medicinal herbs are desired as gifts;
one should give eyes made of gold and silver to a twice-born man,
and during the Aśvinī asterism, a horse should also be given as a gift according to one's ability.
This vow of Aśvinī should be performed with devotion by both men and women.
Chickpeas should be given to horses, while the observer of the vow should consume ghee and curd.
This vow lasts for twelve years and is preceded by the gift of eyes and horses. (14)
Having performed [this], one shall become the best of kings, exceedingly handsome, and a leader among monarchs.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Rādha, the Unborn One indeed commenced his austerity;
one should perform this vow of austerity after having fashioned an excellent lotus.
Having placed the ascetic Brahmā there, the observer of the vow should worship him;
or he should have an auspicious mandala prepared, provided with the seven types of grain.
Having placed the Creator of the Universe upon a water-pot there, he should worship him.
One should give a water-pot, a clean garment, bark-cloth, and likewise a seat;
one should offer fruits as food, sandals, and a sacred thread. Furthermore, one should bestow the gift of a cow and other gifts upon a virtuous Brahmin.
Having enjoyed delightful pleasures, one attains the world of Viṣṇu.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, the great Bhāskara, the jewel of the sky,
was born from the eye of Hara, illuminating the three worlds.
Having worshipped Hari in the form of the four-faced Brahmā together with Gāyatrī,
and having likewise worshipped the Sun along with his chariot, horses, and Aruṇa according to the prescribed rites,
one should observe the vow of eating but once a day and feed virtuous children.

By performing the gift of a golden sun and the offering of gold, the observer of the vow attains the exceedingly prosperous world of Bhāskara. The second day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha is declared to be the Saṃkarṣaṇa-vrata.
In this [age], Śeṣanārāyaṇa himself was born here in the form of Rāma.
In the first yuga, the gods indeed placed Rāma upon a chariot together with Bhadrakā, and having circumambulated the city and other sites, they departed. (24–25)
Having gone to the edge of a body of water, they purified that infinite one.
Then, a great festival should indeed be celebrated by all men. At its conclusion, having installed [the deity] in the temple according to the prescribed rites—
One should perform the *ārārtrika* rite of homage, feed many Brahmins,
and provide food for virtuous women and children. One should also give gifts such as plows and other implements, as well as perform the gift of chariots, fields, villages, and so forth.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, there is the auspicious Viśvakarmavratam;
for on this day Viśvakarmā sleeps, as it is the Aśokaśayana-vrata.
One should [worship] a beautiful four-faced image, accompanied by his wife, seated upon a bed.
Having fashioned [the image] and worshipped the Lord of the worlds, one should pray to the blessed Viśvakarman, the creator of the universe:
"O wearer of the Śrīvatsa, O beloved of Śrī, O abode of Śrī, O Lord of Śrī, O Master! (1.267.30–31).
"O Lord, may my household life, beginning with my home, not come to ruin;
may there never be for me a separation from dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. Likewise, may I have the gift of a house, the gift of a wife, and the gift of the crescent moon. (32)
In this vow, one should indeed perform the gift of a maiden and the gift of gold and other such items.
Since Indra’s birth occurred on the second day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, by worshipping Indra—who is Hari—one shall enjoy the fruit of all sacrifices. (33–34)
And his son, named Jayanta, having fashioned everything— including the chariot of Śacī— out of gold, as well as the thunderbolt, the bow, and the arrow,
and having fashioned a golden elephant, worshipped them according to the prescribed rites. (35)
One should indeed give everything to the preceptor and remain observant of the vow while eating but one meal a day.
(36) Having performed this, the observer of the vow shall attain heaven, the abode of Mahendra, and furthermore, after a long time, liberation leading to the realm of Vairāja. (37)
The vow of the second day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is considered to have been established by Durgā. A gift bestowed on this day shall yield infinite fruit.
Formerly, on the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, Yama was [bound] by Yamunā.

Feasted and honored by her brother in his own home with many delicacies, the sister should observe the vow of Yamadvitīyā in every house. This feeding at the sister’s residence increases one's prosperity. (1.267.40)
After the brother has eaten, garments and ornaments should be given to his sister, and wealth and other gifts as well;
by that, he himself shall become filled with gold, wealth, and grain.
On this lunar day, Yamunā fed King Yama.

He who eats from the palm of his sister’s hand with affection shall become a brother possessed of gold, gems, wealth, grain, and other riches. One should give abundant gifts to one's sister, and even rings should be given to her son.

On the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the ancestors, beginning with Aryaman, were born from the body of Brahmā; indeed, that is the vow of the ancestral Śrāddha. In the morning, one should perform the worship of Sūryanārāyaṇa.
After midday, however, one should perform the *śrāddha* and the water libation (*tarpaṇa*).
One should likewise cause the worship of the ancestors to be performed and offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
The observer of the vow should eat only at night; furthermore, he should give *dhānyaka* as a gift.
One should also give food, clothing, and other such items to a Brahmin;
at that time, the observer of the vow should perform the gift of a cow according to his capacity.
Having remembered all his ancestors who have passed away, he should indeed pay homage to the twice-born.
One should perform [this rite]; one shall obtain health and receive sons and grandsons.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the Kāmadhenus were born;
the Kāmadhenu vow should be performed, and the practitioner of the vow should subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
One should perform the purification with water from a cow's horn, which grants all desires;
one should bathe with cow-horn water and earth, and worship the cow.
One should give gifts of cows and other things for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha.
One should provide grass and other fodder so that the cows may obtain their mouthfuls.
In the evening, one should perform the viewing of the young moon and the offering of *arghya*.
By doing so, the performer of the vow shall indeed become a possessor of cattle, and moreover, exceedingly wealthy.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the Sun was indeed placed upon a whetstone by Viśvakarman and fashioned into a beautiful form.
One should worship Hari in his form as the Sun here with red flowers.
Having fashioned a golden image according to one's means with red perfumes,
one should then offer a full copper vessel filled with wheat and rice to the Sun with devotion, and present the *arghya* with water.
One should offer an image and give a gift according to one's ability to a virtuous Brahmin.
O Lakṣmī, when the vow has been performed in this manner, the observer of the vow becomes like the sun itself on earth—
a twice-born who is difficult to approach and impossible to overcome.
Or else, he may be born as a king, a great universal monarch (cakravartin);
having enjoyed his desired boons here, he goes at the end to the abode of the Sun.
Or, praised by all the gods, he finally goes to the abode of Brahmā.
Then, on the second day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, Hara himself set out for asceticism on the golden mountain at the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.
Thereafter, a golden image of Hara, complete with matted locks, was fashioned.

Śiva should be worshipped with flowers that are very white and fragrant. A canopy should be made with flowers and auspicious floral ornaments, along with various food offerings, incense, lamps, the nīrājana ceremony, and so forth.
Mahādeva is to be propitiated by one observing the vow for the sake of attaining happiness.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the observer of the vow becomes free from disease;
endowed with wealth, grain, and prosperity, he shall certainly live for a hundred years.
In these vows, rites such as the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth should be performed according to one's wealth and other resources.
(63) The Fire-god himself, appearing in various forms month by month, is the body of Hari;
he is to be worshipped by the performer of the oblation who maintains celibacy and other observances. (64)

Whatever procedure has been prescribed for the second lunar days occurring in the bright fortnight, that very same should be performed on those in the dark fortnight by those skilled in the ritual rules.

Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the first part concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, regarding the annual second-day vows: [the accounts of] Brahmā-Sāvitrī, the birth of Lagna-Candra, the birth of the Aśvinī Kumāras, the penance of Brahmā, the birth of Sūrya, the births of Saṃkarṣaṇa and Rāma, Viśvakarmā, and Aśoka—

The two hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Vows of Śayana, Indrajāta, Durgā, Yamayamunā-bhojana, Āryama-pitṛt-patti, Kāmadhenu-utpatti, Sūrya-śāṇollīḍha-tā, and Śambhu-tapa," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*). Chapter 268.
[The Author: Chapter 269.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "Listen, O Lakṣmī! Indeed, hear about the vows of the third lunar day."
By performing which, a man or a woman may attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(1) From the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Gaurī performed a most rigorous penance for the sake of attaining Śaṅkara; that is indeed considered the Gaurī-vrata. (2)
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having fashioned an image of Gaurī together with Śaṅkara—
whether made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay—
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as with auspicious garments and ornaments.
And with darbha stalks, according to the prescribed rite, a maiden who observes a fast— whether seeking a husband,
seeking sons, or seeking a son-in-law—
should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for Mahāgaurī, the consort of Śaṅkara, together with Śaṅkara. 4–5.
Having bowed down again and again, she should pray for that which resides in her mind.
[She should approach] seven, nine, eleven, or even more women of the twice-born;
or women with husbands, or virgins, beautiful as Gaurī and endowed with auspicious marks. (6)
Then, having summoned them with great respect,
she— her mind delighted by ornaments such as vermilion, collyrium, and garments—
should honor those who perform the vow and satisfy them with gifts.
One should offer sweet foods, such as rice-balls (piṇḍakas) and fruits;
by thus satisfying them, the female ascetic shall obtain the fruit [of her vow].
At night, she should keep a vigil with the desire for the complete fulfillment of the vow.
In the morning, having worshipped her again, she should joyfully offer her to the guru;
or else, she should dismiss the image and cast it into a sacred ford or a reservoir of water.
Having thus performed this auspicious Gaurī-vrata for twelve years, [she attains her goal].
A maiden, however, obtains a virtuous husband equal to Śambhu.
For the successful completion of the vow, she should offer twelve cows after making the formal resolve.
What is the use of saying more here? Gaurī is the bestower of good fortune.
Just as it is for women, no other [means] exists in the three worlds.
Gaurī, when propitiated by means of this vow, bestows wealth, sons, a husband, a daughter, knowledge, supernatural powers, fame, happiness, and indeed everything desired. (13–14)
By means of the vows performed by Pārvatī, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Māṇikyā, and Ramā,
she obtained as her husband the Lord Kṛṣṇa, who holds a banner and a bow in his hands;
Hari, whose hands bear the marks of a fish, a trident, a discus, and a svastika.
Therefore, this vow bestows beauty, good fortune, enjoyment, and liberation.
(16) The third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is the Akṣayatṛtīyā vow;
that lunar day is the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, and it renders the merit of [any] act performed there inexhaustible. (17)
In this regard, having fashioned the Tretā Yuga in the form of a golden image,
one should worship Nārāyaṇa as Kṛṣṇa accompanied by Lakṣmī,
with flowers, incense, unguents, and the like, as well as with water from the Gaṅgā and unbroken grains of rice (akṣata).
One should satisfy the illustrious Teacher of the World with various kinds of food;
one should feed the Brahmins with barley-meal, while the observer of the vow himself eats but once a day.
For him who has performed the rite in this manner, the fruit is that of the vow of fasting.
Even the commencement of an undertaking proceeds to completion successfully and without obstacle;
whether a man or a woman, one shall attain the fulfillment of their purpose through this vow on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, under the asterism Punarvasu. (21)
Hari, bearing the axe, appeared in the house of Jamadagni. During this [observance], the practitioner should have a golden image of Rāma made with an axe;
having performed a great worship at midday, he should then take his meal.
From this time forward, until the full moon of the month of Jyeṣ� perfumes,
garments, and even white clothes;
one should also fan the Lord every day with *uśīra* roots and palm-leaf fans.
In the food offering (naivedya), one should present mango juice and other such items mixed with sugar.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, Raṃbhā descended from heaven to earth;
therefore, the fruit of the plantain (raṃbhā-phala) is to be eaten during the vow, and Raṃbhā is to be worshipped with unbroken grains (akṣata) and water.

One should worship the twice-born along with his wife with perfumes, flowers, garments, and other offerings. A woman who performs the Rambhā-vrata here out of a desire for good fortune obtains wealth, sons, intelligence, prosperity, riches, and so forth. (27)
One who seeks the vow obtains a husband, cattle, the earth, a mansion, as well as household utensils;
she attains a delicacy of limb comparable to the plantain tree. In this rite, the fruits of offering are the *raṃbhā* fruit, sugar, and clarified butter.

Then, on the third day of the month of Āṣāḍha, Ramā began her penance for the sake of Keśava; therefore, the Lakṣmī-vrata must be performed by women. [She fashioned] an image of Keśava together with Lakṣmī, made of gold.
One should worship according to the prescribed rite with the sixteen types of offerings, beginning with water for the feet;
one should also worship with meals, gifts of fragrant flowers, garments, ornaments, the waving of lamps (ārātrika), prostrations, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).

There, one should honor and feed a twice-born man accompanied by his wife; one should respect him with the words of the Brahmins, satisfy him, and gladden him. Thus, having propitiated this lady who is the very form of Lakṣmī through the vow, [one attains success].
She should bid farewell to both the Brahmin and the image of Viṣṇu at their home.
A woman who performs the vow while remaining in her household, desiring good fortune,
shall— by the grace of the God of gods— be endowed with wealth and grain.
Accompanied by sons and grandsons, she shall attain the world of Viṣṇu;
a maiden shall obtain a handsome husband who grants her desired and excellent enjoyments.
The vow known as Svarṇagaurīvrata is prescribed for the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.

Since Kālī, having performed supreme penance, became golden-fair (Svarṇagaurī), the observer of the vow should worship Bhavānī with the sixteen types of offerings. At the conclusion of the worship, he should pray: "Grant me a fair complexion. (37–38)
"O lady of virtuous vows, grant me sons, grant me wealth, grant me good fortune;
fulfill my various other desires here. Salutations to you!
Then, one should offer an auspicious *vāyana* (a gift of food) to the Goddess accompanied by Bhava.

This vow is proclaimed to last for sixteen years. At its conclusion, a fortunate woman should perform a great concluding rite (udyāpana) for the virtuous goddess Satī within a Sarvabhadra mandala in a plantain grove.
One should place [the deity] in the center within a golden pitcher endowed with gems and other [precious substances].
Around it, one should worship the fivefold assembly (pañcāyatana) beginning with Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Upon the pitcher, on a fine vessel made of copper and filled with unbroken rice grains (akṣata), [one should place the vessel].
One should worship golden images of Śambhu and Bhavānī with sixteen ritual substances; thereafter,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) using sixteen bamboo vessels filled with cooked food.
Having offered the food-offering to Satī, one should present it to virtuous people;
then one should give excellent betel-leaves to kinsmen and others.
One should give the image to the preceptor and likewise offer a sacrificial fee to the twice-born.
One should perform many acts of giving for the sake of making one’s vows fruitful.
(46) A woman—whether she be a maiden, a married woman, or a widow—shall obtain the full fruit;
having become abundantly enriched with wealth, grain, and other possessions, she goes to the supreme state. (47)
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, there is indeed the vow known as Haratālika.
For it was on this day that the joining of Pārvatī’s hand with the hand of Hara took place.
This very vow called Haratālika increases one's good fortune.
One should perform [the rite] with devotion according to the prescribed rule, preceded by the offering of water for the feet (pādya) and the respectful oblation (arghya).
Here, having placed food along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, bamboo, or even clay— || 1.268.50 ||
Having placed roasted sesame, rice, chickpeas, and so forth,
as well as fruit, clothing, and ornaments, right here in this vessel,
one should indeed give them to the Guru; thereafter, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).

One should feed virtuous Brāhmaṇas, virtuous women, maidens, and children. One should likewise devoutly bestow upon the Brāhmaṇas sixteen vessels for auspicious substances and sixteen bamboo vessels, according to the prescribed rite.
A woman observing the vow should give a more abundant and auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to other Brahmins as well; by that means, she shall attain good fortune.
Having thus performed the vow, the woman, after enjoying delightful pleasures, [shall attain her goal].

By the power of this vow, one shall become the companion of Gauro in the hereafter. Through the grace of the Goddess, this vow is considered to bestow wealth, grain, daughters, and sons in this world, and peace in the next; it grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 55–56.

When the third lunar day of the month of Bhādrapada occurs here in conjunction with the asterism Hasta, the chanters of the Sāman hymns (Sāmaga) should perform the libations for the ancestors, the gods, and the seers (ṛṣis). Furthermore,
a new sacred thread (yajñopavīta) should be worn according to the ritual prescribed in their own Vedic branch.
The vow known as Hastagaurīvrata should be performed for the sake of prosperity;
it shall be a warder-off of poison, the bites of venomous creatures, and the like.
It was [observed] when she assumed ten million forms for the purpose of destroying the demon Mahiṣāsura.
At that time, she became known by the name Koṭīśvarī Durgā,
as it was proclaimed by the wielder of the Pināka bow himself;
for when she assumed the forms of a hundred thousand Caṇḍīs, that indeed became the Koṭīśvarī vow.
Then the virtuous goddess was herself proclaimed as Lakṣeśvarī by the wielder of the Pināka bow.
The vow of Lakṣeśvarī should be observed for a period of four years;
the worship of Lakṣeśvarī must be performed while fasting.
O Lotus-born One, having purified one hundred thousand unbroken grains of rice or sesame seeds, one should cast them here into milk heated over fire until the essence of the substance becomes a firm,
well-formed mass.
Having fashioned a beautiful image of the Goddess from that clay,
adorned with perfumes, flowers, unhusked rice, jewels, hair, garments, and ornaments,
he should invoke Pārvatī there and worship her with a spirit of devotion. (64–65)

One should cause [the deity] to increase [in favor] through perfumes, flowers, water, incense, lamps, food offerings, prayers, various excellent fruits, superior sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and prostrations;
and one should also perform the waving of lights (ārātrika) and prostrate like a staff, while asking for forgiveness.
One should pray for wealth, grain, sons, daughters, a home, and so forth.
Then, one should dismiss Durgā into the midst of water;
after giving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the venerable Guru, one should subsequently perform a night vigil.
"Having given gifts to the Brahmins, she should eat this on the following day.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the Koṭilakṣeśvarī-vrata.
In the home of the woman who performs this vow, Lakṣmī, consisting of wealth and grain, shall always abide."
By the power of this vow, she shines and prospers eternally;
at the end, she goes to the world of Gaurī and indeed attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Īṣa, the Bṛhadgaurī-vrata is observed.
This should be performed for five years, whereby one attains the merit of ten million *kundana* flowers.
One should worship Durgā in the morning with sixteen excellent articles.
Five married women (*suvāsinyah*) should be honored with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste.
With garments, bodices, earrings, necklaces, threads, and ornaments;
likewise, five vessels of metal, small bowls, and cooking pots;
vermilion, cumin, sweets, auspicious substances, and collyrium. (73–74)
One should give to them cakes made from wheat flour, fresh pastries, fruits and the like,
various garments, and indeed five types of woven cloths;
thereafter, one should feed them and eat oneself while remaining silent.
One should keep a vigil at night, interspersed with the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s glories.
One should wear on the neck the fruit [of the tree] or a betel nut that has been offered;
for at night, a fruit worn around the neck bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
Then, at dawn, full of enthusiasm and adorned with ornaments,
she should go to the river accompanied by her female companions and musical instruments for singing; there she should perform her ablutions and address Gaurī, uttering this prayer:
"You have been summoned by me, O blessed lady, and honored according to the prescribed rite.
O goddess, bestower of good fortune, protect me always.
O goddess, forgive whatever was deficient; you may now depart as you please."
Having thus made this petition, having offered salutations with shouts of "Victory! and musical instruments, and having looked upon Gaurī in the water with great enthusiasm, one should dismiss her.
By performing the vow in this manner with devotion, the practitioner, through the grace of the Goddess, [attains his goal].
Having enjoyed pleasures, one shall attain the world of Gaurī at the end of the body.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the Viṣṇu-Gaurī vow is observed;
Viṣṇu was worshipped by Gaurī for the sake of attaining the perfection of the fruits of her asceticism.

Therefore, this auspicious vow named Viṣṇugaurī has been proclaimed. Therein, indeed, Gaurī, together with Viṣṇu, should be joyfully worshipped with sixteen recitations and various kinds of food offerings. (84)
One should feed a young married woman in the form of Gaurī under the name Lakṣmī, O Lord.
One should worship her with auspicious articles for the propitiation of Viṣṇu and Gaurī.
Having bowed to her, one should bid her farewell and give gifts with devotion.
A woman who performs this vow undoubtedly obtains a son.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Haragaurī-vrata is observed.
Gaurī, having ascended the bed of Hara, enters into union with Hara.
Through this union, she became satisfied and endowed with the happiness of her lord.
(88) Having prepared a single bed for Hara and Gaurī during this vow, one should lay them down, worship them with devotion, and serve them with a divine disposition. (89)
By the power of this vow, having enjoyed delightful pleasures and attained the world of Gaurī, one rejoices together with Hara.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the Brahma-Gaurī vow is prescribed.
Brahmā, having arrived, bestowed blessings for the attainment of Śaṅkara.
That vow was then declared: it should be performed according to the proper ritual procedure.
Having fashioned images of Gaurī and Brahmā out of gold, one should worship them.
One should perform the single meal with the sixteen modes of service;
one should give gifts as desired to the guru and feed the twice-born.
By the grace of Brahmagaurī, she rejoices there, united [with him].

On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, Lakṣmī, beautiful with good fortune, became the beloved of Viṣṇu by offering him the garland of choice. Therefore, one should joyfully perform the vow that consists of the beauty of good fortune. (94–95)
There, Lakṣmī should be worshipped by offering an *arghya* of coconut;
with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), sweet foods, ornaments, and so forth,
she becomes pleased and bestows good fortune, even leading one to her own abode.
All the articles for the ritual bath should be given as a gift to the woman.
(97) She should observe the vow of eating only once a day and offer a necklace to Viṣṇu;
that garland of grace should then be placed around her husband's neck, for she is the giver of sons. (98)
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, after midnight,
Satī obtained sons who were Rudras through the yoga with Hara.
Therefore, that third day is said to consist of the vow for the welfare of the family.
When worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, Gaurī becomes the progenitor of the lineage.
Thus, in all vows here, there should be giving, fire-offerings, the ritual dismissal,
the worship of the God and Goddess, and the worship of the Brahmins and the Guru.
One should practice the common observances, such as eating only once a day, with devotion;
these, when performed with faith, shall grant all the desires held in the mind.
For among all the gods, Śrī Hari himself is the inner self of them all.
This worshipful one exists as the bestower of the fruits of all actions.
Whatever object a man, a woman, or anyone else may desire for the sake of their vow, they obtain all of that through the grace of Śrī Hari. (103–104)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Vārṣika Tṛtīyā Vows, including the Gaurī Tapovrata, Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, the Jayantī of Paraśurāma on the first day of the Tretā Yuga, the Kadalīvrata, Lakṣmī Tapovrata, Kālīgaurīvratā, Haragaurīlagnavrata, Sāmaga Śrāvaṇī, Koṭīśvarī, Māhiṣaghnalakṣeśvarī, Bṛhadgaurī, Viṣṇugaurī, Haragaurī, Yogabrahmāśīrgaurī, Viṣṇuvaramālā, and Kulavṛddhi Vratas," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga. 268.
← Chapter 268: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 269 [Author: Chapter 270 →

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, listen; I shall describe to you the vows of the fourth lunar days (caturthī-vratas), by performing which a man or a woman shall attain supreme worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, who became the Master born from the union of the bodily elements within the home of Śaṅkara and Pārvatī—
he indeed exists as Kṛṣṇa in four forms, having the nature of Vāsudeva.
He is the very form of Saṃkarṣaṇa, as well as the form of Pradyumna;
he is the very form of Aniruddha, and therefore he is the leader of the Gaṇas.
He exists as the nature of these four forms, and his vows likewise correspond accordingly.
On the fourth day of the month of Caitra, having properly worshipped Gaṇeśa in the form of Vāsudeva and having given a gift of gold,
one should perform everything from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the dismissal (visarjana).
Having performed everything according to the prescribed rules, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
(6) The vow of eating but once a day should be observed; at the meal, sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas) should be offered.
Likewise, the observer of the vow should offer dūrvā grass and vermilion during the worship. (7)
Other gifts as well should be given for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa;
however, the observer of the vow himself should perform the auspicious breaking of the fast with sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas).
By performing the vow in this manner in the world, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having propitiated Viṣṇu, he shall go to Vaikuṇṭha, honored by the gods.
On the fourth day of Vaiśākha, the one named Saṃkarṣaṇa is to be worshipped;
[one should perform] the various rites beginning with the invocation and ending with the dismissal.
Having performed [the rite], one should worship the god Gaṇeśa and feed many [people].
Likewise, one should make gifts such as conch shells and other gifts according to one's capacity.
By that merit, having become a performer of the vow, one assumes a divine body.
Having attained the world of Saṃkarṣaṇa, he rejoices for many kalpas.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, the Lord Pradyumna is to be worshipped;
having worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas with the sixteen types of offerings.

Having offered fruit, roots, water, and *dūrvā* grass with sincere devotion, the observer of the vow goes by that merit indeed to the heaven of Pradyumna. On the fourth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, Aniruddha is to be worshipped.

One should perform the worship, beginning with the invocation and ending with the dismissal, using various flowers and the like, as well as fruits, food offerings, and so forth; one should give many gifts and perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) and other rites. (15–16)
The observer of the vow should ask for forgiveness and offer alms-bowls made of gourd or *tumbikā* fruit;
he should also give wooden bowls to the virtuous ascetic who maintains his deposits.
Having done this, the observer of the vow should proceed to the supreme abode of Aniruddha.
Having thus performed the Caturmūrti vows for twelve years,
one should perform the great concluding rite (udyāpana) in an auspicious pavilion upon a mandala,
having placed a golden vessel filled with the five gems and other materials.
Then, having installed the five-faced Gaṇeśa according to the prescribed rite,
the practitioner should perform worship with the sixteen supreme articles,
accompanied by the sounds of song and instrumental music, Vedic mantras, and hymns of praise.
One should perform an auspicious great festival with burnt offerings (homa), recitations (japa), feasts, and the giving of gifts for the pleasure of Gaṇeśa and Kṛṣṇa. Thus,
when the concluding rite (udyāpana) has been performed, the full fruit of the vow shall be attained.
Kṛṣṇa himself bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation here and in the hereafter upon the performer of this vow.
Whatever the observer of the vow desires—whether heaven or anything else—he shall obtain it all. Furthermore, another rite known as the Satī-vrata is prescribed for the Jyeṣṭha-caturthī.
Since Satī was born in ancient times from Dakṣa’s daughter, the Brahman woman Siknī,
the observer of the vow should celebrate the festival of Satī’s birth; he should consume only one meal,
or else observe a fruit-fast or a full fast, and perform a grand worship.
Having thus performed the vow and offered gifts to Viṣṇu,
the practitioner of the vow shall rejoice in the world of Gaṇapati’s mother for a duration equal to that.
Likewise, on the fourth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, there shall be another auspicious vow.
Since the day is the very first of the ritual cycle known as Rathantara,
one should worship with a mind purified by faith either the ritual cycle called Rathantara,
or Kālarūpa, or Kṛṣṇarūpa, or Gaṇeśa. (27–28)
One observing the vow should practice eating only once a day; the practitioner shall obtain heaven as the fruit.
On the fourth lunar day of the month of Śrāvaṇa—at dawn, midday, and at nightfall—one should indeed worship Śrī Gaṇeśa according to all the prescribed rites.
When the rising of the moon has thus occurred, the observer of the vow should worship him again.
He should offer the *arghya* water, food, and so forth, and present vermilion and other offerings.
[He should meditate on the deity] as having a protruding belly, four arms, three eyes, and a reddish-pale complexion.
One should meditate upon him as adorned with many precious jewels and possessing a serene countenance;
one should worship him with all the ritual services, beginning with the invocation.
For the sake of pleasing Gaṇeśa, the observer of the vow should offer sweetmeats (modaka) as the food offering.
Having thus performed the vow and eaten the prasāda modakas,
one should sleep on the ground at night and worship again in the morning;
one should give many gifts for the pleasure of Gaṇeśa and Kṛṣṇa.
By the power of this vow, having obtained all the desires of the mind,
one shall attain the supreme station of Gaṇeśa in the highest world.
Therefore, one who desires all these wishes should perform it with diligent effort.
There exists no other supreme vow equal to this.
O Lakṣmī! On this very day, the worship of Dūrvā and Gaṇeśa must be performed;
I shall tell you its procedure, which brings about complete merit. (36–37)
Having appointed a superintendent over the gold and having placed that vessel upon a *sarvatobhadra* mandala made of copper,
one should then set it down and encircle it with red cloth.
One should worship with red flowers and indeed with five kinds of leaves.
The *bilva* leaf, *apāmārga*, *śamī*, *dūrvā*, and *haripriyā*—one should worship with these leaves and flowers, as well as with excellent fruits and other offerings. (39–40)
One should feed [the preceptor] with sweetmeats and other foods, and give an auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should likewise present the respectful offering (arghya), the oblation (upahāra), and a bed with its furnishings.
Having honored the Guru, who is the very essence of Vighneśa, one should offer these to him.
Having thus performed this auspicious vow of Gaṇapati for five years,
one shall enjoy all pleasures here in this world and then go to the realm of Gaṇapati.
In this world one becomes prosperous, and in the next world one possesses great bliss.
On the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
on a Tuesday at midday, the Lord Varāha was born from the nose of Brahmā.
Having fashioned a golden image of the Boar-form, the observer of the vow should worship it.
One should offer saffron-colored garments there to the Lord of Ramā.
One should present milk-rice as an offering, especially water-pots;
likewise, one should cause the hymns of the Varāha incarnation to be sung and perform worship.
Then, one should perform the meal offering with the sixteen excellent services.
[One should worship] the deity who has a human body and a boar's face, possessing four arms and equipped with weapons;
holding the Earth upon the tip of his tusk, he shines as one should offer the gift.
Having thus performed the vow of Viṣṇu, the practitioner shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
Now, on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, there is the excellent vow of the Cow;
it was on this very day that Gaṇeśa was born as the son of Pārvatī’s bed.
O Lakṣmī, the vow of Gaṇeśa should also be observed for four days according to the prescribed rite, preceded by a magnificent festival;
it should be adorned with green creepers, tree branches, plantain trees, and arched gateways.
A beautiful pavilion should be constructed, and the Sarvatobhadra mandala should be prepared;
furthermore, Gaṇeśa should be fashioned from clay or from metal—
whether from gold, silver, copper, or even from gemstone.
Furthermore, it should be adorned with vermilion, saffron, and so forth;
likewise, it should be beautified and worshipped with the sixteen articles.
It should be worshipped every night with sweets such as *laḍḍukas* by the practitioner observing the vow.
He should always be propitiated and prayed to for the attainment of happiness.
Various kinds of gifts should be given, and the observer of the vow should eat only at night.
At the conclusion, the formal dismissal of Gaṇapati should joyfully be performed.
Having thus performed the vow, the practitioner shall indeed attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
When the full year has passed, with the mother’s permission and likewise with faith,
a circumambulation of a cow was performed here on that day by Gaṇeśa.
Therefore, this vow is proclaimed as being named after the cow Bahulā.
Here, she should be worshipped with effort using garlands, perfumes, fodder, and other offerings.
Then one should perform a circumambulation, and if one is able, one should practice giving gifts.
If, however, one is unable [to complete it], one should dismiss her after paying obeisance.
Having performed the vow for five years, ten years, or even sixteen years,
and having performed the concluding rite (udyāpana), one should give a milch cow as a gift.
One should complete the vow; one shall obtain the fruit of attaining a lotus-like wife.
Having enjoyed supreme pleasures here, honored by the hosts of deities, one shall reach Goloka together with one's wife, sons, and others.
On this occasion, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, the vow of Siddhivaināyaka must be observed;
the practitioner of the vow should reverently perform the worship of Śrī Gaṇeśa with all the ritual services beginning with invocation, and with sweetmeat balls (modakas).
One should meditate with a one-pointed mind upon Gaṇeśa, the Lord of Accomplishment (Siddhināyaka).
He is the leader of both Ṛddhi, the daughter of Viśvakarman, and Siddhi;
having been born today through their marriage, Gaṇeśa is the Lord of Accomplishment.
Therefore, one should worship that four-armed god with an elephant's face, who has a single tusk, resembles gold, holds a noose and a goad, has ears like winnowing baskets,
is smeared with vermilion and other unguents, and possesses a beautiful, protruding belly. (65)
Having meditated and offered the *arghya*, the observer of the vow should worship once more.
(66) The observer of the vow should offer twenty-one petals with twenty-one names; hear those names as they are. (67)
One should offer a *śamī* leaf to Sumukha, a *bhṛṅga* flower to Gaṇādhīśa,
a *bilva* fruit to Umāputra, and *dūrvā* grass to Gajamukha;
one should offer a jujube fruit (*badarī*) to Lambodara and a *dhattūra* flower to Harasūnu.
One should offer *tulasī* to Śūrpakarṇa, *śiṃbija* to Vakratuṇḍa;
*apāmārga* to Guhabhrātṛ, and *bārhata* to Ekadantin; *sindūra* to Heramba, and *patraja* to Caturhotṛ.
One should cause the leaf of the Agastya plant to be offered to the peaceful Lord of All;
one should present scents, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and a pair of *dūrvā* blades. One should give five sweetmeats (*modaka*) and offer sweet water.
Having offered betel-leaf, bowed down, and made his formal request, he should dismiss [the deity].
He should present a golden image together with its ritual accessories to a preceptor or a Brāhmaṇa, give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and feed him with sweetmeats and other foods. ||72–73||
Having undertaken this vow for five years on earth,
a person who worships it obtains all desires pertaining to this world and the next.
On this fourth lunar day, one must by no means look upon the moon.
One who sees [this] shall incur a false accusation; of this there is no doubt.
(75) Therefore, for the destruction of that fault, one should recite the eternal mantra:
"Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Nṛsiṃha at the onset of night. (76)
"The lion was killed by the *śarabha*, and the *śarabha* became Śaṅkara;
the moon was held by Śaṅkara—may Hara remove this false curse!
Having uttered this, no false stigma indeed arises among people.

One should pay homage to Śiva, the moon-crested one, endowed with devotion. On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should worship Kapardīśa Vināyaka with the Puruṣasūkta and with ritual offerings.
One should give rice grains to the young student (baṭu), who has been honored with perfumes and flowers, [saying]:
"May this Kapardin Gaṇanātha be pleased by these offerings of rice grains.
May Gaṇeśa, who bears the form of Kṛṣṇa, grant me both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
By performing the vow in this manner, O embodied one, one will certainly attain Goloka.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Nāga-vrata is prescribed;
it should be performed by people in every way for the purpose of destroying snakebites and other such evils.

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the morning vow and having drunk the pure water from the horn of a cow, one should then bathe; thereafter, at midday, one should worship Śeṣa and the other serpents, such as Śaṅkhapāla,
preceded by their invocation and with the various ritual offerings (upacāras).
One should perform the nourishment with milk and give milk to the serpent.
When the Nāga-vrata has been performed in this manner, serpents do not bite at all,
nor do their poisons cause affliction, by virtue of Brahmā’s granting of the boon.

In ancient times, Brahmā said to the serpents, "Do not bite those who worship you during Kārttika. Consequently, they do not bite their worshippers at all. On the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, the vow known as Karaka is prescribed.
In this matter, women alone have the authority; they themselves must perform it.
Having bathed and adorned their bodies, they should worship Gaṇanāyaka.
Beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), they should indeed carry out everything according to the prescribed rite.
In front of that, one should place ten vessels of fully cooked food,
or one should place ten water-filled jars in front of it.
Having uttered, "May the Lord be pleased with me," one should thus offer them.
She should give ten water-pots to married women,
and then, when the moon has risen, she should offer sweet foods.
Having offered the *arghya* according to the prescribed rite, the woman should eat only sweets.

To fulfill the vow, she should give to a twice-born man a jar filled with milk or water, enriched with betel nuts, unbroken rice grains, and gems. Having performed the vow in this manner for sixteen or twelve years, the woman—
Then, having performed the concluding rite (udyāpana), she should complete the vow.
Or rather, a woman desiring good fortune should perform this vow for as long as she lives; indeed, there is nothing equal to this vow for bestowing good fortune upon women. (93–94)
Indeed, there is nothing else in this world that should be performed with such effort as [the worship of] Maṅgala,
the best of planets, who is the very son of the Earth.
On this lunar day, he was born from the drop (bindu) of Śaṅkara.
Therefore, one who desires the highest good should perform the Aṅgāraka vow;
Maṅgala always bestows prosperity upon him and indeed grants every blessing.
One should diligently observe the vow of eating once a day or at night. || 96–97 ||

Likewise, the worship and recitation of the Maṅgala mantra should be performed, for they grant one's desires. At that time, the observer of the vow should also give gifts of red gems, red garments and the like, and red wheat. (98)
The gift of red sesame seeds brings about all forms of prosperity.

From the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa for a full year, the person observing the vow should subsist on a single meal per day for one year, or otherwise on food taken only at night.
The third [year] is by means of unasked food, and the fourth by means of fasts;
thus one should perform this vow for four years without sloth.
This is the Vināyaka-vrata, [performed] in Kāśī because of the manifestation of Vināyaka.
He should worship [the deity] with the sixteen articles on all Caturthī days.
He should give all kinds of gifts according to his capacity and according to his wealth.
At the end of the year or at the conclusion of the vow, he should perform the great rite of completion (udyāpana).
One should have Śrī Gaṇapati fashioned, along with his mouse and a golden chariot;
or else everything may be made of copper, wood, or clay. Having had these made as appropriate, or alternatively, a lotus with well-formed petals, one should proceed.

Alternatively, having placed a suitable and auspicious jar made of copper in the center of a *sarvatobhadra* mandala constructed of grain, one should fill it with rice and install Vināyaka therein. (105–106)
With invocations and other rites, with ritual baths, with vermilion, sandalwood, and the like;
with *dūrvā* grass, flowers, garments, ornaments, incense, lamps, and fragrant substances;
with food offerings consisting of sweetmeats, fruits, betel leaves, and chewing-gums.

One should worship and please the God with offerings of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), with handfuls of flowers of praise (*stutikusumāñjali*), and likewise with vigils; one should also honor Him with songs, instrumental music, and sacred narratives. At dawn, [one should offer] sugar, rice, barley, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and so forth.
One should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite with bilva fruits and white mustard seeds. [The deities to be invoked are:
Gaṇa, Gaṇādhipa, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Tripurāntaka, Lambodara, Ekadanta, Rukmadaṃṣṭra, and Vighnapa.
Brahmā, Yama, Varuṇa, Soma, Sūrya, Hutāśana, Gandhamādin, and Parameṣṭhin— thus with these sixteen names; likewise,
including "Vakra" and "Sutuṇḍa," there are one hundred and eight names.
One should indeed offer oblations into the fire with devotion and perform the final *pūrṇāhuti* offering.
Then, having worshipped the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*) and twenty-four Brahmins,
one should gratify them with sweetmeats (*modakas*), milk-rice (*pāyasa*), vegetables, and fried cakes (*pūrikās*).
Then one should give to the teacher a milch cow accompanied by her calf;
likewise, one should offer a profuse sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability.
Furthermore, having bowed to the Brahmins, one should bestow other gifts upon them as well.
Having dismissed [the guests], he should eat with his kinsmen with a joyful mind.
Having thus performed this vow and enjoyed these excellent pleasures here,
one shall attain union with Viṣṇu through the grace of Vināyaka.
This excellent vow has been proclaimed as bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the fourth day of the month of Pauṣa, having worshipped Vināyaka,
one should feed a single brāhmaṇa and offer sweetmeats (modakas) along with a sacrificial fee.
When this is performed, one indeed becomes a practitioner who is a vessel for all prosperity.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the Gaurī-vrata is highly esteemed;
there, Gaurī is to be worshipped with devotion along with the hosts of Yoginīs.
By men and women with *kunda* flowers, red flowers, and the like;
with red threads, lac-dye, incense, lamps, and excellent food;
as well as with *gūḍa* sweets, *laḍḍukas*, milk, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Women who are worthy of worship and endowed with good fortune, as well as virtuous Brahmins—
gifts should be given to them especially for the increase of one's own good fortune:
gifts, meals, garments, and excellent fruits.
O Lakṣmī! This Gaurī-vrata increases good fortune and health.
It should be performed every year; once performed for Gaurī, it should be repeated again and again.
This is to be understood as the Ḍhuṇḍhi-vrata, wherein Gaṇeśa is worshipped. (124)
He has come to Kāśī and remains there for the purpose of wandering among the devotees of Śambhu.
One who desires their own welfare should perform this vow for that reason;
it is known as the Kuṇḍavrata, the Śāntivrata, and also the Lalitāvratam. (125)
This very same is proclaimed as the sesame vow (*tilavrata*) and the jasmine vow (*kundavrata*).
Whatever bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offering, and libation are performed, they shall become a thousandfold effective through the propitiation of Gaurī and Gaṇeśa. (126–127)
On the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should observe the Saṃkaṣṭahāraka vow by fasting after observing the rising of the moon. Then,
having fashioned an auspicious image of Gaṇeśa out of clay, complete with his weapons and his vehicle.
Having placed him upon the pedestal, one should worship him with the sixteen types of offerings.
One should present sweetmeats and sesame powder mixed with sugar.
One should offer the *arghya* water in a copper vessel blended with red sandalwood.

The observer of the vow should offer *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), *śamī* leaves, and curd as the respectful offering (*arghya*). Then he should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
He should feed virtuous Brahmins, saintly women, boys, and girls.
The observer of the vow should perform the breaking of the fast and give gifts with devotion.
By performing the vow in this manner, one becomes prosperous and shall never encounter distress;
he shall be endowed with wealth, grain, sons, daughters, grandsons, great-grandsons, and so forth.
Furthermore, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, the vow of Ḍhuṇḍhirāja should be performed;
Gaṇeśa is to be worshipped with all kinds of offerings, with sesame flour and sesame seeds, through gifts, fire-oblations, and ritual worship. (134)
Having propitiated Lord Ḍhuṇḍhirāja, one shall obtain all prosperity.
By giving a golden elephant-faced [image] and wealth to a twice-born, the observer of the vow attains many enjoyments; there is no doubt about this.
On whichever month’s fourth lunar day (caturthī) it may fall, if it is joined with Sunday or joined with Tuesday,
it bestows special fruits.
On all such fourth lunar days, Vighneśa is indeed Kṛṣṇa himself.
Likewise, the fivefold abode (pañcāyatana) should be worshipped with a spirit of devotion.
(13.8) At the conclusion of the vow (udyāpana), the observances and self-restraints must be performed; celibacy (brahmacarya) must be maintained, for the fruit shall indeed be eternal. (13.9)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vārṣika Caturthī Vows, including the Vows of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha in the form of Gaṇeśa, the Satī Birth Vow, the Rathantara Kalpa, the Varāha Jayantī, the Gaṇeśa Jayantī, the Cow-Circumambulation, the Siddhivināyaka Vow, the Nāga Vow, the Karakā Vow, the Aṅgāraka Vow, the Kāśī-Vināyaka Vow, the Ḍhuṇḍhirāja Vow, and others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 269.
