Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! to the vows of the five [Tithis], by performing which people attain happiness, liberation, and prosperity. 1.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Hari was born as a fish.
A golden image of the fish should be fashioned, and a great festival for it should be observed.
This fish is indeed the son of Brahmā, who, having slain Hayagrīva, [recovered the Vedas].
He, who is worthy of worship by those desiring prosperity, caused the Vedas to be brought together.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, he who was indeed worthy of worship commanded Matsya to preserve the seeds in a boat for the sake of Satyavrata. (3–4)
Half of his form is human and half is that of a fish;
he is golden and should be worshipped on the bank of the Kṛtamālā river along with Satyaka.
He is auspicious, wearing a crown, and holding a conch in his left hand and a mace in his right.
For the food offering (naivedya), one should provide curd and cooked rice, as well as vada cakes mixed with curd.
One should cause the story concerning the birth of Matsya to be sung and recited.
One should give gifts to the preceptor and eat after the ārārtika ceremony.
This is declared to be Śrīpañcamī, wherein Śrī performed her penance;

therefore, for the sake of attaining the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one should perform this vow and the worship of Śrī with perfumes and other offerings, as well as food offerings such as milk-pudding (pāyasa). 8.
Lakṣmī does not abandon the worshiper who honors her with ornaments, fruits, flowers, incense, and excellent articles. Furthermore,
on this lunar day, the Earth was lifted upon the waters by the Boar.
An auspicious vow for her must be performed through the worship of the deity’s form and other rites;
she should also perform here the Candra-vrata, which destroys the loss [of the moon].
By means of penance and through the grace of Śambhu, the waning of the moon was brought to an end.
And the incarnation of Hayagrīva took place on this fifth lunar day (pañcamī).
One should perform the Hayagrīva vow and worship the horse-faced deity,
[represented by] a golden human form equipped with weapons and accompanied by the Earth.
One should worship Vāsudeva Janārdana, the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa, according to the prescribed rite; likewise, one should feed parched chickpeas and offer gifts of medicinal herbs,
juices, water, and fruits.
The performer of the vow shall always be free from disease and possessed of wealth and grain.
(15) Now, on the fifth day of Vaiśākha, Śeṣa is to be worshipped here by men;
through that, one obtains the desired fruit granted by the hosts of Nāgas. (16)
The Nāgas do not cause any harm whatsoever in the house of one who observes this vow;
indeed, they become protectors in the field, the garden, and likewise in the grove. (17) Then, on the fifth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the wise man should worship the ancestors.

Indeed, the attainment of all desired fruits occurs through the libations to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa). 18. Now, on the fifth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, the Vāyu-vrata is proclaimed. Having gone outside the village, one should remain standing upon a mound of earth. 19.
One should erect a five-colored banner fixed to the tip of a bamboo pole;
one should install it raised high and worship the base of the pole.
In whichever direction the banner goes, being impelled by the wind, [in that direction the victory follows].
One should perform the worship of the lords of those directions at the base of the staff (daṇḍa). In whichever direction the wind blows during the first and subsequent watches of the night,
one should properly offer worship to that respective lord of the direction.

Remaining thus without food for four watches of the night, one should return in the evening, eat, and lie down upon the ground for a moment. Whatever dream arises during that night will certainly come to pass.
If indeed something inauspicious is seen, one should observe a fast;
having performed the worship of Śiva at night, one should feed eight brahmins.
By that, one will enjoy auspicious fruit; one should give gifts such as cows and the like.
This vow has been well-proclaimed as a manifestation of both auspicious and inauspicious results;
it generates good fortune for men and brings happiness both in this world and the next.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, this vow brings about an increase in food.
Indeed, people should perform this rite here, for it brings about an abundance of all kinds of food. On the fourth day, at the end of the day, O Lotus-born One,
one should moisten all the grains with water in separate vessels, and then [place them] in the morning.
At sunrise, he should offer those very same waters to the ancestors, the gods, and the deities, as well as well-prepared, pure foods.
He should also present those very same pleasant dishes to beggars.
Having gone to the temple of Śambhu at night, one should worship the Liṅga with perfumes and other offerings. One should mutter the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" and pray for the attainment of food.
[One should offer] autumnal foods as well as those of the springtime.
"May I be enriched with those [qualities] in birth after birth.
Having thus prayed and given food to the Brahmins while remaining silent, he should eat that very same food; for this vow indeed consists of the preparation of food.

The Jīvantikā-vrata is observed on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa; it produces all kinds of food and grants a favorable rebirth in the next world. On this day, the observer of the vow should worship Indrāṇī with the leaves, flowers, and other offerings of the jīvantī plant.
On both sides of the door, one should draw fierce serpents with cow dung;
having worshipped them and bowed to the twice-born,
one should give gifts of gold, silver, and so forth, which yield infinite fruit.
One should observe the vow of eating but once a day, surrounded by one's wife, children, and friends.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should gratify the nāgas with milk;
for him, his lineage shall remain entirely free from fear of serpents up to the seventh generation. (36–37)
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should worship the best of ṛṣis.
Having bathed early in the morning and having fashioned an altar adorned with flowers out of clay,
and having spread kuśa grass there, one should indeed worship the Seven Ṛṣis.

With various perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and offerings, one should provide *ṛṣyanna* (rice grown by sages) for the meal, especially *nivāra* rice. The observer of the vow should cook the food offering (*naivedya*) from uncultivated grains such as *śyāmāka* and the like. (1.270.39–40)
The observer of the vow, being pleasing in appearance, should feed seven preceptors.
He should fashion seven images of matted-hair ascetics wearing sacred threads, made of gold, placed within jars of copper or clay. (4.1)
Having renounced [all else], one should bathe [the deity] with devotion using the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth.
Having worshipped with the sixteen types of offerings (upacāra), one should present the respectful offering (arghya).
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with sesame seeds, sacrificial oblation (havir), rice, ghee, barley, and other such materials.
Having offered oblations with meritorious mantras and names, one should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
One should give seven cows, adorned with garments and ornaments, to the knower of the Vedas;
indeed, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor for the completion of the vow.
Having fed the gurus and the Brahmins, he should prostrate and dismiss them.
He himself, however, should respectfully eat the pleasing food together with his kinsmen.
By thus performing the vow with all its constituent parts, the practitioner of the vow shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O King, by performing this vow, a woman indeed shakes off even her slightest faults.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, Gopāla Kṛṣṇa himself was born at Kuṅkumavāpī in the temple of Nimbadevānikā.
The four-armed Kṛṣṇa should be fashioned and worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
A great festival should be celebrated with vows, gifts, and feasts;
He should be reverently honored together with His wife, Kaṃbhārā Lakṣmī.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, there is the Upāṅgalalitā-vrata.
Formerly, this vow was performed by Lalitā in order to attain Hari.
O Lotus-born one, having fashioned her golden image according to one's means—

One should worship her according to the prescribed rite with the sixteen types of offerings. To complete the vow, one should give to a Brāhmaṇa palatable food consisting of cooked rice mixed with fruit and ghee, along with a monetary gift (dakṣiṇā).
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, the vow known as Jayā was observed here for the sake of attaining Hari; having worshipped with sixteen excellent articles and other offerings,
and having fed [the deity], one should give the priestly fee and so forth.
Thereafter, the observer of the vow should dismiss [the deities] and then eat himself.
During the Jayā-vrata, one should perform a bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha) which destroys sins;
one shall obtain the fruit of bathing at the concluding purificatory rite (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice.
A sonless man obtains a son, a barren woman becomes pregnant,

a sick person attains health, and the observer of the vow attains worldly enjoyment and liberation. On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having worshipped the Nāgas with devotion—
Having obtained freedom from fear of the *nāgas*, he rejoices together with his kinsmen.

(57) On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is to be worshipped; likewise, the ancestors and the *nāgas* are to be worshipped, for they are considered to be the bringers of happiness. (58)

The Vasantavrata is prescribed for the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha. At that time, worship of Vasanta should be performed, and one should observe the practice of eating only one meal a day.
[One should offer] fresh wheat crops as well as Badarī leaves.

Having constructed a green pavilion with wild dates, black mustard, and various grasses, one should worship it with saffron and other offerings. The observer of the vow should then worship a water-pot filled with colored water.
One should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa and cause Him to engage in play with colored powders.
Having thus performed the vow, one should offer parched grain and dates to the people.
This vow brings about the attainment of worldly enjoyment, liberation, and happiness.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, Kaṃbharā was born as Lakṣmī.
In the morning, her festival should be celebrated at the House of Love (Prema-gṛha), the abode of Om (Om-ālaya). Indeed, the four-armed Mahālakṣmī should be worshipped there with golden [images].
The vow, complete with its constituent parts, should be performed as it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is to be worshipped;
thereafter, the Blessed Lord shall pacify the defects manifested by the Holi festival.
"Thus, one who desires happiness should perform these observances according to their capacity.

(66) Thus ends [the section on] the annual fifth-day observances (*vārṣika-pañcamī-vratāni*) within the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. These include: the Matsya-jayantī, the Śrī-tapovrata, the Vārāha-pṛthvīvrata, the Candrakṣaya-nāśavrata, the Hayagrīva-jayantī, the Nāga-pañcamī, the Pitṛvrata, the Vāyuvrata, the Anna-vṛddhivrata, the Jīvantikā-nāgavrata, the Ṛṣi-pañcamī, the Gopāla-kṛṣṇa-jayantī, the Lalitāvrata, the Jayāvrata, and the Nāgavrata.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now, I shall describe to you the various vows of the Vārṣika-ṣaṣṭhīs.
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall indeed tell you that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(1) In ancient times, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, the birth of Skanda occurred.
This Kumāra-vrata must be performed with worship and other rites. (2)
One should worship the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) together with his peacock and the commander of the army (Senānī).
The observer of the vow should offer meals and gifts with great devotion.
By means of this vow, one becomes strong, heroic, and endowed with all virtues.
A long-lived son is indeed certainly obtained by one who observes the vow.
For the completion of the vow, one should cause a golden image of Śaṅkara, Pārvatī, and Skanda, adorned with all materials,
to be given to the preceptor.
On the sixth lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha, the observer of the vow should worship Kārtikeya;
he obtains the happiness derived from his mother, such as being fondled, protected, and so forth.
On the sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the Sun.
One obtains one's desired objects through the grace of the Sun.
Furthermore, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the Skanda-vrata;
one obtains one's cherished desires and a lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the one born under the Śara constellation (Kārttikeya).
By the grace of the Six-faced One, one obtains all desired objects.
On this very day, one should observe the vow of eating only soup and boiled rice.
The devotee should offer [the food] to Hari and eat it as His prasāda.
(1.271.10) Except for soup and rice, nothing else should be eaten; one should observe the vow of eating only once a day.
By this vow, Śrī Hari will then grant him soup and rice. (11)
On this very day, I shall indeed become Kalki.
One should perform my birth-vow (janmavrata), while I am mounted upon a white horse.
One should worship me with an umbrella, weapons, and adorned with golden necklaces.
I provide protection for the seeker of the vow from the suffering caused by heretics and the wicked.
(13) On the sixth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the observer of the vow should worship Lalitā.
A virtuous woman seeking the vow, having bathed and wearing white garments, (14) should worship.
Having taken sand from the confluence of two rivers, one should fashion a lump;
and having fashioned Lalitā with lotuses,
oleanders, blue water-lilies, jasmine, and ketaka flowers, one should worship her.
Then one should offer one hundred and eight flowers to her.
Standing before her, one should pray to Lalitā, the beloved of Śrī Hari:
"At Gaṅgādvāra, at Kuśāvarta, at Bilvaka, and on the Nīla mountain... (16–17).
"Likewise, having bathed at Kanakhala, she obtained Hari as her husband.
O increaser of good fortune, grant to me also union with Śrī Hari.
Having thus prayed and performed worship, one should place the food offering (naivedya) before [the deity].
One should beautify the area in front with coconut, cucumber, pumpkin, pomegranate, and citron;
with *cirbhaṭṭa* and *karkaṭikā* fruits, as well as with fresh sprouts and leaves, rows of lamps, and archways. (19–20)

The observer of the vow should devoutly feed [the deity] with fragrant incenses, various offerings of food, diverse kinds of sweetmeats, *śaṣkulī* cakes, and *modaka* sweets. He should perform the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) and keep a vigil throughout the night.

Accompanied by her friends, that virtuous woman should not close her eyes while singing, dancing, performing devotional worship, or chanting the Name. On the seventh day, having gone to a river and bathed, she should then worship it.
Having given gifts to the twice-born, having likewise offered oblations into the fire,
and having honored the gods, the ancestors, and human beings,
as well as women in their auspicious finery, the observer of the vow should feed the Brahmins, virgins, virtuous men, and virtuous women.
"May Lalitā be well-pleased with me"; having thus prayed, one should dismiss [the deities].
A man or a woman should indeed observe this supreme vow which bestows good fortune; it cannot be equaled by other vows, austerities, gifts, observances, or restraints. (25–26)
The fruit of which is easily obtained: having departed for the eternal world, the observer of the vow rejoices together with Goddess Lalitā while traveling in a celestial chariot.
This is the Candana-ṣaṣṭhī vow, observed during the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
On that day, Lakṣmī should be worshipped with sandalwood paste, ornaments, and other offerings.
Indeed, when the sixth lunar day is joined with the Rohiṇī asterism, a Saturday, and Mars, it is known as Kāpilā;
on that day, one should worship the Sun with sixteen auspicious articles.
The performer of the vow shall obtain his desired objects; of this there is no doubt.
Even by the Sūrya-ṣaṣṭhī vow alone, through the grace of Bhāskara, [one gains merit];
likewise, recitation, fire-offerings, charity, and the libations offered to the ancestors, gods, and sages [yield fruit].
All auspicious merit performed by one observing the vow is to be known as entirely inexhaustible.
Having worshipped a tawny cow with garlands, saffron, and food, one should indeed present her, along with all her appurtenances, to the preceptor for the satisfaction of the Sun. (31–32)
By performing the vow in this manner, a woman shall obtain supreme happiness;
she shall obtain a husband and a home enriched with juices, food, fruits, ornaments, and other luxuries.
Furthermore, O beloved, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, Kātyāyanī is indeed to be worshipped.

O beloved, Pārvatī herself has declared that Kālī, the mother Kātyāyanī, should be worshipped here with fragrant and auspicious substances and foods of sweet and excellent flavors; or else, O virtuous wife of the twice-born, her image made of sand may be worshipped.
Having given gifts of clothing and ornaments, having bowed and asked for forgiveness, he should dismiss her.
A maiden seeking the vow shall obtain a most handsome husband through destiny;
one seeking a son shall obtain a son by the grace of Kātyāyanī.

On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the high-souled Ṣaṇmukha obtained as his wife Devasenā, who is worshipped by all the gods. One should worship Skanda, accompanied by Devasenā, with ritual offerings.
Likewise, worship of the fire and the fire-oblation (homa) should also be performed with devotion.
In this way, the observer of the vow shall enjoy eternal success as desired by the mind.
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, [this was established] by the wise Kārttikeya.
The Daitya Tāraka having been slain, Brahmā and the other gods performed the worship of Skanda with perfumes,
flowers, and the like, as well as with fruits and other offerings for the one observing vows;
indeed, supreme worship should be performed with garments, ornaments, and weapons.

Sweet food is prescribed as the offering, and the gift of cows and land is traditionally enjoined. If this [day] is joined with Sunday and conjoined with the Śatabhiṣā asterism, it is then called Campā-ṣaṣṭhī; indeed, Hara is to be worshipped on that occasion.

All acts such as bathing and giving gifts are said to become inexhaustible [in merit]. (43) A great worship should be performed for both Hara and Hari; the observer of the vow should, moreover, give various kinds of gifts with sincere devotion. (44)
By this vow, a man or a woman, having obtained happiness here, shall go to the imperishable state.

On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, the Lord of Light, Prabhēśvara, who is the protector of the world and an incarnation of Viṣṇu, should be worshipped; he was indeed born again from the Creator.
This is Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord who brings light to all;
he should be worshipped with the sixteen supreme articles and other offerings by those desiring happiness.
His power of vision shall increase, and he shall become a householder possessed of abundant wealth.
Having had a golden image of Sūrya, adorned with a beautiful crown and accompanied by Brahmā, fashioned, the observer of the vow should give it as a gift to a twice-born man.
The sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha is considered the day of the origin of Varuṇa.

In that [place], the Lord of Waters, who is the Lord of Gods and possesses the form of Viṣṇu, is indeed to be worshipped. Worshipped with red perfumes, garments, flowers, incense, food offerings, and lamps by one observing a vow, he shall grant auspicious and excellent flavors according to one's desire.
And on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should have an image of the Lord Hara Paśupati made,
either of clay or of gold, and worship it;
having bathed it separately with the Śatarudrīya and with the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Having anointed [the deity] with the fragrance of white sandalwood, with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and flowers,
with white dhattūra flowers, and with bilva fruits and excellent leaves,
one should worship and offer sweet foods as the sacrificial oblation (*naivedya*).
Having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), bowed down, and asked for forgiveness, one should then dismiss [the deity].
Having observed this vow, whether man or woman, at the conclusion of their worldly enjoyments, they shall attain the state of Śiva.

Thus ends the section on the annual *ṣaṣṭhī* vows, including the Kārtikasvāmijayantī and Divākaravrata, within the Skanda-vrata in the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 273 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I shall indeed describe to you the vows of the seven Saptamīs of the rainy season, O Lakṣmī! By performing which, the observer of the vow attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform a bath at a sacred ford.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound smeared with cow dung and covered with white clay,
one should draw an eight-petalled lotus there with a pericarp. Having established the Fire-god therein, one should place Ravi (the Sun) on the eastern petal and Hari.
Then, having placed Anala in the southeast, Śukra in the south, Maṅgala and Yama in the southwest, Nirṛti and Rāhu in the southwest (repeated),
and Ketu; and then Śani and Varuṇa in the west, and Anila and Candra in the northwest.
Having established Budha and Kubera in the north, and Guru and Hara in the northeast,
one should worship them all with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, as well as with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, betel, fruits, and mouth-fresheners.
The observer of the vow should perform one hundred and eight oblations with clarified butter;
he should offer eight oblations for each [deity] using the respective name-mantras.
Then, he should perform the final oblation and give an auspicious sacrificial fee.
In this manner, one should perform the vow of worship for the guardians of the directions (dikpālas).
Having performed the vow of eating but once a day, one shall obtain all happiness.
At the end of the body, having pierced the orb of the sun, one goes to the supreme state.

In ancient times, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, Jahnu drank the Jāhnavī and then released her again; this is considered the Gaṅgā-vrata. Having bathed in the Jāhnavī, one should worship Gaṅgā with ritual offerings.
One desiring prosperity should indeed perform the gift of a thousand jars;
this auspicious Gaṅgā-vrata leads seven generations of one's family to heaven.
On this lunar day, the Kamala-vrata is likewise to be understood.
One should fashion an auspicious lotus out of gold weighing a mere sesame seed;
having covered it with a pair of garments, one should worship it with perfumes, incense, and other offerings.
Then, having bowed to the Sun in the evening, one should present the lotus to a brahmin.
One should offer that water-pot, the lotus, and a tawny cow to a twice-born man.
One should observe a fast and break it on the following day.
With devotion, one should feed Brāhmaṇas, as well as virtuous men, women, and chaste ladies.
In this manner, the vow should be performed and likewise a gift of cows should be given;
the woman who observes the vow shall attain worldly enjoyment and liberation, and she shall rejoice in wealth.
On this very lunar day, the auspicious Nimba-vow should be observed.
The worship of the Sun should be performed, especially with neem leaves.
One should likewise eat a neem leaf and sleep on the ground without food.
On the following day, having fed the Brahmins, one should eat together with one's kinsmen.
This Śarkarāsaptamī bestows all flavors upon the earth;
therefore, those who desire such flavors should observe the vow of sugar.
From the hand of the Sun as he drinks the nectar, drops of ambrosia fall.
Rice, mung beans, barley, and sugarcane sprouted upon the earth;
and from the sugarcane, sugar was produced, which is always auspicious and beloved by the Sun.
It is pure for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and should be given for the satisfaction of the deities.
In this matter, the taking of sugar and likewise the eating of sugar must be performed properly by one observing the vow;
it increases the lineage of sons, pacifies all sufferings, and bestows the fruit of a horse sacrifice. 22.
Furthermore, other gifts should be bestowed and virtuous people should be fed.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, Indra himself became the Sun;
one should observe a fast and perform the vow, worshipping Indra according to the prescribed rite.
O twice-born one, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the sun named Vivasvat should be honored with an offering of gold;
having fed the virtuous and the children, the observer of the vow should then eat his meal himself.
(15) On that day, the sun is known by the name Vivasvat.
For one who has attained the royal consecration, worship is prescribed during this vow.
Having worshipped Vivasvat with gold, flowers, and other offerings, one attains union with him and divine, eternal happiness. (26–27)
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the vow known as Arvya is prescribed.
In this context, cotton cloth should especially be given as a gift.
If that seventh day is conjoined with the lunar mansion Hasta, it bestows great merit.
In this [day], charity, recitation, and burnt offerings—all these shall attain imperishability.
This is the Śītalā-saptamī; indeed, Pārvatī is the one to be worshipped.
A garment and food made of flour and other ingredients should be offered to Śītalā.
By this, health shall indeed always prevail within the family of the observer of the vow.
A fast must be observed, and gifts such as fruits and the like should be given.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the Amuktābharaṇa vow is to be performed.
Indeed, the moon was worn upon the forehead by Śambhu as an ornament.
One should perform the worship of Soma and Maheśa with the sixteen [upacāras] and other offerings; having bowed, one should dismiss them for the fulfillment of all desires.
This is considered the "Fruit-Saptamī," consisting of seven fruits;
one should offer these fruits: coconut, eggplant, orange, citron, pumpkin, brinjal, and betel nut.
Having offered here a seven-strand cord with seven knots to Śaṅkara, one should then bind it upon the left hand;
a woman on the left and a man on the right, and thus protect it for a year.
At the conclusion of the vow, the observer of the vow, having fed seven children,
should then eat himself together with his wife for the sake of completing the vow.
He should indeed give fruits to the twice-born for the sake of their satisfaction.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, having performed the vow for seven years according to the prescribed rule, she who possesses it attains union with Mahādeva. During that vow, worship should be performed according to the rule and according to one's wealth.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, the Pañcagavya vow is prescribed.
It is declared that Śubhasaptamī bestows purity as well as merit.
Having bathed and worshipped the Lord Hari and the Sun, the observer of the vow should then proceed.
Having worshipped a tawny cow, he should pray to her; listen, O beloved:
"O auspicious one, I give you away; may Aryaman himself be pleased.
Protect the entire world through the power of righteousness and merit. (41-42)
Having recited this and bowed down, one should offer the liquid to a brahmin.
According to the tradition, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) on that day and perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) on the following day.
After feeding the best of the twice-born, the observer of the vow should partake of the remnants.
By the grace of Śrī, he shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now follows the vow known as Śākāsaptamī on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
The observer of the vow, subsisting on vegetables, should offer seven types of vegetables to a virtuous person.
Then, on the seventh day, one should give food and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a twice-born man;
on the second day, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā). This vow is the destroyer of sins.
The Mitravrata is declared to be observed on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
From Kaśyapa and Aditi was born the sun-god named Mitra.
His supreme vow, accompanied by fasting and festive rites, must be performed;
his worship should be conducted according to the prescribed rules, and one should feed the virtuous with sweet food.
Having given a gift of gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the observer of the vow should then dismiss [the deity];
on the following morning, having again bowed to the Sun, he should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*).
By performing the vow in this manner here, he indeed goes to the world of the Sun.
Whoever is a performer of this vow and is born into a noble family,
on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, the observer of the vow named "Abhaya" should remain standing upon the ground and worship the Sun at the three times of day.
One who observes this vow should fast and feed seven other Brahmins;
he should give milk-rice and a *prastha* measure of sweetmeats (*modaka*) to the twice-born.
The observer of the vow should further offer a liberal sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), such as land or gold.
The Brahmins should likewise grant him blessings and the gift of fearlessness.
This vow is known as Abhaya; it is remembered as the bestower of fearlessness upon all.
This is also called the Mārtaṇḍa vow; the practitioner of the vow should worship Mārtaṇḍa.
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, there is a vow named Sarvāpti.
On that occasion, one should perform the worship of the Sun while observing a fast.
A vigil should be kept at night, and then virtuous people should be fed in the morning.
They should be gratified with milk-rice, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), fruits, and other offerings.
Having dismissed them, the observer of the vow should then eat whatever he desires.
This is indeed the vow named "Bestower of All Attainments," which fulfills all desires.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the vow known as Acalā is prescribed;
one should observe a fast, by which merit becomes unshakable and eternal.
Hara, accompanied by his three-eyed consort, should be worshipped as Trilocana.
This Trilocanājayantī has been composed as the remover of all sins.
This Rathīyasaptamī indeed bestows the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
One should worship the glorious Sun-god, seated upon a chariot yoked with elephants, made of gold.
This is the Bhāskarī-saptamī; on this day,
the observer of the vow himself should place seven leaves each of the *arka* and the *badarī* upon his head and bathe for the pacification of the misfortunes of seven previous births.
This vow for obtaining a son should be performed by one desiring a son.
Sūrya, being greatly pleased, shall become his son through a portion of himself.
Having fasted on the following day, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the morning.
One should feed curd-rice and milk, and honor virtuous men.
By performing the vow in this manner, one shall indeed obtain a long-lived son.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should observe the Arkapuṭa vow.
One should worship the Sun with *arka* leaves and consume *arka* leaves; one should constantly recite the name of the *arka*.
This is considered the *arka-vrata*, which is auspicious and bestows wealth, sons, daughters, prosperity, a husband, and a wife.
Therefore, this vow of sacrifice (yajñavrata) should be performed for the easy attainment of all happiness, as it bestows dharma, artha, and kāma, and destroys all sins.
The propitiation of the Sun (Bhāskara) shall grant the fulfillment of all desires.
Therefore, one should worship the Sun on all seventh lunar days (saptamī).
Likewise, one should perform the drawing of the Sarvatobhadra mandala, the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa),
the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and the ritual services beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).

The performer of the vow should always perform everything according to the prescribed rules, beginning with the food offering (*naivedya*) and ending with the dismissal of the handfuls of rice and flowers (*taṇḍulapuṣpāñjali-visarjana*). One should perform the great concluding rite (*udyāpana*) and feed virtuous children.
Charity, fire sacrifice, chanting, and devotion to Śrī Hari—
these indeed must certainly be performed by one observing a vow so that great satisfaction may arise for Hari.
Through this, there shall be enjoyment and liberation, and the full fruit of the vow will be attained.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Vows such as the Dikpāla-vrata, Jāhnavī-vrata, Nimba-sūrya-vrata, Indra-sūrya-vrata, Vivasvad-abhiṣeka-vrata, Avyaṅga-śītalā-saptamī, Candrābharaṇa-vrata, Śubhaphala-saptamī, Śāka-vrata, Mitrārka-jayantī, Mārtaṇḍābhaya-vrata, Sārvakāmika-āpti-vrata, Trilocanā-jayantī, Bhāskarī-saptamī, Putrapradā, and Arkapuṭa-vrata," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛtayuga in the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*. 272.

Chapter 274 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Lakṣmī! I shall describe to you the vows of the eighth lunar days (Aṣṭamīs), by performing which, O Lotus-born one, the practitioner of the vow attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform the excellent vow for the birth of Pārvatī.
Having constructed a pavilion adorned with plantain pillars and Aśoka archways,
one should prepare a Sarvatobhadra mandala therein and place [the image] in its center.
Having installed a golden image of Pārvatī, one should perform a hundred circumambulations.
One should worship her with the sixteen excellent articles of offering, beginning with water for the feet, and concluding with food.
Having placed her upon a chariot, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and carry out the rites pertaining to the fire.
Devotees should perform a great festival of procession accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and the like.
In every house, [the deity] should be worshipped with rice, parched grain, water, fruits, auspicious substances, saffron, collyrium, ornaments, and so forth. (5)
Then one should increase [the merit] with a coconut fruit or even with a water-pot.
(6) Having thus brought her, preceded by a great festival, either to the water or to the temple, one should worship her and then perform the *ārārtika* rite. (7)
Having fed the Queen of the Gods according to the prescribed rite, one should dismiss her.
One should give all kinds of gifts, as well as clothing and food, to young girls.
By performing the vow in this manner, a woman obtains auspicious good fortune.
A maiden, having observed this supreme vow, shall attain the status of a queen.
Right here, one should practice the consumption of eight *aśoka* buds;
for one who performs this consumption, sorrow never arises anywhere. (1.273.10)
This very same day is known as Mahāṣṭamī; it should be observed with a fast, and the worship of Pārvatī must indeed be performed until the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
Furthermore, one should observe a fast on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha.
That [day] is declared to be Durgāṣṭamī; one should worship Aparājitā.
One should offer an oblation of food mixed with sugar and indeed give gifts at that time.
Furthermore, one should feed young girls on the ninth day, prior to breaking the fast.
The observer of the vow, residing in a celestial chariot of light by the power of Aparājita’s compassion,
may wander through the heavenly worlds and become endowed with both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Upon the arrival of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, one should perform the Trilocana-vrata.
He shall dwell on Kailāsa for the duration of a kalpa, highly honored.
On the morning of the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the white Durgā;
by the grace of the goddess Śuklā, the observer of the vow attains Kailāsa.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the observer of the vow should worship the Goddess;
he should offer an oblation of food accompanied by sugar and feed young girls.
Having given gold as a sacrificial fee and dismissed them, the observer of the vow should eat himself.
Having performed this auspicious vow, one shall attain the world of Durgā.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, the observer of the vow should worship Durgā,
feed her with various kinds of food, and perform the ritual dismissal according to the prescribed rules.
Then, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should perform the breaking of the fast and the vow that increases progeny, known as the Daśāphala-vrata. Indeed,
one should observe a fast and likewise perform the worship of Śrī Hari.
One should worship with ten leaves of black *tulasī* [Kṛṣṇa], namely:
Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Ananta, Govinda, Garuḍadhvaja, Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Hari the Lord. (21–22)
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa day after day with these names,
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) one hundred and eight times in the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
One should likewise offer oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru), flowers, fruits, and sugar.
One should perform this for ten days, and thereafter worship the preceptor.
Having placed a golden Tulasī leaf in a golden vessel or another vessel,
as well as a golden image, one should offer them to the guru.
One should indeed perform the gift of a cow, adorned with garments and ornaments;
for ten days, one should offer milk-preparations and *pūrikā* cakes.
One should personally partake of the consecrated food (*prasāda*) and feed virtuous Brahmins.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give ten *pūrikā* cakes to each of ten virtuous men.
Having thus performed this unsurpassed vow for ten years,
one shall experience all the heavens and attain union with Kṛṣṇa.
A man shall become an attendant of Kṛṣṇa, and a woman shall become a beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
There is no other vow like this that brings about union with Kṛṣṇa. Formerly, the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada was the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī vow.
By means of fasting, the performer destroys the sins of seven lifetimes.
(1.273.30) Having fasted and bathed with sesame seeds in pure water at a river or similar site, one should thoroughly clean the temple by sweeping, washing, and plastering it. (31)
One should beautify [the area] with various colorful paintings, archways, and banners; one should also hang new canopies and the like, as well as figurines.
There should be a throne for the Blessed One and the implements for worship. (32)
One should sweep the area and provide new coverings for the lamps.
Then, the observer of the vow should prepare the offerings, food, garments, and other requisites for worship, either in the center of the assembly hall or in front of the temple. (33–34)
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, adorned with plantain pillars, endowed with cloths, variegated flowers, excellent blossoms, sprouts, and water-pots,
and resplendent with rows of lamps bearing fruits, garlands, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.
One should have that [place] fumigated with incense and place a water-pot (kalaśa) in its center.
Upon that, one should place a copper vessel, and upon that,
the auspicious image of Śrī Hari made of gold, covered with a pair of cloths.
The performer of the vow should worship with offerings such as water for the feet;
furthermore, he should construct a maternity chamber for Devakī within the pavilion. Therein, he should indeed place Devakī together with the infant Kṛṣṇa.
The observer of the vow should represent Yaśodā in Gokula as enchanting and accompanied by her son;
likewise, he should have Vasudeva, Nanda, the cowherds, the cowherdesses,
and the cows made of gold, as well as the bulls, the calves, and the heifers.
One should worship those [images] installed in the pavilion in all the cardinal and intermediate directions;
one should cause musical instruments to be played and have auspicious songs sung.
Having performed the bathing, worship, and other rites for the image, one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony.
At midnight, one should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and pure water.
One should clothe [the deity] in beautiful garments, ornaments, jewels, and necklaces,
as well as saffron, kesara, aguru, sandalwood, and flowers.
Then, having offered necklaces, crest-jewels, flower garlands, and *tulasī* wreaths, as well as incense and lamps, one should present the great food offering (*mahā-naivedya*).
This includes goat meat, ginger, coriander, sugar, and ghee.
One should present the five powders as an offering in a silver vessel.
One should offer rice mixed with milk, *saṃyāva*, and items cooked in ghee.
One should offer water and give betel leaf for the cleansing of the mouth.
One should offer a coconut fruit and a *tulasī* leaf as a priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Then, one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for Kṛṣṇa, who possesses twenty-four forms.
Thereafter, having offered the *arghya* and requested forgiveness, the observer of the vow should then put the deity to rest.
At night, one should keep vigil and listen to the narrative of His deeds.
Then, the observer of the vow should drink the supreme nectar from the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
he should consume a small amount of curd with sugar and partake of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then, having bathed at dawn, one should worship Bālakṛṣṇa;
one should especially offer milk, cooked rice, and sugar.
Thereafter, men and women [should bathe the deity] there with curd, milk, ghee, and water.
First, they should engage in play by means of applying paste, throwing it, and sprinkling water.
(51) Having bathed, one should feed the virtuous, as well as virtuous women, boys, and girls; one should also feed the Brahmins, the devotees, and even the poor, the blind, and the wretched. (52)
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and partake of the prasāda together with one's kinsmen.
Hari is pleased when the vow-observer performs worship in the morning and evening at the conclusion of the rite.
He should be swung daily until the second day of the month of Bhādra.
Having thus performed this vow together with his wife, children, friends, and servants,
a man attains Goloka itself, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
Indeed, there is no other vow in the three worlds that is equal to this.

O Lotus-born one, whatever is performed here that yields a fruit equal to eleven crores, such gifts worthy of a king should be bestowed. O beloved, the vow dedicated to Kṛṣṇa should be observed according to one's capacity and according to the available materials.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the birth of Rādhikā is celebrated.
At midday, the observer of the vow should wear red garments and worship the Lord as well as Rādhā; he should worship the image of Rādhikā together with Kṛṣṇa. ||57–58||
One should offer sweetmeats, pearls, and even fruits as an offering;
whatever is dear to oneself, that the observer of the vow should dedicate.
One should have the verses concerning the birth of Rādhikā sung by the cowherd women and others.
Having observed the vow of eating only one meal a day, he should feed married women.
Having offered his person to the preceptor, the observer of the vow should indeed eat;
or else, he may observe a fast and give red garments.
Having performed this vow in this manner, a woman shall dwell among the retinue of Rādhā;
always becoming a wife of Kṛṣṇa, she shall eternally attain the bliss of Kṛṣṇa.
This Dūrvāṣṭamī vow should likewise be observed by one who observes vows.
On ground where *dūrvā* grass grows, the observer of the vow should worship the arrow of Śambhu (6:3).
With perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, curd, unbroken rice, fruits, and so forth, he should worship with *dūrvā* blades and pray: "O *dūrvā*, you who are ever immortal! (6:4).
Just as you are spread across the earth with branches and sub-branches,
grant me widespread good fortune and a progeny that is undecaying and immortal.
Having fed the Brahmins and the virtuous, and having bid farewell to Śambhu, the observer of the vow [should proceed].
A woman who completes this vow shall become fortunate.
Thus, this meritorious eighth day, which removes sins and bestows progeny, should be observed.
She who does not worship with *dūrvā* grass shall remain a widow for three lifetimes.
This Jyeṣṭhāṣṭamī, joined with the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, consists of a vow;
this vow of Mahālakṣmī lasts for sixteen days from here until the end of Kālāṣṭamī, certainly reaching as far as Punarvasu.
The practitioner of the vow, being skillful, should tie a cord upon his right hand,
provided with sixteen knots and endowed with sixteen strands.
He should daily worship Lakṣmī therein and thereafter perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having constructed a cloth pavilion over a *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala,
one should place the water-pot and the lamp of the deity, and having removed the cord,
one should establish the four beautiful forms of Lakṣmī beneath the jar.
The observer of the vow should perform the ceremonial bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and waters;
having worshipped with the sixteen and other services, he should feed [the deity].
He should keep a vigil at night and offer the respectful oblation (arghya) to the Moon.
O you who arose from the ocean of milk, sister of Mahālakṣmī!
May you be the provider of food and medicine for me; accept this *arghya* of sandalwood paste from me.
O lotus-born one, arisen from the ocean of milk, beloved of Kṛṣṇa!
O you who dwell upon the chest of Viṣṇu, grant me all my desires! O sole mistress, mistress of the world, beloved of Gopāla, the imperishable one;
O goddess who bears the conch, protect me! O Mother of Kṛṣṇa, bestow auspiciousness upon me!
Having thus prayed to Mahālakṣmī and worshipped her with devotion, the women, having fed [the deity],
should offer oblations with bilva, lotus, and kapāvasa, as well as with fuel-sticks,
sesame seeds, ghee, flowers, and various kinds of fruits. (77)
For Viṣṇu, [he should offer] sandalwood, palm leaves, a garland, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata); likewise, dūrvā grass, a safflower thread, a pair [of garments],
a bilva fruit, tulasī, sugar, sweetmeats (laḍḍu), the essence of milk, sesame seeds, and barley.
One should offer water and betel leaf—these sixteen items—to Hari;
likewise, one should offer them to Mahālakṣmī, covering them with a winnowing basket upon a winnowing basket.
Having thus offered these to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, the observer of the vow himself [should partake].
One should conclude the worship and indeed complete that vow.
One should give four images to four Brahmins;
one should give sixteen sets of articles to sixteen virtuous women.
Having gratified them with sweet foods, he should dismiss them along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Afterwards, the observer of the vow should perform the breaking of the fast; indeed, by such a vow, one becomes a lord of ten million in this world and shall dwell in the world of Lakṣmī thereafter.
Indeed, by the grace of the fortune of Kambharā, one enjoys pleasures for a long time.
This is declared to be Śokāṣṭamī; one should perform the worship of Aśoka.
Having observed the vow of eating only once a day and having worshipped Ramā with devotion, [one attains the fruit]. || 84–85 ||
Wherever one may be born, one shall undoubtedly become free from sorrow.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should observe the fast of the Durgā-vrata;
or else, one should perform worship with a single meal according to this prescribed rite. (86)
Having attained prosperity in every respect, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the vow known as Karaka is prescribed;
on that night, Umāpati should be worshipped in every way by those desiring sons. 87–88.
Having given a gift of gold, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite at moonrise.
The observer of the vow, having performed worship in the morning, should then break his fast.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, this is the Śrī Bhagavat-vrata.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was born in the house of Gopāla-Kambharā.
Then all the gods and sages celebrated a great festival;
eager for a vision of him, they arrived having ascended their celestial chariots.
Then they respectfully honored [the deity] with divine flowers and other offerings.
At that time, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should indeed be prepared early in the morning with great care;
then, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was placed within that pavilion in the middle of the palace.

A golden image should be placed here within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala (93). Hari himself should be worshipped in a jar adorned with the five precious gems, fruits, and sprouts, or indeed in a vessel filled with sesame seeds (94).
Endowed with glory, accompanied by his father and mother, that great lord said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī, to my worship which grants liberation along with you;
it bestows prosperity, grants all happiness, and fulfills every desire. (95)
That should be performed by a woman or even by a man seeking the merit of the vow.

Beginning with the invocation, there is the bathing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), water, and so forth, as well as the putting on of garments, ornaments, and other such beautiful accoutrements. (96–97)

One should offer incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, the waving of lights (*ārātrika*), and ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), as well as hymns of praise, worship, betel-leaf, water for consumption, and water for sipping (98). [One should worship] Kṛṣṇa, who embodies all the scriptures and is the abode of Sarasvatī.
One should likewise remember Him as the abode created by all the gods, the dwelling place of Śrī, Ramā, and others, and the Lord of Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, and Māṇikī;
one should give various kinds of gifts and observe the vigil with great festivity. (99–100)
Having bathed in the morning, having performed worship, and having fed [the guests], one should bid them farewell.
By performing the vow of the Jayantī of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in this manner, one obtains a wife, a husband, a daughter, a son, a cow, wealth, and even gold. (101)
The observer of the vow obtains a field, a dwelling, a vehicle, and freedom from disease.
Through this vow, one indeed attains knowledge, existence, great fame, honor, and all prosperity; one truly gains heaven and finds liberation. (102–103)

The birth of Kālabhairava indeed occurs on that very Kālāṣṭamī; he who seeks the fruit of the vow must perform his worship with appropriate offerings. This Śaṅkara himself has become Bhairava in the form of Time (Kāla).
For those observing the vow, no fear of Bhairava and the like shall ever arise.

In the bright fortnight of Kārtika, the Gopāṣṭamī of the cows should indeed be understood; there, one should perform worship of the cows, offer mouthfuls of grass, give gifts of cows, and circumambulate cows. (105–106)

Kṛṣṇa became a cowherd and tended the cows; by always observing the Govrata vow, the goddess Lakṣmī, whose essence is rasa, shall dwell in one's home. On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should indeed observe the Darbhamithunaka vow.
Having fashioned a pair of *darbha* blades named Anaghā and Anagha, he should place them together with the son and grandson [of the *darbha*] upon a ground smeared with cow-dung and other substances;
and he should worship that [pair] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. (108–109)
Having fed the couple and dismissed them after they have received their sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
a man or a woman who has performed the vow shall obtain a son, a daughter, and happiness.
In this very context, one should observe the Kālabhairava-Jayantī vow.
Now, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Durgā-vrata is prescribed by the Sun-god.
This time-bound vow (kāla-vrata) should be performed with worship, fire-offerings, gifts, and excellent meals;
it consists of fasting and keeping a vigil in the presence of Kālabhairava.
Indeed, having performed an action that causes suffering, one attains its destruction through the power of [this rite].
Then, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, there is the Śrāddha known as Aṣṭaka,
which grants satisfaction to the ancestors for a year and increases the lineage of the family.
Everything must be performed according to the prescribed rite specifically after midday.
Since it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, the worship of Śiva should be performed.
Indeed, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should observe the Bhadrakālī vow.
One should worship her who slays hosts of enemies and bestows all desires.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, Hari, the dark Nārāyaṇa,
made his descent from the world of Brahmā into divine Kāśī.
On the ninth day, the Lord performed the transmission of the supreme knowledge (parā-vidyā).
For two days, he observed the vow of incarnation and the vow of knowledge;
he performed worship with the sixteen articles and gave a gift of gold.
The observer of the vow should consume the essence of milk and thereby obtain knowledge and worldly enjoyment.
One should worship Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and Kṛṣṇa. All these queens, together with Kṛṣṇa, become well-pleased. 119.
They lead the man and the woman to their own abode, the supreme, imperishable syllable.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, the Bhīmādevī-vrata is observed;
the worship of Bhīmā should be performed, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should worship Śiva and Śivā;
one should also worship Śītalā with previously prepared sweet foods.
[She is] naked, mounted upon a donkey, and equipped with a broom and a water-pot.
One should recite the mantra of the goddess Visphoṭanāśinī in water without weariness.
For such a person, the goddess Śītalā shall become the bestower of peace from eruptive boils (visphoṭaka).
For one who observes the vow of Śītalā, the entire year shall be filled with peace.
"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, I was indeed born as Ṛṣabha.

A devotee observing the vow must perform the worship of Viṣṇu, which bestows supreme merit. (125) Thus ends the section on the annual eighth-day vows—including the Pārvatī-jayantī, Durgāṣṭamī, Daśāha-phala-vrata, Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, Rādhāṣṭamī, Trūrvāṣṭamī, Jyeṣṭhāṣṭamī, Kaṃbharā-lakṣmī-jayantī, Durgā-vrata, Karakā-vrata, Śrīkṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Bhagavān-jayantī, Kālāṣṭamī, Gopāṣṭamī, Darbha-vrata, and Śrāddhāṣṭamī—within the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 275 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I shall describe to you, my child, the vows of the nine ninth-days;
listen, Lakṣmī! By performing these, one attains both heaven and liberation. (1) In the bright fortnight of Caitra, the Rāmajanma-vrata is prescribed.
The Śrī Rāmanavamī festival should be celebrated with enthusiasm, for it bestows great merit.
(1) One should either observe a fast on that day or, after the midday meal, partake of only one meal.
A very large pavilion should be constructed, featuring a Sarvatobhadra mandala. (3)
Having had a jar fashioned and placed [therein], one should cause the image to be set within a vessel;
it should be adorned with a crown and so forth, as well as a bow and arrows, and other ornaments.
(4) The worship should consist of the sixteen articles, including the waving of lights (*nīrājana*) and other rites.
One should offer as an oblation (naivedya) saffron, cooked rice, sugar, curd, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
(5) One should perform a vigil (jāgara) and on the following day, one should practice giving (dāna).
The observer of the vow should indeed give cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth to the preceptor (guru). (6)
Having gratified the Brahmins and the virtuous, the observer of the vow should break his fast.
By performing the vow of Viṣṇu in this manner, he shall go to the supreme abode.
On this very lunar day, there is also the Hari-jayantī-vrata.
On this very day, Harikṛṣṇa was born in the abode of Dharma.
On this same day, Bhadrakālī, the best of Yoginīs,
was consecrated by Śaṅkara in the sovereignty over all [the other Yoginīs].

This is declared to be the Mātṛvrata; accompanied by Bhairava, the sixty-four Yoginīs should be worshipped together with Caṇḍikā. In the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the goddess Ramā together with Hari.
It bestows enjoyment and liberation, grants sons, wealth, and good fortune, and is auspicious.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight, one should indeed observe the vow of eating but once;
worship and other rites must be performed, as well as the giving of gifts consisting of gold. 11–12.

On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should indeed worship the goddess Umā, the most auspicious, who is established in asceticism; the auspicious vow of eating only at night (nakta-vrata) is prescribed.
One should feed young maidens according to one's capacity and cause various gifts to be bestowed.
The observer of the vow should give an excellent sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and eat milk-rice (pāyasa).
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the observer of the vow should worship Lakṣmī;
likewise, the observer of the vow should worship Indrāṇī seated upon Airāvata.
He shall become a possessor of enjoyments and a traveler in celestial chariots in the world of the gods.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Bhārgavī Śrī;
one should sacrifice to Kumārī Lakṣmī, the destroyer of suffering, with offerings of excellent flavors.
With perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, garments, and woolen blankets,
one should also feed young maidens who are the embodiments of Śrī and the destroyers of suffering.
By performing this vow dedicated to Lakṣmī, the destroyer of suffering, the practitioner goes to the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa.
This Nakula-navamī should likewise be observed by one who has taken a vow;
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Nandā-vrata is proclaimed.
One should indeed worship Nandā—that is, Durgā—according to the rules with the various ritual offerings.
Having obtained the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), the observer of the vow shall go to Vaikuṇṭha.
This Navamī, which destroys suffering, should be observed as *Aduḥkhanavamī*; this Navamī, which ensures one’s husband remains alive, should be observed as *Avidhavānavamī*.
A fast must be observed, and Lakṣmī, along with Satī, should likewise be worshipped. The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is called Mahānavamī;
it is so named because Durgā is worshipped there at the conclusion of the Navarātra vow.
Likewise, Mahālakṣmī is to be worshipped, and the goddesses are to be worshipped by the millions.
All the goddesses— whether married or unmarried— are fully honored with garments,
ornaments, decorations, perfumes, unguents, and liquid offerings.
"By means of vehicles, mounts, food, and other such luxuries," thus [it is said].
(24) O Dear One, in the afternoon, worship of the Śamī tree should be performed in the eastern direction.
In the evening, one should worship the conch, the mace, the discus, and the lotus. (25)
A sword, a bow, arrows, a spear, a trident, a shield, a buckler,
a dagger, an axe, a noose, a staff, a thunderbolt, a mallet; an umbrella,
a banner, an elephant, a horse, a swan, a lute, and a peacock.

A bull, a buffalo, a book, a scale, a cow, and [an image of] the head and so forth—whatever has been protected by her, all that the observer of the vow should worship. Whatever offering is most dear to her, that the observer of the vow should present to her. (27–28)

Having completed the worship at night, after the ritual dismissal (visarjana) in the morning, the observer of the vow should indeed eat cooked food and likewise feed the Brahmins. After giving the priestly fee (dakṣiṇā), he should subsequently give gifts with devotion.
One should indeed complete the vow by casting the image into the water.

(1.274.30) Thus, through this vow, the Mothers—who are the constant givers of happiness to the worlds—being pleased and nourished, and taking refuge in compassion, sustain the children of the worlds. (31)
Having observed the vow and enjoyed excellent pleasures, he shall go to heaven and other realms at the end;
likewise, he shall go to the world of the Mothers, the world of the Satīs, and the world of the Goddesses.
That ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika is Akṣaya; it is a great vow.
One should perform the libation for the gods, sages, and ancestors at the root of the Aśvattha tree (33).
Then, having offered the arghya water to the Sun, one should feed the twice-born and children;
the observer of the vow should perform charity, fire-offerings, and recitation, and should give sacrificial fees (34).
Whatever is performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or in a temple becomes inexhaustible in its spiritual essence.

One should indeed give the gift of a kūṣmāṇḍa fruit, for that yields the primary fruit of sacrifice. In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the vow of Nandinī on the ninth day is proclaimed.
Having fasted and observed the vow, one should then worship Nandā-Lakṣmī.
By giving a gift to a maiden, the fruit shall be equal to that born of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, one should worship Mahālakṣmī.
On the ninth day of the month of Māgha, one should worship Mahānandā;
on the ninth day of Phālguna, one should worship Ānandālakṣmī.
Herein, bathing, recitation, rosaries, giving, fire-offerings, and fasting [are prescribed].
Everything becomes inexhaustible through the grace of Kṛṣṇa’s splendor. (Verse 9) Various kinds of gifts should be given to a worthy recipient at an auspicious place and time.
O Kamalā, I shall tell you who that worthy recipient is—the one who delivers people across [the ocean of existence]. (1.274.40)
Neither by mere learning nor even by austerity alone is one a worthy recipient;
that person in whom both [learning and austerity] reside, and who is endowed with devotion, is indeed a true recipient.
One who studies the sacred texts, observes the rules, practices meditation, is devoted to austerity, and has conquered the senses—[is such a one].

One who is patient by nature, tranquil in disposition, truthful, a twice-born, or a student of the scriptures; one who has heard all the teachings, is free from malice, and takes no pleasure in receiving gifts; one who observes excellent vows, is of virtuous character, and is devoted to worthy recipients—such a person is most great. (42–43)

The virtuous, who are devoted to meditation and delight in serving others, purify those who merely behold them; how much more so those who have entered into their company! By giving to them according to their needs, one attains the supreme goal.
One should offer [the gift] to a learned Vedic scholar who is virtuous and established in Brahman. 45.

Forgiveness, compassion, lack of worldly desire, truthfulness, generosity, good conduct, austerity, and sacred learning—these eight qualities are said here to be the supreme characteristics of a worthy recipient. 46.
One who is a performer of sacrifices, a reciter of the Vedas, a knower of the Purāṇas, a teacher, or a spiritual preceptor;
one who is compassionate toward women, a servant of cows, or a worthy recipient;
one who is naked, destitute of livelihood, afflicted by hunger and thirst, or has come for refuge—[to all such] (one should give). 47.
That which is given to a worthy recipient who performs virtuous deeds is indeed eternal.
(48) Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth, when given to a worthy recipient, are always inexhaustible.
One worthy recipient consists of the Veda; another worthy recipient consists of austerity. (49)
A recipient consisting of devotion is one thing, while a recipient consisting of Brahman is another.
A celibate student, an ascetic, a virtuous man, and a virtuous woman are always considered worthy recipients.
Such a capable recipient will indeed deliver the donor.
By its own splendor, it delivers both the giver and himself.
A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields a hundredfold merit; to one who is a Brahmin in name only, it is twofold;
to a teacher, it is a thousandfold; and among the virtuous, it is remembered as infinite. (51–52)

An offering made into the mouths of Brahmins, who are like sacrificial fires blazing with the fuel of the Vedas, delivers the donor; likewise, an offering made to virtuous women and holy men delivers the giver. Brahmins who have been robbed of their property or stripped of all their possessions are considered the supreme recipients.
To guests who have arrived, to worthy recipients, and to those of meager means;
to those devoted to dharma, devoted to knowledge, devoted to devotion, and compassionate; to those devoted to austerity and those who live on alms—what is given to them yields great fruit. (54–55)
If one abandons a worthy recipient present at hand to go instead to a distant land for the sake of giving, that act burns the family down to the seventh generation.
Furthermore, if there is a fool in one's own house while a man of great learning resides far away... [56]
In this matter, there is no fault in transgression; [the oblation] is poured into the fire, not into the ashes.
(57) Children are vessels for food, women are vessels for adornment, the youth is a vessel for pride, and the elderly are vessels for service. (58)
The virtuous are the recipients of worship; mendicants are the recipients of food;
the suffering are the recipients of compassion; the best of friends are the recipients of truth;
the wretched are the recipients of assistance; and those who have sought refuge are the recipients of protection. (59)
Those who give gifts become vessels for heaven; those who are well-contented become vessels for happiness.

(1.274.60) Giving at marriages, the tying of the girdle, consecrations, and other sacrifices, as well as giving to the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the distressed—that gift is inexhaustible. (1.274.61)
To the reviler, the malicious, the thief, the rogue, the slayer, the destroyer, the cruel, the deceitful, the envious, the one devoid of dharma, the sinner, the rogue, the trickster,
the one who contemplates misfortune, the jealous, and the wicked— 62.

In one who causes suffering, who is full of calamities, who is a malevolent assailant, and who is devoid of devotion—whatever is offered, given, or performed is surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt. This [recipient] weeps when something is being given, thinking, "What evil deed have I committed? (63–64).
A seed sown in salt-waste, or that which is offered as an oblation even into ashes, or that which is given to an unworthy recipient—such things result in total destruction.
Whatever is dear to oneself, whatever belongs to oneself, and whatever is righteous; [these should be given]. (65)
That indeed should be given to a worthy recipient; such a gift alone bears fruit.
There is no end to the merit of what is given with faith and according to the prescribed rules to a worthy recipient.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the vow, the gift, and the worthy recipient.

Thus, in the first section, concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, the two hundred and seventy-fourth chapter titled "Description of the Annual Ninth-Day Vows, including the Śrī Rāma Jayantī, Śrī Hari Jayantī, Bhadrakālī Vrata, Ramā Vrata, Umā Vrata, Indrī Vrata, Duḥkhahā Lakṣmī Vrata, Nakula Vrata, Nandā-Durgā Vrata, Aduḥkha Navamī Vrata, Avidhavā Navamī, Navarātra Navamī Vrata, Akṣaya Navamī, Kūṣmāṇḍa Navamī, Nandinī Navamī, Mahālakṣmī Mahānandā Ānandā Worship, and the True Recipient (Satpātra), etc. is concluded.

Chapter 275: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga — Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Part 1.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, indeed, I shall describe other vows pertaining to the tenth lunar day (daśamī).
O Mahālakṣmī! By performing these, a person shall attain heaven and peace.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should observe the vow of Dharmarāja;
one should worship him with baths, flowers, fruits, perfumes, garments, and ornaments.
One who observes the vow of eating but a single meal should worship fourteen Brahmins;
having fed them and given them sacrificial fees, one shall attain heaven by doing so.
On the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should worship Viṣṇu.
One should perform one hundred circumambulations with the sixteen types of offerings. (4) Having fed virtuous Brahmins, one certainly attains Vaikuṇṭha.
[The month of] Jyeṣṭha, the bright fortnight, the Hasta constellation, Wednesday, and the tenth lunar day—(5)
The *garā*, *ānanda*, and *vyatīpāta* [yogas], occurring when the Moon is in Virgo and the Sun is in Taurus—
this is indeed the highly meritorious *daśayoga*, which destroys ten sins.
It should be understood as the *gaṅgā-daśaharā*, for the Gaṅgā has descended from heaven.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite, one goes to the abode of Hari.
(7) The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha is the anniversary of Manu (Manvādi);
on this day, bathing, recitation, giving gifts, or performing fire-offerings bestow the attainment of heaven. (8)
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, which grants the fulfillment of all hopes,

one should indeed perform the worship of Śiva preceded by gifts, fire-offerings, and other rites. And on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, there is the excellent vow known as Daśāvirbhāva.
Likewise, he should perform a bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and offer libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors.
The practitioner of the vow himself should separately perform the worship of the ten incarnations:
Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, and Trivikrama.
The observer of the vow should worship Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Paraśurāma (Jāmadagni), Buddha, and Kalki;
having worshipped these ten forms made of gold, he should offer them [to a preceptor].
Then, having provided a single meal for a twice-born man, he should feed the virtuous well.
Having thus observed the vow and partaken of the meal, one shall attain Vaikuṇṭha in heaven.
The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is considered Vijayā-daśamī.
Having placed four lumps of cow dung in the courtyard of the house in the morning, [one should proceed].
In the center of these forms of the discus, one should indeed worship all four— Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—
in four earthen vessels provided with lids.
Having taken moist grain along with silver and being clothed in white garments,
one should worship with unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings, and then indeed offer salutations.
At midday, the observer of the vow should feed the children and likewise eat sweet food himself.
Then, in the afternoon, having taken earth from the root of a *śamī* tree situated to the east,
and having brought it to his own home and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite—
if he be a Kṣatriya— he should fully prepare his own army.
Having emerged from the eastern gate of the village, undisturbed,
he [saw] there an effigy of the enemy fashioned from leaves and other materials;
and having mentally visualized that form, he [struck it] with an arrow tipped with a golden shaft.
Thinking "I shall pierce [the enemy]," he would depart for his own home greatly delighted;
thereafter, if he should engage in battle, he will undoubtedly be victorious,
attaining wealth, triumph, a great kingdom, and sons, cattle, elephants, and horses.
One should give goats and sheep here at the end [of the rite] to attain the heavenly realm;
today Śrī Rāma sets forth for victory, and one should perform a festival.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one should observe the Sārvabhauma vow.

There, observing the vow of eating but once a day, at midnight the practitioner should offer an oblation (*bali*) consisting of cakes and other foods in the ten directions, either outside the house or outside the city. On a ground smeared with cow dung, the practitioner should prepare an eight-petaled mandala. (23–24)
One should perform the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna), reciting at that time:
"May Indra, the bestower of desired objects, shake off whatever sin has entered into me;
may Agni, the bestower of desired objects, shake off whatever sin has entered into me. (25)
May Yama, the bestower of desired fruits, shake off whatever sin of mine resides in the south;
may the Rakṣas, the performer of deeds, shake off whatever sin of mine resides in the southwest; and may Yāda, the performer of deeds, shake off whatever sin of mine resides in the west.
May Vāyu, the bestower of desired fruits, shake off whatever sin of mine resides in Vāyu;
may Yakṣa, the bestower of desired fruits, shake off whatever sin of mine resides in Saumya;
and may Īśa, the bestower of desired fruits, shake off whatever sin of mine resides in Īśa.
"May Brahmā, the bestower of desired fruits, shake off whatever sin of mine has gone upward;
may Nāga, the bestower of desired fruits, shake off whatever sin of mine has gone downward.
Having thus offered the *bali* offering in the cardinal and intermediate directions, the observer of the vow then— || 1.275.30 ||
Outside that, one should unweariedly offer the bali-oblation to the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla).
Having returned home, one should keep a vigil during the remainder of the night.
In the morning, having bathed and duly worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas), one should then [honour] the brahmins.
Having worshipped the twelve [deities] and fed them, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Lakṣmī! By performing the vow in this manner, having enjoyed auspicious worldly pleasures and having experienced celestial happiness for a Yuga, one shall become a sovereign emperor.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the two Aśvinīkumāras;
and by worshipping Dhanvantari, one always attains health.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, however, one should worship the Viśvedevas.
One should worship Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, Muni, Guru, Vipra, and Rāma, who are the forms of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
having placed them upon seats of darbha grass with incense, lamps, and food offerings. (35–36)
Having honored them with the sixteen articles, one should dismiss them;
the observer of the vow will in every way become an enjoyer of happiness in both worlds.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should indeed worship the descendants of Aṅgiras.
One should worship with excellent offerings the ten forms: Ātman, Āyu, Manas, Dakṣa, Mada, Prāṇa, Gaviṣṭhaka, Datta, Satya, and Varhiṣmān.
One should present these forms to the twice-born with the sixteen types of services and other offerings.
One who observes this vow thus attains the higher worlds of the Āṅgirases while remaining steadfast in their observance.
On the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should worship Yama;
namely, Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, and likewise Antaka.
Vaivasvata, Kāla, and likewise Sarvabhūtakṣaya;
Audumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, and Vṛkodara; Parameṣṭhin, Citra, and Citragupta—these are the fourteen.
One should worship them, feed them, and satisfy them with water and sesame seeds;
thereafter, one should indeed offer an *arghya* oblation to the Sun from a copper vessel,
using water mixed with red sandalwood, sesame seeds, unbroken rice, and barley.
Afterwards, the observer of the vow, remaining silent, should feed the Brahmins and then eat himself.
Thus, having attained the favor of Dharmarāja,
the observer of the vow enjoys supreme pleasures here, and at the end of the body, attains the abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Vārṣika-daśamī-vratas, including the Dharmarāja-vrata, Viṣṇu-vrata, Gaṅgā-daśaharā, the Manvādi-tithi-sarvāśāpūrti-vrata, the worship of the ten incarnations, the Vijayā-daśamī-sārvabhauma-vrata, the Ārogya-vrata, and the Viśvedeva-Aṅgiras-Yama-vratas," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
