Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, those Ekādaśī vows which were previously described to you—
These vows, indeed, are to be accomplished in three days in their entirety. O Lotus-born One, one should avoid four meals during the three days:
one at the beginning and one at the end, and two in the middle.
Bell-metal, meat, lentil soup, chickpeas, and kodrava grain,
as well as leafy vegetables, honey, food from others, eating a second meal,
and sexual intercourse— on the tenth day, one observing the vow should always avoid these ten things.
One should avoid gambling, sleep, betel nut, and cleaning the teeth;
slander of others, backbiting, theft, violence, sexual pleasure, anger, and false speech on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī).

One should avoid these ten things on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī): bell-metal, meat, liquor, honey, oil, speaking with barbarians, physical exercise, travel abroad, eating a second meal, sexual intercourse, and touching those who are untouchable.
One should observe the vow by eating only once a day or by eating only at night.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer a sacred thread (*pavitra*) to Hari;
it may be made of gold, silver, silk, linen, *kauśa* fiber, or cotton.
The excellent *pavitraka* is made from three hundred and sixty threads;
the ordinary one arises from three strands; and the middling one may be made as desired.
The best has one hundred knots, and the smallest has thirty-six knots.
The best [garment] reaches down to the knees; the least is considered to touch the navel.
(1.276.10) One who performs the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa together with Ramā here on earth shall become happy; O gods, he shall attain the supreme Vaikuṇṭha. (11)
On the twelfth day as well, one should offer the beautiful *pavitra* threads, which indeed bestow happiness and prosperity, to the Guru and also to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada—
One should perform the pastime of the Lord Hari’s taxation on the Yamunā while on a boat.
Having brought yogurt for the purpose of selling it, one should ask the gopīs as they go along, "Give me a tax," and then have them sing his verses. 13–14.
On the day of the vow, the practitioner should indeed offer curd and cooked rice as an oblation to Kṛṣṇa;
he should present gifts of cloth and gifts of curd to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, there is the festival of the worship of Dharma.
At midday, one who seeks the fruits of the vow should perform the rite for the birth of Dharma.
Having fashioned a golden image and placed it within a copper vessel situated inside a pavilion, one should worship it upon a *sarvatobhadra* mandala. (16–17)
Four-faced, four-armed, and four-legged, clad in white garments,
white in complexion; holding a rosary in his right hand and a book in his left,
he bears the personified form of Resolve (Vyavasāya) upon his right side.

Having placed her comfortably on his left side and established devotion in her presence, the observer of the vow should worship her with sincere feeling. Having worshipped her with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), he should then feed her. (1.276.20)
Having performed the vigil and worship at night, one should dismiss [the deities] at dawn;
one should also give other gifts, for this shall be the strength of one's devotion to Dharma.
Along with Dharma, his thirteen wives—Śraddhā and the others—are indeed present.
The daughters of Dakṣa should be properly established, fed, and honored according to the prescribed rites.

These are the lawful wives of Dharma: Śraddhā (Faith), Śānti (Peace), Dayā (Compassion), Gati (Resolve), Medhā (Intelligence), Tuṣṭi (Contentment), Puṣṭi (Prosperity), Maitrī (Friendliness), Lajjā (Modesty), Kriyā (Action), and Unnati (Elevation).

Those [images] of divine form, whether they are called by other names or are golden statues, should be fashioned; their lineage is also extensive. They should be especially worshipped by one who desires the next world.
One should offer excellent gifts intended for that purpose.
(25) Thus, the practitioner should perform the austerity and vow to be accomplished through the Ekādaśikā;
whether he seeks worldly enjoyment or liberation, he shall obtain whatever he desires. (26)
Just as the vows for all Ekādaśīs have been previously described,
those vows should in every way be undertaken here according to the prescribed rules.
The concluding rites (udyāpana) for all of them must be performed according to the injunctions.
The practitioner— whether man, woman, or neuter— shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Observing Ekādaśī, the Pavitrāropaṇa Vow, the Dāna-līlā Vow, the Duties of Vrata, Jayantī, and Other Vows," in the first section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Lakṣmī, listen; I shall describe to you the vows of the twelve [Ekādaśīs], by performing which people go to the eternal abode of Hari. (1)
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should observe the Madana-vrata.
[One should offer] a jar filled with white rice, adorned with fruits and sugarcane,
accompanied by a pair of garments, gold, and a vessel of desirable food.
Having placed [the deity] worshipped with sandalwood and other offerings within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala,
one should install and worship the image of Śrī Kāmadeva accompanied by Rati in a vessel, using all flowers, juices, and fragrances. 3–4.
And one should feed them Rajasic foods and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having worshipped on the morning of the thirteenth day, one should dismiss the Anaṅga [deity].
Having thus performed the vow for a year, [one should give] ghee and a bed with a cow and its calf.
One should joyfully offer gold, desired objects, and pleasure as a gift to the venerable Guru. (6) One should worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, and likewise pray:
"May Hari, who can assume any form at will, be pleased with me; become the bestower of happiness. (7)
The performer of the Madanadvādaśī vow goes to Goloka;
through the service of Kṛṣṇa, a husband and wife attain eternal happiness.
On this very day, there is another vow known as the Bhartṛdvādaśikā vow.
Having caused a pavilion to be constructed, one should prepare a *sarvatobhadra* mandala and a well-spread,
comfortable bed adorned with flowers.
There, one should worship Hari together with Ramā using the sixteen [upacāras] and so forth.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one should place him to sleep together with Ramā.
The observer of the vow should keep a vigil accompanied by song and instrumental music. In the morning, having worshipped Him again with perfumes and other offerings, one should feed Him.
One should offer a golden image of Śrī Hari together with His bed to the venerable Guru.
Having fed the virtuous twice-born, one should dismiss them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
By performing the vow in this manner, the couple shall attain eternal union.
The observer of this vow enjoys pleasures here for seven births and is honored in heaven.
The husband must be worshipped, especially by the wife;
for the husband is indeed Vāsudeva himself and grants all desires.
He bestows all happiness—whether pertaining to the body, worldly, or leading to heaven.
(15) Having worshipped Hari Mādhava on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should offer cooked food with water; thus one shall attain all desires. (16)
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, having fully worshipped Trivikrama, one should offer sweetmeats, water-pots, and other gifts; thus one shall obtain all enjoyments.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the Lord Vāmana.
One should observe the vow of eating only vegetables and practice the vow of abstaining from salt.
(18) The righteous-souled one should give gifts; he should offer to his guru garments, ornaments, a sacred thread, a vessel, a seal-ring, finger-rings, grain, and wealth. (19)
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the observer of the vow should worship Śrīdhara.
Having completed the vegetable-vow (śākavrata), one should then undertake the curd-vow (dadhivrata).
One should offer an excellent sacred thread made of silk to the venerable Guru.
One should give all kinds of gifts according to one's ability so that one may be happy. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, there is the vow of the birth of Vāmana;
one should offer milk-rice to Hari and worship Him with many articles.
One should fashion an auspicious image of Vāmanadeva out of gold,
with a beautiful face, two arms, and holding an umbrella, a staff, a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), and a rosary. At midday, one should worship it in a Sarvatobhadra pavilion.

One should worship Aditi, Kaśyapa, Bali, and the gods with devotion. The observer of the vow should offer an abundance of ghee and white flour, along with powdered sweets and *laḍḍukas* as the food offering (*naivedya*).
Furthermore, the practitioner should subsist on fruit, eat only one meal a day, or observe the *nakta* fast.
If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) should coincide with the Śravaṇa asterism at midday,
or if the twelfth lunar day should occur at midday on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī),
and the Śravaṇa asterism should meet there, that conjunction is known as Viṣṇuśṛṅkhala.
This festival bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants union with Viṣṇu.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, one should worship Padmanābha, feed him sweet foods, and give abundant gifts. (27–28)
One shall attain the state of Śvetadvīpa and the auspicious enjoyments one desires.
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should indeed perform the Govatsadvādaśī vow according to the prescribed rite; therein, one should have a cow made of gold.
One should worship the cow along with her calf with flowers, sandalwood, and other offerings with devotion.
One should feed her auspicious substances and offer water for the feet (arghya) at her hooves.
One should give her balls of black gram and other grains, as well as mouthfuls of fodder such as grass.
Having bowed to them and likewise performed a circumambulation, he should make this resolve:
"O Mother, who embodies all the gods, grant my desire!
O Mother, bestow heaven, liberation, and happiness; salutations unto you, O Mother! (32)
Having performed the worship, one should give gifts of cows according to one's capacity. On that day, one should avoid cow’s milk, buttermilk, curd, and ghee.
One should also avoid food cooked in a pot, food fried in oil, and anything unnatural or transformed.
Or the observer of the vow should worship the deity in embodied form, accompanied by a heifer, at dawn;
indeed, through the service of direct worship, the fruit shall be abundant.
O beloved, [one should worship] Lord Dāmodara on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
One should worship with the sixteen supreme articles and feed Hari.
One should also offer water-pots filled with water, adorned with cloths and sprouts,
and beautified with betel nuts, sweetmeats, gems, fruits, gold, and other such items.
The observer of the vow should joyfully give gifts and feed virtuous people to his guru.
By doing so, he becomes dear to Viṣṇu and endowed with all enjoyments.
On the twelfth lunar day, the king should perform the excellent Nīrājana vow.
The Lord of the World, having arisen from sleep, should indeed be adorned with excellent objects. At the arrival of night, having prepared a new fire and worshipped it according to the mantra,
one should offer oblations of ghee and the like, as well as food fit for sages, accompanied by people holding silver lamps.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, the observer of the vow should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for Hari,
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Ramā, and Pārvatī;
likewise for Brahmāṇī, Caṇḍikā, Gaurī, Māṇikī, and Maṅgalā.

Then one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) for Āditya, Śaṅkara, Yakṣa, Nandā, Gaṇapati, the planets, the Mothers, the ancestors, the mountains, and all the *nāgas*. One should perform the lustration for the cows and address them with the words, "Victory! Homage! (42–43).
He gave bulls, swift horses, and elephants endowed with auspicious marks;
all the royal insignia, such as new umbrellas and other regalia;
the king, the domestic priest, the ministers, the servants, and the women of the inner apartments.
Having worshipped [the deity] as is appropriate, one should sound conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments.
(45) Then the king, adorned with ornaments, should sit upon a new throne; at that time, the assembly hall should be filled with both courtesans and women of noble family. (46)

Likewise, one should increase the prosperity above the head of the lord of men with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and flowers, as well as with golden coins; thereafter, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the king.
At that time, the kings of the earth should listen to the peace-mantras (*śānti-mantra*).

In this manner, this great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) should be performed every day by a king or even by a wealthy person who desires health for a year. For those in whose kingdom, city, or village this supreme propitiation is performed, [well-being shall prevail]. 48–49.
O Lakṣmī! By this rite called Nīrājanā, those diseases go to their destruction.
This should be performed by people in some way or another, even if it is done in a brief form. Indeed, on this very twelfth day, it was formerly established by Viṣṇu.
In the Kṛta Yuga, however, the marriage of Tulasī is the supreme vow.
One should wear a turban of safflower-colored cloth representing Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, as well as a red bodice made of golden thread. (51–52)
One should clothe Tulasī in an auspicious, golden-colored garment;
one should provide her with ornaments, flowers, and other articles of adornment.
Likewise, one should offer sweet rice mixed with jaggery as an oblation.
At the onset of night, in a beautiful pavilion constructed of plantain trees and other materials,
the observer of the vow should worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Viṣṇu and Tulasī;
at the time of the "cow-dust" (godhūli), he should honor them with the sixteen types of ritual offerings.
One should indeed offer to Tulasī golden garments, a necklace, a nose-ornament, bracelets, turmeric, saffron, and so forth;
one should also present fruits such as the āmra and others, along with stalks of sugarcane.
One should offer *khājaka* sweets with yellow centers as an oblation (*naivedya*).
Having performed the *nīrājana* rite for Vṛndā and Kṛṣṇa and having placed a curtain between them,
and having recited auspicious verses, one should present Vṛndā to Śrī Viṣṇu.
One should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, brāhmaṇas, boys, girls, and people according to one's capacity, and should give various kinds of gifts. Indeed,
one should have the verses concerning the wedding of Vṛndā sung by those who are connoisseurs of aesthetic rasa.
In this manner, one should perform the festival which protects unbroken fortune.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, there is the unsurpassed Sādhya-vrata.
Likewise, Manobhava, Prāṇa, Nara, and the heroic Yāta [are the deities].
One should worship these twelve Sādhya deities: Citra, Hayo, Nṛpa, Haṃsa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa, Vibhu, and Prabhu.
Having fashioned them from gold or out of rice grains, one should offer them perfumes and other such gifts.
One should feed many people with desirable food, thinking, "Nārāyaṇa is indeed dear to me.
On this very day, the Āditya-dvādaśī vow should be performed. [The twelve Ādityas are:
Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Śakra, Aṃśu, Varuṇa, and Bhaga.
Having fashioned twelve golden images of those twelve suns— Tvaṣṭṛ, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu— one should worship them and feed [the Brahmins].
One should observe this vow for one year, every month on the day of the bright fortnight.
One should give all kinds of gifts and feed the Brahmins and the virtuous.
Having thus performed the vow and attained the brilliantly shining world of the Sun,
and having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time, one then pierces the solar orb.
Beyond Māyā, one should go to the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
then, right here, one should perform the unbroken vow (akhaṇḍavrata) of Janārdana.
Having fashioned a golden image, one should worship Janārdana.
Then, for one year, the observer of the vow should feed [the Brahmins] every month.
Eating only at night, he should then present that auspicious golden image of a cow together with its calf to his preceptor, and feed the Brahmins with milk-rice and other such foods.
One should pray to Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa: "O Kṛṣṇa! May my vow remain unbroken;
may good fortune, wealth, grain, and constant health be mine.
One should indeed give other gifts for the sake of the next world.
Having performed this, the observer of the vow goes by means of a golden vehicle to the abode of Viṣṇu.
(72) On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, the Rūpavrata is proclaimed.
Having bathed according to the rules on the tenth day, the observer of the vow should take up cow dung. (73)
O Dear One, for a white cow of uniform color, one should then dry one hundred and eight of its dung-cakes while they are suspended in the air.
Having placed them in a copper vessel or a vessel made of clay, one should preserve them for the purpose of the fire-oblation (havana).
On the eleventh day, having fasted and worshipped Viṣṇu with a golden image,
one should offer food and perform a vigil; then on the twelfth day at dawn,
having placed Hari within a water-pot or a vessel, one should worship him with ritual offerings.
Having worshipped the fire produced by the friction of wood,
one should offer oblations of sesame, ghee, and other substances into the pedestal for the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
performing one hundred and eight oblations with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Or one may perform the rite by means of names; one should feed [the deity] with milk-rice and fried cakes (pūrikā).
One should present the pot-image to the preceptor and feed the twice-born.
Having bowed, whether a woman or a man, one should respectfully discharge the vow.
By performing this, one obtains beauty and the most excellent good fortune.
Now, the vow of Sujana-dvādaśī in the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa is described.
Having bathed in the morning and drunk water from a cow's horn, one should offer salutations.
Having performed a circumambulation in that manner, one should undertake the annual vow.
Then, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight in each month, one should perform a gift-offering;
one should give a *prastha* of clarified butter and four *prasthas* of rice.
The observer of the vow should offer four *prasthas* of barley, two *raktikās* of gold,
half an *āḍhaka* of sesame seeds, and a jar full of milk;
likewise, one *māsa* of silver and many kinds of sweet foods.
An umbrella made of half a māṣa of gold, a prastha of excellent molasses,
one pala of sandalwood, and an auspicious garment measuring ten cubits—
such a gift the observer of the vow should give every month according to his capacity. (84–85)
For the sake of purification, the observer of the vow should drink cow’s urine, water, or clarified butter;
likewise, barley-food mixed with curd, sesame and clarified butter with sugar, milk joined with darbha-water, or vegetables as desired. (86)
One should indeed consume [the offering] with devotion every month for a year.
Having worshipped a golden image of the Sun in a copper vessel,
one should present it to the preceptor along with a cow, and then bow down.
Having fed the Brahmins, the virtuous, and likewise the unvirtuous women, he should dismiss them.
One who observes this vow obtains birth in a wealthy and most excellent family, full of all prosperity, where food and drink abound and vigor prevails. (8–9)

In a family that is the locus of the power of passion and served by excellent women, one enjoys countless pleasures here in the eternal heaven; having fully experienced those divine enjoyments, one goes to the everlasting Vaikuṇṭha. (1.277.90–91)
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should worship the Śālagrāma stone;
having placed it in a silver vessel, one should offer gold into its mouth.
One should then feed [the deity] with milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by sugar and clarified butter.

One who observes the vow should give [the image] adorned with garments and ornaments to a knower of the Vedas. By doing so, the observer of the vow shall go to Vaikuṇṭha and become a partaker of eternal bliss.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, [one should offer] a golden image of Hari.
Having worshipped [the deity], one should give [the offerings] to the guru and feed the boys and girls;
for by performing this vow, a person goes to the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, where,
having enjoyed pleasures that are difficult to attain, they experience eternal bliss.
Trispṛśā, Mīlanī, Pakṣavardhinī, Vañjulī, as well as Jayā,
Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā—
these eight Dvādaśīs, which destroy sin, should be observed with a fast throughout the day and night. (96–97)
If Ekādaśī has ended before sunrise, then that Dvādaśī is named Trispṛśā; it yields great fruit.
By the vow of this [day], one enjoys the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. 98.
When the lunar day of Ekādaśī is pierced by Daśamī at dawn, one should completely abandon that [Ekādaśī] and fast on the Dvādaśī;
this is called Sonmīlitā, and it bestows the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices. (1.277.100)
When the eleventh lunar day touches the rising sun at sunrise,
that is Vañjulikā, which bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
When the new moon and the full moon both increase [in duration], that is Pakṣavardhinī.

She indeed bestows all sovereignty and increases one's sons and grandsons. When the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) occurs during the bright fortnight in conjunction with the Maghā constellation, it is called Jayā; it is considered everywhere to be the giver of victory.
If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight should coincide with the asterism Śravaṇa, it is Vijayā;
it bestows the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrtha) and grants happiness and enjoyment.
When it occurs in the bright fortnight conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism (Prājāpatya), [it is likewise auspicious].

That twelfth day (dvādaśī) is known as Jayantī; it bestows the fruits of vows and gifts. When the twelfth day occurs during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) conjoined with Jupiter and the Sun, it is then called Aparājitā; it grants knowledge and liberation and destroys all sins.
When the asterism Anurādhā occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, then two vows should be performed; there is no fault here, as they share a single deity.
And likewise on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada when it is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism.
On the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight during the month of Ūrja, under the final asterism, two vows are observed.

Apart from these occasions, the practice of eating only once a day (ekabhukta) should be performed on the twelfth day, specifically the vow-day of Dvādaśika which is conjoined with the eleventh day (Ekādaśī). || 108–109 ||
"A separate concluding rite (udyāpana) need not be performed; however, a gift should be given according to one's wealth.
Thus, O Kamalā, these vows are to be observed on the twelfth day (dvādaśī).

Thus ends the section on the annual dvādaśī vows—specifically the Madana-vrata, Bhartṛ-dvādaśī, Mādhava-karaka-śā [etc.]—in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
