Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall fully describe to you the vows of the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī-vrata). By performing them according to the prescribed rite, the observer of the vow becomes the most excellent of enjoyers.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship Madana, who consists of sandalwood,
accompanied by Rati, and fan him with a whisk.
One should draw the bodiless god (Anaṅga) upon a wooden board using vermilion, turmeric, and red pigments.
One should have [the image of] Vasanta made, full of passion, beautiful, bearing a flower-bow and quiver,
having the face of a horse, and possessing a bull-banner;
one should worship him with perfumes, garlands, ornaments, garments, edibles, and excellent drinks.
One should worship Madana, Kāma, Manmatha, who is dear to Rati, Anaṅga, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja;
as well as Viṣameṣu, Manobhava, and he whose weapon is flowers. (5)
One should worship with *mālatī* flowers and cause the gift of a goat to be performed.
(6) When [the moon] is conjoined with Saturn on a Tuesday, that is considered the Great Vāruṇī;
if it occurs on the Gaṅgā, it is superior to ten million solar eclipses. (7)
When the auspicious conjunction occurs on the hundredth lunar mansion (Śatabhiṣaj) during the month of Vaiśākha in the year Śani,
it is renowned as the Mahāmaha, which grants liberation to ten million lineages.
When the spring season has arrived, a great festival should be celebrated every year.
Or, having performed it every month until the year is completed,
his desire is always satisfied; here, the beautiful woman grants him the power of passion, and in the next world, the great bliss born of the bodiless god of love.
The Kāmavrata is prescribed for the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha. On that occasion, one should worship Kāma with perfumes and other offerings;
furthermore, one should worship him every month on the thirteenth day with appropriate articles.
At the end of the year, one should give a cow to the preceptor for the successful completion of the vow.
One shall obtain enjoyment, liberation, supreme perfection, and the satisfaction of desires;
as well as heavenly bliss, an excellent woman who grants all desired enjoyments.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, there is a vow for the pacification of misfortune.
Having bathed in a river, one should indeed worship [the deity] with incense, lamps, water, and so forth.
[One should offer] a white mandāra flower, or an arka, or a red karavīra.
Then, having gazed at the sun in the sky, the observer of the vow should pray:
"O Mandāra, Karavīra, and Arka, you who are born from the rays of the Sun;
may you, when worshipped, destroy my misfortune. Salutations be unto you! (15–16)
Thus, the misfortune of the worshipper is surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, Trivikrama should be worshipped here by one seeking the fulfillment of a vow.
Being satisfied, he shall grant the earth and bestow the splendor of enjoyments.
In this case, one should perform the Sāvitrī-vrata according to one's means and desire.
The observer of the vow should worship Sāvitrī and Brahmā with many offerings,
and should present ghee, milk-rice (pāyasa), and fried cakes (pūrikā).
The woman shall always obtain the fruit of enjoyment and liberation, as well as good fortune;
the observer of the vow indeed attains wealth, grain, cattle, sons, and so forth.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should perform [the rite] according to the prescribed rule.
One observing the vow should perform the Jayā-Pārvatī vow while eating but one meal a day.
The images of Umā and Maheśvara may be made of gold, silver, or clay;
they should be placed in a temple of the gods, a stable, or the house of a Brāhmaṇa. 21–22.
Having established them according to the prescribed rite, one should worship them for three days.
On the third day, those two should be joyfully offered to the Guru.
This vow should be performed year after year in this manner for five years.
One should provide various kinds of food and various kinds of gifts.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should cause those two to be presented together with a pair of cows;
for those who observe the vow, there shall be no separation from their spouses for seven births.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one who observes the vow and maintains a fast should perform the auspicious Ratikāma-vrata according to the prescribed ritual.
Whether it be the bride or the groom, [the image should be made] in copper, gold, silver, or clay.
Having established Ratikāma, one should worship them properly with perfumes and other offerings.
One should honor a Brahmin couple and give gifts such as clothing as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, one should feed them and perform the vow for fourteen years.
One should offer two images accompanied by a pair of cows to the venerable Guru.
This vow, which fulfills desires, bestows good fortune, and grants happiness;
it is considered the Gotrirātra-vrata to be performed on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Having fashioned an image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa made of gold or silver,
and having bathed it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should then place it upon a seat within an eight-petaled mandala and worship it with flowers, perfumes, and ornaments.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offer excellent, sweet food;
then, one should present a vessel filled with food and water to the venerable Guru.
One should continue this for three days, and at the conclusion of the vow, one should worship a cow.
Five cows were born when the great ocean was being churned.
Among them, salutations again and again to that cow who is Nandā.
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me. (33–34)
"May cows be at my side; may I dwell in the midst of cows.
Having bowed and circumambulated them, one should cause morsels of food to be given to them.
One should then offer the image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa to the venerable Guru.

Whatever fruit one obtains by performing thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices, that same fruit is obtained by those who observe the vow of the three nights for the sake of the lineage (gotra). On the thirteenth day of both the bright and dark fortnights, the Śrāddha for children and others is most excellent.
One should by all means cause this to be performed so that even the slayers may attain a good rebirth.
The first lunar day of the Kali Yuga is declared to be merit-bestowing for the vow.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, one should observe the excellent three-night Aśoka vow.
Having fashioned an Aśoka tree out of gold and worshipped it with excellent offerings,
a woman devoted to fasting should constantly perform one hundred and eight circumambulations, while praying to me for the removal of her grief.
On the third day, having worshipped Hara on a tree,
she should provide a meal for children and give gifts such as collyrium to worthy recipients and young maidens.
A woman who observes the vow in this manner shall never encounter widowhood.
She shall be endowed with sons, grandsons, and others, and become beloved by her own husband.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, she should light an oil lamp;
having worshipped it, she should then place it outside at the door of her house. 42–43.
"May Yama be pleased with me through this offering of a lamp; one should recite this hymn.
When this is done, O Mahālakṣmī, the affliction of Yama does not arise.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should perform the worship of Dhanada (the Lord of Wealth)."
Wealth is Lakṣmī; wealth is gold; and wealth consists of wives, sons, and so forth.
(45) Through the worship of wealth, one shall attain stability; of this there is no doubt.
Therein, the observer of the vow should worship Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and gold. (46)
One should clean the entire temple and construct an auspicious pavilion.
One should fashion a most beautiful golden image of Hari and Lakṣmī.
One should apply a beautiful tilaka of kunkuma upon Kṛṣṇa.
One should tie a cloth panel inlaid with gold at the edge around one's head. On a suitable body, one should wear other garments and ornaments,
as well as a green silk garment, a saffron-colored sārī, and a beautiful bodice.
One should wear one's own garments, ornaments, and so forth, and adorn the Goddess Śrī;
one should worship her with the sixteen articles of offering and other suitable items, and present them as an offering.
Indeed, one should offer auspicious sweet foods such as *śaṣkulī* and *khājaka*.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with lamps and cause many lamps to be lit everywhere.
With devotion, one should give gifts of new vessels and garments.
For four days, there should be the worship of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
One should especially have [this] constructed, and one shall always be an abode of prosperity (*lakṣmī*).
Having given a gift to the preceptor, one should afterwards conclude the vow.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should eat only once at the beginning of the night.
One should illuminate the house and the temple with thousands or hundreds of lamps arranged in rows, and worship Kṛṣṇa with the sixteen types of offerings and foodstuffs endowed with various flavors.

For the sake of attaining satisfaction, one should worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Māṇikī, Prabhā, Hara, Sūrya, and Hari as well. Having worshipped Him at the onset of night and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), [one should proceed].
Having fed them, the observer of the vow should dismiss them; he shall become possessed of gold and other riches.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Ananga according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship Rati as well in the morning and feed a Brahmin couple.
When the vow has been performed in this manner, one shall become a vessel for all good fortune.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, having worshipped Kamalā and Hari,
one should give a vessel of ghee to a brahmin for the sake of prosperity and success.
The performer of this vow shall become possessed of wealth, grain, and other riches, and shall be happy.
O beloved, beginning on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should perform a bath in cold water at the end of the night in a river for three days.
The observer of the vow should worship the Lord while still wearing wet clothes;
sins from previous births and other lifetimes will surely perish, there is no doubt.
Indeed, the fruit of the Māgha bath shall be the fulfillment of various desires.
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha,
that fruit one does not obtain on earth even by a thousand horse-sacrifices.
There, bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, and worship become infinite.
This very lunar day marks the beginning of the Kalpa and is also the Jayantī of Viśvakarman.
Hari and Brahmā themselves took birth as Viśvakarman.
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed and adorn it with artistic designs.
One should worship Viśvakarman, the architect of this [universe], with all kinds of offerings.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), feed the preceptor, and give gifts to the wise teacher.
During the night, the observer of the vow should keep a vigil accompanied by instrumental music and song.
Having worshipped [the deity] in the morning, fed [him], and praised [him], one should dismiss [the deity].
By performing the vow in this manner, the artisan shall attain the state of Viśvakarman, endowed with wealth, grain, sons, daughters, wives, cattle, prosperity, and other blessings. 68.
One shall be happy and obtain fame for one's own arts both in this world and the next.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna is Śivarātri;
it is a great vow consisting of the manifestation of the Great Liṅga through the splendor of Śiva.
Then, with devotion, one should observe a vow that is stainless and free from food.
In the morning, one should indeed worship Śambhu together with Satī, who is beautifully golden.
At midday, one should offer all kinds of cooked foods with sincere feeling.
One should have the Śatarudra, the Koṭirudra, and the Rudrādhyāya recited.
One should worship all the incarnations of Rudra and the female incarnations of Pārvatī with the sixteen excellent articles of offering, and one should present bhangā as an oblation.
One should worship with rudrākṣa beads, dhattūra flowers, incense such as gajadhūmra and others,
the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), cool sandalwood paste, and so forth. In the evening, one should perform worship with all the materials and services prescribed by the ritual rules.
At midnight, one should joyfully worship Śaṅkara along with his attendants using the Mahābhiṣeka rite and the Rudrasūkta, offering bilva leaves,
jasmine, kunda flowers, dhattūra, and karavīra.
One should bathe Rudra, who possesses eleven forms,

as well as the twelve-fold Ātman and that which is the singular form of Brahman, with milk. Likewise, one should worship him with incense, lamps, fine musical instruments, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and other such offerings.
One should propitiate Śiva and Śivā with dances and hymns of praise.
As for the food offerings, there should be hundreds of wheat-flour dumplings (*kṣaireya-vaṭaka*), sweet dishes, vegetables, sour rice-gruel (*āranāla*), cooked grains (*bhāja*), and fruits. (78–79)
Milk-rice preparations, those with sugar, and those with sugarcane juice; liquids, drinks, foods to be sucked, licked, and chewed; roasted foods;
and bulbs, roots, tubers, leaves, flowers, and sprouts.
One should indeed offer [these] with supreme devotion to Śaṅkara and Śivā.
Here, one should present to Śaṅkara [an image] adorned with ashes, the trident, rudrākṣa beads, the crescent moon, and the serpent Vāsuki, and cause his sacred verses to be sung.
At night, one should hold a festival and keep a vigil together with people;
in the morning, one should perform worship and cause gifts to be given in abundance to Brahmins, renunciants, practitioners of yoga, and likewise to yoginīs.
One should feed and likewise honor virtuous women, chaste wives, ascetics, and holy men;
one should feed and worship gurus, ancestors, the Gaṇas, the elderly, mothers, children, and young girls; as well as maidens, married women, and all living beings.
One should worship those devoted to Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the gods, and Rudra;
one should honor and feed the Brahmins and give gifts in every way.
One should conclude the vow when it is complete and then perform the fire-oblation.
The observer of the vow should perform the auspicious concluding bath (avabhṛtha) with great celebration.
A wealthy observer of the vow should have the Rudra-sacrifice, the great sacrifice, performed.
Thus, on the fourteenth day of Śiva, one should carry out the ritual of feeding.
Having performed the breaking of the fast in this manner, one should partake of food; the fruit will be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One shall attain Kailāsa, Vaikuṇṭha, and the imperishable Goloka.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, there is the vow that bestows wealth.

One should perform worship here and honor Kubera with sandalwood paste and other offerings. Every month, the Lord of Yakṣas himself— the sovereign of Yakṣas, together with his treasures and his retinue— should be worshipped personally with sixteen articles.
The cow, along with her calf, should be honored here with delicious foods;
likewise, the preceptor must certainly be worshipped and provided with food in every way.
Sweet foods and gifts should be bestowed upon the twice-born.
When this vow of eating but once a day has been performed,
one shall attain greatness in this world as well as in heaven, endowed with all prosperity;
having attained a sovereign empire of happiness, he will be like another King of Kings (Kubera).
He shall rejoice together with his family members for eternal years.
In every case, he should perform a vow consisting of eating only at night, eating only once a day, or fasting;
according to his capacity, he may subsist on fruits or water alone.
Subsisting on milk, or consuming curd, or subsisting on water with jaggery.

(96) Thus, in the first section, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [the description of] the annual Thirteenth-day vows (*vārṣikatrayodaśīvratāni*), including the Madana-vrata, the vow for the removal of misfortune, the worship of Trivikrama, the Sāvitrī-vrata, Jayā-pārvatī-vrata, the Rati-kāma-vrata, the Gotrirātra-vrata, the Bālādi-śrāddha, the Kaliyuga-origin day, the three-night Aśoka-vrata, the offering of lamps to Yama, the worship of Dhanalakṣmī, and the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa— [concludes].
Chapter Two Hundred and Seventy-Eight: Description of the Naṅga Vrata, the Kamalāhara Pūjana, the Kalpādi Tithis, the Jayantī of Viśvakarman, the Mahāśivarātri, the Dhanada Vrata, and others.
[From] the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) – Chapter 279.
[The Author: Chapter 280.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe to you the vows (vratas) of the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī).

By performing these rites here, the observer of vows shall obtain what is desired both in this world and the next. (1) Formerly, in a previous age, a great festival was held on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, marking the marriage of Nārāyaṇa with Śrī. (2)
Here, one observing the vow should construct a plantain pavilion while eating only once a day.
Likewise, a water-pot (ghaṭa) should be installed within the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
At its mouth, a vessel of sesame seeds should be placed near the fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
In the interval between Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī, the installation and worship should be performed;
the offering should be made with the sixteen types of service (upacāras).
Then, during the night, the observer of the vow should indeed cause many musical instruments to be played.
One should manifest the splendor of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī;
one should clothe them in garments, ornaments, and fragrant unguents.
Having caused them to perform the worldly customs and having offered the bridegroom’s garland, [one should proceed].

Having completed all the worship of the gods and performed prostrations, he should then change his garment and have [the disciple] hold his hand. Having caused the fire-oblation (homa) to be performed and having had auspicious songs sung, || 8 ||
Having caused her to circumambulate [the fire] and having given her the dowry,
and having honored her according to worldly custom by removing the objects from her head,
he should complete the full *homa* and then settle her within the house.
Having caused Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī to be fed, one should have them sleep in the house.
When morning has dawned, one should indeed untie the knots at the Gaṅgā.
One should give many gifts, such as cows, land, and gold.

One should feed the Brahmins, the gods, the sages, the virtuous, and likewise the chaste women; as well as boys, girls, and others, the wretched, the blind, the destitute, the servants, the mendicants, the helpless, the gurus, and the most eminent elders. (12)

[He saw] those who have gone to the abodes of Brahmā, the beautiful Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the immortal realm; those residing in Śvetadvīpa and the unmanifest state; the Vairājas who dwell in the Satyaloka;
those who go to the world of the Sun; the liberated ones who have arrived; and the divine wives of Viṣṇu.
He should likewise feed his mothers and human women with *śaṣkulīs*,
delightful *khājakas*, *pheṇikās* with a hundred holes,
*ghṛtapūras*, *revālīs*, and *parpikās* filled with yellow essence.
Rice balls, sugar-cane, sugar, and likewise chickpeas;
auspicious garments and also vessels for intoxication; pickled vegetables, knotted sweets, and likewise blooming balls.
The essence of milk, milk-rice, curds, and sandalwood paste; various kinds of vegetables, pearls, powdered sweets, and *modaka* cakes;
as well as split pulses, decoctions, and *rājikā-rāddhaka* preparations. (18)
One should provide excellent whey, fermented rice-gruel drinks, and buttermilk;
one should have water for drinking served and ensure the cleansing of the mouth.
One should cause betel leaves to be given, and likewise cause gifts to be bestowed.
Having fully worshipped Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Lakṣmī, one should bid them farewell.
On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), the observer of the vow should thereafter partake of auspicious food.
Having thus performed the vow consisting of the marriage of Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī—

By their grace, conjugal union here shall become eternal. Moreover, in the abode of Goloka, by the favor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the divine and supreme conjugal union of those who observe the vow shall indeed be eternal. (22–23)

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the Mahālakṣmī vow is observed. On this occasion, a procession for Mahālakṣmī should be performed, and she should be worshipped according to the prescribed rites. Furthermore, the worship of Jānakī and Śivarāja together should indeed be conducted here.
This must be performed by one who has fasted, and especially so by one who has already eaten.
On this occasion, the observer of the vow should perform a night vigil with dance and song.
In the morning, [the deities] should be fed, worshipped, and then dismissed with great devotion.
Having performed such worship of Mahālakṣmī, the man observing the vow, or even the woman, shall indeed obtain wealth, grain, progeny,
and happiness. Furthermore, on this fourteenth day as well, [one should worship] with saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
The worship of Śiva should be performed with perfumes and other offerings, as well as with garments and jewels.
(28) Having offered canopies, banners, and parasols, and having worshipped the Mothers, the man who observes this vow obtains the great merit of the horse sacrifice and other such rites. (29)
In this very place, the observer of the vow should perform the worship of *damanaka* with fragrant flowers;
after the worship, he should offer the *damanaka* to Śiva alone.
[He should also worship] the great golden *liṅga* called Hāṭaka, which came from Pātāla.
Indeed, the Lord Hāṭakeśvara has arrived upon the earth.
He alone is to be worshipped here with excellent articles such as the sixteen [upacāras], including bathing, decoration, food offerings, worship, and the waving of lights (nīrājana). || 31-32 ||
Hāṭakeśa is to be propitiated; he indeed bestows gold.
The observer of the vow, fully endowed with enjoyments, shall go to the supreme Kailāsa.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, at the onset of night—
One should worship the Liṅga with offerings such as perfumes and with Bilva leaves (34).
One should feed it, honor it, offer prayers, and then dismiss it. Thus should the Śiva-vow be performed by one desiring wealth and progeny (35).
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is the Narasiṃha-caturdaśī;
one should perform the festival for the birth of Nṛsiṃha here in the evening.
Eating only once or fasting, [one should worship] Narasiṃha made of gold.
With the sixteen primary services and others, with ablutions such as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth,
with incense, lamps, and beautiful flowers, with foods, drinks, and chewables, with the waving of lights (ārātrika) and the like, and with circumambulations, hymns of praise, and so on. (37–38)
Having worshipped Nṛhari, the observer of the vow should indeed install him at night;
then he should give various gifts there according to his wealth.
[He should worship the Lord] whose hair-ends are like molten gold and whose eyes are like blazing fire.
With claws harder than a diamond, he was a terrifying divine lion (1.279.40).
With thick shoulders, hips, and neck, yet slender at the waist and belly, he had the face of a lion and the body of a man, adorned with every ornament (41).
With a face wreathed in garlands of flames, with a protruding tongue and fangs,
and tearing open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu with the tips of his claws—
thus one should worship Prahlāda and Kaśyapa again in the morning.
One should feed various kinds of food, perform the lustration rite (nīrājana), and offer the formal dismissal. The observer of the vow himself should then break his fast to please Nṛhari;
liberated from the fear of clawed and fanged beasts, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
One who seeks the fulfillment of their vows should perform a pilgrimage here to Oṃkāreśvara;
having bathed the Liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and smeared it with saffron, one should worship it with food offerings, fruits, incense, lamps, garments, and ornaments. (45)
The observer of the vow should worship the liṅga made of flour with the ārārtrika and other rites.
By the grace of Mahādeva, he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whatever he may perform, all that shall become a bestower of knowledge and liberation for men.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should fetch excellent water for the purpose of the bathing procession; for that [water], one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and other rites. On the full moon day, at dawn, one should bathe Śrī Hari with that water.
The observer of the vow should worship with various materials and cause a festival to be held.
On the fourteenth day, performing the "five-fold heat" penance during the day, he should offer a sacrificial cow at the beginning of the night; one should diligently perform this Rudra-vow.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, the observer of the vow, having duly worshipped Rudra with offerings appropriate to the place, time, and worthy recipient, shall obtain all prosperity.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, [one should worship] the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa rite and likewise offer it to Lakṣmī.
Having worshipped Hari and Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rules, both men and women shall attain worldly enjoyment and liberation, which are obtained through their grace.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should perform the supreme Ananta-vrata. Then, the observer of the vow should have an image of the one named Ananta— namely Śeṣa as well as Hari Nārāyaṇa—
crafted out of gold, and subsequently worship it according to the prescribed rite.
Having prepared a thread made of cotton or silk with fourteen well-knotted sections,
and having worshipped it with saffron and other substances, the observer of the vow should bind it upon his own arm—
the woman on the left and the man on the right— and he should then cast the old thread into the water.
Then, having cooked one *prastha* of wheat flour mixed with sugar and clarified butter until it is sweet, he should offer it to Ananta.
Having also fed the children, the observer of the vow should then eat it himself.
One should perform that vow for a period of fourteen years, accompanied by its prescribed sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). Having completed it, the practitioner should then conclude the vow.
He should fashion a Sarvatobhadra mandala using the seven types of grain.
One should place an image of Ananta in a copper jar or vessel,

worship it according to the prescribed rite, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and offer food. One should worship Gaṇeśa, the Mothers, the Kheṭas, and the Guardians of the Quarters individually.
Having performed the *homa* with offerings of clarified butter, the observer of the vow should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
He should present a bed, an image, and a cow to Śrīmukha.
Having fed the children and the virtuous, he should satisfy them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
One should give many gifts and feed virtuous men and women;
thus, one who performs this infinite vow becomes a partaker of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One desiring prosperity should also perform the Kadalī-vrata here.
A man, and not a woman, should bathe and worship Rambhā, who resides within the forest, with perfumes, flowers, grains, sprouts, and so forth;
with curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, lamps, garments, and collections of cooked food. (64–65)
Having bowed and circumambulated her, he should then pray to her:
"O you who are worshipped by Apsaras, daughters of the gods, and daughters of the Nāgas, grant me health of body, beauty, and prosperity; salutations to you!"
Then, having fed four maidens— whether married women or virgins— and having honored them with garments, vermilion, lac, and collyrium,
the observer of the vow, having completed the rite, should return to his own home.

O Lakṣmī! When this vow has been performed in this manner, having obtained supreme good fortune, one shall sport in heaven by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna) and thereafter worship the highest world.
Served by celestial nymphs in the realm of Truth (Satyaloka), one shall enjoy great bliss.
They go at last to the divine world called the Abode of the Imperishable, the station of Hari.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, even those who have killed a Brahmin—whether slain by poison, weapons, water, fire, serpents, beasts of prey, thunderbolts, or other such means—[attain that state]. (1.279.70–71)
One should perform the *śrāddha* rite appropriately according to the rules for the *ekoddiṣṭa* ceremony;
one should feed children with sweets, as well as virtuous men, virtuous women, and the gods upon earth (brahmins).
One should also offer libations (*tarpaṇa*), mouthfuls of fodder to cows, and the ritual offering (*bali*) to dogs and crows.
Having performed these rites and sipped water for purification, the observer of the vow should eat together with his own kinsmen.
By performing the great śrāddha in this manner, having delivered his ancestors and forefathers,
he shall go to the eternal heaven and, at the end, to the abode of Brahmā within Hari.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, having properly worshipped the golden Dharmarāja with perfumes and other offerings, one should feed him excellent, sweet food.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana), and offer gifts to the venerable Guru.
The King of Dharma protects the one who observes the vow and likewise leads him to heaven.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, having performed an oil massage at the rising of the moon,
one should bathe, worship the King of Dharma, and offer libations to Yama.
At dusk, the observer of the vow should light oil lamps for the satisfaction of Yama;
he should place them at a crossroads outside his house. He should feed the Brahmins, perform prostrations, and bid farewell to the Lord Yama.

Having performed the vow in this manner, one shall go to heaven, which is free from fear of hell. Now, on the fourteenth day of that very month, one should perform the worship of Hanumān with oil, vermilion, arka flowers, garlands, mung-bean cakes, and other offerings.
The sons and grandsons of the priests shall attain abundant prosperity;
in the end, they shall reach the eternal and blissful worlds of Vairāja.
[This is] the propitiation of the Tāmasa beings, such as Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and others.
And the accomplishment of the mantras of the *rājasa* deities;
the accomplishment of worldly *sāttvika* [mantras] that produce poison, fire, and paralysis; and the propitiation of the *āveśas*, *ḍākinīs*, and *yoginīs*. (82–83)
One should also perform the practice for those who dwell in cremation grounds and seek Bhairava here at night, according to the instructions and the prescribed ritual.
This includes the respective vows, the offering, the worship, the recitation, the naming, and the dismissal.
The observer of the vow should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and the ritual according to the tantra in the proper sequence.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, at Kāśī, Śrī Śaṅkara himself,
having bathed, performed the supreme Pāśupata vow according to the prescribed rite.
Then, one should perform a great worship here at the *liṅga* with perfumes and other offerings,
using *droṇa* flowers, *bilva* leaves, *arka* flowers,
and *ketaka* flowers; likewise with flowers, fruits, sweet cooked foods, and various kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*).
One who observes the vow of eating only once a day shall attain Kailāsa through the gratification of Śambhu.
Furthermore, one desiring prosperity should perform the Brahmakūrca vow;
he should drink the five products of the cow at night and satisfy the gods in the morning.
Having satisfied the Brahmins, the observer of the vow himself may also eat;
all sins are certainly destroyed by the Brahmakūrca vow.
Indeed, [one should take] the urine of a tawny cow and likewise the dung of a black cow.
The milk of a white cow should be taken, the auspicious curd of a red one;
the ghee of a brindled cow should be taken, and one should mix these with water infused with *kuśa* grass.
By drinking that, sins are destroyed from their very roots, even while still fresh.
Even the "stone-vow" (pāṣāṇavrata) is considered fulfilled here by performing it at night;
having first worshipped Gaurī with perfumes and other offerings, one should offer a cake made of flour cooked in ghee, shaped like a stone and resembling a small ball (piṇḍaka). || 93 ||
The observer of the vow shall attain sovereignty, happiness, good fortune, and his true nature.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, having worshipped a golden bull,
he should observe the vow of eating but one meal and then worship Maheśvara at night.
One should worship with lotus flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
one should feed [the deity] with many kinds of cooked foods, and then one should bid farewell to the deity.
One should give gifts to the preceptor and feed virtuous men and women.
Having thus performed the Śivavrata, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And right here, Hari, Brahmā, Śiva, and Datta, the son of Atri—
these three gods having become one— became known by the name Dattātreya.
Having placed Anasūyā, as well as Atri and Dattātreya,
along with golden vessels upon a jar atop an auspicious mandala within the pavilion,
one should properly worship them in a vessel, feed them, and then dismiss them.
The observer of the vow should give all kinds of gifts and shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, one should perform the Virūpākṣa-vrata;
having bathed, one should worship Śiva Virūpākṣa with all manner of offerings.
One should feed and satisfy Śambhu according to the prescribed rite and bid him farewell;
having given gifts to the twice-born, the observer of the vow rejoices on Kailāsa.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, the libation to Yama is enjoined.
Having bathed before sunrise,
one should offer libations to Yama with sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water; thereafter,
one should feed excellent food to virtuous brahmins, dismiss them, and the observer of the vow should eat himself.
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna is the Śambhunishāvrata;
however, the Śivarātri, observed without water, should be fasted upon with pure devotion.
[One may worship] either a Jyotirliṅga or an earthen [liṅga], as well as Śiva and Śivā in embodied form.

The observer of the vow should worship with perfumes and other offerings, bilva leaves and the like, food offerings, and drinks of excellent flavor; he should feed [the deity], perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), dismiss [the deity], and bow down.
By the power of the vow, the observer of the vow shall attain Kailāsa. (106–107)
The fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna is considered the Durgā-vrata.
On this day, the observer of the vow, eating but one meal, should worship Durgā and likewise feed others.
He should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), bow down, and dismiss the deity; thus he shall become a partaker of Kailāsa. 108.
One who desires the fruit [of their actions] must perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) of their vows.
Here, fourteen water-pots (kuṃbha) are required, along with betel nuts, unbroken rice grains, and sweetmeats;
they should be made of either copper or clay, be free of cracks, new, and accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and fine garments. || 109–110 ||
An equal number of bamboo staffs, purificatory grasses, seats, vessels,
and sacrificial threads were likewise prepared;
and in the pavilion, within the *sarvatobhadra* mandala, there were water-jars accompanied by fruit.
The deities are to be established, worshipped, and fed;
they are to be dismissed and given as a gift to the preceptor. Those who are virtuous, chaste women, Brahmins, and young girls are to be fed. (112–113)

"With enthusiasm, one should in every way perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) along with fire-offerings (homa), recitations (japa), and the ritual union (saṅgama); its fruit is heaven and liberation.

Thus ends the [section on] Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa’s marriage to Lakṣmī and Mahālakṣmī within the annual Caturdaśī vows, in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter Two Hundred and Seventy-Nine: Description of Vows such as the Pilgrimage, the Worship of Śiva, the Worship of Damanaka, the Festivals of Śrī Hāṭakeśvara and Narasiṃha, the Pilgrimage to Oṃkāreśvara, the Pilgrimage for Bathing, the Fetching of Water, the Rudra-vow, the Pavitrāropaṇa, the Anantacaturdaśī, the Kadalī-vow, the Hata-śrāddha, the Worship of Dharmarāja, the Narakacaturdaśī, the Tarpaṇa for Yama, the Oil-Bath, the Worship of Hanumān, the Worship of Bhūtas, Mantra-sādhana, the Pāśupata-vow, the Brahmakūrca-vow, the Dattātreyajayantī, the Śivarātri, and others.
← Chapter 279: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 280 [[Author: Chapter 281 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you the vows of the full-moon day,
by performing which a man or a woman may attain an abundance of merit.
Indeed, the new moon day of the dark fortnight of Caitra is a lunar day marking the beginning of a Manvantara.
On this day, one should offer a jar filled with rice and water for the satisfaction of Soma,
and perform the Śrāddha rite as prescribed for the sake of the gratification of the ancestors.
On the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, it is said to be the "Hanumat-tithi.
Worship with oil, vermilion, vaṭaka cakes, and other offerings is considered excellent;
furthermore, the commencement of the Vaiśākha ablutions is also recommended on this occasion.
On the new moon day of Vaiśākha, a Śrāddha ceremony should be performed to bring satisfaction to the ancestors.
On the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the Kūrmajayantī vow should be observed according to the prescribed rite; therein, one should worship the two-armed form with a human head.

One should worship the Lord, whose form from the waist downwards is that of a tortoise and who is made of gold. The observer of the vow should feed [the deity] with the essence of milk and sweetmeats (modaka) produced from chickpea flour (cāṇaka).
He should perform the lustration rite (nīrājana), perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana), and bestow gifts.
For one who has performed such a vow, residence in Vaikuṇṭha becomes certain.
Here, the vow of Dharmarāja should be observed for the satisfaction of Dharma.
The practitioner of the vow should give cooked rice, a water-pot, and a cow to the preceptor.
One should worship Dharmarāja, feed him, and then dismiss him.
One should give an auspicious black antelope skin, complete with its hooves and horns;
one should also give it along with sesame seeds and cloth, as well as jars filled with clear water.
A person observing the vow should give fruits and gold as a gift;
such a person rejoices in the world of truth (Satyaloka) for as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist. At the end, he attains Vaikuṇṭha and enjoys eternal bliss.
Jyeṣṭhāmā is said to be Bhāvukā; at that time, one should meditate upon Śrī Hari.
One should worship Him in every way during the night, feed [the deity], and then dismiss Him. On the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha, the Vaṭasāvitrika vow should be performed. 12–13.
Fasting, one should sprinkle the banyan tree with waters resembling nectar, and encircle it with a thread while performing one hundred and eight circumambulations.
Or, one may encircle a *pippala* tree; the observer of the vow should then pray to Sāvitrī.
"O Sāvitrī, worshipful by the world, Mother of the World, whose deity is her husband!
O you who reside in the *vaṭa* tree, I offer salutations; grant me non-separation from my husband.
Having thus prayed to Sāvitrī and having fed married women, [he should proceed].
She who observes this vow herself shall become a partaker of good fortune.
Herein, the vow known as the Bilva-trirātra should be performed with devotion. Śambhu is to be worshipped with bilva leaves, and the bilva fruit is to be consumed by the seeker of the vow.
One should perform a bath with *bilva* leaves, and the *bilva* tree itself should also be worshipped.
(18) One should sleep beneath a *bilva* tree, and likewise, the gift of a *bilva* is prescribed.
By performing this for three nights, the observer of the vow shall indeed attain Kailāsa. (19)
This is the lunar day (tithi) of Manu and others; Manu is to be worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
Likewise, gifts should be given, and virtuous, holy men who bestow great merit should be fed.
On this very day, the ceremonial bath and procession for the coronation of the eldest [son] must indeed be performed.
There, the Lord of Ramā should be bathed according to the ritual of consecration (abhiṣeka).
With pure water scented with sandalwood held in a radiant vessel,
one should bathe Kṛṣṇa with a conch shell while reciting mantras in accordance with the Vedas.
Then, one should offer yellow garments to the Lord Śrīpati,
as well as a pale-red turban and various ornaments.
Likewise, one should offer cooked rice, soup, *polikās*, *vaṭikās*, and *kvathikās*.
One should also present side dishes and sweet drinks with the food offering.
In this context, one should have songs sung concerning the water-sports of Śrī Hari.
After bidding farewell to Hari, the person observing the vow should then eat.
Through that, one attains the eternal bliss born of Hari’s grace.
On the new moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, a śrāddha ceremony should be performed for the benefit of the ancestors.
On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, the worship of Guru Vyāsa should be performed.
Just as it is performed for Hari, so indeed should it be done with the sixteen types of offerings beginning with water;
with sandalwood, unbroken rice, *tulasī* garlands, fruits, garments,
saffron, ornaments, food, most delicious meals, excellent coverings, and water.
The observer of the vow should worship the Guru Kṛṣṇa, as well as the Ācārya and the Gurvī, with substances such as gold and silver, as well as lands and other offerings.
For the purification of what is consumed, he should drink the water from the big toe of the Guru’s foot.
The Guru is declared to be Hari himself; one should serve him for the sake of one's own liberation.
Knowledge obtained through the Guru’s grace, or service to him, or the observance of vows—these grant liberation, happiness, merit, and both worldly enjoyment and final release.
On the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform this supreme Gopadmavrata.
[One should meditate upon the Lord] who has four arms, adorned with a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus;
whose face is serene, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who is graced by Ramā and Garuḍa.
Golden-hued, beautiful, made of gold, and adorned with ornaments;
served by sages, gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras—having thus bathed Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and water, [one should worship Him]. (33–34)
Having bathed and being observant of the vow, he should worship while reciting the Puruṣasūkta;
he should adorn [the deity], worship, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and feed [the priests].
The observer of the vow should bow, ask for forgiveness, and then dismiss [the deity].
One should feed and repeatedly please the preceptor, the teacher, or the virtuous man. One should give gifts and eat by the grace of the Lord of Kamalā;
thus the observer of the vow attains eternal desires pertaining to this world and the next.
One desiring prosperity should perform the Kokilā-vrata on this very day.
Until the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, the observer of the vow should bathe in water outside [the village].
The practitioner of the vow should daily worship the cuckoo in the form of Gaurī.
She has golden wings, jewel-like eyes, and a lotus-face as beautiful as coral;
she is richly adorned with the hue and splendor of musk, dwelling in the Nandana forest,
perched upon mango and campaka trees, and warbling sweet songs.
One should meditate upon the goddess Pārvatī, who has assumed the form of a cuckoo;
one should worship her daily with perfumes and other offerings, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and feed her.
At the end of the month, one should then pray to an image made of gold or fashioned from sesame paste.

"O Kṛṣṇā, born from Caitraratha, O Kokilā, beloved of Hara—be a bestower of happiness to me, who have given you to this Brahmin who bears the form of Hara. Thereafter, one should feed thirty or even one twice-born man and a married woman. || 42-43 ||
Having given gifts such as clothing and having bowed, she should dismiss the Goddess.
By means of the performance of this vow, a woman— through the grace of Kokilāgaurī—
attains worldly enjoyment, heaven, great bliss, Kailāsa, and the happiness of a married couple.
One shall obtain good fortune for seven births and, in the end, final liberation. This is also the lunar day marking the beginning of the Manu-period; it is the commencement of the Cāturmāsya.
Here, the festival of Śambhu’s reclining should be performed according to the prescribed rites. (45–46)
One should create an ocean filled with water, and upon it, a bed as is appropriate.
There, Hari or Hara should be laid to rest by a devoted servant.
He should be fed, worshipped, and entreated with sincere devotion.
The observances of the Cāturmāsya must be undertaken by the practitioner during the vow.
(48) Having thus performed the worship, the vow, and the undertaking of the observances, one obtains the divine fruit of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; there is no doubt in this matter. (49)
On the new moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the worship of the lamp should be performed according to the prescribed rite with flowers,
sandalwood paste, rice grains, sugar, fruits, and water.
The lamp bestows vision and splendor, and it shall always grant good fortune.
An offering of lamps should indeed be made to the deity, for that bestows heaven;
(5.1) and here a *śrāddha* ceremony should be performed, which brings divine satisfaction to the ancestors; furthermore, the planting of nine trees should be carried out with great devotion. (5.2)
Making the earth green, the observer of the vow shall attain the green heaven,
served by vehicles, mounts, female slaves, and so forth, and remaining there eternally.
Then, on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, the observer of the vow [should offer] a coconut fruit.
One should worship it, consume it, and give it as a gift with devotion.
(558) In the three eyes of the coconut reside the triad of Hari, Brahmā, and Hara;
they are indeed to be worshipped here within this coconut fruit. (559)
You are Brahmā, Kuṣpara, Viṣṇu, and Śambhu; these three are you.
Viṣṇu is the *sattva* quality residing within you, while the Three-eyed One is the central *kuṇḍala*.
Brahmā is the soul of your matted locks on the outside, and Hari is indeed the soul of the three deities.
Indeed, by worshipping him, one shall obtain eternal worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(5.7) Here, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, there is the vow of commencing the Vedas (*vedopākaraṇa*).
There, the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors must be performed with the Yajurvedic formulas. (5.8)
The worship of the sages should be performed according to the regulations of one's own Vedic branch.

That libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed by those of the Bahvṛca school on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight]. By those of the Sāmaga school, however, that libation should be performed in the month of Bhādrapada.

On the third lunar day, during the second [fortnight] of the bright half of the month when the moon is in the constellation Hasta (Hasta-ṛkṣa), a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed; likewise, the purification of the body (varṣma-śuddhi) should be carried out according to the prescribed rite. Furthermore, libations (tarpaṇa) and worship (pūjana) should be performed with water mixed with *darbha* grass.
Having had a new and auspicious sacred thread (*upavīta*) made, he should wear it;
he should feed virtuous Brahmins, teachers, and chaste women with all kinds of desired foods.
To them, he should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of gold and silver.
The observer of the vow should eat himself along with his kinsmen and others, and thus he shall attain happiness.
Likewise, the protective rite must indeed be performed here according to the prescribed rule,
using black mustard seeds, red cloths, unbroken grains, and sugar.
Having tied it with safflower-colored thread and washed it with water,
one should then place it in a bronze vessel and worship the foremost deities, headed by Viṣṇu, with perfumes and other offerings.
Then, being joyful, one should have it bound upon one's own forearm through the mediation of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born; [he] performs protection with the sacred thread (sūtraka).
On this very lunar day, in former times, the great lord Hayagrīva [appeared] for the destruction of Hiraṇyākṣa and for the protection of the Vedas.
Then the assembly understood with devotion what was to be done for him;
having fashioned a golden image of the horse’s form with a beautiful human-like body,
they worshipped that auspicious object with the sixteen types of ritual offerings.
The observer of the vow should feed [the Brahmins], perform the *nīrājana* rite, and then dismiss them.
By performing the vow in this manner, happiness arises for him in the next world.
On this very day, one should also perform the offering of the *rudrapavitraka*.

On this day, the observer of the vow should worship Śiva and Śivā with various purificatory offerings and bring the Kokilā-vrata to completion. On the new moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should perform the ancestral śrāddha ceremony, including libations and other rites.
One should fetch kuśa grass from a field that has not been cut by a blade, together with its roots.
On the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, one should perform the Umā-Maheśvara vow;
having bathed and put on rudrākṣa beads, sacred ash, and so forth, one should worship Śambhu.
One should worship with bilva leaves rich in fragrance, along with food offerings, incense, and lamps;
one should feed [the deity], bow down, perform the lustration (nīrājana), and then put [the deity] to sleep. One should keep a vigil at night and worship again in the morning.
The observer of the vow should feed [the guests], make requests, and afterwards dismiss them;
he should then perform the breaking of the fast himself, and the observer of the vow shall attain Kailāsa.
Having performed this for fifteen years, he should then carry out the concluding rite (udyāpana).
And having worshipped that auspicious golden image of Umā and Maheśa within the central jar among fifteen jars,
with garments, ornaments, flowers, and the like, with sweet foods, and with pure water. (77)
One should offer to the Guru an image accompanied by [the ritual materials] and complete with a water-pot (ghaṭa).
Having thus performed this vow here, which is a treasury of all prosperity,
the practitioner indeed becomes a recipient of the abundance of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Then, on this very day, one should diligently perform the Śakra-vrata;
one should worship Hari with offerings such as perfumes and with food oblations.
Having offered a golden image of Śakra to the preceptor, one should [also honor] other Brahmins.
A wealthy king should feed [the brahmins] and indeed give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
This rite should be performed every year by one who desires wealth and grain. On the first day of the month of Āśvina, the propitiation of all the ancestors must be performed.
The śrāddha ceremony should be performed, including the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), feeding, and the sprinkling of water.
Various kinds of food, as well as those with the essence of milk, should indeed be given. Virtuous brāhmaṇas should be fed, as well as truthful women and virtuous girls.
Cows are to be satiated with grass, and likewise trees with water and other offerings.
Hari-Kṛṣṇa is to be satiated with food offerings, fruits, and pure water.
Both Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī are also to be satiated. (84–85)
Having thus performed the great *śrāddha*, the fathers, grandfathers,
all those beginning with the respective ancestors, as well as the mothers born of one’s lineage,
attain eternal satisfaction and, in the end, follow after the state of Brahman.
Therefore, the supreme vow is the *śrāddha* [offering], by which they shall attain the state of liberation.
(87) In the month of Āśvina, on the full moon day, the festival of the *rāsalīlā* is celebrated;
at night, upon the rising of the full moon, He performed the *rāsalīlā*. (88)
The Blessed One, together with Rādhā and the gopīs, for a long time [remained there].
He should cause the golden images of Gopī-Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa to shine most brilliantly.
He should wear saffron-colored garments, an upper cloth, and a waist-cloth.
The observer of the vow should wear a yellow bodice, a saffron mark on the forehead,
and black garments of priceless yellow silk;
likewise, he should wear a crown variegated with various jewels, as well as earrings.
In his hand, he should hold a golden flute adorned with jewels.
As an offering of food (naivedya), one should present sweet cakes (parpikā), rice-balls (piṇḍaka), milk-pudding (pāyasa), and so forth,
along with fragrant flowers, oil, and water from land-lotuses.
One should perfume the garments and the temple as well for the Lord of Rādhikā.
Having placed [the image] on a seat in the moon-chamber (candraśālā), one should worship Mādhava at night;
indeed, one should gratify the Lord of Ramā with songs, instrumental music, and dances.
One should offer him freshly harvested flattened rice mixed with sugar and milk,
and have him sing the verses concerning the *rāsa-līlā*.
From that time forward, one who desires prosperity should observe this autumnal vow.

One should indeed begin the Kārtika bath from this very day. On the full moon of the month of Āśvina, the vow known as Kojāgara should be performed while fasting, or one may observe the practice of eating only once a day.
In the morning, one should worship Lakṣmī with various ritual offerings;
one should adorn her and feed her, and worship her again at midday.
At the sight of the moon in the evening, one should [worship] an image of Lakṣmī made of gold.
Having placed them in a vessel or bowl made of copper or even clay,
one should illuminate a thousand, a hundred, or a hundred thousand lamp-bowls.
One should offer *pūrikās* and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to Mahālakṣmī.
One should keep a vigil with dance and song, and having worshipped her in the morning,
the observer of the vow should offer the image to the guru and thus conclude the rite.
During this night, Mahālakṣmī appears with her lotus hands granting boons and fearlessness.
"Who is awake for my sake so that I may observe them?"—thus [I ask]. To that vigilant worshiper of mine, I grant wealth.
By performing this here every year, one becomes prosperous and indeed attains the state of Viṣṇu.
On the first day of the month of Kārtika, the worship of Lakṣmī should be performed especially.
Lakṣmī should be depicted with four arms, seated upon a lotus-throne.
In her right hand there is a lotus, and likewise in her left, a jar of nectar.
On her two lower arms, beautiful bilva fruits and conch shells should be fashioned.
On both her sides, two elephants should be made, both holding water-pots.
Upon her head, a most charming lotus should be depicted. (105–106)
When a beautiful pavilion has been constructed, adorned with plantain pillars and archways,
the observer of the vow should worship her upon the *sarvatobhadra* diagram with the *Lakṣmīsūkta*.
He should also offer ornaments and magnificent garments to Śrī.
One should place on her forehead a crescent moon made beautiful with saffron and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should worship her with fragrant flower garlands, golden ornaments,
lotuses, gems, incense, lamps, liquid offerings, and so forth.
One should likewise have rows of lamps arranged all around according to one's capacity.
Among the food offerings, one should present *śaṣkulīs*, *pheṇikās* with a hundred perforations,
*ghṛtapūras*, *revālīs*, and *pūrikās* made with yellow essence (*pītasāra*).
One should offer her parched grains (*parpikāḥ*), rice-balls (*piṇḍakān*), vegetables (*śākarān*), chickpeas and the like,
as well as cooked rice and other foods to be eaten.
Having presented betel-leaf rolls (*tāmbūlavīṭikām*), one should perform the great lustration ceremony (*nīrājanam*).
Then the observer of the vow should have verses for the worship of Lakṣmī sung;
he should worship the lamps and illuminate all the sites with lamps.
He should perform the worship of Śāradā on the Āyavyaya-etc. diagram.
The observer of the vow should have a golden image of Śāradā fashioned.
[He should offer] betel leaves, areca nuts, cardamom, sugar,
cinnamon, fruits, unbroken grains, saffron, molasses, parched grain, and so forth.

One should worship Śāradā with incense, lamps, and excellent food offerings, as well as with ink, pens, and other such items, using the mantras; one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and then bid her farewell.
For one who performs the vow in this manner, both Lakṣmī and Śāradā remain eternally steadfast.
This [rite] indeed bestows all prosperity and grants the desires for gifts and food.
(1.17) In this very context, an ablution with oil and other substances, along with massage, should be performed by the observer of the vow, by which poverty is certainly destroyed. (1.18)
On the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Festival of the Divine Lamp (Devadīpotsava) is observed.
One should light lamps at sacred fords, in temples, in houses, and so forth.
One should wear ornaments such as a crown [representing] Lakṣmī’s consort and the Lord of Light.
One should offer to Śrī Kṛṣṇa samyāva, pūrikā cakes, boiled rice, kvathikā, soup, sūraṇa, and vegetables such as vṛntāka;
and having offered them according to the prescribed rite, the observer of the vow shall attain heaven and liberation. || 1.280.120-121 ||

On this full moon day of Tripurī, one should worship Tripurāri; the observer of the vow, being happy, should feed various foods and perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana). The conclusion of the Cāturmāsya should be celebrated with festivities by the people.
One should also observe the lunar days (tithis) beginning with Manu and worship Manu;
likewise, Bhaktidevī and Jayantī must be observed here in every way.
When the moon of devotion rises, worship should be performed according to the proper ritual injunctions.
One should feed [the deity] and adorn him with auspicious ornaments;
the observer of the vow should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and then dismiss [the deity], becoming a dweller in the divine abode.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, one should perform the vision of Skanda.
A festival must indeed be celebrated there for the sake of conquering all enemies.
Right here, the Tripura festival should be performed by the offering of lamps.
Even insects, moths, mosquitoes, trees, and climbing plants are born as living beings.
Merely by seeing the lamp, they indeed attain the supreme goal:
the Kṛttikās, the six [Kṛttikās], Kārttikeya, the sword-bearer, Agni, and the Lord of Waters.
[They are honored] with perfumes, flowers, fruits, incense, lamps, food offerings, and drinks.
Lamps should be worshipped and offered in the area outside the house.
Likewise, near the lamps, a beautiful square pit measuring fourteen finger-breadths should be made and sprinkled with sandalwood water.
Having filled [a vessel] with cow’s milk, one should then place a golden fish inside;
having paid homage and worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, one should indeed present it to a Brāhmaṇa according to that rite. By this method, one rejoices in the presence of Hari.
Indeed, this very gift of the milk-ocean is thus proclaimed.
By performing the rite of releasing a bull on this lunar day, one shall attain Kailāsa. On the first day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform the Śrāddha and the libation (tarpaṇa).

The ancestors, being satisfied, go to the supreme station of the Bhāgavatas. On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should give a measure (āḍhaka) of salt enriched with gold to a helpless person for the fulfillment of all desires.
On the full moon day of Pauṣa, one should bathe with waters containing all medicinal herbs.
O Lakṣmī! In ancient times, this world was indeed abandoned by you;
then Viṣṇu, Indra, and Bṛhaspati [acted] for the sake of restoring Lakṣmī once again.
Śukra and Soma joined together under the asterism Puṣya and made diligent efforts;
they further adorned her with festivities and playful celebrations of good fortune,
and by means of their respective qualities and splendors, for the increase of all auspiciousness.
Therefore, the observer of the vow should act accordingly and worship them according to the prescribed rule.
(1.38) Having rubbed his own body with a paste of white mustard seeds, he should bathe with waters containing all medicinal herbs and wear new garments. (1.39)
Having seen auspicious objects, bowed, and touched them, the observer of the vow should then worship Hari, Śakra, Indra, the Moon, Puṣya, and the Ījas with ritual offerings.
Having performed the fire-oblation, he should feed the planets and children with excellent milk-porridge.
Afterward, the observer of the vow should dismiss the deities and partake of the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
This vow indeed destroys misfortune, bestows prosperity, and grants liberation;
likewise, in ancient times, it took place here on Mount Raivata on the full moon day.
Then follows the birth of Ambā and Gaurī; one should perform their worship there.
From this day also begins the commencement of the Māgha bath.
It is also said that on this very day the Holikā-daṇḍa should be erected.
Having given jewels, or wealth consisting of garments, turbans, and footwear,
one rejoices in heaven; likewise, by giving sesame seeds, cotton, and woolen blankets,
and by worshipping Śaṅkara here, one attains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
On the full moon day of Phālguna, the commencement of the milk-vow (dugdhavrata) takes place;
this lunar day is known as the beginning of the Dvāpara Yuga and is auspicious.
On the full moon of Phālguna, however, the worship of Holikā is prescribed.
Having offered oblations into the fire within a heap of wood and other materials using mantras that destroy demons, you were made into Holi by foolish children terrified by the sight of blood.
Therefore, I shall worship you; O Bhūti, grant me prosperity! (147–148)
Having kindled [the fire] with this mantra and having circumambulated it, the observer of the vow should lead forth this Holi,
the Rākṣasī who caused fear to Prahlāda— just as people, their bodies well-charred by Prahlāda, used to set her ablaze. (149)
"This burning of the wicked at the end of the year is Holikā.
This burning of Kāma performed by Śaṅkara is considered Holikā;
however, the narrative of the burning differs according to the distinction between the Kalpas.
Likewise, there is the festival of the swing (dolotsava) here on the full moon day or on the following day,
during the conjunction with the Uttaraphalgunī asterism on Mount Raivata;
having formerly placed Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna upon the swing at the abode of Dharma.
The gods deliberated here: "That festival must be performed.
In the morning, one should perform the worship of the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa with the sixteen types of offerings and with the great *nīrājana* ceremony. (153–154)
With garments, sandalwood, flowers, and the like; with ornaments made of *tulasī* leaves;
with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), fried cakes (*pūrikā*), and fruits such as jujube (*badara*);
and likewise with spring flowers and colored pastes (*raṅgagulālaka*).
One should worship, feed, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and delight [the deity].
One should also have games played with mechanical dolls, and then cause the Lord to sleep.
Having fed the devotees and the children, the observer of the vow should then eat.

In this manner, the observer of the vow should perform, in full detail, the following observances on the lunar days beginning with the first (tithi): anointing the body with oil, ritual bathing, consuming mango blossoms, enjoying the spring festival, and likewise the "dust-worship" (dhūlivandana).
Having awakened Nara-Nārāyaṇa in the morning, the observer of the vow should worship them.
He should bestow many gifts and likewise conclude the vow. [Thereby] he shall obtain a wife, sons, wealth, grain, heaven, and liberation. (1.280.160)

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-saṃtāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, [the following are described]: the *Vārṣika-Pūrṇimā* and *Amāvāsyā* vows; the absence of *Śrāddha* on the new moon day; the lunar days beginning with the *Anvādi*; the *Hanumaj-jayantī*; the commencement of the *Vaiśākha-snāna*; the *Kūrma-jayantī*; the *Dharmarāja-vrata*; the *Bhāvukā-amā*; the *Vaṭa-sāvitrī-vrata*; the *Bilva-trirātra-vrata*; the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of Jyeṣṭhā; the pilgrimage (*yātrā*); the worship of Guru and Vyāsa; the *Gopa-dmaka-kokilā-vrata*; the observances (*niyama*) of the *Cāturmāsya*; the *Śiva-śayana*; the worship of lamps (*dīpa-pūjā*); the *Nārikela-pūrṇimā*; the *Ṛg-yajuḥ-śrāvaṇī*; the *Sāmaga-śrāvaṇī*; the tying of the protective thread (*rakṣā-bandhana*); the *Hayagrīva-jayantī*; and the *Śiva-pavitrā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, regarding those other vows which are observed during the twelve months.
I shall also declare the meritorious duties that must be performed; listen, O Lotus-born One!
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, the Lord, accompanied by Lakṣmī, should be swung with great festivities by the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having rocked the Lord on that swing made of fragrant flowers for two ghaṭikās and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the observer of the vow should bring Him down.
Then, having bowed to Him and asked for His forgiveness, he should offer Him food and dismiss Him.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, during the bright fortnight under the Puṣya asterism, one should perform the chariot procession (rathayātrā).
One should station the chariot together with its horses before Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
and have him wear garments suitable for royalty as well as ornaments.
The Lord should be equipped with excellent golden weapons, such as the preeminent sword and others;
having fed him with curd, rice, and sweetmeats, one should worship him upon the chariot.
After performing the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for Hari four times, again and again, [one should proceed].
One should help [the devotee] descend from the chariot there and have him sing the hymns of praise (kīrtanas).
Then the observer of the vow should take his meal; this is the vow that bestows liberation.
It is observed for one month, beginning from the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha.

The festival of the swing (dolotsava) is considered to last until the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa. When the moon is in the sign of Taurus, one should prepare a well-decorated swing for the ever-new and beloved Śrī Hari, using fresh materials and other offerings. 9.

Every day at evening, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offered the food offering (naivedya), the observer of the vow should swing [the deity] and cause beautiful cradle-songs to be sung while performing a dance.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of Nabhas, one should worship and cause Hari to ascend [the boat].
The month of Śrāvaṇa must be spent by all means through vows, observances, and restraints,
especially by one who desires both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Kārttika should likewise be observed through vows, charity, recitation, and other such practices.
(13) When the sun has entered the sign of Sagittarius (Dhanuḥ) in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and the ascendant is Sagittarius, one should perform an oil massage and bathe Hari with warm water. (14)
Having put on fine garments and placed a small fire before him,
he should perform his daily rites and the adornment of the glorious Lord.
He should offer sweetmeats (*modaka*), fresh butter, ghee, and curd as the food offering (*naivedya*).
One should offer *roṭaka*, fried *vṛntāka* (eggplant), and *taralā*.
One should have [the disciple] drink *kvathikā* and engage him in the study of the *Kṛṣṇa-stotra*.
In this manner, for the duration of one month, one should perform the festival for the sake of instruction.
When the sun’s transit into Capricorn occurs in the month of Pauṣa,
the auspicious time lasts for forty ghaṭikās; during this period,
acts such as giving gifts, ritual bathing, and worship should be performed, as well as offerings of sesame seeds and sweetmeat balls.
Sweet foods should indeed be given, especially to those who are destitute.
One should likewise give mouthfuls of grass to cows and perform the *śrāddha* rite which bestows merit.
On the fifth day of the month of Māgha, one should celebrate the excellent festival of spring.
From that time forward, until the conclusion of Holi, one should always perform worship and offer meals with saffron, colored powders, and fragrant pastes;
one should wear white garments and put on new clothes for Hari.
The observer of the vow should cast colored powders upon the garments of Lakṣmī and Hari;
he should repeatedly scatter gulāla and water from land-lotuses,
wear a crest of mango blossoms, and feed Lord Hari.
One should wear silken garments of the Kaisara variety and worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī; one should sing of the springtime sports of Holi during the month of Phālguna.
Then, from the day of His manifestation until the limit of six days—
While nursing him, the observer of the vow should also cause Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to suckle;
he should feed him milk and other foods, and rock him while singing songs.
He should serve him with the disposition of a child and repeatedly propitiate the Lord.

Starting from the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should perform the monthly anointing of the image of Śrī Kṛṣṇa with sandalwood paste and other substances mixed with saffron. On the days of solar and lunar eclipses, as well as on festival days, one should perform ritual bathing, recitation, and other such rites.
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should offer to Hari auspicious,
soft, and fine cloth made of smooth, delicate threads, dyed with safflower.
During the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, however, one should satisfy the ancestors with ancestral offerings (śrāddha).
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should likewise invoke [the goddess] under the asterism Mūla;
one should worship Sarasvatī, feed her, and offer milk-preparations and other foods. By performing the rite of dismissal under the asterism Śravaṇa, the practitioner of the vow indeed becomes wise.
One’s own birthday should be celebrated with all kinds of festivities:
through acts of charity, feasting, honoring elders, and visiting the deities.
From the eleventh day to the twelfth day, the days dedicated to Hari bestow liberation.

Hari is pleased by those who perform acts of feeding, giving, worship, festivals, and libations; through these, He bestows the state of fearlessness. Indeed, by whatever means Hari may be propitiated for someone, [He grants that person His grace].
For him, there shall be happiness in this world and the next, and an increase in merit; such is the vow.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Lord who reclines upon the waters with the sixteen types of offerings; one shall obtain the fruit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, one who is self-restrained should worship Hari;
through the sixteen types of offerings, he shall enjoy the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should worship the Lord Mādhava.
Through the sixteen primary services and others, one shall attain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, a person should worship Govinda with the sixteen excellent articles; thus he shall win the fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa with the sixteen primary offerings and other services; such a person shall indeed partake in the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should worship Madhusūdana.

Through the sixteen supreme requisites, the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) shall be attained. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship Trivikrama with sixteen types of offerings; the fruit of the human sacrifice (naramedha) shall be attained.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the observer of the vow should worship Vāmana;
by means of the sixteen types of offerings, he becomes a partaker of the merit of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the observer of the vow should worship Śrīdhara.
By means of the sixteen immeasurable objects and so forth, one partakes in the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices (vājimedha).
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should worship Hṛṣīkeśa with the sixteen types of ritual offerings; thus, one obtains the fruit of the Brahmamedha sacrifice.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, one should worship Padmanābha with the sixteen types of offerings and other rites; such a person partakes in the merit of a thousand sacrifices. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one should worship Dāmodara.
Through sixteen types of ritual services and other observances, one partakes in the merit of two thousand horse-sacrifices.
During the vow, one should perform fire-offerings, recitation, austerity, charity, feeding of virtuous Brahmins and others, giving of sacrificial fees, prayer, and keeping vigil. (46–47)
For one with few resources, the fruit is small; for one who is vast [in means], the fruit is great.
When a vow is undertaken with devotion, the fruit attained is liberation.
Having observed the vow for a year, the practitioner of the vow should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having bathed in the morning and put on clean garments, and having applied an auspicious *puṇḍra* mark upon his forehead,
he should have a beautiful, spacious, and square pavilion constructed,
provided with bells, chowries, water-pots, mirrors, and small tinkling bells.
Adorned with flowers, garlands, banners, arches, canopies, and cloths,
and provided with rows of lamps at its four doors and soft carpets;
in its center, one should fashion a *sarvatobhadra* diagram, decorated with grains and other offerings.
Upon that, one should place twelve jars filled with water,
covered with white cloths and endowed with the five jewels.
Therein, one should establish [the image] made of gold, silver, or copper.
One should place the image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa upon a vessel filled with sesame seeds atop a water-pot;
then, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), one should commence the constituent parts of the worship.
One should bathe the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and offer ornaments and garments.
One should offer fragrant sandalwood and the like, as well as incense and lamps. One should present offerings of fragrant liquids, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and provide a meal.
One should offer a drink and betel leaf, put [the image] to rest, and ask for forgiveness.
One should keep a vigil at night and perform the morning fire-oblation (homa).

One should carry out the worship, the feeding, the ritual dismissal (vaisarjana), and the offering to the deity. The observer of the vow should himself perform the breaking of the fast and thus complete the vow.
One should present the image, together with the sacrificial fee, to the preceptor.
(58) Thus, the performer of the concluding rite and the observer of the vow becomes an enjoyer of worldly pleasures;
accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (59)
"O Lakṣmī! Whoever hears this narrative of the vow or recites it, having obtained the fruit of all vows, shall in the end go to the abode of Hari.

Thus ends [the section on] the annual miscellaneous vows, including the swing-vow, the chariot-procession, and the swing-festival, within the first book, "The Succession of the Kṛta Yuga," of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
