Chapter 283 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow, which removes all sins, is meritorious, and utterly destroys all suffering. It is for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise for women.
It bestows the fruits of all desires and grants the rewards of all vows.
It destroys evil dreams, is consistent with dharma, and wards off malevolent planets;
by its performance, even a mountainous heap of ten million sins is pacified.
Having bathed on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa during the Brāhma-muhūrta,
wearing clean clothes, seated on a pure seat, having sipped water (ācamana) and restrained his speech,
he should constantly remember Nārāyaṇa and then perform the worship of the deity.
Having determined the place, time, and other details, one should invoke the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa,
worship Him, and perform the offering of the seat and other requisites.
Having bathed Him with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances, one should present the erotic offering (śṛṅgāra).
With perfumes, sandalwood, flowers, and the like; with garlands, incense, and lamps; with erotic delights, foods, drinks, fruits, betel, and songs;
with dances, hymns of praise, acts of devotion, and likewise with requests for forgiveness.
Having gratified him in front of that [deity] upon a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should duly establish a fire measuring one cubit (aratni).
Having performed the rites up to the portioning of the clarified butter (ājyabhāga) according to the Puruṣasūkta, || 8-9 ||
One should offer oblations to Varuṇa with sesame seeds, flowers, ghee, fruits, juices,
and other sacrificial foods according to one's capacity.
For the destruction of sin, one should perform penance such as purification and the like.
Having completed the *homa*, one should then recite the *Śāntisūkta* once more.
One should worship Śrī Hari and pray for the fulfillment of the vow.
Remaining without food on the full moon day, one should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) on the following day.
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform [the rite]," he should then offer the arghya water to the Moon:
"O Maker of Night, accept this arghya, accompanied by white flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings.
Salutations to you, the possessor of white rays; salutations again and again to the brother of Lakṣmī."
One should keep a vigil during the night with storytelling, chanting, and dancing.
In the morning, one should worship Kṛṣṇa and feed virtuous brāhmaṇas. One should give gifts and sacrificial fees, and a chaste woman should feed the children. (14–15)
The observer of the vow should indeed break his fast together with his servants and others.
Having performed this for a year, on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika,
he should perform the great concluding rite (udyāpana) and have an auspicious pavilion constructed.

In the Sarvatobhadra mandala, within a jar adorned with jeweled petals, and in a vessel of sesame seeds, one should worship the Lord Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. One should perform the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and offer ablutions with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances. || 17-18 ||
One should offer worship with perfumes, ornaments, garments, garlands, incense, lamps, and so forth;
as well as food offerings consisting of various kinds of eatables and drinks, sweet and cool water, betel leaf,
and the offering of fruits and other such items.

Having performed the vigil with dancing, singing, and so forth, as well as the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanā*) and other rites, one should put Kṛṣṇa to sleep; then, in the morning, one should worship him again.
One should give the image to the preceptor (*ācārya*) as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and feed the twice-born.
One should perform oblations in the fire with sesame seeds and other materials, offer gifts,
feed virtuous men and women, and practice the offering of sesame seeds and so forth.
Having thus properly performed the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow, the observer of the vow—
Having enjoyed happiness here together with his sons, grandsons, and family, he partakes of various pleasures and, at the end, goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
By beholding Śrī Hari, he attains everything that is difficult even for yogis to obtain. (23–24)

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall now describe to you the vow of raising the flag (dhvajāropa-vrata), which bestows a kingdom, grants victory, and is the supreme means for pleasing Lord Viṣṇu—whether performed in the temple of the Lord Śrī Hari himself or in the temple of one of his manifestations. ॥241॥
He who performs the gift of a banner shall become worthy of worship by the inhabitants of heaven;
he shall obtain the fruit born of giving a thousand bhāras of gold,
merit equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā, and a reward equal to the worship of Śiva.
The merit arising from the hoisting of the flag shall be equal to the merit of worshipping Tulasī.
Oh, how unprecedented! Oh, how unprecedented! Oh, how unprecedented is this vow!
The hoisting of the flag removes all sins and bestows all merit.
In the month of Kārtika or any other month, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight,
having bathed and performed his regular worship, the observer of the vow should eat but one meal.
He should sleep on the ground at night, remember Nārāyaṇa, and again [remember Him] at dawn.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite on the eleventh day and meditated upon Hari,
one should then perform the worship of Śrī Viṣṇu, including the offering of food and other articles. Then, one should request four Brahmins to recite the benediction (svastivācana).
One should perform the Nāndī-śrāddha and bring forth the two flagstaffs (dhvaja-stambhau).
Having adorned those two with cloths, one should sprinkle them with water while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
[One should likewise worship] the Sun, the Moon, Vidhātṛ, Dhātṛ, and Garuḍa.
One should worship the two flagstaffs with white flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth,

as well as with the fragrances of saffron and sandalwood, turmeric, sugar, and other such substances. Then, having smeared a sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) the size of a cow-hide, [one should proceed].
Having established the fire according to the Vedic mantras, he should likewise offer the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) and so forth;
he should then offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and grain with clarified butter one hundred and eight times,
using both the Puruṣasūkta and the names of Viṣṇu.
Having recited the *irāvatī* section, the observer of the vow should offer oblations;
then again, eight oblations with the mantra "To Vainateya, svāhā";
and thereafter, he should again offer oblations with the hymns "somo dhenuṃ" and "ud u tyaṃ".
Then, from the solar mantra, one should recite the *Śānti-sūktas*.
Having observed the waterless vow (*nirjala-vrata*), one should perform a vigil at night.
On the twelfth day, having risen in the morning and bathed, one should again worship Hari.
Accompanied by auspicious musical instruments, songs, and the like, as well as the recitation of hymns and praises,
one should carry the banner to the abode of Hari and offer salutations once again.
Or, it may be fixed upon the gateway of the temple or atop its pinnacle, joined with a pillar.
One should properly erect the banner and firmly perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
There, one should cast a coconut fruit as a pleasing essence;
then, one should offer it to all and subsequently adorn Viṣṇu.
One should worship Lord Hari with perfumes, flowers, consecrated rice, incense, lamps, fragrant substances, and pleasing offerings of various kinds of food, both solid and soft. Then,
having performed a circumambulation, the observer of the vow should ask the Lord for forgiveness.
O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, wherever the shadow of your banner or the peak of it falls, there and there alone shall the destruction of suffering, poverty, and all faults always occur. (44–45)
May your expansion of sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as your abundance of wealth, grain, and other riches, along with health, vigor, prosperity, and the like, increase further and further.
Your banner stands supreme above all; act likewise toward me as well.
Consciousness is the tail of the banner, while the banner itself consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
The tip of the bamboo is the abode of Brahman, and the bamboo is the path of the rays of light.
The top of the pillar is the abode of Truth, and the wooden plank is the ground of the gods.
The uvula is the wheel of the luminaries, and the pillar is Dharma established by itself;
the goals of human life are at the base of the pillar—salutations to You, the Self, who are the Pillar-Supporter.
You whom the virtuous indeed declare to be the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
"I worship daily the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is accompanied by Lakṣmī.
Having thus offered praise, one should bow to Viṣṇu, the Ācārya, the true Guru, and the twice-born;
one should worship them, feed them, give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
As long as the cloth of the banner moves in the lotus by the wind,
so many nets of sins are destroyed for the one who has offered the banner.
Indeed, for as many days as the banner remains at the temple of the deity, [so many merits are gained].
For as many thousands of yugas as there are [flags], one attains the same form as Hari.
Those who, filled with joy, rejoice upon seeing the raised banner— their sins, even those as firm as adamantine cement, are destroyed.
A banner, by shaking its cloth, shakes away even the heaps of sins of those who offer it;
the one who installs a banner goes to the highest heaven by means of a celestial chariot.
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, there was a man named Sumati born of the lunar dynasty.
King Irīkathāraka and Queen Satyamati were likewise devoted to Hari;
both husband and wife were constantly intent upon the worship of Hari,
remembering their past lives, and bestowing water and food, they performed acts of righteousness.
On every twelfth day of the twelfth month, the king hoisted his banner;
hearing of his fame, the gods sang it, and Vibhāṇḍaka went there.
Having offered hospitality to the sage, the king spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O Blessed One, I have indeed accomplished my purpose through your arrival.
The arrival of the virtuous serves to bring all happiness to householders.
Where there is supreme love for the virtuous, there all prosperity shall abide. (1.282.60)
Splendor, fame, wealth, grain, sons, and prosperity increase,
and auspicious things come daily to that place where the grace of the virtuous truly resides.
He who, with devotion, bears upon his head the water and the dust from the feet of the Great One—
He has bathed in all sacred fords and in the final purificatory rites of sacrifices.
My wife, my sons, and my prosperity have been entrusted to you.
Command me quickly; what very dear service may I perform for you?

Having heard this and touched the head of the king with his hand, Vibhāṇḍaka, being pleased, then said: "O King, all that you have spoken is worthy of your lineage; may you attain many blessings. (64)
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—this is the fourfold aim.
By serving the great, a living being attains eternal happiness.
May you always be well; tell me that which I ask.
There are indeed many kinds of worship that grant satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa;
among them, you consider the hoisting of the flag to be preeminent—how is it that you perform this?
Tell me, how is it that even your wife is always intent on dancing there?
Having heard that, the king spoke of his own wondrous former life:
"In the past, I was a Śūdra named Mālinī, indeed a sinner; I was merciless and a perpetrator of drinking, meat-eating, adultery, theft, and other such acts. (68–69)
Having committed a murder and abandoned my subjects and kinsmen,
I went to the forest and took refuge in a dilapidated temple of Viṣṇu.
Subsisting constantly on fruits and roots, I remained there for twenty years.
I repaired everything that was worn out or broken for him.
That ground was well-prepared and smeared by me for his residence;
trees were planted there and watered with the waters of the lake.
Having made a pact, I took up worn-out clothes and raised a banner;
with the insertion of stakes and shafts, the wall of Viṣṇu was well protected.
This Niṣāda woman, Kokilā by name, was threatened by her kinsmen.
By the turn of fate, the daughter of Dāruka arrived from the Vindhya mountains.
This unchaste woman was obtained by me and protected as my wife; performing service to the gods, we two have entered into the state of husband and wife. (74–75)
While staying there for ten years, once during the night,
intoxicated by drinking liquor and delighted by eating meat, we two—
unaware of each other's thin clothing and deluded— performed a dance.
"We two remained together until the end of the experience of our prārabdha karma.
Then, the terrifying messengers of Yama arrived to take us away.
At that time, Viṣṇu, who was situated in his divine abode, considered them to be his own servants. (77–78)
He dispatched his own messengers bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
They said, "O wicked Yama-messengers, release the two Archanas!
They are my devotees, truly devoted to me, and have taken refuge in me while living in the forest. (79)
Having heard this, the messengers of Yama then said: "These two others are indeed sinners;
since sinners are to be punished by Yama, we shall take these two away.
Having heard them, the Vaiṣṇavas spoke to those who were intent on seizing the sinners.
"Released from sin and devoted to the service of Hari, let these two,
who are being protected by Hari, be set free without delay.
This woman has performed a dance, and likewise this man has performed the hoisting of the banner."
The two [names] of Hari—Saudha and Avana—serve their own purpose and the purpose of others respectively.
Even at the time of death, by hearing or uttering His name even once, one attains liberation and heaven; how much more so for one devoted to serving Him? (83-84)
Even a sinner who serves Kṛṣṇa and serves the ascetics attains the state of a Vaiṣṇava.
He who stays in the temple of Hari for even a moment or half a moment goes to the world of Brahmā; how much more so one who remains for thirty-two years?
They perform sweeping and smearing, and they repair what is worn out or broken;
in the temple, they provide lamps, water, and the shade of trees.
How is it that these two, who possess such great merit, are now joined with the experience of torment? (86–87)
Having spoken thus, they forcibly cast off the nooses of Yama and,
taking us both onto an excellent celestial chariot, went happily to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed divine and great pleasures there, they returned to this earth.
"Even here, this kingdom with its royal banner has been obtained through the grace of service.
Even though it was performed without desire, the great fruit of sovereignty has been attained.
Remembering that, I offer this dance to Ketu."
"By worshipping Govinda even with mere desire, we shall attain the supreme goal;
if such is the result even when one is helpless, how much more so when it is performed with faith!
Having heard this, Vibhāṇḍaka praised them both and departed for the forest.

Know this, O Kamalā: the service rendered to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is indeed considered equal to the Cintāmaṇi jewel for all. For Hari, who is devoted to those intent on devotion to Hari, grants all desires. (92–93)
Whoever hears or likewise recites this sacred narrative,
and the speaker who is devoted to the service of Hari— they too attain the supreme goal.

Thus ends the [section on] the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Vrata, its concluding rite (udyāpana), the raising of the flag on the temple, the smearing [of the deity], and protection, in the first book, the section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 283 [Author:
Chapter 284 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the celebrated Haripañcaka, a vow that bestows happiness upon both women and men, the most excellent of all vows. On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, having bathed, one should perform the worship of the deity.
Even after performing the five sacrifices, one should spend the day eating but once.
On the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), having bathed at dawn and likewise bathed Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) as well as with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha),
one should worship Him with fragrant liquids and other offerings.
Having performed the worship consisting of rites beginning with the invocation and ending with the dismissal,
accompanied by incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, betel, and priestly fees,
the observer of the vow should pray to Śrī Hari before him.
"O Mādhava, from this day forward, I shall remain without food for five nights.
I will perform the vow known as the *Haripañca*, and may it be completed for me.
On the tenth day, one should indeed eat only once and sleep upon the ground at night."
On the eleventh day, one should perform worship at the three periods of the day, offer the three-fold oblation, and keep a vigil at night with songs, dances, and sacred narratives.
On the twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth days, one should likewise perform this triad of rites.
On the full moon day as well, one should perform bathing, worship, and the offering of food (naivedya).
(8) On the night of the full moon, the observer of the vow should likewise keep a vigil;
however, the worship with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other offerings should be performed during the five days. (9)

On the full moon day or on the sixth lunar day, one should bathe Viṣṇu with milk; likewise, having performed an oblation of sesame seeds, a gift of sesame, and the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should feed the Brahmins and worship Hari according to the prescribed rites.
One should feed virtuous men and women and then eat together with one's kinsmen.
(11) In this manner, the auspicious vow should be observed for one year, month by month;
the concluding rite (udyāpana) should be performed in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa with great generosity. (12)
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight during this Śuklapakṣavrata, the practitioner shall remain without food;
then, on the twelfth day, he shall consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having worshipped Hari with flowers and other offerings, he should give [the remains] to a twice-born man.
One should offer milk-rice mixed with sugar, ghee, and fruits (14), accompanied by sweet foods,
vegetables, leaves, and so forth;
it should be joined with fragrant water, excellent jewels, a sacrificial fee, and garments (15).
One should offer a full water-pot to a virtuous knower of the Self;
one should give all one's possessions to the Guru and feed children, both boys and girls. One should feed virtuous men and women, and then partake of the breaking of the fast oneself.
This vow, known as the Haripañcaka, has been declared to you.
For one who performs it, there shall indeed be no return from the world of Brahmā;
he shall obtain the fruit of giving away ten million times ten thousand cows.
Whoever should read this, or hear it, or cause it to be recited, or cause it to be heard, for him too there shall be the merit of the vow, and he shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(19) Now, I shall further proclaim another vow: that of fasting for a month.
O Mahālakṣmī! There is nothing said to be equal to that which is known as Pārāka.
O beloved, in the month of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, or even Āśvina—on the first day of the bright fortnight in any one of these months— || 1.283.20–21 ||
One should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and remain in the presence of Viṣṇu.
Having bathed and meditated upon Viṣṇu at dawn, and having completed one's daily obligatory rites,
one should worship Viṣṇu and perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the month-long fast.

Then the brāhmaṇas should cause him to recite the mantras for the benediction (svastivācana). And the observer of the vow should pray to the God: "O Mādhava! From this day forward for one month, I shall remain without food; grant me my desired wish. || 23-24 ||
From that time until the end of the month, he should reside in the temple of Hari;
he should daily bathe the Lord with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and offer a lamp.
He should consume the tooth-stick of Apāmārga and bathe every day.
One should worship the Lord daily and feed children and Brahmins.
In this manner, one should observe fasts for a month for twelve years;
and every year, one should perform the gift of a cow and the satiation of Brahmins and ancestors.
One should give gifts according to one's ability, such as sacrificial fees, ornaments, and food.
By fasting for one month, the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice is attained;
by fasting for two months, that fruit becomes twofold.
In three months of fasting, the fruit shall be fourfold.
When performed four times, the merit becomes that born of eight Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
When performed five times, the merit becomes that born of an Attyagniṣṭoma sacrifice.
If performed six times, it shall yield the fruit of eight Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices;
if performed seven times, it shall yield the fruit of eight horse-sacrifices (vājimedha);
if performed eight times, it shall yield the fruit of eight human-sacrifices (naramedha).
When performed nine times, it yields the merit born of eight horse-sacrifices (gomedha).
When performed ten times, it yields the fruit of eight Brahma-sacrifices (brahmamedha).
But upon the eleventh *parāka* penance, one attains the same form as Hari.
Upon completing twelve *parāka* penances, one obtains the fourfold liberation.
Those who perform the *parāka* vow are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Whether woman or man, the performer of the vow shall attain liberation.
Or one who reads or hears this narration of the vow shall become a partaker of liberation.
(35) There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no teacher equal to one's mother;
there is no deity equal to Viṣṇu; and there is no austerity higher than fasting. (36)
There is no mother equal to forbearance; there is no wealth equal to fame;
there is no gain equal to knowledge; there is no father equal to Dharma.
There is no brother equal to discernment; there is no vow equal to Ekādaśī.
There is no vessel equal to a Brahmin; there is no beloved equal to a wife.
There is no boat equal to a virtuous person; there is no vow like that of crossing to the further shore.
O beloved, acts such as giving gifts and performing fire-offerings (homa) should be performed when an auspicious day has arrived.
The third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada,
the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, and the fifteenth lunar day (the full moon) of Māgha—
these are declared to be the beginnings of the Yugas, which cause whatever is given on them to become inexhaustible.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of [Kārttika],
the third day of the month of Caitra, likewise the third day of Bhādrapada,
the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and the seventh day of Māgha. 41–42.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the full moon of Āṣāḍha;
the new moon of Phālguna, and the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa;
the fifteenth day of the bright fortnights of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha.

Manu and others have declared that gifts given at sacred sites such as Puṣkara, at rivers such as the Gaṅgā, and in Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, and the land of Kāśī, bring about inexhaustible merit. (44–45)
In Kāñcī, Avantikā, and Dvārakā, what is given becomes inexhaustible:
when given to a guest who is a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, to virtuous men, women, and chaste wives,
and to a god or one equal to a god, such a gift produces inexhaustible merit.

Whatever is given to those practicing celibacy (brahmacārins) shall produce inexhaustible merit. (47) One observing a vow must by all means perform austerity, giving, and worship; eating and all other such acts should be performed so as to bestow inexhaustible merit. (48)

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Haripañcaka Vrata, the Month-long Fasting Vrata, its Concluding Rite (Udyāpana), the Greatness of Gifts on Lunar Days Marking the Beginning of Yugas and Manvantaras," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the vow of worshiping the planets on their respective days;
by performing which all the planets become pleased and bestow prosperity. On Sunday, the vow should be observed with eating only at night or a single meal.
Having bathed in the morning and bowed to the Sun, one should worship him with all available offerings.
(2) Having fashioned a golden image of the Sun seated upon his chariot drawn by ruddy horses, accompanied by Saṃjñā and Chāyā, and adorned with divine garlands and jewels; (3)
Having performed the invocation and other rites, [one should perform] the consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
the ritual bathing, the donning of garments and ornaments, the application of fragrant unguents,
and the offering of incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, fruits, and betel leaf.
One should perform the meditation, circumambulation, hymn of praise, prostration, and so forth, ending with the ritual dismissal (visarjana). Then, at midday and likewise at night,
one should cause all the worship to be performed, including the waving of lights (nīrājana) and the offering of food.
One should bathe the deity at night, and having bathed oneself in the morning, one should awaken [the deity].
One should worship with lotuses and flowers such as the *arka* and *karavīra*.
One should repeatedly offer water and perform the ritual of installation (*upasthāpana*).

One should meditate upon the Sun, whose body is the three Vedas, holding in his hands the gestures of generosity (*dāna*), fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a pair of lotuses, and adorned with earrings, armlets, and bracelets. One should perform oblations according to the rules in the southeast (*vasu*) using red lotuses or sesame seeds.
One should recite for the Sun one hundred and eight times with the mantra: "Svāhā to the Sun!
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! That excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ, we meditate upon; may he inspire our intellects. (1.284.10)

Thus, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the Gāyatrī mantra; likewise, one should address the Shadow (Chāyā) with the name "Svāhā. One should feed, worship, and present the arghya offering to the form of the Sun (Bhāskara).
Having restrained the breaths, sipped water, and washed his hands,
the worshipper should take up a copper vessel capable of holding one *prastha* of water.
[He should also prepare] saffron, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), turmeric, sandalwood, and red sandalwood.
One should cast karavīra, japā, rice, kuśa grass,
śyāmāka grain, sesame, bamboo, and barley into the auspicious water.
Then, kneeling upon the ground, one should hold the water-pot with both hands.
Having lifted the vessel above his head and covered it with a cloth during the formal invitation (*varaṇa*) of the Sun,
and having fixed his gaze and mind [upon him], he should offer the *arghya* water-offering in the form of an *añjali*.
Having also offered a handful of flowers, bowed down, and praised him, he should dismiss [the deity].
Or, one should daily offer this *arghya* to Vivasvat on that day as well.
Pleased by this, he bestows upon him wealth, fame, and happiness every day;
he grants sons, grandsons, and whatever else is desired—he gives everything.
This vow of the worship of the Sun increases longevity and health;
it bestows wealth, grain, cattle, security, land, friends, and a wife;
and it grants splendor, valor, fame, renown, knowledge, prosperity, and enjoyment. (19)
One should perform this supreme rite according to the prescribed method, which brings about the attainment of the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala).
One should present an image of the Sun to the preceptor along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and likewise feed the Brahmins milk-essence and excellent *supolikā* cakes.
The observer of the vow should eat himself and likewise complete the vow.
Then, on a Monday, he should perform the Moon-vow according to the prescribed rite.
Having risen in the morning and bathed, he should bring milk, flowers, and other offerings.
The observer of the vow should worship the golden Soma together with his consort,
accompanied by his twenty-seven wives;
beginning with the invocation, he should perform the worship with the sixteen types of offerings.
One should worship with white water-lilies and offer milk and sugar;
one should perform the lustration ceremony at night on the full moon day when the moon is visible,
[visualizing] his face radiant, crystal-like in hue, with dark curls and earrings.
One should meditate upon the Moon as holding his beloved white water-lily and a garland of pearls.
One should address the offering with the mantra: "Svāhā to Candra, to Rohiṇī, and to the constellations.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter.
One should place a silver vessel and fill it with fragrant milk;
one should offer this *arghya* to the Moon for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
One should thus offer the *arghya* and perform worship daily, or at least on that specific day.
The Moon, the lord of night-lotuses, being pleased, shall grant the food of medicinal herbs.
He indeed bestows wealth, grain, daughters, sons, and good fortune.
One should observe the vow of eating but once a day and offer an image to the preceptor.
One should feed milk and *pūrikā* cakes to children and virtuous people;
however, having oneself completed the vow, one should then partake of the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*).
Now, the vow of Maṅgaladeva must be observed by one who desires happiness.
One should perform this on a single meal for the sake of accomplishing all undertakings.
Having bathed in the morning on the day of the Son of the Earth (Mars), one should meditate upon Maṅgala,
situated in Aries, with limbs clad in red garments, holding a trident, a spear, and a mace in his hands.
One should meditate upon the Lord holding the son of the Earth (Mars), who is marked by perspiration, with his hands.
The commencement of the vow for Mars should take place on a Tuesday during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa or Vaiśākha;
one should observe the vow of Mars at the time of dawn.
Desiring sons, desiring wealth, or desiring prosperity, one should observe the vow.
Having risen, she should run while restraining her speech, using *apāmārga* [broom plant] to brush her teeth.
Then, having bathed, wearing red garments, and adorned with red garlands and unguents, [she should proceed]. (35–36)
One should prepare all the offerings, such as the food oblation (*naivedya*), in red.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and having proclaimed the place and time,
the woman seeking the vow should worship with the sixteen and other services, and then present the water of honor (*arghya*).
Having offered incense and a lamp, one should then present an offering of wheat-based food.
Into a copper vessel filled with pure water,
having cast red sandalwood, red flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and fruits, one should offer the arghya.
"O Son of the Earth, I have sought refuge in you for the sake of a daughter; accept my offering of water (arghya).
O Son of the Earth, grant me a son; accept this arghya; salutations be unto you!
Then, indeed, he drew three lines upon the ground with charcoal from khadira wood.
One should perform this and sweep with the left foot, saying then:
"For the destruction of suffering and misfortune, and for the sake of the continuity of progeny, I sweep away the three lines drawn with my left foot. (41–42)
For the destruction of the suffering of debt and for the accomplishment of one’s heart’s desires,
I wipe away the three black lines produced from the three births.
Having meditated upon Maṅgala with a handful of flowers in hand, one should praise him.
Salutations to you, the remover of debt; may you grant us constant good fortune.
To him who, having entered a retrograde course, bestows suffering upon men—salutations to you, who, when worshipped, becomes the giver of happiness and good fortune. 44–45.
"O Rudra-souled one, whose vehicle is the ram, grant me sons, wealth, and fame.
Having thus praised, bowed, and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should offer flowers.
Having given according to one's capacity, one should accept the blessings of the Brahmins.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and eat what has been offered to him.
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] every Tuesday for the duration of a year.
One should also perform a fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds, saying: "Svāhā to Maṅgala, the embodiment of auspiciousness."
Having worshipped an image of Bhauma made of gold, placed within a jar situated upon a mandala, one should recite the mantra for the attainment of sons and good fortune:
*Oṃ aṅgārakāya vidmahe śaktihastāya dhīmahi.*
One should recite "tanno bhaumaḥ pracodayāt" one hundred and eight times.
Having performed this recitation and worship again, one should offer milk and other foods;
one should present sugar, very sweet food, and wheat-based meals.
One should offer water for drinking, betel-leaf, and a handful of flowers;
then, according to the prescribed rite, one should dismiss him again into the sky at night.
Having bowed, meditated, and offered water, one should present unbroken grains (akṣata) and flowers.

Having prayed for the fulfillment of the vow and its fruit, one should eat, sleep, and remember the planet [Mars]. (53) Thus, whether it be a woman seeking a vow or a practitioner of the vow, through the propitiation of Mars, she obtains children, grain, and so forth, as well as supreme happiness free from obstacles. (54)
Then, on a Wednesday, one should perform the Budha-vrata with a concentrated mind.
Having bathed, one should worship a golden image according to the prescribed sequence,
beginning from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the final offering of handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali).

Having visualized the son of the Moon (Budha) wearing yellow garments, with his right hand in the gesture of fearlessness and his left hand resting upon his knee, one should offer the *arghya* water, saying:
"O Budha, son of the Moon, possessor of great wisdom, remove my suffering and grant me happiness. (56–57)
Then one should offer oblations into the fire with the mantra "svāhā" for Budha one hundred and eight times.
Having worshipped him and fed him, and having requested his forgiveness, one should join the palms in *añjali*.
Having honored him with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should then dismiss him.
The observer of the vow should feed the Brahmins while gazing at the planet Mercury in the sky at night.
Having offered the *arghya* with lotus flowers, he should conclude the vow.
He should feed virtuous men and women and eat himself with due respect. (1.284.60)
In this way, all afflictions caused by the planets are averted for one who performs the vow;
there shall be an increase in sons, cattle, wealth, health, and prosperity.
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the vow of Guru when Guru is [in its period].
Having bathed, the observer of the vow should worship an image of the Guru made of gold.
Beginning with the invocation and continuing with the sixteen auspicious articles,
up until the final offering of handfuls of flowers, he should worship Bṛhaspati.

One should meditate on him with his left hand resting upon a heap of jewels and his right hand scattering all kinds of gems; he possesses a golden luster and a beautiful countenance, and is worshipped with yellow flowers, ornaments, ointments, garments, and other offerings. (64)
One should meditate upon the preceptor of the gods, the treasury of all knowledge and the bringer of peace.
One should feed him milk-rice (*pāyasa*), bow down, and likewise ask for forgiveness.
Then, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra: *svāhā bṛhaspataye*. (65–66)
One should offer oblations with clarified butter, cooked grain, rice-porridge, the essence of milk, sugar-cane juice, and so forth.
In cases of suffering from poison, disease, and the like, or during quarrels arising among one's own kinsmen,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with fuel-sticks made of *pippala* wood for their cessation.
One should also perform oblations for three days with night-blooming flowers soaked in ghee;
thus, the pacification of calamities will swiftly occur.
Furthermore, one should worship and bow at night, and one should practice the visualization of that [deity] in the sky.
Having bowed, the observer of the vow should offer the *arghya* water and pray to the Vidyā;
then he should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*), offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
He should then give a gift to the venerable Guru, including the image and a meal.
Having performed the vow in this manner, one should eat afterwards; thus one shall become happy.
(7.1) Now, on a Friday, one should perform the Śukra-vow according to the prescribed rite.
Having bathed, one should meditate upon the planet Venus, made of gold, clothed in white garments. (7.2)

The observer of the vow should meditate upon [the deity] adorned with white ointments, bestowing wealth with his right hand, and displaying the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyānamudrā*) with his left. Beginning from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up until the final handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should perform the worship.
One should feed [the Brahmins], worship them, ask for their forgiveness, and thereafter bow down to them.
On a Saturday, one should offer oblations with fragrant white flowers;
one should perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings with clarified butter and other substances.
One should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony and offer auspicious water as an *arghya* to the Guru.
At night, one should gaze upon the sky, and having bowed and offered praise, one should bid him farewell.
One should give a gift to the venerable Guru and thus conclude his vow.
The performer of the vow obtains jewels, gems, and the like, and shall become happy.
During the vow, one should practice eating once a day, or eating at night, or fasting, or, according to one's ability, subsisting on water or fruit. (77–78)
Then, on a Saturday, one should observe the vow of Śani.
Having bathed in the morning and bowed to Hari and Hanumān with devotion,
one should prostrate before the image of Śani and worship it made of iron.
The observer of the vow should offer seven black beans during the worship.
Beginning from the invocation and ending with the handful of flowers,
he should perform everything with devotion and offer black flowers and excellent collyrium.
One should offer black garments and ornaments, present black food,
and perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with black sesame seeds and other materials, saying "Svāhā to Śanaiścara.
One should perform one hundred and eight repetitions and recite the mantra according to one's ability.
One should meditate upon him with sword in hand, wearing a black upper garment,
seated upon a chariot, having the color of iron, with a cruel gaze and a fierce face;
beholding him as he moves in a crooked course, one should bow and offer water for the guest-offering (arghya).
Accompanied by black flowers and black beans, grant peace!
Cast a favorable glance, increase valor, prosperity, and happiness!
O Sun, do not bring about what is undesirable; O son of Saṃjñā, salutations be unto you!
"O brother of Yama, accept this kṛśara-rice, water, and so forth.

Having performed his worship in this manner, one should cause gifts to be given to Kṛṣṇa; one should also perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), offer food, and dismiss him according to the prescribed rite.
The observer of the vow should generally eat only once a day, or practice eating only at night; then,
on the morning of the second day, having worshipped Śani with the heart-mantra,
he should feed children, girls, and Brahmins, and perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
By performing this for one year, one shall conquer the miseries of Saturn.
One shall obtain an abundance of happiness and attain a bliss equal to that of heaven.
Thus have the vows been proclaimed; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Complete Rituals for the Vows of the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 284.
← Chapter 284: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 285 [[Author: → Chapter 286
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Svāmin, O Ātha, O Mādhava, O Keśava!
O Lord of Pārvatī and Prabhā, O Master of Lakṣmī and Māṇikī! || 1 ||

"O Lord of the Earth, O Lord of Nectar, O Hari! Tell me the reason why, in the observance of a vow, the pure eleventh day (Ekādaśī) alone is to be accepted and never one that is pierced (by the tenth day). Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall relate a story concerning Brahmā.
On the day of Viddha-ekādaśī, the enchanting daughter of Brahmā remains present at dawn;
she is the destroyer of merit, and therefore she must not be accepted for the vow.
Free from the overlap of the tenth lunar day, it is considered that the fast should always be observed during this vow.
It bestows heaven and liberation; it grants land, sovereignty, and sons;
it gives a wife, wealth, food, a pleasant heart, a healthy body, and well-being. (4–5)

Whether at the time of waning or waxing, or when the dawn has arrived, one should observe the meritorious Dvādaśī; one should avoid it if it is overlapped by the previous day. A man who observes the Dvādaśī overlapped by the previous day cuts away his own merit.

For the destruction of one's lineage and the seizure of one's prosperity, that lunar day was formerly given to the Dānavas; for merit performed on a lunar day joined with the previous [tithi] goes instead to the Asuras. (7–8)
Whatever is given, chanted, offered in sacrifice, bathed in, practiced, or offered as worship to Hari on a *viddha* lunar day goes to ruin, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
(9) There was once a king named Rukmāṅgada, a sovereign ruler of the whole earth, in the land of Surāṣṭra.
Established in the dharma of the great Vaiṣṇavas and devoted to the day of Hari,
that dull-witted man who, having mounted an elephant, beats a drum on the day of Hari, eats today on the day of Viṣṇu. (1.285.10–11)
Whether it be my father, brother, son, wife, or friend, whoever eats on the day of Śrī Hari shall be punished by me— either with a fine, death, or banishment from the city—
and shall be restrained like a thief. (12)
"Give gifts to the Sātvatas and immerse yourselves in the waters of the sacred fords (tīrtha).
Having followed these words of mine, let them remain within my kingdom. Having agreed upon this proclamation, the subjects took refuge in Keśava.
The path to the abode of Śrī Hari was crowded with people traveling there;
indeed, whoever died within his kingdom went to the palace of Hari. At that time, no men from the earth traveled the path of Yama.
The hells became empty, devoid of sinful living beings.
The path to Yama was broken, scorched by the heat of twelve suns.
Indeed, all people, mounted upon Garuḍa, went to the abode of Hari. (16–17)
Then Citragupta also ceased from his work of recording deeds;
indeed, by the grace of Mānava, even men, having shaken off their past karmas,
proceed to the abode of Viṣṇu, while the wooden sandals (carpaṭas) have become useless.
Even the abodes of the gods, such as heaven and the rest, were then empty; for they had become void.
When the celestial realm had become empty and the underworld likewise, Nārada approached Dharmarāja and spoke these words.
How is it that this field of Yama is empty and people do not come here?
Even Citragupta has desisted; he no longer writes down their deeds.
Though they were overcome by illusion and pride, and devoted to evil actions— 21.
"Why do they not come here? Tell me the reason for this.
(22) Yama, filled with dejection, replied: "On earth there is a king named Rukmāṅgada;
he is currently a sovereign ruler and is devoted to Puruṣottama. (23)
One should not eat on the day of Hari;
those mortals who do eat are certainly considered by Me to be deserving of punishment.
Indeed, out of fear of that, all subjects observe the day of Hari.
Even those who fast merely under a pretext go indeed to the world of Viṣṇu.
By that king, through his devotion to Hari, the hells were made empty;
the heavens were also made empty, and the scribes were rendered inactive.
Whatever has been committed or written down [in the form of sin] is wiped away by fasting on the Ekādaśī;
indeed, former sins perish by not eating on the day of Hari.
I have become like a wooden deer, my actions rendered fruitless.
Today I have renounced desire for this inactive office of world-protector.
Indeed, I shall go to the world of Brahmā to inform him of my own suffering.
A functionary who performs no work receives his salary, yet it does not decay.

"Whether he be a human or even Yama himself, such a person goes to a terrible hell. Having spoken thus, O Mahālakṣmī, King Yama himself, along with Citragupta and Nīrava, departed for the abode of Brahmā.
And he beheld him seated, surrounded by beings both embodied and disembodied (31),
being worshipped by various guardians of the world and lords of the quarters,
as well as by the Vedas, scriptures, histories, and the like, along with lakes, rivers, and oceans (32).
[He is perceived] through trees, creepers, grasses, and crops; through forests, wildernesses, and hosts of winds;
through fields, mountains, and plateaus; and through sages, celestial seers, and ancestors;
as well as through the divisions of time such as kalās, days, nights, years, yugas, kalpas, and dissolutions.
Indeed, the Unborn (Aja) is worshipped through pleasure and pain, gain and loss, virtues witnessed by the Nagas,
and other such qualities— both real and unreal, and even those not explicitly mentioned. Among them, the son of the Sun entered [the assembly] with his inner heart broken.
Looking toward the lower part [of his body], he revealed the loss that had occurred.
O Brahmin, he fell down before him, crying out, "Save me! Save me!
He said, "I have turned back, rendered useless; what shall I do with this assignment?"
"I am not worthy of a salary; take this royal robe for yourself.
Having said this, he cast the royal robe before Vidhi.
Citragupta also cast his pen before Vidhi.
The Grandfather consoled the withered Yama;
indeed, he seated him, who was overwhelmed and broken-hearted, upon his throne.
And he asked him slowly: "By whom have you been overcome and driven away?"
"By whom has your divine banner been wiped away, and by whom have you been insulted?
Speak everything in its entirety; tell us the sorrow residing in your heart.
All these people are reflecting upon it—[the sorrow] of him who causes the worlds to weep."
"Why is this son of the Sun dejected in countenance, as if defeated by someone?
Or rather, this proverb is true: 'From an enemy indeed comes fear.
Then, having heard this, Yama said: 'Listen, O Grandfather of old.'"

He who, having been engaged for work, accepts his wages without performing the task, falls into a blind well; so too does he who lives by unjust means. A laborer who, driven by greed, does not carry out his assigned duty [falls likewise].
He who consumes the wealth of his master shall become a wood-worm;
thereafter, he goes to hell for as long as three hundred kalpas.
But he who, intent solely on his own interest, robs his master—
He shall indeed become a rat in village pits for three hundred kalpas.
An official who, having become free from desire, does not perform his master’s work but consumes his master’s wealth,
will turn into a cat in the house.
"Thus, having been appointed by you to govern those who deserve punishment and those who do not—
to join the doer of merit with merit and the doer of evil with evil—
I have today [been sent] there by King Rukmāṅgada."
"I have been defeated in my office and have now been rendered inactive.
Out of fear of Rukmāṅgada, the earth—with its seven islands and the oceans—does not enjoy the day of Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins. (1.285.50)
Even those who are sinful, devoid of virtuous deeds, and destitute of all merit,
indeed go to the abode of Viṣṇu by fasting on the day of Hari.
And even those who have arrived in the city of Yama do so through the merit of their ancestors.

Having abandoned the city of Yama and placed their feet upon my head, they go indeed to the world of Viṣṇu; my sacred field shall thus become empty. By the merit of this vow, a hundred generations of ancestors [shall be liberated]. (52–53)
A hundred maternal grandfathers, a hundred people who are the fathers of one's wives,
a hundred sisters' sons, and a hundred people who are the wives of one's brothers;
a hundred paternal nephews, and a hundred people who are the sisters of one's mother.
And one by one, they each go to the state of liberation of Hari.
This is my supreme sorrow: that after having erased my own record, others go to the highest station through the merit performed by another. (55–56)
"By the greatness of the merit of a single person, those of other lineages attain the supreme state after cutting through my snare; because of that, there is pain in my head.
O Lord, I have no need for such a command."
By fasting on the Ekādaśī day, a single person causes seven generations of his lineage to depart for the abode of Śrī Hari, leaving behind my own world;
this is not achieved by sacrifices, nor by pilgrimages, nor by vows, nor even by recitations. ||58-59||
One does not attain such a state through drowning, fire,
or leaping from a precipice as one attains through the vow of a single day of Hari.
Having become thus hopeless today, I have taken refuge at the lotus-feet of Your Lordship.
"I have come to make a request: do here as you desire.
O Grandfather, act in such a way that Yamakṣetra, Yamamārga, and Yamaśāsana shall not be destroyed, just as they were before. (61–62)
Nowhere has such a thing been seen or heard that is devoid of logic:
whether established in their own duties or engaged in improper acts, whether pure or impure,
they all go to the abode of Viṣṇu after fasting for a day by the king's command.
He is indeed our great enemy and must be captured without a doubt.
For a thousand years he has ruled the circle of the earth;
by his power, most wicked people have been led to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Having mounted upon Garuḍa and assumed a four-armed form,
O Grandfather, he leads the immeasurable world day and night;
if he were to remain for a long time, he would lead everyone to immortality.
This indeed is the supreme punishment; this has been unleashed by your two feet.
By this, our status as guardians of the world has truly been rendered futile.
Blessed is that mother who bore him in her womb—he who effects liberation.
Of what use is a son born who only causes distress to his mother,
by whom neither satisfaction, nor contentment, nor service, nor the destruction of enemies is achieved,
and by whom the lineage of ancestors is not uplifted through either learning or power? (69)
He whose fame does not resound among people, even among those who are knowledgeable, is a man of vain labor;
his mother, who protected the bed of her womb, is likewise in vain.
He is a birth of no purpose, a eunuch, like a disease of the mother's belly.

A son who becomes an adversary to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation is better than that; for in the case of such a son, the suffering merely comes to an end [with his birth]. He who would be a destroyer of dharma in this world—his life is in vain.
But now, the mother of heroes, by whom King Rukmāṅgada—the devotee of Śrī Hari—has been begotten for the very purpose of wiping away the dust from the feet of Malla;
such supreme worship has never before been performed by anyone. (73–74)
"How shall I live while constantly hearing that drum which destroys my path, making me a partaker in the sin of receiving wages in vain?
Having thus complained, he ceased, being exceedingly dejected in spirit.
Then, O Lakṣmī, Brahmā, who brings an end to sorrow, spoke slowly to Sauri:
"What is so wonderful about that for you? Or why are you distressed?
O Lord of Yama, how has this anguish arisen in you regarding virtuous qualities? (76–77)
If people attain the state of liberation with certainty merely by uttering His name,
how could they not reach the supreme state by performing that very vow?
Here, let even a single prostration be offered to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The fruit [of other rites] yields the merit of ten horse-sacrifices, yet that fruit is subject to decay;
it bestows rebirth, whereas a prostration by a person brings about their end. What need has such a person for Kāśī, Gayā, or Kurukṣetra? (1.285.80)
He on whose tongue-tip reside the two syllables "Ha-ri," even if he approaches a menstruating woman or a Cāṇḍālī woman, eats that which is mixed with liquor,
commits great theft for a month, or acts likewise— he indeed partakes in liberation.
Having shaken off the accumulation of sins, one surely goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Since liberation results from the mere utterance of his name, what need is there to mention fasting for him?
Wherever Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is glorified or meditated upon, [there one attains liberation]. 82–83.
Whether out of ignorance, for sport, or even in jest, one who speaks of Hari,
hears of Him, remembers Him, or even laughs at Him, attains the supreme goal.
How then can there be any need for your instruction regarding His devoted followers and those who observe vows?

That you were not ground to powder but were instead bound by his attendants, O Lord, is indeed a supreme honor for us; yet you do not realize it. For the status of a royal servant must be understood through diligent effort. (85–86)
Those who are objects of the king’s favor are certainly not to be appointed here even if they have committed offenses; otherwise, the official is punished.
In this way, even sinners, when they take refuge in service to a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, [are protected].
They go to the abode of Hari; do not issue a command there.
O Yama, I shall fill your house with those devoted to others who are full of faults;
I will never provide assistance to you by means of those devoted to Hari.

There is no subduing of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; indeed, if they should commit an insult against you, I shall not be your helper. O son of the Sun, if I were to provide assistance to you even in this matter, [it would be so].
My staff shall be the end of my body, and there shall be a fall from the station of Brahmā.
What then can be said of you here? Therefore, O sir, observe silence.
Let them go to the abode of Hari; do not obstruct them from the realm of Yama.
"Let your birth from the Sun be fulfilled; the realm of Yama has been emptied by the power of Hari.
Do not grieve over this matter; in due time, what is desired shall come to pass.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Yama’s Grieved Report to Brahmā Regarding the Emptiness of Yamapura through the Power of the Ekādaśī Vow," within the narrative of King Mahābhāgavata Rukmāṅgada concerning the failure to observe the Ekādaśī vow overlapping with the tenth lunar day (*daśamī-viddhā*) in the first section, *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then Dharmarāja spoke to the Grandfather (Brahmā):
"Aha! What a marvel it is, if the King is indeed the bestower of liberation! || 1 ||
Then all the gods would be rendered powerless and their command would be meaningless;
there would not be even the slightest difference between Rukmāṅgada and Hari in that regard.
He is the controller of the city of Yama, the city of the gods, and the city of Brahmā.
The son of the Earth shall be Rukmāṅgada, for he is indeed Hari himself.
Having fed and worshipped that one alone on the day of Hari, I shall have fulfilled my purpose; O Creator, accept [this] from me.
Even if Hari has been remembered, fasted for, or praised by men from the very beginning of time, they are outsiders to me by my decree.
Such a dual nature of ritual conduct is not pleasing to me.
"Appoint another who can endure the state of having his pride shattered.
Having said this, Yama, the lord of the dead, abandoned the cloth and remained silent.
Then Brahmā, in that assembly, reflected upon who should take up the cloth.
Rising up there again and again, he made it public:
"Whoever wishes to take the silk cloth, I shall grant them the kingdom of Yama!
Thus he declared, bound by his vow that the command of King Rukmāṅgada must not be transgressed.
"Let them accept this seat; I give you this empty cloth.
(9) When, even after hearing [the teaching], no one attained his own instruction, he remained in a state dependent on others, intent on serving the teachings of another. (1.286.10)
But then Nārada desired to speak to that Grandfather:
"What god would accept a position of sovereignty dependent upon a mortal?
Therefore, O Grandfather, consider another path in this matter."

"By this [means], the path to Yama shall indeed be blocked, and likewise, the path to heaven shall not be obstructed; act accordingly. Having heard these words of Nārada, which were indeed pregnant with great meaning, [he did so].
For the sake of Vaivasvata’s task and with the desire to honor him,
the Creator of the Universe reflected upon that which would create an obstacle to liberation;
he then brought forth from himself a woman who deludes the world.
The goddess, the most excellent of all women, shone forth, created by the mind.
This Brāhmī, of divine form and adorned with celestial ornaments, was seen by all, their minds struck with wonder, as she had reached the bloom of youth. (15–16)
Then all those present in the assembly, born of Brahmā’s creation, were deluded;
for delusion obstructs liberation, and Mohinī destroys liberation.
Seeing this, the Unborn One (Aja) spoke as that curiosity arose perfectly.
With a mind full of passion here, and with eyes full of passion, one might even think of or gaze upon one’s mother, or even a daughter;
or a daughter-in-law, or a brother’s wife, or the wife of a teacher, or the wife of a king. (18–19)
He who, having reflected even upon a dog-eater’s wife, goes to a terrible hell;
yet that person who, upon seeing this woman, falls into agitation—his merit acquired through many births becomes fruitless, O sons. (1.286.20)
In such a circumstance, ten thousand merits go to destruction.
Then, by that sin, the living being shall attain birth in the animal realm.
Therefore, one should not think of, look at, or speak to a woman with a sinful mind.
One should not contemplate women; one may look at them or speak with them only with a mind free from sin.
If one speaks with a mind full of longing, that person falls from their state in that very instant.
Having spoken thus in many ways, Viriñci [beheld] with the eye of knowledge.
Then, having observed the captivating woman together with her caravan, he reflected for a moment:
"Just as she was fashioned by my mind to cause the intoxication of the heart, so too has she arisen for my bondage; Yama will attain satisfaction [from this]."
"By this [knowledge], the path of Yama will be properly and well-traversed;
one shall never fall empty-handed into either heaven or hell.
Having thus spoken, Mohinī bowed to the four-faced one (Brahmā).
Behold, O Brahmin, this member of the assembly, possessed by a swoon, whose consciousness has become fixed like that of an immobile being.
He is deluded by my form and submerged in the ocean of bondage.
There is no one here today who, upon seeing me, remains as he was. (27–28)
Whether it be slight or great, no one has ever caused agitation in me.
O Brahmā, I was created by you for the purpose of agitating someone;
therefore, O Creator, quickly point out such a person, for I shall agitate him in an instant.
"Even a dull-witted king becomes instantly bewildered upon seeing me on this earth;
how much more so a conscious living being, who was fashioned as a vessel for delusion?
Having spoken thus, she ceased; Brahmā, however, spoke to her with joy.
This is true, O large-eyed one! Your form is enchanting;
indeed, all these members of the assembly appear as if they were inert upon seeing it.
It is exactly so, and may victory always be yours.
"O deluder, accomplish that purpose for which I created you!
In the land of Surāṣṭra there is indeed a king named Rukmāṅgada;
his wife is Sandhyāvalī, who is truly a match for your beauty. (33-34)
O Mohinī, go to the presence of that very Rukmāṅgada, whose son Dharmāṅgada has been born, who is superior in virtue,
who never wavers from his word,
and who is always obedient and wise.
That king will come to the great mountain named Raivata;
deluded by your song, he will enter into union with you.
There, O Goddess, having rendered him helpless, you must speak to him thus: [36–37]
"I shall become your wife, provided that the wager is protected by you;
I will tell you at the proper time, and that must certainly be done by you.
Having heard this, he, being deluded, will agree accordingly.
Then his right hand must be grasped by you with your own hand.
He should be bound to his word with oaths for the sake of observing the agreement.
Thereafter, during the act of sexual union, he should be gratified like one who is utterly innocent.
When deep affection has become firm and the months have passed,
O lovely-limbed one, when he appears truly infatuated with you in love,
you must laugh and remind the king of his own wager and his word.

"O King, that oath which was made by you to uphold my word—fulfill it, O Great King; I believe the time has come. When you had spoken thus, the king, being deluded by his reverence for truth, [remained silent]. (42–43)
"I shall speak; I will protect you. Tell me, what shall I give to you?
When these words have been spoken by you, the king should then be addressed thus:
"In the context of sexual union, fasting is considered a cause of weakness."
"In the conjunction of passion, fasting—which causes hunger—is indeed a great obstacle.
You must never observe a fast on the day of Hari;
for my fast, which causes the exhaustion of sexual pleasure, is an obstacle [to that]."
He who does not serve a woman who is very innocent and endowed with youth,
but instead serves one who is perverse, ill-behaved, and merciless, goes to the Raurava hell.
O King, how indeed could I be able to remain for even three nights without you?
"I am not able to remain even for a single day without you.
O King, for me to fast while I burn with the fire of desire in your absence would result in great sin. (48–49)
If a young woman is to be protected, the pleasure of love should always be given to her;
if one is unable to grant the gift of love, then the young woman should not be protected.
For the sighs born from the burning of passion arise within the heart of the young woman.
It burns away the merits even of those observing vows from their very root.
Therefore, O King, the days of Hari must be observed while one is still in old age;
for when my youth has passed, I shall observe the days of Hari.
"O fair-limbed one! Even when exhorted in this manner, if the king does not carry out your words, then you must speak further words:
'O King, if you do not abandon your fast on the day of Hari...'"

"O King of kings, having severed your own head with your own hand using your excellent sword, place it yourself upon my lap, Dharmāṅgada. O King, if you do not perform this which is dear to me, there will be no healing for your wound. (54–55)
"O Goddess, having heard these words— that you, being devoid of merit, will surely go to hell before long— he will not kill his son; rather,
having obtained the consent of the gods, he will eat [him] on the day of Hari."
Or else, on that day of Hari, his subjects will be liberated;
however, the path of Yama will then be set in motion by people, and it will reach a length equal to the rows of foreheads of those in hell. ||57-58||
When, out of devotion, he does not eat anything on the day of Hari,
then he will slay that very son who has been consecrated to the kingdom.
At that time, the king will depart [from this world], defiled by his subjection to women.
"O King, by these faults— namely, the killing of one consecrated as a sovereign, causing suffering in the hell named Pūyanaraka,
causing the downfall of the ancestors, and even being a self-destroyer—
he shall soon meet his end."
Having gone himself upon the path of Yama, he will fill the Raurava hell;
or else, by the power of his vow, he will quickly depart for the abode of Hari.
If the teaching were obstructed, people would surely devour one another during the observance of the vow.
"The path to Yama shall indeed be opened wide.
Go quickly and wait for Rukmāṅgada on Mount Raivata;
once your task is accomplished, return, and I shall designate a specific day for you at my home. (63-64)
Thus addressed, Mohinī bowed to the Unborn One (Brahmā) and the members of the assembly;
watched by the immortals on the way, she set out for Mount Raivata.
In the third muhūrta, she reached the mountain peak.
The mountain Raivata, whose essence is Mount Mandara, shines resplendent in Saurāṣṭra.
Indeed, this mountain is a treasury of jewels, endowed with many minerals;
it is a playground for the gods and a place of penance for ascetics.
This place of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is like a pleasure garden,
where the Svarṇarakṣā river flows with a golden luster.
There exists the great liṅga Bhaveśvara, and indeed Vāmana as well.
In the form of Dāmodara,
having gone to the banks of the Mṛgīkuṇḍa in the depths of the forest wilderness, the young woman drank the auspicious water, ate the sweet fruit of the *sītā* plant, and performed an excellent song.
Accompanied by melodic modulations (*mūrchanā*) and rhythmic cycles (*tāla*), joined with the sound of the *gāndhāra* note, it was sweet, dispelling fatigue,
and enchanting all living beings.
Hearing this, Śiva, the Lord of Existence, became obscured by a thicket of *ciñcā* trees.
Then, his mind intent on enjoyment, he became exceedingly overcome by passion.
He moved from his own palace toward where Mohinī was singing;
at that moment, Svarṇarekhā became motionless and the forest grew still.
Dāmodara also arrived, due to the confusion caused by the sounds of the forest groves;
the forest deities and Mount Raivata came as well, drawn by the melody.
Immersed in the *mohinī* song, she awaited the arrival of the king.
Rukmāṅgada also desires to go to the forest out of renunciation.

(75) Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between the Grandfather [Brahmā] and King Yama under the pretext of relinquishing his throne, the Production of the Woman Mohinī, the Dispatching of Mohinī to King Rukmāṅgada on Mount Raivata after instructing him, and the Song of Mohinī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 288 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
At that very moment, O Lakṣmī! King Rukmāṅgada,

Protect the burden of the kingdom and accept that which is offered by me.
A father who does not hand over the burden once a worthy son has been fully prepared is a bearer of suffering and is fallen from both dharma and fame. (4)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! At that time, his son Dharmāṅgada ruled the kingdom.
By his father’s command, performing and causing the day of Hari to be observed,
and protecting all subjects in the Bhāgavata dharma,
the son constantly causes the drum to be sounded for the sake of the vow of Viṣṇu’s day.
The king, too, observed the vow of Viṣṇu according to the rules throughout the day;
having abandoned all other vows, he enjoyed the company of his very youthful wife.
Once, during the month of Āśvina, Mohinī [was filled] with every emotion.
She delighted the king again and again with divine pleasures. (4) Although the monarch was exceedingly infatuated, he did not neglect his vow to Hari;
the protector of the earth abandoned his play during the three days beginning with the tenth. (5)

The month of Kārttika has arrived for the awakening of Viṣṇu, who does not abandon his day that cuts asunder birth and death. Whatever meritorious deeds have been performed here by any men during this time—
"Indeed, everything would become inexhaustible and grant the realm of Viṣṇu.
Having reflected thus, the king spoke these words to Mohinī:
"O Goddess, I have enjoyed pleasure with you for many years."
Fearing your disapproval, I have not said anything at all, anywhere.
O fair-browed one, many Kārtika months have passed for me while I was attached to you;
yet not a single Kārtika vow, nor even a month or a fortnight of it, has been performed by me.
Therefore, I wish to observe the Kārtika month with its sacred vows.
For him whose Kārtika passes without vows, that time has gone in vain.
Even those who indulge in liquor, meat, and sexual intercourse may be observers of the excellent Kārtika vows.
Having become pure, they indeed go to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu;
by the offering of a lamp in the month of Kārttika, the donor shall surely ascend to heaven.
Even a poor person may go to heaven by rekindling another's lamp.
By observing the full moon day at Puṣkara, one is liberated from sins committed since birth.
He whose Kārtika month is honored with vows, fasts, observances, worship, charity, and other such acts, attains the supreme goal.
He who observes the *kṛcchra* penance in Kārtika, or is devoted to the *prājāpatya*,
or fasts every other day, or even fasts for three nights;
or who fasts for seven days, ten days, a fortnight, or a month.
A man who subsists on fruit goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
(16) By those established in the vows of eating once a day, eating only at night, or eating only what is unasked for, land, a wife, a son, sovereignty, wealth, and grain are obtained. (17)
The month of Kārtika is meritorious and bestows devotion through vows, gifts, worship, and other such acts.
Within it, the day of Hari is sacred, as is the five-day period [of Kārtika].
Indeed, by observing the Prabodhinī vigil with great devotion, one attains liberation.
In the month of Kārtika, one should avoid oil, honey, soup, and sexual intercourse. (19) One should diligently avoid flat beans, royal foods, and sensual enjoyments.
For men, the initiation undertaken in Kārtika cuts away the bonds of birth. (20)
A person devoid of initiation attains birth in the womb of an animal;
however, one who is initiated on the eleventh day or on the full moon goes to the Imperishable.
By giving jars filled with water, one proceeds to the abode of Hari.
The conclusion of the year-long vows occurs with the worship in the month of Kārttika.
By performing the concluding rite (udyāpana) and all other requirements, the full fruit shall be obtained.
One observing the vow of eating only at night (naktavratin) should feed children and virtuous people with food of the six flavors.
One should cause an ox to be given to a virtuous twice-born man who has not asked for it;
he who eats the food offering (naivedya) should give a cow along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
During the ritual bath with *dhātrī* fruits, people should offer thickened milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and curd.
In that case, when there is a restriction regarding fruits, one should likewise offer fruits.
Upon the renunciation of oil, one should give ghee; upon the renunciation of ghee, one should give milk.
When there is a restriction regarding grains, one should give *śāli* rice or else that specific grain itself.
If one practices sleeping on the ground, one should give a decorated bed provided with a couch;
if one eats from leaves, one should indeed give vessels along with clarified butter.
During the vow of silence, one should cause a bell, gold, or even sesame seeds to be given.
At the morning bath, one should give a horse; for a bath without oil, ghee and roasted barley flour (saktu).
For the removal of nails and hair, one should give a mirror and clay.
For the non-acceptance of footwear, one should give sandals and wooden shoes.
Upon the renunciation of salt and other such items, a cow that yields abundant milk should be given as a gift;
the giver of a lamp should indeed present gold to the image of the deity.
One should also give an umbrella and fly-whisks, and offer garments of fine linen.
One who performs the three-night vow should give a decorated bed;
one who has fasted for seven nights should offer a palanquin and an umbrella;
and one who has fasted for fifteen days should give a vehicle and an elephant.
One who performs a month-long fast (māsopavāsa) should offer his entire household property;
for a single-meal diet (ekabhakta), a goat or sheep; and for a fruit diet (phalāhāra), gold.
For a vegetable diet (śākāhāra), one should give fruit or offer another worthy recipient (pātra).
Thus, one should perform the vow in accordance with the abundance of one’s wealth.
By performing this vow here, a practitioner obtains a kingdom, a wife, wealth, and so forth.
Therefore, O Mohinī, I shall observe the vow during the month of Kārttika.
He whose Kārtika month passes with vows, fasts,
and observances becomes a celestial deity in a divine vehicle and attains the supreme goal.
Therefore, casting aside delusion, give the command regarding the Kārtika vow.
"I shall indeed observe vows for the worship of Hari.
Hearing this unfavorable response, that Mohinī, seeking her own desire, said:
"If you wish me as your beloved, you must certainly not perform any vow. (37–38)
Giving, protection, and warfare—these three are the duties of kings;

(39) O Indra among kings, I am not able to endure even for a moment without you.
O you who possess the luster of the lotus-navelled one, how much less could we endure for a number of months? If this vow were undertaken by you, death would surely befall me;
therefore, let us indeed perform the Kārttika vow in our old age.
Having heard those excellent words from Mohinī, the king then said:
"O fair-browed one, I shall not perform the vow; I shall do as you desire.
Hearing this, Mohinī was delighted and embraced him as they remained in private.
The slender-limbed woman delighted him according to the prescribed methods for inciting passion.
While he was thus enjoying himself, the dawn arrived;
the sound of a drum reached Rukmāṅgada’s ears.

Remember Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the gods of gods.

having completed the collection of śrāddha rites, go to the abode of Śrī Hari.

having fasted on that day, shaking off the web of sins, you shall reach the abode of Hari.
