Having worshipped with garments, flowers, incense, lamps, excellent sandalwood, saffron, food offerings, and fruits, go to the abode of Śrī Hari. Whoever does not follow the word of Rukmāṅgada, which leads to the realm of Hari— || 1.288.50 ||
"He is to be punished by me and even put to death; this I declare according to dharma. Having heard this righteous proclamation from the drum, Rukmāṅgada rose quickly from Mohinī’s bed.
He said at dawn: "In the day of Hari, there shall be the destruction of sins.
I shall remain self-restrained; please forgive me, please forgive me!
This Ekādaśī must be observed; it cuts the bonds and bestows the supreme goal."
O large-eyed lady, you too, together with me, should worship that Adhokṣaja, Hṛṣīkeśa, being devoted to fasting,
so that you shall attain Nirvāṇa, which is free from burning and dissolution.
"Once again sovereignty, once again heaven, or else final liberation.
Mohinī said: "Well spoken by you regarding the vow and worship of Hari!
It cuts through birth, death, and old age; I shall indeed perform it at your command. (55–56)
The promise which was previously made by you on this Raivata mountain—
accompanied by the offering of your hand and marked by your own virtuous deeds—
the time for it has now arrived; therefore, let it be granted by you to me.
"Otherwise, all your merit from birth until now will go to ruin.
Having heard this and remembered it, Rukmāṅga said: "I shall do what is in your mind;
there is nothing that cannot be given by me to you, even at the cost of my life."
"What more need be said of kingdom, city, wealth, or anything else, O beautiful lady?
Mohinī replied, perceiving that the auspicious moment had arrived:
"O Lord, O Beloved, O Dear One, O King, O Master of my life, O Lover of Rati!"
"If I am dear to you, O King, this day of Viṣṇu must not be spent fasting; rather, food must be eaten. For I shall become separated from you, deprived of your company.
Therefore, if you wish to enjoy my company as your beloved for the rest of your life, [you must eat]. (61–62)
"O King, I must certainly dwell in your house until my death.
Therefore, please give up this fast and eat on the day of Hari.
This alone is the boon I requested from you in the past."
If you do not give [it] out of delusion, you will become a speaker of falsehood and go to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings.
[This applies] in the loss of a wife, the loss of a vow, the loss of one's word, or in matters of strength and weakness.
"Virtue and vice have been seen and unseen; having reflected upon them, do what you deem most desirable.
The King said: "O fair-browed one, you were restrained by me during the excellent vow of Kārttika;
how then, my dear, do you now restrain me even on the Ekādaśī?"
"Reflect thus: 'We have become happy through the merit of our vows.
Having become the sister of Dharma and the daughter of Brahmā, such conduct is not fitting for you.
Being one who protects Dharma, why do you create an obstacle to Dharma? (67–68)
"From birth until now, I have never eaten on the day of Hari;
yet today I am dependent upon you—how could I eat on the day of Hari?
In the final stage of my life, I shall serve Svarṇarekhā."

"Devotion, worship, and constant service to Hari were not performed by me in my youth while I possessed the splendor of my prime; how then could I now, in the midst of the forest, perform such loathsome acts? (1.288.70–71)
Do not break your vow, nor do you harbor such persistence;
O fair-browed one, whatever else you desire, I am the giver of royal wealth.
Accept this celestial chariot that travels through the sky like a swing.

Enjoy the essence of the wish-fulfilling vine; do not create obstacles to your vow. A man who eats his own flesh on the day of Hari incurs the same sin as one who destroys the three worlds, and he who engages in sexual intercourse on the day of Hari incurs the same sin.
Whatever sin there is in the neglect of one’s pasture, whatever sin there is in giving false testimony, in misappropriating a deposit, and likewise in betraying trust;
whatever sin there is in a killer, and whatever sin there is in one who reviles his guru— [all these are incurred by him]. (75)
"All that sin resides within you on the day of Hari.
Knowing this, O large-eyed one, how can I consume your sin?
Since you possess such knowledge, why do you destroy your own vow?"
Having heard that regarding the king, Mohinī said: "By eating once a day, by eating only at night, or by whatever offering you have made,
or with fruits, or even by fasting, one must not let the twelfth lunar day pass."
For those who are pregnant, householders, the emaciated, and likewise the sick;
for children, those with trembling limbs, and those who serve on the battlefield; for those intent upon sacrifices and enjoyments, and for women rich in devotion to their husbands. (1.288.79–80)
"O King, it is not proper for young women, wives, or husbands to observe a fast. What is the use of these many words spoken by me?
If you take food today on this Ekādaśī, I shall be pleased."
If you do not give me your own head after having cut it off, I shall have no joy;
O King, if you do not provide a meal on the day of Hari,
then I shall not touch your body, for you would be a speaker of falsehood.
By truth the sun shines, and by truth the moon is radiant;
established in the dharma of truth, the earth sustains the entire world.
By truth the wind blows, and by truth the fire blazes.
All this is established according to its function, having truth as its foundation.
(85) The ocean does not overstep the truth; the Vindhya mountain does not grow beyond it.
Trees, whose conduct is rooted in truth, flower upon reaching their proper season. (86)
Truth alone excels even ten thousand horse-sacrifices;
O King, for one who speaks untruth, everything quickly perishes.
May you not become such a person, O King—for whom I grieve, though it brings great gain.
"Profit is seen in feeding many; therefore, this is my firm resolve.
My father also spoke in this very way, and I speak the truth.
If you have no confidence in this, do as you wish. (88–89)
When Mohinī, having spoken thus, who accomplishes the rites for the ancestors,
ceased speaking, O Lakṣmī, the king indeed fell into deep reflection.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Mohinī’s Obstruction of Rukmāṅgada’s Desire for the Kārtika Vrata, and Subsequently Her Opposition to His Request for Permission to Perform the Prabodhinī Vrata through the Proclamation of Her Own Drum," in the first section, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 288: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 289 [Author: Chapter 290 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, on the tenth day of the month of Kārtika, at dawn, Dharmāṅgada,
having caused a drum to be beaten, made a proclamation while mounted upon an elephant.
"No one should eat on the eleventh day, the day of Hari.
Having taken his army and subjects, he went to the Raivata tirtha,
accompanied by Sandhāvalī, to perform the circumambulation of Mount Raivata.
Starting from the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) and continuing until the full moon (Pūrṇimā), for five days,
the holy places and deities come there to perform circumambulation.
On the Prabodhinī day, at Mount Raivata, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara [arrive].
The ṛṣis, Vasus, Sādhyas, Maruts, and likewise the Munis;
the Pitṛs, Nidhis, Kāṣṭhās, Grahas, Rudras, and Siddhis;
the Kṛttikās, the lunar circle of constellations, and tens of millions of gods. 5.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, pretas, and vināyakas;
kūṣmāṇḍas, vetālas, gaṇeśas, and the hosts of gaṇas; hanūmants, mahālakṣmīs, and likewise the parya-yoginīs.
Durgās, Caṇḍīs, and human deities; rivers, lakes, oceans, mountains, plains, islands, fields, and villages;
cities, forests, days, nights, and even the religious observances of the day. || 8 ||
Likewise, other beings dwelling in the sky and serpents residing in the netherworlds (pātāla),
as well as truthful, virtuous, and devoted women, and maidens who have renounced worldly life— men and women intent on offering their bodies to Kṛṣṇa— proceed [to that realm]. (1.289.10)
There were also forest-dwellers, Kinnarīs, Gandharvīs, and female servants;
likewise, Vaiṣṇavas, Śāṅkaras, Sauras, Gāṇapatyas, and those devoted to Śakti;
Cārvākas, Bījamārgins, Nārasiṃhas, and Rāmiṇas. (11)
The Dāttātreyas, the Kāpilas, the Ārhats, the Bauddhas, and those who have taken refuge in Śiva;
the great gurus, the teachers of Dharma who grant the four aims of human life; the Ābhīras, the Ūraṇavāras, the Gopālas, and the followers of the Vāmamārga. (12–13)
The Mahābhāgavatas, my dancers, and those of the actor caste;
the Aghorapathas, Lambakas, Gāruḍas, and those who have taken refuge in Bhairava;
the Haṃsas, Paramahaṃsas, the Daṇḍins, and the Kuladevins.
Vidyādharas, courtesans, and actresses of many forms; cowherds, artisans, and those accompanied by their wives— belonging to the four castes and following the stages of life—
all come to Mount Raivata in the month of Kārtika for the purpose of circumambulation.
In that place, countless people who offer water, food, clothing, their bodies, and so forth,
come for the sake of merit and liberation, performing the act of self-surrender to the Guru.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Hari, and Nārāyaṇa are the manifest forms [of the Guru].
They come, eager for the circumambulation and the festival, for the sake of the liberation of people.
Likewise, his Saurāṣṭra region is equal to a sacred field of pilgrimage (tīrthakṣetra);
on that mountain, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself is present together with Lakṣmī. (18–19)
The divine realm, together with the sphere of Goloka, shines resplendent upon the summit;
by him who has performed even one circumambulation of that,
indeed, a circumambulation of the worlds of Jīva, Īśa, and Brahmā has been accomplished.
"The merit that is obtained from circumambulating the abode of Brahmā—
that very merit, which wards off the cycle of worldly existence, is obtained here.
Thinking thus, Prince Dharmāṅgada performed a circumambulation.
Having come on the tenth day to the summit of Yoginīparvata to perform [the rite],
he then spent the night in a great garden within a mango grove on the bank of the Svarṇarekhā river, at the side of Māhīṣaparvata.
In the morning, having bathed in the Kuṇḍa and seen Bhaveśvara,
and likewise having seen Nṛsiṃha, Dharmāṅgada beheld Mṛgīkuṇḍa; there he heard a beautiful popular verse.
And here King Rukmāṅgada shines together with Mohinī;
he who is the father of Dharmāṅgada is attended by the daughter of Brahmā.
On the day of Hari, he does not eat, accompanied by the sound of his own drums.
That woman should be enjoyed on the day of Hari (Thursday),
for she is the daughter of Brahmā whom the King made his bride upon the earth;
she is the very one whom he took as his wife when he had gone forth for the sake of penance.
Indeed, Rukmāṅga served him and did not leave Hari’s side.
Thinking, "That daughter of a god must be seen," the people departed.
Dharmāgada also went forth with his army, accompanied by his mother.
To the north of the Suvarṇarakṣā river, on the shore of the lake,
there stands a great celestial palace that shines like that of Vairāja.
There, a divine village belonging to the lords of heaven shines like a celestial chariot.
All divine implements produced in his own world, originating from the objects of Satyaloka, were bestowed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śambhu; likewise,
divine male and female servants— all shone with celestial splendor.
Indeed, everything that exists which is invisible to those with physical eyes was beheld by Dharmāṅgada through the grace of his father;
overcome with great wonder, he prostrated at his father’s feet.
Sandhyāvalī also joyfully prostrated at the feet of her husband;
then the daughter of Brahmā (Sarasvatī) paid homage to her elder sister. By her sister, Mohinī was then honored with the foremost of blessings.
Then, having learned of each other's welfare and their respective circumstances,
they all, immersed in love, went forth to perform the circumambulation;
however, Mohinī at that time did not go for the circumambulation by force.
Then, with joy, Dharmāṅgada bowed at her feet;
in her presence, he inquired about the cause of his mental distress.
Rukmāṅgada then explained everything regarding the nature of his vow.
Having heard that, the people were struck with wonder at her who had restrained her vow.
Then Rukmāṅgada, having conciliated her, spoke these auspicious words:
"O Mohinī, perform the circumambulation of Mount Raivata!"
The vow of Hari’s day, even that of the Prabodhinī, is supreme among the supreme.
One must not eat on the Ekādaśī of either fortnight.
For a living being who performs what ought not to be done, it is recorded as equivalent to the slaughter of a thousand cows.
O Goddess! Even though I know this, how could I eat on the day of Hari?
O Daughter of the Vedhas! When the day of the Lord has arrived, even the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is declared to be equal to forbidden food;
how much more so, then, the eating of ordinary grain-food?

O Goddess, for those who have exhausted their resources, fruits, roots, and the like, as well as milk and other foods, are prescribed during a vow; however, for those possessing wealth, such food is never permitted at all.
For those possessing wealth, eating during a vow leads only to hell.
"Do not be insistent, O you who abide in truth! My vow would be broken.
Whatever else pleases you, that I shall do; of this there is no doubt.
Thus spoke Mohinī while the queen, Dharmāṅgada, and the others were listening.
"O King, among sages, seers, gods, ancestors, moving beings, and stationary things,
nothing other than your food pleases me;
even by the gift of my life itself, there is no purpose for me."
Moreover, this fast on the day of Hari is not seen in the Vedas.
How can you wish to practice a dharma that is outside the Vedas?
Let all these Brahmins listen, having placed the Vedas before them. 48–49.
"The king speaks the truth: 'Shall I not eat on the day of Hari?
For everything, whether stationary or moving, lives by food.
Even the gods in heaven are gratified by food and even by water. (1.289.50)
Ants and other such creatures take food in their mouths with great difficulty;
for the sake of the four-month period and to endure the winter season, they enter their burrows and there gather provisions for their sustenance. (51–52)
Food is indeed the life-breath of living beings; who would not find food pleasing?
Yet the king does not eat food when the day of Hari has arrived.
For ascetics and holy men, however, the renunciation of food is appropriate.
Is the performance of fasting and other such rites by kings indeed Vedic?
A foreign dharma should not be practiced, for it brings suffering and fear;
yet today this very protector of the earth is established in the dharma of an ascetic.
From food arises vital breath; from vital breath, bodily strength and the like.
Through strength, O King, come the duties of royalty; one devoid of it is humiliated.
Knowing this, the king does not understand even though I am instructing him.
"In this matter, all the Brahmins are the authority, not the lady.
Let them speak the truth here; I shall do whatever they say according to the Vedic injunctions.
Then the Brahmins, including Patnīvra, Vasiṣṭha, and others, spoke to the king.
This oath of yours that "one must not eat on the eleventh day" was certainly not established through the vision of the Vedas, but was devised by your own intellect alone. Indeed,
for those who maintain the sacred fires, the consumption of the sacrificial oblation at the two twilights is prescribed.

The consumption of the remnants of the daily *homa* is sanctioned by the Vedas, especially for kings who perform the rites of the obligatory sacrifice. Tell me, however, why fasting has been prescribed for these protectors of the earth? (1.289.60–61)
Whether it be Vedic or non-Vedic, whatever oath has been made by you, let it be fulfilled today by the very word of the twice-born.
There is no violation of your vow here; eat together with the Brahmins and the others.
"You should not feel distress; the word of a Brahmin is most supreme.
For we are seers of the Vedas, and Janārdana is the word of Brahmā.
He who considers anything other than the word of a Brahmin shall enter a demonic womb. (6.3–6.4)
Having heard these words of the Vedic Brahmins, Aṅgada then prostrated himself before the seers of the Vedas and said:
"You are the revealers of the Vedas; you speak with certainty according to the Veda."
"Disregarding the supreme Veda, you have no instruction whatsoever anywhere.
[This applies to] the seer Nārada, as well as Kātyāyana and Vasiṣṭha;
to Brahmā, Mahādeva, and whoever else has gathered here."
Listen to their words regarding the vow performed on the day of Hari.
O twice-born ones, first listen there to the speech of Nārada:
"By men who are constantly endowed with devotion and dedicated to Viṣṇu..."
On every fortnight, one must observe a fast on the eleventh day (ekādaśī).
That man who eats food on the eleventh day is a sinner;
he falls, without a doubt, into the river that carries excrement, urine, and pus.
O lady of excellent complexion, for men who are weakened, a secondary rule has been proclaimed:
O auspicious one, roots, fruits, milk, and water may serve as sustenance.
However, wise men have never considered it proper for anyone to eat on the eleventh day.

O protector of the earth, on the tenth day and for the following three days, a man who subsists on roots and fruits should avoid my bed, my rising, and turning upon my side, as if placing a thorn in my heart. (72–73)
"Without the use of perfumes, betel, flowers, and the like; without sexual union with a woman day or night; and without staying awake for the worship of Viṣṇu, a vow yields only half its fruit.
Therefore, a Vaiṣṇava must observe the fast on the lunar day of Hari while abstaining from these two."
These eternal observances of the devotees of Viṣṇu have been proclaimed:
all the Ekādaśīs are pure, as is the Dvādaśī of Vāmana; and the Navamī on which Śrī Rāmāditya was born bestows divine perfections.
"Furthermore, Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī, the fourteenth day of Nṛsiṃha,
and Śivarātri— these are declared to be the principal vows according to their true nature.
Thus are the words of Nārada, and now those of Kātyāyana.
"May all you sages, who have vision through the Vedas, listen!
Having eaten on the eleventh day, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for a full day and night;
one should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights."
That should be known as a fast, entirely devoid of all enjoyments.
Listen indeed to the words of Vasiṣṭha, O you whose vision is the Vedas:
"O King, having fasted on the eleventh day, likewise on the twelfth day..."

The recitation of that [mantra], its repetition, meditation upon it, listening to discourses concerning it, and so forth— these qualities, as well as others such as compassion and the like, arise from fasting. Now, let the sages, whose vision is the Veda, listen to the words of the Veda.
A man may obtain the merit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices by a single fast on the day of Prabodhinī.
On the day of Viṣṇu’s awakening, one should fast according to the prescribed rules.
Having fasted upon her with devotion to Hari, nothing whatsoever shall be difficult to attain.
And listen to the words of Śiva, O you who perceive through the Vedas:
he is neither a devotee of Śiva, nor of Sūrya, nor of Śakti, but a servant of the Gaṇas. (84–85)
He who eats on the day of Viṣṇu should indeed be known as worse than a beast;
by that wicked sinner, an offense against me has been committed.
He who, relying on the power of my devotion, eats on the day of Hari—
Thus you speak, yet you are also its prohibitors.
How, then, can I place full confidence in you regarding the violation of my vow? You are the guides for all living beings. (87–88)
If they were to be contrary [to the truth], the world would fall into blindness.
Having committed an act that ought not to be done, how could one live for a hundred autumns?
Tell me, are those words of yours non-Vedic?
Therefore, how can I here commit the eating of food that is unfit to be eaten?
And how could I abandon my vow on the basis of the words of those who stand on a wrong path?
It is not fitting for you to speak what is contrary [to dharma] and destructive of one's vows.
Whether they be gods, dānavas, daityas, gandharvas, or rākṣasas;
whether siddhas or even brāhmaṇas—my father and my mother [are not to be harmed].
Nor is Hari, nor Hara, nor Viṣṇu, nor even the father of Mohinī.
"Even if the sages were to say, 'I shall not eat on the day of Hari,' King Rukmāṅgada,
who is renowned for his devotion to Hari,
will never render his vow regarding this observance fruitless. (93–94)
The sun might turn black, Mount Meru might shift from its place, the ocean might dry up, and fire might become cold;
the very elements might become inverted, or even Mohinī herself might die. || 95 ||
Nevertheless, O Brahmins, I shall not abandon my vow on the day of Ekādaśī. A proclamation is being made by the beating of drums throughout the worlds:
"He who eats food on the day of Hari shall be punished, executed, or banished. (96–97)
"If, while this is being proclaimed, I were to be an eater of food on the day of Hari, may my drum become smeared with impurity;
may there be the fault of falsehood, my fame may turn to defilement, and may I have my dwelling in the realm of Yama. (98)
The mother who gave birth would have been born in vain; the ancestors and the gods would be left hopeless.
Yama too would rejoice, and there would be a violation of my vow. Mohinī would have achieved her purpose, and I would become like a dog eating the leftovers. (1.289.99–100)
How could I, a king who upholds the Dharma, become a nourisher of unrighteousness?
For them there are neither Vedas nor those sages, nor even the seers,
who decorate their mealtime on the day of Kṛṣṇa.
Having spoken thus and bowed, the king then fell silent.
Upon hearing this, the Brahmins and the gods joyfully praised the king;
however, Mohinī, her eyes bloodshot with anger and burning within, [remained silent].
While they were all listening, she spoke to her husband;
she was one who accomplished her own ends, a destroyer of Viṣṇu’s vows, and sharp-edged within.

Thus, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, during the encounter between Dharmāṅgada—who was sounding the drum—and his father Ukrmāṅgada at the commencement of the circumambulation of Raivata in the month of Kārttika.
Chapter Two Hundred and Eighty-Nine: The Description of the Dialogue between the Sages and the King Regarding the Obstinate Insistence of Mohinī to Subvert the Ekādaśī Vow.
[The *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 290]
[The Author: Chapter 291.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then, for the sake of accomplishing her own desired goal, Mohinī became enraged.
She made a persistent insistence upon fulfilling her verbal promise to the king.
With eyes reddened by anger, she addressed her husband:
"If you do not carry out my word, you shall become an outcast from dharma."
O King, you offered me your hand for the sake of granting a boon;
if you do not grant it, I shall depart, having achieved my purpose and acquired everything.
I am neither your beloved wife, nor are you my dear husband.
"Fie on you, a double-tongued man who employs the words of dharma as a mere tool!
Today I shall abandon you, who have wavered from truth and are devoted only to your own self-interest.
Having spoken thus, the slender woman, her face cast down in anger, departed in haste.
At that time, Dharmāṅgada, the son of Rukmāṅgada and himself devoted to his father, stood before his mother and bowed to her.
Humble, he said to her: "O Goddess, my dear father, why are you angry?"
"Departure, however, is not appropriate for you; I tell you what is appropriate, O mother. Having heard the words of Dharmāṅgada, Mohinī spoke these words:
"O son, your father is a liar, by whom your hand was made otherwise."
"By whom good deeds were indeed performed, marked by the banner and goad—having placed that hand upon my hand, he offered these words:
'This father of yours will not fulfill [his promise]; what can I say? (9)

I must certainly not dwell here among those who deceive with falsehoods. O son, I do not beg for gold, grain, elephants, horses, villages, or clothing; indeed, I do not beg for anything by which his ruin might occur.
"O son, that by which he might satisfy his body and me, his wife, who am in the bloom of youth—that was what I requested of him; yet, out of delusion, he does not grant it.
For my benefit, I have entreated that best of kings."
"For the sake of pleasure and for the sake of nourishment, he does not even do that for us.
Having fallen from happiness and fallen from truth, I shall abandon him and go to the abode of bliss.
Having heard those deluding words and having bowed down, Dharmāṅgada then spoke:
O Divine Mother, turn back; I shall fulfill your desire,
you in whose truth the worlds— including gods, asuras, and humans— abide,
and by whom the abode of Vaivasvata was rendered empty through the power of Hari.
"His fame shines forth, pervading millions of universes.
How could my father become a liar while I am still alive? Out of compassion for me, please turn back; may it be well. (16–17)
Having heard these words of Dharmāṅgada, she, longing for her own desire, turned back from there; then her son Dharmāṅgada spoke to his father:
"O father, today this mother of mine tells you that I am untruthful."
"O King, while I am present, how can you become a liar?
Give her everything that was promised by you;
I am your servant, O King—let me be sold for even a blade of grass."
"Give [the child] to the goddess if you desire my life; be indifferent [to her].
The loss of fame is a great loss, not the loss of sons or wife.
The gain of fame is a great gain, not the gain of sons or wife. (2.1)
Having heard the words of Dharmāṅgada, Rukmāṅgada said to him:
"O son, let my fame perish, or let me become a liar, or let me go to the blinding hell; how could I eat on the day of Hari?"
Even if I were to enter a loathsome womb known as that of a worm,
I would still never eat on the day of Hari;
for the drum proclaims this for the sake of my vow, and it shall not prove false to me.
Having consumed what is forbidden to eat, what is the use of living for a hundred autumns?
(25) Let falsehood be spoken; I shall not eat on the day of Hari.
Even if censured by people there, or even if separated from Mohinī, (26)
If death should come to me, I shall not eat on the day of Hari;
how could I feel joy upon seeing those who have gone to the city of Yama? O son, those rows of hells which were once empty have been filled by me.
On the day of Hari, when I have eaten, those [houses] would become filled with people;
yet even after causing her son to eat on the day of Viṣṇu,
that wicked mother requests the domain of King Yama to be filled.
"Therefore, I will not give it to Mohinī; this deception has been practiced by the gods.
She is deceitful, and these gods are deceitful; one should employ deceit against the deceitful. One might rather drink poison, enter the fire, or fall from the peak of a mountain."
I would even cut off my own head rather than eat on the day of Hari;
let Mohinī meet her death or go wherever she pleases—
I shall not eat on the day of Hari, for this vow removes both birth and death.
"How could I, having enjoyed that merit and accumulated fame which I have earned through fasting on the Ekādaśī day, bring about their destruction?
Having heard these words of his father, the exceedingly virtuous Dharmāṅgada [reflected].
Then he spoke to Sandhyāvalī, consoling that deluder:
"Act in such a way that my father does not fall away from truth and does not eat [the flesh],
so that there may be well-being for both of us."
Having heard her son’s words, the elder sister, Mohinī, said:
"Follow the king; do not persist in this sinful course.
The king does not partake of food when the day of Hari has arrived."
"O you who abide in truth, choose at will another boon that is very difficult to obtain.
(37) Though I am the eldest, I shall perform the salutation of the feet for my younger sister;
for the sake of her husband, having been married to him, I shall offer my head [in service]. (38)
But you have not been married; otherwise, whence this such persistence?
That sinful woman who, having bound her husband with words and the threat of curses, deceives him and causes him to commit an improper act, shall go to hell. (39)
Having fallen from hell, she becomes a sow for seven and five births;
thereafter she becomes a Cāṇḍālī woman, and after that she becomes a Kāṣṭhilā.
Then she would become a muskrat, and then a crow and a female jackal.
Having become a lizard, she was indeed not purified even in her state as a cow;
yet, O sister, even for an enemy, the granting of right understanding is supreme,
by which there shall surely be the highest welfare and constant happiness for the one who bestows it.
Having heard the words of Sandhyāvalī, the man Mohinī said:
"O elder sister, you are worthy of my respect; I shall do as you say.
However, if the king does not observe the fast on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī), [then I shall follow your advice]. ||43-44||
O Goddess, perform for yourself something even worse than death;
for this [death] brings suffering to me as well and causes great grief to the kingdom.
O Goddess, who desires death, and who does not desire life?
Indeed, every person possessed by fate commits even what is undesirable;
one whose path of action is broken indeed performs that inauspicious deed which is terrible, fallen from the four goals of life, and destructive of fame and fortune. (46–47)
Such as I am—a woman of sinful and wicked conduct, yet desiring the fruits of religious vows—I have acted without compassion.
For as the seed is endowed with such a disposition, so does the resulting action come to be.
With whatever state of mind one should discharge the semen into the womb, [so shall the offspring be].
"By such a disposition, however, the continuum [of existence] would come to be.
(49) "I, having been created by Brahmā with the disposition for the destruction of Rukmāṅgada, thus became one of evil intent, who committed an evil act against the king. (1.290.50)
O Goddess! There is no lunar mansion (*lagna*), no planets, and no auspicious hour (*horā*) that brings merit;
rather, it is through the state of the *niṣeka* (conception) that the child comes to be.
In that regard, neither power, nor courtesy, nor friendship holds any sway whatsoever.
Neither shame, nor affection, nor dharma, nor compassion and the like [will restrain me].
Today I shall tell you that which destroys the lives of the king and his son, and which is an act never to be done by subjects or their wives. (52–53)
O lady of the Mānava lineage, that which cannot even be conceived by the mind or heard by the ear— how indeed could that be performed with the body?
If you do so, there will be fame for you and immediate glory for the king.
"The abiding in heaven for your son is your praise, while for me it is a reproach.
(55) Having heard these deluding words, O beloved, Queen Sandhyāvalī summoned her courage and urged that slender woman, saying, "Speak! Speak! (56)
"Do not speak thus, O young bride! For the sake of the husband, everything may be lost—whether it be one's own death or even the death of a son.
For one who acts for the sake of her husband, there is no pain for me even in the loss of a kingdom. (57)
"For her whose husband is miserable, a downward fate has indeed been proclaimed.
O Caṇḍikā, let that [fate] be yours alone; it shall not be mine, nor for my husband, nor even for my son—whatever [fate] shall belong to you. (58-59)

When happiness has arisen between husband and wife, if the wife becomes an obstacle to liberation and instead becomes a giver of suffering, she is not a wife but a demoness. A wife rescues her husband from sin as he falls into hell.
That other wife is like a creeping vine of karma that causes worldly existence to increase.
She who deceives her husband even with her life or her speech,
having entered a hundred wombs of worms, is born as a Pukkasa woman.
"For in this world, the husband is the deity whom a wife must not deceive.
Therefore, tell me what you desire for the sake of your husband; I shall give it to you—be it wealth, my own body, a son, or whatever else is most difficult to obtain. (63)
"What other deity is there in the world for women besides their one husband?
For his sake, one might renounce everything—even life itself; what could be greater than that?
Having heard this, Mohinī, a casket for enchanting others with her own self-interest, replied: (64–65)
"If you understand this, O auspicious lady— that wealth exists for the sake of one's husband— then I shall beg for a treasure greater than life itself.
Give me the head of my son, which is dearer to me than my heart."
"If the King does not indeed take food on the day of Hari,
then let your husband, the King, grasp a sword in his own hand,
sever the head of Dharmāṅgada, and place it upon my lap."
"Or rather, O blessed lady, do that which he does not eat when it is food.
Having heard those harsh words of Mohinī,
Sandhyāvalī trembled for a moment, thinking her to be a Rākṣasī.
Gathering his composure slowly, he spoke these words of Dharma:
"One should abandon wealth; one should abandon wives; one should abandon life and home;
one should abandon country, king, heaven, friend, and teacher."
One should abandon the sacred ford, one should abandon dharma, one should abandon a beloved son;
one should abandon yoga, one should abandon charity, and one should abandon knowledge and meritorious deeds.
One should abandon austerity, one should abandon all supernatural attainments, and one should abandon even supreme liberation.
One should not abandon the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) during either fortnight.
By the very vow of Ekādaśī, all that is repeatedly attained.
Even in that regard, for the sake of pleasing her husband, a devoted wife should renounce everything.
I shall cause [this] to be given for your satisfaction and for the purification of my husband’s vow, O Caṇḍī;
you are Dharmāṅgada’s head, not a goddess born of the gods.
O Caṇḍī, I shall not waver from the truth for the sake of my husband and for the purpose of my vow.
Having spoken thus, O Lotus-born One, the queen, out of humility, grasped her husband’s feet and spoke these words for the sake of Dharmāṅgada’s head;
indeed, one who is deluded by Mohinī, whose very form is delusion, does not shrink from anything else.
O Lord, eating during the day of Viṣṇu or even the execution of one's own son is better than the abandonment of dharma;
for having slain my son, O King, I have cast my affection for him far away.
"Do not transgress the truth; may unrighteousness not touch you.
In this matter, maternal affection for a son is rendered meaningful for the sake of the husband. This affection is of the nature of dharma, not merely worldly. (1.290.80)
Having given up one's life, or one's beloved, or one's son, or even all one's possessions, the vow of truth must be protected for the sake of Hari, Hṛṣīkeśa, in this world.
Therefore, enough with grieving; protect the truth, O King!

O King, by the preservation of truth, one is united with the body of Viṣṇu. O protector of the earth, I believe that she was instructed and sent by the gods, who are obstacles to your vow, for the destruction of truth regarding Hari’s observance.
"O King, because of the killing of their son, the gods will become face-down;
placing your foot upon their heads, you shall go to the supreme state.
O monarch, the gods, together with their lord, have been thwarted by your virtuous vows."

They are the destroyers of the path to liberation and the subverters of your certainty. Indeed, the deities are the adversaries of those who follow the path of devotion. Therefore, O King, becoming firm, have your beloved son put to death. (85–86)
"O Viṣṇu, fulfill the words of Mohinī indeed by protecting your own truth; for the sake of fulfilling your vow, perform the surrender of your son.
Having heard these words of his wife, King Rukmāṅgada then—
She said this to Sandhyāvalī in the presence of Mohinī:
"O beloved, the murder of a son is a great slaughter, even greater than the killing of a Brahmin.
Having caused the death of your own child here, what destiny will there be for you in the next world? (88–89)
"If I kill my son who has no other offspring, what will be my fate?
Why should I kill my son for the sake of another? Why should I kill him on the day of Hari? I shall not eat on the day of Viṣṇu, nor shall I kill my beloved son."
"I shall tear myself apart, or let this deluder die;
or else, I shall properly conciliate the deluder once more,
for if her mind becomes peaceful through conciliation, it will lead to our welfare."
Having reflected thus, King Rukmāṅgada spoke these words to Mohinī near Sandhyāvalī for the sake of consoling her:

Thus ends the two hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of Dharmāṅgada’s Conciliation of Mohinī, Rukmāṅgada’s Firmness in His Vow, and although Sandhyāvalī gave instruction for the sake of a son, Mohinī’s Request for Her Son’s Head and Sandhyāvalī’s Consent to Give Her Own Head," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! The most exalted devotee of the Lord, King Rukmāṅgada, having resorted to the final Sāman chant, spoke thus to Mohinī.
O fair-browed one, abandon this wicked obsession regarding your son.
What fruit will there be for you here by killing your own son, Dharmāṅgada?
What gain will you obtain by feeding [him] on the day of Viṣṇu?
"Choose another boon, O fortunate one; I shall grant you a boon here before me. Be gracious, O lady of lovely limbs! Grant me the boon of a son.
A virtuous son is difficult to obtain, and the day of Hari is difficult to encounter. (3–4)
"A wife who obeys one's commands is difficult to find, and service to Hari is also difficult to attain.
Why then do you destroy my son or even my vow, which is so dear to me?
(5) Mohinī said: "O King, I have no insistence on that matter."
Dharmāṅgada is not my enemy, nor do I slay your son.
Just as this one is your son, so too is he my son.
How could I kill my own son, who is my protector from hell?
"I have already told you before: 'Eat on the day of Hari.
I do not wish to cause the death of my son; indeed, the accomplishment of my purpose depends upon his eating.
O Lord of the Earth, my task cannot be achieved through the destruction of my son."
"The successful accomplishment of my task depends on eating on the day of Hari.
For that purpose, your wife was sent by the gods to your presence.
Therefore, since your son is indeed dear to you, please eat on the day of Hari."
"Guard the truth with effort; carry out my word.
Seeing her thus firm in her resolve, Dharmāṅgada spoke to her:
"Accept this very thing; do not harbor doubt, O deluded woman! (11)
Having spoken thus, the son took up his sword and said to his father:
"O Father, you must not delay in striking me down.
O King, fulfill the word of my mother; make your promise true."
The self must be protected even at the cost of wealth, wife, daughters, and sons.
Let my death for your sake be such that it grants me the world of Brahmā;
nevertheless, let there be eternal liberation or eternal heaven.
For the sake of truth, cast aside your concern for suffering and carry out my execution.

And those who have been slain for the sake of their father, for the sake of their mother, for the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brahmin, a virtuous man, or a deity, or for the sake of one who has sought refuge, or for the sake of a teacher—[let me be among them]. (15–16)
O King, those who are slain for the sake of dharma go to eternal worlds.
Slay me and protect the truth; do not eat on the day of Hari.
This human sacrifice must be performed for the sake of Hari’s day.
"In this matter there is not even the slightest fault; do not harbor any distress.
At these words, O Lakṣmī, the gods, the hosts of ṛṣis, the sages, the ancestors, the Manus, and the lords of the quarters likewise [spoke].
Celestial beings, those of the wind, those of the earth, and the inhabitants of the netherworld;
those with visible and invisible bodies, as well as the stationary and the moving;
even crores and arbuds of goddesses have arrived for the purpose of the pilgrimage.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, and Nārāyaṇa, standing on the path to Mount Raivata, beheld her filled with wonder;
they were indeed desirous of knowing which was superior: the act of killing or the act of fasting.
"Where, then, is the reality of Dharma in this life, or even in eating? At that moment, the lotus-eyed Lord, situated in the path of the sky,
vanished from sight and remained there, observing the steadfastness of his devotee.
"Eat what Mohinī has prepared, O King; kill me, Father, as your son has commanded.
Hearing this, Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the examiner of truth, [remained silent].
The King, having bowed to Govinda, took up his sword in his hand.
Dharmāṅgada, his speech free from dejection, led his parents and the deities of Raivata and caused them to place their necks upon the path of the sword.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, along with the lamentations of those traveling to the sacred fords.

The entire earth, along with its oceans, cities, and kingdoms, trembled. Meteors fell by the hundreds, and the sky was filled with lusterless planets. The sacred fords became turbid, and the enchanting [Ganges] turned pale.
The work of the gods has not been accomplished, my birth has been made fruitless,
the king has indeed eaten no food, and I have been treated as if I were mere straw.
The king will surely attain liberation, while I, a sinner, shall go to the realm of Yama.

Thus, out of grief, he fell into a swoon upon the surface of the earth. Then, while millions of embodied beings looked on, Kṛṣṇa appeared in visible form and the King, out of joy, severed his son’s head with his sword.
Holding him by his own hand, the King said repeatedly, "I am pleased!
By your son, by your wife, and by you, everything has been accomplished for me.
This which was done for the sake of my vow shall never be performed by anyone else anywhere."
The delusive illusion has been conquered, and my foot is placed upon the head of Yama.
I am pleased; come, along with your sons, wife, friends, and others, to this best of celestial chariots.
Accept the stainless worship of the three worlds and enter my divine form as your dwelling.
The divine king with four arms, as well as his divine wives, sons, and others, all possessing four arms, became dissolved into the form of Kṛṣṇa.
At that time, celestial voices arose, proclaiming the victory of Dharma.
A rain of flowers fell, released by the hosts of gods stationed in the sky.
The fierce kettledrums, struck by the world-protectors (Lokapālas), resounded;
the celestial nymphs sang songs and danced with joy.
Thus the king was honored by Raivata and by those traveling on pilgrimage with the words,
"May you possess an eternal abode, endowed with sons, wives, and all else.
And by his own followers, who were eager for the journey, their bodies were offered into the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Having been consecrated by fire, they performed the concluding rites in the morning;
uttering words of thanks, they proceeded to circumambulate [the sacred site].
On the twelfth day, known as Prabodhinī, they took but a single meal while remaining otherwise without food.
Eating but one meal on the thirteenth, fourteenth, and full-moon days, they circumambulated Mount Raivata and, on the day of the full moon, departed happily.
Mohinī, however, fell into distress; she was ashamed and disgraced.
Having failed to accomplish her task, she became desirous of dying in the forest.
Yama, seeing everything rendered fruitless, spoke indeed to Brahmā:
"The enchantress has become useless, like a barren woman at childbirth."
The world departs for Vaikuṇṭha; no one at all attains me [otherwise].
Even when the king has died, there is no decrease in the devotion of the people.
Having fasted on the day of Viṣṇu, everyone goes to the supreme abode.
"Deluded by passion and intent on death, she does not come into your presence.
I am as inactive as before; what shall I do? Please instruct me.
Having heard these words of Yama, Brahmā spoke to the son of the Sun (Yama).
"Let us go to awaken Mohinī; afterwards, for your sake, we shall do what is appropriate. Fate may intend something else.
Having said this, Aja and the others arrived there in the forest.
Seeing her deprived of luster and her purpose destroyed, the gods, discouraged and dejected, spoke to Sukālī:
"Do not grieve, O knower of dharma! For you have already performed your duty as a human being. (48–49)
"She was sent for the sake of the gods' mission, and although it has indeed been accomplished, you must not grieve; for the king has attained liberation.
Indeed, no obstacle ever arises for those who are devoted to Śrī Hari."
Out of love for his son, Hari protected those devoted to his own vow.
The son, the wife, and the king— these three, being steadfast in the observance of their vows,
were led to his own abode by Viṣṇu, who was thoroughly pleased with them.
Innumerable embodied beings have been led [to liberation] by those who have attained union with them.
Devotion to Hari is certainly the protector and the bestower of liberation at all times.
O Goddess, if the fruit of an action already commenced does not succeed, [it is due to the power of devotion].

If, despite all efforts, there is indeed no fault here for you now, then, for the sake of granting you boons and for the promotion of your happiness, all the gods have arrived; make your request for what you desire. (54–55)
"Whether the task is accomplished or not, wages must indeed be paid;
the circle of dependents must be maintained and likewise protected constantly.
Thus instructed by the gods, she, deprived of her husband, was exceedingly distressed.
The deluding woman, who destroys the joy of her lineage, said:
"Fie on this life of mine here, by which my duty has not been accomplished, and the path of Yama, which must be traversed by people without restraint, has not been prepared! (57-58)
On the day of Hari, nothing was omitted, nor was anything eaten on the day of Hari;
by that king, a devoted worshiper, his beloved son was joyfully sacrificed.
Having placed his foot upon the head [of the son], the king attained the eternal station of Viṣṇu.
"All my possessions have gone there; what fruit, then, is there in my life?
Those servants who, seeking their wages, do not accomplish the business of their masters, become consumers of faults on this earth, O horses. (1.291.60–61)
"I am incapable of accomplishing your task and am the destroyer of my husband and son;
how can I accept a boon from you who dwell in heaven?
For a living being whose pride is shattered, death is in every way better. (62)
Having done this, she wept aloud; then the gods spoke words of consolation:
"O Goddess, you have exerted great effort in accomplishing our task!
Knowing that the fruit depends upon destiny, do not grieve, O deluded one! (63–64)
"Having performed this service for you, we shall indeed be free from debt.
For the sake of your happiness, we shall grant whatever is desired; tell us what is in your heart.
We wish to go with the desire to reach that place where Rukmāṅgada resides."
While Mohinī was thus reflecting in her mind,
the royal priest, who resembled fire, arrived there;
he was Vasu, who had been staying in the Svarṇarekhā lake within a cave of Mount Raivata.
Having dwelt there and restrained his vital breath, he emerged from the midst of the water;
having understood everything through yoga, he spoke to the gods who had granted him boons:
"Fie on this [earth], fie on the host of gods, and fie on karma that produces evil! (68)
"What were they thinking when they came to grant her a boon? Fie upon the lords! Is she, a slayer of her son and husband, to be considered worthy by the gods?
Indeed, there shall be no purification for her in this world, even through self-immolation in fire. (1.291.70)
Having deluded [him] with flattering words and becoming devoted to her own interests, this beloved woman is a slayer of her son and husband, and a destroyer of her own liberation and heaven.
Even in hell there is no dwelling for her; how then could there be one in heaven, in the abode of Hari?
Or let her wander, deprived of a dwelling, in another world or in a state of peace;
for one defiled by the censure of the world, there is no place even here in this world. Fie on the life of her whose actions are so contemptible—what more can I say? (72–73)
Having slain her husband, having slain her son, and having slain her co-wife who was like a mother—
having even destroyed the entire earth, what destiny will she go to?
For she is one who always destroys the very word of Dharma.
She always said to the king, "Let food be eaten on the day of Hari.
When that statement was uttered out of ignorance— "Let food be eaten on the day of Hari"—
the expiation for that is indeed declared to be one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
"This woman is indeed a violator of Hari’s vow for the day;
O Lord of Gods, she must not be touched! How can you grant her boons?
The inhabitants of heaven do not protect one who is joined with sin. (77)
The gods are dependent on dharma, and dharma arises from the words of the Vedas.
(78) Service to the husband is proclaimed as the dharma of women according to the Vedas; the pursuit of her own self-interest is not proclaimed as the dharma of a bride. (79)
Whatever the husband says that must be done by the wife should be performed without hesitation; for that is to be understood as service by which the husband’s satisfaction is achieved.
If the husband’s command is disregarded out of a desire to establish one's own authority, [it is not true service].
The king was constrained by oaths for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose.
This woman is a slayer by her words and a destroyer even by her actions;
she is a destroyer of the family, a sinful body, and a sinner.
How can she, who has committed more than ten thousand murders, become worthy of being chosen as a bride?
Even if a god or a demon were to take her side,
if anyone should make an effort to protect Mohinī— ||| 83 ||
O best of gods, I could even reduce him to ashes in an instant.
The king attained liberation by truly relinquishing his sin upon her;
yet, even for one who takes her side, that sin becomes attached to him.
Having spoken thus, with eyes copper-red with rage, he took water in his hand and threw it upon Mohinī’s head; thereupon a fire blazed forth,
and while the inhabitants of heaven looked on, it consumed Mohinī.
"Stop! Cease your anger, O great ones in the sky!"—as soon as these words were spoken, she became nothing but ashes in an instant;
all the gods, their hopes shattered and hearts broken, returned home. (87–88)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of How Mohinī’s Son’s Head was Cut off with a Sword by the Will of Krūrā Following the Sāman Chant Taught by Rukmāṅgada," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. In this chapter, while the gods looked on, the son of the king and his wife attained liberation; the reproaches of "Fie upon Mohinī! were uttered, and through the curse of the priest, Mohinī was reduced to ashes.
