Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! To the auspicious story of the two daughters of Bhakti, the wife of Dharma, who were born on the middle lunar day of the intercalary month—an account that is most purifying. (1)
In the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, two daughters of Bhakti named Preyasī and Śreyasī were born, both of them being of mental origin. || 2 ||
They constantly served their parents wherever those two were;
indeed, having abandoned them, those parents were unable to sustain their own lives. (3)
Constantly devoted to serving their father and dedicated to their own duties,
they would always bathe in the morning and bow at the feet of their parents.
For the purpose of performing the bathing rites and other ceremonies for their parents, they gave water and other necessities;
and having bathed them, they gave garments for them to wear. || 5 ||
They worshipped with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, jasmine flowers, saffron, and other offerings;
as well as most delicious and refined food offerings, fruit, betel leaf, and water. (6)

Having offered themselves, both performed the massaging of their parents' bodies and other services; they did everything else that was pleasing to their mother and father, except for [certain forbidden] activities.
She attends to the spreading of beds and coverlets, as well as the cleaning of the bowls;
she performs the sweeping of the house, the washing of clothes, and the cooking of food. (8)
Fetching water, milking the wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus), cleaning the food, and likewise bringing flowers and other items for worship. (9)
The chanting of the mantra of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the worship of the gods, the satiation of the ancestors, the sacrifice to all beings, and the honoring of guests. (10)
Generosity, knowledge, self-awakening, and even the spiritual wisdom of Brahman—likewise, all these [were practiced] in household duties and the constant service of their parents. (1.1)
According to their respective wishes, they performed other rites as well day and night;
consequently, they both became recipients of blessings and were greatly beloved.
Just as her name was, so too did virtues take up residence within her;
according to her strength and according to her power, Sundarī remained there with her whole being.
Disregarding her own body, she always served her beloved with devotion, offering all her possessions and enjoyments, day and night, even at great personal hardship. (14)
For she was exceedingly dear to her parents and the object of their supreme affection;
because of that, she became known as "Preyasī" (the Beloved) and "Bhukti" (the Enjoyment). || 15 ||
She always brings about the welfare of her parents, the welfare of others, and the welfare of all distressed people, repeatedly dispelling their sufferings. (16)
Because she perfectly brings about a happiness equal to liberation through her virtuous deeds, that [city] attained the renown of being "Superior Liberation" (Śreyasī). || 17 ||
By a drop of grace from Dharma and Bhakti, their two daughters, Preyasī and Śreyasī, were given the meaningful divine names "Bhukti" and "Mukti" respectively. (18)

For those whose father is Dharma himself and whose mother is the divine Bhakti, what wonder is there in their virtue? Service to these two holy parents—who does it not endow with the highest excellence? (19)
By him who has satisfied his parents, Mādhava is satisfied;
by him all the gods are satisfied, and the entire world is satisfied.
Now, if a daughter were to be born to childless parents, she would be the bestower of satisfaction upon them.
She is indeed declared to be equal to a son; by her, her own aged parents are satisfied through her wisdom, and thus both parents are delivered by her. (22)
That daughter, who is like a son, is entitled to a share of the inheritance;
for although she is a girl in body, she is a son in heart and in soul. (23)
According to the scriptures, she must always be protected by him; through her, heaven for both of them is certain.
For the water, food, and gifts offered by her indeed reach her parents. (24)
For one who indeed has no sons, his daughter should perform the rites:
fame, charity, recitation, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors. (25)
The daughter should perform every rite and wear the sacred thread;
she shall remain in celibacy as long as she serves her parents. (26)
Or, once a son has been born, she may later take it up even by her father’s command;
having completed her period of celibacy according to the prescribed rule, she shall be married.
When one is established in the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), even if impurity such as menstruation occurs, there is no fault because of the power of that ascetic celibacy. 28.
Impurity must be observed for four days;
however, there is no senility, nor any other defect, nor any sin incurred thereby.
By the fire of celibacy, everything pertaining to the body is reduced to ashes.
A dharma equal to the holy life has never existed, nor will it ever exist. //30//

Whether it be a maiden or one joined in marriage, whether she be without a husband or possessed of a husband, whether she be unattached or attached— [the teacher] shall purify her through the practice of celibacy.
Wherever there is devotion to Brahman and the vow of Brahman within the life of celibacy (brahmacarya), whatever indeed exceeds Brahman there is surely reduced to ashes by that destruction. ||32||

The destruction of seeds, the destruction of passion, the destruction of the fertile period, and so forth, are defects; yet in the case of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), these very things—such as the non-emission of seed—are ornaments, for they lead to liberation. //33//
Thus those two maidens devotedly performed service for their parents, remaining constantly established in celibacy within that auspicious house of dharma and devotion. (34)
In the morning, when they had come to bathe in the celestial river in Satyaloka, they heard about Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa from Dundubhi. (35)
The Supreme Person, the source of all abodes and the origin of all incarnations, bestows [his grace] here during this preeminent month of Mahāmāsa. (36)
To the performer of the vow on the middle lunar day, I grant an imperishable abode, prosperity, my own presence,
my very form, and my sovereignty.
I grant my equanimity, my sovereignty, and my world;
I grant my yoga, my power, and my divinity.
I truly bestow upon him my own lap, my own form, my very name, as well as worship equal to mine and preeminence. (39)
I grant my own state, my divinity, and my splendor;
likewise, my divine throne and my all-pervasiveness like my own. ||40||
And during the Madhyāvrata, I bestow the state of being identical with me—that is, identity itself.
Here, in this half-month, I am full, and the vow yields abundant fruit. (4.1)
I shall grant the fruit of true virtue, eternal; let them accept it and strive for it.
This month of Puruṣottama is my most excellent month. (42)
The merit born from that single day surpasses all other merits;
for while others are impermanent, this merit is eternal.
I am indeed the eternal God, and the month is also mine, eternal.
My vow is eternal; may you accept this eternal merit.
By him through whom the mother was satisfied and the father was gratified with devotion—by the grace of mother and father, may they receive eternal fruit. 45.
Having made whatever arrangements they desire, let them perform the vow of the middle way;
I shall fulfill their intentions, whether they be appropriate or otherwise. (46)
Having caused the drum to be sounded in this manner, he maintained silence for a moment and then went forth, taking the leaves, flowers, and fruits offered by the maiden. ||47||
Having made their resolve for the vow on the day of the moon's midpoint, the two maidens went home and duly worshipped the Lord. ||48||
Having had a beautiful golden image of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa fashioned, they performed the invocation ceremony with the sixteen articles. ||49||
Worship performed in sequence is appropriate; first with milk and other liquids, they then bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). ||50||
Then they both bathed with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) and performed the ritual sprinkling;
thereafter, they washed their bodies with a cloth and put on their garments. ||5 1 ||
Then they adorned themselves with ornaments, sandalwood paste, and collyrium, and further embellished themselves with flower garlands and other such items. ||52||
They adorned Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with the finest unguents and perfumed him with sandalwood paste and other fragrant substances. ||53||
They offered to him, who was in the form of Puruṣottama, saffron, unbroken grains of rice, tulasī leaves, and other items such as floral crests. ||54||
They offered incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, sweetmeats such as milk-rice (pāyasa), and presented fruit along with betel leaf and lime powder. ||55||

They respectfully performed circumambulation, prostrated like a staff, offered an apology, presented the waving of lamps (*ārātrika*), offered praise, and made an offering of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). (56)

Having offered the *arghya* and performed the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the attainment of the Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*), they both made their request repeatedly with heartfelt prayers. (57)
The state of maidenhood is indeed always appropriate in the abode of Brahman;
there, the state of liberation is indeed appropriate, adorned with divine conditions and the like. //58//
May celibacy, which is the form of Brahman, and Brahman himself as the Supreme Lord, as well as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Hari, be the protectors of us both. 59.
He is indeed the protector, the impeller, the creator, the ordainer, and the sustainer;
he is the nourisher, the innate lord, and the Lord of the lords of all lords. //60//
Kṛṣṇa is the Lord of syllables, the Brahman-Lord, the Supreme Person; He is the Protector and the Savior.
Apart from Him, there is no other protector for us two. (6.1)
O Lord of Compassion, Lord of Action, Lord of Effort, Giver of Fruit!
O Lord of the Body and the Self, Lord of All, lead me to the Imperishable.
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, you are my own servant; O inner controller residing in the heart, O giver of the merit of vows, O beloved of the heart! ||63||
O dweller in the heart, O knower of the heart, O knower of our inner feelings, fulfill our inner longing! O Lord Kṛṣṇa, taking both our hands, lead us quickly to the Imperishable. (64)
When, having praised him thus, they offered their own blood to his form,
at that moment the beautiful and compassionate one manifested there.
The youth Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Hari, possessed a divine form;
he was a person of divine appearance and limbs seated upon the back of an elephant. 66.
The ends of whose hair are as brilliant as ten million flashes of lightning, while from the roots they possess a lovely, wavy luster that is glossy and black. (67)
His hair is full of wonder, beautified by its wavy style;
moreover, it is auspicious, being drawn back behind the ears and reaching even to their edges. (68)
The forehead-plate, adorned with upward-pointing lines and the moon, is auspicious for those whose eyebrows are like the tips of bows; it removes pride. (69)
On the forehead, the unbroken line of the *sadrekha* indicates the path to Brahman;
reaching the vicinity of the ears, it awakens one to both worlds. (70)
Both ears, beautiful with their two lobes, are enchanting;
the two eyes, resembling bright red lotuses, are long with beautiful lashes. (71)
There are captivating lines, extremely subtle like flashes of lightning; they extend to the tips of the ears, possess graceful curves, and are imbued with emotion, evoking desire. 72.
"Come, come!"—this is indeed the indicator for one residing in the heart;
the pair of eyes and cheeks, deeply red and elevated, signify a smile. (73)
His nose was beautiful, shaped like a sesame flower; his lips were as richly reddened as ripe *bimba* fruits. (74)
A fine, beautiful, and not overly prominent line of beard shone upon him;
likewise, the neck of Hari was like a conch shell, his chest was well-developed, and his shoulders were broad and muscular. (75)
His two arms, like the coils of a serpent, serve as a resting place for rows of moon-like nails;
they are resplendent with the banners, bows, great fish, arrows, and svastikas [of the hand-mudrās]. (76)
The two hands of Hari, joined in añjali, are marked with the lines of the trident, the discus, and the ocean;
both hands consist of rows of hair and possess white and red streaks. (77)
His chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, the Goddess Lakṣmī, and lines of necklaces;
his abdomen was graced with three folds, and upon his navel was the auspicious seat of Brahmā.
The waist is slender and well-concealed, filled with existence, consciousness, and bliss;
the beautiful thighs, resembling the trunks of elephants, are adorned with a line of hair. (79)
His knees are rounded, his shanks are well-developed yet slender, and each foot possesses three prominent ankles that are elevated in the middle and radiant. 80.
O King, his entire body was filled with splendor, nourished and equal to the sixteen digits of the moon, with the radiance of the jewels on his fingernails. (81)
And those two maidens, Preyasī and Śreyasī, beheld the supremely wonderful and beautiful form of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (82)
Having reached Śrī Puruṣottama there, they both rejoiced;
they both placed flower garlands around the neck of Hari. ||83||
And when both were present before him and had attained a state of emotional intensity, Hari said to him with devotion: "By my vow and by your sincere disposition, [I am pleased]. (84)
I lead you both to my own abode, the imperishable, perfectly filled with bliss;
and by means of the state of identity with me, I lead you both into my very form. 85.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished from that place at that very moment;
for both of them became deeply distressed by the separation from him.
At midday, as well as in the evening and at night, they both performed the worship of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rite and kept a vigil. ||87||
They performed divine dancing and singing at midnight;
meanwhile, the Great Lord quickly returned during the night. (88)
White, pervaded by his own moonlight, and the bringer of all blessings, Hari himself shone forth at night, just as he had arrived. (89)
Knowing that Śrī Puruṣottama had arrived at the festival in their home, Dharma and Bhakti bowed to him, realizing he was the Lord Śrī Hari who had come. ||90||
Having obtained Hari, the most excellent Puruṣottama, as their beloved, the two daughters issued the command to lead them to their own abode. (9.1)

When one has accomplished all that was to be done and is established in the supremely perfected, resplendent, and imperishable abode, both enjoyment and liberation are indeed renowned there in that divine realm. || 92 ||
And for the sake of serving both Dharma and Bhakti, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa assumed two forms and offered them even in the house of his parents. (93)
Where there is Dharma and Bhakti, there are both worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti); these two exist in the world, and they also exist in the divine abode. 94.
They both attained all eternal desires together with Brahmā; thus indeed did they reach the abode of the glorious Supreme Self. 95.
And whoever here is possessed of righteousness and devotion toward the Supreme Lord, having attained both worldly enjoyment and liberation, rejoices together with Brahmā. ||96||
Having attained that which is both more dear and more auspicious, one rejoices in the abode of the Imperishable.
O beloved, the listener and the speaker of this obtain the full fruit of the vow. (97)

Thus ends the three hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Service of the Parents by Dharmā and Bhakti, the Two Mind-born Daughters; the Attainment of Śrī Puruṣottama in the Imperishable Abode through the Vow on the Middle Tithi of the Month, and the Renown as 'Enjoyment and Liberation'," in the section on the Greatness of the Month of Puruṣottama within the first book, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (1.307)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! To how the attainment of the status of Vairājñī was achieved by the Vairāja Puruṣa, the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, through his vow. 1.
The Pradhāna-Puruṣa is the son of the Prakṛta-Puruṣa;
indeed, Mahāviṣṇu, known as Hiraṇyagarbha, is his son. (2)
From that, Virāj was born; he is the father of Vairāja and the Ordainer (Vedhas).
His lifespan is indeed one hundred years, according to the calculation of years.
When it becomes full, it then undergoes destruction;
thereafter, another Vairāja arises and attains sovereignty.
In this manner, through the successive process of creation, there is an incalculable number of Vairājas,
day after day, by way of an uninterrupted succession, during the day of Mahāviṣṇu.
Indeed, for each individual Vairāja Īśvara, there is a destruction within a single year of Mahāviṣṇu, specifically thirty-five times sixty-five [days]. (6)
For the Vairājas, these indeed occur in sequence during their hundred-year lifespan:
thirty-six thousand and five hundred [years]. (7)
O beloved, I know all that pertains to the Vairājas;
listen now to the account of this present Vairāja.
In the sovereign empire of Mahāviṣṇu, on the level of the creation of Īśvarī, beyond the eight enclosures (āvaraṇas), there indeed exists the Virāṭ Puruṣa prior to this [creation]. || 9 ||
At the final moment of the final day of his own final year, while the final piercing was occurring within the universe at the very moment of its dissolution. || 10 ||
There was a sovereign named Sahasrākṣa, a turner of the wheel;
that devoted Sahasrākṣa [ruled] over Satya, Pātāla, and the earth.
He always travels by means of a celestial chariot; he hears through the thread of space; he perceives with a transparent substance; and he touches with the swift wind.
In an instant, he carries out the worldly affairs of all people; for one who is endowed with every means of accomplishment, there remains nothing further to be attained. (13)
While he remained in one house, his subjects situated in the four directions conducted their affairs as if they were right before him, knowing him to be within their grasp. 14.
The thousand-eyed one himself goes and returns at the proper time to the assembly of Brahmā in Satyaloka, which is filled with great beings. (15)
By the guardians of the quarters, by the Manus, as well as by the Sun and the Moon, by the sages and the great gods, and likewise by the sovereign kings. (16)
There, at the first location, he did not obtain his own seat;
thus, impelled by the fault of this inequality within his heart, [he moved on]. (17)

Having summoned those who possessed the knowledge of Brahman, he questioned them regarding spiritual prosperity: "How might one attain that supreme state which is even higher than the position of Brahmā? (18)
The Brahmins requested him: "Perform the most excellent sacrifices—the Agniṣṭoma, the Vājapeya, the Rājasūya, and the Vaiṣṇava. (19)
The Great Raudra sacrifice, the human sacrifice, the horse sacrifice, the Vṛṣakratu, the Sautrāmaṇī, the Suteṣṭi, the Vahnihotra, the recitation of prayers (japa), and so forth. 20.
Perform these sacrifices of great undertaking for a hundred years;
by that merit, O King, you shall attain the supreme state beyond that of Brahmā.
"The kingdom will certainly endure; therefore, perform those sacrifices.
Upon the completion of a hundred [sacrifices], you shall attain the station of Indra, and upon a thousand, the realm of the Sun. (22)

Ten thousand reigns constitute a *dhruva-rājya*; a hundred thousand such reigns constitute the station of Brahmā; and when ten million sacrifices have been completed, one reaches the abode of the thousand-faced Brahmā.
When the second half of the sacrifice is completed, the station of Vairāja is attained;
yet, within this world-sphere (golaka), neither the lifespan nor the time available for anyone is such [as to permit its completion]. (2.4)
Therefore, O King, you should enjoy what has been given by him; be one who possesses peace.
For the end of the demoness of craving is not attained through enjoyment. || 25 ||
Having fully experienced all the enjoyments obtained right here, and having utterly destroyed the two great defects of attachment and aversion, accomplish what is beneficial. 26.
"There is someone greater than I in fortune, intellect, or even in the number of followers"—for one who thinks thus, the attainment of happiness will never occur anywhere. (27)
"I am the Great Self, filled with the bliss of Hari"—thinking thus, one should indeed not consider suffering born of the defects of thirst and so forth as misery;
nor should one even regard it as such upon seeing the greater suffering of others. (28)

That happiness which is obtained through what one has earned by oneself is considered to be the giver of peace. (29) He who possesses a sense of sufficiency regarding objects acquired by chance or earned through effort shall always be happy in this world. (30)
Indeed, you possess a firm sovereignty over the three worlds through your unassailable teaching;
if peace is not attained from that, what greater [peace] could there be?
For one who perceives "this is mine" and "that is another," there is nowhere any happiness.

In the world of Māyā, there is everywhere a gradation of degrees in every respect— whether in the primal nature (prakṛti), its transformations (vikṛti), or in effects (kārya)— which are all devoid of any transcendence. Indeed, O King, supreme peace has never been attained by anyone anywhere.
No one shall attain peace if there be a lord of primordial nature (prakṛti), or even a lord of the primary matter (pradhāna); what further talk can there be of anyone else here, O King? (34)
"Therefore, O King, attain peace; do not increase your craving, O Lord. Having thus instructed him, the far-sighted brahmins ceased speaking. (35)
But the thousand-eyed Indra, without even cutting off those ears, caused many most magnificent sacrifices to be performed according to the rules every year. (36)
By these [deeds], he indeed attained the merit acquired by a hundred Brahmās;
then, in the final year of his life, during the intercalary month (adhimāsa) in the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa), ||37||
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, in the morning, he heard the drum of King Sahasrākṣa as he was engaged in sacrifices for Hari. (38)
In the month of Puruṣottama, when the moon had entered the asterism Śravaṇa, during the second intercalary month, on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad). || 39 ||
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of All, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama), shall grant whatever is desired by anyone, even that which is unobtainable for millions of kalpas. (40)
That which cannot be obtained even through ten million sacrifices or ten million gifts, that I bestow here;
in this vow, the king should give charity according to his capacity.
My worship should be performed with whatever offerings are available.
Food should be given to me with appropriate grains and flavorful juices;
(42) a sacrificial fee should be offered to me according to one's faith and wealth.
One should perform service for others for the sake of pleasing Puruṣottama. (43)
If the Emperor, the sovereign of the fourteen worlds, were to worship me, Kṛṣṇa, according to his wealth with the most excellent of offerings;
if he himself, having performed his morning bath, were to bathe me with water containing the five precious gems; ||| 44 ||
And one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with water containing fragrant heartwood.
One should offer fragrant unguent and fresh tooth-sticks;
one should perform the cleansing of the tongue and so forth with mouthfuls of fragrant water. || 46 ||

The king should cause my purification and other rites to be performed with the finest essences of flower-nectar and fragrant waters; he should likewise cause the cleansing of my hands and so forth to be carried out. ||47||
Then, one should effect the purification of the limbs with very fine clay smeared with sandalwood paste, and subsequently bathe them with fragrant waters. ||48||
Then one should bathe [the deity] with milk, curd, honey, sugar, and nectar, as well as with water accompanied by the single-syllable mantra.
The king should have him massaged with the finest fragrant oils, bathe him with waters from sacred fords, and wipe him dry with garments. (50)
Then, she should adorn me with very fine and extremely costly ornaments made of excellent gold and silver, and with soft, variegated, and exceedingly delicate garments. ||5.1||
With golden crowns worthy of a royal throne, bracelets and other ornaments, golden rings, chains and the like, earrings, necklaces, and crest-jewels; 5.2.
With more than ten million precious gems, pearls, and woven ornaments, as well as topazes, corals, lapis lazuli, and sun-crystals (sūryakānta). || 5.3 ||
With moonstones, emeralds, rubies, and crystals, as well as with diamonds, emeralds, pearls, and excellent padmarāgas. ||54||
With sapphire flower-rows, with karketana and bhīṣmaka gems, with pulakas, rubies, gold, and likewise with silver ornaments. ||55||
One should worship the Supreme Lord with ornaments consisting of garlands of gems produced from the ocean, from mines, from fire, and likewise from the sky.
And with other excellent woolens, as well as cottons and silks, those made from tree fibers, others made of gold, those produced from liquids, and indeed those made from bark. ||57||
One should adorn Kṛṣṇa with garments, with fragrant oils, with collyriums, with fresh butter, and with fragrant substances for massaging. 5.8.
One should cause the black [image] to be perfumed with musk, sandalwood, and so forth;
one should worship it with camphor mixed with saffron filaments, along with forehead marks (tilaka) and other offerings. ||59||
With saffron, unbroken grains of rice, and flowers—namely golden campaka, kunda, pārijāta, sthalapadma, kamala, and tulasī leaves. (60)
One should worship the Lord with kalpa-tree flowers and blossoms from golden creepers;
one should cause Him to prosper with golden unbroken rice grains and offer garlands of necklaces. (61)
One should color with pigments the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, the cheeks and temples, the borders of the ears, the arms, the shanks, the nails, and the lips of Lord Hari. (62)
His feet shone with sandals bound with gold, jewels, and gems; his hands were provided with finger-guards, staffs, clusters of ornaments, and bracelets. (6.3)
One should beautify it with a yellow *tilaka* and cause a red moon to be fashioned;
one should also provide incense, lamps, and food in the amount of one hundred and eight.
One should offer what is sour, sweet, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent—according to one's taste and requirement—as something delicious and fragrant. (65)
Eatable, chewable, suckable, lickable, and even drinkable;
food, vegetables, pulses, boiled rice, and excellent fruits. (66)
The king should cause to be offered milk-rice prepared with gold, along with excellent flavors, foods rich in nectar-like essence, and sweet, refined delicacies. (67)
The king should offer to Hari mouth-perfumes, powders, betel, other chewing substances, and other stimulating items. (68)
The king should quickly offer to Hari various cooling drinks, as well as diverse intoxicating beverages enriched with powdered spices. || 69 ||
There were songs performed by the queens accompanied by the sounds of cymbals and other instruments,
along with dances filled with the suggested aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) such as *hāva* and *bhāva*.
The king should have it performed by his female companions and cause it to increase through manifold meditations,
using parched grains, sandalwood powder, unbroken rice, and golden grains.

One should repeatedly honor the deity with precious gems and other offerings; one should cause cries of victory to be raised and perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) at dawn and at night. ||72||
With hundreds and thousands of wicks, camphor, and other substances,
he reverently performed seven circumambulations from the waist up to you, and likewise seven from the head down.
Then one should move through the seven whirlpools, each having seven wheels, and then through the seven waves extending upwards and downwards. ||74||
One should gradually rotate Hari at the two feet in a counter-clockwise direction;
then, one should rotate Hari three times clockwise with a cloth.
Then, one should cause the circumambulation to turn back even with the water from the conch;
one should perform the ārātrika three times with that water. ||76||
Then one should offer incense to the Supreme Lord three times, while sounding the bell and playing other musical instruments as well. (77)
One should sound the dundubhi, jhallarī, ghaṇṭā, and paṭaha drums loudly;
thereafter, one should perform praise, prostration, and a prayer while lying flat like a staff.
Having performed circumambulation and other rites, he should then offer a handful of flowers;
thus the sovereign should worship in the morning, at midday, and at night. (79)
Having adorned his excellent army and having placed Hari upon a palanquin, an elephant, or a chariot, one should parade him through the capital, the gardens, and other such places. 80.
The people shall honor Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the supreme among men;
then, having brought him back to the royal palace, they shall offer him water and other refreshments. ||8.1||
The king should provide rest through such means as massaging his feet, and for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One, he should indeed bestow abundant gifts. ||82||
The gift of elephants, the gift of horses, and the gift of camels and mares; the gift of bulls and goats, and the gift of cows and peacocks. ||83||
The gift of a parrot, the gift of a mynah bird, and even the gift of a peahen; likewise, the gift of male and female servants to men, and the gift of daughters. ||84||
One should also give gifts of vehicles, mounts, and animals;
one should cause excellent items such as woolen blankets, garments, and ornaments to be given. (85)
Heaps of houses, cities, fields, and likewise mountains;
lakes, mines, pits, and forest regions. ||86||
One should give gifts of food and clothing to the twice-born and to the destitute;
likewise, one should bestow trees, creepers, fields, and gardens. (87)
One may give rivers and streams, as well as excavated lakes, heaven, the great world of austerity (mahas), the world of truth (satya), and even the depths of the netherworlds (pātāla). ||88||
One should cause [the recipient] to receive a country, a region, a district, a kingdom, or an island;
if the giver is a leader of the universe, the receiver shall likewise become so. (89)

If one were to take [the earth] for a thousand years and, having resolved it, offer it to Hari, [he would still be] the Lord who sustains the universe, nourishes the universe, and protects the universe. (90)
Hari, who is hungry for meditation, certainly accepts this without a doubt;
he would bestow the crown of sovereignty, as well as queens and sons. (9.1)
One should offer everything to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, the bestower of happiness;
indeed, one should offer treasuries, armies, and kingdoms to Śrī Keśava. (92)
One should give according to one's faith to an authorized recipient who possesses desire; one should also give to a worthy recipient, and one may even give much to women. (93)
One should provide a livelihood for young women, widows, and virtuous wives; one should give food to chaste women, female yogis, and beggars. (94)
He should satisfy the gods and humans of the three worlds with their shares of the sacrifice;
he should gratify all living beings of the lineage of Kaśyapa with food and water.
The king may give all of this, or he may give even one;
provided he does not practice stinginess regarding his wealth, and gives with faith. //96//
The gift of a bronze vessel-casket and the gift of a golden vessel-casket, joined with eight enclosures and having fourteen petals within. 97.
One should offer a casket filled with gold and jewels, as well as other caskets;
the fruit of that is entirely at the will of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (98)
"O best of men, whether with desire or without desire, I shall indeed grant you the eternal [fruit] which bestows great satisfaction, even when the month has exceeded its limit. (99)
May they perform acts of charity, bestow wealth, and cast it into the worthy recipient with the realization of the Blessed One;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa alone is the giver, and I grant them even the kingdom of Vairāja. 100.
Thus does the drum speak when the month of Śrī Puruṣottama arrives;
the thousand-eyed Indra indeed hears that gift of fortune on the first lunar day.
At dawn, that pure king, having heard of the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa from that drum, bowed to Him and worshipped Him. || 10.2 ||
Just as Dundubhi had instructed and according to the king's own faith, the king performed everything—the worship as well as the ritual dismissal. (103)
Then, in the morning, having summoned that twice-born man to the assembly in the world of Brahmā, Satyaloka, he gave a gift to the Brahmin who was devoted to his wife. (104)
O embodiment of Brahma! O best of the twice-born! You alone are the Supreme Person. O soul who presides over the intercalary month! You are the embodied bestower of fruits. 105.
"Having heard the sound of the drum, I shall indeed observe a vow today; for the sake of attaining the station of Vairāja, accept this meaningful gift. (1.06)
"O twice-born one, I am the king of the fourteen worlds, and I grant [this] here in the assembly of Brahmā, with the waters of the celestial river as witness. (107)
"I give fourteen worlds for the attainment of fruit.
"They have been given and accepted," replied the best of the twice-born. (108)
At that moment, the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, possessing the splendor of ten million suns, suddenly manifested in the form of a husband devoted to his wife. (109)
Laughing, Puruṣottama said to that thousand-eyed one:
"O King, a gift has been obtained by me in every respect through the form of a brahmin. (11.0)
The fruit granted by me to you is the eternal station of Vairāja;
at the end of your life, you shall attain that sovereign state of Vairāja.
Having thus granted his favor and revealed his form to the king,
he suddenly vanished while touching the king’s head.
The king performed the vow and the entire worship with faith;
he gave the gift of the universe (brahmāṇḍa-dāna) wherein nothing whatsoever remained. || 1.13 ||
He himself became a servant and a slave to that brahmin;
within a year, the thousand-eyed Indra attained perfection through meditative absorption.
One perceives before oneself the station of Vairāja which was created by one's own self; indeed, that is seen when the previous state of Vairāja has passed away and is near at hand. // 1.15 //
Thus, by that high-souled king who lived in this manner,
the royal body was eventually cast off through the sequence of time and the power of destiny.
Leaving behind this physical sphere, the body of the thousand-eyed one departed by the divine path to that place created by Īśa where he resides. (1.17)
That thousand-eyed one attained the sovereign state of Vairāja, who is today the lotus-navelled Lord, the father of Brahmā. || 1.18 ||
Thus, by virtue of his vow on the first lunar day, he attained the imperial sovereignty of Vairāja,
as well as the status of Hiranyagarbha and other lordships in abundance.
There, he who had been Nārāyaṇa became that consecrated king;
from whose lotus Brahmā was born, and from whose forehead the Lord of Śivā [Śiva] emerged. (1.20)
He from whose heart Viṣṇu emerged and within whose belly this entire world resides—
by the power of his vow, he has indeed become this thousand-eyed king.
Through true devotion to Puruṣottama, Nārāyaṇa was born as the Virāṭ;
thus, on the first day (pratipad) of the middle half of the intercalary month (adhikamāsa).
O beloved, the fruit resulting from the observance of vows, worship, and charity has been told to you;
when Śrī Hari is pleased therein, O Lotus-born One, what will he not bestow? (123)
O Lakṣmī! both its proclaimer and its reciter shall likewise obtain such a fruit; this Puruṣottama declares. (124)
The nihilist, the faithless, the liar, and the defiler—such a reviler of me obtains neither grace nor fruit. (125)

Thus ends the three hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Station of Vairāja-Nārāyaṇa was Attained by King Sahasrākṣa through the Performance of Thousands of Sacrifices in a Former Creation, and Subsequently through the Vows, Gifts, and Other Rites on the First Day of the Bright Fortnight Following the Extra Month, within the Greatness of the Month of Puruṣottama, in the First Section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (1.308)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this divine and captivating narrative of what occurred in the past. A hundred years after this Brahmā, there was another Brahmā. 1.
At that time, as his end approached within the Brahma-egg,
there was on earth a king named Sarvahuta;
he was a devotee of the Lord and intent upon my worship.
He surrendered all his possessions for my sake; he dedicated his mind for my sake.
He wore my necklace, my garland, and my auspicious forehead mark;
and through my grace, he consumed food that purifies the self.
He undertook the Cāturmāsya vow and practiced great generosity throughout the seven continents, the various regions, and the lands of the ocean islands;
wherever his kingdom was established, he did so in every such place.
"Indeed, my food must be given; water must certainly be drunk by me.
As long as the groups of mendicants are not satisfied, they must eat from my own [provision].
Brahmins must eat my food, and likewise the kṣatriya sages."
My food should be eaten in every way by Vaiśyas, Ṛṣis, and Śūdras who act with devotion, as well as by those living the life of celibacy, forest-dwellers,
ascetics, holy men, renunciants, and virtuous women.
By those who are destitute yet resemble guests, by performers of sacrifice and worshippers of the gods,
by those seeking food, by misers, by servants, and by those deprived of a livelihood— by all these, my food alone must be eaten and my water alone must be drunk. (9–10)
"My garments are to be worn by me alone; they must not be taken by anyone else.
For that purpose, throughout my kingdom, at every location and at every moment, I have established food-distributions, clothing-distributions, and water-stations in every way. (11)
Service centers were established and officials were appointed at every location.
One who is hungry shall have a vessel of food, one who is thirsty a vessel of water, and one who is naked a vessel of clothing; these should be joyfully accepted by me. (12–13)
"May he whose heart is miserly, and he who has craving in his mind,
also take my food and water for the sake of destroying that craving and other afflictions.
Thus was it proclaimed by him and written upon a wooden plank against the wall.
"During the four-month period, my food indeed consists of fruit, water, and likewise clothing;
this abundant [gift] is to be accepted by those who beg for dharma, but nothing else should be taken.
While the king was conducting himself in this manner, performing sacrifices with all his possessions, [the sage said: 16.
Whatever is considered meritorious in the Agnihotra sacrifice and other sacrifices,

as well as the offering of materials in the worship of the gods, the expenditure for the sake of giving knowledge to those seeking learning, and the provision of grass for cattle— [all these constitute his merit]. (17)
For the domestic animals and birds, beginning with dogs, there was food consisting of grain-particles;
likewise, water, clothing, and other excellent things were provided as required, so that they brought satisfaction to the guests just like the Sarvahuta sacrifice itself. (18–19)
In villages, hamlets, market towns, fields, cowherd settlements, and riverbanks;
in forests, wildernesses, mountains, and islands, as well as in oceans and desolate battlefields;
in foothills, cities, royal retreats, and places where taxes are collected.

Indeed, throughout all places, King Sarvāhuta held excellent sacrificial sessions and gave abundant gifts. (2.1) That king established sacrificial sessions at the junctions of carriage-roads between villages, at the meeting points of paths through the forests, and at the landing-stages for crossing rivers and streams. (2.2)
In the border regions, at the sites of great caverns, along the paths of caravans,

in the far reaches of the quarters, at sacred fords, and at places frequented by pilgrims— there, in every direction, the name of the Sacrificing King was proclaimed during the worship of the gods. (23)

In the morning, evening, and at midday, the fame of that one who has offered all as an oblation is indeed sung— of him who is established in truth and austerity— among the people, in the great world, in heaven, on earth, and even in the netherworlds.
The gods, the sages, the Daityas, and other embodied beings as well,
having assumed the forms of swans and other creatures, went indeed to witness the sacrifice of all.
Upon seeing the king, radiant with merit, they were struck with supreme wonder.
Adorned by a face-circle enriched with an orb of exceeding brilliance, all the gods shone from afar with great splendor;
however, upon approaching its vicinity, they became devoid of luster. (27–28)
Thus, that king— whose majesty was merit, who fulfilled the multitude of all his purposes, who was like fire, a devotee, and the destroyer of the pride of the gods—
became honored by all the gods and was seated upon half of Indra’s throne. (29)
Even though he was worshipped by the guardians of the quarters, he did not experience even the slightest astonishment. To him, who was free from passion, there was a wife devoted to her husband,
endowed with the quality of magnanimity, named Gaurtambharā.

Even more endowed with exquisite beauty than the goddesses, most beautiful in her physical form and ornaments, able to assume any form at will, possessing all desired enjoyments, acting according to her own will, and supremely virtuous—
she remained thereafter among the goddesses in the assembly of the God of Gods.
There, bashful and with her face cast down, she remained for a moment. She said to her own husband: "I shall sit behind you;
please remain as before upon that excellent seat. (33-34)
"O Lord, O King, act in such a way that Indrāṇī, Vāruṇī, Saurī, Cāndrī, or the wives of other gods shall bow down before me.
The king said to his virtuous queen, "My dear, you are merely a human woman."
Even there, within the assembly of gods, our residence is exceedingly vast.
O auspicious lady, do not harbor longing for the human realm, for that [residence] does not exist there.
Nevertheless, when one’s merit is abundant, it may perhaps be attained.
I shall make an effort to offer praise in the presence of Nārāyaṇa;
yet even when yoga is attained, my thirst will not be quenched in that way.
Constantly, at the proper time, the queen reminds the king of those words.

The king, too, awaited that very occasion when the time had arrived. (39) Once, on the morning of the second day of the dark fortnight of the intercalary month, having bathed, he remained engaged in the worship of the gods. (40)
The learned Queen Gaurtambharā also heard the delightful Dundubhi drum proclaiming the words of Hari;
both of them remained steadfast, their minds fixed upon that sound.
They heard the heart-touching proclamation of the drum:
"I, the month of Śrī Puruṣottama, am the bestower of desired boons upon those people who observe the vow on the second day of the intercalary month. (42–43)
To those who shall perform the vow— whether by eating once a day, or at night, or subsisting on fruits, or consuming only water, or even subsisting on air—
I shall grant sons, wives, wealth, houses, and other such blessings.
Vehicles, mounts, elephants, and so forth; water, fields, lands, and the like;
a region, an island, and the ocean; a terrestrial kingdom and the circle of the earth;
as well as Svarga, Jana, Tapa, and Satya, along with the realms of Indra, Sūrya, and Candra. 45–46.
I shall grant you sovereignty over Sāmrājya, Atala, Pātālaka, and Rasātala;
the lordship over the fourteen worlds, as well as the supreme status of Brahmā (Pārameṣṭhya);
and likewise the realms of Varuṇa, Agni, Īśa, Yama, and Pavana.
I shall grant you the great status of a world-protector, both that of Kaubera and Nairṛta;
the station of a Lokapāla, the realm of Vāsava, the circle of the planets, as well as the domain of Naidheya, Raudra, Māruta, and the vault of heaven.
The eightfold supernatural powers (siddhis) and the quality of creating the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) are granted by my service;
likewise, the capacity for protection and preservation belongs to me, the observer of vows.
I am the deity of the intercalary month, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
"Even for a very slight hardship performed for my sake, I shall grant infinite fruit.
That which I do not give in other months, I give here in abundance.
Here, out of compassion, I am the giver; indeed, I shall give according to my own will. (51–52)
To him who truly bears my word upon his head, I grant a gift, or a reward, or my own favor.
There is no logic of exchange here; rather, my compassion is the logic in this matter.
Out of compassion, I myself, the Lord, bestow upon you everything without exception.
I bestow ten millionfold; I bestow the infinite.
Therefore, let them receive from that Supreme Person exactly as they have intended.
Thus did Śuśruṣatī and Goṛtambharā listen to Sarvahuta.
Having bowed to Dundubhi, they then worshipped him with flowers.
Dundubhi departed elsewhere, and the couple meditated upon the Lord.
They both pondered, "Where then shall we obtain our desired object?
(57) Then Sarvahuta said to Queen Gaurtambharā:
"O Queen, it has been heard that through the vow of the second [lunar day], one's desired goal is attained. (58)
Your mind is capable of remaining in the most exalted position among all the celestial women dwelling on the fourteen levels.
To attain that, we two must perform a vow that will bear fruit.
Dundubhī indeed said this: "Even for a small act, there shall be abundant fruit.
I shall become Brahmā; you shall be my companion.
You shall be Brahmāṇī, my wife, and the mother of the celestial women."
"That being so, your purpose here shall be fulfilled;
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa will grant the fruit of the vow.
Having thus made their formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), they both performed the vow with great devotion.
Having bathed in the morning and meditated upon Hari, one should have a golden image fashioned;
having invoked the supreme deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Puruṣottama, into that form,
and having offered water for sipping, a seat, and water for the feet.
Then the two of them gave him water for sipping from the sacred bathing-place (tīrtha),
and having bathed him with milk, thick curd, ghee, honey, as well as sugar,
they then caused [him] to be adorned.
They bathed Hari with pure, fragrant waters mixed with sandalwood;
they wiped him dry with cloths and adorned him with golden garments, ornaments, and the finest jewels and gems. (66–67)
They worshipped Kṛṣṇa with necklaces, sandalwood scents, liquid extracts, and essences;
with collyriums, oil-essences, flowers, saffron, and grains of rice;
and with crowns, bracelets, and other ornaments.
With necklaces of excellent gems and jewels, with parasols, chowries, and staffs,
and with incense, lamps, fine food offerings, fruits, betel, and aromatic powders, the two of them caused Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), to be satisfied.
Having offered water along with musical instruments, the two performed the *nīrājana* rite.
With devotion, they performed circumambulations, hymns of praise, and prostrations.
They prayed to the Lord Keśava regarding this vow: ||| 71 ||
"Be gracious, O Soul of the Universe; accept this water for honor (arghya) along with fruits and other offerings.
Having said this, the two of them offered a handful of flowers together with gold for the sake of the fruit, and thereafter they performed service.
Likewise, at midday, both performed the worship and other rites;
having worshipped the Lord of Gods in the evening and performed the *ārātrika* ceremony at night,
they observed a vigil with a festival of instrumental music, dance, and hymns of praise.
They gave a golden throne to Kṛṣṇa,
resplendent with umbrellas, chowries, staffs, and other ornaments, brilliantly radiant,
and adorned with garlands of jewels, gems, and fine pearls. (75–76)
And they also gave a residence with fourteen stories,
adorned with golden water-jars, various articles, and furnishings,
and beautified by rooms containing beds, coverlets, food, and other provisions.
Wherever there is a house that is the essence of merit, wherever there is a noble household maintaining the sacred fire-ritual (agnihotra),
wherever there is a hall for the libations to the ancestors and a noble house for giving gifts, and wherever there is even a treasury filled with jewels, gems, and the like— 78–79.
The house, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, was filled with vehicles and conveyances;
it was provided with male and female servants, groves, gardens, rivers, and streams.
Furthermore, there was a house upon the earth known as a "resting place."
There is a house for correspondence and likewise a house for food;
a bathhouse, as well as a secret subterranean chamber and other excellent riches;
and a house where there are trees that grant all desires and a stable for cows.
All these and other such palaces where they dwell—
that great mansion, beautifully adorned and surrounded by a wall—
they both offered as a gift to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Just then, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, arrived there.
He said to them, "I am pleased with your gift and your vow.
Having shown my grace, I shall grant it; choose a boon."
There the couple said, "O Lord, grant us the supreme state of Brahmā;
thereafter, grant us Your own abode, the imperishable and eternal liberation.
Hari said, "So be it," and likewise spoke to Gaurī and Ṛtambharā.
In the future, at the Puṣkara holy site on earth, there will indeed be a Kṣatriya king.
Among the Ābhīras and cowherds dwelling in the Puṣkara forest, there will be a king named Gāyatra, the son of Virāṭ. (87–88)
His wife shall be the queen named Ṛṣī, the daughter of Puṣkara;
from those two shall be born a daughter, a noble maiden named Ārṣī.
She is that very one who will become the cowherd girl Gomatī, also known as Goṛtambharā.
There you shall become Gāyatrī, the one who performs service for Gokula.
This King Sarvahuta shall become Brahmā there;
in the first age, he will go to Puṣkara for the sake of sacrifice.
Together with the gods, sages, seers, ancestors, and others, as well as humans dwelling on the earth—
eighty-four lakhs of embodied beings—
the Creator of the Universe will perform the primordial sacrifice today for the sake of setting the three worlds in motion.
There, when the fires had been drawn forth and the time for initiation had arrived, the Adhvaryu priest summoned Sāvitrī Dīrghasūtrī;
having prepared herself, she did not come to the sacrificial ground at that time. (93–94)
Brahmā, having summoned Śakra, will say:
"O Śakra, quickly bring another wife for my sake, so that the sacrifice may proceed and does not become deficient in time. (95)
"Likewise, act quickly; bring a woman to be my wife.
Thus addressed, Śakra [said]: "He will indeed take you away, for you have come to behold the sacrificial ground, O daughter of Gāyatrī, King of Metres."
That creator of the universe will take as his wife, by the Gāndharva rite, the beautiful daughter of the Ṛṣis, the youthful Gāyatrī.
Thereafter, he will commence the sacrificial fire-ritual with Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
That sacrifice shall indeed take place at Puṣkara for a thousand days.
From that time forth, you shall become Gāyatrī, the consort of Brahmā;
you shall be the Mother of the World, the Mother of the Vedas, and the Mother of Creation.
"You shall be worthy of all worship, worthy of all honor, and one whose mantra is to be recited by the twice-born.
O Ṛtambharā, you shall be the giver of Brahman and the consort of Brahman.
This Brahmā, who offers all oblations, and you, Gāyatrī, are husband and wife."

"By the very power of your second vow, through my grace, you two shall certainly attain my imperishable abode after one hundred years. This is by virtue of the act of giving a mansion equal to a great city. (1.02–1.03)
"I shall grant you a kingdom, a home known as the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa), prosperous and higher than the highest.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa vanished from that place.
Then, when even his elder brother Brahmā had met his dissolution, the couple—
They attained the supreme, eternal, and most excellent station for a long time.
Thus, King Sarvahuta and his wife Gaurtambharā were born as the divine couple Brahmā and Gāyatrī, the parents of the Creator.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this account of the primordial creation,
as well as the virtuous vow for the second day of the month of Puruṣottama;
it bestows the station of the supreme lord (Brahmā) upon both the listener and the speaker.

"There will be no doubt about this," says the illustrious Puruṣottama. (1.08) Thus ends the three hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how, in the past creation, King Sarvahuta and Queen Go-Ṛtambharā attained the status of Brahmā and the descent of Gāyatrī through the second vow of the second fortnight, the giving of the city and its equal, and worship," in the section on the Greatness of the Month of Puruṣottama within the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (1.309)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the narrative of a previous kalpa. At the beginning of creation, there was a sovereign lord of men ruling over a portion of the earth. (1)
He was known by the name Brahmasavitṛ; his wife was a devoted and chaste woman named Bhūriśṛṅgā, who was dedicated to her husband’s service and full of devotion. (2)
She always served her husband, who was the very essence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; the couple were devotees of the Lord and devoted to the duties of household life. (3)
Performing acts of charity and dharma, serving their gurus and people, they lived upon the path of Hari, devoted solely to the service of Viṣṇu. (4)
They honored their guests, were full of humility toward the elders, performed service for the cows, and were compassionate toward all living beings. (5)
They were destroyers of the suffering of the wretched and sustainers of the destitute; they performed service for the virtuous and were restrainers of the wicked. (6)
Let it be that those two were devoted to dharma and intent on protection, for they were indeed removers of suffering;
the king, named Brahmasavitṛ, would always bathe in the waters of the river. (7)
He indeed performed the twilight prayers, the recitation of mantras, the fire sacrifice, and the study of sacred texts;
he also gave gifts of food, gifts of clothing, and gifts of wealth.
The wise man goes to the temples for the purpose of beholding the deities; he offers well-prepared food, fruits, and other such items as an oblation. || 9 ||
At the appropriate time, she indeed performs worship with devotion;
she feeds guests, brahmins, holy men, virtuous women, ascetics, and sages. (10)
He gives sacrificial fees consisting of gold and silver that bring complete satisfaction;
and during food-distributions, he causes foods to be given even from his treasury.
The exceedingly virtuous man listens repeatedly to the petitions of his groups of male and female servants;
having granted what they require, he brings them happiness. 12.
The queen also worships the gods incessantly in her home, and she goes by means of a vehicle to behold the gods. (13)
He always makes his journey on foot, with no other vehicle;
[he offers] water, leaves, fruit, flowers, sandalwood, gold, and sacrificial fees. (14)
Having given [the offering] to the deity and the preceptor, she returns to that house;
having fed the people, she eats, and the king likewise eats thereafter. (15)
During the Cāturmāsya period, the king undertook a vow that unbroken lamps filled with ghee must indeed be offered to Hari in all temples. 16.
In the seven continents and islands, as well as in the islands of the ocean—wherever there were temples within his own kingdom and territory—(he established them). || 17 ||
Of the incarnations of the Supreme Lord, of the lords, and of the yogis;
likewise, of the gods and of all classes of beings, through their wondrous nature. ||18||

And likewise of the manifestations (vibhūtis), the principles (tattvas), the goddesses (devīs), the multitudes of sacred fords (tīrthas), the presiding deities (adhidaivas), and those that are insentient as well as sentient. (19)
And wherever there were celestial abodes, there he established shrines that were marvelous, both stationary and mobile. (20)
He had ghee-lamps made with large pieces of highly radiant [wicks], using purified cow's ghee in golden vessels with excellent wicks. 21.
Having preserved it, he indeed made it manifest and bestowed it upon all the gods;
even if, in his kingdom, it were for some particularly worthy deity. ||22||
If this king perceives that the lamp was not offered,
then he observes a fast and bestows even a thousand pieces of gold;
furthermore, throughout the entire Cāturmāsya period, he proclaims my vow everywhere.
Throughout my entire kingdom, lamps shall be offered by me to the gods. ||24||
May lamps offered by worshippers to the waters of sacred fords, to the trees of shrines, and throughout all temples become my lamps. (25)
May there be sky-lamps on all festival days, beginning with Kārttika;
by means of cow's ghee, may my lights be supreme in every respect. (26)
May there be for me the bathing of the deities with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and may there be sweet foods for me when they are offered to the gods. (27)
May these sixteen services be mine in every way;
may ninefold devotion to Śrī Hari arise through those fed by me, O Lord. (28)
During the Cāturmāsya period, however, vegetables, milk, and juices are for my food at the meals of the brahmins, their virtuous wives, and the gods. (29)
May my food be for the poor, the helpless, and the wretched;
may my morsels of grass be for the cows and the fodder for dogs and other village animals. (30)
May there be for me the giving of grain fragments and the like to pigeons and other birds, and may there be flour-based food for ants and the like. (3.1)
May I likewise attain success in sacrifices and ritual acts through their proper means; and may I perform the waving of lights and other rites in temples every day. (32)
May the gift of water and the gift of clothing always be mine through my prosperity;
may the offering of coins of gold, silver, and so forth also always be mine. (33)
Thus did King Brahmasavitr proclaim throughout the earth;
and his wife Bhūriśṛṅgā undertook a vow together with her husband. ||34||
Having bathed daily, he worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama in a pavilion adorned with plantain pillars, arches, and other ornaments. (35)
Having constantly caused a new mandala to be made and having filled it with the seven kinds of grain, one should prepare the excellent one named Sarvatobhadra.
And having had a golden image of the illustrious Pauruṣottama fashioned, he worshipped it with many kinds of offerings and with great devotion. ||37||
At midday she also provided fifty-six kinds of food;
and in the evening, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), she danced accompanied by ten thousand female attendants. ||38||
Thus, disregarding her own honor, the queen performs this daily for the pleasure of Puruṣottama;
yet even though Kṛṣṇa is delighted by observing the dance accompanied by Sukaṇṭha-miśra, he does not come within the range of her vision. (39)
Those two, the husband and wife, who were thus engaged, ever devoted, and dear to Hari,
heard on the morning of the third day the words of the Goddess.
Just as they heard the proclamation uttered from the drum, which was most wonderful, so too let the citizens, the forest-dwellers, and the denizens of heaven hear it. (41)
"Let men and women listen; I speak as Śrī Puruṣottama, the manifest Lord of the Abode of Brahman, the presiding deity of the intercalary month. (42)
On the third day of the waning fortnight, men and women, endowed with faith, shall perform a vow preceded by the worship of me. (43)
Whether by eating once a day, or by eating only at night, or by subsisting on fruit, or by living on alms, kings or queens shall attain the supreme state. (44)
They shall attain the dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation desired by the world, as well as sons, grandsons, lineages, the expansion of their family, and true fame. (45)
"By my vow, they shall indeed obtain all sovereign powers;
by the vow of a single day, let them grasp eternal happiness. (46)
Endowed with supreme magnanimity, I, the Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, am the bestower of all perfections and the one who unites beings with them. (47)
Today, by the gift of food, I shall bestow the nine eternal treasures;
today, by the gift of gold, I shall bestow the throne of Kubera. (48)
Today, by the gift of liquid, I shall grant the excellent station of Varuṇa;
today, by the gift of jewels, I shall grant the auspicious sovereignty of the Lord of the Gods.
Today, by the gift of merit, I shall indeed bestow the status of Dharmarāja;
today, by the gift of wealth, I shall bestow the eight Vasus in embodied form.
Today, by the gift of my all, I shall bestow the glory of the eight supernatural powers;
today, by the offering of a lamp, I shall grant the state of being the eye of the three worlds.
Today, by the gift of milk, I shall bestow the nature of cool nectar;
today, by the gift of food and water, I shall bestow a meaningful sovereignty.
Today, by the gift of a chariot and other such things, I shall give the celestial vimāna;
today, by the gift of garments, I shall clothe the earth in the sky with cloth.
Today, by the gift of maidens and other such gifts, I shall bestow thousands of women;
today, by the gift of cows, I shall bestow the earth filled with its juices.
Today, by the gift of a house, I shall give the cavernous interior of the universe;
today, by the gift of fruit, I shall give a row of wish-fulfilling trees.
Today, by the gift of ornaments, I shall bestow a well-adorned heaven;
today, through my worship, I shall grant eternal veneration from the three worlds. (56)
"Whatever my devotee desires, I shall grant that very thing; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, Dundubhi became silent for a moment.
King Brahmasavita and his beloved Bhūriśṛṅgā, having bowed to that Dundubhi, who was the messenger of Kṛṣṇa, offered him worship. ||58||
On the third day of the dark fortnight of the intercalary month, the couple observed a vow of eating only one meal, desiring the sun-god. ||59||
O Keśava, by the offering of a lamp during the Cāturmāsya, I become the Sun;
accompanied by my consort, I manifest as the very soul of the eyes for the three worlds.
Having thus resolved, the king and his wife undertook the vow;
having bathed in the morning, they remembered Hari and meditated upon His radiant, desired form.
Having installed the golden Puruṣottama, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, upon an auspicious pitcher within the maṇḍala in the pavilion, the two of them worshipped him with devotion. (62)
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and pure water, and having dressed him in garments,
one should then offer ornaments, flowers, necklaces, and so forth, as well as sandalwood paste.

Having worshipped the Lord with incense, lamps, and other offerings, as well as unbroken rice grains and saffron, one should present fifty-six varieties of food, sweets, delicacies, water, and fruit. (64)
Both of them offered [the gifts] with devotion to Śrī Puruṣottama; they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and made a full circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa). ||65||
Having performed a prostration like a staff, they then offered praise;
they presented an offering of flowers and requested forgiveness. (66)
Likewise at midday and in the evening, they performed worship during the night;
there they held dances with great devotion and kept a vigil. (67)
The Blessed One, Hari, the storehouse of all splendor,
appeared through her worship, her vow, and specifically her Cāturmāsya vow.
"By the gift of this lamp, I am everywhere pleased by your extreme devotion;
for that which is desired by you is the greatest eye-situated place within the three worlds. (69)
"I shall grant you the status of the sun in the sky; together with your wife, you shall become the Sun.
Having spoken thus, Hari vanished from that place. (70)
Having performed the Brahma-savitrī rite, as well as the dance and the all-night vigil,
he, together with Bhūriśṛṅga, bestowed gifts in the morning.
Jewels and gems, cows, buffaloes, elephants, and horses; likewise goats and sheep, as well as vessels of gold and silver and garments. (72)
Male and female servants, couches, houses, and palaces;
fields, groves, gardens, and forests. ||73||
He gave food, wells, tanks, land, cotton, silken garments, as well as woolen cloths, all of which were priceless.
To the Brahmin women, various articles of adornment; and to the ascetics, mats, alms-bowls, water-pots, and so forth. ||75||
To the householders, he gave articles suitable for domestic life;
to those hungry, he gave food, and to those thirsty, he gave water. (76)
To those seeking various forms of happiness, he gave the means for attaining that happiness;
to those seeking wealth, he gave wealth; but to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, he gave everything.
Thus, O Lakṣmī! the supreme gift was performed by Brahmā and Savitṛ;
likewise, it was performed by Bhūriśṛṅgī with the approval of her husband. (78)
Then, after having fed the virtuous ones and others, the husband and wife were about to eat when Śrī Puruṣottama arrived there in the form of a mendicant. (79)
On his chest shines Lakṣmī in the form of a golden line, and on his left thigh shines Śrī in the form of a white mark. ||80||
O lotus-petal-eyed one, on his right hand shine a banner, a fish, a svastika, and likewise a bow, encircled by the radiance of his splendor.
Having seen the monk and recognized him by his marks as Nārāyaṇa, the king and queen fed him and respectfully massaged his feet. (82)
Then, an internal meditative absorption arose within the two forms there;
for the Creator Brahmā beheld the great sphere known as the Sun. (83)
There he beheld his own golden body, higher than the highest, by which the entire world, consisting of light, attains illumination. (84)
Having seen the true nature of her own perception and having beheld the golden wife of the Sun, she attained great satisfaction. ||85||
Hari vanished; at that moment, the two of them arose from their meditative absorption, filled with wonder and amazement, and felt their hearts were fulfilled. (86)
They constantly served Kṛṣṇa and awaited his transformation into the Sun;
meanwhile, by the natural course of time, the end of the kalpa occurred. (87)
The king and queen attained dissolution and assumed divine forms;
they then departed for Mahāstara by means of a sun-crystal chariot. ||88||
Having passed that night at the beginning of the kalpa in the sequence of creation, he, the Lord Brahmā-Savitṛ, became this Sun. (8-9)
And his wife was Bhūriśṛṅgā, born of Viśvakarman;
she was the daughter named Saṃjñā, who had been given by her father to Aṃśumālin.
Bhūriśṛṅga and Savitṛ became Saṃjñā and Sūrya; who else could attain the station of the Sun, those two gods who bestowed their very eyes upon all? (91)
Thus, by the power of offering lamps and by the vow of the third lunar day (Tṛtīyā-vrata), one attains the supreme state as far as heaven shines.
Therefore, lamps should always be offered in the temples of the gods.
By that [means], one shall attain freedom from blindness, luminosity, and divinity. 93.
Just as that King Brahmasavita attained the state of the Sun, such indeed shall be the gain for both the listener and the speaker of this narrative. (9.4)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you this supreme, divine account concerning Sūryanārāyaṇa; it is purifying, merit-bestowing, and beneficial. (95)

Thus ends the three hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the State of Sūryanārāyaṇa, together with the Recovery of His Wife Named Saṃjñā, by King Brahmasavitṛ of the Previous Kalpa and His Consort Bhūriśṛṅga through the Vow on the Third Day of the Second Fortnight and Various Gifts such as Lamps," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-Santāna*, concerning the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama.
