Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To the sin-destroying story of this vow from a previous kalpa, which took place on the ninth lunar day at the very end of the intercalary month. 1.
In a kalpa even more ancient than the preceding one, there was an Indra named Dyumerujit. When his dissolution occurred at the end of that day, he remained by virtue of his residual merit.
Having spent the night in Satyaloka, at the dawn of the new kalpa’s creation, during the first Tretā Yuga, he became a sovereign emperor (Samrāṭ) and a performer of a hundred sacrifices (Śatamakha).
Endowed with charity, righteousness, and compassion, he was intent on protecting the world; having conquered his senses, he was the bestower of honor upon gods, demons, and mortals alike.
Traveling by means of a celestial chariot, he wandered through the three worlds, honoring cows, sacred fords, brahmins, ascetics, chaste women, and holy men.
(5) Indeed, upon the palm of his hand, divine marks in the form of a thunderbolt, an umbrella, and a sword shone forth, clearly indicating his divinity.
(6) His wife was a great queen of celestial complexion and devoted to her husband; she was constantly intent on serving her husband as well as serving the gods. (7)

She follows the duty of hospitality; she is the destroyer of the misery, helplessness, and poverty of the destitute; she brings about the advancement of maidens and is the eternal protector of the female sex. (8) Gandharva women, Naga maidens, goddesses, Dānavīs, Kinnarīs, and even human women indeed dwell there for the sake of instruction. (9) Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Saṃjñā, Svāhā, Arundhatī, Mahendrāṇī, Satī, Lakṣmī, Rohiṇī, Pārvatī, and Svadhā [are also there]. (10)

Prabhā, Māṇikī, Śrī, Jayā, Bhakti, and the Diśas, as well as other rivers such as the Kṛttikās and others, were then her companions. Campā, Dayā, Ramā, Hemnī, Muktā, Godā, Jayantikā, Śānti, Śāntā, Premapātrā, Dīpotsavī, Nandinī, Ojasvatī, Suratnā, Damayantī, Caturmati, Devikā, Kāntikā, Revā, Savitā, and Mūlayoginī [were also there].

Kastūrikā, Maṅgalā, Haṃsā, Ruci, Mañjulā, Nirmalā, Amṛtā, Rālijaṭinī, Pānaputtalī, Vanitā, Miṣṭikā, Puṣpā, Manu, Kṛṣṇā, and Dāsikā were her handmaidens; while Kāntā, Sarasvatī, Padmā, and Śāradā were her attendants. In that kingdom called Prāgjyotiṣa, there were wish-fulfilling trees, jewels, cows of plenty that granted all desires, and celestial creepers. (14–16)

Thus King Śatamakha and Queen Dyurvarṇikā lived on the surface of the earth as husband and wife according to the duties of sovereignty. By the turn of fate, that kingdom became like a fortress against the Snowy Mountain; they established their capital at Sāketa along the Sarayū river.
Having appointed a chief protector and resolved to set out on a journey, they then departed with devotion for the pilgrimage to Badarī.
Accompanied by their two auspicious wives and a limited number of attendants, servants, and maidservants, they proceeded while observing all the prescribed rules of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Morning ablutions, celibacy, the vow of truthfulness, subsisting on fruits, sleeping on the ground, and the renunciation of ornaments, fine seats, and the like;

non-violence, freedom from slander, the wearing of garlands, the chanting of prayers (japa), freedom from passion and hatred, charity, and the worship of the gods and other deities—[these were their observances]. (20–22)
Worship of elders at sacred sites, rendering assistance to the spiritual preceptor at those sites, beholding cows, drinking the nectar of Hari’s feet, listening to sacred narratives;
(23) renunciation of sense objects, conducting oneself like a saintly person, meditating on Nārāyaṇa at night, and auspicious wandering to sacred sites during the day;

(24) performing the evening lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), hymns of praise (*stotra*), chanting (*kīrtana*), and remembrance (*smaraṇa*) [of the Lord], non-agitation toward moving and stationary beings, and forbearance; (25) [Note: The provided text contains a typographical error in verse 25; it reads *jaṃgamānsthāvarānpratyanudvejanaṃ titikṣaṇam* instead of *jaṅgamān sthāvarān pratyanudvejanaṃ titikṣaṇam*. Protecting [the earth], those two became ascetics and went to Badarī. Having sipped water and bathed in the celestial river (Devanadī), they then drank its water.

There they clearly beheld the sages who are the very essence of sacred fords (tīrtha) as well as the fords themselves. Having seen Nara and Nārāyaṇa and performed worship with ritual offerings, they then fed virtuous brahmins and guests. Indeed, this was done by the king and queen for the sake of pleasing Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

Right there, in the presence of the image, he performed dance and song. He offered a pair of golden parasols, two crowns, a pair of earrings for each of the [two] ages, four chowries, a pair of staffs, necklaces, twenty finger-rings, two pairs of bracelets, two sets of chains and waist-bands, a pair of sandals, and likewise two lion-thrones. (29–31)

Abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), excellent vessels of gold, garments of bark, deerskins, and local fruits were all offered, while the words "This is yours" were uttered. Their feet were touched and their water was drunk, thinking it to be the nectar of the feet. Golden garlands were placed at the feet of the two lords of men, and the supreme masters were worshipped with sandalwood and other excellent articles.

Then blessings were received: "O King, may you be blessed with a son! May the queen become a mother of a son! Having heard this praise, they departed. At that time, on the morning of the ninth lunar day (navamī), a drum was clearly heard there, fulfilling the desires of the mind:
"Today, let everyone perform their vows and receive their desired fruits; for this month of Puruṣottama is the bestower of fruits, being itself supreme. (35–37)

"May the auspicious desires residing in the heart be granted by Puruṣottama; and to the seeker of the vow, I shall grant my own abode, glory, and prosperity. For the one who performs the Navamī vow, that which is inaccessible shall become accessible to the intellect, that which is unobtainable shall indeed be obtained, and even that which is inconceivable shall become conceivable. Having spoken thus, Dundubhi looked upon the man, the lord of men.

Having honored the two best of sages, the king and queen departed for the northern region. Having heard their words with great composure and meditated upon them, Nara and Nārāyaṇa then instantly became absorbed within them. Within the hearts of the couple, they beheld those two of divine and most beautiful form—charming, sweet-spoken, with lovely matted locks, robust, youthful, celestial ascetics graced by prosperity.
With their feet worshipped by sages, both were residents of Vaikuṇṭha; they were worthy of a royal palace and deserving of being cherished, protected, and honored.

(44) With eyes as large as lotus petals, faces like the beautiful moon, and abodes of all virtues—dark as rain clouds, heart-stealing, charming, and handsome—they beheld the two children who had been envisioned for them. Then, emerging from meditation and seeing the queen and the king, [they spoke]. (45–46)

Nara-Nārāyaṇa said, "May your resolve bear fruit. Having heard this, they both became exceedingly satisfied; and having performed the rites of the sacred ford (tīrtha), they departed from that place and went to the riverbank. There, having sipped water (ācamana) and bathed, they then worshipped the golden image.
Having bathed Hari with the waters of the Gaṅgā and wiped him with garments, they offered the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then performed the consecration (abhiṣeka) with water.
Having wiped [the deity] clean, offered fine garments and ornaments, prepared the beauty of adornment, and presented incense and lamps;
then, having perfumed [the deity] with sandalwood, unbroken rice, saffron, collyrium, and the essence of liquid [substances], they performed the *ārātrika* ceremony.
They fed the Lord, magnified Him with hymns of praise, and offered handfuls of flowers along with fruits and other offerings.

Having offered betel for chewing, they begged for forgiveness. Thus, after sunrise, when five *ghaṭīs* had passed, at that time they again performed their bathing, worship, and hymns of praise; they presented the food offering (*naivedya*), drinks, betel, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth; likewise, having completed the feeding of the sages, the gods, and the Brahmins, as well as the sacrificial fees, they offered the water of respect (*arghya*), handfuls of flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).

Having offered praise, they performed the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). Thus, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama, and having bowed to Nara and Nārāyaṇa, they completed the rites for the sacred ford (*tīrtha*). Before midday, they arrived by celestial chariot at the renovated capital city of Sāketa, situated along the Sarayū River; there, in a great palace within a garden beautifully adorned with trees and creepers— 56–58.
The two of them had a pavilion constructed, adorned with gold and other precious materials; it was beautified by water-pots, necklaces, ornaments, garments, decorations, banners, and the like.
It was graced with colorful floral designs, sprinkled with fragrant waters, and provided with fire-pits and splendidly decorated altars.
It was made beautiful with mats, couches, stools, and woolen carpets; it was enriched with archways made of auspicious wood and supported by pillars of plantain trees.
It was adorned and beautified with mirrors, moon-shaped ornaments, whetstones, kettledrums, and large drums; with water-wave machines and devices for circulating cool breezes.
It was decorated with various figures of descending deities and others, where the distinction between water and land was made visible through latticed windows.

Furthermore, it was embellished like a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) with instruments for hearing from afar, mirrors for seeing from afar, and other means for achieving the perception of distant objects.
There, in the center of the pavilion, they fashioned a mango tree; in the four side corners, four *aśoka* trees were constructed.

(65) They fastened divine swings to the branches, and upon the chains, they placed the deities in embodied form. There, they prepared soft coverings, and therein [they placed] a golden image in the form of Puruṣottama. (66–67)

The queen and the king likewise lifted and swayed it. There, near the Lord, they prepared a *sarvatobhadra* mandala mixed with the seven grains, gold, gems, diamonds, and other fine materials. In its center, they fashioned an auspicious golden pitcher (68–69).
Adorned with the five jewels, water, flowers, fruits, ritual substances, and garments, they placed upon it a vessel filled with sesame seeds (70).

Thereafter, they both wore rings set with *śrīphala* fruits. They installed a second golden image named Śrī Puruṣottama in that vessel and worshipped it with the sixteen articles of offering. With great devotion, they performed the *ārārtika* ceremony.
At that time, they had dances and songs performed right there, and likewise had a fire sacrifice (*homa*) performed within the sacrificial pit.
They fed the Brahmins, the gods, virtuous women, as well as the poor, the helpless, the weak, the destitute, beggars, and others.

They caused sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to be given and offered handfuls of flowers and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). While they were thus performing their duties there in that beautiful pavilion, a young man of divine form, dark-complexioned and as beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud, was seen—a god with matted hair, accompanied by his younger brother. (74–76)
At the hour of midday, the divine Puruṣottama appeared in bodily form, his face radiant with a smile and encircled by a halo of divine splendor.
His divine eyes were filled with affection; he was robust and accompanied by his robust younger brother. He wore yellow garments and carried a bow, a shield, a sword, a conch, and matted locks.
Adorned with a golden crown and golden earrings, his right hand was raised in blessing, and his mind was overflowing with grace toward those who serve him.

The Lord, who desires to abide and whose exertion bestows peace upon the grove, was born in the pavilion within that garden, resplendent like the midday sun. (80) He was repeatedly addressed there by his younger brother with the words "Rāmāditya," for it is in this supreme Lord, brilliant as the sun, that yogis find delight.
(81) Indeed, this Keśava was born here as Śatamakha; he is celebrated as the first incarnation of Rāma. (82)

Upon seeing the Lord Keśava, a youth, as soon as he was born, both the queen and the king were filled with wonder and amazement. (83) But the Blessed Lord Rāma, out of affection, spoke to his divine parents: "I am pleased; ask for a boon, and I shall grant you whatever you desire.
(84) Since my service has been accepted by you in the form of my physical manifestation, I, the Supreme Person, have appeared before you in person to bestow a boon. (85)

"He who was seen at Badarī as Hari together with Nara, and those two who were seen within my heart in their most beautiful and divine forms—I, that Puruṣottama, have arrived here with my brother. Narāditya, my brother, though he is an ascetic, has also come along with me out of compassion to grant his own vision. Choose a boon; do not delay, for I am now departing."
Having heard this, King Śatamakha and Queen Dyuvārṇikā became greatly agitated and deeply distressed in mind.
"Stay! Stay! Do not go! Do not depart! O Lords, grant us your presence here in our palace at all times.
You are beautiful to behold and most desirable; you shall not obtain [such fortune] again, O Hari. Accept this delightful food, drink, betel, and worship. (89–91)
"Always take your delight here in this garden, granting whatever you desire. My dear sons, why is there such haste? Do not go, my two little sons!
Having spoken thus, the queen, filled with natural affection, drew her two sons close, touched them, and burst into tears.
Her breasts began to flow with milk; she could not bear to let them go. The king, his limbs overflowing with love, as did the others, was utterly enchanted by Hari.
The two Blessed Ones replied, "So be it," in that beautiful pavilion. Then, for a moment, both boys became intent on drinking milk.
Having suckled her milk, the lady Dyudharṇā attained fulfillment, being now possessed of sons named Rāmāditya and Narāditya.
She became happy, and then a great festival of joy took place there. Indeed, at midday, the King performed a celebration marking the manifestation of Rāma.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; the sages beginning with Sanaka; the seers beginning with Nārada; the devotees residing in Vaikuṇṭha;

those whose dwellings are in Satyaloka and other realms; the gods of heaven and human beings; others situated in Pātāla and below; all creatures, both insentient and sentient; holy fords, rivers, mountains, forests, and groves; the Kalpa-trees, wish-fulfilling gems, and the celestial cows—[all these worship Him]. (98–100)

At that festival, the Mantras, the Vedas, the Vittayas, the Tattvas, and all others, as well as the mind-born sons of Brahmā, arrived. The Pitṛs, the kings of the gods, and hundreds of millions of earthly monarchs came on the ninth day to offer blessings upon blessing. On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the intercalary month, when the sun was in the middle [of the sky], they beheld Rāma, just like a human being, on the occasion of the Jayantī of Rāmāditya.
Having received hospitality such as food and other honors, they felt their purpose fulfilled; and having attained Rāma’s favor, they performed beautiful songs and dances.
Śatakratu (Indra) gave gifts of cows numbering in the millions and billions, as did the carpenters, the world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, the gods, and others.
They all departed for their own abodes, and the people returned to their respective worlds. Then, in that pavilion, the midday worship was performed by the queen and the king.

In that same manner, the evening worship at night was completed; then the vigil was observed during the night, and the morning bath and other rites were performed. (107) The worship of the deity’s form, the feeding of worthy recipients, the offering of priestly fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth—all was performed according to the proper rules, and thus the vow was brought to completion. (108) Then he, together with his wife and their virtuous son, performed the ritual breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*). An inconceivable joy arose within him on account of the ninth lunar day (*navamī-tithi*). (109)

"By the vow of the month of Puruṣottama, which bestows sons—thus has this supreme of vows been told to you, O Lakṣmī! This is the most exalted merit of the Rāmādityajayantī vow. Whoever should read or hear this account of the former deeds of Rāma, or cause it to be heard with supreme devotion, shall partake in the merit of that vow. He shall obtain his heart's desire, he shall obtain a kingdom, and he shall obtain sons, wealth, and more. (110–112)
One shall obtain the fruit of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha) performed at Sāketa on the Sarayū river, and one shall obtain a powerful son who resembles Puruṣottama.
By the grace of the Supreme Soul, one shall obtain everything desired—enjoyment, liberation, happiness, heaven, and even the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how, following the sight of Nara and Nārāyaṇa during their pilgrimage to Badarikāśrama, Queen Dyutvarṇā and King Śatamakha of Sāketa performed the vow on the ninth day of the second fortnight, whereby two divine sons named Śrīrāmāditya and Narāditya became the first incarnations of Puruṣottama in the city of Sāketa," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, specifically the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama. || 1.316 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! Vikuṇṭhā, the daughter of Rādhikā in Goloka, was a maiden born by mere resolve; hear now her account, which is endowed with vows.
During the intercalary month, the Lord Puruṣottama became the presiding deity;
accompanied by Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa performed the rāsa dance at that festival. (2)
There arrived crores, billions, and trillions of cowherds, cowherd-maidens, and their wives with their daughters—all endowed with the perfection of beauty and charm. (3)
Beholding the gopīs, Rādhā herself desired a daughter among those who were childless;
the divine daughters of the gopīs then called out to their own mothers. (4)
O Mother, O Ambā, O Jananī—thus indeed do the Mothers bring joy;
yet she who is bereft of a daughter, even if joined with a husband, is not truly complete or happy. (5)
A daughter is the very embodiment of a mother; she is indeed a servant to her mother’s needs.
In every way, through constant companionship, the daughter serves her mother. (6)
At meals, at festivals, on journeys, in secret, in bathing, in the home, on the bed, or while traveling abroad—she is a servant and a daughter in providing assistance. (7)
Among the group of women, only a woman can be a physical attendant;
even among them, one's own daughter is equal [to her], but neither a daughter-in-law nor a servant. (8)
Nor is a housewife like that; rather, she is like a daughter who serves [her parents].
Therefore, a woman without a son possesses only half of good fortune. (9)
In this world, a mother finds greater happiness upon seeing her daughter's face in the morning than even from heaven; she does not find such joy from seeing her son.

Just as there is affection for a son on the part of a father, there is even greater affection for a daughter on the part of a mother. A daughter is like a cow; a young maiden is a servant to her mother. (11)
Thereafter, she should be devoted to her husband; therefore, especially for the sake of her mother, the daughter must certainly obtain a full lifespan and happiness during her maidenhood. (12)
Therefore, a daughter is in every way ten times more beloved [than a son];
she receives from her mother training in the fine arts, skillfulness, domestic duties, and so forth. (13)
A mother always dwells for a long time within her own vessel, which is her daughter;
through a virtuous daughter, she becomes renowned as a mother in both families. (14)
A daughter is fame and glory; a daughter is the funeral cake born of the mother. Seeing and touching their own daughter, mothers rejoice. (15)
A son is the very form of the father, and a daughter is the very form of the mother; a virtuous daughter is honored even by her own mother among those who possess excellent daughters. (16)
Indeed, at the beginning of the assembly and such, she who has no son appears as if withered;
but the mother, standing in the midst of the circle of her sons, shines forth there. (17)
A woman without sons is seen to be like one who has just woken from sleep;
she who has many good sons is honored among the wealthy. (18)
The wealth consisting of a daughter excels all other forms of fortune;
moreover, a woman with many daughters possesses great wealth through her numerous sons-in-law. (19)
His daughters and sons, and their sons in turn, possessed that vast wealth; like the branches of a tree, they sought refuge in its shade by the hundreds of thousands. (20)
A tree without branches indeed has no shade; it provides no shelter and is not held in esteem.
It offers no benefit to others and is likewise regarded as being without offspring. (2.1)
Seeing the supreme happiness of her daughter, the mother indeed attains great joy;
[she wonders], "I have neither daughter nor son, so how is it that Rādhā is the refuge of such happiness? (22)
If a woman who has encountered the suffering of a co-wife should possess a daughter, then indeed that suffering of rivalry ceases upon seeing that daughter. (23)
Virajā, Rukmiṇī, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Śrī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, Jayā, Vijayā, Bhāmā, Maṅgalā, Māṇikī, and Yamī. (24)
Furthermore, there are always countless millions of other co-wives who possess daughters; they are constantly seen by me, who am myself bereft of a daughter. (25)
Therefore, I shall pray for a daughter from Kṛṣṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, so that I may attain preeminence among those who possess daughters, just as I do now. (26)
Having reflected thus, Rādhā, after the great festival,
revealed her own inner state in private in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"O Lord, my beloved daughter—without my daughter, death is better.
Among all those who possess daughters, I do not shine at any festival. (28)
A woman does not shine at all without her offspring, nor does she shine when alone; even a plantain tree does not shine where there are no offspring at its side. (29)
Creepers do not shine anywhere except when supported by the vine of branches;
likewise, a doe does not shine at all without her young fawns. (30)
Lightning shines only where rain falls;
without a stream, the greatness of a river is never established anywhere. (3.1)
Without fingers, a hood does not shine, even if it is adorned;
likewise, without tranquility, knowledge does not shine, however great it may be. //32//
Without liberation, even that supreme knowledge does not shine;
just as eating, without satiety, becomes as if fruitless. ||33||
Just as a bed without a wife causes distress to youth, so too a mother without her daughter brings the sight of sorrow in old age. (34)
Therefore, I desire a daughter who is endowed with all excellent virtues, one who obeys her mother’s commands and follows the dharma of her family. (35)
She was a divine servant who attended to her mother, assisted in household duties, and protected the food, water, sacrificial fuel, leaves, vegetables, flowers, and other provisions. (36)
Sweeping, massaging, protecting the household goods, washing, as well as cooking, refining, and fetching water and so forth— (37).
A daughter who is affectionate and adorned with maternal devotion should perform this;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, O beloved abode of virtues, I have performed it here as a good daughter. (38)
She is the most excellent and renowned, the helper of her mother and father;
by seeing or remembering her, O Hari, peace is attained and desired. (39)
If I am your dear wife, and if you are pleased with me;
if I am your dear servant, and if you, my beloved, are dear to me. (40)
Then Rādhā chose from Kṛṣṇa a daughter of auspicious marks, who would indeed cause me to forget all my other daughters. ||4 1 ||
Having thus entreated the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, her beloved Rādhā embraced Him closely against her chest and served Him with deep devotion. 42.
Kṛṣṇa, having gladdened her, gave her that beautiful daughter—divine, equal in form to Rādhā, and possessing a beauty that surpassed even the form of Rādhā herself. ||43||
Born from mere volition, she was beautiful in her youth as soon as she was born;
divine, possessing a form more exquisite than that of the gopīs of the thousand celestial lotuses. ||44||
As Rādhā is, so is she; as she is, so is Rādhikā.
No internal difference at all shines forth, due to their equality as the Self of all. (45)
All the gopīs and the wives of Kṛṣṇa were bewildered and enchanted;
for a moment, they became as if paralyzed and painted in a picture. ||46||
At that very moment, such a supreme state of all activities, worthy of being witnessed, became paralyzed for everyone and for all their daughters. (47)
Kṛṣṇa too, seeing his daughter endowed with beauty, was indeed filled with joy; for here, the dullness of his worldly inclinations had vanished and steadiness of mind had truly arisen. (48)
Just as his daughter was called with affection and respect by her father Kṛṣṇa as "Vikuṇṭhā," she was likewise called by Rādhā.
Known as Vikuṇṭhā, she was the daughter of Kṛṣṇa and became Rādheyī by name;
all the inhabitants of Goloka arrived to see the maiden. ||50||
Those women praise her, saying, "Oh, how great is Rādhā’s prosperity!
Oh, what a daughter she is, possessing the divine form of Rādhā and being a vessel of supreme beauty! (5.1)
Aha! By whose fortune has this most enchanting woman been born?
He who should possess her would have a fortune even superior to that of Kṛṣṇa. (52)
He whose daughter becomes his wife according to the rites of marriage is indeed Kṛṣṇottama; he is truly Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||53||
Having spoken thus and offered their blessings, the people departed for their respective homes;
Rādhā then caused him to drink the breast milk produced at that very moment.
Kṛṣṇa performed the purificatory rites for her according to the prescribed rules and provided her with food;
his mother delighted her with caresses, protection, and other such attentions. ||55||
Then she performed service to Rādhikā with intense devotion;
having been instructed, she carried out all the household duties. (56)
Thus growing up, that woman of beautiful hips and exceeding youth went constantly with her father to behold the illustrious Puruṣottama. (57)
The Lord of syllables, the supreme Brahman, the glorious Supreme Lord, served by the infinite Kṛṣṇa, and saluted by Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā; 58.
He by whose mere fraction of splendor Kṛṣṇa and others are considered beautiful—that Puruṣottama, who is served by those joined with the beginningless Brahman. ||59||
Every morning Kṛṣṇa always goes to worship the Supreme Lord,
mounted upon a great white celestial winged elephant.
Having accepted the offerings and other gifts, the Blessed Lord, the husband of Rādhikā, returns after honoring her; or rather, it is that daughter of Kṛṣṇa who returns. || 61 ||
Upon seeing Śrī Puruṣottama, Rādhikā’s daughter felt desire; the Lord, having drawn her mind away, established it within Himself. 62.
Vikuṇṭhā meditated upon Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, whom she had seen,
and upon the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, in all her activities.
She sings of, remembers, and even beholds the illustrious Puruṣottama;
thus she constantly attends upon Him for worship.
Having performed this, Kṛṣṇa always goes to His own abode.
Vikuṇṭhā also became absorbed in Him at all times and in all her actions.
She meditated day and night to attain the status of being the wife of Puruṣottama.
At that moment, a great drum of Śrī Hari resounded there.

Today is the beautiful tenth day (Daśamī) of the intercalary month, which bestows great merit. One who performs a vow on this day in the dark fortnight obtains their desired object—whether it be a maiden, a woman, a man, or even a poor person. (67)
"By means of this vow, he shall indeed attain his own desired goal today; of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama, the beginningless Lord of the Imperishable, will surely grant everything that the seeker of the vow desires. (68–69)
"Let people not feel hesitation in making prayers;
indeed, I shall grant whatever has been resolved upon, even that which is secret, to be protected, and not to be disclosed.
Having heard this, that goddess Vikuṇṭhā performed the Daśamī vow.

For the sake of attaining Puruṣottama, she remained awake day and night. In the morning, she performed an auspicious worship of the image of Puruṣottama with the sixteen articles, as well as the offering of food, the waving of lamps, and other rites.
He performed worship with food, drink, sacrificial offerings, fruits, flowers, water, and other items, in the morning, at midday, likewise in the evening, and at night,
within that exceedingly brilliant [temple] filled with the cool-rayed splendor of Kṛṣṇacandra. (73)
At the time called cessation, which signifies the night, Puruṣottama [is present]. 74.
From the imperishable abode, he arrived there at that form known as Mūrti;
he was as radiant as ten million dark-complexioned Kṛṣṇas, lovely, and destined for the fortune of Vikuṇṭhā. ||75||
Laughing, the Lord said to her: "I have come as the bestower of the merit of your vow;
I am pleased by your devotion. Choose a boon, O sinless daughter of Kṛṣṇa. (76)

There is nothing that cannot be given to you by me, for you always remember me; to you who are devoted to no other, who are full of devotion, and who belong to Kṛṣṇa, I shall give whatever is desired.
Then Vikuṇṭhā, both pleased and bashful, said to him:
"O Lord of my life, you abide within my heart; nothing is unknown to you. (78)
Nevertheless, out of affection for your devotees, you indeed entertain this inquiry.
O Blessed One, my Lord, become my master and the lord of my life. (79)
"O Lord, O Master, this garland of choice is offered; please give your command.
"So be it," Hari replied; indeed, Hari spoke even more than that. (80)
Listen: I am not of a single form, for I dwell in various abodes;
I, Śrī Puruṣottama, always dwell in the imperishable abode. 8.1.
I dwell as the second [form] in the abode of Mahāvaikuṇṭha;
likewise, I am the third in Vaikuṇṭha at the end of the watery covering.
I also dwell as the fourth in Vaikuṇṭha known as Śvetadvīpa;
and I also dwell as the fifth in Vaikuṇṭha situated within the Ocean of Milk. ||83||
Therefore, you too must dwell everywhere in your divine form; for it is not possible to remain everywhere with only a single physical form. (84)
Consequently, it must certainly be made to possess manifold forms;
moreover, this is for the sake of service by your beloved Rādhikā. (85)
"You were created by Him; therefore, O beautiful one, you ought not to abandon Him!
You must remain at all times solely for the sake of serving Rādhā. (86)
"Thus, you must remain assuming these six forms in every way;
therefore, out of compassion for me, let these six forms indeed become yours. (87)
Thus addressed, she became sixfold by a drop of his grace;
among them, one was worthy of dwelling in the imperishable abode and superior in every respect. (88)
A realm fit for the Supreme Person, characterized by eternal liberation, came into being;
the Supreme Person took Vikuṇṭhā as his wife. ||89||
The second [form], who was in the nature of a daughter and fit for the service of Rādhikā, Keśava indeed established as that maiden in Goloka. (90)
Just as the maiden Vikuṇṭhā previously remained in that very place,
so too is the third [aspect] of Vikuṇṭhā pervasive and embodied.
There, that pervasive form became twofold in every respect;
it became the abode known as Vaikuṇṭha, which is the form of the divine realm (adhidaiva). || 92 ||
That pervasive abode is called Mahāvaikuṇṭha;
there, she became Mahālakṣmī, the consort of Nārāyaṇa.
The fourth form of Vaikuṇṭhā likewise became twofold:
the Vaikuṇṭha of the water-enveloped realm and the one consisting of light as its presiding deity.
One [form] became all-pervading, while the second was the form of Lakṣmī;
she, Viṣṇu’s consort known as Vikuṇṭhā, serves Viṣṇu with devotion. (95)
Then the fifth form of Vaikuṇṭhā became twofold:
the Vaikuṇṭha known as Śvetadvīpa, which consists of pure light and is the presiding deity. (96)
One [form] became all-pervading, while the second was the form of Lakṣmī;
she, Viṣṇu’s consort named Vikuṇṭhā, serves Viṣṇu with devotion. (97)
And then the sixth form of Vikuṇṭhā also became twofold;
that which is known as Kṣīra-Vaiṣṇava is composed of splendor and is the presiding deity. ||98||
One became the all-pervading [form], and the second was the form of Lakṣmī;
she, Viṣṇu’s consort known as Vikuṇṭhā, serves Viṣṇu with devotion. (99)
Thus, her six beautiful forms as divine women—those consorts of the Lord known as Vikuṇṭhās—reside in the six sacred sites. 10.0.
By the will of Hari, the four Vaikuṇṭhas became divine abodes and their presiding deities. (10.1)
The four pervasive goddesses, having united, became ten at all times; indeed, they assumed distinct forms through their vow to please Hara.
O Lakṣmī! What does the true grace of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Svāmī-Puruṣottama not accomplish? It even becomes the realm of Vaikuṇṭha itself. 102.
"Know yourself to be He, the Supreme Person;
likewise, know that your husband is the Supreme Person. (104)
Knowing this, you worship me there as well as here, O beloved of mine;
I know all of that with the clarity of constant direct perception.
"You do not know all this; my will is the cause therein.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the account regarding the Daśamī vow been told to you. (10.6)
The forms of you, Vikuṇṭhā, became tenfold as fruit;
by my will, they were thus born for the sake of bestowing grace upon me. (107)
Whether one recites it or even hears it, the fruit for that person is likewise;
as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), I grant what is desired and fulfill it out of compassion. 108.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Six Forms of Lakṣmī and the Four Forms of the Deities of the Vaikuṇṭha Abodes," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, concerning the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama, regarding the grace of Lord Puruṣottama who was pleased by the Daśamī vow of the mental daughter of Rādhikā named Vikuṇṭhā, as bestowed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (1.317)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the auspicious story of a female bee in a previous kalpa.
In the first Kṛta age, there was a daughter of Rudra who became a female bee.
That truthful daughter of Mānasa always dwells upon a banyan tree on Mount Mandara, at the incarnation of Rudra, beneath that banyan tree. || 2 ||
Having made her dwelling in the abode of her father, the pure maiden remains there; she is Satyā, who was seen without offspring, and she is Vikuṇṭhā, the daughter of Rādhikā. (3)
Then she repeatedly prayed to Śaṅkara, "May I have a daughter.
Being pleased, Śaṅkara granted her wish, saying, "So be it," and fulfilled her resolve.
In that very Mandara forest, taking refuge under the banyan tree of his own incarnation, Satī, who was of divine form and born of his mind, sported. || 5 ||
A daughter was born, possessed of a splendor exceeding that of ten million moons;
as soon as she was born, she was beautiful, in the full bloom of youth, and as pure as Satī herself.
Possessing even greater beauty than that, an abode of all divine qualities, she—
who possessed divine awakening from the very moment of her birth— bowed at the feet of her father.
She bowed at her mother's feet like a servant girl, and Satī became exceedingly gracious; Rudra, too, was most happy.
Though childless, he became possessed of offspring, his joy being increased;
and there on Mount Mandara, a festival was celebrated by Śambhu in truth.
The gods and goddesses, the humans and the guardians of the quarters, as well as the great sages, the progenitors, and others such as Viṣṇu and Dakṣa. || 10 ||
Couples went there for the great birth festival of the ant; the seven sages performed the consecration according to the rite and placed the sacred thread upon her.
Having been bestowed with spiritual luster, she shone, surpassing all in brilliance;
thus that virtuous woman served her father, who was the very embodiment of Brahman. 12.
Established in yoga, she remains even in meditative absorption as if with her parents;
dwelling at the banyan tree, she has made her hall under the shade of the banyan and takes refuge in the banyan. (13)
Her garments were adorned with banyan bark; she subsisted on the fruit of the banyan tree;
she drank the milk of the banyan tree; and her ornaments were made of banyan fruit. (14)
At the foot of a banyan tree, she wore a garment made from the fibers of a nyagrodha root;
having prepared an altar for the performance of fire-offerings, she was clad in a fine bodice of banyan leaves.

Always possessing the form of a banyan tree, with her arms well-circled by the wood of that banyan, she was a female ascetic; as the daughter of the banyan, she shone, embodying all spiritual perfections. (16)
Whatever one desires, all that appears there:
riches, prosperities, fortunes, essences, objects of enjoyment, and indeed nectar itself. (17)
Various nectars and diverse milks were milked there;
the essences of all trees and all kinds of jewels were also present there. (18)
All objects of enjoyment and requisites appear at that banyan tree;
by the power of yoga, she perceives everything before her. (19)
Having gone to the root-support (mūlādhāra) at the anus-cakra, he meditated upon the divine Gaṇapati;
by contemplating his power, he brought him under control in every respect. 20.
Having gone to the four-faced [deity] in the Svādhiṣṭhāna cakra at the root of the womb, he meditated upon his power and brought everything under his control. 21.
Having gone to the Viṣṇu-cakra at the maṇipūra in the region of the navel, one meditates upon its power and brings everything under control in every way. (22)
Having gone to the unstruck (anāhata) wheel in the heart and meditated upon Śiva residing there, the Yoginī brings even his entire power under her control. ||23||
Having performed supreme *saṃyama* upon one's own self at the *viśuddhi-cakra* located in the throat, one brings the power of the reality of the Self under control in every respect. (2.4)

Having meditated upon the *haṃsa* and likewise the Guru within the *ājñācakra* between the eyebrows, one brings under control even Brahmā and others; such a person attains knowledge and reaches omniscience. (25)
Having gone even to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), she, having reached the world of Brahmā, beholds the glorious Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama. || 26 ||
Sometimes, by means of samādhi, she goes toward the city of Brahmā;
sometimes she goes to the world of Vaikuṇṭha and toward the white city. (27)
He goes to Goloka, the immortal abode, and to Śrīpura, the city of Vāsava;
sometimes to the realm of Śiva, sometimes to that of Brahmā, and to the realms of Sūrya, Candra, and Varuṇa. || 28 ||
The realm of Kubera, the worlds of the gods, and those of Prakṛti and Puruṣa; the world of Sāṃkarṣaṇa, the abode of Pradyumna, and that of Aniruddha. (29)
By means of meditative absorption, he goes to the worlds of the twenty-four principles,
as well as to the abodes of the Asuras, the Nāgas, and the goddesses.
The Yoginī moves through the terrestrial sphere, the celestial sphere, and the entire universe,
by way of the paths of the Iḍā, the Piṅgalā, and the Suṣumṇā.
Relying upon yoga, she went to the worlds of the sun, the moon, and other celestial realms;
by the path of yoga, she proceeded to Saṃyamanī, the city of Dharma.
Assuming many forms, she dwells even in the banyan tree like an ant;
she also resides in other trees, in Vaikuṇṭha, and in Śrīpura.
Having become an ant within the great treasury of Kubera, that Yakṣiṇī remains there as the Yakṣiṇī of Wealth (Dhanayakṣiṇī) and likewise as a protector. 34.
Having thus assumed many forms, she indeed sports as she pleases;
because she was born beneath a banyan tree (vaṭa), she is known as Vaṭasāvitrikā. || 35 ||
That Vaṭayakṣiṇī was the guardian of that banyan tree and gold;
because she dwelt among the trees, she was always known as Vārkṣī and Vamrī. (3.6)
One should always perform the Vaṭasāvitrī-kṛcchra, which bestows union with a husband; by worshipping Vaṭasāvitrī, one never encounters widowhood. (37)
Poverty shall never arise from the worship of Vaṭayakṣiṇī;
the Yakṣiṇī bestows fortune, prosperity, and wealth. (38)
The honored Vārkṣī bestows crops, grains of food, cereals, and so forth;
Vārkṣī exists everywhere within trees in the form of sap. (39)
She who is honored at the banyan tree bestows wealth;
she is Vamrī, the daughter of Satī, skilled in yogic practice, present in every place. (40)
Having traveled by means of the practice of yoga, he beheld in all creations pairs consisting of husbands and wives, even those born of the mind.
O beloved! [These] divine bodies, endowed with merit, belong to the lords, the gods, and humans, as well as to the trees. 42.
Having seen and reflected upon the Dharma, [he realized that] youth without a husband appears as a source of fault for women and devoid of purity within the worlds. (43)
"Therefore, I too must unite with my husband, who shares the same dharma.
Having reflected thus, that female termite, the virtuous daughter of Satī, Susundarī— ||44||
She sat down upon the sacrificial altar beneath a banyan tree on Mount Mandara;
at that moment, ten divine Pracetas brothers arrived at her side. (45)
Having paid homage to Śaṅkara, they again went to his side, accompanied by attendants who were equal to themselves in beauty, endowed with vigor, and matured by youth. (46)
At that time, the mind of the female bee toward them became somewhat affectionate;
with her mind distracted, she kept remembering those very [bees] while at this banyan tree. (47)
He heard the drum sounding loudly, announcing the vow for the intercalary month:
"Today is the Ekādaśī festival, which bestows merit even during an intercalary month. (48)
Whatever is desired by the performer of the vow shall be accomplished without effort.
O Puruṣottama, I, Kṛṣṇa, grant the desired object to the seeker of the vow. 49.
O Dundubhi, I, Śrī Puruṣottama himself, speak here directly:
"May gods and humans receive from me whatever boon they desire. (50)
May men, women, gods, and goddesses come into my presence;
I grant the merit of the Ekādaśī vow as desired by the mind. ॥5 1 ॥
Having heard that drum, the ant quickly approached it;
having honored the drum, the maiden spoke ten times. (52)
Give a husband, give a husband, give a husband, husband, husband.
Give a husband, give a husband, give a husband, husband, husband. ॥53॥
Having heard this, Dundubhi said, "So be it," and departed from there;
she too went quickly to the banyan tree so that the virtuous woman would not know her whereabouts. (54)
Clear-minded, with a joyful heart, and endowed with the wealth of granting boons, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama again heard that musical sound. ||55||
"Pleased by your worship, he will quickly fulfill your heart's desire.
Having heard this, she [saw] the image of Pauruṣottama beneath the banyan tree. ||56||
Having performed [the preliminary rites], he worshipped [him] with banyan leaves, fruits, and other offerings;
having invoked [the deity], caused him to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and offered a seat. ||57||
Having offered water for the feet and the respectful oblation (arghya), he bathed Hari with curd, milk, water,
sugar, honey, and clarified butter.
The Sovereign Goddess wiped the water from her limbs with a cloth; she then put on a washed tiger-skin garment as an undergarment and an elephant-hide garment as an upper robe.
Having offered a sacred thread made of *darbha* grass and dyed with the bark of the *vaṭa* tree,
as well as desired ornaments and golden earrings.
Golden and silver vessels, musk, sandalwood, and unbroken grains of rice;
incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, betel, fruits, and chewing-gum. || 61 ||

Having performed the nightly lamp-offering, prostrating like a staff, and likewise offering circumambulations and hymns of praise, he then presented a handful of flowers and sang a song of glorification.
Having likewise worshipped Keśava at midday, in the evening, and at night, the ant performed a vigil with dancing in the presence of Hari. (63)
Sounding her hand-drum, mingled with the tinkling of small bells, she performed a sweet song accompanied by melodic verses. (64)
Upon hearing that, the forest trees, the creepers, and the grasses approached; even the flower clusters arrived, their consciousness drawn by the sound. (65)
All those forest-dwellers, including their followers and even those who were without a formal group, having been drawn by the mere sound [of his voice], arrived at Vaṭasthala. ||66||
For the worship of Puruṣottamadeva, water is nectar; likewise, the prasāda, other fruits, leaves, flowers, and so forth [are offerings]. (67)
After giving to all of them, Vamrikā then accepted this worship of the Bhāgavata, as did Satī and Śaṅkara. ||68||
Having witnessed this supreme marvel, they both offered praise to their daughter and bestowed blessings upon her:
"O daughter! May you be happy according to your every desire. (69)
Become Vaiṣṇavī, O auspicious one! Become the bestower of happiness to the forest. Become an ascetic woman, the power of Brahman, and beloved by the most excellent of men. ||70||
"O you who dwell upon the banyan tree, worthy of worship and honor, become the bestower of the essence of trees!"—with such words of benediction did Śiva and Pārvatī consecrate her. (71)
Then, having thus performed the worship and the dismissal of Hari,
she withdrew from the assembly and sat down upon the pedestal at the banyan tree.
At that moment, a man possessing a divine form arrived there;
his limbs were proportionate to his beauty, and he was as radiant as ten million Śambhus.
Like a suitable young bridegroom, richly endowed with the exquisite beauty of a moon-like face, he laughed, drew her toward him, and, adorned with the Kaustubha gem, said, "My beloved! (74)
Bowing her face low and recognizing Śrī Puruṣottama, the female bee fell at the feet of him who bears the discus and the lotus. (75)
"Speak, O Goddess! I, Puruṣottama, am pleased by your vow.
Ask for a boon; I shall grant it here, whatever dwells in your mind. (76)
Then the female ant, having bowed at her feet, placed water in her mouth, took the dust upon her head, and placed her lotus-feet upon her breast. (77)
Placing his hands above his throat, fixing his mind within the expanse of his heart, and directing his eyes toward his own eyes, he took hold of Puruṣottama. ||78||
"Take your wife as your maidservant," she said; but Mādhava, Hari, perceiving her true intention, replied, "So be it. (79)
And he said to that female ant: "Remember what you previously requested ten times in my presence: 'Grant me husband after husband. (80)
"I alone shall be your husband, the manifest Śrī Puruṣottama;
become one of divine form and come together with me. (8.1)
In the supreme, imperishable abode, my wife is eternal;
moreover, you shall become her mind-born daughter, Satī, who is always devoted to the service of Śiva. (82)
May the maiden Vaṭasāvitrikā always remain here;
she is the daughter of Rudra, the Yakṣiṇī of the banyan tree, and the guardian of wealth. 8.3.
Even within the mines of the earth, you remain in the form of Rudrī;
remember how, upon seeing Pracetas, your mind became filled with affection. (84)
Therefore, those ten pure Pracetasas shall become your husbands;
however, they are considered unsuitable for you in this present body. (85)
Therefore, O beloved, become the daughter of whichever trees are present here for the purpose of worship; thus it shall be. 8.6.
"By my command, your name shall certainly become Vārkṣī;
O Goddess, become the daughter of a tree, assuming ten forms. (87)
Listen, I shall tell you this: here assume those various forms—trees, pillars, crops, vegetables, and grasses. (88)
Reeds, creepers, stalks, leaves, and bulbous roots—accepting the status of father toward these ten, become tenfold. (89)
Indeed, among those possessing only branches and fruit, and those possessing only flowers and branches;
and indeed, among those possessing only branches and flowers, and those possessing only fruit and branches. (90)
Indeed, [the tree] with branches, fruits, and flowers [is compared] to that without branches, fruits, and flowers;
and indeed, [the tree] with branches but without fruits and flowers [is compared] to that without branches, fruits, and flowers. || 9.1 ||
"O you who possess only branches and leaves, and you who are merely without branches or leaves!
Having become my daughter, grant me juices; let there truly be ten daughters. (9.2)
Having spoken thus with great devotion, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa assumed the form of an ant suitable for his abode, took her with him, and departed joyfully. || 93 ||
One form remained in the guise of a daughter for the sake of Satī, while the other forms became young tree-maidens in the full bloom of their youth. (94)
Then those trees of various species, having come into being, brought [the fruits] and,
according to dharma, gave them to the ten Pracetas.
In every respect, they bestow aesthetic delight and indeed grant the fruits [of their practice], through the instruction of Nārada during the liberation of the Pracetasas. 96.
"Even for those born of trees, liberation will indeed come; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus performed the Ekādaśī vow, the female ant, the daughter of a virtuous woman," 97.
For by means of her spiritual body, she attained the eternal, supreme abode;
indeed, she reached the state of being the consort of Puruṣottama, which bestows desired happiness. (98)
Likewise, the divine female bees and those born from trees arose from a drop of Hari’s compassion;
the divine female bees were the first-born on the altar of Rudra, O excellent one. (99)
At the divine sacrifice of Makha, there were fuel-sticks on the earth;
by hearing and reciting this [text], one obtains the fruit arising from the vow of Ekādaśī. || 100 ||
He who obtains or causes this to be recited becomes possessed of an abundance of wealth and grain;
through the pleasing of Puruṣottama, he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 101 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Satī and Rudra’s Daughter, the Yoginī Vamrī, Attaining a Brāhmī Body Fit for Her Desired Abode of Imperishable Brahman by Performing the Ekādaśī Vow of the Adhika-māsa Month, and Her Subsequent Manifestations as the Wife of the Ten Pracetasas and as the Daughter of a Tree," in the section on the Greatness of the Month of Puruṣottama within the first book, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 1.318.

→ Chapter 320
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story born from the feet of Vairāja,
concerning the goddess Joṣṭrī who emerged at the beginning of creation as his attendant.
The Vairāja Puruṣa, having produced his son Brahmā from the region of his navel,
then presented to him a female servant named Joṣṭrī,
who was born from the feet of the Vairāja and was devoted to the Creator.
In the world of truth (Satyaloka), the Unborn (Aja) caused you— who were always like a maidservant— to dwell there.
Meditated upon by Brahmā with his mind as a servant again and again,
she gave birth in many ways to various classes of beings, born of her own nature, as if in a dream.
Having given birth to his daughter named Aśanā, he bestowed her upon the Ṛṣis;
and having given birth to his daughter named Pipāsā, he bestowed her upon the Pitṛs. Having also given birth to his daughter named Aśanā, he bestowed her upon the Devas. (5)
Having brought forth [the quality of] passion (*rajas*) among ghosts, spirits, and demons, she established the latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Among the mountains, having brought forth the daughter Karā, she established it.
Among human beings, having brought forth the daughter Vyavasāyā, she established it. (6–7)
Among the Dānavas, she forcibly gave birth to a daughter named Prasahyā and entrusted her [to them];
among the Daityas, she gave birth to a daughter named Vilāsā and entrusted her [to them];
and among the beasts and birds, she gave birth to a daughter named Viśvāsā and entrusted her [to them].
Having given birth to that daughter Meghā among the trees and creepers, he deposited her there.
Having given birth to Kardamā among insects, moths, and small creatures, he deposited her there.
Having given birth to his daughter Kumbhikā among those who dwell in water, he deposited her there.
Having thus given birth to twelve daughters according to their respective natures, that female camel gave them, one by one, with great respect, as attendants to the various creatures.
In this way, the female camel remained ever devoted to service for the Creator.
Indeed, he always remained in Satyaloka in the dharma of service.
Just as there are six duties for a Brahmin that grant liberation,
so too is service considered to bring liberation for the fourth caste.
Just as protection is considered to bring about the highest good for Kṣatriyas,
so too does service bestow the highest good upon the class of servants.
And just as giving indeed brings prosperity to the Vaiśya in both worlds.
In this way, the class of female attendants may obtain blessings through service.
(15) Just as for a maidservant, constant adherence to commands leads to liberation, so too does the service of the class of male attendants grant liberation. (16)
Just as virtue within the vow of celibacy provides protection, so too shall service always provide protection for the female servant.
Just as respect for the duties of the householder provides protection, [so too shall it be]. (17)
Just as service performed by a group of attendants becomes a source of protection,
and just as penance is considered to bring happiness to those dwelling in the forest, so too does constant happiness accrue to the one who performs such service. (18–19)
Just as the renunciation of those who possess the spirit of renunciation is considered to bestow supreme bliss,
so too service performed with devotion truly grants joy to the servant.
Just as sacrifice, austerity, meditation, recitation, charity, oblations, and the like [bestow bliss], [so does such service].
Service bestows happiness in both worlds and grants joy everywhere.
(21) Through service, one attains heaven, sovereignty, prosperity, wealth and the like, as well as fame, renown, merit, and the eternal, certain liberation. (22)
Service to Kṛṣṇa, service to one’s mother, service to one’s father, service to oneself;
service to the gods, service to people, service to the elderly, and service to the distressed;
service to one’s husband, service to virtuous women, service to one’s wife, and worship of the Lord. (23)
Service to cows, the earth, the Dharma, the helpless, and those who have sought refuge; honoring the subjects;
service to one's master; service to guests; and the like, such as pleasing others and oneself—these bring happiness in this world and the next, bestow merit, and grant peace. (24–25)

Through the increase of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), however, that which is performed becomes the cause of liberation. Service to the body, service with wealth, massaging the feet and so forth, service to the qualities, service to the objects, service with food, and the offering of water—[all these lead to liberation]. (26)
Service to the household, service to the sick, service to the world, and so forth—
all such acts performed with the vision of Brahman become givers of happiness and givers of liberation.
Therefore, the dharma of service should be understood as being inaccessible indeed to all embodied beings.
Everything else may exist, but service does not occur without faith;
indeed, even if performed, service does not truly become joined [to the goal] without meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
Service may arise from the desire for liberation, or it may also arise from the desire for happiness.
Service may be performed even out of a desire for one's own interest or with a longing for its fruit;
however, that which is performed without desire indeed bestows a reward a millionfold.
For the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is the giver of fruit for an action performed without desire.
Having reflected thus, she caused her daughters to perform service for all people— service by which the inner self is satisfied.
When the virtuous are pleased by such service, they bestow blessings.
The aged Brahmins bestow their blessings upon the one who serves;
by that service, the body attains destruction for the sake of the Supreme.
In this world, it finds companionship; therefore, one should practice service.
Benefiting others never goes to waste anywhere;
even service never becomes fruitless, even after the passage of time.
What is not given does not remain with one; only what is given truly remains.
Non-service does not bring results; service performed brings results.
A living being should always serve their father, guru, and the Imperishable Lord with body, mind, and speech; the fruit thereof shall be eternal. (36–37)
Thus Joṣṭrī always served the Supreme Lord with truth,
and she performed auspicious service to the subjects day after day along with her daughters.
Once, however, an assembly was held in the Sudharmā hall.
Sages, seers, gods, ancestors, humans, and trees;
likewise piśācas and others, as well as bulbous roots, creepers, daityas, and dānavas—all embodied beings dwelling in the fourteen worlds—have arrived. (39–40)
Both invisible and visible, they arrived together with their wives;
all twelve of them came along with those various leaders of the assembly.
Their attendants, appearing as female servants, were daughters of camel-herders who provided food and other necessities.
They attended those assemblies for which they were suitable;
indeed, by performing each respective service, all the various classes [of beings] were gratified.
Being pleased, they bestowed rewards and blessings upon them.
May they all possess good fortune, be filled with eternal bliss,
and be honored for their wealth, grain, fame, renown, dignity, and virtues;
may they be endowed with spiritual accomplishments and sovereignty, and indeed bear beautiful forms.

May these goddesses, who increase the lineage of the camel-leader, who always possess great splendor, who illuminate the world, and who are the servants of [the Lord], remain forever as the attendants of Brahmā, possessing eternal and stable youth. 45–46.
Thus, having received blessings when the assembly had concluded,
all the sisters of their mother’s eldest daughter returned for a moment to her home.
Meanwhile, in Satyaloka, the great drum of Śrī Hari—
The sound uttered by Puruṣottama was heard:
"In this additional month, on the twelfth day, let embodied beings perform my worship and my vow, which is my sole refuge. (48-49)
"I, the Supreme Person, shall grant whatever your heart desires.
You must not be negligent in this matter; though the vow is brief, its hardship is great.
Let those whose fortune is indeed radiant take up that fruit."

Out of compassion, I am Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in every respect; I am the Giver. (5.1) I shall grant perfections, I shall grant my abode, and I shall indeed grant eternal happiness. I shall give everything, and I shall give myself; I shall not, however, give that which is undesired. (5.2)
Perform the vow by eating once a day, or by eating only at night, or by subsisting on fruit;
or by subsisting on water, or on curd, or on grain that has been rinsed;
or perform the vow by eating from a leaf-plate, or with tubers and roots, or by subsisting on air alone.
Even if a vow has been performed by a mere fragment of my grace—
whether with buttermilk or milk, or with sesame seeds and handfuls of beans—
whichever vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) has been undertaken with whatever disposition; ||54–55||
I shall fulfill all his desires in every way.
My worship must be performed in the morning, at midday, and at the onset of night;
likewise, a vigil must be observed and offerings of food must be given.

Gifts should also be given according to one's capacity and according to what has been acquired. (57) One should offer me a handful of flowers, and likewise a handful of unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*); one should offer a handful of water, and one should offer a handful of meditative devotion (*bhāvanā*). (58)
The observer of the vow should offer an añjali of affection, he should offer an añjali of his very self,
and he should offer everywhere the most excellent añjali of total surrender.
I am to be reached through inner disposition, reached through affection, and reached through love.
Whether I am accessible through external objects or accessible through my own self, let it be so.
Long life will pass away, youth will pass away, and all prosperities will go to destruction; yet my compassion is considered eternal.
Yogic practices will fall into decay; nourishment will turn to decrepitude;
the body will become ashes; yet my compassion is considered eternal.
Whatever has arisen—be it merit, sovereignty, wealth, or the like—that shall perish.
My compassion is eternal, for its destruction is never found.
(63) May the wretched take hold of this compassion; may they cast far away their poverty.
By my command and by this very vow, may they indeed become eternally enriched. (64)
Having thus heard the sound of the drum, those twelve daughters of Mātṛvardhana undertook a vow of subsisting on milk for twelve days on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
Even the camel-maiden observed the vow with water, imbued with her sincere devotion.

Having bathed in the morning and remembered Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, they fashioned thirteen golden images and worshipped Puruṣottama. They constructed a pavilion with plantain pillars and archways made of aśoka, mango, and other trees.
Adorned with garlands of flowers, beautified by golden garments and the like,
and decorated with festive lamps, fine jars, archways, and other ornaments;
having had a beautiful mandala called Sarvatobhadra constructed in its center.
Having placed a beautiful golden vessel with five-jeweled sprouts,
cloth, fruit, sandalwood, and unbroken grains (akṣata) in its center,
one should set upon its top a golden bowl containing sesame seeds and sugar.
Having installed the Lord of Gods, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama, there,
they worshipped him with devotion using the sixteen articles of worship.
Having performed the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), they honored him with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with water.
Having bathed Him and performed the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and having adorned Śrī Kṛṣṇa with garments and ornaments,
with saffron, collyrium, sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and sandalwood powder,
one should offer incense and a lamp.
The food offering should consist of excellent milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
sweet foods such as *pūrikās*, fruits such as mangoes, and a drink of sweet nectar-like water.
O Lord, whatever else is desired— be it betel leaf, fruit, or anything else— [should be offered].
Having offered all of those things, they performed the *ārātrika* rite; then, at dawn,
they offered prostrations like a staff, hymns of praise, circumambulations, handfuls of flowers,
requests for forgiveness for their offenses, and the final *arghya*.
They continued their service in that manner at midday and even at night;
during the night, they kept watch, performing dances, singing, and other such acts.
Those twelve maidens were filled with amorous gestures and expressions.

Just as Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Nārāyaṇa, and Śrī Puruṣottama—may that Supreme Person be pleased through the sentiment of the erotic rasa; and being drawn by it, may that compassionate one grant his vision. (78–79)
Thus, with great joy, they performed dancing and singing.
At dawn, during the Brahma-hour,
Hari appeared, laughing— a youth, well-nourished, and handsome, who dwells within the minds of young women.

Exceedingly beautiful beyond measure, with limbs fortified by valor; pervaded by delight in every hair-pore, illuminated by the god of love in every limb—he said repeatedly, "I am pleased, I am pleased! because of his service. (8.1–8.2)
The female attendant chose all her desired boons in every way:
"May I be Indrāṇī, or Śivā, or even Brahmāṇī;
may I be Kṛṣṇā, or Vaiṣṇavī, or Brāhmī, or even beyond that. (83)
"Whatever you may desire, I shall grant it to you this very day; of this there is no doubt.
By means of service, faith, and devotion moistened with affection, you women have conquered the worlds beyond the highest through your twelvefold nature."
Indeed, you who were formerly maidservants have today become non-servants through your service;
therefore, O heart-entrancing ones, choose him who dwells in your minds this very day, and do not delay!
I am the servant of my female attendants and the teacher of the scriptures.
Among friends I am the friend; among the beautiful I am the most excellent.
Among the affectionate I am the affectionate, and among those who seek refuge I am the protector.
For those who have renounced all their possessions for my sake, I am the giver of all their possessions.
I do not obtain such satisfaction through wealth, servants,
or service as I obtain from the service performed by my own self.
I am both the servant and the master where service is not divided.
"Wherever a devotee serves me personally with their own being, let my dear ones speak:
'What shall I give? What shall I say?
What shall I bestow upon my dear ones—my very self, together with my heart'? (90–91)

"All of us, our beloveds, have offered ourselves to the Supreme Self—to the Supreme Beloved, the Beloved of all, our husband, Śrī Puruṣottama. For female servants, likewise, the duty toward the Teacher is indeed total self-surrender. (92)
Likewise, O beloved, it is the duty of those who are dear to offer everything to their beloved;
and likewise, it is the duty of the husband to always accept what has been offered.
Indeed, it is the duty of one who is dear to the beloved to act for the pleasure of the beloveds.
"The beloved is the entire possession of the beloved; the beloved does everything for the sake of the beloved.
And the beloved alone is the entire possession of the beloved—he is indeed a treasure-house of compassion.
Thus, O Keśava, act as you wish in this matter of great significance.
"Your mind and your entire being have been offered to me; do whatever you deem right.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord, then said:
"I know everything, and likewise I accept all within my heart."
Even from without, I take their hands and make them dear to my heart;
by the touch of my hand, may they assume divine forms and become my beloved wives forever in the abode known as the Imperishable.
May my Joṣṭrī be of the nature of light, a power consisting of splendor;
the goddess who bestows all bliss, composed of consciousness, and identical with my own nature.
That conscious one, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, has been created by me as my very self. (99–100)
"Let there also be twelve other wives for me who are eternal;
let those wives dwell in my house there,
each bearing my own name and possessing a form exactly like mine in every respect."

For she indeed never partakes of any other pleasure or the like without me; thus is the meaningful description of "fasting" (anaśana). Now hear about "thirst" (pipāsā) according to its essential meaning:
she who always desires to drink my nectar alone and no other. (102–103)
That wife of mine, Pipāsā, was protected by me in my own form;
and now my wife Aśanā, who always eats me,
enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahmā.
Thus, that wife of mine named Sārthāśanā was protected by me;
and that latent impression (*vāsanā*) which always causes me, her supreme husband, to dwell within her own self—that wife, full of being, was well-protected by me. (105–106)
She whose name must be uttered here, she for whom meditation has been cultivated by me—she, my beloved, indeed comes to my hand, holding my hand.
She is *kaṃ* (bliss), the supreme joy of me; she is *śaṃ* (peace), *lakṣmī* (fortune), and divine prosperity.
She who goes to serve me and receives [gifts] from me is Karāyikā.
(108) She by whom my entire being—consisting of both action and the agent—is made for my sake alone;
she is Vyavasāyā, beloved to me because of the meaningfulness of her resolve. (109)
She who is capable of enduring all my actions is dear to me;
she who intensely endures my pleasure is *prasahyakā*.
She who sports in every way for my sake is divine and devoted to my purpose.
My wife, named Vilāsā, acts as my companion in pleasure;
she is unable to remain alive even for a moment without my breath.
Indeed, I belong to her and she belongs to me as my husband, truly for our mutual happiness.
Thus, having attained confidence, my beloved is full of trust;
for her, there is no life or breath at every moment without me.
She pours forth, she rains down, and she showers her love upon her husband, her lord.
She who shows affection for me is considered by me to be my beloved Meghā. She who restrains herself with devotion toward me in every action—
she whose self-restraint is for my sake— is my beloved Kardamā.
She who daily contemplates her own body as my field for my sake,
just as one holds water in a jar, sustains me within her own self;
she is my wife Kumbhikā, while you are proclaimed to be my wives.
May those twelve divine ones dwell within my imperishable abode.
Furthermore, let them indeed exist in other forms as the twelvefold powers,
assuming different appearances and dedicated to Mahākāla.
From that, it pervaded the universe, encompassing both the eater and the eaten;
indeed, the flow of thirst runs at the forefront of this cycle of existence.
Through latent impression (*vāsanā*), this world—composed of a mixture of the insentient and the sentient—dwells within it.
In this world, there occurs an exchange between two embodied beings.
The year— carried by time, sustained by effort, and prevailing through force— endures and supports them, while also enduring their afflictions and dualities.
Through his playfulness (*vilāsa*), he dispels the weariness of living beings and unites them with life;
through his trustworthiness (*viśvāsa*), embodied beings engage in action out of desire for the fruit.
Through his cloud-like showers of affection (*megha-sneha-vṛṣṭi*), he indeed gladdens all subjects equally.
All beings born of mud abide within me, in that mud.
In these jars, in the globes, and in all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), she who establishes them in their respective places is considered the Protectress, Kuṃbhikā. 123–124.
"Thus, may the powers of Time— which is my own power— perform their functions day by day in the world, dedicated to Time. Then,
where the daughters of Joṣṭrikā lived as they had been...
"May they dwell even within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) by performing the piercing [of the cakras] in that very same manner.
May they dwell there by my desire, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa’s, through their own third forms as the mothers of the camel-boys. || 126–127 ||
Thus, having been properly appointed by me through these three forms,
perform service here to Mahākāla as well as to me.
I am your master, your husband, the glorious Puruṣottama.
"May they sport with me, independent in the supreme syllable.
Likewise, others who have Mahākāla as their companion, being forms of my own power;
and likewise others who always carry out their respective tasks within my creation. (129–130)
"Thus, threefold service has been granted by me to you;
indeed, the eternal fruit of the vow of Dvādaśī has been bestowed.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, [departed].
Having taken those divine ones along and likewise established others there, Hari gave yet others to Mahākāla and departed for the imperishable abode.
O Lakṣmī! Speak: Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of mercy, is the supreme among men.
"What does she give? Out of compassion, she grants an infinite fruit for even a small [offering].
Thus, the entire narrative of the goddess Joṣṭrī has been told to you.
The goddess Joṣṭrī, the bestower of wealth, [praised] the god Indra, the sustainer of vitality.
Having reached the Supreme Person, the great Vedic knowledge increased.
Whoever shall cause this to be heard, or shall hear it, or shall recite it—
for him too there will certainly be a fruit equal to that of the vow.

Thus ends the three hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Puruṣottama-Nārāyaṇa, who was pleased by the service of the twelve daughters beginning with Joṣṭrī— the daughter of Vairāja— and by the vow of the twelfth day, as well as His assuming of the threefold forms," in the section on the Greatness of the Month of Puruṣottama within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
