Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Having seen the excellent Rādhikā possessed of a daughter...
Śrī also spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord and Master of the Gods:
"O Hari, O Beloved, just as a woman who has a daughter shines like Rādhā, she attains honor in every way among all women who have daughters. (1–2)
"O Puruṣottama, by whatever means possible, when shall I become a mother?
Having shown mercy to me, please grant me a daughter who is a source of auspiciousness.
Thus entreated by her, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa then [bestowed] Śrī upon her.
Having granted the boon, saying "So be it," he took delight with her in beautiful play.
(4) By the mere glance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the daughter of Śrī, who graced his couch, became divine;
she was equal to Kṛṣṇa in form and equal to Śrī in beauty. (5)
She suddenly appeared, youthful as soon as she was born;
like a wish-fulfilling cow, she was endowed with all perfections and named Sudughā (the Good Milker).
Indeed, she was summoned by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Śrī herself as "Sudughā."
That dark maiden is a cow that yields all desires;
she is equal to Śrī, her very nature is Śrī, and like Śrī herself she is exceedingly radiant.
Her every limb is well-nourished, and she is endowed with a golden luster.
From the moment of her birth, she was naturally inclined toward the work of milking cows;
she was seen to be full of resolve and likewise beloved by the cattle.
When she was born, a great festival took place there.
In the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s splendor, the sages, demigods, and celestial musicians performed [their roles] (10).
During that great festival, there was the dancing of the goddesses, the singing of the Apsarās, and the exquisite dancing, singing, and instrumental music of the Gandharvas (11).
The sages received blessings that served as protection for the maiden,
while the voices of the hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses became auspicious augurs of prosperity.
Likewise, handfuls of flowers fell upon Sudughā.
Seeing the girl, whose mass of luster was like milk, her companions rejoiced greatly and took delight with her again and again; they entertained her,
she entertained them, and they sported together with her.
Then, desiring to know her purpose, she repeatedly milked [the cow] and reflected with deep feeling: "What must I do here?
Having understood that she had been commanded by her father Kṛṣṇa, and likewise [perceived] his power of yoga.
"O Ūrjāhuti! O Dugha! O Daughter! May you cause Indra to grow with milk!
(16) Thus commanded, Sudughā was then exceedingly joyful; having bowed to her parents, she reflected upon how to bring about the growth and nourishment of Indra. (17)
In whatever spheres and whatever cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa),
and whatever divine sovereignty— the realm of Indra— exists in heaven,
having meditated upon all those kingdoms and their stations with the heart, [he attained them]. (18)
For the sake of their eternal nourishment, she reflected upon a means:
"I am Śrīputrī, the cow of plenty; I exist in the form of milk.
Having bestowed the milk of immortality upon the gods in heaven, I dwell there. (19–20)
At the beginning of the Great Day (Mahārātra), having become immortal through my perfected nature, I dwell there;
and I offer water, funeral cakes, milk-rice, and other such oblations to the ancestors. To cattle, humans, and trees, I give the essence of nectar in the form of milk.
Having bestowed nourishment upon the earth, I provide the nectar of flavor;
having created the nectar of moisture in the water, I effect its sustenance;
and for fire, I grant the sweetness of digestion through the nectar of ripening.
I offer the nectar of the sense-objects to the Self, which dwells within the body.
Indra is the Self; its powers are the senses, which have the sense-objects as their support.
Indeed, by means of those [powers], they become enjoyers of the nectar within the Self itself.
I am the essence within reality, the fresh butter, the clarified butter, and the nectar that accomplishes all;
thus, possessing many forms, I exist as the very nature of action.
For the sake of Indra’s attainment of happiness, I abide as his power (śakti) who yields milk.
In the sacrifice, having become the two offerings of strengthening food (*ūrjāhuti*), I bring about nourishment;
and I act in such a way that Indra’s protection may be complete in every respect.
Having manifested myself again and again everywhere, I shall effect my entry this very day.
Having reflected thus, that cow, who was capable of yielding much milk and assuming many forms,
became visible and invisible at will; she entered wherever she pleased,
and thereafter Indra’s beautiful heaven increased in prosperity.
All the nectars were milked and increased with extreme velocity;
in the worlds, the earth became filled with glory, and prosperity was enchanting.
The gods and goddesses shone forth, becoming more and more resplendent than before.
Even though all these abundant riches were being expended and enjoyed,
they did not diminish even slightly, nor did they ever fail, due to that lineage which was like a cow yielding excellent milk.
Furthermore, there arose a wealth never before seen or heard of, which was directly manifest as bliss.
Thus, when that auspicious time had passed and the first Kṛta Yuga had gone by,
there was a venerable sage named Medhāvī, a great performer of sacrifices.
He performed sacrifices according to the prescribed rites and also caused them to be performed for the sake of rain.
For the sake of sons and others, for the sake of happiness and the like, for the sake of heaven, and for the attainment of merit,
he indeed performed the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice for the sake of a pair of sons and daughters. Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, truly manifested himself in many forms.
He took with his own two hands that well-prepared sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) offered by him, and said:
"I am pleased; choose a boon as you desire.
[Choose] the earth, a kingdom, flavorful juices, sweet milk, heaven, a son, or a daughter."
"I shall give you whatever you desire; do not delay.
(37) Having heard this, the wise Brahmin said to his son: "Give [the wealth] to me.
This sacrifice called Putreṣṭi has been performed by me for the sake of obtaining a son. (38)
The Blessed One said: "Indeed, for seven births there shall be no son for you.
A son is born through the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice, but regarding his long life, there is doubt.
He who gives pleasure at birth but gives pain thereafter, upon death..."
Therefore, O Brahmin, choose a daughter if it pleases you.
O sinless one, the line on your wife’s forehead shines as a sign of a daughter;
she will excel even your son in fame and in service.
"O Brahmin, act in such a way that there shall indeed be no sorrow;
take the consent of your wife. Having accepted those words, the brahmin took his wife's agreement. Then, the Lord indeed granted him a favor for his meal.

Taking [the girl], the Brahmin said to Hari: "O Lord, let my daughter, who is like Śrī herself, be a giver of happiness; may she be peaceful and like a wish-fulfilling cow. She is the power of all beings that bestows the drinking of nectar. (43–44)
"So be it," Hari replied, and he sent forth the cow who yields all desires for the sake of Medhāvin’s daughter. By his command,
that excellent milch-cow appeared upon the bed of Medhāvin’s wife at that time.
That divine being became Mānasī; she shone like another Goddess Śrī.
From the moment of her birth, she was exceedingly beautiful, endowed with youth and fullness of form; she was charming with beauty and grace, casting glances from the corners of her eyes. (46–47)
Endowed with qualities such as cleverness, she was the sole object of praise for her parents;
beautiful with every excellent virtue, she was exceedingly dear to them.
Always cherished like a son, she was never once reproached.

Skilled in the literature of ethics and proficient in the knowledge of the self, she was a servant who always pleased her parents through her service. As time passed, O Lakṣmī, her mother met her death. (49–50)
Her father joyfully nurtured that maiden as if she were his own daughter;
and as time passed, she became like a yoginī, yet she remained by his side,
longing for the happiness of sons and grandsons upon seeing the joy of her friends.
That intelligent maiden, longing for the life of a householder, reflects upon me alone: "How might happiness and good fortune come to pass?
How might there be a husband endowed with virtues and good luck, and sons who grant me joy? (52–53)
For that purpose, which sage or which lord of the gods shall I worship?
I am a young maiden in the midst of my female companions, experiencing great sorrow;
unlike my circle of friends, I am not one who knows the happiness of a husband. (54)
Having perceived his daughter thus distressed with anxiety,
her wise father wandered over the earth searching for a suitor equal to her;
failing to find one, his hopes shattered, he fell into a severe fever.
Even as he was approaching his home, he fixed his mind upon Hari;
he remembered Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person.
He fell in the courtyard of the house, and the messengers of Kṛṣṇa arrived.
Taking that sage by the hand, they went to Kṛṣṇa’s lotus-feet.
Beholding his departure from life, the daughter cried out, "Alas! Alas!
and, placing her father's body upon her lap, she lamented, deeply afflicted with grief.

"Alas, alas, father! Why have you gone away, leaving behind your own daughter who is bereft of her mother, and likewise making me, deprived of my father, truly helpless? I have no brother, no kinsman, no mother, and no protector. (60)
"How shall I remain, O father? I shall die, there is no doubt.
Having heard such lamentation, the ascetics arrived there;
they saw the deceased sage and, filled with grief, cremated him.
Having comforted that maiden, they all went to their own abodes;
the maiden, maintaining her fortitude, performed the funeral rites according to her capacity.
After some time had passed, by the power of destiny, the sage Durvāsas, a disciple of Śaṅkara, arrived.
"O Lakṣmī, he who has been impelled by his future power has arrived at that house!
(64) Seeing him approaching, the young girl paid homage to the sage's feet and reverently worshipped him with offerings of water, flowers, and other honors. (65)
Salutations to you, O son of Atri! From where have you come, O sage?
By serving at your sacred ford, the dawn of my good fortune has occurred.
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my vow has become fruitful.
"Today my merit has borne fruit, since I have seen one such as you.
Having heard this, Durvāsas said to her: "Excellent! May it be well with you, my daughter!
I am coming from Kailāsa and I am going to the Badarī forest."
"If you have a purpose, let it be announced so that the god Nārāyaṇa may be seen.
Medhāvatī said to the sage, "There is nothing at all that should not be reported to the Lord.
Henceforth, through your grace and by the sight of you, there will be auspiciousness."
I have no mother, no father, no kinsman, and no protector at all.
No one desires me for the sake of taking my hand in marriage.
O Brahmin, I am as good as dead; what shall I do? Do what is beneficial for me.
Having heard this, the Sage, after reflecting well upon the means, spoke to his daughter:
"O fortunate one, three months from now is the month of Puruṣottama;
having bathed there at the Janatīrtha, a person is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin."
There is no other month equal to this; indeed, it is the supreme month.
All months, as well as fortnights, lunar festivals, and seasons, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the month of Puruṣottama.
All spiritual practices and thousands of ritual baths in the Gaṅgā and Godāvarī rivers do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the intercalary month.
This month is dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and is known by the name Puruṣottama.
O child! When he is served, everything desired is accomplished.
Therefore, serve that Puruṣottama for a month with diligence;
O daughter! I too shall always serve him just as Puruṣottama does.
"If you desire that which is to be attained, then perform a vow according to your pleasure.
O daughter! I shall go to the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Having spoken thus, she departed quickly; then Medhāvatī followed after her.
Enriched by her anticipation of the intercalary month, she performed auspicious rites that yield fruit at that specific time.
Keeping him in her mind and directed toward him, she practiced a difficult penance:
during the day she stood amidst five fires, and at night she remained in cold water. (79–80)
Free from food, she remained as if absorbed in meditation, her mind fixed on the supreme contemplation.
The Blessed Lord, the husband of Pārvatī, being pleased with her asceticism,
revealed his own form to the young girl so that it might come within the range of her vision.
She paid homage to Hara and worshipped him with flowers and other offerings, as well as with mental devotions.
With a spirit of devotion, she praised him: "Salutations to you, who are easily pleased;
salutations to you, Śaṅkara, the support of the daughter who was without support."
Salutations to you, the three-eyed one who is Sūrya, Agni, and Soma; salutations to Death.
Salutations to you here, who fulfills the desires of Pārvatī and the female ascetic.
O Śaṅkara, effect the deliverance of this maiden who is without a protector.
Having praised him thus and bowed once more, the daughter of the sage fell silent.
Hearing this, Sadāśiva, with a gracious countenance, said to her:
"Choose a boon—blessings upon you! I am pleased and shall grant it to you."
The girl said: "O ocean of compassion, if you are pleased with me, grant me a husband!
Grant me a husband! Grant me a husband! Husband, husband!
Having heard this, Mahādeva then spoke to the daughter of the sage.
"Since you have requested a husband from the Lord five times,
therefore, O daughter, there shall be five righteous husbands for you—
kings who perform sacrifices, who are true to their word, and who are devoted to me."
Now, those five Indras born in the previous kalpa who dwell in Satyaloka— may they become the husbands of your daughter,
indeed with this very body brought to a divine state. (90)
"Come with me today, O Satyabhāmā, to his presence by my aid.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara transformed her into one of a most divine body and led Medhāvatī through the sky on the path to Satyaloka.
He heard a divine drum sounding: "Perform the supreme vow on the thirteenth day of the intercalary month, so that it may grant all desired fruits.
Indeed, by this single vow, may the attainment of a husband be mine."
Having heard this, Medhāvatī said: "How may the attainment of Kṛṣṇa come to pass?
Having heard about this Dundubhi, a desire to know him has arisen within me.
Act in such a way that Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa may meet with me. (94–95)
Śambhu said: "O auspicious daughter! May you have welfare in every way.
I am pleased with your words, which are solely intent upon attaining Kṛṣṇa.
Whether it be a kingdom, heaven, the supreme state of Brahmā, or even the station of Īśvara—"
Everything becomes tasteless without Kṛṣṇa, the supreme among men.
That Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, is attained through devotion.
Perform the vow of the thirteenth lunar day as it was spoken by Dundubhi.

Having observed a fast and subsisted on fruit, one should worship the Supreme Self with sixteen items, feed Him, and likewise delight Him. One should keep a vigil at night and, being fully satisfied, give everything as an offering.

Having spoken thus and sent her to Satyaloka after bestowing the five Indras upon her in the form of wives, Hara spoke again to his daughter regarding the vow of the thirteenth day of the month of Puruṣottama.

Hari shall indeed meet you when he has assumed a human form; there, by the power of your asceticism, you shall be born not from a womb. There, these five husbands, born from portions of the gods, shall be yours.
Born from portions of Dharma, Marut, Mahendra, and the Aśvinīkumāras,
Śrīpati Kṛṣṇa shall then become her protector;
and having attained the happiness born of her husband, she shall thereafter go to the supreme state.
Those who are devotees of Puruṣottama, endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth,
have attained, will attain, and are attaining success both in this world and the next.
We too are all leaders who serve Puruṣottama.
Having spoken thus, Hara, the blue-throated one, quickly vanished.
(106) Having questioned her husbands regarding Medhāvatī, she performed the vow of the thirteenth lunar day according to Śaṅkara’s instruction, observing a fast and keeping a vigil. (107)
Having bathed Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, with the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),

one should offer garments, ornaments, food offerings (naivedya), fruits, betel leaves, and so forth; as well as incense, lamps, beautiful flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), a handful of offerings (añjali), and a request for forgiveness.
Having performed the *ārārtrika* and other rites, he entreated the Supreme Lord:
"O Father, grant me Your vision; be my helper in this worldly existence.
Just then, the Lord of Śrī arrived there, mounted upon Garuḍa.
"I am indeed pleased with you, O daughter, because of this vow on the thirteenth day. I shall always protect you, my child, and I will remain by your side according to the tradition.
Again, that daughter spoke: "O Guru, may my liberation be attained."
"O Father, may it be so for me at the end [of the age]; I desire no other wish.
"So be it," Hari said, and he spoke further in detail:
"Listen, daughter, at the end of the Dvāpara age, I myself shall be the Lord Kṛṣṇa."
"I shall indeed descend to the earth for the purpose of removing its burden.
From the midst of the sacrificial altar of the king named Yajñasena,
you shall be born as a maiden with the luster of gold."
And you shall become known as Yājñasenī, Vairājī, and Kṛṣṇā.
At that very same time, five Indras, portions of the gods and lords of immeasurable prowess, will become your husbands.
"O daughter, when I have, by means of that [deception], caused the Asuras, Daityas, and Dānavas to perish and am about to return to my own abode,
I shall take you away at the proper time and for the proper purpose, having confined you."

Furthermore, you shall regain your abode in Goloka, where your birth took place. Then, O daughter, with my supreme, imperishable, and Brahmanic form, I shall lead you to my own feet— the blissful refuge— within that highest realm.
"Thus, O daughter, this future narrative has been told to you.
Dwell in truth, my daughter; I am now departing for my own abode.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Puruṣottama then vanished from sight.
That daughter of Kṛṣṇa, Yājñasenī, will be a cow that yields milk most easily;
by means of a vow on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the intercalary month,
she shall attain the supreme abode according to the word of Puruṣottama.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this narrative of Śrīputrī.
They are blessed, they are truly born, and they are worthy of worship and sanctification—
those by whom Puruṣottama has been worshipped through various observances.
By hearing or even by reciting [this], one obtains the fruit of the vow here.
One gains the assistance of Kṛṣṇa, which is esteemed by Puruṣottama;
and whether a man, a woman, or another, one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, concerning the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama: the transformation of the cow Sudughā—the daughter of Śrī in Goloka—into nectar-essence by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa for the sake of increasing Indra’s prosperity; her birth as one not born from a womb in the house of the wise sacrificial Brahmin; the death of her parents; the arrival of Durvāsas; the instruction on the vow of the month of Puruṣottama; her penance upon Śaṅkara; her prayer to her husband five times; and [her presence] in Satyaloka.

Chapter Three Hundred and Twenty: The Attainment of the Status of Five Indras; the Vision of Puruṣottama through the Trayodaśī Vow; and the Granting of the Boon that she shall attain liberation after becoming Yājñasenī, the wife of five husbands on earth—thus is the description of these matters.
[The end of] Chapter 320 of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Part 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! By means of the vow of the fourteenth day, an excellent king—
Citradharma had a virtuous son, renowned as Dṛḍhadhanvan. || 1 ||
He attained a kingdom, sons and grandsons, and a devoted wife;
and in the end, he reached the world of the Lord, which is difficult even for yogis to attain.
Endowed with every excellent quality, a master of the Vedas, and a protector of his subjects, he became the son; thus it was that his father perceived him. (3)
Having reflected upon those various dharmas, he consecrated him in his own kingdom; thereafter, he propitiated the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Sovereign. (4)
For that purpose, the forest land is indeed entirely suitable;
[as were the hermitages of] Dhruva, Ambarīṣa, Śaryāti, Yayāti, and Śaśabindu. (5)
Bhagīratha, Śibi, Rantideva, Rukmāṅgada, and others—Divodāsa, Abhayakhaṭvāṅga, and other such most excellent royal sages (rājarṣis)—[all attained their goals]. || 6 ||
These and other kings of great being have gone to the forest in various kalpas and other kalpas, having renounced manifold enjoyments. (7)
Having attained the eternal by means of the transient through the propitiation of Puruṣottama,
I too must therefore perform the service of Hari in the forest.
Having severed the bond known as latent tendencies toward wife, children, home, and the like—having thus resolved in his mind regarding these manifold phenomena—he went to the forest. (9)
Having reached the hermitage of Pulaha, he performed austerities while remembering Hari;
having become pure and possessing a divine body, he went to the abode of Hari. || 10 ||
Then Dṛḍhadhanvā performed the funeral rites for his father;
having established the capital in the city of Puṣkarāvarta, he [ruled] there. || 11 ||
Together with his wife Guṇasundarī, the princess of Vidarbha,
and his four sons, the king ruled over the entire earth.
Once, while Dṛḍhadhanvan was sleeping at night, he had a thought, [he who was adorned] with variegated speech, a variegated chariot, and jeweled earrings of diverse designs. (13)
I have indeed never performed charity, austerity, recitation, or fire-offerings;
nevertheless, by what fortune has this sovereign kingdom come to me? (14)
Rising at the hour of Brahmā, that king, intent on hunting, mounted his horse and went to the shore of a lake in the forest. (15)
At that banyan tree, there was a certain parrot with a human voice;
it recited one excellent verse again and again. (16)
"Even though you possess sovereign power, a kingdom, and a body that grants pleasure, why do you not contemplate the Lord of Lakṣmī? How will you reach the further shore? (17)
Having heard the words of the parrot, the king rejoiced, for they were a means of deliverance;
and having gone out on a hunt, the king reflected upon the parrot’s speech. (18)
He returned home, and at that moment Vālmīki arrived there;
having honored Vālmīki, the king asked him about the parrot's speech.

"What did he say? How did he speak? Who was this Śuka, O Sage? Having heard this and reflected upon it for a moment, Vālmīki spoke to the king: kimuvāca kathaṃ prāha ko'sāvāsīcchuko mune! । śrutvā kṣaṇaṃ ca taddhyātvā vālmīkirāha bhūpatim ॥ 20 ॥
Listen, O King, to the account of your deeds in a previous birth:
in the Dravidian country, on the banks of the Tāmraparṇī river, you were once a twice-born brahmin. (21)
And Sudevā, known as the wife of Gautama and born of Gautama’s lineage, being childless, spoke to her husband in great distress because she lacked offspring. || 22 ||
A lineage that is pure shall lead to happiness both in this world and the next;
without obtaining such an excellent son, life here is indeed fruitless. (23)
Therefore, for the sake of obtaining a virtuous son, we two must constantly propitiate the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣottama, through ascetic penance. (24)
Heeding the words of his lawful wife, on the auspicious bank of the Tāmraparṇī, he subsisted on dry leaves and water, taking food only every fifth day. || 25 ||
For four thousand years they performed supreme austerity;
by that, the worlds trembled, and Mādhava appeared.
Seated upon Garuḍa, Hari said: "O Sudeva! May it be well with you.
O Gautamī! May prosperity be yours as well; do not perform excessive penance. (27)
Having heard this, the two of them bowed to Kṛṣṇa and said, "Victory to you, O Mādhava!
Sudeva said, "O Blessed One, O Lord Hari, grant me a son! (28)
Hari said: "All the letters upon your forehead have been observed by me;
therein, for seven births, there is no happiness from a son for you. (29)
Gautamī said: "If the Lord of Ramā is useless at the forefront of fortune, and if fate alone is to be relied upon, then what is the purpose of Hari? (30)
Having heard this, Garuḍa spoke to Hari, Kṛṣṇa Janārdana:
"O You who cannot endure the suffering of Your devotees! Make the purpose of Hari successful. (3.1)
The greatness of your worship is never, never indeed fruitless;
do not render useless your power to act or to refrain from acting. (3.2)
Seeing Garuḍa’s insistence, Hari said, "So be it";
however, the suffering caused by that will certainly befall the couple. (3.3)
Having spoken thus and mounted upon Garuḍa, Hari departed for Goloka.
After some time had passed, an auspicious son was born to the wife of Sudeva. (34)
As time passed, he grew up, was invested with the sacred thread, and then began his studies.
Once, the sage Devala, the destroyer of sins, arrived there. (35)
Seeing the hand marked with the signs of the parasol, lotus, barley-corn, and chowrie, and with the lines of longevity clearly visible, he then spoke while shaking his head.
"O Sudeva! This son of yours will meet his death in water during his twelfth year; therefore, O noble lady, let there be no grief for you. (37)
Upon hearing this, the two of them lamented, and Devala then went forth.
Then, when the inauspicious time arrived, his son indeed went to the pond. (38)
Having fallen into the bottomless water, he sank and died.
Upon learning of their son’s death from his friends, the father and mother [were overcome]. (39)
Having taken up the corpse there, they both rejoiced and wept profusely; they lamented greatly and abandoned even water and food. ||40||
That month became dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; it was Puruṣottama.
Even though the two of them were unaware, there occurred the service of Puruṣottama. ||41||
Because of that, Hari himself appeared, being exceedingly pleased;
the twice-born man, together with his wife, prostrated like a staff before Śrī Hari. (42)
Hari said: "O Sudeva! You are fortunate at this moment;
I have made this son of yours one whose lifespan shall be twelve thousand years. (43)
O twice-born one, because I have been pleased by the majesty of Puruṣottama, this son has indeed lived for a very long time; may he be a source of happiness to you. 44.
Having always enjoyed incomparable domestic life together with your son, you shall then go to the world of Brahmā and experience great happiness there. ||45||
Having enjoyed [this] for a thousand divine years, you shall go to the earth;
thereafter, you will become a king, a universal monarch (cakravartin) named Dṛḍhadhanvan.
"You shall enjoy the sovereignty of the earth for ten thousand years.
Gautamī, whose name is Guṇasundarī, shall be your wife. There, four sons and one daughter are destined to be born to you."
When you cease [addressing] me, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord. ||48||
"O Brahmin! This son of yours, having become a parrot in that forest, will then awaken others through words concerning devotion that contemplates Kṛṣṇa. (49)
Vālmīki will relate the entire story to you exactly as it happened;
then, having attained detachment and having performed supreme devotion to Hari, [you shall proceed]. || 50 ||
"You shall go with your wife to the supreme liberation, the abode of Hari.
While Mahāviṣṇu was speaking thus, the son of the twice-born rose up.
Upon seeing that son, the couple experienced great joy;
Śukadeva also bowed down to Śrī Hari and to his parents.
Garuḍa and the Brāhmaṇa, together with their wives, bowed down to Hari.
Kṛṣṇa said: "By the effortless observance of the intercalary month (adhimāsa)..."
Indeed, the happiness of sons, wives, spouses, fields, and kingdoms certainly comes to pass; of this there is no doubt—how much more so the life of one's own son? (54)
He who observes even a single fast at Puruṣottama,
having burnt away infinite misfortunes and having obtained treasures of merit— 55.
Having ascended the celestial vehicle, the embodied soul goes to Vaikuṇṭha;
on one side are all merits, but on the other side is Puruṣottama alone. (56)
The Creator weighed [them], and Puruṣottama indeed became the Guru;
He Himself is present in the creation of Īśa, the creation of Jīva, and even in the creation of Brahmā.
(57) The great month of Puruṣottama exists everywhere.
"By the protection of this [image], victory shall indeed be yours here.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, departed for his own abode.
Sudeva, together with his wife, worshipped that [image] for the duration of one month.
Then, having enjoyed all sensory objects day and night for a thousand years,
that best of the twice-born went to the world of Brahmā together with his wife.
Having attained the happiness found there, he returned to earth accompanied by his wife.
He himself is you, the renowned lord of the earth, Dṛḍhadhanvan.
This queen of yours is Gautamī, beautiful in her virtues;
and Śukadeva is your son, who was brought back to life by Hari. 62.
Having lived for twelve thousand years, he went to Vaikuṇṭha;
indeed, having become Śuka himself, he awakened you to the remembrance of Hari.
"O King, your son Sārthaka became a savior from the hell named Pūrna;
thus has been told to you, O King, how this past event truly occurred. (64)
Then Śatadhanvan asked the sage about the procedure for worship;
Vālmīki, however, explained that entire ritual in detail to the king. (65)
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should contemplate the Supreme Brahman;
thereafter, carrying a water vessel for the sake of purification, one should go toward the southwest direction (the quarter of Nirṛti).
Having placed the sacred thread over the ear, one should discharge urine;
having washed the pair of organs with water, one should cleanse them with earth, water, and so forth. (67)
Having performed purification by removing the traces of odor and having taken many mouthfuls of water,
and likewise having cleansed his teeth, he should bathe in the waters of sacred fords and other such places.
Longevity, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, and wealth, as well as sacred knowledge, wisdom, and retentive memory, increase daily for one who bathes. (69)
Having put on clean garments, facing eastward with his topknot tied,
he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with his hand holding a pavitra grass ring.
One should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) along with the dot (bindu) using sandalwood paste or clay;
one should also fashion the conch, discus, and other symbols, and wear a garland of tulasī.
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), the twilight rituals (sandhyā), and the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.
In a clean place, one should prepare a mandala with cow dung and rice grains and the like. ||72||
Having had that [mandala] constructed, one should place a water-filled jar in its center.
Viṣṇu is ever present at the mouth of the jar, and Rudra resides in its neck. (73)
Brahmā stands at its base; the Mothers stand in its center;
and within its belly reside the seven oceans together with the continents of the earth. (74)
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas remain there, together with their auxiliary limbs; likewise, the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Sauryā, Kāverī, and Sarasvatī abide there. (75)
May the rivers that bring about the destruction of sins remain here in this water.
I offer sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and flowers; Oṃ Namaḥ! ||76||
"I offer the food offering, fruit, and betel leaf; Oṃ Namaḥ.
Having thus worshipped, one should then worship the conch with unbroken rice grains (akṣata) and other offerings. ||77||
One should worship the beautiful bell with unbroken grains of rice, saffron, and other offerings;
one should place a vessel filled with sesame seeds and sugar upon the jar. (78)
One should worship that Hari, the deity of the month of Puruṣottama, who is clad in yellow garments, auspicious, golden, and accompanied by Rādhā. (79)
Having performed the extraction of the anus, one should maintain the vital breaths;
indeed, having touched those two skull-halves with the right hand.
Having placed the thumb upon her heart, one should firmly stabilize the vital breaths there, [reciting]:
"May her vital breaths be established; may her vital breaths flow forth. (8.1)
To this one endowed with divinity, Svāhā! To Nārāyaṇa indeed!
Then one should meditate upon the God and invoke the Lord who resides within the heart. 8.2.
I invoke Puruṣottama, accompanied by the glorious Rādhā;
and I offer a seat to this Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. (8.3)
I offer water for the washing of your feet;
I also offer this arghya, accompanied by fruit, to the Supreme Self.
O Lord of Rādhikā, I offer you the waters of sacred fords for sipping;
I offer you milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar. (85)
I shall likewise perform for you the fivefold ablution and the water-bath;
O Keśava, I offer you this yellow washed upper garment. ||86||
O Lord, I offer you the Kaustubha gem, the sacred thread, and ornaments;
I present to you sandalwood paste, the essence of fragrant oils, and other such offerings. (87)
I offer saffron, unbroken rice, and flowers; please accept them.
O Lord, I also offer you incense endowed with divine fragrance. (88)
O Lord Hari, I offer to you a lamp bright with ghee;
O Keśava, I present to you an offering of milk-rice. (89)
O Mādhava, I offer you water for rinsing the mouth, water for drinking, fruit, betel leaf, and likewise a fragrant powder for rubbing the hands. (90)
O Keśava! I offer gold as a sacrificial fee, along with necklaces and unbroken grains;
I perform the lustration ceremony for the Lord of Gods and I circumambulate him. || 91 ||
I offer this handful of flowers and I perform prostration;
O Puruṣottama, forgive whatever deficiency there may be in your worship. (92)
One should perform an uninterrupted fire sacrifice (homa) and maintain a lamp of ghee for the sake of pleasing Puruṣottama and for the attainment of the fruit of all goals. (93)
Thus one should worship him constantly and give gifts according to one's ability; one should feed those worthy of food and bow at the feet of the elders. (94)
The observer of the vow should partake of sacrificial food (haviṣya) that propitiates the gods:
wheat, śāli rice, mung beans, barley, sesame seeds, and sugar. (95)
Millet, dates, wild rice, grapes, and kanda tubers; cucumbers, roots, vegetables, leaves, edible flowers, and radishes. (96)
Plantains, bananas, curd, milk, as well as ginger, the fruit of the mango, buttermilk, jackfruit, and myrobalan (harītakī). ॥97॥
Long pepper, cumin, emblic myrobalan, tamarind, betel nut, and all products of sugarcane—these constitute the sattvic food for one observing a vow. (98)

One should avoid food that is rajasic, such as that prepared with black mustard; tamasic food, such as meat and the like; and food that causes flatulence, such as split pulses and so forth, as well as the food of others. 99.
One should practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, eat from a leaf-plate, observe the vow of eating only once a day, and avoid even the slightest censure of others. (100)
Puruṣottama should be worshipped with the fast, with milk, with curd, with water, with clarified butter, and even with leaves or fruit. (101)
One should take food in such a way that there is no violation of the vow;
by worshipping with a hundred thousand *tulasī* leaves, the merit is infinite.
Even one who observes the vow of the month of Puruṣottama becomes Puruṣottama himself.
He shall indeed become four-armed and will dwell eternally in Vaikuṇṭha.
An unbroken lamp should be offered during the month at Śrī Puruṣottama.
In ancient times, King Citrabāhu reigned in the city of Saubhāgya. 104.
His wife was Candrakalā, and both were indeed very righteous;
then the sage Agastya came to his house. (10.5)
Having honored him with humility, Citrabāhu said:
"Today, indeed, the sovereignty of my home, my birth, and all else have become truly fruitful. (106)
Since you, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, have come to my home today, I give everything today to you, the high-souled Vaiṣṇava. (1.07)
Even a slight offering made to you for Viṣṇu or a devotee of Viṣṇu shall yield fruit equal to Mount Meru; however, a day not offered [to them] is fruitless. (108)
Devotees of Viṣṇu are worthy of service through the actions of speech, mind, and body;
blessed are all the subjects of that king in whose house there dwells a person devoted to Viṣṇu. (109)
One should indeed reside in a Vaiṣṇava land and in a kingdom where the sovereign is a Vaiṣṇava; for a realm that is not Vaiṣṇava should be understood as inauspicious and defective. 110.
The kingdom of a king who has taken refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa prospers.
O Sage! May my fortune, as well as my kingdom, likewise be vast and free from thorns. 111.
"Tell me, by what merit did my wife become devoted to her husband?
Having heard this, Agastya said to him: "In the past, in the city of Camatkārapura..."
You were born of the Śūdra caste as Maṇigrīva, an extreme nihilist, an ocean of evil qualities such as intoxication, meat-eating, sexual indulgence, and theft. 11.3.
This wife of yours is indeed devoted and always possesses a virtuous disposition;
yet you, O King, having been exiled by the monarch, have gone to the forest accompanied by your beloved. (11.4)
While living as a hunter in the forest, you then beheld a sage,
the twice-born Ugradeva, who was thirsty and on the verge of death.
Having risen and lifted up water, he gave him fruit and gladdened him;
the sage, being well-pleased, said: "O Maṇigrīva! Be happy! (116)
"You have granted me my life; tell me, what shall I give to you?
Maṇigrīva then replied, "May my poverty perish! (1.17)
"May my splendors be incomparable; may my desires be fulfilled"—when he expressed this wish, the sage said, "So be it for you. (118)
Indeed, during the upcoming intercalary month at the holy Puruṣottama, a lamp should be offered in the temple for the pleasure of the illustrious Puruṣottama. || 11.9 ||
Your intense poverty shall not perish along with its very root, whether by means of sesame oil, clarified butter, or even ingudi oil. (120)
"Having bathed daily for one month and bowed to the deity while offering a lamp, you shall indeed obtain a great kingdom upon the earth through that act. (121)

Sacrificial rites and other rituals, as well as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances, the recitation of the Vedas, the Śrāddha at Gayā, and likewise the planets at Kurukṣetra—these [are the means]. (1.22)
Holy fords, all forms of charity, and whatever religious acts there may be, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the Lamp of Puruṣottama. || 123 ||
The vow of the intercalary month is supreme; it is a lamp that illuminates from within, bestowing wealth, grain, cattle, sons, grandsons, wives, and fame. 1.24.
This vow destroys barrenness in women and ensures they do not become widows;
it bestows a kingdom, grants desired objects, provides a husband, and provides a wife. (125)
The vow of offering a lamp bestows knowledge, accomplishment, wealth, and liberation.
Thus, you previously offered a lamp to Śrī Hari in the forest. (126)
O Indra among kings! By that merit you obtained a noble kingdom, prosperity, and a devoted wife; by performing it again, you shall obtain them once more. 1.27
Having spoken thus, Agastya, the king of sages, departed for Prayāga;
and by that king as well, Śrī Puruṣottama was reached according to the prescribed rites. || 128 ||
Having performed the offering of lamps, he then attained liberation;
having said this, Vālmīki took the offerings and departed.
Then, when the month had arrived, on the fourteenth day at dawn during the excellent Śrī Puruṣottama festival, Kṛṣṇadundubhi was [confronted] by Dṛḍhadhanvan.
Having heard this, let them perform today itself the vow of the lamp and the night vigil;
by that merit, through my boon, may they attain heaven and liberation. 131.
Having heard this and remembering his entire vow at that time, Dṛḍhadhanvan, together with his family,
remained without food and performed a vigil with lamps.
He celebrated a great festival and gave gifts of cows and land;
at night, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, arrived here.
Garuda led him along with his family to the world of Brahmā;
O Mahālakṣmī, what more need be said regarding the greatness of the intercalary month? 1.34.
Where Śrī Puruṣottama is the creator, the sustainer, and the deliverer;
where Śrī Puruṣottama is the nourisher, the gratified one, the giver, and the enjoyer. (1.35)
O Lakṣmī! whoever hears this, or reads it, or even causes it to be read, shall indeed attain the fruit of the intercalary month and proceed to the world of Brahmā. 1.36.
Having attained heaven according to his desire, as well as the supreme station of Parameṣṭhin,
and having reached the rank of Maheśa and others, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
By those by whom this month has been fully honored, everything has been honored;
by them everything shall be attained, for they have attained Śrī Puruṣottama. (138)
The prosperity of one by whom this intercalary month is disregarded is indeed barren;
all merit performed by him becomes fruitless—of this there is no doubt. (139)
O Lakṣmī! Whatever beings there may be who possess happiness—whether gods, humans, or dānavas—it is the fruit of the month of Puruṣottama, and nothing else. 140.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, within the *Puruṣottama-māsa-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, Dṛḍhadhanvan, having heard a verse spoken by Śuka in the forest and having questioned Vālmīki regarding its meaning, came to know his own history from a previous birth: his state as the Brahmin Sudeva, his possession of sons, and how upon the death of his sons he had restored them to life through the observance of the Puruṣottama month; and that this very son was Śuka, the speaker of the verse, while he himself had now been born as Dṛḍhadhanvan.

He learned the ritual for the worship during the month of Puruṣottama; he also learned what was told by Agastya regarding how, through the offering of a lamp during an intercalary month, the Śūdra Maṇigrīva attained the status of King Citrabāhu and the acquisition of a kingdom in another birth; and furthermore, he learned that after performing the Caturdaśī vow, Dṛḍhadhanvan, together with his family, attained liberation. This is the three hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description [of these matters]. 1.321.
