Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; at the end of the intercalary month, on that day in the abode of the Imperishable (Akṣara-dhāman), the concluding rite (udyāpana) was performed by all in the temple of Puruṣottama.
Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa, and all others residing in Goloka arrived;
Vāsudeva and the other manifestations of the Vyūha came together with their own progeny. || 2 ||
We, Nārāyaṇa and the others, who reside in the world of Mahāvaikuṇṭha, have gone together with you and the subjects to the Imperishable (Akṣara). || 3 ||
Then all those women from the city of Śrīpura in the Avyākṛta and Amṛtadhāma realms, as well as Nyāyeśvara and the others, went there with joy. (4)
Mahāviṣṇu and the others, born from the creation of Hiraṇyagarbha,
along with the Pravairājas and the Āvaraṇas, attained the Imperishable Lord.
Likewise, those residing in Vaikuṇṭha, situated above the watery covering of Viṣṇu, departed;
and those residing in the abode of Sadāśiva, along with the progeny of Mahāmāyā, departed.
Thus those lords and incarnations, having gone to the supreme imperishable state,
performed there the concluding rite for the month of Puruṣottama.
The sages and ascetics in the world of Brahmā, as well as the hosts of Mothers, the ancestors, and the Vaiṣṇava deities, all departed. || 8 ||
The performers of the concluding rite, including the celestial beings, humans, and others, departed;
all the holy fords, the gods, and the goddesses likewise went to their respective quarters.
The principles (tattvas) also went there, as did the rivers and oceans; likewise the mountains, the hollows, the islands, and the continents followed. (10)
The planets, the stars, the circle of constellations, trees, and creepers;
indeed, the divine beings, the excellent devotees, as well as the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas. || 11 ||
Then the medicinal herbs, serpents, nāgas, and stainless birds— those dwelling in water, on land, and in the air— all went forth.

Then those dwelling in the netherworld, those in the crevices, and those divine and non-divine beings went forth for the sake of the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the vow—both the practitioners of the vow and their co-residents, as well as the devotees. || 13 ||
They went with reverence into the presence of Satya in the world of Brahmā;
and they also went for the sake of performing the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the month of Puruṣottama. || 14 ||
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Sūtas and others, as well as gods and humans;
the Bhaṭṭas, Cāraṇas, and servants, and even the fierce followers of Śaṅkara. (15)

These and others went to the festival for the sake of the fruit of completing their vows; listen, Lakṣmī! how they did so in various places according to their ability and according to their wealth. (16)
The concluding rite (udyāpana) was performed by all, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires;
indeed, it was performed by them preceded by the giving of wealth, granting both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (17)
Listen as I relate to you the concluding rite (udyāpana) performed by them, which was spoken by Hari himself regarding the month of Puruṣottama. (18)
On the fourteenth day of either fortnight, on the new moon or the full moon day,
on the eleventh or the ninth, or on the eighth lunar day— the day of the vow— (1.9).
On whichever lunar day there may be auspiciousness, or even on that very lunar day,
one should indeed perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the sake of completing the vow.
In every place, the drum proclaims throughout the month of Puruṣottama:
"Go indeed and perform the auspicious concluding rite (udyāpana). 2.1.
"The full fruit of the month of Puruṣottama shall be attained.
Having heard this from the drum, others also performed the concluding rite (udyāpana) in their own homes. (22)
Having slept on the ground at night and strictly observed celibacy,
they all rose in the morning and then performed meditation upon Hari.
Having performed all bodily rites such as purification and so forth externally, and having then performed the bathing and other rituals according to the body's divine or non-divine nature; 24.

Having performed their recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), twilight prayers (sandhyā), self-study of the scriptures (svādhyāya), libations (tarpaṇa), and so forth—according to local custom, according to their physical capacity, and as was appropriate for them—they [proceeded]. || 25 ||
Having performed the daily worship and the honoring of the elders, as well as the rites of adoration and offering,
they sipped water for purification (ācamana) and prepared the ground with extensive consecration. Then, they constructed a pavilion there, provided with many pillars.
With necklaces of jewels, diamonds, and pearls, and with archways made of mango, aśoka, and other trees.
With plantain trunks, leaves, and the like; with the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavallī);
with water-pots, decorative creepers, and garments adorned with gold. || 28 ||
Having bound it with lamps and adorned it with fragrant scents, one should perfume its interior with the five grains and the seven [herbs]. || 2.9 ||
Or, having caused a Sarvatobhadra mandala to be made with grains,
one should invite devotees of Viṣṇu together with their wives according to one's capacity.
One should place four auspicious jars in the four directions within the mandala, provided with fine cloths, bilva fruits, betel nuts, and betel leaves. ||31||
There, having filled them with unbroken grains mixed with sugar and other substances,
[one should worship] Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from the northeast in due order, one should place [the deity] in the center within an auspicious water-pot (kalaśa) that contains its fruit, is covered with a cloth, and is provided with betel nuts, a golden coin, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
They enshrined Śrī Puruṣottama, who possesses a divine form and is made of gold, together with Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, within a golden vessel adorned with the five jewels. || 34 ||
In this manner, the installation of Śrī Hari was performed by all those observers of vows;
and the preceptor, the guru, was ushered in there for the purpose of worship. (35)
The purification of the body was indeed performed by him for the patron; then the deity was invoked and a seat was offered. (36)
Water from an excellent sacred bathing place was indeed offered for the purpose of washing his feet;
lamps were lit in the four directions, and fragrant incense was burned there. (37)
The *arghya* consisting of fruits and other offerings was presented by the couple, and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) originating from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) was offered to the God. (38)
Curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugar— these, as well as nectar,
were indeed offered as water for the consecration bath to Keśava.
The two deities were wiped with a cloth and adorned with garments and ornaments;
they were made fragrant with sandalwood essence, excellent oils, perfumes, and other scents. ||40||
He was beautifully adorned with saffron, collyrium, powders, sandalwood, and other unguents;
he was further embellished with necklaces of gems, diamonds, and pearls, as well as a sacred thread.
Adorned with a crown, earrings, bracelets, armlets, and chains, he was protected by an umbrella, a staff, a turban, chowries, and armor. ||42||

He was provided with a couch, a bolster, and a mattress, and was beautifully adorned with offerings such as flowers, *tulasī*, and lotuses, as well as with *puṇḍra* marks shaped like the crescent moon. ||43||
Then, in that pavilion, a fire sacrifice was performed using sesame seeds, ghee, and excellent fruits, with the mantras consisting of names ending in the dative case. ||44||
Then, the libation was performed one hundred and eight times with the words:
"May the gods and the ancestors, as well as Puruṣottama, be satisfied. (45)
Then the Lord was honored with the *nīrājana* rite by means of many wicks and fires;
he was saluted, praised, and circumambulated by the Vaiṣṇavas. (46)
Śrī Puruṣottama was honored like a staff-bearer, meditated upon, and Hari was asked for forgiveness; a handful of flowers was offered to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. ||47||
Then the god was feasted, satiated with sweet foods like nectar,
provided with water, offered sweet fruits, and entertained with the chewing of betel.
The Supreme Person was massaged with fragrant unguents on his hands; the Lord was refreshed with comforts and honored by being massaged at his feet. (49)
Thus worshipped by all, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, manifested himself before them; becoming invisible, he granted them infinite fruits.
Then a gift of gold and silver was bestowed upon the preceptor,
and a gift of a cow, adorned with golden horns and ornaments, was also given.
There, a vessel of ghee, cloth, and sesame seeds was given to the Brahmin;
an image was also presented, and the Saṃhitā-śāstra was offered. ||52||
At that time, thirty bronze caskets were indeed given;
each was filled with thirty cakes in their center. ||53||
This gift of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) was indeed fashioned by Puruṣottama; O Lotus-born One, it contains as many apertures as there are in every limb. ||54||
For that many thousands of years one shall dwell in Vaikuṇṭha; thereafter, one dwells in Goloka, and then in the supreme, imperishable abode (Akṣara-dhāman). 55.
Alternatively, cakes that have been cooked by means of the complete collection of ingredients should be given to the twice-born;
then the virtuous Brahmins and the children are to be fed. (56)
With milk-rice, sweet dishes, and side-dishes such as amṛta and others—through these fourfold foods consisting of what is chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked. (57)
Then [one should offer] juices such as milk and water mixed with sugar, cardamom, and so forth;
thereafter, water for rinsing the mouth, betel leaf, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ||58||
Indeed, garments and most excellent ornaments were offered to the goddesses, the deities, and even to the preceptors. ||59||
Indeed, those principles belonging to each respective world which are worthy of being given as gifts—food is offered therein to the elements, to those who have taken refuge, and to guests. (60)
Then, together with his kinsmen and those observing vows, he respectfully partook of suitable food such as fruits and the like—indeed, that which would not cause a violation of his vow. ||61||
Likewise, it was performed at midday and similarly at night;
the deity was worshipped and fed by people engaged in a vigil. ||62||
Singing, dancing, and worship were performed by the people;
having bathed in the morning, [the deity] was honored, asked for forgiveness, and then bid farewell. (6.3)
That Supreme Lord, in the form of an image, was offered to the preceptor.
Having thus performed the concluding rite (udyāpana), they all returned to their own abodes. //64//
And an infinite fruit has been obtained by serving the Supreme Person;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, one should observe this vow according to one's ability. (65)
There shall be the destruction of suffering, poverty, and misfortune, and one shall obtain what is desired;
thereafter, the person observing the vow should perform the relinquishment of the observances (niyamas). //66//
One who observes the vow should eat only at midday or eat only at night, and should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
When food is obtained through the "unasked" (ayācita) vow, one should perform the gift of gold.
One who observes the month-long fast should give as a sacrificial fee a milch cow along with ten thousand coins;
and one who observes the Dhātrī-vow should likewise give curds, milk, and sugar.

O Lakṣmī! In the case of a restriction regarding fruits, one should provide an equivalent gift of fruit. When oil is prohibited, ghee should be given; when ghee is prohibited, milk should be offered. (69)
In the observance regarding grains, one should give those very same grains;
and in the observance of sleeping on the ground, one should give beds, stools, pillows, and coverlets.
In the observance regarding fruits, leaves, and so forth, one should give those to the twice-born;
in the observance of silence, one should offer bells, conchs, and musical instruments to the lotus-born god.
One who wears nails and hair should give a mirror and a hair-comb;
and one should indeed give sandals when sandals and such items are being avoided.
Upon renouncing salt, one should give flavorful juices; upon the gift of lamps, however, one should give lamps.
And fasting on alternate days, one should cause eight jars to be given.
Whatever desirable prosperities belong to kings in this world, all of those should indeed be given as gifts according to one's ability and according to one's wealth. (74)
One who observes the vow while eating only once a day attains the supreme goal like the four-armed Lord;
indeed, by fasting and eating but one meal, one shall obtain all desires.
The gods eat in the forenoon, likewise the sages at midday;
the hosts of ancestors in the afternoon; a man should be one who eats at night. ||76||
One who eats only at night obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice day by day;
one who observes the vow of the twelfth lunar day goes to the abode of Hari on Garuḍa.
Whichever specific rule one may have, one should apply oneself to the giving of that very thing;
by this, the vow becomes complete and shall grant the world of Brahmā. ||78||
O Lakṣmī! With this impermanent body, the state of liberation must always be achieved; for there is nothing equal to the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) in the three worlds. (79)
Even by asceticism performed for a thousand births, that fruit which is attained in this world through service to the Supreme Person is not reached. (80)
By bathing here for three nights, the monkey attained the Imperishable.
Indeed, in the land of Kerala, there was a twice-born man who was exceedingly greedy for wealth. (8.1)
On account of that miserly name, he became notorious among living beings; neither good food nor fine clothing was ever enjoyed by him, nor were the *svāhā* and *svadhā* offerings ever made. (82)
Wealth was guarded on the earth, yet no work of dharma was performed; there were neither vows nor festivals, neither eclipses nor the ritual of the water-pot (kumbha). ||83||
Having repeatedly begged for alms while wandering like a miserable man for wealth, he went to the garden of a gardener, weeping repeatedly in distress. (84)
The gardener, having shown compassion, kept him by his side;
having made him the protector of the garden, the florist departed for the village. (85)
Afterwards, he ate the ripe fruits and bartered for others;
in this manner, ten thousand years passed for that perpetrator of thievery. (86)
He died there in the forest, yet he did not obtain the firewood for cremation;
being led by the messengers of Yama while being beaten, he was taken to the abode of Yama. ||87||
As he was departing, he said: "Indeed, the fruit of my evil deeds has been obtained by me today;
having attained human birth, I have not performed even the slightest meritorious act. (88)
Wealth accumulated through theft and other such means remains useless upon the ground; it is neither maintained nor consumed, and thus no merit has been earned from it. (8-9)
His family was not supported, his wife was subjected to hardship,
and the miser, lamenting thus, then departed for the city of Yama.
Citragupta declared that there were two very severe sins:
the theft of fruit and, moreover, the betrayal of trust. ||9||1||
Having heard this, Yama said to his messengers: "Indeed, designate him as a preta;
however, let this one be a monkey, yet subject to the torments of hell again and again. (92)
Thus, having been sent by messengers to the state of a preta in a waterless forest,
he subsequently became a monkey on the formidable Mount Kālañjara.
There, Indra had previously constructed a sacrificial pit known as Mṛgasutīrthaka;
it was there that [the king] was born as a monkey due to that small amount of merit from his former life. ||94||
Listen to the merit performed in the past through the praise of Puruṣottama:
there was a Vaiśya named Citrakuṇḍala who was devoted to the excellent vows dedicated to Puruṣottama. (95)
In the past, that miser had gone to him for the sake of alms;
out of greed for wealth, the beggar then praised that Vaiśya. (96)
The vow of the month of Puruṣottama which was performed by you according to the prescribed rite—such a thing has never been performed by anyone else here on this earth. (97)
You have achieved your purpose, since you have served Śrī Puruṣottama;
this month of Śrī Puruṣottama is the bestower of fortune and the giver of liberation. ||98||
"Give me some wealth," he entreated for a month;
by that merit, he attained the state of a monkey at this sacred ford (tīrtha). || 99 ||
From birth, there was pain in his mouth arising from blood and wounds;
his teeth fell out, he was overcome by hunger, and he became excessively afflicted by fever. (100)
The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) arrived at the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), having fallen [there].
For five days starting from the tenth day, they remained in the water of the pit. || 101 ||
Having bathed in the waters of the sacred ford, he was born assuming a divine body;
he became four-armed, served by divine goddesses and attendants. || 102 ||
Just as [the merit] arises from bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha), so it arises from bathing performed for five days with due honor;
and just as it arises even from ignorance, how much more so when performed according to the prescribed rite? || 103 ||
They are always fortunate and meritorious, and their existence is fruitful—those for whom the month of Pumuttama has passed with ritual bathing, giving, and recitation. (104)
These [merits] were indeed multiplied ten millionfold for the Supreme Person;
the monkey, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, went to Goloka.
Thus, even though he was a miser and a thief, and had even attained the state of a monkey,
by means of union with Puruṣottama, he reached Goloka itself.
Even by merely hearing the narrative of the month of Puruṣottama, one obtains the full fruit of fasting throughout the month, performing worship, and other such rites. 107.
By hearing the Dharma one understands; by hearing, evil is destroyed.
By hearing, delusion ceases; by hearing, the nectar of knowledge is attained. (108)
One observing the vow should recite or listen to the Veda known as the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā during the month of Śrī-Puruṣottama; for it indeed bestows liberation. 109.
If a woman has not herself observed the month-long festival of Śrī Puruṣottama, yet her husband honors it, she shall obtain that excellent fruit. (110)
If a virtuous woman is always devoted to the duty of fidelity to her husband, the month becomes like her husband, the Supreme Person Śrī Puruṣottama. (111)
Whether he be ugly, ill-behaved, or even of evil character and a drunkard;
whether he be diseased, wrathful, or corpulent; or even mute, blind, or deaf—(11.2).
Whether he be fierce, dejected, miserly, or poor; whether he be contemptible, cowardly, a gambler, a sensualist, or even a libertine; (113)
For a virtuous and faithful wife, Lord Hari is her husband, who must be worshipped constantly as a god;
likewise, for a widow and for a maiden, the husband alone is always Lord Hari.
He is to be served, worshipped, meditated upon, and dwelt upon—both through speech, action, and body, as well as through mental cultivation. || 11.5 ||
A husband’s work must not be made difficult for her, nor should the lord be made to feel anxious;
whether she be a child, a young woman, or an old woman, she should remain devoted and dependent upon her husband. (116)

Whether by desire, greed, or even by force; by a state of wretchedness, or by seeking refuge; by beauty, by residence, or by wealth and the like; or by thirst, or by the nourishment of the sense-faculties and elements. (1.17)

She who does not worship another, even with fine garments, excellent vehicles, mounts, ornaments, millions of diamonds and gems, beautiful dances and songs, or many seats—she indeed possesses the characteristics of a virtuous woman. 118.
A virtuous woman does not indeed adorn herself for the sake of being seen by anyone else;
she does not think of any man other than one who is worthy of her. || 119 ||
She who, upon seeing one who is handsome, youthful, charming, and beloved by women, does not undergo any change of mind—she indeed should be known as a great virtuous woman. 120.
She eats when her husband has eaten; she is sorrowful when he is sorrowful; she rejoices when he rejoices; she sleeps when he sleeps; and she remains awake when he is awake. (121)
Devoted to her elders, she is compliant in her husband’s affairs and does not incur excessive expense;
when her husband returns home, she rises to greet him with a seat and water. (122)
With a serene countenance at the proper time, she should provide food and other necessities; once he has eaten, she should speak no unpleasant words and likewise bestow peace upon him. (123)
She should always be intent on service and always act for the pleasure of her beloved;
as the guardian of the household, she should not spend excessively on material things. 124.
One should wear ornaments and fine attire for the pleasure of one's husband; in the Tretā age and those following, women indeed experience menstruation as their period of ritual impurity.
During those four days, she should not touch any household chores;
having bathed and beheld the Sun and Lord Kṛṣṇa, she should thereafter be devoted to her religious duties.
She who desires a son should engage in sexual union on even nights, while she who desires a daughter should serve her husband on odd nights. (1.27)
Indeed, until the sixteenth night, the power of conception remains;
beyond that, the door of the lotus becomes closed. (128)
She should never be loathsome, nor should she speak harsh words.
She should not draw in the wind from a winnowing basket, nor should she sit upon the bare ground.
She should not sit upon the doorposts, the threshold, the hearth, or the grinding stone.
Or one should not consume very hot food when it has not yet been digested. || 130 ||
By this means she shall have offspring; otherwise, there would be a miscarriage. A co-wife is the seat of jealousy; therefore, a virtuous woman should completely avoid jealousy. || 131 ||
She should not cause domestic distress and should protect the household in every way;
she should not address her husband with harsh words, nor should she revile or treat him with contempt. (13.2)
She should always grant pleasure to her husband, who is her protector;
she may go outside by her husband's command for the purpose of beholding the gods. 13.3.

When her husband has gone to another land, the virtuous wife should conduct herself in every way as one devoid of cosmetic adornments, always carrying out the commands of her mother-in-law and others. 1.34.
She should not remain with soiled garments or limbs, but should maintain her purity;
she should devotedly consume the food, water, and alms-remnants left over by her master. 1.35.
One should bathe without being devoid of clothing, nor should one ever be naked; one should not bathe on a wooden mortar, nor on a pestle, nor in a water-jar or similar vessel, nor on a stone.
A virtuous woman should never sit upon a machine or on a road;
she should drink the water from her husband’s feet, which bestows the fruit of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites. 1.37.
A wife should not perform vows, fasts, or religious observances in violation of her husband's wishes;
she should always eat only after having honored her husband’s feet. (138)
Saramā is one who reviles her husband; Ulūkī is she who fills only her own belly;
Sūkarī is she who stays by the side of another; and Vāgurī is she who eats in secret. (13.9)
A woman who is mute brings contempt; one who is envious of her co-wife becomes unfortunate;
and a woman who is ugly and diseased shall bring suffering to her husband. (14.0)
The husband is Brahmā, Hara, and Viṣṇu; he is the preceptor, the sacred ford, the vow, and the recitation of mantras.
He is purity, heaven, auspiciousness, and charity; therefore, one should serve the husband well. (141)
A body devoid of life is impure; a virtuous wife (*satī*) devoid of her husband is impure.
Yet, a devoted wife (*pativratā*) who is dear to herself leads her husband to heaven.
Upon seeing a *satī*, the messengers of Yama flee far away.
Indeed, for as many hairs as there are on his body, so many tens of millions of ayutas [of years] shall he remain.
A devoted wife who delights in her husband enjoys the happiness of heaven;
a widow, however, should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) every day while remembering her husband. 144.
She should accumulate merit through offerings of *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and water, as well as ground grains, fruits, morsels for cows, and other such acts of giving.
She should present a *brahmāṇḍa* (the cosmic egg) fashioned from bell-metal in the form of a casket.
It was filled with thirty middle-sized cakes and well-wrapped with thread.
The virtuous woman should offer it, honored with unbroken grains, flowers, and saffron;
likewise, a man should be devoted to his wife and dedicated to his wife. (147)
One should always honor one's own life-force, body, field, auspicious sanctuary of peace, and wife, and should regard them with sweetness. 148.
One should give her sweet things, speak to her, and show her affection with love; one should not treat his wife with contempt, nor strike her, nor insult her. (149)
One should always please one's beloved with garments, ornaments such as jewelry, liquid sandalwood paste, flowers, oil, thread, collyrium, and other such things. (150)
One should not cause distress, nor should one eat by force, nor should one restrain her; one should not afflict the wife with hunger, thirst, or through labor. 151.
A husband should not disregard his beloved wife, even if she is humble;
like a creeper that provides support and nourishment, he should cherish her who sustains the lineage and bestows pleasure. 152.
Then, the husband should neither say "No" nor utter "Do not" to his wife;
rather, having uttered "Om," he should bestow whatever wealth or other things she desires. || 153 ||
One should cause great delight in her as she performs her duties of serving food, household chores, sexual pleasure, bodily care, service to her husband, and whatever else there may be. (1.54)

He should not look upon another woman, nor should he engage in sexual union with another; indeed, he should never be fond of any other woman, having abandoned his wife who is like the goddess Lakṣmī. 155.
He shall not provide nourishment for another, nor indeed shall he take pleasure with another woman, even in matters of vehicles, mounts, regions, festivals, or social assemblies. (156)
If one truly desires heaven, one should never be separated from another;
thus, a husband and wife devoted here to dharma are partakers of liberation. (157)
Indradyumna, Śatadyumna, Yauvanāśva, and Bhagīratha—these and other Vaiṣṇava kings and Brahmins appeared in every Kalpa and at the end of every Kalpa. || 158 ||
Having worshipped Puruṣottama, they went into the presence of the Blessed One;
by whomsoever the drum of the month of Puruṣottama was heard. (159)
And everywhere, in each respective place, a festival was indeed celebrated;
and Nārāyaṇa performed the worship of the drum.
Whenever an intercalary month (adhimāsa) should also occur,
at those times the proclamation of the royal command must be made with the sounding of kettledrums and drums.
He is always protected in the imperishable abode by Śrī Puruṣottama, by Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. 162.
Accompanied by Rādhā, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Prabhā,
Māṇikī, Jayā, and Ramā, this Lord,
the Supreme Sovereign, is to be worshipped every day during the intercalary month.
For the sake of food, one should serve and meditate upon the Supreme Person. 164.
The greatness of this month should be heard; this complete chapter and verse shall yield the fruit of all holy places, such as the Gaṅgā—of this there is no doubt.
It possesses the merit of circumambulating the earth and the merit of rescuing the entire universe.
By hearing this, liberation shall likewise be attained within a month.
Likewise, those belonging to the castes and stages of life who have attained excellence in every respect—even common folk following the conduct of beasts—attain liberation upon hearing [this]. 167.
Having caused the *Puruṣottama-māhātmya* to be written along with its binding, one should give it as a gift; by the fruit of this, one's lineage for three generations shall go to Goloka. (168)
In a house where a book concerning this majesty is kept as its foundation, all sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell in every way, the deities also reside there, and Puruṣottama himself is present. (169)
The listener, the speaker, the one who causes others to hear, the one who describes, the one who praises, the protector, the observer of vows, and the giver—all these are supreme among men. (170)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beginningless Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the instructor of the Saṃhitās and Upaniṣads, is especially worthy of worship. 171.
Having heard this, Lakṣmī was exceedingly satisfied and worshipped Puruṣottama;
she worshipped her own husband, Hari, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. || 172 ||
"I have attained my life's purpose by drinking the nectar of your face," she said;
and she worshipped and bowed down to Vyāsa, who was her husband in person. (173)
I am Nārāyaṇa, the speaker, and you are Lakṣmī, the Narāyaṇī. I accept the worship performed by you; what else do you wish to hear? (174)

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the *Puruṣottama-māsa-māhātmya* concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, is described the procedure for the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) of the Puruṣottama-māsa vow performed by all the lords of creation in the imperishable abode (*akṣara-dhāman*); the gifts to be given for the fulfillment of the observances; the fruit of offering lamps; the liberation of the miser; the release of the monkey; the duties of a devoted wife (*pativratā*); the duties of a husband’s devoted wife (*patnīvrata*); the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) consisting of a pair of bell-metal vessels; the worship of the drum (*dundubhi*); and the fruit of hearing [this account] and so forth.
The three hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Definition of the Cetyas and Other Entities," [ends].
Chapter 322 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (*Kṛtayuga-Santāna*).
Chapter 323.
[Author: Chapter 324.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Lord, O Supreme Self, O One higher than the highest!
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Inner Controller, O Supreme Lord!
(1) O Puruṣottama, O Lord of the Self, O Lord of Life, O Beloved, O Giver of Honor! As for what was said by you—that there are thirteen lawful wives—(2)
What are they? From what, when, and where did they arise, and by what cause?
What is their purpose, and by whom was it done? Tell me, if indeed it is something that ought to be told.
By that compassionate one, I have been delivered, purified, and brought to fame.
O Lord, having related the story of the Goddess, the Yoginī who is the Supreme Person,
please tell me in detail for the sake of remembering my lawful wife that divine narrative concerning the wives of dharma, which bestows both heaven and liberation.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate to you the auspicious story of the lawful wives, which bestows liberation;
it indeed took place at the beginning of creation—understand it from me.
The Supreme Person abides in the imperishable, supreme abode;
within that, there exist divine powers by the hundreds of thousands.
Then He formed the intention: "Let me become one, yet may I be born as many."
Then the eternal divine qualities, consisting of power and possessing form, came into being:
faith, friendliness, compassion, peace, contentment, nourishment, exaltation, action, intellect, wisdom, forbearance, and modesty—these are the twelve. (8–9)
There, that which is called "form" is always spoken of under the name of devotion (*bhakti*).
These women are indeed powers (*śakti*) born from the very nature of Hari;
they are eternal even in Hari, appearing as his shadows for the sake of the liberation of the world. (10)
Having assumed a second form, they dwell among the classes of living beings.
When they had thus become endowed with form through the nature of Brahman,
they then prayed to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among men.
O Keśava, since we have been offered as oblations by your mere resolve,
and since we are embodied forms consisting of your own form and go nowhere else,
command us, O Lord, what task is appropriate for those such as us to perform.
Thus entreated, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, reflected and said to them all: "Indeed, become shadow-forms;
let those forms of yours that exist here be composed of shadows."
"May all these circulate within embodied beings during creation"—
having received this hope from Śrī Hari, they became composed of the *guṇas* in the creation; by the will of Śrī Hari, those powers became all-pervasive.
However, among the asuras, daityas, and dānavas,
as well as in the homes of those characterized by darkness (tāmasa), there was no happiness for them in any way.
Then, having all gathered together, they went to the illustrious Badarī forest.
Desiring the Supreme Lord, they performed most fierce penance,
having reached the banks of the Gaṅgā; remaining there without water or food for a period of a thousand years, their minds were fixed solely on Puruṣottama.
Then the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself appeared.
He said to them: "Why, and how, is such a terrible austerity being performed?
By the power of your practice of penance, I have been strengthened. (20–21)
My qualities and my powers are entirely devoted to my growth;
you are always the bestowers of my nourishment and happiness.
Since I have indeed come here for the sake of your assistance, [I am yours]. (22)
"Declare your desire; what is sought through these austerities?
Having spoken thus, Hari remained silent there for a moment.
Then all those Śaktis said, "O Lord! Against the Dānavas and Daityas..."
"O Lord, there is no happiness at all for us among the Asuras!
Because we dwell in unrighteousness, we are indeed miserable there.
Therefore, O Blessed One, draw us away from that and make us happy forever."
Then Hari, having reflected for a mere moment, said to them:
"Observe this great vow on the final day of the month of Puruṣottama; by doing so here on the bank of the celestial river, your desire shall be fulfilled."
Having spoken thus, the Lord vanished;
and when the time for the intercalary month arrived once again,
on its final day, they performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with ritual offerings.
And with various offerings, including flowers and unbroken grains of rice, they all performed worship.
In the evening, the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama appeared there, saying:
"O goddesses, choose a boon; I have come to grant you whatever you desire."
Then, filled with trepidation, they chose the protection of dharma:
"O Kṛṣṇa, we are devoted to dharma; may we be protected in every way.
O Śrī Puruṣottama, you must always provide us with protection. (31)
Having heard this, Hari then said, "So be it.
He further said to all those auspicious Śaktis: "Go to the house of Dakṣa;
let Asiknī be the daughter of you all, and then your father [will be her father]."
"Dakṣa will indeed give thirteen daughters to Dharma as wives;
you shall become renowned by those very names, each according to your respective order.
Then, from my own form, I myself—Hari, the personification of the duty of celibacy—"
"I shall be born as Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, in the Badarī forest. I will always provide protection for you who have acted unrighteously.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa vanished.
Then, abandoning their asceticism, they entered the Asiknī river.
By the mere will of Dakṣa, they then became maidens;
as soon as they were born, they were young women, beautiful and worthy of being chosen as brides.
Remembering their past births, beautiful in form, and having undertaken physical discipline for the sake of dharma—
seeing them thus desirous of dharma and firm in their resolve for dharma,
Dakṣa awaited the auspicious time for the practice of dharma.

Meanwhile, Dharma, having observed the path to Badarī-āśrama by way of the sacred ford (tīrtha), went for a moment’s rest after seeing Dakṣa’s house, which he knew to be adorned with hospitality toward guests. ||40|| He then entered Dakṣa’s residence.
Having recognized and especially remembered his brother Brahmaputra,
Dakṣa was exceedingly pleased upon seeing him and prepared an extensive reception.
Having honored them all, he gave thirteen of his daughters to Dharma.
Having performed the marriage rites for his daughters, Dharma then became fulfilled; taking them with him, he went to Badarikāśrama.
Gaṅgā, having drunk and bathed in the waters, proceeded to Dharmāraṇya.
Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, entered into the Dharma.
At the end of the year, Dharma, accompanied by his wives,
departed for Badarīvana after having visited all the sacred fords.
There, by the will of Kṛṣṇa, both Nara and Nārāyaṇa were born in person from the body through austerity, due to the excellent vow of Puruṣottama.
As the sons of Dharma and the sons of Mūrti, they were most great as soon as they were born.
Those two illustrious youths, ever devoted to the practice of celibacy,
appeared as ascetics for the welfare of the world.
Then, from Faith, Kāma was born as the son of Dharma.
Desire (kāma) is said to be the son of Saṃkalpa, possessing the power of merit and virtue;
from Saṃkalpa was born the son named Resolve (vyavasāya).
Benevolence (maitrī) gave birth to Affection (sneha), and Compassion (dayā) brought forth Assistance (upakāra).
Śānti gave birth to a son named Kṣema, and Tuṣṭi’s son was Santoṣa.
From Puṣṭi was born a son named Lābha, and from Unnati came a son named Abhyudaya.
From Kriyā were born sons named Naya, Daṇḍa, and also Samaya. (50–51)
The awakening of the intellect (buddhi) is Bodha, and both he and Apramāda are the sons of Medhā;
Śubha and Śruta are the two sons of Titikṣā, while Virāma is the son of Hrī.
Niyama is the son of Mūrti, as are Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

O Badrikā, O Lakṣmī! The four lineages of Dharma—Kṛṣṇa, Hari, and the others—dwell there happily, devoted to service and attendance. Now, in the world of Brahmā, within the assembly hall of the Creator in the Satyaloka; ||53-54||
At the conclusion of the month of Puruṣottama, the worship of Puruṣottama was performed with a great festival and vast provisions by gods,
sages, seers, humans, and those of other species. (55)
With great devotion and intense emotion, preceded by the offering of all his possessions,
Dharma, his wives, and his sons, as well as Puruṣottama,
became pleased and attained boundless satisfaction.
At midnight, at the end of the first day, after the worship and the meal,
those invisible beings, desiring to grant an audience to their devotees and to the observers of the vow,
arrived in the sky, distinguished by the sound of singing.
He suddenly manifested in the midst of the devotees of Puruṣottama as a mass of splendor, which instantly pervaded the sky;
that light became condensed, resembling millions upon millions of moons. (59–60)
Then stability manifested and attained a state that illuminated the quarters;
the scales, the musical groups, the modulations, and the sounds became enchanting.
While the gods and others were watching there at that time, the enchanting [voice]—
A single young woman appeared, of divine form and pleasing to the mind;
(62) clothed in celestial saffron garments and adorned with divine ornaments, her beauty was in perfect accord with her form—serene and radiant as molten gold. (63)
Richly endowed with the splendor of every ornament, adorned with all types of jewelry, bearing flowers upon her mass of hair, and graced by a beautiful smile and playful eyebrows;
clothed in spotless garments and decorated with a girdle and anklets. (64)
She bewildered the minds of women even with her loveliness;
playing the lute while her friend sustained its notes, she alone was able to destroy the pride of even the Gandharvas and Apsarases by her singing alone. (65–66)
And twelve other women performed the song of Nārāyaṇa with proper rhythm and measure, truly captivating even the minds [of the listeners].
Their sons, who were highly divine and gracious, also performed as singers.
Amidst the musical instruments, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari was present;
likewise, the intercalary month, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and other divine women were all seen right there in that assembly hall in the house of the Creator.
The Lord, the master of syllables, Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Śrī Puruṣottama,
was seen with lotus-like eyes as he spoke words of blessing.
The four-armed God of Dharma was seen, radiant white in hue.
Speaking with Vedic utterances and displaying his graciousness to the devotees,
Brahmā and the others beheld them and then recognized that as a great marvel.
For a mere moment they were bewildered, but then they were filled with joy and extreme delight toward them.
Having recognized Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and the others likewise bowed to Dharma, his personified form, as well as his sons;
and having prostrated, Śraddhā and the others praised him with the utmost reverence.
O Nārāyaṇa! Salutations to you; salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇī.
O God of Dharma, salutations to you; salutations again and again to those who are righteous. May there be salutations to faith and the other virtues, and salutations to the embodiment of devotion.
Salutations to Rādhā, Ramā, and the other Śaktis, and to the Supreme Person;
salutations to you who have granted us vision, for you are indeed the Supreme Lords who deliver the worlds, and us in particular. (76)
"O gods, you have indeed been made successful here by you through your compassion; if there is a command to be known, let it be instructed.
Having heard this, Puruṣottama then spoke to the gods, headed by Brahmā.

During this month of Puruṣottama, devotion has been offered by you, the leaders of the world, as well as by my subjects, toward this Puruṣottama. Likewise, dharma has been practiced to the utmost degree, and faith and the other virtues have been nourished.
Having been supported along with my family, I have come to grant you my vision;
may there be the greatest welfare for you through my grace.
Otherwise, my vision would not be perceptible even to yogis. (80–81)
"Choose a boon; I am pleased, so choose that which you desire from me.
Hearing these words of grace, they prostrated themselves and performed worship.
They chose [this boon]: "May You dwell forever within our hearts."
May they protect us who abide by your instructions; O Guru, always guard us in our duties.
O Mādhava, lead your devotees—those free from desire—to your divine abode, and fulfill the desires of those with longing. Shower down your grace, shower it down! 83–84.
Having praised him thus, they ceased; and Keśava, the Supreme Person, having granted a boon to Brahmā and the others along with their families, said, "So be it.
Then Hari suddenly vanished, producing a sense of wonder.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, the Lord fulfills all the heart's desires of his devotees moment by moment;
indeed, for those devoted to Puruṣottama, there is nothing that cannot be attained. (86–87)
Whoever shall read or hear this, which brings satisfaction to Puruṣottama,
Hari will indeed fulfill all the desires of his heart.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Dharmadeva, His Wives, and His Sons, and the Granting of a Vision and Boons by Śrī Hari—Who Was Pleased by the Vow of the Puruṣottama Month Performed by Brahmā and Others—Along with Their Families," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama.
Chapter 323. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 324 [Author:
Chapter 325 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Lakṣmī! I become pleased; this is my grace.
When the month of Puruṣottama arrives, grace alone is the cause.
If someone desires to make me exceedingly satisfied during other months," [1]
I become exceedingly pleased even by a single *tulasī* leaf alone.
A person should worship with a leaf joined with a flower-cluster (*mañjarī*), or with two leaves joined with a cluster, or with many leaves joined with clusters. (2–3)
One should worship with a hundred, or a thousand, or even a hundred thousand [flowers];
for upon seeing you, O dear one, I am as delighted by Tulasī as I am by you.
(4) Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, O Puruṣottama, O Keśava! O Lord, why do you regard Tulasī as one who brings you satisfaction, just as you do me?
Tell me everything exactly as it happened, if there is nothing to be hidden.
"If I am considered a worthy recipient, then tell me this secret.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! To the story of former events, told in great detail."
"Just as Vṛndā, who brings me satisfaction, has been accepted by me,
do not entertain doubt regarding that, nor feel envy upon hearing this.
You must always maintain a spirit of friendship with Vṛndā."
For a devoted wife, there is dharma; she never takes account of her own suffering.
But one who is devoted to her husband should always take account of the happiness derived from her co-wife’s union with her husband.
Having heard again and again of the joy arising from her husband’s union with another woman, [she rejoices].
Considering her own self-bliss to be supreme, the devoted wife finds contentment. (1.324.10) "Indeed, thousands upon thousands of wives shall be mine;
even Vṛndā has been made my wife by me, and she too is devoted to me. (11)
Listen, I shall tell you the account exactly as it happened in every detail:
having made the pretext of accomplishing a task, Vṛndā was made my wife by me.
Vṛndā was indeed my wife, equal to Rādhikā in Goloka.
Seeing her own husband sporting with Rādhikā, she was overcome by jealousy in her heart; obstructing her pleasure and unable to speak to me, she did not express what was in her heart. (13–14)

Then, after a moment, although she was summoned by me for dalliance, she did not come. Because of that fault, I thought: "This woman is wicked; she does not deserve to serve me. While I was still reflecting thus, she [then]—
She went to the lower world and attained the state of an asura.
Having obtained Jalandhara as her husband and exhausted her own past misdeeds,
she was enjoyed by me when she took on the form that became the cause of Jalandhara’s death.
Then, purified, that former wife of mine returned to me.
Listen in detail, O Lakṣmī, to how that narrative unfolded!
O Lakṣmī, in the first Kṛta Yuga, Śaṅkara was the benefactor of the world.
The great god Mahādeva, the husband of Satī, roamed through the forest with ease.
In the form of a naked ascetic, out of a desire to purify the forest-dwellers,
the Lord Hara wandered through the lion-forest like a fearless lion.
Having learned that it was the day of Śivarātri, Mahendra and Bṛhaspati descended from heaven to the earth for the purpose of worshipping Śiva in person;
they did so upon seeing Śiva himself moving along the path of the sky. (21)
Guru and Śakra respectfully entered the lion-forest.
Meanwhile, Śambhu, having deliberated for the sake of testing their knowledge,
assumed another form and remained near them,
standing in the path with his head bound by matted locks.
To that man of great splendor, naked, of wondrous form,
long-armed, broad-chested, firm, and naturally terrifying to behold as he blocked the path, Purandara asked: (24–25)
"How is it that you stand blocking the path, O terrifying one?
Here we see Śaṅkara Hara traveling along the path of the sky.
Tell us quickly where he is, for we two attendants are desirous of honoring him. (26)
Thus questioned, the man did not say anything at all; then [the king] spoke again.
Likewise, though questioned by Indra, that great yogi again resorted to silence; he did not speak, but remained silent again and again. (28)
Although questioned, the ascetic said nothing at all; Vāsava became enraged.
Raising his right hand and rebuking Śambhu, he spoke these words. (29)
Raising his hand upward and brandishing his thunderbolt, Hari said:
"O fool! Even though you were questioned, you did not give an answer."
"I shall slay you with my thunderbolt; who will provide you protection?
Having spoken thus, just as he was striving to kill him in his rage, Śrī Śaṅkara then paralyzed him.
Endowed with his vajra-weapon and his body, Mahendra became as rigid as a clod of earth or a piece of wood;
he was utterly consumed by fury.
Even Hara, with his terrifying eyes, quickly became a source of fear.
He blazed forth like the fire of universal dissolution, as if standing there consuming everything.
Then Bṛhaspati, having recognized Śambhu through his pure intellect,
bowed with joined palms to the Lord and prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
With a heart full of fear, he began to praise Hara:
"Salutations to you whose nature is inaccessible, who are independent, and who wear matted locks;
salutations to you, the three-eyed Maheśa, who are clothed in the directions. (35–36)
Homage to the fierce god, the protector of the distressed, the source of bliss;
homage again and again to the three-eyed one, the peaceful, the savior of devotees.
Homage to you, the multiformed one, whose very nature is supreme splendor.
Salutations to you, the Supreme Self, the destroyer of Time, the all-pervading Śarva.
You are Agni, you are the great wind, you are space, you are water, and you are the earth;
you are the sun, you are the moon, and you indeed are the stars. (39)
The wheel of light resides within you; indeed, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and you yourself are one.
Indra, Bṛhaspati, and others are always happy, enjoyers of prosperity, and free from calamities through their constant worship of you.
"How is it then, O Lord, that there is such arrogance here toward the leader of the gods?
Having thus praised him, the Guru prostrated at the feet of Hara;
and having caused Śakra to fall, he spoke again with humility.
Be gracious, O Lord of the World; protect Indra, who has come to you for refuge.
Withdraw your wrath and become peaceful, O Lord, and show compassion toward Indra.
Quickly bring about his pacification, for this fire from the eye on your forehead is [blazing].
"The offense committed against her just now must be forgiven as it was done in ignorance.
Having heard this and recognizing his humility, Śaṅkara, whose forehead blazed with the fire of wrath, slowly spoke these excellent words to his devotee Bṛhaspati.
This anger has emerged from my eyes as a most terrible, embodied flame;
O Bṛhaspati, I do not think it is possible to restrain it once it has gone outside.
Indeed, a snake does not take back the sloughed-off skin once it has been cast away.
"I shall reduce this Hari to ashes, treating him with utter contempt.
Hearing this, Bṛhaspati became afraid and distressed;
yet the Blessed One spoke again, for devotees are always to be shown compassion.
O Śaṅkara, you are named "Bhaktavatsala" (the one who is affectionate toward devotees); make that name meaningful!
You ought to cast Indra and Agni elsewhere, for they are indeed inert matter.
Or else, reduce me, the preceptor of Indra, to ashes as you please.
"O Śaṅkara, you ought not to burn the supreme lord of the gods!
Having heard this most humble plea, Śambhu— the bearer of the name "Benevolent to Devotees" and the remover of the distress of those who bow before him— spoke to Bṛhaspati.
Pleased by your persistence here, by your humility, and by your offering, I grant the gift of life to Mahendra; be free from fear. Let it be proclaimed:
"Indra lives," and "May you also live."
"May you both be happy and perform my worship.
Having performed that worship for which you have indeed come, and having attained my favor, take with you the renown of fearlessness. (53-54)
"I shall myself seize with my own hand the fire of my wrath arising from the eye in my forehead that has gone to heaven and cast it into the salt waters.
Having thus resolved, he cast down the fire of his eye in the form of fiery tears.
Then, having accepted the worship offered by both [the preceptor and Indra] at the western ocean,
Śambhu vanished right there, radiant like a streak of lightning.
Having achieved their purpose, the preceptor and Indra returned to their respective abodes.
Then, that exceedingly terrible water, the turbid impurity of fire, which had been cast forth from the eye in his forehead, fell into the salt ocean. 58.
Having attained the state of childhood, he shone forth immediately;
uttering the word "bāla," that child remained amidst the waves of water like one seated upon a swing.
(59) He sat there, attended by the surging billows of the water.
As soon as he was born, he was like a youth, wonderful and with a body like a thunderbolt.
Laughing repeatedly and uttering sounds that pierced the heavens,
laughing again and again and creating a succession of mirth,
he made all the directions resound and caused even heaven and truth itself to tremble.
The entire earth trembled and all living beings were deafened by that excessive sound of laughter. Along with its army, the netherworld (atala) and other regions shook,
and all the Dānavas as well as all the worlds were struck with terror.
The world-protectors were overwhelmed, and the entire world, with its moving and unmoving beings, trembled; the foremost gods and lords of the worlds quickly shook.
Having assembled at Satyaloka, they went to Brahmā for refuge.
Overcome with fear, they all said: "O Father, danger has arrived!
This sound, produced by a great laughter, strikes terror into the world;
it appears in every way to cause dread—what could this be? Could it be Mahākāla?"
"O Lord! It appears that some great asura has arrived, intent on destroying the universe; therefore, O Foremost Ancestor, protect us!
Having heard these words of the guardians of the gods, the Grandfather of the worlds—
And even though he had fallen into fear, he sought the assistance of everyone. ||68||
Desiring to go to the place where a terrible laughter was being spread, the gods and others descended, having directed their attention toward the quarters of sound. (69)
Aiming for the source of sound that resides beyond speech within the waters of the salt ocean,
they traveled through the sky toward the western direction;
meanwhile, [they encountered] a youth who was laughing and exceedingly harsh.
They beheld him moving fearfully among the waves of the ocean;
then, knowing that the excellent man had arrived,
the Ocean perceived that Brahmā and the others had come and performed the rites of hospitality for them.
Abandoning his laughter, even the child ran there and sat upon the lap of the ocean, crying out, "Father!
Father! Then Brahmā asked the ocean, "From where has this child come, and to whom does he belong?"
The laughter of Śaṅkara, which repeatedly causes the cosmic egg to tremble and pervades all directions—
this very child spoke to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Then the child rose up and ran toward the Creator.
He seized Brahmā by the throat so that he might meet his end;
from the shaking of Brahmā’s throat, water flowed from his two eyes.
Having been drawn out by the ocean, Brahmā was thereby separated from it.
Thus endowed with power, the child named Jalandhara, the son of Hara, was gazed upon by the gods and others;
he was made into a reservoir of water.
Jalandhara is the ocean, and Jālandhara is likewise born from the sea.
He is born as Jālandhara, known as Jālandhara and Jalandhara;
since he is the son of Rudra, he will be fierce in his prowess.
He will be a knower of the scriptures, a conqueror of all, and a master of weapons and missiles.
"He shall be invulnerable to all beings except for Rudra.
Today this son of a Daitya is observed to possess the qualities of a Daitya;
therefore, he will undoubtedly become a lord of the Daityas and a king of the Daityas."
Brahmā spoke again, having seen the fortune of that ocean:
"The wife of Kṛṣṇa who was envious of Rādhā in his abode has indeed become a companion to Rādhikā and Kṛṣṇa’s amorous play in Goloka. (82)
She was brought down from Goloka by the Blessed One to this earth;
born as his daughter in the house of Kālanemi, she, being virtuous and devoted to her husband, will become his auspicious wife—of this there is no doubt. (83-84)
"Let him be made such that, as soon as he is born, he becomes a youth and is consecrated as the ruler of the Daityas' kingdom; let this be ordained by all.
Having received this command from Brahmā, [Viṣṇu] summoned Śukra himself.
Having thus instructed the lord of rivers, they consecrated him in his kingdom.
Then, all the gods, pacifying him with the instruction, "Do not again perform such terrifying laughter," departed for their respective abodes. (86-87)
The Ocean, taking his son with him, went joyfully to his own home;
he nourished Kālanemi with great means and summoned him.
He requested his daughter, named Vṛndā, for the sake of being his wife.
The asura Kālanemi considered Vardhi’s request to be exceedingly desirable.
At that very moment, he gave his daughter to Jālandhara according to the prescribed rites;
then there was a great festival at their wedding. And the ocean also attained happiness upon seeing his son together with his wife.
The Daityas, residing in the netherworld of Pātāla, took refuge with Jalandhara.
Having come to the earth, those powerful lords established their kingdoms;
and all of them became firm-minded in their resolve for victory over the gods.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, within the narrative of Jālandhara and Vṛndā in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*: having observed the amorous dalliance of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, Vṛndā—the consort of Kṛṣṇa residing in Goloka—departed from Goloka due to the fault of jealousy toward her co-wife and took birth as the daughter of Kālanemi. Then, when Bṛhaspati and Mahendra, who had come to see Śaṅkara, beheld Śaṅkara in the Siṃha forest and descended there, they were unable to obtain an answer to their question, "Who are you? from Śaṅkara.
